decisions.title: Adopt scoped task groups as the canonical task-spawn model?
decisions.gist: A scoped task group is the lexical task scope: spawn inside it, collect results through handles/combinators, and guarantee every child is finished, cancelled, or reported before scope exit.
decisions.explainer: Unstructured task spawning makes it easy to leak work: a function returns, its caller does not know tasks are still running, and errors from those tasks are silently dropped. A scoped task group closes that gap at the language level. D-ASYNCRT1=A is already ratified: Jet uses an M:N green-thread scheduler with no function coloring. The task group sits on top as the canonical spawn scope. D-RACEWIN1 and D-CONCCOMB1 become task-scope combinators. D-DEADLINE1 should ride task/#Context propagation. Detached spawn remains an explicit expert escape, not the beginner path. This ballot decides the model, not the final keyword; D-TASKSCOPE1 decides spelling.
decisions.story: I'm making three API calls in parallel. If any one fails, I want the others cancelled immediately. If they all succeed, I collect the results. Today I'd have to manually track tasks and handle cancellation — I want the scope to do that for me.

options.name: Scoped task group as the canonical spawn model
options.detail: Adopt a lexical task scope over the M:N scheduler from D-ASYNCRT1=A. Work created inside the scope must finish, be cancelled, or report an error before the scope exits. Task handles expose explicit wait/join. all/race/any/select are combinators over scope-owned work. Detached spawn remains an expert escape hatch and should require visible intent. Exact keyword/API spelling is decided separately by D-TASKSCOPE1.

options.name: Unstructured spawn + manual join
options.detail: Keep unstructured task spawn as the primary model; programmers join tasks manually. Familiar to Go/thread-pool users; makes task leaks easy to write and hard to detect. Not recommended as the default because it conflicts with beginner-safe lifetime ownership.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Accept the E4 exit criterion slip. D-ASYNCRT1=A already settles the task runtime direction, so deferral is only appropriate if Jet does not want scoped task groups as the default spawn model.
options.code:
// no nursery; E4 criterion missed;
// task-leak hazard remains

comparisons.note: Trio nurseries make child task lifetime lexical: the scope cannot exit while children still run, and cancellation is structured.
Trio originated structured concurrency. `trio.open_nursery()` is the only way to spawn tasks; the nursery guarantees all children exit before the block exits. Proven in production.
comparisons.code:
async with trio.open_nursery() as n:
    n.start_soon(fetch, url1)
    n.start_soon(fetch, url2)
# both done (or both cancelled) here

comparisons.note: `coroutineScope { }` and `supervisorScope { }` provide structured concurrency. `launch` inside the scope is the idiomatic pattern; cancellation propagates automatically.
`withTaskGroup` and `withThrowingTaskGroup` give typed structured task groups. Good mainstream reference for a scoped task API with result collection.

decisions.bestCurrent: Trio proves lexical task lifetime; Swift TaskGroup proves mainstream naming; Go proves why unstructured goroutines need better lifetime ownership.
decisions.recommendation: Adopt scoped task groups as canonical spawn. Jet can keep Go-like simplicity while making task leaks, dropped errors, and forgotten joins structurally impossible.

decisions.title: What spelling should Jet use for the scoped task group?
decisions.gist: The model needs a lexical scope that owns child tasks, but the word `nursery` may be too borrowed and obscure. This decision chooses the final user-facing spelling.
decisions.explainer: `nursery` is precise in Trio, but it is not obvious to most programmers and does not read like Jet systems-language product copy. The concept should survive; the word should be challenged. The spelling should make three facts visible: this is about tasks, it is a group/scope, and child work is owned until scope exit. The choice must not introduce a second spawn model or imply actor supervision unless that is really what it does.
decisions.story: I am new to Jet and I see a block that spawns three API calls. I should understand from the keyword that this block owns a group of tasks and waits/cancels them at the end, without knowing Trio history.

options.name: `taskgroup g { ... }` (recommended)
options.detail: One keyword that says exactly what the construct owns: a group of tasks. It is plain, searchable, close to Swift TaskGroup terminology, and avoids importing Trio jargon. It keeps `task { }` visually related to the scoped form. Downside: compound keyword is less pretty than a short word.

options.name: `task group g { ... }`
options.detail: Most readable English and clearly related to `task`. Downside: two-word keyword phrase adds parser/teaching weight and can look like a declaration rather than a control construct.

options.name: `scope g { ... }`
options.detail: Short and general. Downside: too vague; Jet will have many scopes, and this hides that the construct owns concurrent tasks.

options.name: `nursery n { ... }`
options.detail: Best-known term in structured-concurrency literature through Trio. Downside: obscure to non-Trio users, not self-describing, and product-language mismatch for Jet.

options.name: `with tasks g { ... }`
options.detail: Reads naturally and emphasizes a scoped region. Downside: adds or overloads `with`; less direct as a named API receiver for combinators.

comparisons.note: TaskGroup is mainstream and directly names the idea: a group of child tasks with scoped lifetime.
Nursery is semantically strong but jargon-heavy outside Trio.
coroutineScope is accurate but tied to coroutine vocabulary Jet is intentionally hiding from beginners.

decisions.bestCurrent: Swift TaskGroup has the clearest mainstream name; Trio nursery has the strongest semantics but weaker product language.
decisions.recommendation: Use `taskgroup g { ... }` unless the owner prefers another spelling. It keeps the task relationship obvious and avoids Trio-specific vocabulary.

decisions.title: Add try-both / keep-the-winner as a structured-concurrency combinator?
decisions.gist: Some patterns need to run alternatives concurrently and keep the first to succeed, cancelling the rest. Examples: fallback servers, speculative execution, hedged requests. Today there is no built-in mechanism; the transaction system (`#Transact`) handles rollback but not general success-racing. This decision is whether to add a `race` / `any` combinator and where it lives.
decisions.explainer: This card depends on structured concurrency (D-NURSERY1): a success-race is a nursery operation — spawn alternatives, cancel siblings when one succeeds. Implementing it as a standalone primitive risks I8 (two spawn mechanisms). The correct home is the concurrency combinator set alongside `all`, `any`, `first` — all of which are nursery-level operations. The distinction between first-done-race (returns the first to finish regardless of success/failure) and success-race (returns the first to succeed, retries on error) must be explicit in the API — they are different semantics and should have different names. `#Transact` rollback is orthogonal; this card is not about undoing state.
decisions.story: I have two CDN endpoints for the same asset. I want to fire both requests and use whichever responds first. The slower one should be cancelled. Today I'd write that manually with tasks and channels; I want a one-liner.

options.name: Fold into the structured-concurrency combinator set (race/any), sequence after D-NURSERY1
options.detail: Define `race(tasks)` (first to succeed) and `any(tasks)` (first to finish) as combinator functions in the concurrency stdlib, built on the nursery primitive. No new language syntax — just functions. Sequence after D-NURSERY1. Satisfies I8: one spawn mechanism, multiple combinators over it.

options.name: Standalone language primitive
options.detail: Add `race { }` as a first-class language block, separate from the nursery. Doubles the concurrency surface (I8 concern). Only justified if the nursery model cannot express racing cleanly.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Wait until D-NURSERY1 is implemented and the combinator API is proven before adding racing. The manual pattern works; this is a quality-of-life addition.

comparisons.note: `Promise.any()` returns the first fulfilled promise; `Promise.race()` returns the first settled (either). The naming distinction maps directly to what this card proposes.
comparisons.code:
const result = await Promise.any([
  fetch(cdn1),
  fetch(cdn2),
]); // first success

comparisons.note: `select { }` expression picks the first channel or deferred that is ready. More general but more verbose than a `race` combinator.

decisions.title: Add a bare `undo` keyword for reversing operations, or keep `#Transact` as the sole reversal mechanism?
decisions.gist: The `#Transact` marker already provides transactional rollback. A bare `undo` keyword has been proposed as an alternative spelling — shorter, more imperative. D-SUGAR5 already declined a nearby cleanup-sugar proposal. This reopen asks whether `undo` offers enough over `#Transact` to justify adding it to the surface.
decisions.explainer: I8 is the decisive issue: `#Transact` and a bare `undo` keyword would express overlapping semantics. Unless `undo` covers a strictly different use case (e.g., reversing a single operation mid-function rather than rolling back an entire transaction), it is a second way to do the same job. The keyword would also consume a reserved word in the grammar. D-SUGAR5's rejection establishes a pattern: the owner has already declined nearby sugar. The status-quo is the recommended option unless a concrete use case is presented that `#Transact` cannot express.
decisions.story: I called `db.insert(record)` and now I want to undo just that one operation, not roll back an entire transaction. `#Transact` feels heavy for a single-op reversal.

options.name: Keep #Transact only; reject the undo keyword
options.detail: No new keyword. `#Transact` handles transactional rollback; rollback hooks handle per-operation reversal. The use case in the story is already expressible with a `#SingleUse` or rollback hook. Keeps the surface small; consistent with D-SUGAR5.

options.name: Add `undo` as sugar over #Transact
options.detail: Introduce `undo expr` as a built-in that calls the registered inverse of `expr`. Requires every reversible operation to register an inverse at the type level. Adds a keyword, a registration mechanism, and a new surface concept for a marginal gain over `#Transact` rollback hooks.

comparisons.note: Production systems use explicit transaction scopes for rollback rather than a generic language undo operator.
Ecto.Multi composes operations that can be rolled back as a unit. No bare `undo` keyword; rollback is a first-class concept in the transaction type.
comparisons.code:
Multi.new()
|> Multi.insert(:record, changeset)
|> Multi.run(:side_effect, fn _, _ -> … end)
|> Repo.transaction()

comparisons.note: SQL uses explicit `ROLLBACK` within a transaction; there is no single-statement undo outside a transaction. The analogy maps to `#Transact` + rollback hooks.

decisions.bestCurrent: Database transactions: Production systems use explicit transaction scopes for rollback rather than a generic language undo operator.
decisions.recommendation: Keep `#Transact` as the only reversal mechanism. A bare `undo` keyword is less precise and creates a second rollback path.

decisions.title: Should arbitrary Jet values carry per-value version and conversion history?
decisions.gist: This card bundles two distinct problems that should be decided separately. (a) General per-value history: every runtime value carries version and computation provenance regardless of type — this is expensive, overlaps D-TIMETRAVEL1 / D-PROVENANCE1, and is correctly rejected. (b) Schema migration transparency: after the #[Schema] decode pipeline runs migrations on a blob, the caller cannot observe whether migration occurred — a narrow gap in the ratified D-MIGRATE1 design, not addressed by time-travel or provenance cards. Option A correctly closes (a). No current option addresses (b). The owner is deciding (a) here; (b) needs a separate focused card or a D-MIGRATE2 follow-on.
decisions.explainer: Schema versioning covers the "what shape did this type have at version N" problem for serialized/published data. Per-value history means each runtime value carries provenance of which version it started as and every conversion step it passed through. This is a much heavier runtime model — it affects allocation, copy semantics, and GC pressure for all values, not just schema-registered ones. It also overlaps the time-travel-history card (D-TIMETRAVEL1) and the ask-why card (D-PROVENANCE1). Adding it risks building three overlapping provenance/history mechanisms (I8 concern). The schema migration system is the ratified canonical path for versioned data shapes.
decisions.story: I want to know whether the User object I'm holding was originally a v1 or v2 schema shape and whether it went through the auto-migration — without logging that manually every time.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) Option A does not resolve the story; migration transparency after decode is a real gap in D-MIGRATE1 that needs a focused follow-on card (Option E: migration-status tag at decode time, scoped to #PublishedSchema). (2) Option B's fatal flaw is viral type propagation, not runtime cost. (3) If B and D-PROVENANCE1-B both ship, there are two generic history wrappers — a concrete I8 violation. (4) The E6 defer (Option D) is appropriate for general per-value history but too coarse for schema decode transparency, which is needed as soon as schema migrations ship in production.

options.name: Schema-level versioning only; raise D-MIGRATE2 for decode transparency (recommended)
options.detail: Per-value version and computation history is rejected: extra allocation per value, niche use case, concrete I8 overlap with D-TIMETRAVEL1 and D-PROVENANCE1. The stated story ("did this User go through migration?") is a real gap but requires a narrower follow-on: D-MIGRATE2 targeting a `DecodeResult { value: T, migration: MigrationStatus }` decode-time annotation on #PublishedSchema types only. Zero overhead for non-migrated values. Raise D-MIGRATE2 alongside this decision.

options.name: Opt-in `Versioned<T>` wrapper type
options.detail: A core library Versioned<T> that wraps a value and accumulates conversion history. Fatal flaw: Versioned<User> and User are distinct types. Any function accepting User strips the wrapper silently; history is lost at the first API boundary. For version history to be visible anywhere, the entire call chain must propagate Versioned<T> — viral and impractical. Also risks I8 violation if D-PROVENANCE1 ships a Tracked<T> wrapper.

options.name: Defer to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not attach version/conversion history to values now. Revisit in Epoch 6 if migration/provenance workloads demand it. The migration-transparency story (Option A's D-MIGRATE2 follow-on) is still needed regardless; this option defers both.
options.code:
// Plain values carry no version history.
// Epoch 6 revisit: value-level migration/version provenance.

comparisons.note: Erlang hot-code upgrade supports versioned modules/process state conversion, not arbitrary value history everywhere.
No per-value version tracking; schema versioning is handled by serde with manual version fields or crates like serde_versioned.
Every datom carries a transaction-time timestamp — the DB is the history. Per-value history is the storage model, not a type attribute.

decisions.bestCurrent: Erlang: Erlang hot-code upgrade supports versioned modules/process state conversion, not arbitrary value history everywhere.
decisions.recommendation: Keep schema-level versioning only; raise D-MIGRATE2 for migration-transparency follow-on (Option A). Per-value general history is expensive and overlaps D-TIMETRAVEL1/D-PROVENANCE1.

decisions.title: Decode-time migration transparency: how do you ask a decoded value "were you migrated?"
decisions.gist: When old stored data is auto-upgraded during decode, how does a program find out it happened?
decisions.explainer: Jet already snapshots #PublishedSchema types and auto-applies `migration { }` blocks when decoding old data (D-MIGRATE1, D-MIGRATE2A-F). Today that upgrade is silent: the caller gets a fresh value and cannot tell it started life as an old version. D-SELFVER1=A rejected per-value history but ordered this narrower follow-up: a `DecodeResult { value: T, migration: MigrationStatus }` decode-time answer, zero overhead when nothing migrated, #PublishedSchema types only. (Raised as D-MIGRATE3 — the ordered name D-MIGRATE2 was already taken by the ratified migration-verb family D-MIGRATE2A-F. The struct name `DecodeResult` below is exactly as you prescribed; note it can read like a fallible Result at a glance — say the word if you want a different name, e.g. DecodeTrace.)
decisions.story: Betty runs a SaaS that has stored customer records as JSON for three years. She just shipped schema v3. Her nightly import decodes millions of records; migrations apply silently. Compliance asks her: "how many live records are still arriving in the v1 shape, and which customers do we need to re-export?" Betty has no way to answer — decode hides exactly the fact she needs.

options.name: Separate `decode_traced` — default decode untouched (recommended)
options.detail: One extra method beside `decode`: `json.decode_traced<T>(raw) -> DecodeResult<T> ?`, where `DecodeResult<T>` is a plain struct `{ value: T, migration: MigrationStatus }` and `MigrationStatus` carries `.migrated: Bool`, `.from` (source schema version), and `.steps` (applied migration names) — `.migrated` is false and the rest empty for fresh data and for non-#PublishedSchema types. `decode` stays exactly as it is — zero cost, zero API change for everyone not asking; one canonical way to ask (I8); same method on every codec (json/toml/yaml/csv) since they share the decode machinery. The honest cost: visibility is opt-in — a caller who reaches for plain `decode` silently misses the migration fact (Betty must know `decode_traced` exists), and the codec surface grows to two decode methods to learn.

options.name: `decode` always returns `DecodeResult` for #PublishedSchema types
options.detail: Decoding a #PublishedSchema type returns `DecodeResult<T>`; decoding a plain type returns `T`. Migration visibility is impossible to miss — but the return shape of the same function now depends on whether the type carries a marker: adding #PublishedSchema to an existing struct breaks every `decode` call site in the program (each must add `.value`). A beginner following a JSON tutorial hits the split the moment they adopt schema versioning.

options.name: Observer hook, no per-call value
options.detail: `schema.on_migration(fn (info) { ... })` registers a process-wide callback fired whenever any decode applies a migration; `decode` signatures never change. Good for metrics dashboards, useless for Betty's actual question — "was THIS value migrated?" — because the callback is disconnected from the call site that decoded it. Ambient global state also cuts against effect-visible design.

options.name: Decline — schema tooling only, no runtime answer
options.detail: Keep decode fully silent; point Betty at `jet schema status` (which describes the *code's* schema baseline, not the *data's*). Rejects the gap D-SELFVER1=A explicitly said is real. Listed for completeness.
options.code:
$ jet schema status
  UserRecord  v3 (published 2026-06-30)  2 migrations on file
# says nothing about which stored records are old — the gap stays.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust serde: nothing built in — teams hand-roll a `version: u32` field and match on it.
Protobuf: unknown/renamed fields resolve silently; no per-message answer.
Avro: reader/writer schema resolution is automatic and silent.
Django/Rails DB migrations: migrate the store once, so the question disappears — but Jet migrates lazily at decode, so the question is real and per-value.

decisions.title: Should Jet add proof-based elision of bounds checks for proven-safe indexing?
decisions.gist: Jet indexes are bounds-checked by default (safe, I1). This card asks whether to add a path where static proof of in-range lets the compiler elide the runtime check — zero-cost for proven-safe code, full safety by default.
decisions.explainer: The default array indexing `arr[i]` panics on out-of-bounds — safe. Experts writing tight inner loops want to assert "i is in range" and get unchecked access without writing `@unsafe`. The cleanest route is to tie elision to the refinement-types machinery: when the type of `i` carries a bound proof (e.g., `i: UInt where i < arr.len`), the compiler can drop the runtime check. This is distinct from `@unsafe` manual elision, which carries no proof obligation. It is gated on refinement types being designed and ratified first (D-REFINE1 / c73xs2f). Adding it as a standalone `@unchecked` attribute risks two escape hatches (I8).
decisions.story: My inner-loop index is already validated before the loop — I don't want to pay for a redundant bounds check 10 million times, and I don't want to write @unsafe just because the compiler can't see the proof yet.

options.name: Proof-carrying elision via refinement types (rec, gated)
options.detail: When an index value's type carries a static range proof (from the refinement-types system), sema elides the check. No new syntax, no second escape hatch. Gate this decision on refinement types landing first.

options.name: Checked-only always
options.detail: Keep bounds checks unconditional forever. Safe, simple, but forecloses expert zero-cost paths. Correct for most code; a real cost for hot numeric loops.
options.code: // no change; arr[i] always checks

options.name: @unsafe manual elision only
options.detail: Allow @unsafe blocks to use a raw `.get_unchecked(i)` call. Expert opt-in with explicit audit obligation. Works today without new machinery but requires an @audit annotation and carries undefined-behavior risk if wrong.

comparisons.note: SPARK can prove array index safety statically and remove checks under proof obligations.
Default indexing panics; `get_unchecked` is unsafe and requires the caller to prove safety manually.
SPARK proves array index safety at compile time via contracts; bounds checks are elided when the proof succeeds — same model as option A.
comparisons.code:
pragma Assert (I in Arr'Range);
X := Arr (I);  -- check elided after proof

decisions.bestCurrent: SPARK Ada: SPARK can prove array index safety statically and remove checks under proof obligations.
decisions.recommendation: Gate proof elision on refinement/proof machinery. Jet should not expose unchecked indexing as normal syntax; elision must be front-end-proven.

decisions.title: Should Jet add tracked uncertainty, freshness, and/or precision as first-class type dimensions?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether values should carry metadata dimensions like "this is an estimate", "this may be stale", or "this is accurate to ±5%". These are distinct axes. Option/taint already cover some failure and trust dimensions.
decisions.explainer: Three separate ideas are bundled: (1) numeric precision/tolerance (honest-numbers overlap); (2) freshness/staleness (TTL-secrets overlap); (3) general estimate vs exact (new). All three would require new type-level machinery or effect system extensions. Adding all three risks a proliferation of qualifiers on every value (I8: multiple overlapping mechanisms). Honest-numbers and TTL-secrets are already separate cards; freshness may belong there. A general qualified-value framework would be a large surface area that touches every numeric and IO type.
decisions.story: I'm pulling sensor readings with known tolerance — I want the type system to remind me that adding an exact price to a ±5% temperature doesn't give me an exact result.

options.name: Defer — let honest-numbers and TTL-secrets carry the axes they own
options.detail: Honest-numbers owns numeric precision; TTL-secrets owns staleness/freshness. Let those cards be decided first. A general uncertainty framework is too broad to ballot now without knowing what the specialty cards won't cover.
options.code: // no new surface; revisit after honest-numbers + ttl-secrets decisions

options.name: Pick one axis: freshness only
options.detail: Freshness ("is this value stale?") is the most concrete, most requested axis. Model it as a TTL marker on values that carry a timestamp and expire. Precision and estimate dimensions deferred.

options.name: General qualified-value framework
options.detail: A Qualified<T, Q> wrapper that lets any axis (estimate, stale, tolerance) be composed. Heavy design investment; risks becoming a parallel type system sitting on top of the real one (I8 concern).
options.code:
let temp: Qualified<Float, Tolerance(pct: 5)> = sensor.read()
let bad = temp + exact_val  // type error: mixing Tolerance + Exact

comparisons.note: F# units of measure track one numeric dimension at compile time; uncertainty/freshness usually stay domain-specific.
Libraries like `rounded-hw` track precision as a type parameter but require opt-in; no standard freshness axis.
comparisons.code:
import Numeric.Interval
let x = 1.0 ... 1.1 :: Interval Double

comparisons.note: Tracks dimensional correctness (meters, seconds) but not uncertainty/staleness — orthogonal to this proposal.

decisions.bestCurrent: F#: F# units of measure track one numeric dimension at compile time; uncertainty/freshness usually stay domain-specific.
decisions.recommendation: Defer the general framework. Jet should ship focused types first, then generalize only if repeated axes prove one mechanism.

decisions.title: Should Jet add failure-aware comprehensions that auto-skip failed elements?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether collection-building expressions should have a mode that silently drops elements whose computation failed, collecting only the successes. Today there is no comprehension syntax; the iterator/adapter set is the planned path.
decisions.explainer: Auto-skipping failures in a comprehension is equivalent to `filter_map` with a fallible transform: keep elements where the function returns a value, drop the rest. Adding implicit skip-on-failure as comprehension syntax would be a second way to mean the same thing (I8 concern). The explicit adapter path — `iter.filter_map(fn)` or `iter.try_collect()` — is readable, composable, and doesn't hide control flow. Hidden skip-on-failure makes bugs silent: a whole class of elements can vanish with no error. This card is primarily about whether implicit skip warrants special syntax, not whether the operation exists.
decisions.story: I'm parsing a list of user-supplied URLs — some are malformed. I want the valid ones and want to silently drop the rest, without writing a manual loop.

options.name: Explicit filter_map / try_collect adapter (rec)
options.detail: Add `filter_map` and `try_collect` as standard iterator adapters under D-ITER1. No new comprehension syntax. Callers that want to skip errors call `.filter_map(fn)` explicitly — the intent is visible in the code.
options.code:
let valid_prices: [Price] = raw
    .filter_map(fn(s) -> Price? { parse_price(s) })
    .collect()

options.name: Comprehension syntax with implicit skip
options.detail: A `[expr for x in coll try]` or `[expr for x in coll catch skip]` form that drops failures. New syntax for something `filter_map` already expresses; hides control flow from the reader.
options.code: [parse_price(s) for s in raw try]   // silently drops bad entries

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Decide D-ITER1 (iterators) first. If filter_map lands there, this card is resolved without new syntax.
options.code: // no action until D-ITER1 settles the iterator adapter set

comparisons.note: List comprehensions with a conditional achieve the same thing explicitly; there's no built-in skip-on-exception in comprehensions (that would be a try/except in the expression).
comparisons.code: [parse(x) for x in raw if is_valid(x)]

comparisons.note: `filter_map` is the idiomatic path; `collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()` is `try_collect`. Both are explicit — no hidden skip.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a universal typed "hole" value that propagates through computation instead of failing?
decisions.gist: The decision asks whether Jet should add an absent-value type that propagates silently through expressions. Jet already has propagating absence: `?.` chains through member access (S71) and `?` propagates failures up call stacks. The specific gap is binary arithmetic operators — `T? + T?` does not auto-lift today. A universal absent-propagating type would violate I8 (second absence mechanism alongside T?), conflict with D-VECARITH1 (closed arithmetic operators), and silently bypass D-DIST3 distinct-type safety checks. The ergonomic gap for data-pipeline code is real but closable through T? core library combinators (zip/lift2) with no language change — the question is whether to ship those combinators (option E) or accept the current verbosity.
decisions.explainer: Option<T> and Result<T,E> make failure explicit: the caller must unwrap or propagate with `?`. A universal hole that flows through arithmetic and function calls is a different model — it defers failure to wherever the hole is eventually consumed. This is exactly what SQL NULL does, and the propagation behavior is the source of the most common class of SQL bugs. It also competes directly with Option<T> (I8). The main argument for it is ergonomics in data-pipeline code where many values may be absent; the counter-argument is that it hides which expression produced the hole.
decisions.story: I'm computing a derived column across a dataframe where some source cells are absent — I want the absence to flow through math without wrapping every step in `if let`.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) Gist misframes the question; Jet already has absence propagation via `?.` and `?`. The real question is whether binary arithmetic operators should lift over T?. (2) Option B conflicts with D-VECARITH1=A (arithmetic operators are closed to compiler-provided built-ins) and silently voids D-DIST3 distinct-type safety (Hole<Usd> + Hole<Eur> would propagate where Usd + Eur is E0127). (3) "Hole" is already Jet vocabulary for #Todo typed placeholders (D-TOOL2) — Option B must be renamed. (4) Options C and D are indistinguishable without naming a concrete gate event; Option C should explicitly name D-TABLE1 as its gate. (5) Option E (Option.zip/lift2 combinators) closes the expert data-pipeline ergonomic gap without new types, no I8 cost, and no D-VECARITH1 conflict.

options.name: No hole; ship Option.zip/lift2 combinators for multi-absent arithmetic (recommended)
options.detail: A universal absent-propagating value would add a second absence mechanism alongside T? (I8 violation), silently void D-DIST3 distinct-type safety (Hole<Usd> + Hole<Eur> bypasses E0127), and require a D-VECARITH1 exception to wire arithmetic operators. The ergonomic gap for data-pipeline code is real but closable through core library combinators. A combinator is a small function that combines optional values without new syntax: `zip` turns two optionals into one optional pair only when both are present; `map` transforms the present value; `lift2` applies a two-argument function only when both inputs are present and returns `null` otherwise. These keep propagation visible and type-checked.

options.name: Defer to D-TABLE1 gate
options.detail: The strongest use case is column-absent semantics in table/dataframe operations. Gate this decision on D-TABLE1 (table/dataframe core library design): if the table library requires a language-level absent value, that design surfaces it with real constraints; if it can be built on T? + combinators, this decision closes as A. Concrete gate, not vague deferral.
options.code:
// No action now.
// Reopen D-HOLE1 when D-TABLE1 reaches the Decide lane.

options.name: Typed absent value that propagates through arithmetic
options.detail: Rejected. A compiler-built-in absent type that propagates through arithmetic requires either (a) wiring arithmetic as a compiler built-in (reversing D-VECARITH1=A) or (b) Absent<Usd> + Absent<Eur> propagating where Usd + Eur is E0127 (voiding D-DIST3). Two absence mechanisms violates I8. The D-NUMOPS1 interaction (does propagation short-circuit before or after overflow trap?) is unspecified.

comparisons.note: R and pandas propagate `NA` through data operations, excellent for tables but dangerous as a universal language value.
NULL propagates silently through every expression. This is the canonical example of how invisible propagation creates bugs (NULL comparisons are always false/unknown).
comparisons.code: SELECT price * qty FROM orders  -- NULL * 5 = NULL silently

comparisons.note: Nullable types `T?` require explicit handling at each step; the compiler enforces it. Closer to Jet's current Option model.

decisions.bestCurrent: R / pandas: R and pandas propagate `NA` through data operations, excellent for tables but dangerous as a universal language value.
decisions.recommendation: No universal hole. Ship `Option.zip`, `map`, and `lift2` combinators so multi-optional data flows stay concise without adding a second absence mechanism.

decisions.title: Should Jet add runtime value provenance tracking so you can ask a value where it came from?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether values should carry a provenance chain at runtime. Importantly: D-REPLAY1=A (the commonly cited deferral target) is a compile-time soundness marker only — the runtime replay harness is post-v1, so "defer to replay" does not close this gap today. D-TAINT1=A is a label-tagging system (not a data-flow graph), so "tie to taint" requires reworking the ratified taint design. The narrow stated story (NaN from sensor input) has a zero-cost option via IEEE 754 NaN payload tagging that bypasses all of these dependencies. This card should be decided alongside D-TIMETRAVEL1 to avoid two parallel opt-in instrumentation mechanisms for the same "where did this value come from?" question (I8).
decisions.explainer: Provenance tracking means every value carries a graph of its origin: which function, which input values, which source location. At runtime this is expensive (extra allocation and pointer-chasing on every operation) unless it is debug-only or opt-in. The feature overlaps taint tracking (which tracks data flow for security purposes), the record-and-replay card (D-REPLAY1, which records full program execution), and the time-travel-history card (D-TIMETRAVEL1). Building a standalone provenance system risks a third overlapping mechanism for the same "where did this value come from" question (I8). Taint tracking tied to security already answers a subset; record-and-replay answers the rest for debugging.
decisions.story: I got a NaN in my physics sim. I want to point at the NaN and ask "which input caused this" rather than adding print statements everywhere.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) Option A relies on D-REPLAY1 runtime, which is explicitly deferred to post-v1 — the recommendation is currently a no-op. (2) The physics-sim story uses sensor I/O, making the function ineligible for #Replayable; Option A structurally cannot answer the stated story. (3) Option C conflicts with D-TAINT1=A (label system, not a graph). (4) D-PROVENANCE1 and D-TIMETRAVEL1 are structurally duplicate ballots and should be decided together to avoid a second opt-in instrumentation mechanism (I8). (5) Option E (NaN/poison payload tagging in debug builds) targets the stated story with zero release overhead and no dependency on any unratified card — it should be added and evaluated. (6) Option D's Epoch 6 defer prerequisites: D-REPLAY1 runtime harness shipped + D-TIMETRAVEL1 ratified.

options.name: NaN payload tagging in debug builds + defer general provenance to Epoch 6 (recommended)
options.detail: IEEE 754 f64 NaN has 51 unused payload bits. In debug builds (`jet build --debug-nan-origins`), the compiler stamps a compact source-location index and operation ID into NaN payloads when NaN is produced. A debug-only built-in `value.origin()` decodes the payload to a file/line/operation string. Zero allocation, zero overhead in release, no new type mechanism, no I8 conflict, no dependency on D-REPLAY1 or taint. Directly addresses the stated story (NaN in physics sim, sensor.read()) — the #Replayable function marker cannot apply to sensor I/O, but NaN tagging can. Constrained to float NaN; general value provenance graphs defer to Epoch 6 alongside D-TIMETRAVEL1 ratification.

options.name: Opt-in `#Track` marker on `let` bindings — debug-build instrumentation
options.detail: A `#Track` marker on a let binding instruments that variable to record its computation tree in debug builds. Uses existing marker syntax (#PascalCase, D-ATTR1). Zero release overhead; no type-system contamination. Note: let-binding markers are not established grammar — D-ATTR1/ATTR2 attach to type/function/field declarations, not `let` bindings. This is a new grammar production. Overlaps D-TIMETRAVEL1 option B; must be decided alongside that card to avoid two separate instrumentation mechanisms.

options.name: Defer all provenance to Epoch 6
options.detail: No provenance mechanism now. Prerequisites for reconsideration: D-REPLAY1 runtime harness ratified and implemented; D-TIMETRAVEL1 decided; D-IFC1 decided; debugger card ratified. If all four exist and together answer provenance adequately, closes as superseded. Stopgap: recommend Option A's NaN tagging for the narrow physics-sim story even if general provenance is deferred.
options.code:
// Use taint/replay/debug metadata for narrow provenance now.
// Epoch 6 revisit: runtime value provenance graphs.

comparisons.note: Security taint systems track source labels through values, but full provenance on all values is expensive and noisy.
lineapy builds a computation graph of values post-hoc for data science notebooks; it's a library, not a language feature, and incurs significant overhead.
comparisons.code:
import lineapy
lineapy.save(result, "result")  # stores provenance graph

comparisons.note: Provenance can be modeled via Writer, but it's explicit and opt-in — every function in the chain must propagate the log.
comparisons.code:
import Control.Monad.Writer
compute :: Writer [String] Float
compute = do
  tell ["used sensor"]
  return 42.0

decisions.bestCurrent: Taint-tracking systems: Security taint systems track source labels through values, but full provenance on all values is expensive and noisy.
decisions.recommendation: Ship NaN payload tagging in debug builds for the stated story; defer general value provenance graphs to Epoch 6 (Option A). Option A as previously written (defer to D-REPLAY1) is not actionable — D-REPLAY1=A is a compile-time marker only, not a runtime harness.

decisions.title: Should Jet build a standalone per-variable value history for time-travel debugging?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether the language/runtime should build a standalone per-variable value history mechanism for time-travel debugging. The ballot's current framing — "fold into D-REPLAY1" — is based on a factual error: D-REPLAY1=A is a compile-time static function annotation, not a runtime execution capture system. The replay runtime is explicitly deferred post-v1 with no decision card. The real question is: given that a replay runtime does not exist and is unratified, should Jet build any per-variable history mechanism before that runtime arrives, and if so, at what layer (language surface, debugger protocol, or block annotation)?
decisions.explainer: Per-variable history is what time-travel debuggers provide: step backward through execution and inspect what a variable held at each point. The record-and-replay card (D-REPLAY1) covers this by recording the full execution trace deterministically and letting a debugger replay it. Building a separate value-history capture mechanism alongside record-and-replay would be a second mechanism for the same job (I8). The ask-why card (D-PROVENANCE1) also overlaps. The right call is to decide D-REPLAY1; if deterministic replay ships, time-travel debugging is a UI feature of the debugger, not a language-level mechanism.
decisions.story: My loop variable changed to an unexpected value at iteration 47 of 1000 — I want to rewind and see what it was at iteration 46 without adding a Vec to capture it manually.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): FACTUAL ERROR: The explainer and Option A state D-REPLAY1 "covers this by recording the full execution trace deterministically." This is wrong. D-REPLAY1=A is a compile-time static function marker (#Replayable fn); its card explicitly says "The runtime record/replay harness is SEPARATE post-v1 work." The same error appears in D-PROVENANCE1. GRAMMAR GAP: Option B's `#[History(cap: 100)]` on a let binding is a new grammar production class (statement-level/binding-level markers) not present in any ratified decision. PLATFORM RESTRICTION: rr requires x86-64 Linux; WinDbg TTD requires Windows x64 — unavailable on macOS, ARM, WASM, embedded. Missing Option E (DAP extension, no language surface, all platforms) provides the debugging experience without touching the language surface or creating an I8 conflict.

options.name: Extend DAP with `variableHistory` request — no language surface (recommended)
options.detail: Extend the debug adapter protocol (DAP) that Jet's debugger implements with a `variableHistory` request type. The debugger records variable writes as it steps through execution; the DAP response returns the write history for a given variable in the current session. No language surface, no marker, no grammar change, no new invariant. Works on all platforms (macOS, ARM, WASM, embedded) — unlike rr (x86-64 Linux only) or WinDbg TTD (Windows x64 only). Cost is borne only during debug sessions; zero in release. Different from full replay: the debugger drives capture granularity and timing; no full execution trace required. Implementable before the replay runtime exists.

options.name: Block-scoped `#Trace(window: N)` annotation
options.detail: A `#Trace(window: N)` annotation on a block (not a variable binding — consistent with how Jet uses block-level markers elsewhere) keeps a rolling buffer of the last N writes to every variable inside. Zero cost outside annotated blocks. Works on all platforms. Does not require the replay runtime. Differs from binding-level history (Option B in the old ballot): the marker is on a code block (established grammar), not a variable binding (unestablished grammar). New grammar for block annotations may still be required; validate against current parser before proceeding.

options.name: Defer to Epoch 6
options.detail: No per-variable history now. Revisit in Epoch 6 after replay/debugger infrastructure matures. Time-travel debugging via DAP (Option A) can land independently; full replay-based stepping is a separate, longer-horizon item.

comparisons.note: Elm time-travel debugging works because state updates are messages in a pure architecture.
Record-and-replay for native code; any variable's value at any point is inspectable by replaying — exactly what option A describes.
comparisons.code:
rr record ./my_program
rr replay  # then use gdb to step backward

comparisons.note: Elm's debugger records every message and model state; rewind is built into the dev server. A language-level property, not a separate annotation.
comparisons.code: -- enabled by `elm reactor`; no code annotation needed

decisions.bestCurrent: Elm: Elm time-travel debugging works because state updates are messages in a pure architecture.
decisions.recommendation: Extend the Jet debugger's DAP implementation with a `variableHistory` request — no language surface, all platforms (Option A). Option A as previously written (fold into D-REPLAY1) is not actionable: D-REPLAY1=A is a compile-time static annotation; the runtime replay harness is explicitly deferred post-v1.

decisions.title: Should Jet propagate latency deadlines implicitly through calls via the structured-concurrency context?
decisions.gist: This card asks whether a deadline or timeout set at a task boundary should flow automatically down the call graph — cancelling work when the deadline is exceeded — without callers threading a deadline parameter manually.
decisions.explainer: Structured concurrency (D-NURSERY1) gives Jet task-scoped lifetime management via scoped task groups. The #Context marker already carries cross-cutting values. Deadline propagation is a natural fit: a scoped task group or ancestor context sets a deadline; every I/O wait, channel wait, timer wait, and task join inside checks it and cancels if exceeded. The alternative is explicit deadline parameters, which forces every function in the call graph to accept and forward a deadline. A dedicated Deadline<T> type risks becoming a second propagation channel beside #Context (I8). Exact task-scope spelling is decided by D-TASKSCOPE1.
decisions.story: My API handler has a 200 ms SLA. I want every downstream DB call and HTTP fetch it spawns to automatically cancel if the 200 ms window closes — without passing a deadline parameter into every helper function.

options.name: Deadline on #Context, enforced at wait/IO points (recommended)
options.detail: A parent task, scoped task group, or request handler sets a deadline on #Context. Child tasks inherit it automatically. I/O waits, channel waits, timers, task joins, and explicit cancellation checks observe it. No parameter threading. Pairs cleanly with D-NURSERY1 cancellation.

options.name: Explicit deadline parameter
options.detail: Every function that can wait accepts a deadline parameter. Visible and easy to override per call, but every helper must forward it and one missed parameter silently breaks cancellation propagation.

options.name: Defer until task-scope/#Context surface is ratified
options.detail: Deadline propagation is only well-defined once the task-scope/context model is ratified. This avoids premature spelling but leaves the networking/runtime plan incomplete.
options.code:
// no deadline propagation yet
// call graph can wait forever unless each API invents its own timeout

comparisons.note: Go `context.Context` carries cancellation and deadlines through call graphs and blocking ops check it.
context.Context carries a deadline/cancel signal; every function in the call graph must accept and forward ctx. Correct but verbose — option B's model.
comparisons.code:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parent, 200*time.Millisecond)
defer cancel()
result, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, query)

comparisons.note: withTimeout cancels the entire coroutine scope automatically; inner coroutines inherit the deadline without explicit threading — closest to option A.

decisions.bestCurrent: Kotlin withTimeout inherits through coroutine scope; Go context proves the value of deadline propagation but makes every call thread ctx manually.
decisions.recommendation: Put deadlines on Jet #Context and enforce them at I/O/wait points. Jet improves on Go by making propagation part of structured concurrency instead of another parameter to forget.

decisions.title: Should Jet add language-level support for approximate algorithms, or keep it a library concern?
decisions.gist: Some algorithms trade accuracy for speed under a policy or budget — HyperLogLog for cardinality, t-digest for quantiles, random sampling. The question is whether Jet provides any language machinery for this or leaves it entirely to library code. Currently nothing exists; this is a new idea with no card.
decisions.explainer: A language-level approximation layer would need some way to express accuracy budgets and propagate them — touching the type system, possibly the comptime system, and the standard library. A library-only answer is self-contained and additive: ship HyperLogLog, t-digest, reservoir sampler as stdlib modules with plain Jet types. The language-level route risks a second mechanism for numeric precision alongside the 'honest-numbers' direction and the budgets-as-types card, which would pressure I8. The library path respects I8 and does not require any new surface.
decisions.story: I'm building a dashboard that counts distinct users across billions of events. I need HyperLogLog — I don't want to implement it myself, and I don't want the language to secretly approximate things I didn't ask it to approximate.

options.name: Library-only (no language feature)
options.detail: Ship HyperLogLog, t-digest, reservoir sampler, and CountMinSketch as stdlib modules. No new language surface. Users pick the right sketch for their accuracy/speed tradeoff explicitly. Respects I8 — no second numeric-precision mechanism.
options.code:
import std.sketch.HyperLogLog

let hll = HyperLogLog.new(error_rate: 0.01)
events.each(fn(e) { hll.insert(e.user_id) })
println(hll.estimate())  // prints: ~2_847_391

options.name: Policy/budget-driven auto-approximation
options.detail: Add a language mechanism (annotation or block) that lets code declare an accuracy budget, and the compiler or runtime swaps in an approximate algorithm. Requires new language surface, interacts with the type system and honest-numbers direction, and risks violating I8 by creating a second precision-control mechanism.

options.name: Defer — decide after budgets-as-types and honest-numbers land
options.detail: Both budgets-as-types and honest-numbers will constrain what a language-level approximation mechanism can look like. Defer this card until those designs are stable so we don't have to rework it.

comparisons.note: Pure library: users import sketch types explicitly. No language approximation machinery. The dominant industry pattern.
Library-only: Reservoir, t-digest, etc. as plain structs. No language feature.

decisions.title: Should Jet automatically parallelize proven-pure maps/folds, or keep parallelism explicit?
decisions.gist: Sequential-looking maps and folds could be run in parallel when the compiler proves they are pure. D-REACT1 already rejected hidden async/reactive machinery in favor of explicit parallelism. This card asks whether auto-parallelism on pure pipelines is a different enough case to reconsider, or whether explicit par_* adapters are sufficient.
decisions.explainer: D-REACT1 established that Jet rejects hidden machinery that makes sequential-looking code run differently than it appears. Auto-parallelism is another instance of hidden machinery: a map that looks sequential would actually fork threads. This undermines predictability and debuggability, which the beginner experience depends on. The explicit adapter path (par_map, par_fold) is fully consistent with D-REACT1, keeps the performance model visible, and satisfies I8 — there is one way to mean parallel. The opt-in auto-parallel path requires the compiler to prove purity soundly, which interacts with the effects/dataflow system (not yet designed) and risks a silent footgun if the proof is wrong.
decisions.story: I have a list of 10 million records and I want to transform them in parallel. I don't want to think about threads — but I also don't want the language to silently decide my code is parallel when I'm reading it as sequential.

options.name: Explicit par_* adapters only (no hidden auto-parallelism)
options.detail: Ship par_map, par_fold, par_filter as explicit stdlib adapters. Sequential code is always sequential. Parallelism is always visible at the call site. Consistent with D-REACT1 and predictable for beginners.
options.code:
// Explicit parallelism — user chooses
let totals = orders
  .par_map(fn(o) o.subtotal * tax_rate)
  .par_fold(0.0, fn(a, b) a + b)
println(totals)  // parallel, visible

options.name: Opt-in auto-parallel on proven-pure pipelines
options.detail: Allow a pragma or block that permits the compiler to parallelize pure pipelines automatically. Requires a sound purity proof system (depends on effects/dataflow design). Opt-in means it isn't the default, which partially satisfies I1 — but it still makes code behavior non-obvious to a reader without knowing the pragma is active.

options.name: Defer — decide after effects/dataflow is designed
options.detail: Sound purity proof for auto-parallelism depends on the effects/dataflow system. Deferring keeps options open without committing to a surface that may need to change.
options.code:
// Status quo: no auto-parallelism; explicit par_map available
let results = items.par_map(fn(x) expensive(x))

comparisons.note: Explicit parallelism via par/pseq combinators or the parallel-strategies library. No hidden auto-parallelism in the language; all concurrency is opt-in.
comparisons.code:
import Control.Parallel.Strategies
result = parMap rseq transform items

comparisons.note: Auto-parallelism via @threads on loops — opt-in macro, explicit at call site. Not truly automatic; user annotates.

decisions.title: Should Jet adopt content-addressed definition identity (Unison-style)?
decisions.gist: In Unison, a definition's identity is a hash of its body — not its name. Renaming is free; dependencies are immutable by hash. Jet currently identifies definitions by name within files (file-is-program model). This idea would replace or supplement name-based identity with content hashing. New idea, no card.
decisions.explainer: Content-addressed definitions conflict with Jet's file-is-program model where the source file is the authoritative artifact. A hash-based identity layer would require a persistent codebase database, a rename/alias management system, and tooling that understands both the hash identity and the human-readable name. This is a deep architectural commitment — not a surface feature. It also interacts with the build cache (content-addressed build cache card) and the codemods system. The benefit (free renames, immutable dependency identity) is real but Unison's model is controversial in practice: the codebase-as-database workflow is unfamiliar and tool support outside Unison's own tooling is thin. For v1 this is out of scope and likely incompatible with the file-is-program instinct.
decisions.story: I renamed a core function and now I have to fix 40 import paths. If the function's identity were its body hash rather than its name, the rename would be an alias move and nothing would break.

options.name: Reject for v1 — incompatible with file-is-program model
options.detail: Content-addressed identity requires a codebase database and breaks the assumption that source files are self-contained. Reject for v1. Invest in good codemods / LSP rename instead — that solves the pain without the architectural cost.

options.name: Adopt as an underlying identity layer
options.detail: Add a content-hash layer below the name layer: names are aliases over hashes, and the package system tracks definitions by hash. A large architectural commitment; requires resolving the file-vs-database tension before any other design work can proceed.

options.name: Far-horizon research — no current card
options.detail: Treat this as a far-horizon idea: log it, don't design it now, revisit post-v1 when the codebase model, package system, and build cache are stable. Lower risk than A while keeping the door open.
options.code:
// No current impact. Status quo applies.
// Revisit after: file-is-program model, jetpack, build cache finalized.

comparisons.note: Definitions identified by hash of their AST. Renaming is a metadata operation. Requires the Unison Codebase Manager — no plain text files as the source of truth.
comparisons.code:
-- Unison: renaming is an alias, not a rewrite
move.term math.square math.sq

comparisons.note: Build outputs are content-addressed by input hash. Works because Nix has a single central store. Jet's module/file model is less centralized.
comparisons.code:
# Nix store path encodes content hash
/nix/store/3a7f...-my-package-1.0

decisions.title: How should Jet expose `core / alloc / std` runtime layers to beginners and experts?
decisions.gist: Jet should infer the lowest runtime layer by default, while experts need a visible ceiling they can enforce.
decisions.explainer: Without ring layering, every core library import implicitly requires a heap and OS syscalls. That blocks embedded targets and makes the 'same code from server to microcontroller' goal impossible without ad-hoc #[no_std] patches. The three-ring model (proven by Rust's core/alloc/std split) solves this cleanly: code written against core compiles anywhere; code that imports std is desktop/server only. Jet would express this as platform capabilities gated by which ring a module declares. This interacts with the explicit-allocation card (what 'alloc' means in Jet), the pack.jet platform target field, and the aarch64/QEMU CI work (c57). The ring declaration would live in pack.jet, not in source syntax — no new markers needed.
decisions.story: Doris writes a fixed-point math package for servers and microcontrollers. Most users should get portability automatically, but Doris wants CI to fail if someone imports heap or OS APIs by accident.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) Critical terminology collision: "ring" already means first-party core.* library packages throughout Tower (D-CORENS1); the pack.jet `ring = "core"` field introduces a second contradictory meaning — I8 violation that must be resolved before any implementation. (2) The alloc/core boundary as written ("heap, no OS") does not match Jet's ratified allocation model (D-REGION1=A+B allows arena allocation on bare-metal within what would be called the core ring). (3) Option E (inferred ring ceiling from imports) would eliminate the beginner-default fragmentation problem entirely and should be evaluated before ratifying any explicit-declaration approach. (4) Option A omits I4 compliance (E0410 must be in diagnostics.md with what/why/fix and a ui snapshot). (5) Option C's named gate conditions are already ratified; a specific unratified card ID is needed to make it actionable.

options.name: Infer by default + optional expert ceiling (recommended)
options.detail: Default mode is magic: the compiler infers the minimum layer from imports (`core`, `alloc`, or `std`) and users write no package field. Expert mode adds an optional package ceiling such as `layer: core` or `layer: alloc`; imports above that ceiling are errors. This gives beginner portability with expert visibility/control, and avoids the old "ring" term collision by naming the capability axis `layer`.

options.name: Explicit layer required for packages
options.detail: Every package declares `layer: core`, `layer: alloc`, or `layer: std`. This maximizes visibility but makes beginners choose a target-layer concept before they need it and can fragment libraries that would otherwise be inferred correctly.

options.name: Inferred layer plus per-import assertions
options.detail: No package-wide field. Experts pin individual imports with assertions such as `use core.fs at std` or `use core.math at core`. This makes each capability edge visible near use, but repeats policy across files and is weaker than a package-wide ceiling for CI.
options.code:
use core.math at core
use core.collections at alloc
use core.fs at std

options.name: Target profile controls layer only
options.detail: Do not put layer in package metadata. The selected build target (`embedded`, `freestanding`, hosted) decides what imports are legal. Simple for authors, but experts cannot declare that a library is intended to stay core-compatible across all targets.
options.code:
jet build --target thumbv7m
// compiler rejects imports requiring alloc/std for that target

comparisons.note: `core`/`alloc`/`std` are explicit crates and `#![no_std]` is an expert-visible ceiling.
Imports infer the minimum layer; `pack.jet` may set a maximum.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust’s `core`/`alloc`/`std` split lets libraries target kernels, embedded, and hosted apps.
decisions.recommendation: Use inferred default plus optional expert ceiling (Option A). It keeps beginner magic while giving library authors the explicit control the owner asked for. Rename the concept to `layer` to avoid the existing `ring package` terminology collision.

log.text: Owner asked for inferred magic plus expert visibility/control; ballot updated to make the hybrid the recommended option.
