options.name: Warn only (engines-style)
options.detail: Mismatch prints a warning naming the pinned version, then proceeds with the installed jet. No fetch machinery, but the warning scrolls past and Hank still gets the forty errors — Node's engines shows exactly how this decays into a convention nobody trusts.
options.code:
$ jet run .
warning: project pins jet 0.4, installed is 0.6.1 — output may not build
error[E0xxx]: unknown spelling `…` (x40)

options.name: Dev-shell only — toolchain is an env.jet package
options.detail: The toolchain pins only inside the dev shell: env.jet lists jet@0.4 in packages; `jet dev` / `jetpack enter` use it; a bare `jet run` outside the shell uses whatever is installed. Consistent with 'env.jet is dev shell only', but the beginner path — clone, `jet run` — is exactly the path left unprotected.

options.name: No pin — editions carry compatibility
options.detail: pkg.jet declares `edition: 2027`; one jet binary keeps every edition's grammar alive, so new compilers always build old code. This is the Rust editions bet — but editions cover surface grammar, not stdlib behavior, codegen differences, or pre-1.0 breakage, and they obligate the compiler to carry every historical grammar forever. Editions remain a good complementary idea after 1.0; they are not a substitute for a pin while the language moves fast.

comparisons.note: The gold standard: go.mod's toolchain directive; any Go ≥1.21 auto-downloads and re-executes the pinned toolchain. Clone-and-run just works.
rust-toolchain.toml; works, but only because a separate manager (rustup) intercepts every invocation — a resident middleman jetpack's no-daemon law avoids.
engines is warn-only and widely ignored; teams bolt on nvm/.nvmrc by convention. The cautionary tale for option B.
Flake pin: exact and hermetic, but the pin lives outside the language's own manifest and costs the whole Nix mental model.

decisions.title: Nested variant groups in `enum`: can a variant hold sub-variants so a group name matches its whole subtree?
decisions.gist: Can enum variants nest into groups, so testing `.Fire` also matches `.Fire.Burn` and `.Fire.Scald`?
decisions.explainer: Cross-system code constantly needs a name-tree: damage kinds, permission scopes, diagnostic categories, feature flags. UE ships this as stringly GameplayTags (Damage.Fire.Burn) matched by ancestry, which composes beautifully but renames break silently and there is no counting (two stuns applied, one removed, still stunned). Jet already has closed enums, leading-dot values (D-ENUMDOT1), and the ==-pattern law (S31). This decision adds one axis to `enum`: a variant may group sub-variants, and a group name matches its subtree in == and match arms. No new keyword — the `tag` spelling was killed for colliding with the ratified D-QUAL2 tag qualifier and minting a second closed-name mechanism beside enum (I8). Also on the table: a core `Bag<T>` counted multiset (sibling of Set) so `add`/`remove` counts correctly, and whether `Bag.has(.Fire)` accepts a subtree pattern as sugar for the `any` closure.
decisions.story: Hank is building the damage system for a roguelike. He has two physical damage kinds, two fire kinds, and cold, and armor should soak any physical hit. Today he lists every physical leaf by hand in the armor check; the day he adds a pierce variant he forgets to update it and armor silently stops working against it. He also tracks active damage-over-time in a Set, so a second fire tick and one cure leaves the target un-burning when it should still burn.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: it is the one path that makes the tree a compile-time fact (exhaustiveness, rename-safe, LSP-completable) using machinery beginners already know, with counting handled by a plain core container; the `has` sugar (D) can follow as a library call once A ships. · This ballot was minted from docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Nested variant groups, leaf-only payloads (recommended)
options.detail: A variant may enclose sub-variants in `{ }`; a group name matches its whole subtree in == and match arms; exhaustiveness is checked at the group level; payloads live on leaves only. Ships alongside a core `Bag<T>` counted multiset so add/remove counts correctly. `Bag.has` stays an explicit `any` closure for subtree queries. Renames become refactors, the LSP completes every `.` level, and a value is always a leaf.

options.name: Enum-of-enums (Rust-style nesting, no new syntax)
options.detail: No grammar change: model the tree as separate enums carried as payloads. Ancestor tests become `d is .Physical(_)`; you carry a second type name per group and there is no subtree-level exhaustiveness or dot-path value. Cheapest surface, but the group name is not a value and the compiler cannot see the tree.

options.name: Flat enum + naming convention (status quo, reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Keep `PhysicalBlunt`, `FireBurn` and match ancestry by hand with an else arm. Honest baseline: no new mechanism, but every subtree check is hand-maintained and silently rots when a leaf is added, and there is no counted container so multiset bugs stay.

options.name: Grouping plus subtree-pattern sugar on `Bag.has` (A, extended)
options.detail: Everything in A, and additionally `Bag.has(.Fire)` accepts a subtree pattern as sugar for the `any` closure, so counted-multiset ancestor queries read as one call. More reach, one more thing to learn on the container; the sugar must be exactly equivalent to the closure to avoid a second meaning (I8).
options.code:
active.add(.Fire.Burn)
active.has(.Fire)        // sugar for active.any((t) => t == .Fire)  -> true
active.has(.Fire.Scald) // false

comparisons.note: Swift nests enums inside enums; ancestor matching is by hand (`if case .physical = d`), no subtree exhaustiveness.
GameplayTags are stringly dot-paths matched by ancestry (`.HasTag("Damage.Fire")` catches `Damage.Fire.Burn`). Renames break silently; no compile check.
No grouping axis; nest enum-in-enum and match with a wildcard arm. No subtree name, no counting container in std.
comparisons.code:
enum Damage { Physical(Physical), Fire(Fire), Cold }
match d { Damage::Physical(_) => armor(), _ => {} }

comparisons.note: Discriminated unions with a shared prefix or a nested `kind` field; ancestry is a manual string `startsWith` or a switch group.

decisions.title: `@[Patchable]` derive: generate a typed `T.Patch` change-value you can hold, diff, merge and serialize?
decisions.gist: Should a derive generate a typed `T.Patch` — an all-optional twin of a struct — that you can hold, apply later, diff, merge and log?
decisions.explainer: Jet's ratified `.{ }` copy-update (D-COPYUPDATE1) applies a change now. But a change you hold for later — an undo stack, an audit log, an API PATCH body, optimistic-UI predict-then-reconcile — is hand-rolled per type today: an optional-field struct plus a merge function, written again for every record. UE's insight (GameplayEffect) is that a change should be a data value: previewable, loggable, revertible, sendable. This decision picks a derive on the `@` contract plane (like `@Codable`) that generates a nested `T.Patch` struct whose fields are all optional, plus `apply`/`diff`/`merge`, Codable by construction. No new expression syntax — you build a Patch with ordinary `.{ }`. Killed already: relative magnitudes (`level: +1`), which are literal semantics found nowhere else; `invert(base)`, a footgun valid only against its exact base; duration/stacking policy, which is library speculation.
decisions.story: Doris maintains the employee directory for a mid-size firm. It has an undo button and an audit log. For every kind of record she writes an optional-field struct and a merge function by hand, once per type, forever; and the audit log stores freeform JSON that slowly drifts out of sync with the real field names. She wants one canonical 'here is the change' value she can apply, reverse, and log without writing the plumbing again.
decisions.inWild:
@[Patchable]
struct Employee {
    level: Int
    title: String
    team: String
}

promote :: Employee.Patch.{ level: 4, title: "Senior" }   // ordinary .{ } — set fields = the change
emp2    :: emp.apply(promote)
undo    :: Employee.diff(emp2, emp)      // the patch that gets you back
both    :: promote.merge(relocate)       // right side wins on overlap
audit.log(promote)                       // Patch is Codable by construction
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: one canonical, typed, serializable change value (I8) that reuses `.{ }`, pattern-matching and Codable, and kills the hand-rolled-patch bug class outright; the full apply/diff/merge surface is what the driving use cases (undo, audit, optimistic UI, DB partials) actually require. · This ballot was minted from docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: `@[Patchable]` derive → `T.Patch` struct + apply/diff/merge, Codable (recommended)
options.detail: A derive on the `@` plane generates a nested all-optional `T.Patch` struct plus `apply(base)`, `Type.diff(new, old)`, and `merge(other)`; the Patch is Codable by construction. You construct and read it with skills you already have (`.{ }`, field access, patterns). `apply` is defined in terms of `.{ }` semantics, so there is one meaning of "edited copy" (I8 seam: `.{ }` is change-applied-now, Patch is change-as-a-value).

options.name: Generic library `Patch<T>` type (no per-struct codegen)
options.detail: A single std generic instead of a derive: one type for all structs, no generated code. But field access becomes dynamic/stringly — you lose field-name completion, compile-checked field names, and exhaustiveness. The value is opaque to the type system, which is exactly what a typed patch was meant to fix.
options.code:
p: Patch<Employee> := Patch.new()
p.set("title", "Staff")         // field name is a string; typo compiles
emp2 :: p.apply(emp)

options.name: Manual optional-field structs (status quo, reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Keep hand-writing an optional-field struct and an apply/merge function per record type. No new mechanism, but the plumbing, the diff code, and the audit-log drift all stay, re-implemented everywhere.

options.name: `@[Patchable]` derive, apply-only (defer diff/merge)
options.detail: Generate `T.Patch` and `apply` only; leave `diff` and `merge` to a later library decision. Smallest surface that still gives one canonical change value and Codable serialization. The cost: undo (diff) and combining changes (merge) — two of the four driving use cases — have no answer yet.

comparisons.note: TypeScript `Partial<T>` gives the all-optional twin type for free, and JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) standardizes apply. But there is no diff, no field-wise merge helper, and null-vs-absent is ambiguous.
comparisons.code:
type EmployeePatch = Partial<Employee>;
const next = { ...emp, ...promote };   // apply; no diff, no typed merge

comparisons.note: No built-in. A derive crate or a hand-written struct of `Option<T>` fields plus an apply fn; diff/merge are bespoke each time.
comparisons.code:
struct EmployeePatch { level: Option<i32>, title: Option<String> }
fn apply(e: Employee, p: EmployeePatch) -> Employee { /* per-field ?? */ }

comparisons.note: No built-in partial type. Teams hand-roll an optional-field struct or use key-path writes; no standard diff or merge.
comparisons.code: struct EmployeePatch { var level: Int?; var title: String? }

comparisons.note: A GameplayEffect is data: a modifier list applied to attributes, previewable and reversible — but game-specific, not a general record patch.

decisions.title: Computed struct fields: can a field be a formula over its siblings — `attack: Int => strength*2+gear_mod`?
decisions.gist: Can a struct field be defined by a formula over its sibling fields, recomputed on every read instead of stored?
decisions.explainer: UE's attribute sets bake clamping and derivation into the field so no caller can produce a -3 health. Jet already has the clamping half: `type Health :: Int(0..1000)` (D-RANGETYPE1) and `#Invariant` (D-REFINE1). The missing half is a field defined by its siblings. Today that is a zero-arg method — which works, but is invisible to `@Codable` output and, the moment someone stores the value for speed or serialization, goes stale. This decision adds a computed field: `name: T => expr` where the expression reads sibling fields. It recomputes under `.{ }` and patches, appears in Codable encode, is unsettable (assigning it is an error with a fix-it), and takes no parens. The spelling uses `=>` (already 'computes to', from lambdas); `=` is left free for the eventual field-default decision, which every mainstream language spells with `=`. Cycles are a compile error; derived-from-derived is allowed, dependency-ordered.
decisions.story: Earl is writing the character sheet for a tabletop companion app. Attack power is strength times two plus gear bonus. He stores attack as a plain Int field and computes it in the constructor. A week later a teammate edits strength through a copy-update on the saved character; attack keeps its old value, the sheet shows the wrong number, and the bug hides because everything type-checks.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: the standard cross-language spelling for derived state, it kills the stale-denormalized-field bug class at the source, composes with patches (base/current for free), and keeps one authoring story per job by staying the non-reactive twin of `Computed<T>`. · This ballot was minted from docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Computed field `name: T => expr` (recommended)
options.detail: A field whose value is an expression over sibling fields, evaluated on read. Recomputes under `.{ }` and patches, appears in `@Codable` encode, is unsettable (assignment is a teaching error with a fix-it), takes no parens. `=>` already means 'computes to'; `=` stays reserved for the future field-default slot. Cycles are a compile error; derived-from-derived is allowed, dependency-ordered.

options.name: Keep zero-arg methods (status quo, honest reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Derived values stay methods. Semantically the same result, but the value is absent from `@Codable` output, does not recompute inside a copy-update automatically (the method is fine but a stored cache is not), and reads as `s.attack()` with parens. No new spelling — and the stale-cache bug class stays whenever anyone denormalizes for speed or serialization.

options.name: Computed field, excluded from Codable output
options.detail: Same `name: T => expr` spelling and recompute-in-copy behavior, but treated as transient: never encoded, always recomputed on decode. Simpler contract (no encode ambiguity), but loses the base/current-in-the-wire-format win — a client that only has the JSON cannot read the derived value without the schema.

options.name: `#[Computed]` marker on a method (no new field grammar)
options.detail: Reuse method syntax with a marker that opts the method into Codable output and parens-free access, instead of a new field form. Avoids adding grammar to the struct body, but still reads as a method declaration and introduces a marker to learn; the `=>` field form is the more direct spelling of "this field is derived".

comparisons.note: Swift computed properties are the standard spelling: a stored-free property with a getter body, no parens at the call site.
A `val` with a custom getter — same idea, computed on read, no backing field.
comparisons.code: val attack: Int get() = strength * 2 + gearMod

comparisons.note: Expression-bodied property; recomputes on every access.
No computed fields; you write a method and call `s.attack()`. It is invisible to serde `derive(Serialize)` unless you add attributes by hand.
comparisons.code: impl Stats { fn attack(&self) -> i32 { self.strength * 2 + self.gear_mod } }

decisions.title: Reopen D-EFF4/5: make the effect vocabulary a tree with ancestor subsumption (`#(Fs.Read)` under `#(Fs)`)?
decisions.gist: Reopen the flat effect list: let effects nest so `#(Fs)` accepts any `Fs.*`, and `#(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` callee?
decisions.explainer: D-EFF4/5 deliberately ratified a flat, closed set of ten effects — Net, Fs, Io, Db, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, Log, Gpu — with NO subsumption (calling a `Net` effect under `#(Io)` is E0740). It was chosen for teachability: ten names, no taxonomy arguments. This is the one gameplay-dna transplant that reopens a decided question, and it carries that burden explicitly. The proposal: re-base the ten names as tree roots so `Fs.Read`, `Fs.Write`, `Net.Http.Get` are leaves, and ancestor matching IS subsumption — the exact same rule as the tag trees in D-TAG1, learned once. `#(Fs)` in a signature would accept any `Fs.*` callee; a `#(Fs.Read)` caller would reject an `Fs.Write` callee; `#Grant` (D-SCAP1) gains subtree precision. Existing flat names stay valid as roots, so there is no migration break. It also settles the acknowledged D-EFF2 subsumption documentation gap structurally. Sequence this last, behind D-TAG1/PATCH1/FIELDPOL1.
decisions.story: Walter is hardening a backend service. He has a config loader that should only ever read the filesystem, and he wants the compiler to prove it can never delete a file. Today `#(Fs)` is one indivisible capability: read and write are the same grant, so the loader is trusted with deletes and a stray `remove()` slipped past review would type-check clean. Read/write precision on Fs, Db and Net is the refinement his team asks for most.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A on the merits: it delivers the most-requested read/write capability precision, unifies subtree matching with D-TAG1 into one rule learned once, and settles the D-EFF2 gap structurally with zero migration break — but it reopens ratified D-EFF4/5, so sequence it last behind the other three. · This ballot was minted from docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Effect tree with ancestor subsumption (recommended)
options.detail: The ten ratified names become roots; `Fs.Read`, `Fs.Write`, `Net.Http.Get` are leaves. `#(Fs)` accepts any `Fs.*` callee; `#(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` callee; `#Grant` gains subtree precision. Flat names remain valid as roots, so no existing code breaks. Reverses E0740. Ancestor matching is the same rule as D-TAG1, so a user learns subtree matching once and applies it to enums, tags and effects alike.

options.name: Keep flat, no subsumption (status quo, defer)
options.detail: Do nothing. Ten names, no taxonomy, E0740 stays; the model stays maximally teachable but there is no read/write precision, and the acknowledged D-EFF2 subsumption gap stays a documentation note rather than a structural answer. Walter cannot prove his loader is read-only.
options.code:
fn load(p: String) -> Config #(Fs)   // read and write are one grant
fn read_only(p: String) #(Fs) { remove(p) }  // type-checks — no way to forbid write

options.name: Fixed two-level split on a few effects only
options.detail: Add a curated, closed second level to just the effects that need it — `Fs.Read`/`Fs.Write`, `Net.In`/`Net.Out`, `Db.Read`/`Db.Write` — with no general nesting. Less taxonomy debate than open trees, but the second level is picked arbitrarily by the language and the rule is a special case rather than the general ancestor law shared with D-TAG1.

options.name: Precision via prohibition, not a tree
options.detail: Express read-only by combining the flat name with a D-PROP1 prohibition instead of nesting: `#(Fs) #(!Fs.Write)`. Keeps the ten flat names and adds no hierarchy, but the spelling is compound, `Fs.Write` still has to be a nameable sub-capability (so you half-need the tree anyway), and it does not compose with `#Grant` subtree precision.
options.code: fn read_only(p: String) #(Fs) #(!Fs.Write) { load(p) }  // remove(p) here -> prohibition error

comparisons.note: Deno's permission model splits filesystem into --allow-read and --allow-write, and read/write accept path prefixes — hierarchical capability, granted outside the type system.
GameplayTag subsumption again: a system requiring `Ability.Fire` is satisfied by `Ability.Fire.Fireball`. Same ancestor rule proposed here for effects.
Effects are rows of labels with no hierarchy; you get precise per-effect tracking but express read-vs-write as two unrelated labels, not parent/child.
No effect system; capability is by module privacy and the type of the handle you hold (e.g. `&File` vs write methods). No signature-level effect at all.

decisions.gist: How you ask the compiler to show the facts it proved (inline decisions, resolved ref owners) — the command's exact shape and what it does with no lens named.
decisions.story: Doris maintains a telemetry indexer. A teammate's PR adds `@InlineAlways` to a hot dot-product and a new `&Incident` field whose owner the compiler inferred. Before approving, Doris wants to SEE what the compiler decided — which calls actually inlined, which arena owns that field — without reading generated Rust. decisions.title: Should decode apply migration{} blocks to old stored data at runtime?
decisions.gist: Old stored data currently fails to decode; should the compiler generate the code that upgrades it in place during decode?
decisions.story: Betty (from D-MIGRATE3) ships schema v3 of UserRecord. Her nightly import reads three-year-old v1 JSON. Today that decode simply errors — the migration blocks she wrote only prove a migration EXISTS at compile time. She expected the old records to load and upgrade; decode_traced exists to tell her it happened, but nothing can happen yet.

options.name: Generate the migration chain into decode (recommended)
options.detail: Codegen lowers each migration{} block to a step function; decode of a @PublishedSchema type first tries the current shape, on mismatch walks stored version tags/shape detection oldest to current, applying steps. decode_traced records from+steps; plain decode applies silently. Zero cost for types without migrations (nothing generated).

options.name: Explicit opt-in call: decode_migrating only
options.detail: Plain decode keeps failing on old shapes; a third method decode_migrating<T> applies the chain. Callers must choose migration explicitly; surface grows to three decode verbs (I8 pressure).
options.code:
user :: json.decode_migrating<UserRecord>(raw)?   // applies chain
old  :: json.decode<UserRecord>(raw)               // still errors on v1

options.name: Defer past Epoch 3 (status quo)
options.detail: Keep compile-time-only checks; decode_traced stays always-false until a later epoch. Stored-data users must hand-write upgraders.
options.code:
// no change; v1 JSON keeps failing:
user :: json.decode<UserRecord>(raw) ?? panic("DecodeError")

comparisons.note: serde has no built-in versioning; versioning crates bolt it on manually.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct UserRecord { /* one shape only; old JSON = error */ }

comparisons.note: wire-level field ids + defaults make old data readable by construction.
comparisons.code: message UserRecord { int64 id = 1; string display_name = 2; bool verified = 3; }

comparisons.note: Codable: manual init(from:) branching on version keys.
comparisons.code: init(from d: Decoder) throws { /* if v1 { … } else { … } */ }

decisions.rec: A — the authoring surface (migration verbs) and the transparency surface (decode_traced) are both ratified and shipped; A is the semantics both were designed around, keeps one decode verb (I8), and costs nothing for unversioned types.
decisions.recommendation: A — the authoring surface (migration verbs) and the transparency surface (decode_traced) are both ratified and shipped; A is the semantics both were designed around, keeps one decode verb (I8), and costs nothing for unversioned types.

decisions.title: Memory model v5 — the borrow checker, humanized
decisions.gist: Owner reset (2026-07-03): keep Rust borrow-checker semantics (read-only default, exclusive writers, moves, RAII, zero-cost); fix the experience. Three sigils: bare=read (default, signatures cannot lie), &=write, ^=take — both mirrored at call sites so mutation and moves are always visible. Borrows are second-class (never stored in structs, never returned raw) so lifetime syntax cannot exist; view-shaped APIs use view VALUES (counted Str/List slices, invisible); walls get named escape hatches (Shared<T>, Pool<T>) suggested by teaching diagnostics. ~ deleted; no word spellings.
decisions.explainer: Semantics = Rust verbatim: ownership, shared-xor-mutable, move analysis, deterministic RAII, no GC, no runtime ownership machinery. The five documented Rust pains each get a targeted surface fix: (1) lifetimes — second-class borrows flow only down the stack, so every extent is compiler-obvious; nothing to annotate, nothing to learn; struct fields hold owned values / Shared / Id, never borrows (kills the struct<'a> infection); returns are owned values or library view-values that share storage internally (one Str, one List; no String/&str dualism). Precedent: Hylo second-class references; Graydon's stated preference. (2) invisible moves — every transfer is written ^ at the call site; use-after-move errors point at the ^ the user typed, with a fix menu (copy / reorder / Pool). (3) checker-voiced errors — every borrow error is a what/why/fix teaching diagnostic, I4-pinned. (4) wrapper-assembly escape hatches — Shared<T> (Arc+lock class) and Pool<T>+Id<T> (generational arena; parent pointers/graphs/observers) are named language-level types that diagnostics suggest by name. (5) call-site opacity — & required at mutating calls, so reviewers see effects (Rust's map.insert mutates markerless). Beginner rule set is one sentence: unmarked = looking, & = changing, ^ = giving away, one writer at a time. Deletes from ratified state: ~ glyph, D-CAP8 elevation/freeze + api:explicit, L0201 (heap copies are explicit `copy`), D-REF-SHORTHAND1/2 (no stored borrows to infer owners for), &-as-share (sharing is Shared<T> by name). Keeps: ^ semantics, call-site mirroring where it informs (&/^), D-MUTSELF1 receiver-on-self (&self/^self), copy verb, S63 RAII, #SingleUse resources, arenas/uninit/*T/#Unsafe, S53 posture (borrows cannot cross spawn — unrepresentable, races impossible). Experts lose exactly one Rust feature: storable/returnable raw borrows — replaced by views/Shared/Pool/arenas/raw tier; philosophy C1 already reserves first-class borrows as optional post-v1 tier 2. Implementation reality: closest of all five proposals to the existing AccessConvention Read/Mutate/Move machinery — largely a rename + feature deletion, not a rebuild. On approval, next deliverable is the staged migration path. Full write-up: docs/proposals/memory-greenfield.md.
decisions.story: A beginner reads any signature and knows the whole truth: unmarked can only be looked at, & gets changed, ^ is given away. Their first move error points at the ^ they typed themselves and offers copy/reorder/Pool by name. They never meet a lifetime because the language cannot express one.
decisions.inWild:
fn enroll(party: &Party, player: ^Player)
enroll(&party, ^kai)            // both effects visible at the call

error[E—]: kai was given away on line 1 (`^kai`)
fix: keep a copy:      party.members.push(copy kai)
     or one player referenced everywhere: Pool<Player> (jet explain pools)

fn domain(email: String) -> String { return email.split("@")[1] }   // view; no lifetimes
decisions.detail: Owner directive trail (all 2026-07-03): v1 One-Home rejected; v2 completed-sigils rejected (from-clauses, ~ frequency); v3 progressive-ceremony rejected (copies unclear, read-only-args felt wrong at first); v4 identity-model interrupted; final reset — "use the rust borrow checker system but make it much more ergonomic & beginner friendly… read-only by default… sigils not words… no ~, prefer & or ^". v5 delivers exactly that. Glyph assignment is the live sub-question (options A/B/C). After ratification: follow-on ballots for Shared<T>/Pool<T> APIs, view-value semantics in stdlib, diagnostic voice, then the migration-path plan (owner-gated deliverable #2).

options.detail: Rust semantics, three sigils, second-class borrows (no lifetime syntax can exist), view values, named escape hatches, teaching diagnostics, moves always visible. Note honestly: & means WRITE here — flipped from Rust's read-borrow; Rust immigrants relearn once.

options.name: Same model, swapped glyphs — ^=write, &=take
options.detail: Identical semantics; judge by eye which pair reads better at declarations and call sites.

options.detail: Preserves Rust muscle memory (& never means write) at the cost of a two-char write sigil and an optional-read glyph that adds a fourth spelling.

decisions.title: Shared<T> construction + access API surface (S6 blocker)
decisions.gist: D-MEM1 names `Shared<T>` as the v5 escape hatch for state shared across tasks, but only the TYPE NAME is ratified — its constructor and read/write methods only exist as gallery worked examples, never balloted.
decisions.explainer: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md's D-MEM1 row lists `Shared<T>` by name as a named escape hatch. docs/proposals/memory-v5-gallery.md section 8 ("Web dev — handlers, state, tasks", explicitly marked *(Shared: proposed)* in its own header) shows a consistent worked example: `Shared.new(x)` to construct, `.read(closure)` for a read-locked closure callback, and (per an S6 investigation of D-MEM1's parent proposal doc) `.edit(closure)` for a write-locked closure callback. None of this — constructor spelling, method names, closure-callback shape vs. an alternative (e.g. a guard object with RAII unlock) — has its own ratified decision row. S6 of the memory-v5 migration (Tower card cmemgreenfield) is blocked on this.
decisions.story: Priya is porting a small web server to Jet. Every handler needs read access to shared session state, and one background task needs to mutate it. In Rust this is `Arc<Mutex<App>>` plus `.lock().unwrap()` everywhere; Jet's whole pitch is that `Shared<T>` collapses that ritual into one named concept — but the compiler can't build it until the exact method names are decided.
decisions.detail: Blocks Tower card cmemgreenfield stage S6. The type collapses Rust's `Arc<Mutex<T>>`/`Arc<RwLock<T>>` + explicit lock/unwrap/clone ritual into one CoreLib type; the read/write split matters for allowing concurrent readers.

options.name: Closure-callback API — `.read(f)` / `.edit(f)` (gallery spelling, recommended)
options.detail: Matches the gallery's own consistent worked example across its Shared section. The lock is scoped to the closure's body — impossible to forget to release it, impossible to hold it across a `spawn`/`await` boundary by accident (closures can't smuggle a guard out). `.read` takes a read-lock, allows concurrent readers; `.edit` takes a write-lock, exclusive. `Shared.new(x)` constructs (bare type-name call, no turbofish needed — inferred from `x`).

options.name: RAII guard object — `.read()` / `.write()` return a guard
options.detail: Mirrors Rust's `RwLock::read()`/`write()` directly: returns a guard value that derefs to `&T`/`&mut T` and releases the lock on scope-end (Drop). More flexible (can hold the guard across several statements) but reintroduces the exact footgun class v5's whole `&`/`^` model exists to prevent: a guard can be squirreled away, held too long, or accidentally crossed into another task, deadlocking or violating the borrow that spawned it.
options.code:
state :: Shared.new(App.new())

g :: state.read()
user :: g.sessions.get(req.token)
// g drops here, unlocking

w :: state.write()
w.sessions.insert(token, user)
// w drops here, unlocking

options.name: Single unified method, mutability inferred from body (rejected — ambiguous)
options.detail: One `.access(f)` method whose lock kind (read vs write) is inferred from whether the closure mutates — would require whole-closure-body analysis to decide locking strategy before the closure even runs, and silently changes locking behavior based on incidental code shape. No prior art does this; rejected as a design direction, shown for completeness.
options.code:
state :: Shared.new(App.new())
state.access(s => s.sessions.get(req.token))       // inferred read?
state.access(s => { s.sessions.insert(token, user) }) // inferred write?

comparisons.note: Arc<RwLock<T>> requires explicit lock()/read()/write(), .unwrap() on poison, and Arc::clone at every task-spawn boundary.
sync.RWMutex is a separate value from the data it guards — no compiler-enforced pairing, easy to forget the lock/unlock or lock the wrong mutex for a given field.
Swift's actor model serializes all access through async methods — closest existing-language analogue to a closure-scoped access API, though actors reach further (isolation domains, not just locking).
comparisons.code:
actor App { func getUser(_ token: Token) -> User? { sessions[token] } }
let user = await app.getUser(token)

decisions.title: Pool<T>/Id<T> construction + insert + access + stale-id API surface (S6 blocker)
decisions.gist: D-MEM1 names `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>` as the v5 generational-arena escape hatch, but only the TYPE NAMES are ratified — construction, insert, indexed access, iteration, and stale-id error behavior only exist as gallery worked examples, never balloted.
decisions.explainer: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md's D-MEM1 row lists `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>` by name. docs/proposals/memory-v5-gallery.md sections 6 ("one world, many entities") and 10 ("Graphs & back-references") — both explicitly marked *(Pool/Id: proposed)* in their own headers — show a consistent worked example: `Pool<T>.new()` to construct, `.add(val)` to insert (returns `Id<T>`), `pool[id]` index operator for read+write field access, `.ids()` to iterate live entries, and `Id<T>?` for optional back-references using Jet's EXISTING option syntax (no new syntax needed there). What's completely unspecified anywhere, in gallery or proposal: what happens on a STALE `Id` access (the entity was removed, the generation counter no longer matches) — panic, a checked error return, an effect-tracked fallible op? This is the actual safety mechanism a generational arena exists to provide, and it has zero spec text. S6 of the memory-v5 migration (Tower card cmemgreenfield) is blocked on this.
decisions.story: Marcus is writing a small game in Jet. Entities reference each other (a `target` field on `Player`, a `parent` field on `Node`) — the classic case Rust developers solve with `Rc<RefCell<T>>` graphs or reach for a crate like `slotmap`/`hecs` for. Jet's pitch is that `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>` is first-class and built in, no crate hunt — but the compiler can't build it until insert/access/iteration spellings are decided, and nothing has ever specified what happens when an `Id` outlives the entity it names (the whole safety point of a generational arena).
decisions.detail: Blocks Tower card cmemgreenfield stage S6. Pool<T> owns a collection of T; Id<T> is a lightweight (index + generation counter) handle into it that safely detects use of a removed/replaced slot instead of silently reading garbage or a reused slot's new occupant (the classic ABA bug plain indices have).

options.name: Gallery spelling as-is: `.new()`/`.add()`/`pool[id]`/`.ids()`, stale access is a runtime error (recommended)
options.detail: Matches all 3 gallery worked examples verbatim (sections 6, 10, plus the parent-pointer-tree section). `pool[id]` reads AND writes through the existing index-assignment machinery (already shipped, used throughout the compiler's own examples). Stale-`Id` access (generation mismatch) is a runtime panic with a clear message naming the stale-access class — matches how an out-of-bounds array index already panics in Jet today (consistent with existing runtime-bounds-check precedent, not a new error class). `.remove(id)` (not shown in gallery but necessary for a working Pool — an insert-only Pool isn't really a Pool) needs its own spelling decided here too since nothing shows it.
options.code:
world := Pool<Player>.new()
kai :: world.add(Player.{ name: "Kai", hp: 100 })
world.remove(kai)
world[kai].hp     // panics: stale Id — this entity was removed

options.name: Stale access is a checked/fallible op instead of a panic
options.detail: `world[id]` returns something checkable (`?`-chainable or an effect-tracked fallible call) instead of panicking outright, letting a long-running game loop or server recover from a stale reference instead of crashing. Diverges from existing array-index panic precedent, which is exactly why the plain index operator (`world[id]`) may not be the right spelling for this if fallibility is wanted — might need a distinct method (`.get(id)`) alongside the panicking index.

options.name: Turbofish-explicit construction: `Pool::<T>::new()` (rejected — inconsistent with rest of Jet)
options.detail: Rust-style explicit turbofish construction. Rejected for consistency: every other generic CoreLib type constructed this session (Sender<T>/Receiver<T> via tasks.channel<T>()) already uses the bare `Type<T>.new()`/`Type<T>()` dot-call convention, not Rust's `::<T>::` path syntax — a second construction convention would violate I8.
options.code: world := Pool::<Player>::new()   // inconsistent with Type<T>.new() used elsewhere

comparisons.note: SlotMap<DefaultKey, T> + world.insert(x) -> DefaultKey + world[key] indexing (panics on stale) + world.keys() iteration — the closest prior art, and the gallery's own comparison target.
Arena<T> + arena.insert(x) -> Index + arena[index] (panics on stale) + arena.remove(index) -> Option<T> — remove returns the removed value, a pattern worth considering for Pool::remove.

comparisons.lang: C# (List + generation-tagged struct, common game-dev pattern)
comparisons.note: No language-level generational handle; games hand-roll a (index, generation) struct and check generation on access, panicking or returning null on mismatch — same design space, no built-in precedent either way on panic-vs-checked.
comparisons.code:
struct EntityId { int index; int generation; }
var player = world.Get(id); // null if generation mismatch

decisions.title: policy no_alloc enforcement semantics — what counts as an allocation, local-only or interprocedural? (S7 blocker)
decisions.gist: D-MEM1 ratifies the `policy no_alloc` mechanism and names it the first policy floor, but never specifies what operations trip it or whether the check follows calls out of the module.
decisions.explainer: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md's D-MEM1 row ratifies module `policy` floors with `no_alloc` first, and the surface syntax (`policy no_alloc` as a bare module-top item) is unambiguous and safe to parse — that part isn't in question. What's unspecified: (1) which operations count as "allocation" — String concatenation/interpolation, `[T]`/List `.push`, `Map` insert, a closure capturing by value, `copy` of a heap-owning type, a struct/enum literal with a heap-owning field — none of these are named anywhere as in-scope or out-of-scope; (2) whether the check is LOCAL (only flags allocation-shaped expressions written directly in the module's own function bodies) or INTERPROCEDURAL (walks the call graph — same pattern already used by `@Pure fn`'s effect-purity check, Sema/Effects.rs's `solve()` — and flags a call if ANY reachable callee, in this module, another module, or the stdlib, allocates). The gallery's own framing ("the module claiming embedded-grade guarantees") reads like it wants interprocedural, but that needs its own ruling on opaque/FFI/extern-rust callees (can the compiler even see whether an `extern rust` function allocates?).
decisions.story: Marcus's game has a hot per-frame `integrate` function he wants embedded-grade guarantees on — no surprise heap traffic from an innocent-looking helper call three functions deep. He writes `policy no_alloc` at the top of that module expecting the compiler to catch it. Today nothing defines what "it" catches.
decisions.detail: Blocks Tower card cmemgreenfield stage S7. Once ruled, the actual build is small: one parser item, one sema pass (reusing Effects.rs's existing call-graph/fixpoint machinery if interprocedural is chosen — proven buildable in this codebase already, just needs the ruling on whether to use it here), one diagnostic code, one example + golden.

options.name: Local-only, explicit denylist (recommended for S7's first cut)
options.detail: Flags only allocation-shaped expressions written directly in the policy'd module's own function bodies: String concat/interpolation producing a new String, List/Map insert-that-grows-capacity, a struct/enum literal for any type with a heap-owning field, an explicit `copy` of a heap type. Does NOT follow calls to other functions/modules — calling a helper that itself allocates is the CALLEE's module's problem, not flagged here. Simpler, no interprocedural-analysis edge cases (FFI/extern-rust opacity, recursive call cycles), ships faster, matches how most systems-language "no alloc in this scope" checks actually work in practice (Rust's `#[no_std]`-adjacent tooling, embedded C static-analysis checkers) — they're almost universally local/lexical, not whole-program, because whole-program alloc-freedom for arbitrary stdlib calls is a much bigger claim to make honestly.

options.name: Interprocedural, reuses Effects.rs's existing solve()
options.detail: Walks the call graph the same way `@Pure fn` already does (Sema/Effects.rs), flagging a call under `policy no_alloc` if ANY reachable callee allocates — including callees in other modules and the stdlib. Matches the gallery's "embedded-grade guarantees" framing more literally — a truly alloc-free hot loop can't call an allocating helper and not know it. Needs its own answer for opaque boundaries: does an `extern rust`/FFI call count as "unknown, assume allocates" (conservative, breaks legitimate zero-alloc FFI) or "unknown, assume doesn't" (permissive, could silently violate the claim)? Bigger build: needs the whole stdlib's alloc-shape annotated or inferred once, not per-check.

options.name: No denylist — treat ANY heap-owning type construction as the sole rule (rejected, too broad without a ruling on which types count)
options.detail: "If it's not a plain scalar/fixed-size type, constructing one is an allocation" — simplest rule to STATE but still requires deciding whether that's local or interprocedural (same fork as A vs B), so it doesn't actually resolve the ambiguity, just restates it more generally. Shown for completeness, not a real alternative to A/B.

comparisons.note: Rust's no_std is a library-availability restriction (no std allocator/heap types available at all), not a checked-call-graph analysis — closer to option A's simplicity (you literally can't construct a Vec/String without an allocator crate) than option B's interprocedural reasoning.
comparisons.code:
#![no_std]
// String/Vec/Box simply don't exist without an explicit global_allocator

comparisons.note: Zig requires an explicit Allocator parameter threaded through any allocating call — a caller can pass a failing/panicking allocator to make a whole subtree provably non-allocating, which is closer to option B's transitive guarantee, achieved via an ordinary parameter rather than a whole-program static analysis.
comparisons.code:
fn integrate(alloc: std.mem.Allocator, world: *World) void { ... }
// pass a FixedBufferAllocator or panicking allocator to enforce no dynamic alloc

comparisons.lang: C++ (static analyzers, e.g. embedded game studios' internal tooling)
comparisons.note: Custom clang-tidy-style checks that flag `new`/STL-container-growth call sites lexically, generally NOT interprocedural across translation units — matches option A.
comparisons.code:
// clang-tidy custom check flags `new`, `std::vector::push_back` at the call site
// does not trace into called functions in other translation units

decisions.title: core.fs/core.files merge: the `append` name collides
decisions.gist: Two different stdlib modules both want the method name `append`, with different meanings — merging them under `core.files` (D-FILES-WRITE1) needs one renamed.
decisions.explainer: D-FILES-WRITE1 (ratified) says `core.files` becomes the one file module and folds `core.fs` into it — but a single Rust match arm can't dispatch `(module="files", method="append")` two different ways by argument count without a form of overloading the language doesn't otherwise use (I8 risk). Both spellings already exist in the compiler today in two separate modules: `core.fs.append(path, text)` is a 2-arg whole-file convenience; `core.files`'s handle type (after `.open`/`.create`) has a 1-arg `.append(text)` streaming method. Recommendation: rename the whole-file one-shot function to `append_all`; keep `append` as the streaming-handle method (unchanged). Zero ambiguity, smallest migration, no collision with D-FILES-WRITE1's own decree that `.write` is the handle's overwrite method.
decisions.story: Walter Higgins is porting a log-rotation script to Jet. He already has whole-file code using `core.fs.append(path, "line\n")` to tack one line onto a file, and now wants to switch a long-running job to `core.files.open(path)` streaming handles for a hot loop — he expects both to live under the same module name once D-FILES-WRITE1 lands (`core.files` is decreed as THE file module).
decisions.inWild:
use core.files as fs

// Whole-file convenience — one call, opens+writes+closes:
fs.append("audit.log", "user logged in\n")

// Streaming handle — many writes, one open/close:
h :: fs.open("audit.log")
h.append("user logged in\n")   // same method name, different receiver/arity
h.close()
decisions.detail: Found 2026-07-04 while implementing card cv5syntaxdecrees's decree 5 (D-FILES-WRITE1). Decrees 1-4 and 6 of that card shipped independently; this is decree 5's only blocker.

options.name: Rename whole-file convenience to `append_all` (recommended)
options.detail: `append` is always the handle method; `append_all` is always whole-file. Clean under I8, low migration cost (one stdlib fn + any examples/tests using `core.fs.append(path, text)`), reads unambiguously at a glance.
options.code:
use core.files as fs

fs.append_all("audit.log", "user logged in\n")   // one-shot, opens+writes+closes

h :: fs.open("audit.log")
h.append("more\n")                                // streaming handle, unchanged
h.close()

options.name: Rename handle method, keep whole-file `append`
options.detail: Collides with D-FILES-WRITE1's own text, which already says the handle's overwrite method is `.write` — renaming the handle's append method risks a second collision, and `.write` for append reads as ambiguous (does it append or overwrite?).
options.code:
use core.files as fs

fs.append("audit.log", "user logged in\n")        // whole-file, unchanged name

h :: fs.open("audit.log")
h.write("more\n")                                  // but .write already means overwrite
h.close()

options.name: Keep one name, dispatch by argument count (rejected)
options.detail: Silent overloading by arity — no precedent elsewhere in Jet, violates I8 (one way to mean it). Same name, silently different job depending on receiver/arity.
options.code:
use core.files as fs

fs.append("audit.log", "user logged in\n")   // 2-arg: whole file
h :: fs.open("audit.log")
h.append("more\n")                            // 1-arg: handle — same name, different job

comparisons.note: Whole-file convenience doesn't exist as a free function; it's OpenOptions::append(true).open(path). No collision because there's no free-function form to begin with.
Whole-file convenience is a different verb (appendFile); handle-based writes use write(). No collision because the names differ.
No whole-file one-shot append built in; open(path, "a") then write(). No collision to resolve.

decisions.explainer: Today a script that needs a library needs a pack.jet — a cliff exactly where beginners stand. An inline pin on the use statement (the already-ratified pkg#version pin) lets one file carry its own deps. The lock lives in the user-invisible cache keyed by file content; `jet lock script.jet` materializes a sidecar when someone wants committed reproducibility.
decisions.story: User writes a 40-line log analyzer for a friend. He sends ONE file. The friend runs jet run analyze.jet and it just works — deps fetched, locked, cached. No project, no manifest, no instructions.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Reproducibility — cache lock is per-file-hash; editing the file re-locks. For committed exactness, `jet lock` writes analyze.jet.lock beside the file; jet run prefers it when present. (2) Version drift — bare `use textkit` (no pin) in a script resolves latest-compatible and RECORDS the choice in the cache lock; the teaching hint suggests adding the pin. (3) Upgrade path — `jet init` lifts inline uses into a generated pack.jet deps block, so the script→package rung costs one command. (4) No install-time code execution (PM-I1) applies identically.

comparisons.note: PEP-723 inline script metadata made uv the fastest-growing tool in Python. Demand is proven.
cargo-script languished unstable for a decade; everyone feels the gap.
No single-file story at all; gorun and hacks fill the void.

decisions.explainer: A dev environment is tools + RUNNING THINGS. Nix needed devenv/process-compose bolted on; jetpack builds supervision in. A service is a typed struct: fields are its options (completion + docs in the editor), the supervisor owns lifecycle, health-checks, and logs. Core ships the common set (postgres, redis, mysql, nats, minio…); any package can define a Service.
decisions.story: Priya clones the repo, types jet dev. Postgres 16 comes up with the schema loaded, redis follows, the app starts against them. She never installed either, and `jet services logs postgres` answers her first question of the day.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Supervisor scope — project-scoped processes with sockets/data under .jet/, never system daemons; jetos system services are the system.* namespace, same Service type, different lifecycle owner. (2) Health — a service declares readiness (port/probe); jet dev waits for ready before fn dev(), killing the "app raced the database" class. (3) Magic/expert: beginners write two lines; experts define custom Service types (typed fields, readiness probe, shutdown hook) in ordinary Jet; auditors see every process a project can start by grepping services:. (4) State — service data dirs live under .jet/ and are GC-visible.

comparisons.note: services.postgres.enable = true proved the demand; it is the reason devenv exists apart from flakes.
The YAML sidecar Nix shells need for supervision — the bolt-on this absorbs.
The default answer everywhere else: container-heavy, slow on mac, another language.

decisions.explainer: Secrets are Nix's open wound: the store is world-readable, so agenix/sops-nix exist as third-party duct tape. Jet builds the answer in: a secrets file encrypted to team/machine keys (age-style) lives in the repo; secret("name") references an entry; decryption happens at env entry or service start, in memory, never written to the hangar; reading one from code requires the Secret effect, so the audit question "what can exfiltrate keys" is a grep.
decisions.story: Elena onboards a contractor. He gets repo access and his key added to secrets.recipients — one line, one re-encrypt. He never sees the production Stripe key travel over Slack, and when he leaves, removing the line rotates him out.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Never in the store — hangar artifacts must be secret-free by construction; secrets resolve at activation, not build; a build that tries to read one fails (Secret effect denied in build tier by default, D-BUILDPOLICY1). (2) The Secret effect joins the ratified ten as effect #11 or rides Env — separate is better for budgets (deny: [Secret] for the whole dep graph = D-EFFBUDGET1 integration). (3) Key management: age-style recipients file; CI gets a machine key; no vault dependency for the base tier, adapters (vault/op/kms) as providers for enterprises. (4) Magic/expert: beginners run jet secrets set and it works; experts swap the backend; auditors grep #(Secret) and the recipients file history.

comparisons.note: World-readable store made secrets a third-party problem: agenix, sops-nix — the duct tape this replaces.
Encrypted-file-in-repo with recipient keys — the proven model A adopts, minus the YAML.
The default everywhere else: plaintext .env, .gitignore, and prayer.

options.name: Built-in encrypted secrets + Secret effect gating (recommended)
options.detail: age-style file in repo, recipients management, activation-time decryption, effect-gated reads, provider adapters for vault/kms.
options.code: secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: secret("stripe-dev") }

options.code: env_vars: { STRIPE_KEY: env("STRIPE_KEY") }

options.name: External managers only (adapters, no built-in)
options.detail: Clean scope, but small teams get nothing out of the box — the anti-batteries choice.
options.code: secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: vault("kv/stripe#key") }

decisions.title: U13 follow-up — which cipher backend encrypts the secrets file?
decisions.gist: D-JPK-SECRET1=A needs age-style crypto (X25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305). Zero external crates in the compiler is I6. Pick the backend: FFI-bridge to a vetted crate, shell out to age/rage, or native std-only.
decisions.explainer: The ratified secrets design (encrypted file in repo, recipients list, memory-only decrypt) is cipher-agnostic — everything except the encrypt/decrypt step is already plannable and buildable. But the cipher itself needs X25519 key agreement plus ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD (and scrypt for passphrase keys, bech32 for key encoding), none of which exist std-only in Source/. I6 forbids external crates in the compiler, so the backend choice is an owner call, same shape as the tvix waiver (D-JPK16) and the FFI-bridge stdlib pattern.
decisions.story: Elena runs jet secrets set stripe-dev on a fresh laptop with nothing installed but jet. Option A/C: it just works — the cipher ships inside jet. Option B: jet prints a clear one-line message to install age first, exactly like the Nix-bridge stopgap message she has already seen.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet secrets set stripe-dev
  enter value: ****************
  encrypted to 3 recipients -> .jet/secrets  (never plaintext at rest)

$ jet dev
  secrets: 2 decrypted into the environment (memory only)

fn charge() -> Receipt ? Error #(Net, Secret) {
    key :: secrets.get("stripe-dev")?    // effect-gated read
}
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md §'U13 — first-class encrypted secrets', 'I6 watch — OWNER BALLOT REQUIRED'. The plan builds all non-cipher scaffolding (secrets: field capture in ModuleEval, Secret effect in jet-sema, store format, jet secrets CLI, trust-gate integration, E0986–E0988) regardless of this outcome — only the encrypt/decrypt call is gated. Adversarial notes: (A) the FFI-bridge pattern (Archive.rs/Db.rs/CFFI.rs precedent) emits bridge template text and never touches jet's Cargo.toml, so I6's letter holds; the crate (e.g. age or x25519-dalek + chacha20poly1305) still enters the trust base and the Epoch-3 'replace external deps' mandate applies later. (B) is zero new code in the trust base and ships fastest, but secrets then fail on machines without age — acceptable for the Nix bridge, harsher for a batteries-included secrets story (philosophy: beginner experience ranks above effort). (C) is the only I6-pure end state and the Epoch-3 mandate arrives there eventually; X25519 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are small, well-specified, test-vector-rich algorithms, but hand-rolled crypto needs a real review gate before it guards production keys. A staged A-then-C or B-then-C is a legal answer — say so explicitly if chosen.

options.name: FFI-bridge a vetted crypto crate (house stdlib pattern)
options.detail: Emit bridge template text linking a vetted age-compatible crate (age, or x25519-dalek + chacha20poly1305); never added to jet's Cargo.toml, isolated exactly like Archive.rs/Db.rs. Works out of the box; crate joins the trust base; Epoch-3 native-replacement mandate still applies later.

options.name: Shell out to the age/rage binary (bridge-style stopgap)
options.detail: std::process::Command to age, mirroring the ratified nix-binary stopgap. Zero new code in the trust base, ships immediately; secrets require age installed, with a clear teaching message otherwise — the anti-batteries cost for a first-class feature.
options.code:
// std-only, no crate:
Command::new("age").args(["-R", "recipients", "-o", out]).spawn()?

$ jet secrets set stripe-dev
Error [E09xx]: the `age` tool is needed to encrypt secrets
 Fix: install age (https://age-encryption.org), or ask the owner to enable the built-in cipher

options.name: Native std-only X25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305
options.detail: Implement the ciphers in plain Rust inside the driver. I6-pure, no trust-base growth, matches the Epoch-3 replace-external-deps mandate; both algorithms are small and RFC-test-vectored, but hand-rolled crypto guarding real keys needs an explicit review/audit gate before ship.

comparisons.note: The model U13 ratified: X25519 recipients, small file format, no vault. The question is only where its cipher runs.
Both shell out to or link age — precedent that either A or B is a normal shape for this feature.
Go ships X25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305 in crypto/ — the option-C end state is a proven stdlib choice, not exotic.

decisions.explainer: Deployment artifacts are the third thing every project eventually needs (after build and env). The image namespace is already reserved (§5 unified-ecosystem). This gate fixes its surface: an image module names what goes in (a package target, env slices, files) and what comes out (oci, iso, vm). Because the hangar is content-addressed, images are layered and reproducible for free — nix dockerTools' killer feature with typed fields instead of function soup.
decisions.story: Sam finishes the web app and needs a container for the platform team. He writes four lines, runs jet image server, and gets a 12MB distroless image with exactly the binary and its closure — no Dockerfile, no apt-get layer archaeology, same lockfile provenance as the binary.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Scope discipline — kind: .Oci and .Iso in v1 (containers + jetos installers); VM/disk images later. (2) Contents law: closure of the named target only; adding ad-hoc files is explicit (files: [...]), so images stay minimal and auditable — jet audit image lists every path and where it came from. (3) No Docker dependency: OCI layout built directly from hangar objects; --push speaks the registry protocol. (4) Base-image escape hatch for the messy world: base: oci("debian:12") for teams mid-migration.

comparisons.note: dockerTools.buildLayeredImage — reproducible layered images are beloved; the interface is expert-only function soup.
The default: imperative layers, apt snapshots, non-reproducible by design.
Language-specific image builders proved "no Dockerfile" demand for Go/Java.

options.detail: Typed, reproducible, distroless by default, explicit file additions, registry push built in.

decisions.title: U14 follow-up — which backend builds and pushes OCI images?
decisions.gist: D-JPK-IMAGE1=A promises 'OCI layout built directly from hangar objects, --push speaks the registry protocol'. That needs sha256 digests, gzip layers, and TLS for push — none std-only today. Pick: shell out to skopeo/nix, FFI-bridge a registry lib, or native.
decisions.explainer: The image.* surface (kind/from/expose/env_vars/files/base field-check and capture) builds now with no external need. The build step needs sha256 (layer + config digests) and gzip (layer compression) — both implementable std-only. The push step needs HTTPS/TLS to speak the OCI distribution protocol, which is the genuinely hard native piece. I6 makes any crate an owner call; the split between build (near-native-feasible) and push (TLS wall) is why this is a menu, not a foregone choice.
decisions.story: Sam runs jet image server --push ghcr.io/acme/pulseops:0.4.0. Option A: jet assembles the layout, then skopeo copies it up — works today if skopeo is installed, message otherwise. Option B/C: the whole path is jet's own, nothing external, and CI needs one binary.
decisions.inWild:
module image.server {
    kind: .Oci
    from: packages.pulseops
    expose: [8080]
}

$ jet image server
  -> hangar:.../pulseops-oci-...  (12.4 MB, 3 layers, reproducible)
$ jet image server --push ghcr.io/acme/pulseops:0.4.0
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md §'U14 — image.* OCI containers + ISOs', 'I6 watch — OWNER BALLOT'. The plan lands field-check/capture (E0989/E0990) and the reproducible-layout test regardless; this ballot gates only the tar/digest/compress/push engine. Adversarial notes: (A) matches the ratified nix-binary stopgap pattern and the 'nixpkgs now, jetpack later' interim policy; the UX contract stays jet's so muscle memory survives a later native swap — but the ballot text explicitly promised 'no Docker dependency', and skopeo is a cousin of that dependency; the message must be as clear as the missing-nix one. (B) FFI-bridge (Archive.rs/Db.rs pattern) to an OCI/registry crate keeps Cargo.toml clean but pulls an HTTP+TLS stack into the trust base — the largest surface of the three. (C) split honestly: layout building (tar is already done std-only for archives, sha256 and gzip are small well-specified additions) is native-feasible now; push over TLS is the wall — a legal C variant is 'native build + option-A push until native TLS exists', and the recommendation is exactly that staging.

options.name: Shell out to skopeo / nix dockerTools (stopgap, bridge pattern)
options.detail: jet assembles inputs, skopeo (or nix dockerTools via the bridge) produces/pushes the image. Ships fastest, zero trust-base growth; requires the tool installed with a clear teaching message; leans on the very ecosystem the ballot said images wouldn't need.
options.code:
// push path only:
Command::new("skopeo").args(["copy", "oci:.jet/images/server", &format!("docker://{tag}")]).status()?

$ jet image server --push ghcr.io/acme/pulseops:0.4.0
Error [E09xx]: pushing needs the `skopeo` tool
 Fix: install skopeo, or push from CI where it exists

options.name: FFI-bridge an OCI/registry crate
options.detail: Bridge-template an OCI distribution client (e.g. oci-distribution) for build+push; Cargo.toml untouched, works everywhere jet runs; pulls an HTTP+TLS stack into the trust base — the biggest audit surface on the menu.

options.name: Native: std-only layout build now, native push when TLS exists
options.detail: sha256 + gzip + OCI tar layout in plain Rust (small, spec-pinned, reproducibility test-vectored) — jet image works offline with nothing installed. --push stages through option A's skopeo shell-out until a native TLS story lands; the gate is named, not hidden.
options.code:
// std-only build path:
let layer = tar::pack(closure_paths)?;            // existing archive code
let gz    = gzip::compress(&layer)?;              // new, RFC 1952
let digest = sha256::hex(&gz);                    // new, FIPS 180-4 vectors
write_oci_layout(&out, &[(digest, gz)], config)?;

$ jet image server           # fully native, reproducible digest
$ jet image server --push …  # skopeo until native TLS (named gate)

comparisons.note: dockerTools builds reproducible layered images without Docker — proof the no-daemon build is the right target; its interface is the function soup U14 replaces.
Language-native image builders that assemble OCI layouts and push directly — the option-B/C shape, proven in Go and Java.
The standard daemonless copy/push tool — the option-A engine and the C-variant push stopgap.

decisions.explainer: One machine is system.*; many machines are a map of hostname to system value. Per-host differences are copy-with-update on a shared system module — no overlay/override spaghetti, just the language's own edit-a-copy form. jet push builds every host closure locally (or in CI), ships to each host's hangar over ssh, activates atomically, and rolls back any host whose health probe fails.
decisions.story: Elena runs 2 web nodes and a DB. She edits the nginx module once, runs jet push prod, watches web1 activate and pass health, then web2. The DB host is untouched — its closure hash did not change, so nothing shipped.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Sequencing honesty — this rides jetos Phase 2 (activation/generations); ratify the SURFACE now so system.* design accounts for it, implement after single-host jetos works. (2) Unchanged-host skip falls out of content addressing — deploys are incremental for free. (3) Failure law: health probe fails → that host rolls back to its previous generation and the rollout halts; no partial-fleet mystery states. (4) Secrets integrate per U13 (recipients include host keys). (5) Magic/expert: two hosts need four lines; experts get Rollout knobs; auditors get per-host generation history.

comparisons.note: The NixOS fleet tool this absorbs: hive.nix with per-node overrides.
Flake-based deploys with rollback-on-failure — the health-gate prior art.
The heavyweight answer; fleets of plain machines should not require a cluster OS.

options.name: fleet.* namespace + jet push, staged health-gated rollout (recommended)
options.detail: Ratify surface now, implement post single-host jetos. Copy-with-update per host; incremental by content address.
options.code: module fleet.prod { hosts: { web1: system.web.{ region: "us-east" } } }

options.name: Per-host repos, no fleet construct
options.detail: Each machine pulls its own config (git + jet switch on a timer). Simple, works today, no orchestration, no staged rollout.

decisions.explainer: The owner uses nix shells daily; so does every target user this tool must win. Parity is three flows: (1) ad-hoc tools — jet env -p nodejs ripgrep opens a subshell with those packages from the default source (nixpkgs via the inferred provider today); (2) repo shells — jet env in a repo with flake.nix/devenv.nix and no env.* modules realizes the foreign devShell, prompt and lock jet-side; (3) ephemeral runs — jet run nixpkgs@fastfetch. Export closes the loop: jet bridge flake writes a flake.nix shim exposing this repo's packages/env to Nix consumers.
decisions.story: User keeps his muscle memory: where he typed nix-shell -p ffmpeg he types jet env -p ffmpeg. His work repo is still all-Nix — jet env picks up its devShell unchanged. His Jet side project exports a shim so his Nix-die-hard friend consumes it with nix build. Nobody converted anything, and both tools work the whole time.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet env -p nodejs_22 ripgrep     # nix-shell -p, typed refs, jet prompt
$ jet env                           # flake.nix detected -> its devShell
$ jet run nixpkgs@fastfetch           # nix run parity, nothing installed
$ jet bridge flake                    # writes flake.nix shim for Nix users
$ jet env --pure                    # hermetic: only declared packages
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Mechanism honesty — phase 1 shells out to the nix binary (ratified stopgap: requires Nix installed; clear message otherwise); the UX contract is jet's and survives the core provider absorbing realization later, so muscle memory built now never breaks. (2) Detection order: env.* modules win over flake.nix when both exist; --flake forces foreign. (3) devenv.nix consumption limited to packages/env/services fields it can map — unmappable fields produce a named warning, not silence (no silent caps). (4) The exported shim is generated, never hand-edited, and CI-checkable for drift. (5) Lock: foreign inputs recorded in .jet/lock with their narHashes — one lockfile law holds.

comparisons.note: The flows being matched, verb for verb.
comparisons.code:
$ nix-shell -p nodejs ripgrep
$ nix develop
$ nix run nixpkgs#fastfetch

decisions.explainer: jet = language, jetpack = package engine are ratified canon. The OS name ships on ISOs, boot menus, and headlines — it is the most public name in the family and currently a placeholder. Candidates below keep the aviation canon and are checked for obvious collisions (a real trademark sweep is a pre-release task).
decisions.story: Six months from now someone writes "I daily-drive ____". The word in the blank is this ballot.
decisions.inWild:
MENU (aviation canon, original, no echoes):
  jetos       — literal, matches canon, zero surprise
  Airframe    — the structure everything mounts to; strong OS metaphor
  Jetstream   — fast, always-on current; consumer-friendly
  Flightdeck  — where the whole machine is commanded
  Avionics    — the systems layer of an aircraft; precise but technical
  Mach        — short, fast, memorable; collision: mach kernel
  Contrail    — what a jet leaves behind; generations metaphor, soft
  Tarmac      — where jets live between flights; grounded, humble
  Altimeter   — instrument; too narrow
  Slipstream  — riding the jet's wake; evocative, minor product collisions
decisions.detail: Filter applied: must read as an OS (a place/structure, not an action), survive "install ____", "____ generations", "____ switch", and not collide loudly (Mach = kernel history; Slipstream = several products; Runway = fashion/startup tools — excluded). Shortlist rationale: Airframe is the structural metaphor (the OS is what everything bolts to) and unclaimed in the OS space; Jetstream is the friendliest to consumers; Flightdeck says "control everything" which matches declarative machines; jetos costs nothing and can be renamed only with pain later — decide now.

decisions.explainer: The vision originally implied five file names (pack/env/workspace/host/fleet) and three commands (jet/jetpack/jetos). The owner called the confusion; the fix was already latent: modules are named declarations (U3) discovered by find() (U4), so the namespace states the role and the filename is the USER'S organizational choice. Same for commands: verbs resolve against declared modules, and unknown jet verbs dispatch to the jetpack/jetos binaries git-style — the one-way dependency arrow survives untouched because the compiler execs by name, links nothing.
decisions.story: A beginner learns exactly two names on day one: pack.jet and jet. Six months later she manages a fleet — and has still learned zero new file names and zero new commands, only new module namespaces her editor completed for her.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Revisions required — U10 (jetpack.toml/env.jet as REQUIRED names die; env.jet remains a blessed convention), D-WORKSPACE2 (workspace.jet folds into root pack.jet workspace block), D-PM4 (jet fronts jetpack verbs). (2) The ratified payload/env SEMANTIC separation survives fully — it moves from filenames to namespaces. (3) Verb collisions: jet run file.jet vs jet run nixpkgs@tool disambiguate by ref shape; a user fn named like a tool verb never collides because lifecycle verbs are a closed ratified set. (4) Discovery cost: tools index by module namespace, so "where is the env?" is jet list env, not a filename hunt. (5) Single-binary UX with multi-binary architecture is the D-TOOL-SPLIT industry finding.

comparisons.note: One file (Cargo.toml), one command (cargo, fronting rustc) — the shape that won Rust its tooling reputation.
External subcommand dispatch by binary name — the zero-coupling mechanism proposed here.
The cautionary tale: flake.nix, shell.nix, default.nix, configuration.nix, home.nix + nix/nixos-rebuild/home-manager.

decisions.title: U18 — The two-names rule: one reserved file (pack.jet), one command (jet)?
decisions.gist: pack.jet is the only file name the tool looks for; module namespaces (env.*, system.*, fleet.*) carry every role, discovered anywhere. jet is the only command; jetpack/jetos stay as engines it dispatches to. Revises U10, D-WORKSPACE2, D-PM4.

options.name: Two names: pack.jet + jet (recommended)
options.detail: One reserved file, one command; roles are namespaces; engines dispatched by name.
options.code: $ jet env    # -> execs jetpack enter, invisible to the user

decisions.ratificationNote: Owner amendment folded in: only pack.jet is a reserved filename; every role module (env.*, system.*, fleet.*, build) may live in any file the user chooses (e.g. build.jet) and is discovered by declaration via find(), never by filename. Implementation plans must carry this as an acceptance test.

decisions.title: U18 follow-up — confirm pack.jet, reversing the shipped pkg.jet rename?
decisions.gist: TWONAMES1=A says the one reserved file is pack.jet. But the shipped code retired pack.jet FOR pkg.jet on 2026-06-18 (D-JPK-FILES, 'clean break, no alias'). Confirm the re-reversal to pack.jet, or amend the TWONAMES1 record to keep pkg.jet.
decisions.explainer: History, honestly: payload.jet -> pkg.jet was ratified and shipped 2026-06-18 (D-JPK-FILES; Syntax.rs:1140–1142 records 'the Jet package manifest is pkg.jet … Prior filenames (pack.jet, the U10 interim name) were retired (clean break, no alias)'). The 2026-07-01 vision and the ratified TWONAMES1 text both say pack.jet throughout. One of these must give: either the codebase renames again (every fixture, snapshot, doc, and user habit moves; the old-name teaching error now fires on the name we shipped two weeks ago), or the TWONAMES1 record is amended to read pkg.jet and the vision docs sweep. This is purely a spelling call — the one-reserved-file semantics are identical either way and no other U11–U19 work is blocked on it.
decisions.story: A user who created a project on June 20 has pkg.jet on disk. Under A, her next jet build prints a teaching error telling her to rename to pack.jet — one command, but the tool renamed its own file twice in a month. Under B, nothing changes for her, and the vision docs quietly correct their spelling to pkg.jet.
decisions.inWild:
// Option A — after migration:
$ jet build
Error [E1226]: `pkg.jet` is no longer the manifest name — Jet reads `pack.jet`
 Why: one reserved filename (U18); prior names were retired in a clean break
 Fix: rename `pkg.jet` to `pack.jet`

// Option B — nothing moves:
$ ls
pkg.jet   src/   .jet/
$ jet build      # works as today; vision.md re-spelled to pkg.jet
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md §'U18 — the two-names rename' (and the 'pkg.jet -> pack.jet is a reversal' ambiguity flagged at hand-off). Option A migration, concretely: PAYLOAD_FILE constant in crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs flips to "pack.jet"; ~12+ fixture files rename; all pkg.jet-mentioning stderr snapshots re-bless; docs sweep (spec.md, epoch-5 plans, payload-env-separation.md); E1226 teaching error covers pkg.jet/payload.jet/jet.toml/jetpack.toml by name — the house clean-break pattern, third rename in the file's history. Option B is the zero-churn path: amend the TWONAMES1 ratification record + sweep vision.md/ballot prose to pkg.jet; cost is that the ratified ballot text, the owner's amendment note, and all U18 worked examples say pack.jet — amending a ratified record is its own precedent to weigh. Either way the U18 semantics (one reserved file, roles by namespace, find() discovery) land unchanged; only the string differs.

options.name: Confirm pack.jet (matches the ratified TWONAMES1 text)
options.detail: Rename shipped pkg.jet -> pack.jet: Syntax.rs constant, fixtures, snapshots, docs; E1226 teaches the move (clean break, no alias — house pattern). Cost: second rename in a month for early users; the ratified text stays exactly as written.
options.code:
