options.detail: Expose versioned value APIs for tokens, syntax tree, diagnostics, semindex, and source maps. Internal crates remain private; no AST mutation enters compilation. CLI commands mirror the same model for external tools.
options.code:
tokens :: jc.lex(src)?
unit :: jc.parse(src)?
checked :: jc.check(unit)?
$ jet semindex --json src/run.jet

options.name: Raw compiler crates public
options.detail: Expose internal crates directly. Maximum dogfood reuse, but public stability freezes internals and leaks implementation details.
options.code:
use jet_parser.Parser
use jet_sema.Checker

options.name: CLI JSON only
options.detail: Tools shell out to `jet semindex --json` and `jet fmt/check --json`. Stable and simple, but awkward for in-process tools and compiler-like libraries.
options.code: data :: process.run(["jet", "semindex", "--json"])?

options.name: Mutable AST builder API
options.detail: Users can construct/transform AST nodes. Powerful for standalone tools, but must stay outside compilation or it recreates macro/AST injection pressure.
options.code:
tree := jc.parse(src)?
tree.rewrite(fn(node) => ...)

comparisons.note: Odin exposes parser/checker-adjacent packages for tools.
The compiler API powers many tools but exposes lots of compiler shape.
rust-analyzer provides stable-ish tooling data separate from rustc internals.

decisions.title: Universal trust grants
decisions.gist: How Jet shows and controls package, build, environment, and OS authority.
decisions.explainer: Best of both worlds: magic default summary for Betty, full authority graph for Hank, one revocable model everywhere.
decisions.story: Betty opens a new web-service repo. It wants to fetch npm packages, run one build recipe, start Postgres, and decrypt two dev secrets. She needs one plain trust screen; Hank on security needs the exact hosts, files, commands, cache keys, and revocation handle.

options.name: Code effects only
options.detail: `#(Net, Secret)` stays a language/runtime fact. Jetpack has separate prompts for package fetches, build recipes, services, secrets, and OS activation. This keeps language effects narrow but makes users learn multiple trust models.
options.code:
$ jet dev
package manager asks for network
build asks for script permission
service manager asks to start postgres
program asks for Secret effect

options.name: Unified grants (recommended)
options.detail: One effect/grant graph spans code, packages, builds, envs, services, images, fleets, and jetos activation. Beginners see intent summaries; experts expand to exact authority and policy. Weakness fixed: prompt overload is collapsed by intent, with deep audit one key away.
options.code:
$ jet dev
Trust env.dev?  npm network, vite build recipe, postgres service, stripe-dev secret
  [allow once] [allow for this env hash] [inspect]

$ jet grant inspect env.dev
network: registry.npmjs.org
commands: vite build recipe
service: postgres:5432
secret: stripe-dev
cache key: sha256:...

options.name: CLI permissions only
options.detail: Use Deno-style flags such as `--allow-net` and `--allow-secret` for runtime code. Familiar for scripts, but package/build/env/OS authority remains outside the same model.
options.code:
$ jet run app.jet --allow-net=api.stripe.com --allow-secret=STRIPE_KEY
$ jetpack enter   # separate trust model for packages/services

comparisons.note: Clear scoped runtime permissions, but package/build/env/OS authority is not the same graph.
Install scripts have broad historical trust problems; Jet should default-deny and summarize intent.
Sandboxing is strong, but the authority model is not beginner-visible as one product surface.

decisions.title: Semantic dossier
decisions.gist: Whether every Jet artifact gets one explainable dossier view.
decisions.explainer: Beginner gets one command; expert gets precise lenses and machine-readable facts.
decisions.story: Doris reviews a PR that changes a server type and an env module. She wants API drift, effects, dependency graph, generated code, migrations, performance budgets, and deployment impact without remembering six commands. Earl still wants stable JSON for CI.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dossier src/server.jet
Facts
  public API: 2 changed functions
  effects: Net added to charge()
  generated: 1 Codable derive
  package graph: stripe-sdk updated
  env impact: env.dev gains STRIPE_KEY

$ jet dossier src/server.jet --lens effects --json

options.name: Separate commands only
options.detail: Keep `semindex`, `expand`, `graph`, `audit`, `bench`, and Jetpack explain commands separate. Experts can compose them, but beginners do not know where to start.
options.code:
$ jet semindex --json
$ jet graph
$ jet audit
$ jet expand --facts inline
$ jet explain-build server

options.name: Dossier umbrella (recommended)
options.detail: `jet dossier` is one beginner command over named existing fact lenses. Experts keep stable lens names and JSON schemas. Weakness fixed: no junk drawer because every section must be owned by an existing fact producer.
options.code:
$ jet dossier package api
api - public changes
build - cache/provenance
runtime - effects/budgets
deploy - env/image/system impact

$ jet dossier package api --lens build --json

options.name: IDE-only dossier
options.detail: Show dossiers in editor panels only. This is discoverable in rich UI, but CLI review and CI lose the same first-class view.
options.code:
# Editor: Dossier panel
# CLI fallback: use semindex/graph/audit manually

comparisons.note: `cargo tree` is useful but only covers dependency shape.
Derivation graphs exist, but users often need extra tooling to understand impact.
Jet already has semindex/expand/build/audit facts; the missing piece is one product view.

decisions.title: Strict package graph and catalogs
decisions.gist: How Jetpack prevents hidden dependencies and workspace version drift.
decisions.explainer: Strict by default plus catalogs gives correctness and low-update toil.
decisions.story: Priya maintains a monorepo with 40 packages. A test passes because a root env happened to expose a tool. The release package does not declare it, so CI fails later. She wants strictness without version-update busywork.

options.name: Ambient workspace visibility
options.detail: Packages can see tools/deps installed at the workspace or env root. Beginner friction is low, but hidden dependencies return.
options.code:
module env.dev { packages: [default.protoc] }
# package api can call protoc even though api never declared it

options.name: Strict graph plus catalogs (recommended)
options.detail: Each package sees only declared deps; catalogs centralize shared versions. Weakness fixed: the error offers one command to add the missing dep to the right package or catalog.
options.code:
Error [E12xx]: package api used protoc but did not declare it
 Why: packages only see their own declared graph
 Fix: run jet add protoc --to api, or add it to workspace catalog

$ jet add http --catalog backend

options.name: Per-package locks only
options.detail: Every member owns its versions and lock. Isolation is clear, but monorepo-wide upgrades and duplicate-version control get worse.
options.code:
packages/api/.jet/lock
packages/web/.jet/lock
# http appears at 2.3.0 and 2.4.1 until manually reconciled

comparisons.note: Strict dependency visibility and catalogs are praised for reducing hidden deps and duplicated versions.
Workspaces share resolution, but feature/version unification can surprise users.
Virtualenv isolation helps, but project/workspace version policy is spread across tools.

decisions.title: Explainable lockfiles
decisions.gist: How `.jet/lock` is inspected, reviewed, and merged.
decisions.explainer: Exact machine identity plus human explanation gives reproducibility and reviewability.
decisions.story: Amara rebases a package update and sees a lock conflict. She should not edit hashes or rerun a resolver blindly; she needs to know which package pulled the change, why it is safe, and what command reconciles it.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet lock explain textkit
textkit 1.4.2
  required by: api, cli
  selected by: catalog.text
  integrity: sha256:...
  cache: hit linux.x64

$ jet lock merge
conflict: textkit version vs feature policy
Fix: choose catalog bump, keep old version, or split policy

options.name: Generated lock only
options.detail: Treat lock conflicts as generated-file churn: rerun the resolver. Reproducibility stays, but intent and reviewability stay weak.
options.code:
$ jet update
# .jet/lock rewritten; reviewer sees hashes and versions only

options.name: Explainable semantic lock (recommended)
options.detail: Lock entries carry exact identity plus human rationale: owner package, policy, source, provenance, hash, platform, update command. Weakness fixed: rationale is separate from deterministic identity so review can collapse unchanged metadata.
options.code:
$ jet lock why-dupe regex
regex 1.x used by legacy-parser
regex 2.x used by web-router
Fix: jet update regex --unify, or add split-policy reason

$ jet lock merge --explain

options.name: Human-authored lock
options.detail: Users edit lock decisions directly. This is transparent, but risks invalid/tampered identity and breaks generated integrity.
options.code:
.jet/lock:
  textkit: 1.4.2   # edited manually

comparisons.note: Manifest stays broad, lock stores exact versions.
Package lock records exact install tree and is committed.
Lockfile studies report maintenance and interpretation pain; Jet can make that a product surface.

decisions.title: Migration importers
decisions.gist: Whether Jet adoption gets first-class importers from other ecosystems.
decisions.explainer: Best path: instant on-ramp, editable source, and visible native replacement.
decisions.story: Walter has a TypeScript app, Python data scripts, a Rust CLI, a Nix flake, and a Dockerfile. Jet should let him consume, coexist, and replace incrementally, with generated Jet he can inspect and edit.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet import package.json
$ jet import pyproject.toml
$ jet import Cargo.toml
$ jet import flake.nix
$ jet import Dockerfile

# generated role modules + deps + adapters + TODO diagnostics

options.name: Manual migration guides
options.detail: Document how to rewrite projects by hand. This keeps generated source out, but adoption starts with a cliff.
options.code:
# docs: Translating package.json to pkg.jet
# user writes everything by hand

options.name: Editable importers (recommended)
options.detail: Importers generate role modules, deps, adapters, FFI stubs, and TODO diagnostics. Weakness fixed: output is canonical Jet source, not hidden compat state; `jet migrate native` tracks replacement progress.
options.code:
$ jet import package.json
created pkg.jet
created modules/env.web.jet
created .jet/bindings/js/plotly.jet
TODO [JSMIG1]: package chartjs uses dynamic plugin loading; inspect stub

options.name: Runtime compatibility shims
options.detail: Run foreign ecosystems mostly as-is under Jetpack. Fast start, but projects stay foreign-shaped and native migration is not structural.
options.code:
deps: { app: node@"." }
$ jet run node.app

comparisons.note: Won adoption by coexisting with JavaScript and preserving migration paths.
Can consume many ecosystems, but translating a project still requires Nix knowledge.
Dockerfiles are a universal deployment input; Jet should import them into image role modules.

decisions.title: Federated Jetpack providers
decisions.gist: How Jetpack ingests npm, PyPI, Cargo, SwiftPM, Nix, GitHub, and binary sources.
decisions.explainer: Jetpack gets global reach while keeping one authority graph.
decisions.story: Noor wants numpy, plotly, ripgrep, raylib, and a GitHub binary tool in one reproducible env. She should get reach without inheriting each ecosystem's trust and install behavior.

options.name: Jet registry first
options.detail: Only Jet registry and manual adapters are first-class. Native purity is high, but users cannot tap the world's useful software immediately.
options.code:
deps: { textkit: "1.0" }
# numpy/plotly require hand adapters

options.name: Federated providers under Jetpack authority (recommended)
options.detail: Foreign registries are metadata sources; Jetpack owns fetch, lock, sandbox, build effects, signatures, audit, and replacement overlays. Weakness fixed: broad reach does not grant broad trust.
options.code:
$ jet add py:numpy
locked: pypi numpy 2.1 sha256:...
permissions: native extension, no install script granted
replacement: none yet

options.name: Shell out to native managers
options.detail: Let npm/pip/cargo/swift run their own install flows inside envs. Reach is high, but lock/provenance/sandbox semantics fragment.
options.code:
$ jet env
runs: npm install
runs: pip install -r requirements.txt

comparisons.note: Unmatched reach, high supply-chain exposure.
Strong reproducibility and binary substitution, but separate language and package definitions.
Integrated package/build UX, but mostly Rust-only.

decisions.title: jetos Studio
decisions.gist: Whether declarative OS config gets a first-party GUI over canonical Jet modules.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: GUI-first for beginners, source-first for truth and experts.
decisions.story: Eli wants declarative Linux with rollback but does not want to learn the config language before enabling Steam, Flatpak, fonts, backups, and SSH. Mira is an expert and wants exact source diffs, options, and provenance.

options.name: Text/CLI only
options.detail: Keep OS management like NixOS: source files and commands. Experts are served; mainstream users face the language before the value.
options.code:
$ editor modules/system/laptop.jet
$ jetos switch laptop

options.name: GUI writes Jet modules (recommended)
options.detail: Studio is a source editor over typed modules: toggles, search, conflict fixes, and diff preview write canonical Jet. Weakness fixed: no split-brain JSON; expert mode opens exact module, option, graph, and provenance.
options.code:
jetos Studio:
  Enable OpenSSH [on]
  Preview diff:
    services: { openssh: { enable: true } }
  Apply -> writes modules/system/laptop.jet

options.name: GUI-owned state
options.detail: The GUI stores its own config and exports Jet when asked. Beginner UI is clean, but source of truth splits immediately.
options.code:
.jetos/studio.json
# export to Jet later

comparisons.note: Rollback/declarative power, but code-first OS UX.
Great settings UX, weak declarative reproducibility.
Friendly GUI plus YAML history shows both the promise and split-brain risk.

decisions.title: jetos proof before switch
decisions.gist: How jetos tests OS changes before activation.
decisions.explainer: Keep safe defaults without slowing harmless edits; experts can set policy.
decisions.story: Ren updates GPU drivers and filesystem options. Before changing the boot default, they want a plan, VM boot, service health checks, and rollback proof. A tiny font package change should not feel like launching a moon mission.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetos switch laptop --plan
$ jetos test laptop --vm
$ jetos switch laptop --name pre-gpu
$ jetos rollback

options.name: Build/switch/rollback
options.detail: Offer the NixOS-style baseline: build a generation, switch, and rollback. Good core, but risky classes are discovered after activation.
options.code:
$ jetos switch laptop
$ jetos rollback

options.name: Risk-aware proof pipeline (recommended)
options.detail: Plan/diff always; VM proof and rollback proof required for boot/kernel/filesystem/service-risk classes and CI policy. Weakness fixed: small edits stay light, dangerous edits get proof.
options.code:
$ jetos switch laptop
Plan: boot/kernel risk detected
Fix: run jetos test laptop --vm, or policy override with #Unsafe("reason")

options.name: GUI preview only
options.detail: Show plan and risk in Studio. Friendly, but headless CI and server admins lose the same gate.
options.code:
jetos Studio: preview boot risk
# no CLI proof artifact

comparisons.note: `test`, `build-vm`, and rollback are loved primitives.
Rollout health and rollback are expected for services.
Already models generations/hangar; jetos can add risk-aware activation.

decisions.title: Typed data Core
decisions.gist: Whether data analysis becomes a first-party Core domain.
decisions.explainer: Native typed floor plus foreign accelerators gives reach now and conquest path later.
decisions.story: June reads CSV, joins telemetry, computes stats, calls a Python model for one step, and ships a native dashboard. Jet should not require Python for the whole workflow, but should borrow Python reach while Core grows.
decisions.inWild:
use core.data
use core.stats
use py.numpy as np

fn run() -> Unit ? {
    rows :: data.csv<Row>("events.csv")?
    daily :: rows.group_by(.day).summarize(count: count(), p95: p95(.latency))
    print(daily)
}

options.name: Interop-only data
options.detail: Use Python/R/JS packages for data work. Reach is immediate, but Jet has no native data identity.
options.code:
use py.pandas as pd
fn run() { df :: pd.read_csv("events.csv") }

options.name: Core data floor plus accelerators (recommended)
options.detail: Ship typed tables/series/stats/plot basics in Core; Python/R/GPU bridges accelerate gaps. Weakness fixed: every bridge-heavy workflow exposes native replacement status.
options.code:
rows :: data.csv<Row>("events.csv")?
model :: py.sklearn.load("model.pkl")
jet migrate native --domain data

options.name: SQL-only data
options.detail: Make databases/query blocks the main data story. Strong for DBs, weak for notebooks, files, arrays, and local analysis.
options.code: #Sql<Row> { select * from events }

comparisons.note: Wins data through batteries and ecosystem, but packaging/native deps leak friction.
Strong numeric syntax/perf, smaller ecosystem than Python.
Excellent statistics workflow, less general systems/app story.

decisions.title: Game development lane
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets a blessed game-dev substrate.
decisions.explainer: Substrate plus replaceable backends gives beginner workflow and expert control.
decisions.story: Imani builds a 2D game, then an editor, then a 3D prototype. She needs assets, hot reload, ECS, fixed-step simulation, input, audio, GPU, deterministic replay, and editor hooks without giving up low-level control.

options.name: Graphics bridge only
options.detail: Bless `core.raylib`/graphics wrappers and let game architecture grow in packages. Good for samples, not a world-class game workflow.
options.code:
use core.raylib
fn run() { raylib.draw_circle(...) }

options.name: Stable game substrate (recommended)
options.detail: Core owns assets, ECS, input, fixed-step timing, replay, editor hooks, and budgets; renderer/audio/editor backends are packages. Weakness fixed: engine sprawl is avoided by making Core the substrate, not one monolithic engine.

options.name: Third-party engines only
options.detail: Let Godot/Unity/custom engines bind to Jet. Interop works, but Jet does not become the best language for game code itself.
options.code:
use c.godot
# Jet scripts foreign engine APIs

comparisons.note: Great workflow and editors; language/runtime control is not Jet-shaped.
Powerful but fragmented game ecosystem.
Attract game devs through control and simple builds; Jet can add batteries and safety.

decisions.title: Embedded and freestanding profiles
decisions.gist: How Jet scales down to microcontrollers, kernels, and no-OS targets.
decisions.explainer: One language, invisible defaults for beginners, complete target control for experts.
decisions.story: Tessa writes firmware for a sensor board. She wants no allocator, fixed memory, volatile/MMIO gates, linker script control, panic policy, and the same Jet diagnostics. Her web teammates should never see any of it.

options.name: Freestanding build flags
options.detail: Expose `jet build --freestanding --target ...` and rely on low-level code when needed. Expert path exists; product guidance is thin.
options.code: $ jet build firmware.jet --freestanding --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf

options.name: Typed target profiles (recommended)
options.detail: Board/target profiles make hidden defaults explicit only when embedded/kernels are selected. Expert controls memory, linker, allocator, panic, volatile, and audit output. Weakness fixed: normal Jet never sees target jargon.

options.name: Separate Jet dialect
options.detail: Make embedded Jet a different surface with its own defaults. It can be lean, but violates one-language identity.
options.code:
firmware.jet uses embedded-only syntax
app.jet uses normal Jet syntax

comparisons.note: Excellent target/control story.
Safe and powerful, but many crates/tool concepts surface early.
Ubiquitous control with weak safety/default tooling.

decisions.title: Proof and replay mode
decisions.gist: How Jet turns contracts, tests, budgets, and replay into a correctness product.
decisions.explainer: Progressive proof preserves beginner ergonomics and gives experts real evidence.
decisions.story: Omar ships payment code and a distributed job runner. He wants contract checks, property tests, budget enforcement, deterministic replay, and proof reports before deploy, without raw solver errors becoming the user interface.

options.name: Tests and contracts only
options.detail: Keep today's practical path: tests, contracts, and diagnostics. Useful, but proof/replay are not unified product surfaces.
options.code:
jet test
jet bench
# replay/proof separate or absent

options.name: Progressive proof and replay (recommended)
options.detail: `jet prove` layers contracts, refinements, effects, budgets, property tests, and replay facts. Weakness fixed: beginner face is tests/contracts/replay; deeper solvers are opt-in lenses with Jet diagnostics.
options.code:
$ jet prove src/payments.jet
proved: @Pre/@Post for 12 funcs
checked: 4 budgets
needs test: network timeout path

$ jet prove --lens bounds --json

options.name: Formal verification first
options.detail: Make proof obligations central before code ships. Strong guarantees, but daily Jet becomes proof-tool-shaped.
options.code:
fn charge(...) -> Receipt
proof { forall amount: Money where amount > 0 ... }

comparisons.note: Compile-time memory safety proof is a major adoption driver.
Strong verification, high ceremony.
Practical confidence with shrinking; Jet can integrate it with contracts.

decisions.title: Performance budget profiles
decisions.gist: Whether performance expectations are declared and enforced as product facts.
decisions.explainer: Budgets make performance visible without hiding expert policy knobs.
decisions.story: Mei owns a latency-sensitive HTTP service. She wants startup, allocation, binary size, p99 latency, and generated-unsafe budgets in CI, with local runs that explain what changed.

options.name: Benchmarks only
options.detail: Use `jet bench` and human review. Flexible, but regressions are easy to miss or debate.
options.code:
$ jet bench
p99_latency: 7ms

options.name: Typed budgets (recommended)
options.detail: Budgets attach to packages/envs/services and feed build, bench, dev, dossier, and CI. Weakness fixed: deterministic budgets are hard gates; statistical budgets use pinned baselines and trend policy.
options.code:
$ jet build --release
Error [E14xx]: binary_size budget exceeded: 3.4MiB > 3MiB
Fix: inspect jet dossier --lens size, raise budget, or use profile small

options.name: Optimizer promises
options.detail: Rely on compiler/runtime to optimize without user budgets. Nice default story, but no explicit contract for teams.
options.code:
$ jet build --release
# no declared perf contract

comparisons.note: Simple deployment and predictable operational profile are valued.
Peak performance is excellent, but tuning often spreads across flags/crates/profilers.
Bundle-size budgets are common because teams need explicit gates.

decisions.title: Native replacement overlays
decisions.gist: How Jet replaces foreign packages with native Jet without changing call sites.
decisions.explainer: This turns interop into conquest: same surface, native implementation, proven fit.
decisions.story: A team starts with `js.plotly` and `py.numpy`. Later `core.plot` and `core.linalg` mature. They need to swap implementations without rewriting every import and call.

options.name: Manual rewrites
options.detail: Teams edit imports and call sites when native packages mature. Clear, but migration cost delays replacement.
options.code:
use js.plotly as plotly
# later:
use core.plot as plotly
# fix call mismatches by hand

options.name: Compatibility-proved overlays (recommended)
options.detail: A Jet package declares it replaces a foreign surface only after compatibility proof over public types, effects, errors, examples, and golden fixtures. Weakness fixed: semantic mismatch is visible before the overlay is allowed.
options.code:
core.plot replaces js.plotly {
    surface: generated(js.plotly)
    examples: inherit
}

$ jet replace js.plotly with core.plot
proved: 94% surface compatible
blocked: dynamic plugin API needs adapter

options.name: Permanent interop
options.detail: Keep foreign packages as normal forever. Reach stays high, but native Jet never absorbs the ecosystem.
options.code:
deps: { plotly: js@"plotly.js@2" }
# no native replacement contract

comparisons.note: Preserved JavaScript surfaces while strengthening types.
Can replace package definitions, but not API compatibility.
API compatibility matters; Jet can prove more with examples/effects.

decisions.title: Optional run return and failure annotations
decisions.gist: Whether beginners may keep bare `fn run()` while experts can type an explicit fallible entrypoint.
decisions.explainer: `Unit` is Jet's "nothing meaningful is returned" type, like `void` in C/Java or `()` in Rust. A bare `fn run() { ... }` means `fn run() -> Unit { ... }` by default. The ballot is not asking whether beginners must write `Unit`; they do not. It asks whether experts may opt into the explicit fallible form `fn run() -> Unit ?`.
decisions.story: Priya writes a tiny deploy tool. A beginner should type `fn run() { ... }` and never learn return-type ceremony. Later, Priya wants startup failure to flow with `?`, so she writes the expert form `fn run() -> Unit ?`. Both spell the same entrypoint name; the annotation only states what the function returns and whether failure can escape.

options.name: Bare run by default, explicit fallible run for experts
options.detail: Beginners write `fn run() { ... }`. The compiler treats that as returning `Unit` and infallible. Experts may write `fn run() -> Unit ?` when startup can fail and they want `?` to propagate from the entrypoint. `run` remains the only entrypoint name.

options.name: Bare run only for now
options.detail: Only `fn run() { ... }` is accepted today. Fallible startup must be handled inside the body. This keeps the entrypoint rule tiny, but makes normal CLI/file setup noisier once users need `?`.

options.name: Require explicit return annotations on run
options.detail: Every entrypoint writes its return type: `fn run() -> Unit`. This is explicit, but spends ceremony on every beginner program and conflicts with the magic-out-of-the-box entrypoint goal.

comparisons.note: `main` can omit the return type for the simple path or return `Result` for fallible startup.
comparisons.code:
fn main() { println!("hi"); }
fn main() -> Result<(), Error> { run()?; Ok(()) }

comparisons.note: `main` cannot return an error; startup failures are handled manually.
comparisons.code: func main() { if err := run(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

decisions.comment: But instead of "Unit" use Void

decisions.title: External regex dependency in compile-time path
decisions.gist: Whether a compile-time semantic path may keep an external regex dependency.
decisions.story: Nora adds a compile-time helper and expects the compiler surface to stay std-only. The dependency graph shows regex in `jet-comptime`; if that crate participates in compiler semantics, it weakens I6 and makes future bootstrapping less honest.

options.name: Remove the dependency
options.detail: Replace regex use with a small std-only scanner or parser in the compile-time path. If regex-like power is needed for user code, it belongs in stdlib/runtime code, not the compiler semantic core.
options.code:
// compiler-side scanner: std-only
fn scan_ident(src: &str) -> Token { ... }

options.name: Approve a narrow I6 carve-out
options.detail: Keep regex in `jet-comptime` and document that this crate is allowed an external dependency until a named removal date. The carve-out is explicit and owner-owned.
options.code: // I6 exception: jet-comptime may depend on regex until <date/card>.

options.name: Move regex behind a tool boundary
options.detail: Keep compiler semantics std-only, but let a separate generated-data/tooling step use regex outside the compiler trust boundary. The generated artifact is checked into the repo and audited.
options.code:
$ jet devtools generate-comptime-tables
# tool may use regex; compiler reads generated tables only.

comparisons.note: The compiler has strict dependency policy; procedural tools and libraries have different rules.
The standard toolchain favors small self-contained compiler machinery.

decisions.title: jetos syntax freeze boundary
decisions.gist: Whether jetos-only surface is live syntax law or research-only until the OS lane reopens.
decisions.story: Ari reads the syntax decisions and sees OS configuration examples. Another agent reads the roadmap and sees jetos frozen for research. One starts implementing commands; the other deletes examples. The board needs one boundary.

options.name: Research-only jetos surface
options.detail: Move OS-only spellings to a research appendix and keep only Jetpack-active env/image/generation pieces live. Syntax law stops implying jetos commands/modules are buildable today.

options.name: Frozen but ratified
options.detail: Keep the current jetos surface in syntax law, but mark it frozen and not implementation-ready. Agents may align docs around it, but must not implement new jetos behavior until the freeze lifts.
options.code:
// syntax decision note:
// jetos module syntax is ratified/frozen; implementation work blocked until OS lane opens.

options.name: Make jetos surface live now
options.detail: Treat current jetos examples as active language/product law and unblock implementation cards that use them. This makes the roadmap freeze obsolete and requires immediate cleanup of roadmap wording.
options.code:
$ jetos switch laptop
# live product surface; docs/tests must track it.

comparisons.note: OS module syntax is product law, not research prose.
Accepted proposals distinguish implemented, accepted, and deferred states.

decisions.title: Unsafe gate reason requirement
decisions.gist: Whether every user-written Unsafe gate must include a non-empty audit reason.
decisions.story: Sol reviews generated unsafe blocks before a release. A region labeled only `#Unsafe` says nothing about why the escape hatch exists. A region labeled with a reason can be audited, searched, and challenged.

options.name: Require non-empty reasons everywhere
options.detail: Both block and function Unsafe forms require a non-empty string. The compiler stores the reason for audit output and rejects empty or missing reasons with a Jet diagnostic.

options.name: Allow bare Unsafe with lint
options.detail: Bare `#Unsafe` compiles, but strict profiles and CI can reject it. Beginner code still never sees Unsafe by default; expert experiments are quick, but audit quality depends on policy.
options.code:
#Unsafe { c_call() }
// lint: add an audit reason before release.

options.name: Require reasons for blocks only
options.detail: Unsafe blocks require reasons; `#Unsafe fn` may be bare because the function name is considered the audit anchor. This is less consistent and makes function-level gates easier to under-document.
options.code:
#Unsafe("manual aliasing proof") { ... }
#Unsafe fn fast_copy(...) { ... }

comparisons.note: `unsafe` has no required reason; many teams add comments by convention.
Some Rust teams require SAFETY comments by lint/review.
comparisons.code:
// SAFETY: pointer came from slice bounds check
unsafe { ... }

decisions.title: Collection shorthand and named collection canon
decisions.gist: Whether Jet uses short bracket forms for default list/map and named generic types for specialized collections.
decisions.explainer: The useful split is common-shape shorthand versus specific data-structure name. Lists and default maps are semantic defaults, so shorthand can reduce noise. Specialized collections encode performance/order/hash policy, so their names should stay visible: `HashMap<K, V>`, `Deque<T>`, `Set<T>`. The sharp edge is map shorthand: comma form `[K, V]` is compact but can read like pair/tuple/list; colon form `[K: V]` makes key-to-value meaning clearer and matches map literals/field association.
decisions.story: Bea learns Jet from examples. Lists and maps are everywhere, so short notation helps. But when she reaches `HashMap`, `BTreeMap`, `Deque`, or `SmallVec`, she needs a consistent named-type rule that scales without inventing a new shorthand for every container.

options.name: Hybrid: `[T]`, `[K: V]`, named specific collections
options.detail: Default list and default map get short forms. Specific collection types use Rust-style named generics: `HashMap<K, V>`, `BTreeMap<K, V>`, `Deque<T>`, `Set<T>`. This gives beginners compact common cases and experts visible data-structure policy.

options.name: Rust-style named generics for everything
options.detail: Use `List<T>`, `Map<K, V>`, `HashMap<K, V>` everywhere. Very consistent and searchable; common types are noisier and Jet loses the lightweight feel of list/map shorthand.

options.name: Comma map shorthand: `[T]`, `[K, V]`, named specific collections
options.detail: Matches the proposed `[Map, MapVal]` shape most directly: list has one bracket argument, map has two. Compact and symmetric with generic argument lists, but `[K, V]` can be mistaken for a pair/tuple/list-of-two-types rather than key-to-value mapping.

options.name: No collection shorthand
options.detail: Every collection is a named type. This is maximally explicit, but spends the most ceremony on the two containers users write constantly.
options.code:
let names: List<Text> = List.of("Ada")
let ages: Map<Text, Int> = Map.of("Ada", 36)

comparisons.note: Named collection types make data-structure policy visible.
Short forms for common list/map, named types when policy matters.
Both shorthand and named forms exist for arrays; too many equivalents can fragment style.

decisions.title: Bench marker spelling
decisions.gist: Whether benchmark markers use parenthesized arguments like other marker calls.
decisions.story: Theo writes tests and benchmarks in the same file. `#Test("fast path")` and `#Bench "fast path"` look like two marker grammars even though both attach metadata to a function.
decisions.inWild:
#Test("parses dates") fn parses_dates() { ... }
#Bench "parse throughput" fn bench_parse() { ... }

options.name: Use `#Bench("name")`
options.detail: Bench follows the same parenthesized marker-call shape as Test and other metadata markers. This gives one parser/documentation rule for marker arguments.
options.code: #Bench("parse throughput") fn bench_parse() { ... }

options.name: Bless `#Bench "name"` as an exception
options.detail: Keep the space-string form specifically for benchmarks. It reads nicely, but creates a special marker grammar users must learn.
options.code: #Bench "parse throughput" fn bench_parse() { ... }

options.name: Accept both spellings
options.detail: Both forms compile and the formatter normalizes one. This is a transition path only; as permanent law it is two spellings for one semantic job.
options.code:
#Bench "parse throughput" fn a() { ... }
#Bench("parse throughput") fn b() { ... }

comparisons.note: Attributes use one bracketed argument form.
Attributes with arguments use parentheses.

decisions.title: Runtime profile name canon
decisions.gist: What Jet calls the target environment a program expects.
decisions.explainer: `Runtime profile` means the environment contract for a build target. Examples: `bare` = no OS services, `alloc` = heap but no hosted OS, `hosted` = normal OS process with files/network/time. The audit issue is naming: current prose/examples used `std`, but Jet docs also say user-facing library naming is `Core`, never `std`/`stdlib`. The decision is whether the public profile name should avoid `std` too.
decisions.story: Lena configures a package for normal desktop/server use. Another package targets a tiny embedded board. They need a word for "what runtime services exist here": no OS, heap only, or full OS/filesystem/network. The old ballot called that a ring layer; clearer wording is runtime profile.

options.name: Use `runtime: hosted` for the normal OS profile
options.detail: `hosted` means the program runs with normal OS services. `bare`/`alloc` can name smaller targets later. Core remains the library brand; `std` disappears from user-facing runtime config.

options.name: Keep `layer: std` as a runtime exception
options.detail: `std` remains the public name for the normal runtime layer, with a written exception saying the no-std rule applies only to library names. Existing examples stay familiar to Rust users, but the naming law has a special case.

options.name: Use `runtime: core`
options.detail: The normal profile uses the Core brand. This avoids `std`, but overloads Core-the-library with runtime availability and can make embedded/no-OS profiles harder to explain.

comparisons.note: `std`, `core`, and `alloc` are library tiers; the names are powerful but easy to confuse with target/runtime policy.
Target/environment choices are separate from the standard-library import name.
Hosted versus freestanding is a long-standing environment distinction.

decisions.title: Where should Canvas store breakpoints and watches?
decisions.gist: Blueprint persists breakpoints and watches in editor state. Canvas must support debugger parity while preserving source truth and avoiding accidental committed debug noise.
decisions.explainer: Breakpoints and watches are not program semantics. They should be local dev state anchored to source spans by default, with optional explicit source annotations only if the user wants team-shared debugging probes.
decisions.story: I set a breakpoint on a Canvas node, reload, and it still lands on the same source span. It should not silently edit my program unless I explicitly choose a shared probe.
decisions.inWild:
~/.jet/canvas/debug-state/... anchors source hash + span
// optional later: #[debug_probe] if ratified separately
decisions.detail: Devil pass: source-span drift will destroy trust. Local state must validate source hashes and degrade to invalid breakpoint/warning state when stale.

options.name: Local source-span debug state with explicit shared probes later (recommended)
options.detail: Store breakpoints/watches locally, anchored by file hash and source span. Stale anchors become invalid. Team-shared probes require explicit source annotations in a later decision.

options.name: Always write debug annotations to source
options.detail: Reviewable and portable, but pollutes source with personal debug state.
options.code: #[breakpoint] call()

options.name: Session-only debug state
options.detail: No persistence risk, but misses basic debugger UX.
options.code: // lost after reload

comparisons.note: Blueprint breakpoints persist in editor ini files and can become invalid until compile.

decisions.title: What should Canvas do when a user connects compatible but different pin types?
decisions.gist: Blueprint inserts auto-cast nodes for compatible mismatched pins. Jet must avoid invisible second semantics while preserving the authoring speed of drag-to-connect.
decisions.explainer: Canvas can make conversion authoring fast without making conversion implicit. The graph may suggest and insert a visible conversion node/call that writes ordinary Jet source, or use a compiler-ratified canonical coercion if one exists.
decisions.story: I drag an Int pin into a Float input. Canvas should help me finish the graph, but source review must show the conversion rather than hiding it in graph metadata.
decisions.inWild:
let speed_f = Float.from(speed_i)
move(speed: speed_f)
decisions.detail: Devil pass: Blueprint comfort comes from magic casts, but invisible conversions are exactly where source-backed trust fails. Wrong connections must be impossible; helpful conversions must be explicit.

options.name: Visible conversion nodes only (recommended)
options.detail: Drag-to-connect opens a compatible conversion menu. Selecting one inserts a visible conversion node/call and writes source. Compiler-ratified canonical coercions may render as a small inline conversion badge.
options.code: Float.from(count)

options.name: Allow limited implicit Canvas-only autocasts
options.detail: Canvas creates graph-only cast edges for friendly cases. Fast, but creates behavior source readers cannot see.
options.code: count -> Float input // graph-only cast

options.name: No conversion help
options.detail: Reject every mismatched pin. Safest, but worse than Blueprint and slower than text editing.
options.code: error: expected Float, got Int

comparisons.note: Compatible mismatched pin links create an autocast node.
comparisons.code: Int pin -> Float pin creates conversion node

decisions.title: How should Canvas persist manual layout and comment regions while staying source-backed?
decisions.gist: Blueprint users expect draggable nodes and comment boxes. Canvas law forbids a hidden graph asset or semantic sidecar. We need one shared mechanism for durable layout/comment intent that preserves Jet source as truth.
decisions.explainer: Deterministic layout alone is reproducible but feels less like Blueprint. A binary or JSON sidecar gives perfect visual freedom but violates Canvas acceptance. Source-anchored metadata comments can carry shared visual intent while remaining ordinary source, formatter-visible, reviewable, and removable.
decisions.story: I drag a group of nodes into a readable cluster, draw a comment box named "damage path", commit the file, and another developer opens Canvas. They should see the intent without needing a hidden Canvas asset.
decisions.inWild:
// canvas:region title="damage path" color="#2f80ed" anchors=[span-120-260]
// regular Jet source below remains the only semantic truth
decisions.detail: Devil pass: comments are the hardest source-backed feature. Free-floating geometry cannot round-trip through code naturally. The shared artifact must be text-reviewable and non-semantic; per-user viewport state must stay local.

options.name: Source-anchored hints plus local view cache (recommended)
options.detail: Persist shared layout/comment intent as ordinary Jet comments anchored to source spans. Keep per-user pan/zoom/selection/MRU local. Formatter preserves comments; Canvas ignores hints if stale and falls back to deterministic layout.
options.code:
// canvas:node span=120..180 pos=(420,160)
// canvas:comment span=120..260 title="damage path" color="#2f80ed"

options.name: Deterministic layout only
options.detail: No shared manual positions or regions. Safest source model, but misses expected Blueprint UX for organizing large graphs.
options.code: // no layout hints; graph always auto-layouts from source

options.name: External layout sidecar
options.detail: Store exact geometry in a Canvas file/cache. Best visual fidelity, but conflicts with no hidden source of truth and creates drift/review problems.
options.code: main.jet + main.jet.canvas.json

comparisons.note: Blueprint stores graph layout in the Blueprint asset, which Jet Canvas explicitly cannot copy as hidden semantic storage.

decisions.title: What is Canvas parity for Blueprint collapsed graphs and macros?
decisions.gist: Blueprint has collapsed graphs and macros. Jet already has functions/blocks and has not ratified user macro semantics for Canvas. We need Blueprint organization power without a duplicate semantic mechanism.
decisions.explainer: Collapse should be an editor organization and refactor workflow over source spans. Reusable behavior should become ordinary Jet functions. Visual-only collapse can exist only when it expands back to the same source block without hidden semantics.
decisions.story: I select a validation chain, collapse it to one node while sketching, then either expand it again or extract it into a helper function before committing.
decisions.inWild: fn validate_order(order: Order) -> Result<Order, Problem> { ... }
decisions.detail: Devil pass: macros duplicate functions and become a second language. Canvas should use extract/inline and source blocks first; a separate macro surface belongs behind a later owner decision.

options.name: Collapse as source block; reuse as extract-to-fn (recommended)
options.detail: Collapsed node is a view over a source span. Reusable collapse extracts an ordinary helper function. Tunnel pins are projected params/returns/captures.
options.code: fn helper(a: A) -> B { ... }

options.name: Add visual macro surface now
options.detail: Implement macro nodes with arbitrary tunnels and reuse. Powerful, but creates unratified semantics and risks I8 duplication.
options.code: macro ValidateOrder(...) { ... }

options.name: No collapse until macro design exists
options.detail: Avoids semantic risk, but loses essential Blueprint organization.
options.code: // large graph only

comparisons.note: Macros are reusable collapsed node networks with tunnel nodes and multiple exec outputs.

decisions.title: How should Canvas represent Blueprint-style event graphs in Jet?
decisions.gist: Choose the temporary Canvas projection policy while first-party Event/Hook semantics are decided in D-EVENT1.
decisions.explainer: Canvas does not own event semantics. The core event system is tracked by #286 / D-EVENT1. Canvas can only project ordinary callback functions now, then project the ratified Event/Hook model later.
decisions.story: I add a BeginPlay-like callback in Canvas. In source, I should see the ordinary Jet function that the framework calls, with no hidden asset-owned event body.
decisions.detail: Superseded by owner steer 2026-07-07: event system is a major first-party core language/runtime feature, not a Canvas subset. Canvas #281 is blocked by #286 / D-EVENT1. This Canvas ballot should not decide event semantics; it only decides projection behavior while the core model is pending.

options.name: Event views over ordinary callback functions
options.detail: Canvas groups framework-recognized functions into Event Graph views. Adding an event writes the ordinary function signature from the framework API. This is source-backed and safe today, but only covers callback-style events until the Event/Hook library exists.
options.code: fn on_tick(dt: Duration) { ... }

options.name: New event declaration syntax
options.detail: Add user-typeable event declarations. Ergonomic, but a syntax/API gate and premature before the runtime event model is ratified.
options.code: event Tick(dt: Duration) { ... }

options.name: No event graph concept
options.detail: Canvas only shows functions. Source-pure but fails Blueprint parity.
options.code: fn main() { ... }

options.name: Hybrid: callback views now, first-class Event/Hook model next (recommended)
options.detail: Canvas ships event graphs as views over ordinary callback functions now. In parallel, a separate Event/Hook runtime design defines typed payloads, subscription handles, lifecycle ownership, sync/async dispatch, hook phases, cancellation, backpressure, failure policy, debugger traces, and Canvas projection. Once ratified, Canvas event nodes project the same Event/Hook semantics instead of inventing a UI-only event system.

comparisons.note: Event Graphs expose engine events such as BeginPlay and Tick as nodes.

decisions.title: What source-control model should Canvas expose?
decisions.gist: Blueprint integrates asset checkout/diff workflows. Jet source is text-first and Git-first. Canvas needs conflict safety without adopting asset-lock semantics as truth.
decisions.explainer: Canvas should surface Git text state, transaction diffs, stale revisions, and conflict reloads first. Lock/check-out UI can be an optional adapter over enterprise VCS, not a Canvas storage model.
decisions.story: Before applying a graph edit, I want to preview the exact Jet source diff and know whether my graph projection is stale relative to disk or Git.
decisions.inWild:
Canvas transaction preview:
- let x = old()
+ let x = new()
decisions.detail: Devil pass: asset-style checkout encourages thinking the graph is the artifact. The artifact is the Jet file; Canvas diff must make that obvious.

options.name: Git text diff plus stale transaction guard (recommended)
options.detail: Show exact source diffs, dirty markers, history hooks, and stale edit rejection. Optional lock/check-out adapters may wrap external VCS later.
options.code: git diff -- Source/main.jet

options.name: Blueprint-style checkout abstraction
options.detail: Expose check-out/check-in/lock as the primary workflow. Familiar to Unreal users, but wrong default for Jet source.
options.code: Check Out Canvas Graph

options.name: No source-control UI
options.detail: Keep scope narrow, but misses required stale/conflict UX.
options.code: // rely on terminal git only

comparisons.note: Editor source control supports checkout, status icons, history, and depot diff for assets.

decisions.title: What Canvas extension API is allowed for third-party nodes?
decisions.gist: Blueprint exposes C++ functions and libraries as node palette entries. Jet needs package/function projection and plugin extensibility without creating an unsafe second compiler or hidden behavior layer.
decisions.explainer: The first extension boundary should be facts and metadata: palette entries, docs, schemas, examples, and links to ordinary Jet functions. Providers that execute code, rewrite source, or define new semantics need a separate safety/protocol decision.
decisions.story: A package should make its Jet functions appear as Canvas nodes with docs and pin types, but the call still writes an ordinary Jet function call.
decisions.inWild:
package math exposes fn clamp(x: Float, lo: Float, hi: Float) -> Float
Canvas palette shows clamp node from semindex facts
decisions.detail: Devil pass: plugin nodes can become a second language. Start read-only and source-producing only through ratified edit transactions.

options.name: Read-only palette/schema providers first (recommended)
options.detail: Packages expose ordinary Jet functions/types/docs. Canvas projects them into palette nodes and writes normal calls. No provider-defined behavior or side effects.
options.code: clamp(x, lo, hi)

options.name: Behavior-producing node providers
options.detail: Plugins can define custom node behavior and edit actions. Powerful, but needs safety, protocol, capability, and diagnostics design.
options.code: plugin node emits custom source transform

options.name: No extensibility API
options.detail: Safest short term, but prevents function-library parity.
options.code: // built-in nodes only

comparisons.note: BlueprintCallable/Pure functions and function libraries expose C++ APIs as nodes.

decisions.title: What authority boundary should behavior-producing Canvas actions use?
decisions.gist: Choose how package-supplied Canvas actions may run, edit source, and request authority. Read-only palette entries are just projected Jet functions/types. Behavior-producing actions need an explicit boundary.
decisions.explainer: Rename the extension pieces: a palette entry is metadata projected from ordinary Jet code; a Canvas action is package-supplied behavior that can propose edits or run a preview; an external adapter is a native/tool bridge and must be opt-in. The best hybrid is sandboxed Jet Canvas actions that reuse Jet's existing front end, executable TIR, and JIT for immediate run/preview. Canvas never gets a second compiler or runtime: actions return source transactions or preview requests, Canvas validates through formatter/sema, and AOT remains the build/export path.
decisions.story: Doris installs a physics package. Canvas shows `simulate_step` as a normal node from Jet function facts. If she asks Canvas to set up the simulation graph, the package's Canvas action runs immediately in the Jet JIT sandbox, returns an ordinary source diff, and Canvas rechecks it before writing. Earl can audit the action id, package version, authority list, touched files, generated diff, JIT run result, and whether any external adapter was requested.
decisions.inWild:
package physics exposes:
- palette entry: fn simulate_step(world: &World, dt: Float) -> World
- Canvas action: create_simulation_setup(ctx) -> CanvasEdit ? String
- execution: Jet front end -> executable TIR -> JIT sandbox for preview/run
- write: returned source transaction only, then formatter + sema recheck
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: installing a package makes useful nodes appear; simple actions just work, and prompts appear only when an action asks for extra authority. Expert pass: every action has package id/version/hash, authority manifest, source diff, touched files, diagnostics, JIT/AOT parity evidence, cache key, and audit log. Hybrid pass: one semantic mechanism covers both surfaces: Jet source remains truth, the existing compiler/JIT executes previews, and Canvas accepts only validated Jet diffs. No separate Canvas VM, graph asset, broad editor extension host, or hidden proc-macro-like code execution.

options.name: Static palette entries and edit templates
options.detail: Packages publish metadata and declarative edit templates only. No package code runs inside Canvas. Excellent for audit and simple function-library parity, but cannot perform package-specific analysis, dynamic setup, preview computation, or smart source rewrites.

options.name: Sandboxed Jet Canvas actions using existing JIT (recommended)
options.detail: A package declares ordinary Jet action functions with explicit `canvas.action` authority. Canvas invokes them through the existing checked TIR/JIT path for immediate preview/run. The action cannot write files directly; it returns a CanvasEdit, source diff, diagnostics, or preview value. Canvas then formats, sema-checks, records audit metadata, and rejects undeclared file/tool/network/unsafe authority.

options.name: External adapters for native tools
options.detail: Packages may ship out-of-process adapters for heavyweight native/tool integrations. They run only after an explicit capability prompt naming files, tools, network, cache, and unsafe needs. Canvas still accepts only returned source transactions. Useful as an expert tier, too much authority for the default path.
options.code:
canvas.adapter = "physics-nodegen"
capabilities = ["tool:physicsc", "read:assets/physics", "canvas.source_edit:project"]

Canvas prompt: physics-nodegen wants tool + project edit authority.

comparisons.note: BlueprintCallable exposes compiled engine/module C++ as nodes. Powerful and fast, but authority is bundled with the native module. Jet should copy the palette power, not the broad native trust model.
comparisons.code:
UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
void SimulateStep(UWorld* World, float Dt);

comparisons.note: Extensions run arbitrary extension-host code with broad workspace/process reach, then rely on marketplace trust and workspace trust. Canvas actions should be narrower: declared authority, source-diff output, Jet validation.
Proc macros execute compiler-plugin code and emit tokens during compilation. Canvas must avoid that hidden execution model; actions run as audited Jet code and produce explicit diffs/previews.
Plugins/scripts can mutate documents directly after user trust. Canvas should not grant direct graph mutation; action output is proposed Jet source, then checked.

decisions.title: Time, calendar, timezone, and monotonic clocks
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical time model for calendar depth.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: ceremony-free constructors over a type-safe clock/calendar split.
decisions.story: Marta schedules invoices across time zones and measures request latency. Wall-clock dates, time zones, durations, monotonic instants, and timers must not be interchangeable by accident.
decisions.inWild:
use core.time as time

deadline :: time.now() + time.hours(2)
elapsed :: time.now() - start   // wrong clock? unclear
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: ceremony-free constructors over a type-safe clock/calendar split.

options.name: Hybrid: distinct time types with easy constructors (recommended)
options.detail: Keep separate Instant, DateTime, LocalDate, LocalTime, Duration, and Zone types so wrong-clock bugs are type errors. Add beginner constructors and parse helpers (`time.now_utc`, `time.today`, `time.seconds`) plus expert control over timezone database, monotonic clocks, fake clocks, and schedulers.
options.code:
start :: time.Instant.now()
latency :: start.elapsed()
due :: time.DateTime.now(time.Zone.named("America/New_York")?).plus_days(30)
when :: time.parse_rfc3339("2026-07-07T12:00:00Z")?

options.name: One Time value
options.detail: A single Time type carries clock/calendar data and methods. Fewer names, but bugs move from type errors into runtime meaning.
options.code: t :: time.now(); t.add_days(30); t.elapsed_since(start)

options.name: Durations only for now
options.detail: Ship sleep/timer/duration and defer calendars. Good for runtime loops, weak for apps, logs, files, and jetos schedules.
options.code: time.sleep(time.seconds(1))

comparisons.note: Best current split: Instant, ZonedDateTime, LocalDate, Duration, ZoneId.
time.Time is powerful but mixes many roles in one type.

decisions.title: jetos VM test scenario surface
decisions.gist: How jetos VM test scenarios are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: top-level vmtest remains obvious, while compiling to the same test-target/proof machinery gives CI and expert replay control without a second driver model.
decisions.story: Mara maintains a web service on three jetos hosts. She wants one checked test that boots the database, API, and worker VMs, proves their services, and leaves artifacts CI can replay without writing Python driver strings.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: top-level vmtest remains obvious, while compiling to the same test-target/proof machinery gives CI and expert replay control without a second driver model.

options.name: Hybrid: vmtest declarations as test targets (recommended)
options.detail: Top-level vmtest.<name> declarations are the canonical scenario surface, and the same object is also a normal test target for CI, filtering, artifacts, and package integration. Single-host smoke tests can be authored as shorthand that expands to vmtest; multi-host topology stays explicit. Beginners run one command; experts control host graph, network, replay, timeout, artifacts, and proof capture.

options.name: system.<host>.tests blocks
options.detail: Tests live under each system declaration. This is concise for single-host smoke tests, but multi-host scenarios become split across systems and harder to read as one topology.

options.name: Package-style test targets
options.detail: VM tests are ordinary package/build targets that depend on systems. Good for build graph reuse, but the OS topology is less obvious to beginners and host/service references need extra ceremony.

options.name: External driver file
options.detail: Keep Jet declarations for hosts and point to a separate driver script. This copies NixOS's weakest part: service names and assertions are mostly strings, so Jet cannot catch typos before boot.

comparisons.note: NixOS VM tests declare nodes in Nix and drive them with Python strings.
Scenario resources and probes are declared in one graph, but application assertions often live elsewhere.

decisions.title: jetos VM test assertion API
decisions.gist: How VM tests express checked guest assertions.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: assertion methods give beginner readability, while their underlying check records give expert audit, replay, Studio rendering, and CI artifacts.
decisions.story: Earl changes an SSH service name during a refactor. He wants the VM test to fail at check time if it references a missing service, not after QEMU spends minutes booting a machine and a stringly driver times out.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: assertion methods give beginner readability, while their underlying check records give expert audit, replay, Studio rendering, and CI artifacts.

options.name: Hybrid: typed host handles plus declarative check values (recommended)
options.detail: The test body uses typed host handles and assertion methods. Those methods also produce declarative check values/proof facts, so Studio/CI can render and replay them. Common checks stay one-line and type-checked; experts can write ordinary Jet control flow around them. String shell commands remain an explicit fallback assertion, never the default.
options.code:
run: test {
    devhost.wait_for_boot()
    devhost.assert_unit_active(.openssh)
    devhost.assert_port_open(22)
    check :: devhost.check_file_contains("/etc/ssh/sshd_config", "PasswordAuthentication no")
    assert(check.ok)
}

options.name: Declarative check list
options.detail: Assertions are data entries rather than code. Easy to render in Studio and CI, but weaker for loops, retries, derived values, and multi-step workflows unless it grows a second mini-language.
options.code:
checks: [
    .UnitActive(host: devhost, unit: .openssh),
    .PortOpen(host: devhost, port: 22),
    .FileContains(host: devhost, path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config, text: "PasswordAuthentication no"),
]

options.name: General Jet test functions
options.detail: Use ordinary Jet tests with imported VM helpers. Good reuse, but host topology and artifact capture are less visible unless every project follows conventions manually.

options.name: String command driver
options.detail: Expose low-level machine.shell("...") style commands as the primary API. Flexible, but service/path/command mistakes become guest-time failures and rustc-like subprocess output leaks into user experience.

comparisons.note: Powerful but mostly string-driven from Python; typos often fail after boot.
Typed-ish fluent assertions make multi-step scenarios readable and produce useful traces.
Declarative checks are inspectable, but imperative workflows need another layer.

decisions.title: jetos per-user environment declarations
decisions.gist: How user-level environments are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one reusable source truth for home config, with explicit host overlays and standalone activation using the same generation/proof model.
decisions.story: Betty wants her shell, editor, terminal, and dotfiles to follow her from a laptop to a server without learning home-manager. Earl wants the same user profile to compose into a full jetos host or apply standalone on macOS/Linux with proof and rollback.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one reusable source truth for home config, with explicit host overlays and standalone activation using the same generation/proof model.

options.name: Hybrid: reusable user.<name> profiles with host overlays (recommended)
options.detail: A user.<name> declaration is the canonical per-user environment. It works standalone and can be attached to system.<host>. Host-specific overrides live where the host composes the profile, so one profile can follow a person across machines while experts still control per-host packages, services, secrets, and generated files.

options.name: Only system.<host>.users.<name>.environment
options.detail: User environments live only inside host configs. Simple for OS installs, but loses home-manager's adoption path: applying a user profile without switching the whole OS.

options.name: programs.* modules only
options.detail: Expose app modules but no first-class user profile. Useful for app breadth, but dotfiles, shell, services, and standalone activation lack one shared home environment object.
options.code:
programs.git.enable: true
programs.helix.enable: true
# no reusable user profile boundary

options.name: Separate home.jet files
options.detail: Each user has a separate file format/entrypoint. Familiar to home-manager users, but it creates a second source-of-truth shape beside system.<host> and weakens one-path discoverability.

comparisons.note: Home-manager profiles can be standalone or imported into NixOS, but use a separate module layer.
NixOS system users cover identity and some packages, but not full home environment breadth.

decisions.title: jetos user profile apply command
decisions.gist: How standalone user profiles are built and activated.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: standalone home-manager-class adoption and full OS composition share one user-generation engine.
decisions.story: Doris is not ready to replace her OS, but she wants JetOS to manage her shell, editor, terminal, and app configs today. CI also needs to build the same user generation, inspect the diff, and prove rollback before anything touches her home directory.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetos user plan user
$ jetos user switch user
# writes a user generation, links managed files atomically, starts user services, and records rollback

$ jetos user rollback user
# restores prior user generation without rebuilding the OS
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: standalone home-manager-class adoption and full OS composition share one user-generation engine.

options.name: Hybrid: jetos user commands plus system composition (recommended)
options.detail: `jetos user plan/build/switch/rollback/prove` is the standalone path, and system switching invokes the same user-generation engine when a host imports user profiles. Beginners can manage home config before replacing the OS; experts get proof, rollback, CI, and composition through one mechanism.
options.code:
$ jetos user plan user
$ jetos user switch user

$ jet os switch devhost
# runs the same user-generation proof for users.user.environment

options.name: jetpack env apply
options.detail: Put standalone home environments under jetpack. Good for non-OS adoption, but splits user-generation semantics away from jetos even though rollback/proof are OS-shaped.
options.code:
$ jetpack env plan user.user
$ jetpack env switch user.user

options.name: Only through system switch
options.detail: User profiles activate only when the host system switches. Strong system coherence, but fails the home-manager adoption path for non-jetos machines.
options.code:
$ jet os switch devhost
# updates user.user only as part of host switch

options.name: Generated shell script
options.detail: Build writes an auditable apply script and users run it manually. Easy to inspect, but not a first-class rollback/proof workflow and weak for beginners.
options.code:
$ jetos user build user
wrote apply-user-user.sh
$ ./apply-user-user.sh

comparisons.note: Home-manager has a standalone switch command and a NixOS module integration path.
System switch handles OS generations; user profile rollback is a separate ecosystem concern.

decisions.title: Option priorities, overrides, and module disabling
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos resolves conflicting module option values and explains winners.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: beginner-readable default/force semantics with precise expert ordering when needed.
decisions.story: Gwen has a base desktop module, a plasma-beta variant that forces a different display manager, and a module she must disable. Numeric priorities work in NixOS, but humans cannot read them.
decisions.inWild:
system.devhost { imports: [...] }
// two modules set desktop.displayManager; who wins?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: beginner-readable default/force semantics with precise expert ordering when needed.

options.name: Hybrid: named tiers backed by explicit expert weights (recommended)
options.detail: Common conflicts use named tiers: default, normal, force. Explain output shows all contenders. For rare library authors who need finer ordering, an explicit priority weight can be attached inside the same mechanism and is always shown by name and number. Module disabling uses stable module IDs.
options.code:
desktop.displayManager #Default := .GDM
desktop.displayManager := .GDM
desktop.displayManager #Force := .SDDM
network.firewall.allowedPorts #Priority(1200) += [443]
disable module stylix.kmscon

$ jet os explain desktop.displayManager

options.name: Numeric priorities
options.detail: Expose a number like NixOS. Precise, but weak beginner experience and unexplained magic values.
options.code: desktop.displayManager priority 50 := .SDDM

options.name: Last import wins
options.detail: Simple but brittle; import order becomes hidden semantics.
options.code: imports: [base, plasma_beta]  // later wins

comparisons.note: mkDefault/mkForce are useful; numeric priority internals are not beginner-friendly.

decisions.title: Retired syntax teaching layer after D-S14-PAUSE
decisions.gist: D-S14-PAUSE pauses old-spelling teaching until after Epoch 6, but the implementation still recognizes many retired spellings for teaching diagnostics. Pick the canonical behavior so agents know whether to delete, preserve, or gate that layer.
decisions.story: A new Jet learner types `def main()` after coming from Python, while an agent implementing parser cleanup reads the greenfield law. Today the learner may get a bespoke teaching error, but the spec says retired spellings should be ordinary syntax errors. Both experiences cannot be the default law at once.
decisions.detail: Evidence: Syntax.rs FOREIGN_* constants, lexer tokens for retired words, parser recovery paths, diagnostics entries marked retired by D-S14-PAUSE, and the audit report at docs/plans/epoch-3/language-codebase-syntax-audit-2026-07-07.md. Beginner pass: teaching is useful, but only if it is predictable and documented. Expert pass: parser law must be small, auditable, and not preserve ghost syntax accidentally. Hybrid pass: one semantic language can still offer an opt-in migration/teaching mode if that mode is explicit and tested.

options.name: Strict pause now
options.detail: Honor D-S14-PAUSE literally. Remove or disable retired-spelling recognizers and teaching diagnostics until post-Epoch 6; retired forms fail like ordinary syntax. Smallest default language and strongest greenfield signal.
options.code:
$ jet check old.jet
Error [E0001]: this does not start a Jet item
 Fix: write `fn run() { ... }`

options.name: Curated teaching always on
options.detail: Amend D-S14-PAUSE. Keep a small tested set of high-value teaching diagnostics for common migrations, delete stale/low-value ones, and document the list as first-class compiler behavior.
options.code:
$ jet check old.jet
Error [E00xx]: Jet uses `fn`, not `def`
 Fix: write `fn run() { ... }`

options.name: Opt-in teaching mode (recommended)
options.detail: Default remains greenfield and small; `jet check --teach` or editor teaching mode enables curated migration diagnostics. This keeps the canonical language clean while preserving beginner/migration help when requested.
options.code:
$ jet check old.jet
Error [E0001]: this does not start a Jet item

$ jet check --teach old.jet
Error [E00xx]: Jet uses `fn`, not `def`

comparisons.note: Rust keeps diagnostics helpful for common mistakes, but does not accept or tokenize whole alternate language spellings as a migration surface.
Elm favors small syntax and strong compiler guidance; the language surface stays narrow.
TS migration friendliness is high, but compatibility surface is large. Jet should avoid that default-size cost.

decisions.rec: C — greenfield Jet stays small by default, while migration/onboarding help becomes explicit, documented, and testable instead of half-paused ghost syntax.

decisions.title: Ratify a normalization contract for the content-addressed build cache?
decisions.gist: The build cache (BuildCache.rs / SHA256.rs) is partially implemented but its normalization contract — what counts as 'the same definition' for cache-key purposes — is not specified or tested. This decides whether we lock down a concrete contract now or leave it ad hoc.
decisions.explainer: Without a stated contract, two definitions that are semantically identical (whitespace change, renamed local, reordered doc comment) may or may not produce cache hits depending on implementation drift. A contract at the AST level (after parsing, before sema) is rename-sensitive by default but immune to whitespace and comment changes. Ratifying this establishes a correctness floor for all incremental build work and is a prerequisite for any cross-machine or reproducible-build guarantee. It touches BuildCache.rs, SHA256.rs, and the parser, and pairs with the content-addressed-definitions card.
decisions.story: I rename a local variable inside a function body. Nothing semantic changed. I don't want a cache miss — or worse, a stale hit — because the cache doesn't know whether that rename matters. I need to trust the cache.

options.name: Specify AST-level contract, rename-sensitive
options.detail: Hash the canonical AST (post-parse, pre-sema): strip whitespace and comments, keep all names as-is. Two definitions with different local names get different keys. Simple to implement, easy to test, conservative (avoids false hits). Document the contract and add a normalization test.

options.name: Specify AST-level contract, alpha-rename-invariant
options.detail: Before hashing, alpha-rename all locals to positional names (`_0`, `_1`, …). Two definitions differing only in local names produce the same key. More cache hits but more complex to implement and requires a stable renaming pass before sema.

options.name: Leave ad hoc in BuildCache.rs
options.detail: No ratified contract. The cache continues to work however BuildCache.rs happens to implement it. Risk: silent correctness bugs as implementation drifts; no test surface for the contract.
options.code:
// no contract — cache hits are implementation-defined
// renaming a local may or may not bust the cache

comparisons.note: Nix content addressing normalizes derivation inputs so identical builds share cache entries predictably.

Nix derives cache keys from a normalized derivation ATerm (no whitespace variation); it is rename-sensitive at the attribute level. A clear, auditable contract is what makes Nix's reproducibility claims trustworthy.
comparisons.code:
# derivation hash = SHA256(normalised-ATerm-of-derivation)
# whitespace irrelevant; attribute names are part of the key

comparisons.note: Rust's incremental hashes the HIR with stable IDs; local renames do not bust the hash because HIR is already resolved. Jet can choose either policy but must choose one.
comparisons.code:
// rustc stable-hashes HIR bodies; local var names are irrelevant
// to the incremental fingerprint

decisions.bestCurrent: Nix: Nix content addressing normalizes derivation inputs so identical builds share cache entries predictably.
decisions.recommendation: Specify the AST-level, rename-sensitive contract. Jet should make cache identity explicit enough for agents and humans, not hidden in implementation details.

decisions.title: Add a first-class `workspace.jet` workspace manifest for multi-package repos, or reuse `pack.jet payload:`?
decisions.gist: Multi-package repos need a way to declare a set of member packages. `pack.jet payload:` already handles multi-package core sources. This decides whether to introduce a separate `workspace.jet` root manifest or rely on the existing `payload:` mechanism.
decisions.explainer: The `payload:` field in `pack.jet` lets a single package declare multiple member packages (memory: payload-multi-package-core-source). A `workspace.jet` would be a new top-level file with no associated package, purely grouping independent packages for a shared build/tooling context (shared lock file, cross-member `pub(package)` visibility, unified `jet build`). The key question is whether `payload:` semantics already cover the monorepo case or whether they differ enough to justify a new file type. Under I8, two files solving the same grouping job is a strike unless they cover genuinely different semantic territory. This was a live owner decision in Tower c156.
decisions.story: I have a repo with four separate Jet packages — a compiler, a CLI, a stdlib, and a test runner. I want `jet build` at the repo root to build all of them, with a single lock file and cross-package visibility. I don't want one of them to be the 'master' package that owns the others.
decisions.inWild:
# workspace.jet (proposed)
[workspace]
members = [
    "crates/compiler",
    "crates/cli",
    "crates/stdlib",
    "crates/test-runner",
]

# vs. pack.jet payload: (existing)
[payload]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

options.name: Add `workspace.jet` (separate workspace manifest)
options.detail: A new top-level `workspace.jet` file with no owning package — purely a grouping manifest. Members are independent packages each with their own `pack.jet`. Supports a shared lock file, `pub(package)`, and unified `jet` commands. Clearest model for repos where no single package is 'the root'.
options.code:
# workspace.jet
[workspace]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

$ jet build           # builds all members
$ jet test --all      # tests all members

options.name: Reuse `pack.jet payload:` (no new file)
options.detail: The root `pack.jet` with a `payload:` section already declares member packages. Extend its semantics: if `payload:` is present with no `[package]` section, it acts as a pure workspace root. No new file type; I8-clean if `payload:` already covers this exactly.
options.code:
# pack.jet (workspace root, no [package] section)
[payload]
members = ["crates/compiler", "crates/cli"]

$ jet build           # builds all payload members

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't ratify a workspace surface yet. Multi-package builds work today by running `jet build` in each package directory. Defer until the lock-file and `pub(package)` designs are settled, so the workspace contract is informed by what it actually needs to coordinate.
options.code:
# no workspace manifest; run per-package:
$ jet build -C crates/compiler
$ jet build -C crates/cli

comparisons.note: Cargo uses a root `Cargo.toml` with `[workspace]` members list. The root may or may not also declare a `[package]`. Members share a `Cargo.lock` and `target/`.
npm uses a root `package.json` with a `workspaces` array. The root is itself a package. Closer to Jet's `pack.jet payload:` model than to a separate file.
