decisions.comment: Reconciled 2026-06-27: canonical D-WORKSPACE1 in docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md is B — fully computable workspace.jet. This Tower card's option labels predate the owner-modified ratification; follow D-WORKSPACE1/D-WORKSPACE2 in syntax-decisions.md.

decisions.title: Define a versioned public semantic-index query API?
decisions.gist: The compiler already builds a rich symbol database internally (Source/LSP/SymbolDB.rs: symbols, types, references, call graph). Right now that data is internal-only — no external tool can query it without forking compiler internals. This decision is whether to promote a stable, versioned subset of that data into a public API that tools (IDE plugins, impact analyzers, dossier, ask-your-codebase) can depend on.
decisions.explainer: A public semantic-index API is listed as an Epoch 4 exit criterion. It is the prerequisite for three other queued ideas — impact-analyzer (D-IMPACT1), codemods (D-CODEMOD1), and ask-your-codebase — all of which need reliable, versioned access to compiler facts. The API would live on top of the seam crates (compiler-workspace-seams: jet-sema, jet-foundation) and be versioned independently of the compiler internals. It does not change language semantics or surface syntax, so I1/I8 are not in play. Sequencing risk: if the internal SymbolDB layout changes significantly before the API is frozen, the versioning story becomes harder; starting the freeze now reduces that drift.
decisions.story: I'm writing a refactor tool. I need to know every call site of a function, the type of each argument, and which tests exercise it — without running the compiler myself. I want to query that from a stable interface that won't break when the compiler's internals change.

options.name: Versioned public API over seam crates
options.detail: Expose a stable, versioned query surface (symbols, types, references, call graph) as a public crate built on jet-sema/jet-foundation. Tools depend on the API version, not compiler internals. This is the E4 exit criterion and unlocks impact analysis, codemods, and dossier.

options.name: Keep internal-only
options.detail: No public API. External tools must parse source themselves or shell out to the LSP. Simpler for the compiler team; blocks all downstream tooling ideas indefinitely.
options.code:
// current state: tools use LSP textDocument/references
// (network protocol, not a typed query API, no type info)

options.name: Defer past E4
options.detail: Accept the E4 exit criterion slip. Useful if the internal SymbolDB is still in heavy flux and freezing it now would be costly. Leaves downstream cards blocked.
options.code:
// no change; D-IMPACT1, D-CODEMOD1, ask-your-codebase
// all remain blocked

comparisons.note: rust-analyzer exposes a public `ide` crate with typed queries (find_all_refs, go_to_def, call_hierarchy). Third-party tools depend on it. It is versioned separately from the compiler.
ts-morph wraps the TypeScript compiler API into a stable typed query surface. Tools use it for refactoring and analysis without touching compiler internals.

decisions.title: Should jetpack use content-addressed identity for packages and cache entries?
decisions.gist: Content-addressed store: packages are identified by the hash of their content, not just their name+version. Cache entries, build artifacts, and dependency closures are all hash-named. This gives reproducibility, automatic deduplication, and tamper detection. Partially implemented in the build cache; extending it to full package identity (Nix-style) is the question.
decisions.explainer: The current package cache uses hashes for build artifacts but packages are still identified by name+version strings. Full content-addressing means the package store layout changes: packages live at paths like `store/<hash>-name-version/` and two packages with different contents but the same name+version are never confused. This sequences naturally with a signed package cache (D-c56 equivalent) — the signature vouches for a content hash, not a name. Jetpack memory notes the intent. No Nix dependency required — Jet implements its own store. Blast radius: pack.jet format, lock file schema (src/lock.rs), install paths, jetpack CLI output.
decisions.story: I want to pin a dependency to an exact binary — not just a version string that a registry could silently update. And I want two projects that use the same package to share the cached build without re-downloading.
decisions.inWild:
# pack.jet lock entry (content-addressed):
[deps.serde]
version = "1.0.190"
hash = "sha256:3fb9..."
store-path = ".jet/store/3fb9...-serde-1.0.190/"

options.name: Content-addressed package store (extend current cache)
options.detail: Extend the existing build-cache hashing to cover package identity. Lock file records content hash; install path is hash-prefixed. Enables dedup, tamper detection, and a future signed cache. Changes lock file format — requires migration.
options.code:
# .jet/lock (new schema excerpt):
[[package]]
name = "jet-http"
version = "0.3.1"
hash = "sha256:a1b2c3..."
store = ".jet/store/a1b2c3...-jet-http-0.3.1"

# Two projects sharing the same package reuse the same store path.

options.name: Version-named only (status quo)
options.detail: Packages are identified by name+version. Lock file records the version; cache uses version-keyed directories. Simpler but allows silent content drift if a registry republishes a version. No store-layout change needed.
options.code:
# .jet/lock (current schema):
[[package]]
name = "jet-http"
version = "0.3.1"
# No hash — version is the identity

options.name: Hash lock file only (no store-path change)
options.detail: Record a content hash in the lock file for tamper detection, but keep the store layout version-named. Adds integrity checking without changing install paths. Middle ground — less dedup benefit but lower migration cost.
options.code:
# .jet/lock (hybrid):
[[package]]
name = "jet-http"
version = "0.3.1"
hash = "sha256:a1b2c3..."  # verified on install, store path unchanged

comparisons.note: Full content-addressed store — every package path includes the hash of its inputs. Zero silent drift, perfect dedup. High implementation complexity but proven at scale.
Lock file records content hash (Cargo.lock `checksum`) but store layout is version-named. Option C is what Cargo does — integrity checking without full content-addressing.

decisions.comment: I already ratified a different structure for the install path though, <name>-<version>-<hash>, not has prefix. Ensure we use mine

decisions.title: Should workspace resolution write a separate `.jet/workspace.lock` or fold into unified `.jet/lock`?
decisions.gist: Workspace member discovery needs one durable lock location. A separate workspace lock duplicates package locking; a unified `.jet/lock` keeps one source of reproducibility truth.
decisions.explainer: D-WORKSPACE1/B chose `pack.jet payload:` instead of a new `workspace.jet` file, so the lock should follow the same I8 logic: one package/workspace graph, one lock. The only reason to split is if workspace member discovery has a different lifecycle from dependency resolution. Splitting creates two files CI must validate and two stale states users must debug.
decisions.story: Mara opens a monorepo and runs `jet test`. She wants one lockfile checked into review that tells CI exactly which payload members and dependencies were used, without learning whether a change belongs in package lock or workspace lock.
decisions.inWild:
# pack.jet
[payload]
members = find("./packages")

# recommended lock result:
.jet/lock   # contains dependency pins plus normalized payload-member graph

options.name: Fold workspace graph into unified `.jet/lock` (recommended)
options.detail: One `.jet/lock` file stores dependency pins, payload member paths (normalized), sparse-subtree metadata, and comptime member-expression inputs. Matches D-WORKSPACE1=B: no new workspace file, no new lock file. CI validates one lock with `jet fetch --locked`. Consistent with Cargo (one Cargo.lock for the whole workspace) and pnpm (one pnpm-lock.yaml). When the member expression is a comptime `find()`, the lock records the discovered paths so future builds are hermetic without re-evaluating the expression.
options.code:
# pack.jet
[payload]
members = find("./packages")

# .jet/lock  (one file covers everything)
[workspace]
members = ["packages/a", "packages/b"]  # normalized from find() at lock time

[deps]
core = "1.4.2"

$ jet fetch --locked  # validates both sections

options.name: Separate `.jet/workspace.lock`
options.detail: Workspace member discovery gets its own lock file, distinct from `.jet/lock` which covers dependencies. Isolates member-list churn from dep pins, but creates two sources of truth and two failure modes under `--locked`. Reviewers must understand which lock to check for which change.
options.code:
.jet/lock           # dependency pins
.jet/workspace.lock  # member paths

options.name: Defer member-expression locking — explicit lists only for now
options.detail: Support only explicit member lists (no `find()`/comptime discovery) until D-CTMARKER1/D-CTEFFECT1 implementation lands. Avoids choosing lock shape for computed members now. Blocks the full D-WORKSPACE1=B surface.
options.code:
# only explicit members for now
[payload]
members = ["packages/a", "packages/b"]
# Epoch 3 revisit: find() members + .jet/lock recording

comparisons.note: One Cargo.lock records the whole workspace dependency graph, not a separate workspace lock.
One pnpm-lock.yaml includes workspace package graph and dependency resolution together.

decisions.bestCurrent: Cargo/pnpm: one lockfile covers the complete workspace graph.
decisions.recommendation: Fold workspace member graph into unified `.jet/lock` — one reproducibility file, one CI gate (Option A). I8: one lock mechanism covers both dependency pins and payload-member discovery.

log.text: Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: U22 — Hangar disk contract: GC policy, disk reporting, and the zero-/tmp guarantee
decisions.gist: Decide how hangar disk space is reclaimed (manual verb, safe auto-GC, or explicit roots) and make "no /tmp litter" a tested guarantee instead of a vision bullet.
decisions.explainer: Nix's disk story is a top-three complaint and the owner hits it daily: every nix develop -c litters a ~200 MB /tmp/nix-shell.* directory, hundreds of them fill a 31 GB tmpfs, and the store itself grows until a scary all-or-nothing nix-collect-garbage. The vision claims "no result symlink or /tmp litter" but no mechanism is specified. This ballot fixes three contracts: (1) reclaim policy — what jet gc keeps and when it runs; (2) reporting — jet hangar du showing live vs stale vs build-tmp; (3) hygiene — build scratch lives inside the hangar, is deleted on build exit, and orphans from crashes are swept by the next jetpack command. Retention floor for every option: anything reachable from a lockfile or a jetos generation is never collected.
decisions.story: Earl runs an overnight agent session: four hundred env entries and test runs. On Nix that morning greets him with a 94% full tmpfs and phantom "No space left on device" test failures that look like compiler bugs. On jetpack the same session writes nothing outside the hangar, and the hangar can tell him exactly what it holds and what is safe to drop.
decisions.inWild:
$ df -h /tmp        # after 400 nix develop invocations today
tmpfs  31G  29G  2.1G  94%  /tmp
$ ls /tmp | grep -c nix-shell
147
error: writing to file: No space left on device   # phantom test failure

# the jetpack contract under decision:
$ jet hangar du
hangar: ~/.jet/hangar
  live      (reachable from lockfiles/generations)   3.4 GB
  stale     (unreferenced > 14 days)                 1.1 GB
  build tmp (active builds)                          0 B     # always 0 when idle

$ jet gc
freed 1.1 GB · kept everything a lockfile or generation references
decisions.detail: Raised from the 2026-07-02 vision review (gap 3). Applies to jetpack now and jetos generations later (generations are GC roots; jet rollback must always find its target). Hygiene contract shared by all options, to be enforced by a golden test: a full env-enter/build/run cycle writes zero bytes outside the hangar and .jet/; build scratch is hangar-scoped (~/.jet/hangar/tmp/<build-hash>), removed on success AND failure; orphaned scratch from a killed process is swept opportunistically by the next jetpack invocation, no daemon. Reporting contract: du output is stable, machine-readable with --json (D-JPK-DISPATCH1 contract), and never lies about reclaimable space.

options.name: Manual jet gc only
options.detail: Reclaim happens only when the user types jet gc (retention: lockfile/generation-reachable is kept; the rest goes). Predictable, zero magic — but beginners never type it and rediscover the Nix disk balloon a year in.
options.code:
$ jet gc
freed 1.1 GB

$ jet gc --dry-run
would free 1.1 GB (38 objects, oldest referenced 2026-03-11)

options.name: Safe auto-GC by age + manual verb (recommended)
options.detail: Unreferenced objects age out automatically (default: untouched 14 days), swept opportunistically after jetpack commands — no daemon. jet gc still exists for "free it now". Beginners never think about disk; experts tune or disable per config. Only unreachable objects are eligible, so nothing reproducible is ever lost — worst case is a re-download/re-build.

options.name: Explicit GC roots, Nix-style
options.detail: Projects register roots (.jet/ links into the hangar); gc drops whatever no live project references. Precise, but imports Nix's hardest-to-teach concept — deleted-but-unregistered projects silently pin gigabytes, and users must learn what a root is to understand their own disk.
options.code:
$ jet gc
kept: 12 roots (9 projects, 3 generations)
^ user must now learn what a "root" is
$ jet roots list
/home/earl/old-experiment/.jet   4.1 GB   # deleted from mind, not from disk

comparisons.note: Manual, global, scary: gc deletes everything not rooted; roots are symlink trivia most users never learn; shell litter in /tmp is unmanaged entirely.
comparisons.code: $ nix-collect-garbage -d   # hope nothing you needed was unrooted

comparisons.note: prune verbs + system df — the reporting shape users like; but unreferenced != unwanted bites people constantly (yesterday's image, repulled today).
comparisons.code:
$ docker system df
$ docker system prune

comparisons.note: No GC at all; target/ grows until users delete it by hand. The absence this ballot avoids.
comparisons.code: $ rm -rf target   # the industry standard, sadly

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome). AMENDED by owner 2026-07-03: (1) the verb is `jet clean`, not `jet gc` — one command that both garbage-collects AND optimizes the hangar (hardlink/dedup, `nix store optimise` equivalent); (2) default stale_after is 30 days, not 14. Auto-sweep behavior (opportunistic, no daemon, reachable-never-collected) unchanged.

decisions.title: U24 — Binary cache / substitution: how do machines share built hangar objects?
decisions.gist: Pick the direction for a build-once-substitute-everywhere cache (the cache.nixos.org equivalent). Decided now because it constrains the hangar object format being built today; implementation can land later.
decisions.explainer:
The one Nix superpower the Epoch 5 plan never mentions. cache.nixos.org is why Nix is usable at all: without substitution, every machine compiles the world from source. Jetpack has the same exposure — every core-provider package and every Recipe.cargo/go/cmake adapter builds from source on every machine that lacks the output. The model that fits the hangar: objects are already content-addressed; a cache is any store that can answer "do you have output for platform

?" and hand back bytes whose hash is verified on arrival — hash verification means even an untrusted mirror cannot substitute wrong bytes; signatures answer provenance policy on top. What must be decided NOW regardless of ship date: the hangar object envelope (output hash + platform key + signature slot + provenance link into the lock schema), because retrofitting it after adapters and lockfiles ship means migrating every hangar and lockfile in existence.
decisions.story: Betty's team has nine engineers and a CI fleet. Their env has two adapter builds (a cargo tool, a cmake tool) totaling 40 minutes of compile. With substitution, CI builds each output once per bump; nine laptops fetch verified bytes in seconds. Without it, every laptop and every CI job pays the 40 minutes, every time the lock moves — the exact tax that makes teams abandon source-based tools.
decisions.detail: Raised from the 2026-07-02 vision review (gap 5). Scope of THIS ballot: pick the architecture direction and freeze the object-envelope fields into the hangar/lock schema now; protocol, hosting, and push tooling are Epoch 6 implementation cards. Interacts with: D-JPK-OCITOOL1 (registry push shares the TLS gate), U14 (OCI layouts are hangar objects and should be substitutable like any other), D-JPK-ADAPTER1 (adapter lock identity already includes output hash — the same hash a cache serves). Trust model note for the owner: content addressing makes substitution tamper-evident by construction; the signature layer decides WHOSE builds you accept, not WHETHER the bytes match the hash.

options.name: Output-hash-addressed cache protocol, signed objects (recommended)
options.detail: Any HTTP(S) store answering GET by output hash + platform; bytes verified by hash on arrival, accepted per the configured signing keys. Works for self-hosted, S3-style, and a future jet-hosted public cache. Envelope fields frozen into hangar/lock schema now; protocol ships Epoch 6 behind the same TLS gate as OCI push.
options.code:
# CI, after tests pass:
$ jet cache push https://cache.acme.dev --key ci.key
pushed 2 outputs (codex, weirdctl)

# any machine, any time:
$ jet env
  weirdctl  substituted (890 KB, hash verified, signed: acme_ci)

# miss is never an error — it just builds:
  newtool   no cache hit · building from source (2m10s)

options.name: Registry-coupled cache only
options.detail: The jet package registry serves prebuilt outputs for published packages; nothing else substitutes. Covers registry deps but abandons exactly the expensive cases — adapters and private/unpublished builds — and couples cache trust to registry identity.
options.code:
$ jet env
  textkit    substituted from registry ✓
  weirdctl   adapter — not publishable, no cache path · building (18m)  ← the expensive one

options.name: Dumb hangar mirror (rsync/object store, trust by transport)
options.detail: Sync hangar directories through any file store; whoever can write the bucket is trusted. No protocol to design, but no signatures, no provenance, and partial-sync corruption becomes the user's problem — a footgun dressed as simplicity.
options.code:
$ jet hangar sync s3://acme-hangar
^ anyone with bucket write access now feeds binaries to every laptop, unsigned

options.name: Defer entirely (source builds until Epoch 6)
options.detail: Decide nothing now. The trap is not the missing feature — it is that the hangar object format and lock schema ship without envelope fields, and adding them later migrates every hangar and lockfile in existence.
options.code:
$ jet env    # nine laptops, every lock bump
  weirdctl  building from source (18m)   × 9 engineers × every update

comparisons.note: Substituters + signed narinfo; cachix built a business on hosting it. Proof the shape works at world scale.
Remote cache keyed by action hash; same build-once economics, famously transformative for team CI times.
Registry layers are the degenerate case: content-addressed blobs everyone already substitutes without thinking about it.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U25 — Which platforms are first-class for jetpack? (Linux / macOS / Windows tiers)
decisions.gist: Decide jetpack's platform tiers: is Windows a native tier-1 target alongside Linux and macOS, a documented WSL2 path, or best-effort? (jetos stays Linux either way.)
decisions.explainer: Nix's platform story is a top adoption blocker: macOS is half-supported (nix-darwin, frequent breakage on OS updates), Windows is nothing — the standard answer is "use WSL2", which excludes most corporate and student machines as they actually exist. No env/package tool in this space works natively on all three desktop platforms. jetpack choosing Windows tier-1 would be a differentiator no competitor can answer — and it is a choice about the hangar, providers, services, and adapters, not about jetos: the OS tier is Linux regardless. Tier-1 means: hangar, core provider, adapters (prebuilt/copy/cargo/go/node), services supervision, secrets, and the trust gate all work natively; CI runs the suite per platform; a platform-specific failure is a P1 bug, not a shrug. The Nix bridge is Linux/macOS only by nature — Windows leans on core + adapters + D-JPK-CACHE1 substitution, which is also the exit ramp story.
decisions.story: Mabel teaches a 30-student class; twenty laptops run Windows. With Nix the first lab day dies in WSL2 installs, virtualization BIOS settings, and IT tickets. With tier-1 Windows she says "download jet, run jet dev" and the whole room is compiling in five minutes — same commands, same lockfile, all three OSes.
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 1). Scope: jetpack tiers only; jetos parity bar stays the Linux owner baseline. Platform-conditional surface already exists in adapter design (platforms: [Platform.linux_x64], {target} asset substitution) — this ballot decides which values of Platform the product stands behind. Windows-specific facts for the record: services supervision maps to Win32 job objects; build sandboxing has no user-namespace equivalent (AppContainer is the nearest; honest-warning fallback per U28 applies); path/exec semantics differ (no shebangs, .exe suffix) and are jetpack's to absorb, never the user's. Per philosophy.md, implementation effort is not a factor in this ranking — only reach, beginner experience, and the master-of-ALL goal.

options.name: Linux + macOS + Windows, all tier-1 native (recommended)
options.detail: One product on the three desktop OSes; hangar/core/adapters/services/secrets native everywhere; per-platform CI; platform break = P1. Nix bridge stays Linux/macOS; Windows realizes via core + adapters + cache substitution, with the U23 diagnostic naming any bridge-only package.
options.code:
win> jet dev
First entry to this repo. env.dev wants: ...
Trust and continue? [y/N] y
✓ postgres  healthy on :5432 (native service supervision)
pulseops listening on http://localhost:8080

win> jet env
Error [E1252]: `openblas` needs the Nix bridge, unavailable on Windows
 Fix: `jet add openblas --adapt` can draft a prebuilt recipe

options.name: Linux + macOS tier-1; Windows via documented WSL2 path
options.detail: Native on Unix; Windows users install WSL2 and run the Linux build. Honest and shippable sooner, but inherits every WSL failure mode (IT policy, virtualization, file-system seams with editors on the Windows side) — the exact wall Nix users hit.
options.code:
win> jet dev
'jet' is not recognized...
# docs: install WSL2, then Ubuntu, then jet inside it;
# VS Code needs the Remote-WSL extension; repo must live in the WSL filesystem

options.name: Linux tier-1 only; macOS and Windows best-effort
options.detail: Smallest promise; matches where jetos lives. Concedes the entire differentiator and caps jet's audience at Nix's current audience — hard to reconcile with master-of-ALL.
options.code:
macos% jet dev
⚠ macOS is best-effort: services supervision untested on this platform
# every macOS user reads this and hears "not for you"

comparisons.note: Linux first, macOS strained, Windows never. The gap this ballot decides whether to own.
comparisons.code:
# Windows answer today:
> wsl --install   # + BIOS virtualization + IT approval

comparisons.note: All three tier-1 from day one; widely cited as why Rust onboarding feels effortless everywhere. The model.
comparisons.code: > rustup default stable   # identical on win/mac/linux

comparisons.note: Recent proof the bar moved: single binary, native Windows, no daemon — and adoption followed.
comparisons.code: > uv sync   # works on a locked-down corp Windows laptop

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U28 — Product constraint: no resident daemon, no root for jetpack operations
decisions.gist: Ratify (or reject) a standing constraint: jetpack never runs a daemon and never needs root; root appears only transiently at jetos activation; build sandboxing uses unprivileged mechanisms with an honest fallback warning.
decisions.explainer: Nix's daemon + root exist because /nix/store is system-global and shared: something privileged must write the shared store, dedupe across users, sandbox builds (pre-user-namespace 2006 design), and enforce machine-wide cache trust. Jetpack's hangar is per-user by design, so the daemon's reason evaporates — the cargo/rustup/uv model. This ballot makes that a ratified constraint rather than an accident, because constraints not written down accrete violations: a "small helper daemon" for service supervision, a root hook for a sandbox, a setuid shim for ports. What the constraint costs, eyes open: no cross-user store dedup on shared servers (mitigated by U24 substitution + in-hangar hardlink dedup); sandbox strength rides unprivileged user namespaces on Linux (disabled on some hardened distros) and weaker mechanisms on macOS/Windows; no admin-enforced machine-wide trust policy (org config layer later); concurrent builds coordinate by file locks, not a broker.
decisions.story: Gladys is on a locked-down corporate laptop: no admin rights, software installs need tickets. Nix is dead on arrival — the installer wants /nix and a root daemon. jetpack is one binary in her home directory; jet dev works the first minute. Her company's shared build server pays the flip side: forty users, forty hangars — substitution from the team cache is what keeps that cheap.
decisions.inWild:
# install, no ticket:
$ curl -LO https://jet.dev/dl/jet && chmod +x jet && ./jet env
✓ works — no /nix, no daemon socket, no sudo

# the day root is actually needed, it is explicit and momentary:
$ sudo jet switch --name "pre-gpu-driver"   # jetos activation only

# the honest edge (security-relevant, plainly stated):
$ jet env
⚠ build sandboxing unavailable: this kernel disables unprivileged user
  namespaces. Adapter builds will run unsandboxed — they execute with your
  user's full permissions. `jet config sandbox require` refuses instead.
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 5; tradeoffs walked with owner same day). Contract if ratified: (1) no resident process ever — supervision (U12) parents services from the jet dev session; auto-GC (U22) is opportunistic post-command work; (2) no operation requires root except jetos activation verbs, which use transient sudo and say so; (3) builds are sandboxed by unprivileged user namespaces on Linux, the best available native mechanism per platform elsewhere; where unavailable, jetpack states plainly that builds run unsandboxed and offers `sandbox require` policy to hard-fail instead — never a silent downgrade; (4) concurrent jetpack processes coordinate via hangar file locks. Enforced like an invariant: any future design that wants a daemon or root path comes back to the owner as a ballot.

options.name: Hard constraint, ratified and tested (recommended)
options.detail: No daemon, no root, transient sudo for jetos activation only, unprivileged sandboxing with honest fallback + `sandbox require` policy. CI asserts no-root operation; violations need a new ballot.
options.code:
$ jet env && jet dev && jet gc   # all as plain user, no daemon socket exists
$ sudo jet switch                # the one explicit root moment, jetos only

options.name: No daemon, but optional root helper for stronger sandboxing
options.detail: Default identical to A; hardened-distro users may install a small setuid/root helper that provides namespace-grade sandboxing where unprivileged userns is off. Closes A's weakest edge, but jetpack now ships and maintains a privileged component — the exact attack surface A exists to refuse.
options.code:
$ jet config sandbox helper install   # sudo once; setuid helper owns sandbox setup
⚠ jetpack now has a privileged binary to audit, patch, and trust

options.name: Leave open (no constraint; daemon allowed if a future design wants one)
options.detail: Decide nothing; each future feature picks. History says this drifts daemon-ward one convenience at a time (Docker), and the corp-laptop story silently dies the day the first helper lands.
options.code:
# year two, some feature ships:
$ jet services enable --system   # "requires the jetpack agent; sudo to install"
^ the constraint that was never written down

comparisons.note: Daemon + root default; single-user mode exists but is second-class. Corp-laptop DOA case is common.
comparisons.code: $ sh <(curl -L https://nixos.org/nix/install) --daemon   # wants root, /nix, launchd/systemd units

comparisons.note: The model: one user-owned binary, no daemon, no root, corp-safe. Adoption followed.
The cautionary tale: root daemon became its biggest security and ops liability; rootless mode retrofitted a decade later.
comparisons.code: $ sudo systemctl start docker   # and docker group ≈ root

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U29 — Offline guarantee: once realized, envs work with zero network, forever
decisions.gist: Decide whether "realized once → works offline forever" is a tested product guarantee with an --offline enforcement flag, a best-effort behavior, or an explicit prefetch verb.
decisions.explainer: Lock + hangar already imply this: everything an env needs is content-addressed on disk after first realization. The ballot is whether jetpack promises it. The guarantee: any verb that succeeded against the current lock succeeds again with the network cable cut — jet env, jet dev, jet build, jet run, service startup, all of it. --offline makes the promise enforceable: any operation that would touch the network fails loudly with what it wanted and why, instead of hanging or silently fetching. Guarded by a golden test that realizes an env, severs network, and re-runs the full verb set. What it forbids, permanently: phone-home version checks, lazy metadata refreshes on realize verbs, telemetry in the realize path — the quiet network habits that make tools flaky on planes and in air-gapped CI.
decisions.story: Frank demos on conference wifi that died an hour ago. His repo's lock hasn't changed since yesterday; jet dev brings up postgres and the app from the hangar without noticing the network is gone. The person next to him watches npm install spin on a registry it can't reach.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev            # wifi dead, lock unchanged since yesterday
✓ env.dev realized from hangar (0.1s) · ✓ postgres healthy · app on :8080
# no timeout, no retry spinner — network was never consulted

$ jet update codex --offline
Error [E1258]: `jet update` needs the network (queries github@openai/codex releases)
 Why: --offline forbids all network access
 Fix: drop --offline, or pin the wanted rev explicitly

# air-gapped CI:
$ jet build --offline   # cache miss = loud failure naming the object, never a fetch
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 6). Semantics: verbs classify as realize-class (env/dev/run/build/test/services — never touch network when lock is satisfied; with --offline, hard-fail instead of fetch on any miss) or network-class (update/outdated/add/publish/cache push — honestly network-bound, refuse under --offline with E1258 naming the need). Channel refs (U21) resolve only in network-class verbs, so they cannot break the guarantee. Interlocks: U22 auto-GC must never collect objects the current locks reference (already its retention floor) or GC could break the promise; U24 substitution is an optimization inside realize-class verbs — a cache miss falls back to local build, and under --offline to a loud failure. Golden test shape: realize → deny network at the process level → full verb sweep must pass.

options.name: Hard guarantee + --offline enforcement + golden test (recommended)
options.detail: Realized-once-works-forever is product contract: realize-class verbs never consult the network when the lock is satisfied; --offline turns any would-be fetch into a loud E1258; golden test enforces it in CI permanently.
options.code:
$ jet env --offline      # lock satisfied → identical to jet env
$ jet env --offline      # after a lock bump with an unfetched object:
Error [E1258]: `codex` v0.50.1 is not in the hangar and --offline forbids fetching
 Fix: run `jet env` once with network, or push the object to a reachable cache

options.name: Best-effort offline, no promise, no flag
options.detail: Architecture already mostly delivers it; ship without the contract or the test. Costs nothing today — and erodes silently the first time a feature adds a metadata ping to jet env, which nothing would catch.
options.code:
$ jet dev    # on a plane, some future version:
checking for updates… (30s timeout)   ← the ping nobody balloted

options.name: Explicit prefetch verb required (jet fetch)
options.detail: Offline use is opt-in preparation: jet fetch downloads everything the lock needs; realize verbs may otherwise fetch lazily. Honest, but makes offline a mode users must anticipate — Frank's demo dies because he didn't run the magic verb yesterday.
options.code:
$ jet fetch              # yesterday, with wifi — did you remember?
$ jet dev                # today, offline: works only if you did

comparisons.note: Mostly offline-capable in practice, never promised; eval can still surprise-fetch (flake inputs, tarballs), and failures hang on timeouts instead of failing fast.
comparisons.code: $ nix develop   # on a plane: …waiting on github.com…

comparisons.note: The precedent: --offline exists, fails loudly with the missing crate named, and vendoring is a supported workflow. Users trust it.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build --offline
error: no matching package named `foo` found (offline mode)

comparisons.note: The anti-model: --offline exists but registry metadata habits make it unreliable; nobody trusts it, so nobody uses it.
comparisons.code: $ npm ci --offline   # works, sometimes, depending on cache weather

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: How do the first-party core.* ring libraries reach a build — baked into the compiler, or realized like any package?
decisions.gist: Decide whether core.http, core.regex and the rest ship embedded in every jet binary, get built from source on first use, or ride the pinned toolchain as prebuilt objects.
decisions.explainer: Today the ring libraries (core.http/regex/crypto/db/archive/log/reactive) are compiled into the jet binary via bridge templates; the hangar-realization seam (is_ring_module_staged) exists but always returns false. The card's second facet — 'ships ring packages' — is the question of whether that changes. It interacts hard with U30 toolchain pinning: if ring libs travel with the pinned toolchain object, the stdlib version equals the compiler version by construction, and there is never a Rust build or a network hit on a user's machine to use core.http.
decisions.story: Marion, a data analyst on a locked-down laptop with no internet and no Rust toolchain, clones a teammate's repo that uses core.http and core.encoding.json. She types `jet run .`. Whatever we pick decides whether that just works, downloads something first, or tries to compile a Rust crate she can't build.
decisions.detail: The four models differ on: (1) does a beginner's first offline run of a repo using a ring lib succeed with no toolchain; (2) is the stdlib version coherent with the pinned compiler or a separate matrix; (3) binary size; (4) whether there is one realization path or two. Ranking is on beginner offline experience, version coherence, one-path, and long-term correctness.

options.name: Embedded in the compiler only (status quo)
options.detail: Ring libs stay baked into every jet binary via bridge templates. Always offline, no realization, but the stdlib version is rigidly the compiler version, the binary grows with every ring lib, and 'ship ring packages' — the card's second facet — is declared out of scope.
options.code:
$ jet run .          # offline, fresh laptop
reportgen: running (core.http, core.encoding.json linked from compiler)
# works — but core.http can only ever be the version baked into this jet binary,
# and the binary carries every ring lib whether the project uses it or not.

options.name: Realized source packages, built on first use
options.detail: Ring libs live as core.* source packages in a first-party channel and realize from source into the hangar on first use, like any dependency — including a Rust build for their FFI bridges. Independently versioned. Trades the offline-first-run magic for decoupling.
options.code:
$ jet run .          # offline, fresh laptop, no Rust toolchain
error[E1239]: core.http needs a build toolchain that isn't available
  why: ring libraries realize from source on first use; this machine has no
       realized Rust toolchain and no Nix
  fix: run online once to cache the prebuilt object, or install the toolchain

options.name: Hybrid — prebuilt ring objects ride the toolchain, embedded fallback (recommended)
options.detail: The pinned jet toolchain object (D-JPK-TOOLCHAIN1) carries prebuilt per-platform ring artifacts; realizing the toolchain stages them into the hangar, offline forever (D-JPK-OFFLINE1). is_ring_module_staged flips true when present; the compiler-embedded templates remain the zero-config fallback for a freshly-built dev compiler. Ring version equals toolchain version by construction. One resolution path, two sources, no user-visible difference.
options.code:
$ jet run .          # offline, fresh laptop
reportgen: pins toolchain 0.4 -> realizing jet 0.4.2 (+ core.* prebuilt) ... done
reportgen: running
# core.http is exactly the 0.4 stdlib, staged beside the toolchain, no Rust build,
# no network after the toolchain is realized; a dev-built jet with no toolchain
# object silently uses the embedded template instead.

options.name: Independently-versioned realized packages
options.detail: Ring libs are realized packages with their own version line, decoupled from the compiler (deps: { core.http: "2.1" }). Maximum flexibility, but reintroduces a compiler/stdlib version matrix and a skew failure mode Jet has otherwise avoided.

comparisons.note: The standard library ships inside the toolchain SDK — pin the Go version, get exactly that stdlib, offline. Model C mirrors this.
comparisons.code:
// go.mod
go 1.22   // net/http is whatever 1.22 shipped, no separate version

comparisons.note: std ships with the rustc toolchain (channel-locked); crates.io libs are separate and independently versioned — a blend of C (for std) and D (for the ecosystem).
comparisons.code:
[toolchain]
channel = "1.78"   // std is 1.78's; serde is its own version

comparisons.note: The cautionary tale for A/D: the stdlib is bundled (like C) but pip packages drift, producing the exact compiler/library skew D risks.
comparisons.code: python3.12   # stdlib bundled; `pip install requests` is a separate, driftable version

decisions.rec: C — a beginner's first offline run of any repo using the stdlib succeeds with no toolchain and no network; stdlib version is coherent with the pinned compiler by construction; one realization path; the embedded fallback keeps dev builds friction-free.
decisions.recommendation: C — a beginner's first offline run of any repo using the stdlib succeeds with no toolchain and no network; stdlib version is coherent with the pinned compiler by construction; one realization path; the embedded fallback keeps dev builds friction-free.

decisions.title: When jetpack builds a dependency that wraps a Rust/C crate from source, what toolchain compiles it — and is it pinned?
decisions.gist: Pick whether an extern-rust bridge dependency is compiled by a pinned, realized build toolchain (reproducible) or by whatever cargo/rustc happens to be on the host.
decisions.explainer: D-BFS1 says crate-backed capabilities ship as Jet packages wrapping a vendored, hash-pinned crate via `extern rust`. Building one requires a Rust compiler (and sometimes a C toolchain). The shipped code (build_rlib_from_cargo) shells out to host `cargo` — which means the output hash varies with whatever Rust the machine has, and the build simply fails on a machine with no Rust. That directly undermines D-JPK-CACHE1: content-addressed cache substitution only works if the same source produces the same output hash on every machine, which requires a pinned build toolchain.
decisions.story: Dale, a backend engineer, adds a dependency that wraps a fast Rust checksum crate. It builds on his machine. His teammate on a fresh laptop pulls the lock and expects a cache hit — but her host rustc is a different version, so the output hash differs and she rebuilds the world, or has no Rust at all and it fails.
decisions.detail: This is distinct from U30 (which pins the jet compiler) and from the native-deps stopgap (which covers C system libraries via nixpkgs). Here the question is the Rust compiler used for bridge crates. Rank on reproducibility (cache correctness depends on it), no-Nix/offline coherence, and no host-toolchain leakage.

options.name: Pinned, realized build toolchain (recommended)
options.detail: The Rust toolchain that compiles a bridge crate is itself a hash-pinned hangar object — prebuilt/substituted via D-JPK-CACHE1, or via the standing nixpkgs native-deps stopgap on Nix machines, with the D-JPK-NONIX1 honest error when neither is present. Same source + same pinned toolchain -> same output hash -> cache hits across machines. The toolchain id enters the output provenance.
options.code:
$ jet build     # any machine
  fastsum  building from source (rust 1.79.0 [pinned], hash verified)
$ jet build     # teammate
  fastsum  substituted (hash matches — same pinned toolchain built it)

options.name: Host toolchain (status quo)
options.detail: Keep shelling out to whatever cargo/rustc is on PATH. Non-reproducible: output hash varies by host toolchain, so cache substitution silently misses or mis-serves; fails outright on machines with no Rust. A warn-only lint flags the unpinned build.
options.code:
$ jet build
warning[L02xx]: fastsum built with an unpinned host toolchain (cargo 1.74)
  output hash is not portable; other machines may rebuild
# on a machine with no Rust:
error[E12xx]: fastsum needs a Rust toolchain and none is on PATH

options.name: Prebuilt-only — no local from-source Rust builds
options.detail: No machine ever compiles a bridge crate. Every crate-backed dependency must be published as a prebuilt per-platform object; a machine lacking the object gets an honest error naming the publisher path. Maximally reproducible and zero-toolchain for consumers, but blocks building your own bridge locally.
options.code:
$ jet build
error[E12xx]: no prebuilt object for fastsum on aarch64-linux
  why: this project builds bridge crates ahead of time; nothing compiles locally
  fix: `jet publish fastsum --platform aarch64-linux` from a build host

comparisons.note: Pins the whole toolchain in the derivation so a build is bit-reproducible and substitutable from cache.nixos.org — exactly A's contract.
The status-quo trap of B: `cargo build` uses whatever rustc is installed; nothing guarantees two machines produce the same artifact.
comparisons.code: $ cargo build   # output depends on the host rustc version

comparisons.note: Pins toolchains as explicit build dependencies for hermetic, cache-shareable builds — A at scale.

decisions.rec: A — cache correctness (D-JPK-CACHE1) is meaningless without a reproducible output hash, and that requires a pinned build toolchain; it also removes host-toolchain leakage and gives a clean D-JPK-NONIX1 error path.
decisions.recommendation: A — cache correctness (D-JPK-CACHE1) is meaningless without a reproducible output hash, and that requires a pinned build toolchain; it also removes host-toolchain leakage and gives a clean D-JPK-NONIX1 error path.

decisions.title: Grant command surface
decisions.gist: Choose the command family users use to list, explain, grant, and revoke Jet trust grants.
decisions.story: Mira clones a service. Jet asks for package fetches, a local database, a secret, and a build wrapper. Later she needs one place to inspect and revoke those choices.
decisions.inWild:
jet dev
jet trust list
jet trust explain postgres.service
jet trust revoke postgres.service

options.name: `jet trust` command family
options.detail: Names the product concept directly. Beginner prompts, expert JSON, revoke, explain, and one-shot grants all sit under the same authority graph.
options.code:
jet trust list
jet trust explain --json
jet trust revoke github@acme/web:postgres.service

options.name: `jet grant` command family
options.detail: Names the internal object. Precise for experts, weaker for a beginner seeing a risk prompt for the first time.
options.code:
jet grant list
jet grant explain --json

options.name: `jet config trust` command family
options.detail: Keeps older config-shaped wording, but frames trust as settings instead of authority produced by code, packages, services, envs, images, and builds.
options.code:
jet config trust list
jet config trust revoke postgres.service

comparisons.note: Substituter and sandbox trust are separate knobs; Jet needs one user-facing trust graph.

decisions.title: Grant policy fields
decisions.gist: Choose whether projects may write reviewed trust policy in Jet source.
decisions.story: Noah maintains CI for a service. Local developers can be prompted, but CI must fail instead of prompting unless a reviewed policy permits the exact cache, registry, service, and wrapper facts.
decisions.inWild: policy: { trust: { default: prompt, ci: { prompt: deny } } }

options.name: `policy.trust` field
options.detail: One manifest policy namespace feeds the same grant graph used by prompts, CLI, locks, and audit.
options.code: policy: { trust: { default: prompt, ci: { prompt: deny }, services: { postgres: prompt } } }

options.name: No source policy fields
options.detail: All grants live in trust store, lock, and CLI. Source stays smaller, but teams cannot review repo policy beside package/env/build declarations.
options.code: jet trust grant cache@ci --scope repo

options.name: Role-local trust fields
options.detail: Each package, env, service, and build role writes local trust hints. Local when reading one role, fragmented when auditing one authority graph.
options.code:
module env dev
trust: { services: prompt, secrets: deny }

comparisons.note: Source-reviewed permissions are part of the workflow contract.

decisions.title: Workspace catalog surface
decisions.gist: Choose where shared dependency versions live and how packages opt in.
decisions.story: Priya owns a monorepo with thirty services. Most services share one HTTP version; one audited service pins another. Missing-dependency fixes must name either direct add or catalog opt-in.

options.name: `catalog:` in `workspace.jet`
options.detail: Catalogs live at the workspace authority point. Packages still opt into visible direct deps, so strict visibility remains intact.

options.name: `deps.catalog` inside each package
options.detail: Clear locally, but central version policy scatters across package manifests.
options.code: deps: { catalog: { http: npm@"undici#6.19.2" } }

options.name: CLI-only catalog edits
options.detail: Easy command path, less reviewable canonical source.
options.code: jet add npm@undici#6.19.2 --catalog http

comparisons.note: Workspace dependencies centralize versions while members opt in.

decisions.title: Strict visibility diagnostics
decisions.gist: Choose the diagnostic contract for hidden transitive package use.
decisions.story: Leo imports a package because another dependency already brought it in. Jet must explain transitive deps are hidden, name the asking package, and offer the smallest valid fix.
decisions.inWild:
use leftpad.pad

error[E12xx]: `leftpad` is not visible to package `acme.web`

options.name: Dedicated strict-visibility diagnostics
options.detail: New E12xx diagnostics name requester, hidden package, reason, and direct-dep or catalog fix.
options.code:
error[E12xx]: `leftpad` is not visible to package `acme.web`
fix: run `jet add npm@leftpad --package acme.web`

options.name: Reuse module-not-found diagnostics
options.detail: No new family; hidden packages look missing with extra help text.
options.code: error[E0606]: module `leftpad` not found

options.name: Warning plus resolution failure
options.detail: Splits one user problem into two messages.
options.code:
warning[W12xx]: transitive dependency hidden
error[E0606]: module not found

comparisons.note: Strict deps errors name the missing direct dependency.

decisions.title: Importer command
decisions.gist: Choose how users import foreign project metadata into Jet source.
decisions.story: Sam has a Nix flake and a Cargo workspace. He wants Jet to generate editable package, role, dep, adapter, and TODO files, then safely rerun the importer.
decisions.inWild:
jet import nix ./flake.nix
jet import cargo ./Cargo.toml --update

options.name: `jet import <ecosystem> <path>`
options.detail: Direct migration command. Generated Jet source is canonical; update, dry-run, and conflict rules define repeat behavior.
options.code:
jet import nix ./flake.nix
jet import cargo ./Cargo.toml --update

options.name: `jet migrate <ecosystem> <path>`
options.detail: Names the larger user intent, but migration also includes replacement progress beyond this file-emission job.
options.code: jet migrate nix ./flake.nix

options.name: `jet add --from <file>`
options.detail: Familiar for deps, too narrow for role modules, services, wrappers, FFI stubs, and TODO diagnostics.
options.code: jet add --from ./package.json

comparisons.note: Module commands ingest existing dependency state into canonical files.

decisions.title: Importer TODO diagnostics
decisions.gist: Choose how importer gaps appear in generated Jet projects.
decisions.story: Ari imports a Python package with dynamic metadata and a Node project with lifecycle scripts. Jet should not hide assumptions; it should leave precise review items tied to source spans.
decisions.inWild: warning[W12xx]: importer TODO: dynamic Python metadata

options.name: Dedicated importer TODO diagnostics
options.detail: Stable E/W12xx diagnostics carry what/why/fix, source path, generated target, and migration status.
options.code:
warning[W12xx]: importer TODO: npm lifecycle script needs review
fix: keep generated build recipe or replace with native Jet build code

options.name: Inline generated comments only
options.detail: Readable in files, weak for CI and audit.
options.code: // TODO(importer): postinstall needs review

options.name: Lock/explain TODO facts only
options.detail: Good audit trail, easy to miss while editing generated source.
options.code: jet dossier import

comparisons.note: Plan output surfaces review facts before apply.

decisions.title: Provider trust roots
decisions.gist: Choose how users control registries, mirrors, keys, and allowed providers.
decisions.story: Inez works at a company that allows crates.io and an internal npm mirror, denies public PyPI, and pins registry signing keys. Provider refs already have a spelling; this decides trust-root policy.
decisions.inWild: policy: { providers: { npm: { registry: "https://npm.acme.test" }, pypi: deny } }

options.name: `policy.providers` in source
options.detail: Provider trust roots are reviewable source policy feeding fetch grants, cache, signatures, and lock rationale.
options.code: policy: { providers: { npm: { registry: "https://npm.acme.test" }, pypi: deny, cargo: allow } }

options.name: User/global config only
options.detail: Good for personal machines, weaker for repo-reviewed CI.
options.code: jet trust provider allow npm --registry https://npm.acme.test

options.name: Lockfile-pinned trust only
options.detail: Reproducible after lock, less explicit before first resolution.
options.code: jet lock explain provider npm

comparisons.note: Registry scope config controls fetch source but not a unified trust graph.

decisions.title: Native replacement policy
decisions.gist: Choose how users allow, deny, or prefer proved native replacements.
decisions.story: Gwen depends on an npm HTTP client. Jet finds a proved native replacement. Her team wants replacements active in CI after review, never silent on developer machines.
decisions.inWild: policy: { replacements: { default: prompt } }

options.name: `policy.replacements` field
options.detail: Source policy names allow, deny, or prefer. Compatibility proof remains mandatory; policy only decides activation.
options.code: policy: { replacements: { default: prompt, npm@"undici#6.19.2": prefer core.http.undici } }

options.name: CLI-only replacement grants
options.detail: Useful for local experiments, less reviewable for repo policy.
options.code: jet trust replacement prefer npm@undici#6.19.2 core.http.undici

options.name: Always prompt
options.detail: Beginner-safe but teams cannot encode reviewed choices as project policy.
options.code: Jet can replace npm@undici#6.19.2 with core.http.undici.

comparisons.note: Patch redirects sources but does not prove compatibility.

decisions.title: Replacement proof metadata
decisions.gist: Choose how packages publish compatibility proof for native replacements.
decisions.story: Omar writes a native replacement for a Python CSV library. Users should see which public symbols, effects, errors, examples, and goldens were proved before Jet routes calls to it.
decisions.inWild: replacementProof: { replaces: pypi@"csvkit#2.0.1", public: all }

options.name: `replacementProof:` metadata
options.detail: User-authored proof metadata lives beside the native package and feeds proof runner, lock rationale, and audit.
options.code: replacementProof: { replaces: pypi@"csvkit#2.0.1", public: all, examples: find("./compat/examples") }

options.name: Generated index facts only
options.detail: Keeps source smaller, but package authors cannot publish intent directly in Jet source.
options.code: jet prove replacement core.csv.compat pypi@csvkit#2.0.1

options.name: External proof manifest
options.detail: Clear boundary for large fixture sets, but creates another canonical metadata surface.
options.code: replacement.jetproof

comparisons.note: Publishes compatibility intent for JS types, not runtime behavior proof.

decisions.title: jetos bootloader and kernel defaults
decisions.gist: Choose the first real boot path for jetos systems.
decisions.story: Doris is replacing a NixOS laptop with jetos. She wants one config to build a bootable machine, while her admin teammate needs to see and override the kernel, initrd, and bootloader facts before switch.

options.name: systemd-boot + Linux LTS (recommended)
options.detail: Default UEFI path is systemd-boot, kernel is Linux LTS, initrd is generated from declared filesystems/secrets/services. Expert options can select a kernel package and boot entry fields, but the semantic model stays one boot graph.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.loader: .SystemdBoot,
    boot.kernel: .LinuxLts,
    boot.initrd.modules: ["virtio_blk", "ext4"],
]

options.name: GRUB-first Linux
options.detail: Default boot path is GRUB for broad firmware compatibility. UEFI/systemd-boot remains an override. This prioritizes one mature multi-firmware bootloader as the first target.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.loader: .Grub,
    boot.kernel: .LinuxLts,
]

options.name: Kernel-install abstraction
options.detail: jetos records a boot graph and lets a backend choose systemd-boot or GRUB from firmware facts. Users see boot intent, experts can pin the backend.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.backend: .Auto,
    boot.kernel: .LinuxLts,
]

comparisons.note: NixOS exposes boot.loader.* and boot.kernelPackages as ordinary module options.
Kernel and bootloader are managed by system packages plus grubby/kernel-install.

decisions.comment: I want to use the limine boot loader and cachyos kernel

decisions.title: jetos plan proof provenance API
decisions.gist: Choose how tools read exact jetos plan, proof, and provenance facts.
decisions.story: Hank runs jetos Studio in CI review mode. The GUI and pipeline must read the same plan, diff, provenance, proof, health, and rollback facts that `jet os switch` enforces, with no private GUI state.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os plan devhost --json > plan.json
$ jet os proof devhost --json > proof.json
$ jetos studio
# Studio shows the same plan/proof/provenance artifacts and exact source diff

options.name: Artifacts only
options.detail: Build writes stable JSON files under each generation; users inspect files directly. Lowest surface area, but no canonical command for Studio/CI to refresh proof.
options.code:
.jet/systems/generations/<name>/plan.json
proof.json
provenance.json

options.name: jet os plan/proof (recommended)
options.detail: Add read-only `jet os plan` and `jet os proof` verbs that emit the same stable JSON artifacts build/switch uses. Studio and CI call the verbs; switch still enforces the artifacts.
options.code:
$ jet os plan devhost --json
$ jet os proof devhost --json
$ jet os build devhost

options.name: jet dossier os lens
options.detail: Use the broader D-WD dossier umbrella: `jet dossier os` exposes human and JSON plan/proof sections. Nice consolidation, but less direct for OS workflows.
options.code: $ jet dossier os devhost --json --section proof

comparisons.note: nixos-rebuild shows a derivation path and switch result, but plan/provenance are scattered across store paths and logs.
kubectl diff/apply separates plan from apply and exposes machine-readable objects.
comparisons.code:
kubectl diff -f system.yaml
kubectl apply -f system.yaml -o json

decisions.title: jetos installer user flow
decisions.gist: Choose how the installer asks for disk and host choices.
decisions.story: Betty boots a jetos USB on a new laptop. She wants a guided install that does not mention package graphs, while Earl installing servers needs a scripted path that writes the same transaction and proof.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os image installer devhost
$ jet os vm install devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
# guided default: ext4 root, host devhost, rollback generation recorded

options.name: Guided plus scripted (recommended)
options.detail: One installer transaction model. Beginner guided path asks host and disk; expert CLI feeds the same transaction non-interactively. Both produce the same proof.
options.code:
Install mode: Guided | Scripted
$ jet os install devhost --disk /dev/vda --mode guided

options.name: Scripted first
options.detail: Only a CLI installer is shipped first; graphical/guided UI layers later. Good for CI, weak for beginner drop-in replacement.
options.code: $ jet os install devhost --disk /dev/vda --yes

options.name: Studio installer first
options.detail: The installer is a Studio flow from the start. Best visual continuity, but couples boot media readiness to GUI stack maturity.
options.code: $ jetos studio --installer

comparisons.note: Graphical installers are separate from declarative rebuild; manual install is script-heavy.
Guided install first, advanced storage path available.

decisions.title: jetos installer media format
decisions.gist: Choose the bootable installer artifact format.
decisions.story: Walter wants to download one file, boot it in QEMU, and later write it to a USB stick. CI also needs the same artifact to install onto a virtual disk and reboot.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os image installer devhost
# writes jetos-installer-x64.iso plus SHA/provenance
$ qemu-system-x86_64 -cdrom jetos-installer-x64.iso -drive file=disk.qcow2,format=qcow2

options.name: Hybrid ISO first (recommended)
options.detail: Primary artifact is a bootable ISO named by D-JPK-OSBRAND1. It boots QEMU and physical USB paths; installed disk remains qcow2/raw as target output.
options.code:
jetos-installer-x64.iso
install-target: devhost.qcow2

options.name: Raw disk image first
options.detail: Installer media is a raw disk image. Simple to dd and boot, but less standard for virtual CD installer workflows.
options.code: jetos-installer-x64.raw

options.name: QCOW2 appliance first
options.detail: Ship a prebuilt VM appliance as the first artifact. Useful for demos; not an installer replacement for physical machines.
options.code: jetos-devhost.qcow2

comparisons.note: NixOS publishes ISO install media and can also build VM images.
ISO is the universal live/install artifact; VM disk images are separate.

decisions.title: jetos VM install proof command
decisions.gist: Choose the command that runs QEMU install and reboot proof.
decisions.story: Mara changes filesystem and service options. Before switch, CI must boot an installer, install to a blank virtual disk, reboot from that disk, and verify the guest with one command.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os vm prove devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
# boots installer ISO, installs, reboots from disk, runs guest checks, writes vm-proof.json

options.name: jet os vm prove (recommended)
options.detail: Dedicated OS sub-verb makes VM proof discoverable and keeps install/reboot semantics under jetos. It writes the artifact switch and Studio consume.
options.code: $ jet os vm prove devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2 --reboot

options.name: jet os image --prove-vm
options.detail: Attach proof to image build. Good when every proof starts from media, but hides the fact that proof is a separate install/reboot run.
options.code: $ jet os image installer devhost --prove-vm

options.name: jet prove os
options.detail: Use the broader proof product namespace. Good long-term umbrella, less direct for installer acceptance.
options.code: $ jet prove os devhost --vm-install

comparisons.note: NixOS has VM tests, but usually through Nix expressions and Python driver code.
Packer drives QEMU installs through a declarative template.

decisions.title: jetos VM and installer external tools
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos may depend on QEMU and image-building tools.
decisions.story: Olive runs CI on a clean Linux runner. jetos needs QEMU, firmware, and ISO/disk image utilities, but the compiler must not grow linked external dependencies or silently use random host tools.
decisions.inWild:
devShell: qemu, OVMF, xorriso, dosfstools, e2fsprogs
$ jet os vm prove devhost --offline
# tool provenance appears in proof.json

options.name: Pinned tool packages (recommended)
options.detail: QEMU, firmware, ISO, and filesystem tools are Jetpack-realized tool packages with versions and hashes in provenance. Dev shell may provide them, but proof records exact tools.
options.code:
tools: [core.qemu, core.ovmf, core.xorriso, core.e2fsprogs]
proof.toolchain.tools[].sha256

options.name: Host tools with diagnostics
options.detail: Use PATH tools when present and fail with Jet diagnostics when missing. Simple for local dev, weaker provenance.
options.code:
$ jet os vm prove devhost
Error: qemu-system-x86_64 not found

options.name: Nix-only test harness
options.detail: VM proof runs only through `nix develop`/nixpkgs tools. Good immediate reproducibility, conflicts with no-Nix jetos direction.
options.code: $ nix develop -c jet os vm prove devhost

comparisons.note: Image and VM tests use build inputs from nixpkgs, captured in derivations.
Packer shells out to QEMU and expects the executable/plugins installed.

decisions.title: jetos standard system tree surface
decisions.gist: Choose the full standard OS option tree for users, groups, secrets, boot, and health.
decisions.story: Earl is moving a workstation from NixOS. Packages and networking are not enough: he needs users, groups, filesystems, services, secrets, boot facts, and health checks in one source-backed tree Studio can edit.

options.name: Full-word option namespaces (recommended)
options.detail: Extend D-JPK-OSNS with clear full-word namespaces: users, groups, secrets, boot, kernel, init, health, plus existing filesystem, network, packages, services. One option declaration/setting mechanism; generated Linux files are projections.
options.code:
options: [
    users.user.normal: true,
    groups.wheel.members: [users.user],
    secrets.wifi.source: "secrets/wifi.age",
    boot.loader: .SystemdBoot,
    health.openssh.command: "systemctl is-active sshd",
]

options.name: Dedicated top-level System records
options.detail: Add top-level System fields such as users:, groups:, filesystems:, networking:, secrets:, boot:, health:. More structured at the top level, but it creates a second setting mechanism beside option declarations.

options.name: Keep three namespaces only
options.detail: Keep filesystem/network/packages and encode other facts through services or generated files. This preserves current narrow law but cannot honestly replace NixOS-class systems.

comparisons.note: NixOS has a broad option tree with users, services, boot, fileSystems, networking, and systemd.
Linux splits users/groups/files into separate declarative files; jetos can project one canonical tree into those files.

decisions.title: jetos CachyOS kernel source
decisions.gist: Choose where jetos gets the CachyOS kernel it boots.
decisions.story: Doris chose Limine and the CachyOS kernel for her jetos laptop. The generation proof must name the exact kernel, initrd inputs, patches, and hashes, so the installer can boot the same kernel in QEMU and on hardware.

options.name: First-party kernel package
options.detail: Jet carries or vendors a first-party CachyOS kernel package recipe with exact source, config, patches, initrd inputs, and hashes. Beginners still type `.CachyOS`; experts can audit and override the package path.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.kernel: .CachyOS,
]

proof.kernel.source = "jetos:cachyos-kernel"
proof.kernel.hash = "sha256:..."

options.name: External CachyOS binary repo
options.detail: Jet trusts a pinned CachyOS binary kernel artifact source. Fast to verify and boot when signatures are available, but provenance depends on the external release channel and signature policy.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.kernel: .CachyOS,
]

proof.kernel.source = "cachyos:<version>"
proof.kernel.signature = "..."

options.name: Policy-selected kernel package
options.detail: `.CachyOS` is an alias resolved by project policy to a pinned kernel package. Beginners get the default; expert teams can point the alias at a reviewed package without changing system modules.
options.code:
kernelPolicy.default.CachyOS: packages.cachyos-kernel

options: [
    boot.kernel: .CachyOS,
]

proof.kernel.policy = "kernelPolicy.default.CachyOS"

comparisons.note: NixOS selects a kernel package from nixpkgs or overlays; proofs are derivation/store-path based.
CachyOS distributes kernel packages through package repositories signed by repo keys.

decisions.title: jetos Studio GUI host runtime
decisions.gist: Choose what runs the jetos Studio window.
decisions.story: Betty opens jetos Studio on a fresh laptop to enable OpenSSH and add her user. She expects a real visual control center, while Earl needs the same screen to be scriptable in CI review mode and auditable as exact Jet source, diff, plan, proof, and provenance.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host devhost
# opens Studio: guided controls + source + diff + provenance

$ jetos studio ./machines --host devhost --serve 127.0.0.1:7417
# same projection service available to browser, CI screenshots, and future native shell
decisions.detail: Two-facet pass: beginners need one command that opens a usable GUI with no package-manager ceremony. Experts need an inspectable local protocol, stable JSON facts, deterministic screenshots, and no GUI-owned semantics. The host choice must not create a second configuration language or hide state outside Jet source/proof artifacts.

options.name: Local projection service plus bundled browser shell (recommended)
options.detail: Studio starts a local Jet-owned projection/edit service and opens a first-party web UI in the system browser by default; a bundled native webview shell may wrap the same local protocol when available. One semantic backend powers GUI, browser, CI screenshots, and future native packaging. No hidden GUI state; all edits still write source transactions.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host devhost
opened http://127.0.0.1:7417/studio/devhost

$ jetos studio ./machines --host devhost --headless --screenshot proof.png
# same service, deterministic UI artifact for review

options.name: Native Canvas shell only
options.detail: Studio is implemented as a native Canvas app from the start. Strong visual continuity with Canvas, but Studio readiness becomes coupled to the native Canvas runtime and cannot fall back to a simple browser review surface.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host devhost
# opens native Canvas-backed Studio window
# no browser/local web protocol is part of the contract

options.name: Browser-only local server
options.detail: Studio is always a local web app served by jetos. Simple, source-visible, and CI-friendly, but users do not get a desktop-app window or OS integration unless another layer is designed later.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host devhost
Studio listening at http://127.0.0.1:7417
# user opens browser manually or via auto-open

options.name: External desktop shell dependency
options.detail: Studio ships through an Electron/Tauri-style shell as the primary host. Rich desktop packaging, but the host adds external runtime/tooling authority that must be pinned and audited separately from the jetos projection service.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host devhost
# launches packaged desktop shell
proof.host.runtime = "external-shell:<version/hash>"

comparisons.note: NixOS has CLI and module files as the canonical path; GUI configuration tools are not the source of truth.
A browser UI projects API objects and sends ordinary API edits; the API object remains truth.
A local service/webview style can power desktop UI and browser/remoting from one protocol.

decisions.title: jetos CachyOS kernel bootstrap source
decisions.gist: Choose how the first-party CachyOS kernel package gets real bootable bits for VM/install proof.
decisions.explainer: D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A says .CachyOS resolves to a first-party package. #263 now needs that package to contain real kernel/initrd artifacts, not fixture text, so QEMU can boot and reboot installed jetos.
decisions.story: Doris selected Limine plus CachyOS. She expects jet os vm prove to boot the same kernel the installed machine will boot. Earl needs the proof to show exact source, config, patches, hashes, and whether any binary artifact was trusted.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os vm prove devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
# proof.kernel.source, proof.kernel.config, proof.kernel.hash, proof.initrd.hash
# guest boots the same payload recorded in generation boot/facts.json
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: users still write boot.kernel: .CachyOS or use the default; no package-source ceremony. Expert pass: the package exposes source/config/patch/provenance and can be replaced by policy later. Hybrid pass: one first-party package mechanism feeds build, ISO, VM proof, and installed boot; no separate test kernel.

options.name: Source-built first-party package (recommended)
options.detail: Jet vendors/declares the CachyOS kernel recipe, config, patches, and initrd inputs, then builds boot artifacts into the first-party cachyos-kernel package. Proof records source hashes and build inputs.

options.name: Pinned signed binary bootstrap
options.detail: Jet pins CachyOS kernel/initrd binary packages plus signatures as the first boot source, with source-built recipe still tracked as the replacement target. Fastest honest VM proof, weaker than source-built provenance.
options.code:
proof.kernel.source = "cachyos-binary:<version>"
proof.kernel.signature = "valid"
proof.native_replacement = "source recipe"

options.name: Temporary generic Linux kernel
options.detail: Use a pinned generic Linux kernel only for installer/VM proof until CachyOS packaging lands. This proves the installer path but violates the selected default users will boot.
options.code:
boot.kernel: .CachyOS
vm.kernel = linuxPackages.kernel  # proof-only override

comparisons.note: NixOS kernels are derivation-built from source or overlays; VM tests boot those store paths.
CachyOS distributes signed binary kernel packages; users trust repository signatures unless rebuilding locally.

decisions.title: jetos interactive VM launch command
decisions.gist: Choose how a user opens an installed jetos VM.
decisions.story: Betty has just built a jetos ISO and wants to try the system like a normal OS: boot it, log in, open a terminal, and later start the desktop. Earl needs the same path in CI with exact QEMU args and proof artifacts, without inventing a second runtime separate from `jet os vm prove`.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os image installer devhost
$ jet os vm prove devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
$ jet os vm run devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
# opens QEMU on the installed disk; serial/TTY login uses the same generation proof

options.name: prove plus run (recommended)
options.detail: `jet os vm prove` remains the non-interactive install/reboot proof. `jet os vm run` opens the same installed disk for human use, defaulting to terminal/serial first and later desktop when declared. One harness model feeds proof, CI, and manual use.
options.code:
$ jet os vm prove devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
proved jetos VM install/reboot ...

$ jet os vm run devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
booting devhost generation known-good
login: user
$ jet --version

options.name: prove with interactive flag
options.detail: Keep one verb and add `--interactive`. This avoids a second command, but mixes proof mode and human launch mode in one spelling; CI and users must remember a mode flag.
options.code:
$ jet os vm prove devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2 --interactive
# install/prove first if needed, then leave QEMU open

options.name: studio launches VMs
options.detail: Make Studio the primary human launch path and keep CLI proof-only. Good GUI continuity, but terminal-first users and CI lose a simple command-line launch surface.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host devhost
# click Run VM
# CLI still has only `jet os vm prove`

options.name: emit QEMU script only
options.detail: Proof writes `run-vm.sh` and users execute it themselves. Fully auditable, but beginners do not get a first-class `jetos` launch command.
options.code:
$ jet os vm prove devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
wrote systems/vm-proofs/devhost/run-vm.sh
$ ./systems/vm-proofs/devhost/run-vm.sh

comparisons.note: NixOS can build runnable VM scripts beside test drivers; the script and test share system config.
Packer proves and builds images, while users often run QEMU directly afterward.

decisions.title: jetos default desktop session
decisions.gist: Choose what desktop/window manager a jetos VM boots into.
decisions.story: Betty boots the jetos VM after proving install/reboot. She wants a real graphical session with a terminal and jetos Studio available from the system, not a proof-only shell. Earl needs the same session to be declarative, auditable, and replaceable by policy for workstation images.
decisions.inWild:
system.devhost: {
    services.desktop.enable: true,
    services.desktop.profile: .Default,
}

$ jet os vm prove devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
$ jet os vm run devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
# graphical login/session starts; terminal + jetos Studio are installed apps

options.name: Wayland-first JetOS session (recommended)
options.detail: Default desktop is one JetOS-owned Wayland session profile: display manager, seat/session service, wlroots-class compositor, terminal, browser fallback, and jetos Studio app. Beginners get a graphical system by enabling one desktop profile; experts can replace compositor, terminal, display manager, and session services through the same `services.*` tree and proof artifacts.
options.code:
services.desktop.profile: .Default
proof.desktop.session = "jetos-wayland"
proof.desktop.apps = ["terminal", "jetos-studio", "browser-fallback"]

options.name: KDE/GNOME profile first
options.detail: Default desktop is a mainstream full DE profile. Familiar for users and good hardware coverage, but JetOS proof becomes centered on a large external desktop policy stack instead of a small canonical JetOS session.
options.code:
services.desktop.profile: .Plasma
proof.desktop.session = "kde-plasma"
proof.desktop.external_policy = "desktop-upstream"

options.name: Terminal-first, desktop deferred
options.detail: The VM stays text-login only for now. This keeps the current terminal proof as the whole acceptance surface, but it does not meet the owner goal of opening a desktop/window-manager JetOS VM.
options.code:
services.desktop.enable: false
$ jet os vm run devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
login: user
$

options.name: X11-first session
options.detail: Default desktop starts with Xorg plus a lightweight window manager. It supports older software paths, but makes the first JetOS desktop center on the compatibility display server instead of the modern default graphics path.
options.code:
services.desktop.profile: .X11
proof.desktop.session = "xorg+wm"
proof.desktop.compat = true

comparisons.note: NixOS exposes desktop choices declaratively and can enable a display manager plus desktop manager/window manager in the same system config.
Fedora chooses a mainstream Wayland-first GNOME desktop as the default workstation experience.
comparisons.code: default graphical target + GNOME Wayland session

comparisons.note: Small Wayland compositors give a complete desktop session while keeping policy surface compact and inspectable.

decisions.comment: We should prefer wayland, but we will have gnome de by default, with terminal version as the secondary option/fallback. This way beginners get something easy & experts can get exactly what they want

decisions.title: Typed URL and mime modules: core.url + core.mime
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets typed URL/mime values as new core modules, and under which names.
decisions.explainer: A keeps URL values first-class and discoverable for every consumer (http, web, files, config), and mime is a genuinely separate small domain. Typed values over strings is the owner-preferred direction.
decisions.story: Priya builds a webhook relay in Jet. She concatenates a base URL with a user-supplied path and query params by hand; a space in a param silently produces a bad request that only fails in production. Every serious language gives her a URL type that makes this impossible; today core.http takes raw strings.

options.name: Two modules: core.url + core.mime
