options.detail: WHATWG-class typed Url value (parse/build/join/normalize, typed query pairs, per-component percent-encoding, IDNA) plus a small core.mime (extension↔type table, type/subtype+params parsing). core.http/core.web accept Url and mime types.
options.code:
use core.url as url

u := url.parse("https://api.example.com/notify")?
u.query.add("user", "ada lovelace")   // encoded correctly, by construction
http.get(u)?

use core.mime as mime
print(mime.from_extension("png") ?? "application/octet-stream")   // image/png

options.name: core.url only; mime lives inside core.http
options.detail: Same typed Url module; the mime table ships as http.mime helpers since HTTP is its main consumer. One fewer module name; files/static-serving reach through http for mime lookups.
options.code:
use core.url as url
use core.http as http

u := url.parse("https://api.example.com")?
print(http.mime.from_extension("png") ?? "?")

options.name: Fold both into core.http
options.detail: http.url.parse(...) and http.mime.*. No new top-level modules, but URL values are useful far beyond HTTP (file://, data:, config values, core.web) and burying them hurts discovery.
options.code:
use core.http as http

u := http.url.parse("https://api.example.com")?

options.name: Decline — keep strings
options.detail: URLs stay strings with documented escaping helpers in core.encoding. Cheapest surface, but every consumer re-solves encoding and the beginner footgun stays the default, against I1/philosophy.
options.code: raw :: "{base}/notify?user={encoding.percent(user)}"   // remembering to call percent() is on you

comparisons.note: The URL/URLSearchParams pair is the modern reference; browsers ship it built-in.
comparisons.code:
const u = new URL('https://api.example.com/notify');
u.searchParams.set('user', 'ada lovelace');

comparisons.note: net/url is stdlib and universally used; mime is its own stdlib package.
comparisons.code:
u, _ := url.Parse("https://api.example.com")
q := u.Query(); q.Set("user", "ada lovelace"); u.RawQuery = q.Encode()

comparisons.note: urllib.parse is stdlib but string-tuple based and widely considered clunky — the anti-example.

decisions.title: Human formatting: core.fmt module vs interpolation format-specs
decisions.gist: How Jet spells number/bytes/duration formatting — library functions or string-interpolation syntax.
decisions.explainer: C: A’s functions deliver the daily wins (bytes/duration/thousands) with zero syntax risk now, and the spec-sugar question stays a clean future reopen instead of a silent never.
decisions.story: Ana prints a report: file sizes, elapsed times, row counts with thousands separators, floats to 2 decimals. Today interpolation gives her the raw value only, so she writes arithmetic and string surgery by hand for each cell — the tenth time she has done it.

options.name: core.fmt module, functions only
options.detail: fmt.bytes(n), fmt.duration(ms), fmt.number(n, thousands: true, precision: 2), fmt.ordinal(n), fmt.pad/align helpers. No syntax change; composes in interpolation like any call. Locale-aware variants can join later behind the same names.

options.name: Interpolation format-specs
options.detail: Python/Rust-style mini-language inside braces: {x:.2f}, {n:,}, {s:>10}. Terse at the call site, but it is new user-facing syntax (lexer/parser/formatter/S8 interplay), a second sub-language to learn, and covers only what the spec grammar anticipates (no bytes/duration).
options.code:
print("{name}: {size:.1G}B in {elapsed:dur} ({rows:,} rows)")
// every marker is spec grammar to ratify, document, and format-stabilize

options.name: Both: functions now, spec sugar later
options.detail: Ship A; reopen a spec-syntax ballot only if call-site verbosity proves painful in real code. Keeps today’s decision small without closing the door.
options.code:
print("{fmt.number(rows, thousands: true)}")   // today
print("{rows:,}")                              // possible future reopen

options.name: Decline
options.detail: Raw interpolation only. Every report/CLI author keeps hand-rolling the same helpers — a daily papercut in exactly the beginner path Jet optimizes for.
options.code: print("{(size / 1073741824.0)} GB")   // and now round it yourself

comparisons.note: format-spec mini-language is powerful and famously unmemorizable; humanize is a separate library anyway for bytes/durations.
no format-specs in strings; helpers/libraries do it — humanize is one of the most-imported Go packages.
{:>10.2} exists in format! and still no bytes/duration answer without crates.

decisions.comment: full go-style humanize support in the fmt module/lib.

decisions.title: Terminal and raw IO surface
decisions.gist: Choose the shape of terminal stdout/stderr, TTY facts, colors, progress, raw mode, and key events.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one import for beginner CLIs, but a clean stream/terminal split inside core.io for expert control and audit.
decisions.story: Betty writes a deployment CLI. It prints a progress line, colors warnings only on terminals, flushes before running a child process, and reads one key in raw mode for confirmation. She should not hand-roll ANSI or leak escape codes into logs.
decisions.inWild:
use core.io as io

io.write("Building...")
io.flush()
if io.stdout.is_tty() { io.style(.Yellow).write("warn") }
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one import for beginner CLIs, but a clean stream/terminal split inside core.io for expert control and audit.

options.name: Hybrid: stream backbone plus terminal capability namespace (recommended)
options.detail: core.io owns stdout/stderr/stdin streams, flush, raw bytes, and TTY facts. Terminal capabilities live under `io.terminal`/stream methods, not a separate module: style/progress/raw mode/key events all honor TTY/NO_COLOR by default, with explicit expert overrides for forced color/raw behavior.
options.code:
use core.io as io

io.stdout.write("Building...")?
io.stdout.flush()?
if io.stdout.is_tty() { io.stdout.style(.Green).write("done")? }
key :: io.terminal.raw(() => io.terminal.read_key())?

options.name: Split core.io and core.term
options.detail: core.io stays byte streams; core.term owns TTY/color/raw/key/progress. Separation is clean, but beginners must learn two modules for one terminal program.
options.code:
use core.io as io
use core.term as term
term.style(.Green).write(io.stdout, "done")?

options.name: Decline terminal depth
options.detail: Keep print/eprint/input only. Serious CLIs shell out or hand-roll ANSI/raw mode, so pipes and Windows terminals become user footguns.
options.code: print("\x1b[32mdone\x1b[0m")

comparisons.note: term/console needs x/term or third-party packages; stdlib leaves gaps.
crossterm gives capability breadth as a crate; Jet needs a blessed Core path.

decisions.title: Declarative CLI parser depth
decisions.gist: Choose how core.args grows beyond the typed run(args) layer and simple builders.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: derive ergonomics and builder control feed one checked command-spec model.
decisions.story: Hank ships a CLI with subcommands, env fallbacks, defaults, completion text, and exact errors. Typed entry args cover the common case; library code and custom launchers need the same parser without inventing another command language.
decisions.inWild:
use core.args as args

spec :: args.command("serve").flag("port", default: 8080).subcommand("migrate")
parsed :: args.parse(spec)?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: derive ergonomics and builder control feed one checked command-spec model.

options.name: Hybrid: one ArgsSpec from structs or builders (recommended)
options.detail: ArgsSpec is the single semantic model. Typed `fn run(args: T)` derives an ArgsSpec for beginners; library/tooling code can build the same ArgsSpec dynamically for subcommands, env fallbacks, completions, and tests. No string mini-language.

options.name: Struct-only derive everywhere
options.detail: All parsing starts from structs/enums. Clean for ordinary apps, but generated tools and dynamic command sets cannot compose specs at runtime.
options.code: cmd :: args.parse<DeployArgs>()?

options.name: String mini-language
options.detail: A clap-like DSL string describes commands. Compact, but becomes a second grammar with weak type/source spans.
options.code: spec :: args.spec("deploy --host <HOST> [--dry-run]")

comparisons.note: Builder plus derive coexist; Jet should keep one semantic spec with two ergonomic entrypoints.
Dynamic builders are flexible but weakly typed.

decisions.title: Math library depth and numeric safety
decisions.gist: Choose the Core math surface for libm breadth and integer-safety helpers.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: beginner discoverability without a second numeric-method API.
decisions.story: Doris writes physics and finance tooling. She needs trig/log/hypot, checked/saturating integer operations, gcd/lcm, clamp, and clear NaN/overflow behavior. Bare operators are not enough.
decisions.inWild:
use core.math as math

dist :: math.hypot(dx, dy)
sum :: math.checked_add(a, b)?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: beginner discoverability without a second numeric-method API.

options.name: Hybrid: core.math canonical registry plus discoverability (recommended)
options.detail: core.math functions are the canonical callable surface for libm and explicit checked/saturating/wrapping integer families. Numeric documentation, LSP completion, and optional snippets may surface helpers from values, but emitted code uses the same core.math names so Jet does not grow duplicate spellings.
options.code:
angle :: math.atan2(y, x)
next :: math.checked_add(count, 1)?
cap :: math.saturating_mul(bytes, shards)
// LSP on `count.` may offer "checked_add" and insert math.checked_add(count, ...)

options.name: Numeric methods
options.detail: Put helpers on numeric values. Discoverable after a value, but fragments the surface across types and makes generic numeric docs harder.
options.code:
angle :: y.atan2(x)
next :: count.checked_add(1)?

options.name: Operators and lints only
options.detail: Keep operators and add overflow lints. Beginner code stays terse, but exact overflow intent is not visible at the call site.
options.code: x + y   // maybe checked by profile, maybe not

comparisons.note: Rust names checked/saturating/wrapping arithmetic explicitly.
math and bits are split; integer overflow remains easy to miss.

decisions.title: Randomness modules and distributions
decisions.gist: Choose how PRNG sampling, bytes, shuffling, and security randomness are separated.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: rich sampling UX for ordinary code and hard separation for security-sensitive bytes.
decisions.story: Earl writes a simulation and later adds password reset tokens. If random bytes and deterministic PRNGs share one undifferentiated API, the safe path is invisible.
decisions.inWild:
use core.random as random

seeded :: random.Splittable.new(seed)
token :: ???
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: rich sampling UX for ordinary code and hard separation for security-sensitive bytes.

options.name: Hybrid: reproducible PRNG in core.random, secrets in core.crypto (recommended)
options.detail: core.random owns deterministic PRNGs, distributions, shuffling, sampling, seed splitting, and test fixtures. Secret randomness stays in core.crypto. Shared entropy plumbing may exist internally, but names keep simulation/test randomness and security randomness impossible to confuse.
options.code:
rng := random.SplitMix64.new(seed)
roll :: rng.int(1..6)
items.shuffle(&rng)
token :: crypto.random_bytes(32)
nonce :: crypto.random_nonce(.XChaCha20)

options.name: Single core.random with secure namespace
options.detail: One module owns both random.prng and random.secure. Discoverable, but proximity invites accidental security misuse.
options.code: token :: random.secure.bytes(32)

options.name: Only crypto randomness
options.detail: Use secure randomness for everything. Safe for secrets, poor for reproducible tests/simulations and performance-sensitive sampling.
options.code: roll :: crypto.random_int(1..6)

comparisons.note: rand separates RNG traits and distributions; secrets require OsRng care.
random vs secrets split is the correct beginner lesson.

decisions.title: Regex engine semantics and API depth
decisions.gist: Choose the in-house regex contract before replacing the bridge.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: safe predictable regex for everyone, with migration help instead of importing PCRE footguns into the default path.
decisions.story: Tom filters logs in a server path. Regex must be fast, predictable, Unicode-aware, and impossible to turn into a catastrophic backtracking trap by default.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: safe predictable regex for everyone, with migration help instead of importing PCRE footguns into the default path.

options.name: Hybrid: linear default with explicit compatibility mode (recommended)
options.detail: core.regex is RE2-class and linear by default: captures, named groups, replace, split, flags, Unicode classes. A future compatibility parser may diagnose unsupported PCRE features and suggest safe rewrites; any backtracking/PCRE engine would be explicit, audited, and never the default.
options.code:
rx :: regex.compile("(?<level>INFO|WARN)")?
match :: rx.find(line)?

legacy :: regex.compile_compat(pattern)?
// emits diagnostics for unsafe backtracking features unless explicitly allowed

options.name: PCRE-class full feature engine
options.detail: Lookaround/backrefs maximize compatibility, but catastrophic backtracking becomes a beginner footgun unless heavily gated.
options.code: rx :: regex.compile("(a+)+$")

options.name: Minimal matcher only
options.detail: Ship contains/glob-like matching and defer full regex. Safe but not competitive with existing stdlib expectations.
options.code: if text.contains("ERROR") { ... }

comparisons.note: regexp is RE2-class linear-time stdlib.
Rust regex is linear and omits backreferences/lookaround.

decisions.title: Database rows and migrations
decisions.gist: Choose the database surface above the ratified safe driver floor.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: honest SQL and typed rows now, with generated query plans as an ergonomic front end over the same parameterized mechanism.
decisions.story: Omar builds a service with SQLite now and Postgres later. He needs parameter-only queries, typed rows, transactions, migrations, and schema drift checks without stringly result maps.
decisions.inWild:
use core.db as db

rows :: conn.query("select id, email from users where id = ?", [id])?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: honest SQL and typed rows now, with generated query plans as an ergonomic front end over the same parameterized mechanism.

options.name: Hybrid: typed SQL rows plus optional query builder (recommended)
options.detail: The canonical database path is parameterized SQL with typed row decoding, transactions, prepared statements, migrations, and checksums. A query builder can generate that same SQL/parameter plan for Studio/LSP workflows, but SQL remains inspectable and parameter-only safety remains enforced.
options.code:
rows :: conn.query<UserRow>("select id,email from users where id = ?", [id])?
db.migrate(conn, migrations.from_dir("migrations"))?

plan :: db.query(User).where(.id == id).select(.{ id, email })
rows2 :: conn.run<UserRow>(plan)?

options.name: ORM-style query builder
options.detail: Build queries from Jet expressions. More typed, but creates a second language for SQL and can hide database behavior.
options.code: users.where((u) => u.id == id).select(.{ id, email })

options.name: Raw driver only
options.detail: Expose execute/query returning dynamic rows. Safe params remain, but typed app code does manual casts everywhere.
options.code: row.get_string("email")?

comparisons.note: Typed rows and migrations are loved, but macro/build-time DB coupling is a tax.
Safe params, weak row typing; Jet can improve here.

decisions.title: Structured logging, tracing, and sinks
decisions.gist: Choose the logging API for logs, spans, metrics hooks, and export.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: simple logging calls generate audit-ready structured events for expert observability.
decisions.story: Inez debugs a production incident. Plain print lines are not enough; she needs structured fields, spans, request IDs, JSON output, sampling, and OTel export without every package inventing a logger.
decisions.inWild:
use core.log as log

log.info("started")
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: simple logging calls generate audit-ready structured events for expert observability.

options.name: Hybrid: structured events, spans, and friendly text sinks (recommended)
options.detail: core.log records typed events/spans/fields as the source truth. Text, JSON, and OTel sinks are output formats over those events. Beginners call log.info with plain fields; experts control propagation, sampling, redaction, sinks, trace IDs, and export policy.
options.code:
span :: log.span("http.request", fields: .{ route: "/users" })
log.info("loaded user", fields: .{ user_id: id })
log.sink(log.Json.stdout())
log.export(log.otel(endpoint))

options.name: Printf logging plus JSON sink
options.detail: Keep log.info text-first and add optional key/value args. Familiar, but weaker type/audit story.
options.code: log.info("loaded user", "user_id", id)

options.name: Use print/core.io
options.detail: No logging module. Services and libraries cannot compose observability coherently.
options.code: print("[INFO] loaded user {id}")

comparisons.note: Structured logs are now stdlib-level.
Spans/events are the right model but crate-based.

decisions.title: Collections and iterator adapter depth
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical collection/iterator expansion surface.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: collection-method ergonomics over a single lazy iterator core.
decisions.story: Sam writes data transforms. He expects map/filter/fold/chunk/window/group/sort/dedup/zip/enumerate/collect to work over lists, maps, ranges, files, and streams with one mental model.
decisions.inWild: xs.filter((x) => x.ok).map((x) => x.id)
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: collection-method ergonomics over a single lazy iterator core.

options.name: Hybrid: lazy iterator protocol with eager collection conveniences (recommended)
options.detail: One Iterable/Iterator model powers lazy adapters. Collections expose beginner-friendly adapter methods that return lazy views; `collect`, `to_list`, or terminal reducers make materialization explicit. No comprehension syntax needed now.
options.code:
ids :: users
    .filter((u) => u.active)
    .map((u) => u.id)
    .chunked(100)
    .to_list()

total :: orders.iter().map((o) => o.total).sum()

options.name: Eager collection methods only
options.detail: Every adapter returns a collection. Beginner-simple, but large/streaming workloads allocate unnecessarily.
options.code: ids :: users.filter(...).map(...)

options.name: Comprehension syntax
options.detail: New syntax for collection transforms. Compact, but a major surface and second spelling for adapters.
options.code: ids :: [u.id for u in users if u.active]

comparisons.note: Broad lazy adapters set the bar.
Powerful but split between language loops, list comprehensions, and itertools.

decisions.title: What visible spelling deliberately discards a #MustUse / fallible result?
decisions.gist: D-IGNORERET1=B requires visible discard. This decides the per-call spelling and the method-chain spelling; scoped suppression is `#Suppress`, not `@suppress`.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: the ballot now offers more than three spellings and separates terse sigils from audit-readable words. Adversarial pass on `.ignore("reason")`: method syntax can look like an ordinary user method and reasons can become boilerplate. Patch: sema treats it as a blessed escape only for `#MustUse`/fallible values, requires a non-empty literal reason, emits a lint naming the dropped type, and rejects user-defined `.ignore` from silently intercepting must-use semantics.
decisions.story: Nora writes a telemetry sink. Individual best-effort calls need an audit reason, but long chains should keep reading left-to-right without hiding the discarded result.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Give me other syntax options that read a little better; potentially ok with A but want multiple options.
Agent answer: Updated with six options. Best revised rec: .ignore("reason") — attached to the value being dropped, creates an audit trail, sema treats it as a blessed escape requiring a non-empty literal reason.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): D-LIN1-DROP=A COHESION: that ratified decision rejected both `x.abandon("reason")` (method+reason, the shape of Option D) and `discard(x,"reason")` (vocabulary of Option E) for #SingleUse discard. This ballot proposes both rejected patterns. The design must either unify under `drop(expr,"reason")` (Option H) or explicitly document why fallible-result discard warrants a different form than linear-type discard — without that, I8 is bent. POSTFIX !: `!` is currently OP_NOT (prefix unary only); Options A and B introduce it as postfix for the first time — two meanings, opposite positions, same glyph. MISSING EXPERT TIER: per-call annotation is unworkable for fire-and-forget subsystems; Option I (scope-level suppression) belongs in this ballot alongside the per-call spelling.

Sprint-readiness sweep: story and inWild filled so the ballot is complete for owner decision.

options.name: Method `.drop("reason")` + `#Suppress` scope (recommended)
options.detail: Keep the ratified visible-discard rule, but make the chain spelling a method-like terminal operator: `expr.drop("reason")`. It reads left-to-right in chains and reuses the existing `drop` vocabulary from D-LIN1-DROP. The scoped form is `#Suppress(MustUse) { ... }` or `#Suppress(MustUse) fn ...`, matching Jet marker casing and the owner correction; no `@suppress` attribute exists.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    .drop("telemetry best effort")

#Suppress(MustUse) {
    write_log(event)
    send_metric(event)
}

options.name: Pipe discard `.then(drop("reason"))`
options.detail: Keep `drop` as the vocabulary but make chaining go through an explicit pipeline/combinator step. This is clear that discard is a terminal action, but it introduces a callback-like wrapper for a common review signal and is noisier than `.drop(...)`.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    .then(drop("telemetry best effort"))

options.name: Postfix bang method `.!drop("reason")`
options.detail: Use a visually loud method operator for discards only. Reviewers cannot miss it, and it keeps chaining shape. Downside: `!` already means logical not in Jet; spending it inside method syntax creates another punctuation rule.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    .!drop("telemetry best effort")

options.name: Arrow method operator `-> drop("reason")`
options.detail: A terminal arrow makes the discard look like control flow at the end of a chain. It is visually distinct from ordinary methods, but `->` already carries return/arm meaning; using it in expression chains risks overloading a high-value token.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    -> drop("telemetry best effort")

comparisons.note: Uses `let _ = expr` or `drop(expr)`; no required reason string.
Discard is an audited terminal method or an explicit marker-scoped suppression.

decisions.recommendation: Use `.drop("reason")` plus `#Suppress(MustUse)` (Option A): one discard vocabulary, method-chain friendly, and marker casing matches Jet.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a prelude opt-out directive, and/or let libraries mark names as prelude-injectable?
decisions.gist: The prelude auto-imports `print`, `input`, and a curated set. Two new ideas: (1) a user directive to opt out of the prelude, and (2) a library marker that puts names into scope without a prefix (`#builtin`-style). These can ship independently. This card decides both.
decisions.explainer: Opt-out lets expert users who want explicit imports take full control — a clean I1-compatible escape hatch. Library no-prefix injection is the riskier half: it lets any package pollute the default namespace, violates I8 (arbitrary second paths to a name), and defeats the prelude's curation. A library using this would look like Jet's own prelude to a beginner who can't tell the difference. Interactions: prelude `print`/`input` are ratified; this doesn't touch them. The `#builtin` marker is unratified scratch.
decisions.story: I'm writing a CLI tool with explicit imports everywhere for clarity. I want to put `#NoPrelude` at the top of my file and have zero implicit names — then import exactly what I use.

options.name: Opt-out directive only — no library injection
options.detail: Add a `#NoPrelude` file-level marker that disables auto-imports. Library no-prefix injection is declined (I8 violation — lets packages create arbitrary implicit paths). This is the minimal, safe escape hatch.

options.name: Both opt-out and library injection
options.detail: Libraries can mark exports with a `#Prelude`-style marker to inject names into callers' scope. Powerful but breaks I8 and the namespace contract — any dep can now shadow prelude names.

options.name: Neither — no changes
options.detail: Keep the current curated prelude with no opt-out. Expert users import on top of the prelude; the prelude names are always present. Simplest surface, least flexible.

comparisons.note: Rust offers `#![no_implicit_prelude]` for expert files while preventing dependencies from injecting names into every scope.
`#![no_std]` and `#![no_implicit_prelude]` opt out of std and prelude respectively. Expert escape hatch, not the default.
`{-# LANGUAGE NoImplicitPrelude #-}` disables the Prelude import per-file. Libraries then re-export curated sets (Protolude, Relude).

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust offers `#![no_implicit_prelude]` for expert files while preventing dependencies from injecting names into every scope.
decisions.recommendation: Add opt-out only. This matches the best expert escape hatch while preserving Jet’s curated beginner prelude and blocking package namespace pollution.

decisions.title: Add maturity markers (`#Experimental` / `#Tested` / `#Hardened`) that propagate like effects?
decisions.gist: A maturity lattice lets library authors tag APIs with their stability level, and the compiler warns (or errors) when stable code calls experimental code without an explicit acknowledgment. New; no decision exists. The machinery would ride existing marker and effect-ceiling infrastructure.
decisions.explainer: Propagation rule: calling an `#Experimental` item taints the caller unless the caller also carries `#Experimental` or explicitly acknowledges with a suppressor (e.g. `#[allow(Experimental)]`). The lattice is `#Experimental < #Tested < #Hardened`; unmarked items default to some level (TBD — a separate question). Blast radius: sema (propagation pass), effect ceilings, doc output. Prerequisite: effect ceiling machinery needs to exist or be extended. This interacts with the effect-ceilings card. If the marker propagation model isn't yet shipped, a doc-only convention (Option B) costs nothing and covers 80% of the use-case until the machinery is ready. I1: no safety impact — this is purely about API stability signaling. I8: maturity signaling is a new job; no existing mechanism covers it.
decisions.story: I publish a library. `parse_v2` is solid; `parse_experimental` is still in flux. I tag it `#Experimental` and anyone who calls it without opting in gets a warning at their call site — not buried in a changelog.

options.name: Full propagating marker family
options.detail: Add `#Experimental`, `#Tested`, `#Hardened` as propagating markers riding existing effect machinery. Compile-time enforcement; IDE surfaces stability at call sites. Sequences after effect-ceiling machinery.

options.name: Doc-only convention now, propagation later
options.detail: Define `#Experimental`, `#Tested`, `#Hardened` as documentation-visible markers today (no compiler propagation). When effect-ceiling machinery ships, wire propagation. Low cost; covers the doc/tooling case immediately.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Don't decide until effect-ceiling machinery is finalized. Avoids designing the propagation model twice.
options.code: // no change; stability is communicated via doc comments only

comparisons.note: Kotlin `@RequiresOptIn` makes experimental APIs visible and can require caller opt-in.
`#[unstable]` is a compiler-enforced gate in the standard library (nightly only); third-party crates use `#[deprecated]` or doc comments. No lattice propagation.
`@RequiresOptIn` / `@OptIn` is a propagating annotation lattice — callers must opt in or the compiler warns. Very close to what Option A proposes.

decisions.bestCurrent: Kotlin: Kotlin `@RequiresOptIn` makes experimental APIs visible and can require caller opt-in.
decisions.recommendation: Start doc-visible, propagate later. Jet should not wire a new propagation lattice until machinery is ready, but docs/IDE maturity markers can beat comment-only stability now.

decisions.title: Should Jet pursue refinement types (e.g. PositiveInt proved > 0), and if so as a construction-time subset or a full SMT-backed prover?
decisions.gist: The decision has two forks that should be separated before the owner votes. Fork 1 (mechanism): does Jet add a new `refine` keyword, or extend the ratified `distinct` type (D-DIST1) with an attached invariant clause — these both deliver smart-constructor invariant checking, and I8 says choose one. Fork 2 (power): does the compiler check only at construction (no prover), check linear arithmetic with a bounded pure-Rust prover (I6-clean, no SMT, delivers D-OOBPROOF1=A), or defer to a full SMT solver. The current gist frames the decision purely as "how much proving" — but the I8/mechanism question is equally important and comes first. The expert/beginner split: beginners need "forgot the check = compile error" (all options except A deliver this); experts need "arithmetic on refined values does not require re-checking at every expression" (only the prover options deliver this). Option B gives beginners the compile-time guarantee but gives experts worse ergonomics than the status quo for arithmetic-heavy code.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: B loses real theorem-prover power compared with C. B can validate constructors, literals, and local flow narrowing; it cannot prove arbitrary arithmetic, universal properties, cross-function postconditions, or eliminate bounds checks from a proof. Adversarial pass: a small subset can become a dead-end half-feature. Patch: phrase B as the stable predicate surface/invariant discipline, so a later solver tier can reuse the same predicates instead of replacing them.
decisions.story: I'm writing a billing function and I type fn charge(cents: PositiveInt). A caller passes a value computed from user input. The compiler stops me at the call site: it can't prove the value is positive, and it points me at the one constructor — PositiveInt.new(n) returns PositiveInt ? String — so I write let amt = PositiveInt.new(raw)? once at the boundary. From there it flows through three layers of my code untouched, and nobody re-checks it. When I later guard with if amt > 0 the compiler already knew; when I forgot a guard last week, require() would have blown up at runtime — now it's a compile error with a fix-it pointing at the constructor.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: What are the tradeoffs of option B instead of C? What is lost by going with B over C?
Agent answer: B gives construction-checked refined values, literal checks, and flow narrowing. C can prove `a + b` remains PositiveInt, prove indexing is in bounds, eliminate runtime checks, and verify function postconditions over all inputs. What is lost with B: proof-preserving arithmetic, universal proofs, cross-function theorem reasoning, and check elision. Best sequencing: ship B as the surface; let future C reuse those predicates if a solver/prover tier is owner-approved.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): D-OOBPROOF1=A INCOHERENCE: D-OOBPROOF1 was ratified 2026-06-28 and uses `fn sum(arr: [Int], i: UInt where i < arr.len)` — a relational predicate between two bindings. Option B's construction-time model cannot check `i < arr.len` at construction time (arr is not in scope when i is constructed). If D-REFINE1=B ratifies without relational predicates, D-OOBPROOF1=A stays blocked. `refine` vs `distinct` (I8): D-DIST1/D-DIST3 (ratified) already provide a nominal wrapper; `refine` adds the same pattern with a predicate — I8 demands one mechanism. MISSING OPTION F: Presburger arithmetic (linear integer arithmetic, complete, decidable, pure-Rust, I6-clean) proves `a + b > 0` from `a > 0 && b > 0` and `i < arr.len()` from call-site context — the I6-clean middle path between B and C. `where` keyword: S45 explicitly rejected `where` clauses; using it for `refine T = Base where pred` introduces a rejected keyword in a new position.

options.name: Extend `distinct` with `#Invariant(pred)` + pure-Rust LIA prover — no new keyword (recommended)
options.detail: No new `refine` keyword (I8: `distinct` already provides nominal wrappers). Extend the ratified `distinct` type to carry an `#Invariant(predicate)` clause: `PositiveInt :: distinct Int { #Invariant(it > 0) }`. The compiler generates a smart constructor `.new() -> T ? Error` lowering to `require()/T?E`. Implement a pure-Rust Presburger/linear integer arithmetic (LIA) decision procedure (~3-5K lines, I6-clean, no external crate): proves (a) smart constructor invariants, (b) arithmetic preservation (`PositiveInt + PositiveInt -> PositiveInt` proven from `a>0 && b>0 => a+b>0`), and (c) relational predicates (`i < arr.len`) needed for D-OOBPROOF1=A (already ratified, currently blocked). Non-linear predicates fall back to construction-time checking with a clear diagnostic: "this predicate requires construction-time validation; arithmetic preservation not provable with linear arithmetic." Flow narrowing (`if x > 0` narrows `x: Int` to `PositiveInt`) is a separate sub-ballot — do not bundle.

options.name: Construction-time only — no LIA prover (D-OOBPROOF1=A stays blocked)
options.detail: Add `#Invariant(pred)` to `distinct` but implement only construction-time checking — no prover. Smart constructor `.new() -> T ? Error`. Arithmetic on refined values widens to the base type; caller must re-validate. Literal arguments checked at compile time. D-OOBPROOF1=A (bounds-check elision via `i < arr.len`) is a relational predicate between two bindings — cannot be checked at construction time without `arr` in scope. If B is ratified, D-OOBPROOF1=A has no delivery path.

options.name: Defer refinement types to Epoch 6
options.detail: No refinement syntax now. Prerequisites for reconsideration: Jet has shipped at least one numeric workload where the invariant-duplication cost of `require()` is concretely documented, AND D-OOBPROOF1=A has an alternate delivery path. Without those, defer is equivalent to closing the card indefinitely.

comparisons.note: Liquid Haskell proves rich predicates with SMT-backed refinements, but the model is expert-only.

Bolts refinement types onto GHC and discharges proof obligations to an external SMT solver (Z3). Predicates are written in special comments; the solver proves arithmetic/measure facts. Exactly the model option C describes — and exactly the external-solver dependency I6 forbids us from vendoring.

subtype PositiveInt is Integer with Dynamic_Predicate => PositiveInt > 0. Plain Ada checks the predicate at construction/assignment AT RUNTIME (raises Constraint_Error) — this is essentially option B's construction-time model. SPARK then adds an optional separate prover pass to discharge them statically (option C). The Ada/SPARK split is the clean precedent for shipping B first and treating C as a layered, optional research tier.

No real refinements; simulates them with a phantom 'brand' and a user-written guard that asserts the brand. The type only means anything because one constructor is the sole place that mints it. This is a no-solver pattern very close to option B's smart-constructor discipline — proof its construction-time core is viable without any prover.

Has no refinement types at all; the idiom is exactly Jet's status quo — a newtype wrapping a fallible constructor (NonZeroU32::new returns Option). The ecosystem reaching for newtype+constructor (and never getting compiler-proved arithmetic) shows option A is a coherent, shippable resting point, and that B is the natural, low-cost step beyond it.

decisions.bestCurrent: Liquid Haskell: Liquid Haskell proves rich predicates with SMT-backed refinements, but the model is expert-only.
decisions.recommendation: Extend `distinct` with `#Invariant(pred)` + pure-Rust Presburger/LIA prover (I6/I8-clean) — no new keyword, delivers D-OOBPROOF1=A (Option A). Construction-only (Option B) leaves D-OOBPROOF1=A blocked with no delivery path.

decisions.detail: Two-facet pass: beginners get clean source and sane local persistence; experts can deliberately share source-anchored visual intent for review and teaching.

decisions.title: Canvas multi-file edit authority
decisions.gist: Choose how Canvas applies cross-file edits and refactors.
decisions.story: Hank extracts a shared logging helper from an app package into `packages/logging`, updates `workspace.jet`, edits two `pkg.jet` files, and rewrites imports. He needs Canvas to show the exact touched files and prove the workspace still checks before anything lands.
decisions.detail: Two-facet pass: beginners get preview/proof before broad edits; experts get exact touched files, revisions, authority, and audit payload.

options.name: Previewed source transaction with proof (recommended)
options.detail: Canvas builds an explicit multi-file source transaction, previews the diff, checks touched revisions, formats overlays, runs front-end and package/workspace validation, then writes and reprojects. Authority and touched files are audited.

preview -> diff + touched files + diagnostics
apply -> fmt overlays -> sema/package check -> write all -> reproject
conflict -> no write

options.name: Direct gesture writes
options.detail: Canvas writes all affected files immediately after a drag/drop/refactor gesture. This feels fast but hides authority and makes broad edits too easy to miss.

drag package edge -> writes workspace.jet + pkg.jet immediately
# no required preview, weak audit

options.name: Patch export only
options.detail: Canvas never writes multi-file edits; it emits a patch for the user to apply manually. This is safe but breaks the promise that Canvas can manage the workspace.

POST /canvas/project/transaction -> returns diff only

decisions.title: Canvas visual editor — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: Which editing experience Canvas is built around — four genuinely different editors, one shared look.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — the dual-lens truth you liked, with flow's summoner as the everyday verb, guided's safety exactly where mistakes happen, and workbench's depth one toggle away. One mechanism per job (I8).
decisions.story: Maya opens Canvas to build her first Jet program; Dev, an Unreal veteran, opens it to rewire a 200-node graph. The question is not what Canvas looks like (one visual system, fixed) but what USING it is: does she browse a catalog, summon nodes by typing, edit code and graph as synced twins, or grow a program from type-checked offers? All four options render the full real feature set (typed pins, rails, node search, graph⇄source, inspector, debugger, replay, verbatim E0204). Browse all four side by side: file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#canvas (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid Canvas, modified as follows. Use a Workbench-style persistent project/file viewer for Canvas; the hybrid palette panel becomes the project and file viewer, not a command palette. Keep the rest of the UI hybrid: Code/Split/Graph views, source-backed graph truth, synced replay, and popup panes for palette/project, inspector, and debugger. Commands live in right-click, Ctrl+K, and drag-from-pin release context menus; drag-release menus show only compatible pins/nodes. Nodes need UE5-Blueprint-style polish: consistent shapes and colors communicate semantic role, pin labels are just variable/field names, and types appear on hover only. Variable/const getters render as compact pure capsule/bubble nodes, not full nodes. Simple variables can embed in fields like Scratch nested blocks for graph cleanliness. Visual tone should be streamlined graphite/gray with optional detail toggles.

options.name: Workbench — docked IDE
options.detail:
Core loop: browse the palette catalog, drag a node onto the graph, wire its pins, tune it in the docked inspector. Fixed resizable docks (menubar, palette+project+debugger left, graph center with rail gutter, inspector right) — nothing hides. The Unreal/Blender/VS Code model for people in the editor eight hours a day. Beginner: drag a labelled node from the palette. Expert: Ctrl+K search, tabs, docked debugger. Risk: densest option; most familiar, least novel.

│ palette      │  graph (rail gutter on left edge) │ inspector │
│  search      │   [entry]→[call]→[branch]         │  node     │

options.name: Flow — summon at the cursor
options.detail:
Core loop: type at the cursor to summon the node you're thinking of and keep flowing — never leave the canvas for a panel. Infinite canvas, zero fixed panels; ⌘K or double-click opens a type-filtered summoner AT the cursor; releasing a wire on empty space searches only compatible nodes; inspector pops beside the selection. tldraw/Figma chrome with Unreal's drag-from-pin search promoted to the primary verb. Beginner: double-click → type "print" → Enter (hint bar teaches it). Expert: the whole loop is keyboard, at the cursor. Risk: power hides behind keys/right-click — discoverability rests on the hint bar.

options.name: Dual lens — code ⇄ graph, synced
options.detail:
Core loop: read or write in whichever lens fits the thought — code editor or graph — and the other follows your cursor live. Two equal panes over the same source: click a line, its node lights; click a node, its line scrolls and highlights; a gutter breakpoint mirrors a red halo on the node; replay scrubs both at once. E0204 appears as one truth in both lenses (squiggle in code, red node in graph, verbatim card below). The Enso/Observable model. Beginner: type ordinary Jet, the graph draws itself — no new gesture. Expert: full-speed text editing with a free live map. Risk: sync must be instant — any lag breaks the promise; two panes cost width.

options.name: Guided — grow from typed offers
options.detail:
Core loop: pick a seed, then choose from only the type-compatible offers; the program grows correct-by-construction, one step at a time. A vertical spine of built steps; the value's type rides the connector; the offer tray lists only next steps whose input matches — you never drag a wire, and an invalid wire is unreachable. Diagnostics become refused offers: E0204 shows as a disabled offer with the verbatim why/fix at the exact moment the move would break. The Hazel/Scratch idea with the type system as the snap constraint. Beginner: the strongest story — the first node can't be wrong. Expert: type-to-filter, ↑↓+↵. Risk: linear spine suits growing a function, not reshaping a big graph — needs a hand-off to A/B/C.

options.name: Hybrid — dual-lens core, everything layered
options.detail:
Core loop: read or write in whichever lens fits, summon nodes at the cursor, and the other lens plus any docks you opt into follow — one program, one truth. Takes: dual-lens foundation (synced code⇄graph, one-truth E0204, shared replay) + flow's ⌘K/double-click summoner at the cursor as the primary authoring verb + guided's typed offers where they matter (dragged-pin summon pre-filtered and Hazel-ordered; refused offers teach E0204 at the moment of the mistake; a beginner empty-state seed spine that IS the real graph and graduates seamlessly) + workbench's docks as collapsible, off-by-default panels (palette, inspector, debugger), with a Code–Split–Graph control that collapses to pure editor or pure canvas. decisions.title: jetos Studio — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: Which experience Studio is built around — settings app, review-first changesets, ops board, or an editable source document.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — the document is the app, the rail finds things, the health strip watches the fleet, and nothing lands without the changeset review. Every edit path — widget, alert fix, rollback — funnels through one gate.
decisions.story: User wants to bump devhost's kernel and flip a theme option; later that week a bad generation fails to boot and he needs rollback fast. Four genuinely different apps answer those moments: find-and-flip settings, stage-review-apply changesets, a fleet health board, or config.jet itself rendered as a live document. All four share one visual system and the same truth — every GUI edit rewrites exactly one system.jet line and shows the diff (the real set-option transaction). Browse side by side: file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#studio (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
// config.jet (devhost fixture) — the source every archetype edits
boot.kernel: .CachyOS
boot.loader: .Limine
perf.scheduler: .ScxLavd
desktop.plasma.enable: true
theme.flavor: "catppuccin-mocha"
secrets.wifi: age("wifi.age")
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid Studio, but replace the projectional-document foundation with a normal clean dashboard + sidebar app. Landing page is a simple opsboard-style dashboard: hosts, health, services, generations, alerts, and monitoring status are easy to understand at a glance. Settings live in sidebar categories, with an extensible category/page registry so future Studio modules can add sections without redesign. Changeset is a first-class sidebar page/category for comparing diffs, impact, and generation changes. Settings and monitoring belong in appropriate sidebar categories. Keep the hybrid one-apply-path rule: edits from settings, alerts, rollback, or changeset review stage into the same changeset/apply gate. Visual style follows the cleaner Settings option; information structure follows Ops board where useful. Do not build the projectional config document as the primary UI right now.

options.name: Settings — find it, flip it, apply
options.detail:
Core loop: pick a category, flip one option's control, confirm the single source line it writes, apply. Apple-System-Settings navigator whose sidebar groups map 1:1 to config.jet namespaces; the signature is the pending source tray — a docked bar accumulating the exact +/- lines and impact chips as you toggle, so nothing touches the machine unseen. Kernel change: Boot & kernel → dropdown (tagged rebuild+reboot). Rollback: Generations category → "Roll back to N". The beginner tier: lowest ceremony for changing one thing. Risk: deep tree — search carries it; grouping is editorial, a setting can be "somewhere unexpected."

options.name: Changeset — review before anything lands
options.detail:
Core loop: stage edits from anywhere into one changeset whose primary screen is the diff review plus impact, then apply the whole reviewed set as one build. The GitHub-PR/terraform-plan model: unified source diff with per-hunk include/exclude, beside a plain-language "What this changes" summary and an impact ledger (services restarted, packages rebuilt, reboot needed, generation N+1). Build & switch = merge. Rollback stages the inverse as a reviewable changeset. The safety tier: never surprised by an apply. Risk: heavier for a one-toggle change; authoring via option-key form assumes some fluency (autocomplete helps).

options.name: Ops board — health first, edit on drill-in
options.detail:
Core loop: watch the fleet health board; when a tile goes red, drill into it, fix or roll back from the drawer, watch it go green. Landing screen is KPIs, alerts, per-host generation ribbons (colored run history), and a service grid — the Proxmox/Tailscale/PagerDuty model. Config editing is a drawer opened FROM a red thing; the mock's centerpiece is a kernel panic on gen 42 with auto-fallback to 41 and one-click clean rollback, the diagnosis in what/why/fix voice. Hosts come from workspace.jet. The fleet tier: operate constantly, edit rarely. Risk: drawer editing is intentionally shallow — deep edits should deep-link into A or D.

options.name: Projectional — the file is the app
options.detail:
Core loop: read the config AS the document; edit each value through an inline control so you change system.jet without typing syntax. config.jet rendered line-numbered and syntax-highlighted, but every option value is a live widget in place — toggle, dropdown, stepper, chip list, sealed secret. A Text toggle reveals the exact source the projection produces (one artifact, two surfaces); a git-style gutter marks changed lines; the generation picker turns the document into a time machine ("Restore these values" stages a rollback). The JetBrains-MPS/Dark model — the expert tier, I8-clean (same set-option mechanism, different entrypoint). Risk: real implementation must round-trip through the formatter; densest for beginners.

options.name: Hybrid — projectional doc, health strip, one apply path
options.detail:
Core loop: land on the fleet health strip; read config.jet as a live document the category rail navigates; every widget edit stages into one changeset; open the tray to review the diff + impact, then build — a red alert and a past generation both funnel back through that same changeset. Takes: projectional foundation (inline widgets, git-gutter, Text mirror, generation time-machine) + settings' rail as navigation INTO the document (no separate detail pane — the doc is the detail) + changeset as the only apply path (persistent tray → review sheet: plain summary, impact ledger, per-hunk diff, Build only / Build & switch; rollback stages the inverse) + opsboard's landing strip (hosts, generation ribbons, alerts; a red alert deep-links to the offending option with what/why/fix). Left out: settings' per-change apply, changeset's key/value form, opsboard's shadow drawer editor — one artifact, one gate (I8).

decisions.title: Core process spawning and pipeline surface
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical subprocess API beyond one-shot process.run.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A gives beginners the safe argv-only one-shot they already have, and gives experts a typed ProcessSpec/Child handle for streaming, timeouts, env/cwd, signals, pipelines, and output limits. One semantic mechanism: process.run is sugar over ProcessSpec.run.
decisions.story: Nora writes a Jet build tool. It must run a compiler, stream logs live, kill it after 30 seconds, pass a clean environment, pipe generated code into a formatter, and preserve the child's exact exit status. A capture-everything process.run either hangs, hides progress, or forces her into shell strings.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: a fluent builder can become opaque magic; raw spawn knobs can become a shell footgun. Patch: argv lists only by default, no shell interpolation helper in Core, every knob is a typed field on ProcessSpec, and shell execution remains an explicit expert escape if ever approved separately.

options.name: ProcessSpec + Child handles (recommended)
options.detail: Keep process.run(argv) as beginner sugar. Add process.cmd(argv) -> ProcessSpec with cwd/env/stdin/stdout/stderr/timeout/output_limit methods, spawn() -> Child, wait()/kill()/terminate()/interrupt(), typed ExitStatus, streaming readers/writers, and process.pipeline([...]) for argv-only pipelines without a shell.
options.code:
use core.process as process
use core.time as time

spec :: process.cmd(["cargo", "test"])
    .cwd("crates/app")
    .env_clear()
    .env("RUST_BACKTRACE", "1")
    .stdout(.Stream)
    .stderr(.Inherit)
    .timeout(time.seconds(30))

child :: spec.spawn()?
loop line in child.stdout.lines() { print(line) }
status :: child.wait()?
if !status.success { process.exit(status.code ?? 1) }

pipe :: process.pipeline([
    process.cmd(["cat", "input.txt"]),
    process.cmd(["grep", "error"]),
])?

options.name: Many direct module functions
options.detail: Add process.run_stream, run_timeout, run_env, pipeline, kill, etc. Discoverable in autocomplete, but the surface becomes a pile of near-duplicates and option combinations explode.
options.code:
process.run_timeout(["cargo", "test"], time.seconds(30))?
process.run_env(["env"], ["A=1"])?
process.pipeline([["cat", "x"], ["grep", "y"]])?

options.name: Shell string convenience
options.detail: Expose process.shell("cargo test 2>&1 | tee log") as the powerful path. Familiar for experts, but it makes injection and quoting footguns the blessed default unless gated separately.
options.code: process.shell("cd crates/app && cargo test 2>&1 | tee log")?

options.name: Keep one-shot run only
options.detail: Document that serious process orchestration should use external tools. This keeps Jet worse than Python subprocess, Go os/exec, and Rust std::process for build tools and agent operations.
options.code:
r :: process.run(["cargo", "test"])?
print(r.output)

comparisons.note: subprocess.run/Popen is flexible but easy to misuse with shell=True and text/bytes confusion. Jet can keep argv-only defaults and typed streams.
exec.Command gives explicit argv/cwd/env/stdout fields; pipelines require manual pipe wiring. Jet can wrap that pattern in a typed ProcessSpec and pipeline helper.
std::process::Command is the right safety shape, but verbose for common streaming and timeout cases. Jet can keep the shape and improve ergonomics.

decisions.title: jet dev server — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: Where the dev server's richness lives: in the browser, in the terminal, or mirrored identically in both.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — parity keeps both surfaces honest for free (one poll, one vocabulary), and each side gets its native depth on demand: the full overlay in the browser, the request log in the terminal. No starved surface, no second source of truth.
decisions.story: Kai runs `jet dev app.jet --target=web` with the browser on one monitor and the terminal on the other. On a broken save the last good build keeps serving — but where does he learn what broke, and how much does each surface tell him? Three splits of the same information: rich browser + silent terminal, rich terminal + clean browser, or strict parity where both always show the same status and the same verbatim E0102 frame. Browse: file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#devserver (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev app.jet --target=web
serving http://localhost:8080 — watching app.jet …
# save a typo → E0102. Last good build keeps serving;
# the archetype decides where the error reaches Kai.
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid dev server, with the nicely formatted terminal dashboard header pinned. The header remains visible while request logs, rebuild output, verbose detail, and errors scroll below. Keep mirrored browser status/overlay and terminal depth, but the pinned dashboard header is required as the terminal anchor.

options.name: Quiet terminal, rich browser
options.detail:
Core loop: live in the browser; the terminal is a three-line daemon. Terminal prints URL, watch target, last rebuild — then goes silent. Everything rich is in the page: vite-class full error overlay with the verbatim diagnostic, dim-while-rebuilding, a rebuild toast with timing, reconnect states. Matches how web developers actually work — eyes on the rendered page. Risk: with no tab open an error is invisible until you look (the terminal still prints the diagnostic as fallback).
file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/devserver/quiet.html
options.code:
terminal (steady state)          browser (on error)
 ┌───────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────────────────┐
 │ jet dev  serving      │   │ localhost:8080                 │
 │   :8080               │   │ ┌ Build failed ────── app.jet ┐│
 │   watching app.jet    │   │ │ Error [E0102]: nothing named ││
 │ ✓ rebuilt 0.4s 14:22  │   │ │  `nonexistent_function_xyz`… ││
 └───────────────────────┘   │ │  8 | nonexistent_function()  ││
                             │ │    | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^  ││
  toast: ● rebuilt in 0.4s   │ │ Why / Fix … · Esc dismiss    ││
                             │ └──────────────────────────────┘│
                             └────────────────────────────────┘

options.name: Terminal dashboard, clean browser
options.detail:
Core loop: the terminal is the primary view — a pinned header (status dot, port, client count, last build time) over a scrolling request/rebuild log with timings; the browser shows only a thin error banner pointing back. Best for terminal-centric developers and multi-client debugging: every request and rebuild visible with timing, client count comes free from the 400ms pollers. Risk: pinned header needs cursor-home redraw (std ANSI) and degrades to a plain status line off-TTY; the browser is deliberately information-poor.
file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/devserver/dashboard.html
options.code:
┌ jet dev ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ ● ready   localhost:8080   2 clients   last build 0.4s│
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  14:22:03  GET  /            200  2ms
  14:22:07  save app.jet  →  rebuilt 0.4s
  14:23:01  save app.jet  →  error E0102
  Error [E0102]: nothing named `nonexistent_function_xyz` …
    8 | nonexistent_function_xyz()
      | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

 browser: ● Build failed · E0102 — details in the terminal

options.name: Paired — same truth on both sides
options.detail:
Core loop: glance at the terminal or the browser corner — same status, same error. A one-line terminal status and a browser corner strip mirror each other exactly (building / ok / error / n clients), both driven by the same version poll; on error both expand the identical verbatim diagnostic frame (once in ANSI, once in CSS, same snapshot text). No "which surface is authoritative" question, lowest cognitive overhead. Risk: parity must be genuinely lockstep or it's a lie; the frame is the only detail level — no request log.
file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/devserver/paired.html

options.name: Hybrid — mirrored status with on-demand depth
options.detail:
Core loop: a one-line terminal status and a browser corner strip mirror the same poll; on error the browser strip expands to the full overlay and the terminal can expand to a request log, but the parity line is always the shared truth. Takes: paired's contract (identical state from one poll — they cannot drift) + quiet's full vite-class overlay as the strip's expanded state (room, not a second truth) + dashboard's request/rebuild log behind v/--verbose, printed under the same parity header. Left out: any deliberately starved surface — no mute-daemon terminal, no info-poor browser banner; depth is additive on both sides of one status mechanism (I8).
file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/devserver/hybrid.html
options.code:
terminal (parity line)            browser (strip = collapsed overlay)

                                   │  (app)     ● ready · 2 cl  │
                                   └────────────────────────────┘
 on error — strip EXPANDS to the full overlay:

 ┌ E0102 ─────────────────────┐    │  (app, dimmed)             │
 │ Error [E0102]: nothing      │    │ ┌ Build failed ── app.jet ┐│
 │   named `nonexistent_...`   │    │ │ Error [E0102]: nothing  ││
 │  8 | nonexistent_function() │    │ │  8 | nonexistent_fn()   ││
 │ Why / Fix …                 │    │ │ Why / Fix …             ││
 └─────────────────────────────┘    │ └─────────────────────────┘│

 NO_COLOR: dot → [error]; overlay falls back to terminal diag.

comparisons.note: A's overlay contract: full-bleed error card over the app, code frame, Esc dismiss, auto-clears on the next clean build.
comparisons.code: [vite] Internal server error → overlay with file:line + frame

comparisons.note: B's request log with method/path/status/timing as the terminal's primary content.

decisions.comment: Hybrid devserver, with nicely formatted pinned dashboard header kept as required terminal anchor.

decisions.title: Canvas node states: how a disabled node and a debug-only node are spelled in source
decisions.gist: What Jet source looks like when a Canvas node is switched off temporarily, and how a node can be marked to exist only in debug builds.
decisions.explainer: One attribute family gives both Blueprint states with real syntax that survives fmt/refactors and stays type-checked (a comment marker silently rots when the code around it is renamed); #DebugOnly hides the comptime plumbing beginners should never need to see, while comptime if build.profile remains available to experts if C's value is also ratified later.
decisions.story: Priya is wiring a pricing function in Canvas. A logging call keeps cluttering her test output, so she wants to switch that node off for a while without deleting it — same as unplugging a cable, not cutting it. Separately, she has a sanity-check node that should run in dev builds but must never ship in the release binary. Canvas is source-backed: both states must be spelled in the .jet file somehow, and today Jet has no spelling for either (only build.os exists as a comptime value, no debug/release distinction).

options.name: Comment marker for off, no debug-only yet
options.detail: Disabled node = the statement commented out with a marker comment Canvas recognizes and can re-enable. Zero new language surface; code is genuinely inert because it is a comment. Debug-only nodes wait for a separate build-profile decision.

options.name: #Off attribute statement gate
options.detail: A real attribute the compiler parses and skips (still type-checked, like Rust's #[cfg] siblings or C#'s [Conditional]). Survives formatting and refactors as real syntax; Canvas toggles it. Debug-only becomes #Off("release") or a sibling attribute later.

options.name: build.profile comptime value + comptime if (debug-only), comment marker (off)
options.detail: Adds build.profile (.Debug | .Release) beside build.os; debug-only nodes project as a comptime if rail Canvas renders as a badge, folded at compile time exactly like build.os dispatch. Temporary off stays the A-style comment marker since 'off' is a workspace state, not a program state.

options.name: Both as attributes: #Off and #DebugOnly
options.detail: One attribute family for node states: #Off (skipped every build, still type-checked) and #DebugOnly (compiled only when the build profile is debug; requires the same build-profile machinery as C under the hood but the user never sees comptime if).

comparisons.note: Nodes have a Disabled state (greyed, skipped) and a Development Only mode (hazard-striped, compiled out of shipping builds) — the two states Priya expects.
comparisons.code: Right-click node -> Disable Node / Development Only

comparisons.note: cfg attributes gate code by build profile; debug_assert! is the idiomatic debug-only check that vanishes in release.
[Conditional("DEBUG")] methods compile to nothing in release while the call sites stay type-checked.
comparisons.code:
[Conditional("DEBUG")]
static void AssertBalanced(Cart c, decimal t) { ... }

Costs an npm package.json + lockfile in a tests/ workspace and pinning playwright's browser expectations to the Nix chromium; richer API (auto-wait, tracing) than a hand-rolled driver.

WebSocket session → browsingContext.navigate → input.performActions

decisions.title: jetos is a from-scratch standalone OS; NixOS module system is not a backend
decisions.gist: jetos must be its own Linux system — jet, jetpack, and the hangar all the way down — functionally equivalent to NixOS. Building it by generating a NixOS configuration under the hood produces a reskinned NixOS and is forbidden.
decisions.story: The first working graphical jetos VM was realized by compiling the jetos option tree into a generated NixOS flake. It booted GNOME, but the guest was visibly NixOS: NixOS wallpaper, release codename "Yarara", NixOS module semantics throughout. The owner rejected this outright: adapters may leverage the nixpkgs package ecosystem, but the operating system itself — module/option system, generations, activation, /etc rendering, service units, boot, desktop glue, identity — must be jetos-native.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os vm run devhost --disk ./devhost.qcow2
boots a system whose settings panel reads "jetos" because it IS jetos: hangar store, jetos-generated systemd units, jetos activation — with firefox/steam/plasma fetched from nixpkgs through the jetpack adapter.

options.label: Native jetos system, nixpkgs as package adapter only
options.detail: jetos owns every OS-assembly concern natively; nixpkgs is reached through jetpack providers purely to obtain packages. Functional equivalence to NixOS is proven by behavior, not by sharing its implementation.

options.label: Hidden NixOS realizer (rejected)
options.detail: Compile jetos config to a generated NixOS system, rebrand the output. Fast to ship, but the product is a NixOS fork/reskin.

decisions.comment: Decreed live 2026-07-09: no forked/reskinned NixOS; standalone jetos with nixpkgs adapters.

decisions.title: On-disk package store inside a jetos system: hangar-native, staged
decisions.gist: The jetpack hangar is THE store of a jetos system — its layout, GC, and generation roots. Stage 1 keeps nixpkgs-built closures under a hangar-managed compatibility root so unmodified binaries run; a later stage re-roots/rebuilds packages natively.
decisions.story: Nixpkgs binaries hardcode /nix/store paths internally (ELF interpreters, dlopen paths, wrappers). Running them unmodified requires that path shape to exist on disk. Rather than adopting /nix/store as jetos's permanent format, the hangar owns the store from day one and treats the nix-shaped subtree as the adapter's compatibility root, with native re-rooting as the planned end state.
decisions.inWild:
/hangar/…            ← jetos store: metadata, GC roots, generations
/hangar/compat/nix/store/…   ← stage-1 root for unmodified nixpkgs closures
Later: packages rebuilt against hangar paths; compat root shrinks to nothing.

options.label: Hangar-native, staged compat root
options.detail: Hangar owns everything; nix-shaped compat subtree is an adapter detail with a planned exit.

options.label: Keep /nix/store layout permanently
options.detail: Simplest compatibility, least ownership of the format.

options.label: Hangar-native from day one
options.detail: Rewrite/rebuild every package before anything ships; purest but gates all system work.

decisions.comment: Chosen via session ballot 2026-07-09.

decisions.title: No `nix` binary anywhere in the jetos product path — this epoch builds jetpack's own nixpkgs pipeline
decisions.gist: jetos and jetpack must not shell out to the nix binary. Leveraging the nixpkgs ecosystem requires jetpack to evaluate, fetch, and build nixpkgs packages itself: a Nix-language evaluator (or equivalent artifact protocol), derivation hashing, the binary-cache substituter protocol, and a sandboxed builder — in scope for this epoch, not deferred.
decisions.story: Today the jetpack nix provider runs `nix build nixpkgs#pkg`. That makes the nix binary a load-bearing dependency of every jetos system build. The owner chose the strongest form of independence: the adapter speaks nixpkgs' formats (Nix language, drv hashing, NAR/narinfo caches) through jetpack's own implementation, so no Nix-project executable is required to build or run a jetos system.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack fetch nixpkgs#firefox
  evaluates nixpkgs with jetpack's evaluator, resolves the store hash,
  substitutes the NAR from cache.nixos.org into the hangar compat root —
  no /run/current-system/sw/bin/nix involved.

options.label: Staged: nix CLI now, native later
options.detail: Ship on the CLI, replace it on a scoped later card.

options.label: nix CLI permanently acceptable
options.detail: Never build an evaluator.

options.label: No nix binary at all this epoch
options.detail: The epoch includes jetpack's own evaluation/fetch/build pipeline before jetos ships.

decisions.title: Epoch-7 exit bar: NixOS-class architecture natively + prioritized breadth
decisions.gist: The epoch exits when jetos natively delivers the full NixOS capability architecture (typed module/option system, generations, atomic activation, rollback, fully declarative system) PLUS: a terminal baseline, a graphical baseline, one-line desktop swaps (GNOME/KDE/Hyprland/niri; wayland/x11), and the owner's entire ~/nixos config running natively. Module breadth beyond that grows by demand through a defined process.
decisions.story: NixOS has on the order of 20k options; literal total parity is a multi-year tail. Functional equivalence is an architecture property plus enough module breadth to cover real systems. Nothing is baked into jetos itself: the entire system is driven by the user's jet config files — defaults may exist (terminal and graphical baselines), but composition is wholly the user's, written by hand or through jetos Studio.

decisions.title: Derive output: emit Jet source via $ splice, re-parsed and sema-checked?
decisions.gist: User-authored derives need a way to emit code. D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratifies that output must re-enter lexer/parser/sema (never bypass it). This decision fixes the surface: the `$` splice inside `comptime { }` is the output mechanism. Opens only if D-USERDERIVE1 passes.
decisions.explainer: D-CTCODEGEN1 forbids derives from emitting Rust directly or manipulating the AST in-place — all output must be Jet source that re-enters the front end. The `$` splice already exists for comptime value injection. The question is whether derive output is the same `$` splice mechanism (extended to emit function/impl blocks) or a separate API (typed AST builder). A typed AST builder is a second mechanism for emitting code — I8 violation. The `$` splice path means all derive errors appear in Jet source terms, not in opaque AST operations (I2/I3 compliant). The main risk is that splicing multi-line impl blocks requires the splice to carry statement-level fragments, not just expressions — a small extension to the existing mechanic.
decisions.story: My derive_Serialize function builds up a String of Jet source for the encode/decode methods, then splices it in with `${ ... }`. The parser re-reads it; sema checks the types; if I made a mistake, the error points at the generated Jet, not at rustc output.

options.name: $ splice emits Jet source fragments, re-parsed and sema-checked
options.detail: Extend the existing `$` splice to carry statement- and item-level Jet source (not just expressions). The emitted text re-enters the lexer and parser exactly as user-written Jet would. Sema sees the expanded code; errors appear in Jet source terms. One mechanism for comptime output; I8 satisfied; I2/I3 satisfied.

options.name: Typed AST builder API
options.detail: Derives call a builder API (`ImplBlock.new()`, `.add_method()`, etc.) that constructs a typed AST node directly. No string parsing; type-safe at the builder call sites. A second mechanism for emitting code alongside the `$` splice — I8 tension. Builder API surface must be designed, stabilized, and versioned separately.

options.name: Defer derive output mechanism
options.detail: Approve D-USERDERIVE1 and D-METAREFLECT1 but leave the output mechanism open. Reflection ships; derives cannot emit code yet. Partial; blocks the actual derive use cases; not a useful intermediate state.

comparisons.note: Rust proc-macros receive and emit `TokenStream` — effectively source text in token form, re-parsed by the compiler. The `quote!` macro is the ergonomic surface. Jet's `$` splice is the same concept with Jet syntax.
Zig comptime functions return types directly — a typed approach closer to option B. No string emission; the comptime function is the mechanism. Works because Zig's type system is the API surface.

decisions.comment: Reconciled 2026-06-27 from docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md and decision-ballots.md: derive Trait for T + Jet source-fragment re-entry via $ splice.

decisions.title: Web backend TIR boundary
decisions.gist: Whether browser builds must use the same executable TIR as every other target.
decisions.story: Mara ports a Jet UI from native dev mode to the browser. A branch works in one target and not the other because the web emitter read older AST shapes instead of the checked TIR. That breaks the promise that rustc and target backends never become alternate semantic judges.

options.name: TIR-only web execution
options.detail: All executable web bodies lower through sema/TIR first. Unsupported web features produce Jet diagnostics before emission. This keeps one semantic pipeline and one source of truth across dev, JIT, AOT, and web.
options.code:
$ jet build --target web app.jet
Error [E-WEB001]: this effect is not available in the browser target
Fix: move file IO behind a server boundary or choose a native target.

options.name: Explicit web carve-out
options.detail: Allow the web backend to keep a separate AST emitter for a documented subset. The docs must say web is a distinct semantic path with its own conformance suite. This is a real exception to R7/R12.

options.name: Freeze web target until TIR-ready
options.detail: Stop growing the web backend until all executable emission can come from TIR. This avoids split semantics, but browser examples remain frozen while the backend catches up.
options.code:
