For card #451, each root names either one regular `.jet` file or a directory, and must canonicalize beneath `<project>/examples` or `<project>/tests/ui`; `..`, absolute escape, and symlink escape fail. Directory discovery recursively sorts regular `.jet` files by project-relative byte path; a file root discovers only that file. Each discovered file is an entry compilation unit; its transitive Jet imports join that unit. The same physical file imported by several entries is indexed and edited once. Imports outside editable roots may be read for parsing, name resolution, and semantic identity but never edited; a rule selecting one fails with its path. Non-Jet files are ignored except the exact paired `tests/ui/<name>.stderr` of a touched UI fixture and declared snapshot inputs. Every rule resolves against the currently staged tree after prior rules. Within each compilation unit, every bare identifier in a match template resolves through semindex at the candidate node; that resolved definition anchor, not spelling, controls the match. Every non-capture identifier introduced by a replacement template must resolve uniquely in that same staged compilation unit before an edit is accepted. A rename destination is checked in every affected definition/reference scope and fails on collision or changed binding. A semantic symbol anchor is `(canonical definition module path, symbol kind, current definition span)`; references bind to that anchor through semindex. Independent same-spelled definitions remain independent anchors; selectors either match all and assert the total or narrow with `defined_in`. If a match source or destination resolves to zero or multiple definitions in any unit, the rule fails with unit path and candidates. Rules run in listed order. Within one rule, overlapping/nested edits fail; overlap across rules is intentional sequencing because rule N sees reindexed output from rule N-1. Duplicate ids, unknown fields, ambiguous anchors, unused captures, invalid replacement nodes, and zero matches unless `allow_zero: true` fail. Validation is transactional data, not a code-only check: a `clean` root must finish with zero lexer/parser/sema diagnostics; every touched `fixture` `.jet` must render a complete stderr snapshot. Without `snapshot_after`, generated stderr must equal the existing paired `.stderr` byte-for-byte. With `snapshot_after`, each value is a project-relative path resolved beneath the canonical project; every component must be non-symlink and the final input must be a regular file. Absolute paths, `..`, project escape, symlink, directory, and aliasing the destination `.stderr` fail. That file contains the complete replacement bytes; generated stderr must equal it byte-for-byte, and the paired `.stderr` becomes a planned edit shown in dry-run and committed/undone with source. Dry-run and apply take the exclusive codemod lock before discovery and hold it through discovery, indexing, every staged rule, validation, diagnostic rendering, final hash verification, and output/commit. The lock coordinates codemod processes only; ordinary editors need not honor it. Therefore the engine fingerprints every discovered source, read-only import, existing `.stderr`, and `snapshot_after` input on first read, rehashes all of them after rendering, and refuses with exact drift paths before printing a ready plan or writing anything if any changed. Apply rechecks every destination immediately before its rename and refuses observed drift. This does not close the check-to-rename race with a noncooperating editor: only codemod peers honor the lock, so an editor can still write after the check and be overwritten by the rename. Apply prints that limitation before confirmation; `--yes` accepts it. It writes same-directory temp files, fsyncs file contents, writes+fsyncs a journal containing transaction id, state, every before/after hash, complete before bytes, temp path, and destination, then fsyncs parent directories. Commit uses sequential same-filesystem renames; it is recoverable, not falsely advertised as globally atomic or safe from noncooperating concurrent writers. After each rename it advances and fsyncs journal state. On write/rename/fsync failure, rollback restores a destination only when its current hash equals the transaction's recorded after-hash; any other hash may be an unseen concurrent write, so recovery preserves that destination and the journal, reports the conflict, and refuses further codemod work. A crash leaves the journal. Before any later dry-run/apply/undo, the engine locks and recovers: hashes matching all after states complete the log; mixed/before states attempt the same conditional rollback, restoring only destinations still at recorded transaction hashes. Ambiguous drift or failed recovery preserves the journal, changes nothing further, prints exact paths/hashes, and refuses all codemod work until recovery can succeed. Only successful completion writes+fsyncs the schema-2 replay log and removes+fsyncs the journal. Undo first locks and verifies every current after-hash, then uses the identical temp/journal/fsync/recovery protocol to restore byte-exact before content, including `.stderr`; any mismatch causes zero writes. Dry-run writes no source, snapshot, log, temp, or new journal; after the final stable-snapshot rehash it prints path-ordered rule counts, validation, and unified source+snapshot diffs while still holding the lock.
decisions.story: Maya must update a helper across runnable examples and diagnostic fixtures. One rule renames a semantic function; another changes a call shape while preserving its argument. She needs one reviewed plan where code and every affected UI snapshot move together. Dev needs deterministic discovery, stable symbol identity, exact match counts, crash recovery, and byte-exact undo before approving the apply.

options.name: Typed AST templates
options.detail: Rules are `symbol_rename` or `ast_rewrite`. An AST rule declares `node` as `expr`, `stmt`, `item`, or `type`; `match` and `replace` are current Jet source parsed in that node class. `$name` captures exactly one subtree. `$args...` captures an ordered zero-or-more sequence only where that node grammar has a list. A repeated scalar capture requires structural equality. Bare identifiers, labels, literals, operators, and syntax match exactly after semantic name resolution; comments and layout do not participate. Replacement uses only declared captures, preserves captured bytes when safe, and otherwise formats the replacement node with `jet fmt`; variadic captures splice only into the same list kind. Every root declares `clean` or `fixture`. `clean` requires zero lexer/parser/sema diagnostics after every rule. `fixture` requires the generated final diagnostic output to equal the paired `.stderr` byte-for-byte. If expected output intentionally changes, `snapshot_after` maps the `.jet` path to a repository file containing the complete new `.stderr`; dry-run compares generated bytes to it and shows the paired `.stderr` diff, while apply writes those exact verified bytes in the same transaction. A code-only apply is impossible. Recommended: Jet-shaped patterns are readable to beginners; node classes, semantic anchors, captures, exact counts, and snapshots give experts precise control without regex.

options.name: Finite semantic operations
options.detail: Rules choose a closed registry: `symbol_rename`, `call_rename`, `call_add_named_arg`, `import_move`, or `marker_replace`. `symbol_rename` takes a semantic selector and identifier. `call_rename` changes only calls resolved to the selected function. `call_add_named_arg` parses `value` as one Jet expression, rejects an existing or positionally conflicting label, and inserts through the AST argument list. `import_move` takes exact resolved `from` and `to` module paths and preserves the local alias. `marker_replace` takes exact current PascalCase marker names, changes the marker AST node only, and rejects different argument arity; it does not text-replace comments or strings. No interpolation exists in B. Unknown operations/fields fail. Roots, anchors, ordering, exact `matches`, validation, full snapshot pairing, recoverable transaction, log, and undo are identical to the shared law. This is easiest to discover and audit, but a new migration shape requires a future ratified registry entry.

options.name: Semantic selectors and typed edits
options.detail: Each rule has `select` plus `edit`. Selectors allow only `node`, `symbol_kind`, `resolved_name`, `defined_in`, `called_from`, and exact `argument_count`; globs are project-relative and may narrow but never widen roots. Edits are `rename_symbol`, `replace_callee`, `insert_named_arg`, or `replace_node`. `replace_node.source` is parsed as the selected node class. It may interpolate `$argument[N]`, `$receiver`, or `$node`; indices are zero-based, each placeholder expands to that captured AST subtree, and no other `$` form exists. A missing/out-of-range placeholder, wrong node class, label collision, or marker/value parse error fails. Marker edits use `node: "marker"`, exact PascalCase `resolved_name`, and a complete replacement marker source such as `#New(arg)`; arguments are never implicitly copied. Roots, anchors, ordering, exact counts, validation, full snapshot pairing, journal, log, and undo follow the shared law. This gives experts strongest targeting, but simple work requires learning selector/edit vocabulary.

comparisons.note: Structural templates with holes stay readable across formatting. Option A adds Jet node classes and semantic resolution.
Semantic matchers separate identity from edits. Option C adopts that precision with a deliberately small selector set.
Compiler facts produce checked edits and conflicts stop the run. Jet adds ordered multi-rule objects, paired diagnostic snapshots, and recoverable replay logs.

decisions.title: Generic-module value parameter domain and evaluation
decisions.gist: Choose which compile-time values may specialize a generic module and where those values may be used.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified floor. D-GENMOD1=A approves modules parameterized by types and values. D-GENMOD2=A fixes one `<...>` list, annotation-kind classification, and mirrored instantiation such as `module StringCache32 = Lru<String, 32>`. It supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype parentheses. S26 otherwise says comptime is value-only and never parameterizes/selects types; every option below states whether generic-module parameters create a narrow exception. No option adds a keyword or second generic syntax. `D-GENMOD-IDENTITY1` and `D-GENMOD-BODY1` are proposed companion ballot IDs only: neither is live, queued, nor ratified. The ballots may be presented and ratified in any order, but their implementation dependencies are directional. VALUE1 alone owns value domain, evaluation, substitution/use positions, and canonical value bytes. IDENTITY1 may define its structural choice independently but cannot consume/finalize value-argument identity until VALUE1 ratifies. BODY1 may define declaration/capture law independently, but every selected body feature that reads a value parameter waits for VALUE1. Cross-alias semantic/code/cache dedup waits for IDENTITY1. Nominal struct/enum member emission waits for BODY1 only when its selected option admits those declarations. Type-only/function-only generic-module work need not wait on irrelevant companion outcomes.

Shared resolution law. Parser stores each declaration annotation and alias argument as unresolved syntax with exact spans; casing never determines kind. A bare parameter such as `T` is a type parameter. For `name: Annotation`, sema resolves Annotation in the declaration's lexical scope: a trait/bound makes a type parameter, while an allowed concrete value type makes a value parameter. Unknown, ambiguous, or disallowed annotations reject at the annotation. Once target template resolves, each alias argument is parsed/contextualized by its parameter slot: type slots require a type; value slots accept one ordinary expression delimited by the top-level comma or closing `>`, with nested calls/operators/collections using normal expression grammar. Thus `Ring<Packet, 32 + 32, true>` is unambiguous without uppercase/lowercase guessing. Parameter names still obey D-CASING1 style diagnostics, but spelling never changes semantics. No defaults, named arguments, inference, packs, implicit conversions, or module-valued parameters are introduced.

Option A exact domain. Value parameter annotations are Bool, Int, Char, String, or a named fieldless enum. Int is Jet's checked i64; overflow is a compile-time error. Char is one Unicode scalar. String is its exact UTF-8 scalar sequence; no NFC/case/path normalization occurs. A fieldless enum value includes its resolved nominal type and variant. Float is forbidden because NaN payloads and signed zero defeat obvious equality; lists/maps/structs/payload enums/options/results/functions/types/modules/handles/raw pointers/shared state are forbidden because they introduce mutability, ownership, allocation graphs, or open identity rules. Future additions require another decision.

Option A expression/effect law. An argument must type-check as its annotation and evaluate completely through the existing fuel-limited comptime interpreter before generic-module expansion. Allowed expressions are literals; enum cases; arithmetic, comparison, Boolean, string, and `if` expressions; references to earlier immutable `const`/`comptime` bindings; and calls whose entire reached graph is accepted by Tier-0 pure comptime law. Runtime bindings, ambient state, mutation, task/process/network/time/random access, `#Impure`, Tier-1/Tier-2 effects, `find`, `fetch`, `embed_file`, `embed_bytes`, reflection, panic, fuel exhaustion, division by zero, overflow, and a non-value result reject. Arguments cannot reference the template's parameters, sibling arguments, or declarations inside the uninstantiated template. Evaluation order is source order for diagnostics only; values have no side effects. Existing comptime failures keep their existing exact diagnostic codes; generic-slot type/kind failures use the codes below.

Option A binding/use law and exact amendments. After all arguments validate, sema clones the template and binds each evaluated result as an immutable comptime constant before checking any cloned item. It may appear wherever an ordinary constant of that type is already legal in function bodies, const initializers, array/index/range expressions, `comptime if`, marker value arguments, and nested declarations later admitted by BODY1. It cannot set enum discriminants: Jet has no ratified user-facing enum-discriminant law. It cannot construct an identifier, module/import path, field name, marker name, trait name, type argument, overload set, or dispatch target. Option A and C atomically amend both S26 and S76/D-FIXARR1: today `[T#N]` has a compile-time length but no general named-value const-generic surface; inside a generic-module specialization only, `[T#capacity]` becomes legal when capacity is an Int value parameter, evaluates before body checking, and must satisfy every existing fixed-list range/layout/overflow rule. This is a new narrow named-value use of the S76 spelling, not merely use of an already-open slot. No other type position accepts a value expression; no general const generics, comptime-created types, or type-returning computation becomes legal. Proposed BODY1 decides which declaration kinds may contain these substitutions; any BODY1-selected value-using feature activates only after VALUE1, while nominal identity/dedup separately waits for IDENTITY1 where relevant.

Option A normalization/equality and identity contribution. Evaluation produces one typed GenModuleValue. Bool canonical bytes are domain byte 0x01 plus 0x00/0x01. Int is domain 0x02 plus its signed i64 two's-complement eight-byte big-endian form. Char is domain 0x03 plus its Unicode scalar as four-byte big-endian u32. String is domain 0x04 plus u64-BE UTF-8 byte length and exact UTF-8 bytes. Enum is domain 0x05 plus u64-length-framed resolved package/module/type identity and u64-length-framed variant name. Every field is length-framed where variable; concatenation is ordered by declared parameter position. Two value arguments are equal exactly when their resolved annotation type and Jet value are equal; equal values have identical canonical bytes, unequal values do not. Constant spelling, source path/span, binding name, expression tree, and evaluation route are absent. These bytes are the sole value-argument contribution. Proposed, not-live IDENTITY1 may be decided in any order but may consume/finalize these bytes only after VALUE1 ratifies; this ballot does not decide applicative versus generative module/type identity.

Diagnostics/I4. E0853 remains `generic module argument <N> for <Template> has type <got>, but value parameter <name> needs <want>`; Why says the resolved slot is a value parameter and no implicit conversion occurs; Fix supplies an expression of <want> or changes the declaration. Reserve E0856 for `generic module value parameter <name> cannot use type <type>`; Why lists the selected option's closed domain and identity reason; Fix chooses an allowed type or a type parameter. Reserve E0857 for `generic module argument <N> for <Template> is not a compile-time value`; Why names the first runtime/effect/non-value dependency; Fix passes a literal/immutable Tier-0 value or moves work inside the module. Existing overflow/panic/fuel diagnostics remain canonical but point through a related note to alias argument and parameter declaration. Each emitted code needs diagnostics.md What/Why/Fix, tests/ui source+snapshot, `jet explain`, and AOT/comptime parity tests before shipping.

Beginner pass: literal Int/Bool arguments work like ordinary generic arguments; values become read-only names inside the module. Expert pass: exact evaluation tier, allowed layout slot, canonical bytes, nominal enum identity, errors, and identity handoff are reproducible. Hybrid pass: literals and computed pure constants use one sema/interpreter path; no beginner facade or separate template engine exists.
decisions.story: Priya publishes one ring-buffer module for embedded targets. Capacity changes storage layout, while a checked flag removes bounds-check branches in trusted builds. She wants `Ring<Packet, 64, true>` to produce one ordinary module whose types, constants, and functions all agree on those values. She also needs two imports of the same arguments to mean the same specialization, not two subtly different buffers.

options.name: Closed immutable values plus layout slots
options.detail: Recommended. Bool/Int/Char/String/fieldless-enum values evaluate under Tier-0 comptime and bind as immutable constants. Int additionally enables the narrowly amended `[T#capacity]` generic-module form under S26 + S76/D-FIXARR1. Gives the ratified feature real value specialization while keeping identity closed, safe, deterministic, and explicit.

options.name: Values may affect expressions only
options.detail: Use the same closed types, evaluation, normalization, and diagnostics as A, but preserve S26 literally: parameters may appear in runtime/const expressions and comptime branches, never `[T#N]`, layout, types, or dispatch. Avoids a new type-level exception, but `capacity` cannot define the ring buffer's storage type, so true fixed-size generic modules remain impossible.

options.name: Int-only layout parameters
options.detail: Allow only Int, evaluated under the same Tier-0 law, in ordinary Int expressions and the same narrow S26 + S76/D-FIXARR1 `[T#capacity]` amendment as A. Covers capacities and dimensions with the smallest identity domain, but forces separate modules or type parameters for Boolean modes, string protocol labels, and enum policies despite those values already being safe comptime data.

comparisons.note: Rust permits a restricted structural const domain and uses evaluated values in type identity/layout. A adopts the closed/reproducible part without adding a general const-generic system outside generic modules.
comparisons.code: struct Ring<T, const N: usize> { slots: [T; N] }

comparisons.note: Zig accepts broad comptime values and types. Jet keeps one smaller closed value domain and forbids type-valued computation, ambient evaluation, and arbitrary structural identity.
comparisons.code: fn Ring(comptime T: type, comptime n: usize) type { ... }

comparisons.note: Functor arguments are modules, not scalar values. Jet's ratified type/value module parameters target direct configuration while module-valued parameters remain out of scope.

decisions.title: What declarations and captures belong inside a generic module?
decisions.gist: Choose whether a specialized generic module has the full body and lexical scope of an ordinary module.
decisions.explainer:
D-GENMOD1=A already says instantiation yields a specialized normal module. D-GENMOD2=A fixes unified `<...>` parameters and alias instantiation. BODY1 decides only body item admission, definition-site capture, visibility/coherence consequences, and nested-template cycle lookup. It does not decide value evaluation/normalization/substitution or specialization identity/dedup/fingerprints.

Exact item matrix. A and B admit functions; structs; enums; tags; runtime `const`; `comptime` constants; traits; ordinary trait impls; error-conversion impls; OS-gated impls; tests; benches; ordinary nested modules; nested generic-module templates; and nested module aliases. Existing legal function/type/item markers remain legal only on their existing declaration kinds and keep current semantics; markers are not new items. Tests/benches instantiate only in their existing build modes. C admits functions, structs, enums, tags, runtime `const`, `comptime` constants, and existing legal markers on those admitted declarations. C rejects traits, every impl/error-conversion form, OS-gated impls, tests, benches, ordinary nested modules, nested generic modules, and nested aliases. Every option rejects inline `use`/`pub use` until ordinary module law admits it, plus file/package/build/FFI/C-module/generated-binding/role-module/policy/protocol/state/migration/user-derive/generic-package declarations; those retain their existing homes.

Capture law is independent of argument-value law. Under A/C, non-parameter names resolve in the template definition scope, never alias scope. Under B, only parameters, template-local declarations, and ordinary Core/prelude are visible. Parameters shadow outer names; duplicates use ordinary diagnostics. Public specialized APIs cannot expose private captured declarations. Live open D-GENMOD-VALUE1 owns value evaluation and use; BODY1 does not pre-decide it.

Ordinary orphan law checks expanded declarations: supplied/captured external type and trait remain external, so instantiation never grants an external-for-external impl. Proposed, not-live D-GENMOD-IDENTITY1 gates nominal emission/equality for every specialized struct, enum, tag, and template-declared trait. It also gates whether aliases share a specialization; duplicate nominal declarations; duplicate/coherent trait and error-conversion impls; and semantic/code/cache dedup. BODY1 selects whether these items belong, but they cannot emit until IDENTITY1 ratifies. Functions and constants have no nominal-identity dependency.

Lookup is order-independent: visible top-level/nested templates and aliases may refer forward or backward. Sema collects declarations, builds one dependency graph, then expands in deterministic topological order. Direct/indirect cycles are E0855 at the triggering alias with the full alias/template chain. Source order breaks only diagnostic-order ties, never legality. No expand-until-stable loop. Admitted output enters ordinary sema before codegen.

Dependencies are conditional. VALUE1 is live/open; its selected value behavior remains unresolved. IDENTITY1 is proposed/not live. BODY1 may ratify the matrix and implement function/constant admission, capture/visibility checks, and E0855 independently. Any selected value-using feature waits for VALUE1. Specialized nominal emission/equality, duplicate/coherent impl handling, and cross-alias dedup wait for IDENTITY1.

Diagnostics. E0854 is item-set-only: `generic module <Template> contains a <kind> item, which is not allowed`; Why names the selected closed set; Fix moves it to ordinary module scope or uses an admitted kind. An admitted kind retires its E0854 path; the old snapshot becomes a positive migration test. Reserve E0858 for sealed capture: `generic module <Template> captures <name> from its definition scope`. Why names B's parameter/local/Core-only scope. Fix is per kind and never assumes a value-parameter domain: type -> add a type parameter; trait -> add it as a bound on a type parameter; function -> move/localize helper inside; module -> move needed helpers inside or expose operations through a type parameter trait bound; constant/value -> define it from template-local/Core inputs inside or move the dependent declaration outside. E0858 needs diagnostics.md, `jet explain`, canonical source+snapshot fixtures for value/type/trait/function/module captures, and compiling fixes. E0855 needs its full-chain snapshot.

Beginner: one ordinary-looking parameterized module, private by default. Expert: exact matrix, scope, visibility, orphan, dependencies, and cycle graph. Hybrid: one module mechanism; no template sublanguage or AST/text injection.
decisions.story: Priya maintains a storage library with one key type, one shard count, an Entry type, a Codec trait implementation, constants, and helper submodules that must stay synchronized. She wants to instantiate that family once for production and once for tests. The decision determines whether the family can remain one coherent module, which surrounding names it may use, and whether specialization can accidentally gain authority or violate trait ownership.

options.name: Full ordinary-module parity with lexical capture
options.detail: Recommended. Admits functions, structs, enums, tags, runtime/comptime constants, traits, trait/error-conversion/OS-gated impls, tests, benches, ordinary nested modules, nested generic modules, aliases, and existing legal markers. Uses definition-site lexical capture. Nominal emission and coherent duplicate impl behavior remain gated on IDENTITY1.

options.name: Full declarations, sealed parameter-only scope
options.detail: Admits the same complete item/marker set as A: functions, structs, enums, tags, runtime/comptime constants, traits, all ordinary impl forms including OS-gated, tests, benches, ordinary/nested generic modules, and aliases. Seals scope to parameters, locals, and Core/prelude. Nominal/impl identity still waits for IDENTITY1.

options.name: Data-and-function capsule only
options.detail: Admits only functions, structs, enums, tags, runtime `const`, `comptime` constants, and existing legal markers on those kinds, with definition-site lexical capture. Rejects traits, trait/error-conversion/OS-gated impls, tests, benches, ordinary nested modules, nested generic modules, and aliases via item-set-only E0854. Nominal struct/enum/tag emission still waits for IDENTITY1.

comparisons.note: A functor body is a full module expression: it may define types, values, nested modules, and module relationships. Inputs are explicit module parameters, while ordinary lexical scope remains available.
comparisons.code:
module Make (Key : ORDERED) = struct
  type t = (Key.t * string) list
  module Index = Map.Make(Key)
  let empty = []
end

comparisons.note: Templates can generate types, constants, functions, and nested declarations, but dependent lookup and specialization rules are a major source of surprise. Jet avoids textual substitution and checks one specialized ordinary module in sema.

Rust has no generic modules. Related generic types, traits, impls, and constants stay at module scope, so a family cannot be instantiated and named as one namespace. Jet generic modules exist specifically to preserve that family boundary.

A comptime function can return a type namespace containing declarations and capture parameters. It is powerful, but folds module generation into general compile-time execution; Jet keeps a declarative module mechanism checked by ordinary sema.

decisions.title: Generic-module instantiation and nominal type identity
decisions.gist: Choose whether repeating the same generic-module application means the same module and the same exported nominal types.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-GENMOD1=A makes a parameterized module instantiate to a specialized normal module. Ratified D-GENMOD2=A fixes one unified `<...>` parameter/argument list: parameter annotation kind alone distinguishes type from value parameters; casing is style-only and never identity or semantic classification. This ballot does not reopen that syntax. It closes the missing semantic law: whether module application is applicative (same template and arguments imply one instance) or generative (each alias declaration creates a fresh instance), and therefore what identity exported nominal structs/enums carry.

Current truth is only an MVP. `expand_generic_module_aliases` clones functions into a `CodeModule` named after each alias, substitutes type parameters in function signatures only, and erases templates/aliases before registration. Value arguments, bounds, cycles, body references, exported structs/enums/constants, cross-file templates, JIT parity, stable fingerprints, cache reuse, and semantic-index projection remain staged. Codegen names follow the alias, so two aliases of the same application do not yet have a canonical shared identity or dedup law. D-TYPEALIAS1 remains separate: `alias X = Y` is transparent type naming; `module X = Template<...>` instantiates a module and must not become a disguised second type-alias mechanism.

Exact byte and companion law. frame(B) is unsigned u64 big-endian byte length followed by B. text(S) is frame(exact UTF-8 bytes); no extra Unicode, path, or case normalization occurs. `hex64(H)` rejects anything except 64 lowercase hexadecimal ASCII characters and contributes the decoded 32 bytes; every fingerprint output is exactly 64 lowercase hexadecimal ASCII characters. ResolvedPackageBytes is `text("jet.package.v1") || text(resolved package name) || text(canonical SemVer) || frame(LockedSourceIdentityBytes)`. LockedSourceIdentityBytes is stable and closed: workspace = `text("workspace") || text(workspace identity declared by the resolved workspace graph) || text(package-root WorkspacePath)`; registry = `text("registry") || text(canonical HTTPS registry authority/index identity from the lock resolver) || text(package name) || text(canonical SemVer)`; git = `text("git") || text(canonical credential-free repository identity from the lock resolver) || frame(exact decoded revision object id)`; path = `text("path") || text(locked workspace-relative dependency root) || text(resolved dependency package name) || text(canonical SemVer)`. Whole-tree, file-content, lockfile-content, body-semantic, and interface hashes never enter package/definition/type identity; they belong only to cache invalidation and API compatibility facts. Canonical repository/registry identities are the lockfile's single source keys: lowercase IDNA host, explicit nondefault port only, normalized absolute slash path, uppercase percent escapes, no credentials/query/fragment/dot segments; git ssh/scp spellings normalize to that same credential-free identity before lock write. DefinitionFullKey is text("jet.genmod.definition.v1") plus frame(ResolvedPackageBytes), text(defining WorkspacePath), each framed lexical module segment, text("generic-module"), and text(template name). DefinitionId is lowercase Hex64 SHA-256(DefinitionFullKey). Every store persists schema, id, and full_key and byte-compares full_key on hits; same id with different bytes is ICE 101. No truncation, display name, span, absolute path, import alias, Rust name, map order, or compile order participates.

Type arguments contribute frame(canonical sema TypeFullKey) after transparent aliases resolve. Live open D-GENMOD-VALUE1 exclusively owns value domain, evaluation, selected canonical bytes, and E0853/E0856/E0857. IDENTITY1 may ratify first, but no value-bearing identity ships until VALUE1 ratifies; afterward it consumes exactly VALUE1's selected bytes with no second normalization. `count(N)` is unsigned u64 big-endian. ParameterBytes begins with count(parameter count). Each type parameter is byte 0x01, text(name), byte 0x00 for no bound or byte 0x01 plus frame(resolved trait DefinitionFullKey) for a bound. Each value parameter is byte 0x02, text(name), and frame(annotation TypeFullKey); annotation absence is impossible and rejects before identity. ArgumentBytes begins with count(argument count); each type argument is byte 0x01 plus frame(TypeFullKey), each value argument byte 0x02 plus frame(the complete VALUE1-selected byte string). ApplicationFullKey is `text("jet.genmod.application.v1") || frame(DefinitionFullKey) || frame(ParameterBytes) || frame(ArgumentBytes)`. Counts, kind bytes, names, bound presence, resolved trait identities, and value annotations therefore cannot collide. ApplicationFingerprint is SHA-256(ApplicationFullKey). Under A, InstanceFullKey equals ApplicationFullKey. Under B, InstanceFullKey is text("jet.genmod.instance.v1") plus frame(ApplicationFullKey) and frame(AliasDeclarationFullKey), where the alias key uses the same package/workspace/module/kind/name fields with kind "module-instantiation-alias". InstanceFingerprint is lowercase Hex64 SHA-256(InstanceFullKey). Under C, PackageSealedInstanceFullKey is text("jet.genmod.package-instance.v1") || frame(ApplicationFullKey) || frame(the consuming package's ResolvedPackageBytes). PackageSealedInstanceFingerprint is lowercase Hex64 SHA-256(PackageSealedInstanceFullKey). Every package-sealed store persists (schema, id, full_key), byte-compares PackageSealedInstanceFullKey on every fingerprint hit, and reports ICE 101 if one fingerprint maps to different full-key bytes.

Nominal member identity is conditional on live open D-GENMOD-BODY1. Until BODY1 ratifies an option admitting structs/enums/tags/traits, E0854 remains and no member TypeFullKey exists. After admission, all options preserve Jet's S28 nominal law; no struct, enum, tag, or trait becomes structurally equal by shape. MemberKind is 0x01 struct, 0x02 enum, 0x03 Jet tag, or 0x04 trait; MemberGenericBytes is count(argument count), then each type argument as 0x01||frame(TypeFullKey) and each value argument as 0x02||frame(exact VALUE1 bytes). NominalMemberFullKey is text("jet.genmod.member-type.v1") || frame(option identity basis) || byte(MemberKind) || count(lexical member path segment count) || each text(segment) || text(declared name) || frame(MemberGenericBytes). A's identity basis is ApplicationFullKey; B's is alias-generative InstanceFullKey; C's is PackageSealedInstanceFullKey. TypeFingerprint is SHA-256(NominalMemberFullKey). Trait associated items/signatures, tag qualification, struct fields/layout, and enum variants affect interface/body/cache compatibility but never replace declaration identity with structural equality. An impl mints no type identity: coherence keys on instantiated nominal trait TypeFullKey and target TypeFullKey and applies ordinary orphan/duplicate law. Qualified types preserve written tag order through the existing qualifier TypeFullKey law. Every id collision compares the exact full key.

Cross-file/package law. Loader resolves a template to one DefinitionId before instantiation; re-export/import paths never mint identity. Dependency package identity comes from the resolved package/version/source identity already used by the module graph, so two physical copies of the same resolved package object share and two distinct resolved package versions/sources do not. Private instances deduplicate within the loaded package graph under the chosen option. Public exported types persist their TypeFingerprint into semantic index, interface/API facts, and cache artifacts; readers reject unknown schema or mismatched full keys instead of guessing. Cycles are detected on the active full instance key before body checking and report the complete source-level application chain.

Codegen/cache/LSP law. Sema owns instantiation, bounds, value checking, cycles, privacy, and nominal equality before TIR (I3). Each reachable semantic instance is checked once per canonical identity, lowered once, and codegen emits one specialization per canonical code key; aliases become source-name projections only. If an option makes two nominal instances distinct but their executable bodies safely share, code dedup may use ApplicationFingerprint plus a checked template-body semantic hash only after sema type-erases the distinction; it never changes type equality. Incremental cache keys include compiler ABI/schema, DefinitionId, normalized arguments, checked template-body semantic hash, target/profile/effects/layout inputs, and dependency interface fingerprints. Alias renames invalidate only name/reference projections under A; under B it intentionally creates a new generative InstanceFingerprint and invalidates that alias instance's semantic/type projections; under C, alias rename, import rename, and re-export within the same consuming package preserve PackageSealedInstanceFingerprint; changing the consuming package's resolved source, name, or version changes it. C's semantic, nominal-type, public-interface, and LSP keys use PackageSealedInstanceFingerprint, while checked executable/template-body caches may reuse ApplicationFingerprint across package seals without making types equal. The semantic index records definition, instantiation, alias, argument, exported-member, references, and chosen identity relation; go-to-definition from an alias reaches both alias and template application, find-references joins all aliases only when the chosen option says they share; under C it joins aliases within one consuming package and keeps references from different consuming packages distinct. AOT/JIT/dev/comptime use the same checked instances and cache law.

Diagnostics. E0850/E0851 remain unknown-template/arity and E0852 remains unsatisfied bound. VALUE1 alone defines and imports E0853/E0856/E0857 byte-for-byte; IDENTITY1 neither restates nor widens them. E0854 remains BODY1's staged/item-set error until its selected option admits the relevant member kind. E0855 What is `generic module instantiation forms a cycle`; Why prints the full alias/template/argument chain; Fix names the application edge to remove or replace. E0859 is identity-only: What `generic module identity collided`; Why says two distinct full keys produced one fingerprint; Fix says `report this internal compiler error`; the process exits 101 and never falls back. VALUE1 retains E0853/E0856/E0857 unchanged. Ordinary mismatch between distinct nominal exported types uses the existing type-mismatch diagnostic, but names both fully qualified instance applications and explains whether different arguments or the selected generative rule made them distinct. Every new/changed code needs diagnostics.md What/Why/Fix, UI source, exact snapshot, JSON/LSP parity, and `jet explain` before emission (I4).

Beginner pass: write one module application anywhere; identical applications either work together by the stated rule or produce an error naming both source spellings and why. No fingerprint/cache vocabulary appears in ordinary diagnostics. Expert pass: package/version identity, canonical comptime arguments, public ABI identity, target-independent fingerprints, incremental invalidation, dedup, and semantic-index facts are explicit and inspectable. Hybrid pass: aliases, imports, AOT, JIT, comptime, cache, and editor tooling project one sema identity relation; there is no codegen-only or LSP-only notion of sameness.
decisions.story: Lena publishes a graph package whose generic module bundles Node, Edge, builders, and algorithms for one weight type. Her app instantiates Graph<String> in two files under different local module names. A Node made by the parser must be accepted by the renderer, incremental builds must reuse one specialization, and rename-only edits must not invalidate caches or make the LSP report a false type mismatch. A security library also needs Graph<String> and Graph<Int> to remain unambiguously different types.

options.name: Applicative instances
options.detail: The same DefinitionId plus the same normalized arguments is one module instance everywhere. ParseGraph.Node and RenderGraph.Node are the same nominal type; both aliases project one InstanceFingerprint, one sema check, one TIR/codegen specialization, one cache entry, and joined LSP references. Different arguments or resolved template definitions remain distinct. Recommended: repeated source spelling means one semantic operation, makes imports/aliases harmless, and gives deterministic dedup without weakening nominal types.

options.name: Generative alias instances
options.detail: Each `module Alias = Template<args>` declaration creates a fresh module identity, even when template and arguments match. Uses and re-exports of that alias share its types, but a second alias declaration receives a distinct InstanceFingerprint and nominal members. Code bodies may deduplicate behind the semantic boundary, while types and LSP references stay separate. This supports deliberate abstraction seals, but ordinary aliases unexpectedly create incompatible values and alias duplication becomes semantic.

options.name: Package-sealed applicative instances
options.detail: The same template application shares within one consuming package, but each downstream package gets a distinct nominal module instance even when DefinitionId and arguments match. All structs, enums, tags, and traits remain nominal. Executable/template-body caches may deduplicate by ApplicationFingerprint across package seals without making types equal. This gives packages an abstraction boundary without making every local alias fresh, but values from two packages cannot cross directly and a re-exported public type carries the consumer package seal.

comparisons.note: OCaml distinguishes applicative paths from generative functor applications; stable paths can share abstract types while fresh applications can create new ones. Jet must choose one default because its ratified syntax has no explicit fresh-application marker.
comparisons.code:
module A = F(X)
module B = F(X)
(* type sharing depends on functor/application semantics *)

comparisons.note: Functor application is generative: applying the same functor twice can create incompatible abstract types. B matches that strong abstraction boundary, with corresponding alias ceremony.
comparisons.code:
structure A = F(X)
structure B = F(X)
(* A.t and B.t may be distinct *)

comparisons.note: A monomorphized generic nominal type is identified by its definition and type/const arguments, independent of local aliases. A gives generic modules the same unsurprising identity model.

Template specializations are shared by template identity and arguments across translation units, requiring stable mangling and one-definition discipline. A follows the useful identity/dedup property without exposing mangled names.
comparisons.code:
using A = Graph<long>;
using B = Graph<long>;

decisions.title: Environment removal and enumeration surface
decisions.gist: Choose whether core.env can remove variables and enumerate the process environment, and whether enumeration exposes values.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-OSFACTS1=A keeps environment variables plus cwd/home in core.env and machine/process facts in core.os. It did not authorize unset or enumeration. Existing core.env is get(name) -> String?, set(name, value) -> Void, current_dir(), and home_dir(); generated Rust calls std::env directly. This ballot adds no syntax and does not move system facts. It decides the two remaining #292 gaps and the safety correction required before any environment mutation can remain process-global.

Common substrate for A/B/C. Jet owns one logical process environment. Before user run starts, native launch captures every inherited OS environment entry into a runtime table without decoding it: Unix stores exact name/value byte strings; Windows stores exact name/value UTF-16 code-unit strings. The table preserves inherited spelling, values, and raw encoding. get, home_dir, set, and every core.process child builder read this table. get/home_dir preserve current source behavior: a present raw value that cannot decode losslessly to String is observed as None; vars remains the explicit error-reporting inspection surface. Child spawn takes one owned table snapshot under the read lock, applies ProcessSpec env_clear/env/env_remove overrides, and passes every untouched inherited key/value verbatim through the OS-native process API. No lossy Unicode conversion, normalization, shell, or host-environment reread occurs.

The table is process-global across Jet tasks and protected by one runtime read/write lock. Changes are visible to later Jet get/vars/child calls and cannot alter an earlier returned vars or child snapshot. set and A/B unset mutate only this table after user code begins; they never mutate libc environ or the Windows process environment block. FFI code that directly calls getenv observes the original host environment, not later Jet overlay changes; passing an overlay value to foreign code requires that API explicitly. Programs needing task-local configuration pass values directly; core.env gains no second task-local layer. Comptime, pure evaluation, and the dev interpreter keep their existing ambient-environment denial.

Portable identity and validation. Unix names are exact byte strings and case-sensitive. Windows keys use CompareStringOrdinal ignore-case identity, so Path, PATH, and path are one key; initialization walks environment-block order and the last case-duplicate supplies preserved spelling/value. Jet-written names are Strings but must be nonempty and contain neither NUL nor '='. Jet-written values must not contain NUL. A/B/C export this exact declaration:
```jet
pub enum EnvError {
    InvalidName
    InvalidValue
    NonUnicode
}
``` InvalidName and InvalidValue occur before mutation. EnvError Debug/Display is exactly `invalid environment variable name`, `invalid environment variable value`, or `environment contains a name or value that is not valid Unicode`; it never includes the input, OS bytes, name, value, index, or backend text.

set's current Void signature cannot report a runtime-invalid String. Every outcome selects `set(name: String, value: String) -> Void ? EnvError` in a new major release and edition opt-in under D-REL1/3/5. Existing editions keep the Void source signature. Their invalid call raises existing E3001 at the Jet call span and exits 70. Name message is exactly `core.env.set: invalid environment variable name`; value message is exactly `core.env.set: invalid environment variable value`. The rendered E3001 frame keeps the existing contract: What `panic: {message}` with Jet file, line, function, source context, and debug-safe locals; Why `The program hit a panic, require, or require_eq call that failed, or a bounds/key check triggered at runtime.`; Fix `Fix the logic that led to the failure; the source line and locals show what values were in play.` No new diagnostic code or altered E3001 template is introduced.

The overlay changes one old-edition observable: expert FFI that calls host getenv after env.set no longer sees the Jet write. Keeping post-start OS-global mutation would violate Jet's memory-safety guarantee when foreign threads read the environment. Therefore every A/B/C outcome explicitly ratifies this as a narrow safety exception to the normal compatibility promise: the raw-preserving overlay ships in every supported edition immediately, with no claim that host-environment visibility is backward-compatible. Documented valid Jet behavior—get after set and inherited environment for core.process children—remains. Release notes must name the FFI visibility break and direct foreign APIs to receive values explicitly. The fallible signature still waits for major+edition; the safety substrate does not.

A/B additionally export `unset(name: String) -> Bool ? EnvError`. It uses the same validation and platform identity, returns true exactly when a logical key existed and was removed, false when absent, and is idempotent.

Enumeration law for A/B. vars is an owned snapshot, never a live iterator. One call holds the table read lock, verifies that every current raw name and value decodes losslessly to a Jet String, copies the entire selected result, then releases the lock and sorts. If any name or value is invalid UTF-8 on Unix or contains an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate on Windows, vars returns EnvError.NonUnicode and no element; it never skips, replaces, partially returns, or mutates the table. Raw entries remain available for verbatim child inheritance even when vars fails. Unix sort is ascending lexicographic order of exact UTF-8 name bytes. Windows sort uses CompareStringOrdinal ignore-case first and exact UTF-16 ordinal order as tie-break. Each logical key appears once; map/hash/compile/thread order never participates.

Authority, secrets, and output. Reading/removing inherited environment is existing core.env runtime ambient authority; no workspace manifest, build-time grant, or durable approval is introduced. Neither vars variant logs, prints, audits, traces, serializes, or expands entries by itself. Diagnostics and EnvError never reveal a name or value. A returns names only. B's `@[Redact]` field uses only the already-ratified D-DEBUG-REDACT behavior: auto-derived Debug renders that field as `[redacted]`. It does not invent secret provenance, taint tracking, logging policy, or protection after explicit `.value` access; user code can print or transmit the value exactly as it can after env.get today. Any broader environment-secret taint law needs its own decision.

Release and acceptance. EnvError and A/B unset/vars are new Core items; ordering, raw preservation, overlay visibility, FFI boundary, and child snapshot behavior are compatibility promises. A future live iterator, task-local environment, raw-byte public API, OS-global mutation, alternate ordering, or automatic secret classification needs another decision. Tests cover old-edition valid set compatibility, old-edition invalid-input Jet panic, new-edition fallible set, raw non-Unicode child round-trip, all-or-nothing vars failure, Windows case collapse/order, Unix byte order, concurrent Jet get/set/unset/vars, spawn snapshots, env_clear/env/env_remove composition, no host environ mutation, and exact error rendering.

Beginner pass: set/remove one known variable, list stable names, and spawn a child without platform branches or lock ceremony. Expert pass: raw representation, key identity, ordering, snapshot boundary, FFI visibility, concurrency, child inheritance, invalid encoding, and edition behavior are exact. Hybrid pass: one locked raw-preserving table backs existing get/set and any selected unset/vars; no test-only or platform-only environment mechanism exists.
decisions.story: Mina writes a test runner that must remove CI before spawning a hermetic child and report which environment names influenced the run. Her laptop, Linux CI, and a Windows worker must produce the same ordered audit without accidentally dumping tokens. A library in the same process may read environment variables concurrently, so removal cannot rely on an unsynchronized process-global mutation.
decisions.inWild:
use core.env as env
use core.process as process

fn run() -> Void ? env.EnvError {
    removed :: env.unset("CI")?
    names :: env.vars()?
    print("removed CI: {removed}")
    names.each(name => print(name))
    process.run(["worker"]) ?? panic("worker failed") // receives the same logical environment snapshot
}

options.name: Remove values, enumerate names
options.detail: Recommended. Alongside the common fallible set correction and shared unset, add vars() -> [String] ? EnvError. Deterministic names answer discovery/audit needs; callers retrieve a chosen value through existing get, so a casual print/debug of vars cannot dump every token. Any non-Unicode name or value fails the whole snapshot. This is the smallest useful, safe default without weakening expert access to known values.

options.name: Remove values, enumerate entries
options.detail: Alongside the common fallible set correction and shared unset, core.env exports the exact EnvVar declaration shown below and `vars() -> [EnvVar] ? EnvError`. Entries use the common deterministic name order. Existing auto-derived Debug rendering shows each value as `[redacted]`; explicit `.value` access gives the exact value and receives no new taint or logging semantics. More convenient for forwarding/filtering, but one innocent loop can exfiltrate the entire inherited secret environment.

options.name: Explicit non-goal
options.detail: Do not add unset, vars, or EnvVar. core.env otherwise remains get/set/current_dir/home_dir; programs use known variable names and construct an explicit child environment through core.process.env_clear/env. #292 records removal/enumeration as declined. The common raw-preserving overlay and edition-gated fallible set correction still ship; EnvError exists for set, but removal/enumeration are recorded as declined. This minimizes ambient discovery, but hermetic tools cannot remove an inherited key through core.env and portable audits cannot discover influencing names.

comparisons.note: os.Unsetenv removes a key and os.Environ returns unsorted KEY=value strings. Jet keeps removal but replaces string parsing and nondeterministic order with typed, sorted output; A withholds bulk values by default.
comparisons.code:
os.Unsetenv("CI")
for _, pair := range os.Environ() { fmt.Println(pair) }

comparisons.note: os.environ is a live mutable mapping tied to the process environment. Jet uses an owned snapshot per vars call and a locked logical table so iteration and task concurrency have exact semantics.
comparisons.code:
os.environ.pop("CI", None)
for name, value in sorted(os.environ.items()): ...

comparisons.note: std::env exposes vars/vars_os and process-global set/remove operations whose safety is constrained by concurrent foreign environment access. Jet avoids raw OS strings and post-start host mutation; non-Unicode input fails honestly.

decisions.title: Hand-writable Encode/Decode surface (and whether built-in derives re-enter through it)
decisions.gist: Decide the Jet spelling a person writes to give a type its own wire form, and whether the built-in @Codable/@Encode/@Decode derives generate that same spelling (re-entering the front end, R11) or stay compiler-synthesized Rust that skips it.
decisions.explainer: Today @Codable works by having the compiler write Rust `impl` blocks directly (crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Items.rs::emit_struct_serde) over an internal value tree (jet_std::DataTree), using method names (jet_encode/jet_decode) the docs say `the user never types`. That is the one derive in the language that does NOT follow R11 (architecture.md rule: every build-time code-gen step emits Jet source that re-enters lexer/parser/sema like hand-written code). User-authored derives already follow R11 (D-METADERIVE1=A). This decision fixes (1) whether a person can hand-write a codec for a type the automatic field-walk can't express, and in what Jet syntax, and (2) whether the built-in derives become ordinary derives that emit that Jet source, closing the R11 gap. Note: architecture.md line 188 currently claims @Codable `already works this way` (re-enters); that line is stale and will be corrected to match whichever option is ratified. Ratifying this also fixes an adjacent live bug: the compiler-synthesized impls emit unqualified paths, so decode<T> across an imported module file fails today and only works in the entry file (memory: codable-derive-module-gap).
decisions.story: Ada builds a signup service. Most of her types are plain records: she puts @Codable on `Signup` and `json.to_string(signup)` just works, no ceremony. But `email` is not a plain string — it is an `Email` type that must reject a malformed address on the way in, and should appear on the wire as a bare string "ada@lovelace.org", not as a nested object {"value": "..."}. The automatic field-walk cannot express either the flat wire shape or the validation. Ada needs a way to say, in Jet, `here is how an Email turns into data and back` — and she needs that hand-written codec to compose automatically when `Email` is a field of a derived `Signup`.
decisions.detail: Recommend A. It is the only option where there is exactly one mechanism (I8): a derive is just the compiler auto-writing the same `impl Encode`/`impl Decode` a person could write by hand, re-entering the front end exactly like a user derive (R11, matching the already-ratified D-METADERIVE1 shape). Beginner magic is untouched — @Codable stays zero-ceremony. The expert who needs a custom wire form or validation writes ordinary Jet that composes into any derived parent. B keeps R11 but leaves the hand path second-class (an ‘internals’ module you are steered away from), so the custom-codec story is a demotion rather than a feature and the surface splits in two. C permanently forks built-in derives (compiler-synthesized Rust) from user derives (R11 Jet source), records a standing carve-out in a core safety rule, and gives the expert no override at all — Ada would have to abandon the `Email` type. Effort is not a factor in this ranking.

options.name: First-class Encode/Decode protocol; built-in derives emit it as Jet source (R11)
options.detail: Ratify a user-facing `Encode`/`Decode` protocol: methods `encode(self) -> DataTree` and `decode(tree: DataTree) -> Result<T, DecodeError>`, with DataTree constructors (.Text/.Int/.Float/.Bool/.Null/.Array/.Object), the `?`-chaining accessors already listed in the spec (.text()/.int()/.field(name)/.at(i)), and `DecodeError { path, reason }`. A hand-written impl composes into any @Codable parent because both sides speak the same protocol. The built-in @Codable/@Encode/@Decode derives stop synthesizing Rust and instead generate this exact Jet source, which re-enters lexer→parser→sema like hand-written code — closing the R11 gap and, as a side effect, fixing the cross-module path bug (the generated source resolves names the same way user code does). One mechanism: the derive is the auto-written hand impl. This is the shape the spec already reserved for D-SERDE2 (`encode`/`decode` verbs over DataTree) and matches user derives (D-METADERIVE1).

options.name: Blessed-but-internal encoding module; derives re-enter through it, hand-impl is unblessed
options.detail: Ship the DataTree value tree and the Encode/Decode traits as an ordinary readable Jet module (`core.encoding.internals`), so the built-in derives can emit Jet source that re-enters against it (R11 honored). But the hand-impl path is documented as internal plumbing users are steered away from, not a taught first-class feature. A person CAN read the module and, in a pinch, write against it, but there is no blessed `impl Encode for T` ergonomics story — the intended answer to ‘I need a custom wire form’ stays ‘restructure your type so the field-walk fits’. Keeps the surface small by hiding the protocol, at the cost of leaving Ada's Email case awkward: she reaches into internals rather than using a taught mechanism, and the two surfaces (blessed derive vs unblessed internals) mean encode/decode is learned twice.

options.name: Keep built-in derives compiler-synthesized; record an R11 carve-out; fix only the path bug
options.detail: Accept that the built-in @Codable/@Encode/@Decode derives stay compiler-written Rust over the internal DataTree, and record that as a ratified standing exception to R11 (built-in derives are exempt; user derives are not). No user-facing hand-codec surface ships this increment. Scope the work to fixing the cross-module path bug (qualify the emitted paths so decode<T> works outside the entry file). Ada gets no override: `Email` cannot choose its own wire form and cannot validate on decode through the codec — she must drop the `Email` type and use a plain String, validating by hand somewhere else. Permanently forks two derive machineries (built-in Rust-synth vs user-derive R11 source) and carves a hole in a core safety/trust rule.

comparisons.note: Derive and hand-impl are the SAME trait: #[derive(Serialize)] writes exactly the `impl Serialize` a person could write, and a hand impl composes anywhere the derive would. This is the A shape — one mechanism, derive == auto-written hand impl.
Automatic conformance for plain types; override by writing encode(to:) / init(from:) on the same protocol. Custom and automatic are one mechanism and compose — again the A shape.

A type overrides its wire form by implementing MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON; the struct walker calls into it automatically. Composition-by-interface, like A — but Go bolts custom codecs onto []byte rather than a typed value tree, which is the ergonomics A improves on with DataTree + typed accessors.

decisions.title: Task cancellation model at wait points
decisions.gist: When a task is cancelled (race loser, fail-fast sibling, or handle.cancel()), what happens the next time it hits a wait point (channel recv/send, sleep, task join, I/O): does the wait hand a sentinel back to the task body and let it keep running, or does the task stop right there and unwind — running its Drop-backed cleanup — the way a blown deadline (E3003) already does?
decisions.explainer:
Glossary (terms used below):
- wait point / cancellation point: any place a task can park — channel recv()/send(), time.sleep(), task.wait()/join(), select, I/O. Pure CPU code between wait points never parks.
- unwind: the task stops executing forward at the wait point and runs every value's Drop-backed cleanup on the way out (same machinery as a returned error or an E3003 deadline). No further body code runs.
- Drop-backed cleanup: Jet has no `defer`; a value's close/release runs automatically when it leaves scope on ANY exit path (ratified, syntax-decisions.md line 858). Cleanup fires under all three options below — the question is only whether the code BETWEEN the wait point and scope exit runs.
- sentinel: a stand-in return value meaning 'this wait was cancelled' — e.g. recv() returning None, send() returning false, sleep() returning early.

What already shipped and is NOT reopened: the task/channel/taskgroup model (D-ASYNCRT1, D-NURSERY1, D-TASKSCOPE1), select (D-CONCSELECT1), race winner (D-RACEWIN1), combinators g.all/g.race/g.any (D-CONCCOMB1), and deadlines (D-DEADLINE1 / E3003). Cancel already wakes a parked task correctly — a task blocked in sleep or recv unblocks the instant it is cancelled. This ballot decides ONLY what the woken task does next.

Why it needs a decision now: today the two halves disagree. A blown deadline UNWINDS the task at its wait point and prints E3003 (see examples/features/concurrency/deadline_context.jet). But an explicit cancel is COOPERATIVE — the woken recv()/sleep() returns a sentinel and the task body keeps running until it decides to stop (or never does, if it has no wait point and no check). A deadline is just an ambient cancellation, so the same task can behave two different ways depending on WHY it was cancelled. That is observable, and it is cross-tier: interpreter, JIT, and AOT must agree (R12).
decisions.story: Priya writes a price-quote service. A request fans out to three providers with g.race — first quote wins, losers are cancelled. One provider task, before it loses, has already opened a ledger handle and is parked in a 200ms wait. Priya expects: quote wins, the two losers stop and release their ledgers, done. What she must NOT get is a loser that, after being cancelled, wakes up and still commits a transfer to the ledger — a real side effect from a task the runtime told to stop. Whether that stray commit can happen is exactly this decision.
decisions.detail:
Two-facet pass. Beginner: option A makes the footgun the default — every wait silently returns a sentinel, and if the beginner forgets to check it (or the code past the wait has no check), a cancelled task keeps doing work and commits Priya's stray transfer. That is leaked half-done work, which philosophy.md ranks safety above convenience against. Options B and C make cancel behave like the deadline the beginner already met (E3003): the task just stops at the next wait point and Drop closes the ledger — no sentinel to forget, no stray commit. Expert: all three keep an escape hatch — under A cooperative-continue IS the default; under B/C the shielded region (option C) is the explicit 'let this finish' opt-out for a genuine atomic section. Hybrid/I8: B and C use ONE cancellation mechanism (unwind at wait points, identical to deadlines) instead of two rules for two causes; C adds a scoped opt-out rather than a second system. Recommend C: B's safe, ceremony-free default plus the one control experts need for cleanup-critical sections, and it unifies explicit cancel with the already-shipped E3003 deadline unwind.

Honest cost (behavior change to shipped goldens; difficulty is not an argument, disclosure is): B/C change tasks that are cancelled while still doing forward work. Re-bless expected: examples/features/concurrency/all_failfast.jet (the surviving g.all sibling currently runs to completion; under B/C it unwinds at its sleep) and task_controls.jet (t.cancel() after resume becomes an unwind at the next wait rather than a cooperative flag). race_cancel.jet is unaffected — its loser has no post-wait side effect. Touch points: recv/send/sleep/yield/select cancel handling in BOTH scheduler copies (crates/jet-codegen/src/scheduler.rs and Prelude/Scheduler.rs) and the g.all/race/any result path (JetSchedulerResult::Cancelled is already the wiring). New surface only under C: the shielded-region keyword — spelling is the owner's; candidates in the option.

options.name: Cooperative — wait returns a sentinel, the body finishes on its own terms (Go-style context)
options.detail: A cancelled wait point returns a sentinel and control goes back to the task body: recv() -> None, send() -> false, sleep() returns early. The body decides what to do. Straight-line code with no check keeps running past the cancellation, so transfer() commits after it was cancelled. A task with no wait point and no explicit check is never stopped at all. This is the model that shipped for explicit cancel today; picking A keeps it and lives with the deadline/cancel split (E3003 still unwinds).

options.name: Preemptive at the cancellation point — the task unwinds with Drop cleanup, exactly like a deadline (Trio/Kotlin-style)
options.detail: A cancelled wait point does not return to the body — it unwinds the task then and there, running every Drop-backed cleanup on the way out, and the task's result becomes Cancelled. This is byte-for-byte how E3003 deadlines already behave (deadline_context.jet). The author writes plain straight-line code; no sentinel to check. commit() past the cancelled sleep never runs, so no stray side effect, and the ledger still closes.

options.name: Preemptive by default, with an explicit shielded region for cleanup-critical sections (Trio shield / asyncio.shield / Kotlin NonCancellable)
options.detail: Default is B: cancel unwinds at the next wait point, Drop cleans up. For the rare section that must finish once started — a two-phase commit, a flush, a lock handoff — the author wraps it in a shielded region: cancellation that arrives while inside is deferred until the region exits, so the wait points INSIDE it complete normally, then the task unwinds. One mechanism (unwind at wait points) with a scoped opt-out, not a second system. Recommended: safe default, and the one expert control real cleanup code needs. Shield keyword spelling is the owner's call — candidates below.

comparisons.note: Cooperative — this is option A. ctx.Done() is a channel; a cancelled goroutine keeps running until it checks it. Forgotten checks and work-after-cancel are a well-known Go footgun and the reason context threading is boilerplate.

Preemptive — options B and C. A checkpoint (its wait points) raises Cancelled and the task unwinds through context managers (its Drop equivalent). trio.CancelScope(shield=True) is exactly option C's shielded region.
comparisons.code:
with trio.CancelScope(shield=True):
    await ledger.commit()   # runs to completion even if the outer scope is cancelled

comparisons.note: Preemptive — B/C. Suspension points throw CancellationException, finally/use blocks run cleanup, and withContext(NonCancellable) { } is the shielded region.
Preemptive — B/C. await points raise CancelledError; asyncio.shield(coro) protects a critical awaitable — option C's shield under a different name.

decisions.title: Spelling of the shielded (cancellation-deferred) region
decisions.gist: D-CANCELMODEL1 = C is ratified: cancellation unwinds a task at its next wait point, and a scoped region can defer that unwind until a critical section finishes. This ballot picks the one word a user types to open that region.
decisions.explainer: Shielded region: a block inside a task. If the task is cancelled while execution is inside the block, the cancellation is not lost — it is held until the block ends, then the task unwinds. Waits inside the block behave normally. It is the same job as Trio's CancelScope(shield=True), Kotlin's NonCancellable, and asyncio.shield. The sigil family is already established: #Unsafe("reason") { }, #Context(deadline:) { }. This name joins that family in Syntax.rs with this decision ID (I7).
decisions.story: Priya's task has won nothing: it lost the race, and cancellation is on its way. But it has already begun committing a ledger entry. She wraps the commit in the region so the commit either completes or never starts — cancellation lands the instant the block closes. The word she types should say exactly that to a reader who has never seen it: nothing stops this block early.
decisions.detail: All candidates are semantically identical; this is purely the spelling. Each shows the same commit example. Candidates avoid #Atomic (collides with the atomics/memory-ordering vocabulary) and #Critical (OS critical-section jargon, implies mutual exclusion that this block does not provide).

options.name: #Shield
options.detail: The cross-language term of art (Trio shield=True, asyncio.shield). Verb reads as an action on the block: shield it from cancellation. Short, searchable, already used in the D-CANCELMODEL1 ballot text.

options.name: #Shielded
options.detail: Adjective form: describes the state of the block rather than commanding it. Reads slightly more like prose; one character longer.

options.name: #NoCancel
options.detail: Blunt and literal: cancellation does not land here. Zero metaphor — a beginner cannot misread it. Slightly wrong to a careful reader: the cancel still happens, it is deferred, not refused.

options.name: #Uninterrupted
options.detail: Says precisely what the block guarantees: it runs start to finish. Longest candidate; reads beautifully in docs, is a lot to type at every commit site.

options.name: #Finish
options.detail: Names the promise instead of the mechanism: this block finishes. Shortest to type; pairs naturally with the sentence "cancellation lands after it finishes".

options.name: #Hold
options.detail: Aviation register: holding pattern — the cancellation circles until the block clears. Two syllables shorter than everything but #Finish; the metaphor may not be obvious without docs.

options.name: #Landing
options.detail: Aviation register: final approach — once begun, you land it; nothing aborts the sequence. Distinctively Jet; strongest metaphor, least literal.

comparisons.note: CancelScope(shield=True) — the 'shield' term of art.
withContext(NonCancellable) — the 'no cancel' phrasing.
asyncio.shield(coro) — shield again, as a function.

decisions.title: The value-tree type name a hand codec types: Data or DataTree
decisions.gist: D-SERDE2 = A gives every type a hand-writable encode(self) and decode(tree). The spec text calls the wire tree DataTree, but the only name the compiler lets a user construct and return today is Data. One of them must become the single name users type in every hand codec.
decisions.explainer: The value tree is the format-agnostic middle form: JSON/TOML/YAML/CSV all encode from and decode into it. Its variants are .Null/.Bool/.Int/.Float/.Text/.Bytes/.Array/.Object. The generated Rust type is jet_std::DataTree; the Jet-surface dynamic face is currently spelled Data (bare decode(s) yields it, Data.Text(x) constructs it). The ratified spec sentence (syntax-decisions.md, serde law) says hand-impl verbs are 'over DataTree' — code and spec disagree, and a hand codec forces the choice: the name appears in the signature `fn encode(self) -> <NAME>` of every custom codec ever written.
decisions.story: Ada writes her Email codec. The first line is the signature. Today she must write `fn encode(self) -> Data` even though the docs she read say DataTree; if she writes DataTree the compiler says nothing by that name exists. Whichever word wins is permanent taught surface.
decisions.detail: Pure naming; semantics identical. One name only either way (I8) — the loser becomes a teaching error pointing at the winner, not an alias.

options.name: Data
options.detail: Keep what the compiler already speaks. Short, matches bare decode(s) -> Data reads that already exist in examples. Spec law text is amended to say Data. Cost: 'Data' is a famously overloaded word; reads generic in signatures.

options.name: DataTree
options.detail: Rename the surface to match the ratified law text and the generated runtime type. Self-describing: it is a tree of data, distinct from any user type named Data. Cost: existing examples/goldens using Data re-bless; two more characters.

comparisons.note: serde_json::Value — the tree is named for the format; Jet's tree is format-agnostic so a format-neutral name is needed.
Codable hides the tree entirely behind Encoder/Decoder visitors; Jet exposes the tree as a value, so it needs one good name.

decisions.title: How ?-accessors compose inside a hand-written decode
decisions.gist: decode(tree) returns T ? DecodeError, but the tree accessors (.field/.at/.int/.text/…) return T ? String. Writing `tree.text()?` inside decode is today E2404: `?` cannot turn a String error into a DecodeError. The ratified surface promises ?-chaining in decode; this picks how the two error types meet.
decisions.explainer: DecodeError is the structured error { path, reason } that typed decode reports. The accessors were built for casual dynamic reads (bare decode(s) -> Data), where a plain String reason suffices. A hand codec sits between the two: it reads the tree with accessors and must return DecodeError. Something has to convert.
decisions.story: Ada's decode reads a text node and validates it: `s := tree.text()?`. Under today's types that line does not compile. She should not need a manual error-mapping incantation on every field read — the promise of the surface is that ? just works.
decisions.detail: Three distinct shapes. A changes what accessors return everywhere; B adds one blessed coercion edge; C makes the accessor error type depend on context.

options.name: Accessors return ? DecodeError everywhere
options.detail: One error type for all tree reads; the accessor fills path automatically from where it read (field name / index), which makes casual dynamic reads BETTER (structured paths for free). Cost: casual users see a struct where they saw a String; existing accessor call sites re-check.
options.code:
s := tree.text()?              // ? DecodeError, path auto-filled
age := tree.field("age")?.int()?

options.name: Blessed String -> DecodeError ? coercion
options.detail: Accessors keep ? String; the ? operator inside a fn returning ? DecodeError converts, path empty. Zero churn to existing reads. Cost: a special-case coercion edge in the ? conversion table, and hand codecs get empty paths unless they fill them manually.
options.code: s := tree.text()?              // String auto-wraps into DecodeError { path: "", reason: s }

options.name: Context-sensitive accessor error type
options.detail: Inside a Decode impl the same accessor returns ? DecodeError; elsewhere ? String. No churn, best of both surfaces. Cost: the same expression types differently by context — hardest to teach and to implement honestly (I8 tension: one spelling, two meanings).
options.code:
// inside impl T.Decode:  tree.text() : String ? DecodeError
// elsewhere:              tree.text() : String ? String

comparisons.note: All tree reads speak one error type (D::Error) — option A's shape.
errors are hand-wrapped at every read — the ceremony option A/B avoid.
comparisons.code: if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("email: %w", err) }

decisions.title: Hand-built object nodes: map literal or pair list
decisions.gist: A hand codec that encodes a record needs to build an .Object node. The compiler today takes a Map (Data.Object(map)); the D-SERDE2 ballot text showed a list of pairs. Pick the taught spelling.
decisions.explainer: This is the constructor a custom codec uses for any structured wire form. Whichever shape is taught appears in every non-trivial hand encoder. Key order matters for deterministic output (goldens, diffs, canonical forms).
decisions.story: Ada's Signup type encodes as an object with two fields. She writes the encode body once; every reader of the docs copies it.
decisions.detail: Semantics identical if the map preserves insertion order (Jet Map does). Purely which literal is taught and accepted.

options.name: Map literal
options.detail: DataTree.Object({ "name": v, … }) — matches what the compiler accepts today and how the tree prints; map literal syntax already ratified. Insertion-ordered.

options.name: Pair list
options.detail: DataTree.Object([("name", v), …]) — the ballot's illustrative shape. List-of-tuples reads slightly more wire-like; needs a new accepted constructor form and teaches a second collection spelling for the same job (I8 cost).
options.code:
DataTree.Object([
    ("name", self.name.encode()),
    ("email", self.email.encode()),
])

comparisons.note: json! macro takes map-literal shape — option A.

decisions.title: Decode an arbitrary DataTree subtree through a field type
decisions.gist: Choose the one Jet spelling that asks any Decode type to turn a DataTree subtree into that type.
decisions.story: Ada derives Decode for an Order containing an Address, a list of LineItem values, and an optional coupon. The generated Jet fragment can read each field as a DataTree, but the ratified scalar accessors cannot turn those subtrees into Address, [LineItem], or Coupon?. The derive must emit ordinary Jet that invokes the same Decode implementation Ada could write by hand, so nested validation and DecodeError paths compose without compiler-only helpers.
