message := email.message(from: email.address("login@example.com")?, to: [email.address(user.email)?], subject: "Sign in", text: "Open {link}")?
report := postmark.client(token).send(message)?

options.name: External SMTP bridge
options.detail: Jet exposes A's API but delegates SMTP/MIME to an approved Rust library behind a Core bridge.
options.technical: Approve a new stdlib external dependency outside compiler seams. Jet must still own public types, diagnostics, task/deadline mapping, credential redaction, and acceptance law; raw dependency errors never escape.
options.code:
use core.email as email
mailer := email.smtp_from_env()?
report := mailer.send(message)?

comparisons.note: Python separates EmailMessage construction from smtplib transport. Jet keeps that useful split while adding typed addresses, safe defaults, task cancellation, and honest delivery states.
Nodemailer offers one approachable transport object and rich message options. Jet can preserve that shape without dynamic maps, callback errors, or silent fallback.
comparisons.code: await transporter.sendMail({ to: user, subject: "Sign in", text: link })

comparisons.note: Rust mail libraries provide typed builders and SMTP transports. Jet keeps those strengths behind a smaller surface aligned with Jet tasks, errors, taint, and diagnostics.

recommendation.why: A completes D-AUTH1 with one provider-neutral transport built from Jet's existing audited runtime. Beginners get secure submission; experts retain explicit SMTP security, limits, signing, envelope, and recipient policy.

whyNot.reason: A vendor package and token become mandatory, while private relays, local test servers, and provider-neutral deployments remain unsupported.
It adds an external trust and release boundary although Jet already owns the required sockets, TLS, scheduler, encoding, DNS, files, and crypto primitives.

recommendation.tradeoff: Native SMTP cannot promise provider analytics or inbox placement. Jet reports relay acceptance honestly; provider packages may later reuse the same Message and SendReport types.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep A as the single Core mechanism. Harvest B's transport-neutral message/report types and C's hostile conformance knowledge without requiring a provider or dependency.

harvest.use: Built-in transport and beginner default.
Future packages consume the same Message and return the same SendReport.
Harvest hostile cases into Jet tests without importing dependency/error surfaces.

decisions.title: What exact SMTP configuration, send, report, and trust surface should Jet expose?
decisions.gist: Fix the constructible types and method signatures needed to implement D-EMAIL1 without inventing SMTP spellings in code.
decisions.lesson:
D-EMAIL1 already chose one native Mailer, secure STARTTLS or TLS-from-connect, honest relay-acceptance reports, no hidden retry, and task-aware cancellation. Implementation still needs exact public shapes. A configuration must say where to connect, how TLS starts, how credentials are supplied, how partial recipient rejection is handled, and which certificate authorities are trusted.

Certificate trust and encryption are separate. A custom CA is useful for private relays and local tests, but it must extend trusted roots while preserving hostname verification. A trust-all switch would make encryption unauthenticated and must not exist. Deadlines and cancellation already belong to Jet's ambient task context; duplicating timeout fields in SMTP config would create two competing authorities.

SMTP envelope recipients are separate from visible headers. Bcc must reach RCPT TO but never MIME headers. Relay acceptance is also not inbox delivery, so SendReport must describe server acceptance and rejection without claiming delivery. A disconnect after DATA may be DeliveryUnknown: retrying automatically could send a duplicate.
decisions.story: Mara starts with smtp_from_env and mailer.send(message). Her production team later uses a private relay with a company CA, requires every recipient to be accepted before DATA, and cancels through a request context. The same Mailer must expose those controls without a second expert transport or an insecure test mode.
decisions.inWild:
config := email.SmtpConfig.{
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    security: .StartTls,
    auth: .Password(username: "mailer", password: smtp_password),
    recipient_policy: .RequireAll,
    trust: .System,
    limits: email.Limits.safe(),
}
mailer := email.smtp(config)?
report := mailer.send(message)?
print("relay accepted {report.accepted.len()} recipients")
decisions.detail: Acceptance: every public type, variant, field, constructor, and method below is registered with decision adjacency; smtp_from_env and smtp(config) create the same Mailer mechanism; STARTTLS never downgrades and password auth never occurs before verified TLS; custom CA input extends roots and retains hostname verification; no trust-all option exists; Message owns the default envelope and expert envelope replacement preserves Bcc/header separation; Mailer.send has one signature and inherits the earliest ambient task deadline/cancellation; reports distinguish accepted/rejected recipients and relay acceptance without claiming delivery; EmailError has stable typed variants including DeliveryUnknown; no automatic retry; hostile real-socket/TLS tests cover reply bounds, capability parsing, downgrade, auth order, partial recipients, DATA ambiguity, cancellation, and drop.

options.name: Closed records plus one send method
options.detail: Use constructible records and closed enums for expert policy, while smtp_from_env and message defaults keep beginner use short. Mailer.send(message) is the only send mechanism.
options.technical: SmtpConfig fields: host:String, port:Int, security:SmtpSecurity(.StartTls|.Tls), auth:SmtpAuth(.None|.Password{username:String,password:Secret<String>}), recipient_policy:RecipientPolicy(.RequireAll|.DeliverAccepted), trust:TlsTrust(.System|.SystemPlusCa{pem:[U8]}), limits:Limits. Custom CA never disables hostname verification. Limits is a constructible record for reply-line/reply-count/capability/recipient/message/auth-challenge bounds and Limits.safe() supplies defaults. Message contains its default Envelope. Envelope fields are from:Address and recipients:[Address]; email.envelope validates it; message.with_envelope(envelope) is the expert override and still cannot add headers. Mailer uses a write receiver and `send(message: Message) -> SendReport ? EmailError`; ambient #Context is the sole deadline/cancellation authority. SendReport fields: server:String, accepted:[RecipientReport], rejected:[RecipientReport], response_code:Int, response:String, accepted_at:String. RecipientReport fields: address:Address, accepted:Bool, code:Int, message:String. EmailError variants: Configuration, Dns, Connect, Tls, Auth, Protocol, Rejected, Transient, TimedOut, Cancelled, DeliveryUnknown; each carries operation:String, server:String?, code:Int?, and reason:String. smtp_from_env maps environment into the same SmtpConfig and rejects missing/unsafe values.
options.code:
mailer := email.smtp_from_env()?
report := mailer.send(message)?

custom := message.with_envelope(email.envelope(from, audit_recipients)?)?
report := email.smtp(config)?.send(custom)?

options.name: Fluent builders
options.detail: Keep config and message internals opaque; expose chained with_host, with_tls, with_auth, with_policy, with_ca, and with_envelope methods before send.
options.technical: Every policy becomes a method call returning a new opaque value. Mailer.send remains singular and ambient context still owns cancellation. This avoids public record fields but creates a larger method vocabulary and makes configuration serialization/audit less direct.
options.code:
mailer := email.smtp_builder("smtp.example.com")
    .start_tls()
    .password(username, smtp_password)
    .require_all()
    .system_plus_ca(company_ca)?
    .build()?
report := mailer.send(message)?

options.name: Environment-only Mailer
options.detail: Expose only smtp_from_env and mailer.send(message). Configuration, trust, envelope, and report policy remain opaque environment conventions.
options.technical: Beginners get the shortest path, but private CA roots, explicit recipient policy, reproducible tests, audited configuration, and programmatic multi-relay use cannot be expressed through typed Jet values.
options.code:
mailer := email.smtp_from_env()?
report := mailer.send(message)?

comparisons.note: Rust SMTP libraries commonly use typed transport builders and TLS parameter objects. A keeps typed policy while using one inspectable record and Jet ambient cancellation.
Go exposes tls.Config with RootCAs and ServerName, but net/smtp leaves protocol policy low-level. A preserves verified root extension and hostname checks behind a smaller safe enum.
Nodemailer uses a dynamic transport object and sendMail. A keeps the approachable one-transporter/one-send shape with closed typed fields and explicit acceptance states.

recommendation.why: A supplies the missing expert controls while preserving one beginner path and one send mechanism. Records are auditable and serializable; closed enums prevent downgrade/trust ambiguity; ambient context avoids a second timeout model.

whyNot.reason: It multiplies configuration methods for fields that form one coherent value, making policy discovery, diffing, and audit less direct.
It denies explicit private-CA trust, envelope control, recipient policy, reproducible fixtures, and multi-relay configuration to expert users.

recommendation.tradeoff: A exposes several small records and enums. They are the one canonical typed policy surface and replace environment-string conventions rather than adding a parallel mechanism.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A as the canonical mechanism. Keep C's smtp_from_env as beginner sugar that constructs A, and harvest B's discoverability through docs/completion rather than duplicate builder methods.

harvest.use: Canonical configuration, envelope, reports, errors, and trust.
Completion and examples explain each record field and enum variant.
smtp_from_env constructs the same SmtpConfig and Mailer.

decisions.title: How should SMTP limits, password secrets, and custom certificate trust become exact?
decisions.gist: Complete the missing SMTP configuration law without inventing field names, weakening certificate checks, or creating a second secret mechanism.
decisions.lesson:
An SMTP client reads lines and message data from a server. Every read needs a limit, because a hostile server can send endless lines or an enormous authentication challenge. A Limits value makes those memory and work ceilings visible and testable. Limits.safe() supplies ordinary defaults.

A password must not behave like a normal String. Jet's Secret value prevents ordinary display and debug output. The open question is whether email uses that existing value, makes Secret generic, or adds a narrower password type.

Transport Layer Security checks two things: encryption and server identity. A private certificate authority can extend trusted roots for a company relay. It must never disable hostname verification. SystemPlusCa therefore means system roots plus supplied certificates, not trust every certificate.
decisions.story: Mara uses the safe defaults for a public relay. Her operations team later adds a company certificate authority and lowers reply bounds for a locked-down relay. Passwords must remain redacted in both setups.
decisions.inWild:
limits := email.Limits.{
    max_reply_line_bytes: 512,
    max_reply_lines: 100,
    max_capabilities: 100,
    max_recipients: 100,
    max_message_bytes: 33554432,
    max_auth_challenge_bytes: 4096,
}
config := email.SmtpConfig.{
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    security: .StartTls,
    auth: .Password(username: "mailer", password: smtp_password),
    recipient_policy: .RequireAll,
    trust: .SystemPlusCa(pem: company_ca),
    limits: limits,
}

options.name: Existing Secret, exact limits
options.detail: Keep Jet's existing non-generic Secret for SMTP passwords. Ratify six explicit limit fields and a verified system-plus-CA trust bridge. Beginners still use Limits.safe() and smtp_from_env().
options.technical: Limits fields and safe defaults are max_reply_line_bytes=512, max_reply_lines=100, max_capabilities=100, max_recipients=100, max_message_bytes=33554432, and max_auth_challenge_bytes=4096. Valid ranges are 64..65536, 1..1000, 1..1000, 1..10000, 1..1073741824, and 1..65536. Validation follows field order and returns EmailError.Configuration on the first failure. SmtpAuth.Password stores password:Secret. SystemPlusCa parses PEM certificates, appends them to system roots, and retains DNS-name verification. Empty, malformed, or certificate-free PEM is rejected before SMTP credentials can be sent.
options.code:
password := Secret.from_text(env.get("SMTP_PASSWORD")?)
config := email.SmtpConfig.{
    host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587, security: .StartTls,
    auth: .Password(username: "mailer", password: password),
    recipient_policy: .RequireAll, trust: .System,
    limits: email.Limits.safe(),
}

options.name: Generic Secret payload
options.detail: Make Secret generic and use Secret<String> for SMTP passwords. Limits and certificate trust stay identical to A. Other secret APIs must choose their payload types too.
options.technical: The six Limits fields, defaults, ranges, validation order, and SystemPlusCa law are identical to A. Secret<T> becomes the canonical secret wrapper. Existing bare Secret uses require a ratified default parameter or migration to Secret<[U8]>. Debug, display, clone, serialization, reflection, and error behavior remain redacted for every T.
options.code:
password: Secret<String> := Secret.from_text(env.get("SMTP_PASSWORD")?)
auth := email.SmtpAuth.Password(username: "mailer", password: password)

options.name: Dedicated EmailPassword
options.detail: Add a purpose-specific EmailPassword value for SMTP authentication. Limits and certificate trust stay identical to A. Callers must convert an existing Secret into this narrower value.
options.technical: The six Limits fields, defaults, ranges, validation order, and SystemPlusCa law are identical to A. EmailPassword is move-only, redacted, and non-serializable. Conversion consumes Secret. No plain String constructor exists outside smtp_from_env, which performs the same protected conversion internally.
options.code:
password := email.EmailPassword.from_secret(^smtp_password)
auth := email.SmtpAuth.Password(username: "mailer", password: password)

comparisons.note: Go extends a RootCAs pool and still verifies ServerName. Jet's SystemPlusCa keeps that identity check while hiding certificate-pool mechanics.
Rust secrecy wrappers redact values, while TLS clients use explicit root stores. A keeps both properties behind Jet's smaller existing types.

recommendation.why: A completes the ratified SMTP policy through Jet's existing secret mechanism. It gives beginners fixed safe defaults and experts explicit, bounded, hostname-verified control.

whyNot.reason: Payload generics do not strengthen redaction or SMTP safety. They change every existing secret API and create type choices where one protected byte value already works.
A second protected password type duplicates Secret's semantic job and adds conversion ceremony without a stronger safety boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: Secret does not encode a String payload in its type. SMTP interprets its protected bytes as UTF-8 only when forming authentication data, with invalid bytes rejected as configuration.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A as the one mechanism. Keep B's payload validation at the SMTP boundary and C's purpose-specific handling inside SmtpAuth, without adding public wrapper types.

harvest.use: Store SMTP passwords as Secret and keep safe defaults short.
Validate protected bytes as UTF-8 when SMTP AUTH needs text.
Keep password extraction private to SmtpAuth and transport internals.

decisions.title: Where should optional DKIM signing policy attach?
decisions.gist: Choose where one optional DKIM identity and signing policy attaches to Jet's existing Message, SmtpConfig, and Mailer values.
decisions.lesson:
DomainKeys Identified Mail, or DKIM, lets a receiving mail server verify that a domain approved an email. The sender signs selected headers and the body. The receiver finds the public key in the domain's Domain Name System, or DNS.

A selector is a short key name, such as `login-2026`. Together, selector `login-2026` and domain `example.com` point to `login-2026._domainkey.example.com`. That DNS record publishes the public key. The private signing key stays inside the sending service.

Email can be written in several byte-equivalent forms. Canonicalization turns allowed variations into one stable form before hashing. Relaxed header canonicalization normalizes header names and whitespace. Relaxed body canonicalization normalizes line-end whitespace and trailing empty lines. The same rules must run during signing and verification.

DKIM signs the final serialized email bytes, not the earlier Message fields. A body hash proves the body. A signature covers that hash plus a declared header set. `From` must always be signed. Signing `Subject`, `To`, and content headers prevents useful parts from changing unnoticed.

Jet already has SHA-256, Ed25519 signing, and redacted Secret values. This decision can therefore fix `ed25519-sha256` with relaxed canonicalization. It needs no second algorithm menu. The private key remains a Secret and is copied only inside the signing boundary, then zeroed.

The open choice is policy ownership. Signing can belong to the SMTP configuration, to Mailer construction, or to each Message. Ownership matters because omitted signing can silently send an unsigned login email. It also decides whether one Mailer can represent several domains.
decisions.story: Mara sends passwordless login links from `login@example.com`. Operations rotates DKIM selector `login-2026` and stores the new private key as a secret. Every message from that Mailer must be signed, including retries performed by application code. A separate product later sends receipts from another domain.
decisions.detail: Shared law for all options: DkimConfig fields are domain:String, selector:String, private_key:Secret, and signed_headers:[String]. The key is exactly a 32-byte Ed25519 seed. Signing is fixed to ed25519-sha256 and relaxed/relaxed canonicalization. From is mandatory. Header matching is case-insensitive. Duplicate names, absent mandatory headers, and forbidden hop headers are Configuration errors before any SMTP connection. The signer hashes and signs final MIME bytes, prepends one DKIM-Signature header, wipes every private-key copy, and never places key bytes in diagnostics, debug text, logs, or reports. DNS publishes `v=DKIM1; k=ed25519; p=<base64 public key>` at `<selector>._domainkey.<domain>`. SPF and DMARC remain DNS policy. smtp_from_env accepts DKIM only when SMTP_DKIM_DOMAIN, SMTP_DKIM_SELECTOR, and SMTP_DKIM_PRIVATE_KEY_BASE64 are all present. SMTP_DKIM_SIGNED_HEADERS may replace the safe header list. Partial or malformed environment configuration fails before connecting.

options.name: DKIM belongs to SmtpConfig
options.detail: Add one optional `dkim` field to SmtpConfig. `smtp_from_env` fills it automatically when the complete DKIM environment set exists. An expert passes the same DkimConfig directly. One Mailer then represents one relay policy and at most one signing identity. Every send through that Mailer follows the same rule, so login mail cannot forget signing per message.
options.technical: SmtpConfig gains `dkim:DkimConfig?`. `none` means unsigned mail. `some` means Mailer construction validates domain, selector, key length, and signed_headers. Mailer owns the extracted key and zeroes it on construction failure and Drop. Mailer.send serializes once, canonicalizes those final bytes, signs them, checks the configured message bound again with the DKIM header included, then begins SMTP. No unsigned fallback exists after a signing error. Creating separate Mailers is the explicit multi-domain path.

options.name: DKIM attaches during Mailer construction
options.detail: Keep SmtpConfig limited to SMTP transport policy. Pass optional signing policy beside it when constructing a Mailer. The Mailer still enforces one identity on every send. The visible distinction says transport and authorship are separate concerns, but it widens the already-ratified smtp constructor.
options.technical: The expert form becomes `smtp(config, dkim:DkimConfig?)`. smtp_from_env reads both transport and DKIM environment values before calling that constructor. Mailer owns and wipes the extracted key exactly as in A. Signing order, bounds, canonicalization, error behavior, and multi-Mailer domain separation are identical. The cost is a second authority beside SmtpConfig that must travel with it through factories and tests.

options.name: DKIM belongs to each Message
options.detail: Attach DkimConfig while preparing each Message. One Mailer can then send for several domains. This serves multi-tenant systems directly. It also lets one call omit signing while neighboring calls sign, so policy review must inspect every message path.
options.technical: Message gains a signing attachment operation and carries protected signing state until Mailer.send consumes it. The Mailer signs after final serialization, never serializes the key, and wipes extracted copies. smtp_from_env cannot guarantee signing by Mailer identity alone; it must inject a default into every Message path or reject unsigned messages through another policy field. Adding that rejection field would create a second signing authority, so this option leaves omission under caller control.
options.code:
login := message.with_dkim(login_dkim)?
receipt := other_message.with_dkim(receipt_dkim)?
report1 := mailer.send(login)?
report2 := mailer.send(receipt)?

// This compiles and sends unsigned mail:
report3 := mailer.send(message)?
// Review must catch whether that omission was intended.

comparisons.note: Nodemailer normally places DKIM policy on the transport object. One transport then signs every message, while multiple keys can be selected by policy.
dkimpy signs completed message bytes through a separate signing call. This exposes the protocol boundary, but applications must remember to call it before transport.
Mail libraries commonly separate message construction from transport. DKIM integrations often wrap or extend transport so signing policy applies consistently at send time.

recommendation.why: A makes signing part of the same auditable send policy as relay trust, authentication, recipient handling, and limits. Beginner environment setup and expert records construct one identical Mailer. A login path cannot accidentally omit DKIM on one Message while using a signing Mailer.

whyNot.reason: It preserves consistent Mailer signing, but splits one operational mail policy across two constructor inputs. Factories, tests, and configuration stores must keep those values paired.
It supports several identities through one Mailer, but permits accidental unsigned mail on any call. Preventing that would require another Mailer policy and two competing authorities.

recommendation.tradeoff: A uses one Mailer per signing identity. Multi-domain services create several Mailers, which is acceptable because keys, domains, selectors, and audit policy already differ by identity.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A as the canonical policy owner. Keep signing fields inside one nested DkimConfig, preserving B's conceptual separation without a second constructor authority. Multi-domain experts harvest C's flexibility by creating named Mailers per identity, not by weakening per-send guarantees.

harvest.aspect: One enforced identity policy per Mailer
harvest.use: Keep optional DkimConfig inside SmtpConfig and apply it to every send.

harvest.aspect: Transport and signing remain understandable as different jobs
harvest.use: Preserve that boundary through a nested DkimConfig rather than a second constructor argument.
Use separate named Mailers per identity. Per-message override cannot fit without allowing accidental unsigned mail or adding conflicting policy.

decisions.title: Remove Tower web-push/VAPID entirely
decisions.outcome: Delete web push (VAPID keys, subscribe UI, service-worker push handler, /api/push/*). Keep SSE. Auth secrets stay. Exposed historic keys still scrubbed per D-TOWER-HISTORY1=A when history rewrite runs — no rotation/resubscribe needed because feature is gone.
decisions.comment: Delete web push (VAPID keys, subscribe UI, service-worker push handler, /api/push/*). Keep SSE. Auth secrets stay. Exposed historic keys still scrubbed per D-TOWER-HISTORY1=A when history rewrite runs — no rotation/resubscribe needed because feature is gone.

decisions.title: Should a taking call have a copy shorthand?
decisions.gist: Choose the call-site lens for “copy this value, then give the copy away.”
decisions.lesson:
A taking parameter receives ownership. Jet already writes ^value when the caller gives away an existing value. Jet also has copy value when it must create an independent duplicate.

The combined operation appears often: preserve the original, create a copy, and give that copy to a taking parameter. Every option lowers to that exact sequence. A copied temporary is always transferred into the taking parameter. Only the written lens changes.

^^ is not “more move.” It reads as two ownership steps: the first stroke creates a preserved branch, while the second feeds the new branch into the taking call. The compiler must reject it when independent copying is unavailable. Shared identity remains a different operation.
decisions.story: A student adds one Task to a list that takes ownership. He also needs the original Task for the next exercise. The call should show whether it gives, copies, or shares.
decisions.inWild:
tasks.add(^task)       // list gets original; task is gone
tasks.add(copy task)  // list gets independent copy
share(task)           // both names share one identity

options.name: Keep the copy word
options.detail: Users write copy at the taking argument. It is searchable and already works in any expression. The taking parameter transfers the new temporary by definition.
options.technical: At a taking argument, copy x is surface syntax for the fixed copy-then-transfer operation. It does not create a reusable named temporary.
options.code:
tasks.add(copy task)
task.rename("Read chapter 2")

options.name: Double caret shorthand
options.detail: ^^value is the taking-call lens for copy value. ^ means give this value away. ^^ means preserve this value and give an independent copy away. The full copy form remains available outside calls.
options.technical: In a taking argument only, ^^x lowers exactly to copy x followed by transfer of the temporary. It cannot mean retain, borrow, or shallow alias.
options.code:
tasks.add(^task)   // give original
tasks.add(^^task)  // give independent copy
task.rename("Read chapter 2")

options.name: Written operation stack
options.detail: Users write ^(copy value). This displays both steps even though the taking parameter already fixes the transfer. It is exact but visually dense at common call sites.
options.technical: ^(copy x) is a fully expanded lens for the same fixed copy-then-transfer operation. The written ^ adds no second transfer and changes no lifetime.
options.code:
tasks.add(^(copy task))
task.rename("Read chapter 2")

comparisons.note: Rust moves most values implicitly and uses clone for explicit duplication. Users often criticize clone because cost and identity semantics vary by type.
Swift added explicit copy for consuming contexts. Community discussion still warns that copying a class reference preserves identity rather than cloning the object.
C++ overloads copy and move through constructors and value categories. Experts gain control, but call-site behavior can be difficult to see.

recommendation.why: B makes the three ownership choices form a compact family: plain use, ^ transfer, and ^^ copy-then-transfer. Its meaning stays exact and auditable.

whyNot.reason: A is explicit but misses a concise lens for a frequent ownership boundary.
C is mechanically pure, but punctuation nesting makes the common case slower to scan and write.

recommendation.tradeoff: ^^ must be taught as one operation, not two stronger moves. Diagnostics should always expand it to “copy, then transfer” when copying fails.

hybrid.synthesis: B keeps A's copy word as the canonical general expression and C's exact lowering. ^^ is only the concise taking-argument lens.

harvest.aspect: The copy word is searchable and works outside calls.
harvest.use: Keep copy as the canonical general expression and diagnostic wording.

harvest.aspect: The ownership family becomes compact at call sites.
harvest.use: Use ^^ only where a taking parameter gives it an unambiguous context.

harvest.aspect: The operation order is formally explicit.
harvest.use: Define ^^ as exactly copy followed by transfer, with no alternate lowering.

decisions.title: How one package role holds its fields
decisions.gist: Choose the source shape for one package role.
decisions.lesson:
A package role is one part of a package description. Identity, sources, outputs, and policy are different roles.

This decision asks only how one role holds its fields. It does not decide where files live or how repeated fields combine. The field values remain ordinary typed Jet values, including `Type.{...}` and inferred `.{...}`.
decisions.story: Maya starts Greeter with a name and version. Later she adds sources and outputs. Each part should use the same obvious container shape.
decisions.inWild: Greeter needs identity, sources, outputs, and policy. A reader should spot each role and know where its fields begin and end.

options.name: Typed role field
options.detail: A role is a named field whose expected type supplies the record type. The user writes only the role name and its fields.
options.technical: Each package schema field has a fixed role type. Its `.{...}` body uses existing expected-type construction and rejects unknown fields.

options.name: Named role block
options.detail: A role name opens a body directly. The package schema determines which fields are legal inside that body.
options.technical: Role blocks are package-only declarations. They lower to the same typed role value used by package checking.

options.name: Explicit typed binding
options.detail: Each role is an ordinary binding with its full type. This is explicit, but every package repeats names already known from the role.
options.technical: Role discovery uses the binding's resolved type. A package rejects two bindings that claim the same unique role.

comparisons.note: CUE uses typed fields and lets context supply constraints without repeating a constructor name.
NixOS uses named option paths, but the surrounding schema is often visible only through tools.

recommendation.why: The role name stays visible while expected-type construction removes a repeated type name. It reuses Jet's existing record model instead of creating package-only bodies.

whyNot.reason: The block reads cleanly, but it adds a second way to construct the same typed role value.
The full type is precise, but repeating `identity` and `Package.Identity` adds no information inside a checked package schema.

recommendation.tradeoff: Readers must know that the package schema supplies the type. Exact type information remains available through hover, completion, and inspection.

hybrid.synthesis: Use a typed role field as source truth. Show its full type on demand, and format each role as a clear visual section.

harvest.use: Keep inferred `.{...}` as the written form.
Formatter and editor folding give each role a clear section boundary.
Inspection expands the field to `Package.Identity` or the matching role type.

decisions.title: How one package output is written
decisions.gist: Choose one source shape for every kind of package output.
decisions.lesson:
An output is something a package builds or exposes, such as an executable, library, or service. Every output has a kind and kind-specific fields.

This decision chooses one output representation. It does not choose where outputs are stored, how aliases work, or how entry functions are linked.
decisions.story: Greeter begins as one executable. Maya later adds a library and service. Each new output should follow the first output's shape.
decisions.inWild: Greeter needs an executable named `greeter`, a reusable library, and an HTTP service built from the same package.

options.name: Output type variants
options.detail: Every output is a case of one `Output` type. Expected-type inference removes the repeated `Output` name inside an output collection.
options.technical: `Output` is a closed sum type. Each variant carries a checked record payload and lowers to one package-graph output node.

options.name: Typed output declaration
options.detail: Each output is a named declaration whose type states its kind. The name is not repeated inside the body.
options.technical: An `output` declaration creates a stable package-graph node. Its declared type selects a closed output schema.

options.name: Typed output binding
options.detail: Each output is an ordinary binding of the `Output` type. The right side uses the existing expected-type variant form.
options.technical: A binding becomes a package output only when the package output collection references it. No `Output.Executable` subtype is invented.

comparisons.note: Rust uses one enum with typed payloads for a closed family of alternatives.
comparisons.code: enum Output { Executable { entry: Fn }, Library { ... } }

comparisons.note: Bazel uses a different rule call for each target kind and names each target inside that call.

recommendation.why: A package output is data in a closed output family. Variants preserve that fact, reuse Jet inference, and avoid adding one declaration grammar per build domain.

whyNot.reason: Declarations give outputs strong visual identity, but they create a package-only declaration for values already modeled by one type.
Ordinary bindings are uniform, but names and full subtype paths repeat information the output payload already carries.

recommendation.tradeoff: The output name remains one payload field. Keyed inspection can present it as graph identity without inventing another source representation.

hybrid.synthesis: Use `Output` variants as source truth. Tools present each variant as a named graph node and allow full type expansion on demand.

harvest.use: Keep one sum type with inferred variant names.
Index each output by its checked `name` field in tools and diagnostics.
Inspection expands `.Executable` to `Output.Executable` when requested.

decisions.title: One grammar for CLI subcommands, and fixing the spec mismatch
decisions.gist: The CLI has six shapes for a subcommand, and the shipped binary does not match its own spec: the spec says jet inspect dossier, the binary requires jet dossier. This decides one grammar and which side to align.
decisions.lesson: This is two things at once: pick a consistent subcommand grammar, and fix a real mismatch where the code and the spec disagree today.
decisions.story: A developer reads the docs and runs jet inspect dossier. It fails. The working command is jet dossier. The dispatch code even quotes the doc form in a comment one line above the flat command it actually implements.
decisions.inWild:
Today the shipped binary uses several shapes:

    jet fmt                 // bare verb
    jet trust list          // noun then verb
    jet os vm prove <host>  // noun then noun then verb
    jet dossier             // flat, but the spec says: jet inspect dossier

jet os, jet trust, and jet hangar already group by noun; the inspect and registry families do not.

options.name: Group by noun, and make the binary match the spec
options.detail: Adopt noun-then-verb for tool families, so it becomes jet inspect dossier and jet registry publish. Implement those groups so the binary matches the spec it already documents.

options.name: Keep everything flat, and fix the spec to match
options.detail: Keep jet dossier and jet publish as flat verbs, and correct the spec so it stops promising a grouping the binary does not have. Less typing, but flat does not scale as verbs grow.
options.code: jet dossier   jet publish   jet schema   // flat, spec updated to match

options.name: Leave as-is
options.detail: Keep the six shapes and the spec mismatch. No work, but the docs keep pointing at commands the binary does not have.
options.code: jet dossier   // spec still says jet inspect dossier; mismatch remains

recommendation.why: jet os, jet trust, and jet hangar already group by noun, so grouping the inspect and registry families matches what the CLI mostly does. It also makes the binary match the spec it already ships.
recommendation.tradeoff: Grouped commands are a little longer to type than flat ones. Core everyday verbs (build, run, test, fmt) stay flat, so the extra length only applies to the grouped tool families.

whyNot.reason: Flat is shorter but disagrees with the noun grouping jet os and jet trust already use, and it does not scale as tool verbs grow.
Leaving it keeps the docs pointing at commands that do not exist, which is a real bug, not just an inconsistency.

hybrid.synthesis: A applies B's honesty (code and spec must agree) but aligns to the noun grouping the CLI already uses in most places, rather than flattening everything.

harvest.aspect: Group by noun, code matches spec
harvest.use: The chosen grammar.
Kept: A also closes the mismatch, just toward grouping.
Not kept; the mismatch is a bug worth fixing.

decisions.title: What owns the root command's input types?
decisions.gist: Choose the single source of truth for inputs to the `fn run` command.
decisions.lesson:
A command turns shell text into typed Jet values. One place must own each input's name, type, default, and validation.

Jet already derives the root command from `fn run(args: T)`. This ballot explicitly reopens only where that root input schema lives; it keeps `fn run` as the entry convention. Field mapping and subcommands remain separate.
decisions.story: Maya turns Greeter into a command with `name` and `language` inputs. She later changes `language` to an enum and expects every tool to agree.
decisions.inWild: Greeter needs typed inputs, defaults, errors, help text, shell completion, and direct calls from tests.

options.name: Entry parameter type
options.detail: The parameter type of `fn run` owns command inputs. Fields provide names, types, defaults, and validation once.
options.technical: The compiler derives one command schema from the resolved struct or enum type and lowers parsing through the existing Core arguments engine.

options.name: Command value
options.detail: One root `Command` value owns the external schema and invokes `fn run`. The value and function adapter may repeat input information.
options.technical: The command value stores typed parser nodes and a callable adapter. Sema verifies the adapter accepts the parsed values.

options.name: Command declaration
options.detail: A dedicated root command declaration owns shell inputs and calls `fn run`. It scans clearly, but introduces a second signature language.
options.technical: Command parameters lower to a generated struct and adapter function. Generated names never enter the user's namespace.

comparisons.note: Typer derives command inputs from function annotations and defaults.
comparisons.code: def main(name: str, language: Language = Language.english): ...

comparisons.note: Clap derives a parser from a typed struct, then passes that value to application code.

recommendation.why: The current Jet entry remains an ordinary function, and one type drives parsing, direct calls, tests, help, and completion. Input types never drift between layers.

whyNot.reason: Command values compose, but they repeat function inputs or require an adapter that can drift from application intent.
A declaration reads clearly, but it creates a second parameter system beside functions and generated hidden types.

recommendation.tradeoff: Advanced shell details cannot all fit in ordinary field types. The separate input-mapping decision provides explicit control without moving type ownership.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep the entry parameter type as truth. Generate a typed command value and render a command declaration view for tools and documentation.

harvest.use: Derive every command consumer from the entry parameter.
Expose the generated command schema through Core and inspection.
Render a command-shaped documentation and audit view.

decisions.comment: Providing a type should be optional. just using fn run() {...} should be perfectly valid

decisions.title: Where should complete package merge history be stored?
decisions.gist: Choose the primary artifact that stores every successful contribution and replacement edge.
decisions.lesson:
This ballot holds retained evidence fixed. Every option keeps the final value, every successful contributor, every deliberate replacement, source spans, and value hashes. Failed conflicts remain in diagnostics because no package artifact is produced.

The only choice is where the complete successful history lives. Human views and signatures can be generated from any option.
decisions.story: Greeter builds differently in release. Maya asks why. The answer should identify the file, workspace default, and override that produced the final setting.
decisions.inWild: Greeter combines workspace policy, package roles, provider metadata, and one release override before producing a locked build.

options.name: History inside the package lock
options.detail: The lock stores field history beside the resolved package graph. Copies remain self-explaining, and inspection needs no second artifact.
options.technical: Semantic paths in the lock map to ordered provenance edges with source spans, operation kind, input value hash, and final value hash.
options.code:
$ jet inspect package Greeter --why policy.optimization
.Speed
  default  workspace.jet:18
  override release.jet:4

options.name: Content-addressed history bundle
options.detail: The lock stores one hash pointing to a complete immutable history bundle. Many builds can share it, but copied locks need the bundle to explain themselves.
options.technical: The lock stores a Merkle root. The addressed bundle contains every normalized contribution and field edge; signatures remain optional wrappers.
options.code:
$ jet inspect receipt Greeter
history bundle: 7d9c...
contributors: 14
status: complete

options.name: Append-only merge log
options.detail: The lock keeps the final graph and points into one ordered merge log. Streaming audits are simple, but ordinary inspection must join two artifacts.
options.technical: Each build stores final leaf pointers into an append-only event stream keyed by semantic field path and input hash.
options.code:
$ jet inspect package Greeter --why policy.optimization
.Speed from release.jet:4
  history: build/merge.log#event-18

comparisons.note: Nix can explain derivation inputs, while module-value provenance often requires tracing definitions separately.
Managed fields retain which actor owns each field, supporting conflict reports and audits.

recommendation.why: Keeping history inside the lock makes every resolved package self-explaining. The same edges can generate signed receipts and append-only audit events.

whyNot.reason: A shared bundle is compact, but a lock copied without its addressed history loses local explanation.
A log supports streaming audits, but ordinary field inspection depends on a second artifact and event replay.

recommendation.tradeoff: Locks store more edges. History is bounded to successful package inputs and earns portable explanation, reproducibility, and audit evidence.

hybrid.synthesis: Store complete field history in the lock. Derive a content hash, signed receipt, and append-only audit stream from that one source.

harvest.use: Keep complete history beside the final graph.
Hash the embedded history and emit portable receipt bundles.
Stream the same retained edges without making the log the only copy.

decisions.title: What must every interface lens share?
decisions.gist: Choose how much typed contract stays identical across command, web, GUI, and tool boundaries.
decisions.lesson:
A lens maps an external protocol onto application code. Shell text, HTTP requests, GUI events, and tool calls carry different transport facts.

This ballot decides only what all lenses must share. Authentication, streaming, cancellation, versioning, and source spelling remain separate boundary choices. Every option still calls the same application behavior.
decisions.story: Greeter's `greet` function begins as a command. Maya later exposes the same operation over HTTP and as an agent tool without maintaining three schemas.
decisions.inWild:
fn greet(request: GreetingRequest) -> Greeting ? GreetError { ... }

CLI, HTTP, GUI, and tool boundaries all reach this behavior.

options.name: The exact callable contract
options.detail: Every lens preserves the same application input, output, failure, effects, and function identity. A lens may only parse or render transport data.
options.technical: Boundary mapping must normalize into `GreetingRequest` and project `Greeting` or `GreetError`. Policy may narrow access but cannot change the callable contract.
options.code:
CLI  -> GreetingRequest -> greet -> Greeting | GreetError
HTTP -> GreetingRequest -> greet -> Greeting | GreetError
GUI  -> GreetingRequest -> greet -> Greeting | GreetError
Tool -> GreetingRequest -> greet -> Greeting | GreetError

options.name: Shared domain request and result
options.detail: Every lens shares application request and result types. Each boundary may own extra typed failures, authentication, streaming, and cancellation before or after the call.
options.technical: Adapters must call `greet(GreetingRequest)`. Their external contracts may wrap its result with boundary-specific outcomes.
options.code:
CLI  -> GreetingRequest -> greet -> Greeting | GreetError | CliError
HTTP -> GreetingRequest -> greet -> Greeting | GreetError | HttpError
GUI  -> GreetingRequest -> greet -> Greeting | GreetError | UiError

options.name: Separate interface contracts
options.detail: Each boundary owns its full public input, output, failure, and effect contract. Checked adapters translate those contracts into the shared application function.
options.technical: Each adapter proves a conversion into `GreetingRequest` and a mapping from application outcomes. Interface contracts may evolve independently.
options.code:
CLI  -> CliGreetingArgs -> adapter -> greet
HTTP -> HttpGreetingBody -> adapter -> greet
GUI  -> GreetingForm -> adapter -> greet
Tool -> GreetingToolInput -> adapter -> greet

comparisons.note: WebAssembly Interface Types defines one typed function contract that several component runtimes can carry.
Ballerina gives network resources first-class syntax tied to typed functions.
comparisons.code: resource function post greet(Request req) returns Greeting

recommendation.why: Exact sharing makes one function contract the complete source of behavior truth. Transport policy stays visible around it and cannot quietly change failure or authority.

whyNot.reason: Boundary failures are real, but adding them to each callable view makes the same operation appear to have several public result contracts.
Separate contracts fit each protocol perfectly, but repeat application shapes and weaken one-operation reasoning.

recommendation.tradeoff: Transport-specific failures and policies must live around the shared callable instead of changing it. That boundary remains explicit and separately typed.

hybrid.synthesis: Require the exact application contract in every lens. Model authentication, cancellation, streaming, and transport failures as typed boundary layers around that contract.

harvest.use: Keep input, output, failure, effects, and identity identical.
Place protocol failures and policy in checked layers around the call.

harvest.aspect: Protocols may need distinct wire shapes
harvest.use: Allow typed parsing adapters without letting wire types replace the application contract.

decisions.title: What is the source of truth for the development environment?
decisions.gist: Choose whether local shells, tasks, checks, and CI use one typed environment or separate setup recipes.
decisions.lesson:
A development environment is the tools and services needed to work on a package. It may include Jet, Git, a formatter, a database, and environment variables.

The common failure is drift. A shell setup works locally while CI uses different tools. Another failure is invisible shell mutation through startup scripts.

Jet can model the environment as ordinary typed package data. A shell, task, editor, or CI job then becomes a projection of the same value. Beginners run jet dev. Experts inspect exact tool versions, services, variables, and host changes.
decisions.story: A student clones the todo project on a new laptop. One command should provide the compiler and test database. The same setup must run in the course grader.
decisions.inWild:
git clone todo
cd todo
jet dev

jet test

options.name: Typed environment output
options.detail: The package graph contains an Environment value. jet dev, tasks, editors, and CI consume that same value. Shell commands are generated views, not a second source of truth.
options.technical: Environment contains tools, services, variables, paths, and allowed host capabilities. Every consumer receives its semantic hash. Mutating hooks require explicit audited actions.

options.name: Shell setup recipe
options.detail: The package provides commands to run when entering and leaving a shell. It supports any tool quickly, but behavior is imperative and can differ across shells and operating systems.
options.technical: Hooks run with declared capabilities but remain ordered command actions. CI must execute the same recipe inside its own runner image.

options.name: Separate environment file
options.detail: env.jet owns development setup apart from package outputs. The separation is easy to find, but build, test, and environment graphs can drift or repeat dependencies.
options.technical: env.jet resolves through the same lock receipt but has a distinct root value. Cross-root duplication is diagnosed, not automatically unified.

comparisons.note: Nix devShells can pin complete environments. Users value reproducibility but often repeat per-system keys and package lists across outputs.
comparisons.code: devShells.x86_64-linux.default = pkgs.mkShell { packages = [ jet git sqlite ]; };

comparisons.note: devenv adds services, tasks, and friendly configuration over Nix. Shell hooks remain a common escape hatch with less visible effects.
Devbox gives a simple package list and scripts. Users like onboarding, while application dependencies and development tools can still live in separate files.

recommendation.why: A makes local work, editors, tasks, and CI projections of one checked value. Beginners get one command while experts can audit the exact environment graph.

whyNot.reason: B handles arbitrary setup, but ordered shell mutation hides state and weakens reproducibility across platforms.
C is easy to locate, but it creates a second graph that can repeat or contradict package requirements.

recommendation.tradeoff: A must model tools and services precisely. Truly imperative setup remains possible only as an explicit, capability-scoped action in the same graph.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps C's discoverable environment view and B's escape hatch. Both lower into one typed graph with visible capabilities and one semantic hash.

harvest.aspect: Every consumer uses one environment value.
harvest.use: Make Environment a typed package output.

harvest.aspect: Some setup genuinely requires an action.
harvest.use: Allow explicit audited actions inside the Environment value.

harvest.aspect: Users need one obvious place to inspect development setup.
harvest.use: Provide a generated env view without making it a second source.

decisions.title: What unique job should the pipe family own?
decisions.gist: Choose a job that dot chaining cannot already do.
decisions.lesson:
Dot chaining starts with a value and calls methods now. A generic value pipe repeats that job with different punctuation. Jet should not add a second spelling for the same operation.

A pipe becomes useful when it describes structure rather than one immediate call. It can compose functions, connect incremental streams, or remain limited to alternatives in patterns. Each choice gives the bar family one predictable idea.

This vote chooses the pipe family's job. Later ballots may choose small variations inside that job. They may not turn it into a bag of unrelated operators.
decisions.story: A class reads todo items from text. Students already know functions. They want to combine three small functions once and reuse the resulting flow in several exercises.

options.name: Compose functions
options.detail: |> joins compatible functions into one ordinary function value. Calling that function runs the stages. Dot chaining still invokes methods immediately. The operator never threads a value into an argument slot.
options.technical: a |> b has ordinary type fn(A)->C when a: fn(A)->B and b: fn(B)->C. Existing function-type rules determine effects and ownership. No new Flow type is chosen here.

options.name: Connect incremental streams
options.detail: | connects a stream source, stream transform, and stream sink. Values move incrementally with backpressure. It never applies an ordinary function or replaces dot calls.
options.technical: Both operands must implement closed StreamSource, StreamTransform, or StreamSink contracts. The result is an ordinary StreamPlan value. Buffering and scheduling remain separate decisions.
options.code:
task_stream :: file.lines() | parse_tasks | save_tasks
task_stream.run()?

parse("one task") // ordinary function call stays ordinary

options.name: Alternatives only
options.detail: | keeps its current meaning: peer alternatives inside patterns and choices. Jet adds no general flow operator. Reusable flows use ordinary functions and named composition helpers.
options.technical: Single | remains legal only in alternative-list grammar. |> and other bar operators stay unassigned.

comparisons.note: Elixir's |> threads a value into the first argument. It reads well, but then and tap were added for cases that do not fit that slot.
F# has forward, backward, tuple, and composition operators. Users value flow, while the growing operator family raises learning and debugging costs.
A shell pipe connects reusable processes through one stream contract. Its strength is composition and inspection, not alternate method-call spelling.

recommendation.why: A gives |> a capability dots lack: composing functions before any input exists. The result is an ordinary function, so it adds no second call model.

whyNot.reason: B gives pipes strong runtime meaning, but it serves stream programs rather than ordinary function composition taught across the language.
C is minimal, but it leaves repeated cross-domain workflows without a direct, auditable representation.

recommendation.tradeoff: A needs clear diagnostics for incompatible function inputs and outputs. Jet must resist adding reverse, tap, error, async, and mutation pipe variants.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps one base operation: function composition. It borrows B's stage diagnostics and C's restraint. Pattern | remains context-distinct and |> receives no unrelated variants.

harvest.aspect: Function sequences become named values rather than copied call chains.
harvest.use: Keep |> as ordinary function composition.

harvest.aspect: Connected stages need clear boundary and backpressure diagnostics.
harvest.use: Report the exact stage boundary when composed function types do not match; stream planning stays a library feature.

harvest.aspect: The bar family should stay small and predictable.
harvest.use: Keep pattern | and flow |> only; reject unrelated convenience variants.

decisions.title: What high-level rule separates @ from #?
decisions.gist: Choose a boundary users can predict without knowing compiler internals.
decisions.lesson:
A prefix marker says that nearby code has an extra rule. The confusing part is not the glyph. It is deciding which rule belongs to which glyph.

A usable boundary must be visible from source. “Attribute versus compiler instruction” fails because readers must know implementation details. Two better boundaries are grammatical extent and authority. Extent asks whether a rule attaches to one declaration or wraps a brace scope. Authority asks whether the rule merely checks code or grants power.

This vote chooses the marker system only. If it frees #, D-SHAPE-HASH1 separately decides whether # names build facts, remains reserved, or serves another single job. Effect spelling remains a separate vote.
decisions.story: A student reads a file-writing example. She should know which marker checks a function and which marker changes what code inside braces may do.

options.name: One applied-rule marker
options.detail: @ means “apply this named rule to the next declaration, expression, or brace scope.” The braces reveal extent. The rule name reveals behavior. # is freed but receives no meaning in this vote.
options.technical: Every current @ and # directive migrates to a typed Rule application. A rule declares legal attachment targets. @Unsafe remains the sole user-written unsafe gate.

options.name: Checks use @, power uses #
options.detail: @ may inspect or restrict code but never grant authority. # always grants or changes authority inside visible braces. Readers can ask one question: “Can this code now do more?”
options.technical: Declaration contracts and restrictions use @. Capability grants, unsafe gates, transaction authority, and scoped compiler authority use # with braces. Attached # forms are forbidden.

options.name: Words for power, @ for rules
options.detail: @ applies optional named rules. Built-in power boundaries use plain reserved words followed by braces. This makes dangerous regions loud, while normal extension rules keep one marker. # is freed.
options.technical: unsafe, transact, and grant become closed language constructs. User-defined rules cannot grant authority. This creates a deliberate grammar distinction for authority boundaries.

comparisons.note: Rust uses attributes for metadata and words such as unsafe for semantic power. Users can recognize unsafe without understanding compiler phases.
C# attributes share one bracket form, while checked, unsafe, and lock are language scopes. The boundary follows semantic weight.
Elixir uses @ for module attributes and macros for code transformation. Its flexibility is powerful, but macro behavior can be hard to predict locally.

recommendation.why: A gives one stable reading rule: @ applies a named rule, and braces show its reach. Users never classify compiler internals or guess whether power counts as an attribute.

whyNot.reason: B has a clear authority test, but some rules both restrict and grant, so edge cases would reopen the same classification problem.
C makes dangerous scopes obvious, but every new power boundary expands the reserved-word set and closes extension points.

recommendation.tradeoff: A makes safety depend on strong rule names and diagnostics. Jet should visually emphasize audited rules and show their authority in hover and exact views.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps one grammar and borrows B's authority metadata plus C's loud presentation. Rules remain typed, and dangerous rules receive mandatory brace scopes and editor emphasis.

harvest.aspect: One marker is predictable across declaration and scope rules.
harvest.use: Keep @ as the only rule application syntax.

harvest.aspect: Authority changes deserve a machine-checkable distinction.
harvest.use: Store grants and restrictions in each Rule type and expose them in audit output.

harvest.aspect: Dangerous regions should be visually unmistakable.
harvest.use: Require braces, reasons, and strong diagnostics for authority-bearing rules.

decisions.title: Casing for optional and result values
decisions.gist: A present optional is Val(x) and an absent one is None, both capitalized. A successful result is ok(v) and a failure is err(e), both lowercase. Same job, opposite casing. This decides one casing for both.
decisions.lesson: This is a small, wide change: it touches almost every program, because optionals and results are everywhere. It is split into its own ballot for that reason.
decisions.story: A developer learns that a present value is Val(x), capitalized. They then handle a result and write Ok(v), capitalized to match, and it fails: the real spelling is lowercase ok(v). The two most common wrapper types disagree on capitalization.
decisions.inWild:
Today:

    x: Int? = Val(5)      // present optional, capitalized
    y: Int? = None        // absent, capitalized
    r = ok(value)         // success result, lowercase
    e = err("bad input")  // failure, lowercase

options.name: Both as capitalized choices on their type
options.detail: Write Option.Some(x)/Option.None and Result.Ok(v)/Result.Err(e), or the leading-dot short forms .Some/.Ok. Optionals and results then read the same way, as choices of a type.
options.code:
x: Int?   = .Some(5)
y: Int?   = .None
r: T ? E  = .Ok(value)
e: T ? E  = .Err("bad input")

options.name: Leave as-is
options.detail: Keep Val/None capitalized and ok/err lowercase. No wide migration, but the casing stays a coin flip for anyone guessing one from the other.
options.code: Val(5)  None  ok(value)  err("bad input")   // unchanged

options.name: Make both lowercase
options.detail: Keep the short calls but lowercase all four: val/none/ok/err. Less migration than A, but breaks the rule that a type's choices are capitalized like other enum choices.
options.code: val(5)  none  ok(value)  err("bad input")

recommendation.why: Optionals and results are both choice types, and Jet capitalizes a type's choices elsewhere. Writing them as .Some/.None/.Ok/.Err makes them match every other enum in the language.
recommendation.tradeoff: This edits nearly every file that uses an optional or a result, so it is the widest single change in this set. Teaching errors will map each old spelling to its replacement.

whyNot.reason: Leaving them keeps two of the most common types disagreeing on casing, which is a guess an expert gets wrong half the time.
Lowercasing all four makes them consistent with each other but inconsistent with every other enum choice in Jet.

hybrid.synthesis: A aligns the two types with the rest of the language rather than only with each other, which is what C would do.

harvest.use: The chosen form: capitalized .Some/.None/.Ok/.Err.
Not kept; the change is wide but mechanical with teaching errors.
Kept in A, but the casing chosen matches the rest of the language.

decisions.comment: But ratify "Val" instead of "Some"

decisions.title: Where does an explicit effect set live?
decisions.gist: Choose one signature shape for outside powers such as file, network, and clock access.
decisions.lesson:
An effect is an outside power a function may use, such as reading a file or using the network. Jet infers effects inside private code. Public APIs and course exercises can pin the allowed set.

Square brackets fit the effect set because it is a collection. The remaining question is where that collection belongs. It can decorate the return arrow, follow the result, or appear as an implicit input lane.

All options keep inference, open effect rows, prohibitions, and audit output. This vote changes presentation only. The same spelling must work in declarations, function values, trait methods, and callbacks.
decisions.story: A student writes load_task for a todo program. The signature should show that reading a file is different from adding two numbers.

options.name: Effects inside the arrow
options.detail: The arrow becomes -[Effects]->. Readers see the allowed outside powers on the path from inputs to result. Pure functions keep the ordinary -> arrow.
options.technical: Closed rows use -[File]->. Open rows use -[File, ..E]->. Empty inferred or explicitly pure rows render as ->.
options.code:
fn load_task(number: Int) -[File]-> Task
formatter: fn(Task) -[Log, ..E]-> Text
fn add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int

options.name: Effects after the result
options.detail: The normal arrow always introduces the result. A ! followed by a collection adds the allowed effects. This keeps return types visually stable and makes effectful signatures loud.
options.technical: Function types are Result ! [EffectRow]. ! has no call or error-propagation meaning. Empty effect rows omit the suffix.
options.code:
fn load_task(number: Int) -> Task ! [File]
formatter: fn(Task) -> Text ! [Log, ..E]
fn add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int

options.name: Effects as an input lane
options.detail: Effects appear as an implicit input collection before a | inside the parameter group. This models power as compiler-supplied input while keeping ordinary arguments separate.
options.technical: The left input lane is an effect row, not runtime parameters. Calls do not pass these values. Exact and audit views may materialize authority flow without changing the ABI.
options.code:
fn load_task([File] | number: Int) -> Task
formatter: fn([Log, ..E] | Task) -> Text
fn add([] | a: Int, b: Int) -> Int

comparisons.note: Koka places an inferred effect row between parameters and result. Open rows compose well, although unfamiliar angle syntax raises the learning cost.
Effect-oriented languages put capabilities in function types and handlers. Users gain precise composition but often face dense signatures.
Java checked exceptions repeat declarations through call chains. Scala's CanThrow redesign explicitly targets that inflexibility and boilerplate.

recommendation.why: A gives effects a precise visual home without pretending they are runtime arguments or part of the result. The unchanged -> keeps pure code quiet.

whyNot.reason: B is easy to append, but ! already carries strong error and negation expectations in many languages.
C exposes the capability model elegantly, but empty lanes and callback parameter groups become visually heavier.

recommendation.tradeoff: Decorated arrows are new punctuation. Tooling must render them consistently and explain open rows without requiring effect-system vocabulary.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps the ordinary result arrow from B and the authority-flow model from C. Exact views can show capability inputs while source uses one decorated arrow.

harvest.aspect: Effects visibly sit between input and output.
harvest.use: Keep -[Effects]-> as the source spelling.

harvest.aspect: Pure return syntax should remain ordinary.
harvest.use: Use plain -> when the visible row is empty.

harvest.aspect: Effects are semantically supplied authority, not vague labels.
harvest.use: Expose the capability-flow lowering in exact and enterprise audit views.

decisions.comment: But you must use --[Effects]-> and keep -> ex. fn read_file() --[File.Read]-> Str or fn hello() -> Str

decisions.title: May expected type shorten Type.new to .new?
decisions.gist: Keep .new and choose whether Jet may infer its type from context.
decisions.lesson:
.new stays Jet's name for fresh hidden state. This vote does not rename it. It asks whether the type name may be omitted when the expected type is already exact.

Jet already allows .Active when context proves the enum type and .{...} when context proves a record type. The same rule could apply to .new(...). Beginners avoid repetition. Experts can write Stack<Int>.new(...) whenever they want to pin the type.

Inference must never guess among several types. If the annotation, parameter, or return type does not identify one type, Jet asks for the qualifier.
decisions.story: A class implements a Stack. The variable and function signatures already state Stack<Int>. Students should not repeat that type unless they want to emphasize it.

options.name: Infer the receiver
options.detail: Allow .new(...) only when context proves one result type. Users may always keep Type.new(...) for emphasis. Ambiguous code gets a direct request for the missing type.
options.technical: Expected-type lookup resolves .new as a static member of one known nominal type. It does not search every type or rank candidates.
options.code:
numbers: Stack<Int> :: .new(capacity: 20)
return .new(capacity: 20) // return type is Stack<Int>

x :: .new() // error: name the type

options.name: Always name the type
options.detail: Every fresh-state call remains Type.new(...). Readers never need surrounding context, but annotations and constructor calls repeat the same type.
options.technical: Static member lookup always requires an explicit nominal receiver. Expected types do not participate in member resolution.
options.code:
numbers: Stack<Int> :: Stack<Int>.new(capacity: 20)
return Stack<Int>.new(capacity: 20)

options.name: Infer only at typed boundaries
options.detail: Allow .new(...) in an explicitly typed binding or return. Function arguments and broader expression contexts still require Type.new(...). The rule stays local but creates two classes of expected type.
options.technical: Contextual static-member lookup is enabled only by a written binding type or enclosing function return type. Parameter types do not enable it.

comparisons.note: Swift commonly omits a contextual type before enum cases and some initializers. Users value brevity, while ambiguous overloads produce difficult errors.
Kotlin infers generic arguments but still names constructors. The result is familiar, though type names often repeat around factories.
Zig uses contextual enum and anonymous aggregate literals. The rule is local: omission works only when the destination type is known.

recommendation.why: A extends Jet's existing contextual-dot rule instead of inventing a special constructor keyword. Beginners omit repetition; experts restore the full receiver anywhere.

whyNot.reason: B is locally explicit, but it repeats information already fixed by annotations and parameter types.
C keeps .new, but users must remember why a typed return allows inference while an equally exact parameter does not.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires a clear ambiguity diagnostic. The compiler must never search broadly or select a type by ranking candidates.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps B's fully qualified expert spelling and C's low ceremony. It achieves both through Jet's existing contextual-dot mechanism.

harvest.aspect: One existing inference law covers enums, records, and fresh-state members.
harvest.use: Use exact expected-type lookup for .new.

harvest.aspect: A full type name makes audit intent unmistakable.
harvest.use: Keep Type.new as the explicit lens everywhere.

harvest.aspect: The shortest rule is safest at visibly typed boundaries.
harvest.use: Keep its requirement for one exact written or inferred destination, without limiting which exact contexts count.

decisions.title: How a runtime number becomes a Duration
decisions.gist: Choose the one spelling for building a duration from a number known only while the program runs.
decisions.lesson: Jet already has static unit literals such as `5s`. They remain unchanged. A runtime value cannot be joined to a suffix in source because its number arrives later. The code must name both the `Duration` type and the chosen unit. This ballot decides only that construction. Reading a duration in another unit is a separate choice.
decisions.story: Maya reads a signup timeout from a command-line argument and needs a checked `Duration` for the network request.
decisions.inWild:
timeout :: Duration.seconds(args.timeout_seconds)?
user :: register(signup, timeout: timeout)?

options.name: Type-owned unit constructor
options.detail: The result type and unit appear together. Completion on `Duration` lists every supported unit.
options.technical: Each unit member accepts supported numeric types and returns a fallible result when the value is out of range or not finite.
options.code: timeout :: Duration.seconds(args.timeout_seconds)?

options.name: Number-owned unit method
options.detail: The value leads, which reads naturally in calculations. Numeric completion gains time units alongside unrelated numeric operations.
options.technical: Unit methods are sealed extensions on numeric types and return `Duration`.
options.code: timeout :: args.timeout_seconds.seconds()?

options.name: Value plus unit
options.detail: One constructor accepts a number and enum unit. It is uniform but allows unit names that may not support the number's precision.
options.technical: `Duration(value, unit:)` validates the pair at runtime and has no implicit default unit.
options.code: timeout :: Duration(args.timeout_seconds, unit: .Seconds)?

comparisons.note: Numeric extension properties and functions create durations in named units.
`Duration` exposes type-owned static constructors such as seconds and milliseconds.

recommendation.why: `Duration.seconds(value)` names the result and unit before the runtime number and keeps discovery on one type.

whyNot.reason: Adding every quantity unit to numbers creates a large unrelated method surface.
A loose unit argument weakens per-unit typing and completion.

recommendation.tradeoff: The call is longer than a numeric extension. It stays explicit at the exact place where a runtime number gains physical meaning.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep static `5s` literals. Use type-owned unit constructors for runtime numbers. Keep every conversion checked and explicit.

harvest.aspect: Result and unit share one discovery home
harvest.use: Keep it directly.

harvest.aspect: The numeric value remains easy to follow
harvest.use: Place it as the sole constructor argument.
Give `Duration` one closed family of unit-named members.

decisions.title: How code asks for whole duration units
decisions.gist: Choose the call spelling for reading a duration as a checked whole number in one chosen unit.
decisions.lesson:
This ballot holds the result contract fixed. Every option returns a whole `Int`, truncates toward zero, and fails on range overflow.

The only choice is where the unit appears in the call. Static literals, runtime construction, fractional reading, and rounding policy are outside this vote.
decisions.story: Maya records signup latency in a metrics system that accepts whole milliseconds.
decisions.inWild:
elapsed_ms :: elapsed.in(.Milliseconds)?
metrics.record("signup_ms", elapsed_ms)

options.name: Value in unit
options.detail: One short method keeps the duration first and the requested unit explicit. The fixed result contract supplies the whole-number meaning.
options.technical: `in(unit)` returns `Int ? RangeError` under the held truncation rule.
options.code: elapsed_ms :: elapsed.in(.Milliseconds)?

options.name: Named method per unit
options.detail: The requested unit is part of the method name and easy to scan. Every supported unit adds another method.
options.technical: `in_milliseconds()` returns the same fixed `Int ? RangeError` contract.
options.code: elapsed_ms :: elapsed.in_milliseconds()?

options.name: Unit reads the value
options.detail: The unit namespace owns the operation, which groups unit tools together. The code begins with the requested unit instead of the duration being measured.
options.technical: `Milliseconds.in(duration)` returns the same fixed `Int ? RangeError` contract.
options.code: elapsed_ms :: Milliseconds.in(elapsed)?

comparisons.note: Duration offers `inWholeMilliseconds` and conversion functions for units.
Duration exposes components rather than pretending unit conversion changes the underlying duration.

recommendation.why: `elapsed.in(.Milliseconds)` follows the value being measured and keeps every unit in one closed argument list.

whyNot.reason: One method per unit creates a large family of near-identical names.
Leading with the unit makes value flow less direct and scatters one operation across unit namespaces.

recommendation.tradeoff: The method name alone does not say whole-number. The fixed return type and documentation carry that one settled contract.

hybrid.synthesis: Use `duration.in(unit)` for the fixed checked whole-number reading. Keep units closed and discoverable through completion.

harvest.use: Keep it directly.
Enum completion lists them without multiplying methods.
Accept only the closed `DurationUnit` enum, not strings.

decisions.title: When generic constructor arguments disappear
decisions.gist: Choose how users handle a generic type argument already fixed by constructor input.
decisions.lesson: A generic wrapper such as `Shared<Greeter>` needs an inner type. The value passed to its constructor may already prove that type. Repeating `Greeter` adds noise but can help when inference has several answers. Good inference removes only facts with one answer. It must never guess. Experts still need a direct spelling for ambiguous or intentionally widened types.
decisions.story: Maya shares a `Greeter` between tasks. The compiler already knows the value is a `Greeter`, so she wants no repeated type name.
decisions.inWild:
shared :: Shared.new(greeter)
shared.read(g => print(g.greet("Ada")))

options.name: Infer when unique
options.detail: The constructor omits generic arguments when inputs fix one answer. Ambiguity requires the full type.
options.technical: Inference is one-way from explicit constructor inputs and expected result type. It never searches implementations.
options.code:
shared :: Shared.new(greeter)
empty :: Shared<[User]>.new([])

options.name: Always write the type
options.detail: Every call shows its complete generic result. This maximizes local detail but repeats obvious types throughout ordinary code.
options.technical: A missing generic argument is always an error, even when uniquely determined.
options.code: shared :: Shared<Greeter>.new(greeter)

options.name: Write a visible hole
options.detail: An underscore tells readers that inference occurred. It keeps ceremony while making hidden work explicit.
options.technical: Each `_` creates one inference variable that must have a unique solution before the statement ends.
options.code: shared :: Shared<_>.new(greeter)

comparisons.note: Implicit arguments become holes and unification fills them when enough information exists.
The placeholder `_` may request inference in some generic positions.

recommendation.why: Unique inference removes repetition while a full type remains available exactly when meaning is not fixed.

whyNot.reason: It repeats information the compiler and reader already have.
A visible hole adds punctuation without adding a choice or guarantee.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some result types are not printed in source. Editor expansion and ambiguity errors preserve auditability.

hybrid.synthesis: Infer only from local, explicit facts. Accept a full generic type whenever the user wants to pin or widen it. Reject ambiguity.

harvest.use: Keep it as the default.
Allow the full type in every inferred position.
Use editor expansion instead of source punctuation.

decisions.title: Meaning of public underscore names
decisions.gist: Decide whether a public underscore name is callable without becoming a compatibility promise.
