decisions.lesson: `pub` controls outside access. A leading underscore can separately mark a callable name as unsupported, or it can have no public-contract meaning. Soft-public means outside calls work with an unsuppressible warning, default docs and completion de-emphasize the name, and semantic-version checks permit its removal. Package-internal calls do not warn.
decisions.story: Lena exposes `_scan_token` so a debugger plugin can inspect malformed input. She later removes it in a minor release and needs publish checks to follow the contract callers were shown.
decisions.inWild: The proposal keeps one semantic support flag across docs, completion, policy, dossier, and semver. `pub(package)` remains the hard package-only boundary.

options.name: Soft-public
options.detail: A public `_name` remains callable with one unsuppressible outside warning and no minor-version compatibility promise.

options.name: All public is supported
options.detail: Every public name carries the same compatibility promise, including names beginning with underscore.

recommendation.why: Expert integrations can call a clearly unsupported hook while beginner discovery and semantic-version promises remain focused on supported API.

whyNot.reason: Authors must either make an expert hook a permanent supported promise or block all outside use.

recommendation.tradeoff: Intentional outside callers always retain a warning and must understand that callable does not mean supported.

decisions.title: How do I release a file or lock early?
decisions.gist: Choose the one visible way to end ownership before a long function ends.
decisions.lesson:
Jet already cleans up owned files, locks, sockets, and similar values when their scope ends. Cleanup runs on success, errors, panic, and cancellation.

Sometimes a resource is needed only at the beginning of a long function. A small block can end that ownership early and show the exact lifetime.

Finishing an archive or committing a transaction is different. Those are normal methods with normal result types. Automatic cleanup stays the safety net and never pretends a commit succeeded.
decisions.story: Dev reads a file and holds a cache lock for five lines, then performs a minute of CPU work. The scarce handles should be released before that work begins.

options.name: Use the smallest block
options.detail: The end of a normal block releases everything still owned inside it. The same rule covers files, locks, borrows, errors, and cancellation.
options.technical: No new close or early-drop operation is added. Jet keeps its existing automatic scope cleanup and existing `.drop(reason)` discard meaning.

options.name: Rust directly
options.detail: Host language: Rust. Scope exit cleans up automatically, while `drop(value)` consumes one value early. People love the predictable, zero-cost ownership model.
options.technical: Copy Rust destructor timing and its universal consuming drop function.

options.name: Add a universal `release` operation
options.detail: Write `release(^file)` wherever ownership should end. It is explicit, but adds a second lifetime rule beside normal scope cleanup.
options.technical: The operation only consumes. It never means flush, finish, commit, rollback, or graceful shutdown.
options.code:
file :: File.open(path)?
data :: file.read_all()?
release(^file)
analyze(data)

options.name: Go directly
options.detail: Host language: Go. `defer` places cleanup beside acquisition and runs it when the function returns. People love its small, visible rule.
options.technical: Add a deferred-action stack. A nested helper function is needed when release must happen before the surrounding function returns.

comparisons.note: The best direct ownership implementation. Rust is liked because cleanup timing follows visible scopes.
The best direct deferred-cleanup implementation. Go is liked for a tiny rule placed beside acquisition.

recommendation.why: A uses the cleanup rule Jet already has and shows the exact lifetime with ordinary structure. Nothing can forget to register cleanup or confuse release with commit.

whyNot.reason: Rust has the right model, but its `drop` name conflicts with Jet’s existing deliberate-discard word.
A universal release operation duplicates what a block already says and invites confusion with successful protocol completion.
Function-level defer often keeps resources alive longer than needed and adds repeated cleanup lines.

recommendation.tradeoff: Early release needs a small block. The block is useful because it makes the lifetime and all early-exit behavior obvious.

decisions.comment: But I want to support defer and have one consistent word for closing any type. Add new ballot to choose that word

decisions.title: How do I read a window without copying it?
decisions.gist: Choose the one visible operation for a safe read-only view into existing storage.
decisions.lesson:
A view reads part of an array, buffer, image, or other storage without copying it. The original value still owns the bytes.

Jet prevents the view from outliving its owner. It also prevents the owner from resizing or moving while the view still exists. Several read-only views may overlap safely.

The operation should be visible because a copy and a borrow have different cost and lifetime.
decisions.story: Inez parses two overlapping fields in a network packet. She wants zero-copy speed, but the returned parsed header should own its final data.
decisions.inWild:
bytes :: receive()?

copy :: bytes[0..16]                  // owned copy
header: View<Byte> :: bytes.view(0..16) // borrowed window
version :: bytes.view(4..8)           // overlapping read view is fine

parsed :: parse_header(header)?.to_owned()

bytes.push(0)
error: bytes cannot resize while header or version views it

consume(header)
consume(version)
bytes.push(0) // valid after the final view use

fn bad(local: [Byte]) -> View<Byte> { local.view() }
error: returned view would outlive local

// A custom storage owner uses the same operation.
tile :: image.view(x: 10..20, y: 30..40)

options.name: Ask the source with `.view`
options.detail: Use `source.view()` for everything or `source.view(range)` for a window. The owner is visible, and the result is always a read-only View.
options.technical: This replaces `.over(existing)` only for non-owning views. Type annotations check the result but never create a hidden borrow.

options.name: Swift directly
options.detail: Host language: Swift. Collections expose a safe Span over their storage. People love getting low-level speed without ordinary pointer code.
options.technical: Copy Swift Span’s lifetime tie to its source and bounds checks.

options.name: Construct with `View.over`
options.detail: Write `View<Byte>.over(bytes, range: ...)`. The view type is clear, but the source’s ability to lend storage is less obvious.
options.technical: Keep Jet’s current general `.over(existing)` constructor rule for views.
options.code: header :: View<Byte>.over(bytes, range: 0..16)

options.name: Let the type annotation borrow
options.detail: Writing `header: View<Byte>` automatically borrows the value on the right. It is short, but a type annotation silently changes ownership and cost.
options.technical: Jet inserts a borrow whenever the expected type is View.
options.code:
header: View<Byte> :: bytes[0..16]
// the annotation, not an operation, creates the borrow

comparisons.note: Swift Span is the clearest direct safe-view design. People like its clean collection surface and strong lifetime rule.
Rust slices are the strongest widely used lifetime-checked views. People value compile-time prevention of dangling and alias bugs.

recommendation.why: A reads naturally, makes the owner and borrow visible, and works for arrays, buffers, images, and third-party storage with one rule.

whyNot.reason: Swift supplies the safety model, but a property does not express ranges and multi-dimensional windows as clearly.
`View.over` is explicit, but makes the borrowed view type look responsible for storage owned elsewhere.
Hidden borrowing from a type annotation makes cost and lifetime harder to see.

recommendation.tradeoff: View types do not get a second constructor spelling. Storage owners provide the one `.view` operation instead.

decisions.title: Can normal code use `__name`?
decisions.gist: Choose whether double-underscore names belong to users or to Jet and its tools.
decisions.lesson:
Compilers and debuggers sometimes need hidden names. Reserving one clear spelling prevents a future Jet release from colliding with a user field that happens to use the same name.

Normal private fields already cover application state. Types can expose safe expert operations such as `debug_items()` or `restore(snapshot)` without exposing raw hidden storage.

This vote is separate from `_helper`. One underscore is about support. Two underscores are about who owns the spelling.
decisions.story: Sam’s stack type has private state. A future debugger also needs generated stack details. User code and tool code must never accidentally claim the same name.

options.name: Reserve every double underscore
options.detail: User declarations and access beginning with `__` are rejected. Jet, generated binders, debuggers, and serializers keep a collision-free space.
options.technical: The parser accepts the spelling only long enough to give a clear Jet error. Tool state is exposed through typed inspection channels, not raw source fields.
options.code:
struct Stack { __items: [Int] }
error: __items is reserved for Jet and its tools

stack.__items = repaired
error: normal code cannot access compiler-owned names

options.name: Python directly
options.detail: Host language: Python. Double-leading names are rewritten with the class name. People love deliberate reach-through for debugging, though the storage is not truly private.
options.technical: Copy Python-style name mangling for type fields.
options.code:
# Python
class Stack:
    def __init__(self): self.__items = []

stack._Stack__items = []  # deliberate reach-through

options.name: Type-owned hidden fields
options.detail: A type may declare `__items`, but only its own methods may use it. This adds another privacy level beside Jet’s normal private fields.
options.technical: Name checking gives the declaring type special access to double-underscore fields.

options.name: No special meaning
options.detail: Double underscores are ordinary names. Compiler data uses identities users cannot type. This is flexible, but user APIs can look like compiler hooks.
options.technical: Source names and generated identities live in separate internal tables. Style checks may warn about user double underscores.
options.code:
struct Stack { __items: [Int] }
// ordinary private field; no reserved spelling

comparisons.note: Python is the best-known double-underscore design. It is liked for transparent debugging, even though mangling is not privacy.
C++ reserves underscore patterns for the implementation. Toolchains value never colliding with user names.

recommendation.why: A gives Jet permanent room for generated and tool-owned state without adding another privacy system. Users keep normal private fields and safe typed methods.

whyNot.reason: Python solves inheritance collisions Jet does not have and intentionally leaves raw replacement reachable.
Type-owned hidden fields duplicate normal privacy without giving users a new safe capability.
No reservation works internally, but loses the strong promise that compiler-looking names are never user hooks.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users give up double-underscore spellings. Normal names already cover their needs, while the reservation prevents permanent future collisions.

decisions.title: What if two project parts touch the same thing?
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet combines safe additions, stops on disagreement, or lets file order choose.
decisions.lesson:
Splitting a project means two files may add to the same environment or machine. Adding different named packages is harmless. Setting two different ports for the same service is not.

Jet needs one answer that is easy to predict. Safe additions can combine. Repeated equal facts are fine. A real disagreement should stop with both source locations.

Experts still have full control: create the final value with a normal Jet function before adding it to the project.
decisions.story: Backend adds the API service. Local development wants the same service on another port. Rin needs Jet to explain the disagreement instead of silently choosing whichever file happened to load last.

options.name: Combine safe additions; stop on disagreement
options.detail: Different named items join together. Repeated equal facts are accepted. Unequal facts stop with a clear error showing both places.
options.technical: Single values must agree. Named collections combine by name. Sets combine their members. Ordered steps combine only when their type defines an order. Every result remembers where it came from.
options.code:
// These combine.
dev packages from part A: [api]
dev packages from part B: [debugger]
result: [api, debugger]

// These stop.
api.port from part A: 8080
api.port from part B: 3000
error shows both places

options.name: CUE directly
options.detail: Host language: CUE, implemented in Go. CUE combines files as facts and stops when concrete facts conflict. People love that file order never changes the answer.
options.technical: Jet projects would use CUE’s constraint-combining rules and error model.
options.code:
service: api: port: int
service: api: port: 8080
service: api: port: 3000
// conflict

options.name: GNU Guix directly
options.detail: Host language: Guile Scheme. Each service kind can write its own combine function. People love the freedom to create exactly the extension behavior they need.
options.technical: Every service type chooses how lists of extensions are combined and applied.
options.code:
(service-type
  (compose combine-api-configs)
  (extend extend-api-service))

options.name: Last file wins
options.detail: The later file replaces the earlier value. It is familiar and short, but moving or renaming a file can silently change a build or machine.
options.technical: Discovery order becomes part of project meaning.
options.code:
backend.jet: port 8080
local.jet: port 3000
result depends on which file loads last

options.name: The root combines everything by hand
options.detail: Parts never combine automatically. The root wires every list and setting. Control is obvious, but the root becomes a long import and merge document.
options.technical: Ordinary Jet code builds every final section from each part in a chosen order.

comparisons.note: The best direct order-independent combiner. CUE is liked because data, defaults, and validation use one readable form.
The best direct user-defined service extension system. Guile is liked because the full language remains available.
comparisons.code: service type chooses combine and extend

recommendation.why: A makes splitting safe and boring. Obvious additions combine, disagreements are impossible to miss, and experts resolve them with normal typed Jet code.

whyNot.reason: CUE has the right order-independent behavior, but importing its full constraint language would create a second meaning system.
Guix offers great freedom, but each service having different combine rules makes the whole project harder to predict.
Last-file-wins turns file layout into hidden behavior and makes changes unsafe to review.
Manual wiring is clear at first but recreates the import-tree and merge boilerplate this project should remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must define a simple combine rule for every project field. That rule pays for clear errors, safe refactors, and trustworthy explanations.

decisions.title: What should Jet remember and prove?
decisions.gist: Choose whether one readable record explains dependencies, builds, machine changes, and rollback.
decisions.lesson:
A lockfile usually remembers versions. That is not enough to explain a real build. The compiler, target, settings, permissions, source bytes, and chosen project branch also matter.

Jet can keep one receipt that connects those facts. Beginners see “built” or “switched.” Experts can open the same receipt to learn why something was chosen, rebuilt, or activated.

A build description and its output are kept separate. That lets Jet notice when the same work unexpectedly produces different bytes.
decisions.story: A security update moves PostgreSQL from 16.2 to 16.3. Rin wants a preview showing exactly what changes, then a machine generation that can be proved and rolled back.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet update postgres --dry-run
postgres 16.2 -> 16.3
2 receipt entries change
api and production image rebuild
412 other entries stay exactly locked

$ jet receipt systems.production
project: pulse
source inputs: exact
build tools: exact
target: aarch64-linux
actions: 6
outputs: 6 verified
activation checks: ready
previous generation: 43

$ jet os switch production
checks passed
activated generation 44
rollback available: jet os rollback production

$ jet explain --why-rebuilt packages.api
rebuilt because postgres changed from 16.2 to 16.3
compiler, target, source, and every other input stayed the same

// .jet/lock and receipts are generated state.
// The project source never repeats exact resolved facts by hand.

options.name: One receipt from dependency to rollback
options.detail: Jet records exact inputs, tools, target facts, work steps, outputs, machine checks, and the previous generation in one connected record.
options.technical: The receipt stores small reusable entries rather than copying the whole project for every build. It separately names planned work, produced bytes, and machine activation proof.
options.code:
receipt production@44
  postgres 16.3
  api build action sha256:aaa
  api output sha256:bbb
  image output sha256:ccc
  activation proof passed
  parent generation 43

options.name: GNU Guix directly
options.detail: Host language: Guile Scheme. Guix uses build descriptions, store paths, profiles, and generations. People love reproducible time travel and reliable operating-system rollback.
options.technical: Jet would adopt Guix derivations, profiles, store history, and generation switching.
options.code:
$ guix time-machine -C channels.scm -- build api
$ guix system reconfigure system.scm
$ guix system roll-back

options.name: Bazel directly
options.detail: Host language: Starlark. Bazel remembers an exact action map for builds. People love fast remote caching and strong answers about why a target rebuilt.
options.technical: The action map would cover packages and images. Machine activation would need an added history layer.
options.code:
$ bazel aquery //images:server
// exact tools, inputs, commands, and outputs

options.name: Spack directly
options.detail: Host language: Python. Spack records full compiler, version, feature, architecture, and dependency choices. People love readable package recipes and exact scientific build combinations.
options.technical: Jet would use Spack-style normalized concrete package entries as the main receipt.
options.code:
hdf5@1.14 %gcc@14 +mpi target=aarch64
// full concrete dependency tree

options.name: Separate records for every tool
options.detail: The package lock, build log, image manifest, and machine generation database each keep their own facts. Each piece is smaller, but no single explanation spans the whole project.
options.technical: Tools exchange output digests but do not share one receipt model.
options.code:
.jet/lock
.jet/build-log
.jet/image-manifest
/var/lib/jetos/generations
// four histories to join by hand

comparisons.note: The best complete history and rollback implementation. Guix is liked because builds and operating systems share transactional generations.
The best build explanation and cache implementation. Starlark rules create an exact action map.
The best detailed package-choice record. Python recipes are liked because experts can inspect and extend them easily.

recommendation.why: A makes every Jet command tell the same story, from package selection to machine rollback. Beginners get short answers; experts keep every fact and proof.

whyNot.reason: Guix has excellent history, but broad channel snapshots are less precise than Jet’s existing focused update rules.
Bazel explains builds brilliantly, but machine activation and rollback would remain a separate system.
Spack records packages deeply, but it does not cover complete machine activation history.
Separate records force users to reconstruct one cause across several tools.

recommendation.tradeoff: The receipt contains more than a normal lockfile. Jet can keep the default view tiny and reveal the full record only when asked.

decisions.title: How do users add something Jet did not ship?
decisions.gist: Choose whether extensions are normal Jet code, a plugin language, or built-ins only.
decisions.lesson:
No standard library can know every database, deployment tool, or future service. Users need to teach Jet new project pieces.

The cleanest extension is an ordinary function. It takes a typed setting and returns a normal Package, Service, Image, or ProjectPart. The returned value follows the same checks and combine rules as built-ins.

This keeps beginner use simple. People only write extension code when they are building a reusable extension.
decisions.story: Rin needs backups and PostgreSQL. Jet should not need a compiler release for either, and Rin should not need to learn macros or an untyped plugin API.

options.name: Normal Jet types and functions
options.detail: A library exposes a struct and a function returning Package, Service, Image, or ProjectPart. No macro language, plugin protocol, or whole-project mutation is needed.
options.technical: Extensions return closed typed values. Jet checks their inputs, outputs, permissions, and source package like any built-in value.

options.name: GNU Guix directly
options.detail: Host language: Guile Scheme. Guix service types and functions extend packages and operating systems. People love having macros, modules, procedures, and an interactive prompt available.
options.technical: Extensions would be Guile service types with their own combine and extend functions.
options.code:
(define postgres-service-type
  (service-type
    (extensions ...)))

options.name: Bazel directly
options.detail: Host language: Starlark. Bazel rules declare inputs, tools, outputs, and actions. People love its large extension ecosystem and precise build control.
options.technical: Extensions would be Starlark rules and providers evaluated outside ordinary Jet code.
options.code:
postgres_service = rule(
  implementation = _postgres,
  attrs = {...},
)

options.name: Built-ins only
options.detail: Jet ships every supported package and service kind. The experience stays uniform, but new integrations wait for Jet itself.
options.technical: Only Core and the standard library can create project values.
options.code:
database: Service.postgres(version: 18)
// unavailable until Jet ships it

options.name: Free-form plugins
options.detail: A plugin receives the whole project and may rewrite it. This is powerful, but one plugin can change unrelated values or hide where behavior came from.
options.technical: Plugins are ordered project-to-project callbacks with broad authority.

comparisons.note: The best direct whole-system extension design. Guile is liked because extensions use the same real language as configuration.
The best direct build-rule extension design. Starlark is liked because rules are predictable and shareable.

recommendation.why: A makes extension feel like normal Jet programming. Types, completion, errors, testing, and reuse all work without another language or unsafe project mutation.

whyNot.reason: Guix proves normal-language extension works, but Jet should use Jet rather than embed Scheme.
Bazel rules are precise, but Starlark would become a second language and provider system.
Built-ins only cannot grow into the broad ecosystem Jet needs.
Whole-project plugins gain power by giving up clear ownership, safe combining, and reliable explanations.

recommendation.tradeoff: Extension authors must return one of Jet’s typed project values. That boundary is helpful because every extension remains understandable to the same tools.

decisions.title: What should every project declaration look like?
decisions.gist: Choose one source shape for packages, checks, services, images, and machines.
decisions.lesson:
A good project file should teach itself. Once you understand one package entry, a service or machine entry should look familiar.

Jet already has named values and typed values whose fields Jet knows. Using those ordinary forms gives editors the type of every field, catches misspellings immediately, and lets users call normal Jet functions.

The alternative is special project syntax. It can be shorter, but every new project part adds another mini-language rule.
decisions.story: Rin knows basic Jet but knows nothing about build systems. After reading one package entry, Rin should be able to add a check, service, image, or machine without opening a manual.

options.name: Normal named Jet values
options.detail: Every entry is a name, a type, and its fields: `api: Package.{ ... }`. The same shape works at every level and remains ordinary Jet code.
options.technical: Project and ProjectPart are typed records. Their named sections provide completion, validation, and references. No package-only parser or evaluator is added. Inside Project and ProjectPart, names such as `packages.api` are stable project references. This replaces package and role modules as project declarations; ordinary Jet code modules remain unchanged.

options.name: A special block for each kind
options.detail: Write `package api { ... }`, `service web { ... }`, and `system home { ... }`. It is short, but package files gain a separate set of declarations and grammar rules.
options.technical: Each kind becomes parser-known project syntax that lowers to the same typed values.

options.name: CUE directly
options.detail: Host language: CUE, implemented in Go. CUE uses one record-like form for data, rules, defaults, and validation. People love that files combine without order deciding the winner.
options.technical: The project would be written as CUE values and constraints, then passed to Jet.

options.name: GNU Guix directly
options.detail: Host language: Guile Scheme. Guix declarations are Scheme values and records. People love having the whole language, macros, modules, and an interactive prompt available.
options.technical: Project declarations would use Scheme record constructors and lists.
options.code:
(package (name "api") (source "apps/api"))
(service api-service-type api)

options.name: Short free-form maps
options.detail: Everything is an untyped map. It looks compact, but misspelled fields and wrong value kinds become late, confusing errors.
options.technical: The evaluator discovers meaning from keys at runtime instead of checking a Project type while editing.

comparisons.note: The strongest direct “one shape everywhere” configuration language. CUE is liked because data and rules share the same readable form.
The strongest direct “configuration is normal code” system. Guile is liked for macros, modules, and interactive exploration.

recommendation.why: A is both simple and fully Jet. One pattern teaches the whole product, editors know every field, and experts can use normal functions without learning a plugin language. The same `name: Type.{ fields }` shape works in the root, every part, and every extension library.

whyNot.reason: Special blocks are attractive, but they duplicate ordinary Jet declarations and make each new component another grammar feature.
CUE has excellent records and merging, but it would put another language between Jet users and Jet types.
Guix is powerful, but Scheme constructors and errors would not feel like Jet.
Free-form maps save a few type names while giving up early errors and trustworthy completion.

recommendation.tradeoff: The type name appears once per entry. That small repetition makes every declaration searchable, checkable, and understandable without hidden context.

decisions.title: Where compiled programs carry their command schema
decisions.gist: Choose how a compiled Jet program carries the command schema derived from its entry function.
decisions.lesson:
A command schema is the checked description of a program's commands, flags, types, defaults, help, and schema-known completion values. Plain `fn run()` produces an empty application schema. `fn run(args: T)` derives a typed schema from `T`; the parameter remains optional.

Parsing, help, completion, and inspection must project one schema. A compiled program therefore needs a reliable way to carry that schema beyond the compiler process.

The schema can live inside executable metadata, behind a generated control mode, or in a companion file. The choice determines whether tools execute target code, whether cross-target artifacts remain readable, and whether one program becomes a multi-file bundle. Completion command spelling and automatic installation are separate choices.
decisions.story: Maya builds `greeter` for Linux and Windows, signs both releases, and hands them to an offline operations team. Their tooling must recover the exact accepted inputs without running either program or finding the original source.

options.name: Embedded executable metadata
options.detail: The compiler embeds one versioned schema record in the executable. Host tools read it without loading or starting target code. Linux, Windows, macOS, and WebAssembly artifacts remain inspectable from any supported host. The program stays one file, and stripping, copying, caching, and signing must preserve the record.
options.technical: One canonical JetCommandSchema record uses a format-specific executable metadata container. The record is bound into artifact identity before signing. Strip, copy, package, and cache paths preserve it or fail. Readers reject missing, malformed, unsupported, or duplicate records before producing output. No target instruction executes.
options.code:
release/
  greeter-linux       # executable plus embedded JetCommandSchema v1
  greeter-windows.exe # same logical record in its native container

# Conceptual host-reader results:
read_schema(greeter-windows.exe)
=> { version: 1, options: [name, language] }

read_schema(stripped-without-record)
=> error: command schema is missing

options.name: Generated environment control mode
options.detail: Every compiled program recognizes a versioned environment request and prints its schema before `fn run` or Jet user initialization. The application argument namespace stays untouched. The operating system still loads the target executable, so foreign targets cannot be read and untrusted artifacts cross an execution boundary.
options.technical: Generated startup handles bounded `JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=schema-v1` input before Jet user initialization. The loader, dynamic linker, platform constructors, and runtime startup may still execute. Unknown versions fail nonzero with no schema. The handler bounds request and output bytes. A supervising host tool may enforce a deadline, but startup cannot bound time spent before the handler. Inherited requests are cleared before child processes.
options.code:
$ JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=schema-v1 ./greeter-linux
{"version":1,"options":["name","language"]}

$ JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=schema-v2 ./greeter-linux
error: unsupported Jet command request version 2

$ JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=schema-v1 ./greeter-windows.exe
error: target executable cannot run on this host

options.name: Digest-bound companion file
options.detail: A build emits a versioned schema file beside the executable. Host tools read it without executing target code or parsing executable formats. The executable and schema become one signed bundle that every copy, cache, package, and install operation must keep together.
options.technical: `greeter.jet-command.json` contains the canonical schema and executable digest. Readers verify both before returning facts. Build, package, cache, copy, and signing treat the pair atomically. Missing, mismatched, malformed, unsupported, or duplicate sidecars fail closed. A lone executable has no recoverable command schema.
options.code:
release/
  greeter-linux
  greeter-linux.jet-command.json
  greeter-windows.exe
  greeter-windows.exe.jet-command.json

# Conceptual host-reader results:
read_schema(greeter-linux)
=> { version: 1, options: [name, language] }

read_schema(greeter-linux, mismatched-sidecar)
=> error: command schema does not match executable digest

comparisons.note: WebAssembly custom sections carry tool metadata that runtimes may ignore. This demonstrates format-contained metadata without executing application instructions.
comparisons.code: custom section: name, producers, or tool-defined bytes

comparisons.note: Click invokes an installed program with a special environment variable for completion requests. This demonstrates option B's control-mode boundary.
Native toolchains can move debug facts into a digest-linked companion file. This shows option C's portability and separation risk.

recommendation.why: Embedded metadata keeps a program single-file, preserves application arguments, supports cross-target inspection, and never executes the artifact. One checked record remains available to every completion and audit renderer without a detachable truth source.

whyNot.reason: Generated control code avoids `fn run`, but the host still loads target code. Foreign targets cannot answer, and inspecting an untrusted artifact gains an avoidable execution boundary.
The sidecar is easy to parse, but it turns one executable into a bundle whose halves can be separated. Every transport and trust path must defend that split.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every executable format needs a permanent preservation and signing contract for Jet metadata. That compatibility surface is justified because the command schema is part of the program's public contract.

decisions.title: How users generate completion for a Jet program
decisions.gist: Choose the one command users and shells invoke to render a program's generated completion script.
decisions.lesson:
A shell completion script teaches Bash, Zsh, Fish, or PowerShell what a program accepts. The script can suggest commands, flags, enum literals, and other values already present in the checked command schema. Live values from application code are outside this decision.

Jet already derives that schema from an optional entry parameter. Plain `fn run()` remains valid and yields no application-specific inputs. Typed `fn run(args: T)` yields the inputs declared by `T`.

This decision chooses only the rendering request. The companion carrier decision chooses how the schema travels with a compiled program. Existing parsing, help, and validation continue to project the same schema. Inspection and automatic installation remain outside this decision.
decisions.story: Maya receives the `greeter` executable. She wants Tab to reveal `--language` and its enum values without editing Greeter, maintaining a second declaration, or guessing a hidden protocol.
decisions.inWild:
$ greeter --l<Tab>
--language

$ greeter --language <Tab>
English  French  Spanish

# The chosen request below generates the shell script that supplies those answers.

options.name: Extend Jet's completion command
options.detail: Keep completion generation in the existing `jet self completions` family. Without `--for`, it still renders Jet's own script. With `--for PROGRAM`, it reads that program's canonical schema and renders a standalone script. The application keeps every command and flag name. Jet is needed when generating the script, not when the shell later uses it.
options.technical: Exact grammar: `jet self completions SHELL [--for PROGRAM]`, where SHELL is bash, zsh, fish, or powershell. The renderer obtains one verified schema through the ratified carrier. Stdout contains script bytes only. Human or JSON errors go to stderr. The script contains schema-known candidates only and never reconstructs fields independently.
options.code:
$ jet self completions bash --for ./greeter > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/greeter
$ greeter --l<Tab>
--language

$ jet self completions bash --for ./plain-run
# valid script with only built-in behavior

$ jet self completions bash --for ./not-a-jet-program
error: `./not-a-jet-program` has no readable Jet command schema

options.name: Reserve an application subcommand
options.detail: Every compiled Jet entry program reserves `completion SHELL`. Users invoke the program directly, and Jet is unnecessary after compilation. The command is easy to discover through help, but applications lose the `completion` subcommand name. A user enum variant with that name becomes a compile-time conflict.
options.technical: Exact grammar: `PROGRAM completion SHELL`. Generated entry dispatch handles it before user subcommands and renders from the canonical schema. SHELL accepts the same four values. A user command named `completion` is rejected by a Jet diagnostic. Plain `fn run()` also receives the generated command.
options.code:
$ ./greeter completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/greeter
$ greeter --l<Tab>
--language

$ ./greeter completion nushell
error: unsupported completion shell `nushell`

enum Command { Completion }
error: `completion` is reserved for generated shell completion

options.name: Generated environment request
options.detail: A shell or user sets one reserved environment request while invoking the program. Application arguments remain untouched, and Jet is unnecessary after compilation. The host must load and run the target executable, so foreign targets fail and untrusted artifacts cross an execution boundary.
options.technical: Exact protocol: `JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=completion-v1-SHELL PROGRAM`. Generated startup renders schema-known candidates before `fn run` or Jet user initialization. The handler bounds request and output bytes. A caller may enforce a deadline, but startup cannot bound loader or constructor time. Unknown versions or shells fail nonzero. The request is cleared before child processes.
options.code:
$ JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=completion-v1-bash ./greeter > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/greeter
$ greeter --l<Tab>
--language

$ JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=completion-v1-bash ./greeter-windows.exe
error: target executable cannot run on this host

$ JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=completion-v2-bash ./greeter
error: unsupported Jet command request version 2

$ JET_COMMAND_REQUEST=completion-v1-nushell ./greeter
error: unsupported completion shell `nushell`

comparisons.note: Rust's clap ecosystem can generate scripts ahead of time from one command model. This informs option A's tool-owned renderer.
Cobra applications commonly expose `completion SHELL` as a visible subcommand. This demonstrates option B's discoverability and namespace cost.
Click invokes the program with a special environment variable for script generation and candidates. This demonstrates option C's hidden control path.

recommendation.why: The existing Jet tool family gains one explicit target while application commands and flags remain entirely user-owned. The same route works for cross-target artifacts when the carrier supports static reading, and generated scripts run without Jet afterward.

whyNot.reason: The direct command is discoverable, but it reserves a normal application subcommand forever. That shrinks expert control and creates a second meaning for a name the user's command enum may need.
The environment path preserves argv, but it hides the request and requires loading target code. Cross-target generation fails, and untrusted artifacts cross an avoidable execution boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must be present when a completion script is generated. The produced script is standalone, so normal shell use has no Jet runtime dependency.

decisions.title: What is the one way to write a copy?
decisions.gist: Pick the single way to write a copy: single tilde ~x, a fresh $x mark, the double ^^x, or the copy x word.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's memory model is a borrow checker in plain clothes. A bare name reads a value, & writes it, ^ takes ownership away. A copy makes an independent duplicate, so the original survives. This ballot decides how you write that copy. The owner has already declined two directions: a method x.copy() on 2026-07-15, and a double mark; he wants copy to be a single sigil.

Two shipped decisions disagree. D-CAP2 and S4 made copy x the one copy spelling; D-SHAPE-LIFECYCLE then added ^^x at taking arguments, a second spelling I8 forbids. Corpus data ranks copy the rarest marked ownership op. Receivers run about 50/32/18 read/write/take across 63,949 sites. Rust copy-family calls are about 2.4 per KLOC against 22-plus per KLOC for borrow arguments. In accepted Jet examples copy is 63 uses, the lowest call-site mark.

The owner's rule: the rarest op gets the leftover mark. Tilde is that mark. Math never claimed it: Jet has no bitwise complement, its binary operators are % & | ^ << >>, and ! is reserved for Bool. The question is whether copy becomes ~x, a fresh $x, the double ^^x, or stays the copy word.
decisions.story: Maya loads a grid and calls transform, which takes ownership of its input. She still needs the grid for the next step, so she must hand transform an independent copy while keeping her own. She has already learned ^ to give a value away. She wants one short mark for copy she can reuse at a call and on its own line.
decisions.inWild:
input := load_grid()

// four ways to copy the same value at a taking call:
ops.transform(pool, ~input, 5000)       // A  single tilde
ops.transform(pool, $input, 5000)       // B  fresh mark
ops.transform(pool, ^^input, 5000)      // C  double caret
ops.transform(pool, copy input, 5000)   // D  copy word

// and standalone:
backup := ~input      // A
backup := $input      // B
backup := ^^input     // C
backup := copy input  // D

options.name: Single tilde ~x
options.detail: One tilde prefix marks a copy in any position. The rarest marked ownership op gets the last leftover mark, by the owner's rule. Single keystroke, single sigil, the shape the owner asked for. The copy keyword and ^^ are both retired.
options.technical: ~x is a prefix-verb expression producing an independent duplicate anywhere; at a taking argument the duplicate is then transferred. ~ is unclaimed by math: Jet has no bitwise complement, binary ops are % & | ^ << >>, ! is Bool-only. Prefix ~ coexists with any future infix use, exactly as ^ is both infix XOR and prefix take. A chain needs parentheses: (~input).rotate(). On a non-cloneable type it is E0211.

options.name: Fresh mark $x
options.detail: Give copy the only never-used ASCII prefix, $x. No history to overturn beyond the copy word and ^^. But it has zero mnemonic tie to the caret ownership family, so it reads as an orphan mark.
options.technical: $x is a new prefix-verb expression, an independent duplicate in any position. $ is unclaimed by every plane: % + * ! are math and logic, ~ was deleted by D-MEM1, @ and # are markers. A chain needs parentheses. On a non-cloneable type it is E0211.

options.name: Double caret ^^x everywhere
options.detail: Generalize the ratified taking-call ^^ into the one copy spelling, working in any position. It stays inside the caret family, but it is two keystrokes and reads as a double take rather than a single copy mark.
options.technical: ^^x lowers to an independent duplicate everywhere; at a taking argument the duplicate is transferred, as D-SHAPE-LIFECYCLE defines. The copy keyword is retired. A chain needs parentheses. On a non-cloneable type it is E0211.

options.name: Copy word only
options.detail: Keep the incumbent copy word and retire ^^. One searchable word in every position, the general spelling today. But it is a word, not the single sigil the owner asked for.
options.technical: copy x stays the prefix-verb expression Expr::Copy, parsing on any expression. ^^ is deleted from the grammar. A chain needs parentheses because the verb binds looser than a method call. On a non-cloneable type it is E0211.

comparisons.note: Rust moves most values implicitly and writes .clone() for an explicit copy. Users often criticize .clone() because its cost and identity vary silently by type.
Swift added an explicit copy word for consuming contexts. The community still warns that copying a class reference keeps identity rather than duplicating the object.
C++ copies implicitly through copy constructors. Call sites read clean, but an expensive deep copy can hide behind a plain variable pass.

recommendation.why: A gives copy a single sigil, the shape the owner asked for, and spends the last leftover mark on the rarest marked op, by frequency. Marking copy everywhere also frees unmarked range indexing to become a zero-copy window, a view unification now under study.

whyNot.reason: B is a clean single mark, but a mnemonic orphan: $ has no tie to the ^ ownership family, and it spends the last ASCII prefix on a mark that teaches nothing.
C stays in the caret family, but it is not a single mark; two carets read as a stronger take, not a copy, the direction the owner leans against.
D keeps a searchable word, but it is a word, not the single sigil the owner asked for, and it evicts ^^ from the language.

recommendation.tradeoff: A overturns D-MEM1's decree that ~ is not part of the v5 grammar with no compat ever, the owner's own 2026-07-03 ruling and his to overturn. It also supersedes the D-CAP2 and S4 copy word and retires D-SHAPE-LIFECYCLE's ^^. Un-deleting ~ after S1 removed it means the standard docs, formatter, and grammar sweeps follow ratification. Fix-its that say copy name move to ~name; E0211 stays the non-cloneable error.

decisions.title: How do I read, edit, or copy part of a value?
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet reads, writes, and copies a field or range.
decisions.lesson:
Glossary. An owner is the value responsible for storage. A place is a selectable location inside an owner, such as `packet.header` or `bytes[0..16]`. A projection is the selected part. A range selects consecutive elements. A window is a temporary connection to existing storage. A borrow is temporary permission to use that storage without owning it. An owned copy has separate storage and survives independently. Bounds checking stops access outside storage.

Jet's ratified memory model says bare means read, `&` means exclusive write, `^` means take ownership, and `~` means make an independent copy. A second-class borrow may live in a local binding or pass into a call. It cannot be stored in a struct or returned from a function. Users never write extra lifetime labels.

Many read windows may overlap. A write window must be alone for its selected storage. While any window exists, Jet prevents moving or resizing its owner when that action could invalidate the window. These checks happen at compile time.

This choice decides only read, write, and copy of selected parts. Taking one selected part from a larger owner is not added by either option. Existing `^` rules remain unchanged.

Option A applies bare, `&`, and `~` directly to any place. Option B keeps named `.view` and `.view_mut` operations, while `~` remains the one copy mark. Both check bounds and storage lifetime. Neither lets a window outlive its owner or overlap another write.
decisions.story: Nia writes `wiretap`, a packet inspector for an eight-megabyte capture. She runs `jet run packet.jet`, reads the header, decrypts the payload after byte 16, and saves four tag bytes. The tag must survive after the packet buffer is reused. Her first edit uses a read-only range, so Jet must explain the missing write intent without teaching Rust. The worked file uses 20 elements so every output is visible. The same operations apply to the full capture.
decisions.inWild:
Rust writes a mark at each selected part. `&packet.header` reads without copying. `&mut packet.payload[16..]` edits that range. `packet.payload[4..8].to_vec()` makes independent storage. The compiler prevents windows from outliving `packet` and blocks overlapping writes.

```rust
let header = &packet.header;
decrypt(&mut packet.payload[16..]);
let tag = packet.payload[4..8].to_vec();
```

Go uses `packet.payload[16:]` for both reading and writing. That selected range shares the original array, so assignment through it changes `packet`. The compiler does not block overlapping access. Copying needs new storage and a separate `copy` call.

```go
header := packet.header
patch := packet.payload[16:]
decrypt(patch)
tag := make([]byte, 4)
copy(tag, packet.payload[4:8])
```

Python's ordinary `packet.payload[4:8]` selection copies. Zero-copy work uses a separate object named `memoryview`. A writable memoryview edits its source. Resizing the source while that object exists fails while the program runs.

```python
header = memoryview(packet.header)
patch = memoryview(packet.payload)[16:]
decrypt(patch)
tag = packet.payload[4:8]
```

Jet keeps Rust's compile-time checks. The remaining question is whether users see ownership marks or named window methods.

options.name: One rule for read, write, and copy
options.detail: Use the same rule for a whole value, field, index, or range. Bare reads, `&` edits, and `~` copies. No `View` names or view methods appear in ordinary code. Beginners read without ceremony. Experts see write and copy intent at the exact selection.
options.technical: A prefix mark consumes the maximal place. That means one base name plus following fields, indexes, and ranges. Method calls are not part of a place. Therefore `~packet.header.bytes[0..3]` copies that four-element range. Existing copy precedence remains unchanged. To call a method on a copy, write `(~input).rotate()`. This ballot changes no `^` behavior. Local windows remain second-class and checked against their owner's lifetime.

options.name: Named read and write windows
options.detail: Use `.view` for a read window and `.view_mut` for a write window. The result names `View` or `ViewMut`. `~place` still makes the only owned copy. Bare range expressions are rejected, so every range states window or copy intent.
options.technical: `.view()` and `.view(range)` return second-class `View<T>` values. `.view_mut()` and `.view_mut(range)` return exclusive `ViewMut<T>` values. Both are tied to their owner. Neither may be stored or returned. Passing a mutable window to an `&` parameter still uses `&patch`, preserving D-MEM1 call spelling. An unmarked bracket range is a teaching error. Allowing it would duplicate either `.view` or `~`.

comparisons.note: Rust uses `&` and `&mut` before selected parts, then a named conversion for an owned copy. Its compiler blocks overlapping writes and windows that outlive storage.
Go's range expression shares storage and permits both reads and writes. This is concise, but the compiler does not prevent overlapping access conflicts or stale shared storage.
comparisons.code:
header := packet.header
patch := packet.payload[16:]
decrypt(patch)
tag := append([]byte(nil), packet.payload[4:8]...)

comparisons.note: Python makes ordinary range selections copy and uses `memoryview` for shared storage. The separate type is explicit, but invalid resizing is detected while the program runs.
comparisons.code:
header = memoryview(packet.header)
patch = memoryview(packet.payload)[16:]
decrypt(patch)
tag = packet.payload[4:8]

recommendation.why: A extends the ownership rule users already know to the exact part they selected. Read stays effortless. Write and copy stay visible. One rule covers names, fields, indexes, and ranges without a parallel window vocabulary.

whyNot.reason: It makes safe range work use three mechanisms: `.view`, `.view_mut`, and `~`. Rejecting bare ranges also creates an exception to Jet's rule that unmarked access means read.

recommendation.tradeoff: A changes a bare range from owned data into a borrowed read window. Code that keeps the range while resizing its owner will fail until it copies with `~`. It also supersedes the ratified `.view` spelling. Existing `~` method-chain precedence remains unchanged.

decisions.title: Unmarked parameter: read borrow or plain value?
decisions.gist: Decide what a function parameter with no sigil means: a read borrow of the caller's value, or a plain value with copy-on-write backing.
decisions.lesson:
Glossary. read borrow: the callee may look at the value but not change it; compiles to Rust `&T`, no copy. take (`^`): ownership moves to the callee. copy-on-write (CoW): a value shared until someone changes it, at which point that writer clones the backing store (a detach). detach spike: the allocation that happens on first mutation. reference count (RC): a runtime counter of how many share the backing.

Today's ratified law is D-MEM1 v5: an unmarked parameter is a read borrow, always, with no inference. This ballot asks whether to keep that or make unmarked mean a plain value. Either way, changing the caller's own binding in place still needs `&`.

This choice may amend ratified D-MEM1 v5. The owner has said audit closure likely overrides the earlier ruling, so picking B rewrites the unmarked-is-read law.
decisions.story: Priya is in her first week of Jet. She writes a to-do app: a helper that appends one item to a list, then main prints the list. She writes `add_item(cart, "eggs")` with no sigils, the way she would in Python, and expects the printed list to grow.
decisions.inWild: Any beginner program that passes a String, list, or struct into a helper that changes it: a cart appender, a counter bumper, a config field setter. The question is what happens when the value is passed without a `&` mark and the helper tries to change it.

options.name: Unmarked is a read borrow (current law)
options.detail: An unmarked parameter borrows the caller's value for reading. The callee may read it, never change it. To change it, the parameter and every call site take `&`. Passing a named value to a writer without `&` is a compile error with a one-line fix. Mutation is always visible, and passing never allocates.
options.technical: Unmarked param lowers to Rust `&T`. No RC, no clone, no hidden allocation. A body write or an escape/consume of an unmarked param is a hard error at the definition (E0205 write, E0209 take). This is the D-MEM1 v5 baseline the owner reset to.

options.name: Unmarked is a plain value (copy-on-write backing)
options.detail: An unmarked parameter is the callee's own logical value. Reading and passing never need a mark and never fail with a borrow error, which is the audit's cohesion target: beginner programs see strings, lists, and structs as plain values. The callee may change its copy; the caller's value is untouched. Changing the caller's binding in place still needs `&`.
options.technical: Unmarked param lowers to a CoW value: shared-immutable until first mutation, then it detach-clones the backing. RC tracks sharing at runtime. Ownership analysis should erase counts it can prove single-owner; a real-time `no_alloc` policy may require proof of zero RC and zero detach. `&` is still required to write the caller's binding.

recommendation.why: A keeps mutation visible and passing allocation-free. A named value handed to a writer is a clear compile error with a one-line fix, not a program that compiles, runs, and silently drops the update. It is the borrow rule Priya learns once and applies everywhere.

whyNot.reason: Priya's `push` compiles and runs but silently fails to update the caller — a footgun worse than an error, because nothing points at the bug. CoW also allocates on first mutation (detach spike), and RC traffic must be proven away before a real-time `no_alloc` policy can accept the code.

recommendation.tradeoff: A meets the borrow rule earlier: passing a named value and then writing it is a wall until you add `&`. B removes that wall for reads and passes, in exchange for hidden allocation on mutation and a silent lost-update when a beginner forgets `&`.

decisions.title: Stored and returned safe views
decisions.gist: Decide whether a function may return or store a safe view into someone else's value, and if so, whether the view's source is a public, semver-checked contract.
decisions.lesson:
Glossary. view: a read (or with `&`, write) window into another value's storage, no copy; today it lives only inside one function body. second-class borrow: a view that cannot be returned, stored in a field, or put in a list. zero-copy: reading part of a value without allocating a new one. provenance: which source a view borrows from. semver check: `jet pkg semver` compares a library's public API to its last release and flags breaking changes.

Today's ratified law (D-MEM1 S3) is second-class borrows: no `-> View` returns, no view fields, escape is E2307/E2305. The audit says this blocks general zero-copy and pushes programs toward Shared, IDs, GC, or raw memory. Options B and C reinstate returnable views and so amend D-MEM1 S3; the owner has said audit closure likely overrides.

Composition: all three compose with ratified D-SHAPE-PLACE1 windows (#613). Ordinary in-body place access stays nameless (bare read, `&` edit, `~` copy); a named `View`/`ViewMut` type appears only at the return or field boundary, and only in B and C. Aliasing safety (I1) is unchanged: at most one write view of a value is live at a time. Views do not duplicate `Shared<T>` or `Pool<T>` — those cover many-owners and cross-thread sharing; a view is zero-copy read-through-owner.
decisions.story: Marco writes a log-parser library. Each line yields a timestamp and a message. Today he cannot return a slice pointing into the input buffer, because returned views were deleted (D-MEM1 S3). So every parsed field is copied into a new String, doubling every log line in memory. He wants zero-copy: hand back a view, keep the bytes once.
decisions.inWild: A config or log parser returning the value slice for a key without copying. A tokenizer returning cursors into the source. A downstream package that stores those views and depends on what they borrow. The question: is returning a view allowed, and can a caller see and version-check what it borrows.

options.name: Keep second-class views only (current law)
options.detail: A view never leaves the function that made it. To hand data back, copy it into an owned value with `~` (allocates per call), or invert control: pass a closure that runs while the view is alive. Zero-copy stays a local optimization; a library boundary always copies or inverts.
options.technical: No returnable or stored borrows (D-MEM1 S3). `-> View` and `View` fields are E2307/E2305. Cross-package data is handed back by owned copy (`~`) or closure inversion. This is the ratified baseline.

options.name: Returnable views with public provenance
options.detail: A view may be returned or stored. It carries which source it borrows as public, queryable, semver-pinned metadata. A caller can ask a returned view its source, and the semver check flags any change to what a public function's view borrows as a breaking change. This makes cross-package zero-copy a real, versioned contract.
options.technical: `View<T>`/`ViewMut<T>` become returnable and storable. Each records source-provenance in the public API snapshot; changing it trips the semver check (E2601). Sema still proves owner-outlives-view and keeps at most one `ViewMut` live (I1). Extends D-SHAPE-PLACE1 windows to the return and field boundary.

options.name: Returnable views tied to a named owner (private provenance)
options.detail: A view may be returned or stored, tied to an owner named in the signature with `from name` — no lifetime letters. Same zero-copy power as B, but the borrow relationship is a private compiler check: not published, not queryable, and not part of the semver contract. Downstream tooling cannot see or version-check what a returned view borrows.
options.technical: Returnable views bind to a named owner parameter (`-> View<str> from src`). Provenance is a private sema check, absent from the API snapshot and the semver diff. Same aliasing rules as B; no public `.source()`. Changing `from src` to `from other` is a silent source-compatibility change.
options.code:
fn value_of(src: String, key: String) -> View<str> from src   // owner named, no lifetimes

$ jet run parse.jet
8080

port :: value_of(src, "port")
port.source()               // error: no such method — provenance isn't public

// Author changes the owner:
fn value_of(src: String, key: String) -> View<str> from other

$ jet pkg semver
no API changes.             // callers can break with no version signal

recommendation.why: B makes a stored or returned view a real API contract. A caller can see what a view borrows, and the semver check flags any change to it. Zero-copy parsers, splitters, and cursors stop forcing a copy per field or a closure inversion, and stop being pushed to Shared, IDs, GC, or raw memory.

whyNot.reason: Every returned slice must be copied (allocates per call) or inverted into a closure. So real zero-copy abstractions cannot cross a library boundary — the exact push toward Shared, IDs, GC, and raw memory the audit names.

Same zero-copy power, but the borrow relationship is invisible to tooling and not a semver contract. A library can silently change what a returned view borrows and break callers with no version signal, which is what public provenance exists to prevent.

recommendation.tradeoff: B adds a provenance contract to every public function that returns or stores a view: the metadata is still complexity and it must be semver-pinned. That pinned contract is what makes cross-package zero-copy safe to depend on.

decisions.title: Transitive memory facts across block, function, module, and package scopes
decisions.gist: Choose whether scoped memory facts check lexical bodies, reachable calls, or named memory profiles.
decisions.lesson: All options use one four-level placement rule. Block, function, module, and package declarations remove repetition; this ballot still decides what each memory fact proves.
decisions.story: Priya writes firmware for a heap-less Cortex-M0. She sets memory facts at the smallest useful scope, then calls a dependency whose decode function grows a list. She needs the compiler to say whether her declaration covers only local source or the full reachable call graph.
decisions.inWild: The firmware uses #Policy(no_alloc, zero_rc, arena_bounded(65536)). The same declaration can govern one block, one function, one module, or every source file owned by the nearest package.jet. A dependency helper calls List.push.

options.name: Scoped local checks
options.detail: Each fact checks bodies lexically covered by its block, function, module, or package declaration. Calls outside that lexical scope are not followed, so dependency allocations remain unseen.
options.technical: This preserves D-NOALLOC-SEM1=A. The nearest declaration of each memory-fact key wins, but the checker never computes call-graph closure.

options.name: Scoped transitive facts
options.detail: Each fact checks every call reachable from the marked block, function, module, or package. A violation reports its source, call path, effective declaration, and declaration provenance.
options.technical: Open-world dispatch cannot be proven. Strict code must seal the target set or consume a signed dependency summary, else E0922; this replaces D-NOALLOC-SEM1=A's local-only scope.

options.name: Scoped named memory profiles
options.detail: A named profile bundles memory facts, and the same profile can be placed on a block, function, module, or package. The selected bundle is checked transitively.
options.technical: NoHeap expands to no_alloc, zero_rc, and its configured arena bound. Targets may select a package default, while a nearer declaration of the same profile key wins.

recommendation.why: B keeps each fact explicit and gives every placement the same reachable-call guarantee. One package declaration covers defaults, while a function or block can state a narrower contract.

whyNot.reason: A still misses the dependency allocation reached by read_sensor. Wider placement reduces repetition but does not make the memory guarantee transitive.
C hides the exact facts behind a profile name. Library contracts and diagnostics should state no_alloc, zero_rc, and arena_bounded directly.

recommendation.tradeoff: B must reject unprovable open-world dispatch unless sealed targets or signed dependency summaries close the graph. It also records the effective scope and call path in diagnostics.

decisions.title: Unsafe review policy — gate-only default and optional typed obligations
decisions.gist: Which unsafe checks apply by default, and which package policy may add or remove inside an #Unsafe gate.
decisions.lesson: The #Unsafe gate and typed obligations do different jobs. The ratified gate marks where memory safety is the author's responsibility; typed obligations are extra review records such as valid_ptr, aligned, and no_alias. This decision may make those extra records optional or required by team policy. It may also make the gate's reason optional. Removing the gate itself is a separate amendment to I1 and D-UNSAFE2, represented only by option D.
decisions.explainer: Today D-LL1 and D-UNSAFE2 require every low-level memory operation to be inside a user-written #Unsafe region or #Unsafe fn. #Unsafe("reason") is preferred; bare #Unsafe already compiles with L3101. Ordinary Jet outside those gates remains memory-safe and emits no generated Rust unsafe. Options A through C preserve that boundary. Option D deliberately changes it.
decisions.story: Sam writes a GPIO driver. Sam wants one explicit #Unsafe region and no per-operation paperwork. Sam's employer later requires each pointer operation to record valid_ptr, aligned, and no_alias so code review and CI can audit what remains unproved. The same source model must serve both without making the employer's strict policy the default for every expert.
decisions.inWild: The package contains volatile reads and writes against memory-mapped registers. A solo expert wants the ratified #Unsafe gate only. A regulated team wants CI to reject an operation whose typed obligation is missing and wants jet inspect unsafe to report the effective package or organization policy and its source.
decisions.detail: All policy modes live under the existing pkg.jet policy namespace. Organization policy may require a stricter mode than the package requests and audit output names both sources. A package may never silently weaken organization policy.

options.name: Gate-only default; obligations opt in
options.detail: With no unsafe policy, experts write the ratified #Unsafe gate and nothing else. policy.unsafe = .Obligations makes typed per-operation obligations mandatory and auditable for teams. policy.unsafe = .Relaxed keeps the gate but permits bare #Unsafe without L3101, so one package line removes repeated reason strings. Team or organization policy may require .Obligations and reject either weaker mode. No mode in this option permits a low-level operation outside #Unsafe.
options.technical: Default is D-LL1/D-UNSAFE2 gate checking with no obligation tracking. .Obligations adds the typed obligation checker and makes an undischarged obligation an error. .Relaxed suppresses the existing missing-reason lint only. jet inspect unsafe reports effective mode, policy source, each gated region, and per-operation state when obligations are enabled.

options.name: Obligations by default; package opt-out
options.detail: Every package requires typed per-operation obligations unless pkg.jet selects .GateOnly. .Relaxed selects gate-only checking and also permits a missing reason without L3101. Organization policy may forbid either opt-out. This gives teams strict behavior without configuration, but makes every solo expert opt out before writing ordinary gated low-level code.
options.technical: The absence of policy means .Obligations. .GateOnly disables obligation checking but retains #Unsafe and the existing reason lint. .Relaxed disables obligation checking and the reason lint but retains #Unsafe. Audit output records any package opt-out and whether organization policy allowed it.

options.name: Choose obligations at each unsafe site
options.detail: pkg.jet selects .PerSite, then every #Unsafe region or function says whether it tracks or skips typed obligations. This lets one package mix regulated driver code with short expert-only regions, but it cannot reduce ceremony for the whole package with one line. Every site still has a #Unsafe gate.
options.technical: .PerSite requires an obligations argument on each #Unsafe marker. .Track enables typed checking for that site; .Skip uses the ratified gate alone. Audit output records each site's choice. Organization policy may reject .Skip. Missing site mode is an error so the choice is never inferred.

options.name: Invariant amendment: package-wide gate suppression
options.detail: policy.unsafe = .Unchecked is an explicit package opt-in that permits low-level operations without any #Unsafe region or function. Audit output records the package-wide choice and every low-level operation. Organization policy may deny .Unchecked. This option amends I1's required user-written audited regions and D-UNSAFE2's #Unsafe audit gate; it is not a relaxation allowed by current law.
options.technical: The compiler treats the whole package as an unsafe authority region after reading .Unchecked. use core.mem remains the discovery gate, but lexical #Unsafe gates and reason strings are not required. Generated Rust unsafe may therefore arise from source locations not enclosed by a user-written #Unsafe marker. Ratifying D must explicitly amend I1 and D-UNSAFE2 before implementation.

recommendation.why: A keeps ratified expert behavior as the default, gives teams one enforceable obligations policy, and lets packages remove repeated reason strings without weakening safety outside #Unsafe.

whyNot.reason: B makes every expert opt out of the additional obligation system even though the existing #Unsafe gate already records deliberate entry into the low-level tier.
C repeats the policy choice at every site and does not provide the requested package-wide reduction in ceremony.
D removes the ratified lexical audit boundary, allows generated unsafe outside user-written gated regions, and therefore requires a conscious amendment to I1 and D-UNSAFE2.

recommendation.tradeoff: Under A, teams that want typed obligations must set package or organization policy. The effective policy and its source are included in audit output, so that opt-in is visible and enforceable.

decisions.checkInstructions: Confirm A through C always reject low-level operations outside #Unsafe. Confirm .Relaxed only suppresses L3101. Confirm organization policy can require .Obligations and audit output names the effective mode and source. Treat D as blocked until I1 and D-UNSAFE2 are explicitly amended.
decisions.comment: A but allow the pet site flexibility of c

decisions.title: Choose the opt-in GC scope and migration workflow
decisions.gist: Choose whether `#Policy(gc)` is an inherited package-to-block setting with automatic traced values, a package-only setting, or absent in favor of explicit `Gc<T>` values.
decisions.lesson:
D-MEM1 is Jet's default memory law. A bare parameter is read-only, `&` grants exclusive write access, and `^` transfers ownership. Borrows are second-class, so they cannot be stored in fields or returned.

A tracing garbage collector, or GC, keeps a graph of live heap values and reclaims unreachable cycles. Inside `#Policy(gc)`, each heap-owning value gains stable traced identity without a `Gc<T>` wrapper. Storing a bare read into another GC-managed field or collection creates an edge to that same identity. It does not move or copy the value.

The access law still applies. `&` is required for mutation, `^` transfers a root, and `~` remains an independent deep copy. A traced edge is an owned runtime handle, not a borrow. If a GC-managed value may escape into ownership-only code, the compiler rejects the boundary until ownership is proven or the receiving scope opts in.

D-MARK-SCOPE1 is the common ladder being raised from #644 for eligible markers: package, module, function, and block. A setting inherits inward, while a narrower scope lets one subsystem opt in without changing its neighbors. GC registers in that shared applicability matrix instead of creating another inheritance mechanism.

Trace mode is the exit path. It records each allocation the ownership checker could not prove, including the source site and reason. `jet gc report` turns those records into fixes for moving back to owned values or `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>`.

D-DEP-GC1=A already chose the pure-Rust, std-only mark-sweep collector. This ballot does not approve an external collector or runtime bridge. Either would require its own I6 ballot.
decisions.explainer: This decides both the opt-in boundary and whether opting in changes ordinary values automatically. It also makes GC reporting part of the supported workflow, not an optional debugging extra.
decisions.story: Maya is moving a TypeScript service to Jet. The service has request graphs, caches, and callbacks that share cyclic state. She wants one package setting while porting, then a report that shows how to remove GC one source site at a time.
decisions.inWild: A service package opts into GC once. Most code uses ordinary `Node` and `Request` values. A low-level parser module stays ownership-only, while one embedded plugin uses a function or block opt-in. CI runs `jet gc report --json` and tracks the remaining GC-backed allocation sites until the report is empty.
decisions.detail: The package and source spelling below is the existing `#Policy(…)` family with a `gc` key. `jet clean` remains Hangar cleanup; `jet gc report` is memory analysis.

options.name: Package-to-block ladder with magic and reports
options.detail: `#Policy(gc)` is one inherited setting at package, module, function, and block scope. Heap-owning values gain traced identity, and bare stores create traced edges. `jet gc report` lists every allocation ownership cannot prove and gives a concrete fix.
options.technical: The `gc` policy key uses D-MARK-SCOPE1's applicability matrix. A bare store between GC-managed values preserves identity instead of moving. `&` still gates mutation, `^` transfers a root, and `~` deep-copies. Unproven escape into ownership-only code is rejected.

options.name: Package-only magic
options.detail: Only `package.jet` may opt into automatic GC. Every ordinary heap value in that package uses the GC rules. Source modules, functions, and blocks cannot opt in independently, but `jet gc report` still provides the migration list.
options.technical: The same identity, access, copy, root-transfer, and escape laws as option A apply. Package boundaries are the smallest GC boundary, so one traced subsystem makes the whole package GC-managed.

options.name: Explicit Gc<T> values only
options.detail: There is no GC scope setting. Users import `core.gc` and wrap each traced value in `Gc<T>`. Ordinary values always follow D-MEM1 ownership. `jet gc report` can list explicit GC construction sites, but it cannot offer a package-wide migration mode.
options.technical: This preserves the current explicit handle model. D-DEP-GC1=A remains the backend. No automatic promotion occurs, and module, function, or block markers do not exist.
options.code:
// package.jet — no GC setting exists
payload: { name: "scene-service", version: "1.0.0" }

// Source/scene.jet — every traced value names its wrapper
use core.gc as gc
Node :: { name: String, links: [gc.Gc<Node>] }

fn run() {
    a :: gc.Gc.new<Node>(Node.{ name: "a", links: [] })
    b :: gc.Gc.new<Node>(Node.{ name: "b", links: [] })
    a.with_mut(n => n.links.push(~b))
    b.with_mut(n => n.links.push(~a))
    gc.collect()
    print("a")
}

$ jet gc report
Explicit GC allocations: 2 sites
Source/scene.jet:6:10  gc.Gc.new<Node>
  reason: value participates in cycle a.links -> b.links -> a
  fix: store nodes in Pool<Node> and links as Id<Node>
Source/scene.jet:7:10  gc.Gc.new<Node>
  reason: value participates in cycle b.links -> a.links -> b
  fix: store nodes in Pool<Node> and links as Id<Node>
No implicit GC allocations can be reported because no GC scopes exist.

comparisons.note: Go traces heap values for the whole program. It gives migration projects no per-value wrapper, but it has no module, function, or block opt-out ladder.
comparisons.code:
type Node struct { Links []*Node }
// Ordinary pointers participate in the program-wide tracing GC.

comparisons.note: Library collectors normally expose wrapper types such as Gc<T>. That resembles option C and makes each traced edge visible in the type.
comparisons.code: let node: Gc<Node> = Gc::new(Node { links: vec![] });

recommendation.why: A gives migration projects one package line while preserving the same setting at module, function, and block scope. Its report provides a direct path back to D-MEM1 ownership.

whyNot.reason: B cannot embed GC in one subsystem. A library must opt in its entire package or split the package, even when only one function owns the cyclic graph.
C requires `Gc<T>` ceremony throughout a migration and does not provide the package-level magic the owner requested. Its report also sees only sites users already wrapped explicitly.

recommendation.tradeoff: A makes storage representation depend on an inherited scope setting. Tooling must show that inheritance and report every automatic GC allocation so no hidden site blocks migration.

decisions.title: A defer verb and one close word for resources
decisions.gist: Whether Jet adds a `defer` verb and a single `close` word for every resource type, or only one of the two.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. A resource is a value tied to something outside memory — an open file, a held lock, a live connection. A plain value like a String or Int copies freely; a resource cannot, because two names for one open file would double-close it. `take`, written `^`, hands a resource away: after `close(^file)` the name `file` is gone. `defer` schedules a cleanup statement to run when the scope exits, on every path.

D-SHAPE-RESOURCE1 already frees owned resources at block end. This ballot adds what the owner asked for after ratifying it: a `defer` mechanism and one close word for every type. Today closing is inconsistent — `close(^handle)` for FFI and db, `.drop("reason")` for discard, no `defer`. The `^` at a close call stays the visible mark that a resource is handed away for good.
decisions.story: Sam writes an importer that opens a file, takes a lock on shared state, and opens a database connection. All three must release on every exit — the happy path, a `?` error midway, and an early return. He wants the cleanup to sit next to each acquisition and use one word he does not have to look up per type.
decisions.inWild: An importer in examples/features/io/ that opens a File, takes a Lock on shared state, and opens a Db connection, then must release all three on every return path — success, `?` error, and early exit.

options.name: A defer verb and one close word
options.detail: `close(^x)` is the single word that ends any resource — File, Lock, or Connection. `defer close(^x)` schedules that close at scope exit, written next to acquisition.
