Custom lints require unstable compiler internals (clippy is in-tree); third parties are locked out — the gap Jet can close.
Userland custom rules over a stable AST — massive adoption, but stringly typed and per-file only; no whole-program view.
The message loop grants observe + rewrite together; there is no read-only tier to adopt without the mutation cost.

decisions.title: Epoch 4 exit bar: how much of the build-graph vision ships before e4 is done?
decisions.gist: Pick the finish line for Epoch 4 (metaprogramming): the ratified fn-build MVP, that plus typed targets/actions, or full CMake/Bazel-class build-graph parity.
decisions.explainer: The five fn-build ballots are ratified (D-BUILDENTRY1=B, D-BUILDGEN1=A, D-BUILDPOLICY1=A, D-BUILDSCOPE1=A, D-METADEPTH2=B) with an executable plan (metaprogramming.md §15). The vision doc also holds back six build-graph decision bundles (§12: targets, actions, toolchains, cache, probes, lock) that were deliberately frozen "until the foundation ballots land." They have landed. This decision sets what "Epoch 4 done" means, and therefore which of those six bundles agents must develop into ballots for you now versus later.
decisions.story: Hank maintains a game studio's engine repo: Jet code, shader assets, a test suite, and a handful of C tools. He wants to delete the Makefile. The ratified MVP lets his fn build generate bindings and pick sources — but a test target, an asset-cook step with declared inputs/outputs, and "only rebuild what changed" are exactly the parts of Make he still needs. Where Epoch 4 stops decides whether Hank deletes the Makefile at e4 or waits.

options.name: MVP bar — ship §15 as ratified, all six §12 bundles wait for e5
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits when the five ratified ballots are implemented end-to-end (entry, generate, policy, scope, enforce) plus the explain-build/audit surfaces. BuildPlan stays the three lists. The six §12 bundles get balloted in Epoch 5 beside jetpack. Cleanest scope; but e4's own charter is Jai parity, and Jai ships targets — Hank keeps his Makefile another epoch, and every real project's asset/test steps live in Tier-2 `#Impure` shell-outs in the meantime, which trains exactly the habit the capability model exists to prevent.

options.name: Full parity bar — all six §12 bundles designed, ratified, shipped in e4
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits at CMake/Bazel-class parity: typed targets, declared-I/O actions, toolchain pinning, content-addressed action cache, typed probes, lock/provenance for all of it. "Never reach for Make" is true at e4 exit. The cost is decision-load and design risk, not effort: toolchain registries, remote-cache trust, and probe vocabularies are ecosystem decisions that will be better informed by jetpack's provider model (e5) — ratifying them first risks re-opening them, which is the one thing the ratification process is supposed to prevent.

options.name: MVP + targets/actions — Jai-parity bar; toolchains/cache/probes ride e5 (recommended)
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits on §15 plus two of the six bundles: D-BUILDTARGET1 (executable/library/test/bench/asset targets in BuildPlan) and D-BUILDACTION1 (declared inputs/outputs/argv actions — a step with no declared outputs is not a build step). That is the Jai benchmark e4 is named for, and it is what deletes Hank's Makefile: tests and asset cooks become graph nodes instead of #Impure shell-outs, so the capability story stays honest. Toolchains, cache, and probes are jetpack-shaped ecosystem bundles; they ballot in e5 where the provider model informs them — until then `jet build` is correct-if-slower (no action cache) and probes stay Tier-2 #Impure. Agents develop the two bundles into full ballots immediately; the other four are named and parked, not lost.

decisions.comparisons:
Jai: builds-as-programs with targets and compile options — the e4 charter's benchmark.
CMake/Bazel/Ninja: typed targets + declared-I/O actions + caching; nobody's v1 shipped remote caching.
Cargo: build.rs (ambient, no graph) — the anti-model Jet already rejected.
nob.h (binder idea): C build-as-program; covered by targets+actions, not by the MVP lists.

decisions.title: Single-file Tier-2 build grants: what does the user type to say yes?
decisions.gist: A lone script's fn build wants an ambient effect (exec, env, ...). Pick the CLI spelling that grants it for one run.
decisions.explainer: D-BUILDPOLICY1=A ratified the mechanics: Tier-2 build effects need BOTH a `#Impure("reason")` gate in source AND permission at run time — "a flag or an interactive prompt" for a manifest-less single file. The flag spelling was left open. There is already one ratified grant flag: D-CTEFFECT1's blanket `--allow-impure` (comptime Tier-2, diagnostic E3411 names it). This ballot decides whether that blanket stays the one grant path or is refined into per-effect grants — whichever wins becomes THE spelling (I8: one grant system, E3411's fix text updated to match). Effect names come from the ratified ten-effect vocabulary (D-EFF4: Net, Fs, Io, Db, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, Log, Gpu) — nothing new is minted.
decisions.story: Walter has a 60-line `tool.jet` — no pkg.jet, just a script whose fn build probes pkg-config for a legacy C library before compiling. The probe is `exec`, a Tier-2 effect. His build fn already declares it and gates it with #Impure. Now he runs `jet build tool.jet` on his laptop (interactive) and in CI (no TTY, hermetic by default). What does he type?

options.name: Per-effect `--allow-<effect>` + TTY prompt fallback — supersedes the blanket (recommended)
options.detail: One flag per D-EFF4 effect, lowercase: `--allow-exec`, `--allow-env`, `--allow-net`, `--allow-fs`, ... Grants exactly what is named, for this invocation only, recorded in lock/provenance. No flag + TTY: one prompt listing the declared effects and the #Impure reason. No flag + no TTY (CI): fail, naming the flag to add (the §15.4 not-granted diagnostic). This REPLACES the blanket `--allow-impure` — E3411's fix text is rewritten to name the specific missing effect flag, so there is exactly one grant system (I8), and granting exec never smuggles in env. The honest cost: ten flags are more surface than one, and a build declaring three effects needs three flags in the CI line (or the pkg.jet rung). Tab-completable, greppable, reads instantly to anyone who knows Deno.
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --allow-exec
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0

$ jet build tool.jet          # interactive, no flag
  fn build declares #(Exec) — "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
  allow exec for this run? [y/N] y

$ jet build tool.jet          # CI, no TTY: hermetic by default
Error: this build asks for `Exec`, which nothing has granted
  Fix: pass --allow-exec, or add a pkg.jet with a build: grant

options.name: Keep the ratified blanket `--allow-impure` as the only grant
options.detail: Status quo extended to build entries: one flag opens every effect the build fn declares. Nothing to ratify beyond scope; E3411 already teaches it; shortest to type. But coarse: Walter wants exec, and the same flag also opens env/net/fs if the script (or a future edit to it) declares them — the grant never names what it grants, so reviewing a CI line tells you nothing about what was opened. Provenance still records what ran, but the human said "whatever it wants."
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --allow-impure
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0
# next month someone adds b.env("TOKEN") to fn build —
# the same CI line silently grants that too.

options.name: One list flag `--grant exec,env` — supersedes the blanket
options.detail: Single flag, comma-separated effect list; replaces `--allow-impure` the same way A does. Same granularity as A in fewer characters; but it is a second spelling grammar (list parsing, ordering) instead of plain flags, doesn't tab-complete per effect, and diverges from the Deno convention users will pattern-match against. Everything else behaves like A (prompt fallback, CI failure naming the fix).
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --grant exec
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0

$ jet build tool.jet --grant exec,env,net   # grows into a mini-language

options.name: Prompt-only; no grant flags exist
options.detail: Interactive prompt is the only single-file grant path; CI must create a pkg.jet with a build: block (and `--allow-impure` is retired entirely). Maximally deliberate, but it breaks the ratified single-file story ("a lone script works with no manifest at every rung") the moment that script runs in CI — the exact place hermetic-by-default matters most would force manifest ceremony.
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet            # laptop: prompt works
  allow exec for this run? [y/N] y

$ jet build tool.jet            # CI: dead end
Error: this build asks for `Exec`, which nothing has granted
  Fix: create pkg.jet with `build: .{ allow: #(Exec) }`   # manifest ceremony

decisions.comparisons:
Deno: `--allow-net`, `--allow-read=./data`, `--allow-env` — per-capability flags, the direct precedent; prompts interactively when a flag is missing.
Cargo: nothing — build.rs gets ambient everything, the anti-model.
Nix: sandbox on/off; no per-effect grants.
Jet today: blanket `--allow-impure` (D-CTEFFECT1/E3411) opens ALL declared Tier-2 comptime effects for a run; builds are hermetic unless it is passed.

decisions.title: jet ? help app — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: What jet ? opens: an instant command finder, a full reference book, or a goal-first guide.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — the two-second palette everyone uses, with tasks' goals greeting beginners and browser's full depth one key away, all over a single index. Speed, intent, and depth without three apps.
decisions.story: Ana installed Jet an hour ago and wants "run my file and rebuild on save"; Marco has used Jet for a year and just forgot a flag. Three genuinely different apps serve them: a fuzzy finder that drops over the shell and prefills the command in two seconds, a two-pane reference covering every command, flag, error code and syntax page, or a goal-first explorer that starts from what you want to DO. The axis is speed vs depth vs intent. Browse: file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#help (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
$ jet ?
# what opens? Ana types "watch" or picks a goal —
# either way she should land back at her shell with:
$ jet run --watch src/main.jet▌   ← prefilled, never executed
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid help, modified so the default surface is a command palette categorized like the browser. Remove task-based search/goal home as its own managed surface. Task/outcome phrases can be fuzzy keywords/aliases on explicit command entries, so users can type what they want and still land on concrete commands. Keep explicit command entries, category grouping, command/flag/example/error-code search, Tab inline detail, F1 full two-pane reference, and Enter prefill-never-run.

options.name: Palette — instant overlay, prefill and go
options.detail:
Core loop: summon → type three chars → Enter → back in the shell with the command prefilled. An fzf-style finder drops OVER the shell (no alt-screen takeover; the shell stays dimmed behind). Search spans commands, flags, and examples; Tab peeks flags inline; Enter prefills the shell line and never runs it. The two-second path for someone who roughly knows what they want. Risk: fuzzy ranking quality is the whole UX; prefill-not-run must be unmistakable. NO_COLOR: > selection + [ ] match brackets.
file://~/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/help/palette.html
options.code:
web-api ❯ jet ?
┌─ find a command ─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ > run                                        5 shown │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
> jet [run] <file>      run a file, rebuilding if changed
│ jet [run] --watch     rerun on every save            │
│ jet [run] --release   run an optimized build         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ example  jet run examples/features/basics/hello.jet  │
│ ↑↓ move · ⏎ prefill shell · ⇥ flags · Esc close      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
→ Enter closes overlay, shell line:  web-api ❯ jet run _

options.name: Browser — the full reference book
options.detail:
Core loop: explore the whole tool like a reference book — category → command → man-depth detail. Alt-screen two-pane app (lazygit model): category tree + commands left; usage, description, flags table, runnable examples, see-also right. The reference also covers error codes and syntax — each code page renders the verbatim diagnostic (E0112 shown). Enter on an example still prefills the shell after exit. The learn-it-properly surface. Risk: heavier to invoke; large content to author and maintain. NO_COLOR: ▾/▸ tree glyphs + > selection.

jet ? reference              Build & run › run › usage
┌─ commands ──────────┬─ jet run ────────────────────────┐
│ ▾ Build & run       │ Usage                            │
│ >  run              │   jet run <file> [flags]         │
│    build            │ Run a file, rebuilding first if  │
│    test             │ its sources changed.             │

decisions.title: Compiler-extension v1 boundary: first hook and isolation model
decisions.gist: Choose the first stable compiler-extension contract: what compiler state plugins may observe, and whether they run inside or outside the compiler's trust boundary.
decisions.lesson:
Compiler hooks expose a moving internal pipeline to third-party code. A stable snapshot contract preserves plugin compatibility; process isolation preserves compiler integrity when plugin code fails.

Read-only does not mean weak. A plugin can inspect typed facts, emit findings, and propose edits without changing compiler truth. Mutation creates a second semantic authority and threatens I2, I3, and R12.

The first hook matters because it becomes the compatibility floor. Later stages should extend one capability-negotiated protocol, not introduce separate plugin systems.
decisions.story: A team wants a domain lint that follows resolved symbols and types. Another team eventually wants a code-generation pass. Both need expert reach without letting one faulty plugin crash every beginner build.
decisions.inWild:
Host compiles through sema, freezes a versioned typed snapshot, and sends it to a sandboxed component. The component returns structured findings and edit proposals. Host validates every response, owns diagnostics, and may reject unsupported capabilities cleanly.

plugin request:  protocol=v1, stage=typed, capabilities=[read_types, read_symbols, emit_finding]
plugin response: findings=[{rule, span, message, fix}]
compiler: validates spans/rules, then renders Jet diagnostics
decisions.detail: D-DX5-B already ratified an optional formal API. This ballot does not reopen PATH-discovered jet-* helpers or application target: plugin. It chooses the v1 compiler-extension boundary only. Exact user-facing registration spelling remains a later ballot if new syntax is needed.

options.name: Typed read-only snapshot in sandbox
options.detail: First hook runs after sema. Reuse the shipped WASM Component Model host, but define a compiler-specific versioned snapshot and response contract. Plugins inspect typed symbols, types, effects, spans, and provenance; they return findings and proposed edits. The host validates outputs and remains the only semantic authority. Later parse or codegen capabilities extend the same negotiated protocol.

options.name: All read-only stages in sandbox
options.detail: Ship parse, typed-sema, and after-codegen snapshots together through the WASM Component Model. Plugins still cannot mutate compiler state. Experts gain broad observation immediately, but v1 freezes three large contracts before their shared vocabulary and versioning have proven stable.
options.code:
capabilities = [observe_parse, observe_typed, observe_artifact]
// one sandbox, three versioned snapshot schemas in v1

options.name: Trusted in-process mutable hooks
options.detail: Load native extensions into the compiler and expose mutable parse, sema, and codegen structures. This gives maximum direct control, including arbitrary transforms. A plugin can also invalidate checked facts, diverge JIT from AOT, leak rustc failures, crash the process, or bind itself to private Rust layouts.

options.name: Parse-only sandbox first
options.detail: Expose tokens and syntax trees first through the sandbox. This is a small structural contract and serves formatters or source linters. It cannot support the motivating custom typed lints because names, types, effects, and ownership facts are unresolved.
options.code:
request = { protocol: 1, stage: parsed, syntax_tree }
// no resolved symbol, type, effect, or ownership data

comparisons.note: In-process AST plugins have deep access but track compiler internals closely and share the compiler's crash boundary.
Versioned typed interfaces and isolated execution fit Jet's already-ratified application-plugin substrate, while a compiler-specific world can keep the two mechanisms semantically distinct.
comparisons.code: world compiler-extension-v1 { import typed-snapshot; export analyze; }

recommendation.why: A serves the first real use case, custom typed analysis, while preserving one compiler authority, deterministic replayable inputs, crash isolation, and a stable capability-growth path.
recommendation.tradeoff: V1 cannot perform arbitrary compiler mutations or codegen rewrites. Expert reach grows through reviewed capabilities and validated transformation requests instead of raw internal pointers.

whyNot.reason: B freezes three contracts before one has proven its vocabulary. Broad observation can arrive later through A's same negotiated protocol without creating another mechanism.
C creates a second semantic authority inside the compiler and shares memory, ABI, and crash boundaries. That conflicts with Jet-owned checking and diagnostic guarantees.
D misses the ratified API's first motivating job: custom lints over resolved types and symbols. It would force a second contract almost immediately.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps one sandbox and one negotiated protocol. It starts with typed analysis, then can absorb parse observation and validated artifact transforms as capabilities without exposing mutable compiler internals.

harvest.use: Use as v1's stable contract and safety boundary.
Keep as evolution law: later stages extend capability negotiation instead of creating new plugin systems.
Recover through explicit validated transformation requests and audited host capabilities, never raw mutable pointers.
Add parse observation later as an optional capability when a concrete formatter or source-lint need appears.

decisions.title: Which crypto primitive backend powers `crypto.seal/open` + `sign/verify`? (I6 owner gate)
decisions.gist: D-CRYPTOENV1=A ratified the seal/open + sign/verify envelope. This is an I6 external-dependency approval gate for the underlying AEAD/signature primitives. Pure-Rust is preferred for the native-ize end-state.
decisions.explainer:
Hand-rolling primitive crypto is a footgun (constant-time, audited impls). A vetted backend is required; I6 governs which: runtime-side only, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation. Differentiator is the backend's I6 posture. Blast radius: a stdlib `crypto` module + `.jet/lock` pin.

Recommendation: A — RustCrypto is pure Rust with no C/asm, the closest of the three to the I6 end-state and simplest to re-implement first-party.

options.name: Pure-Rust RustCrypto (aes-gcm/chacha20poly1305/ed25519-dalek)
options.detail:
Audited pure-Rust crates, gated runtime-side like Cranelift.

I6: pure Rust, no C/asm — closest to the native-ize end-state, easiest to re-implement first-party.
options.code:
import crypto
box@ Bytes = crypto.seal(key, plaintext)?
sig@ Bytes = crypto.sign(privkey, msg)
crypto.verify(pubkey, msg, sig)?

options.name: `ring` (C/asm, BoringSSL-derived)
options.detail:
Battle-tested, fast.
I6: pulls in C + assembly, needs a C toolchain, pins a non-Rust core — furthest from the end-state.

options.name: libsodium via FFI
options.detail:
Bind system libsodium through the stdlib FFI-bridge pattern.
Widely audited, misuse-resistant — but an external C library + system dep (nixpkgs-interim), heaviest to native-ize, worst non-Nix story.

comparisons.note: RustCrypto offers pure-Rust AEADs, hashes, signatures, and traits with broad audit attention and no C toolchain.

decisions.bestCurrent: RustCrypto: RustCrypto offers pure-Rust AEADs, hashes, signatures, and traits with broad audit attention and no C toolchain.
decisions.recommendation: Use RustCrypto behind Jet’s misuse-resistant envelope. Jet can expose fewer knobs than Rust while keeping pure-Rust portability.

decisions.title: How does a retained reactive Effect end early?
decisions.gist: Choose the public lifecycle vocabulary for the Effect value already ratified by D-SIGNAL1.
decisions.lesson: D-SIGNAL1 makes Effect a retained runtime value. Retention keeps a reactive callback subscribed until its owner releases it. Automatic cleanup on Drop prevents leaks, but experts also need deterministic early cleanup for views that stay alive while one effect ends. Jet already uses Subscription.unsubscribe()/is_active() for event subscriptions, while dispose() would introduce a second lifecycle vocabulary.
decisions.story: Maya opens and closes a settings panel repeatedly. Each panel creates an Effect that reads a Signal. When the panel closes, the effect must detach immediately so hidden panels stop rerendering and retained nodes can be reclaimed.

options.name: unsubscribe + is_active
options.detail: Effect uses the same explicit lifecycle vocabulary as event Subscription. Drop also unsubscribes idempotently.
options.technical: reactive.effect and @Reactive return Effect. Effect.unsubscribe() detaches dependencies once; Effect.is_active() reports state. Drop calls the same internal operation.
options.code:
effect :: reactive.effect(() => render(state.get()))
effect.unsubscribe()
assert !effect.is_active()

options.name: dispose + is_active
options.detail: Effect uses UI-framework-style dispose(), while event subscriptions keep unsubscribe(). Drop also disposes idempotently.
options.technical: Adds Effect.dispose() as a second public cleanup verb alongside Subscription.unsubscribe().
options.code:
effect :: reactive.effect(() => render(state.get()))
effect.dispose()
assert !effect.is_active()

options.name: Drop only
options.detail: Effects detach only when their owner/value is dropped; no deterministic early-stop method is public.
options.technical: Smallest API, but long-lived owners cannot stop one effect early and tests must rely on scope destruction.
options.code: { effect :: reactive.effect(() => render(state.get())) } // detaches at scope end

comparisons.note: Subscription already exposes unsubscribe() and is_active(), with owner scopes for grouped cleanup.
createEffect is normally owned by a reactive root; explicit roots return a disposer for deterministic cleanup.
State objects use dispose(), a UI-specific lifecycle verb.

recommendation.why: A preserves one explicit subscription lifecycle vocabulary, gives experts deterministic control, and keeps Drop as the beginner-safe default.

whyNot.reason: A second cleanup verb adds vocabulary without different semantics.
Drop-only cannot detach one effect early inside a long-lived owner and makes lifecycle acceptance weaker.

recommendation.tradeoff: Effect becomes a small stateful handle rather than a fire-and-forget call; ignored return values still clean up automatically at end of scope.

decisions.title: Performance-session command and one canonical trace artifact
decisions.gist: Choose how users collect CPU, wall, allocation, task, lock, I/O, native, and browser performance facts without colliding with package profiles.
decisions.explainer:
The identifier deliberately avoids the existing D-JPK-PROFILE1 package-generation surface and build profiles. Every first-party option uses one versioned Jet trace artifact; terminal, HTML, and JSON are projections, not competing truths. Collection occurs only under an explicit command or flag and never exposes generated Rust frames by default.

Fable hybrid review: A quietly forks execution semantics — nothing binds `jet perf run` to `jet run`'s flags and driver, the drift that made cargo bench diverge from cargo test; B entangles observation flags with execution and admits it still needs a separate perf utility surface; C abandons beginners and the merged browser+server artifact. The hybrid keeps the dedicated intent family but law-binds it to the base intents' exact surface and code path, makes `.jtrace` portable and version-honest, turns capture policy into an auditable artifact fact, ties compare to ratified D-PERFBUDGET-BASELINE1/SURFACE1 law, and folds C in as export projections.
decisions.story: Bea sees a slow request, profiles the CLI locally, attaches to the same-user service, merges browser and server spans, compares before and after, and gives CI a stable machine report without recording customer values or secrets.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet perf run api.jet --lens=cpu,alloc,tasks
summary: p99 42 ms; 61% parse; 22 MiB allocated
trace: .jet/perf/20260709T190402Z-7f3a.jtrace
$ jet perf view .jet/perf/20260709T190402Z-7f3a.jtrace
decisions.detail: `.jtrace` v1 is the source of truth and contains Jet source identities, source maps, OTel-aligned spans/metrics, scheduler causality, samples, allocation sites, backend facts, and clock calibration. Files default to `.jet/perf/<UTC>-<id>.jtrace`, mode 0600, ignored build state, latest 20 retained; `--keep` pins and `--out` chooses a path. Values, arguments, environment, request/response bodies, URLs/query strings, SQL, credentials, and secret types are excluded by default. Expert capture requires explicit field/capability allowlists. Same-user attach must pass OS permission checks; otherwise a Jet diagnostic explains required authority. Web collection uses the selected real browser through an authenticated loopback dev session and merges clocks into the same artifact; remote targets require explicit authority.

options.name: Dedicated `jet perf` intent family
options.detail: `jet perf run/test/bench/attach` makes collection unmistakable and keeps package/build profile vocabulary separate. Safe defaults print a short summary and write one trace. Expert lenses, frequency, target, duration, subprocess scope, privacy fields, output, retention, and comparison are explicit.
options.code:
jet perf run app.jet --lens=cpu,alloc,tasks
jet perf test --filter parser --compare baseline.jtrace
jet perf attach 4281 --duration 30s
# different user/denied ptrace -> Jet permission diagnostic, no raw OS error

options.name: Performance mode on existing intents
options.detail: `jet run/test/bench --perf` collects the exact same event model and `.jtrace` artifact. This keeps fewer top-level commands but mixes execution and observation flags and makes attach/view less discoverable.
options.code:
jet run app.jet --perf=cpu,alloc
jet test --perf=tasks
jet perf attach 4281   # attach/view still need a small perf utility surface

options.name: External profilers with Jet source-map export
options.detail: Jet emits symbols/source maps and documented adapters for perf, Instruments, ETW, browser traces, and OTel, but owns no collection or trace UI. Experts keep platform power; beginners face several tools and cross-target reports do not share one artifact.
options.code:
jet build app.jet --emit-profile-map
perf record build/app
jet devtools symbolize perf.data

options.name: `jet perf` family, verbatim base-intent surface, exported projections (hybrid)
options.detail: `jet perf run/test/bench` are law-bound to accept the exact flag and argument surface of `jet run/test/bench` (program arguments after `--`) and execute through the same driver code path, so observation never forks execution semantics and flag drift is impossible; `perf attach/view/compare/export` complete the family. `.jtrace` v1 is self-contained — embedded schema version, toolchain identity, source identities, and source maps — so any artifact views on any machine without the repo, and a reader meeting a newer major version names the required toolchain instead of misparsing. Capture policy is part of the artifact: the ballot's default exclusions apply, and every expert `--capture` allowlist is written into the trace manifest so reviewers audit exactly what was recorded. `jet perf compare` applies the ratified pinned-baseline law: hardware/toolchain identity mismatch is a refusal with an explicit override, and reports evaluate declared perf.* budgets. `jet perf export --pprof/--otel/--chrome` plus `--emit-profile-map` keep expert platform tools (C) as projections of the one artifact, never competing truths; generated Rust frames stay hidden unless `--frames=all`.
options.code:
$ jet perf run api.jet --lens=cpu,alloc -- --port 8080   # full `jet run` surface after --
$ jet perf compare base.jtrace head.jtrace   # hardware identity mismatch -> refusal + override
$ jet perf export last --pprof | pprof -      # projection; .jtrace stays the truth
$ jet perf view head.jtrace --frames=all      # expert: generated Rust frames visible

comparisons.note: Counters, traces, dumps, and profiler APIs form a coherent operational toolbox. Jet should unify those facts around Jet source and structured tasks.
One profile format and strong built-in analysis make production diagnosis approachable. Jet adds async/task, browser, privacy, and performance-budget integration.

decisions.title: Web backend: hybrid JS-DOM for views + WASM for logic?
decisions.gist: Jet has no web target. The proposal is to compile view/UI code to JS DOM operations and logic/compute code to WASM, letting the JS bridge own the DOM while WASM handles the heavy work. This is the proceed/kill gate for any web target at all.
decisions.explainer: A hybrid JS+WASM target is the front door to replacing TypeScript. All-WASM hits a known bottleneck: WASM cannot touch the DOM directly without JS glue, so all-WASM still produces JS glue; the question is whether that glue is generated by Jet or hand-written. All-JS transpile loses the safety and performance properties that make Jet worth using. The hybrid strategy matches how wasm-bindgen and Emscripten actually work in practice. This decision gates the JS/Swift interop card (D-JSWIFTFFI1) and interacts with the one-type-system-wire decision (c23wsw4) and reactive-ui.
decisions.story: I write my app logic in Jet and get WASM performance for data processing. My view layer auto-generates efficient DOM updates. I never write TypeScript.

options.name: Hybrid: JS-DOM for views, WASM for logic
options.detail: Jet's codegen partitions the program: UI/view declarations compile to a thin JS driver that issues DOM operations; pure logic functions compile to WASM. The JS driver calls into WASM for compute. Avoids the WASM-DOM roundtrip bottleneck for event-heavy UI while keeping compute fast.

options.name: All-WASM with generated JS glue
options.detail: Compile everything to WASM; generate the JS DOM glue automatically. Simpler codegen split; JS glue is still emitted, just hidden. The WASM-DOM roundtrip cost remains and is harder to optimize without the partition.

options.name: All-JS transpile
options.detail: Compile Jet directly to JavaScript — no WASM. Simple toolchain; no compile step for small scripts. Loses memory safety enforcement, type-system guarantees at runtime, and performance on compute-heavy paths. Jet becomes a TypeScript replacement without the performance story.
options.code:
// jet build --target js
// -> app.js  (no WASM, no safety guarantees at runtime)

options.name: Defer web target
options.detail: No web backend now. Focus on native and CLI targets first. Keeps the target matrix small; blocks the TS-replacement use case indefinitely. Re-evaluate post-Epoch 3.
options.code:
// status quo: jet has no web/WASM target
// jet build --target web  ->  error: target not supported

comparisons.note: wasm-bindgen compiles Rust logic to WASM and generates JS bindings for DOM calls — the hybrid pattern Jet would adopt. Framework crates (Leptos, Yew) sit on top.
Elm compiles to JS only (all-JS), not WASM. Excellent correctness story but no WASM performance path — the tradeoff of option C.
comparisons.code:
-- Elm: compiles entirely to JS, no WASM
main = Browser.sandbox { init = 0, update = update, view = view }

decisions.gist: Partition inference requires a `Browser` effect (or equivalent named call-graph rule) as its engine — the current D-EFF4 closed set has no such entry. The JS/WASM boundary is bidirectional (WASM→JS exports and JS→WASM callbacks) and interacts with the D-SIGNAL1 reactive graph. Before this decision can be ratified, D-WEBKIND1 (WASM target) and D-JSBIND1 (boundary types) must exist as ballot cards, and the inference engine must be defined precisely enough to snapshot-test.
decisions.story: Priya writes a dashboard. Her chart view responds to clicks in the browser, but CSV export and matrix transforms should run in WASM. She does not want to annotate a hundred helper functions; she wants Jet to send pure compute to WASM and keep browser API code in JS.

comparisons.note: Modern web frameworks infer client/server splits from imports and boundaries, minimizing manual export markers.

options.name: Infer from `Browser` effect + allow module-level target ceilings (recommended)
options.detail: Amend D-EFF4 with a `Browser` effect and use effects as the default partition engine: browser/DOM APIs imply JS; pure/compute code is WASM-eligible. Add the useful part of B as expert control: a module may declare `#Target(Wasm)` or `#Target(Js)` as a ceiling/default, and sema validates it against the inferred effects. This keeps beginner magic (no required module declarations) and gives large teams auditable module-level placement. Per-function `#Wasm`, `#Js`, and `#WasmExport` remain overrides. GATES: D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 still need ballots before implementation.

options.name: Module-level `#Target(Wasm)` / `#Target(Js)` declarations + sema validation
options.detail: Each module declares its default compile target in the header. All functions in the module inherit the default; per-function overrides allowed. Inference validates: a `#Target(Wasm)` module calling a Browser-effect function is a compile error. Explicit, auditable, and no language-gate dependency (no comparison-operator or compiler-type-family changes required). Less magic than Option A for beginners; more auditable for large teams. Does not require amending D-EFF4. Compatible with D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 being raised later.

options.name: Defer web partitioning to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not decide the JS/WASM boundary now. D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 are unraised cards that must precede a sound partition model. D-EFF4 may need amending. D-SIGNAL1=A reactive primitives have no boundary model. D-PLUGIN1's Component Model may or may not compose with the web-backend WASM target. Deciding D-WASM1 before these gates produces a model that will be revised within the same epoch.
options.code:
// No web target partition policy yet.
// Epoch 6 revisit after D-WEBKIND1, D-JSBIND1, and D-EFF4 amendment are settled.

decisions.recReason: Effects already encode the information. Inference gives beginner magic and keeps target details out of normal Jet code; explicit markers remain possible later for exports, not partitioning every helper.
decisions.title: For the web backend, how does Jet partition JS DOM code and WASM logic while preserving expert control?
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: pure inference is not enough for experts. Best shape is inferred default plus explicit markers and a partition report. Compared with Next/SvelteKit, Jet should keep the magic boundary inference but add typed bridge/audit reports. Compared with wasm-bindgen, Jet should require less manual glue and own all diagnostics. Adversarial pass: override markers can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema rejects browser handles in WASM, checks bridgeable types/effects, emits a build manifest, and snapshots boundary diagnostics.
decisions.bestCurrent: SvelteKit / Next.js: Modern web frameworks infer client/server splits from imports and boundaries, minimizing manual export markers.
decisions.recommendation: Use effect inference by default plus module-level `#Target` controls (Option A). Pure B makes every beginner choose a target; hybrid A gives magic out of the box and expert visibility where teams need it.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: We must ensure full expert control & auditability. Reconsider this ballot with devil's advocate, make it best in the world.
Agent answer: Updated. New rec: C, not pure inference. Default is inferred from effects and browser API use; experts can pin #Wasm, #Js, #WasmExport, then inspect `jet build --target web --explain-partition`. Devil's advocate: overrides can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema checks all boundary types/effects, rejects browser handles in WASM, emits a bridge manifest, snapshots boundary diagnostics.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): INFERENCE ENGINE GAP: D-EFF4 (ratified) closed the effect vocabulary at ten effects with no Browser/Dom entry; Option C inference has no implementation foundation without amending D-EFF4 or introducing a parallel ad-hoc tracking pass (I8 violation). Option F (add Browser effect) is the I8-coherent path. PURE ≠ WASM: #Pure (empty effect set) ≠ "WASM candidate" — wasm32-wasip2 allows Net/Fs effects in WASM; correct inference rule is "no Browser effect in transitive closure," blocked on D-WEBKIND1. CALLBACK BRIDGE MISSING: #WasmExport covers WASM→JS direction only; JS→WASM callbacks are absent from all options, gated on D-JSBIND1. D-PLUGIN1 COHERENCE: D-PLUGIN1=B (WASM Component Model) and this web-backend WASM model are two distinct incompatible WASM compile targets — neither ballot acknowledges the other.

log.text: Owner asked why not module-level declarations; Option A now includes module-level `#Target` as expert control while keeping inference default.

Adversarial pass complete: options hardened, challenges documented in detail field.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

use core.http as http

It consumes core.url/core.mime/core.net types and lets experts drop lower to those layers without changing the HTTP model.

Great ergonomics, but split across third-party packages.

decisions.title: Exact shared core.http values, bodies, and errors
decisions.gist: Choose the one typed HTTP model shared by clients, servers, routers, and middleware.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A gives beginners named text/json helpers while experts retain one byte-stream, ordered-header, typed-error model. It replaces current client/server wrapper duplication; it does not alter D-HTTPDEPTH1=A or D-WS1=B.
decisions.story: Mara writes an auth middleware once, tests it without a socket, then uses it around both an outbound API client and an inbound service. Today Jet has separate string-backed client/server values, eager text bodies, lossy header maps, and String errors, so streaming, repeated headers, binary data, cancellation, and safe limits cannot compose.
decisions.detail:
Option A exact law. `core.http` owns nominal `Method`, `Status`, `Version`, `HeaderName`, `HeaderValue`, `Headers`, `Request`, `Response`, `Body`, `Handler`, and closed `HttpError`. Client and server submodules re-export these exact values; no parallel HttpClientReq/HttpSrvReq model remains. Method accepts registered tokens plus `Method.custom(token)?`; Status validates 100..599. Headers preserve insertion order and repeated fields, compare names ASCII-case-insensitively, reject control/whitespace-invalid names and CR/LF/NUL values, and expose first/all/append/set/remove. Request contains method, typed Url, version, headers, Body, peer/local metadata and route params when present. Response contains status, version, headers, Body and trailers. `Handler.handle(take Request) -> Response ? HttpError` is the sole composition unit for client transport, router, middleware, and test doubles.

Body is move-only and byte-native. Constructors: empty(), bytes(take [U8]), text(take String, content_type: Mime = text/plain; charset=utf-8), json<T: Encode>(take T), form(...), multipart(...), reader(take Reader, length: Int?=none). Readers: bytes(limit: Int), text(limit: Int), json<T: Decode>(limit: Int), chunks(max_chunk: Int=65536), copy_to(&Writer, limit:Int). A body may be consumed once; second consumption is BodyConsumed. Unknown-length bodies stream with HTTP framing and never buffer implicitly. Default convenience decode limit is 8 MiB client and 1 MiB server; explicit limits are 0..1 GiB. Dropping/cancelling closes source and returns pooled connections only when framing was fully drained. Secret-bearing Authorization/Cookie/Set-Cookie values redact in Debug, diagnostics, audit, and logs.

HttpError is exactly InvalidMethod, InvalidUrl, InvalidHeader, InvalidStatus, BodyConsumed, BodyTooLarge{limit}, InvalidFraming, UnsupportedEncoding, Resolve{host}, Connect{address}, Tls{stage}, Timeout{phase}, Proxy{stage}, Redirect{reason}, Protocol{version}, Io{operation}, Cancelled, ResourceUnavailable{resource}, and Internal{incident_id}. No OS/backend prose, body bytes, credentials, cookies, URL userinfo/query, certificate private material, or generated Rust appears. HTTP non-2xx is a successful Response, never HttpError. Cancellation is task control where available and projects to Cancelled only at an API boundary that returns HttpError. Public parse failures can identify malformed public fields; authentication/TLS internals remain collapsed. Every variant has stable Display, recovery, diagnostic projection, and tests. Binary bodies never pass through UTF-8 lossiness.

Compatibility: current string helpers become source-migration diagnostics at the next allowed core API break, not permanent aliases. Existing `Client.get/post`, `Server.response/sse/static_file`, and request accessors lower to these same values where signatures remain compatible. Beginner pass: `.text()`, `.json()`, and ordinary handlers need no stream knowledge. Expert pass: repeated headers, trailers, exact limits, readers/writers, cancellation, audit, and connection reuse are explicit. Hybrid pass: helpers construct/consume the same Body and Handler; no framework-only second model.

options.name: Unified typed messages, streaming Body, and Handler
options.detail: One byte-native Request/Response/Body/Handler model serves every HTTP role; ergonomic codecs are checked helpers over it.

options.name: Separate ergonomic client and server values
options.detail: Keep distinct client/server request and response types, adding conversion calls at middleware and test boundaries. Role discovery is explicit, but shared policy can drift and conversion can buffer bodies.
options.code:
srv_req :: http.server.Request
common :: http.Message.from_server(take(srv_req))?
client_req :: common.into_client()?

options.name: Buffered text-first compatibility model
options.detail: Retain current String bodies/maps and add optional stream helpers beside them. Simple calls stay familiar, but binary payloads, repeated headers, bounded memory, pooling, and cancellation have two competing paths.
options.code:
resp.body()       // String
resp.body_stream() // separate semantics

comparisons.note: Request, Response, Header, Body, Handler compose across client/server; Body is streaming and must be closed.
Shared typed parts and handler pipelines preserve streaming/backpressure across roles.

decisions.title: Exact core.http client transport policy
decisions.gist: Choose client pooling, redirects, cookies, proxies, compression, timeouts, and protocol behavior.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A keeps `http.get` ceremony-free but makes one immutable Client policy object the explicit expert path. Defaults are safe, bounded, HTTPS-first, environment-aware, and observable.
decisions.story: Inez calls hundreds of tenant APIs through corporate proxies. She needs safe HTTPS defaults, pooled connections, bounded streaming downloads, controlled redirects, cookies, gzip, per-phase deadlines, HTTP/2, and an audit trail without retrying unsafe writes or leaking credentials across origins.
decisions.inWild:
client :: http.Client.new()
  .timeout(total: 30s, connect: 5s, read_idle: 10s)
  .redirects(.Follow(max: 5, same_origin_credentials: false))
res :: client.send(http.Request.get(url).header("accept", "application/json"))?
decisions.detail:
Requires D-HTTP-CORE2=A. Option A exact law. `Client.new()` owns a Send+Sync pool keyed by scheme, host, port, proxy, TLS identity/policy and protocol; default per-origin idle=8, global idle=64, idle timeout=90s, max concurrent per origin=64, DNS cache positive=60s/negative=5s. `http.get/post` use one process-default Client with identical policy. Keep-alive is default; unread bodies make that connection non-reusable unless explicitly drained within limit. HTTP/2 negotiates ALPN for HTTPS and reuses multiplexed sessions; HTTP/1.1 remains supported; cleartext h2c requires explicit expert policy. No HTTP/3.

Redirect default Follow(max:10): only 301/302/303 rewrite POST to GET; 307/308 preserve method/body only when replayable; cycles and max return Redirect. Cross-origin redirects strip Authorization, Proxy-Authorization and Cookie; downgrade HTTPS->HTTP is denied unless explicit policy. CookieJar is opt-in on custom Client, RFC6265bis domain/path/secure/samesite/expiry bounded to 4096 cookies and 180/domain; shortcut helpers are stateless. Redirect history is inspectable. Automatic retries default only for stale pooled connection before request bytes and idempotent methods with replayable bodies, max one; no status retry.

Timeout has dns, connect, tls, write_idle, first_byte, read_idle, and total phases; defaults total=30s, connect/tls=10s, idle=30s. Zero means immediate, none disables only when explicitly supplied. Task deadline is the upper bound. Proxy policy defaults `FromEnvironment`: HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY/ALL_PROXY and NO_PROXY parsed once per request with lowercase precedence rules documented; credentials redact. Explicit None disables env. CONNECT tunnels HTTPS. SOCKS requires separately ratified support and is absent.

Request bodies support bytes/text/json/form plus streaming reader and multipart parts with known/unknown length. Response decompression advertises gzip and transparently decodes gzip by default, removes Content-Encoding/Length from decoded view while raw metadata remains inspectable; unsupported encoding errors, no silent bytes. `.raw_encoding()` opts out. Upload/download backpressure uses 64KiB chunks and configured caps. TLS inherits D-TLS1 system roots/SNI/hostname validation; custom roots, client identity, pins, minimum TLS and danger overrides use `core.tls` typed policy, never booleans; danger requires #Unsafe. Each response exposes protocol, remote address, redirect history, timings, reused_connection.

No ambient cache. Client clones share pool/jar; policy builders return a new client namespace. Beginner pass: `http.get(url)?.text()` works safely. Expert pass: every pool/proxy/TLS/deadline/redirect/compression/replay/audit fact is controllable. Hybrid: shortcuts send through the same Client implementation.

options.name: Safe pooled Client with explicit policy builders
options.detail: Requests-style shortcuts and one reusable policy-rich Client share transport semantics.
options.code:
res :: http.get(url)?
api :: http.Client.new().proxy(.None).cookies(.Memory).protocols([.Http2,.Http11])
res2 :: api.send(take(req))?

options.name: Global transport policy
options.detail: Pooling and environment policy live in process-global setters. Short calls are compact, but tests/tenants can interfere and authority is hidden.
options.code:
http.configure(proxy: env, redirects: 5)
http.get(url)?

options.name: One connection per request
options.detail: Every request dials independently; streaming exists but pooling, cookie state, multiplexing and shared policy are caller-owned.
options.code:
req :: http.Request.get(url)
http.send_once(take(req))?

comparisons.note: Client scopes pooling, cookies, redirects, proxies and timeouts while top-level helpers stay simple.
Client wraps a reusable Transport with redirect policy and streaming response bodies.

decisions.title: Exact core.http server, router, middleware, and lifecycle
decisions.gist: Choose safe server defaults, route law, middleware composition, streaming, shutdown, files, and logging.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A makes the safe production path the default while retaining exact expert policy on one Server/Router/Handler mechanism. It replaces the current unbounded read-to-String and thread-per-connection behavior.
decisions.story: Omar runs a public REST and SSE service. A slow client must not exhaust memory or threads; route conflicts must fail before listening; middleware must preserve typed errors; shutdown must drain healthy work, cancel stragglers, and publish no partial response; files need traversal-safe ranges and logs must redact secrets.
decisions.inWild:
router :: http.Router.new()
router.get("/users/{id}", show_user)
router.get("/assets/{*path}", http.static_files(root))
app :: http.middleware.recover(http.middleware.access_log(router))
server :: http.Server.bind("127.0.0.1:8080", app)?
server.serve(shutdown: ctx)?
decisions.detail:
Requires D-HTTP-CORE2=A. Option A exact law. Router patterns use literal segments, `{name}` one-segment params, and final `{*name}` catch-all only; percent-decode each segment once after splitting, reject invalid UTF-8/encoded slash ambiguity, dot traversal and duplicate names. Static beats param beats wildcard; then registration order. Duplicate method+equivalent pattern and ambiguous equal-specificity overlap fail at registration with RouteConflict. HEAD falls back to GET without body; OPTIONS auto-lists methods; 405 carries Allow; unknown is 404. Methods get/post/put/patch/delete/head/options plus on(Method,...). Params are immutable typed map. No regex route language.

Router implements Handler. `middleware(fn(next:Handler)->Handler)` wraps handlers; order is declaration order, outermost first request/last response. Built-ins: request_id, recover, timeout, body_limit, cors(explicit policy), compression, access_log(core.log), and static_files. Panic/internal failure closes/publishes nothing if headers unsent and maps to redacted 500+incident; after streaming begins it aborts connection. Middleware cannot read a body twice; buffering requires explicit bounded bytes(limit).

Server.bind(SocketAddr|String, Handler, options=Safe) -> Server ? HttpError; `.local_addr()`, `.serve(shutdown: Context=never)`, `.shutdown(grace:Duration=30s)`, `.serve_listener(take TcpListener,...)`. Defaults: header bytes 32KiB, header count 100, request-line 8KiB, body 1MiB unless route raises it, read-header 5s, read-idle 30s, write-idle 30s, keepalive idle 60s, max requests/connection 1000, global connections 10k with per-IP 256, handler concurrency bounded by task scheduler. Over-limit returns 400/408/413/431/503 as appropriate then closes when framing is unsafe. Parse incrementally; reject request smuggling: conflicting Content-Length, invalid/multiple transfer framing, obs-fold, whitespace-before-colon, CL+TE, invalid chunks. HTTP/1.1 keepalive/pipelining preserves response order; HTTP/2 streams share Handler with per-stream/connection flow control.

Response Body streams bytes/chunks/SSE with backpressure. SSE sets text/event-stream, no buffering, heartbeat optional, cancellation closes generator. Trailers require declaration before headers. Graceful shutdown stops accepts/GOAWAY, lets active requests finish until grace, cancels rest, drains no new keepalive work, returns report counts. TLS uses D-TLSSERVE1 typed material and core.tls policy; cert reload is atomic typed callback, old connections keep old config.

`static_files(root: Path, index=["index.html"], symlinks:.Deny)` canonicalizes beneath root, denies traversal/special files, infers core.mime, supports GET/HEAD, single byte range 206/416, If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since, ETag, zero-copy where safe; directory listing off. Access log is a core.log typed event containing request id, method, redacted path (query omitted by default), route template, status, bytes, duration, peer/protocol/TLS; never Authorization/Cookie/body. Beginner pass: bind router and serve. Expert pass: every parser/limit/scheduler/TLS/shutdown/file/log fact is typed and auditable. Hybrid: built-ins are ordinary Handler wrappers.

options.name: Bounded Handler server with deterministic Router
options.detail: Safe production limits, typed lifecycle, streaming/backpressure and middleware are default parts of one server model.
options.code:
router.get("/users/{id}", show)
server :: http.Server.bind("0.0.0.0:8080", http.middleware.access_log(router))?
server.serve(shutdown: app_context)?

options.name: Minimal listener plus optional framework layer
options.detail: Core serves handlers with basic parsing; routing, middleware, files, limits and shutdown policy live in another package. This splits D-HTTPDEPTH1's batteries-included path.
options.code: http.listen(addr, (conn) => framework.serve(conn, app))?

options.name: Callback server with global defaults
options.detail: Keep `serve(addr,mux)` and configure limits/logging/shutdown globally. Compact, but authority, tests and multiple-server policy become ambient.
options.code:
http.server_limits(body: 1*MiB)
Server.serve(addr, mux)?

comparisons.note: Handler/ServeMux, streaming bodies, Server timeouts and Shutdown form one production server substrate.
Router and middleware lower to one service abstraction with body backpressure.

decisions.title: Temporary production HTTP and compression dependency closure
decisions.gist: Whether generated Jet programs may use a locked audited Rust HTTP stack until native replacement closes in Epoch 3.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation B follows I6's Epoch-3 end state: build the production protocol stack natively now, retaining only already-ratified TLS bridges until their inherited deletion gates close. Option A is ballot-complete as a bridge policy, but grants no package because no exact graph is attached.
decisions.story: Priya ships the same Jet service on Linux, macOS, Windows and WASI. The compiler currently emits a hidden ureq/rustls bridge while the server is an unsafe-in-practice handwritten parser. She needs HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, TLS, pooling, gzip and multipart to use one reviewed dependency closure whose exact packages, features, licenses, advisories, targets and deletion gates are owner-approved before any network fetch.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet audit dependencies --package service
core.http bridge: D-DEP-HTTP2
operation slice: client-http2-gzip
lock/sbom/rustsec/targets: signed, exact match
network: unopened before verification
decisions.detail:
Companion to D-HTTP-CORE2/CLIENT2/SERVER2; each grants nothing until independently ratified. Current truth: client bridge names ureq and TLS bridges name rustls/system roots; server HTTP/1.1 is handwritten std-only, reads unbounded bytes into lossy String, uses thread-per-connection, and does not supply production HTTP/2/compression/parsing. Option A authorizes a generated-program-only bridge, never compiler/seam Cargo.toml deps (I6), containing a minimal maintained pure-Rust HTTP/1.1 parser/codec, HTTP/2 framing/HPACK, async-or-readiness transport compatible with core.tasks/core.net, gzip codec, MIME multipart support, rustls and platform roots. No OpenSSL/C, native assembly, Tokio-only parallel runtime, ambient DNS/RNG, or default features are implicitly approved.

This draft deliberately does not pretend an exact graph exists. Before queue-ready implementation authority, attach: exact direct crate names/versions/default-features/features; complete per-target Cargo.lock checksums; SPDX/license-file hashes; cargo-deny policy; fresh RustSec DB revision and zero-unapproved report; minimal operation slices (client h1, client h2, server h1, server h2, gzip, multipart, TLS client/server); build/process/symbol traces on Linux x86_64/aarch64, macOS x86_64/arm64, Windows MSVC x86_64/arm64, WASI where supported; MSRV/tool hashes; deterministic generator hash; signed DSSE bundle and offline verify-before-fetch. WASI unsupported server/listener operations must return typed UnsupportedTarget, not silently omit behavior. Any advisory/yank/license/feature/graph change requires owner amendment.

Release rejects unsigned, expired, rollback, mixed-lock, extra-feature, unused-direct-crate or network-before-proof state. Generated manifests select only the operation-minimal slice. Cache keys bind source, decision, generator, lock, target, features and toolchain. Dependency errors map through D-HTTP-CORE2 closed errors; backend prose never reaches users.

Epoch-3 deletion gates exist per seam: parser/framing hostile differential corpus and smuggling review; HTTP/2 RFC vectors/flow-control/HPACK review; pooling/redirect/proxy/cookie interop; gzip bombs/truncation/differential; multipart boundary/filename injection; rustls/root bridge inherited native replacement; scheduler/readiness/cancellation; every supported target, independent review, rollback, bridge/lock/SBOM/cache deletion and symbol absence. Beginner: no dependency ceremony. Expert: exact graph, authority, feature, target and audit evidence inspectable. Hybrid: one signed operation-sliced bundle powers shortcuts and expert clients/servers.
