Failed deterministic build budgets still prevent a successful artifact and therefore cannot be bypassed by proof.

options.name: Eager statistical refresh at owning command boundaries
options.detail: Build, development, and benchmark commands eagerly refresh every statistical measurement they can reach. This produces fresher data but makes normal commands do extra work.
options.code:
$ jet build app.jet --release
deterministic budgets: 2 passed
target statistical budgets: 1 warning
# Service, Scene, and Bench providers were not started by build.
options.technical: Keep A's hard deterministic build gates, one evaluator, read-only dossier/Canvas/LSP, and exact #240 Evidence/pass_incomplete/exit law. In addition, build refreshes applicable statistical Target scopes after deterministic gates, dev refreshes all applicable Service/Scene scopes at the same explicit start/ready boundaries, and bench refreshes all Bench scopes. Compatible slices may satisfy matching #240 Evidence exactly as A. No command runs a provider outside the target/service/scene/bench it already owns, so build does not launch services/scenes and editor views remain side-effect free.

comparisons.note: Editors show saved test state and wait for an explicit run action. All options keep editor views read-only.
Bazel reuses command facts only when their build graph and context still match.

decisions.lesson:
Performance budgets become useful only when the right commands measure them at the right time. Deterministic evidence, such as artifact size or compiler facts, should be identical for the same build inputs and can hard-gate every artifact-producing build. Statistical evidence, such as startup time or frame time, varies between runs and needs repeated samples in the runtime context that owns the workload.

Refresh means collecting new evidence. Reuse means accepting existing evidence only when its context still matches: budget definition, source, workload, target, profile, device, and provider facts. Stale or mismatched evidence must never silently pass. Read-only views such as an editor, dossier, or Canvas should display freshness and results without launching benchmarks or services as a side effect. Commands such as bench or dev already own those workloads and are natural refresh points.

Proof aggregation is separate from measurement. A proof command can reuse compatible recorded facts, mark missing required evidence incomplete, and preserve an existing failed result without becoming another hidden benchmark runner. This ballot chooses whether matching command-specific slices can satisfy proof, whether only a whole-policy check can, and how eagerly runtime-owning commands refresh statistical evidence.

recommendation.why: A measures work where users already expect it and safely reuses exact matching facts. It avoids both hidden work and needless repeated checks.

whyNot.reason: B forces a full budget check even when another command already produced the exact fact that proof needs.
C makes ordinary build and development commands run extra statistical work that users did not request.

recommendation.tradeoff: A needs strict rules for deciding when saved evidence still matches. Those checks are necessary to prevent stale results from passing.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps whole-policy checks, lets each command measure only work it owns, and reuses exact matching facts without treating a slice as full coverage.

harvest.aspect: Exact matching facts can avoid repeated work.
harvest.use: Keep fact-level reuse with strict context checks.

harvest.aspect: A full budget check remains the clearest whole-policy report.
harvest.use: Keep that command as the complete policy view.

harvest.aspect: Commands should measure only workloads they already own.
harvest.use: Keep this boundary but do not make every possible measurement eager.

decisions.title: Filesystem watch surface and home
decisions.gist: Where filesystem change notifications live and what the beginner surface looks like.
decisions.explainer: A: discovery beats taxonomy — the person with a path in hand is already in core.files; normalize per-OS quirks and debounce by default.
decisions.story: Lena writes a static-site tool in Jet and wants rebuild-on-save. Today she loops fs.list_dir + mtimes on a timer — wasteful, laggy, and subtly wrong on renames. jet dev itself watches files internally; users deserve the same primitive.

options.name: files.watch in core.files
options.detail: One more capability on the module that owns paths: watch(path) returns a WatchHandle whose events() iterate typed changes (Created/Modified/Removed/Renamed). Debounced by default (beginner-safe); raw stream behind an option.

options.name: New core.watch module
options.detail: Separate module name for the whole watching domain (files now; maybe processes/ports later). Cleaner if watching grows beyond files, but today it is one function and a new top-level name to learn.

options.name: Decline — polling helper only
options.detail: Ship files.poll_changes(path, interval) sugar over mtime polling. No OS notification backends to maintain, but it bakes the laggy/wasteful pattern in as the blessed answer.
options.code: loop ev in files.poll_changes("site/", time.ms(500)) { rebuild() }

comparisons.note: fsnotify is the de-facto standard everyone pulls in — Go not shipping it in stdlib is a known gap.
fs.watch is stdlib but semantics vary per-OS; chokidar exists to paper over it — the lesson is to normalize events in the library.

decisions.comment: also include processes and ports now, not later

decisions.title: Core filesystem depth surface
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical shape for deep file and path operations.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A keeps one semantic path model: typed Path is the backbone for composition and audit, while core.files keeps beginner-friendly string entrypoints that immediately coerce into Path. This reconciles D-PATHFS1 with today's core.files docs without creating two mechanisms.
decisions.story: Marta writes a static-site publisher. She needs to create nested folders, copy an asset tree, atomically write output, inspect mtimes, skip symlink cycles, and clean a temp directory when the build exits. If Jet gives her only read/write/list_dir, she falls back to brittle string paths and shell commands.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: Path-only purity makes beginner scripts noisy; string-only helpers make expert audit and cycle-safe walking weak. The hybrid is one mechanism because every string entrypoint lowers to Path before sema/codegen effects, docs, and audit facts see it. No aliases: names are stable once ratified.

options.name: Path backbone plus string entrypoints (recommended)
options.detail: Ratify typed Path as the internal and expert surface, and keep core.files string helpers as the beginner facade. Add Stat, FileKind, WalkEntry, TempDir, FileLock, and one canonical operation set: stat, create_dir_all, remove_dir, remove_all, glob, walk, symlink/read_link, hard_link, temp_dir/temp_file, lock, canonicalize, absolute, copy_dir, read_at/write_at/seek, fsync, write_atomic.
options.code:
use core.files as files

p :: Path.from("site").join("posts")
files.create_dir_all(p)?              // Path accepted
files.create_dir_all("site/posts")? // String accepted by same coercion

stat :: files.stat(p)?
if stat.kind == .Dir {
    loop ent in files.walk(p)? { print(ent.path.to_string()) }
}

tmp :: files.temp_dir()?              // RAII cleanup
lock :: files.lock("build.lock")?   // advisory, scoped
files.write_atomic(p.join("index.html"), bytes)?

options.name: String-only core.files
options.detail: All operations are module functions over String paths. Very easy to type, but path composition, relative roots, symlink-cycle handling, and audit output stay stringly typed.

options.name: Path-only methods
options.detail: Every deep operation hangs off Path methods. Strong audit and discoverability from a Path value, but beginner one-file scripts must learn Path before simple tasks like mkdir -p or remove_all.
options.code:
root :: Path.from("site")
root.join("posts").create_dir_all()?
root.walk().filter((e) => e.stat.kind == .File)

options.name: Decline depth for now
options.detail: Keep read/write/list_dir/open and document shell/core.process workarounds. This leaves Jet worse than Python pathlib, Go os, and Rust fs for everyday scripting and build tools.
options.code:
process.run(["mkdir", "-p", out])?
process.run(["cp", "-R", src, out])?

comparisons.note: pathlib gives a pleasant Path object, but many APIs still accept strings. Jet can keep that ergonomics while making audit facts typed.
os and filepath are robust but split path values into strings. Jet can be more discoverable with typed Path plus module helpers.
std::path and std::fs have strong types and broad coverage, but error copy is not beginner-facing. Jet keeps the front-end diagnostic contract.

decisions.title: Unified watch surface for files, processes, and ports
decisions.gist: Choose how watch-style change notifications cover files, processes, and ports.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A honors the owner's D-FSWATCH1 comment now: one Watch/Event model, with constructors in the domain where the thing lives. Beginners find files.watch(path); experts compose typed watchers across files, process exit, and port readiness without polling.
decisions.story: Earl builds a dev runner in Jet. It rebuilds when source files change, restarts a child server, waits until port 3000 is accepting connections, and exits cleanly if the child dies. Today he needs three different polling loops and timing guesses.
decisions.inWild:
use core.files as files
use core.process as process
use core.net as net

watch :: WatchSet.new()
watch.add(files.watch("src")?)
child :: process.spawn(["jet", "run", "server.jet"])?
watch.add(process.watch(child))
watch.add(net.watch_port(3000))

loop ev in watch.events() { handle(ev) }
decisions.detail: Devil pass: a single core.watch module looks clean, but it becomes a taxonomy drawer and steals discovery from the domain APIs. Domain constructors plus one shared WatchSet/Event type preserve one mechanism while keeping entrypoints where users already are.

options.name: Domain constructors plus shared WatchSet (recommended)
options.detail: files.watch(path), process.watch(child_or_pid), and net.watch_port(port_or_addr) return typed Watch handles with one shared WatchEvent enum and WatchSet multiplexer. Debounced file events are the default; raw event streams are explicit options.

options.name: One core.watch module
options.detail: watch.files, watch.process, and watch.port live under one top-level module. Easy to enumerate, but the common beginner case imports a taxonomy module instead of the file/process/net module already in use.
options.code:
use core.watch as watch

w :: watch.set([
    watch.files("src")?,
    watch.process(child),
    watch.port(3000),
])

options.name: Only files in Epoch 3
options.detail: Implement D-FSWATCH1 literally and defer process/port watching. This ignores the owner ratification comment and leaves dev-runner tooling polling process/port state.

options.name: Callback watchers
options.detail: Each watch call takes a lambda callback. Good for tiny examples, but harder to compose, cancel, test, and replay than event values.
options.code:
files.watch("src", (ev) => rebuild())?
process.watch(child, (ev) => stop())?
net.watch_port(3000, (ev) => ready())?

comparisons.note: Node has fs.watch and child process events, but port readiness is hand-rolled. Jet can unify these as typed event values.
comparisons.code: fs.watch('src', cb); child.on('exit', cb); net.createConnection(port).on('connect', cb)

comparisons.note: Go pushes file watching to fsnotify and process/port readiness to ad hoc goroutines/channels. Jet can ship the channel-like composition in Core.
notify plus tokio process/net can compose, but through external crates and async runtime choices. Jet keeps a blocking beginner surface and explicit expert control.

decisions.comment: a & b - instead of putting file watcher in file module/lib, put all watcher methods in a core.watcher lib. ALSO, support callback/event triggers with our new event system

decisions.title: Socket layer surface
decisions.gist: Choose the socket API beneath HTTP and services.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: Go-like simple networking with explicit expert hooks for readiness/cancellation/performance.
decisions.story: Nora writes a Redis-like protocol and a health checker. She needs TCP/UDP, Unix sockets where available, timeouts, listeners, addresses, DNS, and TLS handoff without inventing raw OS wrappers.
decisions.inWild:
use core.net as net

conn :: net.tcp_connect("example.com", 443)?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: Go-like simple networking with explicit expert hooks for readiness/cancellation/performance.

options.name: Hybrid: blocking-looking sockets over shared runtime handles (recommended)
options.detail: core.net exposes typed blocking-looking Tcp/Udp/Unix/DNS APIs for beginners. Under the hood the handles are compatible with the task runtime, so experts can opt into readiness, deadlines, cancellation, and high-concurrency serving without a second socket model.

options.name: Async-first sockets
options.detail: Every net op returns tasks/futures. Good for servers, but beginner scripts pay async ceremony before they need it.
options.code: conn :: await net.connect(addr)

options.name: HTTP-only networking
options.detail: Push raw protocols out of Core. That blocks servers, DB clients, and tooling that Go owns today.
options.code: http.get("https://...")?

comparisons.note: net gives blocking-looking APIs multiplexed by runtime; Jet can mirror ergonomics while preserving task law.
std::net is blocking; async ecosystems add split APIs.

decisions.title: DNS resolver trust and platform contract
decisions.gist: Choose how ordinary DNS lookups use the host, validate replies, and fall back.
decisions.story: Mira runs the same service on Linux, macOS, Windows, a VPN, and a corporate split-DNS network. A lookup must honor each host's resolver policy, never silently send private names to a public resolver, reject forged packets, and still allow an expert to query a named DNS server.
decisions.inWild:
use core.net as net

addrs :: net.resolve_ip("db.corp.example")?
records :: net.DnsResolver.at("10.20.0.53:53").txt("_policy.corp.example")?
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: the host resolver is automatic. Expert pass: one typed resolver handle controls server, deadline, and audit-visible behavior. Hybrid pass: both return the same record types and NetError law. Security law: unpredictable IDs; source, ID, QR, opcode, question, class, RCODE, bounds, compression-loop, and truncation validation; UDP TC retries over TCP; no invented public fallback. Platform law: native resolver configuration on Linux, macOS, Windows, BSD; search domains and hosts-file behavior belong only to the system path. Dependency law: std/OS APIs or an owner-approved runtime bridge outside compiler seam crates; never a compiler dependency; any bootstrap bridge carries native-ize ownership.

options.name: System default plus strict first-party wire resolver (recommended)
options.detail: Ordinary calls delegate to the platform resolver and preserve VPN, search-domain, hosts-file, and enterprise policy. `DnsResolver.at` is the single expert escape hatch and uses a strict first-party UDP/TCP DNS client. Missing/invalid host configuration is an error, never a public fallback.

options.name: Strict first-party resolver for every lookup
options.detail: Every call parses platform resolver configuration, then sends validated DNS itself. This gives uniform packet behavior but partially reimplements platform policy and can diverge from VPN, mDNS, hosts files, NSS, and Windows resolver behavior.

options.name: Approved resolver bridge for every lookup
options.detail: A vetted runtime resolver bridge owns platform policy and DNS parsing. It may be bootstrapped behind the Core FFI boundary only after separate dependency approval; the compiler remains dependency-free and the bridge must expose Jet's exact errors and deadlines.

comparisons.note: `net.Resolver` uses system or Go resolution depending on platform/config and offers an explicit resolver hook; Jet should keep one typed result/error law.
`ToSocketAddrs` follows the platform but does not expose TXT/SRV; ecosystem DNS clients add explicit wire resolution.

decisions.title: Socket bytes, text helpers, and close law
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical payload and shutdown model for TCP, UDP, and Unix sockets.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a database driver whose frames contain arbitrary bytes and half-closes its request side before reading the reply. He also writes a beginner echo server that should remain pleasant for UTF-8 text.
decisions.inWild:
conn :: net.Tcp.connect("127.0.0.1:5432")?
conn.write_all(frame)?
conn.shutdown(.Write)?
reply :: conn.read(64.kib)?
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: `read_text` and `write_text` make the echo case obvious. Expert pass: bytes preserve every protocol, partial reads/writes, limits, peer EOF, half-close, local close, and UDP truncation metadata. Hybrid pass: text helpers are checked projections over the same byte operations, not a second transport; the same byte operations are the ratified `Reader`/`Writer` stream contract (D-IO2 `FileReader`/`FileWriter`, D-ENCSTREAM1 codec stream modes), so stream sockets and a wrapped TLS stream compose with the same generic middleware as files and codecs. Datagram law: UDP is packet-oriented, never a byte stream, so it keeps `receive` with source, original length, and `truncated`, and does not implement the stream contract. Socket-only facts (half-close, peer address, readiness) stay first-class inherent methods, never trait-probed capabilities. Unix sockets are available on Unix; unsupported targets reject at compile time when target is known, otherwise return `.Unsupported(.UnixSocket)`. Close law: `close` is idempotent; `shutdown(.Read|.Write|.Both)` is explicit and subsequent misuse returns `.Closed`. Option D subtlety: conformance reuses the reserved `Reader`/`Cursor` core names under D-IO2's user-type-wins guard and adds no new trait or transport; a socket read through generic `Reader` middleware and a direct `conn.read` are the identical byte operation, so there is one canonical mechanism, not two.

options.name: Bytes canonical, checked text helpers
options.detail: TCP/Unix `read(limit)` returns bytes and empty bytes means EOF; `write` returns count; `write_all` loops. UDP packets contain bytes, source, original length, and `truncated`. `read_text` validates UTF-8. `close` is idempotent; `shutdown(.Read|.Write|.Both)` is explicit and subsequent misuse returns `.Closed`. Sockets carry these operations as their own methods only, so generic buffering, framing, or codec middleware cannot compose over them without a socket-specific adapter.
options.code:
chunk :: conn.read(64.kib)?
if chunk.is_empty() { print("peer closed") }
conn.write_all(chunk)?
line :: conn.read_text(8.kib)? // invalid UTF-8 => .InvalidText
conn.shutdown(.Write)?
conn.close()?

packet :: udp.receive(64.kib)?
if packet.truncated { return .PacketTooLarge(packet.original_len) }

options.name: Generic readable/writable stream trait
options.detail: Sockets expose bytes through shared `Reader`/`Writer` traits; text uses Core codecs. This unifies files, TLS, and sockets, but makes socket-only facts such as datagram boundaries, peer address, half-close, and readiness additional capability methods.
options.code:
chunk :: io.read(conn, 64.kib)?
io.write_all(conn, frame)?
net.shutdown(conn, .Write)?
packet :: udp.receive(64.kib)?

options.name: Keep String payloads
options.detail: TCP, UDP, and Unix operations remain UTF-8-only. Arbitrary protocols fail with invalid-text errors and UDP cannot safely represent all datagrams, so Core cannot meet the raw-socket mandate.
options.code:
text :: conn.read()?
// binary frame => error: tcp read: invalid UTF-8

options.name: Byte-canonical sockets that also conform to the shared Reader/Writer contract (recommended)
options.detail: Recommended. Keep every byte and close rule of A, and additionally make stream sockets (TCP, Unix) and the wrapped TLS stream implement the ratified `Reader`/`Writer` core contract (D-IO2, D-ENCSTREAM1) so files, codecs, TLS, and sockets all compose with one generic middleware set. `read_text`/`write_text` stay checked UTF-8 projections over the same bytes. Socket-only facts stay first-class inherent methods, so datagram boundaries, peer address, half-close, and readiness are never capability probes. UDP stays datagram-only and does not implement the stream contract. This dominates A by adding generic composition at no cost to socket richness, and dominates B by keeping datagram and half-close facts concrete instead of trait-probed and text a checked projection instead of a separate codec step.

comparisons.note: Connections read/write byte slices and expose half-close on TCP; text is layered above.
`Read`/`Write` are byte-oriented; `shutdown` selects read, write, or both.

decisions.title: Typed network error law
decisions.gist: Choose what callers can reliably inspect when networking fails.
decisions.story: Asha retries timeouts, reports DNS not-found without retrying, and removes a Unix-socket feature on unsupported targets. String matching would make those decisions depend on OS wording.
decisions.detail: All fallible core.net operations return `? NetError`; stable cases include InvalidInput, PermissionDenied, AddressInUse, AddressUnavailable, ConnectionRefused, ConnectionReset, NotConnected, Closed, Timeout, Cancelled, Unsupported, Dns, Tls, Protocol, and Other. Each carries operation plus relevant address/name and a display message; raw OS code is optional expert audit data, never control-flow law. Compiler diagnostics cover statically known target/API misuse; runtime failures remain values.

options.name: One structured NetError family (recommended)
options.detail: One exhaustive top-level network error with nested DNS/TLS/protocol detail. Stable variants drive logic across platforms; `message`, `operation`, `address`, `os_code` support reporting/audit. Deadline and cancellation are distinct.

options.name: Per-operation error enums
options.detail: ConnectError, ReadError, DnsError, and TlsError precisely enumerate each call. Callers gain narrow types but generic middleware must repeatedly translate them and the same OS event can acquire divergent names.
options.code:
conn: TcpStream ? ConnectError :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)
chunk: Bytes ? ReadError :: conn.read(64.kib)

options.name: Keep String errors
options.detail: Every operation preserves human-readable strings only. This is easy to print but unsafe for retry, fallback, metrics, and cross-platform control flow.

comparisons.note: `net.Error` exposes timeout/temporary behavior while concrete errors retain operation and address.
comparisons.code: if ne, ok := err.(net.Error); ok && ne.Timeout() { ... }

comparisons.note: `io::ErrorKind` gives stable categories plus optional raw OS codes.

decisions.title: Socket deadlines, cancellation, and readiness
decisions.gist: Choose how one socket model serves scripts and high-concurrency tasks.
decisions.story: Leo writes a simple health check, then grows it into ten thousand concurrent probes. The same socket calls must honor the surrounding task budget, permit an explicit per-operation deadline, cancel promptly, and expose readiness without creating async-only socket types.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: blocking-looking calls automatically observe current #Context. Expert pass: named `deadline:` override, cancellation token/context, readiness interest, and scheduler integration use the same handle. Hybrid pass: no AsyncTcpStream type. Precedence: earliest of current context deadline and explicit deadline; cancellation returns `.Cancelled`; expiry returns `.Timeout`; manual socket timeout is persistent configuration and cannot extend a context budget.

options.name: Context-aware calls plus readiness on same handles (recommended)
options.detail: Every blocking-looking operation yields through the shared runtime where available, checks cancellation, and obeys the earliest budget. Experts call `ready` or pass named deadlines on the same Tcp/Udp/Unix/DNS handles. Native-thread fallback preserves semantics without claiming multiplexing.

options.name: Context-only blocking calls
options.detail: Operations observe #Context but expose no readiness or per-call override. Simple and coherent, yet expert event loops cannot integrate sockets without a second lower-level API.

options.name: Separate async socket types
options.detail: Blocking sockets remain simple while AsyncTcp/AsyncUdp own cancellation and readiness. This splits semantics and violates the ratified one-handle hybrid direction.
options.code:
conn :: await net.AsyncTcp.connect(host)
chunk :: await conn.read(64.kib)

comparisons.note: Blocking-looking operations are runtime-polled; context is commonly passed to dialing and DNS while connection deadlines interrupt I/O.
Structured cancellation applies through coroutine context while sockets remain resources.

decisions.title: TLS layering over socket streams
decisions.gist: Choose how TLS wraps sockets without creating a second I/O model.
decisions.story: Noor connects through a preconfigured TCP socket, sets SNI and verification policy, reads binary protocol frames, and needs the same deadline, cancellation, close, and audit behavior before and after TLS.
decisions.inWild:
tcp :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)?
tls :: tls.client(tcp, server_name: "api.example.com")?
tls.write_all(frame)?
reply :: tls.read(64.kib)?
decisions.detail: D-TLS1 remains law: safe HTTPS defaults use rustls and system roots; advanced client TLS configuration lives in core.tls. This ballot only fixes stream composition. Default verification cannot be disabled outside the audited expert/unsafe policy already governing TLS. ALPN, roots, client identity, SNI, protocol versions, handshake deadline, peer identity, and close-notify are explicit expert controls. Runtime rustls bridge remains outside compiler seam crates under the existing approved dependency/native-ize law.

options.name: core.tls wraps the canonical byte stream (recommended)
options.detail: `tls.client` consumes a connected TcpStream and returns TlsStream implementing the same byte/readiness/deadline/close law. Safe defaults verify hostname with system roots. `TlsClientConfig` adds roots, ALPN, identity, and version bounds; insecure verification is unavailable here.
options.code:
cfg :: tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_alpn(["h2", "http/1.1"])
tcp :: net.Tcp.connect(addr)?
secure :: tls.client(tcp, server_name: host, config: cfg, deadline: 3.seconds)?
secure.write_all(frame)?
secure.close()? // sends close-notify, then closes transport

options.name: TLS methods remain inside core.net
options.detail: `net.tls_connect` consumes TcpStream and returns a separate TlsStream API. This keeps current placement but mixes transport and security policy, duplicates read/write functions, and conflicts with core.tls ownership of advanced configuration.
options.code:
secure :: net.tls_connect(tcp, host)?
net.tls_write(secure, text)?
net.tls_close(secure)?

options.name: TLS only through core.http
options.detail: Raw TLS is hidden; HTTPS works but database, mail, messaging, and custom protocols cannot securely compose over sockets.
options.code:
response :: http.Client.get("https://api.example.com")?
// no raw TLS stream for another protocol

comparisons.note: A TLS connection wraps transport I/O while configuration owns roots, SNI, ALPN, and protocol versions.
TLS wraps `net.Conn`, preserving deadline and address behavior while adding handshake/peer state.

decisions.title: Represent the shared byte-stream Reader and Writer contract
decisions.gist: Choose the real generic contract that lets one middleware implementation consume files, TCP, Unix, and TLS streams.
decisions.story: Mina writes a length-prefixed protocol reader against a file capture, then points the same code at a TCP connection and a TLS connection in production. D-NETIO1 promises that this is one generic middleware path, but Jet currently has only concrete FileReader/FileWriter methods and an unrelated binary.Reader cursor; there is no contract a generic parameter can name.
decisions.detail: D-NETIO1=D ratified generic composition while also saying to add no new trait and reuse the existing D-IO2 FileReader/FileWriter law. Repository truth has no generic Reader/Writer law to reuse: FileReader/FileWriter are concrete opaque handles, while core.binary.Reader is a consuming in-memory parser. This ballot clarifies representation without changing byte-canonical I/O, checked text projection, UDP exclusion, or socket-only inherent methods.

options.name: Public io.Reader and io.Writer traits (recommended)
options.detail: Amend the no-new-trait sentence and define two ordinary nominal core.io traits. FileReader, FileWriter, TcpStream, UnixStream, and TlsStream receive real implementations; codecs can implement or wrap them. Beginners keep calling inherent read/write methods with no ceremony. Experts can name bounds and write normal reusable middleware. The compiler uses the existing trait system, so there is no second structural dispatch mechanism.

options.name: Compiler-known structural stream contracts
options.detail: Keep the no-new-trait wording. The compiler treats any approved core handle with matching read/write signatures as Reader/Writer for generic bounds, without a user-declarable trait implementation. Beginner calls remain unchanged and built-in middleware composes, but experts cannot implement the contract for their own safe stream type; Jet gains a second, privileged conformance system beside nominal traits.

options.name: Closed core Stream sum type
options.detail: Keep concrete handles and make middleware accept a core-owned Stream value constructed from file, TCP, Unix, or TLS handles. This supplies one implementation for built-in transports but moves/boxes handles into a closed wrapper and prevents third-party stream participation. Socket-only operations require recovering the concrete handle before use.
options.code:
source :: io.Stream.from(file)
target :: io.Stream.from(tls)
io.copy(&source, &target)?

// peer_addr is unavailable until the TCP handle is recovered

comparisons.note: std::io::Read and Write are nominal traits implemented by files, TCP streams, Unix streams, and TLS wrappers; generic middleware names those bounds directly.
comparisons.code: fn copy<R: Read, W: Write>(r: &mut R, w: &mut W) -> io::Result<u64>

comparisons.note: io.Reader and io.Writer are structural interfaces; files, network connections, TLS connections, and user types compose through the same tiny contracts.
comparisons.code: func Copy(dst Writer, src Reader) (written int64, err error)

decisions.title: Exact Reader and Writer contract law
decisions.gist: Define the exact error, receiver, EOF, partial-write, close, and codec laws for the ratified core.io Reader and Writer traits.
decisions.story: Mina writes one bounded frame relay, tests it against a file capture, then runs it over TCP and TLS. D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A chose public nominal traits, but did not say whether the relay preserves NetError versus IOError, whether reads and writes borrow mutably, what zero bytes mean, or whether closing belongs to generic middleware. Those details decide whether one safe implementation really works across every stream.
decisions.detail: D-NETIO-CONTRACT1=A remains binding direction: public nominal traits under core.io. Clarification is required because its worked example assumed one IOError even though files, sockets, TLS, and codecs currently expose distinct typed failures. Every option below fixes exact namespace, error law, receivers, EOF/limit behavior, partial writes, write_all, close ownership, and codec conformance. All preserve D-NETIO1=D: bytes canonical, UDP excluded, socket-only facts inherent, checked text layered over bytes.

options.name: Associated Error per stream
options.detail: Exact namespace: core.io.Reader and core.io.Writer. Each has associated type Error. read(&self, limit) and write(&self, bytes) use mutable-borrow receivers because cursor/transport state advances without consuming the handle. limit must be positive; read returns at most limit bytes; empty bytes alone means clean EOF; failures retain the concrete FileError/NetError/TLSError/EncodingError. write may return any positive prefix count and zero for nonempty input is an error; write_all is one default trait method that loops until complete or returns Error. close and socket shutdown are not trait members: resource handles own inherent idempotent close, RAII remains fallback, generic middleware never steals ownership. Codecs conform only through explicit Reader/Writer adapter types whose Error is EncodingError and which delegate to one underlying stream; direct encoders/decoders do not claim byte-stream conformance.

options.name: One core.io.IOError for every stream (recommended)
options.detail: Exact namespace and receiver/EOF/limit/partial-write/write_all/close/codec laws match A, but both traits return core.io.IOError. File, TCP, Unix, TLS, and codec adapters convert their native failures into one closed IOError tree carrying operation, source category, address/path, OS code, and cause. This makes Reader-to-Writer middleware use one error type, but callers lose direct NetError/TLSError/EncodingError matching at the generic and inherent byte-operation boundary. Close remains inherent and idempotent; codecs conform only through explicit byte-stream adapters.

options.name: Universal Error at contract boundary
options.detail: Exact namespace and receiver/EOF/limit/partial-write/write_all/close/codec laws match A, but trait methods return universal Error through the ratified Fallible conversion path. Concrete inherent methods keep NetError/TLSError/etc.; only calls through a Reader/Writer bound erase to Error. write_all remains the sole default looping implementation. Close remains inherent and idempotent. Explicit codec adapters implement the traits and erase EncodingError only at the generic boundary.

comparisons.note: Read and Write use mutable receivers, empty successful read means EOF, write may be partial, write_all loops, and Close is outside both traits; Rust unifies failures as io::Error.
comparisons.code:
fn read(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize>
fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize>

comparisons.note: Protocols can preserve concrete associated types, matching Jet's existing associated-type feature and retaining transport-specific failures.

decisions.title: What exact structured IOError tree should every byte stream use?
decisions.gist: Choose the public IOError variants and shared context fields that let files, TCP, Unix sockets, TLS, and codecs implement one nominal Reader/Writer contract without flattening failures into strings.
decisions.lesson:
A byte-stream trait can unify operations only if its error type preserves the facts callers need. The variant answers what kind of failure happened, such as timeout or permission denial. Context answers where and during which operation it happened. An optional operating-system code and cause preserve audit detail without making host-specific text part of program logic.

Clean EOF is not an error: Reader.read returns an empty byte list only after the peer or file reaches end-of-stream. Invalid limits, cancellation, timeout, closed handles, and transport failures must remain distinguishable errors. If adapters collapse NetError, file errors, and TLS errors into Other(message), beginner code can still print the text, but expert code cannot reliably retry, cancel, classify, or audit it.

D-NETIO-CONTRACT2 already ratified one core.io.Reader/Writer contract and the semantic facts IOError must carry. It did not ratify exact constructors or field names. This ballot fixes that public surface before more adapters are wired.
decisions.story: Mara writes one copy function that accepts any Reader and Writer. It works for a file locally, then production reads through TLS over TCP. Beginner code uses ? unchanged. Her service policy retries TimedOut, stops immediately on Cancelled, reports PermissionDenied with a path, and marks Closed as a lifecycle bug. The same match must work across every adapter without parsing messages.
decisions.detail: Acceptance: one public core.io.IOError tree serves Reader/Writer adapters for files, TCP, Unix, TLS, and codecs; exact constructors and fields enter Syntax.rs if user-typeable; read(0) is InvalidInput and empty success means clean EOF only; native errors map losslessly into stable variants/context; beginner Display text remains concise; experts can match kind, operation, resource, OS code, and cause without parsing text; cancellation and timeout never become Other; diagnostics/examples/reference docs and hostile AOT/default-dev tests cover every mapping; obsolete flat adapters are removed rather than retained as a second path.

options.name: Closed variants plus shared IOContext
options.detail: IOError has stable semantic variants and every variant carries the same IOContext record. Beginner code uses ?; expert code matches a variant and inspects one predictable context shape.
options.technical: Public tree: InvalidInput(IOContext), NotFound(IOContext), PermissionDenied(IOContext), TimedOut(IOContext), Cancelled(IOContext), Closed(IOContext), and Other(IOContext). IOContext fields are operation: IOOperation, resource: String?, os_code: Int?, and cause: String?. IOOperation is a closed enum for Read, Write, Flush, Connect, Accept, Close, Resolve, and Codec; adapters select the closest canonical operation. resource contains a path, address, or codec identity when known. os_code is audit data, never portable control flow. cause preserves owned source detail and never contains secrets. Display renders variant + operation + resource, then cause. Existing NotFound(path), PermissionDenied(path), and Other(message) migrate to the context-bearing form; no compatibility alias remains in current-law mode.

options.name: Variants with per-kind fields
options.detail: Keep stable variants, but give each constructor only fields relevant to that kind. Matches are shorter for common cases, while generic logging must normalize several shapes.
options.technical: Examples: InvalidInput { operation, reason }, NotFound { operation, path }, PermissionDenied { operation, path, os_code }, TimedOut { operation, resource, os_code, cause }, Cancelled { operation, cause }, Closed { operation, resource }, Other { operation, resource, os_code, cause }. Every adapter still maps to a typed variant, but adding shared audit data later may change several constructors.

options.name: Keep the three-variant tree
options.detail: Retain NotFound(path), PermissionDenied(path), and Other(message). Network, TLS, cancellation, timeout, closed, and invalid-input failures remain formatted inside Other.
options.technical: No new public constructors ship. Adapter implementations preserve human-readable text but typed programs must parse messages or inspect native errors before conversion. Generic Reader/Writer consumers cannot distinguish retry, cancellation, timeout, or lifecycle policy.

comparisons.note: Go wraps operation, network, source, destination, and cause in net.OpError, then supports errors.Is for timeout and cancellation. A keeps the useful shared context while using a closed Jet enum instead of interface probing.
Rust io::Error exposes a stable ErrorKind plus an optional OS code and source. A makes the kind a Jet variant and the remaining audit facts one typed context.
Python uses an OSError hierarchy with errno and filename fields. A keeps typed classification and resource context without exception subclass ambiguity.

recommendation.why: A provides one semantic mechanism for beginners and experts. ? stays ceremony-free, while every stream adapter preserves the same typed classification and audit context. Shared context also keeps formatter, debugger, report, and policy code uniform.

whyNot.reason: Per-variant records repeat the same operation/resource/cause law and force generic tooling to normalize several shapes. Future shared audit facts would touch every constructor.
It contradicts the already-ratified structured contract: cancellation, timeout, invalid input, and closed lifecycle become unmatchable strings after nominal conversion.

recommendation.tradeoff: A exposes a small IOContext value even for simple path errors. That value is the canonical place for cross-adapter facts and avoids a second native-error channel.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A as the single public tree. Harvest B's concise matching through enum-pattern ergonomics and keep C's short Display text, without flattening stored facts.

harvest.use: Canonical storage and adapter mapping.
Pattern examples bind only fields callers need.
Display remains short while typed context stays available.

decisions.title: Client TLS trust, credentials, and version policy
decisions.gist: Choose how one immutable ClientConfig accepts custom trust, client credentials, and TLS version bounds.
decisions.lesson:
A TLS client authenticates a server through trusted certificate authorities, called roots. System roots cover public websites. Private services may add their own roots or deliberately trust only a private set.

Mutual TLS also authenticates the client. The client sends a certificate chain and proves possession of its private key. That key is secret, while root and certificate data are public.

Version bounds limit protocol negotiation to a closed range such as TLS 1.2 through TLS 1.3. These inputs should become a valid immutable configuration before a socket is consumed. The handshake still performs server-name verification and never exposes an insecure-verifier switch.
decisions.story: Priya connects a hospital service to a private gateway. The gateway uses a private root, requires a client certificate, and permits only TLS 1.3.
decisions.inWild:
roots := tls.RootCertificates.from_pem(ca_pem)?
identity := tls.ClientIdentity.from_pem(cert_chain_pem, private_key_pem)?
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_trust(.CustomOnly(roots))
    .with_client_identity(identity)
    .with_version_bounds(min: .Tls13, max: .Tls13)
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?
decisions.detail: Fixed law remains unchanged: ClientConfig.default(), with_alpn([String]), and tls.client(stream, server_name:, config:, deadline:) are already ratified. Every option preserves built-in certificate and server-name verification. No option permits an insecure verifier. RootCertificates and ClientIdentity are opaque validated values. TlsVersion is closed to supported protocol versions. Invalid PEM, an empty root set, an unusable key, a mismatched certificate/key, an empty ALPN item, or min above max rejects before consuming the TcpStream.

options.name: Validated typed inputs
options.detail: Parse roots and client identity into opaque validated values, then add them through an immutable builder. Trust mode explicitly distinguishes system roots, system plus custom roots, and custom-only roots. Version bounds validate when added.
options.technical: RootCertificates.from_pem([U8]) validates one or more certificate blocks. ClientIdentity.from_pem(cert_chain: [U8], private_key: [U8]) validates the ordered chain, supported key encoding, and certificate/key match; its internal key storage is zeroized on drop. ClientConfig.with_trust accepts .System, .SystemPlus(RootCertificates), or .CustomOnly(RootCertificates). with_client_identity accepts ClientIdentity. with_version_bounds accepts closed TlsVersion values .Tls12 and .Tls13 and rejects min > max. Builder calls return ClientConfig ? IOError and never retain a partially valid value.
options.code:
roots := tls.RootCertificates.from_pem(ca_pem)?
identity := tls.ClientIdentity.from_pem(chain_pem, key_pem)?
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_trust(.SystemPlus(roots))?
    .with_client_identity(identity)?
    .with_version_bounds(min: .Tls12, max: .Tls13)?
    .with_alpn(["h2", "http/1.1"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?

options.name: Raw configuration data
options.detail: Store PEM bytes and version fields directly in ClientConfig. Validate the complete record only when tls.client begins the handshake. The configuration is easy to serialize, but malformed credentials survive until a live connection attempt.
options.technical: ClientConfig carries trust mode plus root_pem, certificate_chain_pem, private_key_pem, min_version, max_version, and ALPN strings as ordinary data. tls.client validates all fields before consuming or registering the transport. Secret key bytes remain redacted from Show, Debug, diagnostics, and audit output.
options.code:
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_raw_credentials(.{
        trust: .SystemPlusPem(ca_pem),
        certificate_chain_pem: chain_pem,
        private_key_pem: key_pem,
        min_version: .Tls12,
        max_version: .Tls13,
    })?
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?

options.name: Platform credential references
options.detail: ClientConfig names roots and client identities stored by the operating system. Jet receives no private-key bytes. This fits managed hosts, but containers, tests, and portable private PKI need platform provisioning first.
options.technical: TlsCredentialRef is an opaque platform reference. ClientConfig.with_trust_ref selects a platform root bundle or custom trust store. with_client_identity_ref selects a certificate and non-exportable key. Missing, ambiguous, inaccessible, or unsupported references fail before transport consumption. Version bounds remain closed typed values on ClientConfig.
options.code:
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_trust_ref(tls.CredentialRef.system("hospital-roots"))?
    .with_client_identity_ref(tls.CredentialRef.system("gateway-client"))?
    .with_version_bounds(min: .Tls13, max: .Tls13)?
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?

comparisons.note: tls.Config groups roots, client certificates, ALPN, and version bounds. RootCAs replaces the default pool unless callers build from system roots explicitly.
comparisons.code: cfg := &tls.Config{RootCAs: roots, Certificates: []tls.Certificate{id}, MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS13, NextProtos: []string{"h2"}}

comparisons.note: ClientConfig is built through states that require roots and client-auth choice before use. Protocol versions and ALPN are configuration facts.
TrustManager and KeyManager separate server trust from client identity, usually through platform key stores. Protocol bounds are configured on each socket or engine.

recommendation.why: A makes invalid trust and credential material ordinary typed errors before networking starts. It supports public roots, private PKI, mutual TLS, hermetic tests, and explicit version policy through one immutable configuration.

whyNot.reason: B keeps malformed certificates and keys inside an apparently usable configuration until a connection attempt, weakening the boundary between configuration and live I/O.
C protects non-exportable keys well, but makes portable services and tests depend on host-specific credential provisioning. It cannot be Jet's only cross-platform expert surface.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts private-key bytes when constructing ClientIdentity. Jet must copy them into redacted, zeroized storage, while platform-only deployments may still need a later credential-reference constructor.

decisions.checkInstructions: Verify that every option preserves system-root defaults, server-name verification, ALPN's ratified [String] shape, immutable config reuse, pre-consumption validation, secret redaction, and one IOError tree.

decisions.title: Verified TLS peer identity evidence
decisions.gist: Choose what verified certificate evidence a TlsStream retains for expert inspection.
decisions.lesson:
A successful TLS handshake proves that the server certificate matches the requested name and chains to the configured roots. Applications sometimes need evidence beyond success, such as certificate fingerprints, issuer data, or the complete chain.

Certificate bytes are public, but retaining them affects audit capability and memory. A compact summary answers common policy questions. A full immutable snapshot also supports pinning reports, compliance records, and protocol-specific certificate processing.

Inspection must never replace built-in verification. The observer sees evidence only after normal certificate and server-name checks succeed. It cannot approve a failed peer or alter the handshake.
decisions.story: Elena operates a payment client. She records the verified leaf fingerprint and issuer, then investigates a rotation by comparing the complete chain without parsing log text.
decisions.inWild:
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?
peer := secure.peer_identity()
print(peer.verified_server_name)
print(peer.leaf.spki_sha256)
for certificate in peer.certificate_chain {
    audit(certificate.der)
}
decisions.detail: The TlsStream return shape and tls.client spelling remain fixed. Evidence is available only after a verified handshake. Certificate objects expose exact DER bytes plus stable derived facts; human-readable subject and issuer text is audit display, never identity control. Private keys and session secrets are never exposed. Renegotiation is unavailable, so a stored snapshot cannot become stale.

options.name: Full immutable peer snapshot
options.detail: TlsStream retains one PeerIdentity snapshot with the verified server name and ordered certificate chain. Each certificate exposes exact DER and stable fingerprints. Experts can derive summaries without losing evidence.
options.technical: peer_identity() returns an immutable PeerIdentity. Fields are verified_server_name: String, leaf: TlsCertificate, and certificate_chain: [TlsCertificate] in wire order. TlsCertificate exposes der: [U8], sha256: [U8], spki_sha256: [U8], dns_names: [String], valid_from_unix_ms: Int, valid_until_unix_ms: Int, subject: String, and issuer: String. Only DER and hashes are stable control data; rendered names are audit text.
options.code:
peer := secure.peer_identity()
require(peer.verified_server_name == host)
require(peer.leaf.spki_sha256 == expected_spki)
audit_chain(peer.certificate_chain.map((cert) => cert.der))

options.name: Compact verified summary
options.detail: TlsStream retains only the verified name, leaf fingerprints, names, issuer, and validity window. This covers routine policy checks while omitting the raw chain needed for independent audit or future derivations.
options.technical: peer_identity() returns PeerIdentitySummary with verified_server_name, leaf_sha256, leaf_spki_sha256, dns_names, valid_from_unix_ms, valid_until_unix_ms, subject, and issuer. Intermediate certificates and raw DER are discarded after verification. Strings remain audit text; hashes are stable bytes.
options.code:
peer := secure.peer_identity()
require(peer.leaf_spki_sha256 == expected_spki)
print("verified {peer.verified_server_name} until {peer.valid_until_unix_ms}")
// complete chain bytes are unavailable

options.name: Post-verification observer
options.detail: ClientConfig accepts an observer called once with the verified chain during the handshake. TlsStream retains no certificate evidence. Callers choose what to copy, but observation becomes callback state rather than a simple stream query.
options.technical: with_peer_observer receives a non-fallible observer of borrowed PeerIdentityView after built-in verification succeeds and before tls.client returns. The observer cannot reject, replace roots, or alter verification. Borrowed certificate bytes become invalid when the callback returns; retained evidence requires an explicit copy.
options.code:
audit := PeerAudit.new()
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_peer_observer((peer) => audit.record(peer.leaf.spki_sha256.copy()))
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?
require(audit.last_spki_sha256() == expected_spki)

comparisons.note: ConnectionState exposes verified chains, peer certificates, and the negotiated server name after the handshake.
ClientConnection exposes peer_certificates as the certificate chain presented by the peer after verification.
SSLSession returns peer certificates and principals after a verified handshake. Callers inspect them outside the trust decision.

recommendation.why: A preserves the actual verified evidence once and keeps inspection separate from verification. It serves simple fingerprint policy and deeper audits without callbacks or message parsing.

whyNot.reason: B answers common checks but permanently discards intermediate certificates and exact DER, preventing independent audit and later derivation from the verified chain.
C avoids retained evidence, but forces ordinary inspection through callback capture and mutable state. It also makes evidence lifetime harder to explain and test.

recommendation.tradeoff: A retains one public certificate chain for the stream lifetime. Long-lived connections therefore keep more memory than a summary-only design, bounded by the verified handshake chain.

decisions.checkInstructions: Verify built-in trust and server-name checks always run first; evidence is immutable; no private key or session secret appears; DER and hashes are stable; display strings are not control-flow law.

decisions.title: Advanced TLS close-notify and truncation law
decisions.gist: Choose how experts half-close TLS writes and prove whether the peer ended the stream cleanly.
decisions.lesson:
TLS has a close-notify alert for ending encrypted application data. Sending it says this side will write no more. Receiving the peer alert proves the peer ended cleanly rather than the transport disappearing mid-record.

The two directions are independent. A request protocol may finish writing, send close-notify, and continue reading a response. A plain close can instead send the alert and release the transport without waiting for the peer.

A raw TCP end without peer close-notify is a truncation failure, not clean end-of-stream. Deadlines and cancellation still bound every wait. Repeated close operations remain harmless under the ratified stream law.
decisions.story: Mateo uploads a signed archive, closes only the request direction, and keeps reading the server receipt. He must reject an abrupt TCP end as truncated TLS.
decisions.detail: Existing close() remains fixed: it sends and flushes local close-notify, closes the transport, and is idempotent. This ballot chooses the additional expert surface and peer-EOF law. Every option uses the same ambient, inherited, or explicit earliest deadline and returns the shared IOError variants. No option treats raw transport EOF as successful TLS EOF.

options.name: Directional write close
options.detail: Add close_write(deadline:) to send and flush close-notify while leaving reads open. Later writes return Closed. Reads return empty bytes only after peer close-notify; abrupt transport EOF returns Protocol truncation.
options.technical: close_write(deadline: Duration) is idempotent, observes the earliest active deadline, and completes only after the alert is flushed and the transport write half is shut down. It does not consume unread peer application data. read continues normally. A verified peer close-notify makes the next exhausted read return []; EOF without that alert returns IOError.Protocol with operation Read and a TLS truncation cause. close delegates to local alert flush when needed, then releases the handle without waiting for the peer.
options.code:
secure.write_all(request)?
secure.close_write(deadline: 2.seconds)?
reply := []
loop {
    chunk := secure.read(64.kib)?
    if chunk.is_empty() { break } // peer close-notify observed
    reply.extend(chunk)
}
secure.close()?

options.name: One bidirectional graceful close
options.detail: Add close_gracefully(deadline:) to send close-notify and wait for the peer alert before releasing the transport. It proves clean closure in one call, but cannot safely discard unread application data.
options.technical: close_gracefully sends and flushes local close-notify, then drives TLS until peer close-notify. If peer application data arrives before the alert, it returns IOError.Protocol rather than buffering or discarding that data. Timeout and cancellation leave the handle closing; a later close may release it. Existing close remains the non-waiting idempotent release path.
options.code:
secure.write_all(request)?
read_complete_response(&secure)?
secure.close_gracefully(deadline: 2.seconds)?
// error if unread application bytes arrive before peer close-notify

options.name: Configuration-selected close policy
options.detail: ClientConfig chooses whether close waits for peer close-notify. Call sites keep using close(), but the same method can release immediately or block according to distant configuration.
options.technical: ClientConfig.with_close_policy accepts .SendOnly or .WaitForPeer(deadline). close always sends and flushes local close-notify. Under WaitForPeer it waits for the peer alert and rejects intervening unread application data. Raw EOF is always Protocol truncation. The policy is immutable and shared by every stream created from the config.
options.code:
config := tls.ClientConfig.default()
    .with_close_policy(.WaitForPeer(2.seconds))
    .with_alpn(["h2"])
secure := tls.client(^tcp, server_name: host, config: config, deadline: 3.seconds)?
read_complete_response(&secure)?
secure.close()? // waits because config selected it

comparisons.note: CloseWrite sends TLS close-notify while keeping reads available. ConnectionState and read errors distinguish protocol state from ordinary use.
send_close_notify queues the alert. Callers continue driving connection I/O and decide whether to wait for the peer alert.
unwrap performs the TLS shutdown exchange and returns the underlying socket. It may block while waiting for the peer.

recommendation.why: A models TLS shutdown's directional nature directly. It supports request-half-close protocols, preserves unread response data, and makes clean peer EOF versus truncation part of normal Reader behavior.

whyNot.reason: B is convenient only after all response data is already drained. Before then it must reject, discard, or buffer application bytes, so it cannot replace directional shutdown.
C hides whether close waits behind shared configuration. The same source call can gain blocking behavior unrelated to the stream's visible lifecycle.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives experts one additional lifecycle method. Callers that require mutual clean shutdown must close writes, continue reading until empty bytes, then call the existing idempotent close.

decisions.checkInstructions: Verify partial alert writes, readiness, cancellation, deadlines, repeated calls, post-close writes, response reads after close_write, peer close-notify, abrupt EOF truncation, and existing close behavior across AOT and dev.

decisions.title: Jetpack package overlays and overrides
decisions.gist: Choose how packages, patches, per-host channel swaps, third-party namespaces, and unfree policy are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: reviewed source truth, reusable overlay composition, and beginner-friendly CLI drafting with no hidden override state.
decisions.story: Marta has one host tree and a plasma-beta variant that uses a different provider pin, disables one package default, applies a source patch, and allows one unfree package. Nix overlays can do it, but nobody can explain the fixpoint. Jetpack should make every override typed and explainable.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: reviewed source truth, reusable overlay composition, and beginner-friendly CLI drafting with no hidden override state.

options.name: Hybrid: workspace policy plus reusable overlay modules and CLI drafting (recommended)
options.detail: workspace.jet owns reviewed policy and named overlay sets. Per-package overlay modules can package reusable override logic, but they must materialize as typed workspace policy facts. CLI commands are allowed only as drafting tools that write source patches/policy, not hidden state.

options.name: Per-package overlay modules
options.detail: Each overlay is a Jet module/package exporting override records. Composable for teams, but common one-repo policy becomes more files and less first-run discoverable.

options.name: CLI grants only
options.detail: Users run trust/override commands and lock records the result. Good for experiments, weak for reviewed source and CI reproducibility.
options.code: jetpack override nixpkgs:kdePackages.plasma-desktop --patch patches/x.patch

comparisons.note: Powerful but untyped fixpoint; Jet should preserve reach while making causes explainable.
Reviewable source policy, but narrow: redirects sources only.

decisions.title: Per-package override record inside an overlay block
decisions.gist: How one package's version pin, build flags, env, and patches are spelled inside a ratified `overlay <name> { }` block, and how two overlays touching the same package resolve.
decisions.explainer: D-JPK-OVERLAY1 ratified the `overlay` block, `provider:` swap, `policy.allowUnfree`, and CLI drafting, illustrating patches as `package("foo").patches += [patch(...)]`. That per-package field spelling was never itself ratified. This decision fixes the full override record (version / flags / env / patches), the patch-source form, and the conflict rule when overlays stack.
decisions.story:
Terms up front. overlay: a named set of package overrides in workspace.jet. provider/channel: which upstream tree and which branch a package comes from (nixpkgs, plasma-beta). override record: the per-package changes an overlay applies. build flag: a compile-time toggle on a package (mpv +vapoursynth). patch: a source diff applied before build. priority tier: who wins when two overlays set the same field (ordinary / Force / Priority(n), already ratified for jetos as D-JOS-PRIORITY1). fixpoint: nixpkgs' untyped self/super overlay chain nobody can explain.

User's ~/nixos has an overlays/ dir. His devhost-plasma-beta host builds the same module set against a plasma-beta nixpkgs input, pins mpv to 0.38.0, turns on the vapoursynth build flag, and applies patches/mpv-osc.patch. Today in Nix that is a lambda `final: prev: { mpv = prev.mpv.overrideAttrs (old: { ... }); }` and when the version that ships differs from what he expected, there is no typed answer to 'why 0.38.0 and not the channel default'. jetos cannot recreate his config without this surface, and the whole point of Beat-Nix is that `jetpack explain` names exactly what each override changed and why the rebuild happened.
decisions.detail: Shared across every option (not itself a choice): (1) Patch source form. A patch is always a file reference in a list -- `patch("patches/mpv-osc.patch")` -- kept as reviewable diffs on disk, matching the D-JPK-OVERLAY1 illustration. Inline heredoc diffs are rejected: they bloat the manifest, evade code review, and break formatter round-trip (memory: formatter-roundtrip-required). A `patches` list composes across overlays by append. (2) Conflict + composition. When two overlays set the same field, resolution REUSES D-JOS-PRIORITY1 rather than inventing a second vocabulary: overlays apply in declared order, within a tier the later overlay wins, `Force(...)` outranks ordinary, and `Priority(n)` gives explicit expert weights. `jetpack explain` lists ALL contenders and names the winner and why -- identical to jetos option-priority explain output. Reuse (not divergence) because it is literally the same semantic job (two facts set one value; who wins + show contenders), and I8 says one mechanism, one mental model across jetos and jetpack. The options below differ only in how the per-package record is spelled and how a field carries its tier.

options.name: Imperative mutation statements (incumbent illustration, made total)
options.detail: Extend exactly what the D-JPK-OVERLAY1 record shows: each override is a dotted statement on `package("id")`. Scalars assign, lists use `+=`. Priority is a method call `.force(...)`. Cost: the package handle `package("mpv")` is repeated on every line -- the repetition the owner cuts elsewhere (U14/U18). Reading 'what does this overlay do to mpv' means scanning scattered statements.

options.name: Keyed override map of typed records (recommended)
options.detail: Name the package once; put every change in one typed dot-construction record (`.{ }`, the only struct-literal spelling). All packages live under one `overrides:` map so an overlay's effect on a package is one readable block. Priority rides on the field: `version: Force("...")`, or a bare value for ordinary, reusing D-JOS-PRIORITY1's `Force`/`Priority(n)`. Anti-repetition, house-style, and the conflict tier is visible at the field. Beginners write a two-line record; experts add `Force`/`Priority(n)` only when stacking overlays.

options.name: Reusable override modules referenced by overlays
options.detail: Make the D-JPK-OVERLAY1 'reusable overlay modules' clause the primary surface: the override record lives in a named `override module` and hosts reference it, so mpv-with-vapoursynth is authored once and shared across devhost and the plasma-beta variant. Same typed fields as B inside the module; the overlay is mostly references plus host-local tweaks. Strong for a many-host tree; for a one-repo override it is an extra indirection and less first-run discoverable (you follow a reference to see what changed).

options.name: Escalating verb fast-path (pin / enable / patch), record only when needed
options.detail: Flat verbs for the common single-change case: `pin("mpv", "0.38.0")`, `enable("mpv", "vapoursynth")`, `patch("mpv", "patches/mpv-osc.patch")`. A package needing several changes escalates to the B record. Beginner one-liners are the draw. Risk: two ways to pin a version (`pin(...)` vs `version:`), an I8 smell -- defensible only if the compiler desugars verbs into the same override facts (ergonomic entrypoint over one mechanism), and even then the default surface grows a second vocabulary the owner would have to learn to read someone else's overlay.

comparisons.note: The parity bar. Untyped fixpoint lambda: any attr, no schema, no per-field explain, conflicts resolved by opaque list order. Jet keeps the reach (version/flags/env/patches) as typed fields so `jetpack explain` can name what changed and which tier won.

Reviewable source policy in a manifest table, but narrow: it only redirects a dependency's source, no version-pin/flags/env/priority in the same place. Option B is the typed-record superset with an explain view.

The precedent this decision reuses rather than diverges from. Named tiers Default/ordinary/Force plus expert Priority(n), explain shows all contenders. Same conflict machinery so a user learns 'why did this win' once for both jetos and jetpack.
comparisons.code:
// jetos:   services.foo.enable: Force(true)
// jetpack: overrides: { mpv: .{ version: Force("0.39.0") } }

decisions.title: Variable and function metadata: how editor-facing facts (category, tooltip, exposure) are spelled in Jet source
decisions.gist: Blueprint lets an author tag a variable with a category, tooltip, and 'designers may edit this' flag from the Details panel. Canvas needs a source spelling for the parts Jet doesn't already have.
decisions.explainer: B keeps metadata honest (sema-checked, formatter-stable, diffable) and gives Canvas a trustworthy write target; A rots silently via typos, C forfeits the designer-tunable surface that makes Blueprint usable by non-programmers — the audience Jet's beginner facet exists for. If B feels heavy, ratify it scoped to the two fields Canvas needs now (category, tunable) and grow by future ballot.
decisions.story: Ana builds a game-balance module her designer teammate tunes through Canvas. She wants `speed` grouped under 'Movement' with a hover explanation, editable from the editor; and `debug_seed` visible but locked. In Blueprint this is checkboxes on the variable. Canvas is source-backed, so whatever the checkbox writes must be honest Jet text the designer's git diff shows.

options.name: Doc comments only — structured keys inside ///
options.detail: No new syntax. Canvas parses conventional keys from the doc comment (category:, tunable:). Zero language surface; the convention lives in Canvas docs. Risk: stringly-typed, unchecked by sema, typos silently ignored.

options.name: #Meta attribute with typed fields
options.detail: One attribute, sema-checked fields, formatter-stable. Unknown keys are compile errors (E-code with what/why/fix). Canvas Details checkboxes write exactly this.

options.name: Existing mechanisms only — no metadata this epoch
options.detail: Category = module/file organization; tooltip = doc comment; tunable = a convention (e.g. a config struct with Codable). Defers the decision; Canvas ships M3 without grouping/exposure flags and revisits after real usage.
options.code: // movement.jet groups movement values; docs are tooltips; nothing new.

comparisons.note: UPROPERTY specifiers (Category, EditAnywhere, ExposeOnSpawn, ToolTip) surfaced as Details checkboxes — the mechanism Canvas designers will expect.
Typed attributes with compile-checked contents; serde's #[serde(rename = …)] shows the one-attribute-many-typed-fields pattern of option B.

decisions.title: Multiple-exec-IN convergence over source-backed spans
decisions.gist: When a user wires two or more execution arrows into the same node, what Jet source does Canvas write — since one node is one statement span, and Jet has no goto.
decisions.explainer:
Glossary. Exec pin: the control-flow arrow socket on a node ("do this, then that"), separate from data pins (values). Statement span: the exact slice of `.jet` source a node projects from — every node is a projection of real source, never a standalone graph object. Convergence: two or more exec arrows pointing at one node, so several places in the program run that same node. Extract-to-function: turning a selected span into a named helper `fn` and replacing it with calls — already shipped in Canvas (matrix row "Extract selection to function", #280). Structured control flow: `if`/`else`, dispatch arms, `loop` — Jet's only control forms; there is no `goto` and no jump-to-label in the language.

The wall. Blueprint lets N exec wires converge on one node; its runtime is a VM that just re-enters that node on each incoming pulse. Jet has no VM and no goto: a node is a statement span, and "run this same span from three places" has exactly one honest spelling in source — a named function called three times. This ballot decides what happens the instant a user tries the Blueprint habit of dropping a second exec wire onto a node that already has one. The matrix row "Multiple exec IN (convergence)" is held at blocked-by-ballot on this decision.
decisions.story: Priya is porting a small chat handler she prototyped in Unreal Blueprint. Her graph has two branches — a Ping arm and a Data arm — and in Blueprint both arms' exec wires ran into a single "Notify + bump metric" node before continuing. In Canvas she rebuilds the two arms, then drags the exec output of the Data arm onto the same Notify node the Ping arm already points at. In Blueprint that just worked. She needs to know what Canvas does with that gesture, and what shows up in her `.jet` file afterward — because in Jet the file is the program.
decisions.detail: Recommend E (hybrid of A+B+D). Devil pass across all five: (C) labeled tunnels introduce goto into a language that has none — it breaks structured control flow, defeats the front end's reachability reasoning, and is the exact spaghetti pattern Godot deleted VisualScript over; reject outright, listed only so the owner sees it was weighed. (D) as a default re-introduces the copy-paste divergence bug Priya is trying to escape — but as an explicit, clearly-labeled expert choice inside a preview it is legitimate (sometimes two arms genuinely should diverge next week). (B) refuse-and-teach stalls the beginner mid-gesture — but its teaching line is exactly what the preview header should say. (A) auto-extract makes the habit work and writes honest DRY source, but fixes every knob: the name is editable, yet the user cannot reuse an existing matching helper or deliberately choose duplication without cancelling and doing something else. (E) keeps A's single mechanism and beginner path — Enter accepts the proposed extract — and puts the expert controls in the same preview: rename, "call existing fn" when the converged span already matches a helper's body (span-equality after formatting), or "duplicate inline instead" as the explicit divergence escape hatch. One canonical write path (the previewed source transaction), three outcomes the user can see as concrete diffs before anything is written. Devil pass on E: three choices could overwhelm a beginner. Patch: the extract diff is the pre-selected default with the name field focused — a beginner who just types Enter gets exactly option A; the alternatives are a small secondary row, not a fork dialog. A genuinely structured join (work after an if/else, not mid-arm) still projects as a single downstream node with no extraction — E, like A, fires only for true non-tail convergence.

options.name: Auto-extract on convergence
options.detail: Dropping a second exec wire onto a node runs the shipped extract-to-function transaction: the converged span becomes a named helper `fn`, and both sites become call nodes pointing at it. Previewed and undoable like every Canvas edit; nothing is written until the user confirms the proposed name and diff. The graph then shows one shared node (the call) reached from N sites — the Blueprint look — backed by honest, DRY source.

options.name: Refuse and teach
options.detail: Canvas projects only structured control flow. A second exec wire onto a node is refused in-UI with a Jet-voice diagnostic that names extract-to-function as the deliberate next step. The user selects the span and runs Extract themselves — two explicit steps, nothing implicit.
options.code:
Gesture: drag Data arm's exec wire onto the Ping arm's `notify` node.
Canvas refuses the drop (wire snaps back) and shows:

  Cannot converge two execution paths on one node.
  A node is one place in your source. To run the same steps
  from two places, make them a function.
  -> Select these steps and choose "Extract to function".

Source is unchanged until the user runs Extract as a separate action.

options.name: Labeled tunnel / jump sites
options.detail: Introduce a new source construct: a label at the convergence node and a jump from each incoming site (goto-like). Multiple sites jump to one label. This is the literal graph shape but requires adding non-structured control flow to Jet.

options.name: Duplicate the span inline
options.detail: Converging N exec wires copies the converged statement span into each site inline — no shared function. Source stays structured and honest, but the shared work is physically duplicated in every arm.

options.name: Convergence preview: extract by default, reuse or duplicate on request (hybrid, recommended)
options.detail: The second exec drop opens ONE preview (the shipped extract-to-function transaction). Default, pre-selected: extract to a named helper — Enter accepts, identical to option A. Same preview offers two expert alternatives, each shown as its concrete source diff: call an existing function (offered only when the converged span textually matches an existing helper body after formatting, e.g. a notify_and_count helper written earlier), or duplicate inline (option D's source, explicitly chosen, labeled with the divergence warning). The preview header carries option B's teaching line, so the beginner learns why convergence means a function. Nothing writes until confirmed; Undo restores exactly.
options.code:
Gesture: drag Data arm's exec wire onto the Ping arm's `notify`/`bump_metric` node.

  Two paths will run these steps. In Jet, shared steps are a function.

  (o) Extract to function   name: [ on_event ]      <- default, Enter accepts
      + fn on_event(id: Id) { notify(id); bump_metric() }
      both arms:  on_event(id)

  ( ) Call existing `notify_and_count(id)`   (its body matches these steps)
      both arms:  notify_and_count(id)

  ( ) Duplicate steps into this arm instead   (copies can drift apart)
      Data arm gains its own notify(id); bump_metric()

Enter -> option A's exact result. Escape -> nothing written.

comparisons.note: N exec wires converge on one node freely; the Blueprint VM re-enters the node per incoming pulse, and there is no source file to keep honest. This is convenient but is the documented root of Blueprint spaghetti — the shared node's upstream context is ambiguous, and refactoring it is manual. Jet has no VM to re-enter; convergence must resolve to real source, which is what option A produces.
comparisons.code:
Ping exec --\
              >--> [ Notify + Bump ] --> ...
Data exec --/
(one node, two incoming exec wires, no source artifact)

comparisons.note: Scratch has no exec convergence: blocks stack linearly and the only way to run the same steps from two places is to define a custom block and call it from both. That custom block is exactly Jet's extract-to-function — option A gives the same mental model ("make it a block, call it twice") with the call performed for the user on the converging gesture.
comparisons.code:
define notify-and-bump (id)
  ... notify (id) ...
  ... change metric by 1 ...

when Ping:  notify-and-bump (id)
when Data:  notify-and-bump (id)

comparisons.note: Earlier Godot VisualScript allowed goto-like sequencing and free exec convergence; Godot removed it, citing unmaintainable graphs. This is the case against option C: adding jump/label sites to reach graph-level convergence trades a structured, analyzable language for the exact pattern a shipping engine deleted.
comparisons.code: (removed from Godot 4 — cited graph maintainability and control-flow spaghetti)

decisions.title: Binary-cache and mirror configuration surface
decisions.gist: Choose where cache order, trust roots, read/write scope, credentials, and private behavior are declared.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option C leaks keys through environment and argv — violating the plan's credential law — and makes cache order an unreproducible per-invocation accident; B strips repositories of any declarable trust posture, so CI and developers silently diverge. A is closest but states no precedence law among mirrors, no offline interaction, no write-grant linkage, and no beginner default.
