recommendation.tradeoff: `project.jet` becomes a new canonical file and replaces current role filenames. The migration is worthwhile because it removes permanent ceremony.

decisions.comment: Ok with this conceptually but need a different word. Parts should be a convenience extensibility and modularity feature but a requirement

decisions.title: What should Jet call one modular graph contribution?
decisions.gist: Choose the public type name for one self-contained piece that joins other pieces into a project's complete checked graph.
decisions.lesson:
Graph: a set of named values connected by references.
Root: the top value containing the complete graph.
Contribution: one value that adds facts to that root.
Closed: the value uses only its declarations and explicit imports.
Composition: the rule that combines contributions.

A team may keep one contribution beside deployment code and another beside monitoring code. Jet checks each value alone, then combines them by one composition law.

Equal facts coalesce. Different facts at the same single-value path produce an error naming both sources.

Jet already uses module for a namespace. Reusing module here would give one word two semantic jobs.

This ballot chooses only the contribution type name. It does not choose filenames, discovery, root name, fields, split policy, or commands.
decisions.story: Mara's shop API gains deployment and monitoring files. Both set `services.api.port` differently. Jet's error must name each self-contained value without forcing Mara to decode product jargon.
decisions.inWild: NixOS users split one machine configuration into modules, which merge through Nix rules and priorities. Terraform modules package declarations behind inputs and outputs. Rust modules and Go packages organize namespaces. npm packages are distribution units. Jet cannot reuse module because that word already names its namespace mechanism. It needs a separate noun for a checked graph contribution.

options.name: Rib
options.detail: Use `Rib`. Aircraft ribs are repeated structural members that join into a larger frame.
options.technical: Rib collides with Golem's Rib programming language and Pixar RenderMan's RIB format. Anatomy and food meanings add search noise.

options.name: Wing
options.detail: Use `Wing`. The word is short, familiar, aviation-rooted, and suggests a substantial part joined to a larger craft.
options.technical: Wing collides with Winglang, a cloud programming language. An aircraft usually has few wings, while a project may have many contributions.

options.name: Bay
options.detail: Use `Bay`. An aircraft bay is a bounded place for one coherent system or payload.
options.technical: Bay has prior container and cloud uses, including OpenStack Magnum's former cluster term. Geography and storage hardware add search noise.

options.name: Section
options.detail: Use `Section`. The ordinary word is familiar and fits one coherent region of an aircraft or technical plan.
options.technical: Section is common in object files, documents, configuration formats, UI types, and cloud product names. Search precision is weak.

options.name: Cell
options.detail: Use `Cell`. The word strongly suggests a small self-contained unit that joins peers into a whole.
options.technical: Jet uses Cell internally for runtime concepts, and Rust exposes `std::cell::Cell`. Compiler discussion and searches would be ambiguous.

options.name: Nacelle
options.detail: Use `Nacelle`. A nacelle is a distinct aircraft housing integrated into a larger craft.
options.technical: Nacelle is unfamiliar to many beginners and more naturally names a housing than its contents. It also names an active commerce platform.

options.name: Config
options.detail: Use `Config` for one layout-neutral typed value that contributes Package facts.
options.technical: Config is distinct from a code module and from a distributable Package. Configs merge by the ratified field law and cannot declare member Packages.

comparisons.note: NixOS modules contribute options and configuration to one system. Jet cannot reuse module because that word already names source namespaces.
Terraform modules package resources behind inputs and outputs. Jet contributions remain ordinary typed values discovered by one root.

recommendation.why: Config is plain English and separates settings contributions from code namespaces and distribution units.

whyNot.reason: Rib is themed and collides with language and graphics names.
Wing is themed and collides with Winglang.
Bay sounds like a location rather than contributed facts.
Section is heavily overloaded and does not state configuration purpose.
Cell collides with memory and runtime vocabulary.
Nacelle requires aviation vocabulary and names a housing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Config is a common word. Type context and Package-qualified documentation must keep it distinct from ad hoc configuration files.

decisions.checkInstructions: Replace contribution placeholders only after ratification. Source discovery and split behavior remain separate decisions. Do not add aliases for rejected names.

decisions.title: What jet split does with inline Package facts
decisions.gist: Decide whether `jet split` extracts inline facts or only moves an already-authored Config.
decisions.lesson: A Config is a typed value contributing facts to one Package. `jet split` is a source refactor that must preserve Package identity and graph fingerprint. The command previews its generated binding, refuses non-closed extraction before writes, and records a ledger that `jet fold` can reverse. This decision controls whether split may create the Config a beginner has not written yet.
decisions.story: Maya starts with a development environment inline in `package.jet`. When the file grows, she asks Jet to move the environment into `package/env.jet` without first learning the manual Config extraction steps.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's S3 transition extracts `package.environments` into `package/env.jet::development`, adds a `Config`, and proves the Package graph hash is unchanged. Experts may author that same Config directly.

options.name: Extract and move
options.detail: Split creates the closed Config needed to move inline facts and records a reversible ledger.
options.code:
$ jet split env --check
Would extract: package.environments
Would create: package/env.jet::development
Would add: Config `development`
package graph before: sha256:39df…
package graph after:  sha256:39df…
No files changed.

options.name: Move Configs only
options.detail: Split moves only an exported Config the author already created. Inline facts fail with a direct prerequisite.
options.code:
$ jet split env
Error: no exported Config owns tier env.
Fix: extract it, then retry.

recommendation.why: The command fulfills the requested growth step and produces the same Config experts write directly.

whyNot.reason: It requires the common one-file growth path to perform a manual extraction before the refactor command can help.

recommendation.tradeoff: Preview must name the generated binding and split must refuse shared bindings, collisions, and open fields before any write.

decisions.checkInstructions: Preserve exact ledger, refusal, precedence, graph-fingerprint, crash-safety, and round-trip laws in technical acceptance. Substitute the type ratified by D-ECO-SLICENAME1 in executable fixtures.

decisions.title: Commands for Package growth and reversal
decisions.gist: Choose the commands that extract Package facts and reverse a recorded extraction.
decisions.lesson: A split moves or extracts facts without changing the checked Package graph. A fold reverses a split through Jet's private provenance ledger. Both commands preview before writing, refuse unsafe boundaries, and preserve the graph fingerprint. This decision names the two commands; D-ECO-SPLITPOLICY1 separately decides whether split may create a Config from inline facts.
decisions.story: Maya's development environment outgrows `package.jet`. She extracts it, reviews the new Config, then restores the original file after a teammate asks for the earlier layout.
decisions.inWild: The proposal uses the same verbs for extracting an environment, a flat member Package, and a System-to-Fleet host map. Reversal always names the generated member file and consumes the recorded split ledger.

options.name: jet split and jet fold
options.detail: Use one extraction verb and one explicit reversal verb for every supported Package tier.
options.code:
$ jet split env
Created package/env.jet.
package graph unchanged: sha256:39df…
Reverse with: jet fold package/env.jet

options.name: jet split with reverse flag
options.detail: Use `jet split` for extraction and `jet split --reverse` for reversal.
options.code:
$ jet split env
Created package/env.jet.

$ jet split --reverse package/env.jet
Restored package.jet.

options.name: Intent-specific verbs
options.detail: Use different verbs for environments, member Packages, and Fleets.
options.code:
$ jet extract-env
$ jet extract-package billing
$ jet make-fleet devhost
$ jet restore package/env.jet

recommendation.why: One split/fold pair applies to every graph-preserving extraction and keeps reversal visible as its own operation.

whyNot.reason: A reverse flag hides a distinct destructive direction behind the extraction command.
Tier-specific verbs create several mechanisms for the same graph-preserving refactor.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users must learn that fold is source-layout reversal, not graph aggregation or runtime behavior.

decisions.title: Reserved Package source-file law
decisions.gist: Decide whether one reserved `package.jet` replaces permanent package, environment, workspace, and OS role files.
decisions.lesson: A script remains complete without any reserved file. When a Package root exists, its reserved filename can supply the expected `Package` type so top-level fields construct it directly. This bare-fields root and inferred construction reuse already-ratified D-DOTCTOR2; they do not create another constructor syntax. Configs may move to discovered `.jet` files, and a leading underscore disables a discovered file. Generated state remains under `.jet/`.
decisions.story: Maya grows a script into a Package, then adds an environment and a System. She needs one place to find the Package root without learning four permanent authority files.
decisions.inWild: The proposal replaces `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and JetOS `config.jet`. During one migration epoch, `jet init --check` previews a reversible fold and `jet init --restore-role-files` restores byte-identical originals.

options.name: One package.jet
options.detail: Use `package.jet` as the sole reserved ecosystem file. Other `.jet` files contribute Configs.
options.code:
// package.jet
systems: .{ devhost: .System.{ packages: [cli] } }

$ jet os plan devhost
Plan: devhost
No machine changed.

$ jet check
Warning [L1320]: this Package uses four retired ecosystem filenames
 What: `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and `config.jet` describe one Package
 Why: `package.jet` is now the one reserved ecosystem source file
 Fix: run `jet init --check`, review the fold, then run `jet init`

options.name: Keep role files
options.detail: Keep `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and `config.jet` as permanent authorities.
options.code:
pkg.jet
env.jet
workspace.jet
config.jet

$ jet explain services.db.port
services.db.port = 5432
winning role file: env.jet

options.name: No reserved file
options.detail: Require users to select an arbitrary Package root file when one cannot be inferred.
options.code:
$ jet --package config/root.jet build
Built Package.

$ jet build
No Package root selected.

recommendation.why: One root file makes later file growth organizational, removes competing identities, and leaves the single-file script path ceremony-free.

whyNot.reason: Permanent role files preserve several authorities and require provenance to explain which file identity won.
The first multi-file Package adds permanent root-selection ceremony to normal commands.

recommendation.tradeoff: One migration epoch must teach and reversibly fold four previously ratified filenames.

decisions.title: Default build profile for everyday commands
decisions.gist: Which build profile the everyday commands (jet run, jet dev, jet build) use by default.
decisions.lesson:
Today the unnamed Default profile optimizes: opt-level 2, thin-LTO, and strip (Source/main.rs). Every `jet run`, `jet dev`, and `jet build` pays optimizer time, even a first hello-world run.

R8 says the default leans toward speed, but that speed is the runtime binary's, not the compile. In the edit-run loop, compile time is the speed a beginner actually feels.

D-BUILDPROFILE1 stays intact: profiles are still selected by explicit flag, never ambient env. This ballot only changes what the unnamed Default profile contains; `--release` remains the optimized profile.
decisions.story: Sam is learning Jet and runs `jet run hello.jet` after almost every edit. Each run waits on the optimizer before printing one line, so the loop feels sluggish from the first program.

options.name: Fast-codegen default, optimize behind --release
options.detail: The unnamed Default profile becomes opt-level 0, codegen-units 256, no LTO. `--release` selects the optimized, thin-LTO, stripped profile that is the default today.
options.code:
# Today (optimized default): the edit-run loop pays the optimizer each time
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~450 ms   (illustrative)

# Option A: opt-level 0, codegen-units 256, no LTO
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~150 ms   (illustrative)

# Shipping build — one flag, fully optimized + thin-LTO + strip
$ jet build --release hello.jet
$ ./hello              # same fast binary today's default produced

options.name: Split by command: run/dev fast, build optimized
options.detail: `jet run` and `jet dev` compile at opt-level 0; `jet build` keeps the optimized profile. An explicit `--profile`/`--release` flag overrides either command's default.
options.code:
# Option B: the command decides the profile
$ jet run hello.jet    # fast: opt-level 0         ~150 ms (illustrative)
$ jet dev  hello.jet   # fast: opt-level 0         ~150 ms (illustrative)
$ jet build hello.jet  # optimized: -O + thin-LTO  ~450 ms (illustrative)

# Override either way with an explicit profile flag
$ jet build --profile=debug hello.jet   # fast build of a build artifact
$ jet run   --release       hello.jet   # optimized one-off run

options.name: Keep optimized-everywhere default (status quo)
options.detail: Every everyday command keeps opt-level 2, thin-LTO, and strip. Fast compiles stay opt-in behind `--profile=debug`.
options.code:
# Option C: every everyday command optimizes (today's behavior)
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~450 ms   (illustrative)
$ jet build hello.jet
$ ./hello              # ~450 ms build; fast small binary

# Fast compile only if you remember the opt-in flag
$ jet run --profile=debug hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~150 ms   (illustrative)

comparisons.note: `cargo build` is unoptimized debug by default; `cargo build --release` opts into optimization. Jet's Default profile is the opposite today, optimizing on every build.
comparisons.code:
cargo build            # debug, fast compile
cargo build --release  # optimized

comparisons.note: `zig build` produces a Debug binary by default; `-Doptimize=ReleaseFast` is the opt-in. Fast iterate, explicit ship.
`go build` has no user-picked optimize/debug split. It is fast by default, with no separate optimized build command in the everyday loop.

recommendation.why: A makes the loop beginners run hundreds of times a day instant, and keeps the optimized binary one keystroke away as `--release`.

whyNot.reason: Two profiles by command means `jet run` and `jet build` of one file can produce different binaries, so a bug seen under one may vanish under the other.
The common path stays slow: every first `jet run` pays optimizer time the beginner never asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A default binaries run slower than today's until `--release`. Everyday commands exist for iterating, not shipping, so compile speed is the right default there.

decisions.title: Backend for the explicit fast AOT debug profile
decisions.gist: D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B already guarantees `jet build --profile=debug` as a fast on-disk AOT artifact. Choose whether rustc or Cranelift emits that existing profile; this does not add a third lens or change any command default.
decisions.lesson: Jet has one compiler core and two feature-identical lenses. The JIT lens runs `jet run` and `jet dev` quickly. The AOT lens emits binaries: `jet build` is optimized by default, while the ratified `jet build --profile=debug` asks for a fast unoptimized artifact. A profile controls optimization intent inside the AOT lens; it is not another feature tier. This ballot chooses only the debug-profile backend. Both choices consume the same sema-approved executable TIR, preserve every feature, and face R12 differential tests.
decisions.explainer: The current transpile path sends even debug-profile output through generated Rust and rustc at opt-level 0. Cranelift already serves the JIT lens and can also emit native objects on supported targets. Using it for debug-profile AOT avoids rustc re-parsing and re-verifying proven TIR, but requires native object/link/debug-info parity and a truthful target fallback. Keeping rustc is the smaller backend set but retains that redundant work. `jet run`, `jet dev`, plain `jet build`, `--profile=debug`, and `--release` keep their ratified meanings whichever backend wins.
decisions.story: Priya uses the JIT loop while editing. CI then needs a real unoptimized binary to run packaging, debugger, and deploy-shape smoke tests, so it invokes the existing debug profile. Priya wants the artifact quickly, with the same behavior and diagnostics as the optimized build, and an audit that names the backend used.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev app.jet                     # JIT lens
$ jet build app.jet                   # optimized AOT
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet   # fast AOT artifact; this ballot chooses its backend
$ jet run --release app.jet           # explicit optimized override

$ jet explain build app.jet
profile   debug
lens      AOT
backend   cranelift | rustc-opt0
parity    executable TIR / R12
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: ordinary run/dev/build defaults stay unchanged; no backend choice is required. Expert pass: the explicit profile selects optimization intent, and build explain/audit output names backend, target support, fallback reason, timings, cache identity, and parity evidence. Backend availability may affect latency, never supported features or program behavior.

options.name: rustc opt-level 0 emits fast AOT
options.detail: Keep Cranelift JIT-only. `jet build --profile=debug` uses the current generated-Rust path with rustc optimization disabled. One native AOT backend covers every target and debug-info path, but rustc still parses and verifies code the Jet front end already proved.
options.code:
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet
# checked Jet -> executable TIR -> generated Rust -> rustc opt-level 0 -> app
$ jet explain build app.jet
lens AOT; profile debug; backend rustc-opt0

options.name: Cranelift emits fast AOT
options.detail: Recommended. On supported targets, lower the same executable TIR through Cranelift to object code and link the debug-profile binary without generated Rust/rustc. Unsupported targets fall back to rustc opt-level 0 and report that fact; they do not lose features or silently switch optimization intent. Optimized AOT remains the existing ship backend.
options.code:
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet
# checked Jet -> executable TIR -> Cranelift object -> app
$ jet explain build app.jet
lens AOT; profile debug; backend cranelift
# unsupported target: backend rustc-opt0; reason shown

comparisons.note: Rust uses Cranelift for faster debug codegen while LLVM remains the optimized release backend. Option B applies that backend split inside Jet's single AOT lens and existing debug/release profiles.
comparisons.code:
cargo +nightly cg_clif build   # debug
cargo build --release          # LLVM

comparisons.note: Zig uses a fast native backend for debug artifacts and an optimizing backend for release. The artifact purpose stays explicit; backend choice does not create a second language.

Go owns direct object emission, so a real binary does not require a second compiler to re-check source. Option B gives Jet's explicit debug artifact that property while retaining optimized AOT for shipping.

recommendation.why: B spends the existing Cranelift investment on the one fast on-disk artifact D-BUILD-DEFAULT1 already guarantees. It removes redundant rustc work where optimization is intentionally disabled while preserving one front end, one executable TIR, two lenses, and full feature parity.

whyNot.reason: A is sound and universal, but every debug artifact still pays generated-Rust parsing and rustc verification after Jet sema has already proved the program.

recommendation.tradeoff: B adds object/link/debug-info conformance work and per-target support accounting. Unsupported targets use the truthful rustc-opt0 fallback until their Cranelift object path passes the same R12 and native evidence gates.

decisions.comment: Owner question q4mspet2 answered with measured numbers: jet check 0.007s vs ~12s rustc path; Cranelift debug AOT lands at about check-plus-link time. His universality point about option A is preserved: B falls back to A's exact rustc-opt0 path on unsupported targets and names the fallback in jet explain build.

decisions.title: One compiler, two lenses
decisions.outcome: One compiler core, two lenses. JIT lens = rapid dev work people love in python/typescript; AOT lens = highly optimized ship binary at the cost of longer build time. Same compiler core prevents drift: there should NEVER be a difference in supported features/functionality between JIT and AOT.
decisions.comment: One compiler core, two lenses. JIT lens = rapid dev work people love in python/typescript; AOT lens = highly optimized ship binary at the cost of longer build time. Same compiler core prevents drift: there should NEVER be a difference in supported features/functionality between JIT and AOT.

decisions.title: Computed module fields: dependency and effect law
decisions.gist: Choose whether computed module fields may depend on other fields and whether locked file or network reads belong in their default evaluation.
decisions.lesson:
A computed module field is a configuration value produced by an expression during planning. Jet already evaluates many field expressions through its shared compile-time interpreter. Literals, conditionals, and pure helper calls work today. This ballot does not invent another evaluator or another field spelling.

Pure evaluation means the answer depends only on declared values and pure code. A dependency graph records which field needs which other field. Jet can evaluate that graph in dependency order. A loop such as `name` needing `label` while `label` needs `name` has no first value, so planning must reject it and print the full loop.

Tier 1 operations read external inputs reproducibly. Examples are embedding a file or fetching content with a required hash. The lock records those exact inputs. Tier 2 operations read ambient state such as an environment variable or unpinned network response. They remain forbidden in module fields under every option.

The choice matters because module files are read as declarations. Beginners need ordinary values and pure helpers to work without build-policy ceremony. Experts need deterministic ordering, exact provenance, and a clear boundary between configuration evaluation and the separate `fn build` authority model.

comptime and `fn build` are different tools; the computed-field law sits on top of comptime, not build. comptime (S26, D-CTEFFECT1) is pure value evaluation: a fuel-limited interpreter runs type-checked Core code and lowers results to constant data, with no authority and no types created. Its only external reads are Tier-1 locked operations (`embed_file`, `find`, `fetch(url, sha256:)`) recorded in `.jet/lock`. comptime values feed constants, markers, and module fields with no ceremony.

`fn build(b: BuildContext)` (D-BUILDENTRY1, D-BUILDACTION1) is a build-time action runner: it registers targets, declares capability-gated cached actions, runs processes, and emits artifacts under `.jet/generated/`. Both are kept. Merging them would give every constant expression filesystem and process authority, or strip build actions of their capability gate, breaking safe-by-default (I1). Module fields evaluate through comptime; build authority stays behind the explicit `BuildContext` grant.
decisions.story: Mara declares one development environment. Its label, prompt, and banner share a computed release name. She wants one source value, clear cycle errors, and no surprising host reads when CI evaluates the same file.

options.name: Pure dependency graph
options.detail: Fields may use any Tier-0 pure expression, top-level immutable compile-time values, pure helper call graphs, and other fields in the same module. Jet evaluates dependencies in deterministic order. A cycle fails before a plan exists and names the complete chain. Tier-1 and Tier-2 reads are rejected.
options.technical: Reuse jet-env-model ModuleEval and jet-comptime. Build a field dependency graph after front-end name/type/purity validation. Evaluate each node once in topological order, using source order to break independent ties. No field gains BuildContext, #Impure, filesystem, network, environment, clock, or randomness authority. Allocate and snapshot exact cycle and forbidden-tier diagnostics before implementation.
options.code:
comptime release = "1.4.0"
module env.dev {
  label: "ledger " + release
  prompt: label + " > "
}

$ jet env
label: ledger 1.4.0
prompt: ledger 1.4.0 >

module env.bad { a: b, b: a }
Error: module fields form a cycle: `a -> b -> a`
 Why: each field needs another field before either has a value
 Fix: remove one dependency or compute both from one top-level `comptime` value

options.name: Independent pure fields
options.detail: Fields may use Tier-0 expressions, top-level immutable compile-time values, and pure helper calls, but cannot name another field. Each field evaluates independently, so module-field cycles cannot exist. Shared values must be lifted to a top-level `comptime` binding.
options.technical: Reuse the current per-field evaluator with a validated top-level immutable environment. Reject a field name during expression resolution. Tier-1 and Tier-2 remain forbidden. `fn build` authority stays separate.
options.code:
comptime release = "1.4.0"
module env.dev {
  label: "ledger " + release
  prompt: label + " > "
}
Error: module field `prompt` cannot read sibling field `label`
 Why: each field evaluates independently
 Fix: compute the shared text in a top-level `comptime` value

options.name: Graph plus locked reads
options.detail: Everything in A also permits Tier-1 file discovery, embedding, and hash-pinned fetches. Every external input is recorded in the unified lock and reproduced offline. Tier-2 ambient reads remain forbidden.
options.technical: Field identity and plan provenance include the exact Tier-1 operation, normalized declared path or URL, content digest, lock schema, and dependency graph. Missing or changed locked inputs fail closed under --locked/offline. No Tier-1 operation falls through to host state or fn-build grants.

comparisons.note: Nix lets configuration values depend on other values, but filesystem and import effects can be less obvious at the use site.
Cargo manifests keep fields independent and literal-like; shared computation usually moves into a separate build script.

recommendation.why: A completes the owner's pure-computed direction with one existing interpreter. Shared field dependencies stay natural for beginners, while experts receive deterministic graph order and exact cycle evidence without granting host authority.

whyNot.reason: It makes harmless field reuse indirect. Users must lift values out of the module solely to avoid a dependency graph the planner can prove safely.
It mixes pure declarations with external input authority. Locked reads remain available through explicit build and input surfaces without widening every module field.

recommendation.tradeoff: A field name becomes part of other fields' dependency graph, so renaming it can break those dependents. That coupling is acceptable because it is explicit, checked, and reported before any plan runs.

decisions.comment: Owner question q7b6hkv9 answered: comptime is the pure value calculator, fn build is the authorized effect runner; both stay (I1). C loses nothing on safety and nothing on effort; it loses on I8: D-CTIO1 comptime bindings already deliver locked reads to fields through one binding line, so C would scatter external-input provenance across every field for one line of convenience.

decisions.title: Should typed project budgets cover compile latency?
decisions.gist: Decide whether Jet projects may enforce cold, unchanged, and representative-edit compile latency, and how each measured workload gets an exact identity.
decisions.lesson:
Compile latency is workload-relative. A cold build, an unchanged rebuild, and a one-file edit exercise different cache paths. A number without source, cache, compiler, target, profile, linker, and host identity cannot be compared safely.

Jet already measures its product compiler in #666. #241 enforces project performance facts, but its closed metric and provider set has no compile workload. Extending that public typed vocabulary requires this decision.
decisions.explainer: All options preserve zero-ceremony defaults. No project receives a compile budget unless its author declares one. Any measurement uses #241's canonical evaluator, pinned baselines, reports, diagnostics, and CI behavior. The choice is whether project-level compile regressions are enforceable and whether representative edits are first-class.
decisions.story: Mina maintains a large Jet service. A harmless generic helper change doubles every developer rebuild, while runtime benchmarks remain green. Mina wants CI to catch that regression with enough provenance to reproduce it.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: no new ceremony or measurement occurs by default. Expert pass: declared probes pin the source tree, edit, cache state, toolchain, target, profile, backend, linker, host, warmups, samples, and phase breakdown.

options.name: Internal Jet SLOs only
options.detail: Keep compile latency entirely in #666's compiler corpus. Projects cannot declare or enforce their own compile-time regressions through performance budgets.
options.code:
$ jet budget check
# Runtime, size, and existing compiler-fact budgets only.
# Compile latency remains a Jet compiler product gate in #666.

options.name: Fixed compile scenarios
options.detail: Add typed Clean and NoChange compiler probes. They are reproducible, but they cannot model the representative edit loop that developers feel most often.
options.code:
Budget.{
    name: "clean-compile",
    scope: .Target("cli"),
    metric: .CompileTime(.P95),
    provider: .CompilerProbe(.Clean),
    comparison: .RelativeTo("ci/linux-x64"),
    limit: .RegressionAtMost(5pct),
}

Budget.{
    name: "no-change-compile",
    scope: .Target("cli"),
    metric: .CompileTime(.P95),
    provider: .CompilerProbe(.NoChange),
    comparison: .RelativeTo("ci/linux-x64"),
    limit: .RegressionAtMost(5pct),
}

options.name: Typed compile workloads
options.detail: Add one CompilerProbe provider with Clean, NoChange, and named Edit workload values. The edit value records a deterministic source patch instead of guessing from timestamps.

comparisons.note: The checked compiler corpus protects Jet's compiler as a product. It does not let one application preserve its own representative edit latency.
comparisons.code:
cold / warm / incremental JIT and AOT corpus
parse / sema / TIR / backend / link timings

comparisons.note: The mined video shows why one total is insufficient. Generics, state machines, linker choice, libc, allocator, profile, and cache state can each dominate.
comparisons.code:
same source + different profile/cache/environment
=> different cause, different useful fix

recommendation.why: C serves both facets with one existing budget mechanism. Beginners pay nothing; experts can prevent the real edit-loop regression, not only clean or unchanged build regressions.

whyNot.reason: A protects Jet's compiler average but gives application teams no enforceable guard for project-specific generic, derive, or module-graph cliffs.
B measures two useful endpoints yet omits the representative edit path where incremental invalidation failures appear.

recommendation.tradeoff: C adds public metric, provider, workload, and edit identity types. Their closed typed form keeps cache state and source changes auditable instead of relying on ambient files or timestamps.

decisions.checkInstructions: Before deciding, compare the beginner default, expert workload identity, cache-key completeness, and whether each option can catch a one-file incremental regression without flaky ambient state.

decisions.title: Default program entry is run.jet
decisions.outcome: Jet’s canonical default program entry file is run.jet, matching the jet run command and fn run entry method. Scaffolding, bare project resolution, and onboarding use run.jet by default; explicit file targets remain available.
decisions.comment: Jet’s canonical default program entry file is run.jet, matching the jet run command and fn run entry method. Scaffolding, bare project resolution, and onboarding use run.jet by default; explicit file targets remain available.

decisions.title: D-LENS-RUN1: jet run = JIT lens, jet build = AOT lens
decisions.outcome: One compiler core. JIT and AOT are lenses only over the same front end and executable TIR — never parallel feature implementations and never a supported-feature gap between lenses. jet run uses the JIT lens; jet build uses the AOT lens. Missing JIT coverage is a compiler defect, not a user fallback to AOT.
decisions.comment: One compiler core. JIT and AOT are lenses only over the same front end and executable TIR — never parallel feature implementations and never a supported-feature gap between lenses. jet run uses the JIT lens; jet build uses the AOT lens. Missing JIT coverage is a compiler defect, not a user fallback to AOT.

decisions.title: One typed contract for user literal prefixes
decisions.gist: Choose one typed literal contract that gives users simple prefixes and library authors full checked control.
decisions.lesson:
A literal prefix turns source text into a value while the compiler checks the program. For example, `sql"..."` can produce a checked `Sql` value.

The compiler must keep text parts and typed holes separate. If it joins them first, the library loses injection safety and accurate source locations.

Beginners should only see the useful prefix. Library authors need explicit control over its name, accepted holes, errors, and generated value.

Jet already has typed text and comptime builders. The choice is how one type claims a prefix without adding macros or another interpolation engine.
decisions.story: Iris uses `sql"..."` in an application. Her database library checks syntax at compile time and keeps each value hole parameterized. Its author can inspect every lowering rule.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: lowercase name inference can collide, tag functions can grant syntax by accident, and joined strings can reopen injection bugs. The winner must reject collisions, preserve hole spans and types, run only at comptime, and use the existing typed-text engine. `Sql.raw` remains the sole audited raw escape under D-TYPEDTEXT1.

options.name: Type-owned contract with beginner shorthand and expert policy
options.detail: A result type derives one `Literal` contract. Users type only the prefix. Authors may accept the unambiguous lowercase default or set an explicit spelling and hole policy. Built-in and user prefixes use one typed-text path. Collisions and unsupported holes fail at the source span.
options.technical: The registry key is the explicit prefix or an unambiguous lowercase type name. The builder receives immutable text segments, typed hole facts, and spans. It returns only its owning type or a registered `LiteralError`. It cannot perform runtime effects or introduce grammar.

options.name: Any comptime tag function
options.detail: Any matching comptime function becomes a prefix. This is concise for authors and exposes functions directly. It also makes syntax capability depend on naming, permits accidental collisions, and leaves result ownership unclear.

options.name: Closed Core prefixes plus expected-type elaboration
options.detail: Only Core owns prefixes. Existing SQL typed text still follows D-TYPEDTEXT1 expected-type elaboration. User libraries cannot add safe domain prefixes, so their custom domains use ordinary constructors without typed holes.

comparisons.note: Tagged templates preserve text and values, but tags run at runtime and ownership follows an ordinary function binding.
Procedural macros offer deep control, but they add a separate token and macro system with macro-specific errors.
comparisons.code: sql!("select * from users where id = {}", id)

recommendation.why: A gives application users one clean prefix while giving authors explicit ownership, policy, errors, and inspection on Jet's existing typed-text path.

whyNot.reason: Function naming grants syntax implicitly and cannot make ownership or collisions clear.
A closed built-in set blocks safe domain literals from user libraries.

recommendation.tradeoff: Library authors must declare a contract and resolve prefix collisions. This visible work protects every simple call site.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, reserve E0358 with the exact what, why, and fix shown here. Bind the prefix registry to Syntax coverage. Prove collisions, typed holes, spans, comptime-only execution, AOT/JIT parity, inspection, and the existing raw escape.

decisions.title: Canvas scope: logic graphs only, or a full visual app builder
decisions.gist: Whether Canvas grows a drag-and-drop app designer beside its logic graphs, and where that designer lives.
decisions.lesson:
Canvas today is a visual editor for Jet logic. Programs appear as node graphs in the style of Unreal Engine's Blueprint, and every visual edit is a source-code transaction, so the graph and the text never drift apart.

RAD (rapid application development) is a different kind of visual tool. In Delphi, Lazarus, or classic Visual Basic you drag a button onto a window, set its label in a property panel, then double-click it. The tool generates the click handler and drops you inside it. App, layout, and code stay one thing.

That loop built the largest hobbyist and small-business software wave in history, and Lazarus keeps devoted users today because no modern tool matches it. Meanwhile Blueprint owns the logic-graph half and its vendor is stepping away from it, which leaves both halves contested.

Jet already has the pieces. The reactive UI kit (signals, renderer, styles, widgets) is the runtime a designer would target. The source-transaction engine is what keeps a visual edit honest. The question is whether Canvas points those pieces at a design surface, and if so, whether inside Canvas or as a separate tool.

The current Canvas roadmap (milestones M2 through M6) is unaffected in every option: nothing here reorders shipped commitments.
decisions.story: Sam, the game-jam hobbyist from the persona audit, wants a settings screen: two sliders and a start button. In Lazarus he would have it in three minutes without reading layout docs. In Jet today he hand-writes widget code, and the visual editor he already uses for logic cannot help him.

options.name: One editor, two surfaces
options.detail: Canvas grows a design surface — component palette, property inspector, callback generation — beside the logic graph, both writing through the same source-transaction engine. Double-clicking a button's handler opens that code as graph or text. You build an app and its logic in one tool. The cost: Canvas's scope grows well past logic editing, and the design surface competes for the same product attention.
options.technical: Design surface targets the reactive UI kit. Widgets and properties are source constructs, layout edits are ordinary transactions on the same file set. Staged strictly after the current M-arc, as its own milestone series.

options.name: Separate designer product
options.detail: A distinct app-designer tool shares the source-transaction engine but ships and evolves apart from Canvas. Canvas stays a focused logic editor. Each tool stays simple on its own. The cost: the double-click-into-your-callback loop now crosses a product boundary, and users juggle two editors for one app.
options.technical: Same engine and file truth, separate front end and roadmap. Cross-tool jump protocol required for designer-to-logic navigation.
options.code:
$ jet design app.jet    # designer: windows, widgets, properties
$ jet canvas app.jet    # canvas: the logic behind them
# double-click Start in the designer -> switches app to canvas

options.name: Stay Blueprint-only
options.detail: Canvas remains a logic editor. UI building stays code plus the reactive kit, and a designer is reconsidered after Canvas M6 ships. Full focus on finishing the committed arc. The cost: the beginner who is best served by drag-and-drop building — Jet's own headline persona — keeps hand-writing layout code for at least an epoch.
options.technical: No change. A future reconsideration would start from this ballot's record.

comparisons.note: Form designer plus double-click-into-callback is the loyalty loop that still holds users decades later.
The mass-market proof that drag-and-drop plus callbacks onboards non-programmers at scale.
Owns the logic-graph half only, and its vendor is stepping away — the opening Canvas already targets.
A design surface detached from logic editing. The round-trip pain of that split is the anti-pattern to avoid.

recommendation.why: The source-transaction engine is the hard-won asset, and pointing it at a design surface makes Canvas the only tool where visual UI building, visual logic, and text are the same file. That is the Lazarus loyalty loop without the code-generation drift that killed most RAD tools.

whyNot.reason: The double-click-into-your-callback jump defines the RAD loop, and option B routes it across a product boundary. Two front ends over one engine also split design attention permanently.
Drag-and-drop building serves the beginner facet better than any feature on the board, and deferring it concedes that ground for an epoch while the market gap is open.

recommendation.tradeoff: Canvas's mission grows from logic editor to app builder, and that larger mission is permanent. Accepted by staging the design surface strictly after the current M-arc, so no shipped commitment moves.

decisions.title: First-party MCP surface with typed defaults and protocol control
decisions.gist: Choose one MCP client and server API that starts simple and exposes full protocol, transport, version, and authorization control.
decisions.lesson:
Model Context Protocol, or MCP, lets clients discover and call tools, resources, and prompts. JSON-RPC is the request and reply envelope that names each operation. JSON Schema describes the allowed input and output data.

A codec converts typed Jet values to exact protocol messages. A transport carries those messages through standard input and output or HTTP. Authorization decides which remote identity may use each operation. An interceptor is an expert hook around message handling.

MCP revisions can change lifecycle rules. Stable `2025-11-25` uses initialization and can use HTTP sessions. The `2026-07-28` release candidate uses a stateless core and extensions.

A beginner should register a typed function and serve it. An expert needs version policy, transports, authorization, cancellation, progress, extensions, raw messages, and audit facts. One protocol core can serve both depths.
decisions.story: Noor serves one repository search function over stdio. The same binary later serves remote clients with OAuth, strict version policy, custom limits, and complete redacted traces.
decisions.inWild:
use core.mcp as mcp

server :: mcp.server("repo-tools")
  .tool("search", search)
server.serve(.Stdio)?

remote :: server.with(McpPolicy.{
  versions: .StableAnd(["2026-07-28"])
  auth: repo_oauth
  limits: strict_limits
})
remote.serve(.Http("127.0.0.1:8443"))?
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: the original lesson treated `2025-11-25` as timeless and made the builder sound closed. As of 2026-07-25, it is stable while `2026-07-28` is a release candidate with breaking lifecycle changes. The winner must use per-revision codecs, stable-by-default negotiation, explicit preview opt-in, bounded schema work, no token passthrough, and one low-level peer beneath the builders.

options.name: Layered typed SDK over one protocol core
options.detail: Typed builders register ordinary functions and cover the common client or server path. Experts use the same public codec, peer, transport, authorization, extension, and interceptor types. Stable revisions negotiate by default. Preview revisions require explicit policy until final.
options.technical: One revision registry owns messages and lifecycle laws. `2025-11-25` keeps session behavior. `2026-07-28` uses its stateless codec when enabled. Schema depth, message size, validation time, deadlines, redirects, origins, tokens, and extension sets are bounded and audited.

options.name: Compiler-discovered MCP markers
options.detail: Markers make registration short and permit generated tables. They also add MCP-specific syntax, hide registry order and policy, and burden functions that applications may call normally.

options.name: Low-level protocol package only
options.detail: Applications get codecs, messages, and transports without builders. Experts get full control, but every project must rebuild schema registration, validation, lifecycle, auth, cleanup, and typed dispatch.

comparisons.note: The stable revision uses initialization, negotiated capabilities, sessions, and Streamable HTTP.
The candidate uses per-request protocol facts, stateless HTTP, discovery, and extensions. It requires a separate revision codec.
Generated services give strong typed calls. MCP also needs runtime discovery and revision-aware JSON schemas.

recommendation.why: A makes the first tool small while preserving every protocol and security control through the same revisioned core and unified grant graph.

whyNot.reason: Markers create syntax and hide policy that an explicit registry can show.
A low-level package alone makes every application rebuild unsafe and inconsistent SDK machinery.

recommendation.tradeoff: Revision negotiation can expose an explicit incompatibility instead of silently adapting unlike lifecycle rules. Preview revisions also require an explicit opt-in.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, test each revision as a separate wire profile. Prove stable defaults, preview opt-in, downgrade refusal, schema bounds, transport cleanup, authorization isolation, redacted traces, unified grants, and `jet inspect dossier` facts.

decisions.title: One authority model for agent command execution
decisions.gist: Choose one process authority model with a safe workspace default and exact expert grants, plans, isolation, and receipts.
decisions.lesson:
An agent can choose commands, so its plan is untrusted input. A familiar command name does not make execution safe.

Authority is the exact set of files, hosts, secrets, programs, devices, and resources a command may use. Isolation enforces that set.

Beginners need one safe workspace command that denies ambient credentials and network access. Experts need exact grants, limits, backend facts, dry-run plans, and machine-readable receipts.

Jet already has `core.process`, native isolation, and one trust graph. The choice is whether agent execution deepens those mechanisms or forks them.
decisions.story: Sam lets an agent run tests. The easy path reads the repository and writes only an isolated build area. A release job later grants one host and one signing key by name.
decisions.inWild:
// beginner-safe workspace policy
result :: process.cmd(["cargo", "test"])
  .under(ProcessAuthority.workspace("."))
  .run()?

// expert expansion on the same policy
release :: ProcessAuthority.workspace(".")
  .write(["dist"])
  .network([Host.https("registry.example.com")])
  .secret([SecretRef.signing("release")])
  .limits(strict_limits)
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a policy object is only useful if defaults deny ambient authority and every host enforces it. Plans can lie if resolution changes after review. Receipts can leak secrets. The winner must bind executable identity, policy, inputs, and backend into one launch transaction. Unsupported enforcement fails before spawn.

options.name: Safe workspace defaults plus exact core.process authority
options.detail: `ProcessSpec` accepts one authority object. The workspace constructor gives a useful read-only repository and private build area with network, home, secrets, devices, and inherited handles denied. Experts widen exact rights on the same object. CLI and MCP tools use the same engine.
options.technical: Resolve executable identity before review and bind it into launch. The plan and receipt share a policy digest. Native enforcement comes from #398. Denied attempts, descendants, limits, outputs, and redaction facts use the D-WD1 grant graph and D-WD2 dossier.
options.code:
// beginner
jet self exec --workspace . -- cargo test

// expert
policy :: ProcessAuthority.workspace(".")
  .write(["dist"])
  .network([Host.https("registry.example.com")])
  .executable([locked.cosign])
print(process.cmd(args).under(policy).plan())

options.name: Separate agent executor
options.detail: A dedicated executor can use agent terms and strict defaults. It duplicates command, child, signal, stream, cancellation, and isolation semantics. The two process systems can then disagree.
options.code:
agent.exec(Command.{ args, authority })?

// ordinary process and agent process now have separate lifecycle laws

options.name: CLI-only sandbox
options.detail: External agents get a safe command, but Jet programs and first-party SDKs cannot use the authority types. Libraries must shell out or launch unrestricted children.
options.code:
jet self exec --workspace . --write src,tests -- cargo test

// no equivalent typed ProcessSpec policy

comparisons.note: Deno grants scoped runtime permissions. Jet also needs executable identity, build authority, process-tree control, plans, and final receipts.
Bazel actions declare inputs and outputs for isolation and caching. Agent work also needs interactive plans and revocable trust.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one safe command and experts exact control without splitting process lifecycle, isolation, grants, or audit facts.

whyNot.reason: A second executor duplicates the most safety-sensitive process semantics.
CLI-only protection leaves Jet programs and SDKs outside the authority boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: `core.process` gains a substantial authority surface. The common constructor keeps that detail outside beginner code.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove no ambient authority, time-of-check binding, and fail-closed hosts. Also prove full-tree cleanup, redacted receipts, denied-attempt facts, shared digests, D-WD1 integration, and API/CLI parity.

decisions.title: Names for the process authority surface
decisions.gist: What the authority, plan, and receipt types are called, and how the CLI spells the same grants.
decisions.lesson:
An agent or a Jet program can start another program. That child may read files, talk on the network, or use secrets. Authority is the exact set of rights the child is allowed to use.

Jet already chose the model. Authority sits on the ordinary process API. Beginners get one safe workspace default. Experts widen exact grants. A dry-run plan shows what would happen. A final receipt records what did happen.

The model ballot sketched names such as `ProcessAuthority`, `Host`, `SecretRef`, `.under(policy)`, `.plan()`, and `jet self exec --workspace`. It did not lock the full public name set.

It never named the plan type, the receipt type, or the grant builders as Syntax-backed spellings. It never said whether network grants take a `Host` type or plain strings. It never fixed how the CLI mirrors the typed API.

Those are user-typeable names and flags. This ballot chooses the public spelling before code lands.
decisions.story: Sam lets an agent run tests in a workspace. Later a release job grants one registry host and one signing key by name. Sam wants the typed API and the CLI to use the same words, so a reviewed plan matches the command that ships.
decisions.detail: Follow-on to D-AGENT-EXEC1=A, same pattern as D-PROCESS-SESSION2 after D-PROCESS-SESSION1. Mechanism is fixed. This ballot locks names only.

options.name: Named types for authority, plan, receipt, host, and secret
options.detail: Every major idea gets its own public name. `ProcessAuthority` holds grants. `ProcessPlan` and `ProcessReceipt` are distinct types. Network and secret grants use `Host` and `SecretRef`. The CLI mirrors the same words as flags. Readers can jump to each type. This is the largest name set.
options.technical: Ships `ProcessAuthority`, `ProcessPlan`, `ProcessReceipt`, `Host`, and `SecretRef` with Syntax.rs decision ids where user-typeable. `.under`, `.plan`, `.run` stay methods. CLI: `--workspace`, `--write`, `--network`, `--secret`, `--executable`, `--limits`.
options.code:
policy :: ProcessAuthority.workspace(".")
  .write(["dist"])
  .network([Host.https("registry.example.com")])
  .secret([SecretRef.signing("release")])

plan : ProcessPlan :: process.cmd(args).under(policy).plan()
receipt : ProcessReceipt :: process.cmd(args).under(policy).run()?

// jet self exec --workspace . --write dist \
//   --network https://registry.example.com -- cargo test

options.name: Authority type only; plan and receipt stay plain data
options.detail: `ProcessAuthority` is the one new named type. Plan and receipt are ordinary records or strings you print. Hosts and secrets are plain strings on the grant methods. Fewer names to learn. Weaker jump-to-definition on plan and receipt fields.
options.technical: One Syntax-backed type: `ProcessAuthority`. `.plan()` returns a structured but unnamed record. `.run()` returns a receipt record. CLI flags still mirror grant verbs.
options.code:
policy :: ProcessAuthority.workspace(".")
  .write(["dist"])
  .network(["https://registry.example.com"])

print(process.cmd(args).under(policy).plan())
receipt :: process.cmd(args).under(policy).run()?
print(receipt.digest)

// jet self exec --workspace . --write dist -- cargo test

options.name: Reuse existing process config names
options.detail: Fold grants into types Jet already has for process limits and environment. No `ProcessAuthority` name. Experts extend the existing process config record. Smallest addition, but authority and ordinary config blur together at the call site.
options.technical: Extend current `ProcessSpec` config/limits records with grant fields. No new authority type. CLI keeps today's process flags plus grant flags without a parallel type vocabulary.
options.code:
child :: process.cmd(args)
  .limits(limits)
  .grants(.{ workspace: ".", write: ["dist"] })
  .spawn()?

// no ProcessAuthority in source

options.name: Typed authority; stringly CLI
options.detail: The Jet API gets the full named types from option A. The CLI stays a thin stringly wrapper with fewer curated flags. Experts script the typed API for exact grants. Beginners still get `--workspace`. The two surfaces can drift unless docs bind them.
options.technical: `ProcessAuthority`, `ProcessPlan`, `ProcessReceipt`, `Host`, `SecretRef` in Jet. CLI guarantees only `--workspace` parity; other grants documented as Jet-first.

comparisons.note: Permissions use explicit allow flags. There is no separate plan type; denial is runtime.
CLI flags name each grant. There is no typed twin inside ordinary application code.
Config and credentials use several file formats. Authority is not one typed process object.
comparisons.code: # cargo config and credential providers are separate surfaces

recommendation.why: A makes the typed API and the CLI speak the same words. Plan and receipt stay searchable types, which matters when agents review a dry-run before launch.

whyNot.reason: Plain strings for hosts and secrets lose checked construction, and unnamed plan or receipt types hide fields from ordinary navigation.
Mixing authority with ordinary process config hides the trust boundary the feature exists to show.
A stringly CLI breaks the ratified API and CLI parity rule from D-AGENT-EXEC1.

recommendation.tradeoff: More public names ship on day one. The workspace constructor still hides that list from beginner call sites.

decisions.title: Names for the expert terminal surface
decisions.gist: What the expert terminal controls are called, and how many new public names ship.
decisions.lesson:
A program that starts another program normally talks through pipes. A pipe is a plain byte channel. It carries output, and nothing else.

Some programs refuse to behave on a pipe. A debugger, a shell, and a password prompt all check whether they are attached to a terminal. On a pipe they turn off colour, drop their prompt, or refuse to read a password at all.

A pseudo-terminal fixes this. It is a fake terminal supplied by the operating system. The child believes a person is typing at a real screen. Unix calls this a PTY. Windows calls it a ConPTY.

Once a terminal exists, three kinds of detail matter. Size is columns and rows, because programs redraw when it changes. Mode says whether the operating system pre-processes keys or hands them over untouched. Raw mode is the untouched kind. An editor needs it to see a single arrow key.

The third kind is the host report. Call it the capability report, or host facts for short. It answers: can this machine give me a terminal at all? Can I resize it? Can I enter raw mode? A stripped container may have no terminal. So the program asks first, then adapts, rather than failing halfway.

Host facts are not settings you choose. They are answers the machine gives back. That is why their shape may differ from the types you use when you set size and mode.

Jet already ratified the beginner half. Writing `.terminal()` asks for safe portable defaults, and that ships today. The ratified text also sketched the expert half with names like `TerminalPolicy`, `mode`, `size`, and `capabilities()`.

It did not say what those names attach to. It never named the type holding columns and rows. It never named the mode that is not raw. It never named what `capabilities()` hands back, nor the terminal handle on the started child.

Those are user-typeable names, so Jet requires the owner to ratify them before code exists. This ballot chooses how many such names ship and what shape they take.
decisions.story: Priya maintains a test runner that drives a debugger. On a pipe the debugger prints no prompt, so her runner hangs waiting for text that never comes. She wants a terminal, raw key handling, and a size she sets herself. She also runs the same suite inside a stripped container, where no terminal exists, and she needs that to fail clearly rather than hang again.
decisions.detail: Owner follow-up: "facts" means the host capability report from `capabilities()`, not a second settings object. Exploration needs a short ask-then-adapt path. Safety needs typed controls on the request side. Option D below keeps growing reports without a breaking struct change, and uses named fact keys so ordinary typos fail at compile time.

options.name: A named type for each idea
options.detail: Every concept gets its own public name. Size, mode, the support report, and the child's terminal handle are four separate named types. Each one can be searched for, jumped to, and documented on its own page. This is the largest number of new names, and the most that a reader must learn before writing expert code.
options.technical: Ships `TerminalSize.{ cols: Int, rows: Int }`, `TerminalMode` with variants `.Raw` and `.Cooked`, `TerminalReport` returned by `capabilities()`, and `TerminalSession` as the handle on `ProcessChild`. Four Syntax.rs entries with decision ids. Field names are fixed by the type, so a wrong field is a compile error naming the type.
options.code:
size :: TerminalSize.{ cols: 120, rows: 40 }

plan :: process.cmd(["lldb", app])
  .terminal(TerminalPolicy.{ size, mode: .Cooked })

report : TerminalReport :: plan.capabilities()
print(report.resize)      // true

child :: plan.spawn()?
session : TerminalSession :: child.terminal
session.resize(TerminalSize.{ cols: 80, rows: 24 })

options.name: One policy record carries everything
options.detail: Only `TerminalPolicy` is public. Columns and rows sit directly on it as ordinary numbers, so no size type exists. The support report comes back as another `TerminalPolicy` describing what the host would actually grant. Fewer names to learn, but the same type means two different things depending on where it appears.
options.technical: `TerminalPolicy.{ cols: Int, rows: Int, mode: TerminalMode, ... }`. `capabilities()` returns `TerminalPolicy` holding granted values rather than requested ones. `ProcessChild.terminal` is typed as the child itself, with resize and mode methods hung directly on `ProcessChild`. One new type plus the mode enum.
options.code:
plan :: process.cmd(["lldb", app])
  .terminal(TerminalPolicy.{ cols: 120, rows: 40, mode: .Cooked })

// same type coming back, now meaning "what you would get"
granted :: plan.capabilities()
if granted.cols == 0 { return Err("no terminal here") }

child :: plan.spawn()?
child.resize(80, 24)

options.name: Borrow the shapes Core already has
options.detail: Jet already ships types for a width-and-height pair and for reporting what a host supports. This option reuses them instead of minting terminal-only twins. Only the mode needs a new name. The smallest addition to the language, at the cost of types whose names never say the word terminal.
options.technical: Size reuses Core's existing two-field extent type; `capabilities()` reuses the existing host-facts record used elsewhere in Core, keyed by fact name. `ProcessChild.terminal` is an existing stream handle. One new public name, `TerminalMode`. Requires an audit that the reused types are a genuine fit and not a coincidence of shape.
options.code:
plan :: process.cmd(["lldb", app])
  .terminal(TerminalPolicy.{ size: Extent.{ 120, 40 }, mode: .Cooked })

report :: plan.capabilities()          // the same record kind used by core.os
if !report.has("terminal") { return Err("no terminal here") }

child :: plan.spawn()?
child.terminal.resize(Extent.{ 80, 24 })

options.name: Typed controls, keyed host report with named facts
options.detail: The things you set are named types, because a wrong field should fail while writing. The things you read back are a host report that can grow. Known facts use named keys such as `TerminalFact.terminal`, so a typo on a known fact fails to compile. Preview facts may use a string form with a nearest-key diagnostic. This keeps strong typing on everyday paths and still lets a new host answer appear without a breaking type change.
options.technical: Ships `TerminalSize`, `TerminalMode`, `TerminalSession`, and `TerminalFact` key constants. `capabilities()` returns a keyed report. `report.has(TerminalFact.resize)` is compile-checked. `report.has("preview_x")` stays open for growth. Documented keys get Syntax.rs entries. String typos suggest the nearest known key.

options.name: Typed stable report plus open preview bag
options.detail: Controls stay named types. The host report also has typed fields for the stable answers every backend must give today: terminal present, resize, raw mode. A separate preview bag holds experimental answers. Everyday exploration uses field access with full type checking. New stable fields still need a release that extends the public type.
options.technical: `TerminalReport.{ terminal: Bool, resize: Bool, raw: Bool, preview: FactBag }`. Stable fields are required. Preview keys are strings with nearest-key diagnostics. More names than D, and each new stable fact is a type change.
options.code:
plan :: process.cmd(["lldb", app])
  .terminal(TerminalPolicy.{
    size: TerminalSize.{ cols: 120, rows: 40 },
    mode: .Cooked
  })

report :: plan.capabilities()
if !report.terminal { return Err("no terminal here") }
print(report.resize)
print(report.preview.has("future_fact"))

child :: plan.spawn()?
child.terminal.resize(TerminalSize.{ cols: 80, rows: 24 })

comparisons.note: The standard library exposes raw file descriptors and leaves naming to the caller. Size is an unnamed four-number packed struct. Readers must know the layout by heart.
comparisons.code:
import pty, struct, fcntl, termios
pid, fd = pty.fork()
fcntl.ioctl(fd, termios.TIOCSWINSZ, struct.pack("HHHH", 40, 120, 0, 0))

comparisons.note: portable-pty names every concept, including a size struct with named fields and pixel dimensions most callers ignore.
node-pty takes a plain options object. Columns and rows are loose fields, and a misspelled key silently falls back to a default.
comparisons.code:
const p = pty.spawn("lldb", [app], { cols: 120, rows: 40 });
p.resize(80, 24);

comparisons.note: creack/pty names the size type but keeps mode as raw operating-system flags, so callers reach for a second package to turn raw mode on.

recommendation.why: D keeps request-side mistakes compile-time hard, keeps ask-then-adapt exploration short, and lets host answers grow without breaking everyday code. Named fact keys remove the old string-typo trap on the known set.

whyNot.reason: A fixed report type makes every new host answer a breaking change to a public type. Callers still read answers by name rather than destructure them.
One type meaning both the request and the grant reads wrong at the call site. Using `granted.cols == 0` as "no terminal" is a sentinel, which Jet avoids elsewhere.
Reuse is right only when the shapes mean the same thing. A terminal size is characters, not pixels or generic extent.
E wins on typed everyday fields, but every new stable host answer becomes a public type change. D gives the same safety on known facts through named keys without that churn.

recommendation.tradeoff: Preview facts still use strings, so a typo there reads as absent. That is limited to experimental keys. Known keys stay named constants. Docs and a nearest-key diagnostic cover the preview path.

decisions.title: One flake-class graph for Jet environments
decisions.gist: Choose one easy Jet environment graph with full expert input, lock, follows, output, and foreign projection control.
decisions.lesson:
A reproducible source graph names external inputs, pins exact revisions, connects shared inputs, and exposes outputs. A lock records the resolved identity.

A follows edge makes two sources share one dependency. This avoids hidden duplicate package worlds and keeps overlays aligned.

Beginners need a small `sources` list and one automatic lock. Experts need named nodes, follows edges, output selection, graph queries, merge facts, and loss-accounted foreign projection.

Jet already has sources, outputs, environment modules, and `.jet/lock`. Ratified flake-parts support also requires expert composition without making Nix the beginner language.
decisions.story: Mina pins nixpkgs and a Rust overlay with two short entries. Riley imports a flake-parts monorepo, inspects every follows edge, and exports a compatible view.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a bridge-only design loses graph intent, a separate flake block creates two locks, and best-effort translation can hide semantic loss. The winner must keep one graph and lock, honor D-ENV-FLAKEPARTS1, report every projection loss, preserve source provenance, and reject ambiguous follows edges.

options.name: Progressive Jet graph with loss-accounted foreign projections
options.detail: Beginners list sources and use automatic exact locking. Experts add typed follows edges, output projections, provider mappings, merge policy, and flake-parts composition in the same graph. Import and export use that graph and produce exact loss reports.
options.technical: `.jet/lock` remains sole identity. Every foreign node maps to a source, follows edge, output, or explicit unsupported fact. Imported arbitrary Nix functions remain in the native compatibility evaluator. They never become opaque native Jet values.

options.name: Separate flake compatibility block
options.detail: Nix users get familiar inputs, outputs, and follows. Jet projects then own two graph vocabularies and must define which lock, source, output, and policy wins.
options.code:
flake: { inputs: { ... }, outputs: fn(inputs) { ... } }
env: { packages: [flake.outputs.rust] }

options.name: Resolved-package bridge only
options.detail: Jet keeps a small native graph and imports final packages from an external evaluator. This cannot preserve follows, output structure, lock reasons, module composition, or round-trip intent.
options.code:
packages: import_flake(".").packages

// graph identity and follows edges are hidden

comparisons.note: Inputs, follows, outputs, and `flake.lock` form one reproducible graph with a functional output layer.
flake-parts composes that graph from modules. D-ENV-FLAKEPARTS1 requires an expert Jet path over the same realization engine.

recommendation.why: A keeps the beginner graph small while giving experts full graph, lock, projection, and flake-parts control through one realization path.

whyNot.reason: A second graph duplicates identity, locking, policy, and outputs.
Resolved packages alone discard graph intent and cannot support honest round trips.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some Nix functions remain evaluator-backed and cannot become ordinary typed Jet values. Their boundaries and projection losses stay explicit.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove one lock, exact follows, and flake-parts use. Prove round trips for representable graph facts. Also prove exact loss reports for evaluator-backed constructs, merge facts, containment, and stable graph and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: One typed environment lifecycle with simple defaults and expert policy
decisions.gist: Choose one lifecycle planner for enter tasks, dotenv, unset rules, default reload, clean-shell checks, trust, and the existing expert hook.
decisions.lesson:
Environment lifecycle actions run when a developer enters or reloads a project environment. They can change files, variables, and services.

A dotenv file supplies named environment values. An unset rule removes an inherited name. Reload evaluates source changes again. A check tests the environment from a clean shell.

A cloned repository must not run code or read secrets silently. Jet therefore needs a plan, typed effects, trust grants, and exact change detection before lifecycle work runs.

Beginners need short fields such as `dotenv` and `checks`. Experts need key allowlists, secret treatment, ordering, reload triggers, cache policy, failure policy, and audit output. One planner can use `#Task`, D-ECO7's hook, and the unified grant graph.
decisions.story: Tess lists `.env`, one setup task, and one check. Reload works by default. A sensitive repo expands key, secret, timing, and failure policy.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: shell strings bypass effects, magic names hide execution, dotenv can import secrets, reload can loop, and a denied hook can leave partial state. Binding owner law requires a first-run prompt with a hash allowlist. Background re-evaluation is on by default and applies at the next prompt. `jet env test` proves a clean shell. The winner must use D-WD1 grants, keep D-ECO7 as the sole arbitrary hook, and publish reload and rollback facts.

options.name: Typed lifecycle fields over one task and grant planner
options.detail: Simple lists cover dotenv files, unset names, enter tasks, and checks. Reload is on by default and applies a background plan at the next prompt. Experts expand key, secret, ordering, reload, cache, and failure policy. An unseen or denied D-ECO7 hook is skipped, and the shell still opens.
options.technical: The planner resolves data changes first, then granted task or hook nodes, then checks. It binds source digests and effects before execution. Hook grants stay scoped per role module and bind the plan hash. Reload coalesces changes and rejects cycles. `jet env test` starts clean. Failure reports exact retained state.

options.name: Embedded shell hooks
options.detail: Existing shell scripts fit directly and experts control their shell. Jet loses typed effects, portable behavior, structured plans, key tracking, and consistent rollback.
options.code:
enterShell: "source .env && ./scripts/setup.sh"
enterTest: "test -f .env"

options.name: Reserved lifecycle function names
options.detail: Authors write ordinary Jet functions with little configuration. Renaming or importing a function can silently change lifecycle behavior, and the module does not show execution order.
options.code:
fn enter() #Fs { ... }
fn enter_test() #Fs { ... }

comparisons.note: Directory entry can load environment code after trust. Jet also needs typed effects, tasks, checks, and structured reload facts.
devenv provides enter hooks, dotenv, tests, and reload behavior through Nix and shell fields.

recommendation.why: A keeps common entry short and gives experts exact lifecycle, trust, secret, reload, failure, and audit control through one ordered plan.

whyNot.reason: Shell strings bypass Jet's type, effect, trust, and rollback facts.
Reserved names hide wiring and make ordinary refactors change behavior.

recommendation.tradeoff: First use can show a trust prompt. Default background reload waits until the next shell prompt before it changes the active environment.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove per-role-module hook grants, plan-hash binding, and denied-hook shell entry. Prove default reload at the next prompt and clean-shell `jet env test`. Also prove plan order, dotenv allowlists, redaction, task effects, cycles, retained-state facts, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: One Service record from simple command to full dev topology
decisions.gist: Choose one Service record with useful defaults and full expert readiness, recovery, watch, resource, dependency, and audit control.
decisions.lesson:
A development service is a long-running process with logs and cleanup. Readiness tells dependents when the service can accept work.

Restart and watch policies control recovery and reload. Ports, sockets, and dependency edges describe resources and start order.

Beginners need a service with only a command. Experts need exact probes, restart budgets, backoff, watch rules, shutdown stages, ports, sockets, dependencies, and receipts.

Jet already has one `Service` record, one service CLI, safe process-tree authority, and ordinary task calls for finite work. The choice is whether that one record grows by progressive disclosure.
decisions.story: Owen starts an API from one `run` field. His full stack later adds database readiness, a migration task, restart limits, file watches, reserved ports, and exact shutdown policy.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: process start is not application readiness. Restart loops can burn resources, watch events can storm, dependency edges can cycle, and port checks can race. The winner must distinguish start from readiness and reserve resources before release. It must bound retries, detect cycles, and honor D-JPK-SERVICEAUTH1 before background spawn.

options.name: Progressive Service record over one supervised graph
options.detail: A `run` field creates a foreground-capable service with safe cleanup and no claimed application readiness. Experts add typed probes, bounded restart, watch, ports, sockets, order, shutdown, and logs. Finite migrations stay ordinary `#Task` calls attached as explicit dependencies.
options.technical: The service planner owns resource reservation, acyclic order, generation identity, readiness transitions, restart budgets, watch debounce, and receipts. Background start uses D-JPK-SERVICEAUTH1 and fails before spawn when safe authority is unavailable.

options.name: Separate ProcessGraph record
options.detail: A graph can model tasks and services uniformly. It duplicates service identity, process ownership, logs, readiness, cancellation, resource claims, and CLI state beside `Service`.
options.code: ProcessGraph.{ nodes: [db, migrate, api], edges: [...] }

options.name: Delegate advanced topology to process-compose
options.detail: Projects gain a mature external supervisor. Advanced behavior then depends on another binary, configuration language, lifecycle, lock, diagnostics, and authority model.
options.code: jet os services export --format process-compose | process-compose up

comparisons.note: It combines dependencies, readiness, restarts, logs, and process supervision in a separate configuration system.
systemd distinguishes process state, readiness, restart policy, resources, and ordering. Jet needs portable typed versions for development.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one command field and experts a complete supervised topology without duplicating service identity, lifecycle, authority, or inspection.

whyNot.reason: A second graph repeats the same service and process facts.
External delegation makes core behavior depend on another configuration and authority stack.

recommendation.tradeoff: The Service type becomes broad. Closed typed policy records and short defaults keep that breadth out of basic declarations.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove start versus readiness, bounded retries, backoff, debounce, resource reservation, and cycle errors. Also prove task and service order, tree cleanup, D-JPK-SERVICEAUTH1 failure, plans, logs, receipts, and dossier facts.

decisions.title: Task metadata with zero-ceremony defaults and exact expert execution
decisions.gist: Choose one `#Task` signature that stays bare and exposes packages, paths, skip rules, cache, authority, resources, and outputs when needed.
decisions.lesson:
A task is an ordinary Jet function exposed to project tooling. D-JPK-TASKRUN1 already makes `#Task fn` the one task identity.

Simple tasks should run with the current environment, project directory, and no hidden cache promise. No metadata is required.

Experts need task-local packages, a working directory, declared inputs and outputs, cache policy, authority, limits, and execution facts. Tooling needs those facts before the body runs.

D-MARKSIG1 gives markers one ordinary call grammar. The choice is whether `#Task` uses that grammar or duplicates task identity in another map.
decisions.story: Rae marks `book` with bare `#Task` and runs it. CI later adds mdbook, inputs, outputs, a platform skip rule, cache, and authority.
