decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: automatic caching can return false results, and runtime provisioning hides the plan. Output globs can capture secrets. Unchecked skip rules can hide required work. The winner must keep bare tasks uncached, use D-MARKSIG1, show skip reasons, and bind facts before execution. Dynamic undeclared access must fail or disable promotion.

options.name: Progressive typed metadata on the existing #Task marker
options.detail: Bare `#Task` stays the beginner form and runs honestly without reusable caching. Experts add closed typed arguments for packages, cwd, inputs, outputs, skip, cache, authority, and limits. Task calls remain the only dependency edges.
options.technical: Metadata uses D-MARKSIG1. Cache keys bind function identity, arguments, locked packages, declared inputs, policy, platform, and compiler. Skip uses typed host or platform facts and reports its reason. Undeclared access fails in strict cached mode. Dynamic tasks may select `.Off`.

options.name: Separate task configuration map
options.detail: The marker stays tiny and a central map can review all tasks. Names, functions, dependencies, arguments, and metadata can drift between two sources of truth.
options.code: tasks: { book: { fn: book, packages: [pkg.mdbook], cwd: "docs" } }

options.name: Provision only inside task bodies
options.detail: Authors use ordinary code for every unusual case. The planner cannot know packages, cwd, inputs, outputs, cache safety, or authority until execution has started.

comparisons.note: Declared actions give strong cache facts, but require a separate build language and explicit metadata for every action.
Recipes are easy to write, but their shell bodies hide inputs, outputs, packages, effects, and portable cache rules.

recommendation.why: A preserves the one-line task while giving experts and tooling exact execution, cache, package, authority, and output facts on the same identity.

whyNot.reason: A separate map duplicates task identity and can drift from the function.
Runtime-only setup hides every fact needed for planning and safe caching.

recommendation.tradeoff: `#Task` gains a broad typed signature. Beginners keep bare `#Task`, and experts reveal only fields they need.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, bind D-MARKSIG1 and keep bare tasks uncached. Prove typed skip reasons, cache keys, undeclared-access errors, output containment, secret exclusion, task-local packages, cwd, authority, limits, dependency calls, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: One managed file graph with safe shorthand and exact sync policy
decisions.gist: Choose one typed file graph for simple managed links and expert seed, copy, generation, permissions, secrets, drift, and conflict control.
decisions.lesson:
Environment files include tool configuration, seed data, generated text, and links to locked content. Jet must know who owns each destination.

A symlink follows its managed source. A seed writes only when the destination is absent. A copy replaces managed output after review.

Beginners need a short map with a safe default. Experts need mode, permissions, secret treatment, generation, conflict policy, atomic updates, drift checks, and exact diffs.

Typed values and ordinary Jet functions can generate content. A separate template language is not required. One file graph can plan and audit every write.
decisions.story: Kai links one tool file with a short map entry. A local settings file uses seed mode, while a generated secret file requires strict permissions and redacted diffs.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: implicit overwrite can destroy local work, and symlink targets can escape the project. Generated content can leak secrets. Seed drift can become invisible, and templates add injection rules. The winner must stop on unmanaged conflicts, use atomic replacement, redact sensitive diffs, bind source hashes, and show exact ownership.

options.name: Progressive typed files map with plan-before-apply
options.detail: A bare value means a managed symlink to immutable content and never overwrites an unmanaged destination. Experts expand the entry with Seed or Copy mode, permissions, sensitivity, generation, and conflict policy. `jet env sync` plans, confirms, applies atomically, and audits drift.
options.technical: Every entry has destination, source digest, mode, ownership, sensitivity, and last applied state. Relative destinations cannot escape their root. Sensitive bytes never enter logs or world-readable stores. Dynamic sources return typed text or bytes before planning.

options.name: Lifecycle tasks only
options.detail: Ordinary filesystem code can express every case. Plans cannot know destinations, ownership, overwrite rules, sensitivity, or drift before the task runs.
options.code:
on_enter: [seed_files]
#Task fn seed_files() #Fs { ... }

options.name: Separate template manifest
options.detail: A template system makes text generation convenient and reviewable. It adds another interpolation language, escaping law, secret path, and ownership model beside Jet values.
options.code: generated_files: { ".env": template("env.tpl", values) }

comparisons.note: Typed declarations manage files and links with source ownership. Jet also needs project sync, seed behavior, and unified trust facts.
chezmoi handles templates, secrets, diffs, and apply workflows through a separate configuration product.

recommendation.why: A makes the common link short and gives experts exact write, generation, secret, conflict, drift, and audit control through one file graph.

whyNot.reason: Imperative tasks hide ownership and overwrite policy until execution.
A template manifest adds a second interpolation and secret-rendering system.

recommendation.tradeoff: An unmanaged ownership conflict stops synchronization and requires a user choice. Jet never guesses which file may be replaced.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove safe shorthand, conflict refusal, and Symlink, Seed, and Copy semantics. Also prove atomic recovery, path containment, permissions, redaction, source hashes, generated values, drift, plan confirmation, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: OCI images as one projection of the environment and image graphs
decisions.gist: Choose one existing image record with a simple environment source and full expert entrypoint, platform, layer, security, and provenance control.
decisions.lesson:
An environment graph already knows packages, variables, files, tasks, services, and locked sources. An Open Container Initiative, or OCI, image packages a filesystem and runtime settings.

A layer is one immutable filesystem change. An entrypoint is the first program the image starts. Provenance records the inputs, builder, and policy that made the image.

Not every environment fact belongs in an image. Host hooks, local secrets, mutable sockets, and unsupported services must fail or require an explicit replacement.

Beginners need `from: env.dev` and a useful shell image. Experts need service selection, platforms, users, layers, ports, health, entrypoints, secret rules, cache, and provenance. Jet can extend its existing image record.
decisions.story: Uma creates a development shell image with one source line. Her CI image later selects the API service, non-root user, two platforms, health probe, and exact layer policy.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: environment projection can copy secrets, activation hooks, host paths, impure outputs, or mutable state into layers. A second container record would split locks and publishing. The winner must classify every fact and refuse non-projectable state. It must use a non-root default, exclude secrets, show the projection plan, and preserve D-JPK-REMOTE1 for remote builds.

options.name: Progressive environment projection in the existing image record
options.detail: `from: env.dev` creates a locked shell image with safe non-root defaults. Experts select services, platforms, users, entrypoints, layers, ports, health, cache, and signatures on the same record. Host-only facts fail with a specific projection error.
options.technical: Projection records included, transformed, omitted, and rejected facts. Secrets use runtime mounts or references and never layers. Hangar owns content, cache, signing, archive, and publish. `.jet/lock` owns exact inputs and platforms. Remote builders use only prior D-JPK-REMOTE1 host bindings and grants.

options.name: Separate container environment records
options.detail: Container users get a focused namespace with its own layers, commands, ports, build, and publish fields. It duplicates image identity, locks, Hangar, provenance, and lifecycle.
options.code: container.api { environment: env.dev, command: api.run }

options.name: CLI-only environment projection
options.detail: One command creates ad hoc images without source changes. The image contract, service selection, platform policy, and security choices disappear from reviewable source.
options.code: jet os image build --env dev --services api

comparisons.note: OCI standardizes image content and runtime configuration. It does not define how a development environment becomes that image.
Nix can build layered images from a package closure. Jet also projects typed services, files, policy, and provenance.

recommendation.why: A makes a shell image one line and gives experts full OCI, security, platform, and provenance control without splitting Jet's image machinery.

whyNot.reason: A container namespace duplicates image identity, locking, storage, signing, and publishing.
CLI-only flags hide the image contract from source review and reproducible builds.

recommendation.tradeoff: A host-only or secret-bearing environment fact stops projection until the user replaces or omits it explicitly.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove shell defaults, service entrypoints, non-root policy, fact classes, secret exclusion, and host-only rejection. Also prove platform locks, deterministic layers, D-JPK-REMOTE1 bindings, Hangar reuse, signatures, publishing, plans, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: Workflow profiles for jet env
decisions.gist: Whether Jet envs get named workflow profiles beyond env.dev / env.test overlays.
decisions.lesson:
A workflow profile is a named slice of an environment you turn on for a job.

Example slices: backend databases, frontend node tooling, or CI-only browsers.

Jet already has role overlays such as env.dev and env.test. Those cover common intents.

Devenv also adds named profiles you combine with flags, and profiles that auto-apply from hostname or username.

Auto profiles save typing. They can also surprise someone on a shared machine if a hostname flips services on.

The choice is how much profile power Jet adds on top of today’s overlays.
decisions.story: Sam maintains a monorepo. On the laptop they want frontend tools. On the CI host they want browsers and stricter env vars. They do not want three separate repos.

options.name: Overlays only
options.detail: Keep env.dev / env.test / env.build. Compose with imports. No named profiles and no hostname or user auto-apply.
options.technical: No new profile syntax. Monorepo uses imports:find and workspace.jet. CI selects jet env test explicitly.
options.code:
$ jet env dev
$ jet env test

options.name: Named profiles with extends, manual only
options.detail: Add named profiles you pass on the CLI. Profiles can extend each other. No hostname or user auto-apply.
options.technical: profiles: on env modules; jet env --profile frontend. Merge law reuses module merge + priority. Auto host/user profiles omitted.
options.code: $ jet env --profile backend --profile testing

options.name: Named profiles plus hostname/user auto
options.detail: Everything in B, plus profiles that activate from hostname or username like devenv. Maximum convenience; more surprise risk.
options.technical: profiles.hostname / profiles.user auto-merge with documented priority. Must show what activated in jet env info.
options.code:
$ jet env
# also applied: hostname.ci-server, user.sam

options.name: Imports-only composition, no profile noun
options.detail: Teach folder imports as the only compose tool. Avoid the word profile to prevent clash with package profiles.
options.technical: Deepen imports for remote locked env modules. Package profiles (D-JPK-PROFILE*) stay a separate concept.
options.code:
imports: find("./frontend")
imports: find("./backend")

comparisons.note: profiles with extends, --profile flags, and hostname/user auto activation.
env role overlays and imports:find without named workflow profiles.

recommendation.why: Named manual profiles cover monorepo and CI slices without surprising auto activation from hostname or username.

whyNot.reason: Overlays alone force awkward env names for every cross-cutting slice a monorepo needs.
Hostname and user auto-apply can enable services without an explicit command, which is a trust hazard on shared machines.
Imports help structure folders but do not give a first-class switch for temporary slices like testing browsers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must teach profile as a workflow idea beside package profiles. Clear CLI naming and docs must keep the two concepts apart.

decisions.title: Language tooling packs for jet env
decisions.gist: How a beginner turns on a full language toolchain in a Jet env.
decisions.lesson:
A language pack is a named preset that pulls the tools people expect for one language.

Think of it as a shopping list the tool fills for you. For Rust that list usually means the compiler, the package tool, the language server, and the formatter.

Without packs, you name every package yourself. That is precise, but beginners must know the whole list.

With packs, one short enable line fills the common tools. Experts still need a way to pin versions and add or remove tools.

The stakes are beginner speed versus expert control, and whether Jet grows a second way to declare packages.
decisions.story: Maya opens a Jet repo to write a small Rust service. She wants cargo and rust-analyzer in one step, like devenv languages.rust.enable, without pasting a twelve-package list.

options.name: Typed language packs on env
options.detail: Beginners enable a language with one typed field. Packs expand into ordinary packages. Experts can still list packages and pin versions. One mechanism underneath.
options.technical: Add languages: map on env modules. Each Lang record has enable, optional version/channel, and optional extra packages. Expansion is pure data into the existing package realize path. No second resolver.

options.name: Explicit packages only
options.detail: Keep today’s model. Docs and jet add helpers teach the lists. No languages field. Beginners paste or generate package lists.
options.technical: No new env syntax. Rely on packages: and overlays. Helpers may print suggested package sets but do not invent a pack type.

options.name: Packs as recipes only, no env field
options.detail: Ship recipe macros or jet add --lang rust that write packages: for you. No lasting languages: field in env modules.
options.technical: Scaffolding writes ordinary packages into env.jet. Re-running the helper can drift from hand edits unless merge rules are defined.
options.code:
$ jet env add-lang rust
# rewrites env.jet packages: [..., rustc, cargo, rust-analyzer, ...]

options.name: Packs plus mandatory explicit confirm
options.detail: languages.enable only prints the package set and refuses until the user pastes it. Maximum explicitness; high ceremony.
options.technical: Enable is a doctor/suggest step, not realize. Conflicts with beginner magic defaults.
options.code:
$ jet env
error: languages.rust.enable needs packages: [rustc, cargo, ...] — paste to confirm

comparisons.note: languages.rust.enable bundles toolchain and helpers with version/channel options.
Usually lists packages by hand in devShell.buildInputs.

recommendation.why: Packs give beginners one clear enable line while still expanding into the same package realize path experts already use.

whyNot.reason: Forces every beginner to memorize toolchain package sets that devenv already proved people want as one toggle.
Scaffold rewrite fights hand edits and hides the live declaration readers expect in env.jet.
Adds ceremony without removing the need for a pack definition, so beginners still stall.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must maintain pack definitions per language. That cost is accepted to keep the beginner path short without a second package system.

decisions.title: Optional environment integrations through Jet-native typed modules
decisions.gist: Choose how simple presets and exact expert controls for platforms, certificates, hosts, and agents fit the existing module and grant systems.
decisions.lesson:
Optional integrations combine packages, variables, files, licenses, secrets, permissions, and host capabilities. Android and Apple toolchains are examples.

A beginner wants one named preset with safe locked defaults. An expert needs exact SDK versions, targets, paths, license decisions, certificates, host mappings, agent tools, and failure policy.

Adding top-level fields for every product would make the environment record grow forever. Raw recipes avoid that growth but lose validation and shared planning.

Jet already has typed modules, imports, packages, files, tasks, providers, and grants. First-party integration modules can compose those facts without creating another mechanism.
decisions.story: Devon imports an Android preset and gets a locked supported SDK. A mobile release environment expands versions, Apple targets, certificates, host aliases, and Codex MCP servers with exact grants.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: closed top-level domains can become a second package system, and direct devenv mirroring freezes foreign names. Generic recipes hide licenses, secrets, host support, and grants. The winner must use typed modules, lower to existing facts, support two depths, and import foreign configs with exact loss reports.

options.name: First-party typed integration modules over existing facts
options.detail: Beginners import a named module with locked safe defaults. Experts pass typed versions, targets, paths, licenses, certificates, hosts, agent tools, and policy. Each module lowers to existing package, file, task, provider, host-check, secret, and grant facts.
options.technical: Integration modules have no private resolver, lock, effect, or activation engine. Their public outputs are typed graph facts. Foreign devenv modules import into canonical editable Jet modules with TODO diagnostics for every unsupported fact.

options.name: Mirror devenv module roots
options.detail: Migration is direct and existing users recognize names. Jet inherits another product's taxonomy, enable flags, nesting, defaults, and compatibility burden as public law.

options.name: Packages and lifecycle tasks only
options.detail: Projects assemble each integration from packages and lifecycle tasks without a curated preset. Beginners repeat fragile recipes, while planning cannot validate licenses, host support, certificates, or agent authority.
options.code:
packages: [pkg.android_sdk]
on_enter: [configure_android]

comparisons.note: devenv offers many named modules with enable flags and nested options. Jet can import them without adopting their taxonomy.
Typed modules compose options and defaults. Jet's modules also lower to one package, task, file, and grant graph.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners curated presets and experts exact integration control while preserving one module, package, file, task, host, lock, and grant mechanism.

whyNot.reason: A direct mirror turns foreign organization and enable flags into permanent Jet law.
Recipes alone cannot provide shared validation, planning, diagnostics, or safe defaults.

recommendation.tradeoff: Only first-party integration schemas receive preset guarantees and tailored diagnostics. Unusual tools use ordinary module composition with less specific guidance.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, prove beginner presets, expert parameters, module composition, one lock, license checks, and host failures. Also prove certificate and secret handling, agent grants, devenv loss reports, TODO diagnostics, and dossier JSON.

decisions.title: Beginner Jet env vs expert flake-parts
decisions.gist: Whether experts can use flake-parts while beginners keep a simple Jet env default.
decisions.lesson:
flake-parts is a Nix toolkit for splitting a project into reusable flake modules.

People use it to assemble languages, services, and shells from small pieces instead of one big file.

Jet already aims for one easy default: typed env modules that just work.

The dual-facet rule says beginners get magic defaults, and experts get explicit control of the same outcomes.

So the question is not whether Jet copies flake-parts as the only UI. It is whether the expert facet may opt into flake-parts composition and interop beside that default.
decisions.story: Alex wants new teammates on jet env with no Nix module homework. Riley maintains a large monorepo already split with flake-parts and needs Jet to consume and extend that graph without a rewrite.

options.name: Dual-facet: Jet default + expert flake-parts
options.detail: Beginners use typed env.* only. Experts can consume and compose flake-parts flakes through an explicit expert path. Same lock and realize engine underneath.
options.technical: Default: env modules + imports:find. Expert: U16/#783 bridge understands flake-parts module flakes; optional emit/import of flake-parts-compatible shards. No beginner requirement to touch flake-parts. I8 preserved: one realize path, two entry surfaces.
options.code:
$ jet env
# beginner repo → env.dev

$ jet env
# flake-parts repo → bridge activates modules; jet env info notes flake-parts

options.name: Jet env only — no flake-parts
options.detail: Experts rewrite flake-parts setups into Jet modules. Bridge may read plain flakes but not flake-parts module composition as a supported expert product.
options.technical: Keep U16 best-effort flake translate. Document flake-parts as unsupported; users flatten manually.
options.code:
$ jet bridge flake
# L0204 / unsupported: flake-parts modules — flatten into env.*

options.name: flake-parts as primary UX
options.detail: Teach flake-parts first. Jet env becomes a thin skin over module flakes. Beginners must learn Nix module composition.
options.technical: Inverts beginner default. Conflicts with epoch-4 vision of typed env without a second language.
options.code:
$ jet env
# requires flake-parts modules even for hello-world

options.name: Emit-only flake-parts, no consume
options.detail: Jet can generate flake-parts shards for Nix neighbors, but cannot activate an existing flake-parts monorepo as a first-class expert path.
options.technical: One-way bridge. Riley's existing repo still needs a rewrite to be consumed.
options.code:
$ jet bridge flake --emit-parts
# writes modules/; cannot jet env an upstream flake-parts tree

comparisons.note: Simple devenv.nix default; flake-parts users often embed devenv as a module inside a larger flake.
Dual-facet: beginner magic defaults; expert explicit control of the same mechanism.
comparisons.code:
module env.dev { ... }  // default
// expert flake-parts via bridge/opt-in

recommendation.why: Keeps the easy Jet env path for beginners while giving experts a real flake-parts consume and compose path on the same lock and realize engine.

whyNot.reason: Forces experts to abandon working flake-parts monorepos even though the owner asked for that expert path.
Makes Nix module composition the default and burdens beginners.
Only helps Jet export outward; it does not load the expert repos people already have.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must maintain flake-parts interop tests and docs. That cost is accepted so the expert facet is real, not a slogan.

decisions.comment: Jet has its own package/module system that should already support single file vs flake parts style devenvs -> ensure alignment with those existing paradigms

decisions.title: Administrator installation for the optional shared-store verifier
decisions.gist: Choose how an administrator installs and identifies the optional multi-user store verifier.
decisions.lesson: Jetpack normally stores packages in each user's private root. A shared store lets several users reuse verified bytes through one privileged broker. The broker rechecks the digest, signature, provenance, and writer authority, never evaluates project source, and records which user and namespace made each request. This ballot chooses who owns the broker's socket-activated service and root-owned store. It does not change the ratified security law. Deferral keeps private stores only; installation choices make the shared workflow available.
decisions.story: Maya runs CI and gives two developers access to one machine. They want one cache without allowing either account to write an unverified object into the other's namespace.
decisions.inWild:
$ sudo jetpack shared-store install
shared verifier: /run/jet/shared-store.sock
store root: /var/lib/jet/shared-store
$ jetpack build --shared-cache
verified by broker as user 1001, namespace team-ci

options.name: Jetpack installs the broker
options.detail: The explicit install command creates the root-owned store, socket unit, service unit, and per-user enrollment records. Users keep the existing rootless default when the install is absent.
options.technical: On Linux, install a root-owned socket-activated transient verifier with peer credentials and a per-user capability record. The verifier rechecks digest, signature, provenance, and writer authority, uses an ephemeral sandbox identity for promotion, and never evaluates user source.
options.code:
$ sudo jetpack shared-store install
installed verifier socket /run/jet/shared-store.sock
$ jetpack shared-store status
ready: peer credentials + writer policy verified

options.name: Platform package owns the broker
options.detail: A system package or image builder installs and upgrades the root-owned units. Jetpack only discovers the socket and registers a user grant. This fits managed fleets but needs a separate installer for each platform.
options.technical: The package owns service files and lifecycle. Jetpack reads a signed broker descriptor, then sends requests over the socket with peer credentials and the broker's tenant/writer checks.
options.code:
$ sudo apt install jet-shared-store
$ jetpack shared-store enroll --namespace team-ci
enrolled with broker /run/jet/shared-store.sock

options.name: Keep shared store deferred
options.detail: Ship only the per-user rootless store for now. No privileged socket, cross-user cache, or administrator operation exists until a later platform decision.
options.technical: The shared-store command reports that the optional broker is not installed and all builds stay in the caller's private namespace.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store status
not installed: using private per-user store
$ jetpack build
cache namespace: user:maya

comparisons.note: The Nix daemon is commonly installed by the operating system and serves multiple users through a privileged service.
Remote and shared caches rely on server-side authentication and provenance instead of trusting a client namespace.

recommendation.why: The command named by the ratified law is self-contained, discoverable, and preserves the safe rootless default when nobody installs it. It lets the verifier own peer identity, tenant scope, and cache-writer checks in one place.

whyNot.reason: A platform package can work, but it splits the product contract across installers and leaves local development without a portable install path.
Deferral keeps the default safe but leaves the requested multi-user boundary and shared-cache workflow unimplemented.

recommendation.tradeoff: The install command needs platform-specific privilege and service-unit code. That cost is accepted because the broker is optional and the unprivileged path remains the default.

reviewPasses.base: Kept the ratified per-user default, transient broker, re-verification, and no-source-evaluation law visible in every option.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Compared self-contained installation, platform-owned installation, and deferral. No fourth deployment model was needed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Recommended the explicit install command while preserving transparent private-store fallback when it is absent.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Gave each option a concrete administrator and developer workflow with the identity and namespace result.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Checked privilege boundaries, user identity, writer authority, service lifecycle, and the case where no broker exists.

decisions.title: Public surface for executable adapter recipes
decisions.gist: Choose how an adapter declares a finite executable build recipe.
decisions.lesson: An adapter turns an upstream source tree into a Jet package. Copying a tree or installing one prebuilt file needs no command execution. A build recipe is different: it lists exact fetch, tool, and install steps that may run a compiler or script. The current data model and trust gate can verify such a graph, but the public environment syntax accepts only copy and prebuilt forms. This choice decides whether users can author finite recipes now, use only signed provider recipes, or defer executable adapters.
decisions.story: Ravi vendors a small C utility and needs Jetpack to run its declared compiler command. The source must be approved by digest and run inside the strong sandbox, not through an implicit shell escape.
decisions.inWild:
packages: [Pkg.adapt(
  name: "wiretool",
  source: "./vendor/wiretool",
  recipe: Recipe.build(steps: [
    .exec(tool: "cc", args: ["-O2", "main.c", "-o", "wiretool"]),
    .install(src: "wiretool", dest: "bin/wiretool"),
  ])
)]

options.name: Expose finite Recipe.build
options.detail: Users may declare fetch, exec, install, and install-tree steps in one typed finite graph. Exact source, tool, capability, platform, and recipe facts enter the grant, and approved execution still requires the strong sandbox.
options.technical: Add the public parser/lowering for `Recipe.build(steps: [...])` over the existing BuildStep model. Reject unknown tools, unlocked fetches, escaping paths, cycles, and partial output. Keep the exact D-JPK-BUILDSCRIPT1=D trust subject.
options.code:
recipe: Recipe.build(steps: [.exec(tool: "cc", args: ["main.c"]), .install(src: "a.out", dest: "bin/a")])
held hook: wiretool (digest + capabilities)
approve and record exact grant? [y/N]

options.name: Provider recipes only
options.detail: Keep user syntax to copy and prebuilt. Providers may supply signed, digest-bound recipes through a separate feed. This narrows the beginner surface but custom local builds wait for provider support.
options.technical: The engine accepts BuildRecipe only from a signed provider record. A user-authored `Recipe.build` remains a typed diagnostic and cannot reach the adapter path.
options.code:
recipe: Recipe.build(...)
Error [E1270]: executable adapter recipes must come from an approved provider feed
Fix: use Recipe.copy(), Recipe.prebuilt(...), or install a signed recipe feed

options.name: Defer executable adapters
options.detail: Ship only non-executing adapters in this epoch. The existing trust and sandbox machinery remains dormant for user-authored build recipes until a later owner decision.
options.technical: Retain AdapterRecipe::Build as an internal reserved variant, but reject it at the public boundary and document the limitation. Copy and prebuilt remain the only production adapters.
options.code:
recipe: Recipe.build(...)
Error [E1270]: executable adapter recipes are not available
Fix: copy the source tree or provide a prebuilt binary

comparisons.note: Cargo build.rs is an executable build hook, so the project must trust an entire dependency unless a separate sandbox is added.
Package install scripts run through a provider-specific approval workflow, often with a separate allowlist.

recommendation.why: The finite graph already has one engine, identity, and trust boundary. Exposing that typed form makes the approved hook path real for local packages without inventing a shell escape or a second build mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Provider-only recipes leave local projects unable to build their own reviewed source and add a separate feed authority before the core path is usable.
Deferral keeps the surface small but leaves the card's executable hook behavior unreachable from production syntax.

recommendation.tradeoff: This adds a public recipe grammar and more diagnostics. That ceremony is accepted because every step remains finite, inspectable, digest-bound, and sandboxed.

reviewPasses.base: Kept the existing finite BuildStep model and exact digest/capability grant law in every option.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Compared a typed user recipe, signed provider recipes, and deferral. No second execution mechanism was needed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Recommended the typed graph while retaining copy/prebuilt as the beginner defaults and requiring explicit approval for execution.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Showed a real local compiler workflow, the resulting approval prompt, and the diagnostics for restricted options.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Checked unlocked fetches, unknown tools, path escapes, shell escapes, and the case where no strong sandbox exists.

decisions.title: Expose explicit environment facet selection
decisions.gist: Choose how a user selects an environment facet when more than one is declared.
decisions.lesson: An environment facet is one named view of an environment source, such as dev, ci, or release. Each facet has its own packages and settings. A plan activates one facet. Jet currently chooses dev, then default, then the first name in sorted order when no choice is given. The model also accepts an explicit name and rejects names that are not declared. This ballot chooses how ordinary users reach that control when one source serves local development and CI.
decisions.story: Mina maintains one repository for local development, CI, and a release shell. She wants CI to use the ci facet on purpose, and she wants a misspelled name to fail before any environment changes.

options.name: Explicit command flag
options.detail: Add one named facet option to environment commands. Users can request the exact facet for inspection, development, or realization, and a bad name fails before state changes. The common case keeps the current automatic default.
options.technical: Add a ratified CLI spelling for a facet name and pass it through every production environment-plan caller to evaluate_env_with_profile_and_facet. The selected facet remains part of JSON and text disclosure. No fallback occurs after an explicit name fails.
options.code:
$ jet env info --facet ci
active facet: ci
packages: core.ripgrep, core.shellcheck

$ jet env info --facet cii
Error [E1337]: environment facet cii is not declared
Why: one environment plan activates one declared env facet
Fix: choose one of the declared environment facet names

options.name: Keep selection API-only
options.detail: Keep automatic selection for ordinary commands and expose the active facet in env info. Hosts and tools may call the typed API with an explicit name, but users do not get a new command option. This keeps the command surface smaller and avoids choosing a long-term flag.
options.technical: The production CLI continues to call evaluate_env_with_profile with no facet. The typed evaluate_env_with_facet API remains available to trusted hosts. E1337 remains a host-facing diagnostic rather than a normal CLI path.
options.code:
$ jet env info
active facet: dev
packages: core.ripgrep

// A host library may select ci explicitly.
evaluate_env_with_facet(source, root, "ci")

options.name: Declare the active facet in source
options.detail: Put the chosen facet in a checked package or environment declaration. Every command then uses that source choice, while an explicit command option could still override it later. This makes the choice reproducible but adds a second source fact and a new conflict rule.
options.technical: Add a new typed field such as active_facet to the environment or Package model. The field must be validated against declared env names, carried into locks, and given an owner-ratified precedence rule against any future command flag.

comparisons.note: Nix develop selects a named flake output with an explicit attribute, while an omitted attribute follows a default convention.
Cargo keeps the ordinary command simple and uses an explicit profile flag when a named build profile is needed.

recommendation.why: A gives users direct control at the moment they need it, while preserving the simple automatic default for ordinary use. It also makes the already-implemented E1337 failure reachable through the real command path.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the CLI small, but ordinary users cannot select a declared facet and the explicit-name diagnostic remains unreachable from production commands.
It makes selection reproducible, but it adds a new source fact, lock identity, and precedence rule for a choice that belongs naturally to the command invocation.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one command option and requires every environment-plan caller to carry the same selected facet. That is acceptable because all callers already share one typed plan and one resolver.

reviewPasses.base: The model already supports deterministic automatic selection and explicit selection. The open choice is the public path to the explicit selector.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The options separate command-time choice, API-only control, and a source-declared choice. They do not propose alternate spellings for the same flag.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A source default plus an optional command flag was not made a separate option because it combines A and C and still needs a precedence ruling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Each option keeps one authority for the selected facet and shows both success and unknown-name behavior.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The ballot checks the missing production caller, the typo failure, the automatic default, and the cost of adding a new public surface.

decisions.comment: Use profile instead of facet. I dont see the overlap in this case as a negative, it keeps things clear that you're selecting a profile in an environment vs selecting a profile for jetos

decisions.title: Core source authority and intrinsic kernel boundary
decisions.gist: Choose whether normal Jet source or compiler templates define Core behavior.
decisions.lesson: Jet's Core library supplies common features such as text, files, tasks, and math. Most Core behavior now comes from snippets stored inside the compiler. The open choice is whether that behavior should stay there, move into normal Jet files, or ship as one complete bundle. Every option must keep offline builds, small output, correct caches, and the same results in every execution mode.
decisions.story: Luna updates a Core text function. She needs the compiler dossier to name the checked source, reachable packages, kernel calls, and cache identity used by every execution tier.
decisions.inWild:
use core.text
use core.compute

fn report(xs: [Int]) -> String {
    total := core.compute.sum(xs)
    core.text.format("total={total}")
}

$ jet build --offline --dossier
frontend: parser -> sema -> TIR
compile core.text: ordinary Jet package
compile core.compute: ordinary Jet package
emit Core: reachable packages only
kernel: 3 audited ABI calls
cache identity: semantic-source sha256:7f4e...a91c

$ jet run
total=6
decisions.detail:
Base — The revised first draft gives one short paragraph of neutral context, then leaves definitions and exact rules to the options. It presents three complete choices with realistic build output and a provisional recommendation.

Boil-the-ocean — The review tested direct source builds, compiler templates, eager bundles, precompiled artifacts, generated fallbacks, and dynamic runtime libraries. It kept three choices that change source authority or reachability, and folded cache tactics into those choices.

Hybrid — The review kept A as the source law, borrowed B's pinned offline delivery and strict compiler boundary, and borrowed C's reusable package artifacts without eager linking. It added the audited kernel, content identity, and differential tier checks to A.

Cooperative — The review strengthened every option on its own terms. B now gets reachable template emission and strong fingerprints, while C gets ordinary source, one bundle identity, and simple offline delivery.

Adversarial — The review attacked A for bootstrap cycles, kernel growth, stale caches, and tier drift. It added a narrow kernel rule, source-bound cache identity, reachable closure proof, and shared Prelude conformance; A still best meets UL3, R10, and I9.

options.name: Ordinary Core packages plus a minimal kernel
options.detail: Normal Jet source defines Core behavior. Jet checks that source through the normal front end, emits only reachable packages and helpers, and keeps only unexpressible operations in a small audited kernel. Users gain inspectable source, exact cache identity, and one meaning across all tiers. The pinned toolchain must carry source and verified package metadata for offline builds.
options.technical: Core source follows parser -> sema -> TIR -> Prelude. Reachable closure controls package and kernel emission. Cache identity covers semantic source, dependencies, toolchain, target, mode, and instances. AOT, dev, interpreter, and web adapters call the same Prelude functions. Differential tests compare every accelerated backend with the canonical Jet path.
options.code:
use core.text
use core.compute

fn total_text(xs: [Int]) -> String {
    n := core.compute.sum(xs)
    core.text.format("total={n}")
}

$ jet build --offline --dossier
core.text      ordinary Jet package      reachable
core.compute   ordinary Jet package      reachable
kernel         3 audited ABI calls
cache          semantic-source sha256:7f4e...a91c

$ jet run
total=6

options.name: Compiler templates with strong fingerprints
options.detail: Compiler templates remain the only broad Core authority. Jet emits only templates for reachable helpers and fingerprints every template, compiler, target, and dependency input. Users gain pinned offline delivery and one compiler-controlled source location. They lose normal Jet source checks, package inspection, and direct Core testing through the front end.
options.technical: Sema records reachable helper identities. Codegen selects matching templates and binds the complete template closure into cache identity. AOT, dev, and interpreter still call shared Prelude functions, but broad behavior remains stored inside compiler code rather than ordinary packages.
options.code:
use core.text

$ jet build --offline --dossier
core.text authority: compiler template
emit: reachable text helpers only
cache: template+compiler sha256:3b19...d044
source check: compiler build, not Core package sema

$ jet run
hello from template-backed Core

options.name: Ordinary source with an eager Core bundle
options.detail: Normal Jet source defines Core behavior, but the pinned toolchain builds and links one complete Core bundle. Users gain inspectable source, one bundle identity, and simple offline delivery. Every program pays for unused Core packages in build work, artifacts, and caches.
options.technical: The toolchain compiles the full Core source graph into one versioned bundle. Cache identity covers the complete bundle. All tiers share that bundle's Prelude meaning, but the build does not use the program's reachable package closure.
options.code:
use core.text

$ jet build --offline --dossier
source authority: ordinary Core packages
compile: core.text core.compute core.db core.net ...
emit: complete Core bundle
cache: full-bundle sha256:91ab...e602

$ jet run
hello
// compute, db, and net were unused but still linked

comparisons.note: Rust stores much of its standard library as normal source. A small set of intrinsics and language items remains compiler-owned, which keeps the special boundary narrow.
Swift uses source-backed library code with narrow compiler builtins and runtime calls. The broad library does not need to live inside compiler templates.

recommendation.why: A is the only option that combines normal source checks, R10 reachable emission, source-bound cache identity, and I9 tier parity. It also makes UL3's minimal kernel boundary visible and auditable.

whyNot.reason: B can emit reachable helpers and reject stale output, but broad Core behavior still bypasses normal Jet package checks. A fingerprint proves identity; it does not make templates inspectable Core source.
C gives Core a normal source authority, but it builds and links packages that the program cannot reach. That breaks R10 and expands artifacts and caches without changing program meaning.

recommendation.tradeoff: Offline toolchains carry reachable Core source and verified package metadata instead of one opaque compiler blob. Jet accepts that visible provenance to keep source, cache, and tier meaning aligned.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep ordinary source as the authority, then use B's pinned delivery and C's reusable package artifacts without keeping broad templates or linking unused packages.

harvest.aspect: Pinned offline delivery and strict compiler fingerprints.
harvest.use: Apply them to the minimal kernel and every semantic source input.

harvest.aspect: Reusable package artifacts from one source version.
harvest.use: Cache them separately, then link only the reachable closure.

decisions.checkInstructions: Choose A, B, or C. The full review still recommends A. A requires ordinary Core source, a minimal audited intrinsic/ABI kernel, reachable package and helper emission, complete semantic cache identity, and shared Prelude behavior across every applicable tier.

decisions.title: How is an ordinary safe compute kernel declared and proved?
decisions.gist: Choose the public representation for compiler-proved ordinary kernels before execution, while keeping raw device code behind #Unsafe.
decisions.lesson: D-COMPUTE-KERNEL1=D says an ordinary Jet kernel is safe only when sema proves bounds, alias and race freedom, captures, barrier uniformity, and control flow. Raw device code remains an audited #Unsafe escape with a typed boundary contract. The current raw contract descriptor records requirements but is not a proof of an ordinary kernel; the public surface must not imply otherwise.
decisions.story: Eli writes a tiled matrix kernel. He wants the compiler to reject an out-of-bounds index, a shared write race, or a divergent barrier before any backend runs. An expert later needs a vendor-specific raw kernel, but that path must carry an audit reason and explicit boundary proof.
decisions.detail: The decision must define kernel declaration spelling, index and shape proof inputs, alias and capture rules, barrier uniformity, effect and placement facts, rejection diagnostics, backend lowering, and the exact boundary between compiler-proved ordinary code and raw #Unsafe code. It must preserve one Prelude semantic law and differential CPU evidence.

options.name: Existing safe functions with compiler kernel lowering
options.detail: Keep ordinary Jet function syntax. A function becomes a kernel only through a checked compute call or compiler-known context; sema emits a typed proof record and codegen lowers the same body.
options.technical: No new user keyword is added. The owning sema pass proves shape/index bounds, non-aliasing, captures, race freedom, barrier uniformity, and control flow before TIR. The proof record is attached to the typed kernel call and every backend consumes it; raw vendor code still requires #Unsafe and a boundary contract.
options.code:
compute.launch(add, grid: shape, args: [a, b])?
// ordinary `add` is accepted only when sema can produce the kernel proof

options.name: Explicit kernel declaration
options.detail: Add a dedicated kernel declaration or marker so authors and tools can see the parallel boundary directly in source.
options.technical: The marker is a new owner-controlled syntax surface. Sema checks the same proof obligations as A, records a stable proof identity, and rejects ordinary function calls that bypass the declaration's effects or placement contract.

options.name: Raw kernels only
options.detail: Do not expose a new safe ordinary-kernel surface in this epoch. All device kernels use #Unsafe with a typed contract and explicit differential tests.
options.technical: This keeps the public language small but leaves safe accelerator work unavailable. The raw contract cannot claim compiler proof; each invocation must surface the audit reason, target, bounds, alias, race, barrier, and CPU-oracle evidence.

comparisons.note: Safe parallel APIs derive freedom from ownership and structured iteration instead of exposing a raw thread contract.
Vendor kernels expose thread indices and barriers directly; safety depends on external review and runtime discipline.

recommendation.why: A preserves the existing beginner surface and makes the compiler own the complete safety proof at the call site. It avoids a second kernel syntax while still allowing explicit expert raw code under #Unsafe.

whyNot.reason: A visible marker improves discoverability, but it adds a new user-typeable syntax choice and another declaration surface before the existing proof seam is exhausted.
Raw-only kernels keep implementation narrow but make safe ordinary kernels impossible and weaken the beginner promise for compute.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires sema to recognize a checked launch context and persist proof facts through TIR, but it adds no syntax and keeps one safe mechanism for ordinary code.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A, B, or C. After ratification, implement only the selected public surface and its sema proof record. Keep raw device code #Unsafe-gated, reject unproved safe kernels, and prove AOT/default jet run parity plus CPU differential behavior.
decisions.comment: You can incorporate parts of a that improve robustness and feature richness, but I think for now having the marker is a good idea

decisions.title: General automatic differentiation in core.compute
decisions.gist: How Jet computes derivatives of a calculation.
decisions.lesson: A derivative tells you how much a result moves when an input moves. Machine learning fits models by following derivatives. Today core.compute can only differentiate three fixed operations: add, multiply and matmul. Anything you build from them cannot be differentiated. This choice picks the shape of the general answer, which decides what users type and how the compiler tracks the work.
decisions.story: Priya trains a small model to rank support tickets. She writes a loss from a matmul, a subtraction, a square and a sum. She asks Jet for the gradient. Today there is no call that answers, because her loss is not one of the three fixed shapes.

options.name: Function transform
options.detail: You pass a function to `grad`, `vjp` or `jvp` and get a new function back. Nothing is stored between calls, so the same code works inside tasks and runs twice with the same answer. You can take a gradient of a gradient by applying the transform again. The cost is that the value you differentiate must live in a function.
options.technical:
`grad(f)` returns a callable with the parameter contract of `f` and a Tensor result. `vjp(f)` returns value and a cotangent-consuming closure; `jvp(f)` returns value and tangent. Reverse mode records a per-call tape owned by the returned closure, so no global or thread-local state exists. The transform is a Prelude function over Jet callable values; it adds no syntax. Higher-order use nests transforms. Effect rows carry through unchanged; a differentiated function must be pure over its Tensor arguments and is rejected otherwise.

Invoking a returned function uses the `.call(…)` spelling from D-CALLVALUE1.

options.name: Explicit tape scope
options.detail: You open a tape, tell it which tensors to watch, run ordinary code, then ask the tape for a gradient. The recording is a value you can see and pass around, so there is no hidden state. The cost is three extra lines around the calculation and a tape you must not reuse after it is consumed.
options.technical: `GradTape.new()` returns an owned recorder. `tape.watch(t)` marks a leaf. Recording happens because watched tensors carry the tape identity, so unrelated tensors cost nothing. `tape.gradient(loss, [w])` walks the recorded graph in reverse and returns one Tensor per requested leaf. The tape is second-class and cannot escape its scope, which keeps recording bounded. Reuse after `gradient` is an E-coded error unless the tape was opened as persistent.
options.code:
tape :: compute.GradTape.new()
tape.watch(w)

pred :: compute.matmul(x, w)
loss :: compute.sum_axis(compute.mul(pred, pred), 0)

gw :: tape.gradient(loss, w)

// reuse without persistent is rejected
// Error [E0xxx]: this tape was already consumed

options.name: Tracked tensors
options.detail: You mark a tensor as tracked once. Every later operation on it records itself. You call `backward` on the result and read `.grad` from the tracked tensor. This is the shortest code to type and the most familiar to people coming from PyTorch. The cost is that recording is implicit and gradients pile up on the tensor until you clear them.
options.technical: `tracked(t)` returns a Tensor carrying a recorder handle. Operations propagate the handle. `backward(loss)` accumulates into each tracked leaf; `grad_of(t)` reads the accumulation. Accumulation is additive, so a training loop must call `zero_grad` between steps. The recorder lives in the tensor rather than in a scope, so lifetime follows ordinary ownership. Concurrent use across tasks requires the tensor to be exclusively owned, which sema enforces.
options.code:
w :: compute.tracked(compute.zeros([4, 1]))

pred :: compute.matmul(x, w)
loss :: compute.sum_axis(compute.mul(pred, pred), 0)

compute.backward(loss)
gw :: compute.grad_of(w)

compute.zero_grad(w)   // forgetting this silently adds to the last step

options.name: Keep one call per operation
options.detail: Nothing changes in shape. Every differentiable operation gains its own `vjp_` and `jvp_` call as it is needed. Users chain those calls by hand to differentiate anything larger. This adds no new mechanism, but a user must write the chain rule themselves for every model they build.
options.technical: The current `vjp_add`, `vjp_mul`, `vjp_matmul`, `jvp_*` and `value_and_grad_mul` set grows one entry per operation. No tape, transform or recorder exists. Composition is the caller's responsibility and is not checked. The public surface grows with the operation table and never closes, because each new operation needs two more names.
options.code:
// Priya differentiates her loss by hand
p :: compute.matmul(x, w)
d :: compute.sub(p, y)
sq :: compute.vjp_mul(d, d, compute.ones(compute.shape(d)))
back :: compute.vjp_matmul(x, w, compute.grad_a(sq))
gw :: compute.grad_b(back)
// one mistake in this chain is silent and wrong

comparisons.note: JAX transforms a function into its gradient function. The transform is pure and composes, so a second derivative is the same call applied twice.
comparisons.code:
gw = jax.grad(loss)(w, x)
hess = jax.grad(jax.grad(loss))(w, x)

comparisons.note: PyTorch marks a tensor as requiring a gradient. Operations record automatically and gradients accumulate on the tensor.
TensorFlow opens a tape scope, watches tensors, then asks the tape for the gradient.
comparisons.code:
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    tape.watch(w)
    loss = f(w)
gw = tape.gradient(loss, w)

comparisons.note: Swift used a function transform with a compiler-checked differentiable attribute, close to option A.
comparisons.code: let gw = gradient(at: w) { w in loss(w, x) }

recommendation.why: A keeps derivative work inside ordinary values with no hidden state, which matches how Jet already treats effects, ownership and tasks. The same code gives a second derivative by nesting, so the surface stays two names wide instead of growing with the operation table. Because each call owns its own recording, two tasks can differentiate at the same time without sharing anything.

whyNot.reason: B is honest about state but makes the user manage a tape that must not outlive its scope or be consumed twice. That is a new lifetime rule to teach, and it gives no benefit A does not already have.

C is the shortest to type but hides recording inside tensors and makes gradients accumulate silently. A forgotten clear step produces a wrong answer with no error, which is the failure mode Jet exists to prevent.
D never closes. The public surface grows by two names per operation and still leaves the user to apply the chain rule by hand, where one mistake is silent and wrong.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires the thing you differentiate to be a function, so a user cannot ask for the gradient of a value they already computed. They must wrap that calculation in a function first.

reviewPasses.base: Wrote the four credible shapes for a general derivative surface. Each carries a worked example over Priya's loss, including the hand-chained version option D forces.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Searched wider designs: compile-time source transforms, a dual-number type, and an overloading graph builder. Compile-time transforms hit ratified metaprogram limits, so they folded into A as an implementation choice.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested combining A with C so a user could differentiate a bare value. That reintroduced hidden accumulation and gave two ways to do one thing, so the options stayed separate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B by making the tape second-class, and C by naming the sema rule that keeps a tracked tensor exclusively owned. Gave D its fairest form: no new mechanism.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on the point that reverse mode still needs a tape. The tape can be owned by the returned closure for one call, so no global state is needed.

decisions.title: How grad is spelled and which inputs it differentiates
decisions.gist: Pick the gradient call shape and the way experts select target inputs.
decisions.lesson: Autodiff APIs settled into three shapes. Julia's Zygote uses one direct call, gradient(f, x, y), one gradient per input, widely praised as the cleanest read. JAX uses a transform, grad(f), which composes but yields the double call grad(f)(x, y) that reads like multiplication with a tuple. Swift spells named arguments, gradient(at: x, of: f). PyTorch hides a tape behind loss.backward(): beginner magic, expert-criticized hidden state. Jet wants one readable call for beginners and explicit targets for experts, with the double-parenthesis shape banned.
decisions.story: Priya trains a support-ticket ranker. Her loss takes weights, a batch, and labels. She wants gradients for weights only, and her teammate Sam just wants a one-line gradient of a toy function without learning any transform vocabulary.
decisions.detail: All options ban the inline double call grad(f)(x, y): a derivative function, where one exists, must be bound to a name before it is called. One mechanism underneath (I8): every spelling lowers to the same jvp/vjp core. Option E exists because the owner asked whether A and B combine; they do, on arity.

options.name: Direct call, Julia shape
options.detail: Beginners write one call that looks like every other Jet call and get every gradient back. Experts add wrt: with parameter names to select targets, and value_and_gradient to keep the loss value. No transform object exists on the surface, so the multiplication-lookalike shape cannot appear.
options.technical: compute.gradient(f, args..., wrt: [names]) evaluates f at args and returns a named tuple of gradients for the selected differentiable Tensor parameters, all of them when wrt is absent. compute.value_and_gradient returns (value, gradients). wrt names are compile-time checked against f's signature; a wrong name is a diagnostic naming the real parameters.

options.name: Bound transform, JAX shape
options.detail: grad(f, wrt: ...) returns a derivative function that must be bound to a name first; calling it inline is a style diagnostic. Composes naturally for higher-order derivatives, but beginners must learn that grad returns a function, and the binding step is ceremony for one-shot use.
options.technical: compute.grad(f, wrt: [names]) => fn with f's input contract returning the selected gradients. The formatter and L-lint flag an immediate call on the result, so grad(f)(x, y) never appears in idiomatic code. Higher-order: gg :: compute.grad(compute.grad(f)).
options.code:
d_loss :: compute.grad(loss, wrt: [w])
weight_grad :: d_loss(w, b, l)
options.tradeoff: Best composition story; worst beginner story.

options.name: Named arguments, Swift shape
options.detail: gradient(of: f, at: x, y) reads like a sentence and can never be mistaken for multiplication. Verbose for the common case, and Jet call sites do not otherwise lead with prepositional labels, so it imports a foreign idiom.
options.technical: compute.gradient(of: f, at: args..., wrt: [names]) with the same semantics as option A. Purely a spelling variant; the labels of/at are fixed words in the signature.
options.code: g :: compute.gradient(of: loss, at: w, b, l, wrt: [w])

options.name: Method on the function value
options.detail: Every differentiable function value carries .gradient and .value_and_gradient methods, so autodiff reads like any other Jet method chain. Most native to Jet's uniform method surface; risks surprising members appearing on every fn value, and needs a rule for which fns are differentiable.
options.technical: loss.gradient(w, b, l, wrt: [w]) with option A semantics. The member exists only on fns whose signature is differentiable (all-Tensor path); elsewhere the member is absent and gets the standard no-such-method teaching diagnostic.
options.code: grads :: loss.gradient(w, b, l, wrt: [w])

options.name: One name, two arities: direct call plus bound transform (recommended)
options.detail: One spelling, compute.gradient, does both jobs. Given the function and its inputs it evaluates immediately, exactly like option A: pure beginner magic. Given only the function (and optional wrt:) it returns the derivative function for binding, exactly like option B: full transform power for composition and reuse. No double-parenthesis shape can appear because the transform result must be bound before call, and the direct form never returns a function. This beats Julia, which lacks the first-class transform, and JAX, which lacks the direct call.
options.technical: compute.gradient(f, args..., wrt: [names]) evaluates and returns the named gradient tuple. compute.gradient(f, wrt: [names]) with zero value arguments returns a derivative fn with f's input contract; the formatter and lint reject calling that result inline. value_and_gradient carries the same dual arity. Both forms lower to the one vjp core (I8). Higher-order derivatives compose through the transform arity: g2 :: compute.gradient(compute.gradient(f)).

comparisons.note: JAX selects function arguments by index and can request one or several gradients.
comparisons.code:
jax.grad(f, argnums=0)(x, y)
jax.grad(f, argnums=(0, 1))(x, y)

comparisons.note: Swift makes the differentiated arguments visible at the call site.
comparisons.code: valueWithPullback(at: x, y) { x, y in f(x, y) }

comparisons.note: PyTorch asks for the input tensors whose gradients the caller needs.

recommendation.why: One name serves the whole ladder: beginners get a direct call that reads like any Jet call, experts get a first-class derivative function for reuse and higher-order composition. Both arities lower to the one vjp core, so no second mechanism exists. The banned inline double call keeps every call site unambiguous.

whyNot.reason: Pure direct call has no reusable derivative function, so training loops re-derive per step and higher-order composition needs new vocabulary later.
Transform-only forces every beginner through bind-then-call ceremony for one-shot gradients.
Prepositional labels import a foreign idiom Jet uses nowhere else, and still lack the transform form.
Members appearing on function values by differentiability is surprising, and the rule for which fns qualify leaks type-system detail into completion.
Accepting E means accepting arity overloading on one core name; if that ever reads as too clever, option A remains the safe subset.

recommendation.tradeoff: One name returning two kinds by arity is a real cost: a reader must see the argument list to know whether a value or a function came back. The bind-before-call rule and the zero-value-argument rule keep the two shapes visually distinct at every site.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compares all-input, named, indexed, and closure-selected targets. Each option uses the same two-argument function and shows the returned gradient shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested target values, closure wrappers, all inputs, named inputs, and indexes. Target values folded into closure selection because a value cannot name a stable function parameter.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested all-input mode with named narrowing. It kept named selection as one contract and treated closure wrapping as an existing composition pattern.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened every option. All-input mode favors short model code, named mode favors intent, index mode favors generated code, and closure mode favors existing language rules.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested parameter renames, reordered parameters, unused inputs, and captured data. It made selector failures compile-time errors and kept named selection as the recommendation.

decisions.title: The vjp carrier: how value and pullback travel together
decisions.gist: Pick what compute.vjp returns and how the pullback is applied.
decisions.lesson: Julia's pullback returns a pair, value and a pullback function, bound to two names and applied later: praised because both halves are named and no call ever touches another call's parenthesis. JAX's vjp returns the same pair; users who inline it get vjp(f, x)[1](seed), a shape nobody defends. Enzyme and Futhark treat vjp as an explicit seeded primitive for experts only. Jet wants named, discoverable halves for beginners and explicit seeds for experts, never an adjacent-parenthesis chain.
decisions.story: Sam has a loss value and wants the gradient too, cheaply. Dana writes a custom training loop and needs to push three different seed vectors through one recorded pass without recomputing the forward run.
decisions.inWild:
// one forward pass, three seeds, no recompute
rec :: compute.vjp(loss, w, b, l)
print(rec.value)
g1 :: rec.pull(seed_a)
g2 :: rec.pull(seed_b)
g3 :: rec.pull(seed_c)
decisions.detail: All options ban inline double calls; a pullback is always a named thing before it runs. One mechanism underneath (I8): grad in D-COMPUTE-GRAD1 is defined as vjp with a scalar unit seed, whichever spelling wins.

options.name: Typed record with pull method (recommended)
options.detail: vjp returns one typed value with named members: .value for the forward result, .pull(seed) to run the recorded pass, and .grads as the beginner shortcut for the unit seed. Discoverable through completion, impossible to mis-order, and the record type gives experts a place for future cost and memory controls. Combines with a two-name destructure: (val, pull) :: compute.vjp(f, x, y) works because the record destructures positionally, so option B is a free subset, mirroring the unified shape recommended in D-COMPUTE-GRAD1 option E.
options.technical: compute.vjp(f, args...) => VjpRun. Members: value: Tensor; pull(seed: Tensor) => named gradient tuple; grads => pull(unit seed) for scalar outputs, diagnostic otherwise. VjpRun holds the tape; dropping it frees the recording under normal ownership rules. VjpRun destructures as (value, pull) for Zygote-style call sites.
options.code:
rec :: compute.vjp(loss, w, b, l)
step :: compute.sgd_step(w, rec.grads.w, 0.01)

// expert seeds
jtj_row :: rec.pull(basis_row)

options.name: Two-name destructure, Julia shape
options.detail: One call returns (value, pull) and the destructure names both halves at the call site. Familiar to every Zygote user and needs no new type; the pullback is a plain function value, so future expert controls have no natural home.
options.technical: compute.vjp(f, args...) => (Tensor, fn(Tensor) => gradient tuple). The formatter flags any expression that calls the second tuple slot without binding it first.
options.code:
(val, pull) :: compute.vjp(loss, w, b, l)
grads :: pull(seed)

options.name: Expert-only seeded primitive, Enzyme shape
options.detail: vjp takes the seed up front and returns gradients directly; no pullback value exists. Simplest surface and one call per seed, but every extra seed pays a full forward pass again, which is exactly the cost the recorded pullback exists to avoid.
options.technical: compute.vjp(f, args..., seed: Tensor) => named gradient tuple. Multiple seeds mean multiple forward passes; a note in docs points batch-seed users at grad or a future batched API.
options.code: grads :: compute.vjp(loss, w, b, l, seed: s)

comparisons.note: JAX returns the primal value and a pullback function as a pair.
comparisons.code:
value, pullback = jax.vjp(f, x, y)
grads = pullback(cotangent)

comparisons.note: Swift exposes a value and a pullback from one differentiation call.
Zygote returns the primal result and a function that applies the reverse step.
comparisons.code:
value, back = Zygote.pullback(f, x)
grads = back(cotangent)

recommendation.why: The typed record is discoverable, safe for beginners through .grads, explicit for experts through .pull(seed), and subsumes the Julia destructure as sugar. It gives future cost and memory controls a typed home.
recommendation.tradeoff: A new public type enters the compute surface; its member set becomes API the freeze must track.

whyNot.reason: Accepting A accepts one more named type in core.compute; if the surface must stay type-minimal, B is the closest subset.
A bare tuple gives the pullback no home for future controls and no discoverable members.
Seed-up-front repays a full forward pass per seed, the exact cost a recorded pullback exists to avoid.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compares a named tuple, a dedicated handle, and a callable closure. Each option shows one score evaluation followed by a value read and a pullback call.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested an unnamed tuple, a named record, a handle, and two closures. The unnamed tuple folded into the named tuple because field names help readers without adding a mechanism.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested a tuple whose pullback also had handle methods. It created two access paths for one value, so the draft kept the tuple and ordinary closure separate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each option. The tuple favors composition, the handle favors lifecycle control, and the closure favors one compact call surface.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested repeated pullback use, saved results, and missing value access. The tuple keeps both outputs explicit without inventing callable-object behavior.

decisions.title: How does durable service authority carry receipts and retention?
decisions.gist: Choose the public authority that carries delivery receipts, retention, and transaction truth through durable service paths.
decisions.lesson: D-SERVICE-DELIVERY1=D gives Jet bounded mailboxes and at-least-once retry with idempotency, but a boolean success result is not a durable receipt. A production caller must know whether a message was accepted, retained, dead-lettered, or rejected. Retention and transaction boundaries must be explicit; hidden global state cannot safely cross restarts or requests.
decisions.story: Nora submits an order while the worker is restarting. She needs a typed answer that distinguishes accepted-and-retained from mailbox-full, duplicate, dead-lettered, and unavailable. A retry must reuse the same authority without creating a second delivery.
decisions.inWild:
runtime := services.runtime(store, retention: time.hours(24))
receipt := runtime.send(order_endpoint, order, key: order.id)?
match receipt {
    .Accepted(id) -> audit(id)
    .Duplicate(id) -> continue
    .Retained(id, until) -> schedule_retry(id, until)
    .Rejected(reason) -> report(reason)
}
decisions.detail: The chosen model must define receipt identity, accepted versus retained state, duplicate replay, dead-letter ownership, retention expiry, durable commit ordering, transaction grouping, crash recovery, and the behavior of a retry after a generation handoff. It must use the existing service runtime and Prelude seam; it must not add actor syntax or a second scheduler.

options.name: Explicit durable authority scope
options.detail: Create one owned service authority scope carrying the durable store, retention policy, and transaction boundary. Send and retry return a typed receipt from that scope; the ordinary in-memory tree remains the bounded local path.
options.technical: The scope contains the service tree, durable store capability, retention facts, and generation authority. Commit order is store record then receipt; a crash before the receipt leaves a retryable idempotency record. Receipts are stable by idempotency key and report Accepted, Duplicate, Retained, DeadLettered, Rejected, or Unavailable. AOT, JIT, interpreter, and live adapters call the same Prelude functions.
options.code:
authority := services.authority(tree, durable_store, retention: .Hours(24))
receipt := authority.send(endpoint, message, key)?
retry := authority.retry(receipt.id)?

options.name: Hidden request delivery context
options.detail: Put the durable store and retention policy in the current task or request context. Existing send calls infer the authority and return a compact status.
options.technical: Every task boundary must install and restore the context. Missing context fails closed. Nested calls, pooled workers, and live subscriptions must preserve the correct authority without ambient leakage.

options.name: External queue adapter
options.detail: Keep the core service tree in-memory and require each application to integrate its own queue or database for durable receipts.
options.technical: The adapter owns commit order, retry, retention, and receipt schema outside the one service Prelude. Jet can type the adapter boundary but cannot prove one delivery law across providers.
options.code:
queue := app_queue.connect(config)?
queue.publish(order, key: order.id)?

comparisons.note: A producer acknowledgment identifies durable broker acceptance, but retention and transaction scope remain explicit broker facts.
An owned capability carries authority without process-global state and makes the commit boundary visible at the call site.

recommendation.why: A makes the durability authority explicit and gives every retry one stable receipt and idempotency seam. It preserves the current simple tree for beginner in-memory services while making durable behavior auditable and tier-parity-safe.

whyNot.reason: Hidden context reduces call-site noise, but pooled tasks, nested requests, and live subscriptions create cross-request leakage risks and make authority hard to audit.
An external adapter can ship sooner, but it fragments receipt, retention, and transaction semantics and leaves the first-party service card without one production law.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one explicit authority value and a durable store capability. That ceremony buys stable receipts, fail-closed missing authority, and one shared implementation across all execution tiers.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A, B, or C. After ratification, implement the selected authority through durable send, retry, dead-letter, retention, generation handoff, and transaction paths. Do not close #1148 or #444 until duplicate, crash, retention, and cross-tier receipt tests pass on AOT and default jet run.

decisions.title: How should service state receive its storage authority?
decisions.gist: Choose the explicit typed handle that gives a service its durable state store.
decisions.lesson:
A service can keep state in memory, but that state disappears when the process stops. A snapshot saves one complete state image. An event log saves changes and rebuilds state by replaying them.

Both choices need a named place for bytes and a rule for interpreting them. That named capability is the storage authority. Injection means the service receives it as an input instead of finding a process-global file or database.

A schema identifies the format. A version or migration rule explains how older data becomes current. The commit point is when a change becomes durable. Corrupt or newer data must refuse startup with recovery guidance. This ballot chooses the public shape for those facts.
decisions.story: Maya runs two copies of an order service during a deploy. She needs each copy to open the same approved store, reject corrupt or newer state before serving requests, and commit one snapshot or event atomically. A hidden file lookup would make the result depend on the process that happens to run it.
decisions.inWild:
store := state.store("orders", root: data_dir)?
tree := services.tree("orders")
services.snapshot(tree, store, schema: "orders.v1")?
services.start(tree)?
services.commit_snapshot(tree, order_state)?

options.name: Explicit state authority on the adapter
options.detail: Pass one typed store handle and schema to the Snapshot or EventLog adapter. The tree keeps the authority, validates it before start, and uses it for every commit and recovery read. Beginners see one explicit setup value; experts can inspect the store, schema, and migration facts.
options.technical: The adapter owns a StateAuthority containing the injected store capability, adapter kind, schema id, schema version, and migration/recovery policy. Empty has no authority. Snapshot commits one complete record. EventLog appends one event record. Reads and writes use one Prelude authority across AOT, default dev, interpreter, and applicable web targets. No ambient path or process-global state is permitted.
options.code:
store := state.store("orders", root: data_dir)?
tree := services.tree("orders")
services.snapshot(tree, store, schema: "orders.v1")?
services.start(tree)?
services.commit_snapshot(tree, order_state)?

options.name: Create a state handle, then attach it
options.detail: Build a typed Snapshot or EventLog handle first, then attach that handle to the service tree. This makes state reusable across trees, but it creates a second setup object and makes ownership and lifecycle less obvious at the beginner call site.
options.technical: The handle carries store, adapter kind, schema, and migration facts. The attach operation consumes or shares the handle under an explicit ownership rule. Every tree operation validates that the handle belongs to the tree authority and has not been attached twice.
options.code:
state := state.snapshot(store, schema: "orders.v1")?
tree := services.tree("orders")
services.use_state(tree, state)?
services.start(tree)?

options.name: Keep adapter markers and inject storage at start
