Undercuts the lint as a teaching tool.

recommendation.tradeoff: One-time example pass across touched features.

decisions.title: One semantic IR for branches
decisions.gist: Choose whether classic if stays a separate AST node or desugars into arm-table IR.
decisions.lesson:
Users type if. Inside the compiler, Jet today has two shapes. Stmt::If is a nested then and else tree. Stmt::Switch is a flat arm list used for tables.

Both mean ordered choice. Dual nodes force duplicate walks in sema, ownership, and codegen helpers.

This decision picks the internal law. User spelling can still include short if forms.
decisions.story: A codegen engineer adds a new branch optimization. They must special-case If and Switch or forget one path.

options.name: Keep dual AST; share helpers
options.detail: Least churn. Document that both mean one mechanism.
options.technical: Stmt::If and Stmt::Switch remain. Shared lower/check helpers.
options.code:
check_if(…)
check_switch(…)

options.name: Early-desugar classic if into arm-table IR
options.detail: Parser may build If. A desugar pass makes one arm-table IR for sema and codegen.
options.technical: Classic two-arm becomes arms + optional else. Spans preserved for diagnostics.
options.code:
if ready start() else wait()
# IR: arms [ready->start, else->wait]

options.name: Single AST node from the parser
options.detail: Parser always builds the arm-table node. One IR from parse through sema and codegen. No desugar pass to maintain. Same runtime forms as B once lowering runs. Up-front cost is parser, formatter, and IDE churn.
options.technical: Stmt::If goes away or becomes sugar only at parse. Spans attach to arms directly. Classic one-line if still parses; it builds the same arm list.

recommendation.why: You asked to spend more up front for a better long-term path. Option C removes a permanent dual-shape seam. Runtime speed still comes from the ratified classifier on D-BRANCH-CODEGEN1, not from parse shape.

whyNot.reason: Keeps two IR shapes forever. Every new branch opt can miss one path.
Reaches the same middle-end IR, but leaves a desugar layer that can drift from the parser over time.

recommendation.tradeoff: Larger first parser and formatter pass. No extra runtime win versus a correct B desugar.

decisions.title: Branch lowering classifier and machine forms
decisions.gist: Lock how Jet picks select, match, tables, or compare chains for each arm table.
decisions.lesson:
On modern optimizers, source if and match often become the same machine code for equality cases. Timing wins come from the right shape: branchless select, data table, jump table, or ordered compares.

A classifier labels each arm table. Then codegen emits the best safe form.

Classes include two-way bool, enum patterns, dense ints, sparse ints, ordered predicates, and mixed heads.
decisions.story: Remy ships a hot protocol demux. Random dense codes want a table. A biased Ok path wants a predicted compare. One blunt always-match rule loses on the biased path.

options.name: Codify today only
options.detail: Enum and Result or Option pattern tables become match. Everything else stays an if-chain.
options.technical: Matches current lower_enum_match / fallible / guard_switch paths.
options.code:
enum table -> Rust match
bool table -> if/else chain

options.name: Full classifier; best form per class
options.detail: Bool2 may select. Enum uses match. Dense ints use data or jump tables. Sparse uses search or hash. Ordered stays compares. Mixed falls back safely. Bind subject once. Avoid needless clone.
options.technical: Classes: C-BOOL2, C-ENUM, C-DENSE-INT, C-SPARSE-INT, C-ORDERED, C-MIXED. PGO weights later.
options.code:
dense value arms -> static table load
ordered guards -> compare chain
enum payloads -> match

options.name: Always if-chain
options.detail: Simplest codegen. Never rely on match or tables.
options.code: all branches -> if/else if

comparisons.note: Dense equality often becomes a table load; jump tables can lose when one arm dominates.
match helps the backend see a switch; if chains often optimize to the same code.

recommendation.why: This is the path to beat careful C and Rust on dispatch: classify, then emit the winning machine form.

whyNot.reason: Leaves dense int and select wins on the table.
Gives up match and table shapes on purpose.

recommendation.tradeoff: More lowering cases to test and bench. Syntax stays one if.

decisions.title: One spelling for domain text and byte patterns
decisions.gist: How writers mark SQL, HTML, shell commands, and byte patterns so each recipe stays explicit.
decisions.lesson:
Some quoted text is not a normal string. It is a recipe in another language.

SQL recipes become checked queries. HTML recipes escape inserts. Shell recipes become argv lists. Byte recipes match bit fields in a buffer.

A typed head names the language. The body is the recipe. Example: SQL.{"select id={id}"} builds a query. [U8].{"{len:U16be}{rest:...}"} matches bytes.

Plain quotes alone stay for ordinary String values and for text-match convenience. Runtime String values still cannot fill a SQL, HTML, or Sh slot.

The choice is whether Jet also keeps short prefixes and silent rewrites, or whether the typed head is the only spelling.
decisions.story: User reviews safety examples and sees sql"…", html"…", Sh.{"…"}, and b"…" side by side. He wants one intentional shape so a typo cannot pick the wrong language.

options.name: Typed head only
options.detail: Domain text uses only Type.{"…"} plus Type.raw. Byte patterns use only [U8].{"…"}. Kill sql"/html"/sh" and silent rewrite of bare quotes into those types. Keep plain quotes for String and for text-pattern convenience. Optional String.{"…"} matches the same text pattern.
options.technical: Amends D-TYPEDTEXT1/2 and D-BINPAT1. Supersedes D-LITERAL-PREFIX1 prefix surface. Sema elaborates typed-text only from typed-literal heads. Bare String into SQL/HTML/Sh remains E0149. Lexer BinStr and hardcoded typed-text prefixes retire.

options.name: Typed head plus silent expected-type rewrite
options.detail: Keep Type.{"…"} as the clear form. Also let a bare quote elaborate when the slot already expects SQL, HTML, or Sh. Kill only the lowercase prefixes. Call sites stay shorter when a parameter is already typed.
options.technical: Keeps D-TYPEDTEXT1 expected-type path. Removes D-TYPEDTEXT2 prefixes. Byte patterns still move to [U8].{"…"}.

options.name: Keep prefixes as sugar
options.detail: Document Type.{"…"} as preferred, but keep sql"/html"/sh" and silent rewrite. Clean example drift only. Byte patterns stay b"…" or switch alone.
options.technical: Status quo for typed text. Optional D-BINPAT1 spelling change only.
options.code:
q :: sql"select * from t where id = {id}" page :: html"

{name}

" cmd :: sh"echo {name}"

options.name: Type-owned prefixes via derive
options.detail: Honor D-LITERAL-PREFIX1. Libraries own prefixes like sql" through a derive contract. Typed heads remain available. Hardcoded parser list goes away by becoming type-owned.
options.technical: Implements ratified D-LITERAL-PREFIX1=A. Opposite of removing prefixes.

comparisons.note: b"…" builds a byte string value. Jet's old b"…" was a pattern mode, not a value.
s"…", f"…", and raw"…" are prefix languages. Jet is choosing typed heads instead of growing that prefix set.
comparisons.code: val q = sql"select * from t where id = $id"

comparisons.note: Sh examples already prefer Sh.{"…"}. SQL/HTML examples still show prefixes. That split is the inconsistency this ballot closes.

recommendation.why: One head names one language. Writers see the type at the recipe. Typos and silent quote rewrites cannot pick SQL, HTML, Sh, or byte-match by accident.

whyNot.reason: Bare quotes at typed call sites still look like String while meaning another language.
Leaves the three spellings and the sql"/b" visual family that caused the review.
Expands prefixes after the owner asked for fewer hidden spellings and more Type.{"…"}.

recommendation.tradeoff: Bindings and untyped slots must write the typed head. Call sites lose bare-quote sugar into SQL, HTML, and Sh.

decisions.title: Code-as-argument spelling: explicit () => blocks
decisions.gist: How a caller passes a multiline code block into a function argument.
decisions.lesson:
A function can take another function as an input. The caller often writes that input at the call site as a short block of code.

The clear spelling is an explicit lambda inside the call's parentheses: `twice(() => { … })`. The block may hold many statements. You can pass several such lambdas in one call, mixed with ordinary values.

An older sugar (D-TRAILBLOCK1) let a bare `{ … }` trail after the call, or even after a bare name with no parentheses. That form only covers one final zero-arg slot, and `twice { … }` can look like a keyword instead of a call.

This decision picks the spelling Jet keeps.
decisions.story: User wants helpers like `twice` to take a multiline body as a normal argument. The call must read as a function call. He wrote the shape he wants: `twice(() => { print("HI"); print("Hello") })` with each statement on its own line.

options.name: Require () => inside the call; drop trailing { } sugar
options.detail: Code arguments use `() => { … }` inside the parentheses. Multiline bodies are normal. Multiple code arguments are ordinary comma-separated args. Trailing bare `{ }` after a call is rejected with a teaching fix that shows the `() =>` form.
options.technical: Amend D-TRAILBLOCK1: remove trailing-block attach in postfix parse/format. Keep zero-param `() =>` lambdas as CallArg values. Retarget E0334/E0335 to teach `callee(() => { … })`. Migrate examples and UI goldens.

options.name: Keep trailing sugar only after visible ()
options.detail: Still allow `name() { … }` and `name(args) { … }` for one final block. Reject bare `name { … }`. Teach `() =>` for multi-block and non-final callbacks.
options.technical: Narrow D-TRAILBLOCK1: trailing block requires a prior `()` argument list. Formatter never emits bare `name { … }`.

options.name: Keep D-TRAILBLOCK1 unchanged
options.detail: Bare `twice { … }` stays legal. Multi-block APIs already use `() =>` inside parentheses. Docs change only.
options.technical: No parser change.

options.name: Allow bare { } inside parentheses as a lambda
options.detail: Treat `{ … }` in value position as a zero-arg lambda so `f({ … }, { … })` works without `() =>`. Quieter, more ambiguous.
options.technical: New primary/block-literal form; resolve vs statement blocks and struct literals.

comparisons.note: Arrow functions are ordinary values inside call parentheses, including multiline bodies.
Trailing closure exists for one final block; multiple closures use the parenthesized form.

recommendation.why: A matches the owner's stated shape: a normal call with an explicit `() =>` multiline body. It stays honest when more than one code argument is needed, and it stops helpers from reading like keywords.

whyNot.reason: Keeping trailing sugar still special-cases one final block and splits the teaching story from the owner's required `() =>` form.
Bare `twice { … }` is the keyword look the owner rejected.
Bare `{ }` as a value hides that the argument is a function, and `() =>` already gives the clear multiline form.

recommendation.tradeoff: One-block UI calls get a little longer (`button("Save", () => { … })` instead of `button("Save") { … }`). That cost buys one spelling for every code argument.

decisions.title: Default auto-derive with reject and override?
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet turns useful built-in traits on by default, and how experts turn them off or replace them.
decisions.lesson:
A derive is a compiler-written implementation of a common trait for a type.

Traits like Printable, Equatable, and Debug describe everyday behavior: show a value, compare two values, or dump a value for debugging. For many structs and enums, the safe default is obvious: walk the fields and do the field-wise thing.

Jet already auto-derives some of these when every field qualifies, and a hand-written impl can replace that default. Less clear: can users reject automatic behavior for a type or package? Should auto-derive be the normal beginner path for every useful built-in trait that qualifies?

This decision picks the default policy and the expert escape hatches. One mechanism should cover magic for beginners, reject for control, and override for custom behavior.
decisions.story: Sam ships a game save format. Most types should print and compare for free. One secret type must not auto-print. Another needs a custom Debug layout. Sam wants defaults on, with clear reject and override paths — not a wall of markers on every type.

options.name: Default-on for qualifying types; reject + override
options.detail: Whenever fields qualify, Jet auto-derives the useful built-in traits. Experts reject auto-derive for a type or package, or override with a hand impl. Beginners write almost nothing.
options.technical: Extend S55 / D-MARK-DEBUG1: keep silent auto for Printable/Equatable/Debug (and any later ratified auto family) when fields qualify. Add an explicit reject spelling (type or package scope). Hand impl remains the override. Reject beats auto; override beats both for that trait.

options.name: Keep today's S55: auto when fields qualify; override only
options.detail: No new reject surface. Auto-derive stays for Printable, Equatable, and Debug when fields qualify. Hand impl still overrides. Types that must opt out use awkward workarounds.
options.technical: No law change beyond clarifying docs. No #NoAuto / package deny. Secret-like types rely on #Redact, non-qualifying fields, or never printing.

options.name: Opt-in markers for every derive
options.detail: Nothing auto-derives. Each type lists the traits it wants. Experts get full visibility. Beginners pay ceremony on almost every type.
options.technical: Reverse S55 / D-MARK-DEBUG1 auto policy. Restore explicit derive markers for Printable/Equatable/Debug. Hand impl still allowed.
options.code:
#Printable
#Equatable
#Debug
struct Player {
    name: String
    score: Int
}

options.name: Package flag off by default; per-type opt-in
options.detail: A package or build flag disables auto-derive globally. Types then opt in one by one. Good for strict codebases; bad for the common beginner package.
options.technical: Introduce package/project auto-derive policy defaulting to off or requiring an enable flag. Per-type markers restore derives. Conflicts with beginner-default philosophy unless the flag defaults on.

options.name: Default-on, package kill-switch, type reject, type override
options.detail: Same beginner default as A, plus a package-level switch that turns auto-derive off for that package. Types can still reject or override one by one.
options.technical: A plus package policy (default on). Package off makes auto-derive opt-in inside that package only. Type reject and hand override still work. One mechanism, three scopes.

comparisons.note: Opt-in #[derive(...)]; no silent auto for user types. High ceremony, high visibility.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Player { name: String, score: i32 }

comparisons.note: Many protocols synthesize members when fields allow; you can write your own implementation to override.
data class generates equals/toString/copy by default; you can override members.
comparisons.code: data class Player(val name: String, val score: Int)

recommendation.why: Beginners get free derives for the common case. Experts can kill auto-derive for a whole package, reject it on one type, or replace it with a hand impl. That matches Jet's two-facet design without a second mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Stops short of a package kill-switch that strict codebases will ask for anyway.
Leaves no clean reject path; secret or intentional non-print types stay awkward.
Pushes beginner ceremony onto every type for the most likely case.
Makes the rare strict package the default, so ordinary projects pay opt-in tax.

recommendation.tradeoff: We must design a small reject spelling and a package policy knob. That is acceptable because both sit on the existing derive mechanism rather than inventing a parallel one.

decisions.title: Package auto-derive switch and type opt-in spelling
decisions.gist: Choose where packages disable auto-derive and how a type turns one trait back on.
decisions.lesson:
An auto-derive is a compiler-written trait implementation. Jet already writes Printable, Equatable, and Debug implementations when every field supports the trait. This default removes routine code from ordinary types.

D-AUTODERIVE1=E fixes the behavior. Auto-derive is on by default. A package can turn it off. A type can reject one automatic trait. A hand-written implementation always wins.

A package manifest stores settings that apply to every source file in that package. A local opt-in restores selected traits for one type after the package switch disables automatic derives.

The remaining choice is syntax, not behavior. The package setting must be easy to find and must not look like package identity. The type spelling must name selected traits clearly.
decisions.story: Sam ships a game-save library. Most projects want free printing and equality. This audited package lists every generated trait. Sam still wants selected records to derive all three built-ins. Secret types use hand-written Debug output.

options.name: Policy block with direct trait markers
options.detail: Put auto_derive in the existing policy block. A type opts in with each trait's own marker. The spelling follows Jet's marker and trait naming law.
options.technical: Use policy: .{ auto_derive: false }. The default is true. Add active type-site rows for Printable, Equatable, and Debug. This narrowly amends D-MARK-DEBUG1 because package-off gives #Debug a required job. #[Printable, Equatable, Debug] records explicit derives. #NoAuto(Trait) rejects only silent auto. A direct opt-in and #NoAuto for the same trait produce a diagnostic. A hand-written impl wins over package policy, opt-in, and reject.

options.name: Payload field with one Auto marker
options.detail: Put auto_derive beside package identity. Use one #Auto marker with a trait list. The local spelling is compact, but it hides the direct trait relationship.
options.technical: Use payload: .{ auto_derive: false }. Add #Auto(Printable, Equatable, Debug) as one type-site rule with a closed built-in trait list. Keep #Debug retired. #NoAuto remains the inverse control. Repeating one trait in both lists produces a diagnostic. A hand-written impl wins over both lists.

options.name: Derives block with body opt-ins
options.detail: Give derive policy its own manifest block. Each type lists opt-ins inside its body. This separates policy, but it adds a manifest section and hides type facts.
options.technical: Use derives: .{ auto_derive: false }. Restore derive Printable;, derive Equatable;, and derive Debug; as explicit built-in requests. These lines remain valid when auto-derive is on. This amends the retired Debug body spelling. #NoAuto continues to control silent auto. A hand-written impl wins.

options.name: Policy block with signed trait markers
options.detail: Put auto_derive in the policy block. A bare trait opts in. A trait with ! opts out. One marker list can mix both choices.
options.technical: Use policy: .{ auto_derive: true|false }. A single reject is #!Printable. A mixed list is #[!Debug, !Equatable, Printable]. Missing traits follow the package default. Positive traits request generation when fields qualify. Negative traits reject only automatic generation. A hand-written impl wins over package policy and either sign. This option amends D-AUTODERIVE1=E by replacing #NoAuto(Trait) with the signed form.

comparisons.note: Rust has no silent derive for user types. Each type names generated traits directly. Package-wide compiler policy uses separate manifest sections.
Swift names a protocol directly on the type. The compiler writes the implementation when fields qualify. A hand-written implementation replaces synthesis.
A data class gets equality and text output automatically. A type can override generated members. Kotlin has no package switch for this behavior.

recommendation.why: The policy block already holds package-wide compiler rules. Signed trait markers use one list for opt-in and opt-out. The same type stays explicit across package defaults.

whyNot.reason: #NoAuto adds a separate negative marker beside direct positive trait markers. Signed names express both directions through one existing marker list.
Payload describes package identity and compatibility. Compiler generation policy has a different job. #Auto also weakens the direct link between a trait and its marker.
A new derives block creates another manifest category for one Boolean setting. Body lines also hide important type facts below the declaration header.

recommendation.tradeoff: This adds ! to applied-rule names and replaces the ratified #NoAuto spelling. The polarity matches effect rejection, but tooling must parse and show the sign.

decisions.title: Should quantity and unit values print with their units?
decisions.gist: Choose what print and Display show for values that carry units or physical dimensions.
decisions.lesson:
A quantity is a number plus a unit the compiler understands.

Jet already checks unit families and physical dimensions. You can write 12meter, divide by 3second, and get a speed. Wrong mixes become clear errors. At runtime the unit metadata erases, so the machine cost stays a plain number.

Printing is the last mile. If print shows only 12, the human loses the unit the compiler just protected. People expect 12 meter, 4 meter/second, or 766 px in logs, demos, and UI text unless they asked for a bare number.

This decision picks the default print and Display behavior for unit and quantity values, and how experts override it.
decisions.story: Riley demos dimensional algebra in a physics toy. The math works. print(recovered) shows a bare number, so the demo fails to teach what was recovered. Riley also draws UI sizes in px and wants 766 px in debug output without hand formatting every value.

options.name: Default Display includes units; override allowed
options.detail: print and Display show value plus unit text for quantities and unit-family values. Derived dimensions print in a readable form such as meter/second. A hand Display overrides.
options.technical: Auto Display/Printable for Quantity and #UnitFamily generated types formats magnitude + canonical unit spelling. Compound dimensions use a normalized product/quotient form. Explicit Display wins. Bare numeric extraction stays available via existing numeric APIs.

options.name: Keep bare numeric print; format helpers only
options.detail: print stays a bare number. Users call helpers or write Display when they want units. Dimension checking stays; presentation is manual.
options.technical: No auto unit-aware Display. Document format helpers if added later. Examples keep string labels beside prints.

options.name: Debug shows units; Display stays bare
options.detail: Everyday print stays numeric. Debug and {value#Debug} show units for developers. User-facing Display must be written when units matter in product text.
options.technical: Auto Debug for quantity/unit types includes unit spelling. Display/Printable remain numeric or absent until explicit. Interpolation {} follows Display rules.

options.name: Units on print, with style controls
options.detail: Default print includes units. Call sites or type attributes can pick short names, long names, or bare numbers without writing a full Display impl.
options.technical: Default like A, plus formatting policy (symbol vs name vs bare) via attribute or format syntax. Still one Display mechanism underneath; styles select rendering.

options.name: Require explicit Display for every unit type
options.detail: No auto unit printing. Authors of each #UnitFamily must define Display. Maximum control; maximum ceremony for demos and science code.
options.technical: Do not auto-implement Display/Printable for unit/quantity types. Missing Display is an error at print sites.

comparisons.note: Units erase at runtime; printing is still a plain number unless you format yourself.
comparisons.code:
let d = 12.0<m>
printfn "%A" d  // numeric unless custom

comparisons.note: Printing includes units by default; very pragmatism-friendly for science workloads.
Lengths are authored and shown with unit suffixes (px, rem). Bare numbers feel wrong in UI work.

recommendation.why: The compiler already knows the unit. Showing it on print finishes the feature people hire quantities for, in science demos and UI sizes alike. Experts still override Display when they need custom text.

whyNot.reason: Leaves the last mile broken; every call site re-attaches knowledge the type already has.
Hides units from the everyday print path beginners actually use.
Useful later, but style knobs can extend A; they need not block the default.
Forces ceremony onto every unit family for the most likely demo and log case.

recommendation.tradeoff: We must pick readable default spellings for compound dimensions. That is acceptable because one Display path serves beginners, and overrides cover special cases.

decisions.comment: A but add the explicit controls to modify style like in option D

decisions.title: Typed JSON on the HTTP client and server
decisions.gist: How a program sends and receives JSON over HTTP without hand glue.
decisions.lesson:
JSON is the text format most web services speak. A program that calls a service gets JSON text back and must turn it into typed values. A program that serves an API must turn typed values into JSON text and label the response with a content type header.

Jet already has both halves separately. `#Codable` on a struct gives typed encode and decode. The HTTP client can fetch text, and the server can return text. The missing piece is the join: today a user reads the body as text with a size limit, then calls the JSON decoder as a second step. On the server, a user builds a JSON string by hand and sets the header by hand.

This decision picks where the join lives. It can be explicit helper methods on requests and responses, a content-type driven automatic decode, or no join at all with the two-step pattern documented. The stakes are daily: calling a JSON API into structs is likely the single most common network job a Jet user will do.
decisions.story: Maya writes a small dashboard that polls a weather service every minute. She defines a `Forecast` struct with `#Codable`, calls `http.get`, and expects to have typed data. Instead she must pick a byte limit for `.text()`, then decode, then handle two different error shapes. Her serve half repeats the same dance in reverse.

options.name: Typed helpers on both sides
options.detail: Add `resp.json<T>(limit)` on the client, `req.json<T>()` on the server, and `server.json(status, value)` for responses. All three ride the existing `#Codable` path. The raw text and byte paths stay for experts. Beginners get one call per direction; the content type header is set for them.
options.technical: resp.json<T>(limit) = body().text(limit) then encoding.json.decode<T>, one Result. Default limit follows the existing body cap. server.json sets Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 and status. req.json<T>() enforces the framing cap already ratified for bodies.

options.name: Document the two-step pattern
options.detail: Ship no new methods. Write one clear docs recipe: read text with a limit, decode with `encoding.json`, and set the header by hand on the server. Every user repeats the glue, but the surface stays smaller.

options.name: Content-type driven auto-decode
options.detail: The response body object inspects the Content-Type header. When it says JSON, `resp.body().value<T>()` decodes without the user naming a format. Less typing, but the behavior of the same call changes with server headers, which can surprise and is harder to audit.
options.code:
// Same call, behavior depends on the server's header
forecast :: resp.body().value<Forecast>() ?? return

comparisons.note: The standard library stops at option B: users call json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&v) by hand every time.
resp.json() made option A the norm; it is one of the most-used methods in the ecosystem.

recommendation.why: The compiler already knows the type through `#Codable`, and the server already owns headers. Naming the format at the call site keeps the behavior auditable while removing the daily glue.

whyNot.reason: The two-step glue stays in every project, with a hand-picked byte limit and two error shapes for one job.
The same call changes meaning based on a remote server's header, which surprises readers and weakens audits.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three new methods widen the HTTP surface. That is acceptable because they compose the two mechanisms Jet already ratified, and the raw paths remain unchanged.

decisions.title: Serve a static directory in one call
decisions.gist: Whether the server can serve a folder of files with one safe call.
decisions.lesson:
Most small web services ship two things: an API and a folder of files (a page, a stylesheet, some images). Serving that folder means mapping request paths to files under one root, guessing content types, and refusing paths that escape the root.

Jet ships the per-file half. `static_file` and `static_file_range` serve one named file each, with range support for media. What is missing is the directory form: one call that says "serve everything under ./public". Users today write a route per file or a hand-rolled loop, and a hand-rolled loop is exactly where path escape bugs live.

The safety rules are the real content of this decision. A directory server must normalize paths, refuse `..` escapes, decide what a request for a bare directory returns, and decide whether symbolic links may leave the root. Those defaults decide whether the beginner path is safe.
decisions.story: Tom builds a club sign-up page: one API route and a `public/` folder with a page, a stylesheet, and a logo. He finds `static_file`, writes three routes, then adds a fourth file and forgets a route. A one-call directory server would have removed the whole class of mistake.

options.name: static_files(root) with safe defaults
options.detail: One call mounts a directory. Defaults: paths are normalized, escapes are refused, dot-files are hidden, symbolic links may not leave the root, and a directory request serves its index.html or 404. Experts opt into different policy with named options. Range requests reuse the shipped per-file machinery.
options.technical: Mount under a prefix; resolve request path against root with canonicalization; reject any resolved path not under root. Content types from the existing mime table. Policy options: index on/off, dotfiles on/off, follow_links on/off.
options.code:
server.static_files("public")
// expert: server.static_files("public", index: false, dotfiles: true)

options.name: Keep per-file helpers only
options.detail: No directory form. Users route each file or write their own loop over a directory listing. The surface stays small, but every hand loop re-invents the escape checks the stdlib already knows how to do.

options.name: A separate static-server command
options.detail: Ship `jet serve-static <dir>` as a tool instead of a library call. Good for quick previews, but it cannot combine with API routes in one program, so the common "API plus assets" job still has no answer.
options.code: $ jet serve-static public --port 8080

comparisons.note: http.FileServer(http.Dir("public")) is the one-call form; its path-escape handling is standard library, not user code.
express.static('public') is among the first lines in most Express apps.

recommendation.why: Directory serving is a solved, safety-sensitive pattern. Owning it in the stdlib puts the escape checks in one audited place and finishes the everyday "API plus assets" job in one line.

whyNot.reason: Every project re-writes path mapping and escape checks by hand, which is where the security bugs live.
A separate command cannot live inside the user's own server, so the most common combined job stays unserved.

recommendation.tradeoff: The stdlib takes on path-normalization policy questions (index files, dot-files, links). That is acceptable because the defaults are deny-leaning and each policy is a named opt-in.

decisions.title: CORS policy helper for browser-facing APIs
decisions.gist: Whether the server gets a built-in, explicit CORS policy helper.
decisions.lesson:
Browsers protect users with the same-origin rule: a page from one site may not read API responses from another site unless that API says so. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how the API says so. The server answers special preflight requests (HTTP OPTIONS) and adds `Access-Control-Allow-…` headers that name which origins, methods, and headers it accepts.

Any project that serves a browser page from one place and an API from another needs this. Getting it wrong in the permissive direction quietly opens the API to any website; getting it wrong in the strict direction breaks the app with opaque browser errors.

Jet's server ships middleware (request wrappers) but no CORS helper, and the docs mark it open with a note that there must be no permissive ambient fallback. This decision picks the shape: an explicit policy value, a dev-only permissive mode, or no helper.
decisions.story: Priya serves her React page from a static host and her Jet API from a small VM. Her fetch calls fail with a console error about missing CORS headers. She hand-writes an OPTIONS route and three header lines, copies them from a forum post, and accidentally allows every origin with credentials.

options.name: Explicit policy value, deny by default
options.detail: A `server.cors(policy)` middleware. The policy names allowed origins, methods, and headers. No policy installed means no CORS headers at all. The dangerous combinations (any origin with credentials) are rejected at construction with a clear error.
options.technical: CorsPolicy { origins: [String] | .Any, methods, headers, credentials: Bool, max_age }. Constructor rejects .Any + credentials. Middleware answers OPTIONS preflight and stamps allow headers on matching routes.
options.code: server.cors(Cors.{ origins: ["https://app.example.com"], methods: ["GET", "POST"] })

options.name: Permissive dev mode only
options.detail: `jet dev` serves permissive CORS headers automatically; production builds serve none and users hand-roll. Local work feels frictionless, but the cliff between dev and production shows up as a breakage at deploy time, and the docs already reject ambient permissiveness.
options.code:
$ jet dev api.jet   # dev server answers preflight for any origin
$ jet build api.jet # production: no CORS, app breaks at deploy

options.name: No helper, documented recipe
options.detail: Keep the surface as is and document the OPTIONS-plus-headers recipe. Every browser-facing project copies security-sensitive boilerplate, and each copy can drift.
options.code:
// docs recipe, pasted into each project
response(204, "").header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin)

comparisons.note: The cors middleware package is near-universal; its default is permissive, which Jet's docs explicitly rule out.
Go's stdlib has no helper; most projects import a third-party middleware, showing the demand is real.

recommendation.why: CORS is security policy that browsers enforce blind. An explicit policy value keeps the beginner from shipping the permissive-with-credentials mistake, while staying one visible line in the program.

whyNot.reason: A dev-only permissive mode hides the policy until deploy day and contradicts the already-written rule against ambient CORS.
A recipe copies security-sensitive boilerplate into every project, where it drifts and rots.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users must still learn what an origin is to fill the policy. That is acceptable because the error messages can teach it, and silence about origins is how APIs get exposed.

decisions.title: web.app must serve, or stop claiming full-stack
decisions.gist: What happens when a user runs a program built with web.app().
decisions.lesson:
`web.app()` is Jet's builder for a whole web application: the user declares pages, routes, actions, assets, and security settings on one value. A builder like this promises that the declared graph becomes a running site.

Today the promise stops at bookkeeping. The runtime records the routes and actions as a graph, and the flagship example ends with `print("web-app-graph-ok")`. Nothing listens on a port; no page is ever served. Meanwhile Jet has a real HTTP server (`core.http.server`) with routing, middleware, and TLS in the same tree.

The pragmatism rule at stake: a feature that looks like a product but stops one step before the job teaches users not to trust the language. This decision picks whether running a web.app serves it by default, serves it on an explicit call, or parks the API until it can serve honestly.
decisions.story: Leo scaffolds a recipe-sharing site with web.app: three pages, two actions, an asset folder. He types `jet run site.jet`, sees `web-app-graph-ok`, opens his browser to localhost, and gets connection refused. He files a confused bug report asking where his site went.

options.name: jet run serves the app by default
options.detail: A program whose entry returns or registers a web.app gets a development server on a local port, wired through the existing core.http.server. The terminal prints the address. Production serving uses the same path with explicit options. Beginners run one command and see their site.
options.technical: Lower the app graph onto core.http.server routes: pages render to HTML responses, actions become POST routes, assets mount via the static path. Port from options or an ephemeral default; print the bound address. One serving mechanism (I8) — no second server.

options.name: Explicit app.serve(port) only
options.detail: The graph stays inert until the user calls serve. One visible line, no ambient behavior. Beginners must learn that building an app does not run it, which is one more chance to stop at a confusing dead end.

options.name: Park web.app until serving exists
options.detail: Remove or gate the builder so no user can reach the dead end. Honest, but it deletes a surface that examples and tests already exercise, and the graph model itself is sound.
options.code: // web.app() → E-code: "web.app cannot serve yet; use core.http.server"

options.name: jet dev auto-serves; jet run serves plainly
options.detail: Matches the existing jet dev convention. When the entry builds a web.app and the file defines no fn dev(), jet dev serves the graph on a local port with live reload and prints the address. jet run serves the same graph without dev extras — for a server app the running server IS the program, which is also the deployment path. fn dev() and an explicit app.serve(port) remain the expert overrides.
options.technical: Same lowering as A: app graph onto core.http.server — pages render to HTML responses, actions become POST routes, assets mount via the static path. jet dev wraps that server with the existing core.web.devserver live-reload plumbing, no fn dev() required. One serving mechanism (I8); today nothing lowers the graph onto any server, under either command.
options.code:
$ jet dev site.jet
# serving http://127.0.0.1:8080 (live reload)

$ jet run site.jet
# serving http://127.0.0.1:8080

comparisons.note: The framework's entire pitch is that declaring pages IS the app; `next dev` serves them with zero extra wiring.
Explicit app.run() is the option B shape; beginners forget it often enough that the CLI grew `flask run` to compensate.

recommendation.why: The builder's one promise is a running site, and jet dev is the command that already means "develop against a live server". D finishes the promise through the server Jet already ships, on both commands, with the dev niceties where developers actually live.

whyNot.reason: Puts the development default on jet run alone and leaves jet dev — the established dev-server entry — out of the story.
Keeps a silent dead end: build an app, run it, get nothing. The explicit call survives as the expert path either way.
Deletes a sound graph model instead of finishing its last step, and the gap this card exists to close stays open.

recommendation.tradeoff: jet run and jet dev gain behavior that depends on what the program builds. Acceptable because the terminal states the bound address, and fn dev() plus explicit serve options remain the expert overrides.

decisions.title: Browser demo: Jet owns click, state, and render
decisions.gist: Who owns the button click and the counter state in the flagship browser demo.
decisions.lesson:
Jet compiles to WebAssembly so a program can run inside a browser page. A minimal interactive demo needs three parts: an event handler (the click), some state (the count), and a render (paint the new count).

In the flagship click demo today, hand-written HTML and JavaScript own two of the three parts. The host page declares `let n = 0`, listens for the click, and calls into Jet only to re-paint. A reader who opens the example to learn "how do I handle a click in Jet" finds the answer written in JavaScript.

Jet already has the pieces to own all three: `web.on` attaches a handler from Jet, `core.reactive` signals hold state, and the reactive render already repaints. The Linux desktop (GTK) counter example already works exactly this way. This decision picks which wiring the flagship browser example teaches.
decisions.story: Ana knows some JavaScript and wants to try Jet for a browser widget. She opens the click example to copy the pattern. She finds the counter logic in the HTML file, not the Jet file, and concludes Jet cannot handle events in the browser yet.

options.name: Wire the demo with web.on and a signal
options.detail: Rewrite the flagship example so Jet attaches the click with `web.on`, keeps the count in a reactive signal, and repaints through the existing reactive render. The HTML shrinks to a shell div. No new API; the docs and the demo start telling the same story as the GTK example.
options.code:
count :: reactive.signal(0)
web.on("#btn", "click", () => count.set(count.get() + 1))
ui.reactive_render(root, () => counter_view(count.get()))

options.name: Uniform on_click across UI backends
options.detail: Extend the UI node tree so the same `on_click` the GTK backend uses also works on the web backend, then use that in the demo. One event mechanism across desktop, terminal, and browser. More design work: it must map tree nodes to DOM nodes and route events back.
options.technical: Requires stable node identity across renders on the DOM backend, an event dispatch channel from JS to the wasm side, and a ruling on which events the portable set includes.
options.code: button :: ui.button("Count", on_click: () => count.set(count.get() + 1))

options.name: Keep the host-page pattern, label it
options.detail: Leave the example as is and label it "host-page integration": the surrounding site owns events, Jet renders. Honest about today, but the flagship then teaches that interactive Jet-in-browser is someone else's job.
options.code: // README note: "state and events live in your page's JS"

options.name: A now, B ratified as the destination
options.detail: Rewrite the flagship today with web.on and a signal (A), and in the same ruling commit to B: one portable on_click across GTK, web, terminal, and future mobile backends, designed on its own card. The demo respells to the portable form when B lands. Write-once-run-everywhere stays the ratified goal; the flagship stops teaching that JavaScript owns the click in the meantime.
options.technical: A needs no new surface. B's design card owns: stable node identity across renders on the DOM backend, an event dispatch channel from JS to the wasm side, and the portable event set. Ratifying D makes B's card ratified scope, not an idea.

comparisons.note: Wasm UI frameworks own events end to end; needing hand-written JS for a counter is treated as a framework failure.

recommendation.why: The owner's goal — write it once, deploy anywhere without Electron/Tauri-style parallel clients — is exactly B. D buys that destination as ratified scope while A fixes what the flagship teaches today with zero new mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Fixes the demo but leaves the write-once destination unratified, so the web-specific spelling could quietly become permanent.
Right destination, but it blocks the flagship fix on real design work (node identity, event routing), leaving the example wrong until then.
Keeps teaching that Jet cannot handle a browser click, which is false.

recommendation.tradeoff: The demo carries the web-specific web.on spelling until B lands, and B's design card must actually be scheduled. Acceptable: one example respell, and the ruling itself keeps B from rotting into a someday-idea.

decisions.title: One-call UI mount over measure/layout/paint
decisions.gist: Whether showing a UI tree takes one call or three pipeline steps.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's UI works in two layers. The user builds a tree of nodes (a column, a label, a button). A backend (terminal, GTK desktop, browser DOM, or a null backend for tests) turns that tree into pixels in three steps. Measure asks each node its size, layout assigns positions, and paint draws.

The three steps are a real pipeline that experts sometimes need to drive by hand — for custom layout, for tests that inspect geometry, or for animation timing. But every shipped example and the beginner docs snippet write all three calls verbatim just to show a static screen. The pipeline is identical boilerplate each time.

This decision picks whether the stdlib ships a default entry that runs the pipeline for you. The manual steps stay either way; the question is only what the first line of every UI program looks like.
decisions.story: Sam wants a two-line terminal dashboard: a title and a count. The tree takes three lines. Showing it takes four more: create a backend, measure, layout, paint. He copies those four lines from an example without understanding them, which is the definition of ceremony.
decisions.inWild:
// Every example today, verbatim
backend :: ui.tui()
root :: ui.column([ui.label("Deploys today"), ui.label("{count}")])
size :: backend.measure(root)
backend.layout(root, size)
backend.paint(root)

options.name: ui.mount(backend, tree)
options.detail: One call runs measure, layout, and paint (and present, where the backend has one). Re-render on state change keeps using the existing reactive render. The three manual stages remain public for experts. Every example's boilerplate collapses to one line.
options.technical: mount = measure(root) → layout(root, size) → paint(root) → present?. Idempotent on re-call; reactive_render internally reuses it.
options.code:
backend :: ui.tui()
ui.mount(backend, root)

options.name: backend.run(() => tree) owns the loop
options.detail: The backend takes a closure that builds the tree and runs the whole app loop: first paint, event wake-ups, and re-renders. Closest to app frameworks, but it takes over the program's control flow, which overlaps with the reactive layer Jet already ships.
options.code: ui.tui().run(() => ui.column([ui.label("Deploys today"), ui.label("{count.get()}")]))

options.name: Keep the manual pipeline
options.detail: Document the three calls as the way. The surface stays smallest, and every program keeps four lines of copied ceremony the compiler could have absorbed.
options.code:
size :: backend.measure(root)
backend.layout(root, size)
backend.paint(root)

comparisons.note: runApp(widget) is the one-call mount; the measure/layout/paint pipeline exists underneath and stays reachable for experts.
Appending a node mounts it; no user calls layout or paint by hand. The pipeline is real but owned by the engine.

recommendation.why: It removes the exact four copied lines from every program while adding no control-flow opinion. It composes with the existing reactive render instead of competing with it.

whyNot.reason: A run-loop entry takes over the program's control flow and overlaps the reactive layer, creating a second update mechanism.
The ceremony stays in every beginner's first UI program, copied without understanding.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more name in core.ui that experts will rarely call. That is acceptable because the manual pipeline stays public and unchanged.

decisions.title: game.run drives a real frame loop
decisions.gist: Whether game.run runs a playable loop or a fixed three-frame transcript.
decisions.lesson:
A game is a loop: read input, update the world, draw a frame, repeat until the player quits. Everything else in a game engine (scenes, assets, entities) hangs off that loop.

Jet's `core.game` has the hangers but not the loop. `game.run` executes exactly three frames when no count is given, headless, and stops. That is a deliberate testing shape: deterministic transcripts golden-test well. But the same API names (`scene`, `on_frame`, `input`, assets) read like an engine, so a user who builds a pong clone discovers the ceiling only at the end. Separately, a thin raylib bridge can open a real window and draw, but nothing connects it to `game.run`.

Ratified law already says backends are chosen by a typed `game.Backend` value (D-GAME-BACKEND1). This decision picks what `game.run` means under a real backend: loop until the player quits, stay a transcript tool with honest naming, or park the surface.
decisions.story: Nadia teaches a weekend game-dev class and picks Jet for its clean syntax. Her students build paddle movement with on_frame, run it, and get three silent frames and an exit. The class switches to Love2D after lunch.

options.name: Loop until the backend says stop
options.detail: Under a windowed backend, game.run repeats on_frame until the window closes or the program quits, with frame timing owned by the backend. The headless backend keeps a frame budget (default stays small and deterministic) so goldens and tests do not change. One API, both worlds.
options.technical: Backend contract gains should_continue() and present(). Headless returns false after the budget; windowed returns !window_should_close(). Frame pacing (vsync/FPS cap) is backend policy. Existing three-frame goldens keep passing via the headless default.

options.name: Rename to a simulation harness
options.detail: Keep the three-frame transcript and rename the surface to say what it is (for example game.simulate), with docs stating that playable games await a renderer package. Honest, no new runtime work, but Jet ships no path to a playable game and the examples stay demos of a test tool.
options.code: game.simulate(scene, frames: 3, (frame) => { ... })

options.name: Park core.game until a renderer ships
options.detail: Gate the module behind an explicit experimental flag so no one mistakes it for an engine. Removes the trap and also removes the deterministic testing value the transcript already provides.
options.code: // use core.game → E-code: "core.game is experimental; enable with ..."

comparisons.note: The canonical beginner loop is while (!WindowShouldClose()) — option A adopts exactly this stop condition through the backend.
The framework owns the loop; users only fill update and draw callbacks. That callback shape is what game.run already has.
comparisons.code:
function love.update(dt) ... end
function love.draw() ... end

recommendation.why: The callback API is already the right shape; only the stop condition is fake. Letting the ratified backend value own continuation turns the existing surface into a real engine floor without a second mechanism.

whyNot.reason: It makes the docs honest but leaves Jet with no answer for the games domain, which the audit graded blocked.
It throws away working deterministic testing to avoid finishing one contract method.

recommendation.tradeoff: The backend contract grows and the raylib bridge must implement it, including frame pacing. That is acceptable because headless behavior and existing goldens stay unchanged.

decisions.title: #CLI field markers for short flags and env fallbacks
decisions.gist: How a typed CLI struct declares -v short flags and environment fallbacks.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's typed command-line path is ratified: put `#CLI` on a struct, and each field becomes a `--flag` or `--option` with help text from `#Doc` and defaults from `#Default`. The entry function's parameter is the whole CLI spec.

Real tools need two more everyday features. Short flags: seasoned users type `-v`, not `--verbose`. Environment fallbacks: deployment scripts set `PORT=8080` instead of passing a flag. Jet's lower-level builder (`core.args`) already supports both with `.flag_short` and `.option_env`.

The typed path cannot express either, so a tool that needs them must abandon `#CLI` entirely and rewrite its whole interface on the builder. That is the gap: the two APIs are one mechanism by law (`#CLI` lowers to the builder), but the typed spelling covers less than the thing it lowers to. This decision picks how fields opt into shorts and env fallbacks.
decisions.story: Omar ships an internal deploy tool with `#CLI` and is happy. Ops asks for `PORT` env support so the container platform can configure it, and `-n` for dry-run because they type it fifty times a day. Omar rewrites the whole interface on the builder and loses the derived help.

options.name: Per-field markers #Short and #Env
options.detail: Two new field markers inside the existing bracket list. `#Short("n")` adds a one-letter alias; `#Env("PORT")` reads the variable when the flag is absent. Each lowers to the builder method that already exists. Explicit, per field, no surprises, and precedence is spelled in the help text.
options.technical: Codegen maps #Short → .flag_short/.option_short and #Env → .option_env on the existing lowering. Precedence: flag beats env beats #Default. Duplicate short letters are a compile error with the two fields named.

options.name: Auto-derive shorts from first letters
options.detail: `#CLI(shorts: true)` gives every field a short flag from its first letter. Zero per-field typing, but two fields starting with the same letter collide, and adding a field can silently change another field's short. Env support would still need a marker anyway.

options.name: No markers; builder is the answer
options.detail: Keep `#CLI` minimal and document that shorts and env mean dropping to `core.args`. The typed path stays small, but the most common growth step for a real tool remains a full rewrite.
options.code:
// docs: "need -n or PORT? use core.args:"
spec :: args.spec().flag("dry-run").flag_short("n").option_env("port", "PORT")

comparisons.note: Per-field attributes are the settled shape: #[arg(short = 'n', env = "PORT")]. Auto-short exists and is documented as collision-prone.
Both spellings are given per option; env fallback is not built in and every project glues os.environ by hand.

recommendation.why: Per-field markers keep the typed struct the single source of truth and lower onto builder methods that already exist. The growth step becomes one word instead of a rewrite.

whyNot.reason: First-letter shorts collide, and adding a field can silently reassign another field's short. It also solves nothing for env fallbacks.
It keeps the cliff where a tool's most common growth step abandons the ratified typed path entirely.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two new user-typeable markers must enter the ratified syntax table. That is acceptable because they ride the existing bracket-list marker rail and add no new grammar shape.

decisions.title: Number formatting inside string interpolation
decisions.gist: How a user prints a float with two decimals inside a string.
decisions.lesson:
String interpolation puts a value inside text: `"total: {x}"`. Jet ratified a strict shape for the braces (S8): exactly one value, no expressions of arbitrary form, and one optional selector spelled with `#`, currently only `{value#Debug}` (D-ATTR4).

The most common formatting job in any program is a number with fixed decimals: prices, percentages, timings. Today that job cannot be spelled in the braces at all. The user imports `core.fmt` and writes `fmt.decimal(x, 2)` around the value, or pre-formats into a variable. `"{x:.2}"` is a hard error by design.

The question is whether the braces gain a formatting spelling, and if so which one. The ratified `#` selector rail already exists, so one option extends it. The other school adds a colon mini-language like Rust and Python, which is powerful but is effectively a second small language inside strings. This is new user-typeable syntax, so the owner decides.
decisions.story: Ines writes a receipt printer for a food stall. Every line has a price. She writes `"{item}: {price:.2}"`, gets a syntax error, searches the docs, imports core.fmt, and wraps every price on eleven lines. Her receipt code is now half formatting calls.

options.name: Format selectors on the # rail
options.detail: Extend the ratified selector: `{price#Fixed(2)}` for decimals, and later siblings like `#Percent(1)` if wanted. One value plus one named selector — the brace grammar shape does not change. Selectors map one-to-one onto the existing core.fmt functions, so there is one formatting mechanism.
options.technical: Grammar: interpolation hole = value ('#' selector)? — already the D-ATTR4 shape. #Fixed(n) lowers to the fmt.decimal path. Unknown selector is a registered compile error listing the valid set.
options.code:
print("{item.name}: {item.price#Fixed(2)}")
print("total: {total#Fixed(2)}")

options.name: Colon spec mini-language
options.detail: Adopt the `{x:.2}` family like Rust and Python: width, fill, alignment, precision in one compact code string. Familiar to many and very dense, but it is a second little language with its own parser, error space, and learning cliff, and it duplicates what core.fmt already does.
options.code:
print("{item.name}: {item.price:.2}")
print("{qty:>5} x {name:<20}")

options.name: No syntax; keep fmt calls
options.detail: The braces stay value-only. Formatting stays an ordinary function call, which is explicit and searchable, and the most common formatting job keeps paying an import plus a wrapper on every use.
options.code:
use core.fmt as fmt
print("total: {fmt.decimal(total, 2)}")

comparisons.note: f-strings use the colon mini-language; it is loved for density and routinely cited as unreadable for anything past precision.
Interpolation takes named arguments instead of a code string — the same direction as the # selector rail.

recommendation.why: It finishes the most common formatting job in one readable word, rides the selector rail the owner already ratified, and keeps core.fmt as the single formatting mechanism underneath.

whyNot.reason: A colon mini-language is a second language inside strings, with its own parser and error space, duplicating core.fmt.
The everyday job keeps paying an import and a wrapper per use, which the audit measured as real ceremony.

recommendation.tradeoff: Named selectors are wordier than `:.2` and will grow one selector per common format. That is acceptable because each selector is searchable prose, not code-string punctuation.

decisions.title: core.args finishes --help and exit
decisions.gist: Whether the argument-parser library can print help and exit for you.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has two ways to read command-line flags. The high road is `#CLI` on a struct: the compiler derives the flags, prints `--help`, and exits. The floor under it is the `core.args` builder: the program declares flags one call at a time and then parses.

The floor recognizes `--help` but refuses to act on it. Parsing never prints and never exits; the caller must test `parsed.flag("help")`, print the help text, and return. That is a deliberate property — a library that exits the process is hard to test and hard to embed. But it means the documented library path leaves the most common CLI behavior half-done, and every program that uses the builder hand-rolls the same three lines.

This decision picks whether the builder gains a convenience entry that finishes help and exits, while the pure non-exiting parse stays for tests and embedding.
decisions.story: Ruth needs repeated flags, so `#CLI` does not fit and she drops to the builder. Her tool ships, a teammate runs `--help`, and gets a parse error output instead of help, because Ruth forgot the hand-rolled branch the docs example carries.

options.name: parse_or_exit alongside parse
options.detail: One new method: `spec.parse_or_exit(argv)` prints help and exits 0 on `--help`, prints the error and exits 2 on a bad flag, and returns parsed arguments otherwise. The existing pure `.parse` stays untouched for tests and embedding. Programs choose which behavior they want with one word.
options.technical: Exit codes: 0 for help/version, 2 for usage errors (BSD convention). Uses the process-exit path already in core. Help text is the same spec.help() output.
options.code:
parsed :: spec.parse_or_exit(io.args())
// --help now prints and exits; bad flags print the error and exit 2

options.name: parse result carries a handled action
options.detail: Keep one parse method, but its result can say "help was requested" as a distinct case the caller matches on. Nothing ever exits for you. More explicit, still testable, but the three-line branch survives in every program — the ceremony this card exists to remove.

options.name: Leave the floor as is
options.detail: Point everyone at `#CLI` for finished behavior and keep the builder purely mechanical. But the builder is the only path when a tool needs features `#CLI` lacks. The gap lands on exactly the users with the least choice.
options.code: // docs: "handle --help yourself when using core.args"

comparisons.note: parse_args() prints help and exits by default; the non-exiting form exists for tests. That split is option A's shape.
flag.Parse() prints usage and exits 2 on error by default, with ContinueOnError as the library-friendly override.

recommendation.why: One added word gives the finished behavior every interactive tool wants, while the pure parse keeps the library testable and embeddable. Both audiences get their path with no mode flags.

whyNot.reason: It renames the ceremony instead of removing it; every program still writes the help branch.
The builder is the only path for tools #CLI cannot express, so leaving it half-done taxes the users with no alternative.

recommendation.tradeoff: A library method that can exit the process is a small purity loss. That is acceptable because the name says so, and the non-exiting parse remains the default teaching form for tests.

decisions.title: Checked subprocess runs: fail on nonzero exit
decisions.gist: Whether a failed subprocess can stop the script by default.
decisions.lesson:
Scripts run other programs: a compiler, a copy, a deploy step. Every program reports success or failure through its exit code — zero means success, anything else means failure.

In Jet, `process.run` returns Ok whenever the child could start and finish, even when the child failed. The result carries a `success` field the caller must remember to test. The distinction is real: the run mechanism worked versus the command did its job. But the common script intent is to run a step and stop on failure. Today that intent needs an explicit if-check after every call. Forgetting the check does not error — the script continues on garbage, which is the worst failure mode.

This decision picks whether Jet adds a checked form where a nonzero exit is an error the `??` operator can catch, keeping today's inspect form for callers who want the full result.
decisions.story: Dev writes a release script: build, sign, upload. The signing step fails on a expired key, returns exit 1, and the script uploads the unsigned build anyway, because `process.run` said Ok and Dev never tested `.success`.

options.name: run_checked treats nonzero as an error
options.detail: A sibling entry: `process.run_checked(cmd)` errors when the child exits nonzero, carrying the exit code and captured stderr in the error. `??` then does what scripts mean: stop or fall back. Today's `run` stays for callers who inspect the full result.
options.technical: Error variant carries code, signal if any, and bounded captured stderr. run_checked is run + one branch; no new process machinery.
options.code:
process.run_checked(Sh.{jet build app.jet}) ?? return
process.run_checked(Sh.{sign build/app}) ?? return
process.run_checked(Sh.{upload build/app}) ?? return

options.name: A .ok() adapter on the result
options.detail: Keep one run method; add `result.ok()` that converts a failed run into an error after the fact. Composable and small, but the call site reads as two steps, and forgetting `.ok()` is exactly as silent as forgetting the if-check today.
options.code: process.run(Sh.{sign build/app}).ok() ?? return

options.name: Make run itself checked; opt out to inspect
options.detail: Flip the default: `run` errors on nonzero, and a named option or sibling gives the raw result for callers who expect failure (test runners, linters that use exit codes as data). Strongest safety, but it changes the meaning of every existing run call and punishes the inspect use case with ceremony.
options.code: process.run(Sh.{grep -q pattern file}) ?? return   // grep exit 1 = 'not found', now an error

comparisons.note: check=True is the documented right default for scripts; the unchecked form exists for exit-code-as-data callers.
set -e makes nonzero exits fatal script-wide; its absence is the classic source of continue-on-failure bugs.
comparisons.code:
set -e
sign app   # script stops here on failure

recommendation.why: It gives scripts the stop-on-failure meaning in one word per call, with the error shape the `??` rail already handles, and changes nothing for existing code.

whyNot.reason: The adapter is as forgettable as the if-check it replaces; the silent failure mode survives.
Flipping the default breaks the exit-code-as-data callers and every existing run call site.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two run entries exist where one could. That is acceptable because they express two genuinely different intents, and the names say which is which.

decisions.title: Interactive prompt helpers in core.io
decisions.gist: Whether asking yes/no, picking from a list, and reading a password are built in.
decisions.lesson:
Interactive command-line tools ask the user things. Three asks cover almost every installer, setup wizard, and destructive command. A confirmation: proceed, yes or no. A choice: pick one option from a short list. A secret: type a password without echoing it to the screen.

Jet's `core.io` has the raw parts. `input(prompt)` reads one line. Styles, progress bars, and TTY detection ship. The `live` terminal surface can read raw keys. But the three everyday asks are missing, so each tool re-invents them. Each hand-rolls y/n parsing, re-prompts, and menu numbering. For secrets, each must figure out terminal echo control or leak the password to the screen.

The secret case is the sharp edge. Echo control is platform-fiddly, and a wrong hand-rolled version shows passwords in terminal history. This decision picks whether the stdlib owns these three prompts.
decisions.story: Kim writes a database reset tool for her team. She wants one confirm before dropping data and a password prompt for the admin login. Her hand-rolled confirm accepts an empty line as yes, and her password prompt echoes in plain text during a screen-shared demo.

options.name: Three helpers: confirm, choose, input_secret
options.detail: `io.confirm(prompt)` returns a Bool with a safe default of no. `io.choose(prompt, items)` numbers the items, re-prompts on bad input, and returns the pick. `io.input_secret(prompt)` reads without echo and errors when there is no terminal. All three respect the existing TTY and NO_COLOR facts.
options.technical: confirm default is no; Enter alone returns the default shown in brackets. choose returns the index (or the item) and re-prompts on out-of-range. input_secret uses termios echo-off on the existing terminal surface; non-TTY stdin is a typed error, never a silent echo.

options.name: Secret input only
options.detail: Ship only `input_secret`, since echo control is the part users cannot safely write themselves. Confirm and choose stay hand-rolled. Smallest addition, but the two most common asks keep differing tool to tool.
options.code:
pw :: io.input_secret("admin password: ") ?? return
// confirm and choose: still DIY

options.name: Leave prompts to packages
options.detail: Keep core.io as is and let a future package own interactive prompts. No stdlib growth, but the safe-echo primitive stays missing too, and today no such package exists — the friction stays for every current user.
options.code: // future: use pkg.prompts as prompts

comparisons.note: getpass.getpass is standard library precisely because echo control is unsafe to hand-roll; confirm/choose live in packages.
comparisons.code:
from getpass import getpass
pw = getpass("admin password: ")

comparisons.note: Confirm, Select, and Password are the three primitives the ecosystem standardized on — the same trio as option A.

recommendation.why: The trio covers nearly every interactive tool, the secret one is a safety primitive users cannot write correctly themselves, and all three sit on TTY facts core.io already owns.

whyNot.reason: It fixes the safety edge but leaves the two most common asks inconsistent across every tool.
No such package exists, and the echo-control primitive belongs where the terminal surface already lives.

recommendation.tradeoff: core.io grows three names with small policy choices baked in (default no, numbered menus). That is acceptable because the raw input and live-key paths stay for tools that want different policy.

decisions.title: Listing declared project tasks
decisions.gist: How a user discovers which #Task tasks a project declares.
decisions.lesson:
Jet projects can declare named tasks with the `#Task` marker: build steps, code generation, scheduled jobs. A task runs with `jet run --task NAME`.

Discovery is the gap. Nothing lists the declared tasks. The only way to see them is to ask for a task that does not exist: the unknown-task error (E1294) helpfully prints the declared names. So the working discovery method is deliberately typing a wrong name, and the compiler already computes the exact list the user wants.

Every task runner treats listing as a first-class verb, because "what can I run here?" is the first question in any inherited project. This decision picks the spelling: a top-level command, a bare flag form, or status quo.
decisions.story: Ravi joins a team and clones their service. The README says "run the usual tasks." He types `jet run --task help`, gets an error listing eleven task names, and bookmarks that error as his team's de facto documentation.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet run --task deploy-staging
# works, because Ravi pair-programmed once and memorized it
$ jet run --task hlep
# error E1294: unknown task "hlep" — declared tasks: build-assets,
# deploy-staging, deploy-prod, gen-docs, ...
# ^ the only listing the toolchain offers

options.name: jet tasks lists them
options.detail: A top-level verb: `jet tasks` prints each declared task with its doc line, marking scheduled ones. It reuses the same list the E1294 error already computes. Discoverable in `jet help` next to the other verbs.
options.technical: Reuses list_task_names from the compile path; output is name, #Doc text, and #Every schedule when present. Non-project directory is the same error jet run gives.
options.code:
$ jet tasks
build-assets     bundle css/js into build/
deploy-staging   push current build to staging
gen-docs         regenerate API docs (every day 06:00)

options.name: Bare --task prints the list
options.detail: `jet run --task` with no name lists tasks instead of erroring. No new verb, but the listing hides inside a flag form nobody would guess, and `jet help` gains nothing to point at.
options.code:
$ jet run --task
build-assets, deploy-staging, deploy-prod, gen-docs

options.name: Keep the error as the listing
options.detail: Change nothing; the unknown-task error keeps doubling as discovery. Zero surface growth, and the first question in every inherited project keeps requiring a deliberate mistake.
options.code:
$ jet run --task ?
# error E1294 ... declared tasks: ...

comparisons.note: npm run with no arguments lists the scripts; it is many developers' first move in a new repo.
comparisons.code:
$ npm run
Scripts available via `npm run-script`: build, test, deploy

comparisons.note: just --list is the canonical answer and doubles as the project's task documentation.
comparisons.code:
$ just --list
Available recipes:
    build
    deploy env

recommendation.why: A visible verb answers the first question a newcomer asks, reuses a list the compiler already computes, and gives the docs and `jet help` something to name.

whyNot.reason: A no-argument flag form is undiscoverable — the exact problem this card exists to fix.
Discovery by deliberate mistake stays embarrassing and teaches users to rely on error text.

recommendation.tradeoff: The top-level command list grows by one verb. That is acceptable because task running is already a first-class jet run feature and the verb only reads.

decisions.title: Compile-checked literal regex patterns
decisions.gist: Whether a regex written as a literal can fail at compile time instead of run time.
decisions.lesson:
A regular expression (regex) is a small pattern language for matching text: `\d+` means one or more digits. A pattern can be malformed — an unclosed group, a bad escape — and then it cannot be used at all.

When the pattern arrives at run time (typed by a user, read from a config), failure must be a runtime Result. But most patterns in real programs are literals written by the programmer. Their validity is knowable the moment the compiler sees them. Jet today treats both the same: every one-shot call like `re.find("\\d+", line)` returns a Result, and example code answers it with `?? panic("bad pattern")` on every line.

That tax teaches a bad habit — panic on a thing that cannot fail — and buries real error handling in noise. Jet already has compile-time machinery for literals; typed literal heads and binary patterns check their strings during compilation. This decision picks whether literal regex patterns join them.
decisions.story: Elena writes a log filter with six small regexes, all literals. Her code has six `?? panic("bad pattern")` arms that can never fire. During review a teammate asks which of the six can actually fail, and nobody can answer without reading the regex engine docs.
decisions.inWild:
// Today: every literal pattern pays the fallible ceremony
ids :: re.find_all("\\bID-\\d{4}\\b", text) ?? panic("bad pattern")
when :: re.find("\\d{2}:\\d{2}", line) ?? panic("bad pattern")
level :: re.find("ERROR|WARN", line) ?? panic("bad pattern")
decisions.detail: Ratification comment (owner, 2026-07-28) corrects option D's spelling: a bare string literal is NEVER implicitly a regex. Regex requires the typed-literal form like other typed string literals; only the HEAD is inferable. In a pattern-typed position the head may be omitted via the leading-dot form: re.find(.{"\\d{2}:\\d{2}"}, line). Explicit Regex.{"..."} works everywhere. Option D text below is amended to match; the pre-correction wording treated bare literals as implicit typed literals and is retired.

options.name: Literal patterns check at compile time
options.detail: When the pattern argument is a string literal, the compiler validates it during compilation. A bad literal is a registered compile error pointing at the exact spot in the pattern. The call then returns the match directly, no Result. Runtime-built patterns keep the fallible path unchanged.
options.technical: Sema validates the literal with the same linear-engine parser; diagnostic carries the pattern offset. The one-shot API becomes infallible only for literal arguments; a non-literal argument keeps today's Result signature via the existing compiled-pattern path.

options.name: A typed literal form Regex.{"..."}
options.detail: Follow the typed-literal-head family: `Regex.{"\\d+"}` builds a checked pattern value at compile time, and the infallible methods live on that value. Consistent with SQL and HTML typed literals, but every call site grows a wrapper, and the one-shot string forms keep their tax.
options.code:
time_pat :: Regex.{"\\d{2}:\\d{2}"}
when :: time_pat.find(line)   // infallible

options.name: Keep runtime Results everywhere
options.detail: All patterns stay fallible regardless of origin. One uniform signature, and the `?? panic` noise stays on every literal call in every program, teaching that panic is normal error handling.
options.code: when :: re.find("\\d{2}:\\d{2}", line) ?? panic("bad pattern")

options.name: Typed literal required; the head is inferable (ratified spelling)
options.detail: A regex is always a typed literal, like other typed string literals — a bare string is never implicitly a pattern. In a pattern-typed positional or named argument, the head may be omitted with the leading-dot form: .{"..."}. The pattern is compile-validated and the call returns the match directly, no ??. The explicit Regex.{"..."} head is the same construct for named reusable pattern values and anywhere inference cannot see the expected type. Runtime-built strings keep the fallible Result path unchanged.
options.technical: One-shot re.* pattern parameters take the pattern type, so .{"..."} resolves against them like enum variant shorthand resolves against an expected enum. Sema validates the literal with the linear-engine parser; the diagnostic carries the offset inside the pattern. Passing a bare string literal where a pattern is expected is a compile error whose fix text shows the .{"..."} form. Non-literal patterns keep todays Result signature via the compiled-pattern path.
options.code:
when :: re.find(.{"\\d{2}:\\d{2}"}, line)   // head inferred — compile-checked, cannot fail

time_pat :: Regex.{"\\d{2}:\\d{2}"}          // explicit head, reusable value
first :: time_pat.find(line)                  // infallible

bad :: re.find(.{"(unclosed"}, line)
// error: this pattern has an unclosed group at position 1

user_pat :: re.compile(user_input) ?? return  // runtime patterns stay fallible

comparisons.note: The ecosystem's answer is a macro or lazy static with unwrap — acknowledged boilerplate that option A removes at the language level.
Regex literals /\d+/ are parsed with the program; a bad literal is a syntax error at load, not a runtime branch.

recommendation.why: The literal case is B with the head inferred, so A and B were never rivals. D gives the beginner path zero ceremony with compile-checked literals, and gives experts one blessed spelling for a named, reusable, checked pattern value — consistency with the typed-literal family for free.

whyNot.reason: Alone it leaves checked patterns anonymous: no blessed spelling for a named, reusable compile-checked pattern value.
Alone it adds a wrapper at every call site and leaves the one-shot string forms — the beginner path — still paying the ?? panic tax.
Keeps teaching panic-on-impossible as normal style, which the audit called out in shipped examples.
