Declarations are package-scoped facts; the checked/unchecked flag is per root per package view (own + dependencies' declared leaves). pkg.jet budgets and #Caps/#Grant arguments resolve against the same names. Tree matching unchanged.

options.name: Mandatory declarations for every leaf
options.detail: Every dotted leaf must be declared before use, everywhere. Maximum typo protection and a complete effect inventory per package. The cost: the invent-a-leaf-inline idiom dies, and every quick script with a custom effect writes a declaration first. The beginner path gains a ceremony step the closed roots were designed to avoid.
options.technical: Same declaration form as A; no per-root freedom. Undeclared leaf anywhere is an error. Requires the prelude to be complete for stdlib leaves before landing, or every existing program breaks at once.

options.name: Status quo: freeform leaves
options.detail: No declarations. Leaves keep minting on use. The docs warn about typos, budgets keep comparing strings, and the effect keyword stays reserved for a future that never gets scheduled. Zero new surface; the security-surface string matching stays.
options.technical: No change. The FS.Raed class of bug remains unfindable by the compiler.
options.code:
fn warm_cache(path: String) =[FS.Raed]=> Bool { ... }
// compiles forever; the budget backstop silently does not apply

comparisons.note: Permissions are strings on the command line; a typo in --allow-net silently over- or under-grants. The cautionary tale for option C on a real security surface.
comparisons.code: deno run --allow-net=api.exmaple.com app.ts   # typo: grant never matches

comparisons.note: Capabilities are handles minted by the host, not strings — misspelling one is impossible by construction. The direction option A moves toward while keeping Jet's readable names.
comparisons.code: // wasi: fd = preopened directory handle; there is no name to misspell

recommendation.why: Optional declarations put typo checking exactly where names carry authority, and the prelude makes the protection free for the roots everyone uses. The one-line app-local leaf survives, so the lightweight idiom and the security backstop stop being enemies.

whyNot.reason: Mandatory declarations tax every quick script and kill the inline leaf idiom, buying little beyond option A once the prelude covers the stdlib roots.
Effect names gate real authority, and string-matched authority with silent minting is how the FS.Raed bug ships and hides for months.

recommendation.tradeoff: The per-root rule has a mixed moment: the first declaration under a root flips that root to checked for the package. A team adding its first declaration must therefore declare the leaves it already uses. The error's fix text lists them.

decisions.title: Marker/trait name-collision law, and the two worst renames
decisions.gist: One naming law so markers and traits stop sharing names by accident — and whether to rename the two worst offenders now.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has two Pascal-case vocabularies that meet in user code. Traits are contracts: `Comparable`, `Printable`. Markers are `#` rules: `#Comparable`, `#Codable`, `#Task`. Some markers *are* trait requests — `#Comparable` on a struct derives the `Comparable` trait, and user derives already work exactly this way (`derive T.Wire` defines it, `#Wire` applies it). For those, sharing the name is correct: the marker is the trait, applied.

The trouble is the names that collide by accident. "Tag" means three unrelated things today. It is the `tag` keyword (erased qualifiers), serde's `#Tag("type")` (the discriminant field a serialized enum writes), and the spec's own name for nested enum groups. `#Task` marks a scheduled entry-point function, while `Task<T>` is the concurrency handle — same word, unrelated machinery, both near any async code. When one word means three things, error messages, docs, and searches all degrade at once.

A naming law fixes the future: a marker that derives trait X is spelled `#X`, and a marker that is not a derive may not take a trait's name. Cheap, permanent, and it turns the marker/trait relationship from a coincidence into a rule the spec can state in one line.

The remaining question is the past: whether to rename serde's `#Tag` and the scheduled `#Task` now. Greenfield policy makes renames ordinary errors with fix text, not migrations — the cost is real but small, and it only shrinks with time in one direction.
decisions.story: Noor searches the docs for "tag" to understand a serialization error. She gets the tag keyword page, the enum-groups section, and the serde marker — three unrelated mechanisms wearing one name. The error she is chasing involves exactly one of them, and nothing in the word tells her which.

options.name: Law + rename the two offenders
options.detail: Adopt the naming law for all future markers. Rename serde's #Tag to #Discriminant (the standard term for the variant field) and the scheduled #Task to #Job (a scheduled unit of work, distinct from the Task handle). Old spellings error with fix text pointing at the new name. "Tag" shrinks to two meanings, and the remaining pair (tag keyword, spec prose for enum groups) is a docs cleanup, not surface.
options.technical: Registry renames with retirement rows (E-code teaching the new spelling). Spec prose for D-TAG1 groups switches to "variant groups" in the same pass. The law lands in the marker-authoring section of the spec and as a registry lint.

options.name: Law only; keep today's names
options.detail: The naming law prevents every future collision, and the three-way "tag" overload plus #Task/Task stay as grandfathered exceptions the docs must forever disambiguate. No respell cost now; the two worst offenders remain the two worst offenders permanently, and each new user meets them.
options.technical: Spec law + registry lint only. Docs add disambiguation boxes to the tag keyword page and the scheduling page.

options.name: No law, no renames
options.detail: Names stay first-come, first-served. Nothing breaks, nothing improves, and the collision count grows with every rule added — each future marker author re-argues naming from scratch in review.
options.technical: Status quo.
options.code:
// next year, plausibly:
#Stream fn ingest() { ... }   // and Stream<T> gains its own #Task problem

comparisons.note: serde contains the same concept inside its own namespace — #[serde(tag = "type")] — so 'tag' never collides with a language keyword. Jet's flat marker plane has no namespace to hide in, which is why the law matters more here.
Annotations live in packages; two @Task annotations coexist by import path. The namespacing Jet chose not to have is exactly what a naming law substitutes for.
comparisons.code:
import org.quartz.Task;    // vs
import myapp.Task;         // collision resolved by package, not by law

recommendation.why: The law costs one spec line and prevents every future collision; the two renames retire the only overloads bad enough that new users meet them in week one. Greenfield policy makes the respell ordinary errors with fix text, and that price only grows if deferred.

whyNot.reason: Grandfathering the two worst offenders means every future reader of docs, errors, and search results pays the disambiguation tax the law was written to end.
Without the law, each new rule re-fights naming in review, and the collision count only goes up.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing examples, snapshots, and docs that use #Tag and #Task respell now. Two retirement diagnostics join the registry and stay for an epoch.

decisions.title: Whole-number literals beside a fixed-width integer
decisions.gist: Whether writing 1 next to a 32-bit number is allowed, or needs its type spelled.
decisions.lesson:
A whole number in Jet is normally an `Int`, which is 64 bits wide. For hardware, file formats, and foreign libraries, Jet also offers a fixed-width menu: `I8`, `I16`, `I32`, `U8`, and the rest. A `U8` holds 0 to 255. An `I32` holds about minus two billion to plus two billion.

These are separate types on purpose. Mixing widths by accident is how programs lose data or wrap around silently. Jet keeps them apart, and conversion is always spelled out.

Now the wrinkle. When you type the numeral `1` in your source, it has no width yet. It is just a number the compiler can see. The compiler must decide what type to give it. That decision is called literal typing.

Jet already makes that decision in one place. If a function takes an `I32` and you call it with `2`, the call compiles. The numeral takes the width the function asked for.

But in arithmetic it does not. Here is the whole problem:

    fn increment(x: I32) => I32 { return x + 1 }

That line is rejected today. The message says `+` cannot combine `I32` and `Int`. The workaround is to write the width on the numeral: `x + I32.{ 1 }`.

So the same numeral is fine as an argument and rejected as an operand. This ballot decides whether that gap closes, and which way.

One thing must not change either way. Jet arithmetic stops the program on overflow at every width, and a value never narrows behind your back. Any option here has to leave that alone.

One more piece of today's behaviour matters for the options below. Two different named widths never mix either. `I32 + I16` is refused, even though every `I16` value fits in an `I32` with nothing lost.
decisions.story:
Priya is writing a driver for a temperature sensor. The chip reports readings as `I32` counts, and her calibration step adds a one-count offset. She writes `raw + 1` and the compiler refuses it. She tries `I32.from_int(1)` and now holds a fallible result to unwrap, for a constant she typed herself.

She has written three spellings of the number one and shipped nothing. A test in this repository, `cffi_named_pure_callback_has_stable_c_symbol`, is written the way Priya expected and fails for the same reason.

options.name: A numeral takes the width of what it sits beside
options.detail: `x + 1` compiles when `x` is an `I32`, and the `1` becomes an `I32`. This is the rule Jet already uses for arguments, now used for operators too. A numeral too large for the width is a compile error naming the width and the limit. Nothing else about the fixed-width menu changes: two named widths still never mix, and no value ever narrows on its own.
options.technical: Expected-type propagation extends from call arguments into binary operand positions. When exactly one side is an untyped integer literal and the other has a concrete integer type, the literal takes that type. The range check runs at compile time against the destination width and reports E0135-class out-of-range. Two concretely typed operands of different widths remain E0109. D-NUMOPS1 trap-on-overflow and S42 separation are untouched, because only compile-time-known literals participate.

options.name: Keep the rule; teach it in the error
options.detail: Nothing about the language changes. `x + 1` stays an error, and the fix text stops saying "make both sides the same type" and starts showing the exact line to type: `x + I32.{ 1 }`. The repository test that assumes otherwise is corrected to spell the width. You always read a numeral's type off the numeral itself.
options.technical: Copy-only change in the E0109 handler: when one operand is an untyped integer literal and the other has a concrete width, render a fix that reproduces the literal in typed-head form. Registered fix text plus UI snapshot per I4. The cffi fixture is rewritten to `x + I32.{ 1 }`.

options.name: Narrow types do their arithmetic at full width
options.detail: Fixed-width values widen to `Int` whenever they take part in arithmetic, and the result narrows back when it is stored somewhere with a declared width. `x + 1` compiles because both sides are `Int` by then. This is how C and Java behave, so it will feel familiar. The cost is that overflow is no longer caught at the width you declared, only where the result lands.
options.technical: Integer promotion on every arithmetic operator: operands below platform Int width widen to Int, the operation runs at Int, and assignment or return into a narrower declared type performs a checked narrowing. This contradicts D-NUMOPS1's trap-at-every-width rule, which would need an explicit amendment. Intermediate results no longer wrap or trap at the declared width.
options.code:
fn increment(x: I32) => I32 { return x + 1 }        // ok, computed at Int width

byte :: U8.{ 200 }
sum: U8 :: byte + 100                                // 300 computed, then trapped at the store
mid :: byte + 100 - 100                              // ok: intermediate 300 never trapped

options.name: Keep the rule; let the tools write the width for you
options.detail: The language keeps its current rule, and the tooling removes the typing. A lint flags a bare numeral beside a fixed-width value, and the formatter and the editor fix rewrite it to `I32.{ 1 }` on save. You type what you meant and the file ends up spelling the width. Every source file still reads with the width visible on the numeral.
options.technical: B's diagnostic plus a machine-applicable fix. The lint fires on an untyped literal operand facing a concrete integer type, and the rewrite inserts the typed head with the same numeral. The formatter applies it only when the literal fits the target width; otherwise the error stands. No sema or lowering change.

options.name: Give the numeral its smallest type, then widen it losslessly
options.detail:
The numeral `1` becomes the narrowest type that holds it, and then widens to the other side when nothing can be lost. `x + 1` works when `x` is an `I32`, because a small unsigned number fits an `I32` exactly.

The catch is that "smallest" cannot be decided without looking at the other side anyway. The narrowest type for `1` is an unsigned byte, and an unsigned byte does not fit in an `I8`. So `x + 1` would be refused when `x` is an `I8`, which is the plainest case there is.

The second catch is the value that does not fit. When `x` is a `U8` and you write `x + 300`, the numeral becomes a 16-bit number, `x` widens to meet it, and the sum is 16 bits wide. The mistake is accepted and the expression quietly changes width.
options.technical: Literal gets the minimal-width type containing its value, then implicit lossless widening applies to the operator. Signedness makes minimal-width ill-defined without the destination: min(1) = U8, and U8 does not widen to I8 or I16-signed-narrow cases cleanly, so a signed destination narrower than the promoted literal is rejected. Out-of-destination-range literals promote the whole expression rather than erroring, deferring the diagnostic to the store and losing the declared width as the trap point.
options.code:
fn increment(x: I32) => I32 { return x + 1 }   // ok: 1 is a byte, widens to I32

fn tick(x: I8) => I8 { return x + 1 }          // refused: a byte does not fit I8

byte :: U8.{ 200 }
sum :: byte + 300                              // accepted, and sum is 16 bits wide
out: U8 :: sum                                 // the error lands here, not at the 300

options.name: Lossless widening is implicit everywhere, numerals included
options.detail:
Any whole number, written or stored, moves on its own into a wider type that holds every one of its values. `x + 1` works. So does `I32 + I16`, giving an `I32`. Nothing ever narrows on its own, and a mix with no common wider type, such as `U8` with `I8`, is still refused.

This answers the whole family of complaints, not just the numeral one, and it removes the conversion ceremony from cases that provably cannot lose anything.

Two costs. The separation of named widths in S42 is deliberate, and this ends it. And floats would then disagree with whole numbers: mixing `F32` with `Float` stays a compile error under the ratified float rule, so the two halves of the numeric menu would follow opposite laws.
options.technical: Implicit widening coercion on integer types ordered by value-set containment: In widens to Im when every value of In is representable in Im. Applies to literals via the same rule after minimal-width assignment. Expression type is the join; no common supertype is E0109. Amends S42 separation. Puts D-FLOATW1 under pressure, since F32-with-Float remains explicit under the ratified float rule, and the two would need reconciling in the spec.

comparisons.note: An integer literal takes the type of its neighbour, and an out-of-range literal is a compile error. This is option A.
comparisons.code:
fn increment(x: i32) -> i32 { x + 1 }   // 1 is an i32
let b: u8 = 200 + 100;                  // error: literal out of range

comparisons.note: Narrow types widen to int for arithmetic and narrow back on assignment. This is option C, including the silent wrap.
comparisons.code:
unsigned char b = 200;
unsigned char s = b + 100;   /* 300 computed as int, then wraps to 44 */

comparisons.note: An untyped constant takes the type it is used at, but two named types never mix, even at the same width.
comparisons.code:
var x int32 = 5
x = x + 1        // ok, 1 is untyped
var y int = 1
x = x + y        // error: mismatched types

comparisons.note: Closest to today's Jet: strict named widths, but literals are typed by context, so the arithmetic case still works.

recommendation.why: Jet already gives a bare numeral the width the context asks for when it is a call argument. Option A applies that same rule to operators, so one law covers both places instead of two.

whyNot.reason: It teaches a rule the language does not actually hold. `increment(2)` compiles and `x + 2` does not, and better wording cannot explain that difference to a beginner.
Arithmetic would stop trapping at the width the programmer declared, which contradicts the ratified trap-on-overflow rule and hides the exact class of bug the fixed-width menu exists to expose.
It leaves the same inconsistency as B and adds a tool that edits the source. A beginner who reads the rewritten line still cannot say why the argument form needed no rewrite.
The narrowest type for a numeral cannot be picked without looking at the other side, so it refuses the plain `I8` case and it accepts an out-of-range numeral by widening the whole expression.
It ends the deliberate separation of named widths and leaves whole numbers and floats under opposite laws, since mixing F32 with Float stays explicit under the ratified float rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: A numeral's type now depends on what sits beside it, so a line read in isolation says less about itself. That is already true of arguments, so the language gains one rule instead of a second exception. A also leaves `I32 + I16` refused, which option F would fix.

decisions.title: Lossless widening covers floats too (amends D-FLOATW1)
decisions.outcome: Implicit lossless widening covers floats as well as whole numbers. An F32 moves on its own into Float, exactly as a narrow whole number moves into a wider whole number; nothing ever narrows on its own. This amends D-FLOATW1, which today makes mixing F32 and Float a compile error with a convert fix-it. Owner words (2026-07-28): "Ok, again we want beginner magic out of the box and full expert control. So let's go with option f but for both int and floats". With D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F this is the ruled surface: one widening law across the whole numeric menu.
decisions.comment: Implicit lossless widening covers floats as well as whole numbers. An F32 moves on its own into Float, exactly as a narrow whole number moves into a wider whole number; nothing ever narrows on its own. This amends D-FLOATW1, which today makes mixing F32 and Float a compile error with a convert fix-it. Owner words (2026-07-28): "Ok, again we want beginner magic out of the box and full expert control. So let's go with option f but for both int and floats". With D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F this is the ruled surface: one widening law across the whole numeric menu.

decisions.title: Does automatic widening cross between whole numbers and decimals
decisions.gist: Whether a whole number can meet a decimal number without you writing a conversion.
decisions.lesson:
You have just ruled that a number widens on its own whenever nothing can be lost. A 16-bit whole number becomes a 32-bit one by itself. An `F32` becomes a `Float` by itself. Nothing ever narrows on its own.

That rule was written about whole numbers meeting whole numbers, and decimals meeting decimals. It does not say what happens when the two kinds meet, and the rule as stated answers that question by accident. Here is why.

A `Float` is a 64-bit decimal. It can hold every 32-bit whole number exactly, all four billion of them. So under a strict reading of "widens when nothing is lost", an `I32` would move into a `Float` on its own.

But `Int`, the everyday whole number, is 64 bits. A 64-bit decimal cannot hold every 64-bit whole number exactly. Above about nine thousand million million, values start rounding. So `Int` would not move into `Float`.

That is the awkward part. Read strictly, the rule gives the automatic conversion to `I32`, which is an expert's type for hardware and foreign libraries, and refuses it to `Int`, which is what every beginner writes. The magic would land on the wrong side.

So this needs a deliberate pick rather than a strict reading. There is also a separate and much smaller case worth noticing: a bare numeral. When you write `price * 3`, the `3` you typed has no kind yet, so letting it become a decimal costs nothing and converts nothing you stored.

One more thing matters, because this is the ground where MATLAB and Python are strong. Both let a whole number meet a decimal with no ceremony at all. Both pay for it in the same place: above the exact range, the value quietly rounds and nothing tells you. Jet can take the convenience without taking the silence, because it already stops the program on whole-number overflow rather than wrapping.
decisions.story:
Ana is pricing an order. She writes `total :: price * 3` where `price` is a decimal, and the compiler tells her to write `3.0` instead. She fixes it and moves on, slightly puzzled, since she meant three either way.

Later she writes `total :: price * quantity`, where `quantity` is a whole number she read from a form. Same message. This time the fix is a real decision, because a whole number and a decimal are genuinely different things and she has to say which she wants.

options.name: Strict reading: cross whenever nothing is lost
options.detail:
One law, applied without exception. A whole number moves into a decimal whenever every one of its values is held exactly. `I32` and everything narrower crosses into `Float`. `Int` does not, because a 64-bit decimal cannot hold every 64-bit whole number.

The law is easy to state and never loses a value. The cost is where the magic lands. The expert's `I32` gets it and the beginner's `Int` does not, which is the opposite of what we are aiming for.
options.technical: Containment ordering extended across the integer and float families. Lossless pairs: I8, I16, I32, U8, U16, U32 into Float; I8, I16, U8, U16 into F32. Lossy and therefore refused: I64, U64, Int into Float; I32, U32 into F32, since F32 is exact only to 2^24. Expression type is the join. Error copy must explain why the narrower type crossed and the default did not.

options.name: Widening stays inside its own kind
options.detail:
Whole numbers widen among whole numbers. Decimals widen among decimals. Crossing between the two is always something you write. One sentence, no exceptions, no cases to remember.

The cost is that the smallest version of the friction stays. Writing `price * 3` is still refused and still asks you for `3.0`, even though the numeral you typed has no kind and converting it loses nothing.
options.technical: Containment ordering applies within the integer family and within the float family only. Cross-kind requires the destination-owned conversion, Float.from_int and its siblings, per D-SHAPE-CONVERT1. The current E0109 cross-kind copy stays as it is, including the "write 2.0 instead of 2" fix line.
options.code:
counts :: I32.{ 1000 }
scale :: 2.5
out :: counts * scale                    // refused
out2 :: Float.from_i32(counts) * scale   // what you write

price :: 19.99
with_fee :: price * 3                    // refused: write 3.0
with_fee2 :: price * 3.0                 // what you write

options.name: Every whole number crosses into a decimal
options.detail:
Any whole number meets any decimal, `Int` included, and the result is a decimal. This is what C, Java, and JavaScript do, so it will feel like arithmetic simply working. The beginner never meets the wall.

The cost is real and it is the kind Jet exists to prevent. Above about nine thousand million million, a whole number quietly loses its exact value on the way into a decimal. That range holds account identifiers, database keys, nanosecond timestamps, and currency held in the smallest unit.
options.technical: Implicit conversion from every integer type to the float type of the other operand. I64, U64, and Int into Float round beyond 2^53, and I32 into F32 rounds beyond 2^24. No diagnostic is possible at the conversion site, because whether a given value rounds is a runtime fact. This is a deliberate exception to the no-silent-loss posture and must be stated as one in the spec.
options.code:
id :: 9007199254740993        // an Int, exact
rate :: 1.0
out :: id * rate              // ok, and out is 9007199254740992.0

// the last digit is gone, and nothing warned you

price :: 19.99
with_fee :: price * 3         // ok
total :: price * quantity     // ok for any whole number

options.name: Numerals cross; stored values do not
options.detail:
A numeral you type takes whichever kind the other side is, so `price * 3` works and means what you wrote. A value you stored as a whole number still needs an explicit conversion to become a decimal.

This puts the magic exactly where nothing is at stake. A numeral has no kind until it is used, so giving it one converts nothing and can lose nothing you were holding. A stored whole number is a thing you chose, and turning it into a decimal stays a decision you write down.
options.technical: Within-kind containment widening as in B, plus untyped numeric literals resolving against the expected type across both families. A literal is checked at compile time for exact representability at the destination, so an out-of-range or inexact literal is a compile error rather than a rounded value. Stored values keep D-SHAPE-CONVERT1's destination-owned conversion. This is the same context rule the ratified numeral ruling already uses.
options.code:
price :: 19.99
with_fee :: price * 3         // ok, 3 is a decimal here

small :: F32.{ 1.5 }
out :: small + 2              // ok, 2 is an F32 here

n :: 5                        // a stored Int
bad :: price * n              // refused: write Float.from_int(n)

counts :: I32.{ 1000 }
bad2 :: counts * price        // refused: it is stored, so you say so

options.name: Everything crosses, and a cross that cannot be proved exact is checked
options.detail:
Any whole number meets any decimal, `Int` included, so the ordinary line works with nothing written. Where the compiler can prove the value survives, as with an `I32` into a `Float`, the conversion is free and nothing is checked.

Where it cannot, as with a 64-bit whole number, the conversion is checked as it happens and stops the program if the value would not survive. You get the convenience of MATLAB and Python, and you never lose an identifier in silence.

Experts opt out per operation, the same way they already opt out of overflow trapping.
options.technical: Cross-kind implicit conversion for every integer and float pair. The compiler proves exactness statically where the source value set is contained in the destination: I8, I16, I32, U8, U16, U32 into Float, and I8, I16, U8, U16 into F32 emit no check. The remaining pairs emit a round-trip check on conversion and trap on mismatch, reusing the D-NUMOPS1 trap path and its per-operation escapes. Numerals keep their compile-time exactness check and never emit a runtime check.
options.code:
counts :: I32.{ 1000 }
scale :: 2.5
out :: counts * scale         // free, an I32 fits a Float exactly

price :: 19.99
qty :: 5
total :: price * qty          // works, and qty is checked as it converts

id :: 9007199254740993        // an Int past the exact range
bad :: id * 1.0               // stops here, instead of quietly dropping a digit

// expert escape, the same shape as the overflow escapes:
fast :: price * approx(qty)   // no check, loss accepted on purpose

comparisons.note: A whole number meets a decimal with no ceremony, and the result is a decimal. Above the exact range the value rounds and nothing is reported.
comparisons.code:
>>> 9007199254740993 + 1.0
9007199254740992.0        # a digit is gone, no warning

>>> 9007199254740993 == 9007199254740992.0
False                     # comparison is exact; only arithmetic loses

comparisons.note: Everything is a double unless you say otherwise. An integer meeting a scalar double takes the integer type, rounds, and saturates. Two different integer classes are an error.
comparisons.code:
>> int8(5) * 2.5
ans = 13            % int8: computed as 12.5, rounded, silently

>> int8(127) + int8(1)
ans = 127           % saturates instead of trapping

>> int8(1) + int16(1)
Error: Integers can only be combined with integers of the same class

comparisons.note: The array world moved toward weak literals in 2024. A written numeral takes the array type, an out-of-range numeral is an error, and stored values promote by a fixed table.
comparisons.code:
>>> np.int8(1) + 1
np.int8(2)                # the numeral is weak, no promotion

>>> np.uint8(1) + 300
OverflowError             # out of range for the dtype

>>> np.int64(1) + np.float32(1)
np.float64(2.0)           # stored values promote to hold both

comparisons.note: Every whole number converts into a decimal on its own, and the loss above the exact range is silent. This is option C.
comparisons.code:
long id = 9007199254740993L;
double d = id;   /* becomes 9007199254740992.0, no warning */

comparisons.note: None of them cross on their own. All three type a written numeral from context, which is option D.

recommendation.why: It is the only option that matches MATLAB and Python for convenience and then beats them where they lose. The ordinary line works with nothing written, and a value that cannot survive the crossing stops the program instead of rounding in silence.

whyNot.reason: It hands the automatic conversion to `I32`, an expert type for hardware and foreign code, and refuses it to `Int`, which is what a beginner writes. The magic lands on the wrong side.
It leaves the smallest and most common friction in place. `price * 3` still asks you to retype the numeral, and `price * quantity` still needs a conversion written out.
This is exactly what MATLAB and Python already do, including the silent rounding above the exact range. Copying it means matching them rather than beating them.
It is safe and it is simple, but it still refuses `price * quantity`, which is the line a MATLAB or Python user writes without thinking about it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A crossing from a 64-bit whole number carries a check and can stop the program. That is the same bargain overflow trapping already makes, and the check is provably unnecessary for `I32` and narrower, so it never appears on those paths.

decisions.title: Widening where several branches produce one value
decisions.gist: Whether a value built from two branches of different number widths takes the wider one, or is refused.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has one default whole-number type, `Int`, plus a sized menu for experts: `I8`, `U8`, `I32`, `U64`, and friends. The number in the name is how many bits of storage a value gets. A `U8` holds 0 through 255. An `Int` holds every whole number up to about nine quintillion.

Widening means moving a value into a type that holds every value the old type could hold. Moving 200 out of a `U8` into an `Int` cannot lose anything, so Jet does it silently. Moving the other direction could lose data, so Jet never does it on its own.

The ratified rule D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F applies that idea in four places: operators, arguments, returns, and assignments. The same rule also gives a written numeral its smallest fitting type first. So the expression `40 + 2` is a `U8`, because 42 fits in one byte.

A join is a fifth place, and the rule never named it. A join happens when one value has more than one producer. In `answer :: if ready -> 40 + 2 else -> 0` there are two producers. The first is a `U8`. The second is a plain `Int`.

Today Jet compares the two branch types for exact equality. It sees `U8` beside `Int` and reports E0124. Nothing was lost and no value was in danger, so the refusal reads as a compiler bug to whoever wrote four ordinary numerals.

The same arithmetic is accepted one line earlier, as a binding or an argument, because those places already follow the widening rule. This decision picks the rule that joins follow.
decisions.story: Priya writes firmware dashboards in Jet. She reads a byte from a sensor register, then picks a retry budget with `budget :: if aggressive -> 8 + 8 else -> 0`. Jet refuses it and tells her the branches produce `U8` and `Int`. She never asked for a byte anywhere; she typed four plain numbers. Her fix is to spell a width she does not care about, in code that had no sized types in it.

options.name: One join law wherever a value has several producers
options.detail: Every place a single value comes from more than one producer follows the widening rule already used by operators. That covers `if` and `switch` value branches, loop values, and the elements of a list. One side widens to the other. Jet never invents a third type and never narrows. Priya's `backoff` becomes an `Int`, because a byte fits in one.
options.technical: Branch and element joins call the same value-set containment join as binary operators: `Type::numeric_join`, one step, no least-upper-bound search. E0124 stays for pairs with no containment, such as `U8` beside `I8`. List element joins reuse the same call, so `[byte, 300]` yields `[U16]` instead of an error. No narrowing path is added.
options.code:
backoff :: if register > 200 -> 40 + 2 else -> 0   // Int
sizes   :: [U8.{1}, 300]                          // [U16]
mixed   :: if flag -> U8.{1} else -> I8.{1}       // still E0124: neither holds the other

options.name: Control-flow branches only
options.detail: `if` and `switch` value branches and loop values widen; collection literals keep exact matching. Priya's code compiles. A list holding a byte beside 300 still fails, so the rule has to be learned twice: once for branches, once for collections.
options.technical: Join applied in `infer_if_value`, `infer_switch_value`, and yielding-loop item typing only. `infer_list_lit` keeps exact-equality element checking and its current E0074/E0124 paths.
options.code:
backoff :: if register > 200 -> 40 + 2 else -> 0   // Int
sizes   :: [U8.{1}, 300]                          // refused: element types differ

options.name: Exact match stays, with a teaching error
options.detail: Branch types must be identical. Priya keeps her error, but the message names the wider type and offers the exact edit that fixes it. The sized menu stays strictly separated once a value has several producers, which is easy to state and easy to predict.
options.technical: E0124 keeps exact equality. The fix line gains the computed widening target and a suggested edit, for example annotating the narrow branch or wrapping it in the destination constructor. No inference change.

options.name: A numeral with no sized neighbour stays Int
options.detail: Drop the smallest-fitting-type step when nothing sized sits beside the numeral. `40 + 2` becomes an `Int`, so Priya's two branches already agree and no join rule is needed. The cost is that a numeral no longer arrives pre-sized, so a byte-typed destination must be reached through the surrounding context instead.
options.technical: `minimal_integer_literal_type` narrows only with a fixed-width peer; with no peer both operands stay `Int`. The expected-type channel must then thread destination width into literal arithmetic, or `accept_u8(1 + 2)` regresses to E0112 since `Int` does not widen to `U8`.

comparisons.note: Branches must already have one type; there is no implicit widening, so the programmer writes a cast.
The conditional operator applies the usual arithmetic conversions, so the result silently takes the wider type.
comparisons.code:
unsigned char b = 200;
int r = flag ? b + 1 : 0;   /* both arms promote to int */

comparisons.note: Literals have no fixed type until the whole expression is solved, so both branches settle on one type together.
comparisons.code:
let b: UInt8 = 200
let r = flag ? Int(b) + 1 : 0   // conversion is explicit; literals adapt

comparisons.note: Branches produce a union of both types, which is a third type Jet deliberately refuses to invent.
comparisons.code: const r = flag ? small : big;   // type is `Small | Big`

recommendation.why: A value with two producers asks the same question as an operator with two operands. One law answers both, so nobody has to learn where the sized menu stops mixing. Priya's numerals stay numerals, and the widening she gets can never lose a value.

whyNot.reason: A list holding a byte beside 300 still fails, so the same pair is legal in a branch and illegal one line later in a list.
It keeps a refusal the writer cannot act on without naming a width their code never mentioned, in the beginner-facing form of `if`.
It reopens the ratified smallest-fitting-type step, and `accept_u8(1 + 2)` compiles today only because that step exists.

recommendation.tradeoff: A branch result becomes width-sensitive: adding a branch can widen the whole value's type. That is acceptable because a widening never loses a value and never reaches for a third type.

decisions.title: What type a numeral takes when nothing typed sits beside it
decisions.gist: Whether plain numbers with no other type around them keep the default whole-number type or shrink to their smallest fit.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's default whole-number type is `Int`. It holds every whole number up to about nine quintillion. Experts can also name an exact size. A `U8` holds 0 through 255. A `U32` holds 0 through about four billion.

Say a written number sits next to a sized value. The ratified rule D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F gives that numeral its smallest fitting type first. Then it widens one side to the other, if nothing can be lost. That is what makes `byte + 1` work when `byte` is a `U8`.

The rule as implemented applies that first step even when there is nothing sized to fit. So in `1000000 * 1000000` each numeral shrinks to a 32-bit unsigned number, because a million fits there. Both sides are then 32-bit, so the product is 32-bit too.

Jet traps on overflow at every width, by ratified design. A million times a million is a trillion, which no 32-bit number holds. The program stops. At compile time it stops the build.

The same first step turns `0 - 17` into unsigned-byte subtraction, because `0` and `17` both fit in a byte. Unsigned bytes cannot hold minus seventeen, so that traps too.

Both expressions are ordinary arithmetic with no sized type anywhere in the source. Today they fail. This decision picks what a numeral means when nothing beside it asks for a size.
decisions.story: Tomas checks a throughput budget in a build script: `comptime budget = 1000000 * 1000000`. The build stops with a compile-time overflow, naming a 32-bit range he never wrote. He tries `0 - 17` in the next line and that stops too. Nothing in his file mentions a fixed width; both are plain numbers, and both would be fine in a pocket calculator.

options.name: A numeral with no sized neighbour is an Int
options.detail: The smallest-fit step only runs when something sized sits beside the numeral, which is the case it was designed for. With no sized neighbour, numerals keep the default `Int`. Tomas gets a trillion and minus seventeen. `byte + 1` still works, because `byte` is the neighbour that asks for a byte.
options.technical: `minimal_integer_literal_type` narrows only when the peer operand resolves to a fixed-width integer; with no peer both operands stay `Int`. Amends D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F's "after minimal-width assignment" clause to "after minimal-width assignment against a typed peer". Destination-driven cases keep working through the expected-type channel: a `U8` parameter or annotation still pushes `U8` into the literals.
options.code:
budget :: 1000000 * 1000000   // Int, 1000000000000
offset :: 0 - 17              // Int, -17

fn tick(byte: U8) => U8 { return byte + 1 }   // unchanged
fn take_u8(value: U8) {}
take_u8(1 + 2)                // still U8: the parameter asks for it

options.name: Keep smallest-fit, and size the result to the value
options.detail: Numerals still shrink, but a numeral-only expression is folded at compile time and typed by its *result*, not its inputs. A trillion becomes a 64-bit number; minus seventeen becomes signed. Nothing traps, and small constants stay small, which matters for packed data and hardware registers.
options.technical: Constant-fold integer expressions whose leaves are all bare numerals, then assign the minimal type containing the folded result (signed when negative). Requires the fold to run before type assignment in sema, and a rule for what happens when a folded constant meets a sized peer later in the expression tree.
options.code:
budget :: 1000000 * 1000000   // folds to 1000000000000, takes I64
offset :: 0 - 17              // folds to -17, takes I8
mask   :: 255 & 15            // folds to 15, takes U8

options.name: Keep today's rule and refuse instead of trapping
options.detail: Numerals keep shrinking. An expression the compiler can prove overflows its own inferred width becomes a compile error naming that width and value, not a run-time trap. Tomas still cannot write his multiplication, but he learns exactly which width was chosen and why.
options.technical: Constant-evaluate numeral-only integer expressions during checking and report a registered diagnostic naming the inferred width, the computed value, and the containing range, with a fix-it that annotates a wider type. The trap stays for values that are not compile-time known.

options.name: Numerals are always Int; sized types are reached only by conversion
options.detail: Drop smallest-fit entirely. Every numeral is an `Int`, and a sized value comes from its own constructor. Simplest rule in the language, and the beginner never meets a width. The cost falls on expert code: `byte + 1` needs the numeral spelled as a byte.
options.technical: Remove literal narrowing; `Int` never widens to a narrower type, so mixed expressions with sized operands need an explicit constructor or conversion. Reverts the part of D-INTLIT-WIDTH1=F that closed the original `x + 1` complaint, so that ergonomics loss returns.

comparisons.note: An unsuffixed integer literal defaults to `i32` when nothing constrains it, and constant overflow is a deny-by-default compile error.
comparisons.code:
let x = 1000000 * 1000000;   // error: this arithmetic operation will overflow
let y = 0 - 17;              // fine: both are i32

comparisons.note: Untyped constants are arbitrary precision until they need a type, so a constant product cannot overflow on the way.
comparisons.code: const budget = 1000000 * 1000000   // exact; only assignment to a sized type can fail

comparisons.note: Literals default to `Int` (64-bit) unless context asks otherwise, and overflow traps at run time.
comparisons.code:
let budget = 1_000_000 * 1_000_000   // Int, fine
let offset = 0 - 17                  // Int, -17

comparisons.note: Integer promotion pulls small operands up to `int` before arithmetic, so byte-sized inputs never do byte-sized math.
comparisons.code:
unsigned char a = 0, b = 17;
int d = a - b;   /* -17: both promote to int first */

recommendation.why: It fixes the broken case by narrowing the rule to the case it was written for: a numeral takes a size from a neighbour that has one. With no neighbour there is nothing to match, and the language default is the honest answer. Tomas's arithmetic works and expert `byte + 1` is untouched.

whyNot.reason: It types an expression by its answer, so the same numerals mean different widths depending on the arithmetic around them, and folding has to precede checking.
It turns ordinary arithmetic into a compile error and asks the writer to annotate around a width the compiler invented.
It reopens the `x + 1` complaint that D-INTLIT-WIDTH1 was ratified to close, and puts conversion ceremony back into every expert expression.

recommendation.tradeoff: A numeral-only expression is `Int`-wide even when its values are tiny, so packed or register-sized code must name its width in the destination. That is acceptable because the destination is exactly where a width belongs.

decisions.title: Distributed compare if + Void-or-value tables
decisions.gist: How multi-arm if tables compare a subject and produce a value.
decisions.lesson:
An if table picks one arm. Today Jet writes if subject == { value -> body }. The == is a marker that means each arm head is compared to the subject.

You often want other comparisons too. Writing if n < { 16 -> 0 32 -> 1 } should mean n < 16, then n < 32, without repeating n each time. That is a distributed compare: the operator before the brace applies to every bare arm value.

A bar | joins several values for the same arm (a union). And and or (&& and ||) add extra true or false checks on that arm.

The same table should work as a statement or as a value. When arms give values of one type, the if expression has that type. When arms only do work, the type is Void.
decisions.story: User is writing a browser hex color helper. He wants return if n < { 16 -> 0 ... } and return if n == { 0 -> "0" ... } in the same style as statement tables, and he needs that shape to compile for the web target.

options.name: All comparisons distribute; tables yield Void or a value
options.detail: Any comparison can sit before the brace. A bare arm value becomes subject OP value. Bar joins those with or. And and or combine extra checks. The same spelling works in expressions. Web must emit value if.
options.technical: Amend D-IF3/D-MATCHARM2/S68. Marker ops: == != < > <= >=. arm_atom_to_cond(subject, value, op). Drop E0328. parse_if_expr accepts subject OP { value-arms }. Desugar to Expr::If chain. Pattern heads remain ==-only.

options.name: Keep == only; rewrite with full predicates
options.detail: No new marker ops. Writers repeat the subject on every arm as a full boolean. Expression dispatch stays blocked.

options.name: Distribute comparisons only in statements
options.detail: Allow if n < { … } as a statement, but keep expression position on subjectless or two-arm forms only.

comparisons.note: case / when uses ===; no distributed < table.
when can be an expression; comparisons are written in full on each branch.

recommendation.why: One table spelling for statements and values matches how people already write == dispatch, and distributed compares remove repeated subjects without a second mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Forces repeated subjects and leaves the showcase expression form illegal.
Splits statement and expression surfaces, so return if n < { … } still fails.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors must learn that bar always means or of subject OP atom, including for !=, which is rarely useful with multiple alternates.

Method API (Constraint.gte/eq, Layout.h/v/add/value/suggest) remains desugar underlayment. self.width vivifies as the binding’s container box (same box id as binding name). GATE 1/2 unchanged.

decisions.title: comptime retired: implicit folding + #Known marker; 'when' rejected
decisions.outcome: Retire the comptime keyword. Beginner default is implicit compile-time folding (no keyword). The explicit demand form is the marker-plane #Known. 'when' is rejected as the comptime-if replacement; the conditional's exact spelling remains open and needs a follow-up owner confirmation before parser work. Owner words (2026-07-28): 'Ok let's go with known as a keyword. NO to using when instead of comptime if. I guess if markers are the more coherent system, let's go with that then' and 'I REALLY LIKE how the no keyword plays into our philosophy of beginner magic out of the box and full expert control.'

decisions.title: Stable identity for UI nodes across re-renders
decisions.gist: How a UI node keeps the same identity when the tree is rebuilt on each render.
decisions.lesson:
A UI tree is a picture of the screen right now. Many backends rebuild that picture on every update. Click handlers hang on real screen objects (DOM nodes, GTK widgets). If the picture is new but the identity is lost, the click dies or the handler is attached twice.

Identity is the answer to: which screen object is the same logical button as last time? One common answer is the path in the tree (first child of the root row, and so on). Another answer is an explicit key the author writes on the node. A third answer mixes both: use the path by default, and let a key override when the author moves nodes around.

Jet's DOM runtime already stores painted boxes by render path in jetDomBoxRegistry. GTK already has an on_click that takes a numeric id. The portable on_click design must pick one identity rule that every backend can honor, so a button keeps its handler after a redraw.
decisions.story: Maya ships a counter button on the web demo. Each click updates a signal and re-renders the tree. After the second click the button looks fine, but the handler is gone — or worse, every click fires three times because each render added another listener.

options.name: Render path is identity
options.detail: The path in the tree names the node. No extra key in beginner code. Moving a node to a new path is a new node. Authors who reorder lists can get surprising remounts.
options.technical: Keep jetDomBoxRegistry keyed by render path. Portable on_click attaches by path. GTK maps path (or a derived stable i64) into its existing id. No new syntax.

options.name: Explicit key on every interactive node
options.detail: Authors always write a key for nodes with handlers. Reorders keep the handler. Beginners must learn a key before their first click works well. Forgetting a key is an error or a silent path fallback — either costs ceremony.
options.technical: New optional or required key field on interactive UI nodes. Registry keys by author key. Duplicate keys are a diagnostic.
options.code:
ui.button("Save", key: "save", on_click: () => save())
// Reorder siblings; handler stays on key "save".

options.name: Path by default; optional key override
options.detail: Simple screens need no key. Lists and reorders opt into a key. One mechanism, two spellings of identity. Cost: authors must know when the default path is not enough.
options.technical: Registry key = author key if present, else render path. Duplicate keys diagnostic. Matches common React-style practice without requiring keys everywhere.
options.code:
ui.button("Save", on_click: () => save())
ui.for(items, (item) =>
  ui.button(item.name, key: item.id, on_click: () => open(item.id))
)

options.name: Backend-local identity; no portable rule
options.detail: Each backend keeps its own rule. Portable on_click cannot promise the same remount behavior. Authors debug web and GTK separately. Breaks the point of one portable handler.
options.technical: Document divergence. Rejected by I8 / D-WEB-CLICK-OWN1 destination B unless owner accepts non-portable remounts.

comparisons.note: Reconciles by position; keys opt in for lists.
Element identity follows Element tree; keys preserve State across moves.
comparisons.code:
ElevatedButton(onPressed: save, child: Text('Save'))
ListView(children: items.map((i) =>
  ElevatedButton(key: ValueKey(i.id), onPressed: () => open(i.id), ...)).toList())

recommendation.why: Beginners keep zero ceremony. List and reorder cases get an explicit key without a second click mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Reordered lists remount by path and surprise authors who did not ask for that.
Forces a key on every click before a beginner needs list identity.
Gives up portable click lifetime, which this card exists to deliver.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors must learn when to add a key. That cost is paid only when path identity is wrong, not on the first button.

decisions.title: How a browser click reaches Jet handler code
decisions.gist: How a DOM click reaches Jet handler code with production speed, safety, and expert control.
decisions.lesson:
Jet UI must win on the web the same way it wins on the desktop. A button click starts in the browser. The handler runs as Jet code inside WebAssembly.

That crossing must be fast enough for dense UIs: editors, games, trading boards, and design tools. It must be safe when a node unmounts mid-click. Authors must write almost nothing for the common case.

Stable node identity is already decided (path by default, optional key). This ballot picks the pipe under that identity: how JavaScript names the Jet handler and when the handler runs.

Beginner magic means on_click on the node just works. Expert control means you can opt into ordered scheduling, filters, and batching without a second event system.
decisions.story: Priya ships a collaborative editor with thousands of interactive nodes. A Save click must hit the Jet handler in microseconds. A list reorder must not call a freed handler. Experts on her team also need clicks ordered with animation frames. A demo-only bind will not carry that product.

options.name: Handler-id table only
options.detail: Each on_click gets a numeric slot. JavaScript calls one wasm export with that id. Fast and clear. No built-in path to ordered batching with the rest of the UI scheduler.
options.technical: DomRuntime listener → jet_ui_dispatch(id, event). Unmount clears the slot. Matches GTK id-shaped handlers.
options.code:
element.addEventListener("click", () => wasm.jet_ui_dispatch(id, ev))
// missing slot → no-op

options.name: Raw closure handle only
options.detail: JavaScript holds an opaque wasm callable. Direct, but easy to leave stale after remount. Weak audit story for a market-facing runtime.
options.technical: externref / callable export. Drop must clear listener and handle together.
options.code: element.addEventListener("click", (ev) => wasmCb(normalize(ev)))

options.name: Selector bind (web.on) only
options.detail: Portable on_click is sugar over CSS selectors. Fragile under dense trees. Not acceptable as the long-term web channel for a language that aims to replace everything.
options.technical: Generated selectors; collisions on duplicates.
options.code:
ui.button("Save", on_click: () => save())
// lowers to web.on("#jet-el-12", "click", …)

options.name: Queue-only dispatch
options.detail: Every click is enqueued and drained later. Great for ordering. Adds latency and machinery to the default button path.
options.technical: JS posts {kind, nodeId}; Jet scheduler invokes handlers.
options.code:
queue.push({ kind: "click", target: nodeId })
// drain loop runs on_click later

options.name: Node-keyed slots by default; expert scheduler opt-in
options.detail: Default path: O(1) dispatch by stable node identity into a handler slot table. Unmount clears the slot. Beginners only write on_click. Experts opt the same handlers into the shared UI event scheduler for ordering, coalescing, and frame alignment — one mechanism, two strengths.
options.technical: Hot path: jet_ui_dispatch(node_or_handler_id, event) sync. Slot free on unmount/remount. Expert: ui.events.schedule / backend policy routes selected events through the shared drain without a second author-facing API. Never selector identity. Full I9 meaning across web and native backends that share the slot model.

comparisons.note: Synthetic events + delegation; production apps still need stable identity and careful unmount.
Events become messages on a queue — strong ordering, always async relative to the DOM callback.
Closures need explicit drop; stale handles are a real class of bugs.

recommendation.why: E is built for real products: microsecond default clicks, safe unmount, zero beginner ceremony, and expert scheduling without a second event system. It matches Jet's beginner-magic / expert-control law and the already-ratified stable node identity.

whyNot.reason: Fast table alone leaves experts without a first-class ordered path.
Opaque handles are the stale-handle footgun at scale.
Selector identity will not dominate dense, dynamic UIs.
Queue-only taxes every click with latency the default path does not need.

recommendation.tradeoff: The runtime must implement both the hot slot path and the opt-in scheduler route cleanly. That cost buys one author-facing model that can win demos and trading floors.

hybrid.synthesis: E keeps A's O(1) table as the default and harvests D's queue only where experts ask for ordered drain.

harvest.aspect: Numeric/slot dispatch is simple and fast.
harvest.use: Default hot path.

harvest.aspect: Queued drain gives ordering and batching.
harvest.use: Expert opt-in on the same handlers.

harvest.aspect: Author spelling stays on_click on the node.
harvest.use: Keep the portable spelling; drop selector identity.

decisions.title: Which UI events every backend must support
decisions.gist: Which events portable UI nodes support, and what a backend does when it cannot produce one.
decisions.lesson:
A click is not the only UI event. Hover, focus, text input, and key repeat exist on some devices and not on others. A terminal UI may have enter and focus-like selection. It may never have hover. A phone may have tap and long-press.

Portable handlers need a declared set. For each event outside a backend's power, the language needs a rule: error at build time, ignore at run time, or map to a cousin event. Without that rule, authors write on_hover and only find the gap on the device that lacks it.
decisions.story: Priya writes on_click and on_hover for a toolbar. It feels great in the browser. On the terminal backend the hover handler never runs, and she thinks her logic is wrong. She needs a clear rule up front.

options.name: Small core only: click (and submit-like activate)
options.detail: Every backend must support click/activate. Other events stay backend-specific modules (web.on, gtk.…). Portable code stays honest. Authors leave the portable layer for rich events.
options.technical: Portable node fields: on_click (and maybe on_activate). Hover/focus/key are not portable fields. Document backend modules for the rest.
options.code:
ui.button("Go", on_click: () => go())
// hover stays: web.on(sel, "mouseenter", ...)

options.name: Wide portable set; missing events are compile errors
options.detail: Authors can write many on_* fields. Building for a backend that cannot produce one fails with a teaching diagnostic. Safest. Forces ifdef-like splits or feature gates per target.
options.technical: Sema checks target backend capability matrix. Unsupported handler → diagnostic with snapshot.
options.code:
ui.button("Go", on_hover: () => hint())
// jet build --target terminal → error: hover not supported on terminal

options.name: Wide portable set; missing events no-op at runtime
options.detail: Same spelling everywhere. Unsupported handlers never fire. Easy to write once. Easy to ship a dead hover on terminal with no warning.
options.technical: Backend registers only capabilities it has. Others attach as no-ops. Optional runtime warning under a debug flag.
options.code:
ui.button("Go", on_hover: () => hint())
// terminal: builds clean; hint() never runs

options.name: Core click plus capability traits per backend
options.detail: Portable core is click. Rich events live behind explicit backend capability traits or target packages the author imports. Expert control stays visible. Beginners see one click path.
options.technical: on_click on ui.*. Hover etc. require importing ui.web or a Hoverable capability in scope. I8: one click mechanism; extras are opt-in modules.
options.code:
use ui.web.hover
ui.button("Go", on_click: () => go(), on_hover: () => hint())

comparisons.note: Gesture detectors vary by platform; some no-op or are absent on desktop vs mobile.
Modifiers apply widely; unsupported ones degrade per platform.
comparisons.code:
Button("Go", action: go)
  .onHover { hovering in showHint(hovering) }

recommendation.why: Keeps portable click small and safe, and makes richer events an explicit opt-in instead of a silent or noisy surprise.

whyNot.reason: Pushes all non-click events back into ad hoc web.on-style binds forever.
Forces target splits early for common hover/focus experiments.
Silent no-ops hide bugs when a backend cannot produce the event.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors import a capability module for rich events. That ceremony protects the beginner default.

decisions.title: Portable on_click identity, dispatch, and event set
decisions.gist: How portable on_click names widgets, reaches Jet from the host, and which events every backend must honor.
decisions.lesson: A UI backend paints a tree of nodes. Click handlers need a stable node id across re-renders. They also need a channel from the host into Jet code. A closed event list keeps missing events honest. Portable on_click is one method on every backend. Backends that cannot produce an event leave that handler unbound.
decisions.story: Maya ships a counter demo for web and desktop. She wants one `app.on_click(btn, …)` line. Today web uses `web.on("#btn", "click", …)` while GTK uses widget ids — she cannot teach one story.
decisions.inWild: ui_web_click.jet still binds with web.on while ui_native_linux.jet uses on_click. Without identity and dispatch law, a portable respell either breaks re-render or invents a second click API.

options.name: DOM-only: CSS selectors + JS bridge forever
options.detail: Keep web.on selectors as the web identity; GTK keeps integer ids. Document the split. Fast for web, no portable surface.
options.technical: No shared on_click. Rejects D-WEB-CLICK-OWN1=D destination B.
options.code: web.on("#btn", "click", ev => count.set(count.get() + 1))

options.name: Stable node id + host callback table + closed Click set
options.detail: Every backend node carries a stable i64 id across reconcile. Hosts call into a registered Jet callback table by that id. The portable set is Click (and later Focus/Input as separate cards). A backend that cannot emit Click leaves on_click unbound and documents it — never fakes clicks.
options.technical: Identity: JetUiNode.id assigned at construction, preserved on reconcile match (same key path as GTK). Dispatch: host → extern "C"/wasm import → look up id → invoke Fn(). Event set v1: Click only on on_click; unknown host events ignored. Terminal/null backends: on_click registers but never fires unless the backend can produce Click.
options.code:
app.on_click(btn, () => count.set(count.get() + 1))
// same on GtkBackend, web backend, and future mobile

options.name: String keys everywhere, free-form event names
options.detail: Identity is an author string; events are arbitrary strings. Maximum flexibility. Typo-prone; breaks I8 closed surfaces.
options.code: app.on("save-btn", "click", …)

options.name: Hybrid: B identity/dispatch + Click-only v1 + explicit unsupported
options.detail: Same as B, and each backend publishes which portable events it supports. Unsupported on_click on a headless null backend is a documented no-op with a debug trace, not a type error — beginners keep one API; experts query capability.
options.technical: Harvest A’s honesty about host limits and C’s desire for discoverability without free-form strings. Capability query is optional follow-up; v1 law is B plus no-op semantics for unsupported backends.
options.code:
backend.on_click(btn, handler)  // Click only
// Terminal without pointer: register succeeds; handler never runs

comparisons.note: Stable keys across reconcile; synthetic events.
Widget pointers / ids for signal connect.
addEventListener + element identity.

recommendation.why: D keeps one portable on_click (D-WEB-CLICK-OWN1=B destination), stable ids, and a closed Click set while staying honest when a backend cannot fire.

whyNot.reason: Leaves the web/desktop fork that the parent ruling already rejected.
Almost complete; D only adds explicit unsupported/no-op honesty for headless backends.
Free-form strings fight I8 and turn typos into runtime misses.

recommendation.tradeoff: Headless demos that call on_click will compile but never fire until the backend can produce Click — that must be documented in the example.

hybrid.synthesis: D is B’s identity and dispatch with A’s honesty about host limits, without C’s open strings.

harvest.use: Unsupported backend = no-op, not a fake event.
Core portable law.
Closed enum + docs, not free-form names.

decisions.title: Who guarantees the working memory the compiler needs for nested code
decisions.gist: What happens when a deeply nested program runs the compiler out of its scratch memory.
decisions.lesson:
A running program keeps a stack: a block of memory where each active function call parks its local values. Every call pushes a frame; every return pops one. The block has a fixed size, chosen when the thread starts.

On Linux the first thread of a process gets about 8 megabytes. A thread created later gets 2 megabytes by default. Nothing warns you which one you are on.

Compilers walk nested code by calling themselves. A list inside a call inside an `if` inside a lambda becomes one nested chain of calls, so nesting in the source turns into depth on the stack. Each of Jet's checking frames is large, because it carries types, spans, and scope maps.

When the frames no longer fit, the operating system stops the process immediately. There is no error to catch and no diagnostic to print. The output is one line: `fatal runtime error: stack overflow`. That is a crash, not a refusal.

Jet hits this today. The `jet` binary survives because it checks on the process's first thread, with 8 megabytes. Calling `jet::compile` from a 2-megabyte worker thread aborts on a ten-line program. Our own test suite trips it, and one test file already sets a bigger stack by hand to dodge it.

That matters beyond tests. An editor server, a build server, or any embedder calls the compiler from a pool thread. Jet promises that every refusal is a diagnostic with a code and a fix. A crash keeps that promise only by luck, depending on which thread called in.
decisions.story: Marcus runs a build server that embeds the Jet compiler and answers requests on a thread pool. One generated file with deeply nested data takes the whole server process down. His log shows a single line about a stack overflow: no file, no line, no error code, and no way to tell the user what to fix. Locally the same file compiles, because his terminal runs the compiler on the process's first thread.

options.name: The compiler owns its stack and names a depth limit
options.detail: `jet::compile` runs the checking passes on a thread it creates itself, with a stack large enough for realistic code. Past a published nesting limit it stops and reports an ordinary diagnostic naming the limit. Every caller is safe without configuring anything, and absurdly nested input gets a product error instead of a crash.
options.technical: The public entry points spawn one worker with an explicit stack size (32 MiB) and join it, so callers keep the current synchronous signature. Sema and the TIR evaluator keep a depth counter beside the existing fuel counter and emit a registered diagnostic past the limit, with a UI snapshot. The limit is documented in docs/spec/diagnostics.md and chosen to sit well inside the reserved stack.

options.name: Grow the stack on demand
options.detail: The recursive passes check how much room is left before descending, and add a fresh chunk of memory when it runs low. Depth is then bounded by available memory rather than a fixed reservation, so no realistic program is refused and no memory is reserved up front.
options.technical: Adds a stack-probing dependency (the `stacker` crate, as rustc uses) or a hand-rolled equivalent, called at each recursive entry in sema, TIR lowering, and the evaluator. Requires a new external dependency in a compiler seam crate, which I6 gates on owner approval. Missed call sites still crash, so coverage must be audited.

options.name: Publish a depth limit and refuse past it
options.detail: Keep whatever stack the caller happens to have, and count nesting instead. Past a conservative published limit the compiler reports a diagnostic. The limit must be low enough to be safe on a 2-megabyte thread, so some legal deeply nested code is refused on every platform to protect the smallest case.
options.technical: Depth counter and registered diagnostic as in A, with the limit derived from the 2 MiB worst case rather than a reserved stack. No thread spawning, no new dependency. Frame sizes then become a hard product constraint: any frame growth lowers the limit users see.
options.code:
// same diagnostic as A, but the ceiling is much lower
// Error [E0xxx]: this code nests 70 levels deep; the limit is 64

options.name: Callers configure the stack
options.detail: Document that the compiler needs a large stack, and let each caller arrange it. Our test harness and any embedder set the size themselves. Nothing changes inside the compiler, and a caller who misses the note gets today's crash.
options.technical: Document a minimum thread stack in docs/spec/architecture.md; set RUST_MIN_STACK in the test harness and spawn sized threads in the CLI, LSP, and build paths. The failure stays an abort with no diagnostic, and the contract lives only in prose.
options.code:
# test harness and embedders opt in by hand
RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432 cargo test

std::thread::Builder::new()
    .stack_size(32 * 1024 * 1024)
    .spawn(|| jet::compile(source))?;

comparisons.note: Runs the compiler on a spawned thread with a large explicit stack, and additionally grows the stack on deep recursion.
comparisons.code:
// rustc_interface: spawn with an 8 MiB (or RUST_MIN_STACK) stack, then
// ensure_sufficient_stack(|| ...) around deeply recursive work

comparisons.note: Reserves a large stack and enforces a published bracket-depth limit, reporting a normal compiler error past it.
comparisons.code:
// error: bracket nesting level exceeded maximum of 256
//   note: use -fbracket-depth=N to increase maximum nesting level

comparisons.note: Counts recursion instead of trusting the stack, and raises a catchable error at a documented limit.
comparisons.code:
>>> sys.setrecursionlimit(3000)
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

comparisons.note: Goroutine stacks start tiny and grow automatically, so depth is bounded by memory, and a runaway hits a documented 1 GB ceiling.

recommendation.why: It makes the guarantee the compiler's own promise instead of the caller's homework, so Marcus's server, the editor, and the test suite are all safe by default. Nested input past the limit becomes a diagnostic with a code and a fix, which is what every other refusal in Jet already is.

whyNot.reason: It needs a new external dependency inside a compiler seam crate, and one missed recursive call site still aborts the process.
Sizing the limit for a 2-megabyte thread refuses code that fits comfortably everywhere else, and every frame that grows lowers it again.
It leaves a crash reachable from any caller who never reads the note, and prose cannot enforce a memory contract.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each compile pays one thread spawn and reserves address space it usually will not touch. That is acceptable because the reservation is virtual until used, and one spawn is invisible next to checking a program.

decisions.title: Fence spelling and expression entries
decisions.outcome: Respell the D-EACH1 fence as symmetric $[ ... ]$ (open $[, close ]$). Expression-position fences accept arbitrary expression entries separated by top-level commas; binding fences still require plain names. Statement fanout semantics unchanged: one statement copy per entry, lock-step across fences.
decisions.comment: Respell the D-EACH1 fence as symmetric $[ ... ]$ (open $[, close ]$). Expression-position fences accept arbitrary expression entries separated by top-level commas; binding fences still require plain names. Statement fanout semantics unchanged: one statement copy per entry, lock-step across fences.

decisions.title: Variadic newline print
decisions.outcome: print and eprint accept one or more arguments; each argument renders on its own line (print(a, b) == print(a); print(b)). Single-line composition stays with interpolation.
decisions.comment: print and eprint accept one or more arguments; each argument renders on its own line (print(a, b) == print(a); print(b)). Single-line composition stays with interpolation.

decisions.title: Task group helper set
decisions.outcome: Ship the full ergonomic group set: tasks.spawn_group(n, fn) => [Task<T>] plus list methods join_all/wait_all (consume), detach_all (consume), cancel_all, pause_all, resume_all (borrow). Beginner magic first: handles.cancel_all() must work without writing a loop.
decisions.comment: Ship the full ergonomic group set: tasks.spawn_group(n, fn) => [Task<T>] plus list methods join_all/wait_all (consume), detach_all (consume), cancel_all, pause_all, resume_all (borrow). Beginner magic first: handles.cancel_all() must work without writing a loop.

decisions.title: Remove S75 fan-out operator
decisions.outcome: Remove (not deprecate) the S75 fan-out operator f.[a, b, c] and its E0961/E0962 diagnostics. Keep S76 [T#N] fixed-size lists and their typed literal heads.
decisions.comment: Remove (not deprecate) the S75 fan-out operator f.[a, b, c] and its E0961/E0962 diagnostics. Keep S76 [T#N] fixed-size lists and their typed literal heads.

decisions.title: Labeling a loop that produces no value
decisions.gist: How to name a pure-effect loop so `break(name)` and `next(name)` can target it.
decisions.lesson:
When loops nest, `break` and `next` normally act on the innermost one. To act on an outer loop instead, that loop needs a name: `break(outer)` exits the loop named `outer`.

Today a loop gets its name from binding syntax. Writing `found :: loop { … }` does two jobs at once: it declares that the loop's break payload lands in `found`, and it makes `found` a target for `break` and `next`. When the loop produces a value, this is elegant — the name of the destination is the name of the loop.

The wrinkle appears with loops that produce nothing. A logging sweep or a retry driver is pure effect; it has no value to bind. To label it today you must still write `sweep :: loop { … }`, which binds the empty value Void to `sweep`. The binding is harmless but dishonest: it looks like data flow and is really only a control label.

The question is whether that dishonesty matters enough to give loops a second way to get a name, or whether one slightly awkward spelling is better than two mechanisms.
decisions.story: Marco writes a crawler: an outer loop over sites, an inner loop over pages. When a site returns a rate-limit error he wants `next(sites)` — skip to the next site. His outer loop returns nothing, so to name it he writes `sites :: loop site; queue { … }` and now has a binding `sites` that holds Void forever. His reviewer asks what `sites` stores. The honest answer is: nothing, it exists only so `next` can aim at it.

options.name: Keep binding-as-label, accept the Void binding
options.detail: No change. A labeled effect loop binds Void to its name. One mechanism covers both value loops and labels; the cost is an occasional binding that exists only for control. The compiler already accepts it and the unused Void value is inert.
options.technical: No grammar or sema change. Optionally suppress unused-binding lints for Void-typed loop bindings that are used as control targets.

options.name: Head label only: loop(name)
options.detail: A loop is named in its head, mirroring how exits already target: `loop(sites) site; queue { … }`. The binding form stops being a control target — `found :: loop` still binds the payload, but `break(found)` no longer resolves to it; you would write `found :: loop(search) { break(search, -1) }`. One naming mechanism, but value loops that want a targeted break now carry both a binding and a label.
options.technical: Grammar: optional `( name )` immediately after KW_LOOP. Loop names move to a control-label namespace; D-LOOPLABEL3's binding-name targeting is retired.

options.name: Both: binding names value loops, head label for effect loops
options.detail: Value loops keep the elegant `found :: loop { break(found, -1) }`. Effect loops gain `loop(sites) …` so nobody binds Void as a label. Every loop has exactly one natural spelling, but the language now has two labeling mechanisms and style guides must say when each applies.
options.code:
found :: loop { break(found, -1) }   // value loop: binding is the label
loop(sites) site; queue {             // effect loop: head label
    next(sites)
}
options.technical: Both mechanisms feed one label namespace; a loop with both a binding and a head label is an error to keep targeting unambiguous.

comparisons.note: Python has no labeled break at all. Breaking out of nested loops requires a flag variable, an exception, or refactoring into a function — a long-standing, frequently-cited pain point. Any of these options beats it.
Rust labels at the head with a lifetime-style tick: `'outer: for … { break 'outer; }`. Labels live in their own namespace and never pretend to be bindings.
JavaScript uses statement labels (`sites: for (…)`), also purely in a label namespace. They work but read as an obscure corner because nothing else in the language uses labels.

recommendation.why: One mechanism stays one mechanism. The Void binding is rare, inert, and two characters of noise; both alternatives buy honesty in that rare case by adding a second naming plane that every reader must then learn. Naming the destination and the loop with one word is also a genuinely good idea — it reads as 'exit toward found' — and both alternatives weaken it.

whyNot.reason: It taxes the common elegant case (value loops with targeted breaks now need a binding plus a separate label) to fix the rare awkward one.
Two labeling spellings for one concept is exactly the surface split I8 forbids, and every style discussion about which to use costs more than the Void binding ever did.

recommendation.tradeoff: Labeled pure-effect loops keep binding Void to a name that is only a control target. That is accepted as the cheapest honest price for a single naming mechanism; a lint exemption keeps the binding quiet.

decisions.title: One loop header shape carries two different meanings
decisions.gist: Whether the three-slot loop header keeps two meanings, loses one, or is redesigned so one shape always means one thing.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has one loop keyword. The header is what sits between `loop` and the body, and semicolons separate its parts.

Start from what repetition is. Every loop has a driver: run forever, run while a test holds, or run once per item that a source hands you. Jet spells these `loop { … }`, `loop n > 0 …`, and `loop i; 0..10 …`.
