The C-style counter — `loop i := 0; i < n; i++` — is not a fourth driver. It is a test-driven loop plus two conveniences. The counter variable lives only inside the loop, and the advance runs on every path back to the test.

Now the shape problem. A surface is honest when one shape always means one thing. Today the three-slot header has two readings: binding; source; stride — or init; test; advance. Slot two flips between data and a test. Slot three flips between a count and an action. Only the `:=` in slot one says which reading applies.

People read code by silhouette first and tokens second. Two constructs with one silhouette and two meanings interfere, the way false-friend words do across languages. A two-character token is too small a cue to flip the meaning of a whole line.

One more asymmetry hides in the logic of `next`, the skip-to-the-following-pass word. In a counter loop, `next` runs the advance and then retests, so the increment cannot be skipped. In a bare test loop, `next` only retests. Any option that removes the counter form must say what protects that edge.

The choice: which header design gives one shape one meaning, keeps counters expressible, and protects the `next` edge.
decisions.story: Priya learned Jet from the examples and reads `loop i; 0..10; 2` correctly: walk the range by twos. A teammate writes `loop size := 1; size < budget; size *= 2`. The same silhouette now means start, test, advance, and Priya misreads slot three as a stride. Later the teammate rewrites it as a bare test loop, puts `next` above the doubling line, and ships a loop that spins forever. Both failures trace back to the same header design.

options.name: Keep both dialects, unchanged
options.detail: Nothing changes. Readers keep telling the families apart by spotting `:=` in slot one. Programmers arriving from C, Go, or JavaScript keep a familiar one-line counter, and the `next` edge stays safe. The cost is permanent: every reader of every three-slot header pays the which-dialect check, and the misreading Priya hit stays writable forever.
options.code:
loop i := 0; i < n; i++ draw(i)       // counter dialect
loop chunk; chunks; 4 upload(chunk)    // source dialect, same silhouette
options.technical: No change. Parser keeps disambiguating on ColonEq in the first clause (Parser/Statements/control.rs).

options.name: Retire the counter form; visible state plus a test loop
options.detail: Three slots always mean binding; source; stride. Counters with irregular advance move their state above the loop and advance in the body. Every program stays expressible and the state becomes visible. Two honest costs the old ballot hid: the variable now leaks into the enclosing scope, and `next` no longer runs the advance — the skip-the-doubling spin from the in-the-wild example becomes writable.
options.technical: Remove the init;test;advance parse. A teaching diagnostic on `loop name := …` shows the rewrite. Migration of existing code is mechanical.

options.name: Keep the advance, drop the init slot: loop test; advance
options.detail: The header keeps only what belongs to the loop: its driver test and its continuation action. Starting state was always just a binding, so it moves above the loop. `next` still runs the advance first, so the spin bug stays impossible. Costs: the variable leaks into the enclosing scope, and two-slot headers still carry two readings — a name starts a source loop, an expression starts a test loop — so the dialect split shrinks but survives.
options.technical: Grammar: `loop expr ; assignment` when the first clause is not a bare name list. A test that is only a Bool variable needs parentheses or a comparison, or it parses as a source binding. The advance clause runs on body completion and on `next`.

options.name: One meaning for three slots: binding; source; step rule
options.detail: The counter dissolves into data. Slot three accepts a whole number — today's every-Nth stride — or a step rule like `s => s * 2` that computes the next value from the current one, with a range giving the start and the stop bound. Counting, striding, and irregular growth all read in one dialect, one line. The binding stays loop-scoped, and `next` means advance-the-source everywhere. Counters juggling several variables, or tests that are not range bounds, use the visible-state rewrite from option B.
options.code:
loop size; 1..<budget; s => s * 2 probe(size)   // start 1, stop at budget, doubling
loop i; 0..10; 2 audit(i)                        // stride unchanged
loop chunk; chunks; 4 upload(chunk)              // every 4th chunk
options.technical: A step-rule stride is legal only on range sources: the range supplies start and stop test; the rule supplies the advance. Int strides keep today's index-stride law over any source. The counter form retires with a teaching diagnostic. Pointer-chase loops (`node = node.next`) get a Core generated-sequence (Swift's sequence(first:next:) shape); name settled at implementation. Yield arrows keep working since this stays a source loop.

options.name: Keep both, split the silhouettes: parenthesized counter head
options.detail: The counter form survives but must wear parentheses: `loop (i := 0; i < n; i++)`. The paren group reads as one machine-with-state unit; bare slots always mean binding; source; stride. The interference dies at a glance because the shapes differ before any token is read, and the `next` edge stays safe. Cost: the language keeps two loop dialects forever, the counter gains ceremony, and semicolons mean statement-separation inside the parens but slot-separation outside.
options.technical: Grammar: KW_LOOP `(` init `;` test `;` advance `)` body. `loop(` is unclaimed surface after D-LOOPLABEL4=A. Old bare counter headers get a teaching diagnostic pointing at the paren form.

comparisons.note: No C-style loop; `range` covers regular counters. Irregular ones fall to `while` with a manual advance, and `continue` above the advance line spins — exactly the hazard option B imports.
comparisons.code:
size = 1
while size < budget:
    if not ready(): continue   # spins: size never doubles
    probe(size)
    size *= 2

comparisons.note: Removed the C-style for loop in Swift 3. `stride(from:to:by:)` and `sequence(first:next:)` cover counters and generated sequences — option D's shape, shipped at scale and considered an uncontroversial cleanup.
comparisons.code: for size in sequence(first: 1, next: { $0 * 2 < budget ? $0 * 2 : nil }) { probe(size) }

comparisons.note: Keeps the advance co-located with the loop in a visually distinct continuation slot, so `continue` cannot skip it — the direction options C and E take.

One `for` keyword carrying both dialects, disambiguated by header shape — option A shipped. Its spec needs three separate header forms explained, and Jet's current ambiguity is inherited from this design.
comparisons.code:
for i := 0; i < n; i *= 2 { }
for _, v := range items { }

recommendation.why: One shape keeps one meaning across every loop: binding, source, step. The counter concept dissolves into data, so the advance is a visible named rule at the header instead of hidden mutation in a body. `next` keeps a single law — advance the source — so the spin bug cannot be written. The binding stays loop-scoped. And it beats Python on Python's turf: exponential growth stays one line with no mutable state.

whyNot.reason: Two meanings stay behind one silhouette, cued by a two-character token. The which-dialect reading tax lands on every reader of every three-slot header, forever.
The cheapest surface, but it trades a reading trap for a runtime trap: `next` above the advance now spins forever, and the counter leaks into the enclosing scope.
It protects the `next` edge but still leaves two readings for one slot shape, and a plain Bool-variable test collides with a source binding, needing a parse tiebreak nobody will remember.
It kills the interference but signs Jet up for two loop dialects permanently, plus ceremony, with semicolons meaning different things inside and outside the parens.

recommendation.tradeoff: Slot three becomes two-typed — a count or a step rule — and counters that juggle several variables or non-range tests lose their one-line spelling and take the visible-state rewrite. Accepted: those loops are rare, stay fully expressible, and every remaining header reads in one dialect.

decisions.title: Two ways to map: eager loop-yield vs lazy adapters
decisions.gist: Whether Jet keeps eager loop comprehensions and lazy method pipelines side by side, and how the split is taught.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has two spellings for 'transform every item'. The loop form, `doubled :: loop v; values -> v * 2`, runs immediately and produces a complete List. The method form, `values.map(v => v * 2)`, produces a lazy pipeline: nothing runs until something pulls from it, for example `.to_list()` or a fold.

Eager means the work happens at the line where you wrote it, and you hold real data afterward. Lazy means the pipeline is a recipe; work happens later, possibly fused with more steps, possibly never. Lazy pipelines avoid building throwaway middle lists when you chain several steps.

Both behaviors are useful. The concern is that nothing in the spelling says which is which. A reader sees `map` and, if they come from Python, expects a list; they get a pipeline object. A reader who writes a loop-yield inside a hot path materializes a full List where a lazy chain would have avoided it.

The question is not whether both should exist — they serve different jobs — but whether the current split is discoverable enough, and whether anything should change in spelling, defaults, or teaching.
decisions.story: Ana ports a Python script. She writes `evens :: values.map(v => v * 2)` and then `print(evens)`, expecting a list like Python's comprehensions give her. She gets a pipeline value, not data. Her fix is `.to_list()`, but nothing told her at the `map` call; she found out at the print. Meanwhile her teammate Ken writes a loop-yield over ten million rows, chains three more transformations after it, and builds four full lists where a lazy chain would build one.

options.name: Keep the split, document it as the plane boundary
options.detail: Loop-yield is the beginner plane: eager, immediate, holds data. Adapters are the expert plane: lazy, fusable, allocation-free until pulled. Nothing changes in the language; the spec and docs state the rule in one sentence so the split is a teachable boundary instead of folklore.
options.technical: No compiler change. Spec section under S19/D-COMPREHENSION1 states the eager/lazy boundary; hover docs on adapters say 'lazy — pull with .to_list(), fold, or a loop'.

options.name: Make adapters eager; opt into laziness with .lazy()
options.detail: `values.map(f)` returns a List, matching what Python-trained users expect everywhere. Chained pipelines that should not build middle lists opt in: `values.lazy().map(f).filter(g).to_list()`. Beginners never meet a pipeline object uninvited; experts type one extra word. Cost: innocent-looking chains like `xs.map(f).filter(g)` now build a full middle list unless the author remembered `.lazy()`.
options.code:
evens :: values.map(v => v * 2)        // a real List now
hot :: readings.lazy()
    .map(r => r.celsius)
    .filter(c => c > 30)
    .to_list()                          // one pass, no middle lists
options.technical: Adapter methods on List/Set/Map return collections; `.lazy()` enters the pipeline plane where current adapter semantics apply. Iterator sources (files, channels) stay lazy — eagerness applies only to in-memory collections.

options.name: Keep the split, add a boundary lint
options.detail: Semantics unchanged. A lint fires exactly where the confusion bites. Using a pipeline value where a List is expected teaches `.to_list()`. Materializing a loop-yield only to chain more adapters onto it teaches starting the pipeline at the source. Legal code that is plausibly intended stays quiet.
options.technical: Two lint sites in sema: pipeline-typed value reaching a List-typed or Printable sink; loop-yield binding whose only use is a single adapter chain.

comparisons.note: Python splits the same way: comprehensions are eager, `map()`/generators are lazy. It is a known stumbling block — `map` returning a non-list surprises learners — and comprehensions won the culture war precisely because they hand back real data.
comparisons.code:
evens = [v * 2 for v in values]   # eager, everyone's default
evens = map(lambda v: v * 2, values)  # lazy iterator, surprises

comparisons.note: Rust is lazy-only with explicit collection: `.iter().map(f).collect()`. Nobody is surprised because there is no eager spelling to contrast with — but every beginner must learn `.collect()` on day one.

Kotlin made collection operators eager and gave laziness its own entry word, `asSequence()`. This is option B's shape, shipped at scale; the middle-list cost on long eager chains is real and documented.
comparisons.code:
val evens = values.map { it * 2 }          // eager List
val hot = readings.asSequence()
    .map { it.celsius }.filter { it > 30 }.toList()

recommendation.why: Beating Python for its own users means the obvious spelling hands back data, everywhere, with no pipeline object arriving uninvited. Eager `map` plus an explicit `.lazy()` entry word gives beginners Python's comfort. Experts get a single visible switch for fused, allocation-free chains — clearer control than semantics that depend on which of two spellings was used. The loop-yield and eager adapters then agree with each other, and laziness becomes something you can point at in the code.

whyNot.reason: Documentation cannot fix a surprise that arrives at runtime distance from its cause; the reader meets the pipeline object long after the `map` call that created it.
A lint at the sink still teaches after the surprise exists, and its second half polices style on legal code, which erodes trust in lints.

recommendation.tradeoff: Chained eager adapters build intermediate collections unless the author writes `.lazy()`. That is accepted: the cost is visible and local, Kotlin demonstrates it works at scale, and hot paths get one obvious word to reach for.

decisions.title: Mandatory braces for control-flow bodies
decisions.gist: Whether every if/else/loop body must be wrapped in { }, and whether the formatter collapses short bodies onto one line.
decisions.lesson:
A body is the code a control statement runs when its condition holds. Jet today allows two spellings for a one-statement body. You can write braces: `if n < 0 { return 0 }`. Or you can write the statement adjacent, with no braces: `if n < 0 return 0`.

The adjacent form saves four characters. Its cost is that the body's boundary is invisible. The reader must infer where the guarded code ends. Editors and merge tools must infer it too.

This failure has a famous name: Apple's goto-fail bug. A duplicated line after a braceless `if` shipped inside TLS verification, because nothing marked where the body ended. Jet's own repository holds a live specimen today: a stray closing brace beside a braceless guard in git_diff_review.jet. The parser reports that failure 21 lines away from its cause.

Mandatory braces mean the compiler rejects the adjacent form everywhere. The formatter then owns compactness instead: any single-statement body that fits the 100-column width is printed on one line, braces included. So `if n < 0 { return 0 }` stays exactly one line. The change trades four characters per guard for one body shape, machine-checkable boundaries, and a formatter that makes the compact spelling automatic.
decisions.story: User is reviewing a contributor's patch to a CLI adapter. The diff shows `if root_name != "before" panic(...)}` — a stray brace after a braceless guard. The build fails 21 lines below the real mistake, and he spends ten minutes finding it. He asks why a guarded body has no visible boundary in the first place.

options.name: Mandatory braces + fmt collapses fitting one-liners
options.detail: The adjacent form becomes an error with a teaching diagnostic, and fmt auto-fixes it by wrapping braces. fmt also canonically prints any single-statement control body on one line when it fits 100 columns. Writers lose nothing vertically; every body gains a visible boundary; formatted style is uniform with zero judgment calls.
options.technical: Retire D-IFGUARD1's adjacent spelling and the adjacent loop body. New diagnostic (registered code, what/why/fix, UI snapshot) for an unbraced body; `jet fmt` rewrites source form to braced. S44 amendment: single-statement if/else/loop bodies use collapse-if-fits (canonical), replacing author-choice preservation for those bodies. Arrow arm bodies (`->`) are expression arms and keep their existing rules.

options.name: Mandatory braces, fmt preserves the author's line choice
options.detail: Same brace rule as A, but fmt keeps a body one-line or multi-line exactly as the author wrote it (current S44 behavior). Authors keep control of vertical shape. The cost is two coexisting printed styles for identical code, and review debates about which to use.
options.technical: Brace enforcement and diagnostic identical to A. S44 unchanged: a single-simple-statement one-line body stays one-line only if authored that way; multi-line stays multi-line.

options.name: Keep the adjacent form (status quo)
options.detail: No grammar change. The adjacent guard remains the compact spelling and the brace form remains legal. Existing code is untouched. The boundary-invisibility failure class stays open, including the goto-fail pattern the repo has already reproduced once.
options.technical: No change to D-IFGUARD1 or S44. Optionally add a lint recommending braces around adjacent bodies that sit next to closing braces.
options.code:
if n < 0 return 0                    // stays legal
if index == 0 root_name = piece else pieces.push(piece)

comparisons.note: Braces are mandatory on every if/for body; gofmt owns layout. The rule is widely credited with eliminating dangling-body bugs, and nobody writes a linter for it because the compiler is the linter.
Braces mandatory; rustfmt always expands bodies to multiple lines, so guard-heavy code pays 3 lines per guard. Jet's collapse-if-fits keeps the safety without that vertical tax.
Optional braces produced the Apple goto-fail TLS vulnerability: a duplicated statement after a braceless if silently escaped the condition.

recommendation.why: One body shape with a visible machine-checked boundary removes the stray-brace failure class the repo has already hit, while collapse-if-fits keeps every current guard exactly one line, four characters wider.

whyNot.reason: Preserving author line choice keeps two printed styles for identical code, so files drift and reviews relitigate layout; A's canonical collapse makes the compact form automatic instead of optional.
The adjacent form's invisible boundary already produced a live parse bug in this repo, and it is the goto-fail shape. A lint would still ship two spellings of one body.

recommendation.tradeoff: Adjacent one-line if/else pairs get 8 characters wider, and the formatter overrides author intent on body layout for single-statement control bodies. Accepted because uniform output is the point of a zero-config formatter.

decisions.title: Loop header clause separator: comma or semicolon
decisions.gist: Which symbol separates the clauses of a multi-part loop header, and how the two-name iteration form is spelled under that choice.
decisions.lesson:
A loop header can carry several clauses that do different jobs. Take `loop i := 0; i < 3; i += 1 { }`. The first clause binds a counter. The second is the test rerun before each pass. The third advances the counter after each pass.

Today those clauses are separated by semicolons (D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1). This is the only place a Jet author types a semicolon. Everywhere else commas separate things: call arguments, struct fields, bound names.

That last form is the crux. In `loop key, value; map` the comma groups two names being bound, and the semicolon splits the name group from the source. If commas also separated clauses, `loop a, b, c` could mean two names iterating one source, or one name with a source and a stride. The parser could not tell without type information, which Jet forbids.

So switching to commas requires a respelling of the name group, such as parentheses: `loop (key, value), map`. The reward is one meaning per symbol across the language: comma always separates header clauses and list items, and the semicolon is freed to mean only a statement boundary. That matters if one-line bodies with `;` inside braces are adopted later. A semicolon header would then mix two semicolon meanings on one line; a comma header keeps them apart.
decisions.story: User is teaching a friend Jet. She writes `loop i := 0; i < 3; i += 1 { sum += i; print(sum) }` from an example and asks why the same symbol splits the header clauses and the body statements. He has no answer except history: C spelled for-loops that way in 1972.

options.name: Comma clauses, parenthesized name group
options.detail: Commas separate header clauses. Multi-name binding wraps its names in parentheses, matching how grouped things look everywhere else. Every header is unambiguous at parse time, and the semicolon disappears from loop headers entirely.
options.technical: Clauses split on depth-0 commas; Jet expressions have no top-level comma so this is unambiguous. Two-name form becomes `loop (key, value), source`. S19 and D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 amended; old `;` headers get a teaching diagnostic plus fmt auto-fix. All loop examples, goldens, and formatter emission updated.

options.name: Comma clauses, bare names with a shape rule
options.detail: Commas separate clauses and the two-name form stays bare: `loop key, value, map`. A shape rule decides the reading: when every clause before the last is a lone name, they are bindings. Saves the parentheses but the rule is invisible, and `loop a, b, c` reads two ways to a human even when the parser has picked one.
options.technical: Grammar rule: N leading clauses that are bare identifiers followed by one expression clause parse as an N-name binding over that source. A bare-name source variable (`loop x, xs, 2`) collides with three-clause counted form when `xs` is also a lone name; needs a tie-break and a diagnostic explaining it.

options.name: Keep semicolon clauses (status quo)
options.detail: No change. Semicolons keep separating header clauses, commas keep grouping bound names, and the C-family muscle memory for counted loops keeps working. The semicolon stays a header-only symbol, and any future one-line body semicolon shares a line with it.
options.technical: No grammar, formatter, or migration work. D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 stands as ratified.

comparisons.note: Both spell counted loops with semicolon clauses; Go dropped the parens but kept the semicolons. This is the muscle memory option C preserves.
No clause headers at all — iteration is always over an object, and tuple unpacking uses bare commas: the same bare-comma binding Jet's two-name form copies today.
Removed the C-style for(;;) loop entirely in Swift 3, arguing the semicolon header was the language's least consistent corner. Iteration and while cover the same ground.
comparisons.code:
for i in stride(from: 0, to: 10, by: 2) {
}

recommendation.why: One meaning per symbol across the whole language: comma separates clauses and list items, semicolon means only a statement boundary. The parenthesized name group keeps every header unambiguous to both the parser and a human reader.

whyNot.reason: The bare-name shape rule makes `loop a, b, c` two-faced: readers must run the disambiguation rule in their head, and a rename can silently change which form a header is.
Keeps the language's only author-typed semicolon as a header-only special case, and collides with body semicolons on one-line loops if those are adopted.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two-name iteration gains a pair of parentheses, and every C-family newcomer must unlearn `for(;;)` muscle memory once. Accepted for symbol-level consistency across the surface.

decisions.title: Expert spelling for declared view provenance
decisions.gist: How an expert writes down which inputs a view may borrow from.
decisions.lesson:
A view is a lightweight window into memory that another value owns. The owner is the value that really holds the data. Provenance is the compiler's record linking each view to its possible owners. While a view is live, Jet freezes every possible owner: none may move, resize, or be dropped.

Jet infers provenance silently (ratified as D-MEMPROVENANCE2 option A). Sema reads each function body and records which inputs a returned view can come from. A view that might come from either of two inputs gets both recorded — a source union. Rust states the same relation with lifetime annotations such as `'a`. Jet bans that notation, and inference took its place.

Inference has a blind spot: it states what a body does today, never what an author promises. Three walls follow. A library's borrow contract shifts silently whenever a body is edited — a breaking change no signature shows. A callback type has no body to read, so callers of a view-returning callback freeze every non-scalar argument. A trait object's method has no single body either, so a view-returning call through it is refused outright (error E2305).

The fix is a declaration: the author names which sources a view may borrow from. Sema checks every return path against the declaration and teaches on escape. Callers rely on the declared set, trait implementations are held to their trait's declaration, and open dispatch becomes checkable. The same spelling covers view parameters, aggregate slots, and static storage. Inference stays the default; a beginner never writes any of this. This ballot picks the spelling.
decisions.story: Mira ships the zero-copy parser from D-MEMPROVENANCE2 as a library. Callers depend on which buffer each view borrows from, but that fact is inferred from her bodies. Any refactor silently changes her public contract and breaks downstream builds. Her next feature is pluggable decoders behind a trait, and every view-returning decoder call dies with E2305. In Rust both are one lifetime annotation. Jet gives her no spelling at all.
decisions.detail:
Relation to the ratified record: D-MEMPROVENANCE2=A stays law. Inference remains the only thing a beginner sees; the hidden relation machinery is unchanged. That ratification rejected mandatory owner notation in routine APIs. This ballot adds only the opt-in declared form option A left without a spelling. Undeclared code behaves exactly as today.

Parity checklist — every borrow relation safe Rust can state, and its home here. Returned borrows and source unions: a declaration on the return. Borrow-carrying structs and enums (Rust `struct Foo<'a>`): per-slot declarations at the signatures that produce or accept them; type definitions never carry owner parameters. Outlives relations between inputs (Rust `'b: 'a`): two slots declared against one shared source. Lending traits, trait objects, and lending iterators (Rust GATs): a declaration on the trait method that binds every implementation. Higher-rank callbacks (Rust `for<'a>`): a declaration on the function type's own named parameters. Static storage (Rust `'static`): a static path as a source. Owned-only generics (Rust `T: 'static` bounds): already covered by owned and sendable facts (E1102); no new syntax.

Out of scope exactly as in safe Rust: self-referential values route to Pin (D-PIN1) and Pool/Id, and variance stays internal to sema, never user-facing.

options.name: Trailing `from` clause — on results, parameters, traits, and function types
options.detail: One word, four placements, one rule: a `from` clause after a type names the sources its views may borrow from. Results declare contracts where callers read them. View parameters declare required sources, which spells Rust's outlives relations. Trait clauses bind every implementation, so trait objects lend. Function-type clauses make callbacks precise. Beginners still write nothing.
options.technical: Grammar: `from src (| src)*` after a return type, a view-typed parameter's type, a trait-method return, or a function type's return. src = parameter name, `self`, or `static.<path>`, each with optional field/index/range projections. Per-slot form for aggregates: `from (text: primary, meta: fallback)`, keyed by output path; a bare clause binds every view slot in the type. Checking: each return path's inferred sources must be a subset of the declaration; declaring wider than the body is legal and reserves evolution room; a violation reports the offending return with a fix-it. Parameter clauses are call-boundary requirements: the argument must derive from the named source — sharing one source name across slots expresses Rust's `'b: 'a`. Trait clauses bind impls after receiver substitution and retire E2305 for declared methods, including lending-iterator shapes (Rust GATs). Function-type clauses quantify per call (Rust `for<'a>`). Type definitions never carry owner parameters; relations attach at signatures. API digests publish declared relations flagged `declared`; changing one stays a breaking provenance change.

options.name: Lender-marked parameters — `from` as a parameter prefix
options.detail: Instead of describing the result, mark the inputs that lend: any view in the result may borrow from any `from`-marked parameter. It is the shortest spelling and can never drift out of sync with the parameter list. But one mark serves every output slot, so per-slot relations, parameter requirements, and static sources have no home.
options.technical: Prefix `from` on parameter declarations, on `self`, and on function-type parameters. The declared relation for every view slot in the result is the union of the marked parameters. No per-slot form, no parameter-to-parameter requirement, no static sources — those cases fall back to inference or stay rejected. Checking and publication law otherwise identical to option A.

options.name: Type-attached `from` — the clause lives inside the view type
options.detail: The relation travels with the type itself: `View<str from left | right>`. Nested lists, options, tuples, and function types need no extra rule, because the fact sits wherever the type is spelled. The cost: the most-read line of an API carries the machinery, deep nesting repeats it, and named view-holding structs still need signature-level declarations anyway.
options.technical: Type grammar gains `View<T from srcs>` and `ViewMut<T from srcs>`, legal anywhere a type is written, including function types and aggregate element positions. Named structs and enums do not carry owner parameters; signatures producing or accepting them still need slot declarations, so this form is a superset of option A's grammar only for anonymous positions. Checking and publication law identical to option A.

options.name: Path-keyed `from` block — one table after the signature
options.detail: Every declaration lives in one block after the signature, keyed by output path — nothing inline, ever. Multi-slot APIs read like a table, and every function states its whole borrow story in one place. Simple cases pay one extra line, and the contract sits apart from the return type it governs.
options.technical: `from { <path>: src (| src)*, ... }` after the signature. `result` names the whole return, `result.text` one slot, a parameter name states a call-boundary requirement, `static.<path>` a static source. Trait methods and function types take the same block; function types inline it after their return type. Checking and publication law identical to option A.

comparisons.note: One lifetime variable links a result to its inputs; traits, closures, and structs carry the same variables. Fully general, and the single most-cited learning cliff in the language.
The origin of a returned reference is named in the return type by parameter name — no abstract variable in the common case.
comparisons.code: fn choose(a: String, b: String) -> ref [a, b] String

comparisons.note: Lifetime-dependency attributes on nonescapable returns name the source value; inference covers the common cases.

recommendation.why: One English word in four placements covers the entire safe-Rust lifetime surface. Returns, aggregate slots, parameter requirements, statics, lending traits, and callbacks all use the same clause. The common case stays one short clause on the exact line callers read. It is the only option that is both complete and lightest where reading actually happens.

whyNot.reason: One mark for all outputs cannot state per-slot relations, parameter requirements, or static sources — parity with Rust fails exactly where the hard programs live.
The relation inflates every nested type and the most-read API line, and named view-holding structs still need signature clauses — so the type-position form buys nothing the trailing clause lacks.
Forcing a block on every declaration turns the common single-source case into two lines of ceremony and moves the contract away from the return type it governs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Opted-in signatures grow a trailing clause, and a second provenance vocabulary now exists beside silent inference — readers must learn that a missing clause means inferred, never none.

decisions.title: Writing many members that share one prefix
decisions.gist: How you list several names that all hang off the same thing.
decisions.lesson:
A prefix is the part before the dot. In `default.git`, `default` is the prefix and `git` is the member. Jet code reads members off a prefix constantly: a package source, a module, a settings group.

When you want many members from one prefix, you repeat the prefix. Ten packages from `default` means typing `default` ten times. The repetition carries no information, and a typo in one of the ten is easy to miss.

A spread is a shorthand that writes the prefix once and the members once each. The compiler expands it back to the long form before anything else runs, so it is a typing convenience, not a new runtime idea.

Jet used to have a similar-looking operator called fan-out, spelled `f.[a, b, c]`. That one meant something different: it CALLED `f` on each entry, producing `[f(a), f(b), f(c)]`. The owner removed it. jetpack's config files happened to use the same brackets, but they meant member spread, never calls. So the bracket spelling is now free, and the meaning jetpack needs has never actually been decided.

One detail matters for every option below. When a spread sits inside a list, it should flatten into that list rather than nest a list inside it. `[default.[a, b], mine.c]` should mean three packages, not a two-item list beside one package.
decisions.story: User keeps this repository's development shell in `env.jet`. It pins nineteen packages, every one of them from the `default` nixpkgs source. He also writes host configurations that pull packages, services, and user settings from the same few sources. He wants to name the source once per group, not once per line, and he asked for that spreading back specifically for jetpack.
decisions.inWild:
// env.jet — this repository's own development shell, after the removal.
module env.dev {
    sources: { default: github@NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable }
    packages: [
        default.cargo,
        default.clippy,
        default.rustc,
        default.gcc,
        default.clang,
        default.lld,
        default.nodejs_22,
        default.nixfmt,
        default.ripgrep,
        default.jq,
        default.gh,
        default.fd,
        default.bashInteractive,
        default.zsh,
        default.fish,
        default.util-linux,
        default.wasm-tools,
        default.tree-sitter,
        default.pkg-config,
    ]
    prompt: "jet"
}

// The word `default` appears nineteen times and says nothing nineteen times.

options.name: Bracket member spread, everywhere in Jet
options.detail: Write the prefix, a dot, then the members in brackets. It works in any Jet code, not only config files. Inside a list it flattens, so you can mix spreads and single members freely. You gain one short mechanism that reads the same wherever prefixes repeat. You lose the ability to ever reuse this bracket spelling for anything else.
options.technical: Sigil `.[` reuses the slot freed by D-VERDICT-1324-1. Entries are plain member names only, never expressions or calls; a non-ident entry is a registered sema error. Desugars in sema before type inference: in list position it splices into the surrounding `ListLit`, elsewhere it produces a fixed-size `[T#N]` list (S76). No TIR, codegen, or engine work, so tier parity is structural.

options.name: Grouped map in the config data
options.detail: No new operator. The config fields that take a list also accept a map from prefix to members. The grouping lives in the data shape you already write. You gain a spelling that needs no language change and reads clearly in settings files. You lose the shorthand everywhere outside jetpack, and each field that wants it must opt in.
options.technical: `packages`, `services`, and peer fields gain a second accepted shape: `{ prefix: [name, …] }`, merged into the same `Pkg` list the flat form produces. Implemented in `jet-pkg-model` and `jet-env-model` only. No Syntax.rs entry, no parser change, no I7 decision beyond this one.

options.name: Prefix block
options.detail: Open a block that names the prefix once. Inside it, bare names resolve against that prefix. It covers packages, services, and options with one construct instead of one spread per list. You gain the most saving on large config files. You lose local clarity: a bare name inside the block means something different from the same name outside it.
options.technical: New keyword-led block `with <path> { … }`, a user-typeable keyword needing its own Syntax.rs entry (I7). Name resolution inside the block tries the prefix first, then the enclosing scope, which introduces a shadowing rule the language does not have today. Sema rewrites the block away before inference.

options.name: Write every prefix out
options.detail: No shorthand at all. Every member carries its own prefix, which is what the repository does right now. You gain a surface with nothing extra to learn and no expansion rule to reason about. You lose exactly what was asked for: the prefix keeps repeating on every line of every package list.
options.technical: The state after D-VERDICT-1324-1 with the callers migrated. `Merge::parse_package_list` already handles the flat `source.name` form, so nothing is built and nothing is removed.
options.code:
packages: [
    default.cargo,
    default.clippy,
    default.rustc,
    default.ripgrep,
    default.jq,
    default.fd,
]

comparisons.note: The language jetpack's package sources come from spells this with a prefix block, the model option C follows.
comparisons.code: with pkgs; [ cargo clippy rustc ripgrep ]

comparisons.note: Names the prefix once at import, then uses bare members. The saving is real, and so is the loss of provenance at the use site.
comparisons.code: from validators import length, charset, entropy

comparisons.note: Braces after a path expand to several members of that path. Closest in shape to option A, though it applies to imports rather than values.

recommendation.why: It is the spelling already written in this repository's `env.jet` and every jetpack fixture, so the owner's existing files become correct again rather than being rewritten twice. One mechanism serves config files and ordinary Jet code, and the sigil is free because the call fan-out that held it is gone.

whyNot.reason: It helps only the jetpack fields that opt in, so ordinary Jet code keeps repeating prefixes and the language gains nothing.
A bare name inside the block means something different from the same name outside it, which hides where a value came from at the place you read it.
It is the state the owner just asked to change, and it makes a nineteen-package list say `default` nineteen times.

recommendation.tradeoff: The `.[ ]` brackets are spent for good, so no later feature can claim them. That is acceptable because the one feature that held them was removed by owner ruling, and no other pending surface wants that sigil.

decisions.title: Jet as guest: #Import / #Export parity for the native library edge
decisions.gist: Whether Jet's foreign edge uses matching Import and Export spellings so both directions read as one system.
decisions.lesson:
Jet talks to other languages over the C ABI: a shared calling convention for scalars, strings, and C-layout records. Crossing that edge has two directions.

Import means a Jet program calls a function that already lives in a foreign library. Export means a foreign program calls a function that lives in Jet. Same phone line, opposite ends.

Today only import exists. The everyday overlay spelling is `#Extern module c.<lib>`. Generated caches live under `.jet/bindings/`. Call sites use `use c.<lib>`. A separate fourth tier, `#FFI(c)`, pastes a foreign body inside a Jet function — that is not how you consume a library.

Maximum parity means the two directions share names, shape, type law, and on-disk layout. The natural twin words are Import and Export. This ballot picks how far that twinning goes, including whether today's `#Extern` becomes `#Import`.
decisions.story: Priya rewrites a pricing kernel in Jet inside a Java host. Her Jet code still imports libc and a Go helper with the existing binders. She wants `#Import` and `#Export` to feel like one dial turned two ways — not `#Extern` in, something else out.

options.name: Exact twins: #Import(c) / #Export(c) (retire #Extern)
options.detail: One marker family for both directions. #Import(c) declares a foreign symbol Jet will call. #Export(c) offers a Jet function foreign code will call. Same C-safe type law, same expert args for symbol and ABI. #Extern is renamed to #Import (module form: #Import module c.<lib>). Generated inbound caches stay under .jet/bindings/; outbound products land under .jet/exports/ with a re-import #Bindgen so use c.<lib> round-trips. #FFI(c) stays the inline-body escape — not the library Import path. Beginners learn two words that face each other.
options.technical: Amends S59 / D-FFI-UNIFY1 overlay spelling: #Extern module → #Import module; per-function foreign decls may use #Import(c) fn … = "sym". #Export(c) fn … { body } lowers to non-mangled extern "C". Emit .jet/exports/c/<lib>.{h,a|so|dylib|dll} plus .jet/bindings/c/<lib>.jet #Bindgen for round-trip. Teaching diagnostic maps #Extern → #Import. #Bindgen remains compiler-only in generated caches (E3207). #FFI(c|cpp) unchanged as the inline fourth tier.

options.name: Module twins only: #Import module / #Export module
options.detail: Parity at the module keyword, not on each function. #Import module c.<lib> replaces #Extern module. #Export module c.<lib> lists what this package offers out. Function bodies stay unmarked on the export side. Same trees and type law as A. You get matching words at the module level, but reading a function no longer shows it has foreign callers, and renames need a second edit in the export module.
options.technical: S59 overlay rename only: #Extern module → #Import module. New #Export module c.<lib> { fn price(...) => Int; } resolves bodies by name from package modules. No #Import(c)/#Export(c) function markers. Same emit layout as A.

options.name: Keep #Extern; add only #Export(c)
options.detail: Leave the ratified import spelling alone. Export gets #Export(c) without renaming Import. Directions work, but the words do not match: Extern in, Export out. That is the asymmetry this question is pushing against. Smaller syntax churn; weaker everyday rhyme.
options.technical: No S59 rename. New #Export(c) marker + .jet/exports/ emit + round-trip #Bindgen only. #Extern module and #FFI(c) unchanged.

options.name: Mirror #FFI instead: #Export(c) as reverse of #FFI(c)
options.detail: Treat #FFI(c) as the import-side twin. That marker pastes a foreign body into Jet; #Export(c) would offer a Jet body out. The rhyme is real at the inline-body tier, but it is the wrong tier for library migration. Everyday import is use c.<lib> and #Extern/#Import modules, not #FFI. Teams would learn Export against a rare escape hatch instead of against the normal Import path.

comparisons.note: Import overlay is #Extern, not #Import. Generated caches are #Bindgen under .jet/bindings/. No export twin yet.
Export uses //export; import of C uses import "C". Words differ, but both sit on the function. Jet can do better with literal Import/Export twins.
comparisons.code:
//export price
func price(cents int64) int64 { return cents / 100 }

comparisons.note: import and export are exact spelling twins for opposite directions of the same module edge — the parity target here.
comparisons.code:
import { strlen } from "./libc";
export function price(cents: number): number { ... }

recommendation.why: Option A gives the parity you asked for: the same word family on both ends of the C edge. #Import(c) brings a foreign symbol in; #Export(c) sends a Jet symbol out. Renaming #Extern to #Import finishes the rhyme instead of papering over it. #FFI(c) stays the rare inline-body escape, not the Import twin.

whyNot.reason: Module-only twins match keywords but hide foreign callers at the function, so everyday reading and renames stay split across two places.
Keeping #Extern while adding #Export leaves the exact asymmetry you called out: two directions, mismatched words.
Pairing Export with #FFI mirrors the wrong import tier — inline foreign bodies, not the library Import path migration teams live in.

recommendation.tradeoff: Renaming #Extern to #Import is a clean break on ratified S59 spelling, with a teaching diagnostic for the old word. That churn buys a durable Import/Export rhyme instead of a permanent Extern/Export mismatch.

decisions.title: How Jet libraries reach foreign package registries
decisions.gist: How a Jet library gets published so Python, Node, JVM, and .NET developers can install it with the tools they already use.
decisions.lesson:
Every language ecosystem has a package registry and an install command. Python has pip, Node has npm, the JVM has Maven, and C# has NuGet. Developers only adopt what arrives through those doors.

A compiled language can hide inside those packages. Rust took this road: many popular Python and Node packages are Rust inside, installed as ordinary wheels and npm modules. Users never learn Rust exists; they just get faster libraries. The authors, meanwhile, chose Rust for the core. That is how a language wins share invisibly.

For Jet this means: once a Jet library exports a native C surface, glue code can wrap it for any host. The wrapper becomes a wheel, an npm module, a JAR, or a NuGet package. Each ecosystem has fiddly rules — platform tags, binary loading, version matrices — that decide whether the consumer's install just works.

This ballot picks who produces that wrapper: the Jet toolchain itself, a scaffold each team maintains, or the community.
decisions.story: Sam maintains an open-source data library written in Jet. A Python data scientist finds it on a benchmark page. If she can type pip install and use it within the same minute, Sam gains a user and Jet gains a beachhead inside her company.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet publish --to pypi
  built fastpricer-1.4.0-cp3-abi3-manylinux_x86_64.whl
  uploaded to pypi.org

# the consumer, who has never heard of Jet:
$ pip install fastpricer
>>> import fastpricer   # just works

options.name: First-party jet publish --to <registry>
options.detail: One command builds the ecosystem-correct artifact — wheel, npm module with native glue, JAR with library loading, NuGet package — straight from the same typed export surface the compiler already checks. The glue can never drift from the library. Publishing becomes a one-command habit, so far more Jet ships into foreign registries.
options.technical: Packaging generators consume the D-ADOPT-GUEST1 export facts: Python abi3 wheels with manylinux/musllinux tags, Node N-API prebuilds, JVM JNI loader JARs, NuGet runtimes/ layout. Registry credentials follow each ecosystem's standard auth.
options.code:
$ jet publish --to pypi
$ jet publish --to npm
$ jet publish --to maven
  # artifact + glue generated from the export surface, then uploaded

options.name: Scaffold generators the team maintains
options.detail: Jet generates a starter packaging project once, and the team owns it afterward. Every team re-solves the same platform-matrix and binary-loading problems alone. The scaffold drifts from the export surface with every release, so consumers hit broken installs that Jet's reputation pays for.
options.code:
$ jet new binding-python
  wrote python-pkg/  (yours to maintain from now on)
# six months later: export surface changed, wheel builds stale glue

options.name: Community-owned; Jet ships only the C export
options.detail: Jet's job ends at the .so and header. Whether wheels or npm modules exist depends on volunteers per ecosystem. The invisible-adoption channel opens years late or never, and install quality varies wildly between ecosystems.
options.code:
$ pip install fastpricer
  ERROR: No matching distribution found
  # nobody wrapped it for PyPI yet

comparisons.note: One command turned Rust-inside-Python into the normal case; PyO3 wheels made Rust invisible to pip users.
Prebuilt N-API binaries per platform; npm consumers never see a compiler.
Generates Kotlin, Swift, and Python bindings from one interface definition — one source of truth for many hosts.

recommendation.why: The whole value is that a foreign developer's first minute is flawless: install, import, run. Only compiler-owned packaging keeps the glue permanently in sync with the exported types, so that first minute never breaks. One-command publishing also multiplies how many Jet authors actually ship to foreign registries.

whyNot.reason: Scaffolds rot: every release risks glue drift, and every author re-learns platform tags and binary-loading rules alone, with consumers paying for the mistakes.
Rust needed maturin before Rust-inside-Python became normal; shipping only a header outsources the decisive channel to chance.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet's toolchain owns four ecosystems' packaging rules, and when those ecosystems change their rules, publishing correctness depends on Jet updating promptly.

decisions.title: What LTS cadence and support window does Jet promise at GA?
decisions.gist: Choose how often Jet names an LTS compiler line and how long it receives active and maintenance fixes after 1.0 GA.
decisions.lesson:
An LTS line is a specific compiler release family, such as 1.4.x, that keeps receiving selected fixes after newer feature releases exist. Cadence answers how often a new LTS starts. The support window answers when fixes stop. Active support normally includes security, critical correctness, supported-host, and toolchain fixes. Maintenance support is narrower: security and severe data-loss or compiler-correctness fixes.

Jet editions are separate. An edition controls source compatibility. An LTS line controls how long one compiler family is serviced. D-REL4 already forbids a pre-GA LTS and says the window is set at GA. This ballot supplies that missing promise.
decisions.story: Mina's company qualifies a Jet compiler for a regulated product. Qualification takes three months, so she cannot move to every feature release. She needs the next baseline date, the security-fix window, and the number of overlapping LTS lines. She also needs to know when an upgrade project must begin.
decisions.inWild:
Example if Jet 1.0 GA ships in October 2027:

line       starts       active until   maintenance until
1.0 LTS    Oct 2027     Oct 2028       Oct 2030
next LTS   Oct 2028     Oct 2029       Oct 2031

`jet --version --support` and the signed release manifest name the line, phase, exact end date, supported editions, hosts, and replacement LTS. The public calendar lists dates at least twelve months ahead.

options.name: Annual LTS, 36 months total
options.detail: Make 1.0 GA the first LTS. Start one successor LTS every twelve months in the same published month. Give each line twelve months of active support and twenty-four months of maintenance, for three years total and at most three overlapping LTS lines. Current non-LTS releases remain available, but the latest stable plus every live LTS receives applicable security fixes. Publish exact dates, phases, supported editions and hosts, and the replacement line.
options.technical: Active: security, critical compiler/runtime correctness, supported-host/toolchain breakage, and severe performance regressions; no new language behavior. Maintenance: security plus critical data-loss, memory-safety, type-safety, or miscompilation fixes. Patch releases preserve D-REL1. An LTS keeps the editions and target matrix it advertised; dropping either before EOL needs the existing security/safety exception process and a migration notice. Calendar changes require at least six months' notice and cannot shorten an existing line.
options.code:
Jet 1.0.x LTS
active:      2027-10-01 .. 2028-09-30
maintenance: 2028-10-01 .. 2030-09-30
replacement: Jet 1.4.x LTS (example; exact SemVer chosen by shipped release)

options.name: Annual LTS, 24 months total
options.detail: Start an LTS every twelve months, with twelve months active and twelve months maintenance. At most two LTS lines overlap. This gives enterprises a predictable yearly baseline while reducing the age of code Jet must patch.
options.technical: Use the same active and maintenance definitions as A, but end support after two years. Publish exact dates and never shorten a live line. Customers that qualify slowly must begin migration within the first LTS year to keep overlap with the replacement.

options.name: Biennial LTS, 48 months total
options.detail: Start one LTS every twenty-four months. Give it twenty-four months active and twenty-four months maintenance, for four years total and at most two overlapping lines. Enterprises upgrade less often, but each baseline waits longer for a successor and carries an older compiler, Core, host, and toolchain contract.
options.technical: Use the same fix classes and no-shortening rule as A. The longer active phase accepts supported-host and toolchain compatibility fixes for two years. Feature releases between LTS lines are not promoted later; the next scheduled line is cut from then-current stable after its release gates pass.

comparisons.note: Node's official policy promotes even-numbered major lines to LTS and gives them twelve months of Active LTS plus eighteen months of Maintenance. Its public schedule records exact transition and end dates. https://github.com/nodejs/Release

Go supports each major release until two newer major releases exist and issues minor revisions for critical problems, including security problems. This is simple, but it ties the time window to release cadence instead of fixed enterprise dates. https://go.dev/doc/devel/release
comparisons.code: support Go N until Go N+2 ships

comparisons.note: Rust ships stable every six weeks and officially supports the newest stable release, so each version's support is about six weeks. That fast train is useful for current users but is not an enterprise LTS promise. https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/appendix-07-nightly-rust.html
comparisons.code: stable every six weeks; previous stable reaches EOL

recommendation.why: A gives adopters a predictable yearly qualification target and a full two-year migration overlap after the replacement LTS starts. Three years is long enough for regulated and air-gapped estates without binding Jet to four-year-old host and toolchain assumptions. It also keeps editions separate from servicing, so source compatibility does not depend on choosing an old compiler forever.

whyNot.reason: Two years leaves only one year of overlap after the replacement starts. A slow qualification or skipped annual cycle can put an enterprise against EOL before its replacement is approved.
Four years improves stability but makes Jet promise old hosts, toolchains, runtime dependencies, and security backports for too long at GA, while a two-year cadence delays a fresh qualified baseline.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must service up to three LTS lines at once and publish backport eligibility clearly. The fixed three-year promise is worth that bounded cost because the adoption pack explicitly targets enterprises that qualify toolchains slowly.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A, B, or C. After ratification, record the relative policy in release-policy.md. When the GA month is fixed, publish the first dated calendar and signed support metadata without reopening this cadence decision.

decisions.title: What Jet 1.0 promises about formatter output, JSON output and the editor protocol
decisions.situation: Jet's release policy promises that code which compiles keeps compiling, but it promises nothing about the formatter, the JSON that tools print, or what editors receive. A toolchain update could therefore reformat a whole codebase or silently break a build script that reads a JSON field. You decide what Jet 1.0 promises for tool output. We recommend that machine output only ever gains fields, that new fields and new formatting styles first ship as an opt-in preview, and that messages stay free to improve.
decisions.gist: After Jet 1.0, how should formatter output, JSON output and the editor protocol stay stable across toolchain updates?
decisions.lesson: Jet ships its compiler, formatter, JSON reports and editor server in one binary. Today the promise covers only source code. A lets machine output gain fields but never lose one before 2.0, and tries every new field and style in an opt-in preview first. B numbers each output's layout and keeps the previous layout for one support line. C keeps today's source-only promise.
decisions.explainer:
Jet's release policy describes source compatibility after 1.0. Code that compiles in an edition keeps compiling on every later toolchain that supports that edition. Exit codes are also documented as stable. Nothing is said about the formatter, the JSON that commands print with --json, receipts and maps, or the language server that editors talk to.

These outputs have different readers. Programs read JSON and the editor protocol, so a renamed field breaks them silently. Version control reads formatter output, so a style change produces huge diffs. People read diagnostic messages and help text, which should keep getting clearer.

Option A combines the two strongest proven promises. Machine output follows the Cargo and Language Server Protocol rule: within 1.x a field may be added but never removed, renamed or given a new meaning. Every new field and every new formatting style first appears only under --preview, the opt-in that Black and Ruff use for formatting and that Rust uses for unstable output. A preview item graduates after real use, so a poor shape is fixed while it can still change.

Option B is the Kubernetes promise. Each machine output carries a schema number. A breaking change ships as a new number, and --json=N selects the previous one for one long-term-support line. Scripts that pin a number keep working for that window; scripts that do not pin break at the change.

Option C keeps today's policy: only source is promised. Under A and B, human-readable text may improve in any release. Nothing binds before the owner declares 1.0; until then the golden tests below run as practice.
decisions.story: Bea's CI reads the JSON check report and fails a build whenever a diagnostic has severity error. After a minor update the field is renamed, every build passes silently, and broken code reaches production. In another team, a patch update reformats 4,000 files and buries a real change in the diff.
decisions.inWild:
# rustfmt: formatting is tied to a style edition, so updates do not reformat
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2024/rustfmt-style-edition.html
style_edition = "2021"

# Black: next year's style is opt-in until it becomes the stable style
# https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/future_style.html
black --preview src/

# Cargo: --message-format=json only gains fields; old consumers keep working
cargo build --message-format=json
decisions.detail:
Replaces D-TOOL-STABLE1 (OptionQuality1, 2026-10-07); revised 2026-10-10 because the owner did not ratify the posted A. Mapping: new A is the posted A plus an opt-in preview stage; B and C are unchanged. The withdrawn freeze-everything option stays withdrawn: no surveyed toolchain freezes diagnostic text.

What changed in A. The posted A carried one loss: a mistaken field stays until 2.0. The preview stage attacks the cause rather than the symptom. A new field or style is visible only to people who pass --preview, so it can be renamed or reshaped after real use. It becomes stable only when it graduates. The residual loss is a field that passes preview and still proves poor; that is now rare and still costs nobody a broken script.

Why that residue cannot reach zero. Removing or renaming any stable field breaks every script that reads it without pinning. The only way to remove a field earlier is B's numbered schemas, which break every unpinned script at each change. A therefore keeps the mistaken field beside its replacement, marked deprecated, until 2.0, exactly as source deprecations already wait for a major version.

Current state: release-policy.md covers SemVer, editions, the post-1.0 source guarantee, deprecation, LTS, the version banner and exit codes. Patch releases may fix diagnostic text. Nothing covers formatter output, --json shapes, receipts, .jetmap or the language server. Some outputs already carry a schema_version field (the Canvas protocol, semindex); under A that field identifies the output and never changes within 1.x. D-ADOPT-LTS1=A sets the LTS calendar. Card #1349 owns the enterprise adoption pack.

Sources: Gleam's Louis Pilfold asks what 1.0 promises when one binary ships compiler, build tool and language server (RntfkL8lUY4 49:21-49:47, claim languages-a:G56). Also release notes taught by running changes (learning-compilers:OZ1), and 20-year-old C that still builds (systems-perf:SP2-DaJWWePhRsM-07; v3-S1:DAJ-07).

Proven right ways. rustfmt ties formatting to a style edition from Rust 2024, after years of complaints about reformatting on update; its stability rule allows output changes only to fix output that was wrong.

Black promises one stable style per calendar year and ships next year's changes under --preview. Ruff's formatter uses the same preview gate. The Language Server Protocol marks new features as proposed before finalizing them, and new fields are optional. Cargo and rustc keep --message-format=json backward compatible by adding fields only; unstable output needs an explicit unstable flag. GitHub's REST API also evolves by adding fields.

Known wrong ways. gofmt promised stable output, but Go 1.19's doc-comment reformatting still produced large diffs because the change shipped as default rather than opt-in. Kubernetes-style versioning (option B) works for pinned clients, but its own deprecation guide documents breakage for clients that never pinned.

options.name: Machine output only gains fields; new fields and styles try out under --preview first
options.detail:
Every --json output, receipt, map file and the editor protocol may gain fields in any 1.x release, but never removes, renames or changes the meaning of one. A new field or a new formatting style first appears only under --preview. It graduates to stable output after at least one minor release of real use.

A stable field that still proves poor gets a better field beside it and stays, marked deprecated, until 2.0. The formatter's output for an edition never changes on later toolchains, except to fix output that changed meaning or failed to parse. Diagnostic wording and help text may improve in any release.
options.technical: One schema declaration per machine output, with golden tests that fail when a stable field is removed, renamed or retyped. Each field carries a stability marker (preview, stable or deprecated); `jet inspect schema` lists them. --preview is one global flag accepted by every command that prints machine output, and by jet fmt. Formatter rules are keyed by edition; preview rules live in a separate set that the next edition adopts. release-policy.md gains a Tool output section. No --json=N selector exists.

options.name: Numbered schemas; previous one kept for one LTS line
options.detail: Every --json output, receipt, map file and the editor protocol carries a schema number. Minor releases only add fields. A breaking change needs a new number, and the previous one stays selectable for one LTS line. A script that does not pin a number gets the newest schema. Formatter output and messages behave as in A.
options.technical: Each machine output declares schema: N; jet ... --json=N selects an older supported schema. Golden tests pin each schema. Formatter rules are keyed by edition. The version banner lists supported schemas.

options.name: Promise source code only
options.detail: Today's policy stays. Tools may change any output in a minor release. Scripts and editors follow the release notes.
options.technical: No policy change.
options.code:
jet check --json
// fields may change in any minor release

comparisons.note: rustfmt output is tied to a style edition; JSON diagnostics only gain fields, and unstable output needs an opt-in flag. This is option A.
Style changes ship under --preview first and become the stable style later. A uses the same gate.
New features are marked proposed first; new fields are optional, so old editors keep working.
Every API is versioned; old versions stay served through a deprecation window. This is option B.

recommendation.why: A keeps every script and editor working through all of 1.x with nothing pinned, never reformats a project on update, and keeps messages free to improve. The preview stage lets new fields and styles be corrected while they can still change, which removes most of the old cost of an add-only promise.
recommendation.tradeoff: A field that passes preview and still proves poor stays beside its replacement until 2.0.
gains: No CI script breaks on any 1.x update, pinned or not.
Toolchain updates never reformat a project.
New fields and styles are fixed during preview, before they are promised.
Error messages can keep getting clearer.

losses.loss: A field that graduates from preview and still proves poor stays in the output until 2.0.
losses.mitigation: Preview catches most mistakes before they are promised. For the rare one left, a better field ships beside it at once and the old one is marked deprecated. Removing it earlier would break unpinned scripts, which is the very harm this promise prevents.

whyNot.reason: B breaks every script that reads plain --json at each schema change, and keeps old schemas only for one LTS line.
C lets any minor update break CI scripts and reformat whole codebases.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Add a Tool output section to release-policy.md naming each machine output, the add-only rule, the --preview stage and the formatter rule. Check that a golden test fails when any stable --json field, receipt field, .jetmap field or language-server field is removed, renamed or retyped. Check that a preview field appears only with --preview, and that jet inspect schema lists preview, stable and deprecated fields.

Check that formatter rules are keyed by edition, that an edition's golden formatting corpus is unchanged across toolchain updates, and that jet fmt --preview applies only the preview rule set.

surface.gist: After Jet 1.0, how should formatter output, JSON output and the editor protocol stay stable across updates?
surface.lesson: Today only source code is promised. A lets machine output gain fields but never lose one, after an opt-in trial. B numbers each output layout. C stays source-only.

current.code:
jet check --json   // fields may change
jet fmt            // style may change on update

wild.note: Formatting follows a style edition; JSON only gains fields; new style is opt-in first.

options.name: Add-only output with a preview trial
options.gist: Machine output only gains fields; new fields and styles try out under --preview first.
gains: No script breaks, pinned or not.
No surprise reformatting.
Mistakes get fixed during preview.
losses: A rare poor field that passes preview stays until 2.0.

proposed.code:
jet check --json            // stable fields only
jet check --json --preview  // plus fields on trial
jet fmt --preview           // next style, opt-in

options.name: Numbered schemas
options.gist: A breaking change gets a new number; the previous one stays for one support line.
gains: Mistaken fields can be fixed before 2.0.
No surprise reformatting.
losses: Unpinned scripts break at each change.
Old schemas served for one support line.

proposed.code:
jet check --json     // schema 2
jet check --json=1   // previous schema

options.name: Source only
gains: Tools may change freely.

recommendation.why: A keeps every script and editor working through 1.x with nothing pinned. The preview trial fixes most mistakes before they are promised.
gains: Stable automation without pinning.
Better messages over time.

losses.loss: A rare poor field that passes preview stays until 2.0.
losses.mitigation: Its better replacement ships beside it at once; removing it early would break unpinned scripts.

whyNot.reason: B breaks unpinned scripts at each change and still retires old schemas.
C breaks scripts and reformats code silently.

recommendation.tradeoff: A rare poor field lingers until 2.0.

designAway.loss: A mistaken field stays in the output until 2.0.
attempts: Number the schemas and keep one previous number per LTS line; kept as option B, with its unpinned-script breakage.
Ship every new field and style under --preview first, as Black, Ruff, Rust and the editor protocol do. Kept: most mistakes are now fixed before they are promised.
For a stable field that still proves poor, ship the better field beside it, mark the old one deprecated, and remove it in 2.0. Kept for the residue.
designAway.result: Reduced to a rare case; the residue is irreducible because any earlier removal breaks unpinned scripts.

designAway.loss: Freezing formatter output per edition would stop the style from improving.
attempts: Ship style improvements under jet fmt --preview and adopt them in the next edition, as Black does per year and rustfmt does per style edition.

designAway.loss: Freezing message wording would stop diagnostics from improving.
attempts: Freeze every output; withdrawn, no surveyed toolchain does it.
Promise machine outputs and formatting only; human text stays free.

decisions.title: Interpolation debug-label shorthand
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets a one-character way to print a variable's name and its value together while debugging.
decisions.lesson:
String interpolation lets you drop a value into text: print("total is {total}") prints the value of total inside the sentence.

While debugging, people rarely write sentences. They want a quick dump that shows which variable they printed and what it held, like: total = 42. Today that takes typing the name twice — print("total = {total}"). The two copies drift apart: rename the variable or tweak the expression, and the label silently lies.

A debug-label shorthand makes the compiler write the label for you. You mark the interpolation hole, and Jet prints the expression's own source text, an equals sign, then the value. One keystroke replaces the duplicated name, and the label can never go stale.

Jet already has one interpolation add-on rail: selectors, spelled with a hash inside the braces. {price#Fixed(2)} formats a number with two decimals; {value#Debug} shows a value's developer-facing form. Selectors change how a value renders. A debug label is different: it adds new text (the name) rather than reformatting the value. The options below differ on whether the label rides that existing rail or gets its own tiny mark.
decisions.story: Priya is a data analyst three weeks into Jet, chasing a wrong total through a pricing script. She peppers the code with print lines. Every line means typing each variable's name twice, and yesterday a stale label sent her down the wrong path for an hour: the print said discount but the hole actually held surcharge. She wants the label to come from the code itself, for free.

options.name: Trailing equals: {expr=}
options.detail: A single equals sign at the end of the hole prints the expression text, then ' = ', then the value. It is the cheapest possible spelling at the exact moment users want zero friction. Python programmers already know it. The cost: interpolation gains a second modifier mark besides the hash selector rail.
options.technical: Renders expression source text verbatim, then " = ", then the value through the same Display path as a bare hole. Composes with selectors: {x=#Fixed(2)} labels then formats. Registered in Syntax.rs under I7; misuse (empty hole, pattern position) gets one diagnostic with snapshot.
options.code:
print("{base=}")            // base = 104.5
print("{order.tier_rate()=}") // order.tier_rate() = 0.15
print("{discount=#Fixed(2)}") // discount = 15.68

options.name: Selector spelling: {expr#Label}
options.detail: The label rides the existing hash-selector rail next to #Debug and #Fixed. Nothing new to learn beyond one more selector name, and the error listing valid selectors makes it discoverable. The cost: seven extra characters per debug line, and the rail's meaning blurs — every other selector reformats the value, while this one injects new text.
options.technical: One more row in the selector registry; unknown-selector diagnostic E0914 already lists the valid set. Same rendering law as option A.
options.code:
print("{base#Label}")      // base = 104.5
print("{discount#Label}")  // discount = 15.68

options.name: Decline: keep typing the name
options.detail: No new surface. Users keep writing print("x = {x}"). The language stays one mark smaller, but the duplicated-label papercut and its stale-label bug stay forever, felt most by beginners who debug with prints the most.
options.code: print("base = {base}")   // fine until someone renames base

comparisons.note: f-strings added the trailing-equals form in 3.8; it is now the most-taught debug idiom in the language.
dbg!(x) prints file, line, expression text, and value — a macro rather than an interpolation mark.

recommendation.why: A debug shorthand only earns its keep if it is nearly free to type. One trailing character wins that test, and the largest beginner population arrives already knowing this exact spelling from Python.

whyNot.reason: Seven extra characters at the highest-frequency debug moment, and it bends the selector rail: every other selector reformats a value, this one injects new text.
Keeps the duplicated name and the stale-label bug this decision exists to remove; the papercut lands hardest on beginners.

recommendation.tradeoff: Interpolation gains a second modifier mark besides the hash rail. It is one fixed character with one meaning, ratified in Syntax.rs, and it composes with selectors instead of competing with them.

decisions.title: Map spelling: keep [K: V] or move to a comma-style form
decisions.gist: Whether the map type keeps its bracket-and-colon spelling, [K: V], or changes to look more like other comma-separated generic types.
decisions.lesson:
A map stores key-to-value pairs, like a phone book from names to numbers. Jet spells the map type [K: V] — for example [String: Int] — and a map value ["ana": 31, "bo": 27]. Lists use the matching sugar [T], as in [Int].

Jet uses two punctuation marks around collections, each with one job. The comma separates items in every sequence: list elements, call arguments, and also the entries of a map. The colon pairs a name or key with its value. That pairing colon appears in type annotations (x: Int), named tuples ((x: 1, y: 2)), struct literals (Point.{ x: 1 }), and each map entry ("ana": 31).

Inside a map literal both marks appear on their usual duty: colons pair, commas separate. The place the spelling can look odd is the type position. Named generics such as Lru<K, V> take comma-separated angle-bracket parameters, while the map sugar writes [K: V] with a colon. This ballot decides whether that colon is a win (the type mirrors the literal) or a loss (it breaks the comma rule of other generics).

One more fact matters: the compiler is never confused, but a reader can be, in two places. First, trait bounds also put a bracket list after a colon — <T: [Hash, Eq]> means 'T constrained by these traits', which looks like an annotation with a map type (x: [String: Int]) but pairs nothing. Second, map keys are expressions, so [limit: 3] means 'key = the value of variable limit'. The same word-colon-value shape in parens or braces — (limit: 3), Point.{ limit: 3 } — declares a field named limit instead.
decisions.story: User, the language owner, is reading an audit report that quotes the cache type Lru<K, V> in one sentence and the map type [K: V] in the next. The two spellings carry the same two type parameters with different punctuation. He flags that maps look inconsistent with everything else that separates with commas, and asks for the choice to be put on the board.

options.name: Keep [K: V] (status quo)
options.detail: The type keeps mirroring the literal: you write ["ana": 31] daily, so the type [String: Int] reads as 'a map shaped like that'. The colon stays on its one job — pairing — and entries stay comma-separated like everything else. The angle-bracket difference against Lru<K, V> remains, accepted as the price of the sugar.
options.technical: No change. D-LISTMAP-CANON1=A, S38, S64 stand as ratified.
options.code:
ages: [String: Int] = ["ana": 31, "bo": 27]
empty :: [String: Int].{}

options.name: Retire the sugar: Map<K, V>
options.detail: The map type becomes an ordinary named generic, punctuated exactly like Lru<K, V>. Every generic type now reads one way. The loss: the type stops mirroring the literal (which keeps its colons), and the everyday collection gets a heavier name that beginners must discover instead of a shape they already type.
options.technical: Amends D-LISTMAP-CANON1=A and S64; [T] list sugar would stand alone. Migration sweep across examples, tests, docs, and formatter.
options.code:
ages: Map<String, Int> = ["ana": 31, "bo": 27]
empty :: Map<String, Int>.new()

options.name: Comma type form: [K, V]
options.detail: The type swaps its colon for a comma so brackets always separate with commas. But [Int, String] now reads like a list of two different things, not a pairing. The type also stops matching the literal: the same key-value relationship gets a colon in values and a comma in types.
options.technical: Amends D-LISTMAP-CANON1=A and S64; grammar must disambiguate from any future heterogeneous-list spelling. Literal S38 unchanged.
options.code: ages: [String, Int] = ["ana": 31, "bo": 27]  // type comma, literal colon

options.name: Comma everywhere: positional pair literals
