options.detail: Both type and literal drop the colon: ["ana", 31, "bo", 27] alternates keys and values by position. It is the only option that fully removes the colon. The cost is that nothing marks which item is a key, so one missing element silently shifts every later pair.
options.technical: Amends S38, S64, D-LISTMAP-CANON1=A. Odd-length literals need a new diagnostic; nested pairs become visually ambiguous.

comparisons.note: Type and literal both use the colon pair — exactly Jet's current design.
Type and literal disagree: the type hint separates with a comma while the literal pairs with colons.
No literal and no sugar; the named generic is precise but heavy for the everyday case.

recommendation.why: The colon is not a separator — it is Jet's one pairing mark, used identically in annotations, named tuples, struct literals, and map entries. Entries already separate with commas. The current spelling follows both rails at once, and the type mirrors the literal users type daily.

whyNot.reason: Loses the lightweight sugar that parallels [T] lists, and the type stops mirroring the literal — Python's exact mismatch, which its own users cite as confusing.
[K, V] reads as a two-item list, and the same key-value relationship would be punctuated one way in types and another in values.
Positional pairs hide which item is the key; one dropped element silently shifts every later pair — the exact bug class the colon prevents.

recommendation.tradeoff: Maps keep a bracket sugar that other named collections like Lru and Deque do not get. That asymmetry is accepted because lists and maps are the two everyday collections and earn their shorthand.

decisions.title: Map merge when both sides share a key
decisions.gist: When two maps merge and share a key, which value wins.
decisions.lesson:
A map stores keys with values. Merge builds one map from two. When both sides share a key, Jet needs one clear conflict rule.

Beginners should overlay configs with no ceremony. Experts sometimes need a per-key choice. One method can do both: a default rule for the common case, and an optional callback when you need control.
decisions.story: Devon merges default settings with user settings. Both maps have theme. If the wrong side wins, dark mode vanishes after every load. Later Devon also merges inventory counts and must add quantities on clash instead of picking one side.

options.name: Right wins only
options.detail: merge always keeps the right map on overlap. Simple overlays work. No per-key control on the same call.
options.technical: Map.merge(self, other) copies self then other; duplicates take other. Full I9 Prelude.
options.code: defaults.merge(user)  // theme = dark

options.name: Left wins only
options.detail: First map keeps its values. Feels like fill-in blanks. Opposite of common overlay order.
options.technical: Duplicates keep self.
options.code: defaults.merge(user)  // theme = light

options.name: Error on conflict
options.detail: Overlap is always an error. Safe for strict joins. Painful for normal config overlays.
options.technical: Result or runtime error on duplicate keys.
options.code: defaults.merge(user)  // error: key theme on both

options.name: Callback always required
options.detail: Every merge takes a conflict function. Maximum control. Beginners must pass a lambda for basic overlays.
options.technical: merge(other, (k, a, b) => …) with no defaulted form.
options.code: defaults.merge(user, (_k, _a, b) => b)

options.name: One merge: right-wins default, optional conflict callback
options.detail: defaults.merge(user) overlays with right wins — beginner magic, no ceremony. Experts pass an optional conflict callback on the same method for per-key control. One name, one idea, two strengths.
options.technical: Map.merge(self, other, conflict: ((K, V, V) => V)? = None). Absent/None → right wins. Present → callback result. Label conflict: at call site. Full I9 in Prelude. No second method name.

comparisons.note: dict | is right-wins with no callback.
Map.merge/3 optional conflict function — closest to E.
comparisons.code: Map.merge(defaults, user, fn _k, _a, b -> b end)

comparisons.note: extend is right-wins; custom combine is manual.

recommendation.why: E is one mechanism: beginners get right-wins overlays with zero extra args; experts pass an optional callback for per-key policy. That is beginner magic plus expert control without splitting the surface.

whyNot.reason: Right-wins alone leaves experts without a first-class per-key path.
Reverses usual overlay order and invites silent wrong themes.
Punishes normal override merges that are not errors.
Forces a callback on every simple overlay.

recommendation.tradeoff: The signature grows one optional labeled argument. That is the cost of keeping a single merge name for both audiences.

hybrid.synthesis: E is A for the default path and D when the callback is supplied — one signature, not two methods.

harvest.use: Default when conflict is omitted.
Optional conflict: argument on the same merge.

decisions.title: Name of the bounded cache collection
decisions.gist: What Jet calls its built-in size-limited cache, currently named Lru.
decisions.lesson:
A cache keeps recent results of expensive work so the program can reuse them instead of recomputing. A useful cache must be size-limited, or it grows forever. When a full cache gets a new entry, an old one must go. Choosing which one to drop is called eviction.

Jet's Core library ships one such collection today. It evicts the entry that has gone unused for the longest time. The classic computer-science name for that rule is Least Recently Used, shortened to LRU. Jet currently names the whole type after the rule: Lru<K, V>.

That name tells an expert the eviction rule instantly. It tells a beginner nothing: it is an unexpanded acronym, and nothing in it says 'cache'. Jet's naming law elsewhere favors plain words — membership is has, storage is add. The question is whether this type's name should say what it is (a cache) or how it evicts (LRU), and in which words.
decisions.story: Sam is building his first Jet web scraper and wants to avoid re-fetching pages. He searches the Core docs for 'cache' and finds nothing by that name. The type he needed was sitting in the collections table the whole time, labeled Lru — three letters he has never seen before and does not think to click.

options.name: Cache<K, V>
options.detail: The plain word. A beginner searching for a cache finds a type called Cache. Jet ships one cache mechanism, so the plain name is unambiguous today. The eviction rule moves to the doc line: 'a size-limited map that forgets the least recently used entry when full.' Other eviction rules, if ever ratified, become constructors on this one type. No new type names would appear.
options.technical: Rename in jet-foundation Collections, comptime dispatch, and the D-COLLBREADTH1 row; method law (has_key, add, add_new) unchanged. Future policies as constructors: Cache.new(cap) stays least-recently-used; a hypothetical Cache.by_frequency(cap) would be a later ballot.
options.code:
cache :: Cache.new(256)
page :: cache.get(url) ?? fetch(url)

options.name: RecentCache<K, V>
options.detail: Says both what it is and roughly how it evicts, in plain words, no acronym. The cost: the compound reads oddly — it is not a 'recent cache', it is a cache that keeps recent entries — and beginners searching 'cache' must still scan past the modifier.
options.code: cache :: RecentCache.new(256)

options.name: LruCache<K, V>
options.detail: The industry compound: Android and Rust's ecosystem both ship an LruCache. Experts recognize it on sight, and 'Cache' is now in the name for searchers. The confusing part the owner flagged — the unexpanded acronym — stays, and stays first.
options.code: cache :: LruCache.new(256)

options.name: Keep Lru<K, V>
options.detail: No change, no migration. The shortest spelling for people who already know the term, and the name is honest about the eviction rule. Fails the beginner test outright: it cannot be explained without first expanding an acronym.
options.code: cache :: Lru.new(256)

comparisons.note: Ships the compound LruCache — option C's exact precedent.
The dominant crate is named lru with type LruCache; std ships no cache at all.
comparisons.code: let mut cache: LruCache<String, Page> = LruCache::new(cap);

comparisons.note: Hides the acronym behind a decorator use-site; most users say 'cache' and never learn what LRU means.

recommendation.why: A beginner's search word is 'cache', and Jet ships exactly one cache, so the plain word is both findable and unambiguous. It matches the existing naming law that picked has and add over jargon. The eviction rule is one doc sentence away for experts.

whyNot.reason: The compound misreads — the cache is not recent, its entries are — and it still buries the search word behind a modifier.
Keeps the unexpanded acronym the owner flagged, and puts it first, where a beginner's eye lands.
The name cannot be explained to a beginner without expanding an acronym; the owner already judged it confusing.

recommendation.tradeoff: The name stops stating its eviction policy. Accepted: policy is a doc-line detail for experts, and a second policy, if ever ratified, arrives as a constructor on the same type rather than a competing name.

decisions.title: When pause stops a task on each engine
decisions.gist: When does pause stop a task, and must every Jet engine use the same rule?
decisions.lesson:
Jet can run one program on more than one engine. Ahead-of-time and just-in-time engines run compiled code. The interpreter steps a slower form on some fallback paths.

Pause means: this task should stop soon. Cancel means: this task should stop and must not resume.

A wait point is a place where the task already yields. Examples are sleep, channel receive, and similar waits.

If engines pause at different times, the same source lies about its meaning. Jet forbids that drift.

Beginners need one rule that just works. Experts sometimes need a stronger pause that can stop a tight loop. This ballot also keeps one shared text form for paused and cancel flags.
decisions.story: Nia calls pause on a pool of workers while she debugs. She expects the same stop rule on every engine. She also wants a strong pause mode when she hunts a hot loop that never waits.

options.name: Wait-point pause on every engine
options.detail: Every engine pauses only at the next wait. A tight loop with no wait keeps running. One shared rule. No strong pause for hot loops.
options.technical: Document cooperative pause as the only law. Unify the trace string in Prelude.

options.name: Different pause strength per engine
options.detail: Compiled engines may stop sooner. The interpreter stays wait-only. Honest about today. Breaks one meaning across engines.
options.technical: Needs an owner carve-out from execution-tier parity. Trace string can still be shared.
options.code:
// JIT may stop earlier
// interpreter only at waits

options.name: Forced stop on every engine
options.detail: Pause always stops soon, even in a tight loop. Best for some debuggers. Costs interrupt checks on every engine all the time.
options.technical: Interrupt or signal checks on AOT, JIT, and interpreter.
options.code:
tasks.pause_all(workers)
// even while true { n = n + 1 } stops soon

options.name: Fix the text only; leave pause timing open
options.detail: Only share the paused and cancel text form now. Pause timing stays as today until a later card. Smallest change. Leaves the stop rule unclear.
options.technical: One Prelude formatter. No pause behavior change.
options.code: print(task)  // both engines call the same formatter

options.name: Same wait-point default; optional strong pause
options.detail: Default: every engine pauses at the next wait. One beginner rule. Experts pass an optional strong mode that also checks in tight loops. The paused and cancel text always comes from one shared formatter.
options.technical: Default cooperative wait-point law on all tiers (I9). Optional labeled mode on pause APIs, e.g. mode: .WaitPoints | .CheckLoops, default .WaitPoints. Strong mode adds portable yield or back-edge checks on every engine — never engine-specific timing. Trace flags only via Prelude.

comparisons.note: Cancel is seen at wait or call points. A tight loop can delay it.
comparisons.code: // check ctx when you Read, Wait, or select

comparisons.note: Cancel is cooperative at await points.

recommendation.why: E gives beginners one pause rule that matches on every engine. Experts get a stronger mode when they ask. The text form stays shared. That is magic for the common case and control for hard debug work.

whyNot.reason: Wait-only with no expert mode leaves hot-loop debug weak.
Different stop times per engine break one program meaning.
Forced checks on every pause tax the default fast path.
Leaves the pause rule unclear after this card.

recommendation.tradeoff: Strong mode needs portable interrupt or yield checks on every engine. Default pause stays cheap and cooperative.

hybrid.synthesis: E uses A's shared wait-point default and borrows C's strong stop only behind an explicit expert mode.

harvest.use: Default beginner path.
Optional strong mode.
Always ship with E.

decisions.title: One spelling for field defaults
decisions.gist: Should struct fields use the same = default spelling as function parameters, retiring #Default?
decisions.lesson:
A default is a value used when the caller or input leaves something out.

Jet already has defaults in two places. Function parameters use name: Type = value. The caller may skip that argument.

Struct fields use a different marker today: #Default(value). That fills a missing key when decoding JSON or when a CLI flag is absent.

Two spellings for the same idea force people to remember which form belongs on a field. Markers also compete for attention on crowded fields that already need docs, rename, env, and similar tags.

This choice decides whether fields keep the marker, switch to = like parameters, and whether writing Type.{ name: "web" } may omit other fields that declare defaults.
decisions.story: Maya ships a small HTTP tool. She wants port to default to 3000 on the CLI struct and the same default when her config JSON omits port. She also wants Config.{ name: "api" } in tests without restating every field. Today she writes #Default(3000) on the field and still fills every field in source literals. She asks why the language uses a second spelling for the same idea.

options.name: Keep the split
options.detail: Fields keep #Default for wire and CLI absence. Parameters keep =. Source literals still require every field. No migration. Marker congestion stays.
options.technical: Preserves D-SERDE5 and D-CLIFLAG1 as written. S61 remains call-site only. Construction omission stays illegal (E0303).

options.name: Fields use = for absence only
options.detail: Replace #Default(expr) with field: T = expr for decode and CLI absence. Retire the #Default marker. Source Type.{ … } still requires every field unless you write a constructor function.
options.technical: Amend D-SERDE5 / D-CLIFLAG1: field = is the absence default. Migrate examples and diagnostics. Construction law unchanged. Free Default marker name in Policy/Syntax.

options.name: Fields use = for absence and construction
options.detail: Same as B, and omitted fields in Type.{ … } fill from their = defaults. One spelling covers params, wire, CLI, and partial construction. Biggest beginner win; largest migration.
options.technical: Amend D-SERDE5 / D-CLIFLAG1 / construction (E0303). Field = is compile-time constant like today's #Default. Required fields remain those without =. Partial literals legal when every omitted field has =.

options.name: Allow both spellings
options.detail: Accept #Default(expr) and field = as synonyms forever. Softens migration but keeps two ways to say one thing and does not free the marker.
options.technical: Violates I8 preference for one mechanism. Docs and fmt must pick a canon anyway. Marker name stays reserved.

comparisons.note: Data/class fields commonly use = for construction defaults in one spelling.
comparisons.code:
data class Serve(val port: Int = 3000)
// Serve(name = "api") fills port

comparisons.note: No field =. serde uses attributes; Default trait is a separate mechanism — closer to today's Jet split.
Params use =; fields use #Default; construction does not fill from #Default.
comparisons.code:
fn f(x: Int = 0) {}
struct S { #Default(0) x: Int }

recommendation.why: Owner wants one short spelling and a freed marker. C makes field = mean the same idea everywhere a value can be omitted — call site, wire, CLI, and source construction — which matches how beginners already read =.

whyNot.reason: Keeps the confusing split and the marker congestion the owner called out.
Fixes spelling for wire/CLI but still forces full literals in source, so the everyday Type.{ … } story stays incomplete.
Two spellings forever; does not free #Default; fights I8.

recommendation.tradeoff: C is a breaking syntax migration across serde, CLI, and construction, with a large example and diagnostic update. That cost buys one mechanism and an empty marker slot for more important tags.

decisions.title: Collapse every fitting braced block
decisions.gist: Should jet fmt put any braced block that fits the line width onto one line, not only control bodies?
decisions.lesson:
jet fmt rewrites Jet source into a canonical layout so projects do not argue about spacing.

Card #1335 already made braces mandatory for if/else/loop bodies and told fmt to collapse a single-statement control body when it fits the width.

Other braces still keep authored multiline shape: match arms, function bodies, and marker blocks such as #Unsafe("…") { … }.

This choice is whether "fits means one line" becomes the rule for every brace pair, or stays limited to control bodies.
decisions.story: Rio runs jet fmt before every commit. A one-line #Impure("probe") { … } block keeps getting expanded across three lines, while a matching if body collapses. They want one predictable rule: if the contents fit, the braces stay on one line.

options.name: Control bodies only (status quo)
options.detail: Keep #1335. Only if/else/loop single-statement bodies collapse. Arms, functions, and marker blocks keep authored layout.
options.technical: No amendment beyond D-IFBRACE / #1335 collapse-if-fits for control bodies.
options.code:
if ok { print("ready") }          // collapses
#Impure("x") {\n  work()\n}       // stays multiline if authored that way

options.name: Every fitting braced block collapses
options.detail: Any { … } whose contents fit the width budget becomes one line: controls, arms, function bodies, marker regions. Comments or over-width contents keep multiline. Nested blocks collapse inside-out.
options.technical: Amend fmt law after #1335. Re-bless snapshots/goldens. Width budget unchanged (S44 / 100-col).

options.name: Collapse list with opt-outs
options.detail: Collapse controls, arms, and marker blocks, but never collapse multi-statement function bodies even when they fit. More special cases to learn.
options.technical: Partial extension of #1335 with an fn-body exception. Extra fmt classification.
options.code:
#Impure("x") { work() }    // collapses
fn run() {\n  print("hi")\n} // stays broken even if it fits

comparisons.note: Uses width heuristics; does not force every small block onto one line the same way.
Already collapses fitting single-statement control bodies only.

recommendation.why: Owner asked for one rule: if it fits, it is one line, including marker blocks. B matches that without a special-case menu.

whyNot.reason: Leaves the inconsistency that motivated the card.
Adds another exception beginners must memorize.

recommendation.tradeoff: Large snapshot and golden churn when fmt rewrites the corpus. That is accepted to get a uniform brace rule.

decisions.title: BuildContext defaults for CLI and effect knobs
decisions.gist: How a project sets default build flags and effect grants once inside fn build.
decisions.lesson:
A build flag is a switch you pass on the command line. Examples are --release, --profile=debug, and --allow-exec. Effect grants are the yes-you-may switches for risky build steps such as running a process or reading the network.

Today those switches are typed again on every jet build line, or they live in package files that this card does not own. Many projects want one shared default: set the knobs once, then run a plain jet build.

fn build(b: BuildContext) is Jet's build-time entry. BuildContext is the typed toolbox that fn build uses to register targets and actions. This ballot picks whether BuildContext also carries project defaults for ordinary CLI and effect knobs. It also picks which knobs it may set, and what happens when you pass a flag on the command line.

The rule must stay Jet-facing. It must not leak rustc flags. Explicit command-line intent should stay stronger than a project default unless you pick a lock option on purpose.
decisions.story: Omar maintains a tools package. Every CI job repeats jet build --release --allow-exec --allow-fs. He wants those defaults declared once beside fn run, then a plain jet build in scripts. He still needs a one-off jet build --profile=debug to win over the project default when he debugs.

options.name: Typed default methods; CLI always wins
options.detail: BuildContext gains small methods such as default_profile and default_allow. Beginners set defaults in fn build. Any matching flag on the command line overrides the default. Effect grants still name each effect. No way to lock out CLI.
options.technical: Add BuildContext methods for profile/release-class knobs and for default --allow-* grants that apply when CLI omits them. Merge order: batteries/command defaults, then fn build defaults, then explicit CLI (CLI highest). Does not amend D-BUILDFLAGS1's per-effect naming. I2: Jet knobs only.

options.name: One defaults record; CLI always wins
options.detail: One call passes a BuildDefaults record for profile and allows. Same override rule as A: CLI wins. Slightly more ceremony than methods. Easy to extend with new fields later.
options.technical: b.defaults(BuildDefaults.{ profile: .Release, allow: [.Exec, .FS] }). Same merge order as A. Missing fields mean no default for that knob.

options.name: Defaults plus optional CLI lock
options.detail: Same defaults as A or B, plus an expert lock that rejects conflicting CLI flags. Strong for sealed CI images. Easy to surprise a developer who passes --profile=debug and gets an error.
options.technical: b.default_profile(.Release, lock: true) or defaults(..., lock_cli: true). Locked knobs: CLI match ok; CLI conflict is a diagnostic. Unlocked knobs keep CLI-wins.

options.name: Profile defaults only; effects stay CLI/pkg
options.detail: BuildContext may set profile/release defaults. Effect grants stay on --allow-* and package grants (D-BUILDFLAGS1). Smaller surface. Omar still repeats allow flags in CI.
options.technical: Methods or record for Build profile knobs only. No default_allow on BuildContext. Effect path unchanged.
options.code:
b.default_profile(.Release)
$ jet build --allow-exec --allow-fs

options.name: No BuildContext defaults
options.detail: Keep defaults in CLI and package files only. Rejects the owner ask for this card. Avoids a second defaults channel next to package profiles.
options.technical: Close or re-scope #1370. No new BuildContext default APIs.
options.code:
// no b.default_* 
$ jet build --release --allow-exec --allow-fs

comparisons.note: Shared flag tables set once; tools reuse them without retyping every switch.
comparisons.code: // conceptual: shared flags struct applied to multiple targets

comparisons.note: Permissions are explicit --allow-* flags; projects often wrap them in tasks rather than locking them in code.
Profile defaults live in Cargo.toml; CLI --release still selects the release profile.

recommendation.why: A matches the owner ask: BuildContext methods, shared defaults beside fn build, and explicit CLI still wins. Typed methods stay small and Jet-facing without a lock footgun.

whyNot.reason: A record works, but methods match how BuildContext already adds targets and stay shorter for the common case.
CLI lock fights the stated rule that explicit CLI overrides still win, and it surprises local debug flags.
Leaves effect grants as repeated CI noise, which is half of the pain this card names.
Rejects the BuildContext defaults the owner asked to track on this card.

recommendation.tradeoff: Authors must learn a few default_* methods. That cost buys one place for shared knobs without sealing out CLI overrides.

decisions.title: Shared-in-Shared cycles: reject or execute
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet rejects cyclic Shared payloads at compile time or executes them with full tier parity and a free-or-leak proof.
decisions.lesson:
Shared<T> is Jet's synchronized shared handle. A value of type Shared<T> can be passed into many places at once. Each place can read or edit the same T under the Shared contract.

A cycle appears when T itself contains Shared<T>, or Shared of something that eventually points back. Example: struct Node { next: Shared<Node>? }. Two nodes can each hold the other. Reference counting alone cannot free that pair: each handle keeps the other alive.

Terms: Shared-in-Shared means a Shared field whose payload type contains Shared again. A cycle is a live graph of Shared handles that points back to itself. Free means the last reachable handle ends and storage is released. Leak means storage stays after the program dropped every named handle.

Mental model: either the type system forbids building that cycle, or the runtime must define how cycles die (for example a weak link, or a collector that finds unreachable cycles).

Tiny example:

struct Node { next: Shared<Node>? }
a :: Shared(Node.{ next: Absent })
b :: Shared(Node.{ next: Present(a) })
a.edit(n => { n.next = Present(b) })

Stakes: without a clear rule, beginners can build graphs that never free, and experts cannot audit ownership. #1353 proved sema accepts the type today while neither default jet run nor AOT executes the constructing function cleanly.
decisions.story: Mira ships a graph editor. Each node holds Shared handles to neighbors. On Linux CI, jet run --release hits an ICE. On her laptop, default jet run says the function is unsupported. She cannot tell whether closing the last window frees the graph or leaks it. She needs either a clear compile error naming the cycle, or a working Shared cycle story with a free-or-leak measurement she can trust.

options.name: Reject Shared-in-Shared / cyclic Shared at sema
options.detail: Sema diagnoses Shared fields whose payload can form a Shared cycle. Construction that would close a cycle is a named diagnostic with what/why/fix and a UI snapshot. Beginners never build an un-freeable graph by accident. Experts who need graphs use an explicit non-Shared edge or a later weak-handle design under a different card.
options.technical: Add a structural check on type definitions and Shared constructors: if a Shared payload's type graph can reach Shared of a type that reaches back, emit a registered diagnostic (new E-code). Keep I9: every tier refuses the same programs. No interpreter/JIT special case. Docs name the rule; example shows the diagnostic.
options.code:
struct Node { next: Shared<Node>? }
// error: Shared cycle in Node.next — use an explicit weak edge or a non-Shared id

options.name: Full I9 execute Shared cycles + free-or-leak measurement
options.detail: Make Shared-in-Shared constructible and runnable on AOT, default jet run, and interpreter ambient with one Prelude meaning. Ship a proof that either frees the cycle when last external roots drop, or documents a deliberate leak with a measurable test. Weak references may be part of the mechanism if needed for free.
options.technical: Close the Items.rs / quick-run gaps for Shared-bearing recursive types. Define cycle lifetime in Prelude (collector, weak back-edge, or owned break). Prove free vs leak with an example golden and a runtime measurement. I9 required end to end.

options.name: Both now: beginner-safe Shared + expert cycles on this card
options.detail: One Shared mechanism (I8). Beginner path never builds an immortal graph by accident: either construction that would cycle needs an explicit expert form, or cycles free when external roots drop — with a clear diagnostic if the beginner form is wrong. Expert path ships in the same delivery: intentional Shared graphs (weak back-edges or equivalent), full I9 on AOT / jet run / interpreter, and a free-or-leak proof. No follow-on card for the expert surface. No parking in jit_gaps.
options.technical: Implement reject-or-require-opt-in for the accidental beginner cycle, plus the expert cycle/weak API, Prelude free-or-leak law, I9 adapters only, example+golden, and a free-or-leak measurement test — all acceptance for this card.
options.code:
struct Node { next: Shared<Node>? }  // beginner: clear diagnostic or free-safe
struct Node { next: Shared.Weak<Node>? } // expert: intentional cycle, frees — ships here

options.name: Leave constructible; document ICE/unsupported as known gap
options.detail: Keep today's sema acceptance. Document that constructing Shared cycles may ICE or hit quick-run unsupported. Do not add a diagnostic or an execution path on this card.
options.technical: Docs-only. Violates I2 spirit (rustc/ICE as user path) and I9 (tiers disagree). Not a product outcome.
options.code: // status quo from #1353 — not recommended

comparisons.note: Rc/Arc cycles need Weak to free. Strong-only cycles leak until the process exits.
comparisons.code: struct Node { next: Option<Rc<RefCell<Node>>> } // leaks without Weak

comparisons.note: Class cycles need weak/unowned for ARC to free.
comparisons.code: class Node { weak var next: Node? }

comparisons.note: GC collects pointer cycles; no Shared handle distinction.

recommendation.why: Matches the owner rule: beginner magic and full expert control in one delivery. C (revised) keeps Shared one mechanism, stops accidental leaks for beginners, and ships expert cycle graphs now with I9 and free-or-leak proof — not a later card.

whyNot.reason: Reject-only gives beginner safety but denies expert graphs entirely. Owner wants expert control out of the box.
Execute-all as the silent default risks beginner immortal graphs unless free law is perfect; revised C keeps beginner default safe and still ships B's expert power now.
Documenting ICE/unsupported violates I2 spirit and leaves both facets unfinished.

recommendation.tradeoff: This card's scope grows: reject/opt-in beginner path plus expert cycle API, I9, and free-or-leak proof all close together. That is the point — no deferred expert half.

hybrid.synthesis: Harvest A's beginner non-leak default and B's full execute/I9/free-or-leak expert path into one option that ships both now.

harvest.aspect: Beginners never accidentally immortalize a graph.
harvest.use: Default/diagnostic path for ordinary Shared.

harvest.aspect: Intentional cycles run on every tier with free-or-leak proof.
harvest.use: Expert Shared cycle/weak surface on this card.

decisions.checkInstructions: Pick A/B/C/D. Guidance already recorded: both beginner magic and full expert control now — no later. Recommended revised C. After ratify: implement the whole dual surface on this card (I9 + free-or-leak); do not split expert to a follow-on.

decisions.title: Full and short ballot contract
decisions.gist: Choose how Tower enforces complete short ballots and reviewed full ballots.
decisions.lesson: Tower's current Learn this first rule asks for a long lesson, so ballots can bury the decision under definitions. The open choice is how much review Tower should require before a ballot reaches you. Every ballot will use /simple and start with a short paragraph that gives only the context needed to compare its options.
decisions.story: User opens a difficult architecture ballot. He wants a clear lesson, strong alternatives, visible review evidence, and a recommendation that already survived several different attacks.
decisions.inWild:
$ tower decision add --file cache-policy.json --by sol
ballot profile: full
base            complete
boil-the-ocean  recorded
hybrid          recorded
cooperative     recorded
adversarial     recorded
recommendation  B

$ tower decision add --file naming.json --by sol
ballot profile: short
owner request: "Make this a short ballot."
base: complete
reviews: skipped by owner request
decisions.detail:
Base — The revised first draft makes Learn this first a short orientation, not a glossary or tutorial. It still defines full and short profiles, owner authorization, review order, summaries, colors, and final recommendation proof.

Boil-the-ocean — The review tested guidance-only rules, hard CLI gates, separate commands, profile fields, automatic review agents, and one universal full format. It kept three choices that change enforcement or owner control and removed duplicate command spellings.

Hybrid — The review combines flexible draft creation with strict ready-state checks. It also joins short context, structured review data, fixed UI order, and skill instructions without creating a second ballot system.

Cooperative — The review strengthens guidance-only mode with clear skills and makes all-full mode consistent and predictable. It strengthens the recommendation with explicit owner authorization, one-paragraph context, legacy safety, and accessibility rules.

Adversarial — The review attacks long lessons, context that is too thin, fake review evidence, old ballot breakage, and color-only meaning. It adds a one-paragraph cap, /simple for every field, a required owner quote for short mode, unchanged ratified history, labels and icons, and full-path tests.

options.name: Enforced profiles with visible review records
options.detail: Tower stores full or short as an explicit profile. Every field uses /simple, and Learn this first gives context in one short paragraph at most. Full is the default and requires the complete base plus all ordered review summaries before ready state. Short requires a recorded owner request and the complete base. Users gain durable process, visible reasoning, and one clear interface. Drafts stay open while work is incomplete.
options.technical: Add ballotMode: full|short. The lesson accepts one paragraph at most; the skill targets a few sentences, and the CLI keeps its plain-language limits. Full stores reviewPasses in fixed base, boilOcean, hybrid, cooperative, adversarial order. Each entry contains a one-to-two-sentence summary. Short stores shortAuthorizedBy with the owner's words and rejects reviewPasses. addDecision and update --ready enforce the contract for new or edited open ballots. Ratified history stays valid. Focus Mode renders labeled color blocks: slate, violet, cyan, green, orange, then blue recommendation and muted-red rejections. Text and icons preserve meaning without color.

options.name: Skill guidance without a CLI gate
options.detail: Tower skills tell agents to use /simple, keep Learn this first short, and run the ordered reviews. The data model and ready-state gate stay unchanged. Users gain fast adoption and flexible prose. They cannot tell whether every review ran, and later agents can omit the process without an error.
options.technical: Update tower-ballot and tower skills only. Store optional summaries in detail, hybrid, or recommendation fields. Do not add ballotMode, owner authorization, reviewPasses, lesson validation, or dedicated Focus Mode sections.
options.code:
# tower-ballot skill
1. Write one short Learn this first paragraph.
2. Write the complete base.
3. Run boil-the-ocean.
4. Run hybrid.
5. Run cooperative.
6. Run adversarial.

$ tower decision add --file ballot.json --by sol
# CLI accepts long lessons or missing review evidence

options.name: Require full review for every ballot
options.detail: Tower requires short context, the complete base, and all four reviews for every ready ballot. Users gain one strict path and never need profile authorization. They lose the owner-requested short path for small, clear decisions and must record reviews even when the owner asked for a short ballot.
options.technical: Add one-paragraph lesson validation and require reviewPasses for every narrative decision. Do not add ballotMode or shortAuthorizedBy. Drafts remain exempt. Ratified history remains valid.

comparisons.note: A pull request can require named checks before merge. Tower can use the same model: drafts stay flexible, while ready ballots must show required review evidence.
comparisons.code:
required checks: scope, tests, security, review
merge: blocked until every check reports

comparisons.note: An architecture decision record keeps context, options, and reasons. Tower adds ordered challenge passes so the owner can see how the recommendation improved before the verdict.
comparisons.code:
status: proposed
context: ...
options: A | B | C
decision: B
consequences: ...

recommendation.why: A makes the owner's requested order and evidence part of Tower's ready-state contract. It keeps short ballots owner-controlled, gives every ballot clear prose, and shows how full review improved the recommendation.

whyNot.reason: B can produce excellent ballots when every agent follows the skill, but Tower cannot detect a skipped pass or an unauthorized short ballot. The process would drift again.
C gives strong and consistent review, but it removes the short profile that the owner specifically requested. Small decisions would carry review records even when the owner chose less ceremony.

recommendation.tradeoff: New and edited open ballots must carry explicit profile data, and full ballots carry five short stage summaries. That extra visible record is the cost of a durable review contract.

hybrid.synthesis: Use flexible drafts from B, strict ready-state evidence from C, and an owner-authorized short profile so one Tower mechanism serves both decision sizes.

harvest.aspect: Draft authors need room to work before every field exists.
harvest.use: Keep --draft exempt until decision update --ready.

harvest.aspect: A single strict full path prevents review drift.
harvest.use: Make full the default and gate all five stage summaries.

decisions.checkInstructions: Choose A, B, or C. The full review recommends A. If A wins, update schema and CLI validation first. Learn this first must use /simple, contain one paragraph at most, and explain only the situation needed to compare options. Every other ballot field also uses /simple. Then update the ordered UI, accessible colors, skills, docs, targeted tests, and independent review. Do not change ratified history.

decisions.title: Which surface should expose compiler-owned type facts?
decisions.gist: Choose the focused spelling for layout and future small compiler facts. Full reflection stays explicit in every option.
decisions.lesson: This is a surface decision, not a data-model decision. Every option returns the same typed `LayoutInfo` and uses the same target-layout engine. The choice is how code asks for a focused compiler fact without making metaprogramming noisy, hidden, or collision-prone.
decisions.explainer: Voting for any option also ratifies the shared inner API: `.kind`, `.size`, `.alignment`, `.stride`, `.target`, `.guarantee`, `.source`, `.fields`, and typed field selection with `[.field]`. Known fields never become strings. The focused path is exactly the `reflect().layout` object, not a second mechanism.
decisions.story: Mira binds `Packet` to C. She wants one readable compile-time check for size and one rename-safe field offset. Later, a tool author needs every field and marker. Mira should get easy magic. The tool author should get an explicit, extensible reflection root. Both must read the same facts.
decisions.detail: Exact byte facts exist only for layouts and targets Jet guarantees. Plain layout returns unknown optional physical facts. Every answer names its target, guarantee, and source rule. Completion, hover, go-to-definition, diagnostics, CLI text, and JSON are part of this decision.

options.name: Compiler dunder member
options.detail: Write `T.__layout` for the focused view and `T.reflect()` for the full model. Jet owns every `__*` declaration. User code may read only documented compiler members, and completion shows them in a visible Compiler facts group.
options.technical: This amends D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 from access-forbidden to declaration-reserved. Unknown dunders fail; users and libraries cannot define them. `T.__layout` is a compiler-provided projection of `T.reflect().layout`.
options.code:
size :: Packet.__layout.size
alignment :: Packet.__layout.alignment
offset :: Packet.__layout[.count].offset

meta :: Packet.reflect()
fields :: meta.layout.fields

options.name: Single meta sigil member
options.detail: Write `T.$layout` for the focused view and `T.reflect()` for the full model. `$` means a compiler-known value at this member position. Existing `$name` remains the splice of a user-known compile-time binding.
options.technical: This broadens D-CTMARKER1 into one known-value law. Prefix `$name` materializes a known binding; member `T.$name` selects a documented compiler-known fact. Users cannot declare `$` members. Completion shows them in a visible Compiler facts group.
options.code:
size :: Packet.$layout.size
alignment :: Packet.$layout.alignment
offset :: Packet.$layout[.count].offset

meta :: Packet.reflect()
fields :: meta.layout.fields

options.name: Explicit reflection only
options.detail: Add no focused magic member. Every caller writes `T.reflect().layout`; tools keep the returned object when they need several facts. This preserves the current dunder and dollar rules unchanged.
options.technical: No new token role or reserved reference surface is needed. `reflect()` remains an ordinary compiler-provided method in the user member plane. Its layout projection has the same type and tooling contract as A and B.
options.code:
layout :: Packet.reflect().layout
size :: layout.size
alignment :: layout.alignment
offset :: layout[.count].offset

meta :: Packet.reflect()
fields :: meta.layout.fields

comparisons.note: Closest to A in ownership. Python reserves documented dunder names for the system, but layout is fragmented across `ctypes.sizeof`, `alignment`, and field descriptors. A keeps the ownership signal and groups the facts.

Closest to B in visual signaling. Zig marks compiler built-ins with `@`, but exposes a flat catalog and uses a string for field offsets. B puts the sigil after the inspected type and keeps field identity typed.
Closest to C in explicit grouping. Swift uses a generic `MemoryLayout<T>` namespace and typed key paths. C is shorter because the inspected type comes first and the field selector is contextual.
No option copies Rust's fragmented surface. Rust separates size, alignment, and offset and adds turbofish or a macro. All Jet options return one typed object instead.

recommendation.why: B is shortest, visually explicit, and coherent with Jet's existing compile-time `$` signal. `Packet.$layout` reads as a compiler-known fact, while `Packet.reflect()` remains the obvious expert root. It avoids underscore noise and prevents collision with user members.

whyNot.reason: A has strong precedent and preserves `$` as splice-only, but leading dunders are visually heavier and many developers expect tools to hide them. Jet can fix discovery, but cannot remove that learned friction.
C is architecturally clean, but it makes a common focused check spell the whole metaprogramming path. Beginners pay expert ceremony even when they need one compiler fact.

recommendation.tradeoff: B widens a ratified sigil law and needs `T.$name` member grammar. The compiler-fact catalog must stay small and closed, or `$` becomes a flat magic namespace.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared the user's dunder idea, a single-sigil member, and explicit reflection only. Every option now shares one typed fact model and one full reflection root.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested `@`, `#`, `?`, `!`, `^`, `~`, `%`, free functions, static namespaces, scalar magic fields, and CLI-only access. Existing sigils conflict, new sigils lack meaning, and flat queries fragment one fact set.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass keeps focused access for the common fact and `reflect()` for expert enumeration. It rejects aliases: the focused member must be an exact projection of the full object, not a second API.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gives dunder visible completion and gives reflection-only callers a short local binding. It gives the sigil option one precise known-value law instead of calling it mere punctuation.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested name collisions, hidden completion, unknown fields, rename, targets, plain layout, columnar layout, strings, and catalog growth. B wins only if `$` members stay compiler-owned, documented, grouped, and few.

decisions.checkInstructions: Choose A, B, or C. Voting for any option also chooses the shared typed selector and tooling contract described above.

decisions.title: How should Jet calls spell generic type arguments?
decisions.gist: Choose one rule for every generic call. Inference stays the normal path in both options.
decisions.lesson: A generic function can often infer its type arguments from inputs or the expected result. Some calls have no such evidence, and expert code sometimes needs to pin the choice locally. This decision chooses whether Jet permits that explicit call-site escape everywhere or never permits it.
decisions.explainer: This ballot resolves a real contradiction. S45 first chose inference-only calls. D-SERDE6 later authorized `call<T>(...)` for every generic call, but a later summary described `decode<T>` as an exception. The winning verdict supersedes every conflicting clause. Jet will have no API-specific exception.
decisions.story: Noor writes a generic parser. Most callers write `parse(text)` because inputs and expected results identify the type. In a pipeline with no useful expected type, Noor wants either one local type argument or a separate annotated binding. Both can work. Jet needs one predictable rule across free functions, namespaced calls, and methods.
decisions.detail: Option A keeps inference as the default and allows explicit `<...>` after any named or member callee. Option B removes call-site arguments everywhere, including decode. Neither option changes generic declarations or generic types such as `fn id<T>` and `Box<Int>`.

options.name: Infer by default; allow explicit arguments
options.detail: Normal calls omit type arguments. Any generic free function, namespaced function, or method may add `<T>` when inference lacks evidence or local clarity matters. Jet uses `call<T>(...)`, never Rust's `call::<T>(...)`.
options.technical: A balanced `<...>` is a call argument list only when it is adjacent to the callee and immediately followed by the call parentheses. The formatter emits `call<T>(...)`. Spaced `a < B > (c)` remains comparison syntax. Arity and bounds fail in sema with what, why, and fix text.
options.code:
values := empty<Int>()
row := json.decode<Row>(text) ?? panic("bad row")
page := query.fetch<Page<User>>()

// Still preferred when inference is clear:
copy := identity(value)

options.name: Inference-only calls
options.detail: No call may carry type arguments. Inputs and expected result types must determine every generic parameter. Underconstrained code adds a result annotation or uses a type-owned API. Existing `decode<T>` calls migrate with no compatibility spelling.
options.technical: The parser always reads `<` after a value as comparison syntax. Sema diagnoses missing inference evidence and suggests an exact binding annotation. APIs whose main purpose is to create or inspect a type should prefer a type-owned shape.
options.code:
values: [Int] :: empty()
row: Row :: json.decode(text) ?? panic("bad row")
page: Page<User> :: query.fetch()

// Type-owned redesign when that reads better:
row := Row.decode(text) ?? panic("bad row")

comparisons.note: Closest to A. Kotlin normally infers function type arguments but permits explicit arguments when needed.
comparisons.code:
val box = emptyBox<Int>()
val copy = identity(value)

comparisons.note: Closest to A. C# documents both `Swap<int>(...)` and the shorter inferred call.
comparisons.code:
Swap<int>(ref a, ref b);
Swap(ref a, ref b);

comparisons.note: Closest to B. Generic function calls infer their arguments; callers use contextual types or a different API shape when inference is insufficient.
Closest to A, but Rust often needs the extra `::` separator. Jet can keep explicit control without copying that punctuation.
comparisons.code:
let values = Vec::<i32>::new();
let item = parse::<Item>(text);

recommendation.why: A gives beginners the shortest call through inference and gives experts a precise local override. Kotlin and C# show that optional explicit arguments can stay uncommon without becoming confusing. One general rule is cleaner than a decode-only exception.

whyNot.reason: B makes ordinary calls clean, but it forces distant result annotations or API redesign when a generic parameter has no input evidence. That removes useful expert control without improving the common call.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one parser ambiguity around `<` and comparison. Jet must make adjacency, formatting, completion, and diagnostics exact so the escape never makes ordinary expressions surprising.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared general optional arguments with a complete inference-only rule. It rejected any API-specific exception because one call grammar must apply everywhere.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested Rust turbofish, keyword arguments, brackets, type-owned factories, and result annotations. None beats plain `<T>` as an optional local override while keeping inferred calls unchanged.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested explicit arguments only for result-only parameters or selected Core APIs. It rejected that split because users would need to memorize which generic calls permit the same syntax.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gives inference-only code exact expected-type inference and useful fixes. It gives optional-explicit code the same clean default, so the comparison turns only on the expert escape.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested nested `>>`, methods, bad arity, failed bounds, comparisons, formatter stability, and misleading decode precedent. Option A survives only with a strict adjacency and diagnostic contract.

decisions.checkInstructions: Choose A or B. The verdict will become canonical S33 and will explicitly supersede conflicting S45, D-SERDE6, parser comments, examples, and summaries.

decisions.title: Argument labels and parameter contracts
decisions.gist: Choose how calls bind names and require clear arguments.
decisions.lesson: Jet labels now check spelling at one fixed position. They cannot skip defaults or reorder arguments. This makes policy-heavy APIs longer than Python and prevents label-only safety contracts.
decisions.story: Maya opens a service connection. She wants a five-second timeout but accepts every other safe default. The call should name only the changed policy.
decisions.inWild: client :: connect("db.internal", timeout: 5, tls: true)?

options.name: Named binding with parameter zones
options.detail: A written label binds by name and can skip defaults. `/` ends positional-only parameters. `*` starts label-only parameters. Unmarked parameters accept either form. A public label defaults to the local parameter name; `timeout seconds: Int` keeps public label timeout while local code uses seconds.
options.technical: Sema builds one parameter map before type checking and rejects unknown, repeated, missing, forbidden, or unlabeled-after-labeled arguments. Supplied expressions run left to right. Unbound defaults then run at call time in declaration order and may use earlier bound parameters. Public labels and zones are callable type identity; function types reuse parameter grammar. Local names and default bodies are not identity. Inferred function values retain defaults; annotated values expose only defaults written in their type. Public-label changes break callers; local-only renames do not when an external label stays stable.
options.code:
fn connect(host: String, /, *, timeout seconds: Int = 30, tls: Bool = true) => Client ? ConnectError
client :: connect("db.internal", tls: true, timeout: 5)?

forced: fn(*, force: Bool) => Void = save
forced(force: true)
// forced(true) is rejected

options.name: Named binding without zones
options.detail: A written label binds by name and can skip defaults. Every parameter still accepts positional calls. This keeps declarations small but cannot require labels or protect positional compatibility.
options.technical: The binder maps labels to parameter names. There is no label-only or positional-only declaration. Public labels are part of callable type identity and function types spell them with the same parameter grammar. Renaming any public parameter remains a source change for labeled callers.
options.code:
fn connect(host: String, timeout: Int = 30, tls: Bool = true) => Client ? ConnectError

client :: connect("db.internal", tls: true)?
legacy :: connect("db.internal", 30, true)?

options.name: Mandatory external label contracts
options.detail: Each declaration writes a public label or `_` for positional use, even when public and local names match. The rule is explicit per parameter but adds text to ordinary declarations.
options.technical: This follows a strict Swift-style external and internal name split. A public label binds by name. `_` forbids a label. Every parameter and function type declares its public call contract separately; no label is inferred from the local name. Public labels are part of callable type identity.
options.code:
fn connect(_ host: String, timeout seconds: Int = 30, tls enabled: Bool = true) => Client ? ConnectError

client :: connect("db.internal", timeout: 5, tls: true)?

options.name: Keep fixed positional binding
options.detail: Labels remain optional spelling checks at fixed positions. Existing calls stay unchanged. APIs still cannot skip an earlier default or require a policy label.
options.technical: S61 stays unchanged. Labels never reorder. Only trailing defaults can be omitted. Function types keep erasing labels because labels remain positional spelling checks rather than a call contract.
options.code: client :: connect("db.internal", EncodingLimits.safe(), 5, true)?

comparisons.note: Python uses `/` for positional-only parameters and `*` for keyword-only parameters. Named arguments can reorder calls and skip defaults.
comparisons.code:
def connect(host, /, *, timeout=30, tls=True): ...
connect("db.internal", tls=True, timeout=5)

comparisons.note: Swift gives each parameter an external call label and an internal name. `_` removes the external label.
comparisons.code:
func connect(_ host: String, timeout seconds: Int = 30)
connect("db.internal", timeout: 5)

recommendation.why: A reaches Python's call power with one familiar contract and adds an optional stable public/local name split. Jet then adds static types, effects, ownership, and better diagnostics without longer common calls.

whyNot.reason: B cannot require a clear policy label or protect a positional-only compatibility boundary.
C repeats a public-label choice on every parameter and makes ordinary declarations longer.
D keeps the exact API weakness that caused this decision.

recommendation.tradeoff: The declaration and function-type grammars gain two parameter separators. Public labels and zones affect callable assignability. Authors can preserve callers by writing a stable external label and changing only the local name.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared name binding, per-parameter labels, and the current rule. It recommended named binding with explicit contract zones.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested automatic labels, Boolean-only labels, builder objects, and overloads. Those choices either missed general APIs or added a second mechanism.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined named binding with Python-style zones. This gives short normal calls and explicit expert contracts through one binder.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review added an optional public and local name split to the recommended option. The mandatory-label option remains more verbose for ordinary declarations.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested public and local renames, mixed positional and labeled calls, spreads, side-effect order, defaults, generics, assignment, and function-value calls. Label and zone identity, explicit function-type grammar, unlabeled-after-labeled rejection, source-order supplied evaluation, declaration-order default evaluation, and one pre-type-check binding map close those risks.

decisions.title: Exact numbers in JSON
decisions.gist: Choose how JSON keeps exact integers and decimals.
decisions.lesson: JSON number text can exceed Int or lose meaning in Float. Python can parse those tokens as Decimal or arbitrary integers. Jet must keep exact values without an untyped callback bag.
decisions.story: Noah reads invoices from a payment service. An amount such as 12.340 and a large invoice number must survive decoding without binary rounding.
decisions.inWild:
invoice :: json.decode<Invoice>(payload)?
print(invoice.amount) // Decimal("12.340")

options.name: Typed decoder reads number tokens
options.detail: DataTree keeps the ratified Int and Float meaning. A typed Decimal or BigInt decoder reads the original number token before tree conversion. Typed whole-value and stream decoding stay exact.
options.technical: One tokenizer feeds either the ratified DataTree builder or a typed visitor. The visitor projects number text directly into the requested Decimal or BigInt field before any Float conversion. Both destinations share limits, paths, errors, duplicate-key rules, and stream behavior. json.canonical(json.parse(text)?)? keeps the one-call behavior required by D-JSONCANON1.

options.name: Amend DataTree and JCS together
options.detail: Edition 2027 adds BigInt and Decimal tree variants. Dynamic tree work becomes exact. Ratifying this option also amends the canonical JSON law with one checked projection rule.
options.technical: D-JSONCANON1 is amended as follows: json.canonical keeps direct support for ordinary parsed Int and Float values, including -0.0 and 1e30. BigInt and Decimal canonicalize only when exactly representable as a finite Float. Otherwise EncodingError has kind Unsupported and the value path. BigInt reason is `JCS requires BigInt exactly representable as IEEE 754 binary64; encode this integer as Text`. Decimal reason is `JCS requires Decimal exactly representable as IEEE 754 binary64; encode this decimal as Text`. No rounding is allowed.
options.code:
tree :: json.parse(payload)?
amount :: Decimal = tree["amount"].decimal()?
canonical :: json.canonical(tree)? // exact Float projection or EncodingError Unsupported

options.name: Exact numbers by parse policy
options.detail: Callers request exact numbers when they need them. Existing Int and Float defaults remain small. Exact work gains an extra option and can be missed at a money boundary.
options.technical: json.parse and json.reader accept a checked JSONNumberPolicy. `.Native` returns Int or Float. `.Exact` returns Int, BigInt, or Decimal. The policy becomes part of stream state and error identity.
options.code:
tree :: json.parse(payload, numbers: .Exact)?
invoice :: tree.decode<Invoice>()?

options.name: Require quoted exact values
options.detail: Exact Decimal and BigInt values stay JSON strings. This preserves current DataTree. It rejects normal numeric input from common services and remains worse than Python.
options.technical: Decimal accepts DataTree.Text and DataTree.Int. Fractional DataTree.Float remains rejected. Schemas must encode exact fractional values as strings.
options.code: invoice :: json.decode<Invoice>("{\"amount\":\"12.340\"}")?

comparisons.note: Python json.loads can send integer and fractional number tokens to arbitrary-precision constructors.
JavaScript JSON.parse converts every number to binary64 Number. Large integers can lose precision before application code sees them.

recommendation.why: A gives typed Decimal and BigInt fields exact standard JSON numbers without changing the ratified DataTree or one-call JCS contract. One tokenizer and one error model still serve whole-value and stream APIs.

whyNot.reason: B reopens D-JSONCANON1 and changes the dynamic tree contract to solve a typed-decoding need.
C makes correctness depend on a caller option at the exact boundary that needs a safe default.
D requires nonstandard quoted numbers and remains worse than Python's direct numeric parsing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Dynamic DataTree users still receive Int or Float. Exactness is guaranteed when the destination type requests Decimal or BigInt.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared typed token decoding, exact tree values, an opt-in policy, and quoted strings. It recommended typed token decoding.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested raw number text, arbitrary rational values, schema-only decoding, and callbacks. BigInt and Decimal already cover the required domain without new numeric types.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review uses one tokenizer with two checked destinations: the ratified DataTree builder and an exact typed visitor. Limits and diagnostics remain shared.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened exact tree values by requiring an explicit D-JSONCANON1 amendment. That option remains available without hiding the conflict.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested JCS values such as -0.0 and 1e30, scale, exponent text, limits, streams, and old editions. Typed token projection preserves exact fields without breaking ratified canonicalization.

decisions.title: How typed policies apply to callables
decisions.gist: Choose how a typed policy wraps a function without changing its callable contract.
decisions.lesson: A callable is a function that can be stored and passed. A policy adds caching, retry, tracing, registration, or routing around that call. Signature-preserving means the policy keeps parameter labels, defaults, access modes, generic types, effects, errors, and returned-view relations. The choice is where the policy is named. An ordinary wrapper is explicit but can repeat a signature. A declaration marker is concise but hides behavior at call sites. An application expression is local and reusable. A registry is distant. The compiler must reject hidden authority and changed lifetimes.
decisions.story: Mina maintains a service client used by a command tool and a web worker. She wants retries and tracing on both call sites, but a policy must not change labels, error handling, or the borrowed response view.

options.name: Explicit ordinary wrappers
options.detail: Policies are ordinary functions that take a callable and return another callable. The call site names every wrapper, so behavior is easy to see. The cost is that a wrapper may need to repeat the target signature, and repeated signatures can drift.
options.technical: No callable-policy syntax or new type is added. A wrapper is accepted only when its checked signature matches the target, including labels, defaults, access, effects, errors, generic parameters, and view provenance.

options.name: Declaration policy marker
options.detail: A function declaration names its policy beside the function. Calls remain ordinary and keep the original signature. This is concise for a function with one stable policy, but the declaration carries behavior that is less visible at each call site.
options.technical: A ratified marker attaches a typed policy value to a function declaration. Expansion happens after signature checking. The policy may observe and return the declared result, but may not widen effects, errors, access, or view provenance.

options.name: Explicit policy application
options.detail: A policy is applied where a callable value is created. The source shows both the target and the policy, and the result can be passed to several callers. It adds one expression form, but keeps behavior local and inspectable.
options.technical: The policy application receives a typed callable value and returns the same full callable signature. The compiler records the source identity and policy chain. Policy code cannot create a type, add authority, or erase labels, effects, errors, or view relations.
options.code:
load_user_with_retry :: apply(retry(3), load_user)
load_user_traced :: apply(trace("users.load"), load_user_with_retry)

user :: load_user_traced(id: account.id)
// The applied value keeps the original named parameter and default.

options.name: Registry by callable identity
options.detail: A policy is registered for a named function, and later calls use the registered behavior automatically. This keeps call sites short, but behavior depends on distant configuration and can surprise readers or tools.
options.technical: Registration is checked against the complete callable signature and source identity. Duplicate or conflicting registrations are errors. The registry cannot cross package or authority boundaries without an explicit import.
options.code:
policy.register(load_user, retry(3))
policy.register(load_user, trace("users.load"))

user :: load_user(id: account.id)
// A reader must inspect the registry to know that retries and tracing run.

options.name: Declared default, call-site override
options.detail: One policy mechanism with two attachment points. A declaration marker sets the default policy, so plain calls get safe behavior with no ceremony. An explicit application at a call site replaces that default with the exact chain it names.
options.technical: The marker and the application use the same typed policy values and the same signature-preservation law. A plain call runs the declared chain. An application such as apply(p1, p2, f) builds a callable whose chain is exactly p1 then p2; the declared default does not stack under it. An application with no policies yields the bare function. No policy may widen effects, errors, access, or view provenance.

comparisons.note: Decorators attach wrappers above a function and can change its runtime behavior or signature unless the author preserves metadata by convention.
Rust normally uses explicit higher-order functions or macros. A macro can preserve a surface, but the compiler does not provide one general decorator contract.
Swift commonly uses explicit wrappers, property wrappers, and result builders. These are separate mechanisms with different type and lifetime rules.

recommendation.why: The declared marker gives every plain call a safe default with no ceremony. The explicit application gives any call site exact local control. Both spellings use one typed policy value, so the language keeps one mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Repeated wrapper signatures create a migration and drift surface for labels, defaults, effects, errors, and returned views.
A declaration default alone cannot be changed or removed at a call site, so an expert loses exact local control.
Application alone gives no default, so a library author cannot ship safe behavior for plain beginner calls.
A distant registry hides behavior from call sites and makes package, source, and tooling inspection harder.

recommendation.tradeoff: A reader of a plain call must check the declaration to learn the default chain. Any call site where the chain matters can repair this locally, because an applied chain is the whole chain.

reviewPasses.base: The ballot compares explicit wrappers, declaration attachment, explicit application, and identity registration. Each option keeps the full callable contract visible in its own way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked labels, defaults, access modes, generics, effects, errors, returned views, package boundaries, and source identity. No option may hide these facts.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review first kept application alone. The owner then proposed a declared default with call-site override; that combination is now option E with a replace rule, and it becomes the recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Each option was strengthened with a concrete beginner call and an expert inspection rule. The recommendation favors local behavior over distant registration.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack checked policy-added authority, changed errors, hidden defaults, label loss, view lifetime, duplicate registration, and policy behavior across package boundaries.

decisions.title: Two markers spell #Policy: pick the one owner of the name
decisions.gist: Which mechanism keeps the name #Policy: call wrappers, or compiler rules.
decisions.lesson: D-CALLPOLICY1 ratified #Policy(retry(3), trace("users.load")) as the marker for callable wrapper chains. A shipped marker already spells #Policy(no_alloc): a scoped compiler rule, legal at the same grammar position. Same name, two meanings. The ratified ballot never checked against the shipped marker. Separately, D-AUTHORITY-MEM1 already retires four of the old marker's six keys, so the old #Policy is shrinking either way.
decisions.story: Ana reads a codebase and sees #Policy(no_alloc) on one function and #Policy(retry(3)) on the next. One forbids the function something at compile time; the other wraps its calls at run time. Nothing on the page says these are different machines.

options.name: One grammar, told apart by argument shape
options.detail: Both meanings keep the name. A bare name like no_alloc means a compiler rule; a call like retry(3) means a wrapper chain. No rename, no migration. The cost is a silent rule: adding parentheses to an argument flips which machine reads it, and no error says so.
options.code:
#Policy(no_alloc)          // compiler rule
#Policy(retry(3))          // wrapper chain
#Policy(no_alloc, retry(3)) // both machines, one list

options.name: Rename the wrapper marker
options.detail: The shipped compiler-rule marker keeps #Policy. The new wrapper marker takes a fresh name: #Wrap, #Around, #Apply, #Relay, or #Escort. This reopens D-CALLPOLICY1's spelling, ratified two days ago, and the wrapper cards re-land on the new name.

options.name: Retire the old marker; #Policy means wrappers only
options.detail: MEM1 already moves the four memory keys onto the rights tree as denials. The two survivors follow their own laws home: the unsafe permission becomes an authority manifest entry, and explicit_units becomes a typed setting on the fact plane. The PolicyKey table deletes, and #Policy has exactly one meaning: the ratified wrapper chain.
options.technical: no_alloc, zero_rc, arena_bounded, gc: rights-tree denial rows per D-AUTHORITY-MEM1 and D-AUTHORITY-MEM2. unsafe: an allow/deny entry in the authority manifest per D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1. explicit_units: a typed setting per D-CONF-KEY1. Scope inheritance (organization to block) rides the manifest and scope law that already governs those planes. The denial row rides the signature effect arrow, in the return position. It never stands above a function; only markers stand there.

options.name: Merge: compiler rules join the wrapper chain grammar
options.detail: One registry row, one list: #Policy(no_alloc, retry(3)). Compiler rules and runtime wrappers become entries of one chain. The reader still cannot tell which entry does what, and the two behaviors share nothing but a comma.
options.code:
#Policy(no_alloc, retry(3), trace("users.load"))
+fn load_user(id: UserId) => User ? DbErr { ... }

comparisons.note: Decorators wrap calls, and linter pragmas constrain code, and they never share a name. The split option C creates is the split Python already has.
Attributes share one syntax for both kinds, like option A, and readers must know each attribute to know its machine.

recommendation.why: Every old key already has a better home under this week's ratified law, so the collision resolves by finishing that migration. The name then has one meaning, the newest ratified spelling stands unchanged, and no shape rule or rename is needed.

whyNot.reason: A silent shape rule flips meaning when parentheses appear, with no error. Two machines behind one name is the confusion, not a fix for it.
It reopens a spelling the owner ratified two days ago, and the newest ruling owns the name.
Compile-time constraints and runtime wrappers share nothing but a comma. One list with two behaviors hides which entry does what.

recommendation.tradeoff: The old marker cannot delete until the unsafe and explicit_units keys land in their new homes, so #1396 gains two small dependencies on the authority and settings cards.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared shape disambiguation, renaming the new marker, retiring the old marker, and merging, and recommended retiring the old marker because its keys already have ratified homes.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review hunted more options: banning #Policy at Function scope for rules, and a mandatory prefix like #Policy(rule: no_alloc). Both were folded into A as tactics, since each still leaves two machines behind one name.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested C plus a temporary shape rule during migration. Rejected: greenfield law forbids a transition grammar, and the migration is one coherent change.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with a rich name menu (#Wrap, #Around, #Apply, #Relay, #Escort) and confirmed any of them reads well at the call site. B still reopens a two-day-old ratification.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked C's claim that every key has a home: unsafe and explicit_units were unhoused. The ballot was repaired to name their exact destinations, the manifest and the settings plane, and the recommendation survives with those two dependencies made explicit.

decisions.title: Source count is evidence, not a hard ceiling
decisions.outcome: Do not use a hard 1:1 source-count ceiling. Count syntax, but judge added syntax by clarity, readability, reasonability, and the guarantees it makes explicit. Preserve Jet's useful explicit structure.
decisions.comment: Do not use a hard 1:1 source-count ceiling. Count syntax, but judge added syntax by clarity, readability, reasonability, and the guarantees it makes explicit. Preserve Jet's useful explicit structure.

decisions.title: What zip does when the lists are different lengths
decisions.gist: What happens when you zip lists of different lengths.
decisions.lesson: `zip` walks several lists at once and hands you one item from each. Today Jet stops at the shortest list and says nothing. The extra items vanish, and every pair after a missing item can line up the wrong values. This choice decides whether Jet reports that, prevents it, or lets it pass.
decisions.story: Sam builds a class report. He has one list of student names and one list of scores. Bob missed the test, so the scores list is one shorter. Sam's report prints, looks fine, and quietly gives Bob the next student's score. Nothing warned him.

options.name: Stop at the shortest, stay silent
options.detail: Today's behavior. Zip pairs items until one list runs out, then stops. No error, no warning. Fast and simple, and wrong quietly.
options.technical: Current `jet_iter_zip` in Prelude/Core/Collections.rs delegates to Rust's `Iterator::zip`. No sema check, no diagnostic, no runtime cost.
options.code:
names.zip(scores)   // 2 pairs, no message
// Bob silently gets Cara's score

options.name: Different lengths stop the program
options.detail: Zip requires every list to be the same length. A mismatch stops with a friendly report naming both lengths, the same way indexing past the end already does. You can never ship the wrong pairing.
options.technical: Runtime length check before iteration; friendly report in the S39 out-of-bounds family, exit 70. Lazy `Iter` sources with unknown length check as they run and stop at the first shortfall.

options.name: A warning you can silence
options.detail: Zip still stops at the shortest, but the compiler warns when it can prove the lengths differ, and a lint fires otherwise. Existing code keeps working and you get told.
options.technical: Comptime length proof where both operands are literal or const; otherwise an L05xx lint on any zip whose operands are not proven equal. No runtime check, no runtime cost.

options.name: Three named verbs, no default guessing
options.detail: You say what you mean at the call. `zip` requires equal lengths. `zip_short` stops at the shortest on purpose. `zip_pad` fills the gaps with a value you supply. Nothing is silent and nothing is guessed.
options.technical: `zip` carries option B's check. `zip_short` is today's behavior under an honest name. `zip_pad(other, fill: T)` yields the longer length. All three are D-ITERTOOLS1 adapters returning lazy `Iter`, unchanged in every other respect.
options.code:
names.zip(scores)              // error: lengths differ (3 vs 2)
names.zip_short(scores)        // 2 pairs, on purpose
names.zip_pad(scores, fill: 0) // 3 pairs, Bob scores 0

comparisons.note: Silent truncation by default. `strict=True` was added in 3.10 to raise instead, and `itertools.zip_longest(fillvalue=)` pads. The default stayed silent for compatibility, which Jet does not owe.
comparisons.code:
zip(names, scores)              # silent, 2 pairs
zip(names, scores, strict=True) # ValueError
zip_longest(names, scores, fillvalue=0)

comparisons.note: Silent truncation, no strict form. Rust accepts this because its zip is an iterator primitive and pairing errors are expected to be caught by types.
Silent truncation. Swift's answer to the shifted-pairing bug is to push you toward a dictionary or a struct instead.
`List.map2` truncates, but Elm's culture is to model paired data as one list of records, so the mismatch rarely arises.

recommendation.why: Option D removes the guess. Each of the three real intentions gets its own verb, so reading the call tells you what happens when the lengths differ. The dangerous case needs the most typing and the safe case is the short plain name, which is the ordering Jet wants everywhere.

whyNot.reason: It ships a wrong report with no signal. Jet already stops on a missing map key and teaches manual index loops, so staying silent here contradicts how the rest of the language behaves.
Stopping is right for the mistake but leaves no spelling for stopping at the shortest on purpose, which is a real and reasonable thing to want.

A warning that can be silenced still lets the wrong pairing reach production, and the proof only works when both lengths are known at compile time. The common case of two lists built at runtime gets a lint that authors learn to ignore.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three names instead of one. That cost is paid once when learning and repaid at every call, because the reader never has to remember which silent rule applies.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared today's silence with a hard stop and recommended the hard stop, on the grounds that Jet already stops on a missing map key.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the padded variant and the warning option, and checked Python's strict flag, Rust, Swift, and Elm.
