Returning a length-tagged result and returning an optional were tested and dropped, because both push a check onto every caller for a mistake most callers never make.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Combining the hard stop with named opt-outs proved stronger than either alone, which produced option D. A hard stop with no escape and a silent default with a lint each solved one half of the problem.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Each option was strengthened on its own terms, giving silence its zero-cost case and giving the warning exact comptime length proof. Both survive as coherent choices and both still let a wrong report ship.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The recommendation was attacked on lazy sources whose length is unknown before iteration. Option D was repaired to check as it runs and stop at the first shortfall, keeping the guarantee without materializing the input.

decisions.title: Zip family: n-ary inputs and typed padding
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet zips any number of lists and fills missing items.
decisions.lesson: Python has two useful shapes: `zip(a, b, c)` pairs any number of inputs, and `zip_longest(a, b, c, fillvalue: x)` keeps the longest input. Jet currently has one receiver plus one other, and D-ZIPLEN1 names three safe behaviors but does not define n-ary types or padding for heterogeneous inputs. This decision completes that family without silent truncation, guessed values, or a dynamic `Any` row.
decisions.story: Maya builds a report from names, scores, and regions. The report needs one row for each position, must keep each column type, and must stay clear when one source ends first.
decisions.inWild:
names :: ["Ada", "Lin"]
scores :: [12, 18, 25]
regions :: ["US", "CA", "GB"]

rows :: zip(name: names, score: scores, region: regions)
loop name, score, region; rows {
    print("{name}: {score} ({region})")
}

short :: zip_short(names, scores, regions)
optional :: zip_pad(names, scores, regions)
filled :: zip_pad(
    name: names,
    score: scores,
    region: regions,
    fills: (name: "(unknown)", score: 0, region: "??"))

options.name: Keep pair methods
options.detail: A list method takes one other list. `zip`, `zip_short`, and `zip_pad` stay pair operations. This keeps the smallest surface, but it cannot express Python's common three-list call.
options.technical: The receiver contributes the first list and the call accepts one `[U]`. `zip_pad` keeps two typed fill values for heterogeneous pairs. No free n-ary entry point exists.

options.name: Homogeneous n-way rows
options.detail: A variadic family accepts any number of lists when every element type is the same. Each row is a list, so the call is short, but mixed columns such as names and scores fail.
options.technical: Use the existing homogeneous `...T` parameter shape. `zip(xs: ...[T])` returns `Iter<[T]>`, and one `fill: T` value fills every missing position.

options.name: Fixed arity overloads
options.detail: Ship checked forms for two, three, four, and a published maximum number of inputs. Mixed columns keep their types, but a call above the maximum fails and the family grows one arity at a time.
options.technical: Each supported arity has an ordinary signature and a named tuple result. No heterogeneous type pack is needed, but the API and codegen have a fixed upper bound.

options.name: Dynamic Python rows
options.detail: Accept any number of inputs and return dynamic rows. This matches Python's runtime freedom, but Jet loses static column types, field access, and early fill errors.
options.technical: The row uses `DataTree` or a top type. This conflicts with Jet's closed dynamic value law and moves type checks from sema to every caller.

options.name: Typed n-way family with optional padding
options.detail: Accept any number of lists and keep each column's type. Free functions cover Python's call shape, and methods remain equivalent convenience forms. `zip_pad` uses `None` by default and accepts typed fills when concrete rows are needed. The default changes only padding; strict and short behavior stay unchanged.
options.technical: An inferred heterogeneous pack preserves `T1, T2, ...` and creates a named row. `zip` requires equal lengths. `zip_short` ends at the first end. `zip_pad` runs to the longest input. Omitted `fill` means explicit `None` and yields optional columns. `fill: value` works when one value fits every column. `fills: (field_1: T1, ...)` gives one typed fill per column. Free and method forms call one Prelude implementation. Zero inputs return empty `Iter<Void>`; one input returns identity `Iter<T>`.
options.code:
rows :: zip(name: names, score: scores, region: regions)
same :: names.zip(scores, regions)
short :: zip_short(names, scores, regions)
method_short :: names.zip_short(scores, regions)
optional :: zip_pad(names, scores, regions)
method_filled :: names.zip_pad(scores, regions,
    fills: (a: "(unknown)", b: 0, c: "??"))
filled :: zip_pad(
    name: names,
    score: scores,
    region: regions,
    fills: (name: "(unknown)", score: 0, region: "??"))
// the last row is ("(unknown)", 25, "GB")

comparisons.note: `zip` accepts any number of iterables and stops at the shortest. `itertools.zip_longest` keeps the longest and uses `None` or one supplied fill value.
comparisons.code:
zip(names, scores, regions)
itertools.zip_longest(names, scores, regions, fillvalue=None)

comparisons.note: Rust's standard `Iterator::zip` is binary and truncates. Multi-input zip needs a separate adapter, and typed padding needs a caller-chosen representation.
comparisons.code:
left.iter().zip(right.iter())
// a third input needs another adapter

recommendation.why: Only E gives arbitrary input count, heterogeneous static rows, Python's free-function call, and method convenience. It keeps D-ZIPLEN1's explicit verbs and makes missing data visible as `None` or a typed fill.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the requested n-way Python shape unavailable and forces callers to nest pair calls or write manual loops.
It accepts many lists, but it rejects the normal mixed-column case and returns list rows instead of typed columns.
It keeps typed rows only up to an arbitrary cap and duplicates the family for every new arity.
It copies Python's runtime freedom by giving up Jet's type safety, field access, and sema checks.

recommendation.tradeoff: The compiler must infer one heterogeneous input pack and generate named row types. `fills:` adds words for concrete heterogeneous padding, while default `None` keeps the no-fill call short.

hybrid.synthesis: Use E's typed heterogeneous pack with Python's `None` default and an expert per-column fill pack. Both forms call one zip Prelude operation, so convenience does not create a second semantic path.

harvest.use: Keep `zip_pad(a, b, c)` short and return visible optional columns when no fill is given.
Keep `fills:` typed per column so concrete rows do not use dynamic values or guessed defaults.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared pair-only, homogeneous variadic, fixed-arity, dynamic, and typed n-way families. It recommended E because only E covers mixed columns and arbitrary input count.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review checked common fills, per-column fills, optional `None`, free functions, method calls, input labels, and zero or one input. It added explicit `fills:` and stable generated row fields.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined E's typed pack with Python's `None` default and an expert per-column fill pack. One Prelude operation serves both forms.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each alternative on its own terms. Pair methods stay clean, homogeneous rows stay simple, fixed arities stay easy to lower, and dynamic rows stay flexible.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked arbitrary arity, lazy length mismatch, omitted fills, bad fill types, method and free-function drift, and dynamic fallback. E now defines strict checks, optional rows, typed fills, stable fields, and no silent cap.

decisions.checkInstructions: After ratification, test two, three, and many inputs; zero and one input; strict, short, and padded behavior; optional `None`; common fills; and per-column fills. Test free and method forms, lazy sources, AOT, default `jet run`, interpreter deopt, JIT, and web where applicable.

decisions.title: How a plain function earns a dot
decisions.gist: Whether `print(x)` can also be written `x.print()`, and how a function earns that.
decisions.lesson: Jet names work two ways. A method belongs to a type and is called after a dot. A plain function stands alone and takes the value inside its parentheses. Only methods get a dot today. The dot is also how editors show you what you can do with a value, so plain functions stay invisible until you know their names.
decisions.story: Priya is three days into Jet. She types `total.` and her editor lists every method on a number. She wants to print it. Printing is a plain function, so nothing in that list mentions it. She has to already know the name to find it.

options.name: Any function is callable either way
options.detail: Every plain function whose first value fits can be called with a dot, and every method can be called as a plain function. No declarations. This is what D and Nim do.
options.technical: Method lookup falls back to searching every visible free function whose first parameter accepts the receiver. Resolving `text.parse()` against `Int.parse`, `Float.parse`, and `Bool.parse` needs return-type-directed inference, which D-LAMBDAINFER1 refuses. Retires E0311. A receiver marked `&` in D-MEM1 would write through a call site that shows no sigil.
options.code:
total.print()   // finds core.io.print
print(total)    // same call
add(total, 3)   // methods also callable this way

text.parse()    // ambiguous: Int, Float, or Bool?
v.scale(2.0)    // writes to v, decided by a sigil in another file

options.name: Core writes a second dot-only function
options.detail: Nothing changes about lookup. Core declares extra dot-callable wrappers using the form Jet already has. You get the dot, but the same work is now written twice.
options.technical: Uses D-EXTMETH1's top-level `fn Type.method(self)` form. No parser, resolution, or inference change. The wrapper is a separate declaration from the plain function, so the two can drift. D-EXTMETH1's same-module orphan rule also blocks users from giving a Core type a dot from their own module.

options.name: Mark the receiver in the signature, first value only
options.detail: One function, written once, marked to say which value is the subject of the call. Both spellings work. The mark must sit on a read-only value, so a dot from a plain function can never change what is before it. The owner chose the `#Root` spelling on 3 August 2026, from a menu including Datum, Subject, Pivot, and Anchor.
options.technical: A `#Root` rule at the reserved `RuleSite::Parameter` site (Policy.rs:161, unused today), on the first parameter. Six laws follow. One: the marked parameter must be bare read access (D-MEM-PARAM1), so `&` and `^` are E-coded. Two: dot-callability is import-scoped, never global. Three: a collision with a real method is an error, never a silent shadow. Four: resolution is never return-type-directed, so two candidates is an error listing both. Five: `jet inspect` and LSP report which module a dot came from. Six: `jet fmt` never rewrites between the two spellings.

options.name: Mark the receiver anywhere in the signature
options.detail: Everything in the marked-receiver option, except the subject need not be the first value. The signature can be ordered for reading while the dot is chosen for chaining.
options.technical: Identical laws to E, minus the first-position restriction. Cost: at a plain call `write(path, text)` the argument order no longer predicts the dot form `text.write(path)`, so a reader moving between spellings must check the signature. Every language with this feature restricts it to the first argument; none has tried this.
options.code:
fn write(path: Path, #Root text: String) => Void ?

text.write(path)      // chain the text
write(path, text)     // or read it as an ordinary call

options.name: Leave it alone
options.detail: Plain functions stay plain. Chains end by wrapping the result in a call. One spelling per call, and a dot always means a method.
options.technical: D-UFCS1's decline stands, as does D-SHAPE-PIPE1=C's ruling that reusable flows use ordinary calls and named intermediate values.
options.code:
print(orders.filter(o => o.state == .Paid).map(o => o.total).sum())

report :: orders.filter(o => o.state == .Paid).map(o => o.total).sum()
print(report)

comparisons.note: Rejected implicit either-way calling twice, because it made every plain function a possible method and destroyed local reasoning. It instead shipped an explicit marked receiver parameter in 2023, which is the shape of options E and F.
comparisons.code: void f(this Self&& self);   // C++23: the receiver is marked, not guessed

comparisons.note: Extension functions declare a receiver and resolve at compile time, which works well. Its known trap is that a real method silently wins over an extension, so adding a method quietly changes call sites. Law three exists to prevent that.

Extension methods carry a marked first argument and built the whole LINQ chaining ecosystem, so the shape is proven at scale. Its weakness is opacity: which methods exist depends on imports, and origin is hard to see. Law five answers that.
comparisons.code:
static int Twice(this int x) => x * 2;
5.Twice();

comparisons.note: Full symmetry, and it works there because the standard library has almost no methods, so nothing collides. Jet has methods on every core type, so that model does not transfer.

The original either-way design. It enabled excellent chained pipelines, but codebases drift between both spellings for the same call with no canonical form. Law six keeps the author's choice instead of churning it.

recommendation.why: Marking the receiver gets the discoverability and the left-to-right reading without letting the compiler guess. One function is written once and read two ways, and the mark is visible where the function is defined. The read-only law then buys a reasoning rule no other language offers: if a dot changes the value before it, that dot is a method.

whyNot.reason: Guessed either-way calling needs inference Jet refuses, and it hides D-MEM1 sigils, so `x.f()` could write to x based on a sigil declared elsewhere. C++ rejected this exact design twice on reasoning grounds.
It writes the same work twice, and the two declarations can drift apart. It also cannot give a Core type a dot from a user's module, because the orphan rule blocks it.
It is strictly more powerful and can be adopted later without breaking anything written for E, so there is no reason to buy the extra reasoning cost before an API needs it.
It leaves the discoverability gap that started this. A beginner typing a dot cannot find printing, and a chain that reads left to right still ends by being read inside out.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core must decide, function by function, which functions get a subject, and an unmarked function stays invisible from the dot. That work is the feature: the alternative is a dot whose meaning is assembled by search instead of written down.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft weighed guessed either-way calling against the status quo and recommended writing a second dot-only function in Core, because it needed no language change.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review found `RuleSite::Parameter` reserved and unused, which made a marked receiver reachable without new grammar, and added options E and F. It also surveyed C++, Kotlin, C#, Nim, and D, and turned each failure into a law rather than a warning.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Writing a second function in Core was tested against the marked receiver and lost, because one definition read two ways cannot drift while two declarations can. The read-only rule was then folded in from the memory model rather than invented.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Guessed either-way calling was steelmanned as the honest end state for a chain-shaped language, and the status quo as the only option with exactly one spelling per call. Both remain coherent and both were kept.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The recommendation was attacked for deferring work to Core reviewers one function at a time, and that holds and is accepted. It was also attacked on whether the read-only law blocks useful mutating chains; it does, and that is the point, since mutation stays on real methods.

decisions.title: How many symbols does a Jet binding need?
decisions.gist: How many symbols Jet uses to name a value and to change it.
decisions.lesson: Jet spells a local binding three ways today. `name :: value` names a value that never changes. `name := value` names a value that can change. `name = value` changes a value that already exists. Jet also bans one name hiding another (E0118). The compiler therefore always knows whether a name is new. This choice picks how many of those three symbols Jet keeps, and which symbol does which job.
decisions.story: Priya runs a two hour Jet workshop for people who know a little Python. Six minutes in, a student types `total = 0` and the file will not build. Priya then spends ten minutes on three symbols, before anyone has printed a number.

options.name: Keep three symbols
options.detail: Nothing changes. `::` names a fixed value. `:=` names a changing value. `=` changes a value that already exists. Because `=` can never make a new name, a misspelt write is an error today, with a spelling suggestion. The price is that the everyday case uses `::`, which is the least familiar of the three.
options.technical: Three legal binding events exist: declare fixed, declare changing, and write. `=` requires the name to already exist, so a misspelt write raises E0107 with a suggestion. Writing a `::` name is E0111. Redeclaring a live name is E0118. A census of the repository shows 667 `::`, 72 `:=`, and 24 plain writes across `examples/` and the test corpus.
options.code:
tax_bp :: 875        // fixed
subtotal := 0        // changing
subtotal = 12        // write

tax_bp = 900         // E0111: tax_bp cannot change
subtatal = 12        // E0107: unknown name; did you mean `subtotal`?

options.name: Two symbols: `::` and `:=`
options.detail: Drop `=` from bindings. `::` names a fixed value. `:=` names a changing value and also changes it. Fixed values stay clearly marked, and the two symbols look alike, so the pair is easy to teach. The price is that a misspelt write quietly makes a new name instead of raising an error.
options.technical: `:=` declares when the name is new in the current scope and writes when the name is already live and changeable. Writing a `::` name stays E0111. E0107 no longer fires on a misspelt write, because every `:=` is a legal declaration. Jet has no unused name check, so nothing else catches it.
options.code:
tax_bp :: 875        // fixed
subtotal := 0        // changing
subtotal := 12       // write, same symbol

tax_bp := 900        // E0111: tax_bp cannot change
subtatal := 12       // no error: a new name quietly appears

options.name: Two symbols: `=` and `:=`
options.detail: Drop `::`. `=` names a fixed value, and also writes a changing one. `:=` is the one mark that says a name may change. Beginners type the symbol they already know, and get the safe default. Jet already uses `=` to define types, module aliases, field defaults, and short function bodies, so bindings would match. The price is that a misspelt write quietly makes a new name.
options.technical: `=` declares a fixed binding when the name is new, and writes when the name is already live and changeable. Writing a fixed name stays E0111. E0107 no longer fires on a misspelt write. This spelling matches `type Key = Int`, `module m = other`, `field: Int = 3` (D-FIELDDEF1), and 238 expression bodies in `examples/`.
options.code:
tax_bp = 875         // fixed
subtotal := 0        // changing
subtotal = 12        // write

tax_bp = 900         // E0111: tax_bp cannot change; declare it with `:=`
subtatal = 12        // no error: a new fixed name quietly appears

options.name: Two symbols: `::` and `=`
options.detail: Drop `:=`. `::` names a fixed value. `=` names a changing value and writes it, exactly like C or Java without a marker. Anyone arriving from a mainstream language writes changing code with no new symbol at all. The price is that the familiar symbol is the unsafe one, and a misspelt write quietly makes a new name.
options.technical: `=` declares a changeable binding when the name is new, and writes otherwise. Writing a `::` name stays E0111. E0107 no longer fires on a misspelt write. Compound writes such as `+=` and `++` keep working unchanged, because their target is still a changeable binding.
options.code:
tax_bp :: 875        // fixed
subtotal = 0         // changing, declared
subtotal = 12        // write, same symbol

tax_bp = 900         // E0111: tax_bp cannot change
subtatal = 12        // no error: a new changing name quietly appears

options.name: Three symbols, remapped: `=`, `:=`, `<-`
options.detail: Keep three jobs, but move them. `=` names a fixed value, so the everyday case uses the familiar symbol. `:=` names a changing value. `<-` writes into a changing name, and can never make one. Every check in option A survives, and the first hour only needs `=`. The price is a new arrow that no other popular language uses this way.
options.technical: `<-` is unused in Jet today. It joins the existing arrow family, where `=>` gives a callable result and `->` picks a control arm. `<-` requires the name to exist, so E0107 still fires on a misspelt write. The lexer must split `<-` from `<` followed by a negative number, so `x <- 1` and `x < -1` need a firm rule.
options.code:
tax_bp = 875         // fixed
subtotal := 0        // changing
subtotal <- 12       // write

tax_bp <- 900        // E0111: tax_bp cannot change
subtatal <- 12       // E0107: unknown name; did you mean `subtotal`?

comparisons.note: The same three symbols as Jet today, from the Newsqueak and Limbo line. `::` is a compile time constant there, not a runtime fixed value.

Two symbols, and no fixed local at all. Merging declare and write into `:=` created the well known shadowed `err` bug. Go needs a separate `shadow` analyser, and a Go 2 proposal asked for explicit shadowing.
One symbol declares and writes. A misspelt write makes a new name and reports nothing. The later `:=` covers expressions only, and its addition was heavily contested.
comparisons.code:
total = 0
totla = total + 1   # no error, silently wrong

comparisons.note: Words mark the binding and `=` writes. Old sloppy mode let a write make a global by accident. Strict mode made that a `ReferenceError`, which is the same protection option A keeps.
All three mark changeability with a word, and all three keep declare and write apart. `let mut`, `var`, and `var` cost more to type than a symbol, but the split is never lost.
`:=` writes and `=` compares. The split is a stated safety goal, so a comparison can never be mistaken for a write.
`=` binds and rebinds, and `^` pins a name so it compares instead. Rebinding by default is a known source of confusion for people arriving from Erlang.

recommendation.why: Jet has exactly three legal binding events, and three symbols give each one its own spelling. The third symbol is what makes a write checkable. Because `=` can never make a name, a misspelt write is E0107 today, with a spelling suggestion. Any two symbol form must let one symbol both declare and write, so that error disappears and the program runs on a stale value. The learning cost stays small, because a beginner meets `:=` only at their first counter.

whyNot.reason: A misspelt write becomes a new changing name with no error, and Jet has no unused name check to catch it.
It reads best, but it still loses the misspelt write error, and it puts the write on the same symbol as the fixed declaration.
It gives the shortest and most familiar symbol to the changing case, which inverts the safe default, and it also loses the misspelt write error.
It keeps every check and reads well, but it spends a brand new arrow on a rare event, and `x <- 1` against `x < -1` is a real reading trap.

recommendation.tradeoff: The recommendation accepts one inconsistency. Everywhere else in Jet, `=` defines a thing: `type Key = Int`, `module m = other`, `field: Int = 3`, and 238 short function bodies in `examples/`. In a local binding, `=` instead overwrites. That mismatch is the honest cost of keeping writes checkable. If you would rather remove the mismatch, option E removes it without losing a single check, and option C removes it by giving up the misspelt write error.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft framed the question as three legal binding events against the number of symbols, and measured the repository: 667 fixed declarations, 72 changing declarations, and 24 writes. It recommended keeping three symbols because only three symbols keep a write from making a name.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the remapped three symbol option E, after confirming `<-` is unused in Jet today. It also tested a single symbol form with inferred changeability, and dropped it because the owner fixed the scope to symbols only.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested whether option C could keep the misspelt write error by adding an unused name check. It could not, because a misspelt write in option C is a legal fixed declaration, and an unused name warning fires after the wrong value has already shipped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened every option, adding that Jet already spells type aliases, module aliases, field defaults, and short function bodies with `=`. It also credited option D for asking nothing new of people arriving from C or Java, and option B for teaching as a matched pair.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the write error claim, since Jet bans shadowing and a misspelt write therefore cannot hide an outer name. The claim survived because Jet has no unused name check, so the misspelt name is never reported and the intended value silently stays stale.

decisions.title: What list remove takes: a position or a value
decisions.gist: Whether `xs.remove(3)` deletes the item at slot three or the item equal to three.
decisions.lesson: Jet's `List.remove` takes a position. Python's takes a value. The names match, the meanings do not, and both compile when the list holds numbers. Nothing warns you. This choice decides how Jet names the two operations so the mistake cannot be written.
decisions.story: Maya moves a scoring script from Python to Jet. It held `scores.remove(3)` to drop the score of three. In Jet the same line deletes the fourth score instead. Her totals are wrong and nothing failed.

options.name: Keep remove as a position
options.detail: Nothing changes. `remove` takes an index, and authors coming from Python learn the difference once. The trap stays for anyone who does not.
options.technical: Current `list_method_return` behavior in crates/jet-foundation/src/Collections.rs. No migration, no new names.
options.code:
scores.remove(3)      // drops slot 3
// no spelling for dropping the value 3

options.name: Two names that each say what they take
options.detail: `remove_at(index)` deletes by position and `remove_value(value)` deletes the first equal item. Neither name can be read the wrong way, and `remove` alone stops with a report naming both.
options.technical: `remove` becomes E-coded with a fix listing both spellings. `remove_value` requires `T: Eq`. Every in-repo caller migrates in one change, per greenfield law.

options.name: Follow Python's naming
options.detail: `remove(value)` deletes by value and `pop(index)` deletes by position, matching Python exactly. Python authors are right by default.
options.technical: Inverts today's meaning of `remove` and widens `pop`, which currently takes no argument and returns the last item. Silently changes the meaning of existing Jet code that uses `remove`.
options.code:
scores.remove(3)   // [10, 7, 22]  drops the value
scores.pop(2)      // drops slot 2

options.name: Position keeps remove, value goes through a filter
options.detail: `remove(index)` stays. Deleting by value is `retain`, which keeps every item passing a test. One verb covers dropping one item, several, or none.
options.technical: `retain(pred)` mirrors Rust. Removing one occurrence needs extra care from the author, since a predicate drops every match.
options.code:
scores.remove(3)                  // drops slot 3
scores.retain(s => s != 3)        // drops every 3

options.name: One name, and the label must be written
options.detail: `remove` keeps its short name, and the call must say which meaning it wants. `remove(at: 3)` deletes the slot. `remove(value: 3)` deletes the first item equal to three. A bare `remove(3)` stops, because the call carries no label. Nothing new has to be named, and the reader sees the meaning at every call.
options.technical: Uses the label-only zone from D-APILABEL1=A: `fn remove(*, at: Int = …, value: T = …)`. The `*` marker rejects a positional argument, so `remove(3)` is a label error naming both spellings. `remove_value` needs `T: Eq`. Sema adds one check for exactly one of `at:` and `value:`, since the signature alone cannot state that rule.

options.name: One default meaning, and an enum to say otherwise
options.detail: `remove(x)` deletes the first item equal to `x`, because that is what most code does. `remove(i, .Slot)` deletes a slot instead. `remove(x, .Val)` says the default out loud when a reader needs it. The short call stays short, the rare case names itself, and a Python author is right by default.
options.technical: `fn remove(x: T, by: RemoveBy = .Val) => T?` over `enum RemoveBy { Val, Slot }`. When `by` is `.Slot`, the first argument must be `Int`, which sema checks and reports on its own, because one parameter cannot hold both `T` and `Int`. This inverts today's index meaning, so every in-repo caller migrates in one change. Measured default: see the census in the recommendation.
options.code:
scores :: var [10, 7, 3, 22]

scores.remove(3)          // [10, 7, 22]  the item equal to 3
scores.remove(3, .Val)    // [10, 7, 22]  the same, said out loud
scores.remove(3, .Slot)   // [10, 7, 3]   the fourth slot

names :: var ["ada", "grace"]
names.remove(1, .Slot)    // drops "grace"
names.remove(1)           // type error: 1 is not a String

comparisons.note: Splits by name: `remove` is by value and `pop` is by index. Clear once learned, and the source of the collision with Jet.
comparisons.code:
scores.remove(3)  # by value
scores.pop(3)     # by index

comparisons.note: `remove(i)` is by index and there is no by-value verb; `retain` filters instead. Same shape as option D.
No remove at all. Authors use `splice` for position and `filter` for value, which is widely considered a wart.
`remove(at:)` names the argument at the call, so the reader always sees which is meant.
Swift has no unlabeled `remove` on an array. `remove(at:)` is the only spelling, and the label is required. The label carries the meaning, and no default meaning exists.

Java gave both meanings the same name and no way to say which. `remove(2)` on a list of numbers silently takes the slot. Effective Java calls the fault giving two very different operations one name, and option F answers that by keeping the name and adding the word.

recommendation.why: Option F keeps one short verb and lets the rare reading name itself. The default follows the measurement, not taste. Across four corpora, deleting by value beats deleting by slot. It leads 861 to 572 in 268 Python packages, 350 to 46 in the Ruby standard library, and 1285 to 146 in a real Node tree. Jet agrees, with 33 of its 36 `remove` calls already naming a thing. The Python standard library is the one near-even case, at 112 to 124.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a silent wrong answer for the most common migration path into Jet, and offers no spelling at all for deleting by value.
It spends two longer names on a problem one short word already solves, and the plain verb `remove` never returns.
It picks the same default as F but gives the slot reading no spelling of its own, so the position case has nowhere to go.
A predicate drops every match, so removing one occurrence becomes fiddly. It also leaves `remove` meaning position, which the measurement says is the rarer reading.
Requiring a label on every call charges the common case for a rare confusion, and a bare `remove(x)` reads clearly once the default is the measured one.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bare `remove(3)` on a list of numbers still carries a meaning the call does not show. The default now matches Python, so the larger audience is right without doing anything, and anyone who wants the slot writes `.Slot`. Today's index meaning inverts, so every in-repo caller changes in one pass. On any list whose items are not numbers, the wrong reading is already a type error.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft weighed keeping today's index meaning against adopting Python's names, and recommended explicit names because both existing meanings read wrong to half the audience.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added Rust's retain shape and checked JavaScript. It also tested a compile-time guard that fires only for number elements, and dropped it, because the trap must not depend on the element type.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review added option F, which keeps one name, sets a default meaning, and gives the other meaning an enum. It replaced the earlier label-only shape, because a required label taxes every call for a confusion that only bites lists of numbers.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Each option was strengthened on its own terms, and a corpus census was run to settle the default rather than argue it. Python, Ruby, Node, and Jet's own code all show deleting by value ahead of deleting by slot.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The recommendation was attacked for keeping a call whose meaning is not visible. The type system absorbs most of it, since a wrong reading is already an error unless the items are numbers, and the remaining case now defaults to the measured majority.

decisions.title: Does Jet need a user-facing Never type?
decisions.gist: Decide if Jet names code that never returns.
decisions.lesson: `()` means a function returns one value with no useful information. Some code never returns because it panics, exits, or loops forever. This choice sets whether Jet exposes that difference as a type or keeps it inside compiler control-flow analysis.
decisions.story: Sam writes a command-line tool that loads a file or stops with a clear error. He wants the success path to return `String` without adding a type that beginners must learn.
decisions.detail: This choice affects return checking, value branches, panic paths, callbacks, and generic code. It does not reopen tuple syntax.

options.name: No Never type
options.detail: Do not add a user-facing `Never` type. Keep `()` for no-information results and treat non-returning paths as compiler control-flow facts.
options.technical: Add no `Never` token or type entry. Sema marks known non-returning expressions and statements as terminating. APIs cannot name non-returning behavior.

options.name: Public Never type
options.detail: Add a type with no values. Functions that never return can name it, and its expressions can stand in for any result type.
options.technical: Add `Never` to the type system and `Syntax.rs`. A `Never` expression is unreachable after evaluation and can satisfy any expected result type without producing a value.

options.name: Compiler-only bottom fact
options.detail: Do not expose `Never`, but give the compiler one formal fact for code that cannot return. Users get the benefit in expressions without learning a new type.
options.technical: Sema uses one internal bottom result for panic, exit, proven infinite loops, and other terminating paths. It unifies with an expected result type and never lowers as a runtime value.

comparisons.note: Rust exposes `!` for functions and expressions that never produce a value.
TypeScript exposes `never` for impossible values and non-returning functions.
comparisons.code: function stop(message: string): never { throw new Error(message) }

comparisons.note: Go has no bottom type. A function can call `panic` without naming that fact.

recommendation.why: C gives the compiler one honest rule for code that cannot produce a value. Users do not type `Never` during normal work, but value branches and later generic checks still have one sound rule.

whyNot.reason: A keeps the surface smallest, but separate special cases can grow across `if`, loops, panic, callbacks, and generic checks.
B gives experts a clear contract, but it adds a rare public type and invites confusion with `()`.

recommendation.tradeoff: The compiler has an internal bottom fact that users cannot name. Experts who need a named non-returning contract would need a later ballot.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft separated no-information returns from paths that never return. It compared no public type, public `Never`, and a compiler-only bottom fact.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested an effect marker, a `!` spelling, and inferred annotations. Those choices either add another surface or duplicate the same type decision, so they stay out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The strongest hybrid is the compiler-only bottom fact with no public spelling. It keeps the semantic value of `Never` without adding beginner syntax.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option A is smallest, while Option B gives experts the clearest contract. Option C keeps one compiler rule while hiding rare detail.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The final attack checked panics, infinite loops, value branches, callbacks, generics, and web code. C still needs cross-tier tests, but it avoids public syntax and keeps the door open.

decisions.checkInstructions: After ratification, test panic and exit paths, infinite loops, value branches, callbacks, generic calls, and exhaustive dispatch. Prove AOT, `jet run`, the interpreter, JIT, and web where applicable.

decisions.title: How should one Jet file launch as an executable script?
decisions.gist: Choose how one Jet file launches directly.
decisions.lesson: An operating system needs a launch instruction before it can execute a source file. Jet already accepts a file as a direct run command. This choice can add direct launch without creating separate script semantics.
decisions.story: Mina writes a backup tool in one Jet file. She wants cron and teammates to run that file directly, while Jet keeps the same arguments, errors, and exit status.
decisions.inWild:
$ chmod +x tools/backup.jet
$ tools/backup.jet --source ./photos --dest /mnt/archive
scanned 1842 files
copied 17 files
exit 0

options.name: First-line shebang
options.detail: Allow one operating-system shebang at the start of a Jet file. Unix hosts launch it directly. Every host can still use the direct Jet file command.
options.technical: The lexer accepts #! only at byte zero and only through the first line ending. It records the line for spans but emits no program token. The canonical line is #!/usr/bin/env jet. Jet then uses its existing direct-file resolver and jet run semantics. Arguments after the file remain program arguments. No dependency or option grammar exists in this line.

options.name: Generated launcher
options.detail: Keep Jet source unchanged. A Jet command creates an executable launcher beside the file and forwards all work to the normal run path.
options.technical: A command such as jet script install backup.jet --as backup creates a platform launcher. The launcher pins the source path and toolchain identity. Source files never contain launch metadata.
options.code:
fn main() {
    print("backup complete")
}

$ jet script install backup.jet --as backup
installed ./backup
$ ./backup
backup complete

options.name: Command only
options.detail: Add no direct source launch. Users run jet file.jet. Distribution uses the existing package and native executable path.
options.technical: The lexer and source format do not change. Shell jobs, cron entries, and users must name the Jet command or use a separately maintained wrapper.
options.code:
fn main() {
    print("backup complete")
}

$ jet backup.jet
backup complete

# cron
0 2 * * * jet /srv/backup.jet

comparisons.note: Python files commonly use a shebang for direct Unix launch. The interpreter ignores that first line as launch metadata.
Deno scripts use a normal shebang and keep runtime permissions in the launch command when needed.
Rust normally compiles source into a separate executable. Direct source launch needs an outside tool or wrapper.

recommendation.why: A adds direct launch with one ignored first line and reuses the existing Jet file command. It creates no generated wrapper, project file, or second runtime path.

whyNot.reason: B adds a command and generated artifact for a job the operating system already supports. Source moves can also leave stale launchers.
C keeps the grammar smallest, but it does not meet the direct executable-script workflow required by cron, tools, and normal Unix use.

recommendation.tradeoff: The shebang is meaningful only on Unix-like hosts. Windows keeps the direct Jet file command and packaged executable path.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a first-line shebang, a generated launcher, and command-only use. It recommended the shebang because Jet already owns direct file execution.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested inline dependency headers, file associations, shell wrappers, and automatic native compilation. Dependency headers duplicate package facts, while the other tactics fit options B or C.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept the shebang for source use and left native packaging for distribution. Combining both inside one source contract would add policy that the launch line does not need.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened generated launchers with pinned toolchains and gave command-only use its strongest grammar argument. Both still add more user work than one first-line marker.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested missing env, spaces, moved files, line endings, source spans, and Windows. A byte-zero rule plus the direct-file fallback keeps failures clear and spans correct.

decisions.title: Comprehension guard spelling in the loop head
decisions.gist: Choose how a yielding loop head spells its item filter.
decisions.lesson: A yielding loop can keep or skip items with an `if` guard in its head. Today the guard parses only without a comma, while every other head clause uses commas (D-LOOP-COMMA1). The natural comma spelling misparses as a stride and fails with an unrelated error about value `if` branches. The guard form is Jet's cheapest collection transform, and it beats Python when people can find it. Zero examples show it today.
decisions.story: Mina converts a Python script to Jet. Commas separate every loop clause she has seen, so she writes the guard with a comma. The compiler answers with an error about `if` branches needing values. The working spelling appears nowhere in the docs, so she gives up and writes a method chain that costs more than her Python original.

options.name: Comma-less guard stays canonical
options.detail: Keep the shipped spelling: the guard follows the source with no comma. Add the missing docs, examples, and a teaching diagnostic for the comma spelling. This is the cheapest form at 14 tokens, one under Python. The cost is a head with two separation laws: commas everywhere, except before the guard.
options.technical: No grammar change. The parser adds one lookahead so `, if` in a yielding head produces a teaching diagnostic naming the comma-less form, instead of parsing a stride. Formatter output is already stable for the shipped form.

options.name: Guard is a comma clause
options.detail: The guard becomes an ordinary comma-separated head clause, so one law covers the whole head. The natural spelling works on the first try. It costs one comma token, landing at 15, level with Python. The formatter rewrites the old comma-less spelling.
options.technical: In a yielding head, `, if` always begins a guard clause and never a stride. A stride expression may not begin with a value `if` unless parenthesized; measured strides are numeric, so the loss is theoretical. One guard per head; combine conditions with `&&`. The formatter canonicalizes the comma-less form to the comma form.
options.code:
names :: loop u, users, if u.active -> u.name   // canonical, 15 tokens
evens :: loop n, nums, if n % 2 == 0 -> n * n
pairs :: loop (key, value), scores, if value > 0 -> key

options.name: Retire the header guard
options.detail: Remove the guard from the head. Filtering uses `next` in the body, the same skip word every loop already has. The head grammar shrinks, but the common filtered transform grows to about 19 tokens and loses to Python by 4.
options.technical: The parser removes the head guard production. Existing guard code migrates to a body `if` with `next`. No new token.

comparisons.note: The guard trails the source with no separator. It is the most used transform surface in the measured corpus.
comparisons.code: names = [u.name for u in users if u.active]

comparisons.note: Commas separate generators and guards alike inside a comprehension. This is the precedent for one separator law.
comparisons.code: names = [name u | u <- users, active u]

comparisons.note: No comprehension exists; filtering rides a method chain with a closure per step.
comparisons.code: let names: Vec<_> = users.iter().filter(|u| u.active).map(|u| u.name.clone()).collect();

recommendation.why: Commas separate the positional clauses whose meaning comes from position; the guard announces itself with a keyword, exactly like the yield arrow that already takes no comma. The shipped form is the consistent one, and at 14 tokens it beats Python outright.

whyNot.reason: The comma before a self-announcing keyword is redundant punctuation, and its uniformity claim fails because the yield arrow already attaches without one.
It retires Jet's cheapest transform, drops the common case to 19 tokens, and loses to Python by 4.

recommendation.tradeoff: The natural first guess with a comma stays an error. A precise teaching diagnostic that says remove the comma closes that gap at first compile.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared the shipped comma-less guard, a comma guard clause, and retiring the guard. It recommended the comma clause because one law should govern the head.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a Python-style guard after the yield expression, a `where` keyword, and filtering only through fallback-next. Each reorders or duplicates an existing mechanism, so all folded into the three options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested accepting both spellings at once. Two canonical spellings for one clause violate the one-form rule, so the loser becomes a teaching diagnostic either way.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with zero migration and a one-token lead, and C with the smallest grammar and a uniform body-skip story. B kept its first-guess advantage.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The owner challenged the comma's benefit, and the attack confirmed the uniformity claim fails: the yield arrow already attaches without a comma, so the head is positional commas plus keyword-marked trailers. The recommendation moved to A; both options still need the same stride carve-out for a head-position value if.

decisions.title: Bindingless loops with an implicit subject
decisions.gist: Choose whether a loop may omit its binding and read the current item directly.
decisions.lesson: A subject is the value a bare `.member` reads from. Dispatch arms already have one: in `if user == { .active -> … }` the bare member reads from `user` (D-IFDIST1). This ballot decides whether a yielding loop that names no binding makes the current item its subject. The body stays an inline arm, not a lambda, so `?`, `next`, and `break` keep working. Today every loop names a binding even when the body reads it once.
decisions.story: Mina writes a loop where the binding `u` appears four times in fifteen tokens: once declared, three times read. She wants the loop to read like its sentence: loop the users, keep the active ones, give the names.

options.name: Bare-member subject
options.detail: A head with no binding makes the item the subject, and bare `.member` reads from it. This reuses the dispatch-arm rule people already learn, and it is the cheapest form measured: 11 tokens against Python's 15. Scalar items still name a binding, because a bare member needs a member to read.
options.technical: Grammar: `loop source [, if guard] -> arm` with no binding clause; the comma-less source position is unambiguous because a condition loop cannot yield (E0072). Inside a bindingless head and body, bare `.member` always resolves against the subject; type names spell statics. Nested loops under a bindingless loop must name bindings; the compiler teaches this. `(key, value)` sources always name bindings.
options.code:
names :: loop users, if .active -> .name
totals :: loop orders, if .paid -> .total
upper :: loop words -> .to_upper()

doubled :: loop n, nums -> n * 2
// A scalar transform names its binding; there is no member to read.

options.name: Named `it` subject
options.detail: A head with no binding introduces the implicit name `it`, as Kotlin does. Scalars work naturally, and no dot rule changes. The cost is a pronoun in every position, 13 tokens instead of 11, and a contextual name that can collide with user code.
options.technical: `it` is a contextual identifier bound to the item inside a bindingless yielding loop. A user binding named `it` shadows it and gets a warning. Nested bindingless loops are rejected the same way as option A.

options.name: No implicit subject
options.detail: Every loop names its binding. Nothing new to learn or resolve, and every read names its source. The guarded transform stays at 15 tokens, level with Python and never ahead.
options.technical: No change. The binding clause remains required in every yielding head.
options.code: names :: loop u, users, if u.active -> u.name   // 15 tokens, the floor

comparisons.note: Single-parameter lambdas get the implicit name `it`. Concise, but the pronoun repeats at every read.
The underscore stands for the parameter once per use. It cannot be read twice, which confuses beginners.
Closures get positional names. Terse, but `$0` reads as nothing to a beginner.

recommendation.why: It reuses the bare-member rule dispatch arms already ratified, so the language grows a home, not a mechanism. At 11 tokens it beats Python by 4 on the corpus's most common transform, and the body keeps inline `?`, `next`, and `break`.

whyNot.reason: It mints a contextual pronoun that collides with user names, repeats at every read, and still costs two tokens more than the bare member.
It leaves the most common transform at parity, never ahead, and keeps four spellings of a binding the body reads once.

recommendation.tradeoff: Scalar items have no member to read, so scalar transforms keep a named binding. The sentence-form win applies to record sources, which dominate the measured corpus.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a bare-member subject, a Kotlin-style `it`, and requiring bindings. It recommended the bare member because dispatch arms already teach that exact rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested Scala's underscore and Swift's positional names. Both mint a new sigil family that reads as nothing, so they folded into option B as the named-pronoun representative.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested shipping A and B together. Two spellings for one subject violate the one-form rule, and `it` adds nothing the named binding does not already give scalars.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with its natural scalar story and C with its zero-rule clarity. B's scalar win is real and is recorded in A's tradeoff honestly.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack found scalar sources, nested subject shadowing, and collisions with expected-type static shorthand. The repairs: scalars name bindings, nesting requires names, and inside bindingless bodies the subject always owns bare members.

decisions.title: Bare-member shorthand for one-parameter callable arguments
decisions.gist: Choose whether `.member` may stand for a one-parameter lambda at a call site.
decisions.lesson: Jet's method-chain pipeline costs 33 tokens on the task Python's comprehension does in 15, because every step writes a full lambda to read one member. This ballot decides whether a bare member chain may stand for that lambda when the expected argument is a one-parameter callable. The same desugar is proposed for bindingless loops in D-LOOP-SUBJECT1; this ballot owns the call-site half on its own.
decisions.story: Mina keeps the pipeline style for a long transformation because each stage reads separately. Every stage needs a whole lambda whose body is one member read, and the ceremony triples the cost of her Python original.

options.name: Member chains
options.detail: Where the expected argument is a one-parameter callable, a bare member chain stands for that lambda, including method calls along the chain. The pipeline drops from 33 tokens to 15. Anything beyond a member chain still writes the lambda.
options.technical: The rule fires only when the expected parameter type is known and is a one-parameter callable. The shorthand is a member chain on the parameter: fields, methods, and their arguments. Operators, literals, and multi-parameter callables are excluded; write the lambda. Function types have no static members, so the expected-type static shorthand (D-SHAPE3a) cannot collide here.
options.code:
names :: users.filter(.active).map(.name)
shouting :: users.map(.name.to_upper())
oldest :: users.max_by(.age)

total :: orders.fold(0, fn (sum: Int, o: Order) => Int = sum + o.total)
// Two parameters: the shorthand never applies.

options.name: Single member only
options.detail: The shorthand allows exactly one bare member: `.name` works, `.name.to_upper()` does not. The rule is smaller to state, but the lambda returns the moment a chain grows one link, and readers must learn where the cliff is.
options.technical: Same expected-type rule as option A, restricted to one field or one zero-argument method. Any longer chain is an error that teaches the full lambda.

options.name: No shorthand
options.detail: Arguments always write full lambdas. One spelling for callables everywhere, nothing contextual to resolve. The pipeline stays at 33 tokens, half again dearer than TypeScript on the same task.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: names :: users.filter(fn (u: User) => Bool = u.active).map(fn (u: User) => String = u.name)

comparisons.note: Key paths pass a member read where a function is expected. Adopted widely because pipelines are mostly member reads.
The implicit `it` shortens the lambda but keeps a pronoun at every read.
Method references pass an existing accessor by name. The double colon adds ceremony Jet's dot form avoids.

recommendation.why: Pipelines are mostly member reads, and the shorthand removes exactly that ceremony: 33 tokens fall to 15, under TypeScript's 22. It reuses the bare-member atom Jet already owns instead of minting a key-path sigil.

whyNot.reason: Half the measured pipeline steps call a method on the member, so the cliff lands in the middle of real code and the rule's value halves.
The audit's most-written style stays Jet's dearest spelling, and the pipeline keeps losing to every measured peer.

recommendation.tradeoff: Bare `.member` gains a second contextual meaning: static shorthand under a non-callable expected type, lambda under a callable one. The two contexts cannot overlap, and sema owns one diagnostic for the unknown-type case.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared member chains, a single-member form, and no shorthand. It recommended chains because measured pipelines are member reads with occasional method calls.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested Swift key-path sigils, Scala underscores, and bound method references. Each mints a new sigil or duplicates the dot form, so all folded into the three options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed this desugar and D-LOOP-SUBJECT1 are one rule in two homes. The ballots stay separate so each home is judged on its own evidence.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C with its uniform-spelling clarity and B with its smaller rule. Both stand, and both leave the pipeline losing to TypeScript.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack targeted inference: generic adapters may not know the parameter type mid-inference, so the rule fires only on a known expected type, and the diagnostic teaches the lambda. Operators like `!.active` stay excluded.

decisions.title: Jet library reuse and linking model
decisions.gist: How Jet reuses compiled dependencies, and whether Jet ships its own dynamic libraries.
decisions.lesson: Rust ships every dependency as source, and each project compiles all of it again. Clean builds are slow and binaries are large. Rust also has no fixed binary layout, called an application binary interface or ABI, between compiler versions. Compiled Rust libraries therefore cannot be shared safely. Jet already plans a Nix-style package store with binary caches. This choice decides how Jet reuses compiled dependency work, and whether Jet ever promises a stable binary layout of its own.
decisions.story: Priya runs three Jet services that share twelve packages. Every clean build today would compile all twelve from source, in each service, on every continuous-integration run. She wants the second build to reuse the work the first build already did. She also asks whether her team can ship a plugin as a compiled Jet library.
decisions.inWild:
# pkg.jet
Package.{
  name: "flightdeck",
  deps: .{ http: "2.1", json: "1.4", metrics: "0.9" },
}

$ jet build
  http 2.1, json 1.4, metrics 0.9: restored from cache (0.2s)
  flightdeck: compile + link (3.1s)

options.name: Sealed package objects
options.detail: Each dependency compiles once into a sealed object keyed on the exact compiler version, target, and profile. Later builds restore it from the local or shared cache instead of recompiling. A compiler upgrade simply rebuilds once. You never think about it; builds just get faster.
options.technical: Per-package compile actions lower into the ratified jetpack action IR (E4-JP2). Identity covers package sources, dependency artifact digests, compiler identity, target, and profile. Artifacts link statically. Generic function bodies travel as typed IR inside the artifact and instantiate at the use site. Sema and diagnostics always run; no cache path bypasses them.
options.code:
$ jet build          # first build on this machine
  http 2.1: compile (1.8s)
  json 1.4: compile (1.1s)
  flightdeck: compile + link (3.1s)

$ jet build          # second build, or a teammate via shared cache
  http 2.1, json 1.4: restored from cache (0.2s)
  flightdeck: compile + link (3.1s)

$ jet build          # after a compiler upgrade
  cache empty for Jet 1.4.2 — rebuilding dependencies once

options.name: Sealed objects plus pinned Jet dynamic libraries
options.detail: Everything in the sealed-objects option, plus a way to build a Jet dynamic library that another Jet program loads at run time. Both sides must use the exact same compiler version. Loading a mismatched library is a checked error, not a crash. This serves plugins and game mods.
options.technical: Same artifact identity as sealed objects. The loader verifies compiler identity and package digests before mapping the library. No layout promise crosses compiler versions.
options.code:
$ jet build --emit jet-shared plugins/echo
  built target/echo.jetso (Jet 1.4.2)

# in the host program
plugin := Plugin.load("target/echo.jetso")?

# mismatched compiler version
error[E0912]: echo.jetso was built by Jet 1.4.1, this program uses Jet 1.4.2
  fix: rebuild the plugin with the same Jet version

options.name: Public stable Jet ABI
options.detail: Jet commits to a fixed binary layout and evolution rules, like Swift did in version 5. Anyone can ship a compiled Jet library, including closed-source vendors, and any later Jet compiles against it. Every future change to layout or calling rules must stay compatible forever.
options.technical: Requires a versioned layout specification, resilience rules for public types, and a frozen calling convention. Every public type pays an indirection cost unless marked frozen, following Swift's library-evolution model.
options.code:
# vendor ships a binary-only package, no source
$ jet add sensorlib --binary vendor/sensorlib.jetso

# five years later, Jet 3.0 must still load it unchanged
sensor := Sensor.open("lidar0")?

options.name: Source-only, whole-program
options.detail: Keep today's model. Every build compiles the whole program and all dependencies from source. Speed comes from the fast development loop and incremental checking only. Clean builds and continuous integration pay the full cost every time.
options.code:
$ jet build     # every clean build, every CI run
  http 2.1: compile (1.8s)
  json 1.4: compile (1.1s)
  flightdeck: compile + link (3.1s)

comparisons.note: Ships source only. The rich stable ABI proposal, crabi, has stayed an open experiment since 2022.
comparisons.code: cargo build   # recompiles every crate, per project

comparisons.note: Committed to a stable ABI in Swift 5. Apple ships Swift libraries with the operating system, and pays a permanent indirection cost on resilient public types.
comparisons.code: @frozen public struct Point { var x, y: Double }

comparisons.note: Binary caches substitute build results keyed on exact inputs. No ABI promise exists; identity does the work. Jet's ratified package store already follows this model.

recommendation.why: Sealed package objects remove the recompile tax on every machine and in continuous integration, using the store and cache machinery already ratified. Jet promises nothing about binary layout, so the language stays free to evolve.

whyNot.reason: No shipped Jet feature needs run-time loading of Jet libraries today, and jet dev already covers live reload. A dormant loading surface would sit untested in the product.

A public ABI freezes layout and calling rules before the language has settled, and Swift paid a permanent performance and design tax for that promise. It also conflicts with Jet's greenfield law until the owner declares a compatibility baseline.
Clean builds and continuous integration keep paying the full recompile cost that drives people away from Rust.

recommendation.tradeoff: No compiled artifact survives a compiler upgrade. Every upgrade rebuilds or re-downloads the world once. That is accepted because the rebuild is automatic and correctness never depends on layout luck.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared source-only builds, sealed cached objects, pinned dynamic libraries, and a public stable ABI. It recommended sealed objects because they cut recompilation without freezing the language.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested shipping typed intermediate code per package, per-module granularity, and caching only checker summaries. All three folded into the sealed-objects option as artifact-format details, not separate owner choices.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a partial stable ABI covering only a frozen core subset, and rejected it because public types leak the full promise. It also confirmed pinned dynamic libraries compose cleanly on top of sealed objects later.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each option on its own terms: dynamic libraries best serve game mods, a stable ABI best serves closed-source vendors, and source-only stays the simplest mental model.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked cache poisoning, unreproducible outputs, and generic functions; the ratified writer-authority and repro-cache decisions answer the first two. Generic bodies travel as typed intermediate code and instantiate at use sites, so sealed objects survive.

decisions.title: What a Library output hands to another language
decisions.gist: Whether Jet can be compiled into a library that C, Python, or Swift calls directly.
decisions.lesson: D-LIB-REUSE1=B already settled how Jet reuses Jet. Sealed package objects restore from cache, and no binary layout is promised. It said nothing about the other direction. Today nothing lets a C or Python program call into compiled Jet code. Jet's foreign-function work all runs inbound: Jet calls C, Python, Dart, and Rust through generated bridges. This choice decides whether the arrow ever points outward, and through which door.
decisions.story: Marcus maintains a log parser for a data team. He rewrote it in Jet and it is four times faster. The team's pipeline is Python and will stay Python for years. He wants to ship the parser as something their Python code imports, without rewriting the pipeline or standing up a server.
decisions.inWild:
# what Marcus wants to hand his team
import flightlog

records = flightlog.parse(open("gate.log", "rb").read())
print(len(records), "records")

# what he can do today: nothing.
# Jet reads C, Python, Dart and Rust.
# Nothing reads Jet.

options.name: WebAssembly is the only door out
options.detail: Library stays a Jet-to-Jet output. Any other language reaches Jet through the sandboxed WebAssembly component Jet already builds. One export path, one safety story, no new memory contract. Marcus ships a component, and his team loads it with a Python WebAssembly runtime.
options.technical: Reuses target: plugin (D-PLUGIN1=B, D-DEP-WASM1=A) and its ApiFreeze-frozen pub surface (D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1=A). No native artifact, no header, no calling convention of Jet's own. Host capabilities stay at zero, so the guest cannot open files or sockets.
options.code:
# pkg.jet
name: "flightlog"
target: plugin

pub fn parse(bytes: [Byte]) -> [Record] { … }

$ jet build
  built target/flightlog.wasm (component)

# Python side needs a wasm runtime and a byte copy per call
import wasmtime

options.name: Native library plus a C header
options.detail: Library can also produce a static and a shared native library, with a generated C header beside it. The exported surface is the entry module's pub items. Any language with a foreign-function interface can call it. Marcus gets a .so and a .h, and writes the Python wrapper himself.
options.technical: The boundary uses the C calling convention, not a Jet ABI. Jet promises nothing about its own layout, so the no-stable-ABI stance under D-LIB-REUSE1=B is unaffected. The exported surface freezes through Sema::ApiFreeze, so a breaking change is a diagnostic. Ownership of returned buffers is stated in the header and enforced in sema.

options.name: Native library plus generated bindings per language
options.detail: Everything in the header option, plus Jet generates the caller-side binding file for each language you name. Marcus writes no wrapper. He names python in the output, and jet build produces the module his team imports. The same generator that reads foreign libraries today runs in reverse.
options.technical: Mirrors the ratified inbound binder direction (D-FFI-UNIFY1=A, D-FFI-PY1=A) with one shared surface description. The native artifact and the C header are still produced, so a language with no generator is never blocked. Binding files are build outputs, never checked-in source. The frozen pub surface is the single source for header, bindings, and version check.

options.name: Cross a process boundary, never a memory boundary
options.detail: Jet never links into a foreign process. Other languages reach Jet by running it as a service and calling it. Jet generates the client for the caller's language. No memory contract ever crosses a language line, so no foreign bug can corrupt Jet's heap. Marcus ships a small service and a Python client.
options.technical: Reuses the ratified Service output and service topology (D-SERVICE1=D, D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A). Transport is local by default. No header, no calling convention, no shared allocator. Every call pays serialisation and a context switch.
options.code:
# pkg.jet
outputs: .{ api: .Service.{ entry: serve, clients: [python] } }

$ jet build
  built target/flightlog-service
  built target/clients/flightlog.py

# Python side
import flightlog
records = flightlog.connect().parse(data)   # over a local socket

comparisons.note: Emits staticlib and cdylib with a C boundary. Callers get a header, and each ecosystem builds its own wrapper generator on top, such as PyO3 or cbindgen.
c-archive and c-shared build modes generate the header for you, but the runtime must start before the first call.
Exports to C only through explicit annotations, and its own stable interface stays Swift-to-Swift.
comparisons.code: @_cdecl("parse") public func parse(_ p: UnsafePointer<UInt8>) -> Int32

comparisons.note: export fn produces a C symbol, and the generated header is a first-class build output rather than a side tool.
comparisons.code: export fn parse(ptr: [*]const u8, len: usize) callconv(.C) i32 { … }

recommendation.why: Generated bindings are the only option where the caller writes no glue. It also finishes an arrow Jet already draws in the other direction, using the same frozen public surface for the header, the bindings, and the version check.

whyNot.reason: A WebAssembly component forces the caller to adopt a runtime and copy bytes across the guest boundary. Marcus cannot hand his team something they simply import.
A raw header stops one step short of usable. Every ecosystem then writes its own wrapper generator, which is the same work done many times outside Jet.
A process boundary adds a socket, a lifecycle, and serialisation cost to a call that was a function. It also cannot serve a caller who must run in one process, such as a game host.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet takes on the ownership rules at the boundary: who frees a returned buffer, and what a foreign caller may hold across calls. That contract is stated in the exported surface and checked in sema, so it is a design cost, not a safety hole.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared no native export, a C header, generated bindings, and a service boundary. It recommended generated bindings because the caller writes no glue and the inbound binder machinery already exists.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a Jet-specific foreign protocol, a C++ class surface, and a Python-only special case. All three folded into the bindings option as generator targets rather than separate owner choices.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review confirmed the bindings option already contains the header option, so both artifacts ship together and a language with no generator is never blocked. It also kept the WebAssembly path alive for untrusted callers, since that path is already ratified law.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each option: WebAssembly gives one safety story, a header is the widest common denominator, and a service isolates faults completely. Each remains the strongest choice for its own audience.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked layout leakage and buffer ownership. The boundary uses C's frozen convention rather than Jet's, and the exported surface must state ownership so sema can check it.

decisions.title: What a loaded Jet library is allowed to do
decisions.gist: The powers a Jet library gets when a running Jet program loads it.
decisions.lesson: D-LIB-REUSE1=B ratified that a Jet program can load a Jet library while it runs. Both sides must come from the same compiler version, and a mismatch is a checked error. It did not say what the loaded code may then do. Jet already has a second way to load code: a sandboxed WebAssembly plugin with zero host powers, and no gate to widen that. Two ways to load code need one clear boundary between them.
decisions.story: Rosa ships a flight-sim game in Jet. She wants community aircraft mods that run at full speed inside her render loop. A mod needs to read its own model and texture files. It must never read her players' save files or open a network socket she did not expect.

options.name: Declared effects, granted at load
options.detail: A loadable library declares what it does, in the same way any Jet package does. The host states what it grants when it loads one. A library asking for more than the host grants is refused before it runs, with a clear error. Rosa grants read access to the mods folder, and nothing else.
options.technical: Reuses the existing package effect declaration and effect checking (the machinery behind E1258). The compiler already proves a package cannot use an effect it did not declare, so the declaration in the artifact is enforceable, not advisory. Load compares the artifact's declared effect set against the host's grant, then refuses or proceeds. Artifact provenance and signature verification come from D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1=D.

options.name: Loading native code is an audited trust decision
options.detail: Loading a Jet library is a trust act the host author signs, in an audited region with a written reason. The loaded code then runs with the host's full powers. Untrusted third-party code must use the sandboxed WebAssembly plugin instead. Rosa writes one audited line, and accepts every mod she ships.
options.technical: Spelled like the existing audited region: an explicit block with a required reason string, which appears in audit output. No effect comparison happens at load. The sandboxed plugin path stays the only route for code the host author has not vetted.

options.name: Same powers as linking
options.detail: A loaded library behaves exactly like a library linked at build time. Same process, same powers, no gate and no ceremony. Whoever loads it takes responsibility. Rosa writes one line and every mod can do whatever her game can do.

options.name: Same contract as the sandboxed plugin
options.detail: A loaded Jet library gets exactly what a WebAssembly plugin gets: no host powers at all. The host passes in every value the library needs, and takes back every result. The two loading paths then differ only in speed and portability, never in what code may do. Rosa hands each mod its textures and gets back draw commands.
options.technical: One capability law across both substrates, matching the ratified zero-capability plugin contract and its E1258 refusal to widen. All input and output crosses the boundary as values. No ambient file, network, process, or clock access exists inside a loaded library.

comparisons.note: dlopen gives the loaded object every power the process holds. Nothing is declared and nothing is checked.
A guest gets only the imports the host passes in. This is the model Jet's ratified plugin target already follows.
comparisons.code: // host chooses which imports exist; the guest cannot reach anything else

comparisons.note: The security manager tried to police loaded code at run time with a policy file. It was deprecated for removal because run-time policy proved unenforceable in practice.
Mod hosts hand the guest a restricted environment table. Enforcement is a convention of the host, not the language.

recommendation.why: Jet's compiler already proves a package cannot use an effect it did not declare. That turns the declaration inside an artifact into an enforceable fact, so the host can grant a precise set instead of choosing between all powers and none.

whyNot.reason: An audited trust act is all-or-nothing at the load site. It teaches hosts to sign one blanket reason rather than say what a mod may do.
A mod can then read save files and open sockets the host never intended, and nothing in the artifact or the audit output says so.
Zero powers blocks the ordinary case of a mod reading its own assets, and it copies the WebAssembly contract without adding anything the WebAssembly path lacks.

recommendation.tradeoff: The grant is only as good as the artifact's provenance, because a file that was not built by this compiler could claim anything. That is acceptable because the load already verifies compiler identity, digest, and signature before mapping anything.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared granted effects, an audited trust act, unrestricted loading, and full sandbox parity. It recommended granted effects because Jet's effect checking makes a declared set enforceable rather than advisory.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a signed publisher allowlist, a per-call permission prompt, and a separate process per mod. The first folded into provenance checks, and the other two were dropped as run-time policy Java already proved unworkable.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested granted effects combined with an audited region for hosts that want no gate. The audited form collapses into a grant of everything, so it needs no separate spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each option on its own terms. Unrestricted loading is simplest, sandbox parity gives one law for both substrates, and an audited act names a human behind every load.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked forged effect declarations and stale grants. Compiler identity, digest, and signature verification happen before mapping, so a forged artifact fails the pin rather than the grant.

decisions.title: How a package asks for a loadable library, and what it is called
decisions.gist: The word for a loadable Jet library artifact, and where a person asks for one.
decisions.lesson: D-LIB-REUSE1=B ratified that Jet can build a library another Jet program loads while it runs. Nothing yet says how a person asks for one, or what the file is called. Jet already has nine closed output kinds, and Library is one of them. The manifest vocabulary is also settled: a package states its facts in text, and commands act on them. This choice fits the new artifact into that vocabulary before any parser work starts.
decisions.story: Rosa is setting up her flight-sim game for community mods. She opens a mod package's manifest to say what it should build. She wants one obvious line, and she wants a reader of that manifest to know at a glance that this package ships something loadable.
decisions.inWild:
# a community mod package, today
name: "skyhawk"
version: "0.3.1"
deps: .{ simkit: "^4" }
outputs: .{ ??? }        # nothing here means "a thing Rosa's game loads"

# and on the command line
$ jet build
  built target/skyhawk          # an executable. not what Rosa needs.

options.name: A field on the Library output
options.detail: Library already exists as an output kind. A field on it says this library is also loadable at run time. No new word enters the language, and a reader sees the fact in the manifest. The file is called skyhawk.jetlib.
options.technical: Adds one manifest field to the ratified Library output payload under D-ECO-OUTPUT-PAYLOAD1=A. The closed nine-kind set from D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A stays closed.
