No token, keyword, or sigil enters Syntax.rs, so I7 needs only this decision identifier. Suffix candidates for the owner: .jetlib, .jlib, .jetso, .pylon.
options.code:
# pkg.jet
name: "skyhawk"
outputs: .{ mod: .Library.{ entry: Skyhawk, loadable: true } }

$ jet build
  built target/skyhawk.jetlib (Jet 1.4.2)

# the host
mod := Mod.load("./mods/skyhawk.jetlib")?

options.name: Its own output kind, named for the mount
options.detail: A loadable library is a different thing from a library you link, so it gets its own name in the closed set. An aircraft carries an external store on a pylon, and a pylon is cleared for one airframe. That matches a file cleared for one compiler version. The file is called skyhawk.pylon.
options.technical: Adds a tenth kind to the closed Output set, which D-ECO-OUTPUT-KINDS1=A explicitly allows by ratified addition. Kind-name candidates for the owner: Pylon, Hardpoint, Jetway, Pod, Attach. Matching suffix follows the chosen noun.
options.code:
# pkg.jet
name: "skyhawk"
outputs: .{ mod: .Pylon.{ entry: Skyhawk } }

$ jet build
  built target/skyhawk.pylon (Jet 1.4.2)

# the host
mod := Mod.load("./mods/skyhawk.pylon")?

# a stale file
error[E1xxx]: skyhawk.pylon was built by Jet 1.4.1; this program uses Jet 1.4.2
  fix: rebuild the mod with the same Jet version

options.name: A build flag, nothing in the manifest
options.detail: The package says nothing. Whoever builds it asks for the loadable form on the command line. This keeps the manifest vocabulary untouched, and lets one package be built either way. The file is called skyhawk.jetso.
options.technical: One new value on an existing build flag, with no manifest field and no new output kind. The fact lives only in a build invocation, so a reader of the package cannot see it. Suffix candidates for the owner: .jetso, .jso, .jetlib.
options.code:
# pkg.jet — unchanged
name: "skyhawk"
outputs: .{ mod: .Library.{ entry: Skyhawk } }

$ jet build --emit shared
  built target/skyhawk.jetso (Jet 1.4.2)

# and Rosa's build script must remember the flag, forever
$ jet build          # silently builds the linkable form instead

options.name: Any library is loadable, with no declaration
options.detail: Nothing is declared and no flag is passed. Any Library output can be loaded, and the compiler produces the loadable form when a host asks for it. The least ceremony possible. A package cannot state that it is not meant to be loaded.
options.technical: The loadable artifact becomes a derived output of every Library, produced on demand and cached under the same artifact identity. No manifest field, no flag, no new kind. Package authors lose the ability to refuse run-time loading.
options.code:
# pkg.jet — unchanged, nothing added ever
name: "skyhawk"
outputs: .{ mod: .Library.{ entry: Skyhawk } }

# the host names a package, not a file
mod := Mod.load("skyhawk")?
  # builds or restores the loadable form on first use

comparisons.note: The manifest declares the artifact shapes, and the file suffix follows the platform.
A build mode flag decides, and nothing in the module file records the choice.
The package manifest names the product and its kind explicitly.
Loadable code is the normal unit and needs no separate declaration, which is the closest match to the no-declaration option.

recommendation.why: A field on Library keeps one word for one concept and keeps the ratified nine-kind set closed. The fact stays in the manifest where a reader finds it, which is the settled rule that facts live in text.

whyNot.reason: A tenth kind splits one concept into two words. Every reader must then learn when a library stops being a Library.
The manifest no longer says what the package ships. The fact survives only in build scripts, which is exactly where facts get lost.
Every library silently becomes a loading target, and an author has no way to refuse. Run-time loading is a real surface and should be stated.

recommendation.tradeoff: The word Library then covers both a package you link and a file you load. That is acceptable because both are the same code, and the field says which artifacts the build produces.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a field on Library, a new output kind, a build flag, and no declaration at all. It recommended the field because it adds no new word and keeps the fact in the manifest.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a marker on the entry module, a separate loadable manifest file, and a naming convention by folder. All three moved the fact away from the output list without making it clearer.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a field plus an override flag for one-off builds. The flag adds a second source for one fact, so the field alone stands.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each option. A dedicated noun reads well aloud, a flag keeps one package flexible, and no declaration is the shortest path for a mod author.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the field for overloading one word across two artifact shapes. Both shapes come from the same code and the same frozen surface, so one word stays honest.

decisions.title: How a host grants and calls a loaded library
decisions.gist: How a host grants paths and calls a function from a loaded mod.
decisions.lesson: A loadable library is compiled Jet code that a running host uses. An exported function is an entry point, such as on_tick(dt). An effect is a power such as file read or network access. D-LIB-DYNTRUST1 says the library declares effects and the host grants an equal or narrower set before mapping. It does not ratify the grant spelling. bd19-rev flagged the path gap. Read access to ./mods must not become read access to every file. This ballot chooses the call and grant shapes while keeping Mod.load(path)?.
decisions.story: Rosa maintains a flight-sim game with community mods. Each frame, the host loads f16.jetlib, grants read access to ./mods, and calls on_tick(dt). She wants a beginner path that reads like a normal method call and an expert path that can bind or select exports without hiding authority.

options.name: Typed member call with a load grant
options.detail: Jet checks the exported surface and exposes each public function as a typed member. The load line shows the file and its grant in one place. Beginners write mod.on_tick(dt); experts can bind mod.on_tick before a call. The cost is one grant record at every load site.
options.technical: grant: is a load-only named argument. Its value maps effect names to normalized path sets. The loader checks declared effects against the grant before mapping. mod.on_tick resolves only an exported function with a checked signature. A path grant covers descendants of ./mods, not sibling paths.

options.name: Lexical grant block with typed members
options.detail: The host opens one trusted region around the load and its calls. Authority ends at the closing brace, which makes review scope clear and can cover several mods. The loaded value still has typed members. The cost is a block for a single load.
options.technical: #Grant(caps: .{ read: ["./mods"] }) reuses the existing scoped-grant marker and adds path entries. The marker supplies the library's load-time authority; it does not change the library declaration. The loader checks each load inside the block before mapping. The handle and loaded values cannot escape the block.

options.name: Explicit export handle with a load grant
options.detail: After loading, the host asks for one exported function and binds it to a name. This fits dispatch tables and repeated calls because the function handle is explicit. It adds a line and moves a fixed export name from compile time to load time.
options.technical: mod.export("on_tick")? returns a typed function handle after the loader checks the frozen export table. The handle carries the export signature and the library lifetime. A missing name or wrong signature is a checked error. The grant remains path-scoped at the load call.
options.code:
mod := Mod.load("./mods/f16.jetlib", grant: .{ read: ["./mods"] })?
tick := mod.export("on_tick")?
tick(dt)

options.name: Dynamic named call with a grant record
options.detail: The host passes an export name and arguments to one dynamic call. This fits mod registries that discover names at run time. A typo becomes a checked run-time error, and the fixed on_tick case reads less like an ordinary call.
options.technical: mod.call("on_tick", dt)? resolves the name against the frozen export table and checks the argument shape before entering the library. The call returns the exported result or a checked call error. The grant record still maps read to normalized paths. The host cannot use this call to bypass the declared-effect check.
options.code:
mod := Mod.load("./mods/f16.jetlib", grant: .{ read: ["./mods"] })?
mod.call("on_tick", dt)?

// typo: checked error before entry
mod.call("on_tik", dt)?
error: export on_tik was not found

comparisons.note: Rust hosts open a library, get a named symbol, and call the typed handle. The unsafe boundary and ABI rules remain visible.
Lua exposes module functions as table fields, so mod.on_tick(dt) is the easy call shape. Hosts often pass a restricted environment separately.
A component host gets an export from an instance and passes imports at instantiation. It favors explicit handles over ambient grants.
comparisons.code:
instance := linker.instantiate(module, imports)?
tick := instance.export("on_tick")?
tick(dt)

recommendation.why: Option A keeps the common mod call as a normal typed member call. Its load line shows the exact path grant, so authority and code use stay together. Binding the member gives experts a named function without adding a second call mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Choosing A accepts one visible grant argument at each load. That repetition is useful because authority stays beside the load.
B hides the grant in a surrounding block. It can cover several loads, but a distant block can make one mod's authority harder to audit.
C adds an export lookup and shifts fixed-name errors to load time. It helps registries but adds ceremony to the common fixed export.
D supports name-driven registries, but it gives up compile-time export-name checks. A typo and argument mismatch surface later than typed member access.

recommendation.tradeoff: Option A adds a named argument and path normalization to every dynamic load. It accepts that repetition to keep authority local, preserve typed calls, and let experts bind a checked export.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared typed member access, a lexical grant, an export handle, and a dynamic call. It recommended the typed member form because it serves the fixed mod path and still lets experts bind the function.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The broad pass tested interface binding, a capability object, and a first-call prompt. Binding folded into typed members, the object duplicated the grant record, and the prompt delayed authority until after load.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested a typed member call inside a lexical grant block. It kept the block as a separate option because its wider scope changes audit behavior, not just spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened every option for its target user. A serves fixed mods, B serves grouped loads, C serves expert dispatch tables, and D serves name-driven registries.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested forged effect claims, sibling paths, missing exports, and wrong arguments. The recommendation keeps identity and effect checks before mapping, and keeps every call typed or checked before entry.

decisions.title: Calling a returned function value
decisions.gist: How you call a function that another call just returned.
decisions.lesson: Some calls return a function as their result. Today the only spelling to use that result at once is a second parenthesis pair, as in `grad(loss)(w, x)`. The owner review of the autodiff ballot found that shape foreign and hard to read. This choice picks one clear spelling for calling a function value that is not a plain name.
decisions.story: Priya reads a Jet tutorial that computes a gradient. The line `compute.grad(loss)(w, x)` stops her cold. She cannot tell what the second parenthesis pair belongs to, and she has never seen that shape anywhere else in Jet.

options.name: Uniform call, status quo
options.detail: Any expression followed by a parenthesis pair is a call. This is the smallest rule and matches Python, JavaScript, Rust and Swift. Docs teach the two-line form that binds the returned function to a name first. The cost is that the `)(` shape stays legal and will keep appearing in real code and tutorials.
options.technical: The parser postfix loop already produces a call-of-value node when `(` follows any expression. Nothing changes in parser, sema, formatter, or grammars. The style guide and formatter would steer toward bind-then-call.
options.code:
dloss :: compute.grad(loss)
gw :: dloss(w, x, y)

// also legal, and the shape in question
gw :: compute.grad(loss)(w, x, y)

options.name: Chained .call, ban the double parenthesis
options.detail: A call result is invoked with a chained `.call(…)`, and a parenthesis pair directly after a call is an error with a fix. `compute.grad(loss).call(w, x)` reads as the chain it is: build the gradient function, then call it. Plain names and stored fields keep the direct spelling, so `f(x)` and `w.step(4)` do not change. The cost is one extra word at a rare call site.
options.technical: Every function-typed value carries a builtin `.call(…)` member with the callee's parameter contract. The parser rejects `(` directly after a call expression with an E-coded error whose fix-it inserts `.call`. Member lookup on structs wins over the builtin, so a user field named `call` keeps its meaning. The ban covers any call result, including a `.call` result, so longer chains stay in `.call` form. Formatter, tree-sitter, tmGrammar, and LSP completion learn the member.

options.name: Dot-call sigil
options.detail: A function value is called with `.(…)`, a dot directly before the parenthesis. Elixir uses this exact shape to separate named calls from value calls. It is shorter than `.call`, but it is a sigil a reader must already know. A beginner cannot guess it, and it can read as a typo.
options.technical: A new `.(` token sequence in postfix position lowers to the same call-of-value node. Parser, formatter, both grammars, and highlighting change. The `)(` shape is rejected the same way as option B.
options.code: gw :: compute.grad(loss).(w, x, y)

options.name: Pipe operator
options.detail: A new `|>` operator feeds a value into a function from the left. It reads in data-flow order and many functional languages ship it. It is a whole new operator with language-wide reach. It only moves one argument, so multi-argument calls still need another rule, and the `)(` shape survives without a separate ban.
options.technical: `x |> f` rewrites to a call of `f` with `x` as the first argument. This adds an operator to the expression grammar and touches precedence, formatter, grammars, and docs. It does not remove the call-of-value shape on its own.
options.code:
gw :: w |> compute.grad_wrt_w(loss)   // one value pipes cleanly
// multi-argument calls still need bind-then-call or a ban like option B

comparisons.note: A proc is called with an explicit method. The direct parenthesis spelling does not exist for proc values.
Function values have a named `invoke` method, and `f(x)` is sugar for it. The explicit form is always available.
A function value is an object with a named calling method. There is no direct parenthesis call on values at all.
Function values must be called with a dot before the parenthesis, which separates them from named calls.
Any expression can be called directly, so the double parenthesis appears wherever a call returns a function.

recommendation.why: B says in one word what the second parenthesis pair only implies. The line reads as a dot chain, which is how Jet users already read everything else. The rule bans exactly the shape the owner review found foreign and changes nothing else in the language. Ruby, Kotlin and Java all ship this shape, so it carries mainstream precedent.

whyNot.reason: A keeps the `)(` shape legal, so tutorials and real code will still show it. Teaching an idiom around a confusing legal shape is weaker than removing the shape.
C replaces one cryptic shape with another. A sigil the reader must already know fails the beginner test that started this decision.
D is a language-wide operator decision far bigger than this question. It also does not remove the `)(` shape on its own, so the confusion survives.

recommendation.tradeoff: Calling a returned function costs one extra word, and function values gain a reserved member name. A user field named `call` keeps its meaning because struct member lookup wins, but that shadowing rule must be documented.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the uniform status quo, a chained `.call` method, the Elixir sigil, and a pipe operator. It recommended `.call` for readability at a rare but load-bearing call site.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested Haskell-style juxtaposition, Ruby bracket calls, and a Kotlin `invoke` name. Juxtaposition breaks the whole call grammar, brackets collide with indexing, and the name choice folded into option B.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested allowing `.call` everywhere alongside direct calls. That makes two full spellings for every call, so option B stays a targeted ban on the call-result position only.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened A with a formatter hint toward bind-then-call, C with full tool support, and D with its honest data-flow reading. Each option now shows its best form.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked B with a struct field named `call`, longer call chains, and lambda results. Member lookup precedence and applying the ban to every call result repair all three, so B survives.

decisions.title: Exponent operator spelling
decisions.gist: Which spelling raises a number to a power.
decisions.lesson: Jet has no power operator today. Powers go through `math.pow` and `math.int_pow` function calls. Scientific, engineering, and data users type powers constantly, so the spelling shapes everyday code. The infix `^` currently means exclusive-or, a bitwise operation that is rare outside low-level bit work. Typing `3 ** 2` today parses as a multiply followed by a raw-pointer sigil and fails with a confusing unsafe-pointer error.
decisions.story: Maya, a mechanical engineering student, ports a beam-deflection script from MATLAB. She types `L^3` exactly the way her textbook writes it. Today Jet quietly computes an exclusive-or of two numbers instead, and her deflection results are wrong with no error at all.

options.name: Infix `^` becomes exponent; xor moves
options.detail: `^` reads as power, the way mathematics, MATLAB, Julia, R, Lua, and Excel all write it. Exclusive-or gives up the glyph and gets a new spelling in its own decision. Gain: ported formulas from math tools work unchanged, and `L^3` means what the textbook means. Loss: any existing xor code must migrate, and the glyph now has an infix meaning (power) and a prefix meaning (take).
options.technical: Infix `^` reparses as BinOp::Pow. Compound `^=` becomes power-assign. Prefix `^` (the take capability sigil, D-MEM1) is untouched; parser position disambiguates, exactly as it disambiguates xor and take today. Xor respelling is D-XORSPELL1. Precedence, associativity, and Int typing are D-EXPSEM1.
options.code:
area :: side ^ 2
volume :: side ^ 3
growth :: principal * (1.0 + rate) ^ years

options.name: Add `**`; xor keeps `^`
options.detail: The Python, JavaScript, and Ruby spelling. Gain: nothing existing moves, and Python migrants recognize it instantly. Loss: `**` exists in those languages only because C had already spent `^` on exclusive-or. Jet is free of that history and would be adopting the workaround instead of the math spelling. MATLAB, R, and Julia users must retrain their fingers.
options.technical: New token `**` plus compound `**=`. Today `3 ** 2` lexes as `*` then prefix `*`, which is never valid, so the token is free. `^` stays BinOp::BitXor.
options.code:
area :: side ** 2
volume :: side ** 3
growth :: principal * (1.0 + rate) ** years

options.name: No operator; keep `math.pow`
options.detail: Powers stay function calls. Gain: no grammar change and no xor migration. Loss: everyday formulas stay noisy, nested powers become unreadable, and both Python and MATLAB migrants hit friction on day one. This works against the goal of being the best language for scientific and data work.
options.technical: Status quo. `math.pow(Float, Float)` and `math.int_pow(Int, Int)` remain the only power surface.
options.code:
volume :: math.pow(side, 3.0)
growth :: principal * math.pow(1.0 + rate, years.to_float())

comparisons.note: The math-tool family all spell power with a caret.
The C-descended family uses double-star because C spent the caret on xor.
No power operator at all; a function call is the only spelling.

recommendation.why: Jet targets scientific, engineering, and data work, where formulas are written and read as math. `^` is the spelling every math tool and every textbook uses, and Jet has no C legacy forcing the workaround.

whyNot.reason: `**` is a historical workaround for languages that had already spent `^` on xor. Jet has no such debt, and the math-tool audience reads `^` natively.
Function calls make everyday formulas noisy and unreadable, which directly hurts the audience this language is built for.

recommendation.tradeoff: Exclusive-or must move to a new spelling and existing xor code migrates. That is acceptable because xor is rare outside expert bit work, while powers appear in everyday beginner code.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared `^`, `**`, and function-only, and recommended `^` because the target audience reads and writes formulas the math-tool way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a named infix word `pow`, superscript unicode digits, and supporting both `^` and `**`. The word is noisy in formulas, unicode is untypeable, and dual spellings violate the one-spelling rule, so none joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested `^` for floats with `**` for integers and rejected it: one operation with two spellings by type is worse than either option alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with its Python-migrant familiarity and free lexer slot, and strengthened C by noting it needs no migration at all. Both remain weaker for formula-heavy code.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on the double life of the glyph: prefix take versus infix power. The parser already runs exactly this split for xor today, and no ambiguous program exists, so the recommendation survives with the xor migration as its accepted cost.

decisions.title: Exponent semantics: grouping and integer results
decisions.gist: How power expressions group, and what type integer powers return.
decisions.lesson: Tools disagree about power expressions in two places. First, grouping: does `2^3^2` mean `2^(3^2)` (512) or `(2^3)^2` (64), and does `-3^2` mean `-(3^2)` (-9) or `(-3)^2` (9)? Second, integer results: does `2^10` stay an exact integer, and what happens on a negative exponent like `2^-1`? These choices decide whether ported formulas compute the same numbers they did at home.
decisions.story: Priya ports a statistics routine that computes `-x^2 / 2.0` inside a normal-distribution formula. In Python and MATLAB that means minus the square. If Jet groups it the other way, her probabilities silently come out positive-shifted and every downstream chart is wrong.

options.name: Math convention: right-grouping, exact integers
options.detail: `2^3^2` is 512 and `-3^2` is -9, matching Python, Julia, Ruby, and written mathematics. Integer base with a non-negative integer exponent stays an exact integer. A negative integer exponent returns a Float, the way Python does. Gain: textbook formulas and Python ports compute identical numbers. Loss: MATLAB users get 512 where MATLAB gave 64 on chained powers, a rare shape.
options.technical: Right-associative. Power binds tighter than unary minus but looser than postfix and prefix capability sigils. `Int ^ Int(>=0) -> Int`, exact under the default Int. `Int ^ Int(<0) -> Float`. Any Float operand makes the result Float.
options.code:
print(2^3^2)   // 512
print(-3^2)    // -9
print(2^10)    // 1024, exact Int
print(2^-1)    // 0.5, Float

options.name: MATLAB convention: left-grouping, float results
options.detail: `2^3^2` is 64, evaluated left to right, and `-3^2` is -9. Every power returns a Float, because MATLAB numbers are all doubles. Gain: chained powers match MATLAB exactly. Loss: `2^10` stops being an exact integer, which poisons index math and big exact arithmetic, and Python ports of chained powers change value.
options.technical: Left-associative. Power binds tighter than unary minus. Result type is always Float regardless of operand types.

options.name: Excel convention: unary minus wins
options.detail: `-3^2` is 9 because the leading minus binds tighter than the power, and chains group left. Gain: spreadsheet migrants get Excel's numbers. Loss: this contradicts written mathematics and every programming language, so textbook formulas silently compute wrong values. Included for completeness because spreadsheet users are a real audience.
options.technical: Left-associative. Unary minus binds tighter than power. Result is Float.
options.code:
print(-3^2)    // 9.0, unlike every textbook
print(2^3^2)   // 64.0

comparisons.note: Right-grouping, minus applies last, ints stay exact until a negative exponent.
Left-grouping, everything is a double.
The odd one out: a leading minus beats the power.

recommendation.why: Written mathematics and the largest migration source (Python) agree on right-grouping with minus applying last. Exact integer powers keep index math and combinatorics correct under the default Int.

whyNot.reason: Forcing every power to Float breaks exact integer arithmetic, and left-grouping matches only MATLAB against math convention and Python alike.
Excel's grouping contradicts textbooks and every programming language, so it silently corrupts ported formulas for everyone except spreadsheet migrants.

recommendation.tradeoff: MATLAB migrants who chain powers without parentheses get 512 where MATLAB gave 64. That shape is rare, and a formatter hint can suggest explicit parentheses on chained powers.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared math-convention, MATLAB, and Excel packages and recommended math convention for textbook and Python parity.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review considered requiring parentheses on any chained or minus-adjacent power, making ambiguity a compile error. It was folded into option A as a possible formatter hint rather than a hard error, to keep textbook formulas typeable.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested right-grouping with always-Float results and rejected it: exact integer powers are load-bearing for the arbitrary-precision Int direction.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by noting MATLAB parity matters for whole-script ports, and C by naming spreadsheet users as a genuine audience. Both still lose on silent number changes for the majority.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's negative-exponent rule: an Int silently becoming Float can surprise. Python behaves identically and the alternative, a runtime error, is harsher for beginners, so A survives unchanged.

decisions.title: Integer power when the exponent sign is unknown
decisions.gist: What an integer power returns when nobody knows the exponent sign until the program runs.
decisions.lesson: You already chose that `2 ^ -1` is 0.5 and returns a Float. That rule reads the minus sign in the source text. Jet checks types before the program runs. When the exponent is a variable, no one knows its sign yet. The compiler must still pick one result type. This choice decides that type, and what happens when the exponent turns out to be negative.
decisions.story: Sam writes a loop that doubles a counter: `total = 2 ^ step`. The variable `step` comes from a file. Sam expects exact whole numbers. One day the file holds -3. Jet must either hand Sam a fraction, stop the program, or refuse to compile the line.

options.name: Stay exact, stop on a negative exponent
options.detail: An integer raised to an integer stays an exact integer. If the exponent turns out negative while the program runs, the program stops with a clear message. A written minus sign still gives a Float, so `2 ^ -1` is still 0.5. Gain: counting and sizing code keeps exact whole numbers, which is what almost every loop wants. Loss: a negative exponent from data stops the program instead of returning a fraction.
options.technical: `Int ^ Int -> Int`. The result type never depends on a runtime value. A written negative literal exponent keeps the ratified `Int ^ Int(<0) -> Float` rule, decided in sema from the source text. A runtime-negative exponent traps, using the same trap family as divide by zero and overflow. The trap message and its diagnostic code come from one Prelude symbol shared by every tier.

options.name: Always return a Float when the sign is unknown
options.detail: If the compiler cannot see that the exponent is zero or more, the answer is a Float. Nothing stops the program. Gain: a negative exponent from data returns a fraction, exactly like the written case, so one rule covers both. Loss: ordinary counting code quietly loses exact whole numbers. `2 ^ step` in a loop returns 1024.0 instead of 1024, and large values lose digits.
options.technical: `Int ^ Int -> Float` unless sema proves the exponent is a non-negative constant. Proof comes from literals and from constant folding only. A variable of type Int always widens. Float results follow the platform double rules, so exactness is lost above 2^53.
options.code:
let step = config.read_int("scale_step")
print(2 ^ step)   // 1024.0, a Float, even when step is 10

let n = 10
print(2 ^ n)      // 1024, exact: n folds to a constant
print(2 ^ 62)     // exact
print(2 ^ step)   // loses digits past 2^53

options.name: Make the author state the intent
options.detail: Jet refuses to compile `2 ^ step` when nothing proves the sign of `step`. The message offers two fixes: check the sign first, or make the base a Float. Gain: no surprise fraction and no surprise stop, because every power says what it means. Loss: real ceremony on ordinary code. Every power over a variable needs an extra line, even where a negative value is impossible in practice.
options.technical: `Int ^ Int` is an error when sema cannot prove the exponent is non-negative. Proof comes from a literal, a constant, a checked branch, or a non-negative integer type. The error carries a registered code with a fix that offers a guard or a Float base.

options.name: Split the spellings
options.detail: `^` means exact integer power and only accepts an exponent that cannot be negative. A separate `math.pow` covers fractions and negative exponents, and always returns a Float. Gain: each spelling has one meaning and one result type, with nothing to learn about proofs. Loss: `2 ^ -1` stops meaning 0.5, which reverses a rule you already chose, and textbook formulas need rewriting.
options.technical: `^` takes a non-negative integer exponent type. A negative literal is a compile error. `math.pow(base, exponent) -> Float` covers every other case. This retires the ratified `Int ^ Int(<0) -> Float` rule and needs that decision amended.
options.code:
print(2 ^ 10)         // 1024, exact Int
print(2 ^ -1)         // compile error, use math.pow
print(math.pow(2, -1))// 0.5, a Float

let step = config.read_int("scale_step")
print(math.pow(2, step))  // always a Float

comparisons.note: Types are checked while the program runs, so the sign is always known. Jet cannot copy this directly.
The exponent type cannot hold a negative number, so the question never arises. Overflow stops the program in debug builds.
There is no power operator. The library function takes and returns floating point numbers only.
There is no power operator. The library covers floating point, and exact integer power needs a written loop.
The power function is floating point only. Exact integer power is not in the standard library.

recommendation.why: Almost every power over a variable is counting, sizing, or scaling, and those need exact whole numbers. Option A keeps them exact. A negative exponent from data is a bad input, and Jet already stops on divide by zero and overflow, so the behaviour is familiar. The written rule you ratified stays untouched.

whyNot.reason: It quietly turns exact counting into floating point. `2 ^ step` returning 1024.0 breaks index and size code, and silently loses digits past 2^53.
It puts a guard or a conversion on every power over a variable. That is ceremony on ordinary code, and the beginner surface pays for a rare input.
It reverses your ratified rule that `2 ^ -1` is 0.5, and it splits one idea across two spellings.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bad configuration value stops the program instead of returning a fraction. That is accepted because a negative exponent in integer code is a data fault, and a clear stop beats a silent change of number type.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft framed the gap left by the ratified rule: the written case is decided, the computed case is not. It compared staying exact against widening to Float, and recommended staying exact.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the author-states-intent option and the split-spelling option. It also tested returning an optional or a checked result, and dropped that because it adds a new mechanism for one operator.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested proving the sign from checked branches and adding that proof to the exact option. The proof rule was folded into option C, because bolting it onto A would make the same line compile or fail depending on distant code.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened every option: constant folding for B, a two-way fix hint for C, and a clean library boundary for D. Each option now reads as the strongest honest version of itself.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the recommendation with the config-file case, where a bad value stops a running program. The stop survived, because every alternative changes the result type of ordinary counting code.

decisions.title: Respell exclusive-or after `^` becomes power
decisions.gist: Where bitwise exclusive-or lives once `^` means power.
decisions.lesson: If D-EXPOP1 gives `^` to the power operator, exclusive-or needs a new home. Exclusive-or keeps a bit where exactly one input has a one bit: either, but not both. It is rare in everyday code but essential in hashing, graphics, checksums, and hardware work. The rest of the bitwise family is sigil-spelled (`&`, `|`, `<<`, `>>`) with compound assignments. On Bool, `!=` already is logical xor. Gate ops like nand and nor have operator spellings only in hardware languages and compose from these primitives.
decisions.story: Tomás writes a fast hash for a game asset cache. His inner loop xors a rolling state with each chunk. He needs a spelling that reads clearly in a dense loop body and does not tangle with the new power operator one line above.

options.name: Infix `~|` with compound `~|=`
options.detail: A new sigil built from the family it belongs to: `|` keeps a bit when either or both inputs have it; `~|` keeps a bit when either input has it, but not both. Gain: the spelling teaches itself as the exclusive variant of or, and the compound `~|=` reads unmistakably as an or-family update. Loss: no language spells xor this way, and Verilog readers arrive expecting `~|` to mean nor, since their tilde negates a result.
options.technical: New token `~|`, BinOp::BitXor in the old `^` precedence slot, compound `~|=`. Both glyphs are free in infix position today; prefix `~` (copy) is untouched. If gate operators were ever wanted, Verilog's `~&`/`~|` spellings would be unavailable, an accepted cost since gates compose from primitives.

options.name: Infix `~` with compound `~=`
options.detail: Bare tilde, the choice Lua made when its caret became power; prefix `~` stays the copy sigil, the same position-split infix-and-prefix `&` lives with. Gain: one glyph, direct precedent. Loss: bare tilde says nothing about or-ness, and C and Python readers expect it to mean complement. Worse, the compound `~=` means not-equal in Lua itself, a false friend planted in the precedent's own community.
options.technical: Infix `~` becomes BinOp::BitXor with compound `~=`. Parser position disambiguates against prefix copy. The retired `~~` connector is only a teaching diagnostic.

options.name: Infix word `xor`
options.detail: `a xor b`, the Ada, Pascal, and VHDL spelling. Gain: reads exactly as pronounced and can never be mistaken for any sigil meaning. Loss: it becomes Jet's only word-spelled binary operator, since and/or are `&&` and `||`, so the bitwise family splits into words and sigils, and there is no natural compound assignment.
options.technical: New keyword `xor` in the old `^` precedence slot. No compound spelling; write `a = a xor b`.

options.name: Method `a.xor(b)`; no operator
options.detail: Exclusive-or leaves the operator family and becomes an integer method. Gain: zero new grammar and autocomplete discoverability beside future bit helpers like rotate and popcount. Loss: xor becomes the only bitwise operation without an operator, and chained bit expressions turn into nested calls exactly where operator shape matters most.
options.technical: Fixed-signature method on all integer widths. A fuller bits toolkit can grow beside it independently of this ballot.

comparisons.note: Faced the same collision and chose bare tilde; note Lua's own `~=` means not-equal.
Word-spelled xor operator; VHDL also has nand, nor, xnor words.
Caret means xor because power has no operator there.
Tilde negates a result there, so its `~|` is nor, not xor.

recommendation.why: `~|` is the only candidate that says what it means: the exclusive variant of `|`, learnable from its own glyphs. Its compound `~|=` stays visibly an or-family update, and it avoids every false friend the bare tilde carries.

whyNot.reason: Bare tilde reads as complement to C and Python eyes, and its compound `~=` means not-equal in Lua, the very community its precedent cites.
A lone word operator splits the bitwise family's shape and loses compound assignment, a real cost in accumulator loops.
Making xor the only operator-less bitwise operation breaks family symmetry exactly where dense expressions need operator shape most.

recommendation.tradeoff: The spelling is a Jet invention, and Verilog readers must unlearn `~|` as nor. That is acceptable because the glyph pair teaches itself to everyone else, and the hardware audience overlap is far smaller than the C, Python, and Lua audiences the alternatives confuse.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a word operator, a method, and a bits-module function, recommending the word. The owner rejected that menu, prompting a family-wide audit of every logical and bitwise spelling.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The audit found infix tilde and tilde-pipe both free. Bare tilde joined with Lua precedent; the owner then challenged its compound as unreadable, surfacing tilde-pipe, which self-describes as exclusive-or and joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested operator plus a discoverable method alias and rejected the alias: one operation, one spelling. It confirmed gate ops stay compositions, with the Verilog family noted for the future.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened bare tilde with its one-glyph brevity and real precedent, the word with its VHDL pedigree, and the method with bit-toolkit discoverability. Each remains weaker on family shape or false friends.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked `~|` as an unprecedented invention and via the Verilog nor reading. Novelty is mitigated by self-description, the nor collision touches the smallest audience, and no parse ambiguity exists, so `~|` survives as the recommendation.

decisions.title: Floor division operator
decisions.gist: How to spell whole-number division that rounds down.
decisions.lesson: Floor division divides and rounds toward negative infinity, so `7 /% 2` is 3 and `-7 /% 2` is -4. Python and Lua spell it `//`, but in Jet `//` starts a comment and cannot be an operator. Doc comments (`///`, S49) and doctests (D-TEST4) already work today, so the comment marker is settled and only the floor-division spelling is open. Floor division pairs with floored modulo (D-MODSEM1) so that `a == b * (a /% b) + a % b` always holds.
decisions.story: Ana lays out a photo grid. She computes `row :: index /% columns` and `col :: index % columns`. With a floor pair these are correct for every index she will ever pass, and the two spellings visibly rhyme.

options.name: `/%` with compound `/%=`
options.detail: A new two-glyph operator: divide, then the `%` reminds you it is the partner of modulo. Gain: a first-class operator for an everyday operation, visibly paired with `%`, and the spelling is free today because `a /% b` currently parses as an error. Loss: no other language uses this exact spelling, so every migrant learns it once.
options.technical: New token `/%`, BinOp slot, compound `/%=`. Works on Int and Float; floors toward negative infinity in both. Satisfies `a == b * (a /% b) + a % b` with floored `%` (D-MODSEM1). Division by zero traps like `/`.
options.code:
print(7 /% 2)    // 3
print(-7 /% 2)   // -4
print(7.5 /% 2.0) // 3.0
page := index
page /%= per_page

options.name: Infix word `div`
options.detail: `a div b`, the Pascal and SQL spelling. Gain: pronounceable and precedented. Loss: it does not visually pair with `%`, it reads as prose inside dense arithmetic, and word operators need D-XORSPELL1-style precedent to feel at home in Jet.
options.technical: New keyword `div`, same precedence as `/`. No compound spelling.
options.code:
print(7 div 2)    // 3
print(-7 div 2)   // -4

options.name: Function only: `math.floor_div`
options.detail: No operator; a named function does the job. Gain: no new grammar. Loss: an operation this common in index math, pagination, and time arithmetic deserves better than a function call, and the identity with `%` becomes invisible.
options.technical: Status quo plus a `math.floor_div` fixed signature for Int and Float.
options.code:
print(math.floor_div(7, 2))   // 3
print(math.floor_div(-7, 2))  // -4

comparisons.note: Spells it with double slash, which Jet's comments make impossible.
Word operator.
Percent-bracketed operator family.

recommendation.why: Floor division is everyday index math and deserves an operator. `/%` visibly pairs with `%`, keeps the division-family look, and the spelling is unclaimed by any current syntax.

whyNot.reason: A word operator reads as prose inside arithmetic and hides the pairing with modulo.
A function call is too heavy for an operation that appears in every pagination and grid loop.

recommendation.tradeoff: The spelling is novel, so every migrant learns it once. That is acceptable because the glyphs teach themselves: divide, in the manner of modulo.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared `/%`, the word `div`, and a function, recommending `/%` for its pairing with modulo.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested reclaiming `//` by moving comments to `#` or `--`. Both evict ratified syntax (markers, decrement) for one operator, and doc comments plus doctests already work on `///`, so reclaiming was rejected outright.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping `/%` plus a `math.floor_div` alias and rejected the alias: one operation, one spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened `div` with its Pascal and SQL pedigree and the function option with zero grammar cost. Both still hide the modulo pairing that makes the floor pair teachable.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked `/%` as line noise and probed whether `a /% b` could ever parse ambiguously today. It cannot, because `%` has no prefix form, and the noise concern fades against the pairing it buys, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Modulo semantics: `%` floored, `%%` truncated
decisions.gist: What `-7 % 2` returns, and how to spell the other remainder.
decisions.lesson: Two remainder definitions exist. Floored modulo follows the divisor's sign, so `-7 % 2` is 1; clock, index, and wrap-around math want this one. Truncated remainder follows the dividend's sign, so `-7 % 2` is -1; C, Rust, and JavaScript ship this one. Jet's `%` is truncated today, which silently breaks even/odd checks and array wrap-around on negative numbers. Python, Ruby, and Lua chose floored for exactly that reason.
decisions.story: Ben writes a music sequencer. Beat position is `tick % 16`. When the user scrubs backward past zero, ticks go negative. With truncated remainder his sequencer indexes step -1 and crashes; with floored remainder it wraps to step 15 and just keeps playing.

options.name: `%` floored, `%%` truncated
options.detail: The everyday spelling gets the answer that index, clock, and parity math want: `-7 % 2` is 1. The C-style remainder stays available as `%%` for ports and specialist code. Gain: the beginner default is the correct one for wrap-around math, matching Python. Loss: code ported from C, Rust, or JavaScript changes meaning on negative operands unless it switches to `%%`.
options.technical: `%` becomes floored on Int and Float, with `%=` following. New token `%%` is truncated remainder with `%%=`. Identity `a == b * (a /% b) + a % b` holds with floored floor division (D-FLOORDIV1). Both trap on zero divisor. Prelude jet_rem splits into jet_mod (floored) and jet_rem (truncated) per I9 across all tiers.
options.code:
print(-7 % 2)    // 1
print(-7 %% 2)   // -1
print(step(-1))  // 15, wraps correctly

options.name: Keep `%` truncated only
options.detail: Status quo, matching C, Rust, and JavaScript. Gain: no migration and C-family ports keep their meaning. Loss: the beginner default stays wrong for wrap-around and parity math on negatives, the single most reported modulo trap across languages, and Python ports silently change meaning instead.
options.technical: No change. Floored modulo would remain unspelled or become a math function.
options.code:
print(-7 % 2)    // -1
print(step(-1))  // -1, indexes out of range

options.name: `%` floored only, no `%%`
options.detail: One remainder, the floored one; truncated becomes a method for the rare port that needs it. Gain: smallest surface, one obvious spelling. Loss: C-family ports lose a direct spelling, and systems programmers reaching for hardware-native remainder get a method instead of an operator.
options.technical: `%` floored everywhere. `a.rem_trunc(b)` fixed signature covers the truncated case.
options.code:
print(-7 % 2)          // 1
print((-7).rem_trunc(2)) // -1

options.name: `%` truncated, `%%` floored
options.detail: Keep C meaning on the short spelling and add the floored one at `%%`, roughly R's arrangement. Gain: zero migration for existing Jet code and C ports. Loss: the beginner-facing default stays the trap, and the correct-for-indexing operation hides behind the longer spelling.
options.technical: `%` unchanged; new `%%` floored with `%%=`.

comparisons.note: Floored on the everyday spelling.
Truncated on the everyday spelling.
Floored, spelled with doubled percent.

recommendation.why: The short spelling should give the answer wrap-around, clock, and parity math need, which is what beginners write first. Keeping truncated at `%%` preserves an explicit spelling for C-family ports and hardware-native code.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the most famous modulo trap as the default and silently changes the meaning of Python ports.
Dropping the truncated operator entirely pushes systems code to a method for a real hardware operation.
It optimizes for existing C habits over the correctness of the beginner default, against the mission.

recommendation.tradeoff: C, Rust, and JavaScript ports change meaning on negative operands until they switch to `%%`. That is acceptable because the compiler can lint suspicious negative-capable `%` during migration, and the scientific audience mostly arrives from Python.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared four arrangements of floored and truncated remainder and recommended floored on `%` with truncated on `%%`.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added Euclidean remainder (always non-negative) as a candidate meaning. For positive divisors it equals floored, and positive divisors dominate real code, so it was folded into option A's technical notes rather than added as a fifth option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested `%` floored plus a compile warning whenever a possibly-negative dividend meets `%`. The warning punished correct code, so it was cut; the migration lint in the tradeoff is one-time instead.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B and D on zero-migration grounds and C on smallest-surface grounds. Each still leaves either the default wrong or systems code underserved.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with the performance cost of floored modulo over the hardware instruction and with double-glyph confusability. The cost is one branch, unmeasurable outside hot loops where `%%` remains available, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: What `Int / Int` returns
decisions.gist: Whether 7 / 2 is 3.5 or 3.
decisions.lesson: With floor division getting its own operator (D-FLOORDIV1), plain `/` no longer has to do double duty. Today Jet truncates: `7 / 2` is 3, the C behavior. Python 3 famously changed `/` to always return a float precisely because silent integer truncation was its most common beginner bug, and moved whole-number division to a dedicated operator. This decision sets what a calculator-shaped expression returns in Jet.
decisions.story: Leo, in his first week of programming, computes an average: `total / count`. With truncating division his average of 7 and 2 is 4 with no warning. His spreadsheet says 4.5. He concludes the language is broken, and he is not entirely wrong.

options.name: `/` always returns Float
options.detail: `7 / 2` is 3.5, the Python 3 and calculator answer. Whole-number division is `/%`, an explicit choice. Gain: the single most common beginner numeric bug becomes impossible, and averages, rates, and ratios are correct by default. Loss: code wanting integer division must say `/%`, and C-family ports of `/` on ints change type.
options.technical: `Int / Int -> Float`. `Int /% Int -> Int` (D-FLOORDIV1). `/=` on an Int binding whose division produces Float is a type error pointing at `/%=`. Large default-Int values may lose precision crossing to Float, exactly as Python accepts.
options.code:
print(7 / 2)     // 3.5
print(7 /% 2)    // 3
average :: scores.sum() / scores.len()   // 8.5, correct

options.name: Keep truncating `Int / Int -> Int`
options.detail: The C, Rust, Go, and Java behavior. Gain: no migration, integer expressions stay closed over Int, systems code keeps its habits. Loss: the averages bug stays the default experience for every beginner and data user, which is the audience this language is built to win.
options.technical: No change. Truncation toward zero, trap on zero divisor.
options.code:
print(7 / 2)     // 3
average :: scores.sum() / scores.len()   // 8, silently wrong as a mean

options.name: `Int / Int -> Int`, flooring
options.detail: Keep division closed over Int but round down instead of toward zero, aligning with floored `%`. Gain: internal consistency with D-MODSEM1 and no type change. Loss: `7 / 2` still is not 3.5, so the beginner trap survives, and it now differs from both C and Python at once.
options.technical: Floors toward negative infinity, making `/` and `/%` identical on Int, which duplicates one mechanism under two spellings.

comparisons.note: Changed this exact default after two decades of the truncation bug.
Truncating integer division.
Division is numeric, never silently whole.

recommendation.why: Every math tool the target audience comes from answers 3.5. With `/%` available for explicit whole-number division, keeping the truncation trap would preserve a famous bug purely for C-family nostalgia.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the beginner-hostile default that Python 3 spent a painful decade migrating away from, with the benefit of hindsight available for free.
It makes `/` and `/%` the same operation on Int, two spellings for one mechanism, while still giving the wrong average.

recommendation.tradeoff: Integer-heavy code must write `/%` to stay in Int, and enormous default-Int values lose precision when `/` produces a Float. Both are explicit and visible, unlike the silent truncation they replace.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared float-producing, truncating, and flooring division and recommended the float result for calculator correctness.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added exact-rational results as a candidate: `7 / 2` as a Rational preserving exactness. It was rejected as a new core numeric type with pervasive cost, better raised someday as its own proposal, not smuggled through an operator ballot.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested context-dependent division, Int in Int contexts and Float otherwise. Result types that depend on surrounding inference make errors non-local, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with systems-code closure over Int and C with its consistency story beside floored modulo. Neither fixes the average that is simply wrong.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on precision loss for huge arbitrary-precision Ints and on `/=` breakage. The type error on `/=` is loud and mechanical to fix, Python demonstrates the precision tradeoff is livable, so A survives.

decisions.title: Bitwise NOT: extend `!` to integers
decisions.gist: How to flip every bit of an integer.
decisions.lesson: Jet has no bitwise complement at all today. `!` works only on Bool, and `~`, the spelling C and Python use for complement, is Jet's copy sigil. Complement builds bit masks: clearing a flag is `flags & !mask`. On a Bool, `!` already flips the single bit, so extending it to flip all bits of an integer is one rule, not two. Rust ships exactly this design.
decisions.story: Rosa writes a driver for a sensor board. To clear the interrupt-enable bit she needs `status & !INTERRUPT_MASK`. Today Jet gives her no spelling for the complement at all, and she hand-writes the inverted constant, which breaks the day the register grows.

options.name: `!` flips bits on integers
options.detail: One prefix operator: on Bool it flips the truth bit, on integers it flips every bit. Gain: no new sigil, one consistent rule, and Rust proves the design works at scale. Loss: readers from C and Python expect tilde and must learn that Jet's tilde means copy, and a stray `!` on an integer is no longer caught as a type error.
options.technical: UnOp::Not extends from Bool to all integer widths as bitwise complement, matching Rust's `!`. On the default arbitrary-precision Int, complement is defined as `-x - 1`, the two's-complement identity, so it is width-independent. Fixed-width types flip their exact bits.
options.code:
print(!true)         // false
print(!0b1010)       // ...11110101 (two's-complement -11)
cleared :: status & !ENABLE

options.name: Method `x.flip_bits()`
options.detail: No operator; complement is an integer method. Gain: keeps `!` Bool-only so an integer `!` stays a type error, and the name says what happens. Loss: mask expressions read worse (`status & ENABLE.flip_bits()`), and complement becomes the only bitwise operation without an operator.
options.technical: Fixed-signature method on integer types; same `-x - 1` definition on default Int.
options.code: cleared :: status & ENABLE.flip_bits()

options.name: No complement; masks via xor
options.detail: Skip it; experts write `x xor all_ones` or precompute inverted constants. Gain: zero surface growth. Loss: every driver, protocol, and graphics programmer rebuilds a basic operation by hand, and the width of all-ones is a per-type trap.
options.technical: No change. The all-ones value differs per width, which is exactly the bug the operator prevents.
options.code: cleared :: status & (ENABLE xor 0b1111_1111)   // must match width by hand

comparisons.note: One `!` for logical and bitwise NOT, chosen deliberately over C's tilde.
Separate tilde operator for complement.

recommendation.why: Flipping bits is what `!` already does on Bool, so one rule covers both, with Rust as working precedent. No new sigil is spent, which matters in a language where tilde and caret are already claimed.

whyNot.reason: A method call in the middle of a mask expression is heavier than the operator every peer language provides.
Hand-built all-ones masks are width traps, recreating the exact bug a complement operator exists to prevent.

recommendation.tradeoff: An accidental `!` on an integer now compiles instead of erroring. That is acceptable because the same is true in Rust and the confusion is rare, while the Bool-only rule left a real operation unspellable.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared extending `!`, a named method, and no complement, recommending the extension for its one-rule consistency.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review searched for a dedicated sigil: tilde is the copy sigil, doubled `!!` reads as double negation, and inventing a new glyph fails the no-unprecedented-sigils bar. None were menu-worthy.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested operator plus method as a teaching alias and rejected the alias: one operation, one spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by naming its discoverability and its preservation of `!`-on-Int as an error, the strongest honest case against the extension.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's meaning on arbitrary-precision Int, where bit width is unbounded. The two's-complement identity `-x - 1` is total and width-free, Python defines tilde identically for its big ints, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Three-way comparison: operator or method
decisions.gist: How custom ordering is written for sorting.
decisions.lesson: A three-way comparison answers less, equal, or greater in one step. Its real job is custom sorting: define ordering once and every sort and comparison derives from it. Ruby, PHP, and C++ spell it `<=>`, the spaceship operator. The spelling is free in Jet — `a <= > b` is invalid today, so no conflict exists. The question is whether ordering deserves an operator or stays a named method, since ordinary user code compares with the six operators and rarely needs the three-way form directly.
decisions.story: Sam sorts a leaderboard by score, then by name for ties. He writes one ordering rule for his Player type and expects `sort` to use it. He touches the three-way form once, inside that rule, and never again in the rest of the program.

options.name: `compare` method returning Ordering
options.detail: Ordering is a named method and an Ordering type; no new operator. Gain: the three-way form appears exactly where it is defined and read, in ordering rules, where a named method with combinators like `then` reads better than operator chains. Loss: Ruby and PHP migrants type `<=>` and get a parse error, and dense comparator bodies carry method-call weight.
options.technical: Core `Ordering` type (Less, Equal, Greater) with `then` and `reverse`. Fixed-signature `compare` on ordered core types; user types define `compare(self, other)` and the six comparison operators plus sorting derive from it.

options.name: Spaceship operator `<=>` plus Ordering
options.detail: The Ruby and C++ spelling as a real operator, sugar over the same method. Gain: comparator bodies get shorter and migrants keep their muscle memory. Loss: an operator visible to every learner for an operation used almost only inside ordering rules, and Jet gains a three-glyph sigil whose meaning cannot be guessed from its parts.
options.technical: New token `<=>`, lexed before `<=`. Desugars to `compare`. Everything else as option A.

options.name: Neither; six operators only
options.detail: No Ordering type, no three-way form; custom sorting takes a key function or a Bool less-than rule. Gain: nothing new. Loss: tie-breaking multi-field sorts through Bool rules are error-prone boilerplate, and library authors lose the single-definition derivation that every peer language provides.
options.technical: Sorting APIs accept key extraction or a `less` predicate only.

comparisons.note: Spaceship operator returning order.
Named method plus Ordering enum with combinators; no operator.
Dropped its three-way cmp entirely; key functions dominate.

recommendation.why: Three-way comparison lives inside ordering definitions, read by library authors, not beginners. A named method with combinators covers that audience fully without spending a three-glyph operator on the everyday surface.

whyNot.reason: The operator's entire benefit is brevity inside comparator bodies, too small a payoff for a new learner-visible sigil.
Bool-rule comparators are the worst of both worlds: verbose, error-prone on ties, and without single-definition derivation.

recommendation.tradeoff: Comparator bodies stay slightly wordier than Ruby's. That is acceptable because the `then` combinator keeps multi-field ordering flat and readable, which is the case that actually matters.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared method-only, spaceship-plus-method, and neither, recommending the method for audience fit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added Python-style key functions as a candidate and folded them in: key-based sorting composes with a compare method and belongs in the sorting API design regardless of this ballot.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping the method now while reserving `<=>` for later and rejected the reservation: unratified futures are not law, and the spelling stays free either way.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with Ruby and PHP migration comfort and C with zero surface growth. B still buys brevity only inside rare comparator bodies; C still leaves tie-breaking to hand-rolled Bool logic.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A by asking whether deriving six operators from one method is magic beginners cannot trace. The derivation is the same one every peer language ships and diagnostics can name the source method, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Default Int overflow model: arbitrary precision
decisions.gist: What happens when the default Int gets too big.
decisions.lesson: Jet's default Int is fixed-width today and the program stops with a panic when a result overflows (D-NUMOPS1). Overflow is not a beginner mistake; it is a machine limit leaking through. Python removed the limit entirely: its int grows as needed, so factorials, big powers, and money math in small units just work. The cost is a check on arithmetic and a slower path for huge values. This decision sets the default; fixed-width expert types exist regardless.
decisions.story: Nadia, a biology student, computes 25 factorial for a probability. It is a 26-digit number. In Python she has the answer before her coffee cools. In Jet today her program panics mid-run with an overflow message she has no tools to understand.

options.name: Int grows without limit; fixed widths are the expert opt-in
options.detail: The default Int is arbitrary precision with a fast path for machine-sized values, exactly Python's model. Overflow stops existing for beginners. Experts who need exact machine behavior reach for fixed-width types, where overflow traps by default and wrapping or saturating is an explicit named choice. Gain: a whole class of runtime crashes disappears and exact math just works. Loss: arithmetic carries a small-versus-big check, and foreign-function boundaries must range-check.
options.technical: Small-int fast path in machine words, spilling to heap digits past roughly 63 bits, per I9 identical across AOT, JIT, interpreter, and web. Fixed-width `I8..I128`, `U8..U128` keep trap-on-overflow plus explicit `wrapping_*` and `saturating_*` methods. Amends D-NUMOPS1 for default Int only. Crossing to fixed-width or FFI range-checks with a real diagnostic.
options.code:
print(factorial(25))     // 15511210043330985984000000
print(2 ^ 200)           // exact, 61 digits
sensor: U8 = 300         // error: 300 does not fit in U8

options.name: Keep fixed-width Int with panic on overflow
options.detail: Status quo. Gain: predictable machine-speed arithmetic everywhere and no representation split. Loss: correct-looking math crashes at runtime on big inputs, the message teaches machine trivia beginners should never need, and Python migrants lose exactness they took for granted.
options.technical: No change. D-NUMOPS1 stands as ratified.
options.code:
print(factorial(25))
// panic: attempt to multiply with overflow

options.name: Fixed-width Int that wraps silently
options.detail: The C model: overflow wraps around modulo the width. Gain: fastest possible arithmetic, no checks at all. Loss: factorial(25) returns a confidently wrong number with no error, the worst possible outcome for scientific work and a direct violation of safe-by-default.
options.technical: Wrapping two's-complement arithmetic on the default Int.
options.code: print(factorial(25))   // 7034535277573963776, silently wrong

options.name: Fixed-width Int that saturates
options.detail: Overflow pins the result at the maximum value. Gain: no crash and the error stays visible as an extreme value. Loss: silently wrong results that additionally look plausible in aggregates, and no mainstream language uses this default, so it surprises everyone equally.
options.technical: Saturating arithmetic on the default Int.
options.code: print(factorial(25))   // 9223372036854775807, silently wrong

comparisons.note: Default integers grow without limit; the scripting standard.
Fixed-width, panics in debug, wraps in release; experts choose explicitly.
Doubles by default, lossy past 2^53; BigInt bolted on later.

recommendation.why: The mission is magic for beginners with expert control behind opt-in. An Int that simply holds the answer is that magic, proven by the exact languages Jet aims to beat, while fixed-width types keep every expert capability explicit.

whyNot.reason: A panic explains a machine limit to a person doing math homework; the crash is safe but the experience fails the mission.
Silently wrong answers are disqualifying for a language whose pitch is trustworthy computation.
Saturation is silent wrongness with a plausible face, and no precedent recommends it as a default.

recommendation.tradeoff: Default-Int arithmetic pays a small-versus-big check and FFI boundaries need range checks. That is acceptable because hot numeric code moves to fixed-width or Float types anyway, which is where experts already live.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared unlimited growth, panic, wrap, and saturate, recommending unlimited growth as the mission answer.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added checked-Result arithmetic and compile-time range types as candidates. Both push expert ceremony into everyday sums, so they were folded into the fixed-width expert surface where they belong.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested panic-by-default with an opt-in BigInt type and rejected it: the beginner still crashes first, and two integer defaults split the ecosystem, the JavaScript BigInt lesson.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with its predictable performance and Rust precedent, the strongest honest rival. It still trades a beginner-facing crash for a cost experts can already escape.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on hot-loop performance, memory layout of spilled ints, and I9 parity cost across four tiers. The small-int fast path bounds the common case, Python and Erlang prove the model at scale, and parity work is implementation effort, which never ranks a ballot, so A survives.

decisions.title: What `*` means between two matrices
decisions.gist: Which multiplication the `*` key writes when two matrices sit beside it.
decisions.lesson: Jet has no matrix arithmetic today. Matrix work goes through functions such as `compute.matmul(a, b)`. Two multiplications exist in this field. One composes two matrices as transformations. The other multiplies matching cells. Every language must decide which one the `*` key writes, and how the other one is written. Two square matrices accept both meanings without complaint, so a wrong choice returns a wrong number instead of an error.
decisions.story: Priya ports a physics notebook from MATLAB. She writes `a * b` for two three-by-three rotations. The line is well shaped under either reading, so nothing warns her. Her simulation drifts for a week before she finds the cause.

options.name: `*` composes; a leading dot multiplies cells
options.detail: The spelling MATLAB and Julia use, and the one a textbook writes. `*` between two matrices is composition. A leading dot asks for cell-by-cell work: `.*`, `./`, `.^`. Ported formulas read the same in Jet as on the page. The cost is that `*` reads two ways, and two square matrices accept both.
options.technical: New infix tokens `.*`, `./`, `.^` with compound forms. `*` between `Matrix<M, K>` and `Matrix<K, N>` gives `Matrix<M, N>` on the D-TYPE2-MEASURE1 substrate; a mismatch names both inner sides. `^` on a square matrix is repeated composition. Amends D-LINALG1, which today defines `*` as element-wise plus matrix-times-vector and puts matrix-times-matrix on `.matmul()`.
options.code:
oriented :: pose * spin          // Matrix<3, 3>, composed
lit      :: gain .* spin         // Matrix<3, 3>, cell by cell
scaled   :: gain ./ spin
raised   :: gain .^ 2
squared  :: pose ^ 2             // pose * pose

wide :: Matrix<4, 2>.zeros()
bad  :: pose * wide
// Error: inner sides 3 and 4 do not match.

options.name: `*` always multiplies cells; composing is `.matmul`
options.detail: Every arithmetic operator means cell by cell on every math value, everywhere. Composition is the named method `.matmul(b)`. No symbol changes meaning and no new symbol is added. The cost is that the textbook formula becomes a chain of method calls.
options.technical: `*`, `/`, `^`, `/%` and `%` are cell-by-cell on equal shapes. `.matmul(b)` matches inner sides and composes outer sides. Matrix power is `.power(n)`. Amends D-LINALG1 by removing its matrix-times-vector reading of `*`, so the symbol never changes meaning by operand type.
options.code:
oriented :: pose.matmul(spin)    // Matrix<3, 3>
lit      :: gain * spin          // Matrix<3, 3>, cell by cell
scaled   :: gain / spin
raised   :: gain ^ 2             // every cell squared
squared  :: pose.power(2)

bad :: gain * Matrix<4, 2>.zeros()
// Error: cell-by-cell work needs equal shapes; 3 by 3 and 4 by 2 differ.

options.name: `*` multiplies cells; a new `@` composes
options.detail: Python added exactly this in 2014, after twenty years of one library shipping both readings of `*`. The two multiplications are visibly different in the source and neither changes meaning by operand type. The cost is one more symbol, and `@` is not a symbol mathematics uses.
options.technical: New infix token `@` at the same precedence as `*`, left grouping, with compound `@=`. `Matrix<M, K> @ Matrix<K, N>` gives `Matrix<M, N>`; `Matrix<M, N> @ Vec<N>` gives `Vec<M>`. All other operators stay cell-by-cell. Amends D-LINALG1's matrix-times-vector reading of `*`.
options.code:
oriented :: pose @ spin          // Matrix<3, 3>
lit      :: gain * spin          // Matrix<3, 3>, cell by cell
chained  :: pose @ spin * gain   // groups left to right: (pose @ spin) * gain
raised   :: gain ^ 2             // every cell squared

bad :: pose @ Matrix<4, 2>.zeros()
// Error: inner sides 3 and 4 do not match.

options.name: The type says which multiplication it is
options.detail: Two shape-typed values share one storage. `Matrix<M, N>` is a transformation and multiplies by composition. `Grid<M, N>` is a table of numbers and multiplies cell by cell. No symbol is overloaded and none is added: `*` asks the type, which is the rule the rest of the language already follows. Crossing between the two is one written word and copies nothing.
options.technical: `Matrix<M, N>` and `Grid<M, N>` are two readings of one `Tensor<T>` buffer (D-COMPUTE-TYPE1). `m.cells()` gives a `Grid` view, `g.as_map()` gives a `Matrix` view; both are views under D-SHAPE-PLACE1, not copies. `*` dispatches through the ordinary operator hook (D-OPDEF1) rather than a closed compiler table. `^` composes on `Matrix` and raises each cell on `Grid`. `/` between two `Matrix` values is refused, naming `.solve` and `.cells()`. Amends D-LINALG1's closed-family operator table.
options.code:
oriented :: pose * spin                       // Matrix values compose
lit      :: gain.cells() * spin.cells()       // Grid values multiply cells
back     :: lit.as_map()                      // read the result as a map again
raised   :: gain.cells() ^ 2                  // every cell squared
squared  :: pose ^ 2                          // pose * pose

bad :: pose / spin
// Error: two transformations do not divide.
// Use `.solve(...)` for a system, or `.cells()` to divide cell by cell.

options.name: A leading dot means element by element, for operators and for calls
options.detail: Julia's full rule. `*` composes, and a leading dot on any operator or any function call means it applies to every element. One idea covers `a .* b`, `a .+ 1`, and `sqrt.(a)`, so no function needs an element-by-element twin. The cost is that `*` still reads two ways for two square matrices.
options.technical: Extends option A: the dot prefix generalizes to call position, so `f.(x)` applies `f` to every element of `x` and composes with the existing operator dots. `*` behaves exactly as in option A.
options.code:
oriented :: pose * spin          // composed
lit      :: gain .* spin         // cell by cell
shifted  :: gain .+ 1.0          // add to every cell
roots    :: math.sqrt.(gain)     // one rule, applied to a call

bad :: gain .* Matrix<4, 2>.zeros()
// Error: element-by-element work needs equal shapes.

options.name: The type says which; the dot asks for cells where the plain operator would compose
options.detail:
Option D decides the meaning, and the leading dot from option A returns as the one way to override it. `Matrix` composes under `*`. `Grid` and lane vectors multiply cells under `*`, which is already law (D-VECARITH1). A leading dot is legal only on a `Matrix`, where it means cells: `pose .* spin`. Where `*` is already cell by cell the dot is refused, so no meaning has two spellings.

The textbook line types as written. A ported MATLAB line types as written. Two square matrices never accept both readings.
options.technical: Extends option D. New infix tokens `.*`, `./`, `.^`, `.+`, `.-` with compound forms, accepted ONLY where the left operand composes under the plain operator (today: `Matrix<M, N>`). On `Grid`, lane vectors, and scalars the dot form is a sema error naming the plain operator. Call-position dot (`f.(x)` from option E) is NOT adopted: call fan-out was retired by ratified D-VERDICT-1324-1, and `.[` already carries member spread under D-SPREAD1=A. `^` stays take in prefix position (D-MEM1=A) and power in infix position; `.^` must be lexed against that.

comparisons.note: `*` composes and a leading dot means cell by cell. The oldest form, and the one textbooks match.
comparisons.code:
C = A * B;
D = A .* B;

comparisons.note: Same as MATLAB, plus the general rule that a dot on any call applies it to every element.
comparisons.code:
C = A * B
D = A .* B
E = sqrt.(A)

comparisons.note: `*` is cell by cell and `@` composes. The `@` symbol was added to Python because an earlier matrix type gave `*` the other meaning, and both readings shipped side by side.
comparisons.code:
C = A @ B
D = A * B

comparisons.note: `*` is cell by cell and composition gets its own spelled symbol.
comparisons.code:
C <- A %*% B
D <- A * B

comparisons.note: The type carries the reading. A matrix composes; asking for its array view multiplies cell by cell, over the same storage.
comparisons.code:
C = A * B;
D = A.array() * B.array();

recommendation.why:
It keeps every gain of the current recommendation and pays back its one cost. The type still settles what `*` means, so the two-square-matrix trap cannot happen and no symbol reads two ways. The dot returns as a real override, so a person porting a formula writes the line they know on the value they hold, with no conversion step.

The dot is not a new idea here. `.[` already spreads a member across a list, and `.Variant` already reaches into a type. Distributing an operator across cells is the same idea, one level down.

whyNot.reason: Two square matrices accept both readings, so a person who meant cells gets a composed answer and no error.
The textbook formula becomes a method chain for the scientific audience the ratified `^` spelling was chosen to serve.
It adds a symbol mathematics does not use, and a reader arriving from MATLAB still types `*` and quietly gets cells.
Correct, but a porter must write `.cells()` at the crossing point, so a formula that reads the same in every other language does not read the same here.
Its call half reintroduces call fan-out, which ratified D-VERDICT-1324-1 removed, and `*` still reads two ways for two square matrices.

recommendation.tradeoff: Five new infix tokens, and a MATLAB porter who writes `.*` on a Grid gets an error instead of a result. That error is the teaching moment and needs registered what/why/fix text under I4. `.cells()` stays for a chain that is cellwise throughout; the dot is for one expression.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the textbook `*` against a cell-by-cell `*` with a named `matmul`, and recommended the textbook reading because the ratified `^` spelling already chose the mathematics-tool audience.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added Julia's general dot rule as option E and the type-carried reading as option D. It folded away a Unicode multiplication sign and a no-operators-at-all surface, since neither changed who decides the meaning of a line.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review found that option D already is the combination: it keeps the textbook line of option A and the one-meaning-per-symbol promise of option B. The recommendation moved from A to D.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with the point that a named multiply never guesses, and C with Python's history, where `@` was added because one library shipped both readings of `*` at once.
