reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked D for making data work wordy at every crossing. Reductions and cell helpers now sit on both types, so a crossing appears only where two values combine cell by cell, and the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: How a matrix is written down
decisions.gist: What separates one row of a matrix from the next in source code.
decisions.lesson: A matrix is a grid, and source code is lines of text. Jet builds every other typed value with `Type.{ ... }`, and rows must be told apart inside those braces. The spelling decides whether a small matrix reads like the grid it is. It also decides whether a matrix can sit on one line as a function argument. A vector is a plain comma list under every option.
decisions.story: Ravi writes a two-by-two rotation directly inside a call and wants it on one line. He also keeps an eight-by-two design matrix at the top of the same file. That one should look like the table the numbers came from.

options.name: A line break ends a row
options.detail: Rows sit under each other, so the source shows the grid. Nothing is counted by eye and no separator is learned. The cost is that a matrix cannot be written on one line, so a small rotation inside a call spans four lines.
options.technical: Inside `Matrix<M, N>.{ ... }` a newline ends a row and commas separate cells within a row. The declared shape checks the row count and each row width. `Vec<N>.{ ... }` stays a comma list.

options.name: A semicolon ends a row
options.detail: The MATLAB and Julia spelling. A matrix fits on one line anywhere an expression fits, and ported code carries over unchanged. The cost is a tall literal: it becomes one long line, or the reader counts semicolons to find the rows.
options.technical: Inside `Matrix<M, N>.{ ... }` a `;` ends a row. Jet already uses `;` as a within-header separator in a loop head, so the character is not new. A newline is ordinary whitespace here.

options.name: Each row is an ordinary list
options.detail: Nothing new is learned: a matrix is built from list values, the way NumPy builds one. The cost is two extra brackets on every row, and the value reads as a list of lists rather than as a grid.
options.technical: Inside `Matrix<M, N>.{ ... }` each element is a `[Float#N]` row and the element count is `M`. Both counts come from the declared shape.

options.name: No literal at all; build with named functions
options.detail: Matrices come from `Matrix.rows(...)`, `Matrix.columns(...)`, or a flat list plus a row count. No grammar is added and the building step names itself. The cost is that the most common small matrix stays a function call, so the grid never appears in the source.
options.technical: `Matrix.rows(a, b, c)` and `Matrix.columns(a, b)` take fixed lists and infer the shape from their measures. `Matrix.of(flat, rows: n)` checks that the length divides evenly.
options.code:
design :: Matrix.rows([1, 4], [1, 7], [1, 8])       // Matrix<3, 2>
flat   :: Matrix.of([1, 4, 1, 7, 1, 8], rows: 3)    // Matrix<3, 2>
apply(turn: Matrix.rows([0, -1], [1, 0]))

options.name: A row ends at the line end, or where a semicolon says so
options.detail: One idea with two ways to say it: a row ends where the line ends, or where a `;` ends it. A tall matrix is written as the grid, and a small one fits on one line inside a call. Nothing is counted by eye in either shape.
options.technical: Inside `Matrix<M, N>.{ ... }` both a newline and a `;` end a row, and a `;` at a line end is redundant rather than wrong. Commas separate cells within a row. The declared shape checks the row count and each row width, so a short row names the row index and both counts. `Vec<N>.{ ... }` stays a comma list.

comparisons.note: Semicolons end rows and spaces separate cells. The space rule is a known trap, because a leading minus reads as either a separator or a sign.
Semicolons end rows on one line, and a line break ends a row in the multi-line form. Both spellings are ordinary.
Rows are lists inside a list. No grammar is involved, and the brackets are the price.
A flat vector plus a row count, filled down the columns by default. The fill order surprises people.

recommendation.why: It writes both shapes people actually need. A design matrix read from a table looks like that table, and a two-by-two rotation fits inside the call that uses it. Neither form asks the reader to count separators, because the declared shape checks every row and reports the row that is short.

whyNot.reason: A two-by-two inside a call has to break over four lines, which pushes small matrices out of expressions.
A tall literal becomes one long line, or the reader counts semicolons to find where the rows are.
Every row carries two extra brackets, and the value reads as a list of lists instead of a grid.
The most common small matrix stays a function call, so the grid never appears in the source at all.

recommendation.tradeoff: A row ends in two ways, which is one more thing to read. It stays one rule stated twice: a row ends where the line ends, or where a semicolon says it ends.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the line-break grid against the MATLAB semicolon and the list-of-lists spelling, and recommended the line break because a design matrix should look like its source table.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added constructor-only building as option D and tested MATLAB's space-separated cells. Spaces were dropped, because a leading minus then reads as either a separator or a sign.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the line break with the semicolon into option E, which writes the tall grid and the one-line matrix with one rule. The recommendation moved to E.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: list rows add no grammar at all, and a ragged row is caught by the declared shape under every option, not only under C.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what a short row reports. Option E now states that the error names the row index and both counts, which is what makes the missing separator readable, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: When two different shapes may combine
decisions.gist: Whether a short side repeats itself to meet a bigger one, and when.
decisions.lesson: Subtracting a column mean from every row of a table is everyday work. The mean has one row; the table has eight. Letting the short side repeat is called broadcasting, and it saves a written loop. It is also the best known source of quiet wrong answers in array code, because a repeat that was never intended still produces a well-formed result. Jet knows every shape at compile time, so this choice decides how much of that convenience is worth keeping.
decisions.story: Sara centres eight brake readings by their column means. In an earlier Python project she wrote the mean the wrong way round, got an eight-by-eight answer instead of eight-by-two, and lost an afternoon to a chart that looked plausible.

options.name: A short side repeats itself, on the shapes as written
options.detail: The NumPy and Julia rule. Any axis of extent one repeats to meet the other side, and a plain vector takes whichever axis fits. Nothing is written and everything lines up. The cost is that a vector with no stated direction guesses, and a guess that goes the wrong way still produces a well-formed answer.
options.technical: Axes align from the last one. An axis of extent one repeats. A `Vec<N>` is treated as a row when the column count is `N`, and as a column when the row count is `N`. All of it resolves at compile time on the D-TYPE2-MEASURE1 substrate.
options.code:
mean :: x.mean(along: .Rows)     // Matrix<1, 2>
centred :: x - mean              // Matrix<8, 2>

gain :: Vec<8>.{ 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 }
y :: Matrix<8, 1>.zeros()
odd :: y - gain                  // Matrix<8, 8> — accepted, and rarely meant

options.name: Only a single number spreads; every other repeat is written
options.detail: A number combines with any shape. Anything else must have equal shapes, and a repeat is spelled out. Nothing ever expands behind your back. The cost lands on the most common line in this area: centring a table by its column means has to say the repeat out loud.
options.technical: Scalar with matrix is allowed. Two matrices must have equal shapes. `m.repeat_rows<N>()` and `m.repeat_columns<N>()` produce the expanded value, checked against the declared measures.
options.code:
mean :: x.mean(along: .Rows)                 // Matrix<1, 2>
centred :: x - mean.repeat_rows<8>()         // Matrix<8, 2>
halved  :: x / 2.0                           // a number still spreads

slip :: x - mean
// Error: 8 by 2 and 1 by 2 differ. Write `.repeat_rows<8>()` to repeat the row.

options.name: A vector repeats along the one axis it matches
options.detail: A number spreads everywhere. A vector whose length matches exactly one axis repeats along that axis. A vector whose length matches both axes is refused, and the message names the two ways to say which was meant. The cost is that two one-wide axes can still expand each other into a bigger result.
options.technical: `Vec<N>` with `Matrix<M, N>` repeats down the rows; `Vec<M>` with `Matrix<M, N>` repeats across the columns. When `M == N` the combination is refused and names `.as_row()` and `.as_column()`. Matrix-with-matrix follows the extent-one rule.

options.name: Nothing repeats; the operation names the axis
options.detail: Shapes must match exactly for every operator. When a shorter value is meant to apply along an axis, the operation says which axis by name. Every repeat is visible at the place it happens. The cost is that ordinary arithmetic turns into method calls, and the axis is already visible in the shapes.
options.technical: Operators require equal shapes, except with a single number. `x.minus(v, along: .Rows)` and `x.times_cells(v, along: .Columns)` carry the axis as a named argument and check the length against that axis.
options.code:
centred :: x.minus(mean, along: .Rows)
scaled  :: x.times_cells(gain, along: .Columns)
halved  :: x / 2.0

slip :: x - mean
// Error: 8 by 2 and 1 by 2 differ. Use `x.minus(mean, along: .Rows)`.

options.name: A one-wide axis repeats, and direction is always part of the type
options.detail: An axis of extent one repeats silently, so centring a table stays one clean line. Nothing is ever guessed, because every value states its direction in its own type: a bare vector says `.as_row()` or `.as_column()` before it meets a matrix. A combination that would repeat both sides into a bigger result is refused and names the spelling that means it.
options.technical: Matrix with matrix follows the extent-one rule on the D-TYPE2-MEASURE1 substrate. `Vec<N>` has no direction, so it never combines with a matrix directly; `.as_row()` gives `Matrix<1, N>` and `.as_column()` gives `Matrix<N, 1>`, both views. When both sides carry an extent-one axis on different sides, the combination is refused and names `.outer(...)`. Reductions such as `.mean(along: .Rows)` already return a directed result, so the common path needs no extra word.

comparisons.note: Axes align from the last one and a one-wide axis repeats. A vector has no direction, which is why the one-column and one-dimension mix-up is the most reported array bug.
comparisons.code:
x - x.mean(axis=0)          # fine
y - g                       # y is (8,1), g is (8,) -> (8,8), rarely meant

comparisons.note: Since R2016b the same repeat happens automatically, but every value is already a matrix with a direction, so the direction is never guessed.
A short vector is recycled down the columns whether or not the length divides evenly, with a warning at most. A long-standing complaint.
comparisons.code:
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3)
m - c(1, 2)     # recycles down the columns, warns

comparisons.note: Repeating happens only where a dot asks for it, so the expansion is visible in the source.

recommendation.why: It keeps the line people write every day, subtracting the column means from a table, and removes the step where a direction is guessed. Direction lives in the type, so a reader can see from the shapes which side repeated. The one silent expansion that grows both sides is refused and names the spelling that means it.

whyNot.reason: A vector with no stated direction guesses an axis, which is the step that turns an eight-by-two answer into an eight-by-eight one.
Centring a table by its column means, the most common line in this area, has to spell out the repeat every time.
It refuses only the case where one length matches both axes, and still lets two one-wide axes expand each other into a bigger result.
Naming the axis on every operation turns ordinary arithmetic into method calls, and the axis is already readable in the shapes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A hand-built `Vec<N>` must say `.as_row()` or `.as_column()` before it meets a matrix. Reductions already return a directed result, so that word appears only where a bare vector enters an expression.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the NumPy repeat rule against a numbers-only rule, and recommended the numbers-only rule because a wrong repeat still produces a well-formed answer.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the axis-as-argument option and the direction-in-the-type option. It tested a marked region where repeating is switched on, and folded it away because a marker moves the question rather than answering it.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined free repeating with typed direction into option E, which keeps the clean centring line and deletes the guessing step. The recommendation moved from B to E.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, since a written repeat is always readable, and strengthened C, since compile-time shapes already catch most mismatches without any rule at all.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review found that option E still let two one-wide axes expand each other into a bigger result. Option E now refuses that case and names the outer-product spelling, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: How you read one cell, one column, and one window
decisions.gist: The spelling that picks part of a matrix out of the whole.
decisions.lesson: Reading part of a matrix is constant work: one cell, a whole column, a block of rows. Jet already settled what a partial read gives you. A bare projection is a read window, `&` makes it writable, and `~` copies it. Today a matrix cell is read with a function call, and only the first axis can be windowed. This choice is the spelling inside the brackets, and whether a single index drops that axis while a range keeps it.
decisions.story: Tom pulls the second column out of a design matrix to plot it, then doubles that column in place to change its units. Today he writes `compute.get(t, [0, 1])` for one cell, and the language can only window the first axis for him.

options.name: One bracket, one slot per axis
options.detail: Rows and columns get a slot each inside a single bracket. A range in a slot picks a band, and `..` means the whole axis. A single index drops its axis, so one cell is a number. The cost is that the two most common reads, a whole row and a whole column, are written as punctuation.
options.technical: `m[i, j]` gives the cell type. `m[range, j]` and `m[i, range]` give `Vec<N>`; `m[range, range]` gives `Matrix<M, N>`. `..` in a slot means that whole axis. Every result is a place under D-SHAPE-PLACE1, so `&m[.., 1]` is the write window and `~m[.., 1]` copies. Ranges are ordinary values (D-RANGE-VALUE1).
options.code:
cell   :: m[0, 1]              // Float
column :: m[.., 1]             // Vec<8>
block  :: m[0..<4, 0..<2]      // Matrix<4, 2>
&m[.., 1] *= 2.0               // write window over that column

options.name: Chained brackets, a row at a time
options.detail: A matrix reads like a list of rows, so `m[0]` is a row and `m[0][1]` is a cell. Nothing new is learned beyond list indexing. The cost is that the two axes stop looking alike: a row is punctuation and a column needs a method.
options.technical: `m[i]` gives `Vec<N>` and `m[i][j]` gives the cell type. `m[range]` windows the first axis, matching today's `Tensor` behaviour. Columns are only reachable through `.col(j)`.
options.code:
cell   :: m[0][1]              // Float
row    :: m[0]                 // Vec<2>
column :: m.col(1)             // rows come first, so a column needs a method
block  :: m[0..<4]             // Matrix<4, 2>

options.name: Named methods only
options.detail: Every read says what it is in words: `m.at(i, j)`, `m.row(i)`, `m.col(j)`, `m.window(...)`. Nothing has to be decoded and the argument order is labeled. The cost is that a method call is not a place, so editing a column in place needs a second surface that the bracket form does not need.
options.technical: Reads are methods returning views. A method call is not part of a place under D-SHAPE-PLACE1. So `&m.col(1)` is not a write window. In-place edits use named mutating methods such as `m.scale_column(j, by: v)`.
options.code:
cell   :: m.at(0, 1)
column :: m.col(1)
block  :: m.window(rows: 0..<4, cols: 0..<2)
m.scale_column(1, by: 2.0)     // the in-place edit needs its own method

options.name: Labeled slots
options.detail: Each slot carries the axis it means: `m[row: 0, col: 1]`. The order can never be swapped by mistake, and a single-axis read needs no filler. Jet already writes labeled arguments this way. The cost is two labels on every read, and the labels stop helping past two axes, where they turn into invented names.
options.technical: `m[row: i, col: j]` and `m[col: j]` are index expressions with labeled slots, following the existing labeled-argument surface. Omitting a label means that whole axis. Results are places, so `&m[col: 1]` is a write window.
options.code:
cell   :: m[row: 0, col: 1]
column :: m[col: 1]
block  :: m[row: 0..<4, col: 0..<2]
&m[col: 1] *= 2.0

options.name: One bracket per axis, with named readers for the whole-axis case
options.detail: Brackets carry cells, bands and windows, and `.row(i)` and `.col(j)` are the readable names for a whole axis. A single index drops that axis and a range keeps it, so a one-row matrix and a plain row are both writable with no extra flag. Everyday reads are words and precise reads are brackets.
options.technical: `m[i, j]` gives the cell type; `m[i, ..]` and `m[.., j]` give `Vec<N>`; `m[0..<1, ..]` gives `Matrix<1, N>`. `..` means the whole axis. `.row(i)` is `m[i, ..]` and `.col(j)` is `m[.., j]`. All bracket results are places under D-SHAPE-PLACE1. So `&m[.., 1]` is the write window and `~m[.., 1]` copies. A method call is not a place, so an in-place edit is written on brackets. Ranges are ordinary values (D-RANGE-VALUE1).
options.code:
cell   :: m[0, 1]              // Float — a single index drops that axis
column :: m[.., 1]             // Vec<8>
kept   :: m[0..<1, ..]         // Matrix<1, 2> — a range keeps the axis
block  :: m[0..<4, 0..<2]      // Matrix<4, 2>
first  :: m.row(0)             // the readable name for m[0, ..]

&m[.., 1] *= 2.0               // write window: doubles the column in place
keepsafe :: ~m[0..<4, ..]      // an owned copy that outlives `m`

comparisons.note: One bracket with a slot per axis. A single index drops that axis and a slice keeps it, which is the rule most array users already carry.
comparisons.code:
cell = m[0, 1]
col  = m[:, 1]
kept = m[0:1, :]

comparisons.note: Parentheses with a slot per axis, and a colon for the whole axis. Indexes start at one.
One bracket per axis, but a single-column read silently becomes a plain vector unless a flag says otherwise. That flag is a long-standing complaint.
comparisons.code:
col  <- m[, 2]
kept <- m[, 2, drop = FALSE]

comparisons.note: One bracket per axis with a colon for the whole axis, and a view is asked for by name when no copy is wanted.

recommendation.why: The two reads people write most, a row and a column, become words instead of punctuation, and everything else stays one bracket with one slot per axis. Because a range keeps its axis, a one-row matrix and a plain row are both writable without the extra flag other languages carry. Bracket reads stay places, so the same line that reads a column can edit it.

whyNot.reason: Without the named readers, the two most common reads are written as punctuation and `m[.., 1]` has to be decoded.
A row is punctuation while a column is a method, so the two axes stop looking alike in the source.
A method call is not a place, so editing a column in place needs a second surface that brackets do not need.
Every read grows two labels, and the labels turn into invented names as soon as a value has more than two axes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A single index drops its axis, so `m[0, 1]` is a number while `m[0..<1, 0..<1]` is a one-by-one matrix. That difference is learned once, and it removes the flag other languages need for the same job.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one bracket with a slot per axis against chained brackets and named methods, and recommended the slot form because both axes then read alike.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added labeled slots, which Jet can already write, and checked whether an index needs a new value type. Ranges are already values under D-RANGE-VALUE1, so nothing new was needed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the bracket form with named row and column readers, and folded in the rule that a range keeps its axis while a single index drops it. The recommendation moved to that combination.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened D, since labeled slots read well for two axes and refuse a swapped argument order outright, and strengthened C for the same clarity in words.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the drop rule with the single-row case that other languages need a flag for. A one-wide range keeps the axis, so no flag is needed and the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: How you solve a system and fit a line
decisions.gist: The spelling that answers a system of equations and fits a line to measurements.
decisions.lesson: Fitting a line to measurements is the most common reason anyone reaches for a matrix. The algebra is one step: solve a system of equations. A square system has one exact answer. A tall system, which is what measured data gives, has no exact answer and takes the closest one instead. Those are two different questions with two different ways to fail, and this spelling decides whether a reader can tell which one ran.
decisions.story: Ana fits a line to eight brake tests. Her system is tall, so no exact answer exists and she wants the closest one. In R she writes `lm(dist ~ speed)` and is finished. In Jet today she writes a chain of fallible function calls.

options.name: A backslash solves
options.detail: The MATLAB and Julia spelling. `x \ y` answers exactly when the system is square and takes the closest answer when it is tall. Ported code carries over and the fit is one short line. The cost is a symbol nobody can guess, which also hides which of the two questions was answered.
options.technical: New infix `\` at division precedence. `Matrix<N, N> \ Matrix<N, K>` is the exact solve; `Matrix<M, N> \ Matrix<M, K>` with `M > N` is the closest answer. Both are fallible: a square system that cannot be solved and a tall system with dependent columns both report failure. A wide system is refused.
options.code:
exact :: a \ b ?? panic("singular")     // a is Matrix<2, 2>
fit   :: x \ y ?? panic("no fit")       // x is Matrix<8, 2>: the closest answer
print("intercept {fit[0, 0]}  slope {fit[1, 0]}")

options.name: Two named methods, one per question
options.detail: `x.solve(y)` answers a square system exactly. `x.least_squares(y)` takes the closest answer for a tall one. The call says which question was asked, so a reader never has to check a shape to know what came back. The cost is that people arriving from MATLAB will look for a backslash first.
options.technical: `.solve(y)` accepts `Matrix<N, N>` only; on a tall matrix it is a compile error naming `.least_squares`. `.least_squares(y)` accepts `Matrix<M, N>` with `M >= N`. Both are fallible and report a dependent-column failure rather than a quiet answer. `\` is registered as an unknown operator whose message names both methods. Expert routes reuse the same names on a stored factorization: `x.qr().least_squares(y)`.

options.name: One named method that reads the shape
options.detail: `x.solve(y)` answers exactly when the matrix is square and takes the closest answer when it is tall. One name to learn, and the shape picks the behaviour at compile time. The cost is that a reader of the call cannot tell which of the two questions was answered without going to find the shape.
options.technical: `.solve(y)` accepts `Matrix<M, N>` with `M >= N` and chooses the exact or closest route from the measures. Fallible in both routes. The compiler can report the chosen route on request, but the call site does not carry it.
options.code:
exact :: a.solve(b) ?? panic("singular")     // a is Matrix<2, 2>: exact
fit   :: x.solve(y) ?? panic("no fit")       // x is Matrix<8, 2>: closest
print("intercept {fit[0, 0]}  slope {fit[1, 0]}")

options.name: Free functions in the module
options.detail: `la.solve(x, y)` and `la.least_squares(x, y)` sit beside the other library entries, and the module name says where the work happens. The cost is that the surface stops reading like the rest of the matrix API, which is method-shaped, and a call breaks a chain in the middle of an expression.
options.technical: Module-level functions with the same shape rules and the same fallible results as option B.
options.code:
exact :: la.solve(a, b) ?? panic("singular")
fit   :: la.least_squares(x, y) ?? panic("no fit")
print("intercept {fit[0, 0]}  slope {fit[1, 0]}")

options.name: A fitting surface above the algebra
options.detail: `la.fit(speed, stop)` answers the question people actually have and hands back a value with a named intercept, slope and prediction. This is the level R users work at, and it is one line. The cost is that it answers only the straight-line case, and it puts model fitting inside the algebra surface.
options.technical: `la.fit(xs, ys)` returns a `Fit` value carrying `.intercept`, `.slope`, `.predict(x)` and `.residuals()`. The algebra stays available underneath through the option B method pair, which the fit calls.
options.code:
line :: la.fit(speed, stop) ?? panic("no fit")
print("intercept {line.intercept}  slope {line.slope}")
print("12 mph stops in {line.predict(12)} feet")

// The algebra is still reachable:
beta :: x.least_squares(y) ?? panic("no fit")

comparisons.note: One backslash covers both questions and picks by shape.
The same backslash, with a factorization available by name when the same system is solved many times.
comparisons.code:
beta = X \ dist
F = qr(X); beta = F \ dist

comparisons.note: Two separate named functions, one per question, in the linear algebra module.
`solve` does the algebra, but the everyday answer to this exact task is a model-fitting function, not matrix algebra at all.
comparisons.code:
beta <- solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% dist)
fit  <- lm(dist ~ speed)

recommendation.why: The two questions fail in different ways, so the call should say which one was asked. A reader of `x.least_squares(y)` knows a closest answer came back without going to look at a shape. A square system that cannot be solved reports failure instead of quietly returning an approximation, which is the mistake this area is known for.

whyNot.reason: A backslash is a symbol no new reader can guess, and it hides which of the two questions the shape decided to answer.
One name covers two questions, so the call site no longer says whether an exact answer or a closest one came back.
Free functions read against the rest of the matrix surface, which is method-shaped, and they break a chain mid-expression.
It answers only the straight-line case and moves model fitting into the algebra surface, while still hiding which algebra ran.

recommendation.tradeoff: People arriving from MATLAB and Julia will type a backslash and not find it. That character reports a message naming both methods, so the search ends on the first attempt.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the backslash against a pair of named methods, and recommended the pair because the two questions fail in different ways.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added free functions, a single shape-reading name, and a fitting surface above the algebra. It also tested a factorization-first surface and folded it into option B as the expert route for repeated solves.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested pairing the named methods with the fitting value. The fitting value stays its own option, because it answers only the straight-line case and would move model fitting into the algebra surface.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened A, because one symbol covers both questions the way two whole fields already write them. It strengthened E with Rs evidence that most people want the fit, not the algebra.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what a MATLAB reader does when the backslash is missing. That character now reports a message naming both methods, and `.solve` on a tall matrix names `.least_squares`, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Whether matrix types are always there or asked for
decisions.gist: Whether a program can write a matrix without importing anything first.
decisions.lesson: Every Jet program starts with the names the language always provides: numbers, text, lists, `print`. Everything else is asked for with `use`. Matrix work spans a wide range. A two-by-two rotation inside a game loop is arithmetic. A determinant, a decomposition and a fast Fourier transform are a library. This choice decides which of those a program gets without asking, and therefore how much every beginner sees in front of them forever.
decisions.story: Ben writes a twenty-line script to fit a line through eight readings. The first thing he has to work out is whether a matrix is already there, or which module holds it. Every extra step at that point is a step where he goes back to Python.

options.name: Everything is always there
options.detail: Types, literals, arithmetic, and the whole algebra library need no import. Nothing stands between a person and a matrix. The cost is that determinants, decompositions and transforms sit in front of every beginner, and most programs never touch one.
options.technical: `Matrix<M, N>`, `Vec<N>`, and the full `core.linalg` surface enter the always-available name set. Every name appears in completion and in the beginner listing.

options.name: Everything is asked for
options.detail: One import brings the whole surface, exactly like every other core module. The file states what it depends on, which a reader auditing a program can see at a glance. The cost lands on the smallest use: a matrix literal does not type-check until the import is written.
options.technical: `Matrix<M, N>` and `Vec<N>` resolve only through `use core.linalg`. An unimported use reports the ordinary unknown-type message naming the module.

options.name: The small fixed sizes stay; the general shapes are asked for
options.detail: Today's fixed graphics types stay always available, and the shape-typed general forms need the import. Game and graphics code changes nothing. The cost is two families of matrix type living side by side, when the small ones are already names for the general ones.
options.technical: `Vec2/3/4` and `Mat3/Mat4` stay in the always-available set as D-LINALG1 has them. `Matrix<M, N>` and `Vec<N>` resolve through `use core.linalg`.

options.name: Arithmetic is always there; the algebra is asked for
options.detail: Types, literals, indexing, transpose, `+ - *` and reductions need no import, the way `+` on numbers needs none. Solving, determinants, decompositions and transforms come with `use core.linalg`, the way `sqrt` comes with `core.math`. A rotation or a small sum never meets an import, and the always-available set grows by two names rather than by a library.
options.technical: Always available: `Matrix<M, N>`, `Vec<N>`, their literals, indexing and windows, transpose, `+`, `-`, `*`, `.mean()`, `.sum()`. Asked for with `use core.linalg`: solving, least squares, determinant, inverse, decompositions, eigenvalues, transforms. Shape-typed matrices are fixed size, so they sit in the heap-free `core` runtime layer (D-RINGLAYER1); the dynamic `Tensor` stays in the allocating layer.

options.name: `core.compute` owns them
options.detail: One import covers every array shape, from a two-by-two rotation to a device tensor, and `core.linalg` stops being a separate name. The cost is that a rotation then arrives with the device, placement and transfer surface attached, which a rotation has no reason to see.
options.technical: `Matrix<M, N>` and `Vec<N>` resolve through `use core.compute`, which already owns `Tensor<T>` under D-COMPUTE-TYPE1. `core.linalg` retires and its fixed types move across.

comparisons.note: Matrices are the base type of the language. Nothing is imported, ever, and that is the whole pitch.
Arrays and their arithmetic are always there; decompositions and solvers need one standard-library import.
Everything is asked for, including the array type itself. This is the single most repeated line in scientific Python.
comparisons.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])

comparisons.note: Matrices, arithmetic, determinants and solving are all in the base language with no import.

recommendation.why: It follows the split Jet already uses for numbers: arithmetic is always there, and `core.math` is asked for when `sqrt` is needed. A person writing a rotation or a small sum never meets an import, which is where scripting users are lost. The names in front of every beginner grow by two types instead of by a whole library.

whyNot.reason: Determinants, decompositions and transforms sit in front of every beginner, and most programs never use one.
A matrix literal does not type-check until an import is written, which is ceremony on the smallest possible use.
It keeps two families of matrix type, and the small fixed ones are already names for the general shape-typed ones.
It ties a two-by-two rotation to the device, placement and transfer surface, which a rotation has no reason to see.

recommendation.tradeoff: A line has to be drawn between arithmetic and algebra, and it has to hold as the library grows. The line is written out: types, literals, indexing, transpose, `+ - *` and reductions are always there, and everything else is asked for.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared putting the whole surface always in reach against putting all of it behind an import, and recommended the import to keep the beginner listing small.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the split home, the two-family option matching today's fixed graphics types, and folding the whole surface into `core.compute`.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the two, giving arithmetic to the always-available set and algebra to the import, which is how numbers and `core.math` already divide. The recommendation moved to that split.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: one import is one line, and it makes the dependency visible to a reader auditing what a program touches.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the split as a line that will drift as the library grows. Option D now writes the line out as a list, and the fixed-size types also fit the heap-free runtime layer, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Plain short names for the named Core containers
decisions.gist: What each named container type is called.
decisions.lesson: Core ships eight named containers beside the bracket forms for list and map. Several names are computer-science jargon. Deque, Bag, BitSet, and ByteBuffer do not tell a new reader what the type does. This choice picks the one canonical name for each container. The names appear in code, docs, errors, and search results every day.
decisions.story: Mia is new to programming. She needs a line of jobs where the first job in is the first job out. She scrolls the container list and stops at Deque. The name tells her nothing. She leaves the editor to search the web instead of writing the next line.
decisions.inWild:
// A build farm, written with the current names.
pending :: Deque.from(jobs)          // what is a Deque?
urgent  := PriorityQueue.from(jobs)
retries := Bag.from(failed_ids)      // a bag of what, kept how?
flags   := BitSet.from(ports)
wire    := ByteBuffer.from(packet)

options.name: Owner slate: Set, Rank, Queue, PriorityQueue, Tally, Cache, Bits, Bytes
options.detail: Rename the jargon rows to one short word each. Deque becomes Queue. SortedSet becomes Rank. Bag becomes Tally. BitSet becomes Bits. ByteBuffer becomes Bytes. Set, Cache, and PriorityQueue keep their names. Every name is one common word except PriorityQueue. Queue names the both-ends structure, so it also covers last-on-first-off use without a separate Stack type.
options.technical: Amends the D-COLLBREADTH1 and D-ITERTOOLS1 rosters. Type names only; no keyword or sigil change, so Syntax.rs is untouched. HashMap and BTreeMap stay reserved. One rename sweep across Prelude, sema, docs, examples, and snapshots.
options.code:
pending :: Queue.from(jobs)          // take front, add back
urgent  := PriorityQueue.from(jobs)  // most important first
scores  := Rank.from(results)        // unique, always in order
retries := Tally.from(failed_ids)    // counts repeats
flags   := Bits.from(ports)
wire    := Bytes.from(packet)

options.name: Keep the current names
options.detail: No change. Set, SortedSet, Deque, PriorityQueue, Bag, Cache, BitSet, ByteBuffer stay. Readers who know other languages find familiar words. Beginners keep hitting Deque, Bag, and ByteBuffer, which do not describe behavior in plain English.
options.code:
pending :: Deque.from(jobs)
urgent  := PriorityQueue.from(jobs)
scores  := SortedSet.from(results)
retries := Bag.from(failed_ids)
flags   := BitSet.from(ports)
wire    := ByteBuffer.from(packet)

options.name: Descriptive slate: Roster, Rail, Priority, plus Queue and Stack aliases
options.detail: SortedSet becomes Roster. Deque becomes Rail, with Queue and Stack as thin aliases that signal which ends you use. PriorityQueue becomes Priority. Tally, Bits, and Bytes as in option A. Beginners searching for a queue or a stack find those exact words. The cost is three names for one structure and one invented word, Rail.
options.technical: Queue and Stack are transparent aliases of Rail with the same methods. Alias rows join the D-COLLBREADTH1 roster.
options.code:
pending :: Queue.from(jobs)     // alias of Rail
undo    := Stack.from(edits)    // alias of Rail
urgent  := Priority.from(jobs)
scores  := Roster.from(results)

options.name: Industry slate: match Rust and Java spellings
options.detail: Rename toward the names experienced developers already know. HashSet, BTreeSet, VecDeque, BinaryHeap, Multiset, Cache, BitSet, ByteBuffer. Zero learning cost for people arriving from Rust or Java. Maximum jargon for beginners, and several names describe the implementation rather than the behavior.
options.code:
pending :: VecDeque.from(jobs)
urgent  := BinaryHeap.from(jobs)
scores  := BTreeSet.from(results)
retries := Multiset.from(failed_ids)

comparisons.note: Ships jargon and plain names side by side: deque and heapq are jargon, while Counter is exactly option A's Tally.
comparisons.code:
from collections import deque, Counter
retries = Counter(failed_ids)

comparisons.note: Names containers after their implementation: VecDeque, BinaryHeap, BTreeSet. Precise for experts, opaque for beginners.
Keeps the surface tiny: Array, Set, Dictionary in the standard library; Deque and Heap live in a separate package.

recommendation.why: Every renamed row becomes a word a beginner already knows: Queue, Rank, Tally, Bits, Bytes. Names that were already plain stay put, so the change is small and complete.

whyNot.reason: Keeps Deque, Bag, and ByteBuffer, the exact names that send new readers to a search engine instead of the next line of code.
Buys Stack discoverability at the price of three names for one structure and the invented word Rail, which explains nothing by itself.
Optimizes for people who already know another language and abandons the beginner facet that Jet leads with.

recommendation.tradeoff: Queue names a both-ends structure, so it also supports last-on-first-off use that a strict queue would not. PriorityQueue stays the one long compound name. Both accepted by the owner in chat on 2026-08-05.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the owner slate, the current names, and a descriptive slate, and recommended the owner slate for plain-word coverage.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested acronym names such as FIFO and FILO and an industry slate matching Rust and Java. FIFO cannot name the priority structure, so only the industry slate joined the menu as option D.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested Rail with Queue and Stack aliases on top of the owner slate. The owner rejected the extra aliases, so the hybrid stays recorded as option C rather than the recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each option: B gained its familiarity argument, C its search-discoverability argument, D its zero-relearning argument for experienced arrivals.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked Heap as a shorter PriorityQueue name, but its plain meaning is a disordered pile and it collides with memory vocabulary. The remaining Queue wrinkle is recorded in the tradeoff and survives.

decisions.title: How a file declares an app program
decisions.gist: How a source file tells the toolchain it is an app to serve, not a script to run once.
decisions.lesson: Today a web app is a function named `app` that returns `WebApp`. The toolchain sniffs for that name and splices in a hidden `run() { app().serve() }` entry. So the entry that actually runs is one you never wrote. Files can also hold `run`, `dev`, and `app` together, which forces a precedence table nobody should have to learn. This choice picks one visible rule for what an entry is.
decisions.story: Mia builds her first site and `jet run site.jet` serves it, which feels great. Later she adds a plain `fn run()` to print a debug line. Her server silently stops serving, because the hidden rule says her new function now outranks `app`. Nothing in her file explains what happened.

options.name: Named builder function (today)
options.detail: Keep `fn app() => WebApp` as a magic name. The toolchain detects it and synthesizes a hidden serving entry. You can also write `run` and `dev`, and a fixed precedence table decides which one wins. Gain: shipping code keeps working unchanged. Loss: three competing entry names, an invisible synthesized entry, and the silent-outranking trap in the story.
options.technical: Detection is name plus return type. A file with `app` and no `run` gets `fn run() { app().serve() }` appended before load. `run` beats `app`, and `dev` beats both under `jet dev`.

options.name: The entry returns the program
options.detail: One entry, `run`. Its return type says what the program is. No return means a script that executes and exits. Returning `App` means the value describes an application, and the runtime serves it. `jet dev` serves the same value with watch, reload, and hot swap added. An expert can still write `fn dev()` to replace the dev default entirely. Gain: one visible rule, no hidden entry, no precedence table. Loss: existing `fn app()` files migrate.
options.technical: The runtime interprets the entry's returned value. Tooling such as `jet explain --web-graph` statically evaluates the returned builder chain, and reports a diagnostic when the chain is not statically known. `fn <command>()` remains the ratified override hook for a command's default metaprogram, today only `dev`.

options.name: Marker on the entry
options.detail: Keep one entry name but mark it: `#App fn run()`. The marker, not the type, declares the program kind. Gain: the declaration is loud and searchable. Loss: the marker duplicates what the return type already proves, so the two can disagree, and every new program kind needs a new marker ratified.
options.technical: Sema must reconcile marker and return type and diagnose mismatch. The marker namespace grows one entry per program kind.

options.name: No magic: call serve yourself
options.detail: No detection at all. A server is a script that happens to call `.serve()` at the end. Gain: nothing is hidden, and the beginner rule is just "programs run top to bottom". Loss: the app description never escapes the entry, so `jet dev` cannot re-serve the same value in watch mode, and `jet explain` cannot read the graph without guessing where the chain is. Every command that wants the graph re-sniffs the body.
options.technical: Static graph extraction must pattern-match a call chain inside an executed body, which breaks as soon as the chain is built through a variable or helper.

comparisons.note: The entry is a value of type Program. The runtime interprets it, and the same value drives dev tooling like the time-traveling debugger.
comparisons.code:
main : Program () Model Msg
main = Browser.sandbox { init = init, update = update, view = view }

comparisons.note: An app is a value conforming to App. The framework runs it, and previews reinterpret the same value without a second entry point.
Routes and pages are exported descriptions. `next dev` and `next build` reinterpret the same exports rather than asking for a second program.

recommendation.why: The signature the user writes is the whole rule. The return type separates a script from an app, and the same value feeds run, dev, build, and explain. New program kinds arrive as new types, which the language already knows how to extend.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a hidden synthesized entry, a name sniff, and a precedence table, and the story's silent-outranking trap stays in the product.
The marker restates what the return type already proves, which creates a disagreement case to diagnose and a marker to ratify per program kind.
Serving inside the body hides the app from every tool. Dev mode, graph explain, and deploy all need the description without executing it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The returned builder chain must be statically known for tooling to read the graph. A chain built through arbitrary runtime control flow gets a diagnostic asking for a static description.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared today's named builder with a value-returning entry and recommended the value form, because one visible signature replaces a hidden entry and a precedence table.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the marker form and the fully explicit serve-yourself form. A manifest-declared entry kind was folded into the marker option, since both restate what the type proves.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested marker plus value together and rejected it as two spellings of one fact. It kept one hybrid piece: the expert `fn dev()` override survives inside the recommended option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the explicit form with a documented chain-extraction convention and strengthened today's form by documenting its precedence. Both still hide the program from at least one tool.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked static extraction with chains built via helpers and conditionals. The repair is a named diagnostic that asks for a statically known chain, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: One App type or one type per target
decisions.gist: Whether Jet has one App type for every target, or a separate type per platform.
decisions.lesson: The app builder currently returns `WebApp`, a type whose name bakes in where the program runs. Native UI, and any future platform, would each need a sibling type. Where a program runs is already stated elsewhere, by the `#Target` marker or the package manifest's `target:` field. This choice decides whether the platform lives in the type name or stays where it is.
decisions.story: Ravi ships a web dashboard as a `WebApp`. His team then wants the same product as a native desktop app. The program is the same routes, views, and actions, but the type name says web, so the retarget starts with a rename and a fork.

options.name: One type per target (today's path)
options.detail: Keep `WebApp` and add siblings like `NativeApp` as platforms arrive. Gain: each type lists only what its platform supports, so misuse fails at the name. Loss: one product forks per venue, shared code needs a common wrapper, and every new platform mints a new type with its own builder surface.
options.technical: Each target type carries its own builder methods and its own runtime interpretation. Cross-target code must be generic over an app trait or duplicated.

options.name: One App, target set by marker or manifest
options.detail: One `App` type describes any application. The platform comes from the existing `#Target` marker or the manifest's `target:` field, never from the type. Using a capability the chosen target cannot honor is a compile-time diagnostic that names the target. Gain: one program retargets by changing one setting, and beginners learn one type. Loss: some misuse surfaces at target check rather than at the type name.
options.technical: Sema checks the app value's capabilities against the resolved target and reports a registered diagnostic on mismatch, for example `.csr()` under a native target. `WebApp` is deleted, and in-repo examples migrate in the same change.

options.name: Target as a type parameter
options.detail: One generic type, `App(Web)` or `App(Native)`, so the platform is visible in the signature but the type is shared. Gain: misuse still fails at the type, and shared code can be generic. Loss: the platform now threads through every signature that touches an app, and the same fact is stated twice once a `#Target` marker or manifest is present.
options.technical: Capability methods constrain the parameter, so `.csr()` exists only on `App(Web)`. Sema must still reconcile the parameter with `#Target` and the manifest, and diagnose disagreement.

comparisons.note: One app type runs on mobile, web, and desktop. The target is a build setting, not a type, and unsupported plugins fail per target at build time.
comparisons.code:
void main() => runApp(const MyApp());
// flutter build web | apk | macos — same MyApp

comparisons.note: One Application class, targets picked in the project file. Platform-only APIs are guarded per target rather than by separate app types.

recommendation.why: The platform is deployment information, and Jet already has a ratified home for it in `#Target` and the manifest. One App keeps one program retargetable by one setting, which is the one-mechanism rule applied to applications.

whyNot.reason: It forks the product per venue and mints a new type and builder surface for every future platform.
It states the target twice once a marker or manifest exists, and threads deployment info through every signature that touches an app.

recommendation.tradeoff: A target-only capability is caught by the target check instead of by the type name. The diagnostic must therefore name the capability, the target, and the fix plainly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared per-target types with one marker-driven App and recommended one App, because the platform already lives in `#Target` and the manifest.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the generic `App(Target)` form and considered a structural capability-set type. The structural form was folded into the generic option, since both move deployment into signatures.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested one App with an optional visible parameter for experts. It was rejected as two spellings of one fact, which invites disagreement between parameter, marker, and manifest.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened per-target types with a shared app trait, and the generic form with parameter inference. Both still fork or thread the platform through code that never cares about it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked one App with capability misuse caught late and with mixed-target workspaces. Registered per-target diagnostics and the manifest's per-member target answer both, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: One word for named auxiliary entries
decisions.gist: Pick one word for named auxiliary entry functions across the marker and the CLI.
decisions.lesson: A named auxiliary entry is a function you can invoke by name, like a database migration. Today the marker says `#Job fn`, but the CLI says `jet run --task` and `jet tasks`. Two words for one thing means every user learns the pair and every doc explains it. This choice picks the single word.
decisions.story: Priya writes `#Job fn migrate()` and then types `jet run --job migrate`, which fails. The flag is `--task`, and nothing connects the two words. She files it as a bug, but it is a naming split we shipped.

options.name: Unify on job
options.detail: The marker stays `#Job fn`, and the CLI becomes `jet run --job <name>` and `jet jobs`. Gain: the word you write is the word you type, and it does not collide with anything else in the language. Loss: the two CLI spellings change, and shipped docs and muscle memory migrate once.
options.technical: Rename `--task`/`--task=` to `--job`/`--job=` and `jet tasks` to `jet jobs`. Migrate help text, examples, snapshots, and docs in one change, with no alias left behind.

options.name: Unify on task
options.detail: The CLI stays, and the marker becomes `#Task fn`. Gain: the smaller diff, since only the marker changes. Loss: `Task` is already Jet's concurrency type, so `#Task fn` reads as an async declaration and the collision follows the word into docs, search, and teaching forever.
options.technical: Rename the `#Job` marker to `#Task` and migrate examples and snapshots. The concurrency `Task` type keeps the same spelling in the same files.

options.name: A fresh third word
options.detail: Retire both words for something unclaimed, for example `#Op fn` with `jet run --op` and `jet ops`. Gain: no collision with anything, ever. Loss: both surfaces migrate, and the new word teaches nothing that `job` does not already teach.
options.technical: Rename marker and CLI together and migrate all consumers. The word must be registered in Syntax.rs with this decision id.

comparisons.note: A Job is a run-to-completion unit of work, distinct from long-running services. The word carries exactly this meaning to a large audience already.
Cargo shipped `cargo check` and kept every verb aligned with its docs. Verb-flag drift is treated as a bug, not a style choice.

recommendation.why: Job matches the marker already in the language, reads as a schedulable unit of work, and collides with nothing. The word you write becomes the word you type everywhere.

whyNot.reason: Task is the concurrency type, so the same word would name two unrelated mechanisms in the same file.
A fresh word migrates both surfaces and buys nothing that job does not already deliver.

recommendation.tradeoff: The CLI flag and the list command change spelling once, and anything that memorized `--task` or `jet tasks` must relearn one word.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared unifying on job against unifying on task and recommended job, because task collides with the concurrency type.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the fresh-word option and considered keeping both words with aliases. Aliases were dropped as a standing greenfield violation rather than an option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested job in the CLI with task kept as a doc synonym. It was rejected, since a sanctioned synonym recreates the split this ballot exists to close.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened task with its smaller diff and prior CLI familiarity, and the fresh word with a collision-free future. Both still lose on the type collision or on teaching cost.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked job with the scheduling connotation of cron jobs. That connotation matches these entries, which can be scheduled or invoked by name, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Whether jet env lists integration checks as jobs
decisions.gist: Whether the env check list is renamed to jobs, and whether it stays merged.
decisions.lesson: A project declares its own jobs. The environment model also declares checks, such as an Android SDK check or a vault check. `jet env` prints both in one list under the heading `tasks`. The word `task` is being retired from this surface in favour of `job`, so this list needs a decision: what heading it uses, and whether the two kinds stay merged.
decisions.story: Rae runs `jet env` to see why a build will not start. The list shows a vault check beside two of Rae's own jobs, all under one heading. Rae fixes the vault check, reruns, and cannot tell which entries were the project's and which came from the environment model.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet env
tasks:
  android-sdk-check   ok
  vault-check         failed
  build-assets        ok
  publish-docs        ok

// build-assets and publish-docs are the project's own #Job entries.
// android-sdk-check and vault-check come from the environment model.

options.name: Rename the heading to jobs and keep one list
options.detail: The heading becomes `jobs` and both kinds stay together. Gain: one word across the whole surface, and one place to look. Loss: a reader still cannot tell a project job from an environment check.
options.technical: Rename the machine key and the human heading from `tasks` to `jobs` in the env report. Merged ordering is unchanged.
options.code:
$ jet env
jobs:
  android-sdk-check   ok
  vault-check         failed
  build-assets        ok

options.name: Rename the heading and split the two kinds
options.detail: The heading becomes `jobs` for the project's own entries, and environment checks get their own heading. Gain: a reader sees which entries they wrote and which the environment supplies. Loss: two headings to read, and any script reading the machine key must handle both.
options.technical: Rename the project key to `jobs` and emit environment checks under a separate `checks` key. Both keys appear in the machine output, so a consumer reads the one it means.
options.code:
$ jet env
checks:
  android-sdk-check   ok
  vault-check         failed
jobs:
  build-assets        ok

options.name: Keep the heading tasks
options.detail: Nothing changes here. The word `job` applies to what a program declares, and this list keeps its own name. Gain: no script that reads the machine key breaks. Loss: one surface keeps the retired word, so a reader meets both words.
options.technical: No change. The env report is documented as using its own vocabulary, separate from the #Job surface.
options.code:
$ jet env
tasks:
  vault-check         failed
  build-assets        ok

comparisons.note: npm keeps one word for the things a project declares and reports tool checks separately, so a reader is never asked to tell them apart in one list.
comparisons.code:
$ npm run
Scripts available:
  build
  test

comparisons.note: Nix flakes name each output kind separately, so a reader sees which part of the system produced an entry.

recommendation.why: It fixes both problems at once. The word matches the rest of the surface, and a reader can tell an entry they wrote from an entry the environment supplied, which is the confusion the story describes.

whyNot.reason: It fixes the word but keeps two different kinds of thing under one heading, so the reader still cannot tell which entries are theirs.
It leaves the retired word on a surface a user reads, which is the thing the retirement set out to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Splitting the list means a script that reads one key now reads two. That is acceptable because the machine output names both keys explicitly, so a consumer states which kind it wants instead of guessing from a merged list.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared renaming the heading against splitting the list, and recommended doing both because the merged list is the reason the report is hard to read.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added keeping the heading unchanged, and tested a single list with a per-entry source column. The column was folded into the split, which states the source once per group instead of once per row.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept the split and asked whether the two groups should share one exit status. They already do, so no change was needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the merged option by sorting the project entries first. A reader still has to know the names to tell the groups apart.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what a script does when an environment check is added upstream. Under the split it reads the key it means and is unaffected, so the split remains the recommendation.

decisions.title: Jobs as program subcommands, with a typed scope
decisions.gist: Whether jobs become subcommands of the program itself, and which audience a bare `#Job` gets by default.
decisions.lesson: A job is a named auxiliary entry, like a database migration. Under this design the job dispatcher is program semantics, not a build artifact. The same argv contract holds on every tier, so `jet run app.jet -- migrate` on plain source and `./myapp migrate` on the built binary hit identical routing. That retires the separate `--job` flag. The marker's argument is a real enum, `.Ship`, `.Dev`, or `.Internal`, so the audience is typed and extendable. The open choice is the default for a bare `#Job`.
decisions.story: Sam deploys a compiled app, and release night needs the migration job. Meanwhile a teammate left `#Job fn wipe_test_data()` in the same package. Whether that second job silently ships as `./myapp wipe_test_data` is exactly the default this ballot picks.

options.name: Bare word table, everything ships
options.detail: Every `#Job` becomes a subcommand on every tier, and hiding one uses an untyped marker word like `#Job(hidden)`. Gain: maximum magic, what works in dev works in production with zero extra marks. Loss: the word table is a closed compiler list rather than a type, and the teammate's wipe job ships unless someone remembers a word for it.
options.technical: Marker arguments are bare identifiers validated against a compiler table. New audiences mean compiler changes, and tooling cannot complete or type-check them.

options.name: Typed scope enum, ship by default
options.detail: The audience is the enum, and a bare `#Job` means `.Ship`. Gain: the beginner's first job survives deploy with no extra marks, and the enum gives experts typed control. Loss: the default answers the story badly, since the wipe job ships unless its author remembered `.Dev`.
options.technical: The scope is a Prelude-owned enum. Dispatch and `--help` derive from it identically on every tier under the parity rule.
options.code:
#Job fn migrate() { ... }             // = #Job(.Ship), ships
#Job(.Dev) fn wipe_test_data() { ... } // author must remember this
#Job(.Internal) fn tick() { ... }      // never a subcommand

options.name: Typed scope enum, dev by default
options.detail: A bare `#Job` means `.Dev`, a subcommand everywhere the toolchain runs the program, but stripped from release builds. Shipping is the explicit act, `#Job(.Ship)`. The release build prints what it stripped and names the fix. Gain: full magic while developing, and a production binary whose surface is deliberate. Loss: the release-night migration needs `.Ship` on it, one mark, taught by the build output.
options.technical: Dev tiers, `jet run`, `jet dev`, and debug builds, dispatch every job. Release builds dispatch `.Ship` jobs only and list stripped jobs in the build summary. `.Internal` jobs are callable from code and the scheduler, never from argv. The enum is Prelude-owned, so all tiers share one meaning.

options.name: Typed enum, no default
options.detail: A bare `#Job` is a diagnostic, and every job states its scope. Gain: no default to argue about, and every audience is visible at the declaration. Loss: the very first job a beginner writes fails to compile until they learn an enum, which is ceremony the magic facet exists to avoid.
options.technical: Sema rejects a scope-less `#Job` with a fix-it listing the three variants.
options.code:
#Job fn migrate() { ... }
// error: `#Job` needs a scope — .Ship, .Dev, or .Internal

comparisons.note: Management commands ship with the deployed app and run in production, which teams rely on for migrations. Nothing separates dev-only commands, so they ship too.
comparisons.code:
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py wipe_test_data   # also there, forever

comparisons.note: Scripts run from source with no build, and the runner strips nothing, so dev scripts ride into every environment that has the manifest.
comparisons.code:
npm run migrate
npm run seed:demo

comparisons.note: Feature flags gate code out of release binaries explicitly, and cargo reports what a build included. Deliberate release surface is the norm.

recommendation.why: While you develop, every job just works from plain source with no build and no flags. What ships is exactly what was marked to ship, the build says what it stripped, and the enum keeps the whole surface typed and extendable.

whyNot.reason: An untyped word table is a closed compiler list, and its ship-everything default sends the wipe job to production.
The typed enum is right, but ship-by-default still answers the story with an exposed wipe job.
Requiring a scope on the first job a beginner ever writes is ceremony before the first success.

recommendation.tradeoff: A production-needed job carries one explicit `.Ship` mark. The release build's stripped-jobs summary teaches that mark at exactly the moment it matters.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft exposed every job with an untyped hide word. Owner review reshaped it, a typed scope enum, tier-uniform argv dispatch, and a safe release default became the frame.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass compared ship-by-default, dev-by-default, and no-default over the enum, and kept the word-table form as the baseline. A per-package manifest allowlist was folded into dev-by-default, since the `.Ship` mark is that allowlist at the declaration.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combined the enum with tier-uniform dispatch and the stripped-jobs build summary, which became the recommended option. It also merged the old dev-time flag path into program argv, retiring the second invocation spelling.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened ship-by-default with the zero-marks deploy story and no-default with total explicitness. One still ships the wipe job, and the other taxes the first job ever written.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked dev-by-default with the forgotten `.Ship` on release night and with job names colliding with run flags. The build summary names the stripped job and its fix, and the dispatcher reserves job names before flag parsing, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.comment: Enum must cover all cases

decisions.title: How CLI arguments reach an app entry
decisions.gist: How command-line arguments flow into the parameters of an entry that returns an App.
decisions.lesson: Script entries already turn their parameters into typed command-line flags, so `fn run(count: Int)` accepts `--count=3` with type checking. An app entry returns a program value instead of running to completion, which raises the question of whether the same parameter magic applies. This choice decides how a served app receives arguments, and what happens when an argument does not fit.
decisions.story: Leah serves her app locally and wants it on another port. She expects `jet run site.jet -- --port=9000` to just work, the way flags already work on her scripts. If apps need a different ceremony for the same idea, that is the day the language stops feeling coherent to her.

options.name: Parameters are flags, one rule for every entry
options.detail: The script rule applies unchanged: app entry parameters become typed flags, values flow in before the value is built, and defaults keep the zero-argument path working. An incompatible argument is a launch-time diagnostic naming the flag, the expected type, and the fix. Experts customize names, validation, and help text with the ratified CLI field markers. Gain: one rule, no new ceremony. Loss: the signature becomes the binary's public flag surface.
options.technical: Argument mapping runs before the entry is called, identically for Unit and App entries. The extraction of the static app graph is unaffected, since parameters only feed builder arguments. Field markers from the ratified CLI field-marker decision provide renames, validation, and docs.

options.name: The builder reads arguments explicitly
options.detail: App entries take no parameters, and the value asks for arguments itself, for example `.port(args.get("port"))`. Gain: the app value owns its whole configuration in one visible chain. Loss: apps and scripts follow different rules for the same idea, argument reads scatter through the chain untyped until checked by hand, and the beginner's expectation from the story breaks.
options.technical: An `args` accessor is exposed to the builder chain. Type checking happens per read site, and there is no derived `--help` surface unless each read also declares metadata.

options.name: Apps take no CLI arguments
options.detail: Served programs configure through the manifest and environment variables only, never argv. Gain: deployment config lives in declarative files, which some platforms prefer. Loss: the quick local override in the story requires editing a file or exporting a variable, and scripts and apps split into two rules.
options.technical: App entries must have an empty parameter list, enforced by a diagnostic. Config values arrive through the manifest's settings or the environment API.

comparisons.note: The dev server accepts direct flags for the quick path and a config file for the durable one. Users reach for the flag first.
Server config arrives as typed CLI flags on the runner, and the app object stays free of argv handling.

recommendation.why: It is the rule users already learned on scripts, applied without exception. Compatible arguments flow in with types checked, incompatible ones fail with a named fix, and the expert path is the already-ratified field markers rather than new machinery.

whyNot.reason: It splits apps from scripts, moves type checking to each read site, and loses the derived help surface.
It removes the quick local override entirely and forces file edits or environment exports for a one-off port change.

recommendation.tradeoff: The entry signature is the binary's public flag surface, so renaming a parameter renames a flag. The field markers give experts stable names when the signature needs to move.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared extending the script flag rule against builder-owned reads and recommended the shared rule, because one mechanism should serve both entry kinds.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the no-argv option and considered a dedicated config-struct parameter. The struct form was folded into option A, since a struct parameter already works under the field markers.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested auto-mapped parameters plus a builder-side args accessor together. It was rejected, because two ways to read the same flag invite drift between them.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened builder reads with a typed accessor sketch and the no-argv form with twelve-factor deployment practice. Both still break the expectation the script rule already set.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked flag-surface stability across refactors and collisions with job subcommand names. Field-marker renames and reserved-word checks in the dispatcher repair both, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Which commands an entry function can override
decisions.gist: Whether test and bench, like dev, can be customized by writing a function named after the command.
decisions.lesson: Each toolchain command runs a default metaprogram over your code. For `jet dev` that default is watch and hot swap, and a user-written `fn dev()` already replaces it. Test and bench have no such hook, so custom setup like starting a database before a suite means wrapper scripts outside the language. This choice decides how far the override rule extends, and what an override receives.
decisions.story: Noor's integration tests need a database container running first. Today she wraps `jet test` in a shell script that every teammate and CI job must find and remember. The setup she wants is ten lines of Jet, with nowhere to put them.

options.name: Dev only (today)
options.detail: Keep the override hook for dev and nothing else. Gain: test and bench runs are always the stock harness, so a green run means the same thing everywhere. Loss: real setup and teardown needs live outside the language in wrapper scripts, and dev stays an unexplained special case.
options.technical: No new detection. The dev override remains the single command hook.
options.code:
fn dev() { devserver.start(port: 4000) }   // works today
fn test(suite: TestSuite) { ... }          // never called, silently dead

options.name: Every command overridable, bare replacement
options.detail: Writing `fn test()` or `fn bench()` replaces that command's default entirely, the way `fn dev()` does. Gain: one uniform rule with full control. Loss: the override starts from nothing, so reaching the actual discovered tests means reimplementing discovery, and most overrides would rebuild the harness badly.
options.technical: Detection matches the dev rule, name only. The override body receives nothing and must locate and execute blocks through library calls if it wants them.

options.name: Every command overridable, suite handed in
options.detail: Same uniform rule, but the override may declare a parameter and receive the command's discovered work as a value, a `TestSuite` or `BenchSuite`. Discovery, filtering, and reporting stay the compiler's job, and the override orchestrates around them. A no-parameter override still fully replaces the default. Gain: setup, teardown, custom order, and custom reporting become ordinary Jet code. Loss: a bad override can skip work and print green.
options.technical: The suite value carries the discovered blocks after `--filter` is applied, with `run()`, iteration, and result access. `jet test --default` and `jet bench --default` ignore overrides, and verification contexts use that flag so an override can never mint CI green. Suite types are Prelude-owned under the I9 parity rule.

options.name: Hooks instead of overrides
options.detail: Keep the stock harness in charge and expose fixed extension points, like `#TestSetup fn` and `#TestTeardown fn`. Gain: the harness can never be skipped, so green stays trustworthy without a flag. Loss: every new customization needs a new ratified hook, and reordering or custom reporting never fits a fixed hook list.
options.technical: Each hook is a new marker with its own detection and ordering rules. The hook set grows per use case and per command.

comparisons.note: A crate can replace the default test harness per target, and most never do. The escape hatch existing does not corrupt ordinary runs.
conftest.py customizes collection, fixtures, and reporting in the language itself, which is a large reason teams standardize on it.
TestMain receives the run as a value and wraps it with setup and teardown. Discovery stays the toolchain's job.

recommendation.why: It makes the override rule one sentence covering every command, and hands the override the discovered suite so orchestration is ordinary code. Discovery stays the compiler's job, and the default flag keeps verification honest.

whyNot.reason: It leaves real setup needs in wrapper scripts and keeps dev as an unexplained exception to its own rule.
A bare override cannot reach the discovered blocks, so any useful customization starts by reimplementing discovery.
Fixed hooks grow a marker per use case and still cannot express reordering or custom reporting.

recommendation.tradeoff: An override can skip the suite and print green. The `--default` flag exists for verification contexts, and a run under an override says so in its output.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared dev-only against a uniform override rule and recommended uniformity with a suite parameter, because setup needs are real and discovery should not be reimplemented.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added bare replacement and fixed hooks. A manifest-declared harness path was folded into bare replacement, since both swap the whole runner without reaching the discovered blocks.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced the recommended option itself, combining uniform overrides with the suite value from the Go TestMain shape. Bare and hooked forms stayed as separate options.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened hooks with a minimal two-hook set and dev-only with its trustworthy-green property. Both still fail custom ordering and reporting, which the story generation needs.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked false green from overrides that skip the suite. The `--default` flag, an override notice in output, and verification contexts pinning `--default` repair it, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Bench runner parity with the test runner
decisions.gist: Whether `jet bench` gains the same targets and selection that `jet test` already has.
decisions.lesson: `jet test` accepts a file, a directory, or a project, walks directories recursively, and selects by name with `--filter`. `jet bench` accepts exactly one file, cannot walk a module, and cannot run a single region. The two markers were ratified as siblings, but their runners drifted apart. This choice decides whether and how the runner surfaces stay parallel.
decisions.story: Owen keeps a bench block beside each hot function across a dozen files. Before merging an optimization he wants one number per region, but `jet bench` takes one file at a time. He writes a shell loop, loses the summary, and stops running benches at all.

options.name: Status quo, one file at a time
options.detail: Keep bench as a single-file command. Gain: nothing moves. Loss: module-wide numbers need shell loops, one region cannot be run alone, and the sibling markers keep strangers for runners, which is drift and not a decision anyone made.
options.technical: No change. The asymmetry stays undocumented behavior.
options.code: for f in src/*.jet; do jet bench "$f"; done   # Owen's shell loop

options.name: Parity where meaning carries over
options.detail: Bench accepts the same targets as test, a file, a directory walked recursively, or a project, and gains `--filter` for region names.
