Assertion-specific flags stay test-only, since coverage and snapshots have no bench meaning, and benches always run one at a time for timing integrity. A standing rule keeps future runner surface changes applied to both commands or explicitly carved out. Gain: the sibling promise becomes real and stays real. Loss: none beyond the migration itself.
options.technical: Bench reuses the test runner's target resolution and recursive walk. `--filter` matches region names after discovery. `--shuffle`, `--coverage`, and `--update-snapshots` remain test-only. Multi-file output is one line per region plus a per-file heading, and `--json` emits one record per region.
options.code:
jet bench src/                       // every region under src/, serial
jet bench src/ --filter="fib"        // just the fib regions
jet bench .                          // whole project, one summary

options.name: One command for both
options.detail: Fold bench into test, for example `jet test --bench`, so one runner owns both modes. Gain: a single surface can never drift. Loss: the command stops matching the marker you wrote, and timing runs inherit test defaults like parallelism that corrupt measurements. It also reverses the direction to keep the two parallel.
options.technical: One discovery pass tags blocks by kind, and a mode flag selects which kind executes. Timing integrity needs mode-conditional defaults inside one runner.
options.code:
jet test src/ --bench --filter="fib"   // benches via the test command
jet test src/                           // tests only — flag decides meaning

comparisons.note: `cargo test` and `cargo bench` share the same target and filter grammar, so knowledge transfers between them with one word changed.
comparisons.code:
cargo test parser::
cargo bench parser::

comparisons.note: One command runs both, with `-bench` selecting regions by regex. It works, but timing runs inherit test flags and the pairing confuses newcomers.

recommendation.why: The markers were ratified as siblings, so the runners should keep the same promise. Parity restores directory and project targets plus name selection, keeps timing-hostile test flags out, and pins the pair against future drift.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a shell loop where a command should be, and leaves the sibling promise broken by accident.
It reverses the direction to keep the two parallel, and timing runs inherit test defaults that corrupt measurements.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two commands must now evolve together, so every future runner change pays a small check against the parity rule or names an explicit carve-out.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the status quo with target-and-filter parity and recommended parity, because the single-file limit is drift rather than a ratified design.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added folding bench into test and considered a shared lower-level runner command. The shared runner was folded into the merge option, since both trade the marker-matching command away.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested parity plus a merged discovery pass internally. It kept shared target resolution as an implementation note and rejected surfacing one command, which is the merge option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the status quo with scripting composability and the merge with a never-drifts guarantee. Neither survives the story or keeps timing defaults clean.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked parity with long project-wide bench runs and filter-name collisions across files. Serial execution with per-file headings and path-qualified names in output repair both, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Arrow loop bodies in statement position
decisions.gist: Whether a loop can take a `->` body as a statement, the way if arms already do.
decisions.lesson: The arrow already gives lightweight bodies in two places. An if arm runs `-> expression` with or without braces, and a finite loop yields values with `loop x, xs -> expression`. But the loop form is legal only where the values are collected. A loop that just does something still requires braces, even for one call. This choice decides whether the arrow body also works as a plain statement, and on which loop headers.
decisions.story: Dana writes `if hit -> score += 1` all day, so she types `loop pair, joined -> print(pair)` and gets an error. The braces she must add hold one statement. The language taught her a rule and then applied it to only half the constructs.

options.name: Status quo, braces for statement bodies
options.detail: Arrow loops stay expression-only. Gain: the arrow on a loop always means values are being collected, one signal with one meaning. Loss: the one-statement loop keeps ceremony the if arm does not, and the story's inconsistency stays in the product.
options.technical: No change. Statement-position arrow loops keep their current diagnostic.
options.code:
loop pair, joined { print(pair) }        // required
loop pair, joined -> print(pair)         // error, today and after

options.name: Statement arrows on finite-source loops only
options.detail: The arrow body becomes legal as a statement, but only on the loop headers that can already yield, finite sources. Gain: the statement form and the value form stay one grammar rule. Loss: condition-only and infinite loops still demand braces, so Dana's rule breaks again one construct later, on `loop running -> tick()`.
options.technical: Statement position discards the body value. A non-unit body in statement position gets a lint naming the `::` collection form. Condition-only and bare infinite headers keep their brace requirement.
options.code:
loop pair, joined -> print(pair)     // ok
loop n < 10 -> n += 1                // still an error
loop running -> tick()               // still an error

options.name: Statement arrows on every loop header
options.detail: In statement position, every loop header takes an arrow body, finite, condition-only, or bare infinite. Value position stays exactly as ratified, finite sources with non-unit yields. Gain: one sentence covers the arrow everywhere, a lightweight body for any control-flow construct. Loss: the same spelling collects in value position and discards as a statement, which one docs paragraph must teach.
options.technical:
The grammar allows `-> statement` after any loop header in statement position, with the body value discarded. A non-unit body in statement position gets a lint naming the `::` collection form and the `&` write form. The write form binds each element through the memory model's write handle, `loop v, &values`, so in-place change is a visible header fact. The infinite-yield bar stays for value position, since an infinite collection cannot terminate.

The body rule is line-based per D-BODY-ARROW1. A loop whose whole form fits one line uses `->`. A longer body uses a brace block opening on the next line, one statement per line. The formatter picks by width and round-trips both forms, with a stability test.

options.name: A second separator for statement bodies
options.detail: Keep the arrow for yields and add a different spelling for one-statement bodies, for example `loop pair, joined: print(pair)`. Gain: collecting and discarding never share a spelling. Loss: a new sigil to ratify and teach, two lightweight-body forms in one language, and the if arm already discards with the arrow, so the separation is not even consistent.
options.technical: A new separator token enters the grammar, Syntax.rs, the formatter, and the teaching surface, duplicating the arrow's role.
options.code:
loop pair, joined: print(pair)       // new spelling
doubled :: loop v, values -> v * 2   // arrow kept for yields
if hit -> score += 1                 // but if still discards with ->

comparisons.note: Match arms take one expression or a block after the arrow, in statement or value position alike, and the value is simply discarded when unused.
The one-line body after a colon works on every compound statement, if, for, and while, so the rule transfers between constructs.
comparisons.code:
for pair in joined: print(pair)
while running: tick()

recommendation.why: It finishes the rule the if arm already teaches, a `->` body is the lightweight form of any control-flow body. Statement position discards, value position collects, and the ratified value-form restrictions stay untouched.

whyNot.reason: It keeps brace ceremony on one-statement loops and leaves the arrow rule applying to only half the constructs.
It moves the inconsistency one construct over, since condition-only and infinite loops still refuse the body form the user just learned.
A second separator duplicates the arrow's job and still disagrees with the if arm, which discards with the arrow today.

recommendation.tradeoff: One spelling collects in value position and discards in statement position. The discard lint on non-unit statement bodies keeps the accidental case loud, and one docs paragraph teaches the split.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the status quo with statement arrows on all headers and recommended all headers, because the if arm already set the discard rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the finite-only middle ground and a second-separator spelling. An expression-statement rule making bare arrow loops expressions everywhere was folded into option C, since discard-in-statement-position is that rule.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested finite-only statement arrows plus a separator for the infinite headers. It was rejected as two body spellings split by header kind, which is harder to teach than either pure option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the status quo as a one-signal reading of the arrow and the separator option with never-ambiguous collection. Both still contradict the if arm the user learned first.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the collect-versus-discard split and nested arrow chains like a loop feeding an if. The non-unit discard lint answers the split, nesting already parses in value position today, and the formatter stability test guards round-trips, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.comment: Same rule as the more general arrow syntax for non pattern matching/if statements. For inline/fitting/single item statements/expressions, use arrow. For multiline, auto convert to {…} block

decisions.title: One line-based body rule for every head
decisions.gist: Whether every body is `-> body` when it fits one line and a brace block past that, with `=` retired from bodies.
decisions.lesson: A body follows a head, a function signature, an if condition, a loop header, or a dispatch arm. Today three spellings split that job. Functions use `= expression`, effect guards use a bare statement with no arrow, and arms use `->`. This choice tests one line-based rule instead. A body that fits on one line is `-> body`. A longer body is a brace block that opens on the next line. The formatter picks by width, so the writer never chooses. Values route to any consumer and drop otherwise, on every form alike.
decisions.story: Ana writes `if err -> return err` on day one and loves it. Then she writes a one-line function and must switch to `=`, and a one-line guard where the arrow is suddenly illegal. Three spellings, one idea. She asks which one the language actually believes in.

options.name: Keep the three spellings (today)
options.detail: Functions keep `=`, effect guards stay arrowless, arms keep `->`. Gain: each spelling carries a nuance, the equation reading on functions and the bare guard's brevity. Loss: the beginner learns three body forms for one idea, and the formatter cannot collapse or widen a body without changing which spelling it uses.
options.technical: No change to D-ARROW-CONTROL1, D-IFGUARD1, or the function grammar.

options.name: One line-based rule, arrow or block
options.detail: Every head takes `-> body` when the whole form fits one line, and a brace block otherwise, with the body starting on the next line. Functions join the rule, effect guards gain the arrow, and `=` retires from bodies to mean values only. The writer never chooses, since the formatter widens or collapses by line width. Gain: one sentence teaches every body in the language. Loss: the equation reading of `= expression` disappears.
options.technical:
Amends D-ARROW-CONTROL1, D-IFGUARD1, and the D-IF3 effect form. Inside arm tables `->` stays before a block, since it also separates head from body. Self-delimiting heads take the bare block. Marker-scoped regions such as `#Unsafe("reason") { … }`, `#Test("name") { … }`, and `#Bench("name") { … }` always keep braces, even for one statement. Their braces state the extent of a fact, the audited region, the registered test, the timed region, and are not bodies, so the arrow never applies to them.

Blocks hold one statement per line under S6, and a block's final expression is its value. A dropped non-unit arrow value in statement position gets a lint naming `::` collection and the `&` write form. The formatter emits the arrow form for one-line bodies, widens past width to a block, and round-trips both, with a stability test.

options.name: Blocks only for functions, arrows only for control flow
options.detail: Functions always take a brace block, and the arrow stays a control-flow mark. Gain: the arrow keeps one narrow meaning, and function bodies have exactly one shape. Loss: the most common function, one expression, pays braces and an extra line, and the guard split with `if` remains untouched.
options.technical: The `=` form is deleted and one-line function bodies are written as blocks. Control flow keeps today's arrow rules unchanged.

comparisons.note: Arrow functions use one rule, an expression body or a brace body, and it transfers to every arrow a user ever writes.
comparisons.code:
const area = (w, h) => w * h
const log = (m) => { console.log(m) }

comparisons.note: The equation form is today's Jet function spelling. Kotlin accepts carrying it as a permanent second body form beside braces.
comparisons.code: fun area(w: Int, h: Int): Int = w * h

comparisons.note: Match arms keep the fat arrow before both expressions and blocks, which is the same head separator rule this ballot keeps inside arm tables.

recommendation.why: One structural sentence covers every body, the arrow for one line, braces past it, chosen by the formatter and never by the writer. Each symbol keeps one role, `=>` for callables, `->` for bodies, `=` for values.

whyNot.reason: Three spellings for one idea tax the beginner and block the formatter from resizing a body without respelling it.
It taxes the most common function shape with braces and an extra line, and leaves the guard split in place.

recommendation.tradeoff: The equation reading of `= expression` is given up, and `=> Int -> body` places two arrows adjacent. Each arrow keeps one fixed role, which is what keeps the adjacency readable.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft extended the arrow to function bodies for uniformity and recommended it over the equation form and braces-only functions.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested unifying on `=` instead, which dies on `if c = a` colliding with assignment, and a marker-based body form, which restates what the grammar already shows. Both folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried value-marking arrows and owner review killed them for forcing a value-versus-action choice on every body. The line-based rule replaced them, with the arrow kept inside arm tables as the head separator.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the equation form with its math reading and Kotlin precedent, and braces-only with its narrow-arrow economy. One keeps three spellings for one idea, the other taxes every one-liner.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked the arrow adjacency in `=> Int -> body`, S6 legality of collapsed blocks, silent value drops, and one-line `#Unsafe` regions losing their audit weight. Fixed symbol roles, the width-based formatter, the discard lint, and the marker-region carve-out that keeps scope braces mandatory repair all four, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: One-line function bodies: two ratified rulings disagree
decisions.gist: Which mark attaches a one-line function body: the arrow or the double colon.
decisions.lesson: Two ratified decisions give the same surface two different answers. D-BODY-ARROW1=B says every head takes `-> body` on one line, and functions join that rule. D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A says a one-line function body binds with `::`. Neither is built yet, and neither appears in the syntax record. Two cards wait to build opposite spellings. A third card teaches the formatter to emit `= expr`, which both rulings retire. One ruling must win before any of them starts.
decisions.story: Mia writes her second Jet file. She types a one-line function and the formatter rewrites it. Later she reads a one-line `if` and sees a different mark for what looks like the same act. She asks which mark means body. Today Jet has two ratified answers for her, so nobody can teach her one.

options.name: The arrow takes every body
options.detail: One sentence teaches every body in the language. A head takes `-> body` when the whole form fits one line, and a brace block otherwise. Functions, guards, loops and arms all read the same. The cost is two arrows in one function line: `=> Float` names the result and `->` opens the body. The reader must hold two arrow meanings on the same line.
options.technical: Honors D-BODY-ARROW1=B as ratified and drops D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A. `=` retires from bodies and keeps its slot-fill jobs: reassignment, parameter defaults, field defaults, enum discriminants, index write. Card #1454 builds it. Cards #1812 and #1512 retarget.

options.name: The double colon defines, the arrow maps
options.detail: Two words with two jobs, and each says what it does. `::` gives a name a meaning, so a function body binds like every other definition. `->` sends a head to a body, so guards, loops and arms keep the arrow. A function line then carries one arrow, not two. The cost is that the body rule needs two sentences instead of one.
options.technical: Honors D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A for function bodies and keeps D-BODY-ARROW1=B for control heads, with a named scope boundary between them. Both ratified texts survive under that boundary. `=` still retires from bodies. Matches D-ALIAS-OP1=B, which already binds an alias with `::`. Card #1812 builds the function half; card #1454 builds the head half.

options.name: The double colon takes every body
options.detail: Every one-line body binds with `::`, heads included. One mark, one sentence, and it is the mark a beginner already met on day one. The cost is heavy. A guard reads `if ready :: run()`, which says a name is being defined when none is. Arm tables lose the arrow that separates head from body.
options.technical: Overturns D-BODY-ARROW1=B in full and extends D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A past its stated scope. It also reopens D-ARROW-CONTROL1=A, which gave `->` the selected-value and yielded-value job. Arm tables would need a separate rule, because `->` there separates head from body inside a block.

options.name: The equals sign keeps function bodies
options.detail: Nothing changes. A one-line function body stays `= expr`, which is what ships today and what most languages with this form use. The formatter work on card #1512 lands as written. The cost is that `=` then means both define and fill, and Jet already chose `::` for every other definition, including aliases.
options.technical: Overturns both D-BODY-ARROW1=B and D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A. It also breaks the rule D-ALIAS-OP1=B set on 2026-08-06, where a new name arrives through `::` and `=` only updates what exists. Card #1454 and card #1812 both close as rejected.

comparisons.note: Expression-bodied members use an arrow. The result type sits before it, so one line carries one arrow.
comparisons.code: public double Area(double r) => 3.14 * r * r;

comparisons.note: Same arrow form. The return type is a bare word, not an arrow, so the two never collide.
Uses the equals sign for a one-line body, and keeps braces for longer ones.
comparisons.code: fun area(r: Double): Double = 3.14 * r * r

comparisons.note: Added an endless method in 3.0 with the equals sign, after twenty-five years of braces only.
A one-line body is a keyword, not a sign. It reads as prose and never collides with a type arrow.

recommendation.why: Each mark says one thing. `::` gives a name a meaning, in a binding, an alias, and now a function body. `->` sends a head to a body, in a guard, a loop, and an arm. A function line keeps one arrow, so `=> Float` still reads as the result and nothing competes with it. This is also the newer ruling, and it is the one that examined function bodies directly.

whyNot.reason: It puts two arrows on one function line. `fn area(r: Float) => Float -> 3.14 * r * r` asks the reader to hold two arrow meanings three words apart.
It reads `if ready :: run()` as a definition when nothing is being defined, and it takes the arrow out of arm tables, where the arrow separates head from body.
It keeps `=` meaning both define and fill. Jet already ruled the other way for aliases on 2026-08-06, so this answer splits one rule across two surfaces.

recommendation.tradeoff: The body rule takes two sentences, not one. That is acceptable because the two sentences name two different acts, and each mark then means exactly one thing everywhere it appears.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft set the two ratified rulings side by side and recommended the double colon for function bodies, because it matches the alias rule ratified one day earlier.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the current equals form and a colon-everywhere form, so the menu covers all four end states a card on the board could build. It also gathered five peer languages; none uses a double colon, and the arrow languages all keep a bare return type, which Jet does not.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review found that the two rulings need not fight, because a named scope boundary keeps both ratified texts alive. That boundary became the recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave the arrow its real prize, one sentence for every body, and gave the equals sign its peer evidence from Kotlin and Ruby. Neither answer survived the two-arrow line or the alias rule.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the boundary as arbitrary, and it held, because the split is by act and not by construct. It also tested the return type against the body mark and found no parse ambiguity.

decisions.title: Markers must live in the registry — no drift, no exceptions
decisions.outcome: D-MARK-REG1 — mandatory registration: a marker exists if and only if it is a registry row. No marker may be parsed, checked, formatted, highlighted, or reflected outside Policy::APPLIED_RULES; every active row must be fully implemented end to end or retired. Drift in either direction is a defect enforced by CI guards (name-literal scan, per-row end-to-end coverage, generated editor grammars). Owner words (2026-08-05): 'We must make all markers REQUIRED to be registered in the registry, no exceptions for drift, no tolerance. Not acceptable to have marker drift from registry.'
decisions.comment: D-MARK-REG1 — mandatory registration: a marker exists if and only if it is a registry row. No marker may be parsed, checked, formatted, highlighted, or reflected outside Policy::APPLIED_RULES; every active row must be fully implemented end to end or retired. Drift in either direction is a defect enforced by CI guards (name-literal scan, per-row end-to-end coverage, generated editor grammars). Owner words (2026-08-05): 'We must make all markers REQUIRED to be registered in the registry, no exceptions for drift, no tolerance. Not acceptable to have marker drift from registry.'

decisions.title: Impure joins the reason law
decisions.gist: Whether an Impure block must say why.
decisions.lesson: Three block markers unlock checked power: Unsafe, Nondeterministic, and Impure. The first two demand a written reason. Impure's reason is optional today, which contradicts the block-plane ruling that names it beside the other two. This ballot settles Impure's obligation.
decisions.story: An auditor sweeps a service for authority blocks before a release. Every Unsafe block explains itself in one line. A bare Impure block says nothing, so the auditor must reconstruct intent from diff history.

options.name: Reason required
options.detail: Every Impure block carries a written reason, exactly like Unsafe and Nondeterministic. A bare block becomes an error whose fix asks for the reason. All three authority gates then read identically.
options.technical: The registry signature becomes reason: String with no default. Existing bare blocks migrate with a one-line reason added.

options.name: Reason stays optional
options.detail: The signature keeps its optional reason. The spec records Impure as a lighter gate than the other two, and audit sweeps accept bare blocks.

options.name: No reason parameter at all
options.detail: Impure becomes a plain switch with no reason slot. Writers who want to explain themselves use an ordinary comment; the gate stops pretending to collect audit text.

comparisons.note: The undocumented_unsafe_blocks lint makes every unsafe block carry a SAFETY comment. Teams enable it because bare unsafe rots.
comparisons.code:
// SAFETY: the pointer is live for this call
unsafe { ptr.read() }

recommendation.why: One law for all three authority gates is easier to teach and to audit, and it matches the block-plane ruling already on the books.

whyNot.reason: A lighter gate splits the authority story into two rules and leaves audit sweeps blind on one of three gates.
Removing the slot forbids even willing writers from explaining themselves where the gate is, and comments are invisible to tooling.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing bare Impure blocks need a one-line reason added during migration.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared requiring the reason with keeping it optional and recommended requiring it, for one authority law.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested reason-required-under-policy-only and a lint-level nudge. Both re-create the split rule this ballot exists to close, so option C was added instead as the honest opposite.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried optional-with-audit-flag, where bare blocks pass but audits list them. That is B with extra machinery, so it was folded into B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C: comments are cheaper and the block already draws the eye. It still loses tooling visibility.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with reason fatigue producing copy-paste reasons. The same risk already exists for Unsafe and has not materialized in the examples, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.comment: Let’s make them optional BUT ones that are not provided should be easily auditable with tool chain and can be considered warnings or errors with build settings or ci/cd pipelines

decisions.title: How a SQL block names its row type
decisions.gist: The lawful spelling for the row type on an inline SQL block.
decisions.lesson: An inline SQL block can name the row type it produces. Today that is written with angle brackets, the only marker in the language that takes them. The registry row declares no parameters, so the spelling is typeable but never ratified. This ballot picks the lawful spelling.
decisions.story: Ana writes a dashboard query and wants each row typed. She copies the angle-bracket spelling from the one existing example, and nothing in the spec says whether that spelling is law.

options.name: Ordinary call argument
options.detail: The row type rides the one marker call grammar: SQL takes the type name as its argument. The angle spelling retires with a teaching fix. No new grammar anywhere.
options.technical: Registry signature: SQL(row: Type = none). Type-valued marker arguments follow the ratified argument-type ruling; the compiler checks the query's columns against the named type.

options.name: Ratify angle brackets
options.detail: Markers gain a type-parameter feature and the angle spelling becomes law. SQL reads like a generic call from host languages, and the signature schema grows to carry it.

options.name: No argument; the binding's declared type decides
options.detail: The block takes no type at all. The row type flows from the declared binding type. An unannotated binding in expression position is an error that asks for one.

comparisons.note: The row type is a generic argument on the query call.
comparisons.code: let rows = sqlx::query_as::<_, Row>("SELECT id, name FROM users");

comparisons.note: The row type is the ordinary generic argument of Query.
comparisons.code: var rows = conn.Query<Row>("SELECT id, name FROM users");

recommendation.why: The one call grammar already carries every other marker argument, and a type name is an ordinary argument under the ratified argument-type ruling. It works in every position with no new grammar.

whyNot.reason: A type-parameter feature for exactly one marker is a second grammar bought for one registry row.
Context typing fails in positions without a declared type, so a beginner hits an error the explicit argument never causes.

recommendation.tradeoff: SQL blocks read slightly less like generic calls from host languages that use angle brackets.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the call-argument spelling with ratifying angle brackets and recommended the call argument for grammar economy.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a named argument, a scope member inside the block, and full inference. The first two are spellings of A and were folded in; inference became option C.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried the call argument with inference as a fallback when the argument is omitted. Two ways to say one thing violates the one-mechanism rule, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with its host-language familiarity and C with its zero-ceremony reading on annotated bindings.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with type-versus-value ambiguity in the argument slot. The argument-type ruling already gives type names a lawful value form there, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: One placement law for markers; the five forms retire
decisions.gist: One rule for where a marker sits.
decisions.lesson: The compiler's marker table gives every marker one of five written forms: Bare, Call, BareOrCall, Block, and Prefix. The audit found the five forms describe one shape. A marker sits right before the code it rules. This ballot decides whether the spec keeps five categories or one law. No current spelling changes under any option.
decisions.story: Sam adds a new marker row to the compiler. Under five forms, Sam must first pick a category, and that pick quietly invents grammar. Under one law, Sam declares a name, a signature, and legal targets. The written shape then follows on its own.

options.name: One placement law
options.detail: A marker, or one bracket group, sits right before its target. Parentheses appear exactly when arguments are written. Empty parentheses are an error the formatter fixes. The form column leaves the registry. Every current spelling stays legal.
options.technical: The registry row schema becomes: name, signature, legal targets, repeatable, status, inheritance. Formatter layout rule: own line above types, functions, and methods; inline before fields, parameters, bindings, statements, and blocks. S82 is rewritten to the one law.

options.name: Keep the five forms
options.detail: The spec keeps Bare, Call, BareOrCall, Block, and Prefix as documented law. Every new marker picks one category. Nothing changes today, and the category stays a coarse reading aid in the registry.

options.name: Two grammars: attached and scoped
options.detail: Attached markers get the one placement law. Scoped block markers keep a separate grammar section because a brace body follows them. Two rules replace five.

comparisons.note: One attribute grammar covers every attribute. Placement legality is per-attribute data, never a grammar class.
Attributes declare their legal targets in data (AttributeUsage), not through written-form categories.

recommendation.why: One sentence teaches the whole plane, and every future marker is a data row instead of a grammar decision. The audit showed the categories already collapsed: Known is filed Prefix while Track is filed Bare for the same written shape.

whyNot.reason: Five categories describe one shape, so each category names a difference that does not exist, and the table already holds contradictory filings.
A scoped rule differs only in what its target is, not in where the marker sits. A second grammar section rebuilds the split this rebuild removes.

recommendation.tradeoff: The registry loses a coarse hint about how each marker is usually written. The signature and legal-target columns carry that information with more precision.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one placement law against the current five forms and recommended the law because every form reduces to marker-before-target.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested postfix pragmas, always-bracketed lists, and keyword-per-marker designs, all rejected as respellings that break ratified stacking or casing law. Option C was added as the strongest genuine split.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried the one law plus a dedicated scoped-block appendix. That is option A with clearer spec prose, so it was folded into A's technical detail.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: the form column does feed tooling menus today. A keeps that value because completion menus read the legal-target column instead.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with empty-parentheses ambiguity and same-line declaration markers. Both resolved as formatter rules, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Repeating one marker on one target
decisions.gist: What happens when the same marker is written twice on one target.
decisions.lesson: Today the same marker can be attached twice to one declaration, and the compiler accepts it silently. Some markers repeat with real meaning: a function can state several Pre contracts. This ballot decides the default rule and how meaningful repeats are declared.
decisions.story: Riley merges two branches. Both branches added Inline to the same function, so the merged file carries it twice. Nothing warns, and the duplicate ships as noise the next reader must puzzle over.
decisions.inWild:
#[Inline, Inline]              // merge artifact — accepted silently today
fn price(cents: Int) => Int = cents * 3

#[Pre(n > 0, "n must be positive"), Pre(n < 100, "n must stay small")]
fn take(n: Int) => Int = n     // two contracts — repetition with meaning

options.name: Error by default; the registry marks repeatable rows
options.detail: Writing one marker twice on one target is an error with a remove-the-repeat fix. Rows where repetition carries meaning are marked repeatable in the registry: Pre, Post, and allow.
options.technical: The check joins the E0999 family and runs in the shared validation pipeline, so it covers every site. The repeatable column is ordinary registry data under D-MARK-REG1.
options.code:
#[Pre(n > 0, "n must be positive"), Pre(n < 100, "n must stay small")]
fn take(n: Int) => Int = n      // legal: Pre is repeatable

#[Inline, Inline]
fn price(cents: Int) => Int = cents * 3
// error: `#Inline` is already applied to this function — remove the repeat

options.name: Keep silent acceptance
options.detail: The duplicate stays legal and the last copy wins. No new error, no new registry column. A lint could flag it later without a ballot.
options.code:
#[Inline, Inline]     // compiles clean; the second copy wins
fn price(cents: Int) => Int = cents * 3

options.name: Error for every marker; no repeatable rows
options.detail: All repeats are errors with no exception column. Several contracts combine into one condition with and, carrying one combined message.
options.code:
#Pre(n > 0 and n < 100, "n must be between 1 and 99")
fn take(n: Int) => Int = n   // one contract, one blunt message

comparisons.note: Repeating is an explicit opt-in on the annotation declaration; unmarked annotations cannot repeat.
AllowMultiple is false by default on every attribute; repeats are opt-in per attribute.

recommendation.why: A silent duplicate is nearly always a typo or a merge artifact, and the registry already owns per-row facts. Meaningful repetition stays first-class for contracts.

whyNot.reason: Silence hides mistakes today and lets two copies quietly disagree later when one of them gains arguments.
Merging contracts into one condition produces one blunt failure message where separate contracts each explain their own violation.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more registry column, and every future row must state whether it repeats.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared erroring with today's silent acceptance and recommended the error because duplicates are almost always accidents.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a warning-only rule and a formatter-dedupe rule, folding both into B since neither stops the copies from diverging. Option C was added as the strict alternative.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried error-by-default with a formatter auto-remove fix. That is option A's fix-it text, so it was folded into A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a future lint and strengthened C with its one-law simplicity and zero new columns.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with repeated Doc lines and several allow lints on one declaration. Marking allow repeatable resolves it, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Two mechanisms share the name HTML
decisions.gist: Separate names for the page-pairing marker and the inline HTML block.
decisions.lesson: A file-level marker pairs a Jet web file with its host page. A block marker embeds inline HTML. Both are spelled HTML today, and the block form has no registry row. One name for two mechanisms breaks the one-name-one-meaning rule the marker renames established.
decisions.story: Kim reads a teammate's web module. The top of the file says HTML with a path, and the middle of a function says HTML with a brace body. Kim assumes they are one feature and hunts for a connection that does not exist.

options.name: Block keeps HTML; the pairing marker gets its own name
options.detail: Inline HTML keeps the name that says what the block contains. The file-pairing marker takes a name that says what it does. Candidate names, owner picks one at ratification: Page, Hosts, Mount, Serves.
options.technical: Both mechanisms get registered rows with full signatures. The old file-level HTML spelling retires with a teaching fix to the chosen name.

options.name: Register both under one name
options.detail: Two rows share the name HTML with site-dependent signatures. On a file it means pairing; on a block it means inline HTML. Nothing renames, and readers carry the double meaning.

options.name: Retire the pairing marker
options.detail: Page pairing moves to the package manifest. Source files stop naming their host page, and HTML means only the inline block.

comparisons.note: The file format owns the pairing, and the embedded template block has its own name. Two jobs, two names.

recommendation.why: Each name then says exactly one true thing: the block contains HTML, and the file marker names the page it serves. The rename is one teaching fix.

whyNot.reason: One name meaning two things at two sites is exactly the confusion the marker hygiene ruling paid to remove.
The manifest is far from the code it describes, and a reader at the top of the file loses the pairing information they want most.

recommendation.tradeoff: One rename with a teaching fix for existing files.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared renaming the pairing marker with registering the shared name twice and recommended the rename for one-name-one-meaning.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested renaming the block instead and folding pairing into Target, rejecting both because the block's name is its content and Target rules build partitions. Option C was added from this pass.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried the rename plus manifest pairing as an override for generated sites. That is a future manifest feature independent of this naming choice, so it was set aside.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B, since site-dependent signatures become expressible after the registry rebuild, and strengthened C's single-source-of-truth story.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A over churn in existing web examples and candidate-name collisions. The sweep found few files, and none of the candidate names collide with registry rows or traits, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: How fine a Duration measures
decisions.gist: The smallest slice of time a Duration can hold.
decisions.lesson: A Duration in Jet counts whole milliseconds. That is the smallest slice it can hold, so a Duration cannot say 250 microseconds, and `core.time` has no way to build one. Eleven compared languages all measure finer. This choice decides how fine Jet measures, and it cannot be changed later without changing every stored Duration.
decisions.story: Mira times a database call to tune an index. The call takes 400 microseconds. Jet reports it as 0 milliseconds, so every run looks the same and she has nothing to tune against. She drops to raw integers and carries her own unit by hand.

options.name: Nanoseconds, in a 64-bit count
options.detail: A Duration counts whole nanoseconds. It reaches about 292 years, which covers timeouts, benchmarks and retry schedules, and it matches what an operating system clock actually reports. Gain: every measurement a program can take is representable, and no unit is lost on the way in. Loss: a Duration can no longer hold a span longer than 292 years, so calendar-scale arithmetic must use dates rather than durations.
options.technical: `Duration` becomes an i64 nanosecond count. `DurationUnit` gains `Nanoseconds` and `Microseconds`. `core.time` gains `nanoseconds` and `microseconds` constructors beside the existing four. `in(unit)` keeps returning a whole number and keeps refusing a span that leaves the range. Existing millisecond values scale by 1_000_000 at construction; no stored format changes, because Duration is not serialized as a raw count.
options.code:
gap :: time.microseconds(400)
print(gap.in(Unit.Nanoseconds) ?? 0)   // 400000
print(gap.in(Unit.Milliseconds) ?? 0)  // 0, still whole

budget :: time.hours(2)
print(budget.in(Unit.Seconds) ?? 0)     // 7200

options.name: Microseconds, in a 64-bit count
options.detail: A Duration counts whole microseconds. It reaches about 292 thousand years, so calendar-scale spans stay representable. Gain: fine enough for almost every measurement a program takes, with a range nobody will hit. Loss: nanosecond timing is still lost, which is the resolution a profiler and a hardware clock report, so benchmark work still rounds.
options.technical: `Duration` becomes an i64 microsecond count. `DurationUnit` gains `Microseconds`. `core.time` gains a `microseconds` constructor. A nanosecond reading from the clock is rounded to the nearest microsecond on the way in, which is a lossy conversion the caller cannot see.
options.code:
gap :: time.microseconds(400)
print(gap.in(Unit.Microseconds) ?? 0)   // 400

// A nanosecond reading rounds on the way in.
print(time.start().elapsed().in(Unit.Microseconds) ?? 0)

options.name: Two numbers: whole seconds and a nanosecond part
options.detail: A Duration carries a whole-second count and a nanosecond remainder, the way an operating system reports time. Gain: full nanosecond resolution with no range limit worth worrying about, so both a benchmark and a century are exact. Loss: a Duration stops being one number, so comparing and adding cost more, and the type is harder to explain than a count.
options.technical: `Duration` becomes a struct of an i64 second count and a u32 nanosecond remainder, matching the shape of a POSIX timespec. Arithmetic normalizes the remainder. `in(unit)` keeps its contract.
options.code:
gap :: time.nanoseconds(400)
print(gap.in(Unit.Nanoseconds) ?? 0)    // 400

long :: time.hours(1_000_000)
print(long.in(Unit.Hours) ?? 0)          // 1000000, still exact

options.name: Keep milliseconds, and record the decline
options.detail: Duration stays a whole-millisecond count. Sub-millisecond timing is recorded as a deliberate decline with this decision id, so it stops being scored as a gap. Gain: nothing changes, and the type stays the simplest thing it could be. Loss: Jet cannot express a measurement that eleven compared languages can, and anyone timing a fast operation leaves the type behind and carries raw integers.
options.technical: No change. `microseconds` and `nanoseconds` are marked declined against this decision id in the Core surface ledger.
options.code:
// Timing a fast call stays outside the type.
started :: time.start()
lookup(index, key)
print(started.elapsed().in(Unit.Milliseconds) ?? 0)   // 0

comparisons.note: A duration is a 64-bit nanosecond count, reaching about 292 years.
A duration is whole seconds plus a nanosecond remainder, with no practical range limit.
A timedelta stores days, seconds and microseconds, so microsecond is the finest slice.
A duration carries seconds and attoseconds, finer than a nanosecond.
A TimeSpan counts 100-nanosecond ticks.

recommendation.why: A nanosecond count is what the operating system clock reports, so nothing is lost between the clock and the type. It stays one number, which keeps comparison and arithmetic cheap and the type easy to explain. The 292-year reach covers every span a Duration is for; a longer span is a calendar question, and dates answer that.

whyNot.reason: It rounds the clock reading on the way in, and the caller cannot see it happen. Benchmark work is exactly where that matters.
It gives up one number for a range nobody reaches. Two fields cost more on every compare and add, and are harder to explain.
It leaves Jet unable to express a measurement all eleven compared languages can, and pushes timing work out of the type entirely.

recommendation.tradeoff: A Duration can no longer hold more than about 292 years. That is accepted because a span that long is a calendar question, and `Date` answers it exactly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared nanosecond, microsecond and two-field representations against keeping milliseconds, and recommended nanoseconds for matching what the clock reports.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a floating-point second count and a unit carried alongside the number. The float was dropped because it loses exactness at large spans, and the carried unit because it makes two durations of the same length compare unequal.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a nanosecond count that widens to two fields past its range. It was rejected because a type that changes shape at a threshold is harder to reason about than either shape alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened every option, giving D an explicit decline id and giving C the timespec shape that makes it genuinely exact at both ends.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the 292-year reach with scheduling and archival cases. Those are calendar spans measured between dates, not durations, so the limit survives.

decisions.title: Public-key encryption in Core: keep one mechanism, or add the RSA shape
decisions.gist: Decide whether Core gains an RSA-style public-key encrypt and decrypt surface.
decisions.lesson: Core already encrypts to a recipient's public key. The mechanism is a sealed box built on X25519. Eleven other languages expose a second shape as well: make a key pair, encrypt with the public half, decrypt with the private half. That shape is RSA. Adding it needs either a large-number library Core does not have, or a second way to do work the sealed box already does. Card #1473 blocks on this and records six ledger rows as unimplemented.
decisions.story: Ravi moves a payment service to Jet. The bank he talks to hands out an RSA public key and will not change. Ravi searches Core for a way to encrypt with it, finds only the sealed box, and cannot tell whether Jet declined RSA on purpose or forgot it.
decisions.inWild:
// What Core has today: encrypt to a recipient, decrypt with the matching secret.
use jet.crypto.[seal, open, keypair]

keys :: keypair()
box  :: seal(keys.public, "card token")
plain :: open(keys.secret, box)?

// What Ravi needs, and cannot write today:
bank_key :: rsa_public_from_pem(read("bank.pem")?)?
blob     :: bank_key.encrypt(payload)?   // no such call exists

options.name: Decline RSA, and say so
options.detail: Core keeps the sealed box as its only public-key encryption. The six ledger rows close as a stated refusal with a reason and a pointer to the sealed box. Ravi still cannot talk to the bank from Core.

options.name: Add RSA on a new library
options.detail: Core gains generate_key, public_encrypt, private_decrypt, and their partners, built on a vetted outside large-number library. Ravi's code works. Core takes its first outside cryptography dependency, and two mechanisms now do one job.
options.technical: This adds an external crate to the Core build. Invariant I6 keeps compiler seam crates on path dependencies only, so this needs a named carve-out. Invariant I8 keeps one mechanism per job, so the sealed box and RSA both need a stated role.
options.code:
use jet.crypto.[rsa_generate_key, rsa_public_encrypt, rsa_private_decrypt]

keys :: rsa_generate_key(2048)?
blob :: rsa_public_encrypt(keys.public, payload)?
back :: rsa_private_decrypt(keys.secret, blob)?

options.name: Add RSA, written inside Core
options.detail: Same surface as option B, with the large-number arithmetic written by hand inside Core. No outside library joins the build. Hand-written large-number arithmetic is where timing leaks live, so this trades a dependency for a safety risk.

options.name: Decline in Core, ship an interop package
options.detail: Core keeps one mechanism, as in option A. RSA lives in an ordinary Jet package outside Core, built on the existing bridge that already carries outside libraries. Ravi adds one dependency and his code works. Core stays small and beginners never meet RSA.
options.technical: The package uses the standard bridge template that other outside libraries already use, so no new dependency enters any crate under `crates/`. The refusal note in core.crypto names the package, so the ledger rows close as routed rather than missing.

comparisons.note: Go ships RSA in its standard library and also ships a modern sealed-box style package. Both live side by side, and its own docs steer new code away from RSA.
libsodium refuses RSA on purpose. It offers one sealed-box shape and tells callers to use a separate library when a peer demands RSA.
comparisons.code:
crypto_box_seal / crypto_box_seal_open
// no RSA at all

comparisons.note: Rust's standard library ships no cryptography. RSA arrives as a separate crate that projects add when a peer needs it.

recommendation.why: Ravi can talk to the bank, Core keeps one public-key mechanism, and no outside cryptography library enters the compiler build. The refusal becomes a route instead of a dead end.

whyNot.reason: It leaves a real interop need with no answer, so anyone who must meet an RSA peer leaves Jet for that work.
It puts an outside cryptography library in the compiler build and gives one job two mechanisms in the same namespace.
Hand-written large-number arithmetic in Core carries timing-leak risk that no test in this repo would catch.

recommendation.tradeoff: RSA users add one dependency instead of finding the call in Core. That is accepted because RSA is interop with older peers, not the shape Jet teaches.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared declining RSA against adding it on an outside library, and recommended declining, because the sealed box already performs the same job.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added a hand-written option and a package option. It also tested hiding RSA behind an expert door in Core, which was dropped because it still puts the library in the build.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review joined the refusal with a route, so Core stays one mechanism while the interop need still gets an answer. That became option D.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the outside-library option by pairing it with a named expert module and a steer in the docs. It still adds a second mechanism to the same namespace.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what happens when no package exists yet. The answer is that card #1473 must name the package and its first release, so option D now carries that requirement.

decisions.title: Set's last 4 order-dependent methods: decline, ship all, or ship the order-producing pair
decisions.gist: Whether Set answers shuffle, sort, indexof, and indexed directly, when a Set keeps no positions.
decisions.lesson: Card #1478 shipped 11 more Set methods and closed most of the surface ledger. Four names remain: shuffle, sort, indexof, and indexed. A hash-backed Set keeps no positions, so today all four route through to_list. The usage-frequency report ranks sorting among the most common operations in all real code, and dedupe-then-sort is an everyday idiom. A fifth name, flatten, stays declined either way: Set elements must be Hash and Eq, so a Set can never hold nested containers.
decisions.story: Sam is building a card-shuffling game in Jet. The deck lives in a Set so duplicate cards are impossible. Sam types deck.shuffle() expecting a shuffled hand back, the way deck.to_list().shuffle() already works, and wonders why Set itself has no shuffle.

options.name: Decline all 4, route through to_list
options.detail: None of the 4 names add a workflow Jet is missing. shuffle and sort already exist on List. Calling to_list first, then shuffle or sort, reaches the exact result Set.shuffle or Set.sort would compute. indexof and indexed ask for a position, and a hash Set keeps no position for any element. A direct answer would only expose an implementation detail, not a meaning a caller can rely on.
options.technical:
shuffle, sort: both already exist on List, and Set already converts to a list. A Set-native shuffle or sort would be a second spelling of the same List call, reached one method earlier.

indexof, indexed: Rust's HashSet keeps no stable enumeration order across inserts and removals. A Set-native indexof or indexed would return a real Int, but that Int would carry no meaning beyond this one call. A List's index or enumerate answers over a sequence with a real position instead.

flatten: declined regardless of outcome. Diagnostic E0506 requires Set elements to implement Hash and Eq, so a Set element can never be a list or another set. flatten needs a Set of nested containers to unpack, and Jet's type checker never allows that Set to exist.

options.name: Ship all 4 on Set with a documented arbitrary order
options.detail: Set gains shuffle, sort, indexof, and indexed directly. Each one runs by first walking the Set in whatever order Rust's HashSet currently keeps, then applying the same List logic. The docs would say the starting order before shuffle or sort is arbitrary, and that indexof or indexed answers that same arbitrary order.
options.technical: Each of the 4 names ships as a new sema case, routed through the same to-list-then-List machinery already built for filter, map, fold, each, all, min, and max. indexof and indexed need one more caveat in the docs: the position they return stays valid only until the next add or remove on that Set.

options.name: Ship sort and shuffle, each returning a List; decline indexof and indexed
options.detail:
sort and shuffle both turn an unordered Set into an ordered List, and that is a real, common step: dedupe with a Set, then sort the result. Both ship directly on Set and return a new List, running the same List logic to_list plus sort runs today.

indexof and indexed stay declined for meaning, not tidiness. A hash Set has no positions, so the number they return changes after any add or remove. Code that needs positions converts to a List, where the position is real.
options.technical:
Set.sort() and Set.shuffle() route through the same to-list-then-List machinery already built for filter, map, fold, each, all, min, and max. Each returns a fresh List and never mutates the Set. sort's output is deterministic no matter what internal order the Set walks. shuffle's output is uniform for the same reason.

indexof and indexed stay declined: Rust's HashSet keeps no stable enumeration order, so any Set-native position is an implementation leak dressed as an answer.

comparisons.note: Kotlin's Set inherits Iterable, so sorted and withIndex exist on Set too, always over an unspecified encounter order.
Swift's Set exposes sorted and enumerated the same way, both documented as running over the Set's undefined order.

recommendation.why: Sorting is a top-tier operation in the usage-frequency report, and a Set exists to dedupe, so Set-to-sorted-List is among the most common things a Set does. Option C makes that one call while running the same List mechanism underneath. It still refuses to hand back a position that means nothing.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a top-tier operation behind a to_list detour on every dedupe-then-sort, taxing the most common Set workflow to avoid a second spelling of one mechanism.
indexof and indexed would return positions that silently change after any mutation. That reads like a real index, and a beginner has no way to know it is not.

recommendation.tradeoff: Set gains two names whose results are Lists, not Sets. Docs must say the input order never matters: sort is deterministic and shuffle is uniform.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft grouped shuffle/sort with indexof/indexed as one order-dependent family and recommended declining all four through to_list.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked whether sort deserves its own bucket, since a sorted result is deterministic regardless of a Set's internal order. That split later became the seam option C ships along.
reviewPasses.hybrid: After the owner's philosophy question, this pass was rerun with frequency as the scale: sort and shuffle ship directly, while indexof and indexed stay out. The earlier sort-only hybrid grew to include shuffle because both produce an order rather than pretending to read one.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option B: shipping all four lets a newcomer from Kotlin or Swift type the name they already know without a to_list detour, and matches those two languages exactly.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether Set.sort hides the arbitrary internal order from learners; the output is fully determined by the elements, so it does not. It re-confirmed declining indexof and indexed, since to_list keeps the arbitrary order visible instead of minting an index that quietly changes.

decisions.title: Iter's last six ledger gaps: decline or ship
decisions.gist: Whether Jet adds six more Iter methods that rename features it already has, or add a second consumption model.
decisions.lesson: Card #1479 gave Iter thirteen new methods. The surface ledger still lists six more names other languages ship on their iterator type. Five of the six are synonyms: fill, cycle_n, and duplicate are repeat; tostring is join; clip and iterator are to_list and collect; compact is filter. The sixth, next, asks for a hand-held cursor Jet's Iter model does not have. Jet's philosophy sets friction in proportion to frequency, and a synonym cuts no friction: the canonical call is already the same length.
decisions.story: Sam is porting a Python generator pipeline to Jet. Python's iterator protocol calls next(it) by hand to pull one item at a time and keep the cursor between calls. Sam reaches for it.next() on a Jet Iter and finds nothing, then wonders whether Jet's iterators are missing basic stepping.

options.name: Decline all six, route each to what Jet already ships
options.detail: None of the six cuts any friction. The five synonyms rename calls that are already one short method under the canonical name, so shipping them saves zero keystrokes and doubles what a reader must learn for each capability. next would add a second, stateful way to consume a sequence beside the for-loop and the lazy adapters. Every workflow next serves already has a one-call route: chunk for pairwise reads, take and skip for bounded steps, a loop for walking.
options.technical:
Synonym declines: fill/cycle_n/duplicate -> Iter.repeat(n). tostring -> Iter.join(sep). clip/iterator -> Iter.to_list()/collect(). compact -> Iter.filter(f).

Consumption-model decline: next. Jet's for-loop and iterator adapters consume a full Iter value each time; there is no live cursor object a caller holds and advances by hand. Adding next(self) would need a second, stateful iterator protocol running beside the existing one — a second mechanism for the same job, unlike the one-mechanism spellings above.

options.name: Ship all six as new Iter methods
options.detail: Iter grows five methods that duplicate repeat, join, to_list, and filter under new names. It also grows a sixth, next, that adds a stateful cursor object living beside the existing for-loop and lazy-adapter model. Every sequence workflow now has two ways to repeat, render, materialize, and filter. It also gains a new way to walk a sequence that behaves differently from every other Iter consumer.
options.technical:
fill, cycle_n, and duplicate each ship as one more case in Iter's method table. Every one calls the same repeat logic repeat already uses.

tostring ships as a second text-rendering method beside join. clip and iterator ship as two more spellings of to_list and collect. compact ships as filter with a fixed predicate.

next ships as a new stateful method with a held cursor value and a new Prelude function. It also needs matching AOT, JIT, and interpreter lowering that mutates and returns that cursor across calls. No other Iter method has this shape.
options.code:
nums :: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

five_pairs := nums.fill(2)
line := nums.tostring()
materialized := nums.clip()
nonzero := nums.compact()

it := nums
first := it.next()
second := it.next()

comparisons.note: Python's next(it) advances a live generator/iterator object and raises StopIteration at the end; Jet's for-loop and lazy adapters already own that walk without exposing a mutable cursor.
comparisons.code:
it = iter([1, 2, 3])
first = next(it)
second = next(it)

comparisons.note: Ruby's Array#cycle(3) repeats the whole array three times, the same job Jet's repeat(n) already does under a different name.

recommendation.why: Friction in Jet shrinks in proportion to frequency, and every operation these six names cover is already one short call under its canonical name. A synonym cuts nothing and grows the beginner surface. next would buy a second consumption model whose workflows already have one-call routes.

whyNot.reason: Shipping the six saves no keystrokes anywhere, since repeat, join, to_list, and filter are already the same length. It adds five duplicate names to learn plus a stateful cursor unlike every other Iter consumer.

recommendation.tradeoff: A programmer arriving with fill, compact, tostring, clip, or next as muscle memory looks up the canonical name once. If a stepping workflow ever appears with no one-call route, the answer is a new adapter, not a cursor.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft grouped the six names into a synonym set (four names already answered by repeat, join, to_list, or filter) and a model-mismatch case (next), recommending decline for both groups.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked whether next could ship as a read-only peek instead of a full stateful cursor. A peek still needs somewhere to remember the last position between calls, which is the same held-cursor problem, so the finding stood.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid shipping the synonym names as thin aliases was tested and dropped. An alias saves no keystrokes, since the canonical call is the same length, so it fails the friction-per-frequency test while doubling the names a beginner must learn.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option B: a newcomer typing fill, compact, tostring, clip, or next by muscle memory from another language would find it immediately instead of detouring to repeat, filter, join, or a for-loop.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether declining next leaves a real workflow stranded. Every pattern the six names cover already has one working route — pairwise stepping is one chunk call — so no workflow is stranded.

decisions.title: The small-cluster ledger's 75 remaining names: decline or ship anyway
decisions.gist: Whether Jet adds 75 competitor names across 15 small modules that a check already found a working route for.
decisions.lesson: Card #1481 checked 81 rows the surface ledger flagged as missing across 17 small modules. Four were real gaps and now ship. The other 75 already have a working Jet route. Two lenses grade every row. First, frequency: does declining tax a path real code takes often? Second, name quality: is Jet's existing spelling actually the better API? Where a competitor's spelling is better, Jet replaces its own name outright — it never keeps two.
decisions.story: Priya ports a Go service to Jet. She reaches for sync.Lock, testing.Run, and reflect.Set out of habit, and cannot find any of them under core.sync, core.testing, or core.reflect. Each time the missing name turns out to already have a working Jet answer, once she knows where to look.

options.name: Decline all 75; keep whichever spelling is the better API
options.detail:
Every one of the 75 names already reaches its result in equal or fewer keystrokes under Jet's canonical name, so declining taxes no frequent path. The only cost is one docs lookup, and the core-library reference names the existing route beside each declined name.

Each pair was also judged on merit: had a competitor spelling been the better API, Jet's would be replaced outright, never aliased. In this sweep the current names win or tie every head-to-head: v4 over uuid4, query_one over first, next over read, float_range over uniform.
options.technical:
core.sync (12 names: broadcast, clear, lock, put, rlock, signal, trylock, unlock, wait, thread, timer, locked). Jet's core.sync is CRDT data sync — SyncText, SyncCounter, SyncMap, SyncList. The competitor evidence is Go, Python, and Ruby's sync or threading package: Mutex, RWMutex, Cond, Event. That is a different domain; it only shares the word "sync". Jet's safety design omits raw shared-memory locks. core.tasks owns concurrency instead. put duplicates the already-shipped map_set.

core.encoding.xml (9 names: close, copy, end, flush, indent, name, nodetype, write, clear). close, flush, and write already ship as XMLWriter.finish, flush, and write. end, indent, name, and nodetype ask for incremental SAX-style tag control. Jet parses every format into one shared DataTree value instead, by design (D-SERDE13=B). copy and clear each have one witness language and no consistent competitor meaning.

core.process (8 of 9 names: id, kill, wait, spawn, output, success, exitcode, start). id, kill, wait, spawn, output, and success already ship on ProcessChild, ProcessResult, and ProcessSpec. exitcode already ships as ProcessResult.code. start already ships as ProcessSpec.spawn(). Only exited, a non-blocking poll, was a real gap. It ships with this card.

core.db (8 names: close, commit, name, first, raw, rollback, copy, count). close, commit, and rollback already ship on DBConnection and DBScope. first already ships as query_one(). count duplicates query(...).len(). raw would open an unaudited escape from the portable DB-plugin-wire protocol every backend goes through. name and copy have no consistent competitor meaning.

core.testing (7 names: benchmark, fail, main, run, runtests, skip, stop). Jet already defines and runs tests through #Test and #Bench marker blocks, plus the jet test and jet bench commands. Every one of these 7 names asks for that same capability, spelled as a function call instead of a marker.

core.reflect (8 names: clear, copy, equal, get, set, getfile, getmodule, loadfile). reflect.of(x) is deliberately a read-only structural snapshot. It keeps no runtime type registry and allows no field write by string name (I1). get, set, clear, copy, and equal would all need that registry. getfile, getmodule, and loadfile ask for dynamic runtime code loading, which a compiled, ahead-of-time language does not do.

core.http (4 names: cancelrequest, copy, first, postform). first already ships as HTTPHeaders.first. postform already ships as the request builder's .form(...) call. cancelrequest duplicates the deadline every request already takes. copy has one witness language.

core.tls (4 of 6 names: start, handshake, verifyhostname, copy). start already ships as tls.client(). handshake happens inside client() automatically, by design; there is no separate step. verifyhostname is mandatory already, visible as TLSPeerIdentity.verified_server_name; Jet gives no way to turn it off. copy has one witness language. The other 2, ciphersuites and tlsversion, are real gaps needing a native TLS-bridge change; they move to a follow-up card, not this ballot.

core.uuid (3 of 5 names: join, uuid1, uuid4). uuid4 already ships as v4. uuid1 is MAC-address-based, an older and weaker format; Jet declines it in favor of the already-shipped, safer v7. join matches no real UUID operation in any compared language. parse and v5 were real gaps. They ship with this card.

core.binary (2 names: pipe, readchar). JetReader is a fixed in-memory byte-buffer parser (D-SHIFT1), not a stream. pipe asks for a stream-to-stream copy, a different mechanism. readchar asks for character decoding, which belongs to core.text's Cursor, not a byte reader.

core.encoding.csv (3 names: flush, read, fieldsizelimit). flush already ships as CSVWriter.flush. read already ships as CSVReader.next, matching every other stream reader's name. fieldsizelimit already ships as the shared EncodingLimits.max_item_bytes, one cross-format limit instead of a CSV-only one.

core.random (2 names: random, uniform). Both already ship, as float() and float_range(a, b).

core.args (2 names: parse, parseargs). Both already ship as ArgsSpec.parse(argv), Jet's one declarative CLI-parsing route.

core.encoding.json (1 name: dump). Already reachable as to_string() plus a file write, or the streaming JSONWriter.

core.mem (2 names: replace, copy). replace duplicates the take operator (^) plus assignment, which already swaps a value out. copy has one witness language and duplicates plain assignment for Copy values.

options.name: Ship all 75 as new, second spellings
options.detail: Every declined name ships anyway, even where Jet already reaches the same result another way. A newcomer from Go, Python, or Ruby can type the exact name they already know, in every one of the 15 modules, without learning Jet's existing spelling first.
options.technical: Each name ships as its own new function or method. Where a Jet spelling already exists, the new name routes to the same result. v4 stays, and uuid4 becomes a second name for it; query_one stays, and first becomes a second name for it. Where none exists yet, real new surface ships instead: raw shared-memory locks for core.sync, dynamic module loading for core.reflect, a second XML DOM alongside DataTree for core.encoding.xml.
options.code:
// Every module keeps its existing name AND gains the competitor's name.
uuid.v4()
uuid.uuid4()              // new: identical result, second spelling

reader.next()
reader.read()              // new: identical result, second spelling

// Modules with no existing answer gain a new mechanism outright.
lk := sync.Lock.new()
lk.lock()                  // new: a raw mutex, alongside CRDT SyncMap

v := reflect.of(config)
v.set("port", 9090)        // new: field write by string name, breaks I1

comparisons.note: Go's sync package is OS-level locking; its separate CRDT-style types live in third-party packages. Jet keeps the CRDT half under core.sync and the safety half under core.tasks, never both under one name.
unittest defines a test as a class with methods Python's own runner discovers and runs. Jet's #Test marker plus jet test plays the same role without a base class to inherit.

recommendation.why: Declining costs no friction anywhere: every one of the 75 results is already equal or fewer keystrokes under Jet's canonical name. The sweep's four real gaps ship with the card, and the two real TLS gaps moved to a follow-up card, so real friction still gets fixed. Safety declines (raw locks, reflect writes) keep the beginner default safe: concurrency routes through core.tasks, and reflection stays read-only by design.

whyNot.reason: It gives every reader two names for one result while cutting no friction, since the existing call is already as short. For core.sync and core.reflect it also reopens raw locks and string-keyed field writes that Jet's safety design deliberately left out.

recommendation.tradeoff: A reader who reaches for a familiar name from Go, Python, or Ruby and does not find it must learn Jet's existing spelling once. docs/reference/core-library.md names the existing route right next to every declined name.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft grouped the 75 names by module and matched each to its existing Jet route, recommending a decline with the route named for every one.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked whether any module deserved a partial ship — for example shipping core.sync's raw lock as an expert escape hatch. Declined: Jet's whole concurrency story routes through core.tasks, and a second raw-lock mechanism would fork that story for one competitor package.
reviewPasses.hybrid: After the owner's philosophy question, every pair was regraded by frequency and by name quality, and no declined name beats its Jet route on either scale. The regrade also fixed the standing rule: when a competitor's spelling is the better API, Jet renames its own, never aliases.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option B: a beginner arriving from Go or Python reaches for the name their prior language taught them, and if that name does not exist, they have to search. That friction is real for exactly one lookup per name, once.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Shipping reflect.set or a raw core.sync lock as an audited #Unsafe escape hatch was tested and dropped. No request for either has ever reached the backlog, so it would be speculative scope, not a real gap.

decisions.title: Collection helpers: run at once, or only when read
decisions.gist: Decide when list helpers like map and filter do their work.
decisions.lesson: Today list.map(f) returns a lazy view. The work happens only when something reads the view, and reading it twice does the work twice. The eager choice runs the work at the call and returns a plain list. The lazy spelling stays available behind one visible word. This amends the ratified lazy default from D-ITERTOOLS1.
decisions.story: Marcus filters a list of orders, then counts the result twice while debugging. Under the lazy default his filter runs twice, and a print inside it fires twice. He spends an hour filing a bug against his own code. Under the eager default the second count is free and the print fires once.
decisions.inWild:
open_orders :: orders.filter((o) => o.open)
print(open_orders.count())
print(open_orders.count())   // lazy: filter runs AGAIN here

loop o; open_orders { ship(o) }   // lazy: and a third time here

options.name: Eager on containers, .lazy opt-in
options.detail: Helpers on a real list, map, or set run at once and return a plain collection. Writing .lazy first gives the same vocabulary as a deferred view for large or infinite work. Streams and file lines stay naturally lazy because they arrive over time. Gain: no invisible re-running, results are inspectable in a debugger. Loss: long chains build intermediate lists unless the optimizer fuses them.
options.technical: Amends D-ITERTOOLS1. [T].map returns [T]; [T].lazy.map returns Iter<T>; Iter adapters unchanged. Sources that are already streams (files.lines, Stream, channels) keep returning Iter. The optimizer may fuse adjacent eager adapters when the intermediate is unobservable.
options.code:
names :: users.filter((u) => u.active).map((u) => u.name)
print(names.len())   // free: names is a plain list

big.lazy.map(parse).filter(ok).first(10)   // deferred, visibly

options.name: Keep the lazy view default
options.detail: Status quo. Helpers return a lazy Iter view, and collect, to_list, or a reducer materializes it. Gain: chains never build intermediate collections, matching Rust's zero-cost model. Loss: reading a view twice silently repeats the work and its effects. This is the documented multiple-enumeration trap that bites C# LINQ users at every level.
options.technical: D-ITERTOOLS1 as ratified. Adapter methods return Iter<T>; to_list()/collect()/reducers materialize.
options.code:
names :: users.filter(active).map(name)   // no work yet
print(names.count())   // work happens
print(names.count())   // work happens again, silently

comparisons.note: Collections are eager; asSequence() opts into lazy with the same method names. Widely praised as the beginner-safe split.
Enum is eager, Stream is lazy, same shape. Laziness is a module choice you can see.
LINQ is lazily deferred by default. Silent multiple enumeration is one of its most documented bug classes.
comparisons.code:
var q = xs.Where(p);
q.Count(); q.Count(); // enumerates twice

recommendation.why: Eager defaults make results real things a beginner can print, count, and debug. The deferred trap disappears, and experts keep the identical lazy vocabulary behind one word.

whyNot.reason: The lazy default trades an invisible correctness hazard for a performance property most code never needs. When the work is big, .lazy is one visible word away.

recommendation.tradeoff: Chained eager helpers can allocate intermediate lists. Accepted: fusion can remove most of it, and the hot-path escape is explicit and cheap.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared eager-with-opt-in against the ratified lazy default and recommended eager on the multiple-enumeration evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered a caching lazy view that memoizes on first read, and per-call-site inference from the expected type. Both were rejected as hidden machinery and folded into the two honest models.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed A is already the hybrid: eager containers plus naturally lazy streams plus an explicit lazy view. No stronger combination emerged.
