options.detail: Defaults stay as ratified, and a package policy flips a project into the exact world. Teams that care opt in once per package. Two worlds then exist, and any code snippet means different things depending on an invisible setting.
options.technical: A policy key switches literal typing and the division landing type per package scope.
options.code:
policy: .{ exact_math: true }
// same source now means different values in different packages

comparisons.note: Decimal literals are exact rationals by default, so a tenth plus two tenths equals three tenths. Floats exist and are opt-in. This is the closest shipped precedent.
Exact int by default, binary float for fractions, with Decimal and Fraction as opt-in library types. This is option B, and its float surprises fill beginner forums.

recommendation.why: It finishes the move the bigint Int decision started: the default world is simply correct, and every restriction is chosen on purpose. Beginners get right answers; experts lose nothing and gain a visible audit of where approximation enters.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the single most famous beginner footgun as the default experience, in a language whose constitution ranks the beginner experience above performance.
One spelling with two meanings across packages breaks reading, teaching, and copy-paste, which is worse than either consistent world.

recommendation.tradeoff: Exact rational arithmetic costs more than machine floats, and long chains can grow big denominators. The small-value fast path and the one-word Float escape bound the cost, and the constitution spends performance rank to buy beginner rank.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the exact default against the ratified status quo and recommended exact, because the bigint Int precedent shows the default-correctness move works.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the per-package policy shape and considered decimal-only exactness without fractions; the latter folded into A's printing rule since both keep exact values underneath.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested exact decimals with approximate division. Splitting literals from division reintroduces the surprise at the first divide, so it folded into B rather than standing alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, whose model is Python's and battle-tested, and C, which gives teams an explicit contract. Both remain honest choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with denominator blowup in long simulations and with FFI boundaries expecting floats. Fast paths plus the one-word Float escape answer the first, and crossings already range-check under ratified law, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Primary dirty units for Jet incremental builds
decisions.gist: Which units Jet marks dirty so an edit does not force a full rebuild.
decisions.lesson: Swift and Xcode often rebuild far more than the edit needs. Progressive caches fail, so teams treat clean builds as ritual. Jet already plans query caches, module checks, and sealed package objects. This choice locks how those layers share dirty work. It must match C++-style small units without a second build system.
decisions.story: Priya changes one helper inside module util.math. She wants Jet to recheck that module and its dependents only. She does not want the whole app or every package to rebuild. She also wants a warm second build to restore sealed package objects when nothing in them changed.
decisions.inWild:
# edit only util.math
$ jet build --timings
# expect: util.math dirty; dependents rechecked; unrelated packages restored from cache

$ jet build --timings   # no edits
# expect: no world recheck; sealed objects hit cache

options.name: Three-layer dirty model
options.detail: Editor and warm check reuse item and file queries. Batch builds dirty a Jet module when its interface fingerprint changes, and recheck dependents only. Link and distribute sealed package objects under the ratified library reuse law. Small edits stay small. Package cache stays honest.
options.technical: Layer 1: jet-queries + IncrementalSemaCache item reuse (D-LSP1 path, promoted to batch by #1026). Layer 2: module interface fingerprint invalidates importers only. Layer 3: D-LIB-REUSE1=B sealed package artifacts for compile/link restore. No path skips sema or diagnostics on a cache hit that still needs checking.
options.code:
# util.math changes a private fn body → item/module local recheck
# util.math changes a pub signature → dependents recheck
# unrelated pkg.ui → sealed object cache hit

options.name: Package-only dirty units
options.detail: Any file change dirties the whole package artifact. Simple mental model. Small modules inside a large package still pay a full package tax. Fine editor reuse may still exist, but batch builds stay coarse.
options.technical: Invalidation key is package source digest only. Module fingerprints are not used for batch dirty sets.
options.code: # one-line edit in util.math rebuilds all of package util

options.name: File-only dirty units
options.detail: Dirtiness is per source file with no module interface layer. Easy to implement. Cross-file modules and generic APIs still force broad conservative rechecks. It underuses Jet modules as units.
options.technical: Query keys stay file-scoped. No module interface fingerprint. Package sealed objects may still cache link outputs.
options.code: # changing math.jet always rechecks every file that imported any symbol from it

options.name: Whole-program always
options.detail: Every build rechecks the full program. Maximum simplicity and no cache bugs. Large projects become Swift-like multi-minute no-change builds. Rejects the video lesson.
options.technical: No batch incremental sema. Caches may still store final binaries only.
options.code: $ jet build   # always full check, even with zero edits

comparisons.note: Translation units and interfaces limit rebuild fan-out when headers stay stable.
comparisons.code: # change .cpp → rebuild one object; stable .h → dependents stay

comparisons.note: Crate-level artifacts with fingerprint invalidation; fine queries inside rustc.
Module planning and weak incrementality often rebuild too much; clean becomes ritual.

recommendation.why: Three layers match Jet's existing law: queries for warm work, modules for batch dirty sets, sealed packages for link restore. Priya's one-module edit stays bounded. It is the C++-style split without a second build tool.

whyNot.reason: Package-only dirty sets punish large packages for a one-module edit.
File-only dirty sets ignore Jet modules as the natural interface boundary.
Whole-program always recreates the Xcode no-change multi-minute failure mode.

recommendation.tradeoff: Module interface fingerprints must be exact. A wrong fingerprint either trusts stale code or over-invalidates. Hostile tests on #1023 own that risk.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared three-layer dirty sets, package-only, file-only, and whole-program builds. It recommended three layers.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested function-only dirty sets as a fifth default. That stays an internal query optimization under layer 1, not a separate owner default.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept three layers and required sealed package hits to still honor sema when interfaces change. No merge created a fourth product mode.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened package-only with internal file tips and file-only with import graphs. Each still misses module-scale batch dirty sets.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested wrong interface fingerprints and cache hits that skip diagnostics. Hostile corpus rules on #1023 repair those, so three layers remain.

decisions.title: How Jet fails when type checking gets too hard
decisions.gist: What Jet does when a type check would take too long or get too complex.
decisions.lesson: Swift sometimes says it cannot type check an expression in reasonable time. The span is often too wide. People then reshape working code to please the compiler. Jet diagnostics are a product. The checker must stay honest and local. This choice sets the bound and the failure shape.
decisions.story: Omar writes a nested UI builder that type-checks on a small sample and hangs on a real screen. He needs a clear error at the real problem site. He must not be told to rewrite style because the compiler gave up.
decisions.inWild:
# pathological nested builder
ui.column:
  ui.row: ... # deep inference

# required outcome under the winner:
error[E????]: type check hit its bound near this call
  --> app.jet:84:12
   |
84 |   ui.row: ...
   |            ^
 Why: this expression exceeded the type-check bound
 Fix: split the expression or add a type annotation here

options.name: Bound plus pinpoint diagnostic
options.detail: Type checking has an explicit bound. When the bound hits, Jet emits a normal diagnostic at the best local span. The message never says the compiler merely gave up on the whole program. Users annotate or split at that site. Refactoring only to soothe the checker is treated as a Jet defect to fix.
options.technical: Sema carries a type-check bound (steps or recursion depth) separate from comptime interpreter fuel. Diagnostics use a registered code with What/Why/Fix and a UI snapshot (I4). No approximate types. I3 stays: codegen never invents unchecked meaning.
options.code:
error[E????]: type check hit its bound near this call
 Fix: add a type annotation or split this expression

options.name: Unbounded complete checking
options.detail: The checker always runs to a full answer or an ordinary type error. No complexity bound. Some programs may hang the compiler. Matches classic batch compilers. Fails Omar's hang case.
options.technical: No type-check fuel. Process-level timeouts stay outside sema.
options.code: $ jet check app.jet   # may not return

options.name: Timeout with guessed types
options.detail: On timeout, Jet invents approximate types and continues. Builds feel fast. Wrong programs may pass. Breaks sema-as-gatekeeper.
options.technical: Would violate I3. Listed to reject clearly.
options.code:
# warning: approximated types after timeout
$ jet build   # may ship wrong code

options.name: Ban deep type-level builders
options.detail: Jet forbids language features that create SwiftUI-like checker explosions. Strong prevention. Also blocks useful nested DSLs that stay within a bound. A bound with pinpoint errors already covers the failure mode.
options.technical: Syntax or sema rejects nested builder depth above a fixed limit even when checking is cheap.
options.code: error: nested builder depth 8 is not allowed

comparisons.note: Unable to type check this expression in reasonable time often points at a wide span.
comparisons.code: error: unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time

comparisons.note: Mostly completes or gives a normal error; pathological cases still exist but culture rejects compiler-soothing refactors as the product.
comparisons.code: error[E0277]: the trait bound is not satisfied

comparisons.note: Instantiation depth and complexity limits emit local diagnostics.
comparisons.code: error TS2589: Type instantiation is excessively deep

recommendation.why: A bound with a pinpoint diagnostic keeps sema honest and local. Omar sees where to annotate. Jet never ships guessed types. Useful nested DSLs still work when they stay within the bound.

whyNot.reason: Unbounded checking allows compiler hangs on real UI code.
Guessed types after timeout break sema as the only gatekeeper.
A hard ban on deep builders blocks healthy DSLs that a bound already keeps safe.

recommendation.tradeoff: Bounds need tuning on a corpus. Too tight annoys experts. Too loose still feels like a hang. #1023 owns measurement after ratification.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared bound-plus-pinpoint, unbounded checking, guessed types, and a hard builder ban. It recommended bound-plus-pinpoint.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested process kill-only timeouts and always-require-annotations modes. Those folded into ops policy and local annotation fixes under option A.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept option A and allowed shallow DSL nesting inside the bound. No guessed types were added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened unbounded checking with external watchdog scripts and strengthened the builder ban with allow-lists. Each still hangs or over-blocks.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested wide spans and silent approximates. Option A requires a registered local diagnostic and forbids approximates, so it remains.

decisions.title: One authority model for effects, caps, policy, budgets, and trust
decisions.gist: Whether Jet builds all authority checks on one shared model.
decisions.lesson: Nine parts of Jet decide who may do what. Effect rows, #Caps and #Grant, the #Policy ladder, package budgets, build effects, comptime purity, the REPL gate, plugin sandboxes, and the trust store each carry their own vocabulary and rules. They already obey the same law: a scope may only shrink what its parent allows, and every exception is written down. This choice decides whether that law gets one implementation or stays spread across nine.
decisions.story: Maya runs a small billing service with two dependencies and a deploy agent. Her auditor asks one question: what can this system touch? Today the compiler, the package manifest, the build runner, and the trust store answer in four vocabularies. She wants one answer she can hand to the auditor.

options.name: One substrate
options.detail: All nine mechanisms become readers of one rights tree, one holds-set relation, one tighten rule, and one gate record. Nothing users type changes. The compiler, the budget, the sandbox, the REPL, and the trust store give the same answer with the same names. Ratified-but-unbuilt work (the agent executor, jetos install trust, the sandbox proof) lands on this substrate instead of adding more copies.
options.technical: One foundation module owns the root table, the subsumption lattice (effect_covers), the scope ladder (D-MARK-SCOPE1), and the gate ledger. Effects.rs, Policy.rs, EffectBudget.rs, BuildEffects.rs, both purity checkers, and the REPL authorizer become consumers. Semantics live in the substrate per I3/I9; generated Rust stays byte-identical.

options.name: Law on paper only
options.detail: The spec states the attenuation law and each mechanism must cite it, but every engine keeps its own code. Cheapest to adopt. Drift between the copies remains possible, and the ratified agent and jetos work still each build their own engine.
options.technical: A spec section names the law and lists the nine mechanisms as instances. No shared code. New authority features must reference the section in their ballots.

options.name: One vocabulary, nine engines
options.detail: Merge the six closed name tables into one rights tree so every surface uses the same names, but keep each mechanism’s own checking engine. Users see consistent words. The same tighten law still runs in nine places with nine error surfaces, and boundary features still need bespoke types.
options.technical: EFFECT_ROOTS, BuildEffect, PolicyKey, trust authority kinds, and plugin capabilities merge into one table in jet-foundation. Resolution code stays where it is.

options.name: Keep nine models
options.detail: Decline. Each boundary keeps its own model and vocabulary. No re-founding work. The word capability keeps six meanings, the spec and code keep drifting, and every future boundary (agents, jetos, remote builders) adds another copy.

comparisons.note: One runtime policy oracle over ambient authority. Retired: hand-written policy for real dependency trees collapsed to grant-everything, and every sensitive call site had to opt in forever.
comparisons.code: grant { permission java.security.AllPermission; }; // what real policy files said

comparisons.note: The compiler checks the trust chain across the whole import graph. The strongest prior art for making authority a static, transitive fact rather than a runtime hope.
comparisons.code: {-# LANGUAGE Safe #-} -- a Safe module cannot import untrusted code

comparisons.note: Default-deny with explicit allow flags works, but the grant unit is the whole process, so one needy dependency widens everyone.
comparisons.code: deno run --allow-net app.ts  // every module now has the network

recommendation.why: One substrate makes every authority answer agree, heals the drift at its root, and lets the ratified agent, jetos, and sandbox work land as instances instead of copies ten, eleven, and twelve. It also makes the safety story teachable in one sentence.

whyNot.reason: Paper cannot stop drift. The spec already said ten roots while the compiler shipped twenty-eight, with the stale count baked into user-facing explain text.
Shared names with nine engines still checks one law nine ways, keeps nine error surfaces, and leaves boundary features building bespoke authority types.
The fragmentation is already user-visible, and two more authority consumers are ratified and about to be built on nothing.

recommendation.tradeoff: A single substrate concentrates risk: a bug in the shared lattice touches every check at once. That is acceptable because one heavily tested lattice is safer than nine partly tested ones, and the golden suite pins generated output byte-for-byte.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one substrate, a documented law, a shared vocabulary without shared engines, and the status quo. It recommended the substrate because agreement between checkpoints is the point.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested a dynamic runtime authority object and split language-side and toolchain-side substrates. The runtime shape repeats the SecurityManager failure and was rejected, and the split shape was folded into option C as its strongest form.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried document-now-unify-later and vocabulary-now-substrate-later stagings. Both let the agent executor build on the old engines meanwhile, creating the tenth copy this ballot exists to prevent, so no hybrid survived.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a conformance test suite that checks each engine against the documented law, and strengthened C by including the manifest schemas in the merged vocabulary. Both improvements are kept in those options as written.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with substrate bugs propagating everywhere and the refactor disturbing erasure. The golden suite pins byte-identical output and phase A changes no surface, so A remains the recommendation.

decisions.title: Heal the effect root table: FFI languages become leaves
decisions.gist: What the closed list of effect roots actually is.
decisions.lesson: D-EFF4 ratified ten closed effect roots. Since then, sixteen language-binding ballots each added a root (Go, Java, Lua, and so on), plus Browser and Secret, without amending D-EFF4. The code now has twenty-eight roots, the spec and the E1221 explain text still say ten, and D-FFI-PY1 promised a Py root that was never added. This choice picks the true closed list and where foreign-language calls live in it.
decisions.story: Tom reads the Jet book, learns the ten effect roots, and audits a teammate’s service. He finds =[Java]=> in a signature. No documentation he owns mentions a Java effect, and jet explain tells him the vocabulary has ten roots. He no longer trusts the list he learned.

options.name: One FFI root, languages as leaves
options.detail: The closed table becomes thirteen roots: the ratified ten plus FFI, Browser, and Secret. The sixteen language roots become leaves: FFI.Go, FFI.Java, FFI.Lua, and the promised FFI.Py and FFI.Octave arrive as leaves too. A bound like =[!FFI]=> forbids all foreign calls at once. Existing rows migrate in one pass and the old flat spellings are deleted.
options.technical: Amends D-EFF4/D-EFF5 (root list) and the effect clause of each D-FFI-*1 ruling. Honors D-FFI-PY1 and D-FFI-OCTAVE1 by delivering their effects as leaves. Ancestor subsumption (D-EFFTREE1) already gives FFI covering FFI.Go. E1221 text and the stale Effects.rs comments are corrected in the same change.

options.name: Bless the flat thirty
options.detail: Keep every language as its own root and add the missing Py and Octave. Amend D-EFF4/5 and the explain text to list thirty roots. No migration. The teaching story grows from ten words to thirty, and forbidding all foreign calls takes sixteen prohibitions.
options.technical: Facts.rs becomes the ratified list verbatim. D-EFF4/5 amended to thirty. No row changes anywhere.

options.name: Ten teaching roots, system roots documented apart
options.detail: Keep the ratified ten as the beginner vocabulary. Everything else (language roots, Browser, Secret) becomes a documented system register that ordinary teaching never mentions. Code keeps compiling as today. Two registers of the same kind of name is a second vocabulary wearing a disguise.
options.technical: No code change. Spec gains a system-roots appendix. E1221 text says ten user roots plus system roots.

comparisons.note: Preview 1 shipped a flat rights bitmask per handle. The grain was wrong and unwinding it took a full redesign. Grant shape calcifies early.
comparisons.code: // preview1: fd_rights: u64 bitmask -> preview2: typed interfaces

comparisons.note: STORAGE bundled all files under one grant. Narrowing it later (Scoped Storage) took years of migrations.

recommendation.why: One FFI root restores a small closed list that teaches in a breath, makes forbid-all-foreign-calls one word, and honors the two rulings whose promised roots never shipped. The tree already supports it: leaves and subsumption are ratified and built.

whyNot.reason: Thirty flat roots make the closed set a memorization exercise and a sixteen-term prohibition row the price of purity from foreign code.
Two registers of one vocabulary is drift by design. The audit that found this problem started from exactly such a split.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing =[Go]=> style rows migrate to =[FFI.Go]=> in one repository-wide pass. That is churn without behavior change, accepted because the flat spellings were never ratified as a set.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the leaf collapse against blessing the flat table and recommended the collapse for teachability and single-word prohibition.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the two-register option and tested folding all foreign-language effects into Exec. The Exec fold was rejected because a JVM call and spawning a process are different risks an auditor must tell apart.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried A with Browser and Secret also demoted to leaves under IO or a new Data root. Neither has a natural parent among the ten, so the hybrid was rejected and both stay roots.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with its real virtue: a flat table has no hierarchy rules and never surprises anyone with subsumption. C gained its clearest framing as a documentation-only fix.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether FFI subsumption hides which language a dependency uses, and it does not: exact leaves stay in rows, budgets, and the ledger. The migration was checked against the examples and formatter round-trip traps, so A holds.

decisions.title: Memory floors ride the rights tree
decisions.gist: Whether memory floors and effect rules share one ladder.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two tighten-only ladders. The effect system checks rows and #Caps regions on one lattice. The #Policy ladder checks memory floors (no_alloc, zero_rc, arena_bounded, gc) and the unsafe mode on a second lattice with its own error code. Both enforce the same rule: inner scopes may only tighten. This choice decides whether the memory floors become denials on the rights tree (new Mem leaves) or keep their separate engine.
decisions.story: Ana writes firmware for a flight-data recorder. Certification asks: prove this package never allocates after boot and never touches the network. Today those are two proofs from two systems with two vocabularies. She wants one proof from one system.

options.name: One ladder, spellings kept
options.detail: Mem.Alloc, Mem.Rc, and Mem.Gc become rights on the tree. #Policy(no_alloc) keeps its exact spelling and meaning but now records a Mem.Alloc denial on the same ladder #Caps uses. Nothing users type changes, diagnostics keep their codes, and a certification audit reads one ledger.
options.technical: Amends D-MEM-FACTS1=B in substrate only: same facts, same transitivity, expressed as tree denials. PolicyKey memory variants retire; the unsafe mode stays a policy value (it is a gate mode, not a right). arena_bounded(N) carries its limit as gate data. E0355 remains the diagnostic for policy-shape errors.

options.name: Full respell as effect denials
options.detail: Retire the memory keys from #Policy and write floors as prohibitions: =[!Mem.Alloc]=> on functions, deny: [Mem.Alloc] in manifests. One mechanism and one spelling, but the friendly floor words (no_alloc) disappear and arena limits need a new home.
options.technical: Amends D-MEM-FACTS1 and D-POLICY-WORD1. #Policy keeps only non-memory arguments. arena_bounded needs a parameterized-denial form the row grammar does not have today.

options.name: Two ladders stay
options.detail: Decline. Memory floors keep their own lattice and error family. The certification story stays split and the substrate keeps two implementations of the tighten rule.

comparisons.note: Fused all of aliasing and authority into one six-mode lattice that every beginner faces. Lesson taken: fold the substrate, not the beginner surface — the floor words stay.
comparisons.code: iso | val | ref | box | trn | tag  // mandatory vocabulary, day one

comparisons.note: no_std and #![forbid(unsafe_code)] are separate systems from the borrow checker. Certification audits there also stitch multiple proofs.

recommendation.why: One ladder gives embedded and certification work a single proof and deletes a duplicate lattice. The floor words stay because they read better than row noise, and the unsafe mode stays a gate setting, which keeps the model honest.

whyNot.reason: It trades the ratified, readable floor words for row noise and has no good answer for parameterized floors like arena_bounded.
It keeps two implementations of one rule and a permanently split audit story for exactly the users who audit hardest.

recommendation.tradeoff: Mem joins the root table, so the closed list grows by one root. That is acceptable because the alternative is a whole parallel lattice for three names.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared substrate fold, full respell, and status quo, recommending the fold because it unifies proof without touching ratified spellings.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested an Unsafe root and per-type floors such as no_alloc on a struct. Unsafe stays a gate with modes rather than a held right, and per-type floors are not this decision, so both were folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried A plus optional row spellings (=[!Mem.Alloc]=> as sugar for the same denial). That reintroduces two spellings of one mechanism, against I8, and was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a concrete manifest form for limits and strengthened C by naming its real virtue: zero migration risk to certified code. Both are reflected in the option details.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A on arena_bounded, since a limit is not a set-membership fact; the denial carries its limit as gate data, as grants entries already carry per-dependency data. Tighten-only (D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1) survives unchanged as the ladder law, so A holds.

decisions.title: Name the authority value that crosses boundaries
decisions.gist: What the carried rights-set value is called, and whether it is one type.
decisions.lesson: When rights cross a boundary the compiler cannot see past — into a spawned process, a plugin, or a session — they must travel as a value. Jet has four designs for that value today: the unnameable #Grant handle, the ratified-but-unbuilt ProcessAuthority, the plugin capability list, and the REPL grant copy. The type name Capability is currently accepted anywhere a type is legal but can never be constructed. This choice picks one type and its name.
decisions.story: Priya builds a CI agent in Jet. She spawns a build in a workspace, hands a plugin its rights, and opens a debug session. Three handoffs, and today each would use a different type with a different shape. She wants to write one thing three times.

options.name: Authority — one Prelude type
options.detail: One type named Authority carries a rights set across every boundary. The #Grant handle has this type, process.workspace() returns it, plugins receive it, sessions hold it. It can only be narrowed, never widened, and it never participates in dispatch. The dead-end phantom is fixed by making the real type exist.
options.technical: Amends D-AGENT-EXEC2 naming: ProcessAuthority becomes Authority (ProcessPlan and ProcessReceipt stay). Reopens the type-unification audit’s post-v1 note on typed handles, value form only. Facts stay facts (D-FACTMODEL1): Authority is ordinary data, no type selection, no dispatch. Narrowing is the only operation family (with/without). Construction keeps the ratified PascalCase convention from D-AGENT-EXEC2: Authority.workspace(...), not a lowercase namespace call.
options.code:
a :: Authority.workspace()         // proposed
a2 :: a.with(FS.Write, "out/")      // extend only within holds; else E0712
process.run("jet build", a2)
plugin.load("lint", a2.without(FS.Write))

options.name: Caps — match the marker
options.detail: Same one-type design, named Caps to rhyme with #Caps(...). Shortest name, already half-taught by the marker. The rhyme cuts both ways: #Caps narrows a static scope while the value crosses runtime boundaries, and one word for both may blur that line.
options.technical: Identical semantics to option A. Amends D-AGENT-EXEC2 naming the same way.
options.code:
c :: Caps.workspace()
process.run("jet build", c.with(FS.Write, "out/"))

options.name: Clearance — plain-word metaphor
options.detail: Same one-type design, named Clearance: what you have been cleared to do. Reads naturally in security prose and to newcomers. It is a fresh word with no anchor in existing Jet surface, so it adds a vocabulary item instead of reusing one.
options.technical: Identical semantics to option A.
options.code:
c :: Clearance.workspace()
process.run("jet build", c.with(FS.Write, "out/"))

options.name: Bespoke types per boundary
options.detail: Honor D-AGENT-EXEC2 exactly as ratified: ProcessAuthority for processes, plugin capabilities for plugins, session grants for the REPL, and the #Grant handle stays unnameable. Each boundary gets a type shaped for its job. Three shapes to learn, and narrowing rules are re-stated per type.
options.technical: No amendment. The phantom-type regression is fixed separately by scoping marker-argument names to marker positions (card #1501).

comparisons.note: One handle type with a rights mask; duplication may only reduce rights. One narrowing rule serves the whole OS.
Linear capability values threaded from main, no ambient authority anywhere. Proof the value form works in a language, unproven at ecosystem scale.
Everything the guest may touch is a handle it was explicitly given at instantiation.
comparisons.code: // no ambient open("/etc/passwd") inside the sandbox

recommendation.why: One type with one narrowing rule serves processes, plugins, and sessions alike, lands the ratified agent design as an instance, and turns the Capability dead end into a real, teachable thing. Authority is the plainest word for exactly what the value is.

whyNot.reason: Caps names the static marker; reusing it for the runtime value blurs the static/boundary line the model works hard to keep sharp.
Clearance is a good word with no anchor: it adds vocabulary where Authority reuses the concept the whole model is named for.
Three bespoke shapes re-state the same narrowing law three times and leave the phantom type a permanent trap to re-fix.

recommendation.tradeoff: Renaming ProcessAuthority amends a ratified naming ruling before any code exists. That is the cheapest possible moment to amend it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft posed one-type-versus-bespoke and a name menu, recommending one type named Authority.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass weighed Warrant, Permit, and Leash, folding them into C as the best fresh-word representative. A generic parameterized form like Authority[FS.Read] re-enters the withdrawn typed-handle design and touches the facts-never-dispatch wall, so it stays out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried one type with per-boundary aliases (ProcessAuthority = Authority). Aliases are exactly the parallel-spelling drift greenfield law forbids, so the hybrid was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave D its best case: boundary-shaped types can carry boundary-only fields without polluting a shared type. The answer, kept in A’s technical notes, is that boundary data rides the constructor rather than the type.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with dispatch creep and with revocation. Authority is data and never a dispatch input, and scope end already revokes while boundary values die with their boundary, so A holds.

decisions.title: One manifest schema for what a package may do and delegate
decisions.gist: How pkg.jet spells every grant the package makes.
decisions.lesson: Four separate schemas in pkg.jet answer authority questions: effects allow/deny, per-dependency grants, trust prompting (allow/prompt/deny), and provider allow/deny for package sources. Each has its own parser, its own malformed-block error, and its own documentation. They are one kind of record: this subject holds these rights, decided by this default. This choice decides whether the manifest keeps four spellings or gets one.
decisions.story: Sam reviews a new dependency for work. He opens pkg.jet to answer: what does this package let its dependencies do? The answer is spread over effects:, grants:, policy.trust, and policy.providers, each shaped differently. He wants one block to read top to bottom.

options.name: One authority block
options.detail: A single authority: block holds every grant the package makes: its own bound, per-dependency grants, trust defaults, and provider bounds. Old keys are migrated in one pass and deleted. A reviewer reads one block; the lockfile and the ledger mirror its shape.
options.technical: Amends D-EFFBUDGET1 (key spelling only; E1220/E1221 semantics unchanged) and D-JPK-POLICYSURFACE1/D-JPK-GRANTSCHEMA1 (trust and providers relocate from policy:). policy: keeps floors and unsafe mode. One parser, one malformed-block diagnostic family.

options.name: Keep keys, share the schema
options.detail: Every current key stays where it is, but all four validate through one shared record shape and report through one diagnostic family. Reviewers still hunt four places; tooling and docs get one model underneath.
options.technical: One internal grant-record type; E1221 and the two Bad*Policy manifest errors converge on it. No manifest migration.

options.name: Four schemas stay
options.detail: Decline. Each block keeps its own parser and errors. The next authority surface (agent workspaces, jetos app grants) adds a fifth shape.
options.code:
// Status quo, plus the fifth block that is already coming:
// agents: { workspace: ..., allow: ... }   // D-AGENT-EXEC1 will need a home

comparisons.note: All grants in one place (flags) is the readable part of its design, even where the grain is wrong.
One manifest block for all permissions made review a habit; scattered grant surfaces never became one.

recommendation.why: One block makes package review a top-to-bottom read, gives the coming agent and jetos grants a ratified home instead of a fifth schema, and lets the lockfile and ledger mirror one shape.

whyNot.reason: It fixes the plumbing and leaves the reader’s problem: four places to check before trusting a package.
It guarantees a fifth shape the moment agent grants land, which is the pattern that produced this ballot.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every in-repo manifest migrates once and external examples in docs are rewritten. Accepted: greenfield law prefers one canonical current form over parallel spellings.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one merged block, shared-schema-hidden-keys, and status quo, recommending the merged block for reviewability.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a separate authority.jet file and inline per-dependency grant blocks. The separate file splits the manifest story and was rejected, and inline grants were folded into A as formatting freedom rather than schema.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried A for effects and grants but leaving trust in policy:. That keeps two homes for allow/prompt/deny decisions and died on its own test: where would a reviewer look for service trust?
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the observation that it is zero-migration and fully invisible to users, now stated plainly in its detail. C gained its honest framing: it is the default outcome of doing nothing.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass confirmed that moving trust out of policy: amends the ratified one-policy-namespace ruling, and the ballot names that amendment rather than hiding it. Floors stay in policy: so tighten-only stays meaningful, and A holds.

decisions.title: One audit ledger for every authority gate
decisions.gist: Where the record of every granted exception lives.
decisions.lesson: A gate is any written widening of authority: an #Unsafe reason, a per-dependency grants: entry, an --allow flag, a trust grant. The ratified lint ruling already states the law for one gate kind: every bypass is spelled at the site and lands in the audit record. Today each gate kind keeps its own record: unsafe inspection, the lockfile, the trust file, session flags. This choice decides whether those records become one ledger with one reader.
decisions.story: An auditor gives Maya’s billing service two hours. Their first question: list every exception this system granted itself. Today that answer is assembled from jet unsafe, the lockfile diff, ~/.jet/trust, and shell history. She wants one command.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet inspect authority              # proposed
gates:
  src/dma.jet:41   #Unsafe "MMIO: board manual §4.2"  obligations: discharged
  pkg.jet          grants image-codec: FS.Read        lockfile: recorded
  build            --allow-net (jet build, 2026-08-06)
  user             trust grant build ./vendor-tool (2026-08-02)

options.name: One ledger, one reader
options.detail: Every gate kind records to one ledger and jet inspect authority reads it all: unsafe gates with obligation status, dependency grants, build and session flags, trust grants. The lint ruling’s bypass law becomes the stated law of every gate. Existing per-kind views keep working as filtered views.
options.technical: Generalizes D-LINTPOLICY1’s recording clause to all gates. Sources stay where they are (source markers, lockfile, trust store); the ledger is the merged, provenance-keeping read model. No new write surface.
options.code:
$ jet inspect authority --scope package
$ jet inspect authority --kind unsafe     # today's jet unsafe, preserved
$ jet inspect authority --json            # CI diffs the ledger

options.name: Ledger in artifacts only
options.detail: The merged record exists but only as a build artifact (lockfile section and receipts), with no new command. CI can diff it; humans assemble the story from files, as today.
options.technical: Same merged record, serialized into the lock and receipts. No CLI addition.
options.code:
# CI-only consumption:
$ git diff jet.lock   # shows new grants and new unsafe gates as diff lines

options.name: Per-kind records stay
options.detail: Decline. Unsafe, budget, trust, and session records stay separate with separate readers. Nothing new to learn, and the auditor’s question stays a four-source scavenger hunt.
options.code: $ jet unsafe && git diff jet.lock && cat ~/.jet/trust && history | grep allow

comparisons.note: Unsafe hygiene is culture plus scattered tools (Miri, cargo-geiger). No single ledger; audits re-assemble it every time.
comparisons.code: $ cargo geiger   # counts unsafe, one dimension only

comparisons.note: Grants exist only as the command line; nothing records what a past run was allowed to do.

recommendation.why: The model’s law has two halves and this is the second one: widenings are not only written at the site but readable in one place. One reader turns a scavenger hunt into a command and makes the exception list diffable in CI.

whyNot.reason: Artifacts serve machines. The human question — what did we grant ourselves — deserves a first-class answer.
Four separate records is how exceptions hide; the audit that motivated this found the trust store, budget, and unsafe views already disagreeing in vocabulary.

recommendation.tradeoff: The ledger merges records of different lifetimes (source, lock, machine, session), so provenance labels must be carried honestly. Accepted: provenance is exactly what an auditor needs anyway.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one reader, artifact-only, and status quo, recommending the reader as the second half of the bypass law.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested failing builds on unacknowledged new gates and a web view of the ledger. Enforcement is a later lint-style policy layer and the web view is presentation, so both folded out of this decision.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combined A and B: the reader consumes the same merged record the artifacts carry, so B is A’s storage half rather than a rival. The options were rewritten to make that explicit.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave B its best case (zero new surface, CI-first teams already live in diffs) and C its honest one (nothing new to learn). Both survive in their details.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A on privacy and staleness. Unsafe reasons stay package-local unless published and session entries carry their lifetime label, so A holds.

decisions.title: Retire the word capability from surfaces or reserve it for one thing
decisions.gist: What the word capability is allowed to mean in Jet.
decisions.lesson: The word capability means six unrelated things here: the unnameable grant-handle type, a marker-argument enum, borrow-diagnostic wording, the product claim manifest, the capability ledger card, and the remote-builder capability model. A word that means everything explains nothing, and two of the six sit in user-facing diagnostics. This choice picks one meaning or retires the word from surfaces.
decisions.story: Leo hits two errors in one afternoon. One says a value needs a write capability (borrowing). The other says his #Grant handle, a Capability, escaped its region (authority). Same word, unrelated systems. He searches the docs for capability and gets both chapters interleaved.

options.name: Retire from surfaces
options.detail: No user-facing surface uses the word capability. Borrow diagnostics say write access. The authority value takes whatever name D-AUTHORITY-NAME1 picks. The product claim manifest becomes feature claims; internal cards rename at next touch. Docs may still say capability-based when describing the design tradition.
options.technical: Diagnostic copy is snapshot-tested product text (I4): the &/^ wording change re-blesses those snapshots. No grammar change; no code identifier named Capability remains reachable by users.

options.name: Reserve for the authority value
options.detail: Capability becomes the authority value’s name (overriding the NAME1 menu) and every other use renames. The industry term lands on exactly the industry concept. The borrow wording still changes, and the word’s six-way history keeps echoing in old docs and searches.
options.technical: Binds NAME1 to the name Capability. Same renames elsewhere as option A.
options.code:
c :: capability.workspace()
process.run("jet build", c.with(FS.Write, "out/"))

options.name: Leave the word alone
options.detail: Decline. All six meanings stay. Cheapest today; the docs search problem, the interleaved chapters, and the double-meaning diagnostics remain.
options.code: // Leo's afternoon stays as-is: two systems, one word.

comparisons.note: Called its aliasing modes reference capabilities; the overlap with object-capability security confuses newcomers to both fields to this day.
comparisons.code: iso, val, ref  // "capabilities" that are about aliasing, not authority

recommendation.why: Retiring the word ends the collision at its root: each concept gets a word that means only itself, and the borrow diagnostics get plainer at the same time. Access is what & takes; authority is what a scope holds; neither needs the loaded word.

whyNot.reason: It rescues the word by spending it on one meaning while five renames happen anyway, and it preempts the NAME1 menu from inside a different ballot.
Six meanings in one project is a documentation and teaching tax that compounds with every new page.

recommendation.tradeoff: Searches and older external writing that say capability will not match surface text. Accepted: docs keep the term as a described tradition, so discovery survives.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft posed retire, reserve, and decline, recommending retire because both shipped diagnostic uses read better without the word.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested namespaced uses such as borrow capability versus authority capability, and rejected them because qualified jargon is still jargon in an error message. Product-manifest rename wording folded into A as detail.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested retiring the word everywhere except documentation titles. That is option A as written, since surfaces retire the word while prose may describe the tradition, so no separate option was needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: if the industry word must live somewhere, the authority value is its one honest home, and the option now says so plainly. C’s cost was restated without exaggeration.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A on discoverability for newcomers who search the word capability, and on snapshot churn. Discovery survives through descriptive prose and re-blessing snapshots is the normal cost of copy changes, so A holds.

decisions.title: One scope marker: #Caps absorbs #Grant
decisions.gist: Whether one marker or two set the rights of a block.
decisions.lesson: Two markers set what a block may do. #Caps(Net) narrows the block to a list of rights. #Grant(caps: FS) sets a list and binds a handle that ends with the block. Both check the same rule with the same names, but they use two spellings and two error families. This choice decides whether the two markers merge into one.
decisions.story: Ines reviews a teammate’s service. One function narrows with #Caps, the next grants with #Grant, and she has to stop and ask why. The answer is history, not meaning. She wants one marker whose one difference — a named handle — is visible in its head.

options.name: One marker, optional handle head
options.detail: #Caps does both jobs. A bare list narrows, as today. A name before the list binds the handle: #Caps(g: FS, Net). #Grant is deleted and every use migrates in one pass. One spelling, one error family, one thing to teach.
options.technical: Amends D-EFF1 (region form), D-SCAP1 and D-ARROW-CONTROL1 (the caps: head moves to a name head on #Caps). The handle keeps S63 scope-end revoke and E0711/E0712 checks; E0741 merges into the same check. REPL host gating keys off the same marker.

options.name: One marker, handle always bound
options.detail: Same merge, but every #Caps block binds a handle, named or not: #Caps(_: DB.Read). One form with no optional part. The common narrow-only case pays a head it never uses.
options.technical: Same amendments as option A. The anonymous head spelling follows the existing wildcard convention.
options.code:
#Caps(_: DB.Read) { db.query(id) }   // handle unused
#Caps(g: FS, Net) { backup() }

options.name: Keep both markers
options.detail: Decline. #Caps narrows and #Grant grants, and the two verbs teach the two directions. The cost stays: two spellings and two error families for one relation, and every reader must learn why.
options.code:
#Caps(DB.Read) { ... }
#Grant(caps: FS, Net) { ... }        // unchanged

comparisons.note: One operation — duplicate a handle with fewer rights — serves every narrowing job in the OS. One verb, learned once.

recommendation.why: Under the one law both markers set the holds of a block, so one marker is the honest spelling. The optional name head keeps the narrow-only case clean and makes the handle case visible at a glance.

whyNot.reason: A forced anonymous head taxes the most common case for a symmetry no reader asked for.
Two spellings for one relation is exactly the surface debt this proposal exists to delete, and the grant-versus-narrow story dissolves once the attenuation law holds everywhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: The word Grant leaves the marker surface, so the grant idea lives in manifests, flags, and the trust store only. That is acceptable because the block form never granted beyond what the outer scope held.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft posed merge-with-optional-handle, merge-with-mandatory-handle, and keep-both, and recommended the optional-handle merge.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a fourth shape: block-level effect rows (=[Net]=> on a block) instead of any marker. It was rejected because a row states a contract on a signature while a block sets a scope, and mixing the two spellings blurs where contracts live.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried keeping #Grant as sugar for the handle form of #Caps. Two spellings for one meaning is the drift this ballot deletes, so the hybrid died on its own test.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C: two verbs can teach direction, and its detail now says so plainly. It also strengthened B with the wildcard-head convention so the forced head is at least familiar.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A on REPL gating, which today keys off #Grant, and on migration blast radius. The gate keys off the handle head with no behavior change, and the migration is one mechanical pass over a small marker population, so A holds.

decisions.title: Where a bounded arena limit lives after memory keys leave #Policy
decisions.gist: How code declares: this function may allocate at most N bytes.
decisions.lesson: D-AUTHORITY-MEM1 chose option B: memory floors become effect denials, written =[!Mem.Alloc]=> on functions and deny: [Mem.Alloc] in manifests, and the memory keys leave #Policy. The ratified option text left one hole it named itself: arena_bounded(65536) carries a number, and denial rows carry none. Until the number has a home, the memory-floor implementation card cannot start.
decisions.story: Sam ships a firmware package for a device with 64 KB of spare RAM. The embedder asks for a written promise: this package never allocates past that line. Sam had #Policy(arena_bounded(65536)); after MEM1 that spelling is retired and nothing yet replaces it.

options.name: Parameterized denial row
options.detail: The denial row grammar gains arguments. A plain denial stays =[!Mem.Alloc]=>; a bounded one is =[!Mem.Alloc(above: 65536)]=>, and manifests write deny: [Mem.Alloc(above: 65536)]. One mechanism carries both the floor and the number, in the one place a reader already checks.
options.technical: The rights tree row for Mem.Alloc accepts an optional above: Bytes argument. The authority gate records the number in the audit ledger with the denial. Sema enforces the unbounded form statically where it can and the bounded form at the allocator, on every tier. The row rides the signature effect arrow, in the return position, never a line above the function.

options.name: A typed setting on the fact plane
options.detail: The bound becomes a typed build fact, arena_ceiling :: Bytes, on the settings plane the build/config law just created. The denial row stays parameterless. The reader must now check two places to learn one memory law: the row for the floor, the setting for the number.

options.name: One surviving #Policy spelling for bounds
options.detail: #Policy(arena(65536)) stays only for the bounded case. This reopens what MEM1 retired two days ago: the memory keys were removed from #Policy so that memory law has one mechanism. The friendly spelling returns, and so does the second mechanism.
options.code:
#Policy(arena(65536))
fn decode_frame(input: Bytes) => Frame { ... }

options.name: No declarative bound: an arena API in code
options.detail: The bound is not a declaration. Code opens a bounded arena and runs inside it: arena(65536).run { }. Simple and explicit, but a manifest can no longer promise a cap to an embedder, which is the case MEM1 exists for.

comparisons.note: Allocation bounds are values in code: a FixedBufferAllocator over a fixed buffer, like option D. Zig has no declarative package-level cap.
comparisons.code:
var buf: [65536]u8 = undefined;
var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&buf);

comparisons.note: The cap is an external runtime flag (-Xmx), not a fact the code carries. Nothing in the package declares it.

recommendation.why: MEM1 chose one mechanism for memory law: the rights tree. Giving the denial row an argument keeps the number inside that one mechanism, visible at the same line a reader already checks, and the audit ledger records it with the denial.

whyNot.reason: It splits one memory law across two planes, so the floor and its number live in different places and can drift apart.
It reopens the retirement MEM1 made two days ago and restores the second mechanism that vote removed.
It loses the declarative promise. A package could no longer state its cap to an embedder, which is the very case this law serves.

recommendation.tradeoff: The row grammar gains arguments, and every consumer of rights rows — sema, the gate, the audit ledger, reflection — must carry the number through.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a parameterized row, a settings-plane fact, a surviving #Policy key, and a code-only arena API, and recommended the parameterized row for staying inside MEM1's one mechanism.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a refinement-type spelling on the function's return type and a comptime assertion. Both were folded out: they state the bound where no embedder or manifest can read it.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested row-plus-API: the declarative row for promises and the arena API as its runtime enforcement. That is not a separate option; option A already implies an enforcing allocator, so the pairing was noted inside A's technical text.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: typed settings are real law now and give the bound a typed home with provenance. It still leaves the floor and the number in two places.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether above: opens the row grammar to arbitrary predicates. The repair is a closed argument list registered per right, and with that fence the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: A package deny is a compile-time prohibition for every effect
decisions.situation: A package may deny effects its code must never use, such as the clock or the network. Jet's checker enforces denials of memory use while compiling. Every other denial is caught only when the program starts. So the checker reports a file as fine, and the run then refuses it. The vote decides whether every package denial is checked while compiling; we recommend it is.
decisions.gist: Should the checker report a denied effect, or only the run?
decisions.lesson: A package can deny an effect, such as the clock or the network. Today the checker enforces only memory denials. Other denials are caught when the program is started, so the checker passes code that will be refused. This vote decides whether every denial is checked at once.
decisions.story: Ana's service denies the clock for reproducible output. Her editor and checker show no problems. The first deploy stops at start-up with a refusal she never saw.

options.name: Every denial is checked
options.detail: Each entry in the package deny list becomes a whole-program prohibition, exactly like writing -[!E]> on every function. jet check, jet build and jet run report a reachable use with E0749 and the call chain. E1803 keeps undecided rights and CLI --deny denials. Extends D-AUTHORITY-MEM1=B and D-MEM-FACTS1=B from memory to every root.
options.technical: Effects/Checks.jet:2316-2318 today turns manifest deny entries into memory declarations only. It widens to every denied right, with provenance naming the package deny. The E1803 gate already computes reachable direct effects before the run (Driver/Pipeline.jet:4197-4220), so no new analysis is added. Probe p3 (deny: [Time], time.sleep): jet check prints ok; jet run refuses with E1803.
options.code:
authority: { deny: [Time] }
// jet check: E0749

options.name: Only memory denials are checked
options.detail: Keep today's split. Memory denials are compile-time prohibitions; other denials are refused only by the pre-run authority gate, E1803.
options.technical: No code change.
options.code: authority: { deny: [Time, Mem.Rc] }

comparisons.note: forbid is a crate-wide compile-time rule that inner code cannot relax. https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/lints/levels.html

recommendation.why: A deny list is a promise about the code, not about one run. Checking it early gives one meaning and the exact call chain.
gains: One meaning for deny.
Errors arrive at check time with the call chain.

losses.loss: Tests and builds now fail on a reachable denied call.
losses.mitigation: The run already refuses the same programs, so only the timing of the report moves.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a checker that says ok to programs the run refuses.

recommendation.tradeoff: Stricter checks and builds, in exchange for one meaning of deny.

current.note: The checker passes this file. Starting it is refused because the clock is denied.

wild.note: A crate-level forbid lint is checked by the compiler across the whole crate. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/lints/levels.html.
wild.code:
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
// any unsafe block fails to compile

options.name: Every denial is checked

gains: The checker and the run agree.
The report names the call chain that reaches the effect.
losses: Tests and builds now fail on a reachable denied call.

decisions.title: Concurrency re-founded on the existing type machinery
decisions.gist: Whether the compiler tracks concurrent work with the type machinery it already has.
decisions.lesson: Jet tracks three facts about concurrent work: what state a task is in, what must still be done with it, and where its data may travel. Today each fact has private one-off code. The same three facts already have general machines: typestate, single-use obligations, and crossing checks. The unjoined-task check is a line-for-line copy of the single-use check. Protocols already compile onto typestate plus obligations. This choice decides whether concurrency moves onto those machines internally, with no surface change.
decisions.story: Maya drops a task handle in one function and a protocol handle in another. She gets a warning for the first and an error for the second, in different words. Both mistakes are the same: work she started was silently thrown away. She asks why the language treats them as different things.

options.name: One substrate for all three facts
options.detail: Task lifecycles become typestate rows. The join duty becomes the same obligation every single-use value carries. The five separate send-safety checks become one crossing plane. Every concurrency error then speaks one language. Nothing on the page changes.
options.technical: Phase A deletes task_lint_span, type_holds_task_handle, and PendingTaskSpawn.consumed in favor of the State.rs automaton and the D-LIN1 obligation pass. Sendability registers in FactRegistry as a plane. All knowledge erases before codegen: I3 and I9 are untouched, and all existing goldens stay green.

options.name: State and duty only
options.detail: Merge the lifecycle and join tracking onto typestate and obligations, but leave the five send-safety checkers separate. The twin passes merge. The crossing question keeps five vocabularies, and each new parallel surface still writes its own checker.
options.technical: Same phase-A deletions as option A, minus the FactRegistry plane. E1101, E1102, E1111, E1130, and the cell rules keep their own provers.

options.name: Keep the separate machines
options.detail: Status quo. Each concurrency feature keeps its private checker. The twin passes stay duplicated, and each new feature builds checker number six. The two copies have already drifted once: one is a warning, the other an error.
options.code:
h :: tasks.spawn(() => push_profile(user))
// stays L1101 (warning) while the protocol twin stays E0140 (error)

comparisons.note: Send and Sync prove crossing safety once, as knowledge on the type, and every API reuses them. Rust never unified the join duty, so dropped handles silently detach.
comparisons.code: fn spawn<T: Send>(f: impl FnOnce() -> T + Send) -> JoinHandle<T>

recommendation.why: The duplicate passes prove the general machines already fit. One substrate makes every future concurrency feature a set of table rows instead of a new checker, and every error teaches the same three words.

whyNot.reason: It leaves five copies of the crossing question, so the next parallel surface still hand-rolls checker number six and users still meet three vocabularies.
The duplicated passes have already drifted once into warning versus error, and every unbuilt ratified feature would deepen the divergence.

recommendation.tradeoff: A large internal migration must land with every test and golden held green. That is accepted: effort is expendable, and the outcome is one engine instead of ten.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared full adoption, a partial merge, and the status quo. It recommended full adoption because the twin passes show the machines already fit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a brand-new unified concurrency checker and a runtime-tag approach. The first is option C with more code, and the second breaks zero-cost erasure, so both were folded away.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid that merged state and duty now but staged the crossing merge later was tested. It re-creates the seam it deletes, so it survives only as option B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option C was strengthened: separate machines let one feature evolve alone without cross-plane review. That freedom is what produced the warning-versus-error drift, so it stands but does not win.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack targeted churn risk to shipped diagnostics and typestate fit for group lifecycles. Phase A holds goldens green and the group automaton has two states, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: What happens to a dropped task handle
decisions.gist: Whether dropping a bound task handle without joining it is an error, an automatic join, or a warning.
decisions.lesson: Under the proposed spawn surface, an unbound task joins at the end of its scope on its own. A bound handle is different: the writer took the handle, so the writer owns it. Today dropping it only prints warning L1101, and the program may exit while the task still runs. Jet already has a hard rule for values that carry unfinished work: a single-use value must be consumed, error E0140. That error names the unjoined task as its example. This choice amends the shipped L1101 rule.
decisions.story: Ben starts a task that writes a report to disk, binds the handle, prints a status line, and returns. The warning scrolls past in test output. In production the process exits first, and the report is half-written.

options.name: Dropping a bound handle is an error
options.detail: The join duty becomes the same rule every single-use value follows. Dropping a bound handle fails to compile. The fix text names the three exits: join it, use its result, or call detach for fire-and-forget. No work is ever lost silently, and the choice is always visible on the page.
options.technical: Extends D-LIN1 to Task<T> and to the list forms from D-VERDICT-1323-1. Handles consumed by all, race, or any discharge at those calls. Amends the L1101 behavior in the spec's task section. Unbound spawns are untouched: the scope joins them per D-CONC-SPAWN1.

options.name: Scope exit joins the bound handle too
options.detail: Dropping a bound handle means the scope waits for it at the end, the same as an unbound spawn. No error, no lost work. The cost: binding a handle then ignoring it silently blocks the scope, and the reader cannot tell a joined handle from a forgotten one.
options.technical: Bound and unbound handles behave the same at scope exit. detach remains the only fire-and-forget spelling. A failure from the implicit join reports at the scope end.

options.name: Keep the warning
options.detail: Status quo. The warning stays advisory, and a dropped bound handle still races program exit. The same mistake on a protocol handle stays a hard error, so the two rules keep teaching opposite lessons.

comparisons.note: A dropped JoinHandle silently detaches, and the must-use lint is ignorable. This is a documented community regret.
comparisons.code: tokio::spawn(async { write_report(report).await }); // dropped, detached, panic swallowed

comparisons.note: Spawning is only possible inside a nursery that joins its children, so lost work cannot be written at all.
comparisons.code:
async with trio.open_nursery() as n:
    n.start_soon(write_report, report)

recommendation.why: Binding a handle is a claim of ownership, so silence is the one wrong answer. The error reuses a rule the language already enforces everywhere else, and the fix is one visible call.

whyNot.reason: It erases the difference between a handled task and a forgotten one, and hides a wait the reader cannot see.
A warning lets real work vanish, and E0140 already names the unjoined task as the mistake it exists to stop.

recommendation.tradeoff: Fire-and-forget code must write .detach() once per spawn. That one visible call is the price of never losing work silently.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared error, auto-join, and warning for a dropped bound handle. It recommended the error because the single-use rule already exists and names this case.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added cancel-on-drop and process-exit-blocks-on-tasks as candidates. Both punish the common case to rescue the rare one, so they were folded into option B's discussion.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid making the drop an error in libraries but a warning in the entry function was tested. Two severities for one mistake is the current defect restated, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened: with unbound spawns already scope-joined, joining bound ones too is consistent. Consistency loses to legibility here, because the binding is the reader's signal of intent.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack claimed the error punishes quick scripts. A quick script writes the unbound form and gets the scope join free, so the error only fires where the writer claimed the handle.

decisions.title: How spawn authority may be written and passed
decisions.gist: Which positions may name a taskgroup, now that it is understood as a borrow of its scope.
decisions.lesson: A taskgroup value is the right to start children inside a scope. The board already rejected freely storable groups, because stored authority would let children outlive their scope. That rejection stays law here. Today a group may be a named free function's parameter, but the same parameter on a method hits a generic 'no such type' error. The model behind this slate says a group is simply a borrow of its scope. This choice decides how far the writable positions extend.
decisions.story: Ravi builds a crawler as methods on a Crawler struct. His free function drain(group: TaskGroup) compiles, but moving it onto the struct as a method gets 'there is no type called TaskGroup'. He cannot tell whether the language forbids it or forgot it.

options.name: Any borrow position, never stored
options.detail: A group parameter works on free functions and methods alike, because both are ordinary borrow positions. Storage, return, capture, and fields stay banned with the existing teaching error. Helpers can live where the code lives.
options.technical: Amends D-TASKGROUP-PARAM1=A by lifting its named-free-function restriction to all direct parameter positions, including method receivers' parameter lists. The storage ban and its E1110 rationale are unchanged. Spawns through a parameter group still own their captures.

options.name: Param-only, hole fixed
options.detail: Keep today's named-free-function rule exactly, and route the method-position case to the E1110 teaching family instead of the generic no-such-type error. Helpers that spawn must stay free functions.
options.technical: No amendment to D-TASKGROUP-PARAM1=A. Registration's owner-type gate keeps rejecting methods, but with the taskgroup teaching text instead of falling through to E0119.

options.name: Leave as is
options.detail: Status quo. Free-function parameters work, methods fall into the generic 'no such type' error, and the illegal-position list in the spec keeps omitting methods. The hole stays undocumented.

comparisons.note: A nursery is an ordinary object you pass anywhere, including methods. Scope safety comes from its lifetime, not from restricting where its name may appear.
comparisons.code:
async def drain(self, nursery, recv):
    async for job in recv:
        nursery.start_soon(self.handle, job)

recommendation.why: If a group is a borrow, it should work wherever borrows work. Methods are the natural home for code that belongs to a type, and the storage ban alone carries the structural guarantee.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a fence the borrow model no longer needs, so helpers must stay free functions for no reason a user can see.
A raw no-such-type error on a position the spec never mentions fails the rule that diagnostics are products.

recommendation.tradeoff: The parameter whitelist in registration grows one case and needs matching tests. Accepted: the structural guarantee never rested on the free-function restriction.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared extending to methods, fixing only the error text, and the status quo. It recommended extension because the storage ban alone carries the guarantee.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review re-tested the rejected storable-group design and a group-in-closure extension. The first stays rejected by ratified decision, and closures reopen escape, so neither entered the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid extending methods now and lambdas later was tested. Lambda capture is exactly the escape door the ban exists for, so the hybrid collapsed into option A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened: param-only keeps the whitelist tiny and auditable. That virtue is real but invisible to users who just meet a wall between functions and methods.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack tried to smuggle storage through method receivers on stored structs. Receivers hold self, not the group; the group stays a direct parameter, so no new escape exists.

decisions.title: How a program reads what happened to a task
decisions.gist: Whether task results and control state become typed enums instead of formatted strings.
decisions.lesson: A task ends one of four ways: it finishes with a value, panics, is cancelled, or blows a deadline. The runtime already knows which. Jet programs cannot see that fact directly: trace() returns the string 'paused=false,cancel=true' and exception() returns the string 'cancelled'. Select and the event system each carry their own separate outcome words. This choice amends the trace and exception surface ratified under D-COROUTINE1 and decides whether these facts become real values.
decisions.story: Ana cancels a slow worker during shutdown and needs to know whether it finished its batch or stopped early. Her working code compares a method result against the literal string 'cancelled' and hopes the spelling never changes.
decisions.inWild:
h.cancel()
if h.exception() == "cancelled" {   // string-matching a fact the runtime
    print("worker stopped early")     // already holds as an enum
}
print(h.trace())                      // "paused=false,cancel=true"

options.name: Typed outcome and status
options.detail: Two small enums replace the strings. outcome() consumes the handle like join and says how the task ended, carrying the value. status() borrows the handle and answers live questions: running, paused, cancel requested. Select and events adopt the same outcome words. The strings retire.
options.technical: TaskOutcome mirrors the runtime's existing result: Finished(T), Panicked(reason), Cancelled, DeadlineBlown. TaskStatus covers the control plane trace() encodes today. trace() and exception() are deleted, not aliased. One outcome vocabulary is shared with select results and the event dispatch states.
options.code:
h.cancel()
match h.outcome() {              // proposed: consumes, like join
    .Finished(batch)  => print(batch.count)
    .Cancelled        => print("worker stopped early")
    .Panicked(reason) => print("failed: " + reason)
    .DeadlineBlown    => print("out of time")
}

options.name: Outcome enum only
options.detail: The terminal outcome becomes a typed enum, but the live control strings stay. Cancellation queries become honest values while pause state remains a formatted string to parse.
options.technical: TaskOutcome ships as in option A. trace() keeps its current string contract; exception() retires into the enum.
options.code:
match h.outcome() { .Cancelled => print("stopped") }
print(h.trace())   // still "paused=false,cancel=true"

options.name: Keep the strings
options.detail: Status quo. Programs keep string-matching 'cancelled' and parsing key-value traces, and the four outcome vocabularies in the runtime, select, events, and user code stay unaligned.
options.code: if h.exception() == "cancelled" { print("stopped") }

comparisons.note: Join returns a Result whose error distinguishes panic from cancellation. Programs match on it; nobody parses strings.
comparisons.code: match handle.await { Ok(v) => .., Err(e) if e.is_cancelled() => .. }

recommendation.why: The runtime already holds these facts as enums, so this only stops hiding them. Matching an enum is beginner-friendlier than string comparison, and one vocabulary lets task, select, and event results compose.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the pause trace as a string to parse, so the control plane stays folklore while the outcome plane becomes honest.
String-matching 'cancelled' breaks silently on any wording change and cannot carry the finished value.

recommendation.tradeoff: The trace and exception methods disappear, and their few call sites migrate in the same change. Accepted: both appear only in one audit example today.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared full enums, outcome-only, and strings. It recommended full enums because the runtime already stores the facts this way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a single merged state-plus-outcome enum and a record type. The merge conflates a live query with a terminal consume, so both folded into the two-enum shape.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid keeping trace() as a debug-only formatter over TaskStatus was tested. It survives as a print of the enum, not a contract, so it needs no separate option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option C was strengthened: strings never break callers when new states appear. That forward-compatibility is real and is kept by marking the enums open for future variants.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack asked how outcome() interacts with the join obligation and double reads. It consumes the handle exactly as join does, so use-after-move already covers it and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: One answer to 'may this value move to another worker'
decisions.gist: Whether five separate send-safety checkers become one registered knowledge plane.
decisions.lesson: When data moves to another task, a parallel worker, or a graphics kernel, the compiler must prove the move is safe. Jet proves it five separate times today: task captures, parallel adapters, kernels, local cells, and pinned reactive boxes each have their own checker and their own error words. The stored fact is a bare yes-or-no flag on each local. The same mistake therefore reads completely differently depending on which door it walks through.
decisions.story: Omar wraps a counter in a closure. tasks.spawn rejects it citing sendability, para_map rejects it citing worker transfer, and a kernel rejects it citing a capture proof. Three vocabularies, one mistake: his closure grabs data that cannot safely travel.
decisions.inWild:
counter := 0
nums.para_map((n: Int) => { counter += 1; n * 2 })   // E1111 wording
tasks.spawn(() => { counter += 1 })                   // E1101 wording
#Kernel(.parallel) fn step() { counter += 1 }         // proof-record wording

options.name: One plane, one error family
options.detail: Crossing safety becomes a registered fact about a type, like its state or its unit. One prover answers every boundary, and every rejection speaks one language: what cannot cross, which boundary, and the fix. New parallel surfaces reuse the plane instead of writing checker six.
options.technical: Sendability moves from a per-local flag into the fact registry as a plane. The task, parallel-adapter, kernel, cell, and fixed-backing provers fold into one, absorbing E1111 and the kernel wording into the E1101 and E1102 family. Snapshots migrate in the same change. Ratified semantics from D-PARCAPTURE1=D and the kernel decisions are preserved exactly; only the prover and the error voice unify.

options.name: Merge the provers, keep the codes
options.detail: One internal prover answers every boundary, but each door keeps its current error code and wording. Users still meet three vocabularies; the compiler stops maintaining five copies.
options.technical: Same internal fold as option A. E1101, E1102, E1111, and the kernel proof keep their registered texts and snapshots.
options.code:
// identical rejections as today at each door,
// produced by one prover instead of five

options.name: Keep five checkers
options.detail: Status quo. Each boundary keeps its own checker and vocabulary, and the flag stays a bare boolean outside the fact registry. Each future surface adds another copy.
options.code: // the three rejections above stay three different lessons
