comparisons.note: One trait, Send, answers every crossing question, and every concurrency API composes with it. Nobody re-proves sendability per API.
Reference capabilities prove race freedom entirely in the type system, but six user-facing modes proved too heavy. The lesson: keep the guarantee, infer the vocabulary.

recommendation.why: One question deserves one answer with one voice. The registered plane also makes crossing facts nameable and reflectable, which the bare boolean can never be.

whyNot.reason: It fixes the compiler's cost but not the user's: the same mistake still teaches three different lessons.
Five drifting copies of one question is the defect this slate exists to remove, and checker six is already foreseeable.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rewording absorbed diagnostics re-blesses their snapshots and touches teaching material in one migration. Accepted: error text is product copy, and one lesson is the better product.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one plane with one voice, an internal-only merge, and the status quo. It recommended the full unification for the single-lesson payoff.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested exposing a user-visible Sendable-style trait and per-boundary capability annotations. Both add ceremony the inference already avoids, so they were folded into the plane's expert reflection story.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid unifying wording but keeping split provers was tested. Shared wording over divergent provers re-creates today's drift risk in reverse, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option C was strengthened: per-boundary checkers can tailor fixes, like the disjointness hints on group borrows. The unified family keeps per-boundary fix lines, so the advantage transfers.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack claimed one family flattens genuinely different failures, like view escape versus mutation. The family keeps distinct fix texts per cause; only the frame sentence unifies, so it survives.

decisions.title: Transaction commits: what the law says versus what ships
decisions.gist: Whether the transaction law is amended to match the shipped commit, or the runtime rewritten to match the law.
decisions.lesson: Inside a #Transact block, reads and writes to Shared values commit together. The ratified text of D-STM1 says the commit is 'retried on conflict'. The shipped runtime never retries: it takes all the locks in one fixed address order, applies the buffered writes once, and releases. Both designs are atomic and deadlock-free. They differ in one observable way: a retrying commit may run the block body more than once. Only the owner can pick which one is law, so this ballot amends D-STM1=A either way.
decisions.story: Priya transfers money between two shared accounts inside #Transact. Reading the spec's retry line, she adds a log line to count retries. It never fires, because the runtime runs her block exactly once. The spec and the runtime told her two different stories.

options.name: Law says: one run, ordered commit
options.detail: Amend the D-STM1 text to the shipped behavior: the block body runs exactly once, and the commit takes locks in a fixed order. Log lines never duplicate. Under heavy contention, transactions wait on locks instead of retrying.
options.technical: D-STM1=A's 'retried on conflict' clause is replaced by: participants sort by stable address, all write locks acquire together, buffered deltas apply, locks release. Body-runs-once becomes part of the ratified law. A future optimistic mode would need a new ballot.

options.name: Runtime learns to retry
options.detail: Rewrite the runtime to match the ratified text: run the block against a snapshot, validate at commit, and rerun the whole block on conflict. Readers never block writers. The body must tolerate re-running, so log lines may duplicate.
options.technical: Requires read-set tracking and validation on every Shared touch inside the block. The E0746 wall already bans irreversible effects inside #Transact, but reversible ones like logging re-run. The retry loop needs a starvation policy.

options.name: Amend now, keep the retry door open
options.detail: Adopt option A's text today, and record retry as an explicitly open future mode behind its own ballot. The law matches the runtime now, but the door stays marked rather than closed.
options.technical: Same amendment as option A, plus a recorded open question naming optimistic commit as a possible future expert mode.
options.code: // behavior today: identical to option A

comparisons.note: STM retries safely because the type system bans all side effects inside a transaction. Jet bans only irreversible ones, so logs and metrics would visibly re-run.
comparisons.code: atomically $ do { modifyTVar from (subtract amt); modifyTVar to (+ amt) }

recommendation.why: Body-runs-once is the stronger promise for an imperative language: every allowed effect happens exactly as written. The shipped design already delivers atomicity and deadlock freedom without it.

whyNot.reason: Re-running bodies makes logging and metrics duplicate, the classic reason imperative transactional memory failed elsewhere.
A door marked 'maybe retry later' invites code that hedges for both laws. If retry is ever wanted, a new ballot can say so then.

recommendation.tradeoff: Under heavy write contention, ordered locking waits where optimistic designs might scale better. Accepted: correctness of effects beats throughput of a contended corner.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared amending the text, implementing retry, and amending with a marked door. It recommended the amendment because body-runs-once is the stronger user promise.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested hardware transactional memory and a hybrid lock-then-retry escalation. Both inherit the duplicate-effect hazard and add platform variance, so neither entered the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid running read-only transactions optimistically and writers through ordered locks was tested. It splits one law into two observable behaviors, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened with its best case: read-heavy workloads never block. Even there, the duplicated-effect hazard remains user-visible, so it stands but does not win.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack tried a starvation case: many small ordered commits blocking one large one. Address-ordered acquisition guarantees progress and cannot deadlock, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Typed schedules, one job vocabulary, services on the substrate
decisions.gist: Whether schedules become typed data, jobs and tasks become one vocabulary, and services build on groups.
decisions.lesson: A scheduled job and a spawned task are the same unit of work started by different hands. Today the schedule marker parses its own private duration table, the docs and CLI present jobs and tasks as different things, and the ratified service plane is unbuilt. This choice decides three linked things: the schedule value becomes typed data on the one time rail, the vocabulary collapses to one word, and services build as supervisor tasks that own groups. The worker cap moved to D-CONC-SPAWN1; literal spelling stays with D-TYPE2-TIME1.
decisions.story: Sofia ships a nightly scraper. Her schedule line works, but jet dev, the future service runtime, and jetos each need their own reading of it, and the spec admits only one reader exists. When she asks what a job is versus a task, the docs give two answers.

options.name: Typed data, one word, services on groups
options.detail: The schedule value behind the unchanged marker becomes a typed value every consumer reads: jet dev, services, jetos timers. Hours and days work because the one time rail covers them. A job is a task the runtime starts — one vocabulary, finishing card 1448's cleanup. The service plane then builds as supervisor tasks owning groups, restart rules as data.
options.technical: The private suffix table in the schedule checker dies; the marker's value type becomes Duration or wall-clock time on the D-TYPE2-TIME1 rail. Amends D-SCHEDULE1=A's value grammar, not its placement rules. D-SERVICE1=D and its five sibling decisions build on the group substrate with no new mechanism. Aligns D-TAG-SURFACE1 and D-TASK-META1.

options.name: Typed value only
options.detail: The schedule value becomes typed and every consumer can read it, but the vocabulary stays split and the service plane keeps waiting for its own separate design pass.
options.technical: Only the value grammar of D-SCHEDULE1=A changes. Card 1448 and the service decisions proceed on their own paths.
options.code:
#[Job, Every(2h)] fn refresh_cache() { … }
// docs still explain jobs twice; services still unplanned on the substrate

options.name: Decline
options.detail: Status quo. The private suffix table stays and tops out at minutes, the two vocabularies stay, and the service plane waits.
options.code: #[Job, Every(120min)] fn refresh_cache() { … }   // 2h spelled the long way

comparisons.note: A semaphore-limited dispatcher bounds coroutines as data, not hand loops. Beginners reach for it because it is one argument.

recommendation.why: One typed value feeds every consumer the spec already promises, one word ends a documented confusion, and the largest unbuilt ratified block gets its foundation for free.

whyNot.reason: It fixes the table but leaves the naming confusion alive and the service plane without a substrate decision.
It keeps a duration table that cannot spell two hours, in a language with a ratified time system.

recommendation.tradeoff: The schedule checker and its errors are rebuilt against the time rail, and that work waits on the D-TYPE2-TIME1 outcome. Accepted: building it twice is the alternative.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the full adoption, a value-only fix, and decline. It recommended full adoption because the three pieces reinforce each other.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested cron strings, calendar rules, and per-job time zones. All are future value shapes the typed rail can add without new syntax, so the menu stayed small.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid shipping the vocabulary cleanup separately was tested. It is card 1448's existing path, so option B already covers it and no new option was needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option C was strengthened: the private table is tiny and shipped. Tiny is not the bar; it cannot spell two hours, and every future consumer would re-read a raw string.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack asked whether typed schedules break the wall-clock string form. The daily form stays as a typed wall-clock value with the same spelling, so nothing user-visible breaks there.

decisions.title: One lifecycle law for streams and tasks
decisions.gist: Whether a stream producer follows the same cancellation and cleanup law as a task.
decisions.lesson: A generator function yields values into a Stream. Its producer already runs on the task scheduler, pauses until the consumer pulls, and is shut down when the iterator is dropped. That shutdown law was written separately from the task cancellation law, in different words, in two decisions. The two implementations have already drifted: a field audit found the ahead-of-time build and the development build free the producer differently. This choice decides whether one law governs both.
decisions.story: Lena breaks out of a loop over a stream of parsed lines. On the ahead-of-time build the producer's cleanup runs as the spec promises. On the development build it does not. Nobody changed her code; the two builds carry two copies of one law.

options.name: A stream is a task
options.detail: One law: dropping the iterator cancels the producer, which unwinds at its next wait point running its cleanups, exactly as any cancelled task does. The generator decision's separate shutdown wording is replaced by a reference to the task law. The drift class dies by construction.
options.technical: Amends D-STREAMYIELD1's independent pull-and-cancellation wording to delegate to D-CANCELMODEL1=C: the producer is a scheduler child, drop-close is a cancel, yield is a wait point. Subsumes the open generator-lifecycle defect card 1392. Tier parity follows because all tiers already share the task cancel path.

options.name: Two laws, drift fixed case by case
options.detail: Keep the generator decision's own shutdown wording and repair the current build divergence as an ordinary bug. Future changes to either law must remember to mirror the other.
options.technical: Card 1392 is fixed against the generator decision's text as written. The two wordings remain authoritative for their own surfaces.
options.code: // same program; correctness depends on two texts staying in step

options.name: Defer until the defect closes
options.detail: Fix the build divergence first under the current wording, then revisit unification later with fresh evidence. The two-copies risk stays alive in the meantime.
options.code: // same program; decision postponed

recommendation.why: The producer already runs on the scheduler, so the unified law describes what the machine does. One law cannot drift against itself, and the open defect becomes a consequence instead of a special case.

whyNot.reason: Two texts for one behavior is how the current divergence happened, and nothing stops it happening again.
Deferring keeps the duplicate law alive precisely while the defect it caused is being fixed.

recommendation.tradeoff: The generator decision's wording changes even though its observable promises stay. Accepted: the promise is easier to keep when it is written once.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one law, two laws, and deferral. It recommended one law because the producer already runs on the task scheduler.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested making streams eager buffers and a dedicated coroutine object. The first changes ratified pull semantics and the second was already declined by the coroutine decision, so neither entered.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid keeping separate wording but adding a conformance test between the two laws was tested. A test guards drift but cannot remove its source, so it folded into option B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened: separate wording lets generators evolve without touching the cancel law. No such divergent evolution is wanted; parity is the requirement, so it does not win.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack asked whether cancel-at-yield could strand a producer holding a resource between yields. Unwinding runs the deferred cleanups exactly as task cancel does, so the case is covered.

decisions.title: Channels, draining, and select
decisions.gist: How Jet spells channels, draining them, and waiting on several sources at once.
decisions.lesson: Channels today live behind a module import. The receiver's type cannot be written in a signature. Draining a channel is a manual receive-or-break line users copy between projects. Waiting on several sources is a builder chain hung off a group, and it accepts a read arm that every build silently drops. Jet already has one branching shape: the arm table. This choice decides whether channels become plain builtin values and select becomes an arm table.
decisions.story: Kofi writes a worker that drains a job queue and also listens for a control message. He cannot put the receiver's type in his helper's signature. His wait code is a builder chain he re-reads three times to trust.

options.name: Builtin values, loop, arm-table select
options.detail: channel<T>() is builtin, no import. Draining is loop job, rx until the channel closes. select is an arm table that works anywhere in a task, on plain endpoints, with the same head-arrow-body shape as if. The arm binding mirrors the loop binding. Receiver and Sender become nameable. The builder chain, the dead Channel table entry, and the silently dropped read arm are deleted.
options.technical: Amends D-CONCSELECT1=A (the fluent builder and its read arm are replaced) and narrows D-TASKRUNTIME1's module surface. select arms are S68 arm-table arms. after takes a Duration literal on the D-TYPE2-TIME1 rail. Cancellation at a select wait follows D-CANCELMODEL1=C unchanged. Fixes the interpreter-tier select gap as part of the migration.

options.name: Fix the gaps, keep the builder
options.detail: Receiver becomes nameable, the drain loop lands, and the dead entries go. The builder chain stays as the select surface, still hung off a group, still fluent.
options.technical: Table and loop changes only. D-CONCSELECT1=A stands unamended; the read arm is deleted as a stub.

options.name: Leave as is
options.detail: Status quo. Receivers stay unwritable in signatures, the drain dance stays idiomatic, and select keeps accepting an arm that no build runs.
options.code: // the inWild example above remains the answer

comparisons.note: Ranging over a channel and a select statement with case arms are the two shapes every Go program uses. Both read as control flow, not as method chains.

recommendation.why: The two most common channel shapes become one loop line and one arm table, in the branching shape users already know. The surface stops lying about a dead handle and a dead arm.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the least readable part: a wait that is control flow, spelled as a method chain, reachable only through a group.
A signature that rejects a value users hold daily, plus a silent no-op arm, fails both the honesty and the teaching bars.

recommendation.tradeoff: select becomes a reserved word and a new statement form, with parser, formatter, and snapshot work. Accepted: waiting on several sources is control flow and should read like it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the arm-table redesign, a minimal fix, and the status quo. It recommended the redesign because both common shapes collapse to known forms.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested send arms, else arms, and receiver fan-out clones. All are real future extensions the arm-table shape admits cleanly, so they were noted for later cards, not packed into this menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid keeping the builder as sugar over the arm table was tested. Two spellings for one wait violates the one-mechanism rule, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened: the builder is expression-shaped and returns a value directly. The arm table is also an expression under S68 value arms, so the advantage transfers.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack asked how select interacts with cancellation and closed channels. A select wait is a wait point under the ratified cancel law, and a closed source arm stops matching, both already defined.

decisions.comment: This syntax is absolutely not valid, need a new ballot to ensure it is properly integrated with valid jet syntax

decisions.title: Shared values read and write like values
decisions.gist: Whether shared state drops its closure ceremony and becomes plain field access.
decisions.lesson: Shared<T> is Jet's one shared-mutation cell. Every touch today takes a closure: read with a lambda, edit with a lambda. A counter bump is a closure call. The compiler already knows which statements touch shared values, and the transaction machinery already orders locks. This choice decides whether shared access becomes plain reads and writes, with each statement one atomic step and #Transact for multi-step commits.
decisions.story: Noor keeps a hit counter and a config name in shared state. Her counter bump is config.edit(c => { c.hits += 1 }). She writes the closure dance so often she made an editor snippet for it.
decisions.inWild:
config :: Shared.new(AppConfig.{name: "jet-server", hits: 0})
label :: config.read(c => c.name)
config.edit(c => { c.hits += 1 })

options.name: Plain access, statement steps
options.detail: shared expr builds the cell. Reads and writes are plain field access. Each statement is one atomic step. Several statements commit together under #Transact. The closure forms are deleted. Expert guards and Condition stay for manual control. Race freedom does not move: the compiler still checks every crossing and orders every lock.
options.technical: Amends D-SHARED-API1=A (read/edit closures deleted) and D-TXN2 (the #Transact name becomes optional, kept for on_commit and on_rollback). A statement touching several shared cells acquires locks in address order, the same engine as D-CONC-STM1. Guards from D-SHAREDGUARD1 stay.

options.name: Keep the closures
options.detail: Status quo. The closure scopes the lock visibly, and nothing changes. Every read of one field stays a lambda, and the counter bump keeps its snippet.
options.code:
label :: config.read(c => c.name)
config.edit(c => { c.hits += 1 })

options.name: Guards first
options.detail: Delete the closures the other way: every access goes through an explicit guard binding whose scope is the lock. Most explicit, most lines. The beginner counter bump becomes three lines.
options.technical: guard_read and guard_edit become the only access forms; read and edit are deleted.

comparisons.note: Mutex access is explicit lock then plain field access on the guard. Explicit, but the lock call is the ceremony users complain about first.

recommendation.why: Shared state is the beginner's first wall today. Plain access removes the wall while the compiler keeps every safety proof: checked crossings, ordered locks, one clear multi-step spelling.

whyNot.reason: The closure tax on every touch is the single loudest ergonomic cost in this area, and it proves nothing the compiler does not already know.
It makes the simple case three lines to make the lock visible, which experts already have through the guards that stay.

recommendation.tradeoff: Lock scopes become implicit per statement, so a reader sees locking only at the shared binding and in #Transact blocks. The expert guards keep manual scoping available.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared plain access, the closure status quo, and guards-only. It recommended plain access because each statement maps to one atomic step the machinery already supports.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested an actor-style mailbox and a software-transactional-everything design. Actors are a declined mechanism, and whole-program transactions break the effect wall, so neither entered.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid keeping read for multi-field snapshots was tested. A #Transact block already gives a consistent multi-field read, so the extra form died.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened: the closure shows the lock scope on the page. That visibility survives in guards for experts, so the everyday tax still loses.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack hunted torn reads across two statements. Two statements are two steps by definition; the fix is the #Transact block, which the proposal teaches beside the feature.

decisions.title: The spawn surface: four spellings, or the ratified taskgroup block
decisions.gist: How Jet code starts tasks and fans work out.
decisions.lesson: Two ratified decisions, D-CONC-JOIN1 and D-CONC-SCHED1, already cite a spawn surface named D-CONC-SPAWN1. That ballot was never raised. The ratified D-CONC-GROUP1 blessed the older taskgroup block instead. The board now holds two spawn surfaces, and each one deletes the other's work. This ballot settles which one is law, so the concurrency implementation cards can start.
decisions.story: Rio writes a crawler. They want many fetches in flight with a cap of four workers. Today they import core.tasks, open a taskgroup block, and wrap every call in a lambda. They ask why starting work needs this much ceremony when calling a function needs none.
decisions.inWild:
use core.tasks as tasks
taskgroup g {
    a :: g.task => sum_range(1, 25)
    b :: g.task => sum_range(26, 50)
    results :: g.all([a, b])
    print(results[0] + results[1])
}
h :: tasks.spawn(() => work())
h.join()

options.name: Four spellings: task, all, race, any, group
options.detail: Starting work looks like calling a function. No import, no lambda wrapper. task f() starts one child. all, race, and any fan out and need no handles. group g(limit: n) covers dynamic counts with a worker cap. The taskgroup block, g.task, g.all, and tasks.spawn are deleted. D-CONC-GROUP1's law survives: a group may still be named in any borrow position, now as the Group value.
options.technical: task expr spawns a child of the current scope; an unbound handle is joined at scope end per D-CONC-JOIN1. all/race/any keep their ratified fail-fast, cancel-losers, first-Ok meanings. group g(limit: N) { } joins every child at the closing brace. Group can never be stored. Amends the spelling of D-TASKSCOPE1, D-NURSERY1, D-CONCCOMB1, and D-TASKGROUP-PARAM1; their laws carry over.

options.name: Keep the ratified taskgroup block
options.detail: D-CONC-GROUP1 stays as ratified and the proposal's spawn section is struck. Spawning keeps the core.tasks import, the taskgroup block, and the lambda wrapper. D-CONC-JOIN1 and D-CONC-SCHED1 must then be corrected, because their ratified text and code samples show the four spellings.
options.code:
use core.tasks as tasks
taskgroup g {
    a :: g.task => sum_range(1, 25)
    b :: g.task => sum_range(26, 50)
    results :: g.all([a, b])
}
h :: tasks.spawn(() => work())
h.join()

options.name: Handles only: task everywhere, combinators as calls
options.detail: One spawn form: task f() returns a handle. all, race, and any become ordinary functions over handles, not blocks. The grammar gains one form instead of four. The cost: race and any must not start work early, so their arguments go back inside lambdas, and every fan-out is handle bookkeeping.
options.code:
a :: task sum_range(1, 25)
b :: task sum_range(26, 50)
(x, y) :: all(a, b)

winner :: race(() => slow(), () => fast())

options.name: One keyword, nested: task, task.all, task.race, task.any, task.group
options.detail: Option A surface, spelled under one keyword. task f() starts one child. task.all, task.race, and task.any fan out with no handles. task.group g(limit: n) covers dynamic counts. Only task becomes a reserved word; all, race, any, and group stay free for user names. This spelling came from owner feedback on this ballot.
options.technical: Same laws as option A: scope-end joins per D-CONC-JOIN1, the ratified fail-fast, cancel-losers, and first-Ok meanings, and group joins at the closing brace. The parser reads task and an optional selector, so the grammar gains one head form, not four. Autocomplete after task. lists the whole concurrency surface.

comparisons.note: launch and async inside a coroutineScope block; children are joined at scope end, like option A's group.
async let spawns a child with no lambda; TaskGroup covers dynamic counts. Swift ships both, close to option A.
comparisons.code:
async let a = sumRange(1, 25)
print(await a)

recommendation.why: It keeps everything option A wins: spawning reads like calling a function, and the two newest ratified decisions keep their surface. It reserves one word instead of four, so all, race, any, and group stay available as user names.

whyNot.reason: It reserves all, race, any, and group as block keywords. Those are common user identifiers; any and all are everyday function names.
It keeps the import and lambda ceremony, and it forces corrections to two newer ratified decisions that already show the bare spellings.
Fan-out becomes handle bookkeeping, and race and any need lambdas again so they do not start work early. The ceremony returns through the back door.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every fan-out site pays a short task. prefix, and D-CONC-JOIN1 and D-CONC-SCHED1 need their code samples respelled to the nested forms.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the proposal's four spellings with the ratified taskgroup block and recommended the four spellings, because two newer ratified decisions already cite them.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a handles-only surface, which became option C, and a keep-both surface. Keep-both was folded out because two spawn forms for one job break the one-mechanism rule.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested four spellings plus a kept tasks.spawn expert call. It lost: task f() already is the low-level form, so the extra call would duplicate it exactly.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, whose block is explicit about scope and keeps ratified text, and C, which is the smallest grammar. Each still pays lambda ceremony at every spawn.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the four new grammar forms of A as scope creep against formatter round-trip and tier parity. All four lower to the same scheduler calls that exist today, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Task failure: the one ? rail, or a separate outcome type
decisions.gist: What a program reads when a task it waits on has failed.
decisions.lesson: Today a task failure hides in strings: exception() returns text like "cancelled", and a child panic can kill the process. The ratified D-CONC-OUTCOME1 answered this with a separate TaskOutcome type read through outcome(). The final proposal replaced that with a simpler law: join() is fallible like any other call, on the same ? rail every other error uses. The two answers delete each other's work, so one must win before the outcome card can be built.
decisions.story: Priya fans out three scrapes and one times out. She wants the other two results and a fallback for the third. Today she compares exception() against the string "cancelled" and hopes the spelling never changes.

options.name: join() is fallible: T ? TaskFailure
options.detail: One rail for every error in the language. join() returns T ? TaskFailure, so ?? gives a fallback and the arm table tells failures apart. TaskFailure is a normal enum: .Cancelled, .DeadlineBlown, .Panicked(reason). It converts up to app error families like every other error. trace(), exception(), and the separate TaskOutcome and TaskStatus types are deleted.
options.technical: all { } returns its tuple on the same rail. A joined child's panic becomes .Panicked(reason) instead of killing the process. Conversion rides the one rail of D-FAIL-CONV1. Amends D-COROUTINE1's handle surface and retires D-CONC-OUTCOME1's TaskOutcome/TaskStatus surface.

options.name: Keep the ratified TaskOutcome type
options.detail: D-CONC-OUTCOME1 stays as ratified: outcome() consumes the handle and returns a typed TaskOutcome, with TaskStatus for the running states. Failure reading is a second door beside the ? rail: results travel one way, task failures another. The trace() and exception() strings still retire.

options.name: Failure on the rail, plus a status() probe
options.detail: join() returns T ? TaskFailure as in option A. A non-consuming status() probe is added for liveness: running, paused, finished. Failure travels the one rail; watching a live task is a separate read. The probe is a second window onto the task, and supervisors are its only known reader today.

comparisons.note: JoinHandle.await returns Result<T, JoinError>; JoinError tells cancellation from panic. The same one-rail shape as option A.
try await task.value throws like any call; CancellationError rides the normal error path.

recommendation.why: A task failure is an error, and Jet's failure law says every error is one report on one rail. With option A the fallback, the arm table, and the conversion rules a person already knows all work on tasks unchanged.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a parallel concept beside results: a second consuming read with its own type, which ?? and error conversion cannot touch.
The probe adds a second window whose one known reader is a supervisor, and the service-plane cards own supervision. The core task type should not carry it.

recommendation.tradeoff: D-CONC-OUTCOME1, ratified days ago, is retired, and the outcome-card work already sliced against it must be re-sliced onto TaskFailure.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the ratified TaskOutcome type with fallible join() and recommended the rail, because it reuses the failure law instead of adding a parallel concept.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested exceptions, a status-code integer, and callback-style completion handlers. All were dropped: each is a second failure vocabulary that the ratified failure law forbids.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option C: rail plus a liveness probe. It stays on the menu because liveness is a real need, but supervision cards already own it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B, whose consuming outcome() is race-free and whose enum is honest. It still leaves the fallback operator and error conversion useless on tasks.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with a joined child that panics, which must become .Panicked(reason) on every tier instead of killing the process. That work equals what OUTCOME1 needed, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The select wait in valid Jet syntax
decisions.gist: How Jet spells waiting on several channels at once.
decisions.lesson: D-CONC-CHAN1 was ratified with a note from you. The direction stands: channels are builtin values, a loop drains a receiver, and waiting on several sources becomes an arm table. But the worked spelling in that ballot is not valid Jet. S68 law says if is the only branching keyword. S68 arm heads are values, patterns, or Bool expressions, never a binding paired with a source. This ballot picks the spelling that makes the ratified wait table real inside that law.
decisions.story: Kofi writes a worker. It drains a job queue, listens for a control message, and retries after 100ms of silence. He wants wait code he can read once and trust, in the same shape the rest of his Jet code uses.

options.name: select is the readiness table
options.detail: A new select table stands beside if. The if table branches on values. The select table branches on which source is ready. Each arm head is a binding and a source, in the exact shape the drain loop already uses. An after arm takes a normal time value. An optional else arm makes the wait non-blocking. The chain, the dead read arm, and the group requirement are deleted.
options.technical: Amends one S68 sentence: if remains the only value-branching keyword, and select is the one readiness table. Arm heads are binding, source pairs mirroring loop binding, source. after takes any Time delta expression (D-TYPE2-TIME1=A). else fires when no source is ready at entry. Expression position follows the if value-table law: arm results unify, or the table yields unit. select is reserved only at statement or expression head. Member and field names such as query.select() stay legal. A closed source stops matching. Cancellation at the wait follows D-CANCELMODEL1=C.

options.name: A Core function and the if table
options.detail: No new keyword. A builtin function waits on the sources and returns one event value. The existing if table then tells the arms apart. The event type names its arms by position, because a type cannot borrow the names of your local bindings. Every wait costs one extra line, and the arms read First and Second instead of jobs and control.
options.technical: tasks.select2, tasks.select3, and so on, one per arity, each returning a generated enum with positional variants plus TimedOut. after is a named argument taking a Time delta. The if dispatch over the result is ordinary S68. No parser or grammar change.

options.name: The readiness table rides subjectless if
options.detail: No new keyword. A subjectless if table whose arm heads are a binding and a source is the wait. A comma head can never be a Bool expression, so the parser knows this table waits. The table shape, the after arm, and the else arm are exactly option A's. The cost: an if statement can now block, and the reader learns that from the arm shape, not the keyword.
options.technical: Amends the subjectless table law (D-IFGUARD1): a table whose every head is binding, source is one atomic readiness wait. Mixing readiness heads and Bool heads in one table is a registered diagnostic. after takes a Time delta expression (D-TYPE2-TIME1=A). else fires when no source is ready at entry. Expression position follows the if value-table law. The whole table compiles to one wait, so there is no test-then-read race. select stays a free identifier everywhere. Cancellation at the wait follows D-CANCELMODEL1=C. A closed source stops matching.

options.name: Merge the sources, loop the result
options.detail: Waiting on several sources becomes stream composition. A merge builtin joins the sources into one stream, a tick source supplies the timeout, and the drain loop is the wait. Repeating waits read well. A single one-shot wait still needs the merge, a next call, and the same positional variant names as option B.
options.technical: merge(a, b, ...) yields a stream of a generated positional enum. every(duration) is a tick source on the Time rail. One-shot wait is merged.next() with a fallback. No parser change. The stream machinery follows the ratified stream lifecycle law (D-CONC-STREAM1).

comparisons.note: Go spells both common shapes as control flow. Ranging drains a channel, and select with case arms waits on several. Neither is a method chain.
Rust has no select in the language, so a macro fakes the table shape. The macro body has its own grammar that rustfmt and rust-analyzer handle poorly.

recommendation.why: One branching keyword stays the whole law. The wait keeps option A's table shape, named sources and all, without reserving a word or amending the S68 keyword sentence. The comma head marks the wait, and the arm head is the drain loop head, so learning one form teaches the other.

whyNot.reason: It reads the same as D but reserves select and adds a second branching keyword, which costs an S68 amendment for no extra clarity.
The arms lose the source names, an arity family of functions grows without bound, and every wait costs an extra binding line.
It answers a control-flow question with stream plumbing. A single wait needs a merge call, a next call, and nameless positional variants.

recommendation.tradeoff: An if can now block. The arm shape announces it, but readers must learn that one table form waits. Accepted: the shape is loud, the after and else arms flag it further, and the keyword count stays at one.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a select keyword table, an arity function family dispatched by if, and merged streams. It recommended the keyword table because the wait stays control flow with named sources.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested Bool readiness heads inside a plain if table and an alternation form in the loop head. Bool heads lie about atomicity and the loop alternation cannot format, so both were folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Option D came from your direction on this ballot: it merges the if keyword with option A arm shape. The comma head keeps the whole table one atomic wait, so the earlier atomicity objection does not apply.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B gained a named TimedOut variant and keyword arguments, and option C gained every(duration) ticks that make timeouts ordinary sources. Positional variant names remain the floor for both.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack on D asked whether a reader can mistake a waiting if for a testing if. The comma heads, the after arm, and the mixed-table diagnostic mark the wait, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Build/config: one plane of typed facts
decisions.gist: One model for build and config: typed facts on one plane, read by one parser.
decisions.lesson: One file, package.jet, is read by two parsers. The compile path reads the legacy flat vocabulary (payload:, effects:, build:). Tooling, Canvas, and migration read the ratified role-typed vocabulary (identity:, outputs:, policy:) from D-SHAPE5a/b. Fields the legacy parser lacks — outputs:, defaults:, members: — never reach the build. Every new config feature must pick a side and invent its own checking. This ballot decides the foundation the other D-CONF ballots build on: is configuration one plane of typed compile-time facts, or a separate world beside the language?
decisions.story: Ana maintains a web service. She writes her manifest in the ratified shape the newest docs show, with an outputs: block. The Canvas panel accepts it. jet build reads the same file with the older parser, which has no outputs: vocabulary, so her declared output never drives the build. She files a bug that is really an architecture gap: one file, two parsers, two truths.

options.name: One fact plane, one parser
options.detail: Adopt the model. Configuration is the program's knowledge about itself: every build fact (identity, machine, profile, settings, policy) is a typed value on one registered plane, with one contribution law and one audit command. The ratified role-typed Package shape becomes the only manifest vocabulary; the legacy flat parser is deleted. build.os, which already works this way, becomes the plane's first row. Later D-CONF ballots (fact reads, settings, contribution law) land on this substrate.
options.technical: Internal fact registry follows marker law zero (D-VERDICT-1455-1) and the type-v2 plane law (D-TYPE2-PLANE1): every fact nameable, reflectable, registered. Facts are comptime values; they erase at codegen, so I9 tiers see one folded program. S26 stands: a fact never creates or selects a type. Implements D-SHAPE5a/b and D-ECO-DECL1 on the compile path; deletes crates/jet-pkg-model/src/PackageManifest as a parser.

options.name: Port the parser, skip the plane
options.detail: Fix only the split: wire the compile path to the ratified Package parser and delete the legacy one. Do not register a fact plane. Settings, merge rules, and fact reads stay future one-off features, each designed on its own when it arrives.

options.name: A separate config language
options.detail: Give configuration its own small declarative dialect, the way CUE and Nix sit beside a host language. The manifest stays data with its own grammar, checker, and tooling, deliberately walled off from Jet source.

options.name: The build script owns config
options.detail: Zig's answer: make fn build(b: BuildContext) the one configuration surface and shrink the manifest to bare identity. All targets, profiles, and switches are imperative calls. Full power of the language, applied everywhere.

comparisons.note: Types and values live on one lattice; validating config is the same operation as type checking. Jet gets this free because package.jet is typed Jet source.
comparisons.code: port: int & >1024   // schema and value are one kind of thing

comparisons.note: One language for build and program — but the build graph is a program, so IDEs could not see the config without running it. Zig later added a serialized escape hatch.
Declarative manifest plus an escape-hatch script (build.rs). The split is sound; the failures are unreadable feature strings and unsandboxed script authority.

recommendation.why: A gives every current and future config feature one home: typed declaration, one contribution law, one explain command. The ratified precedents (build.os, D-MARK-SCOPE1, D-SHAPE5) already behave this way; A names the model they share and deletes the second parser.

whyNot.reason: B fixes today's split but leaves the next feature to invent checking and merging again. The two-parser split was exactly this pattern once.
A second language doubles what a user must learn and forfeits the type checker Jet already has. CUE's own lesson is that typed config wants the host checker.
An imperative script hides the effective config from every tool that does not execute it. Zig paid this cost and had to bolt on a data escape hatch.

recommendation.tradeoff: The fact registry becomes a load-bearing seam: every config feature must register a typed fact instead of hand-rolling a field. That constraint is the point — it is the same law zero the marker plane ratified.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the fact plane with a parser-only fix and a separate config language, and recommended the plane because ratified precedents already behave that way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added option D, the Zig-style build-script-owns-config answer, and folded a YAML-manifest variant into C because it differs only in grammar.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested plane-plus-script: keep the plane and let fn build contribute facts. That is already A's design (contributions are one moment on the plane), so no new option was needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B by scoping it as a shippable first step, and strengthened D by citing BuildContext defaults (D-BUILDCTX-FLAGS1) as its existing beachhead.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's registry as ceremony for tiny scripts. Rung-0 scripts declare nothing and read fallback facts, so the ceremony is zero until a fact is written and A survives.

decisions.title: Fact reads: $build.* opens the cage
decisions.gist: Whether a program can read its own facts, and what the read looks like.
decisions.lesson: Exactly one fact is visible to programs today, in one position: build.os as the subject of a #Known if dispatch (D-OSTARGET2). Everywhere else build is an ordinary identifier and the read is E0107. build.profile is ratified as not user-typeable (spec.md:813, D-CANVASSTATE1). So a program cannot read its own name or version, and the string drifts in source. The metaprogramming rethink (D-META-ONE1, S4) gives $ one meaning: read a compile-time value here. This ballot opens the record and picks the spelling, amending D-OSTARGET2 and D-CANVASSTATE1 by name.
decisions.story: Ben ships a command-line tool. His --version output says 0.3.0 while package.jet says 0.3.2, because the release script bumped the manifest and nobody touched main.jet. A user reports a bug against a version that does not exist.

options.name: $build.* — fact reads ride the one splice
options.detail: Facts are read with the metaprogramming splice: $build.package.version, $build.os, $build.settings.tls. The $ carries the compile-time meaning, so build stays an ordinary identifier — no reserved word, and a user module named build keeps working. One spelling covers compiler facts, identity, settings, and stamps, and it is the same $ a derive body already uses. Every read folds to a constant. Bare scripts read fallback identity (file name, 0.0.0).
options.technical: Amends D-OSTARGET2: the dispatch subject respells to #Known if $build.os == { ... }, and value-position reads become legal. Amends D-CANVASSTATE1: $build.profile is exposed. Rides D-META-ONE1/S4 ($ = read a compile-time value here); if the owner declines that law, option B is the fallback spelling. Reads fold before codegen; all I9 tiers see one program. The record is closed and documented.

options.name: Bare build.* reserved namespace
options.detail: The record opens without a sigil: build.package.version reads like any field chain. It is cleanest on the page, but build must become a reserved namespace, so any user module or binding named build breaks. Compile-time reads also look identical to runtime field access.
options.technical: Same two amendments as A. Additionally reserves build as a namespace (new cost; today it is an ordinary identifier per D-OSTARGET2).

options.name: No reads — keep restating
options.detail: Today's rule, kept on purpose. The manifest is write-only for programs, build.os stays legal only as a dispatch subject, and build.profile stays hidden. Version strings and switches are restated in source by hand or by release scripts.

comparisons.note: @import("builtin") exposes target and mode as typed comptime values; the @ sigil marks the compile-time boundary the way $ would.
env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") reads the manifest through a string-keyed macro; typos fail at expansion with no schema.
debug.ReadBuildInfo() returns version and VCS facts — at runtime, through reflection over the binary.

recommendation.why: A opens the record with the sigil the metaprogramming law already gives compile-time reads. The $ marks the fold boundary visibly, costs one character, and deletes B's reserved-word migration entirely — build stays an ordinary identifier.

whyNot.reason: Reserving build breaks existing user code to buy one character of cleanliness, and hides the compile-time boundary the $ makes visible.
Keeping the drift is a choice to keep a known bug class. Every peer language grew a read path because users need one.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every fact read carries a sigil, and the ratified #Known if build.os spelling respells to $build.os — a one-time migration of the one existing dispatch form. A depends on the metaprogramming $ law; declining it falls back to B.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a bare readable record with an explicit import and the status quo, and recommended the bare record.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a core.build import and a marker-demand-only spelling; both folded into usage patterns of the record, not designs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass ran after owner feedback pointed at the metaprogramming $ law: respelling the record as $build.* keeps the record and deletes the reserved-word cost. The $ spelling became option A; the bare namespace became option B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B (no sigil noise on every read; field-chain familiarity) and C (release scripts can inject versions via generated source today).
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's dependency: what if the metaprogramming one-splice law is declined? The ballot names B as the recorded fallback so the record opens either way, and A survives.

decisions.title: Typed settings replace feature and env strings
decisions.gist: How a package declares switches like tls on/off, and how code branches on them.
decisions.lesson: Build.{ features: [...] } sends strings to rustc as --cfg flags, but no Jet construct can read a feature, so the field configures nothing a program can see. Build.{ env: {...} } copies user strings onto the compiler's own process environment — the security audit flagged it as an injection path (rustc-build-profile-env-injection). This ballot amends D-BUILDPROFILE1 by name: both string tables are deleted. It decides what replaces them. The replacement block is spelled settings:, so the ratified noun Config (D-ECO-SLICENAME1, a typed contribution value) and the configs: field keep their exact meaning.
decisions.story: Cara ships an HTTP library with optional TLS. She declares features: ["tls"] the way Cargo taught her, then searches the docs for the Jet spelling of #[cfg(feature)]. There is none. She ships two nearly identical packages instead, and her users pick the wrong one.

options.name: Declared typed settings
options.detail: The package declares each setting with a type and a default in a settings: block. Profiles and the command line contribute values by the contribution law. Code branches with #Known if and the dead arm is not compiled, or reads the value as a constant. Undeclared settings are compile errors. features: and env: are deleted, which also closes the audited injection path.
options.technical: Settings are Tier-0 comptime values (Bool, Int, Char, String, fieldless enum) on the fact plane — the same value set D-GENMOD-VALUE1 ratified. #Known if folding on closed values is the ratified D-OSTARGET2 mechanism; no new dispatch is added, S26 stands. CLI spelling: --set key=value. The fact-read spelling ($build.settings.tls vs bare) is decided by D-CONF-READ1. Amends D-BUILDPROFILE1: the features and env fields of Build.{} are removed.

options.name: Readable feature strings
options.detail: Keep Cargo-shaped feature names but add the missing reader: build.features.has("tls"). No declaration block, no types, no defaults beyond absent-means-off. A typo in the string is silently false forever.

options.name: No switches at all
options.detail: Go's answer: delete features: and env: and add nothing. Conditional compilation exists only on the compiler's own facts (build.os, the machine). Libraries that want a switch split into two packages. Radically simple, and the audited hole still closes.

comparisons.note: Features are additive strings unified across the whole graph; the leaks across dev/build boundaries needed RFC 3692 to start fixing. Typed, scoped settings avoid the class.

Compile-time vs runtime config is a folder convention (config.exs vs runtime.exs); getting it wrong bakes secrets into releases. In Jet the boundary is typed: comptime facts here, core.env behind the Env effect there.
comparisons.code: # config/runtime.exs — the convention the type system never checks

comparisons.note: #ifdef branches on raw tokens before the grammar exists; every tool must run the preprocessor to know what a file means. #Known if folds on typed values after sema.

recommendation.why: A makes a switch a typed value with a home, a default, and an audit chain. The library-switch use case works with one package. The injection finding closes because no user string reaches the compiler's environment.

whyNot.reason: Strings keep the typo-is-silently-false trap and cannot carry values like a URL or a shard count. It repairs half the defect and keeps the other half.
It solves the security hole by amputation. The two-packages-per-switch world is the one Cara already lives in, and it is why Cargo grew features.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every setting must be declared before use, so a quick experiment costs one manifest line. That line is also the documentation, the type, and the default.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared typed settings with readable strings and deletion, and recommended typed settings because they close both the readability gap and the injection finding.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested per-file settings and dependency-set settings (Cargo's dep-features). Both folded into A: scope handles the first, and downstream contributions to a dependency's declared settings handle the second.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested A-with-B's spelling (typed settings, string lookup syntax). The string lookup re-opens the typo trap that types close, so it was rejected.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C with Go's record: build-tag simplicity has held for a decade. It also gave B its honest gain: zero manifest ceremony for the first flag.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's graph story: two packages contributing different values to one dependency's setting. The contribution law answers it — contributions carry homes, same-layer conflicts are errors, jet explain names both writers — and A survives.

decisions.title: One contribution law for every fact at every scope
decisions.gist: One rule for which written value wins when several places set the same fact.
decisions.lesson: Three ratified rules touch this today. D-MARK-SCOPE1: in source, the nearest scope wins for policy keys, and jet explain shows overrides. The Config composition law (ecosystem-shape; D-ECO-COMPOSE2 is the expert escape): unequal facts at one path are a hard error naming both sources. D-JOS-PRIORITY-SURFACE2: jetos option contributions are plain values unless an expert override adds a priority. Settings (D-CONF-KEY1) have no rule yet. This ballot sets one law for all facts and amends the composition conflict rule: across layers a deliberate override becomes legal; within one layer conflicts stay errors.
decisions.story: Devon sets metrics: true in the release profile. The fleet config pins it off for a canary group. On his laptop he passes --set metrics=true. Three writers, one fact. He needs to know who wins, and he needs the answer to be the same rule he already learned for #Policy.

options.name: Nearest in source, most explicit across layers, .Force pins
options.detail:
One law with two halves and one audited exception. In source scopes, the nearest scope wins — D-MARK-SCOPE1's rule, extended to all facts and to the full six-rung ladder: item, block, function, module, file, package. Across contribution layers, the most explicit writer wins: a profile beats the declared default, and a flag typed today beats every standing file. Two writers at the same layer with different values stay a hard error naming both sources — the ratified composition conflict rule, kept per layer.

At system and fleet layers, the ratified OptionValue override (.Force) pins a value against later layers, including the CLI, and jet explain names the pin.
options.technical:
Source scopes: item < block < function < module < file < package (innermost wins). D-MARK-SCOPE1 ratified four rungs (block, function, module, package); item (one declaration, the marker placement unit) and file (the #PubFile precedent) are added as a named extension. Contribution layers: declaration < profile < workspace < environment < system < fleet < CLI (most explicit wins); .Force at system/fleet outranks CLI.

Amends the Config composition conflict rule (ecosystem-shape law; D-ECO-COMPOSE2 escape): cross-layer setting overrides become legal; same-layer conflicts still error with provenance. The noun Config (D-ECO-SLICENAME1) is untouched. Keeps the D-JOS-PRIORITY-SURFACE2 surface unchanged. Safety facts tighten-only everywhere; no ambient contributions (D-BUILDPROFILE1 clause).

options.name: Numeric priorities everywhere
options.detail: NixOS all the way down: every contribution at every scope and layer carries a priority, defaulting by position. One uniform mechanism, but every user must learn the priority table before their first override, and everyday code grows priority noise.

options.name: Conflicts are always errors (the current composition law, everywhere)
options.detail: Extend the ratified composition rule unchanged to every fact: contributions must agree; two different values for one fact is a hard error naming both writers, at any layer. No silent override anywhere — not even a profile over a declared default. Every override becomes an explicit conflict to resolve by editing a file. This is today's ratified law for Config facts, applied to the whole plane.

comparisons.note: mkDefault (1000) and mkForce (50) are the priority spelling A keeps for system/fleet. NixOS's regret is not priorities — it is five parallel composition mechanisms beside them.
Order-independent unification kills the last-file-wins bug class, but plain defaults-then-override needs special defaults machinery even there.
Profile precedence is fixed and undocumented in places; there is no explain command, so effective values are folklore.

recommendation.why: A states as one law what Jet ratified in three pieces: D-MARK-SCOPE1's nearness in source, the composition conflict rule per layer, and D-JOS's audited pin. The beginner story stays one sentence: the value written closest to the act wins, and jet explain shows the chain.

whyNot.reason: Numbers in everyday code tax every user for a problem only fleets have. NixOS shows the table becomes folklore.
Extending pure conflict everywhere refuses the commonest act in configuration — a profile overriding a declared default on purpose — and turns it into an error to hand-resolve.

recommendation.tradeoff: The law has two directions (innermost wins in source, outermost-explicit wins across layers) plus one pin. That is three things to teach, softened because each was already ratified separately and one explain chain shows them all.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared nearest-wins, priorities-everywhere, and conflict-everywhere, and recommended nearest-wins as the generalization of ratified precedent.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested last-write-wins (rejected: ambient order, banned by D-BUILDPROFILE1) and per-fact custom merge functions (rejected: Gradle-shaped unbounded logic). Owner feedback then added the missing source rungs — item and file — completing the ladder.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced A's current form: nearness kept for source scopes, C's per-layer conflict rule kept within each layer, and B's priorities kept as the system/fleet pin only.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass rewrote C honestly as the ratified composition law extended unchanged, not an exotic import — its no-silent-override guarantee is real. It strengthened B by noting one mechanism is easier to specify than two.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's original framing twice: it called the CLI the nearest scope (backwards under D-MARK-SCOPE1) and pinned the amendment on the noun ballot D-ECO-SLICENAME1 instead of the composition law. Both are restated — two directions plus a pin, amendment on the composition rule — and A survives.

decisions.title: Settings and module value parameters: one substrate
decisions.gist: Whether settings and generic-module value parameters become one mechanism.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two features that accept the same five value types (Bool, Int, Char, String, fieldless enum), evaluate them with the same purity rules, and reject the same expressions. One is generic-module value parameters (D-GENMOD-VALUE1). The other is settings (D-CONF-KEY1). Today they are checked by two code paths and cannot mix: no fact is a legal value argument. This ballot decides one substrate or two, and names the two D-GENMOD-VALUE1 clauses that one substrate amends.
decisions.story: Elin tunes a cache per deployment. Her module takes a slot count: module cache<slots: Int>. Her package declares a setting cache_slots. She writes module tuned = cache<$build.settings.cache_slots> and wants it to just work — a fact is a value, and the parameter wants a value.

options.name: One substrate
options.detail: One value substrate: settings and module value parameters share one evaluator, one fuel budget, one diagnostic family. Nothing on the module page changes — cache<slots: Int> is spelled exactly as ratified. The one visible gain: a fact becomes a legal value argument, so module tuned = cache<$build.settings.cache_slots> works. Each profile produces its own cached specialization, and jet explain traces the value into the instantiation.
options.technical:
Amendment one: D-GENMOD-VALUE1's closed-expression rule extends to admit facts as value arguments. Today it rejects any non-literal reference.

Amendment two: the ratified [T#capacity] layout carve-out (S26/S76/D-FIXARR1) extends to fact-fed Int parameters. A build fact may size a fixed array, exactly as a different literal instantiation does today. A profile change produces a different cached specialization; the existing E0859 fingerprint path keys on argument values.

Unchanged: the parameter-list grammar keeps no defaults and no named arguments; defaults and names live at the settings declaration only. S26 otherwise stands: values specialize bodies and the one ratified layout slot, never type identity or dispatch.

Spelling note: the examples use the ratified D-GENMOD2 punctuation. D-CONF-GENSPELL1 decides the final spelling (<types>(values) and :: binding); this ballot is independent of that choice.

options.name: Two mechanisms, a documented wall
options.detail: Keep them separate on purpose: module parameters are code, settings are data, and never the twain. Facts stay illegal as value arguments, and module instantiation stays hermetic — a module's meaning never depends on who built it. The wall is written into the spec so the sameness of the rules is declared a boundary, not a seam.

options.name: Full syntactic unification
options.detail: Go further: the package itself is spelled as a generic module with value parameters, and settings are its parameter list. One concept on the page, but the whole ratified manifest surface (identity:, the D-ECO nouns) is respelled for no new power.

comparisons.note: Functors are the ancestor of D-GENMOD; nobody feeds build config into them because the build system is a separate world. Jet can close that gap.
comparisons.code: module Tuned = Cache(struct let slots = 64 end)

comparisons.note: comptime values flow freely from build options into generic code — the composition A wants — because there is one value world.

recommendation.why: The rule sets are already identical; A makes the identity real and buys composition — facts flow into modules, and explain chains reach instantiations. One diagnostic family teaches both features, and both amendments are small and named.

whyNot.reason: The wall preserves two copies of one rule set and forbids the composition users will ask for first. A coincidence this exact is a seam.
It respells the ratified D-ECO manifest surface for zero new capability. The unification A buys is semantic, not orthographic.

recommendation.tradeoff: Instantiation errors can now involve facts, so diagnostics must name the contributing home in the message, and a fact-sized [T#capacity] layout can change between profiles. Both costs are visible in jet explain, but they are real.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared unification with a documented wall and recommended unification because the two rule sets are already identical.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added option C, the full syntactic merge, found while testing how far the identity extends. It also tested facts-in-type-position and rejected it against S26 without balloting.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested A-plus-C for new packages only. Two manifest spellings for one ecosystem violates one-mechanism (I8), so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: hermetic instantiation is a real guarantee — a module's meaning never depends on the build that ran it. Owner feedback drove a clarity rewrite: the lesson now states the unification in plain terms and the example uses the $ fact-read spelling.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass surfaced two silent amendments the first draft skipped: the closed-expression rule and the [T#capacity] layout carve-out reaching facts. Both are now named in A's technical text with the fingerprint answer, and A survives with the amendments owned.

decisions.title: Provenance facts: a binary names its own build
decisions.gist: Whether a binary can name the exact source and toolchain that built it.
decisions.lesson: No comptime path exists for build provenance. A program cannot learn the git commit or toolchain that built it, so crash reports carry only a hand-maintained version string. Comptime inputs are closed today to embed_file/embed_bytes (D-CTIO1) and find (D-CTFIND1/2, Tier 1 under D-CTEFFECT1). This ballot proposes, as a named amendment to that closed input list, one more Tier-1 locked input: the repository state. It also decides what stays out for reproducibility.
decisions.story: Fatima runs three replicas of a service. A crash report says version 3.0.0. Two commits shipped under 3.0.0 last week because a hotfix did not bump the version. She bisects blind between them at 2am.

options.name: Source and toolchain stamps, no timestamp
options.detail: Two facts join the plane: build.stamp.git (the commit hash, -dirty suffixed for an unclean tree, absent outside a repository) and build.stamp.toolchain (the jet version). Each read is recorded in .jet/lock, so a --locked rebuild reprints the same stamp. A build timestamp is deliberately absent: wall-clock time is not a fact about the source, and the lock cannot pin it.
options.technical: Amends the closed comptime-input list (D-CTIO1/D-CTFIND1/2 family): the repository state becomes a Tier-1 locked input under D-CTEFFECT1 — hashed, recorded in .jet/lock, reproducible from the lock; never Tier 2, never #Impure. build.stamp.git is a String? fact; optional facts are readable on the plane but are not legal module value arguments, so D-GENMOD-VALUE1's Tier-0 set is unchanged. build.stamp.toolchain is a String fact.

options.name: Stamps plus a lock-pinned timestamp
options.detail: Everything in A, plus build.stamp.at: a timestamp captured once when the lock is written and replayed from the lock afterward. Rebuilds stay reproducible because the value comes from the lock, not the clock — but the fact describes the lock file's history, not the source.
options.code:
print("built {build.stamp.at}")   // when the lock was cut,
// not when this binary was built — a fact that lies politely

options.name: No stamp facts
options.detail: Provenance stays a tooling concern: jet inspect names the commit and toolchain from the lock and receipts, but no program can read them. Crash banners keep hand-maintained strings, and the 2am bisection stays blind. The comptime input list stays exactly as ratified.

comparisons.note: Stamps vcs.revision into every binary by default; the ecosystem treats it as table stakes for operations.
No first-party answer; the vergen build script fills the gap with env-var stringly plumbing.
SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH exists because timestamps are the classic reproducibility leak — the reason A excludes them.

recommendation.why: A gives crash reports and support tooling the one fact they need — which source built this binary — while keeping the same-input-same-binary law intact. The dirty suffix keeps the stamp honest during development.

whyNot.reason: A pinned timestamp is a fact about the lock file, not the source. It answers no question bisection asks and invites time-based logic that reproducibility forbids.
Provenance only an operator can query never reaches the crash report, which is where Fatima meets it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The ratified comptime input list grows by one entry, and builds outside a repository read an absent value, so banner code handles the missing case once with ??.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared stamps-without-timestamp, stamps-with-timestamp, and tooling-only provenance, and recommended the first for reproducibility.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested richer stamps (branch name, remote URL, builder identity) and folded them out: branch and remote are mutable labels, and builder identity is a receipt concern (D-ECO-RECEIPTSTORE1).
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested A plus an opt-in timestamp behind a flag. A flag that breaks reproducibility when set is a trap with a switch, so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C: receipts (ratified, unbuilt) will carry full provenance for operators regardless, and C alone leaves the ratified comptime input list untouched.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass caught the first draft calling stamps Tier-0 while D-CTEFFECT1 makes ambient reads tiered; A now names the amendment and places stamps at Tier 1, locked like find. It also caught String? against the Tier-0 value set, answered by barring optional facts from module arguments, and A survives as restated.

decisions.title: One meaning for the word profile
decisions.gist: End the name clash: profile names four ratified things today.
decisions.lesson: Four ratified features share one word, across five surfaces. Build profiles are optimize bundles (release, debug, ci) behind --profile and its sugar --release (D-BUILDPROFILE1). TargetProfile (crates/jet-foundation/src/TargetProfile.rs:12) is a board/triple machine identity for firmware builds — internal, its user surface deliberately unbuilt. Environment profiles own the profiles: field (D-ENV-PROFILE1) plus --env-profile and an env-namespace --profile flag (D-ENV-FACET1). Package and user profiles share a generation engine (D-JPK-PROFILE1). This ballot decides which meaning keeps the word, and what the others are called.
decisions.story: Gus builds firmware for a sensor board. He reads about build profiles in the CLI help and meets target profile in the freestanding docs (D-WD11). He guesses jet build --profile=board.sensor_v1, gets E1219 unknown profile, and files a docs bug that is really a naming bug — the word taught him the wrong flag.

options.name: Profile means the optimize bundle; the rest are renamed
options.detail: release, debug, and ci keep the word, matching --profile and its ratified sugar --release. The board identity is a machine description; before its unbuilt surface ships, it is renamed into the machine vocabulary and selected beside triples with --target. Environment profiles become presets (amends D-ENV-PROFILE1's field and flag spelling). Package/user profiles are already generation snapshots and take the generation word (amends D-JPK-PROFILE1's wording only). Each rename is an amendment named here; none changes behavior.
options.technical: TargetProfile renames into the machine axis (--target=<triple|board>), not the targets: manifest field (artifact kinds, D-TGT1-4) and not build-graph targets (D-BUILDTARGET1) — those two keep their own words, and E1216 stays as-is. The board surface is unbuilt (TargetProfile.rs:3-4 defers user diagnostics to a follow-up surface ballot), so this rename lands before any user meets the old name. D-ENV-PROFILE1: profiles: becomes presets:. D-ENV-FACET1: --env-profile and the env-namespace --profile flag become --preset. D-JPK-PROFILE1: prose adopts generation.

options.name: Machines keep profile; bundles become modes
options.detail: The firmware side takes the word when its surface ships; release and debug become modes with a --mode flag. The unbuilt concept gets the word, and the common ratified surface is respelled — including the --release sugar for --profile=release.

options.name: Keep all four meanings
options.detail: Do nothing. Docs disambiguate with build profile, target profile, environment profile, and package profile on every mention, and E1219 keeps catching the crossover guess at run time instead of the vocabulary preventing it.

comparisons.note: Profiles are exclusively optimize bundles; targets are exclusively machines. The clean split is why nobody confuses them.

recommendation.why: A gives each question one word: profile answers how hard to optimize, target answers what machine, preset answers which environment. It keeps the ratified --profile/--release surface unchanged and renames the three others while two of them have no shipped user surface to break.

whyNot.reason: It respells the common ratified surface (--profile=release, --release) to hand the word to a surface that has not shipped.
The clash keeps generating the exact error Gus hit, and every doc pays a four-way disambiguation tax forever.

recommendation.tradeoff: Four amendments land at once (TargetProfile, D-ENV-PROFILE1, D-ENV-FACET1, D-JPK-PROFILE1 wording), and board names join triples under one --target flag, so that flag accepts two name shapes for one question.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft treated this as a two-meaning clash (bundles vs boards) and recommended renaming the board side to target.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass found the clash is four-way across five surfaces, not two-way: environment profiles hold profiles: (D-ENV-PROFILE1) plus two selection flags (D-ENV-FACET1), and package/user profiles (D-JPK-PROFILE1) also hold the word. A was widened to rename all of them, each as a named amendment.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested renaming only the board side and leaving environment profiles alone. That leaves profiles: in env modules one field away from build profiles, so the four-way fix was kept.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C: E1219 does catch the crossover today with a real diagnostic, and the board surface being unbuilt means the collision is mostly latent. It strengthened B by noting mode is Xcode's word for the same bundle.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's flag sharing: --target must tell a board name from a triple, and no manifest declares boards today. Sequencing answers it — the board surface is unbuilt, so its follow-up ballot defines the declared home and name shapes, and the rename lands before anything breaks.

decisions.title: The manifest vocabulary
decisions.gist: What the fields of package.jet are called, judged as one coherent set.
decisions.lesson: The manifest's field names grew in layers and it shows. Identity alone has three live spellings: the legacy payload: block, the ratified identity: .{ } wrapper (D-SHAPE5a/b), and bare name:/version: lines (examples/jetpack/epoch5/package.jet). The corelib doctrine (D-CORE-DOCTRINE1) gives the yardstick: plain words, zero-config defaults, no wrapper ceremony. This ballot picks the whole vocabulary as one set, so every field is judged with its neighbors, not renamed one at a time.
decisions.story: Priya opens her first package.jet after a jet init. She wants to bump the version. Today the answer depends on which parser her tools use: payload: { version: }, identity: .{ version: }, or version: — three spellings for one fact, and the docs show all three.
decisions.inWild:
// three live spellings of one fact today
payload: { name: "aviary", version: "0.4.1" }      // legacy parser
identity: .{ name: "aviary", version: "0.4.1" }    // D-SHAPE5 wrapper
name: "aviary"                                      // epoch5 example, bare
version: "0.4.1"

options.name: Bare identity, ratified nouns
options.detail: name: and version: sit at the top level with no wrapper — the two facts every reader wants first, spelled with zero ceremony. The block nouns keep the ratified vocabulary where it wins: deps:, outputs:, settings:, build:, policy:, members:. The identity: wrapper is deleted. One manifest reads top to bottom: who I am, what I need, what I make, how I am tuned.
options.technical: Amends D-SHAPE5a/b's field list: identity: .{ } is removed; bare name:/version: (already parsed, epoch5 path) become the only spelling. All other ratified block nouns keep their D-SHAPE5/D-ECO decision IDs unchanged.

options.name: Keep the identity wrapper
options.detail: The ratified D-SHAPE5 shape as written: identity: .{ name, version } groups the who-am-I facts in one typed block, symmetric with every other role block. The manifest is a record of records, uniform but one level deeper for the two most-read fields.

options.name: One Package literal
options.detail: Implement D-ECO-DECL1's normative-future spelling now: the whole manifest is one typed value, Package.{ ... }. Maximum honesty — the file is literally a Jet expression — at the cost of one indent level everywhere and a wrapper around the entire file.
options.technical: Implements D-ECO-DECL1 (ratified as future source behavior) as the present spelling. The file is one expression; a manifest error is a plain type error on a Package literal.

options.name: Verb scheme
options.detail: Rename the block nouns to reading verbs: needs: for dependencies, makes: for outputs, keeps settings:/build:/policy:. The file reads as a sentence — birdfeed needs httpkit, makes serve. Friendlier first read; breaks from the ratified D-ECO noun set and from what peer tools call these things.

comparisons.note: [package] wraps name/version in a section — the wrapper B keeps. Nobody reads it aloud; tools and humans both say name and version.
go.mod is bare directives, no wrapper at all — the shape A takes for identity.
build.zig.zon is one anonymous struct literal — option C's shape.

recommendation.why: A puts the two facts everyone reads at the top with zero ceremony and keeps every ratified noun that already earns its place. The manifest reads top to bottom as who I am, what I need, what I make, how I am tuned.
