options.technical: A code { … } block is a first-class comptime value of a code type. It composes, so a helper function can return one. This is the quotation form used by Scala 3 and Template Haskell. It sits close to a stage type, which S26 does not currently name.

options.name: Keep strings
options.detail: Leave emit() as it is. Nothing breaks, and the mechanism is already shipped and understood. Every derive author keeps doubling braces, keeps writing quotes inside quotes, and keeps finding mistakes only when someone uses the derive.
options.technical: The re-lex and re-parse path at Bundle.rs:1654-1697 stays, with E2710 as the failure mode. The second splice implementation in apply_dollar_splices stays beside Expr::ComptimeSplice.

options.name: Generic modules do the job
options.detail: Delete derives and express the same work as generic modules, which already take parameters and already hold real code. This removes a mechanism instead of improving one. It cannot read a type's shape, so it cannot replace #Codable.
options.technical: A generic module is parameterised by types and values, never by a type's field list. Making it read TypeInfo would turn it into a derive under another name.

comparisons.note: String mixins let you build source by joining text. Errors point into the joined result, and tools cannot see inside until it is already text.
Scala 2 macros were untyped and unsound. Scala 3 replaced them with typed quotation, which is option B's shape.
A macro returns a syntax tree, not text, so Xcode shows the expansion inline.

recommendation.why: Option A gives every benefit the string form lacks and adds no new concept. The body is code, so the parser, formatter, and editor already know what to do. It also deletes the second splice implementation and the E2710 error class.

whyNot.reason: It adds a code value and moves close to a stage type. A block of items covers both derives and b.generate, so nothing needs a first-class value yet.
Doubling every brace is a tax on every derive author, and the mistake is found by the user of the derive, not its writer.
A generic module cannot read a type's field list, so it cannot express #Codable. Deleting derives would remove capability.

recommendation.tradeoff: A derive body can no longer generate arbitrary text, so a generator that assembles code from a data file must produce items rather than characters. That is the intended limit, and it is what makes the body checkable.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared real code against strings and recommended real code, because a string is only checked when someone uses it.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the nestable code block and the delete-derives option. It also tested a text form with checked interpolation, which was folded into option C.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review asked whether option B could ship later on top of option A. It can, because a code value is an extension of an item template, not a different design.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting that emit is shipped, understood, and covered on every execution tier today.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested code that must be built from a schema file at build time. Option A handles it by generating items in a loop, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.comment: Both option A and b. A is the simple case, b is the expert case

decisions.title: What a user-written rule may do
decisions.gist: How much power a rule written by a user gets, compared with a rule written by the compiler.
decisions.lesson: A marker applies one named rule to the next thing you write. Today the compiler owns 99 of them and a user owns none, except through a derive, which only works on types and only adds methods. This choice decides what a user-written rule may do: record a fact, add code, or both, and at which sites.
decisions.story: Ravi runs a platform team. Every service function that touches the network must carry a timeout. He can check this in the build entry, but only at the root, and the error points at a function far from the rule. He wants the rule to sit on the function it governs.

options.name: Rules may record facts and add code
options.detail: A user declares a rule with a signature and legal sites, exactly like a compiler rule. A rule with no body records a fact. A rule with a body adds code. This is the same power the compiler has, so #Codable and #Inline stop being special.
options.technical: The four checks of D-MARK-FORM1 run unchanged against the declaration. Law 1 still holds: a rule adds items and facts, and can never change or shadow what the user wrote. Additive-only is checked, not trusted, as D-BUILDGEN1 already requires.

options.name: Rules may record facts and reject code
options.detail: A user rule can record a fact and raise a diagnostic, but never add code. This gives Ravi his timeout rule at the right site with a good error. Nobody can generate code, so #Codable stays a compiler feature and boilerplate stays hand-written.
options.technical: This is D-METADEPTH2's read-only enforcement moved from the build entry down to the attachment site. The diagnostic API keeps the code, what, why, and fix shape that I4 requires.

options.name: Types only, as today
options.detail: Keep the current rule. A user rule is a derive: it attaches to a type and adds methods. Functions, fields, blocks, and files stay closed. This is the smallest change and keeps every current guarantee. Ravi's rule stays in the build entry.
options.technical: known_derive_names stays the only dynamic half of the marker vocabulary, as it is today at Bundle.rs:1234-1239.

options.name: Nothing: the compiler owns every rule
options.detail: Close the door fully and delete user derives too. The vocabulary becomes one closed table with no exceptions, which is the simplest thing to audit. Every library that needs a rule must ship a build entry or a patch, and #Codable-style boilerplate stays a compiler privilege.
options.technical: This retires D-METADERIVE1 and the reserved D-CTMARKER1 door. The registry becomes fully static, so the CI drift guards in D-VERDICT-1455-1 get simpler.

comparisons.note: A derive macro is the successful case because its scope is closed: input is a type, output is an impl. An attribute macro can rewrite the function it sits on, and reading the code no longer tells you what runs.
An annotation processor may add new files and may never change the annotated class. That rule is why reading a Java class is still reliable.
A source generator adds a partial class. The author must open the seam with the partial keyword, so the extension is never a surprise.

recommendation.why: Option A is the only one where a user rule and a compiler rule are the same kind of thing. That is what makes the vocabulary one table instead of two. Law 1 keeps it safe: a rule adds, and can never change what you wrote.

whyNot.reason: It fixes Ravi's case and leaves boilerplate as a compiler privilege. A library author still cannot ship the derive their users need.
It keeps the rule that a derive works on types only, which is why org rules live in the build entry, far from the code they govern.
It removes a shipped capability and makes every library that needs a rule fork the compiler or ship a build entry.

recommendation.tradeoff: A user rule that adds a method can collide with a hand-written one. The collision must be an error naming both sites, which costs a diagnostic and a check. That is the price of not letting generation shadow anything.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared full user rules against types-only derives. It recommended full rules, because the closed table is the cause of the drift and the missing surfaces.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the reject-only option and the close-the-door option. It also tested rules limited to new sites, which was folded into option A as a site list.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping option B first and option A later. That is the implementation order, not a separate choice, so the options stayed as written.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option D by noting a fully static table makes the drift guards simpler and the audit surface smaller.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested whether an adding rule becomes an attribute macro. It cannot, because Law 1 forbids changing or shadowing user code, and additive-only is checked.

decisions.title: Who may declare a text block language
decisions.gist: Whether a library may add a checked text block such as GraphQL, the way the standard library adds SQL.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two text blocks: #SQL and #HTML. Inside them you write another language, and Jet checks it. The list is closed to two entries, fixed in the compiler. D-DSLBLOCK1=A ratified that closure to stop libraries from changing Jet's grammar. This ballot asks whether the closure can be narrowed to what it was protecting, without opening the grammar.
decisions.story: Mei ships a GraphQL client. Her users write query strings that fail at run time on a typo. She wants a #GraphQL block that checks the query against the schema at compile time, exactly as #SQL checks a query against a table. She cannot, so her users keep shipping typos.

options.name: Open the text region, keep the grammar closed
options.detail: A library may declare a block rule. Jet reads the block boundary with its own grammar and hands the inside to the library as text. The library checks it and adds code. Jet's grammar never moves, because the braces are always Jet's braces.
options.technical: Amends D-DSLBLOCK1=A. The closure narrows from the marker name to the grammar. STDLIB_DSL_BLOCK_MARKERS retires. The block body is one lexical region delimited by the marker grammar, so no library can change how Jet parses anything outside it.

options.name: Open it, but only under a grant
options.detail: Same power as option A, but a project must permit each block language in its manifest before the block parses. This makes the surface visible in one file per project. It adds a step for every user of every library that ships a block.
options.technical: Amends D-DSLBLOCK1=A and adds a manifest key. The grant rides the existing chain from D-BUILDSCOPE1: flag, then package, then workspace.

options.name: Keep it closed, add rows by ballot
options.detail: The list stays in the compiler. When a block language earns its place, it is added by a decision, as SQL and HTML were. This keeps the audit surface at two entries and keeps every block checked by the compiler team. Mei waits for a ballot.
options.technical: D-DSLBLOCK1=A stands unchanged. Each new row is a syntax decision under I7 and a compiler patch.
options.code:
// Only SQL and HTML exist.
#SQL<Row> { select id from users }

options.name: Retire text blocks
options.detail: Delete #SQL and #HTML and let every embedded language be an ordinary checked function call on a string. This removes a mechanism and one closed table. It also loses compile-time checking of the query, which is the reason the blocks exist.
options.technical: Retires D-DSLBLOCK1 and D-SQL-ARG1. Checking moves to a comptime function over a string literal, which cannot report a span inside the string as precisely.
options.code:
// proposed under D
rows :: sql.query<Row>("select id, name from users")?

comparisons.note: #lang lets a file choose its whole reader. It is the most powerful version of this and the reason Racket tooling must be built per language.
A function-like proc macro takes a token stream, so sqlx can check a query at compile time. The cost is a separate crate and expansion the reader cannot see.
String mixins let any library assemble source text. This is the version Jet refuses, because the grammar and the tooling lose their footing.

recommendation.why: D-DSLBLOCK1 was written to stop third-party grammar mutation, and option A keeps that stop exactly. Jet still parses the block boundary, so no library can change how any other file reads. What opens is the inside of one clearly marked region, which is text either way.

whyNot.reason: The grant protects against grammar mutation, which option A already prevents structurally. It taxes every user for a risk that is no longer present.
It makes every embedded language wait on the compiler team, and the surface frequency audit shows embedded query languages are common work.
It removes compile-time checking of the query, which is the only reason these blocks exist rather than plain strings.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bad block library can give bad errors inside its own region. Jet cannot check another language for the author. The block still reports a span, so the error lands in the right place even when its text is poor.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared opening block rules against keeping the closed list. It recommended opening, because the ratified closure protects the grammar and the grammar does not move.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the grant option and the retire option. It also tested a curated registry of blessed block libraries, which was folded into option C.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested option A with an opt-out for projects that want no block languages. That belongs in lint policy, not in this decision.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting two entries are trivially auditable, and every shipped block is checked by the compiler team.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested whether a block rule can become a reader macro. It cannot, because Jet owns the delimiters and the region never extends past them.

decisions.title: One effect model, or two
decisions.gist: Whether compile-time code declares what it touches the same way run-time code does.
decisions.lesson: Run-time code says what it touches with an effect set, written =[FS]=>. Compile-time code says the same thing a different way: a fixed list of allowed calls, three tier names, and its own diagnostics. Two vocabularies describe one idea. There are also two checkers, which report the same mistake as E0951 or as E3401. This choice decides whether they merge.
decisions.story: Lena writes a build step that reads a schema file. She already knows how to declare a file effect, because she does it in every service she ships. At compile time none of that applies. She learns a second vocabulary to say the same sentence.

options.name: One model at both stages
options.detail: Compile-time code declares effects with the same syntax as run-time code. The three tiers stay exactly as ratified, but they stop being a separate vocabulary and become what the effect set already says. One checker, one diagnostic family, one thing to learn.
options.technical: Amends D-CTCORE1: the allow-list of pure Core calls retires, because the effect set already carries the fact. D-CTEFFECT1's tiers are unchanged in meaning. Tier 0 is an empty effect set. Tier 1 is a recorded effect. Tier 2 needs #Impure plus permission. The two checkers at Sema/Purity.rs and Comptime merge, retiring one diagnostic family.

options.name: Merge the checkers, keep both vocabularies
options.detail: Fix the duplication that hurts most: two checkers proving the same property with two diagnostic families. Users still learn tier names at compile time and effect sets at run time, but a mistake now reports once, with one message.
options.technical: Effects.rs's fixpoint absorbs Purity.rs's recursive walk. E3401 and E0951 collapse to one family. D-CTCORE1 and D-CTEFFECT1 stay as written.
options.code:
// Surface unchanged; one error instead of two spellings of it.
#Known cfg :: embed_file("app.toml")

options.name: Keep both
options.detail: Leave the two models alone. Compile-time and run-time really do differ: one runs on the build machine, one on the user's machine. Separate names make that difference obvious. The cost is two checkers, two diagnostic families, and a second vocabulary to learn.
options.technical: D-CTCORE1 and D-CTEFFECT1 stand unchanged. The Purity and Effects duplication stays, as flagged in authority-one-model.md:118.

comparisons.note: build.rs has no effect declaration at all. Any build script may read anything, which is the documented supply-chain hole.
comptime code is restricted by what the evaluator supports, not by a declared effect. The rule is real but unwritten.
comparisons.code: comptime { const x = readFile(); }  // rejected, no declaration involved

comparisons.note: Builds are pure by default and impure inputs must be pinned by hash. This is the same tier idea Jet ratified, expressed once rather than twice.

recommendation.why: The stage a function runs at does not change what it touches. An effect set already says the thing the tier names say, so one vocabulary covers both. This also deletes the allow-list, which is the last place where being allowed at compile time is a hard-coded list rather than a declared fact.

whyNot.reason: It repairs the duplicated checker and leaves the duplicated vocabulary, so a user still learns two ways to say the same sentence.
The difference it preserves is when the code runs, which the tiers already record. It pays two checkers and two error families for a distinction the effect set carries.

recommendation.tradeoff: The tier a call needs becomes a property of its effect set rather than a name in a table. Reading a build file then requires reading the effect set to see the tier. jet inspect audit-effects already prints exactly that.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one shared effect model against the current pair. It recommended sharing, because an effect set already carries what the tier names say.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the merge-the-checkers option. It also tested a stage-annotated effect set, which was folded into option A as the tier reading.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping option B first as a safe internal step toward option A. That is the implementation order, not a separate choice.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting that separate names make the build machine and the user machine visibly different.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested whether the allow-list is doing work the effect set cannot. It is not, because every listed call is pure and an empty effect set says so.

decisions.title: Where a compile-time value may be used
decisions.gist: Whether an array size or an enum number may be computed, or must be typed as a literal.
decisions.lesson: Jet can compute values at compile time. It does this for bindings, for #Known if, and for module parameters. Two places refuse to use it: the length of a fixed array and the number on an enum variant. Both demand a literal you type by hand. The evaluator exists and these two parsers do not call it.
decisions.story: Tomas writes a signal-processing library with a lane count. He wants a buffer twice as long as the lane count. He writes [Float#(LANES * 2)] and gets E0963. He types 16 instead, adds a comment saying keep this in sync with LANES, and waits for the day someone forgets.

options.name: Any compile-time value, anywhere a constant is legal
options.detail: Both sites call the evaluator that already exists. An array length or an enum number may be any expression the compiler can compute. The rules that follow are unchanged: the value must be known, and it must be an integer. Only the shape of what you may type changes.
options.technical: Retires the literal-only checks at Parser/Types.rs:447-478 (E0963) and Parser/Items/enums_traits.rs:124-148 (E0035). Resolution happens where module value parameters already resolve, so generic-module substitution still works. S26 is untouched: the value stays a value and never selects a type.

options.name: Named values only, no arithmetic
options.detail: Both sites accept a literal or the name of a compile-time value, but no expression. This closes the worst case, where a number is copied by hand, and keeps the parser simple. Tomas must still declare a second name for every derived size.
options.technical: The array-size site already accepts a bare name for module substitution. This extends the same rule to enum numbers and stops there. No expression evaluation enters either parser.

options.name: Leave both as literals
options.detail: Keep the current rule. A reader sees the real number in the source with nothing to work out, which matters most for a memory layout. Anyone who needs a derived size keeps a second name and a comment, and the compiler cannot catch a mismatch.
options.technical: E0963 and E0035 stand. The evaluator stays uncalled at these two sites.
options.code:
// today
struct Frame { samples: [Float#16] }   // keep in sync with LANES by hand

comparisons.note: An array length is an ordinary comptime expression, because there is one evaluator and every constant site calls it.
const generics arrived years after arrays, so a computed length was a long-standing gap that needed a separate feature.
comparisons.code: struct Frame<const N: usize> { samples: [f32; N] }

comparisons.note: The preprocessor supplies arithmetic the language lacks, which is why sizes are macros and errors point at expanded text.

recommendation.why: The evaluator is built, tested, and used elsewhere. These two sites reject expressions because their parsers never call it, not because a rule requires it. Option A deletes two special cases and gains a capability, and it keeps every rule that follows the value.

whyNot.reason: It still forces a second declaration for every derived size, so the mismatch it is meant to prevent can still be written by hand.
The readability it protects is real but small, and it is paid for with a hand-copied number the compiler cannot check.

recommendation.tradeoff: A reader may have to follow a name to learn a buffer size. jet inspect expand already prints the folded value, and the layout lens shows the real number.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared full expressions against literals and recommended expressions, because the evaluator already exists and is simply not called.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the named-values-only option. It also tested a separate const-generic feature, which was dropped as a second mechanism for one job.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested allowing expressions for array sizes only, since that site already accepts names. Splitting the two sites would leave one special case standing.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting that a literal size is the clearest thing to read in a memory layout.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested whether an expression at these sites can affect dispatch or create a type. It cannot, so S26 stands untouched.

decisions.title: How a generic module instance names its types
decisions.gist: Whether a user must type a name the compiler invented.
decisions.lesson: A generic module is a template with type and value parameters. Writing module three_ints = fixed_buffer<Int, 3> builds a real module. Its types get names the compiler mints, and today the user must type those minted names to build a value. The name has a shape nobody would choose to write.
decisions.story: Aria uses a fixed-size buffer module. She writes the instance, then tries to build one of its structs. Completion offers her M5Three4IntsBuffer. She copies it, because she has no other way, and her code now contains a name she cannot explain to a reviewer.

options.name: Members are reached through the instance
options.detail: An instance is a module, so its types are its members. You write three_ints.Buffer, exactly as you already write three_ints.echo for a function. The minted name becomes an internal detail the user never sees or types.
options.technical: Type members resolve through the module path the same way function members do. The mangled symbol stays for codegen and stops being a user-facing name. Resolution errors name the module and the member, never the mangled form.

options.name: Instances may name their exports
options.detail: The instance declares which members it publishes and under what names. This gives full control and reads clearly at the use site. It adds a declaration to write for every instance, including the common case where the member name is already right.
options.technical: The alias form grows an export list. Members not listed stay reachable through the module path, so option A's rule is still the default beneath it.

options.name: Keep the minted names
options.detail: Leave the current behaviour. Every instantiated type has one unique name in one flat namespace, which is simple to implement and never collides. Users keep typing names the compiler invented, and those names appear in reviews and in error messages.
options.technical: GenericModules.rs keeps producing the flat mangled name as the user-facing spelling.
options.code:
// today
buffer :: M5Three4IntsBuffer.{items: fixed}

comparisons.note: A functor application produces a module, and its types are reached through it. Nobody writes a mangled name.
comparisons.code:
module M = Make(Int)
let x : M.t = M.empty

comparisons.note: Monomorphised names exist only in symbols and backtraces. Source always says Vec<i32>.
Mangled names leak into linker errors, and every C++ developer learns to read them. That is the outcome to avoid.

recommendation.why: The instance is already a module and its functions are already reached through it. Types are the only members that behave differently, and there is no reason for the difference. Option A removes a name from the user surface and needs no new syntax.

whyNot.reason: It solves a naming problem that option A already removes, and taxes every instance with an export list for the common case.
It puts a compiler-minted name in user source, in code review, and in error text. No reader can tell what M5Three4IntsBuffer means.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two instances of one template give two distinct types with the same member name. The error when they are mixed must name both instances, which is a clearer message than a mangled-name mismatch.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared member access through the instance against the minted names. It recommended member access, because functions already work that way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the export-list option. It also tested importing members into scope by default, which was dropped because it hides where a type came from.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested option A with an optional export list on top. The list can be added later without changing option A's rule.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting a flat unique name never collides and is trivial to resolve.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested two instances of one template used together. Member access names the instance, so the error says which one, and the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: One registration table, or four
decisions.gist: Whether the four registries proposed this week become one table.
decisions.lesson: Four proposals in two days each build a table of registered facts with one law. The marker registry holds rules on code. The plane registry holds knowledge about values. The rights tree holds what a scope may do. The build fact plane holds what the build knows. Each cites the others as precedent. Each is a separate Rust table. This choice decides whether they share one.
decisions.story: A reviewer opens the four proposals in one sitting. Each says a thing exists only if it is registered, is nameable, and is reflectable. Each says it extends the others. No two share a line of code. The reviewer cannot tell whether this is one design or four.

options.name: One table, four uses
options.detail: One declaration kind covers all four. A marker rule, a knowledge plane, a right, and a build fact are rows of the same kind, separated by what they attach to. Reflection, jet inspect, and the drift guards are written once and serve all four.
options.technical: One declaration form in the Prelude with a target kind. The four ratified laws collapse into one law with four instances. Each sibling proposal keeps its own surface and its own ballots; only the substrate merges.
options.code:
// proposed
marker Inline(mode: InlineMode = .Hint) on [.Function, .Method, .Constant]
plane Exactness on [.Value]
right FS.Read on [.Scope]
fact build.os: OsName

options.name: One law, four tables
options.detail: Write the shared law once in the spec and require every registry to obey it. Each area keeps its own table and its own code. This costs nothing to coordinate and lets each proposal ship on its own clock. Four copies of reflection and four drift guards remain.
options.technical: The law enters docs/spec/philosophy.md. Each of the four registries implements it separately, as each proposal currently plans.
options.code:
// Four tables, one written rule they all cite.
// Policy.rs, the plane registry, the rights tree, the fact plane.

options.name: Two tables: rules on code, facts about values
options.detail: Split by what the row attaches to. A marker and a right attach to code you write. A knowledge plane and a build fact describe a value or the program. This matches how the two groups are used and keeps each table smaller.
options.technical: Two declaration kinds, two reflection surfaces. The line between them is real but not sharp: a unit dimension is a fact about a value that is written as a marker on a type.

options.name: Leave them separate
options.detail: Each proposal builds what it needs. This is the fastest path for all four, and no proposal waits on another. The same law gets written four times, and a fifth proposal will write it a fifth time.
options.technical: No coordination. Four tables, four reflection paths, four sets of drift guards, four diagnostic families.
options.code: // Today's path, continued.

comparisons.note: One binding table serves every phase. A macro, a value, and a type are entries with different phases, not different tables.
An annotation is a type. Placement and retention are themselves annotations, so the mechanism describes itself with one table.
Three planes for one concept: user attributes, pragmas, and built-in attributes. D's own leadership names this as the fragmentation to avoid.

recommendation.why: The four laws are already one law, written four times by four authors who each noticed the others. Merging the substrate costs one coordination pass now and saves four copies of reflection, four drift guards, and the fifth table the next proposal would mint.

whyNot.reason: A written law with four implementations is what happened in July. D-MARKSIG1 ruled one registry and the compiler drifted, because nothing failed when it did.
The split it draws is not sharp. A unit dimension is a fact about a value and is written as a marker on a type, so it belongs to both halves.
It guarantees the same audit runs again. Four tables today became four because nobody stopped to merge three.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three sibling proposals gain a shared dependency, so none can land its substrate alone. Their surfaces and ballots stay independent, so only the internal table is shared.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one shared table against four separate ones. It recommended sharing, because the four ratified laws say the same thing.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the two-table split and the leave-them-separate option. It also tested a generated shared table, which was dropped as a fifth artifact.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested one table for markers and planes now, with rights and build facts joining later. That is the implementation order under option A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option D by noting that four independent tables let four proposals ship without waiting on each other.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested whether merging blocks the sibling slates. It does not, because their surfaces and ballots stay independent of the substrate.

decisions.title: The word that declares a rule
decisions.gist: What keyword introduces a rule declaration in Jet source.
decisions.lesson: If rule rows move from Rust into Jet, a word has to introduce them. The word appears in the Prelude beside every rule the compiler applies, and in library source wherever an author writes one. It is read far more often than it is written. Today the concept is called a marker in the spec, in the glossary, and in diagnostics, but no keyword exists.
decisions.story: Noor opens the Prelude for the first time to learn what #Inline really does. The first word on the line tells her what kind of thing she is reading. She has never written one, and she should still know within a second whether this declares a rule, a type, or a function.
decisions.inWild:
// The same declaration under each candidate word:

marker Inline(mode: InlineMode = .Hint) on Function, Method, Constant
rule   Inline(mode: InlineMode = .Hint) on Function, Method, Constant
derive Inline(mode: InlineMode = .Hint) on Function, Method, Constant

// At the use site nothing changes under any option:
#Inline
fn hot(a: Int) => Int = a * 2

options.name: marker
options.detail: Use the word the whole project already uses. The spec says marker, the glossary says marker, the diagnostics say marker, and the audit that opened this door is called the marker plane. Nobody has to learn a second name for one thing.
options.technical: Zero churn in docs, diagnostics, and card titles. Other plain candidates considered and rejected: tag, which S54 already uses for taint values; note, which reads as a comment; annotate and decorate, which name the act rather than the thing.

options.name: rule
options.detail: Use the word the ratified law itself uses. Law zero says a marker applies one named rule to the next thing you write, and the registry is called APPLIED_RULES in code. Rule says what the thing does, where marker only says how it is written.
options.technical: Matches Policy::APPLIED_RULES and RuleSite, RuleSignature, RuleStatus in the current source, so the compiler-side names stop disagreeing with the user-side ones. Costs a rename across spec, glossary, and diagnostic text.

options.name: derive
options.detail: Reuse the keyword that already ships. A user already writes derive to declare a rule that adds code. Extending it to rules that record a fact adds no word at all. It reads oddly for #Inline, which derives nothing.
options.technical: Keeps KW_DERIVE and the existing parse entry. The word's plain meaning narrows to generation, so a fact-only rule reads as deriving nothing from nothing.

options.name: No keyword: the target clause declares it
options.detail: A rule is recognised by its on clause, with no introducing word. This spends no keyword and reads compactly. A reader scanning a file has to reach the middle of the line to learn what kind of declaration it is.
options.technical: Parsing needs lookahead to the on clause, which the parser can do but which no other Jet declaration requires. It also leaves the concept without a name to say aloud.

comparisons.note: An annotation is declared with @interface, which reuses an existing word and confuses every learner about what it is.
A decorator has no declaring keyword at all. It is an ordinary function, and readers cannot tell one from a plain function until they read the use site.
define-syntax names the thing precisely. The word is long, and nobody misreads what a definition is.

recommendation.why: Marker is already the project's word in the spec, the glossary, the diagnostics, and the audit that opened this door. Choosing it means no rename and no second name for one concept. The keyword and the sigil then teach each other: you write #Inline because someone declared a marker.

whyNot.reason: Rule is a better description of the behaviour, but it renames a word used across the spec, the diagnostics, and every card title in this area.
Derive means generate from a shape. A fact-only rule such as #Inline derives nothing, so the word would mislead in the common case.
It saves a word and costs a reader the first thing they need, which is what kind of declaration they are looking at.

recommendation.tradeoff: The compiler-side names stay RuleSite and APPLIED_RULES while the user-side word is marker. That mismatch is internal and can be renamed later without touching a line of user source.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared marker against rule and recommended marker, because the project already uses that word everywhere it matters.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added reusing derive and using no keyword. It also tested tag, note, annotate, and decorate, which are recorded in option A's technical notes.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested marker for fact rules and derive for code rules. Two words for one declaration kind would reintroduce the split this slate removes.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option B by noting that rule matches the compiler-side names and the wording of law zero itself.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested whether marker misleads once rules can add code. It does not, because the marker is the attachment and the body is its rule.

decisions.title: One mark for compile time
decisions.gist: Whether one sigil marks compile time, and whether it is written once or at every mention.
decisions.lesson: Jet spells compile time four ways today. A binding that must be computed now is #Known x :: 5. A branch is #Known if. A compiler fact is T.$layout. A value carried out of a compile-time block into emitted code is $ratio. Two of the four already use the sigil. This choice picks one mark, and decides whether the mark belongs to the binding or to the name.
decisions.story: Bo has used Jet for a month and can write #Known. He reads a derive and meets $name, which he has never seen. He reads a layout example and meets T.$layout, which looks related but is a third thing. He asks which one means compile time, and the honest answer is all of them.

options.name: The mark belongs to the binding
options.detail: The sigil is written where a value is bound, and where a compiler fact is read. Ordinary uses stay plain, exactly as they are today. This is the smallest move from what is ratified, and existing code reads almost unchanged. Two rules remain: one for binding, one for carrying a value out of a compile-time block.
options.technical: Amends D-VERDICT-1308-1 and D-VERDICT-1308-2 by replacing the #Known spelling only. D-CTMARKER1 survives unchanged: $name still marks a value crossing out of a compile-time-only scope. T.$layout is unaffected. #Known leaves the marker registry, so the marker plane loses the row that needed a Prefix form.

options.name: The mark belongs to the name
options.detail: The sigil is part of the name and is written at every mention. A reader can tell from any single line whether a value was computed before the program ran. The rule for carrying a value out of a compile-time block disappears, because there is nothing to carry: the name is the same name everywhere.
options.technical: Amends D-VERDICT-1308-1, D-VERDICT-1308-2, and retires D-CTMARKER1 outright rather than generalizing it. There is no scope-crossing concept and no splice rule left to state. Sema treats the sigil as part of the identifier, so a plain name and a marked name can never denote the same binding.

options.name: Keep #Known, and use it everywhere
options.detail: Go the other way. Make the marker the single mark and retire the sigil, so a carried value becomes #Known(name) and a compiler fact becomes T.#layout. One mark, and it is the one most users already know. Every use gets longer.
options.technical: Amends D-CTMARKER1 and D-LAYOUT-FACTS1=B. #Known keeps four legal sites and gains more. The marker plane keeps a row whose meaning is a stage rather than a rule about a target, which is why it needs the Prefix form nothing else uses.

options.name: Keep all four spellings
options.detail: Leave it alone. Each spelling is short, each is ratified, and no existing code or documentation moves. A reader learns four marks for one idea, and cannot tell from the mark which one applies where.
options.technical: D-VERDICT-1308-1, D-VERDICT-1308-2, D-CTMARKER1, and D-LAYOUT-FACTS1=B all stand unchanged.
options.code:
#Known limit :: 1000
#Known if debug { … }
print("{$ratio}")
layout :: T.$layout

comparisons.note: The mark belongs to the binding. A constant is declared with const and then used plainly, so a reader cannot tell a constant from a variable at the use site.
Quotation and splice are a paired notation, so the mark appears wherever a stage boundary is crossed rather than on the name.
The sigil is part of the name. A global is $x and an instance variable is @x at every mention, so scope is visible on every line.

recommendation.why: Option B is the only one that makes the claim true. If the mark is part of the name, then reading a marked name is ordinary use and the carrying rule has nothing left to say, so a whole concept leaves the language. It also answers the question a reader actually has at a use site, which is whether this value existed before the program ran.

whyNot.reason: It moves the spelling and keeps two rules: one for binding and one for carrying a value out of a compile-time block. The reader still cannot tell a compile-time value at its use site.
It keeps a stage inside the marker plane, which is why #Known needs four sites and a Prefix form no other row uses. It also makes every use longer.
Four marks for one idea is the finding, not the baseline. A reader must memorise all four to know which applies where.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every mention of a compile-time value gains a character, so code that leans on named constants gets slightly noisier. That is the cost of making the stage visible on every line, and it is the same trade Ruby made for scope. Option A is the right pick if that noise matters more than deleting the carrying rule.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed one sigil and claimed the carrying rule would disappear. Review found that this is only true if the mark belongs to the name, so the draft was split into options A and B.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the keep-#Known option and the keep-all-four option. It also tested a stage keyword, which was dropped because a word cannot attach to a member the way T.$layout does.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested marking the name only where a value leaves a compile-time block. That is option A exactly, so it added no fifth choice.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option A by confirming against comptime_block.jet that plain uses are what ships today, so A is the smaller migration.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether a marked and an unmarked name could denote one binding under B. They cannot, because the mark is part of the identifier, so the ambiguity never arises.

decisions.title: What a derive body holds
decisions.gist: Whether a derive body is the implementation, or something that produces one.
decisions.lesson: A derive says: implement this trait for this type. Today its body is a small program that builds a string of Jet source and calls emit. The header already names the trait and the type, so the body has to repeat both inside the text it builds. This choice decides what a body holds.
decisions.story: Sam reads a derive for the first time. The header says derive T.Wire. Three lines later the body writes impl $tname again, inside a string, with every brace doubled. He cannot tell which part is the rule and which part is the thing being written.

options.name: The body is the implementation
options.detail: The body holds the members, and nothing else. The header already said which trait and which type, so no inner impl is written. Compile-time control flow inside the body generates one member per field when a derive needs that.
options.technical: The body parses as a member list at definition time. Compile-time control flow uses the same verbs as run time, marked by the stage sigil. A member that already exists on the type is a collision error naming both sites, since Law 1 forbids shadowing.

options.name: The body holds one or more impl blocks
options.detail: The body contains ordinary impl blocks, written in full. A derive can then implement more than one trait, and the code looks exactly like hand-written code. The trait and type are written twice for the common case, which is one trait.
options.technical: Keeps the derive header as a trigger only. A multi-trait derive becomes possible, at the cost of repeating the header's information in every single-trait derive.

options.name: The body returns a code value
options.detail: The body is a comptime function that returns generated code as a value. Helper functions can build and combine pieces, which suits a derive assembled from many parts. It adds a code type, and the simple case gains a wrapper.
options.technical: Introduces a first-class code value, the quotation form used by Scala 3 and Template Haskell. This is the strongest option for composition and the only one that adds a new kind of value to the language.

options.name: Keep emit and strings
options.detail: Leave the body as a program that builds text. It is shipped, understood, and can generate anything at all, including code shapes no template form anticipated. Every author keeps doubling braces and keeps finding mistakes only when someone uses the derive.
options.technical: The re-lex and re-parse path stays, with E2710 as the failure mode when generated text does not parse.

comparisons.note: A derive macro must build the whole impl block as tokens, including the trait and type the attribute already named.
An extension macro returns member declarations only. The compiler attaches them, so the member list is all the author writes.
A source generator emits a partial class, so the author writes the members and the compiler joins them to the original type.
comparisons.code: public partial class Bar { public void Hi() {} }

recommendation.why: The header already carries the trait and the type, so option A is the only one that does not write them twice. It makes the common derive three lines, and it reads as what it is: the implementation. Swift and C# both landed on member lists for the same reason.

whyNot.reason: It repeats the header's information in every single-trait derive, which is nearly all of them, to buy a multi-trait case that a second derive already covers.
It adds a code value to the language. Nothing in the reported cases needs composition that a member list plus compile-time control flow cannot express.
A string is only checked when someone uses the derive, so the author is not the person who finds the mistake.

recommendation.tradeoff: A derive can no longer produce arbitrary text, so a generator that assembles code character by character must instead produce members. That is the limit that makes the body checkable when it is written.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a member list against the current string form and recommended the member list, because the header already names the trait and type.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the explicit impl option and the code value option. It also tested a body that returns a list of members, which is option C without the new type.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a member list with an optional escape to a code value for hard cases. The escape can be added later without changing option A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option D by noting that emit can generate shapes no template form anticipated, which is real power.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested a derive that must generate a nested type and an impl on it. A member list covers it, because a type is a member of the module the derive contributes.

decisions.title: How a rule declaration carries its facts
decisions.gist: The shape of a rule declaration, and how it says where the rule may be written.
decisions.lesson: A rule row carries a name, the arguments a user writes, the targets it accepts, whether it repeats, and its status. Today that is a Rust macro call. If rows become Jet declarations, the shape has to be decided. The risk is inventing a small grammar of clauses that exists nowhere else in Jet.
decisions.story: Noor opens the Prelude to learn what #Inline really does. She reads one line. She should learn what arguments the rule takes, where it may be written, and whether it may be repeated, using only syntax she already knows from reading ordinary Jet.

options.name: Named parameters, marked by the compile-time sigil
options.detail: The rule's own arguments and the facts about the rule share one named-parameter list. A fact about the rule carries the compile-time mark, so a reader can tell at a glance which parameters a user writes and which describe the rule. No clause grammar is invented.
options.technical: Introduces no keyword beyond the declaring word. $sites takes [Site], the existing 18-member RuleSite enum published as a Prelude enum under D-RULEARG-TYPES1=A. A new fact about rules is a new named optional parameter, not a new clause. The $ mark is the same rule as $limit and T.$layout, applied to a parameter list, so it depends on D-META-STAGE1.
options.code:
marker Inline(mode: InlineMode = .Hint,
              $sites: [.Function, .Method, .Constant])

marker Pre(condition: Any, message: String,
           $sites: [.Function, .Method], $repeatable: true)

marker Unsafe(reason: String, obligations: ObligationMode = .None,
              $sites: [.Function, .Method, .Block, .Operation])

options.name: Two parameter lists
options.detail: The rule's arguments come first, then a second list holds the facts about the rule. The split is visible without reading any sigil, and the two kinds of parameter can never collide by name. Two lists on one declaration appear nowhere else in Jet.
options.technical: Needs a second parameter-list position in the grammar, which no other Jet declaration has. It does remove any chance that a rule wanting an argument literally named sites collides with the fact of the same name.
options.code:
marker Inline(mode: InlineMode = .Hint)(sites: [.Function, .Method, .Constant])

marker Pre(condition: Any, message: String)(sites: [.Function, .Method], repeatable: true)

options.name: A clause after the signature
options.detail: The sites follow a word such as on, with further facts as trailing words. It reads close to English and is the shortest form. It invents a clause grammar that exists nowhere else in Jet, and every new fact about rules needs a new word in it.
options.technical: Adds on and repeatable as declaration-level words under I7, each needing a Syntax.rs row. The site list stops being an ordinary argument, so reflection needs its own path to publish it.
options.code:
marker Inline(mode: InlineMode = .Hint) on [.Function, .Method, .Constant]

marker Pre(condition: Any, message: String) on [.Function, .Method] repeatable

options.name: A scope block of members
options.detail: The declaration opens a block and each fact is a member line, using the dot-member form Jet already has for test scopes. It scales when a rule carries many facts. Nearly every rule uses two facts, so almost all of them cost four lines instead of one.
options.technical: Uses the ratified dot-scope member form from D-DOTSCOPE1=B, the same shape as #Test("name") { .timeout(2s) }. This is the better shape if the row schema ever grows well past its current six fields.

comparisons.note: Placement is declared with a separate annotation on the annotation, carrying an array of constants. Reflection reads it as a real value.
AttributeUsage takes a flags enum, so the target set is one value built with the or operator.
There is no declaration at all. A proc macro states its targets in documentation, and a wrong placement fails inside the macro body.
comparisons.code:
#[proc_macro_attribute]
pub fn audited(attr: TokenStream, item: TokenStream) -> TokenStream

recommendation.why: Option A introduces no keyword and no grammar. A rule declaration becomes an ordinary Jet declaration with named parameters, which is syntax every user already reads. The compile-time mark does the separating work, and it is the same mark this slate establishes everywhere else, so it teaches itself.

whyNot.reason: Two parameter lists on one declaration exist nowhere else in Jet, and the collision it prevents is avoided by the sigil at no cost.
It invents a clause grammar for one declaration kind, and every future fact about rules needs another word in it. That is the keyword soup the move out of Rust is meant to end.
It costs four lines for a row that almost always carries two facts, and Jet has no other declaration that states its own signature in a block.

recommendation.tradeoff: A rule that genuinely wants a user-facing argument named sites must pick another name, because the reader distinguishes the two kinds by sigil rather than by position. No current rule has that problem, and the collision is a compile error rather than a silent mistake.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft used a trailing on clause. It was rejected on review because it invents a clause grammar Jet has nowhere else.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added two parameter lists and the scope block. It also tested facts declared as markers on the declaration, which makes the plane bootstrap on itself.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested named parameters now with a scope block later for rules with many facts. The block can be added without changing option A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option D by noting it is the right shape if the row schema grows well beyond six fields.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested a rule legal at all eighteen sites and a rule wanting an argument named sites. A named list covers the first, and the second is a rename caught at compile time.

decisions.title: How much is derived without asking
decisions.gist: Whether every trait the compiler can derive is derived unless you refuse it.
decisions.lesson: Jet already derives four traits without being asked: Debug, Printable, Equatable, and Comparable. A type refuses one by writing an exclamation mark before the name, and a package can switch the defaults off. Codable and the rest still need an explicit marker. This choice decides where the line sits between derived-unless-refused and asked-for.
decisions.story: Mira writes a struct and sends it as JSON. She has already learned that printing and comparing just work. Encoding does not, so she adds a marker she did not need for the other three. Nothing about her type made encoding harder; the line was drawn somewhere she cannot see.

options.name: Everything derivable is derived unless refused
options.detail: If the compiler can derive a trait from a type's shape, it does. A type refuses one trait with the exclamation mark it already uses, and a project switches any of them off in settings. Only traits that cannot be derived structurally stay opt-in, because there is nothing to derive.
options.technical: Amends D-AUTODERIVE1=E by widening the default set from four traits to every structurally derivable trait, Codable included. The refusal spelling and the package switch are unchanged, as ratified by D-AUTODERIVE-SYNTAX1=D. Eligibility gates still apply: a type whose fields are not derivable simply does not get the trait, silently, exactly as today.

options.name: Widen to a named set
options.detail: Add the traits people reach for most, such as Codable and Hashable, and keep the rest opt-in. This removes the common ceremony and keeps a written list of what appears without asking. The list is another closed table, and the question returns for the next trait.
options.technical: Amends D-AUTODERIVE1=E by naming a larger default set. The set stays a compiler-side list, which is the closed-table pattern this slate removes elsewhere.

options.name: Keep the four
options.detail: Leave the line where it is. Printing and comparing are safe to assume; sending a type over a wire is a decision worth writing down. Users keep adding a marker for encoding, and the reason the line sits there is not visible from the code.
options.technical: D-AUTODERIVE1=E stands unchanged at Debug, Printable, Equatable, and Comparable.
options.code:
#Codable
User :: struct { name: String, visits: Int }

options.name: Ask for everything
options.detail: Nothing is derived unless written. Every generated implementation is visible in the source, which is the most auditable outcome. It puts four markers on almost every type and makes the beginner path longer than any peer language's.
options.technical: Retires the default-on half of D-AUTODERIVE1=E. Every struct that prints or compares carries explicit markers.
options.code:
#[Debug, Printable, Equatable, Comparable, Codable]
User :: struct { name: String, visits: Int }

comparisons.note: Nothing is derived by default, so almost every type in the ecosystem carries a derive line, and forgetting one is a common first error.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct User { name: String }

comparisons.note: Printing and JSON encoding work on any struct with no declaration at all. Field-level tags refine the result. This is the closest shipped model to option A.
Codable conformance is one word, but it is still a word. Swift synthesises the members once you name the protocol.
comparisons.code: struct User: Codable { let name: String }

recommendation.why: The line between the four and the rest is invisible from the code, and nothing about a type makes encoding harder to derive than comparing. Option A removes the ceremony most users pay most often, keeps the refusal spelling already ratified, and gives a project one switch. It matches Go, where a struct is printable and encodable on sight.

whyNot.reason: It moves the line and keeps it invisible, and the default set stays a closed compiler list that needs a ballot to grow.
It keeps a boundary no reader can see, and encoding is the trait users reach for most after printing.
It makes the beginner path longer than any peer language's, and the owner's own ruling on implicit folding put the default on the magic side.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every type becomes encodable unless refused, so a type that should never cross a wire relies on a written refusal rather than on silence. That is a real widening of the default surface, and `#Redact` and `#!Codable` become the controls that matter. The honest cost is that forgetting to refuse is now the risky direction, where today forgetting to ask is merely inconvenient.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared widening the default set against keeping four traits. It recommended widening, because the current line is invisible from the code.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the named-set option and the ask-for-everything option. It also tested per-module defaults, which the package switch already covers.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested deriving everything except Codable. That is option B with one member, and it keeps the invisible line the finding is about.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting that sending a type over a wire is a decision a reviewer may want written down.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked accidental exposure: a type encodable by default may leak fields. The tradeoff now states this plainly, and #Redact plus #!Codable are named as the controls.

decisions.title: Alias declarations: bind with :: or keep =
decisions.gist: Which mark a type alias uses: the binding mark :: or the current =.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two marks for giving something a value. name :: value binds a new name. name = value changes something that already exists. A type alias introduces a new name for a type. Today the alias line spells it with the update mark: alias Parsed<T> = T ? AppError. This ballot decides whether alias keeps = or moves to the binding mark ::.
decisions.story: Mia is three days into Jet. She learned that total :: 0 binds a new name and total = total + 1 updates it. Then she reads alias Parsed<T> = T ? AppError in a teammate's file and pauses. Nothing is being updated here, so why the update mark?

options.name: Keep alias X = Y
options.detail: The alias line keeps =. It reads like the alias forms in Rust, TypeScript, and Go, so imported habits work unchanged. It also matches the function expression body fn f() => T = expr, where = likewise means 'is defined as'. The loss: = does two jobs. In statements it updates an existing thing, but on an alias line it introduces a name.
options.code:
alias Parsed<T> = T ? AppError
alias Rows = [[String]]

retries :: 3          // a new name binds with ::
retries = retries - 1 // = updates it

options.name: Bind with alias X :: Y
options.detail: One rule: every new name arrives through ::. The alias line reads exactly like a value binding, so what Mia learned on day one carries over. = keeps its single job of updating what already exists. The loss: people arriving from Rust or TypeScript will type = out of habit, and the alias line no longer matches the function body =.
options.technical: Amends D-TYPEALIAS1 spelling only. Scope is unchanged: transparent aliases for shortening generic spellings, not newtypes. A diagnostic on alias X = Y offers the :: fix.
options.code:
alias Parsed<T> :: T ? AppError
alias Rows :: [[String]]

retries :: 3   // same mark, same meaning: a new name

options.name: Drop the keyword: Parsed<T> :: T ? AppError
options.detail: A type alias becomes a plain binding whose right side is a type. It is the shortest spelling. The loss: nothing marks the line as an alias, so a reader cannot tell a type alias from a value binding until they resolve the right side. The keyword also fences aliases to their ratified narrow scope, and losing it opens a side door toward general type programming.

comparisons.note: Type aliases use =.
Every compile-time definition - constants, types, procedures - binds with ::.
Type aliases use =.

recommendation.why: Every new name in Jet arrives through one mark. A beginner who knows retries :: 3 reads the alias line correctly on first sight, and = keeps its single job of updating what already exists.

whyNot.reason: It keeps = doing two jobs. The alias line looks like an update but updates nothing.
Without the keyword a type alias is indistinguishable from a value binding at a glance, and the fence that keeps aliases in their narrow ratified scope loses its anchor.

recommendation.tradeoff: The alias line now differs from Rust and TypeScript muscle memory, and from the function body form fn f() => T = expr, which keeps its ratified = spelling.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keeping = against binding with :: and recommended :: because an alias line introduces a name rather than updating one.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added dropping the keyword entirely as option C. A colon-free alias X Y form was also tried and cut as unreadable rather than genuinely distinct.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid accepting both marks on alias lines was rejected. One construct with two spellings breaks the one-spelling rule (S14).
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option A gained its strongest case: = matches the ratified function expression body and every mainstream alias syntax, so imported intuition works unchanged.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack pressed the function body = as a counterexample to 'definitions bind with ::'. The claim was narrowed to name introduction - the body = defines a body, not a name - and the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: fmt simplify: catalog, surface, and default
decisions.gist: Whether jet fmt may rewrite code to its simplest ratified spelling, and how you turn that on.
decisions.lesson: jet fmt fixes spacing and layout but never changes the shape of your code. A simplify mode would re-emit the most concise ratified spelling with the same meaning. The starter catalog has four rewrites. Braced single-return bodies become = expr one-liners (card #1512). Else-if chains become one arm table. A struct literal drops a type name the context already knows. A listed run of integers in a fence becomes a range. Each rewrite cites its ratified law and proves the same program. The ballot picks the catalog, surface, and default.
decisions.story: Priya inherits a Jet service written by three people in three styles. She wants one command that makes the whole repo read like current canonical Jet, without changing what it does.

options.name: Opt-in flag: jet fmt --simplify
options.detail: Plain jet fmt stays exactly as it is. The rewriter runs only when you ask for it with one flag. Teams canonicalize a repo in one deliberate run, and nobody's code changes shape mid-edit. The in-repo corpus migrates once with the flag as part of this work.
options.technical: The flag shares the fmt engine and AST. Each catalog rewrite carries its decision ID and an AST-equality check: emit, re-parse, compare. The ratified branch-shape law (D-BRANCH-FMT1=C, fmt does not change branch shape) stays intact for default runs. The catalog grows only by ratified law, never by heuristic.

options.name: Simplify is the default fmt
options.detail: Every jet fmt run emits the simplest spelling. One canonical form everywhere, enforced by the tool everyone already runs. This amends the fresh branch-shape ruling, and code changes shape under your cursor on every save.
options.technical: Explicitly amends D-BRANCH-FMT1=C (ratified 2026-07-28): fmt would now change branch shape. Same catalog, same AST-equality proof. An escape flag to skip simplify would be needed for teaching material that shows the verbose forms.
options.code:
$ jet fmt src/        # every run rewrites shape

fn mirror(p: Point) => Point = .{x: -p.x, y: p.y}

options.name: A separate command: jet simplify
options.detail: The rewriter gets its own verb next to fmt. The split makes the intent loud, but there are now two commands that both reformat code, and every guide must explain when to run which.
options.technical: Same engine and catalog under a second CLI entry. fmt law untouched. Editors would need a second format-on-demand action.
options.code:
$ jet simplify src/
$ jet fmt src/        # still needed for layout

options.name: Lint hints only, no batch rewriter
options.detail: No rewriter. Lints point at the simpler spelling and editors offer a quick fix, one site at a time. Nothing ever rewrites your file wholesale, but a repo can never be canonicalized in one run.
options.technical: One L-code per catalog entry, each citing its decision ID. Quick-fix payloads reuse the same AST emitters, so a later batch mode could still be built on top.
options.code: src/geo.jet:4: L0510 this body can be `= expr` (jet fmt cannot fix this automatically)

comparisons.note: gofmt fixes layout only. The shape rewriters live in a separate opt-in tool, gofmt -r and gopls modernizers, and Go has kept that split for a decade.
rustfmt never changes shape. cargo clippy --fix applies shape rewrites as an explicit second step.

recommendation.why: One flag gives whole-repo canonicalization on demand while plain fmt stays predictable. It honors the fresh branch-shape ruling instead of amending it, and it still lets this repo migrate to one canonical form in a single run.

whyNot.reason: It amends a branch-shape ruling you ratified nine days ago, and code changing shape on every save punishes people mid-edit.
A second command that also reformats is two tools for one job, and every guide must teach the split.
Site-at-a-time hints can never canonicalize a repo, so the one-canonical-form goal stays out of reach.

recommendation.tradeoff: fmt gains a mode, so its docs and tests cover two behaviors. Accepted: the default stays frozen and the mode is one flag with one catalog.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an opt-in flag, a default rewrite, a separate command, and lint hints. It recommended the flag because repos canonicalize on demand while the default stays predictable.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-rewrite flags, a config-file toggle, and an editor-only action. All collapsed into the four menu options because they only move where the same switch lives.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of the flag plus D's lint hints was tested: the lint names the simpler spelling and the flag applies it. It was folded into option A's technical path since the lint codes can land later without a new ballot.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened with an escape flag for teaching code, and option D with quick-fix payloads that reuse the batch emitters. Both remain honest versions of themselves.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack tried a rewrite that changes comment placement or drops a needed paren, breaking the same-program promise. The AST-equality check after every rewrite catches both, so the flag survives with the catalog gated on ratified law.

decisions.title: Map type spacing: [K:V] or [K: V]
decisions.gist: Whether the map type is written [K:V] with no space or stays [K: V].
decisions.lesson: The map type is spelled with brackets and a colon. A map from names to ages is [String: Int] today, with a space after the colon, and the formatter enforces that space. This ballot decides whether the type form tightens to [String:Int]. Map literal entries like ["ana": 31] and field declarations like age: Int are separate forms. They keep their spacing unless an option says otherwise.
decisions.story: Sam scans a signature: fn tally(votes: [String: Int]) => [String: Int]. The space inside each bracket pair makes every map read as two pieces, and the whole signature as four. Sam wants each type to read as one compact shape.

options.name: [K:V] in type position
options.detail: Type spellings tighten: [String:Int], including empty-literal heads like [String:Int].{}. A type now reads as one compact unit. Literal entries and field declarations keep their space, so value-position colons stay consistent with fields. The loss: the type no longer mirrors the literal's spacing exactly.
options.technical: Amends the written form of the S64 / D-LISTMAP-CANON1 canonical map type. The formatter emits no space around the colon in type position only. Nested forms follow the same rule: [[U8]:String].
options.code:
votes: [String:Int]
ages :: [String:Int].{}
ages["ana"] = 31
print(["ana": 31])   // literal entries keep the space

options.name: Tight everywhere
options.detail: Types and map literal entries both drop the space: [String:Int] and ["ana":31]. One spacing rule for every map colon. The loss: literal entries stop matching record fields like .{x: 1} and field declarations like age: Int, which keep their space. The inconsistency moves into value code everyone writes daily rather than going away.
options.code:
votes: [String:Int]
print(["ana":31])
point :: Point.{x: 1, y: 2}   // fields still spaced

options.name: Keep [K: V]
options.detail: The status quo. One universal rule with no exceptions: a colon is always followed by a space, in types, literals, and fields alike. The loss: type signatures stay visually wide, and a map type keeps reading as two pieces.
options.code: fn tally(votes: [String: Int]) => [String: Int] { ... }

comparisons.note: Dictionary types are written tight.
comparisons.code: var votes: [String: Int]   // Swift's own formatter keeps the space

comparisons.note: Type hints keep a space after the colon only in annotations, not in dict display.

recommendation.why: A map type reads as one compact shape, the way Sam scans it, while every value-position colon keeps the one-space rule it shares with fields.

whyNot.reason: Tightening literals breaks their rhyme with record fields and field declarations, so the spacing inconsistency moves into everyday value code.
The type form stays wide, and a signature with two maps keeps reading as four fragments.

recommendation.tradeoff: The type no longer mirrors the literal exactly: [String:Int] against ["ana": 31]. That gap is accepted because type position and value position already read differently.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared tightening the type form against the status quo and recommended the tight form because a type should scan as one unit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added tight-everywhere as option B. Spacing both sides of the colon ([K : V]) was also tried and cut as a wider spelling nobody asked for.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A width-dependent hybrid - tight when short, spaced when long - was rejected. Spacing that depends on content makes two spellings of one type.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The status quo gained its strongest case: one universal colon rule with zero exceptions is the easiest rule to teach and to format.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack used nested and generic forms such as [String:Lru<K, V>], where inner commas still carry spaces. The tight bracket pair still delimits the map cleanly, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Expression fences: expand integer-literal ranges
decisions.gist: Whether $[0..3]$ in an expression fence expands to one entry per number.
decisions.lesson: A fence repeats a statement once per entry: print(pick_str($[0, 1, 2, 3]$)) runs four prints. Binding fences already accept a name range: $[ t1..t8 ]$ makes eight names. But in an expression fence, 0..3 is a single Range value, so $[0..3]$ makes one statement copy that receives a Range. This ballot decides whether integer-literal ranges expand into entries, and how a real Range still passes through a fence.
decisions.story: Priya tests a function against inputs 0 through 9. She writes print(pick_str($[0..9]$)) expecting ten runs, because $[ t1..t8 ]$ taught her that fences understand ranges. She gets one run, with a Range as the argument.

options.name: Integer-literal ranges expand; parentheses keep a Range
options.detail: A bare ascending integer-literal range entry expands to one entry per number: $[0..3]$ means $[0, 1, 2, 3]$, matching the binding-fence rule. To pass a real Range through a fence, parenthesize the entry: $[ (0..3) ]$ stays a single Range value.
options.technical: Expansion applies only when both endpoints are integer literals and the range ascends: lo..hi with lo <= hi, or lo..<hi with lo < hi. Any other range entry is a normal expression entry. The formatter keeps entry-level parentheses around a range entry - they carry meaning there. Amends D-VERDICT-1320-1; binding-fence rules and E0369 are unchanged.
options.code:
print(pick_str($[0..3]$))    // pick_str(0), pick_str(1), pick_str(2), pick_str(3)
run($[ (0..3) ]$)             // one copy: run(0..3) with a Range value

options.name: Status quo: a range entry is a Range value
options.detail: No change. Every expression entry substitutes token for token, so 0..3 stays one Range argument and repeated inputs are written out. The gain: zero special cases in the fence rule. The loss: the binding fence and the expression fence read the same but treat a range differently, which is the trap Priya hit.
options.code:
print(pick_str($[0, 1, 2, 3]$))   // spell out every input
run($[ 0..3 ]$)                    // one copy: run(0..3)

options.name: Explicit expansion mark
options.detail: Bare ranges stay Range values. A marked entry expands - for example $[ each 0..3 ]$ becomes four entries. The gain: no bare spelling silently changes meaning, and expansion is visible at the entry. The loss: a second mark for a meaning the binding fence already carries bare, so the common case pays ceremony.
options.code:
print(pick_str($[ each 0..3 ]$))   // four copies, marked
run($[ 0..3 ]$)                     // one copy: a Range value

comparisons.note: The ratified precedent: a range in a binding fence already means one name per step.
Hardware languages expand a literal range into repeated statements at compile time.
comparisons.code: for (i = 0; i < 4; i = i + 1) begin : gen ... end

recommendation.why: Both fence positions keep one story - a range in a fence means one entry per step - and the parenthesized escape keeps every Range expressible.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the trap Priya hit: the same spelling means expansion in one fence position and a single value in the other.
It adds a second mark for a meaning the binding fence already carries bare, so the common case pays ceremony to avoid an ambiguity parentheses already resolve.

recommendation.tradeoff: Parentheses become meaningful inside a fence entry: $[0..3]$ and $[ (0..3) ]$ differ. That is accepted because passing a literal Range through a fence is rare, and the parenthesized spelling states it plainly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared bare expansion against the status quo and recommended expansion so both fence positions treat a range the same way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added an explicit expansion mark as option C. Comptime expansion of any known iterable was considered, folded into C as its natural extension, and set aside as scope creep.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid expanding literal ranges bare while requiring a mark for computed ranges collapsed into option A, which restricts expansion to integer literals outright.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The status quo gained its strongest case: token-for-token substitution with zero special cases is the simplest possible law and stays literally true.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack pressed the parenthesized escape: a formatter that strips parentheses would silently change meaning. Option A now names the formatter obligation to keep entry-level parentheses, and the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Choose the expression fence glyph after the @ swap
decisions.gist: Choose the marks that open and close an expression fence.
decisions.lesson: A fence copies one statement for each entry. That meaning is settled. The old fence uses `$`, but `$` now belongs only to typed environment reads in config files. This choice repairs that conflict.
decisions.story: Mara updates eight account tasks after the compile-time mark changes to `@`. Her fence still contains `$`, so the source now teaches two conflicting rules for the same mark.
decisions.inWild:
use core.tasks as tasks

fn run() {
    from :: Shared.new(Account.{balance: 1000})
    to :: Shared.new(Account.{balance: 0})
    @[ t1..t8 ]@ :: tasks.spawn(() => transfer(from, to, 100))
    @[ t1..t8 ]@.wait()
    from_bal :: from.read(a => a.balance)
    to_bal :: to.read(a => a.balance)
    print(@[ "from={from_bal}", "to={to_bal}", "total={from_bal + to_bal}" ]@)
}

// Output
from=200
to=800
total=1000

options.name: Symmetric @ fence
options.detail: Write `@[ entries ]@`. The fence uses the compile-time mark at both ends. The matching marks keep a wide or nested expression fence easy to scan.
options.technical: This amends only the spelling in D-VERDICT-1320-1. The one-copy and lock-step laws stay unchanged. `@[` and `]@` become longest-match tokens, and `]@` suppresses line termination.
