Sources: syntax-decisions.md:5826 and :5838 and :6636. Lexer digraphs: crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:241 and Terminators.rs:121. Parser: crates/jet-parser/src/FencedNames.rs:122. Grammars: editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js:23 and editors/zed/languages/jet/highlights.scm:130.

options.name: Dollar fence carve-out
options.detail: Keep `$[ entries ]$`. A named exception says the two digraphs are fence tokens, not bare environment marks. Existing source stays unchanged, but ordinary Jet still shows `$` outside config files.
options.technical: This option amends D-ONCE-DOLLAR1 with one exception. The current lexer already gives `$[` and `]$` dedicated tokens at crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:242 and crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:254. The formatter reads the same constants at crates/jet-parser/src/Formatter/Statements.rs:74. The editor lists both digraphs at editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js:23.

options.name: @ plus normal brackets
options.detail: Write `@[ entries ]`. The opening `@` marks compile-time expansion, while normal brackets close the entry list. This form is viable, but its closing edge has no matching mark.
options.technical: This form is lexically viable. The lexer already emits `At`, `LBracket`, and `RBracket` at crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:241 and crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:252. The fence pass must match the outer bracket by depth because entries can contain lists and indexes. No new close token can suppress a line break. The parser must instead keep the bracketed fence segment open by context. Current pairing expects a dedicated close token at crates/jet-parser/src/FencedNames.rs:124.

comparisons.note: Prefix `@` marks compile-time names and fact reads after D-ONCE-AT1. Option A makes statement expansion use the same visible mark.
Normal brackets already close lists and member spreads. Option C borrows that close, while option A keeps fences visibly distinct.
comparisons.code:
items :: [first, second]
use default.[cargo, ripgrep]
@[ first, second ]@ :: work()

recommendation.why: Option A follows the ratified mark law without an exception. A fence performs compile-time statement expansion, so `@` names its role. Matching edge marks also preserve the strong visual boundary chosen by D-VERDICT-1320-1.

whyNot.reason: It leaves `$` in ordinary source after D-ONCE-DOLLAR1 made that use a teaching error. Calling the digraph special weakens a simple language-wide rule.
It is viable, but the unmatched close makes fences look like marked lists. It also loses the dedicated close token that controls line termination.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each fence carries a closing `@` that normal bracketed forms do not need. The extra mark is accepted because it makes the expansion boundary explicit at both edges.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a symmetric `@` fence with a dollar carve-out. It recommended `@[ ]@` because the fence is compile-time expansion.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review checked words, braces, normal brackets, and the retired `<: :>` pair. Only `@[ ]` added a distinct viable design; the other forms either mint more syntax or revive a retired mark.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested `@` only at the opening edge. That form became option C, but it did not improve the symmetric recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the dollar option with its best case: digraphs are tokens, not bare `$`. It also confirmed that normal brackets can be matched by depth.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review tested editor support, nested brackets, line breaks, and the risk that `@` has too many roles. Dedicated symmetric tokens keep the parser boundary clear, so option A survives.

decisions.title: The default error on the exported web wire
decisions.gist: How an exported `Err` becomes a value that JavaScript and a Wasm host can use.
decisions.lesson: `JetErr` is Jet's default error value: a message, optional code, and optional recursive cause. The internal shape is settled. No ratified law covers how a compound default error crosses an exported web boundary. JavaScript and Wasm need one stable wire value that preserves these facts. The boundary therefore needs one versioned encoding, while adapters may present native errors or data.
decisions.story: Rui ships one profile loader as a browser app and a Wasm library. A missing profile is normal input failure, not a code stop. Rui needs JavaScript callers to use normal `try` and `catch`. A Wasm host needs stable fields for logs and retry rules. One wire must keep both code and cause chain.

options.name: Native `JetError` chain
options.detail: JavaScript gets a normal rejected Promise with a typed `JetError`. Beginners use `try` and `catch`. Experts read `message`, `code`, and recursive `cause`. Wasm hosts get the same fields as a plain record. The shape has no version tag, so future wire changes can break machine clients silently.
options.technical: Map `Err` to a `JetError` that extends JavaScript `Error`. Set `name`, `message`, and `code`, with absent code as `null`. Map one Jet cause to `Error.cause`. A raw Wasm host sees `{message, code, cause}`. The JS bridge throws once for the web edge. No full `jet.report/v1` object crosses.

options.name: `jet.report/v1` envelope
options.detail: JavaScript still gets a typed `JetError`, but its `report` field uses the existing machine-report schema. Tools can share one decoder with compiler and test reports. The schema gives every failure a full report frame. `JetErr` lacks why, fix, and source, so the boundary must add generic values or the schema must change.
options.technical: Encode the outer error as `jet.report/v1`. Set `moment` to `run`, `severity` to `error`, and `what` from `message`. Set `why` and `fix` to boundary text. Flatten the recursive Jet cause into the schema's `cause` array. A missing Jet code needs `null` support or a reserved placeholder. The JS bridge throws `JetError` with this report. A Wasm host receives the report object.

options.name: Tagged outcome at the raw edge
options.detail: The Wasm host gets an explicit success or failure record. Experts can branch without exceptions. The JavaScript adapter still throws a typed `JetError`, so browser code keeps target-native rejection. The outer tag makes every fallible export uniform, but it wraps successful values too.
options.technical: Use `JetOutcomeWire<T> = {tag: "Ok", value: T} | {tag: "Err", error: JetErrWire}`. `JetErrWire` has `message`, `code`, and recursive `cause`. The raw Wasm adapter returns the tagged record. The JS bridge unwraps `Ok` and converts `Err` to `JetError`. This option has no schema tag for `JetErrWire` itself.

options.name: Versioned `jet.err/v1` plus native adapters
options.detail: The wire mirrors `JetErr` and adds one stable schema tag. JavaScript gets a native `JetError` with `message`, `code`, and recursive `cause`. Experts can inspect those fields or call `toJSON()`. A Wasm host gets the same record as data. `jet.report/v1` remains a renderer shape, so no why, fix, or source data is invented.
options.technical: Define `JetErrWire = {schema: "jet.err/v1", message: String, code: String|null, cause: JetErrWire|null}`. Define a fallible edge as `{tag: "Ok", value: T} | {tag: "Err", error: JetErrWire}`. The JS bridge maps `Err` to `JetError` and maps cause nodes to `Error.cause`. The Wasm host decodes the tagged value. A report renderer may adapt the value to `jet.report/v1` when full What, Why, Fix, or source data exists.

comparisons.note: `Result<T, E>` is a strong Wasm precedent. `Ok` becomes a JavaScript value. `Err` becomes a JavaScript exception carrying the converted error. The boundary favors native JavaScript control flow, but the error shape depends on `Into<JsValue>`. Source: https://rustwasm.github.io/docs/wasm-bindgen/reference/types/result.html

`google.rpc.Status` is a durable cross-language shape. It has an integer code, a message, and repeated typed details. It separates stable classification from extensible detail. It does not model one linked cause directly. Source: https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/rpc/status.proto

JavaScript `Error` supports a recursive `cause` value. The platform keeps the outer message useful for people and the cause useful for machines. It is strong for native JS ergonomics, but it is not a versioned wire schema. Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Error/cause

Problem Details is the established HTTP JSON shape. It uses `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, and `instance`, with extension members. It is strong for HTTP responses, but `JetErr` does not carry all of those facts. Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html

recommendation.why: D keeps D-FAIL-MODEL1's value facts and D-FAIL-EDGE1's target-native delivery. One small recursive record maps exactly to `JetErr`. The schema tag prevents silent drift. JavaScript beginners use normal `try` and `catch`. Experts read stable fields or call `toJSON()`. Raw Wasm hosts branch on the explicit outer tag. `jet.report/v1` remains a renderer schema, so it does not force invented why, fix, or source fields.

whyNot.reason: A native error chain feels right, but it has no version tag or raw decoding contract. A host must guess field meaning, and a future field change can break it silently.
B gives tools one decoder, but `JetErr` does not contain why, fix, or source. Generic values would misstate the report. It also turns one recursive cause into many diagnostic objects.

C gives Wasm hosts control, but it adds a wrapper to every success and still leaves the error record unversioned. JavaScript callers gain a second public branch model when native rejection already fits the target.

recommendation.tradeoff: The wire adds one small schema tag and a boundary adapter. JavaScript receives a rejection instead of a fulfilled result for `Err`, and Wasm hosts decode one outer tag. This cost buys stable machine data without changing Jet's internal carrier or success ABI.

reviewPasses.base: The first pass compared four boundary contracts. Only D covers the JS and raw Wasm hosts without changing the internal value or bending the report schema.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The wide pass tried JS-only exceptions, binary status codes, RFC 9457, and a bare record. Each misses a host, adds a second schema, invents facts, or drifts unversioned.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Combining A native errors, C tagged edge, and a versioned record reproduces D exactly. The B envelope on top only reintroduces invented diagnostic fields.
reviewPasses.cooperative: C strengthened with the versioned record and a throwing JS adapter becomes a usable contract. It is then the D design plus a success wrapper with worse beginner ergonomics.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack targeted versioning overhead, adapter drift, and recursive decoding bugs. D survives: one fixed tag field, a wire record that mirrors the settled JetErr, and one shared encoding both adapters consume.

decisions.title: How a plane, a right and a build fact are written in Prelude source
decisions.gist: Which written form carries a non-code registry row and its law columns.
decisions.lesson: Marker rows now live in Prelude Jet source. The same registration table also holds knowledge planes, scope rights and build facts. Those ten rows still sit in a Rust array. Each carries the two law columns the ratified fact law asks for. One says which way its facts move for free. The other names the written words that move them the other way. This ballot decides the written form those rows take, so the law reads in source.
decisions.story: Sam wants to know why a range narrows for free but never widens. Today the answer is a Rust file Sam cannot open. Sam wants to read one line that says the direction and the escape words, next to the marker rows that already read that way.

options.name: One new word: fact
options.detail: A non-code row is written `fact Name(...)`, with the same dollar-marked facts a marker declaration uses. What it attaches to is one more fact. Gain: the word matches what the row is, and one word covers all three kinds. Loss: one new keyword.
options.technical: Add KW_FACT and a fact_decl parser reusing marker_decl_param_list. Registry.rs reads Prelude/Facts.jet the way Policy reads Prelude/Markers.jet. NON_CODE_ROWS and PRELUDE_GATES are deleted.
options.code:
fact Exactness($holds: .Value, $safe: .Gain, $gates: [approx, raw, wrapping])
fact Rights($holds: .Scope, $safe: .Shrink, $gates: [Unsafe, Impure, Grant])
fact Sendability($holds: .Value, $safe: .None, $proved_by: ownership)

options.name: Three new words: plane, right, fact
options.detail: Each kind gets its own word, so the declaration names the kind without a fact. Gain: the reader sees the kind at the left margin. Loss: three keywords for one table, and a fourth kind later needs a fourth word.
options.technical: Add KW_PLANE, KW_RIGHT and KW_FACT, all parsed by one shared routine. The keyword sets RowTarget.
options.code:
plane Exactness($safe: .Gain, $gates: [approx, raw, wrapping])
right Rights($safe: .Shrink, $gates: [Unsafe, Impure, Grant])
fact BuildSettings($safe: .Shrink, $gates: [Force])

options.name: Reuse the marker word
options.detail: A non-code row is a marker declaration with no site and a fact naming what it holds. Gain: no new keyword, one form for the one table. Loss: the word marker stops meaning a thing a writer types before a target, which is what it means everywhere else.
options.technical: No parser change at all. Registry.rs reads the same Prelude/Markers.jet and splits the rows on the $holds fact.
options.code: marker Exactness($sites: [], $holds: .Value, $safe: .Gain, $gates: [approx, raw, wrapping])

options.name: Leave them in Rust
options.detail: The ten non-code rows stay a Rust array. Gain: no new syntax and no work. Loss: half the one table reads in source and half does not, and the fact law stays unreadable to the people it governs.
options.code: // crates/jet-foundation/src/Registry.rs keeps NON_CODE_ROWS.

recommendation.why: One word for one table matches the ratified ruling that the four kinds differ only in what they attach to, and it keeps a fourth kind from needing a fourth keyword.

whyNot.reason: Three words for one table teach a split the table does not have.
Calling a knowledge plane a marker breaks the one word a beginner already learned.
Half the table readable in source is the drift the registration card set out to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new keyword, and the word fact is already used in prose for what these rows hold.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one new declaration word with leaving the ten non-code rows in Rust, and recommended the new word so the whole table reads in source.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review asked whether the row could be a type declaration or a package setting. Both were dropped: a row is compiler vocabulary, not a user type, and a package file cannot carry compiler law.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested writing the planes now and the rights later. It collapsed, because the two law columns are the same columns for all three kinds and a split leaves a second Rust table alive.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option D: no syntax, no work, and the guard in Registry.rs already checks the law columns. It still leaves half the one table unreadable to the people the law governs.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked option A with the prover rows, which carry no direction and no gate. They already state a none direction and name a prover, so the shared form holds and A stands.

decisions.title: Where Panic sits in the closed effect table
decisions.gist: Whether `Panic` is an effect root that code must name.
decisions.lesson: An effect is a right a function needs, such as `FS` for files. Card #1567 heals the closed table to thirteen roots. A panic is not a right. It is a program stop: `jet_panic` renders E3001 and leaves with code 70. Today `Panic` ships as a root in `Prelude/Effects.jet`, so a `#Grant` region or a signature must name it. Two shipped examples already fail the front end for that reason. This choice sets what `Panic` is in the table, and who must type it.
decisions.story: Ravi opens Jet for the first time and runs the shipped effects example. It does not run. The front end stops at line 16 and asks him to grant `Panic` in a block about files and console output. Nothing in that example is about stopping. He came to learn `#Grant`, and the first rule he meets is about panics.

options.name: Panic is a deny-only row: nobody grants it
options.detail:
`Panic` stays in the vocabulary, but only a denial may name it. No grant and no signature ever lists it. The two shipped examples compile again with no edit.

You keep the guarantee that matters. A function promises no stop with `=[!Panic]=>`. A package promises the same in one manifest line. Tools still project the inferred row, so an audit can still see which functions can stop.

The loss: a signature no longer warns a reader that the call can stop. A reader learns that from the deny surface and from tooling instead.
options.technical:
Table: thirteen grantable roots, plus `Panic` as one deny-only row. Gate law: the positive subset checks (E0740, E0741, E0712, E0747) drop the `Panic` root from the inferred set before they compare it with a bound.

The prohibition path does not change. `=[!Panic]=>` and `effects: { deny: [Panic] }` keep E0749, with the `#Pre` and refinement discharge from D-NOPANIC1=D. Seeding stays at `check_panic_call` in `CheckerItems.rs`, so the projected row and the `__jet_panic__` reach edge are untouched.

Naming `Panic` in a positive list becomes proposed error E0751, whose fix names `=[!Panic]=>`. Records the row as deny-only in the D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1 table.

options.name: Panic is the fourteenth root and every gate names it
options.detail:
The compiler keeps today's rule and the corpus moves. Every `#Grant`, every `#Caps` block, and every signature row that can reach a stop adds `Panic`.

The gain is plain reading. A signature that lists `Panic` tells a caller that the call can stop, with no tool needed.

The cost, counted on master: the 611 example files hold 64 effect-gate sites, and 108 of them hold 561 explicit `panic(` calls. Twelve files hold both a gate and a stop, covering 21 gate sites; the test corpus adds 8 more. Reach crosses files, so the real set is larger than any text count.

The burden also grows later. Today only an explicit `panic` seeds the row. If a failed bounds check or key check joins it, most ordinary code needs the word.
options.technical:
Table: fourteen roots. `Panic` keeps ordinary root behavior in E0740, E0741, E0712 and E0747, and keeps `!Panic` denial.

Migration is mechanical: add `Panic` to every gate that reaches a stop, such as `#Grant(caps: FS, IO, Panic)` and `=[Fortran, IO, Panic]=>`. Generated binder output must carry it too, because reach crosses files. Golden output for the two failing examples updates in the same pass.

Amends the D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1 root count from thirteen to fourteen, and keeps D-NOPANIC1=D as ratified.

options.name: Panic leaves the effect model
options.detail:
A stop is not a right, so it leaves the table. Nothing grants it and nothing denies it. Both examples compile again, and the table is exactly the thirteen roots card #1567 names.

The loss is the guarantee. `=[!Panic]=>` stops parsing, `effects: { deny: [Panic] }` is deleted, and E0749 goes with them. No function and no package can promise that it never stops.

This reverses the ratified ruling D-NOPANIC1=D and removes shipped enforcement. The stdlib rule that expected failure returns `T ? E` becomes an honor rule again, checked only by review.
options.technical:
Table: thirteen roots. The `effect Panic` line leaves `Prelude/Effects.jet`, and `Effect::Panic` leaves the enum.

The seeding at `check_panic_call`, E0749 and the prohibition path are deleted. The `__jet_panic__` reach edge stays, because the legacy `reaches_panic` fact and the autodiff panic rule read it. `tests/ui/panic_effect_prohibition.jet` and its transitive sibling are deleted.

Needs an owner amendment that reverses D-NOPANIC1=D by name.

options.name: Panic becomes the leaf Exec.Stop
options.detail:
The stop moves under the root that already owns leaving a process. `Exec.Exit` is a shipped leaf, and `Exec.Stop` joins it. The table is exactly thirteen roots, with no extra row.

Denial reads `=[!Exec.Stop]=>`, and a manifest denies it the same way. Grants never need the name, as in option A, so both examples compile again.

The loss is subsumption. `=[Exec]=>` covers every leaf, so a function that runs a program silently admits stops. `=[!Exec]=>` promises no subprocess, and now promises no stop as well. Two unrelated facts share one word.
options.technical:
Table: thirteen roots. `Exec.Stop` joins `Exec.Exit` in `BUILTIN_EFFECT_LEAVES` in `effects_surface.rs`.

Gate law matches option A: the leaf drops out of the positive subset checks and is enforced only through prohibition. D-EFFTREE1 ancestor subsumption makes `Exec` cover `Exec.Stop`, in a bound and in a denial alike.

`=[!Panic]=>`, `deny: [Panic]`, the E0749 text and both shipped ui tests migrate to the new name. Amends D-NOPANIC1=D on spelling only, and leaves its enforcement rule intact.

comparisons.note: A checked exception must be declared with `throws`, and the declaration spreads to every caller. An unchecked `Error` needs no declaration at all. That spread is the cost option B accepts.
A returned `error` carries expected failure, and the signature shows it. `panic` sits outside that model and never appears in a signature.
comparisons.code:
func ParsePort(raw string) (int, error) { ... } // expected failure, in the signature
func mustPort(raw string) int { panic("bad port: " + raw) } // stop, not in the signature

comparisons.note: `panic!` sits outside `Result` and never appears in a signature. Panic freedom needs the third-party `no_panic` crate, which works outside the type system.
comparisons.code:
fn parse_port(raw: &str) -> Result<u16, PortError> { ... } // expected failure
fn must_port(raw: &str) -> u16 { panic!("bad port: {raw}") } // stop, unmarked

comparisons.note: Koka gives divergence its own row, apart from the rows for input and output. The compiler infers that row, so a programmer never grants it. This is the split option A adopts.
comparisons.code:
fun fib(n : int) : div int { ... }        // divergence row, inferred
fun add(x : int, y : int) : total int { x + y }  // no effect at all

recommendation.why: A panic hands out no authority. It ends the program at the shared boundary with E3001 and exit code 70. A grant cannot make a stop legal, so asking a person to grant one teaches nothing. D-NOPANIC1=D already calls `Panic` a deny-only row, and milestone M12 names it a deniable row. Option A keeps every enforcement surface, removes every word a person must type, and both shipped examples pass with no edit.

whyNot.reason: It taxes the widest surface in the language to state a fact the compiler already infers. On master that is 21 gate sites across 12 example files, plus 8 more in tests. It reaches most ordinary code once bounds and key checks join the row.

It deletes the only shipped enforcement of the panic rule: `=[!Panic]=>`, the manifest deny list and E0749. It also reverses D-NOPANIC1=D, and option A already removes the whole typing burden without giving that up.

Subsumption makes one word carry two unrelated facts. `=[Exec]=>` would admit stops in any function that runs a program, and `=[!Exec]=>` would promise no stop by accident. The rename buys a tidy root count and no new power.

recommendation.tradeoff: A signature stops advertising that a call can stop. A reader learns it from the deny surface, from the projected row, and from tooling instead. We accept that because the row was never a grant, so no reader could act on it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft set out three routes: keep `Panic` as a root and migrate the corpus, drop it from the model, or make it deny-only. It recommended deny-only after reading D-NOPANIC1=D, which already calls the row deny-only.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a `#Grant`-only exemption and a per-package strict mode, then folded both away, because neither fixes the E0740 failure without making one signature mean two things. It added option D, the `Exec.Stop` leaf, from the shipped `Exec.Exit` precedent.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass split the question into table shape and gate law. Options A and D share one gate law and differ only in the name, so D stayed as the naming alternative rather than a second law.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each loser: B gained the caller-visible reading argument, C gained the divergence argument that Rust and Go show, and D gained the exact thirteen-root count. Each detail now states its own strongest case.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A for losing audit value, and for opening a path to more ambient rows. The repair names the limit: only a row that hands out no authority qualifies, and the closed table names exactly one.

decisions.title: What replaces the word capability in the three places a user still types it
decisions.gist: The new name for three user-typed spellings of the old word.
decisions.lesson: The project retired the word `capability` from what a user reads. That pass covered diagnostics, help text, docs and examples. Three places are different: a user types them, so renaming one changes real programs and scripts. This choice picks the replacement for those three, or decides to keep them.
decisions.story: Ari reads a permission error, and it now says `authority`. Ari searches the docs for `authority`, finds the guide, then writes the marker the guide describes. The compiler answers that the name does not exist, because the thing a program types is still spelled `Capability`. Ari now has two words for one idea and no way to tell which is current.

options.name: Rename all three to authority
options.detail: The three become `Authority.FS`, `.authority()` and `--authority-json`, matching the word a reader now sees everywhere else. Gain: one word for one idea, so a reader who follows a diagnostic finds the thing they must type. Loss: existing programs and scripts that use the old spellings stop working and must be edited.
options.technical: Rename the `Capability` fact menu to `Authority`, `BrowserCapabilities` to `BrowserAuthority` with `.capabilities()` becoming `.authority()`, and the CLI flag to `--authority-json`. Greenfield cutover per AGENTS.md: remove the old spellings rather than keeping aliases. E0119 pins the marker prefix, so its snapshot moves with it.

options.name: Rename the marker menu only, and leave the two library and tool names
options.detail: `Capability.FS` becomes `Authority.FS`, because that is the one a diagnostic sends the reader to. The browser reader and the flag keep their names. Gain: the confusing case is fixed with the smallest change to working programs. Loss: the old word survives in two places, so a search still returns both.
options.technical: Rename only the fact menu and its E0119 snapshot. `BrowserCapabilities`, `.capabilities()` and `--capabilities-json` stay, documented as names taken from the browser protocol rather than from Jet's own vocabulary.

options.name: Keep all three and say why in the docs
options.detail: Nothing a user types changes. The docs state that `Authority` is the word for the idea and that these three names are historical. Gain: no program or script breaks. Loss: a reader who follows a diagnostic still cannot find the name to type, which is the problem the retirement set out to fix.
options.technical: No code change. The retirement stops at read-only surfaces, and a note records that the typed names were deliberately left.

options.name: Rename the marker menu to rights
options.detail: The menu becomes `Rights.FS`, keeping `Authority` for the value a program passes around and using a different word for the menu of facts. Gain: two related but distinct ideas keep distinct names, so a reader is not left wondering why one word means both. Loss: a third word enters the vocabulary a reader must learn.
options.technical: Rename the fact menu to `Rights`, matching the rights-tree wording already used in the authority substrate work. `Authority` stays the name of the handle a program holds. The two library and tool names follow option B and stay.

options.name: One word everywhere: ability
options.detail: Every surface a user reads or types uses one word. The menu becomes `Ability.FS`. The carried value becomes `Abilities`. The marker becomes `#Abilities`. The browser reader becomes `.abilities()` and the flag `--abilities-json`. Read-only wording that today says authority is rewritten to say ability. Gain: one short plain word for the whole idea, with no echo of auth or authorization. Loss: this is the widest rename, and it amends three ratified rulings.
options.technical: Amends D-AUTHORITY-NAME1 (`Authority` becomes `Abilities`), D-AUTHORITY-WORD1 (the reader-facing replacement word becomes ability), and the marker name from D-AUTHORITY-SCOPE1 (`#Caps` becomes `#Abilities`; the one-marker law is unchanged). Greenfield cutover per AGENTS.md: old spellings removed, no aliases. The E0119 snapshot moves, and one wording pass rewrites authority to ability across diagnostics, help text and docs. WebDriver's wire format still says capabilities; the Jet-side reader renames anyway, and the docs note the protocol word once. No `Ability` symbol exists in the codebase, so the rename is collision-free.

comparisons.note: Deno spells permissions one way in the flag, the prompt and the API, so a reader who sees the prompt can guess the flag.
comparisons.code:
deno run --allow-read=/etc main.ts
await Deno.permissions.query({ name: "read" })

comparisons.note: Android uses one word in the manifest, the request call and the dialog. The word is long, but a search finds all three.
WebDriver's own wire format calls them capabilities, which is why the browser reader carries that word. It comes from the protocol, not from Jet.

recommendation.why: One word for one idea, on every surface at once. A reader who meets ability in an error can type it, search it, and pass it. It also avoids the auth echo: web programs already use core.auth, and the word authority reads as authorization vocabulary there.

whyNot.reason: It settles on authority, which sits beside core.auth in the one domain where the two are easiest to conflate. The word is also longer and stiffer than ability.
It keeps three words alive at once: authority in the menu, capabilities in the reader and the flag. A search returns all of them, and none is clearly current.
It leaves the exact failure the story describes: a diagnostic sends the reader to a word that no program can type.
It grows the vocabulary to two words on purpose. Rights is also legalistic, and it has only ever lived inside the substrate design papers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Option E is the widest cutover: it renames the menu, the value type, the marker, the reader, the flag and the read-only wording in one change, and it amends three ratified rulings. That is the price of ending at exactly one word. A lowercase search for ability also matches inside words like capability, though the typed names are unambiguous.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared renaming all three against renaming only the marker menu, and recommended the menu because it is the only one a diagnostic sends a reader to.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added keeping all three with a documentation note, and renaming the menu to `rights`. It also tested keeping an alias for one release, which was dropped because the project's greenfield rule forbids deprecated spellings.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested renaming the menu and the flag while keeping the browser reader. The flag is read by scripts and gains nothing a reader needs, so it was folded into option B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the rename-everything option by pairing it with a migration note in the release docs. It still renames two names borrowed from the WebDriver format.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what a reader does after seeing `authority` in an error under each option. Only the options that rename the marker menu answer that, and keeping all three fails it outright.

decisions.title: String's remaining 34 ledger gaps: decline, ship, or ship the high-frequency few
decisions.gist: Which of String's 34 remaining ledger names ship directly on String, and which route to an existing mechanism.
decisions.lesson: Card #1476 gave String 30 methods. The surface ledger still lists 34 more names other languages ship on their string type. Each name already has a Jet route somewhere else. The usage-frequency report (docs/research/corelib-api-usage-frequency-2026-08-06.md) ranks how often real code performs each operation. Jet's philosophy sets friction in proportion to that frequency: the most common work must be the shortest call.
decisions.story: Priya is writing a log cleaner in Jet. She trims a line, then wants the number inside it. She types line.trim().to_int(), the way Ruby's to_i chains, and wonders whether Jet forgot number parsing on text or expects a detour through another type.

options.name: Decline all 34, route each to what Jet already ships
options.detail: None of the 34 names add a workflow Jet is missing. Mutation verbs like clear and push do not fit an immutable String. Sequence names like map, fold, and first already exist on List and Iter once text becomes a list of characters or bytes. parse, tofloat, match, and matches already live on Int, Float, and core.regex. concat duplicates the plus operator and interpolation. The rest are niche buffer operations two languages ship, covered today by slice, replace, and the shipped surface.
options.technical:
Immutable-string declines: clear, push, pop, remove, and write. String is an immutable value. Rebuild text with plus, replace, or slice instead of mutating it in place.

Iter and List declines: all, map, fold, skip, chunk, droplast, indexed, flatmap, each, max, min, scan, first, last, get, and codepointat. These are sequence operations, not text operations. Call chars or bytes first, then use the existing List or Iter method.

Number-parsing declines: parse and tofloat. Int.parse and Float.parse already convert text to a number with one error type.

Pattern-matching declines: match and matches. core.regex already owns pattern matching under D-REGEXENGINE1.

Concatenation decline: concat. The plus operator and string interpolation already join text.

Validity decline: isvalid. A live String is always valid UTF-8 by construction. String.from_bytes already reports invalid bytes as an error when text is built from a byte buffer.

Niche buffer declines: replacerange, isprint, intern, indexofany, lastindexofany, chop, and rpartition. Each is a low-traffic operation only two of eleven compared languages ship.

options.name: Ship all 34 as new String methods
options.detail: String grows a second copy of the Iter vocabulary, a second parse path, and a second match method, all living beside the mechanisms Jet already ships elsewhere. Every text tutorial now has to say which of two spellings to use for map, parse, or match, and the answer changes by container.
options.technical: Each of the 34 names ships as a string_method_return case in Collections.rs plus a matching jet_str_* Prelude function in UnicodeString.rs. Sequence names like map, fold, and first duplicate the List/Iter case arms already registered for those same names. parse and tofloat duplicate Int.parse and Float.parse. match and matches duplicate core.regex.is_match and core.regex.matches. concat duplicates the existing plus operator lowering for String plus Add.

options.name: Ship the high-frequency names as direct spellings; route the rest
options.detail:
The frequency report marks parse-to-number as a dominant string operation and regex tests as heavy, recurring work. Those names ship directly on String: to_int and to_float (the ledger's parse and tofloat, spelled to match to_string) plus match and matches. Each one is a spelling of a mechanism Jet already ships — Int.parse, Float.parse, and the one core.regex engine — so no second mechanism appears.

Every other name stays routed. Mutation verbs clash with immutable String. Char-level sequence work sits below the frequency line, where one chars() call is proportional friction. concat stays declined because plus and interpolation are already the shortest spelling.
options.technical:
to_int() and to_float() call the same Prelude parse functions Int.parse and Float.parse use today. They return the same result with the same error meaning. matches(pattern) answers a yes-or-no test by routing to core.regex.is_match. match(pattern) returns the first match through the same engine. Both carry the engine's existing bad-pattern error shape.

Declines unchanged from option A: mutation verbs (clear, push, pop, remove, write); the sequence family, still one chars() or bytes() call away; concat; isvalid; and the niche buffer names.

comparisons.note: Ruby puts number parsing and regex tests straight on String, the shape option C adopts. Jet keeps the parse error where Ruby's to_i silently returns 0 on junk.
Kotlin's CharSequence mirrors most of Iterable, so all, map, and first exist twice: once as a sequence operation and once as a string operation.
Rust keeps text parsing on the destination type through FromStr, the route option A keeps and option C shortens with a direct String spelling.

recommendation.why: The frequency report shows parse-to-number is everyday string work and regex tests recur constantly. Option C makes those the shortest possible calls, which is what friction-proportional-to-frequency demands. Underneath, each new name is a spelling of one existing mechanism, so the expert model stays single-engine.

whyNot.reason: It weighs all 34 names the same and leaves dominant operations behind a detour, taxing the most common text work to keep a rule tidy.
It ships a second copy of the sequence vocabulary and synonyms that save no keystrokes, growing what a beginner must learn without cutting friction anywhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: Docs must say plainly that to_int, to_float, match, and matches are the one parse mechanism and the one regex engine. Char-level sequence work still detours through chars().

reviewPasses.base: The first draft grouped the 34 names into six families, each already answered by an existing Jet mechanism, and recommended declining all of them.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked isprint and indexofany for a real gap instead of a duplicate. Both still routed to an existing mechanism or a two-witness niche buffer method.
reviewPasses.hybrid: After the owner's philosophy question, this pass was rerun with the usage-frequency report as the scale. Parse-to-number and regex tests crossed the dominance line, and that split became option C, now the recommendation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option B: shipping the full 34 would let a newcomer type any name they already know without a detour. Option C keeps that welcome exactly where the traffic justifies it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked option C as reopening dual mechanisms. It survives: the four new names call the one parse mechanism and the one regex engine, and every still-declined name keeps a one-call route.

decisions.title: Where shared Prelude semantics live in the source tree
decisions.gist: Which folder holds the one shared implementation every execution tier calls.
decisions.lesson: Invariant I9 demands one implementation of every language behavior, and it names the folder: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude. The compile-time interpreter lives in a crate that is not allowed to depend on the codegen crate. So a behavior that the compile-time interpreter must also run cannot live in the named folder. The outcome carrier hit this wall. The code now lives in the foundation crate, which every engine can reach. The invariant's purpose is intact; only its named path is wrong.
decisions.story: An agent finishes the outcome carrier and must make the compile-time interpreter call the same jet_partial function the compiled program calls. The named Prelude folder is unreachable from that interpreter's crate. The agent either duplicates the function, breaks the crate seam, or moves the file. Duplication is the exact drift I9 exists to prevent, so the agent moved the file and flagged the invariant text.

options.name: Amend I9: shared semantics live in the Prelude parts
options.detail: The invariant stops naming one folder. It instead says: semantics live only in the embedded Prelude parts, and today those parts live in jet-foundation and crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude. Every engine must call those functions. Nothing moves. The carrier stays where every tier can already reach it.
options.technical: I9 text change only. The prelude assembly order in Codegen/mod.rs and Codegen/Web.rs remains the single source of truth for what is a Prelude part. A new part is legal in either crate; the comptime-reachable parts must sit in jet-foundation.

options.name: Move every Prelude part into jet-foundation
options.detail: One folder again, but a reachable one: all Prelude semantics migrate from the codegen crate into jet-foundation. The invariant keeps naming exactly one home. Larger one-time move; the codegen crate keeps only emit and marshalling.
options.technical: Relocate crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/** into jet-foundation prelude modules; codegen includes them verbatim as it already does for Outcome.rs. No behavior change; include order preserved; golden output byte-identical.
options.code:
// I9 (amended): Semantics live only in crates/jet-foundation/src/prelude/**.
// jet-codegen embeds those files verbatim; no semantic code remains in codegen.

options.name: Keep I9's folder; carve out the carrier by name
options.detail: The invariant text stays. A ratified carve-out names Outcome.rs as the one permitted exception, with its reason. Every future comptime-reachable behavior needs its own carve-out, so this choice recurs.
options.technical: No code change. The carve-out record must name the file, the I6 seam reason, and its removal condition (a future dependency restructure that makes the named folder reachable).

comparisons.note: Rust's core library sits below every backend for the same reason: the lowest crate everyone may depend on holds the shared meaning.
comparisons.code: // libcore is reachable from every consumer; codegen backends never define language semantics.

recommendation.why: Option A states the real rule the code already follows: one embedded Prelude, every engine marshals onto it. It fixes the text without moving working code or inviting repeat exceptions.

whyNot.reason: A large file move with zero behavior change; the single-folder purity it buys is cosmetic, and the move risks churn in every open branch.
A named exception recurs every time the compile-time tier needs a new behavior, and a growing exception list is weaker law than an accurate rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two legal homes instead of one folder. That is acceptable because the prelude assembly list, not the folder path, is what engines actually share.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared amending the text, moving all parts to the foundation crate, and a named carve-out, and recommended the amendment because it matches the shipped, working shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested two more shapes: letting comptime depend on codegen, and duplicating the carrier per crate. Both die on ratified law — the I6 seam and I9's anti-drift purpose — so neither joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tried A now with B as a scheduled migration. That adds a standing obligation with no behavior gain, so the passes stayed separate options.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by noting verbatim embedding makes the move mechanical, and C by giving the carve-out a concrete removal condition. Both stand as their best selves.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A: two homes could invite semantic code sprawl into any foundation file. The repair names the prelude assembly list as the authority — a file is a Prelude part only when embedded — so A survives.

decisions.title: How block-construct markers are stored after parsing
decisions.gist: Whether a parsed block construct also keeps a separate marker record.
decisions.lesson: Card #1456 unified marker reading. One shared reader reads every hash-name marker, and bindings keep a plain list of marker records. Block constructs like #Unsafe and #Context still have their own dedicated tree nodes. Those nodes store the marker's arguments as typed fields. Storing a second marker record beside those fields would say the same fact twice. This choice decides the one storage shape for block constructs, plus #Todo, #Tainted, and the tag-prefix operator in expression position.
decisions.story: Priya writes a formatter pass that must find every marker in a file. Bindings hand her one marker list. Block constructs hand her twelve different node shapes. She asks which shape is the one truth, and today the answer differs by position.

options.name: The construct node is the record
options.detail: Dedicated nodes keep their typed fields, and no separate marker record is added. The registry still owns every name. Tools get one uniform accessor that yields any construct's marker row and arguments, derived from the fields. Gain: no fact is stored twice, and the checker keeps precise typed fields. Loss: the uniform view is an accessor, not a stored field.
options.technical: Stmt variants keep their shapes. A registry-derived accessor (marker_row()) maps each block-construct node to its Policy::APPLIED_RULES row plus argument values. The retained markers: Vec<Marker> list stays binding-only. The shared parse-path reader from #1456 is unchanged.

options.name: Retain a marker record on every construct
options.detail: Each block node carries the parsed marker record beside its typed fields. Gain: every marker in a file is findable the same way, as a stored value. Loss: the same fact lives in two places. An edit that changes one copy and not the other ships silent drift, and every consumer must know which copy is authoritative.
options.technical: Add marker: Marker to the twelve block-construct Stmt variants plus the #Todo, #Tainted, and tag-prefix expression nodes. A single-writer rule makes the record authoritative; fields become derived views. Formatter and reflection read the record; sema reads the fields.

options.name: One generic marker-block node
options.detail: Dissolve the dedicated variants into one node: a marker record plus a body, the same shape bindings use. Gain: one storage mechanism for every marker position. Loss: construct-specific typed fields leave the tree. Every checker and codegen consumer reads arguments through accessors, and the one-time refactor crosses parser, sema, TIR, and formatter.
options.technical: Stmt::Marked { marker: Marker, body: Block } replaces the twelve variants. Typed argument accessors are generated from the registry row schema, so malformed arguments are still rejected at parse time. Sema match arms key on marker.name instead of variant.

comparisons.note: Attributes stay uniform token records on every node, read on demand through typed parsers — the shape option C proposes.
comparisons.code: #[cfg(unix)] fn f() {}  // syn: Attribute { path: cfg, tokens: (unix) }

comparisons.note: Each statement kind is its own typed AST node with dedicated fields — the shape option A keeps.
comparisons.code: // SwiftSyntax: GuardStmtSyntax { conditions, body } — no generic wrapper

recommendation.why: The node already records every fact the marker states, in typed fields the checker verifies. The registry supplies the name. Nothing is stored twice, and the uniform tooling view is one derived accessor.

whyNot.reason: It stores the same fact in two places, and the two copies can drift apart silently.
It trades precise typed fields for accessor indirection across the whole checker, with no user-visible gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: Tools that want one flat marker list call a shared accessor instead of reading one stored field. That accessor is written once and derived from the registry, so it cannot drift.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared typed fields, a duplicate record, and one generic node. It recommended typed fields because no fact is stored twice.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested erasing markers after checking and a side table of records. The first lost the source shape the formatter needs; the second folded into option B as the same duplication.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass added a registry-derived accessor to option A, yielding any construct's marker row in one call. This closes option B's uniformity gain without duplicate storage.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option B a single-writer rule with fields as derived views. Option C gained typed accessors generated from the registry row schema.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked option A with the formatter walk and a future reflection walk; the shared accessor answers both. Drift between fields and registry names is already caught by the D-MARK-REG1 scans, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Where should an interpreter view-bounds failure be tested?
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet proves an interpreter view-bounds failure.
decisions.lesson: The interpreter already performs the shared bounds check. D-INTERP-DIAG1, ratified on card #1483, maps this runtime failure to a panic with exit 70. Card #1616 still requires a compile diagnostic snapshot. Both requirements cannot be true at once.
decisions.story: Mara runs a program that creates a view outside a list. Jet must stop before any invalid access. She also needs a test that fails if one execution tier ever accepts the view.
decisions.inWild:
values := [1]
outside :: &values[2..2]

$ jet run --interpret main.jet
Error [E0953]: can't view 1 items from 2 to 2 (inclusive)
# exit 70

options.name: Test the runtime trap in the runtime suite
options.detail: Keep the ratified exit-70 runtime trap. Delete the stale compile-diagnostic fixture and prove the same message and failure across AOT, default run, and forced interpreter. This keeps each test suite about one product surface.
options.technical: Retarget #1616 to the tier-parity runtime test. Amend #1601 criterion 3 to remove tests/ui/view_mut_bounds_interpreter.stderr. Preserve D-INTERP-DIAG1 and the shared E0953 bounds predicate.
options.code:
assert_tiers_fail(
  source: "outside :: &values[2..2]",
  code: "E0953",
  exit: 70,
)

options.name: Teach the diagnostic suite to capture runtime traps
options.detail: Keep the ratified exit-70 runtime trap and keep the UI fixture. Change the snapshot harness so a nonzero interpreter run records panic output instead of reporting no errors. One suite then covers compile reports and runtime traps.
options.technical: Preserve D-INTERP-DIAG1. Extend diagnostic_snapshots only for RunOutcome::Ran with a nonzero exit. The golden stores stderr and exit status, not a Problems value.

options.name: Turn the failure back into a compile diagnostic
options.detail: Restore the old Problems/E0953 snapshot. The interpreter rejects the view before execution, so the diagnostic suite remains unchanged. This reopens the ratified rule that runtime interpreter failures use panic output and exit 70.
options.technical: Amend D-INTERP-DIAG1 for view bounds. Source/Interpreter.rs must return RunOutcome::Problems for this case instead of RunOutcome::Ran.
options.code:
$ jet check main.jet
error[E0953]: can't view 1 items from 2 to 2 (inclusive)

comparisons.note: Rust tests compile diagnostics and runtime panics in separate suites. An out-of-bounds dynamic index is a runtime panic.
comparisons.code:
let xs = vec![1];
println!("{}", xs[i]); // panics when i is outside the vector

comparisons.note: A dynamic bounds failure is tested by running code and checking IndexError, not by a parser snapshot.

recommendation.why: The bounds check already works. A runtime parity test proves the safety contract at the surface where it occurs and keeps the ratified exit-70 rule intact.

whyNot.reason: It makes one snapshot harness interpret two different products. Future readers cannot tell whether a fixture tests a compiler report or a runtime failure.
It reopens a ratified interpreter rule even though the current runtime behavior is safe and consistent.

recommendation.tradeoff: The stale UI fixture is deleted. The same case remains protected by a stronger three-tier runtime test.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a runtime parity test with a mixed snapshot harness and a compiler diagnostic. It recommended the runtime test because the failure occurs during execution.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested keeping both suites and removing the case. Keeping both duplicates proof, while removing it loses tier safety coverage.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the useful part of the stale fixture with the runtime test: keep the exact E0953 message, but assert it in the three-tier runtime matrix.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the mixed harness option by limiting it to nonzero interpreter outcomes. It still gives one suite two meanings.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked whether deleting a golden weakens diagnostics. It does not, because no compile diagnostic exists under ratified law and the runtime test checks code, message, exit, and tier parity.

decisions.title: What the environment-module selector flag is called
decisions.gist: The command-line flag that picks one environment module needs a name that no longer says profile.
decisions.lesson: The ratified one-word ruling keeps the word profile for exactly one meaning and renames the rest. The rename card found a flag the ruling's fold list mislabeled: --env-profile does not select a preset composition, it selects one env.<name> module from the manifest. Folding it into --preset would make one flag mean two different things. The flag kept its old spelling, so a user still types the retired word today.
decisions.story: Rowan keeps two environment modules in one package: env.dev with a local database and env.ci with a hermetic one. To enter the second, Rowan types jet enter --env-profile ci. Every other surface stopped saying profile; this flag still does, and Rowan wonders whether it is the old system or the new one.

options.name: --env <name>
options.detail: The flag names the axis it selects: an environment module. Short, matches the env.<name> spelling in the manifest, and cannot be confused with --preset. The loss: --env reads slightly generic next to commands that already live inside an environment.
options.technical: Rename EnvProfileFlag and its parse row to Env; retired --env-profile teaches the replacement with a registered diagnostic, same pattern as the E1300 row --profile already has.
options.code:
$ jet enter --env ci
entered env.ci (hermetic database)

$ jet enter --env-profile ci
error[E1301]: `--env-profile` is retired
  fix: type `--env ci` — the flag now names the environment module directly

options.name: --enter <name> positional on enter
options.detail: jet enter ci: the subcommand already means entering an environment, so the module name rides as its positional argument and no flag exists at all. Smallest surface. The loss: other commands that accepted --env-profile (run, test) still need a spelled flag, so this option only removes the flag in one place.
options.technical: enter takes an optional positional env module; other commands keep a flag (whatever this ballot picks for them) — so option B must pair with A or C for the general case.
options.code:
$ jet enter ci
entered env.ci (hermetic database)

$ jet test --env ci   # non-enter commands still need the flag

options.name: --environment <name>
options.detail: The full word, no abbreviation. Unambiguous and self-teaching, at the cost of eleven characters where every sibling flag is short. Tab completion softens the cost.
options.technical: Same mechanical rename as option A with the long spelling; --env could be accepted as its documented short form only if the owner wants both, which reintroduces two spellings for one thing.
options.code:
$ jet enter --environment ci
entered env.ci (hermetic database)

comparisons.note: nix develop .#ci selects a named devShell with a positional attribute — the enter command and the selector are one gesture, like option B.
--profile selects optional service groups; the overload of the word profile across tools is exactly why Jet retired it.

recommendation.why: The flag's whole job is picking an env.<name> module, and --env says exactly that in the manifest's own spelling. It works uniformly on every command, not just enter.

whyNot.reason: It only removes the flag on enter; every other command still needs a spelled flag, so the ballot's question returns immediately.
The long word buys no clarity over --env, because the manifest itself spells the axis env.

recommendation.tradeoff: --env is one more short global flag to learn. That is acceptable because it replaces a retired spelling users must unlearn anyway.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared --env, an enter positional, and --environment, and recommended --env for matching the manifest spelling on every command.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a namespaced preset value and keeping the old flag; neither joined the menu because one re-merges the two axes and the other keeps a retired word.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review paired option B's positional on enter with option A's flag elsewhere. That is two spellings for one selection, so the combination was rejected and the options stayed separate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by noting enter is by far the most-typed site, and C by noting completion erases its length cost. Both stand as real choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked --env as colliding with the env.jet file and manifest env blocks. That is agreement — flag, file, and block name one axis — so A survives.

decisions.title: One law for every compiler-held fact
decisions.gist: Whether one written law governs every fact the compiler holds.
decisions.lesson: The compiler proves facts about the program: a value's range, a scope's rights, a task's duty, a place's write window, a build setting. Four ratified rethinks each gave their facts a rule, and all four rules say the same thing in different words. A fact may move toward safety silently. Every move away from safety needs one written word at the site. This ballot decides whether that sentence becomes one recorded law, or stays as four separate rules.
decisions.story: Ana learns Jet from the book. The numbers chapter says knowledge is conserved. The security chapter says rights only shrink. The packages chapter says policy only tightens. The concurrency chapter says a task must be joined. Four chapters, four rules to memorize. Her teammate asks what the safety model is, and she cannot answer in one sentence.

options.name: One written law in the spec
options.detail: The spec states the law once: a fact moves toward safety silently, and every move away is one written word, recorded for audit. The four ratified per-plane rules become named instances of it. Teaching, docs, and diagnostics can point at one sentence. Gain: one safety story. Loss: the law is prose only, so a future plane could forget to follow it.
options.technical: The law enters docs/spec/philosophy.md and syntax-decisions.md as a recorded decision. D-TYPE2-EXACT1, D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1, D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1, D-CONF-MERGE1, D-FLOWTYPE1, and D-CONC-JOIN1 are listed as instances. No ruling changes.

options.name: Law plus a guarded registry
options.detail: Everything in option A, and the plane registry enforces it. Every registered fact plane must name its safe direction and its gate words in its registry row. A plane without them fails the same guard that already protects marker law zero. Gain: no future plane can drift from the law. Loss: registry rows carry two more required columns.
options.technical: The D-META-REG1 table gains two columns per plane: safe_direction and gates[]. A CI guard mirrors the marker drift-guard: a plane row missing either column fails the build. Existing planes are backfilled in the same change.

options.name: Keep four separate rules
options.detail: No umbrella law. Each rethink keeps its own rule, vocabulary, and chapter. Gain: nothing moves, and no wording debate happens now. Loss: the same law stays written four times, new planes copy whichever wording their author read last, and the one-sentence safety story never exists.

comparisons.note: Pony unified its concurrency and memory safety into one deny-capability table. One rule made the system teachable where prior actor languages had scattered rules.
comparisons.code:
// Pony reference capabilities: one matrix of what is denied.
// iso, trn, ref, val, box, tag - every alias rule reads off one table.

comparisons.note: Rust never stated one law across borrow checking, Send/Sync, const rules, and unsafe. Each is taught separately, and learners report the total model as the hard part.

recommendation.why: The registry guard is what made marker law zero real, and the same guard makes this law real. Implementation cards #1517-#1579 are about to add planes, so the check must exist before they land.

whyNot.reason: A prose-only law repeats the pre-law-zero marker story, where five ad-hoc forms grew because nothing checked new arrivals.
Keeping four wordings leaves the fifth rethink free to mint a fifth, and the one-sentence safety story never exists.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every plane author must declare a safe direction and gate list, even for a plane with no gates. That is two lines per plane, and it is the audit trail working.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a spec-prose law with keeping four separate rules and recommended the written law for the one-sentence safety story.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the guarded-registry option and considered a diagnostics-only variant. The diagnostics-only variant was folded into the vocabulary ballot D-FACT-WORD1, where it belongs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested prose law now with a guard later. It collapsed into option B, because the guard is two registry columns and delaying it invites drift during the #1517-#1579 builds.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C: it costs nothing today and avoids a wording debate. It still leaves the law unwritten while sixty implementation cards build fact planes.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked B with planes that have no meaningful safe direction, such as pure bookkeeping rows. The registry accepts a declared none value for such planes, so the guard survives and B stands.

decisions.title: One word for the one-way rule
decisions.gist: Which word names the safe move and the escape in errors and docs.
decisions.lesson: Five words currently name the same one-way rule. Policy and config say tighten. Rights say attenuate. Flow types say narrow. Number knowledge says conserve. Facts erase. A user who meets all five reasonably believes Jet has five different rules. This ballot picks one word pair for the law in diagnostics and docs. Exact operation names stay: flow narrowing keeps its technical name, and no user-typed spelling changes.
decisions.story: Sam hits three errors in one afternoon. One says a package may only tighten policy. One says rights may only attenuate. One says a conversion would lose knowledge. He searches the docs for three different rules and files a confused issue asking how they relate. They are the same rule.

options.name: Tighten and loosen
options.detail: Facts tighten silently. A gate loosens, and loosening is always spelled. Two ratified rules already say tighten, so this option renames the least. Plain everyday words. Gain: smallest migration, reads naturally at every plane. Loss: tighten reads oddly for duty, where the safe move is finishing a job rather than shrinking something.
options.technical: Diagnostic copy and docs adopt tighten and loosen as the law words. attenuate, conserve, and law-level narrow retire from prose. Operation names stay: flow narrowing, widening conversions, and every user-typed spelling are untouched.

options.name: The ratchet and the release
options.detail: Facts ratchet toward safety. Every escape word is a release, and a release is always written. One vivid picture that works for all four planes, including duty. Gain: memorable, teaches itself, names the gate family too. Loss: ratchet is a workshop metaphor, not a plain word, and it translates poorly.
options.technical: Docs name the law the ratchet. Diagnostic copy says moves toward safety and names the release word. The gate ledger and the release family share the release name.

options.name: Toward safety and away
options.detail: No metaphor at all. Diagnostics say a fact only moves toward safety here, and name the written word that allows the move away. Gain: nothing to learn, no metaphor to translate, works for every plane including duty. Loss: longer phrases in error text, and no single noun for the law when docs need to cite it.
options.technical: Diagnostic copy adopts the toward-safety phrase. Docs cite the law as the one-way law. attenuate, conserve, and tighten retire from law-level prose but stay legal in local descriptions.

options.name: Keep the five words
options.detail: Each plane keeps its own vocabulary and only the docs note the family resemblance. Gain: zero migration, each word stays locally precise. Loss: the confusion in the story stays real, error copy never converges, and every future plane picks a sixth word.

recommendation.why: Tighten is already ratified language in two places, it is a plain everyday word, and one word pair makes every error teach the same law. The duty plane reads acceptably as tightening what the value may still do.

whyNot.reason: Ratchet is a metaphor the simple-prose rule would flag, and it adds a word to learn where a plain one exists.
The toward-safety phrase is honest but wordy, and the law still needs a noun the docs can cite.
Keeping five words preserves the exact confusion this ballot exists to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: Duty errors fit the tighten frame least naturally, so their copy leans on the owes phrasing rather than the law word. That is one plane with softer wording, against four that align exactly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared tighten, ratchet, and keeping five words, and recommended tighten for continuity with ratified text.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the no-metaphor toward-safety option and tested narrow and widen as the pair. Narrow lost because flow narrowing already owns that word as an operation name.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested tighten in errors with ratchet as the doc nickname. Two names for one law recreates the original problem, so the hybrid was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened D: local words are locally precise, and attenuate is standard security vocabulary. It still leaves users finding five rules where there is one.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked tighten with the duty plane, where nothing shrinks. The owes phrasing repairs duty copy without breaking the law word, so A survives with that carve-out recorded.

decisions.title: One ledger for every gate
decisions.gist: Which escape words land in the one audit list.
decisions.lesson: A gate is one written word that moves a fact away from safety: #Unsafe, #Scrub, approx, .Force, grants, detach. The ratified authority ledger (D-AUTHORITY-GATE1) already collects the rights gates behind jet inspect authority. The other gate families, such as taint scrubs and precision drops, live only in source text. This ballot decides how far the one ledger reaches. It generalizes D-AUTHORITY-GATE1 and changes no gate spelling.
decisions.story: Priya reviews a payment service before a compliance audit. She needs every place the code stepped off the safe path: unsafe regions, dependency grants, scrubbed customer data, forced build settings, and precision drops in the interest math. Today that is one CLI command, a lockfile diff, a trust file, and a repo-wide grep, assembled by hand into a spreadsheet.
decisions.inWild:
# today - the exceptions live in four places
jet unsafe
git diff jet.lock
cat ~/.jet/trust
rg "#Scrub|approx\(|wrapping\(" src/

# the authority ledger (ratified) covers only the rights rows:
jet inspect authority

options.name: Full ledger, grouped by kind
options.detail: Every gate lands in one ledger: unsafe regions, impure marks, grants, trust and .Force, taint scrubs, duty drops, and precision demotions. jet inspect gates prints counts per kind with security kinds expanded first, and filters select one kind. Gain: one list is the whole audit, and CI can refuse new gates without sign-off. Loss: numeric code can log thousands of demotion rows, so the tool must summarize well.
options.technical: The gate record generalizes D-AUTHORITY-GATE1. Each entry: site, gate word, kind, reason where ratified law requires one. Compile-time only; no runtime cost. jet inspect authority remains as the rights-kind filter of the same ledger.
options.code:
$ jet inspect gates
rights   2   src/dma.jet:41 #Unsafe "MMIO: manual 4.2"
              pkg.jet grants image-codec: FS.Read
taint    1   src/etl.jet:88 call of #Scrub(Pii) fn hash_email
build    1   pkg.jet stamp.at forced via .Force
exact   214  (summarized; jet inspect gates --kind exact)
duty     1   src/jobs.jet:12 detach

options.name: Security gates only
options.detail: The ledger holds the gates a security reviewer needs: unsafe, impure, grants, trust, .Force, and taint scrubs. Precision demotions and duty drops stay in code only, found by grep. Gain: a short, high-signal list with no numeric noise. Loss: simulation and money code lose the precision audit, and the law's on-the-record clause holds for only half the gate family.
options.technical: Same record shape as A, restricted to the rights and taint kinds plus .Force. approx, wrapping, and detach never enter the ledger.
options.code:
$ jet inspect gates
src/dma.jet:41  #Unsafe "MMIO: manual 4.2"
src/etl.jet:88  call of #Scrub(Pii) fn hash_email
pkg.jet         grants image-codec: FS.Read
pkg.jet         stamp.at forced via .Force
# precision drops: rg "approx\(" src/   (outside the ledger)

options.name: Keep the authority ledger as ratified
options.detail: No generalization. jet inspect authority ships as D-AUTHORITY-GATE1 wrote it, and other gates stay source-only. Gain: nothing new to build or decide. Loss: the audit crawl in the story stays real for every non-rights gate, and each future plane will propose its own inspector.
options.code:
$ jet inspect authority
gates:
  src/dma.jet:41  #Unsafe "MMIO: manual 4.2"
  pkg.jet         grants image-codec: FS.Read
# scrubs, demotions, forced settings: grep by hand

comparisons.note: cargo-geiger counts unsafe but nothing collects allows, feature forcing, and lossy casts in one place. Auditors assemble the picture from separate tools.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo geiger        # unsafe only
$ rg "as f32" src/    # lossy casts by grep

recommendation.why: The law says every gate is on the record, and one grouped ledger is that clause made real. Certification work reads one list, and the kind grouping keeps numeric rows from burying security rows.

whyNot.reason: Half a ledger reopens the audit crawl for exactness and duty, exactly where money and simulation code need the record.
Stopping at the ratified rights ledger invites one bespoke inspector per future plane, which is the fragmentation this slate exists to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: Heavy numeric code produces large exact-kind sections, so the default view must summarize them to counts. That is a presentation cost, accepted to keep the record complete.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a full ledger with the ratified rights-only ledger and recommended the full ledger for the one-list audit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the security-only middle option and considered a per-plane inspector family. The inspector family was rejected as the fragmentation pattern itself.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the kind grouping and summarized counts from a separate presentation idea into option A, so the full ledger ships with noise control built in.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: a short list auditors actually read beats a complete list they skim. The counts-first default in A answers the same concern.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with ledger bloat from hot numeric loops and with reason-ceremony creep. Summarized counts answer bloat, no gate gains a new required reason, and A survives.

decisions.title: One way to read what the compiler knows
decisions.gist: How code reads a compiler-held fact: the $ sigil, reflection methods, or tools only.
decisions.lesson: The compiler knows a value's range, a function's effects, a type's states and units. Reading that knowledge is currently uneven. Build facts read as $build.profile (D-CONF-READ1). The metaprogramming rethink made $ the one mark for a compile-time name (D-META-STAGE1). Type reflection is partly typed and partly strings, and state names cannot be written at all. This ballot picks the one reading surface. It extends D-CONF-READ1 and D-META-STAGE1 and completes D-TYPE2-PLANE1's typed reflection.
decisions.story: Marco writes a derive that generates an audit table for every type in his payments package. He needs each field's range, unit, and tags. Today the ranges are readable, the units arrive through a different call, and the state names come back as mangled strings he must parse.

options.name: The $ mark reads every plane
options.detail: Reading a fact is one act, one mark: T.$range, f.$effects, Order.$states, $build.profile. Every registered plane answers as typed values, in comptime code and derive bodies. The string fallback dies. Gain: one lesson covers every fact read, and the build-fact spelling generalizes instead of staying special. Loss: the $ position grammar grows from build facts and splices to member position on types and functions.
options.technical: Extends D-META-STAGE1: $ marks a compile-time name, so a fact read is $ in member position. Facts return typed values from the D-META-REG1 registry. Comptime only; S26 holds, facts are values and never mint types. TypeInfo remains the aggregate view and loses its string fallback.
options.code:
// one act, every plane (proposed):
Severity.$range          // 0..10
send_report.$effects     // [Net, DB.Read]
Order.$states            // [.Draft, .Confirmed, .Shipped]
Meters.$dimension        // Length
$build.profile           // ratified today - same act, build subject

options.name: Typed reflection methods only
options.detail: Complete D-TYPE2-PLANE1 as written: T.reflect() returns fully typed data for every plane, and the string fallback dies. The $ mark stays where it is ratified, on build facts and splices. Gain: no grammar change, one aggregate object per type. Loss: two reading stories remain, because build facts read with $ and type facts read with a method.
options.technical: TypeInfo gains typed fields per registered plane: ranges, dimensions, states, effects, marker args. No new $ positions. Reflect.rs string paths are deleted.
options.code:
// reflection completes, $ stays build-only:
info :: Order.reflect()
info.states              // [.Draft, .Confirmed, .Shipped] - typed
info.fields[0].range     // 0..10
$build.profile           // still the separate build spelling

options.name: Tools read facts, code does not
options.detail: jet explain and the language server answer what is known here, but programs cannot read facts beyond today's ratified surfaces. Gain: zero language change, and no risk of programs depending on checker internals. Loss: derives and comptime code keep parsing strings or go without, and the phantom reflection gap stays.
options.code:
$ jet explain value order
order: Order   state: Confirmed (set at line 12)
               tags: Pii (from field email)
// in code: only today's partial reflect() remains

recommendation.why: The metaprogramming rethink already ratified $ as the one mark for a compile-time name, and a fact is a compile-time name. One act for one idea is the whole point of the capstone.

whyNot.reason: It keeps two reading stories, so the build plane stays a special case forever and the one-lesson claim fails.
It leaves derive authors parsing strings, which is the exact defect the evidence table documents.

recommendation.tradeoff: The $ member-position grammar must be specified carefully so it cannot be mistaken for runtime field access. Accepted: the mark is already defined as compile-time-only, and the checker rejects runtime positions.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared $ reads with completing typed reflection and recommended $ reads for the one-act story.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the tools-only option and tested a facts() standard-library call. The library call was folded into option B as the same design behind a longer name.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review confirmed A already contains B: the aggregate reflect() view remains as the bulk read, and $ is the per-fact read. No separate hybrid option was needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: tools cover the human questions and freeze no surface. It still leaves generated code without typed fact access, which derives need today.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A for grammar creep and for programs branching on checker internals. The mark stays comptime-only under S26 and facts never dispatch under D-FACTMODEL1, so the walls hold and A survives.

decisions.title: Home the orphan facts, retire the phantom types
decisions.gist: Which stray compiler facts join the registry, and phantom fact names stop compiling in signatures.
decisions.lesson: Some compiler-held facts live outside every registry: send-safety is a stray flag, #Track provenance and view provenance are unreadable, maturity and failure attribution are unregistered. Separately, about eighteen fact-menu names such as Capability and State are accepted in function signatures today, then every call fails, and no value can ever exist. This ballot decides which orphans become registry rows and confirms that phantom names are refused at the signature with a fix-it.
