decisions.story: Lena writes fn audit(c: Capability) after reading an error message that mentioned Capability. It compiles. Every call site then fails with a type error, and there is no way to make the value. She loses an hour before learning the name was never a type.

options.name: Home the user-facing orphans
options.detail: Facts with user-visible meaning join the registry as typed, readable rows: send-safety, failure attribution, #Track and view and unit-scale provenance, and maturity. Prover internals such as uninit tracking and exhaustiveness stay engine-side, matching the prover wall in D-FACT-OWN1. Phantom fact-menu names are refused at the signature with a fix-it naming the real path. Gain: every fact a user can meet is nameable and readable. Loss: prover internals stay unreflectable.
options.technical: Each homed fact becomes a D-META-REG1 registry row with typed members. Marker-argument menus stop resolving as general types in core_type_known; the diagnostic names the real value type where one exists, such as the authority value.

options.name: Home everything
options.detail: Every fact the compiler holds joins the registry, including uninit tracking and exhaustiveness. Phantom rejection lands the same way. Gain: complete uniformity, and tools can show even prover internals. Loss: registry rows for facts no user can act on, and the prover wall blurs, because engine-internal state becomes a public surface the checker must keep stable.
options.technical: As A, plus registry rows for definite-assignment and exhaustiveness facts. Those rows expose intermediate prover state, which then falls under reflection stability rules.

options.name: Phantom fix only
options.detail: Refuse phantom names in signatures with fix-its, and home nothing. Gain: the user trap closes with the smallest change. Loss: send-safety stays a stray flag while the concurrency cards build on it, and provenance, attribution, and maturity stay unreadable.

recommendation.why: Homing the user-facing orphans finishes what the four rethinks started, and the prover wall keeps engine internals free to change. The phantom fix closes a real beginner trap the audit documented.

whyNot.reason: Publishing prover internals freezes checker implementation details as API, trading engine freedom for reflection nobody asked for.
It leaves send-safety as a stray flag exactly while cards #1557-#1565 build the crossing checker on top of it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The line between user-facing fact and prover internal is a judgment call recorded per fact. Accepted: the ballot lists the assignment explicitly, so the line is written down, not folklore.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft homed every orphan and refused phantoms. The recommendation later narrowed after the prover wall took shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review split homing into user-facing and everything variants and added the phantom-only floor. It also checked for further orphans and confirmed maturity and unit-scale provenance belong on the list.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested phantom fix now with homing later. That is option C wearing a schedule, and it leaves the concurrency cards building on the stray flag, so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: complete uniformity is the simplest rule and tools benefit. The stability cost to the checker stands, because published shapes cannot change freely.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's fix-it quality: a refusal without a real alternative just moves the dead end. Each refused name must name its living counterpart, the menu without one says so plainly, and A survives with that requirement recorded.

decisions.title: The ownership wall: prover, not plane
decisions.gist: Whether the borrow checker stays its own engine or becomes a registered fact plane.
decisions.lesson: Fact planes fold facts through code with small per-operation rules: ranges add, units multiply, rights meet as sets. The borrow checker is different. It tracks places, aliases, and time: which windows overlap, which owner moved, which view outlives what. That is flow analysis, not algebra. This ballot decides whether that difference becomes a recorded wall, so no future card tries to rebuild ownership as a plane, while the facts ownership proves still register like all others.
decisions.story: Next spring an agent picks up a card that says unify the fact planes. Without a recorded wall it spends a week flattening the borrow checker into plane rules, breaks view invalidation, and the review has no ratified sentence to point at when rejecting the patch.

options.name: Ratify the wall
options.detail: The borrow checker is a prover, never a plane. The sigil surface stays closed as ratified. The facts the prover publishes, such as sendability, view provenance, and moved-ness, register as read-only rows so tools and other planes can consume them. Gain: the engine stays free to be a real program analysis, and its outputs still join the one model. Loss: one mechanism is formally outside the plane registry.
options.technical: Records: ownership checking follows D-MEM1, D-SHAPE-PLACE1, and D-MEM-VIEWRET1 as its own analysis. Published facts enter the D-META-REG1 table as prover-supplied rows. No plane algebra is defined for windows.

options.name: Ownership becomes a plane
options.detail: Windows and moves register as a plane with combination rules, and the checker becomes that plane's algebra engine. Gain: complete uniformity, one registry with no exceptions, window facts reflect like all others, and one guard checks every plane including this one. Loss: alias analysis does not decompose into per-operation rules, so the registered algebra must delegate to the engine, and forcing the frame invites a rebuild that loses precision.

options.name: Leave it undecided
options.detail: No ruling either way. Gain: no decision to maintain. Loss: the question returns on every unification card, and the next agent has no ratified sentence to cite, which is how the week in the story gets spent.
options.code: // status quo: the boundary lives in reviewers' heads

comparisons.note: Rust's borrow checker is its own engine, and Send/Sync are auto-derived facts published from it. The split works and nobody proposes merging the two frames.
comparisons.code:
// borrowck: flow analysis over MIR
// Send/Sync: structural facts other systems consume

recommendation.why: The evidence shows ownership already obeys the one-way law at its surface while its engine is genuinely different inside. Naming that split keeps both truths and stops future rebuild attempts.

whyNot.reason: It gains a registry entry and risks a precision-losing rebuild, because alias analysis has no per-operation rule table to register.
It spends future reviewer time relitigating a boundary this audit has already proved twice.

recommendation.tradeoff: The registry carries prover-supplied rows that no plane algebra backs, a small irregularity accepted to keep the engine honest.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft stated the wall and recommended it, with full absorption as the alternative.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the leave-undecided option and checked whether duty should sit behind the same wall. Duty stays a plane, because discharge rules are per-operation and D-CONC-UNIT1 already ratified that.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the published-facts-register clause from a separate idea into option A, so the wall and the registry stop being rivals.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with the uniformity argument and the reflection gain. Both survive in A through the published rows, without forcing the engine into the plane frame.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A as an excuse wall that future proposals could hide behind. The wall is scoped to the alias engine only, and its published facts must register, so nothing else can shelter under it and A survives.

decisions.title: One flow-fact store with one join rule
decisions.gist: How the checker stores per-binding facts that change along control flow.
decisions.lesson: Six separate stores track facts that change as code flows: moved bindings, uninit fields, typestate, optional narrowing, taint, and view windows. Each store hand-writes its own branch-merge logic, and two of the merges are dead code, so typestate and partial-init simply keep whatever the last-walked branch left. This is machinery, but it decides whether the concurrency and type-v2 cards build one engine or six more copies.
decisions.story: A user writes an if/else where one branch confirms an order and the other cancels it. After the join the compiler believes whichever branch it happened to walk last. The bug report lands next winter, and the fix gets written twice, once per store, because there is no shared join.

options.name: One store, planes supply joins
options.detail: One flow-fact store on the checker holds every per-binding fact. Each plane supplies only its join rule for branch merges, and the walker applies joins uniformly at every if, loop, and arm table. The six stores and the twelve one-off checker columns migrate in. Gain: joins can no longer be forgotten, and new planes get flow tracking for free. Loss: one large internal migration through the checker.
options.technical: Store keyed by binding and plane. Join called at every control-flow merge point by the shared walker. Sema-only; no TIR or codegen change; generated Rust stays byte-identical. Lands as phase A of the implementation shape, before cards #1517-#1579 build on it.

options.name: Shared join contract, separate stores
options.detail: The stores stay where they are, but each must implement one join interface, and a guard test lists every store and asserts its join is live. Gain: the dead-join class of bug dies with a much smaller change. Loss: six data shapes remain, new planes still hand-roll storage, and the walker still calls six merge paths.
options.technical: A JoinFacts trait over the existing stores plus a registry-driven test that fails when a store lacks a live join. No storage migration.
options.code:
// each store implements join(); a guard test enumerates them
// State.rs join_after: now called, or the build fails

options.name: Fix the two dead joins as bugs
options.detail: Wire up the typestate and uninit merges, change nothing structural. Gain: the known soundness holes close this week. Loss: the seventh store gets hand-written by the next card, and the next forgotten join waits there.

recommendation.why: The concurrency and type-v2 cards are about to add more flow-tracked planes. One store built first means those cards add join rules, not storage engines, and the forgotten-join bug class ends.

whyNot.reason: It keeps six shapes and six merge paths, so every new plane still pays the storage tax the capstone exists to delete.
It patches two symptoms of a structure that has already produced dead code twice, and leaves the structure.

recommendation.tradeoff: One wide internal migration through the checker before feature cards land. Accepted: effort is expendable, and the migration is phase A with every test staying green.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the unified store with fixing the dead joins and recommended the store for the by-construction guarantee.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the shared-contract middle option and checked whether view facts belong in the store. They do as storage, while their invalidation logic stays with the ownership prover per D-FACT-OWN1.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested contract-now, store-later. Sequencing both costs more than building the store once before the feature cards, so the hybrid was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: it is the honest minimal soundness fix and ships immediately. It still leaves the next plane hand-rolling store number seven.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A over loop fixpoints and merge-order subtleties that six bespoke stores currently dodge. The shared walker must document its fixpoint rule once, which is strictly fewer places to get it wrong than six, so A survives.

decisions.title: Adopt the one-tree name model
decisions.gist: Is a name one thing: a member at one point in one tree?
decisions.lesson: Today a name can reach you through five doors: two import forms, a file-reference declaration, automatic discovery, and the prelude. The shadowing rule has one law and four exceptions. Inside the compiler, six separate stores resolve names, and two of them disagree about package visibility. This ballot decides the founding model. The other eight D-NAME ballots each stand alone, but they all read cleaner on top of this one.
decisions.story: Maya teaches Jet to a high-school class. A student asks: where does the name print come from, and why does use sometimes take quotes? Maya has no one-sentence answer today. Under the model, she says: every name lives in one tree; you declared it, your project has it, or the prelude aliases it.

options.name: Adopt: one tree, one law, one ledger
options.detail: A name is a member at one point in one tree. A declaration attaches it. An alias (use, prelude) only points at it. Declarations never collide; a declaration replaces an alias, never another declaration. The four shadowing exceptions become one rule. Inside the compiler, sema writes one name ledger and every engine and tool reads it. The six follow-up ballots then shape the surface.
options.technical: Law: attach/alias. E0118 and E0105 become the collide clause. D-PRELUDE-LAW1 user-wins, the Reader/Cursor guard, and FFI in-situ shadowing become the replace clause. D-GENMOD-IDENTITY1 (aliases never mint identity) becomes a theorem. Backend: generalize reference_anchors and import_targets into one sema-owned table; codegen, JIT, interpreter, LSP, REPL, and devserver consume it. One mangle function. Fixes the pub(package) divergence: codegen filters today read bare is_pub only (Codegen/Imports.rs:83).

options.name: Law and ledger only, surface unchanged
options.detail: Adopt the attach/alias law and the one compiler ledger, but keep today's import and visibility spellings exactly as they are. The compiler gets simpler and the exceptions get one explanation. The page a user reads does not improve.
options.technical: Same internal consolidation as A. S16, D-VISDEFAULT2, and the prelude table stay untouched. The six follow-up ballots would be moot.

options.name: Reject: keep five doors
options.detail: Keep today's model. Each door and each exception stays its own rule. No compiler consolidation is scheduled. The duplicated resolvers keep drifting; the pub(package) divergence stays open until fixed piecemeal.
options.technical: No change. The B1-B9 duplicate list from the audit remains the maintenance surface.

comparisons.note: Zig removed usingnamespace because hidden name origins forced the compiler to discover namespace contents. One visible tree avoids that whole class.
comparisons.code:
// Zig: @import returns a value; a file is a struct
const scoring = @import("scoring.zig");

comparisons.note: Go's one loved property: every non-universe name is greppable to its source. The tree keeps that property with jet project parts.

recommendation.why: One sentence answers every beginner question about names, and one ledger ends the compiler's six-store drift. Every ratified naming rule already fits the law, so nothing fights it.

whyNot.reason: An internals-only rethink leaves the five doors on the page. The owner has rejected exactly that shape of outcome before.
The five doors and four exceptions stay unexplained, and the sema/codegen visibility divergence stays live.

recommendation.tradeoff: The follow-up migrations touch many examples and snapshots at once. That is accepted: each follow-up ballot is one coherent greenfield change that deletes the replaced form.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared adopt, internals-only, and reject, and recommended adopt because the law already covers every ratified rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a two-tree design (project tree plus separate core universe) and a Zig-style files-are-values design. Both folded into A: roots are just top members of one tree, and module-as-value is already ratified for generic modules.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review asked whether B plus one surface fix beats A. It does not: the surface wins come from the follow-up ballots, which need the model named and ratified first.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: today's doors each have a ratified rationale and shipped tests. It still leaves four shadowing exceptions and two disagreeing visibility checkers.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the ledger as a new mechanism, but it generalizes the existing reference_anchors and import_targets tables and deletes six ad-hoc stores. Mechanisms fall from six to one, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Project files visible without imports
decisions.gist: Do your own project files need an import line?
decisions.lesson: Today a second file in your project needs a use line with quotes, or a module declaration that only imports. U3 already rules that discovered modules merge into one whole and never import each other. This ballot decides whether that rule reaches every file, and fixes the explicit spellings an expert keeps. It amends S16 (D-S16-USE, D-MOD1/2, D-MOD-DIR) and U3/D-SHAPE-MODULEINTERNAL1's outermost-construct and discovery-naming clauses, and touches D-CALLDUAL1's scope wording. The project-wide refusal switch is its own ballot, D-NAME-AUDIT1.
decisions.story: Sam is thirteen and writes a game. The main file grows, so Sam cuts the enemy code into enemies.jet. Today the game breaks until Sam learns two import spellings and picks the right one. Under option A the game keeps running, because enemies was already part of the tree.

options.name: Whole project tree, with a full ledger
options.detail:
Every project file is a module named by its filename; a directory is a namespace. Siblings and subdirectories are visible everywhere in the project with no use line. The file-reference module declaration is deleted.

Three exits ship with the magic. jet imports FILE prints every name a file resolved, the member path, the source file, and the door it came through. use project.path is the explicit spelling for any member, including _name internals. use "…/file.jet" as name imports any file by relative path; only out-of-tree files need it, and the ledger flags them.
options.technical: Deletes the file-reference module declaration and in-tree quoted imports (S16, D-MOD1, D-MOD-DIR). The quoted form survives with one job: importing a file outside the project tree, with as required. module name { } inline grouping stays, but nests under its file's namespace — this amends U3's single-outermost-construct and declared-name-discovery clauses. The common case, one declaration matching the filename, keeps its path unchanged. Project roots enter file scope as implicit aliases, so D-CALLDUAL1's no-global-search wording gets one edited sentence. Collisions stay E0105/E0118.

options.name: Same directory only
options.detail: Files in the same directory see each other with no import line. Anything in another directory still needs a use line with a tree path. Smaller magic radius; deep projects keep import ceremony. The jet imports ledger and the explicit spellings apply the same way.
options.technical: Same deletions and exits as A. Cross-directory reach requires use grades.curve or use project.grades.curve.

options.name: Keep explicit imports
options.detail: Every cross-file name keeps an import line, as today. The two spellings could still be merged editorially, but a beginner's second file still fails until an import is learned.
options.technical: No change to S16. The tree model still holds; the project root is simply not ambient. jet imports still has value as a resolution viewer.

comparisons.note: Python requires imports even for sibling files, and sys.path rules are a famous teaching wall. The loved part is only that a file is a module.
Rust requires mod declarations to mount files, and mod.rs versus file naming confused a generation. Jet's U3 discovery already removed the mount step for declared modules.
Java's compact source files auto-see their package neighbors; the same code stays valid in a full project. Growth without rewrites is the goal here too.
comparisons.code: // same file compiles in both modes

recommendation.why: Splitting a file is the third most frequent operation in real code, and option A makes it free. Provenance survives and improves: jet imports lists every resolved name with its source, and the explicit spellings cover every case, including files outside the tree.

whyNot.reason: A directory boundary is an arbitrary magic radius. The first subdirectory brings the ceremony back, at the exact moment a project starts to grow.
It keeps ceremony on the most common growth step and keeps two import spellings alive for the same job.

recommendation.tradeoff: A large project sees more ambient roots, so a new file can collide with an existing module name. That is accepted: the collision is a clear E0105 at compile time, and the D-NAME-AUDIT1 switch restores strictness without changing meaning.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared whole-tree, same-directory, and explicit imports, and recommended whole-tree because it deletes two spellings and frees the most common refactor.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested an opt-in marker per file and an editor-inserts-imports answer like goimports. Both folded into A's exits: the switch is the opt, and tooling needs no inserted lines when the tree is ambient.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review first proposed a package.jet compile switch for explicit imports, then demoted it to a lint and split it into D-NAME-AUDIT1. A compile mode would make one source mean different things per package.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C with Go's provenance argument: an import line per file is greppable. A keeps the property through jet imports, which lists the exact resolution per file with its source.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked name collisions, accidental coupling, and untracked out-of-tree reach. Compile-time E0105, the _name exit, pub fences, and the ledger's out-of-tree flag contain all three, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Where the prelude lives
decisions.gist: Is the prelude a readable Core module or a compiler table?
decisions.lesson: The prelude is the set of names every file sees with no use line. Today it lives as a closed list inside the compiler's Rust source, and each call site matches those names by string. The ratified list, its membership criteria, and its epoch-gated growth (D-PRELUDE-LAW1, D-CORE-PRELUDE1/2) are not in question here. This ballot only picks the home: where the list is written and how the compiler applies it. It amends the D-PRELUDE-LAW1 mechanism and D-PRELUDEX1 wording, not their rulings.
decisions.story: Ana reviews a security-sensitive service. She asks: exactly which names can appear in this code without an import, and what do they resolve to? Today the answer lives in compiler source she has to trust. Under option A she opens one short Core file and reads the whole list.

options.name: A readable Core prelude module
options.detail: Core ships one short prelude module: the ambient basics are declared there, and the rest are pub use aliases into the ratified Core tree. The compiler opens it for every file. The full ratified list moves — including the four comptime-gated names, whose gate lives on the declarations and is untouched by aliasing. Growth stays ballot-gated as decided. Your declaration still replaces a prelude alias, with the ratified warning. #NoPrelude still opts a file out, and anyone can read what is ambient.
options.technical: core/prelude.jet carries the whole D-PRELUDE-LAW1 registry (always-ambient and comptime-gated names) plus the ratified D-CORE-PRELUDE1/2 additions. Names with no module home (print, panic, require) are declared in the prelude module itself; their meaning stays in Prelude/CoreLib per I9. Member spellings follow the ratified D-CORE-TREE1 tree and are settled by card #1576. Sema injects the aliases once at file scope instead of per-call-site string matching (core_surface.rs:183 and the scattered shadow guards retire). Libraries still cannot inject: only Core owns the file, enforced as today.

options.name: Keep the compiler table
options.detail: The list stays in compiler source, matched per call site. Behavior is identical for users who never ask where names come from. Reading the ambient surface keeps requiring compiler-source trust, and the per-builtin shadow guards stay scattered.
options.technical: No change. PRELUDE_ALWAYS_IDENTS and PRELUDE_COMPTIME_IDENTS remain the registry; ratified additions extend the Rust arrays.
options.code:
// user code identical; the list lives in
// crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_surface.rs

options.name: Mode-gated prelude
options.detail: Two ambient sets: a bigger list for single-file programs, the small ratified list inside packages. Scripts get more magic; the same code can stop compiling when it moves into a package, which breaks grow-without-rewrite.
options.technical: Java JEP 512 shape. Requires defining the mode boundary and a migration lint for names that fall out of scope on package promotion.

comparisons.note: Rust's prelude is an ordinary module of re-exports, grown per edition with a migration lint. That is the proven growth path Jet's epoch gating already mirrors.
comparisons.code: // std::prelude::rust_2021 is just pub use lines

comparisons.note: Elixir's Kernel is readable source with per-name opt-out. Jet's #NoPrelude plus shadowing gives the same exits.

recommendation.why: The ambient surface becomes something a person can read, hover, and audit, while the list, its criteria, and its growth gate stay exactly as ratified. The compiler deletes scattered per-builtin guards.

whyNot.reason: A closed compiler table is the one shape every audit flags: names users see but cannot read the source of.
Code that compiles alone must keep compiling inside a package. Two ambient sets break that promise at the worst moment.

recommendation.tradeoff: The compiler must bootstrap the prelude module before user files, adding one ordering rule to module loading. That is accepted; Units.jet injection already proves the pattern.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a Core module, the current table, and a mode-gated set, and recommended the module because it makes the ambient surface readable without changing the list.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-project prelude extension and a no-prelude-ever design. Both were rejected as ratified-law violations: D-PRELUDEX1 forbids injection, and the ambient floor is already decided.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review took C's growth idea and folded it into A: any future bigger-script set would be another readable Core module behind its own ballot, not a compiler mode.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: a table is trivially fast and cannot be shadowed by a broken Core checkout. A keeps both properties because Core ships with the compiler.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked bootstrap ordering, user edits to a vendored file, and the comptime-gated four. Core is compiler-shipped and read-only, and the gate rides the declarations, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The visibility set
decisions.gist: How many ways can Jet spell who sees a name?
decisions.lesson: Today visibility has six spellings: pub, priv, #PubFile, pub(package), soft-public pub _name, and the module-level _name discovery skip. Two of them give the underscore different meanings. Private-by-default (S18) is not in question. This ballot picks the set of marks. It amends D-VISDEFAULT2 and D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1, and option A redefines the current pub module spelling, which today makes the module visible while members still need pub. Option C would also amend D-PUBPKG1.
decisions.story: Ben publishes his first Jet library. He wants: a public API, one internal helper he may delete, and one function only his workspace uses. Today that tour needs four spellings and a file marker. Under option A it is pub, _name, and pub(package) — each with one meaning.
decisions.inWild:
// today, one library file
#PubFile
fn api() { }                 // public because of the marker
priv fn secret() { }         // opt-out keyword
pub(package) fn shared() { } // wait - was pub redundant here? (E0414)
pub fn _legacy() { }         // soft-public, warns outside
// elsewhere: module _draft skips discovery - same _, different meaning

options.name: Four marks, one meaning each
options.detail: pub opens an edge; pub(package) fences at the package; _name means internal everywhere - skipped from discovery, callable, warns outside, never a promise. pub module makes a public-by-default subtree at the attach point, replacing the #PubFile file marker. priv keeps its one existing job - opt a member back to private inside such a subtree. On a file that is its own module, a leading pub module line does what #PubFile did. Fewer spellings, and the underscore stops meaning two things.
options.technical: Deletes #PubFile and the separate L0601 soft-public rule; the E0412-E0418 family retargets from the marker to pub module. priv stays legal only inside a public-by-default subtree, exactly today's E0413 shape. _name unifies D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1 and U3's discovery skip into one story. This redefines today's pub module (module visible, members still private) into public-by-default; the old meaning falls out of pub on the declaration plus per-member defaults.

options.name: Keep today's six spellings
options.detail: No change. Each spelling has a ratified rationale and shipped tests. The underscore keeps two meanings, and library files keep the marker-plus-keyword pattern.
options.technical: S18, D-VISDEFAULT2, D-PUBPKG1, D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1, and U3 stay as written.

options.name: Minimal: pub and underscore only
options.detail: Two marks: pub opens, _name is internal. pub(package), #PubFile, and priv are deleted. The workspace fence disappears, so package-only APIs become soft convention instead of a checked rule.
options.technical: Amends D-PUBPKG1 in addition to D-VISDEFAULT2 and D-SHAPE-INTERNAL1. E0605 package enforcement retires.

comparisons.note: Go has one visibility idea (capitalized exports) and it is loved for zero ceremony. But its missing package fence bred internal/ directory conventions.
comparisons.code: func Letter(n int) string  // public by case

comparisons.note: Rust's pub(crate), pub(super), pub(in path) zoo is the cautionary tale. Jet already rejected everything but pub(package) (E0411).

recommendation.why: Every mark keeps exactly one meaning, the file marker stops fighting the module tree, and the checked package fence survives. Ben's tour is pub, pub(package), and _name.

whyNot.reason: Six spellings for three ideas, and the underscore means two different things depending on where it appears.
Deleting the package fence trades a checked boundary for a naming convention, which the enterprise pass cannot accept.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing #PubFile and priv code migrates to pub module in one greenfield change. That is accepted; the migration is mechanical and examples are few.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the unified mark set, the status quo, and a Go-style minimal set, recommending the unified set for one-meaning-per-mark.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested visibility-by-casing and per-item export lists in a module head. Casing collides with the ratified casing law; export lists duplicate pub use doors, so both folded away.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option A's pub module: it keeps #PubFile's real value (public-by-default regions) but moves the flip to the attach point the tree already has.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: every spelling is shipped, tested, and ratified, so keeping them costs no migration. It still leaves two meanings of underscore.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked pub module: _name alone is callable, not private, so the first draft lost true privacy inside public subtrees. Keeping priv inside the flip repairs it, and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: use inside module bodies, and one meaning for .[ ]
decisions.gist: May a module body hold use lines, and what does .[ ] always mean?
decisions.lesson: Two small gaps sit on the walk. First: use and pub use inside a module body are rejected today with a message citing a ratification that already happened; the generic-module law keeps the exclusion 'until ordinary modules admit it'. Second: the sigil .[ ] is ratified twice - member spread in expressions (D-SPREAD1) and grouped use lists (D-CORE-USELIST1) - but no spec sentence says they are the same operation. This ballot admits inline use and writes the one sentence. It lifts D-GENMOD-BODY1's exclusion clause.
decisions.story: Rio builds a report module and wants its imports next to its code, the way every other block keeps its own locals. Today the compiler says no and cites a decision that was ratified and shipped in June. Rio pastes the error into chat and asks if the compiler is broken.

options.name: Admit inline use, write the .[ ] sentence
options.detail: A module body is a namespace like any other, so use and pub use work at every level, with the same meaning as at file top. The spec gains one sentence: .[ ] always means 'these members of that prefix' - values in expression position, aliases after use. Both changes remove exceptions; neither adds a spelling.
options.technical: Lifts the parser rejects at Parser/Modules.rs:805 and :858 and the D-GENMOD-BODY1 exclusion clause. Alias scope is the enclosing module body. The .[ ] sentence lands beside D-SPREAD1 and D-CORE-USELIST1 in the spec and amends neither: expression entries stay bare members (E0961), use entries keep as and dotted paths. No grammar change; both forms are already ratified.

options.name: Only inline use
options.detail: Admit use and pub use inside module bodies, but leave the .[ ] relationship unwritten. The user-facing gap closes; the spec keeps two unconnected rulings on one sigil.
options.technical: Same parser change as A; no spec sentence.

options.name: Neither
options.detail: Keep the exclusion and the silence. Module authors keep writing qualified paths inside bodies, and the stale error message needs a text fix at minimum.
options.technical: No change beyond correcting the E0003 message's dead reference to D-MOD4.

comparisons.note: Rust allows use at every module level and nobody debates it; imports live beside the code they serve.

recommendation.why: Both halves delete an exception: module bodies stop being the one namespace level that refuses aliases, and the sigil stops needing two unrelated explanations.

whyNot.reason: It closes the user gap but leaves the next reader of the spec to rediscover that the two .[ ] rulings share one law.
It keeps a parked feature whose stated blocker shipped in June, and the stale error text keeps telling users a false reason.

recommendation.tradeoff: Inline aliases add one scope level to import resolution. That is accepted; the one-ledger resolver treats every namespace level identically anyway.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft paired the inline-use unpark with the .[ ] spec sentence and recommended both, since each deletes an exception without adding a spelling.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review looked for other walk exceptions to fold in and found the two-step dot-access rule already superseded by ratified deep paths; no third item earned a seat.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested splitting the two halves into separate ballots. They stayed together: both are walk-law cleanups, and neither is contested enough to need its own page.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: the exclusion has a ratified sentence guarding it, so keeping it is coherent. It still rests on a blocker that no longer exists.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked alias leakage from module bodies into siblings. Aliases scope to their body under the attach/alias law, so nothing leaks, and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Finish the retirement of role modules
decisions.gist: Does module mean only code, as the ecosystem ruling already decided?
decisions.lesson: The module keyword serves two grammars today: code namespaces, and role declarations like module env.dev for environments, systems, and images. The ecosystem slate (D-ECO-DECL1, D-ECO-FILEROOT1, ratified 2026-07-15) already ruled the other way: Packages and Configs are typed values, package.jet is the one reserved file, and env.jet folds in. But U3's reserved-namespace text, U8, and D-JPK-MODBODY1 were never edited, and the code still ships both worlds. This ballot finishes one ruling or reverses it; there is no coherent both.
decisions.story: Priya reads the spec to learn modules. Section one says modules hold code and never import each other. Three pages later a module declares an environment with a packages: list. She asks which sentence is true. Today the honest answer is both, in different files, depending on the year.

options.name: Finish it: module means code
options.detail: Complete the ratified ruling. Ecosystem entries are typed values in package.jet; role declarations like module env.dev respell as those values. U3's reserved-namespace paragraph, U8, and D-JPK-MODBODY1 are edited to match. The ENV_FILE, CONFIG_FILE, WORKSPACE_FILE, and pkg.jet readers are deleted, and the repo's own env.jet migrates. One keyword, one grammar.
options.technical: Implements D-ECO-DECL1 and D-ECO-FILEROOT1 on the module plane. The reserved namespaces env/system/image/workspace stop being module-name prefixes; their vocabulary lives in the ratified manifest types (D-CONF-NAME1). The peek-past-brace dual parse in the module grammar retires.

options.name: Keep role modules, amend the ecosystem ruling
options.detail: Reverse course: role declarations stay modules, and D-ECO-DECL1's retirement of package-as-module is amended back. The module keyword keeps two grammars, and the spec text becomes internally consistent the other way.
options.technical: Amends D-ECO-DECL1 and D-ECO-FILEROOT1. ENV_FILE and friends become canon again; package.jet-as-sole-file is dropped.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Leave both worlds in place for now. The spec keeps two true stories about one keyword, and every tool that reads manifests keeps supporting two file sets. The drift the audit measured continues to spread.
options.technical: No change. The known drift list: spec.md:1059, roadmap.md, epoch-4 plans, Loader.rs:928 doc versus :956 message, and dual manifest files in core.archive.

comparisons.note: Nix let one deployment idea grow overlapping composition layers, and every layer became a permanent teaching tax. Two manifest worlds is the same road.
comparisons.code: // override vs overrideAttrs vs overlays vs modules

recommendation.why: The choice was already made and ratified; only the follow-through is missing. Finishing it gives module one grammar and deletes a whole family of dual-file readers.

whyNot.reason: It reverses a ratified slate to preserve a grammar fork, and keeps the manifest vocabulary split across two syntaxes.
Deferring keeps two true stories in the spec, and the audit shows the drift is already spreading into plans and messages.

recommendation.tradeoff: The repo's own env.jet and every fixture migrate in one change. That is accepted: migration churn is not a product tradeoff, and the ledger records provenance.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft framed this as finish-or-reverse and recommended finishing, because D-ECO-DECL1 is ratified law with the follow-through unbuilt.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a third design: role modules as sugar that desugars to the typed values. It folded away because two spellings for one manifest violates the one-spelling law.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested finishing the values while keeping env.jet as a second reserved file. D-ECO-FILEROOT1 already names package.jet as the single file, so the hybrid contradicts law.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: role modules are shipped, tested, and pleasant to read. The strongest honest B still needs an amendment ballot against a two-week-old ratified slate.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's migration surface: the repo env.jet, fixtures, devserver scanners, and jetpack readers all move at once. The change is large but mechanical and provable, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Names round-trip as paths
decisions.gist: Do reflection and diagnostics print a path you can type back in?
decisions.lesson: Reflection today returns bare names: reflect.of(x).type_name() gives Point, so two Point types in different modules reflect identically. Diagnostics mostly print bare names too. The tree model gives every member one canonical path. This ballot decides whether reflection and diagnostics print that path. It amends D-METAREFLECT1 (comptime T.reflect()) and the D-ANY-JAI1 runtime reflection surface by adding a field to each; nothing ratified is removed.
decisions.story: Devon debugs serialization in a service with geo.Point and ui.Point. The log says encoding failed for Point. Which one? Today the reflected name cannot say. Under option A the log says project.geo.Point, and Devon pastes that path straight into the REPL.

options.name: Paths everywhere, leaf stays
options.detail: T.reflect() gains .path, the canonical typeable spelling; .name stays the leaf. Runtime reflect.of follows. Diagnostics print the path whenever the bare name is ambiguous in scope, and the bare name otherwise, keeping short errors short. Hover, jet project parts, and JSON project the same spelling.
options.technical: Adds .path to the D-METAREFLECT1 surface and a path field to the D-ANY-JAI1 runtime surface. Diagnostic rendering rule: leaf name when unique among visible names, canonical path otherwise. The name ledger supplies the path; no second naming model is minted (the D-LAYOUT-FACTS1 pattern: one model, focused projections).

options.name: Keep bare names
options.detail: Reflection and diagnostics keep printing leaf names only. Errors stay short in every case, and same-named types stay indistinguishable in logs, tooling output, and derives that key on the reflected name.
options.technical: No change to D-METAREFLECT1 or the runtime surface.
options.code: print(reflect.of(p).type_name())   // "Point", either one

options.name: Paths in tools only
options.detail: Hover, parts listing, and LSP output print paths; the reflection API and diagnostics keep bare names. Tool users get disambiguation; programs and logs that use reflection do not.
options.technical: Ledger-backed paths surface in jet-semindex projections only. The reflection API is unchanged, so derive authors still cannot name a type unambiguously.
options.code:
// hover: project.geo.Point
print(reflect.of(p).type_name())   // still "Point"

comparisons.note: std::any::type_name returns a full path and people rely on it in logs. Its instability warning shows the spelling must be the canonical source path, never a mangled one.
getName versus getSimpleName is the same leaf-versus-path split; both exist because each has real callers.

recommendation.why: A name that cannot be typed back in is half a name. Paths make logs, derives, and errors unambiguous exactly when it matters, while unique leaf names keep everyday errors short.

whyNot.reason: Two same-named types stay indistinguishable everywhere reflection reaches, including generated code that keys on the name.
It fixes the read-only tools and leaves programs, logs, and derives with the ambiguity the tools no longer have.

recommendation.tradeoff: Snapshot tests that quote reflected names re-bless once. That is accepted; the change is one string field and a rendering rule.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared paths-everywhere, status quo, and tools-only, recommending paths-everywhere so every surface prints one spelling.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested making .name itself the full path with no new field. It folded away: ratified derive examples splice $name as a leaf into generated code, and breaking that costs more than a second field.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved A's diagnostic rule to leaf-when-unique, taking C's short-error virtue into A. The ballot was revised to carry that rule.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: short names are friendlier in beginner errors, and most programs have one Point. The unique-leaf rule in A preserves exactly that behavior.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked path stability across refactors and generic instances. Paths follow the ledger through renames, and generic instances print their binding name per the ratified identity law, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The underscore ladder
decisions.gist: What do _, _name, __name, and the dunder shapes each mean?
decisions.lesson: Greenfield includes the unclaimed lexical space. Today _ discards (ratified), and _name gets one internal meaning if D-NAME-FENCE1 passes. __name is already Jet's: D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 rejects every source-written double underscore and reserves the space for generated code, debugger metadata, and tools. Nobody has ruled on the dunder and sunder shapes (__name__, _name_), and the reserved space has no visible structure. This ballot writes the ladder into the spec as one law. Option A keeps D-SHAPE-DUNDER2; options B and C amend or repeal it.
decisions.story: Marta reads a stack trace with __jet_lambda_7 in it and knows on sight the compiler made that frame. Her student asks why print has no __init__ around it, and the answer is one sentence. One underscore talks to humans; two is the machine. Jet never asks you to type the machine's names.

options.name: One law: _ human, __ machine, dunders mean nothing
options.detail: The spec states the ladder once: zero underscores is a name, one underscore is a message to humans (discard, internal), two underscores is the machine's space. Dunder and sunder shapes are defined as nothing, on purpose — an explicit wall, so no meaning gets discovered later. The reserved space gains one visible product: every generated symbol a tool can show starts with __jet, so machine names are recognizable in traces, dumps, and generated-code review.
options.technical: Keeps D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 word-for-word; __name__ was already rejected as a double underscore, and _name_ falls under the single-underscore internal rule with the trailing character meaningless. Adds the __jet scheme as the one mangling law — the B5 cleanup target: the ~30 inline user_ format bypasses and the JIT's private scheme derive from the ledger under one prefix. Protocol members stay trait members; compiler facts stay $ reads (D-FACT-READ1), so no dunder has a job left.

options.name: Carve __name__ back: visible protocol members
options.detail: Python's shape: compiler-provided members live at __name__ and users read them in source (Point.__fields__, run.__doc__). Discoverable and collision-free. But it puts machine names in human mouths, invites silent typos, and duplicates the ratified $ read surface, which already answers what the compiler knows.
options.technical: Amends D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 to allow the dunder shape in read position. Every dunder member would race the $ fact surface (D-FACT-READ1, ratified): two spellings for one read is an I8 violation waiting for a carve-out.

options.name: Repeal the reservation: __ returns to users
options.detail: Delete the D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 wall. __name becomes ordinary user space, and the compiler hides its generated names outside the identifier space entirely, as symbols no source can spell. Users gain a prefix convention; tools lose the on-sight distinction between human and machine names.
options.technical: Amends D-SHAPE-DUNDER2 to repeal it. Mangling moves to non-identifier symbols, which complicates every surface that prints a name a user might paste back — the round-trip property D-NAME-REFLECT1 is buying.
options.code:
fn __fast_path() { }   // legal under C — user code
// traces now show human and machine names with no visible difference

comparisons.note: Dunders gave Python a protocol namespace but put the machine's names in everyone's mouth: __init__ is typed daily, and a typo like __lne__ silently never fires. Users also mint their own dunders against the docs' advice.
comparisons.code:
def __init__(self): ...
def __lne__(self): ...   # never fires, no warning

comparisons.note: C reserved _Name and __name by rulebook, and users collide with the rule constantly — the result is undefined behavior. Jet's reservation is enforced at parse, so the collision is a friendly error instead.
Dart fused privacy into the underscore, so renaming _x to x changes the API. Jet keeps the fence (pub) and the promise (_) as separate marks.

recommendation.why: The ladder is one sentence a beginner keeps and an auditor uses: one underscore talks to humans, two is the machine. Every shape gets exactly one meaning, and nothing new is spent — no sigil, no keyword, no carve-out.

whyNot.reason: Dunders would be a second spelling for the ratified $ read surface, and Python's own experience says machine names in human mouths breed silent typos.
It trades a ratified, parse-enforced reservation for a convention, and gives up the on-sight trace distinction for nothing the tree needs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Defining the sunder shapes as meaningless closes a door: no future _name_ convention can arrive without amending this ruling. That is the point — an explicit wall beats an accident — but it is a real commitment.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the one-law ladder, a Python-style dunder carve-back, and repeal, recommending the ladder because it spends nothing and settles every shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review swept the wider space — trailing underscore, double-trailing, mixed shapes — and found no job the trait, $, or fence planes had left over. Defining them all as nothing closed the sweep.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested A plus a single dunder (only __doc__). Even one reopens the two-spellings split with the $ surface, so the hybrid collapsed back to A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: dunders are self-documenting in a way $ reads are not, and Python users arrive knowing them. The $ surface is ratified law, so B would need to unseat it, not join it.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the __jet prefix as mangling leakage into user sight. It appears only in surfaces that already show machine frames — traces, dumps, generated review — never in diagnostics about user code, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: One law for everything Jet says to a human
decisions.gist: Does one rule govern every error message from every Jet tool?
decisions.lesson: A compile error in Jet has one tested shape: a code, the problem, a why, and a fix. The rest of the toolchain does not follow it. Today six different error styles ship: the compiler frame, lowercase `error:` prints, jetpack's indented style, a `what:/why:/fix:` outlier, the `panic:` frame, and bare unlabeled lines. This choice decides whether one law covers everything Jet says, or only part of it.
decisions.story: Maya is new to Jet. Her first compile error teaches her the shape: a sentence, a code, a why, a fix, and `jet explain`. Then her first test fails. The runner prints `left: 1, right: 2` with no file and no line. She concludes tests speak a different language — because today they do.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build app.jet
Error [E0102]: nothing named `pirnt` exists here
  --> app.jet:2:5
 Why: only functions that have been defined can be called
 Fix: did you mean `print`?

$ jet test orders.jet
totals: FAIL
  left: 101, right: 100

$ jet logs web
  error[E1274]: no build log for `web`

$ jetpack-bin verify
build-plugin manifest changed after verification

options.name: One law, whole toolchain
options.detail: Every error, warning, stop, and test failure from any Jet tool is a registered report: one code, one What/Why/Fix, one frame, rendered by one renderer per surface. Status lines, progress lines, and usage echoes stay plain — they are instructions, not reports. The six styles collapse into the compiler's frame.
options.technical: Scope: jet CLI, test harness output, fmt, jetpack, jetpack-bin, jet-rt, dev server, REPL. The terminal renderer owns the `jet explain` pointer line: toolchain commands print it once per run; release binaries omit it; `--no-hints` turns it off. The 184 uncoded `error:` sites in Source/ get rows or adopt an existing row. Extends I4 to every moment; restates D-FAIL-MODEL1's law for non-failure speech. Exit codes already have one law (D-FAIL-EXIT1); jetpack adopts ExitCodes.
options.code:
$ jet test orders.jet        # after
totals: FAIL
  Stop [E3001]: expected 100, got 101
    --> tests/orders.jet:14 in totals

$ jet logs web               # after
Error [E1274]: no build log for `web`
 Fix: run `jet build web` first.
run `jet explain E1274` to learn more

options.name: Compiler and runtime only
options.detail: The law covers `jet check`, `jet build`, and `jet run` output. The tools — test harness, fmt, jetpack, doctor — keep their own styles. Less migration, but the beginner still meets a second error language at the first failed test, and CI still parses several formats.
options.technical: No change to the test harness, jetpack Output.rs, or the ad-hoc `error:` sites. The registry stays compiler-only.
options.code:
$ jet test orders.jet        # unchanged
totals: FAIL
  left: 101, right: 100

$ jet logs web               # unchanged
  error[E1274]: no build log for `web`

options.name: One frame, optional codes
options.detail: Every tool adopts the visual frame — severity word, sentence, Why, Fix — but tool errors do not need registry rows or codes. The page looks uniform. But a message without a code has no `jet explain` path, no machine identity, and no snapshot duty, so the words drift again.
options.technical: Renderer shared; registry duty stays compiler-only. `--json` output for uncoded messages carries a null code.
options.code:
$ jet logs web               # option C
Error: no build log for `web`
 Fix: run `jet build web` first.
# no code — `jet explain` cannot answer for this message

comparisons.note: rustc has one excellent frame with codes, but cargo, clippy, and the test harness each print their own style. Users learn several error languages; CI parses several formats.
comparisons.code:
error[E0425]: cannot find value `pirnt` in this scope   (rustc)
test result: FAILED. 1 passed; 1 failed                  (libtest)
error: no such command: `buld`                           (cargo)

comparisons.note: Famous for one friendly error frame — but it covers the compiler only. The runtime and tooling never joined it.
comparisons.code:
-- NAMING ERROR ---------------------------------------- Main.elm
I cannot find a `pirnt` variable.

recommendation.why: The beginner learns one error language once, and it then holds everywhere: compile, run, test, tools, web, editor. Every message gains a code, an explanation path, and a snapshot that keeps its words honest.

whyNot.reason: It keeps six styles alive. The first failed test — the second error a beginner ever sees — still speaks a different language.
A frame without a code has no `jet explain` answer, no machine identity, and no snapshot duty. The words drift back apart.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every real tool error must get a registry row, which is authoring work per message. That work is one-time, and the snapshot suite then guards it forever.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared whole-toolchain law, compiler-only law, and frame-without-codes, and recommended the whole-toolchain law for one learnable shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-tool registries and a style guide without enforcement. Both re-create the drift this ballot ends, so they folded into options B and C.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested option A with option C's loose codes for rare messages. The exemption for status lines and usage echoes already covers the honest cases, so the hybrid collapsed into A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: it is the smallest migration and touches no tool. It still leaves test failures — the most-read message after compile errors — outside the law.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with the ceremony risk: does every `can't read file` need a row? The status-line exemption and reuse of existing codes answer it, so A stands.

decisions.title: Where a diagnostic's text lives
decisions.gist: One home for every diagnostic's code and words, instead of two unsynchronized copies.
decisions.lesson: Today a diagnostic's words live twice. The compiler renders inline Rust strings; `jet explain` re-parses a 252 KB markdown chapter on every call. A manual checklist keeps the copies in sync, and it has not. 328 codes have no explanation prose, three registered codes are emitted nowhere, and no test compares the copies. This choice picks the single home for diagnostic text.
decisions.story: Priya renames a concept across forty diagnostics. She edits the Rust strings, misses their markdown twins, and ships a `jet explain` that contradicts the error on screen. Nothing failed, because nothing checks.

options.name: Typed rows in the compile-time program
options.detail: The registry becomes typed rows — code, severity, moment, What/Why/Fix templates with named holes, optional structured fix — declared in the compile-time program, on the one registration table the metaprogramming slate ratified. Emit sites reference a row and fill its holes. The spec chapter, the error pages, and `jet explain` are generated from the rows, so the words cannot drift: there is nothing to drift from. This amends the I4 "Adding a diagnostic" process in the spec: the spec chapter becomes generated output of these rows.
options.technical:
Extends D-META-REG1's table with the diagnostics plane — the one table its proposal diagnosed but never balloted. Message templates are plain strings with named holes, not D-META-CODE1's derive-body law.

Bootstrap: at stage 0 the build generates a typed Rust table from the declarations, the same embed-and-rebuild pattern the Prelude uses. That step dies at self-hosting (#813).

Coverage runs both directions: every emitted code has a row; every row is emitted or marked retired or reserved. I4 snapshots stay mandatory per row. `reject` (D-META-USER1) mints user rows on the same rails. The declaration word is not chosen here: it needs its own Syntax.rs row and decision ID (I7), landed with D-META-REG1's table.

options.name: Markdown stays the source
options.detail: Keep `docs/spec/diagnostics.md` as the registry. Add the missing reverse check (every spec row must be emitted or marked retired) and generate a typed table from the markdown at build time. Cheapest change — but the compiler's inline strings remain a second home for the same words, so the drift this ballot exists to end continues.
options.technical: Build step parses the markdown once into a generated Rust table; `jet explain` stops re-parsing per call. Emit sites keep their own strings unless separately migrated.
options.code:
| E3010 | runtime | index out of range | the list has {len}... | reading past... | check the position... |
// + build.rs parse -> generated table; emit sites unchanged

options.name: One Rust static table
options.detail: One typed table in `jet-foundation`; markdown and explain generated from it. Ends the split brain — but parks the diagnostics table in Rust while every other rule table moves into the compile-time program. Self-hosting then ports it separately, and user rules cannot share its rails.
options.technical: A `const REPORTS: &[ReportRow]` table; emit sites reference rows by constant. Spec chapter generated by a test, like `docs/reference/errors/` today.

comparisons.note: All compiler messages live in one JSON file; the build generates the typed accessors. One home, no drift, easy localization later.
rustc keeps a per-code markdown file in-tree and a macro registry; `--explain` reads the markdown. Two artifacts, but both live beside the code and CI checks the pairing.

recommendation.why: One home ends the drift by construction and turns the 328 prose-less codes into a visible authoring worklist. The table lands on the substrate every other rule table now uses: built once, ported once, shared with user rules.

whyNot.reason: The compiler's inline strings remain a second copy of the words. The checklist survives, and so does the drift.
It fixes the split brain but strands the table in Rust while D-META moves every sibling table into the one program. Diagnostics would be ported twice and user rules could not share the rails.

recommendation.tradeoff: The registry becomes a build input of the compiler, so bootstrap ordering needs care, and the 328 prose-less codes become a visible authoring backlog instead of a hidden one.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared Jet rows, markdown-as-source, and a Rust table, recommending Jet rows for one home on the ratified registration table.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-crate registries and a database file. Both add homes instead of removing them and folded away.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested C-then-A: land a Rust table now, migrate to rows with the D-META cards. That is sequencing inside option A's implementation, not a distinct destination, so it folded into A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: it is the only option needing no compiler change, and the reverse check alone would catch today's three ghost codes. It still leaves two homes for the words.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's bootstrap: the compiler needs rows before it can compile the program that declares them. The stage-0 generated table answers it, and the marker table (#1539) crosses the same bridge first, so A holds.

decisions.title: The severity law: words and levels
decisions.gist: One law for severity levels and frame words — including what heads a stop the test runner contains.
decisions.lesson: No ratified law governs severity. The code has a two-value enum, a second copy of that enum, and three code prefixes, each freelancing. Three frame words are ratified in use: `Error` at compile time, `Stop` for a runtime breach, `Warning` for a lint. One new case forces the question: D-FAIL-BREACH1 makes a failed `require` a stop, and the ratified failure model names a test body as a boundary that contains it. A word must head that contained report. This ballot ratifies the whole severity law: the levels and the words.
decisions.story: Ben's test calls `require_eq(total(cart), 100)` and it fails. The runner prints `totals: FAIL` and, underneath, the report with the file, line, and caret. Ben reads the first word of that report. Which word is it?
decisions.inWild:
$ jet test orders.jet          # today — no report at all
totals: FAIL
  left: 101, right: 100
1 passed, 1 failed

options.name: Two severities, reuse the ratified words
options.detail: The law: two severities — blocking and advisory — and the three ratified words. A failed assertion is a broken promise — a `Stop`, the same word the same `require` prints in production (D-FAIL-BREACH1 already binds them to one family). An error value a test did not expect renders as the `Error` frame it would print at the program edge. The ledger line (`totals: FAIL`) already says this happened inside a test. No new word.
options.technical: Severity stays two-valued; the duplicate enum in Source/Compiler.rs is deleted. The moment (compile/run/test/tool) is row metadata, carried in JSON, not a new frame word. E and L code prefixes stay; W0410 stays frozen. A stop contained at the test boundary keeps its word and code (E3001 family).
options.code:
totals: FAIL
  Stop [E3001]: expected 100, got 101
    --> tests/orders.jet:14 in totals
      |
   14 |     require_eq(total(cart), 100)
      |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

options.name: A new word: Fail
options.detail: Test reports get their own head word, `Fail`, and their own code block. The word matches the ledger line. But it teaches a fourth word for a distinction the model says does not exist: the assertion that stopped the test is the same breach that would stop the program.
options.technical: A `Fail` frame word mapped to the blocking severity; a reserved code range for test-only reports. This re-carves the E3001 family D-FAIL-BREACH1 ratified, so picking it amends that ruling by name.
options.code:
totals: FAIL
  Fail [E4001]: expected 100, got 101
    --> tests/orders.jet:14 in totals

options.name: Reuse the words, add a Note severity
options.detail: Option A's words, plus a third severity `Note` for advisory information that is not a lint — future doctor output, deprecation timelines. Nothing today emits one: deopt is ratified silent, doctor prints a Warning. The slot is speculative.
options.technical: Severity becomes three-valued; LSP maps Note to Information. No current producer.
options.code:
totals: FAIL
  Stop [E3001]: expected 100, got 101
    --> tests/orders.jet:14 in totals

Note [N0001]: (no producer exists today)

comparisons.note: libtest prints `thread panicked at 'assertion failed: ...'` — the production panic voice inside test output. One voice; users never questioned it.
comparisons.code:
thread 'totals' panicked at 'assertion failed: `(left == right)`
  left: `101`, right: `100`', tests/orders.rs:14

comparisons.note: `go test` failures print the test's own log lines under a `--- FAIL:` ledger header — ledger plus detail, no third vocabulary.

recommendation.why: The assertion that fails a test is the same broken promise that stops a program, so it wears the same word. One word fewer to teach, and the ledger line already carries the test context.

whyNot.reason: A fourth word teaches a difference the model does not have. The same `require` would print `Stop` in production and `Fail` in a test — two words, one event.
No producer for `Note` exists today. A severity nobody emits is a slot added on speculation; it can be balloted when a real producer appears.

recommendation.tradeoff: `Stop` under a `FAIL` ledger line reads slightly formal for a test. The gain is that the beginner's runtime knowledge transfers to tests unchanged.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared reusing the ratified words, a new Fail word, and a Note severity, recommending reuse because the assertion is the same breach either way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested severity-free frames (color only) and per-moment code prefixes. Color-only fails NO_COLOR and new prefixes re-open a settled allocation, so both dropped.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested Fail as a ledger-only word with Stop in the frame — and found that is exactly option A, since FAIL already heads the ledger line.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: matching the ledger word has a real readability draw, and a test-only code block would make test reports easy to filter in JSON. The moment field already gives that filter.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with the beginner read: does `Stop` under `FAIL` confuse? The words sit two lines apart with the ledger naming the test, no ambiguity was found, and A stands.

decisions.title: A failed test shows a real report
decisions.gist: How a failed test presents the report: full frame, compact line, or a flag between them.
decisions.lesson: A `require` in production prints a full frame: message, file, line, and caret. The same `require` under `jet test` throws the frame away and prints `left: 101, right: 100` — no file, no line. Ratified law (D-FAIL-BREACH1) already makes the failed `require` a stop report, so the report is owed; this ballot decides its presentation. The golden-test helper also returns a bare true-or-false, so a missing golden file and a real mismatch are the same silent false.
decisions.story: Dana's test has thirty `require_eq` calls. One fails. The output is `left: 101, right: 100`. She adds print statements to find which line failed — in a language whose compile errors point at the exact character.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet test orders.jet
totals: FAIL
  left: 101, right: 100
1 passed, 1 failed

// golden helper today: returns Bool — missing file and mismatch are both `false`
require(testing.golden("totals.txt", output))

options.name: Full report, same renderer
options.detail: Assertion and golden failures render the one report frame — code, message with expected and got, file, line, caret — under the ledger line, from the same renderer production stops use. The golden helper produces a report that says which of two things happened: no golden file exists yet, or the output changed. Passing tests print exactly what they print today.
options.technical: The test-mode branch that drops the frame is deleted; the harness frames the same report the production path builds (E3001 family per D-FAIL-BREACH1). Golden failures include the diff path. Test reports ride `--json` like every report; the JETTEST2 prove record stays and is untouched. Tests may assert an expected code on an expected failure.
options.code:
totals: FAIL
  Stop [E3001]: expected 100, got 101
    --> tests/orders.jet:14 in totals
      |
   14 |     require_eq(total(cart), 100)
      |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
1 passed, 1 failed

options.name: Compact line plus location
options.detail: Keep the one-line `left/right` shape and add the file and line. Smaller output, but no caret, no code, no why or fix, no JSON row — a second voice for the same event, kept on purpose.
options.technical: The test-mode branch gains file:line interpolation. No registry row; `--json` still skips test failures.
options.code:
totals: FAIL
  left: 101, right: 100 (tests/orders.jet:14)
1 passed, 1 failed

options.name: Compact by default, full behind a flag
options.detail: Option B's line by default; option A's frame under `--verbose`. Two output modes for one product: snapshots, docs, and muscle memory must cover both, and the beginner — the person who most needs the caret — gets the compact one.
options.technical: A harness flag switches renderers. JSON emits the full report regardless of the flag.
options.code:
$ jet test orders.jet
totals: FAIL
  left: 101, right: 100 (tests/orders.jet:14)

$ jet test orders.jet --verbose
totals: FAIL
  Stop [E3001]: expected 100, got 101
    --> tests/orders.jet:14 in totals

comparisons.note: libtest shows the panic message with file:line but no source excerpt; pretty-assertions exists because users wanted more, not less.
comparisons.code:
thread 'totals' panicked at tests/orders.rs:14:
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: 101
 right: 100

comparisons.note: Prints expected/received plus a source excerpt with a caret — the frame option A proposes — and it is the output developers cite as a reason to use it.

recommendation.why: The failed check points at its own line with the same frame every other Jet failure uses. Nothing new to learn, nothing to bisect by hand, and test failures finally exist in JSON for CI.

whyNot.reason: It patches the location in but keeps a second voice: no code, no explanation path, no machine row. The one product stays forked at its most-read seam.
Two modes for one message doubles snapshots and docs, and hands the compact mode to the beginner who most needs the caret.

recommendation.tradeoff: Failure output gets taller — about six lines per failed assertion instead of one. Passing runs are unchanged.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the full frame, a compact line with location, and a flag-switched pair, recommending the full frame from the shared renderer.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested diff-style output for golden failures and structural diffs for collections. Both are message content inside option A's frame, not separate surfaces, and folded in.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested A's frame with B's one-line summary as the frame's message line. That is what A already is: the sentence carries expected and got.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: thirty failures at six lines each is real scroll, and B keeps failure walls short. Failing thirty at once is the rare case; the common case is one failure you must locate.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's height claim with property tests, which can fail many times per run. The harness already stops at the first failing case per test, so the wall does not materialize and A stands.

decisions.title: One JSON shape for every report
decisions.gist: The one machine-readable shape every Jet command uses for reports, replacing four incompatible ones.
decisions.lesson: A CI script reading Jet output today needs four parsers. There is the `--json` envelope from `jet check`, a crypto-only line format that preempts it, the Canvas panel's private shape, and a binary-only test report. The spec documents a fifth shape that exists only in a dead file. jetpack ignores `--json` on its error paths entirely. This choice picks the one shape and how it is framed.
decisions.story: Sam writes a CI annotator that marks failing lines in pull requests. Compile errors need parser one. A crypto diagnostic breaks it — parser two. Test failures are not in JSON at all, so Sam writes a regex over human output. The regex breaks on the next wording fix.
decisions.inWild:
{"schema_version":1,"diagnostics":[...]}            # jet check --json
{"schema":"jet.diagnostic/v1","code":"E2702",...}   # crypto only, different shape
{"code":...,"rendered":...}                          # Canvas panel, third shape
JETTEST2<binary>                                     # jet test proof report
# spec documents a fifth shape; its implementation is a dead, never-imported file

options.name: JSON lines: one report object per line
options.detail: Every report is one self-contained JSON object on one line: schema tag, code, severity, moment, what, why, fix, location, span, optional structured fix, cause chain. Commands stream them as they happen — live test runs and the dev loop included. Command envelopes keep their small status payloads; every report inside any command is this one object. Amends D-DX1 (the shipped envelope becomes a status wrapper; reports move to lines).
options.technical:
One shared writer emits every report line. The crypto shape, the Canvas shape, the dead file, and the ten hand-rolled envelope sites are deleted. The Canvas panel consumer migrates in the same change.

Every field delta vs the shipped shape is named. `message` renames to `what`, because registry field names win. `detail` stays. The promised `suggestions` array is kept as `fix_edits`, plural. A `schema` tag replaces `schema_version`.

D-DX1 is ratified in spec prose with no board record, so this ratification also mints the record it amends. jetpack's error paths honor `--json`. Gate audits (D-FACT-GATE1) emit the same object. The JETTEST2 prove record is untouched; JSON test reports are additive.

options.name: One envelope object per command
options.detail: Keep the shipped envelope (`{"schema_version":1,"diagnostics":[...]}`) and extend it to every command. One parse call for one-shot commands — but streaming surfaces must buffer: a long test run or a dev loop emits nothing until it ends, and a crash loses the buffer.
options.technical: The report object inside the envelope is the same as option A's. Test and dev buffer reports and emit one document at exit.
options.code:
$ jet test orders.jet --json
{"schema_version":2,"reports":[{"moment":"test","code":"E3001",...}],"passed":1,"failed":1}

options.name: Envelope for one-shot, lines for streaming
options.detail: `jet check` and `jet fmt` keep an envelope; `jet test` and `jet dev` stream lines. Each command uses its natural framing — but consumers must know which command produces which framing, so every consumer writes both parsers anyway.
options.technical: Same report object in both framings; a per-command table in the spec says which framing each command uses.

comparisons.note: `--message-format=json` streams one JSON object per line. Every Rust CI tool parses it with a per-line loop; the framing has held for years.
`go test -json` streams line events for live CI progress — the buffering problem option B walks into is the one Go solved this way.

recommendation.why: One object, one framing, every command. A consumer is a per-line loop that works for a compile check, a live test run, and the dev loop alike, and never loses output to a crashed buffer.

whyNot.reason: Buffering breaks live test and dev output, and a crash mid-run loses every buffered report.
Two framings means every consumer writes two parsers — the situation this ballot exists to end, minus two shapes.

recommendation.tradeoff: The shipped envelope goldens re-bless once, and existing scripts that parsed the old envelope update once.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared JSON lines, one envelope, and a mixed framing, recommending lines for streaming and single-parser simplicity.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested SARIF as the native format. It is verbose and single-document, better served later as a converter over jet.report lines, so it folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested lines plus a closing status line per command — and adopted it into A: the status payload rides its own small schema-tagged line.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: one `JSON.parse` call is the simplest possible consumer for one-shot commands, and most CI calls are one-shot. The buffering cost on test and dev remains.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with interleaving: parallel test workers writing lines concurrently could tear. The writer serializes lines through one lock, as the terminal renderer already must, so A stands.

decisions.title: The editor gets the whole report
decisions.gist: What the language server sends the editor for each diagnostic: the whole report, or today's first line only.
decisions.lesson: The registry stores a What, a Why, and a Fix for each diagnostic. The language server sends the editor only the What. The Why and Fix never arrive; the quick-fix edit is recovered by pattern-matching the Fix sentence for phrases like `replace X with Y`. This choice decides what the editor receives.
decisions.story: Ana hits E0321 in Zed. The squiggle says what is wrong. On the terminal the same error would tell her why and hand her the fix. In her editor — where she actually works — that half of the product is missing.
