options.name: Full report, structured
options.detail: The editor receives everything the terminal knows. The What is the message. The Why and Fix show on hover or expand. The code links to its explanation page. The quick-fix edit comes from the row's structured fix — the same edit `jet fix` applies, no scraping. Related locations ride the standard field editors already render.
options.technical: message = what. why/fix ride the standard diagnostic fields editors show on expand. codeDescription.href points at the code's explanation. relatedInformation replaces the hardcoded empty list. The code action reuses the row's structured fix. Editors that ignore a field lose nothing.
options.code:
{"range":...,"severity":1,"code":"E0321","source":"jet",
 "message":"<what>",
 "codeDescription":{"href":"<explanation for E0321>"},
 "relatedInformation":[{"location":...,"message":"the conflicting definition is here"}],
 "data":{"why":"<why>","fix":"<fix>","fix_edits":[{...}]}}

options.name: What plus quick fix only
options.detail: Today's payload, kept on purpose: the message and a quick-fix action. Why and Fix stay terminal-only; a user who wants them runs `jet explain` in a terminal. Smallest payload — and the editor surface stays half a product.
options.technical: No payload change. The prose-scraping edit derivation stays, or is separately replaced.
options.code: {"range":...,"severity":1,"code":"E0321","source":"jet","message":"<what>"}

options.name: Terminal frame embedded in the message
options.detail: Send the fully rendered multi-line terminal frame — What, arrow, Why, Fix — as the message string. Everything arrives with no editor cooperation, but every squiggle tooltip becomes a seven-line block, and machine consumers must parse prose out of the message again.
options.technical: message = the rendered frame minus color. No structured fields.
options.code:
{"message":"Error [E0321]: <what>
  --> app.jet:2:5
 Why: <why>
 Fix: <fix>"}

comparisons.note: Sends structured diagnostics with related locations, and carries the full rendered message for clients that want it. Editors show the short form, expand to the long one.
Every diagnostic links its rule page via the standard code link; one click from squiggle to essay.

recommendation.why: The registry's whole product reaches the surface where people actually read diagnostics. The fix becomes real data instead of scraped prose, so the editor's edit and `jet fix` cannot disagree.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the editor at half the product and keeps prose scraping as the only source of the edit.
A seven-line tooltip on every squiggle, and the structure is flattened back into prose that tools must re-parse.

recommendation.tradeoff: The payload grows by the Why and Fix text per diagnostic. Editors that ignore the extra fields behave exactly as today.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the structured full report, the status quo, and an embedded terminal frame, recommending the structured report.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested hover-only delivery of the why and fix. That hides them from diagnostic panels and quick-fix flows, so it folded into B as a variant.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined A with C's rendered frame as an optional extra field for thin clients, mirroring rust-analyzer. Adopted into A's technical shape as an optional field.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: it is zero migration and no editor shows nothing it shows today. It still cannot show the Why or apply an unscraped fix.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's payload growth on huge diagnostic sets. Why and Fix are bounded registry prose rather than source dumps, so size stays small and A stands.

decisions.title: Script mode: bare statements are the fn run body
decisions.gist: Whether a file of bare statements runs as a program, and how far that rule reaches.
decisions.lesson: Today a Jet file may hold only definitions, so the smallest program needs a fn run() wrapper (E0003). The approved direction makes a file of bare statements a script that jet run executes, defined as sugar: the bare statements are the body of an implicit fn run(). Three owner rulings are law in every adopting option. An imported script never runs. Mixing bare code with an explicit fn run is an error with an auto-wrap fix. Diagnostics nudge promotion without punishing the script rung. This ballot picks the rule's reach.
decisions.story: Ana is teaching her first Jet class. She wants each student to create hello.jet, type one print line, and see output within a minute. Today she must first explain what fn run() { } means before anyone sees anything run. Later, a student pastes a classmate's script into a project with use, and the class needs the compiler to say clearly why an imported script does not run.

options.name: Adopt for jet run only
options.detail:
A file with bare statements runs with jet run (and jet dev through its existing fall-back to run). The three owner rulings apply in full: importing a script is a friendly error, mixing bare code with fn run is an error with a jet fix auto-wrap, and errors nudge promotion.

But jet test file.jet on a script stays an error until a later decision. You gain the zero-ceremony rung now with the smallest ruling. You lose the rhyme's reach: a script with a #Test block cannot run its tests without first promoting to fn run.
options.technical:
Sugar law: bare statements form the body of an implicit fn run(); declarations stay at file level. The implicit entry is the fallible form (fn run() => () ?, D-S80-RUN1), so ? works at a script's top level. A file with any bare statement is a script and may only be the direct jet run target; use and package discovery report the new import error. Explicit fn run beside bare code is the new mixing error; jet fix wraps under D-REL5 authority.

Amends S12 (adds the implicit spelling) and the E0003 copy. U7, D-VERDICT-678-1, D-BUILDSCOPE1, and D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1 are unchanged.

options.name: Adopt for the whole verb table
options.detail:
Same script rule as option A, plus the whole verb rhyme lands now. jet run runs the implicit entry, jet dev hot-reloads the script, and jet test runs the script's #Test blocks. A script may hold any ordinary declaration beside its loose code: fn helpers, struct, #Test, use, #Job fns, fn build, fn dev. Only an explicit fn run conflicts, because two entries would exist.

You gain one complete law stated once, and a script rung that grows tests before it needs promotion. You lose nothing at the beginner surface. The cost is deciding dev and test behavior on scripts now.
options.technical: Everything in option A, plus two verbs. jet test file.jet runs the script's #Test blocks; package-level jet test keeps D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1's plural rule. jet dev file.jet hot-reloads with the fn dev override per U19. The implicit fn run counts as the zero-config entry in D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1's five-step rule. The import-error rule attaches to whichever file-import spelling the open D-NAME-FILES1 slate (card #1625) ratifies. This option needs declarations in scripts, so it assumes D-ENTRY-ORDER1 lands outcome A or B, not C.

options.name: No script mode — better wrapper help instead
options.detail: Keep fn run() mandatory. Sharpen the on-ramp instead: E0003 gains a fix that offers the auto-wrap, and jet fix file.jet writes the fn run() wrapper for you. You gain one unchanged entry story and no new file category. You lose the zero-ceremony rung: the first minute of Jet still starts with explaining a function. Notebook and REPL cells would also need their own future rule instead of riding this one.
options.technical: No grammar change. E0003 copy gains a jet fix hint; jet fix learns the wrap rewrite under D-REL5. S12 unchanged. The notebook and REPL substrate question returns later as a separate design.

comparisons.note: Any file runs top to bottom, but import also runs it — the guard idiom exists to patch that footgun. This design keeps the run half and blocks the import half by rule.
comparisons.code:
# tools.py
print("cleaning…")   # runs on import too!

if __name__ == "__main__":   # the patch everyone must learn
    main()

comparisons.note: Only main.swift may hold top-level code; every other file needs declarations. Close to this design, but the rule keys on a file name instead of how the file is used.
comparisons.code:
// main.swift
print("Hello")   // legal here, error in any other file

comparisons.note: fn main() is always required. Great for large programs, and exactly the ceremony this proposal removes from rung zero.

recommendation.why: One law stated once covers the whole verb rhyme: jet run, dev, and test all work on the file the beginner already has. The script rung can grow a helper and a test before promotion, which is exactly the nudge-not-punish ruling. Notebooks and the REPL inherit a complete substrate, not a run-only slice.

whyNot.reason: It ships the same mechanism but leaves jet test and jet dev on scripts undefined, which guarantees a second ballot and an awkward gap where a script's own tests cannot run.
It keeps the wrapper ceremony in the first minute of Jet and leaves notebook and REPL cells without a law to ride.

recommendation.tradeoff: Option B must define dev and test behavior on scripts now, so its implementation cards touch three verbs instead of one. That is accepted: the semantics are one desugaring, and splitting the decision would reopen this same question within weeks.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared run-only adoption, whole-verb-table adoption, and a no-script-mode alternative, with the owner's three rulings written into both adopting options. It recommended the whole table because the law is one desugaring either way.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested four more shapes: a special file name (Swift main.swift style), a #Script marker, a jet script subcommand, and shebang-only scripts. All four add a naming or ceremony surface without changing semantics, so they folded into the existing options rather than widening the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested adopting run now with test and dev pre-approved to follow, which is option B with a second ratification, so no separate option was added. It also moved C's jet fix wrap into A and B as the mixing-rule fix.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A as the smallest ruling that still delivers rung zero, and strengthened C by giving it the auto-wrap fix so its on-ramp is two commands, not a lecture. C remains the honest keep-today option, not a strawman.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked B where scripts meet packages — import, package discovery, and an explicit fn run beside bare code — and all three land on the ruled errors. It also confirmed the implicit entry slots into D-ECO-OUTPUT-DEFAULT1's existing zero-config step, so B survived and the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Script visibility: what a name can see inside a script file
decisions.gist: Whether a script name exists only after its line, or declarations are visible file-wide with statements in order.
decisions.lesson: A script file mixes two kinds of code: declarations (fn, struct, #Test) and loose statements. Jet's current file law is order-independent — a declaration is visible anywhere in its file, before or after its line. Statements inside a function body always run top to bottom. A script holds both kinds, so it must pick a visibility law. Every option shares one rule: a loose binding is a local of the implicit run body, never visible inside a fn, or scripts would grow hidden mutable globals.
decisions.story: Sam is three days into Jet. His script grew a repeated block, so he makes his first function — and pastes it at the bottom, under the code that calls it, like the tutorial showed. Whether that file runs, or errors telling him to reorder, is this decision.

options.name: Strict top to bottom
options.detail:
A script name exists only after its line, declarations included. The story is one sentence: the file runs like you read it. The cost lands on real beginner programs. A helper pasted below its call errors and must move up. Two functions that call each other cannot be written at all — no reorder fixes them.

Reordering code changes meaning, so refactors can break a working script. Promotion changes the law mid-ladder: the same functions become order-free the moment they move into a module file. Notebook cells inherit order fragility for functions, not just state.
options.technical: Sema resolves a script in one pass. A reference before the defining line is a compile error naming both lines, with a move fix. Mutual recursion between script declarations is unrepresentable. Module files keep today's order-independent law, so the script regime differs from every other Jet file.

options.name: Declarations file-wide, statements in order
options.detail: Declarations follow the existing file law and are visible anywhere in the script. Loose statements run top to bottom as the implicit run body. This adds zero new law: declarations already work this way in every Jet file, and statements already run in order in every function body. A helper pasted below its call works. Mutual recursion works. The cost is a teaching sentence: fn greet is reachable from line one, but a loose binding is not — it is body code, and the shared-rule error explains that when it bites.
options.technical: The desugaring is exact: declarations stay at file level, loose statements become the fn run body in written order. Sema is unchanged for declarations and unchanged for bodies — a script is the composition of the two existing laws. Promotion to fn run or to a module file never changes what any name can see. Notebook cells: function and type cells are order-free, only state cells are ordered.

options.name: Statements only — no declarations in a script
options.detail: A script admits loose statements and use imports, nothing else. The first fn or struct is an error pointing at promotion. There is one category of code, so the visibility question disappears. The cost: the script rung can never hold a helper or a #Test block, so it dies at roughly five lines and the promotion nudge becomes a wall. That collides with the ruling that diagnostics never punish the script rung.
options.technical: The parser rejects declarations (except use) in a file that has any bare statement, with a promotion fix. The implicit run body is the entire file. This option excludes D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1 option B: script tests need declarations, so ratifying both together is a contradiction the boards must not allow.

comparisons.note: Strict top to bottom for everything, patched by habit: put all defs first, call at the end. Notebook cells famously break when re-run out of order.
comparisons.code:
greet("Ada")        # NameError: name 'greet' is not defined
def greet(name): print(f"Hello {name}")

comparisons.note: Function declarations hoist file-wide while statements run in order — the same split as option B. It is one of the few beginner-loved parts of the language's scoping.
comparisons.code:
greet("Ada");                 // works: declarations hoist
function greet(n) { console.log(`Hello ${n}`); }

comparisons.note: main.swift is strict top to bottom for statements, but functions defined anywhere in the file are callable — Swift chose option B's split for its script file.
comparisons.code:
greet("Ada")   // works in main.swift
func greet(_ n: String) { print("Hello \(n)") }

recommendation.why: B is the only option that adds no new law. It is exactly the desugaring: file law for declarations, body law for statements. Real beginner programs — the pasted-below helper and mutual recursion — run instead of erroring, and promotion never changes what a name can see.

whyNot.reason: It breaks the helper-below-use script every beginner writes, forbids mutual recursion outright, and flips the visibility law underneath the user at the promotion step.
It caps the script rung at a handful of lines and turns the promotion nudge into a wall, against the never-punish ruling.

recommendation.tradeoff: B keeps two kinds of code in one file, so the docs owe one sentence: declarations are file-wide, loose bindings are body locals. That is accepted because both halves are laws Jet users must learn anyway, and the shared-rule error teaches the split at the exact moment it matters.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft worked strict order against file-wide declarations on three beginner programs: helper below use, mutual recursion, and a mid-file binding. It recommended file-wide declarations because that is the desugaring with no added law.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested statements-only scripts, Python-style runtime binding, and full hoisting where bindings also lift; statements-only was genuinely distinct and became option C. Runtime binding is option A with later errors and hoisted bindings recreate hidden globals, so both folded.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested A's one-sentence story on top of B's semantics: keep file-wide declarations but lint, not error, when a helper sits above first use in teaching mode. That is a formatter or lint choice, not a visibility law, so it was noted for the docs and no hybrid option was added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with its best honest case — the file reads exactly as it runs, matching Python intuition — and gave it a precise two-line error with a move fix. C was strengthened as the only option with a single code category and zero visibility teaching.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked B's split with a beginner reading a loose binding from a helper; the shared-rule error covers it with two concrete fixes. It also tested notebook cells, where B keeps function cells order-free while A reproduces the out-of-order fragility notebooks are hated for, so B survived.

decisions.title: One run, one claim — adopt the law for the dev loop and testing
decisions.gist: Make every dev verb one run with a different observer, and every check one claim with different inputs and evidence.
decisions.lesson: Jet ships seven dev verbs and seven check forms. The audit found they are one machine wearing coats. Each coat grew its own seams: two assertion vocabularies are ratified at once, the bench marker duplicates the test marker, and the test harness drops the file and line from failures. This ballot adopts the model that names the machine. Later ballots pick each surface change; this one only sets the law that guides them.
decisions.story: Ana learns Jet in week one. She knows `jet run`, then meets `jet dev`, `jet test`, `jet bench`, `require`, `#Test`, `#Bench`, budgets, and Check Outputs as nine separate things to memorize. Under the law she learns two ideas instead: a verb picks what watches the run, and a check picks where inputs come from. Everything else is a cell in that grid.

options.name: Adopt the whole law
options.detail: One program, one meaning, one claim. Verbs choose the observer of a run. Claims choose their inputs and their evidence grade. Nothing else may vary. Every later card in this area builds on one substrate: one harness, one report frame, one watch choreography. Beginners learn two ideas. Experts lose nothing; every current control stays.
options.technical: Run observers: none, watcher, claim harness, measurer, stepper, prompt, recorder. Claim inputs: caller, author, docs, generator, stored artifact, measurement, prover. Evidence words stay the ratified jet prove set: proved, passed, observed, met. I9, D-DEVMODE1, D-FAIL-BREACH1, and D-ONECORE1 already state the tier half of this law.
options.code:
# One grid, spoken by the tools themselves
$ jet run app.jet            # observer: none
$ jet dev app.jet            # observer: watcher + session
$ jet test app.jet           # observer: claim harness
$ jet bench app.jet          # observer: measurer
$ jet debug app.jet          # observer: stepper
$ jet prove app.jet          # the evidence ledger over all claims

options.name: Adopt the run half only
options.detail: Verbs become observers of one run, but the check forms stay as they are. The watch loop unifies and the session improves. The claim seams stay: two assertion vocabularies, a duplicate bench marker, and a test report that drops the frame. Half the confusion remains.
options.code:
$ jet test app.jet
# still today's harness:
double: FAIL
  left: 6, right: 7        # no file, no line, no caret

options.name: Adopt the claim half only
options.detail: Checks unify into one claim construct, but the verbs stay separate machines. Tests gain the full report frame. The dev loop keeps two watch choreographies, a dead-end session, and no path to the recorder. The teaching story stays fragmented.
options.code:
$ jet dev app.jet
watching app.jet ... (Ctrl-C to stop)
# still a dead end: no way to run claims inside the warm session

options.name: Decline the model
options.detail: Keep the area as it is. Each ratified-but-unbuilt card (test report frame, bench parity, script mode, prelude assertions) builds on today's seams. The seams are then load-bearing and cost more to remove later.
options.code: # No change. The twelve-row evidence table in the proposal stays live.

comparisons.note: One toolchain where run, test, bench, and fmt share flags and one config. Watch is a flag on every verb, so new verbs compose for free.
Cargo never named the machine. Watch, bench, and test extension went to third parties (cargo-watch, criterion, nextest), which now define those loops.

recommendation.why: The grid already exists in ratified law: I9 owns one meaning across tiers, and jet prove owns the evidence words. Adopting the law makes the unbuilt cards land on one substrate instead of rebuilding seven coats. Beginners get a two-idea mental model; experts keep every control.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the claim seams in place, so the test report stays poorer than the production report and two assertion words ship.
It leaves the dev loop fragmented, so the session stays a dead end and the watch loop stays duplicated.
The ratified-but-unbuilt cards then harden today's seams, and the same unification costs a migration later.

recommendation.tradeoff: The law constrains future tools: a new dev feature must be an observer, and a new check must be a claim. That is the point, but it does close the door on parallel mechanisms.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared adopting the full law with adopting each half and with declining. It recommended the full law because both halves share one substrate and one teaching story.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review looked for a third axis beyond observer and inputs-evidence. Tier is already owned by I9 and D-ONECORE1, and no distinct fourth option emerged.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The halves were tested as staged adoption: run half now, claim half later. Staging was folded into options B and C rather than a new option, because the substrate work overlaps and staging doubles it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option D was strengthened: today's tools do ship and the pragmatism audit found the dev loop healthy. Options B and C were given their strongest scopes so each half stands alone if picked.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack asked whether the law is empty naming, so the test was whether it forbids anything. It forbids second harnesses, second report shapes, and second watch loops — exactly the defects in the evidence table — so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: One assertion word for code, tests, and scripts
decisions.gist: Pick the one word that states a runtime fact everywhere: require, assert, or a fresh word.
decisions.lesson: Two assertion families are ratified at once. S43 gave Jet `require` and `require_eq`, and they ship today. D-CORE-PRELUDE1=A later added `assert` and `assert_eq` to the prelude with a rich structural diff; they are not built yet. No ruling retires either family. One fact needs one word, chosen before the second family ships. The winner keeps the ratified rich diff and the one stop family from D-FAIL-BREACH1 (registered E30xx codes, `.expect_fail`).
decisions.story: Sam writes a first test and types `assert`, the word from every other language they know. Jet answers with an unknown-name error and teaches `require`. Next month the prelude ships `assert` too, and Sam's codebase uses both words for the same fact. Every reader now wonders whether the two words differ. They never did.

options.name: assert / assert_eq everywhere
options.detail: Adopt the word every mainstream language uses. Migrate every `require` and `require_eq` in examples, docs, and tests, then delete them. Beginners type the word they already know and it works. Amends S43 wording, the D-PRELUDE-LAW1=A ambient registry (swap require for assert), and the D-FAIL-BREACH1=A wording that names require.
options.technical: The ambient prelude registry becomes print, input, panic, assert. assert_eq keeps the sema arity and type checks (E0104, E0108) and gains the ratified structural diff. Failures stay one stop family with registered codes on every tier.

options.name: require / require_eq everywhere
options.detail: Keep the shipped word. Amend D-CORE-PRELUDE1=A to drop `assert` and `assert_eq` before they are built; the ratified structural diff moves onto `require_eq`. Zero migration of existing code. Beginners who type `assert` keep getting a teaching error that names `require`.
options.technical: No registry change. The rich-diff work lands on require_eq. D-FAIL-BREACH1 wording stays as written.

options.name: claim / claim_eq — a fresh single word
options.detail: Name the construct after the model: a claim about the program. One new word replaces both families. It reads well beside the evidence ledger (`jet prove` grades claims). Cost: nobody arrives knowing it, and every arriving user first types assert and hits a teaching error. Amends the same set as option B plus D-CORE-PRELUDE1.

options.name: Keep both words
options.detail: Ship `assert` beside `require` with identical meaning. No migration. Every codebase then mixes them, style guides must pick one anyway, and readers keep asking what the difference is. This is the status quo the two ratifications drift toward.
options.code:
require(amount > 0)
assert(amount > 0)   // same meaning, forever explained in FAQs

comparisons.note: One family, assert and assert_eq, used in code and tests alike. The shared word is why tests read like code.
One function, std.debug.assert, plus std.testing.expectEqual in tests. Two vocabularies split by context — a common complaint.

recommendation.why: The word a beginner already knows should be the word that works. `assert` is that word in Python, Rust, C, Java, and JavaScript. It is also the family the owner already ratified for the prelude with the rich diff, so the migration finishes a decision instead of reversing one.

whyNot.reason: It keeps a rarer word and forces every arriving user through a teaching error for the common one. It also reverses the ratified prelude addition.
A fresh word makes every arriving user learn Jet-only vocabulary for the most common statement in testing. The model does not need its name in the code.
Two words for one fact is the defect this ballot exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every existing example, doc, and test that spells `require` migrates in one greenfield change. That churn is internal and accepted; the final surface is judged on its own.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keeping require, adopting assert, and keeping both. It recommended assert because arriving users already know it and the prelude ratification already points there.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the fresh-word option, claim, which matches the model vocabulary. An expect family was checked and rejected because `expect(...).snapshot()` and `.expect_fail` already own that word.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A split-meaning hybrid was tested: require for contracts, assert for tests. It was folded out because D-FAIL-TIER1 already gives contracts their own forms (#Pre, #Post), so the split has no home.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option A was strengthened: zero migration, and require reads naturally in precondition prose. Option D was given its honest best case: no breakage and full familiarity, at the price of permanent duplication.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack asked whether the migration silently touches ratified wording in S43, D-PRELUDE-LAW1, and D-FAIL-BREACH1. It does, the ballot now names all three amendments, and the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Benchmarks are measured tests — one marker, one verb
decisions.gist: Spell a benchmark as a test with a .measure member, and run measurement as a mode of jet test.
decisions.lesson: The code already says the two are one: a `#Bench` body type-checks exactly like a `#Test` body, and the AST comment calls the nodes identical. But `#Bench` is a separate marker with no members, so `.setup` inside it is an error, and `jet bench` is a separate verb on the wrong build profile. Enforcement is split too: the spec orders one path through typed budgets, yet the old paths stand, their ratified deletion unfinished. If a benchmark is a test with a measurement, the spelling should say so.
decisions.story: Mia benchmarks a parser. Loading the fixture costs more than parsing, so her numbers measure file reads; in a test she would write `.setup`, but in `#Bench` that is error E0614. She also compares numbers with a friend's release build, not knowing `jet bench` ran the ordinary profile. Then she wonders why her benchmark never ran under `jet test` even though it would have caught the crash she shipped.

options.name: .measure member; #Bench and jet bench both retire
options.detail: One marker, one verb. A measured claim is `#Test` with a `.measure` member; new members are the ratified extension axis (D-DOTSCOPE1: an API decision, not a syntax one). Plain `jet test` runs it once as a correctness claim, so a crashing benchmark is a failing test. `jet test --measure` is measurement mode: warmups, auto-scaled iterations, the optimized profile the spec promises, tier labeled in every line and artifact. Limits live only in typed budgets. Typing `jet bench` or `#Bench` becomes a teaching error naming the new spelling.
options.technical: Amends D-BENCH-MARKER1=A (marker retired) and D-BENCH1 wording; subsumes D-BENCH-PARITY1=B (one verb cannot disagree with itself). Completes D-PERFBUDGET-BENCHMIGRATE1=B and paired D-PERFBUDGET-GAMEMIGRATE1; the Budget scope spelling .Bench(name) migrates with the marker. Fixes the spec.md:2235 profile drift. Measured claims report through the one frame and the one machine shape (D-REPORT-TEST1=A, D-REPORT-MACHINE1=A).

options.name: .measure member; jet bench survives as sugar
options.detail: Same marker unification as A, but the verb stays: `jet bench` means exactly `jet test --measure`. People who reach for the word keep it, at the cost of two spellings for one command forever, and docs must explain that bench is test.

options.name: #Bench stays as sugar for a measured test
options.detail: The substrate unifies (one harness, members work, budgets only, honest profile) but both surface words survive: `#Bench("x") { }` is sugar for `#Test("x") { .measure }` and `jet bench` for `jet test --measure`. Zero migration, and the surface keeps teaching that benchmarks are a different thing when they are not.

options.name: Status quo plus the profile fix
options.detail: Keep `#Bench` as a separate construct with no members. Only fix the drift: run the optimized profile and label the tier. The enforcement split and the missing member vocabulary stay, and the ratified prototype deletion still has no destination shape.

comparisons.note: Benchmarks live in the testing package and run through the one test verb with a flag. One vocabulary, one harness; b.ResetTimer is their setup escape.
comparisons.code: go test -bench=Parse   # benchmarks are tests, selected by flag

comparisons.note: #[bench] stayed nightly for a decade, so criterion (a third-party crate) owns benchmarking with a separate harness and verbs. The lesson: keep measurement inside the test family or lose it.

recommendation.why: It is the model's own spelling: a measured test is a test, so it uses the test marker and the test verb. Every seam goes — the second node, the banned members, the split enforcement, the wrong profile, and the parity gap between two verbs that should never have been able to disagree. Measured claims also start running as correctness claims, which no other option gives for free.

whyNot.reason: Keeping the verb as sugar preserves two spellings for one command and re-opens the door this ballot closes.
Marker sugar keeps teaching that benchmarks are a separate construct, which is the exact misconception the unification removes.
It fixes the honesty bug but keeps the duplicate construct, so the ratified prototype deletion still lacks a destination and members stay banned.

recommendation.tradeoff: The words bench and #Bench stop working and become teaching errors. Every arriving user knows the word benchmark, so the teaching error must name the new spelling well; that discoverability duty is accepted.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft kept #Bench as the measured-test marker for word familiarity. The owner's consistency test overturned it: if a benchmark is a test with a measurement, the spelling must say so.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review checked a separate-tool shape, the criterion model, and rejected it as a new mechanism. It also confirmed Go as the strongest precedent: benchmarks ride the one test verb behind a flag.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Options B and C are the hybrids: substrate unification with one or both surface words kept as sugar. They stay on the menu as honest smaller steps that A subsumes cleanly.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option D was strengthened to include the tier label and profile fix so honesty does not depend on the bigger unification. Options B and C carry their real virtue: zero relearning for arriving users.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack was discoverability: users type jet bench everywhere else, so retiring the verb risks a dead end. The repair is the ratified teaching-error pattern that names the new spelling — the path jet serve already walks — so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Watch is a modifier on every runnable verb
decisions.gist: Let --watch attach to test, bench, and check the way it already attaches to run, with honest partial-run output.
decisions.lesson: Today `--watch` works on `jet run` and `jet dev` is the watch loop. Tests and benches cannot watch; a user edits, switches windows, and re-runs by hand. The engine (one WatchSession graph) already exists and already powers two hand-copied loops. The strongest cross-language lesson in the research: when watch is a flag it composes with every verb forever; when it is a verb or a third-party tool it fragments. The risk to manage is false green: a partial re-run must never read as a full suite.
decisions.story: Leo is deep in a refactor with forty tests. He wants the failing three to re-run on every save. Today he re-types `jet test` after each edit or keeps `jet dev` open in one pane and tests in another. With `--watch` on `jet test`, the affected tests re-run on save and the output says exactly what was and was not covered.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet test app.jet --watch          # today: unknown flag for test
$ jet bench app.jet --watch         # today: unknown flag for bench
# Meanwhile jet run --watch and jet dev already share the WatchSession engine,
# with the loop choreography copy-pasted in CmdDevTools.rs and CmdCompile.rs.

options.name: --watch on run, test, bench, check; jet dev stays the session
options.detail: Every runnable verb accepts `--watch`, riding the one engine. Re-runs select only affected claims from the watch graph and say so, with the full-suite spelling printed beside the count. `jet dev` remains the resident session verb, unchanged, per D-CLI-DEVSERVE1=A. Internal to this option: the duplicated web loop dies and one choreography serves native and web.
options.technical: One watch choreography in one home; the native and web loops consume it. Affected selection comes from WatchGraph reverse edges. Partial runs always print the affected count and the full-suite command. --watch=off keeps its meaning.
options.code:
$ jet test app.jet --watch
3 passed  (0.4 s)
— lib/parse.jet changed —
2 claims re-run (affected); full suite: jet test
2 passed

options.name: Fold watching into jet dev lenses
options.detail: Plain verbs never watch. `jet dev --test` and `jet dev --bench` run those observers inside the session. One loop, one verb, but every watching intent now routes through dev, and a user who only wants watched tests must learn the session verb and its flags.
options.code:
$ jet dev app.jet --test
watching app.jet ...
3 passed
— lib/parse.jet changed —
2 claims re-run (affected)

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: Watch stays on run and dev only. Test and bench users keep hand re-running or wire their own file watchers, which then define the loop's semantics outside Jet.
options.code:
$ jet test app.jet --watch
tower: unknown flag ... # user installs a shell watcher instead

comparisons.note: --watch is a flag on run, test, bench, and serve. It composed with new verbs for free and no third-party watcher emerged.
Cargo shipped no watch. cargo-watch, then bacon, then each IDE defined the loop, each differently.
comparisons.code: cargo watch -x test   # third party, one of several

comparisons.note: Watch mode with affected-only selection from the module graph is the ergonomic peak of test tooling, and its known trap is partial-run green read as full green.
comparisons.code: jest --watch   # p pattern, t name, f failures-only

recommendation.why: It gives every verb the loop with one engine and zero new verbs, keeps `jet dev` exactly as ratified, and closes the third-party-watcher door before it opens. The honesty line neutralizes the one known trap of affected-only re-runs.

whyNot.reason: It makes the session verb a prerequisite for watched tests, adding a learning step for the most common watching intent.
It leaves the loop to hand re-running or external watchers, which then own the semantics Jet should own.

recommendation.tradeoff: Affected-only selection depends on the watch graph being right; a missed edge silently skips a test until the next full run. The printed affected count plus the full-suite line keeps that visible, and CI always runs the full suite.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the modifier form, the dev-lens form, and the status quo. It recommended the modifier because it composes with every current and future verb.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a dedicated `jet watch <verb>` prefix form, the dotnet shape. Rejected: prefix verbs compose badly with flags and add a verb where a flag serves.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A and B combine naturally: the session can also run claims via keys (that is D-RUN-SESSION1), while plain verbs watch via the flag. The ballots stay separate so either can land alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened: one resident process is cheaper than N watchers, and dev already owns the loop. Option C was given its honest case: fewer flags, no false-green risk.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack ran two watchers on one directory, jet dev beside jet test --watch, and they do not fight: each holds its own graph and shares only the filesystem. Rebuild cost is bounded by the shared build cache, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: One resident session with in-session keys
decisions.gist: Give jet dev single-key verbs (re-run, restart, tests, failures) and let the prompt and stepper attach to the same warm session.
decisions.lesson: The `jet dev` session already holds the resident program, the live heap, `#Persist` state, and the hot-swap baseline. But it is a dead end: it can only re-run the program. Running tests means a second cold process, and the REPL and debugger own separate engines. The research is one-sided here: the fastest loops ever shipped put the verbs inside the running process. The ratified script-mode law makes a REPL line bare code, which is the substrate that lets tools attach.
decisions.story: Priya is fixing a bug with `jet dev` open. To check her fix against the tests she switches panes and runs `jet test` cold, twelve seconds. With session keys she presses `t` and the claims run in the warm session in milliseconds. Three fail; she edits and presses `f` — only those three re-run.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev app.jet          # today
watching app.jet ... (Ctrl-C to stop)
✓ ran in 38 ms
# and that is everything the session can do: wait for saves, or die.
# Tests? Second terminal, cold process. REPL? Separate engine. Debug? Separate engine.

options.name: Full session model: keys plus attaching tools
options.detail: In-session keys for the loop verbs — `r` re-run, `R` restart fresh, `t` tests, `f` failed claims only, `q` quit. The REPL prompt and the stepper attach to the same warm session instead of owning parallel engines, on the ratified script-mode substrate. Canvas projects this session rather than keeping its own weaker debug endpoint. Every swap and restart stays announced exactly as today.
options.technical: Keys act on the resident module and heap; t and f run the claim harness inside the session at the current tier. Attachment rides the session snapshot (generation, artifact token, persist). The canvas debug endpoint becomes a projection of the one session, removing the second stepper vocabulary. Key vocabulary is claimed here; future lenses extend it by ballot.
options.code:
$ jet dev app.jet
watching app.jet ... (Ctrl-C to stop)
✓ ran in 38 ms
  r re-run   R restart fresh   t tests   f failed claims   q quit
[t]
3 passed  (12 ms, warm)
[f]
no failed claims

options.name: Keys only
options.detail: The keystroke menu lands (`r R t f q`), but the REPL, debugger, and canvas keep their separate engines. Most of the daily win at a fraction of the work, and the engine duplication the audit found stays in place.
options.code:
$ jet dev app.jet
  r re-run   R restart fresh   t tests   f failed claims   q quit
[t]
3 passed  (12 ms, warm)

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: The session stays a save-watcher. Tests stay cold, the prompt and stepper stay separate, and the canvas keeps its sessionless debug endpoint.
options.code:
$ jet dev app.jet
watching app.jet ... (Ctrl-C to stop)
# t does nothing; Ctrl-C, then jet test, twelve cold seconds

comparisons.note: One verb, then in-session keystrokes: r reload, R restart, q quit. The loop living inside the process is the framework's signature feature.
comparisons.code: flutter run   # then: r / R / q

comparisons.note: Watch mode's interactive menu — f failures-only, t name filter, p path filter — is the part users praise most.
The whole system was the live session; the debugger was the editor. The power was real and so was the trap: state that drifted from source. Jet's session stays a cache over source files.
comparisons.code: "edit a method in a running image; proceed the halted frame"

recommendation.why: The session already exists and holds everything warm; the keys and attachments turn stored state into saved seconds on every edit. Unifying the engines also deletes the duplicate stepper and prompt paths the audit found, which is the model's whole point.

whyNot.reason: It keeps three engines for one program, so the canvas stepper and the REPL stay divergent and the duplication debt stays.
It leaves the warm session unable to do the one thing users want most while iterating: run the claims that just broke.

recommendation.tradeoff: Warm-session test runs execute on the dev tier. D-DEVMODE1 already demands tier output be identical, so this is safe by law, but any parity gap now shows up in test results too — which makes those gaps louder, not quieter. CI still runs cold and full.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the full session model, keys only, and the status quo. It recommended the full model because the session state already exists and the engines are already duplicated.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a client-server split: a session daemon that all verbs talk to, the language-server shape. Folded into A as an implementation detail, not a distinct surface.
reviewPasses.hybrid: B is the hybrid: keys without attachment. It stays on the menu as the honest smaller step, and A subsumes it cleanly if picked later.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option C was strengthened with its real virtue: no raw-mode terminal handling, no key vocabulary to teach, and panes compose fine for experts with two monitors.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack was state leaks between warm runs, the reused-worker trap; the repair is that t re-runs setup from source, R gives a guaranteed-cold path, and warm runs are labeled. The image-drift trap is fenced because the session is never the source of truth, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.comment: But use Title Case/Pascal Case

decisions.title: The recorder on user verbs — the Epoch 6 time-travel on-ramp
decisions.gist: Put --record on the verbs users hold and let jet debug replay the artifact, without building per-variable history.
decisions.lesson: Time travel is deferred to Epoch 6 (D-TIMETRAVEL1=C) behind two named prerequisites: the D-REPLAY1 replay harness, shipped, and a mature `jet debug`, carded. The capture format also exists — D-JREPLAY1=A ratified `.jetproof-replay` — but only `jet prove` can produce or consume it. Capability-gated effects make recording cheap: log the chokepoint, not syscalls. This ballot decides how much of the on-ramp lands now. It builds no reverse-step and no variable history, and the ratified capture preflight (E3625 refusals, E3627 consent) is untouched.
decisions.story: Diego has a property test that fails once in five hundred generated cases and never under a debugger. With the recorder he runs `jet test svc.jet --record=flaky`. The failing case lands in an artifact. `jet debug svc.jet --replay=flaky` steps that exact run through the ratified replay adapters, at his desk, as many times as he needs.
decisions.inWild:
# Today the capture format is ratified but lives only under jet prove:
$ jet test svc.jet --record=flaky     # no such flag
$ jet debug svc.jet --replay=flaky    # no such flag
# D-JREPLAY1 states both halves of the closure this ballot amends:
#   "no option creates `jet replay`, changes `jet run`"          (producer)
#   "consumption stays exactly `jet prove <target> --replay`"    (consumer)

options.name: --record= on run, dev, test; jet debug --replay=
options.detail: The recorder becomes an observer on the verbs users hold. `--record=NAME` writes the ratified `.jetproof-replay` artifact; `jet debug --replay=NAME` steps the recorded run through the ratified replay adapters. This amends two D-JREPLAY1=A clauses, both named here: the producer clause (no option changes `jet run`) and the consumer clause (consumption stays exactly `jet prove --replay`). Nothing else changes: not the format, the `=ARTIFACT` grammar, the E3625 refusals, or the E3627 consent rule. Refused programs stay refused; they are Epoch 6 scope. Reverse-step stays deferred per D-TIMETRAVEL1=C.
options.technical: Capture uses the ratified dev-tir-v1 and aot-native-v1 adapters and the closed frame-kind set. Replay grants zero ambient effects and uses the virtual clock, as ratified, honoring the recorded-adapter-first order. One format; jet prove --replay and jet debug --replay= are its two consumers.
options.code:
$ jet test svc.jet --record=flaky
$ jet debug svc.jet --replay=flaky
(jet) continue
paused at svc.jet:41 — the recorded run stops here
(jet) locals
queue_len: 4096   last_msg: "…"

options.name: jet debug --replay= only
options.detail: The debugger learns to step a recorded run, but capture stays under `jet prove --capture=`. Only the D-JREPLAY1 consumer clause is amended, and it is named here. The catch: the person with the flaky run must know the prove surface to make an artifact, so most recordings never happen.
options.code:
$ jet prove svc.jet --capture=flaky   # capture stays here
$ jet debug svc.jet --replay=flaky    # new: step the recording

options.name: Wait for Epoch 6
options.detail: Nothing lands now. Epoch 6 starts time travel from a design instead of a used recorder, and the debugger gains its replay muscle latest.
options.code: # status quo: .jetproof-replay reachable only via jet prove

comparisons.note: Records nondeterminism at the syscall boundary, then replays deterministically under gdb. Gold standard, but expensive because the OS boundary is wide. Jet's capability chokepoint is far narrower.
Got session replay nearly free because effects are data — the language design, not tooling, paid the cost. Jet's effect capabilities are the same lever.
comparisons.code: -- import/export of the full message history in the debugger

comparisons.note: Showed the real UX prize is asking new questions of an old run. That prize needs recordings users actually make, which needs capture on everyday verbs.
comparisons.code: record once, add print statements to the past run later

recommendation.why: The deferral names a shipped replay harness and a mature debugger as prerequisites; the harness shipped, and option A gives the maturing debugger its replay muscle plus artifacts in users' hands. Epoch 6 then starts from used recordings and real bug reports instead of a cold design. The capability chokepoint makes the cost small now.

whyNot.reason: Capture hidden behind the prove surface means the flaky-test user never records, so the on-ramp exists but goes unused.
It leaves the ratified format without a user-facing producer for another epoch and the debugger without its replay muscle.

recommendation.tradeoff: Recording effect frames can capture sensitive payloads (requests, file reads). The artifact stays local and opt-in per run, and the flag's docs must say plainly what is stored. That documentation duty is accepted.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared record-on-verbs, replay-only, and full deferral. It recommended record-on-verbs because the deferral's prerequisites are exactly what it ships.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested an always-on flight recorder (record the last N seconds by default). Rejected here: it changes the default run's cost and privacy posture, so it belongs to Epoch 6 with data, not to the on-ramp.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of A and B — record on debug and test but not run — was tested. It misses the headline user, the crashing long-running service under jet run, so it was folded out.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option C was strengthened: the run_gaps parity debt makes dev-tier replay weaker today, and waiting lets #1543 land first. That argument is real and is why A ships capture on AOT too via the ratified aot-native-v1 adapter.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack found the original story impossible: a long-running service reaches FS, tasks, and Net, which the ratified preflight refuses (E3625, E3627). The story was rebuilt on a recordable target, both amended D-JREPLAY1 clauses are now named, and the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Table-driven claims: .cases with an ambient case binding
decisions.gist: Add a .cases member so one test runs a table of inputs, each row reported on its own line.
decisions.lesson: Jet has nothing between one literal test and a full property generator. A person with five known input-output pairs today copies the test block five times or hand-rolls a loop that dies at the first failure and reports one line for all five. The surface-frequency audit watchlisted table-driven tests as a loved convention with no Jet equivalent. The member grammar is already ratified: D-DOTSCOPE1 says scope vocabulary grows by members, and each addition is an API decision. This ballot decides the shape of that member.
decisions.story: Ana tests a rounding function with six edge values. She writes one block with a `.cases` table and one assertion line. The run prints six lines, one per row; the negative-half row fails alone, named by its inputs, while the other five stay green. Without the member she would have six near-identical blocks or one loop that stops at the first bad row.

options.name: .cases with ambient case
options.detail: The member takes a list of records. The block body runs once per row with `case` bound ambiently — no lambda, no parameter, the same no-ceremony shape the ratified `err` binding uses in fallbacks. Each row reports as its own claim line, named by its fields, and fails alone. `.cases` composes with `.setup`, `.skip`, and `.measure` like any member.
options.technical: Rides D-DOTSCOPE1 (member spelling, typo teaching, completion) and the D-FAIL-BIND1 ambient-binding precedent. Row identity is the rendered field list; selection and shuffle treat each row as one claim. Under jet test --json every row is one D-REPORT-MACHINE1 report line.
options.code:
#Test("rounding") {
    .cases([
        .{ give: 1.5,  want: 2 },
        .{ give: 1.4,  want: 1 },
        .{ give: -1.5, want: -2 },
    ])
    require_eq(round(case.give), case.want)
}

$ jet test app.jet
rounding[give: 1.5]: pass
rounding[give: 1.4]: pass
rounding[give: -1.5]: FAIL …

options.name: .cases with a named parameter
options.detail: Same table, but the row binding is named by the author in the member head: `.cases(row, [...])`. Nothing is ambient, at the cost of one more word in every table and a second spelling question (what to name it) with no payoff beyond explicitness.

options.name: Decline — literals and generators only
options.detail: Keep the input axis as it is: literal blocks for single cases, typed-parameter property tests for many. Tables stay hand-rolled loops or copied blocks, and per-row reporting stays unavailable.

comparisons.note: Table-driven tests are the community's signature idiom, but they are hand-rolled: a slice, a loop, and t.Run per row for naming. Jet can ship the idiom without the boilerplate.
parametrize is the loved form: declarative rows over one test body, each row reported alone. Its weakness is stringly row ids; typed records fix that.
comparisons.code:
@pytest.mark.parametrize("give,want", [(1.5, 2), (1.4, 1)])
def test_round(give, want): assert round_(give) == want

recommendation.why: One member closes a watchlisted gap with zero new grammar: the member spelling, typo teaching, and completion are already ratified law. The ambient binding copies a shape the owner already picked for `err`. Per-row reporting is the whole value, and it falls out of rows being ordinary claims.

whyNot.reason: The named parameter adds a word to every table and a naming question to every author for no gain the ambient form lacks.
It keeps the copied-block and dead-loop patterns for the most common shape of real-world test, with no per-row failure reporting.

recommendation.tradeoff: An ambient name is one more implicit word inside `#Test` blocks. It is scoped to blocks that declare `.cases`, mirrors the ratified `err` precedent, and shadows nothing outside the block; that small implicitness is accepted.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the ambient binding, a named parameter, and declining. It recommended the ambient form because it matches the ratified err shape and keeps tables one line per row.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested generator-style tables (rows produced by an expression, not a literal list) and found the member already allows it — any list expression works — so no separate option was needed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid allowing both ambient and named forms was rejected: two spellings for one binding is the duplication disease this audit treats.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option C was strengthened: property tests plus literals do cover correctness eventually, and every added member grows the vocabulary a beginner meets. Option B carries the honest virtue of explicitness.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack asked whether ambient case collides with a user binding named case; it shadows only inside blocks that declare .cases, the containment the err precedent survived. Row identity under shuffle and filter was repaired by treating each row as one ordinary claim, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.comment: Named parameter should be OPTIONAL -> default name is case, providing a name as an arg overwrites the name so we can have the best of both worlds with beginner magic and expert control

decisions.title: List and tuple shapes join the test grammar
decisions.gist: Whether list and tuple shapes can stand in arm heads and `==` tests.
decisions.lesson: Arm heads and `==` tests know enum shapes, ranges, or-patterns, and string patterns, but not lists or tuples. Lists destructure only beside `::`, exact length only. This ballot adds list and tuple shapes to the test grammar, with a rest spelled `...rest`. Binds and loop heads change nothing. An earlier draft also rewrote binds; the adversarial syntax audit killed that half, and it is withdrawn.
decisions.story: Priya routes network frames. Empty, single, and longer frames take different paths. A list cannot stand in an arm head today, so she tests lengths by hand and indexes each element out. She wants the frame's shape on the page.

options.name: List and tuple shapes in tests, rest is three dots
options.detail: Arm heads and `==` tests accept list and tuple shapes. The rest capture is `...rest`, matching the three-dot capture convention the language already has. Two dots stays discard-only. Binds, loop heads, and the exact-length list bind are untouched, so nothing a beginner writes today changes.
options.technical: `...rest` follows the ratified three-dot capture family: `...xs` spread (D-VARIADIC1) and `{rest:...}` string-pattern tails (D-PARSESTR1, D-BINPAT1). Two-dot `..` stays discard-only (S74 struct binds, E0326/E0327). Amends the S68 arm-head grammar and D-DESTRUCT1's dispatch-arm list only. E0307 exhaustiveness gains list arms. Byte patterns already share the one engine and need no new rule.

options.name: Also rewrite binds (the withdrawn draft)
options.detail: The earlier scope: every pattern form also becomes legal on the left of `::`, so `[head, ...rest] :: queue ?? return` and string patterns as binds. The adversarial audit found statement-start collisions for the leading dot, quote, and bracket forms, and a backwards reading order the owner also rejected.
options.technical: Requires new statement-start dispatcher arms for `.`-leading, string-leading, and bracket-leading binds, colliding with D-DOTSCOPE1 scope-member statements and list literals. Kept on the menu because it was the ratified S74 direction generalized.
options.code:
[head, ...rest] :: queue ?? return
"v{major:Int}.{minor:Int}" :: version ?? return usage()

options.name: Keep the split
options.detail: No change. Lists stay bind-only and exact-length, and shape routing stays hand-written length tests with indexing. The promised S74 refutable bind still has zero code and still needs an answer somewhere.
options.technical: No grammar change. Card #1652 (S74 form unbuilt) stays open with no landing zone.

comparisons.note: Slice patterns with a named rest live in match arms; the rest is `..` there, but Rust has no three-dot spread to stay consistent with.
match brought list patterns with a starred rest, reusing the unpacking star — the same reuse-the-spread-glyph move as option A.
comparisons.code:
match queue:
    case []: idle()
    case [only]: single(only)
    case [head, *rest]: stream(head, rest)

recommendation.why: Shapes belong where tests happen, and the three-dot rest reuses the capture glyph the language already ratified twice. Nothing a beginner writes today changes.

whyNot.reason: The audit found real parser collisions at statement start and a reading order that puts the shape before the subject. Tests give the same power more clearly.
It keeps hand-written length tests and leaves the S74 promise with no landing zone.

recommendation.tradeoff: The test grammar grows while the bind grammar stays small, so the two are no longer mirror images. Accepted: the asymmetry is the point — `::` always succeeds, tests carry the shapes that can miss.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft added list and tuple shapes to both tests and binds with a two-dot rest. It recommended the full merge before the audit ran.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review checked byte patterns, string patterns, and spread for glyph consistency. It surfaced the two-dot versus three-dot split and moved the rest to `...rest`.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A staged hybrid, tests now and binds later, collapsed into option A once the audit showed binds gain nothing tests lack. The bind half is preserved as option B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned as the ratified S74 direction generalized, and its parser costs were written down rather than waved at. Option C gained the honest note that `.len()` tests already work.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The audit attacked statement starts, the `..` overload against ranges and spread, and garden paths at `[`. Option A survives because tests sit behind `==` where the grammar already parses patterns.

decisions.title: A search that finds nothing takes a written route
decisions.gist: What a value loop is worth when it ends without finding anything.
decisions.lesson: A search loop walks a source and breaks with the first hit. The ratified idiom (D-LOOPSTATE1) wraps the search in a labeled value loop and writes `break(label, Val(x))` and `break None` by hand. It works today and stays. This ballot decides whether a single finite loop can be the search directly: `break v` for the hit, and a mandatory fallback route for the found-nothing case. Nothing about the type is inferred silently.
decisions.story: Ana looks for the first admin in a user list. In Python she uses for-else and has to look up which way the else fires. In Jet she wants the fallback to read like every other fallback she writes.

options.name: Finite value loop with a mandatory route
options.detail: A finite loop in value position may exit with `break v`, and the `??` route is required, not optional. The loop's type is the break value's type, and the written route answers exhaustion — so the reader never infers what running out means. The routes `next` and `break` are illegal right after the loop's closing brace, because they would read as controlling the loop that just closed; the labeled idiom covers those cases.
options.technical: In value position, a finite-source braced loop whose exits are `break v` types as V, and the statement is legal only with a `??` route answering exhaustion. Narrows S23/E0075: the payload-break rejection keeps applying to yielding (arrow) loops, so the bindingless arrow forms (D-LOOP-SUBJECT1, D-LOOP-STMT-ARROW1) cannot host `break v` and are unchanged. `?? next` and `?? break` are rejected immediately after the loop's `}` with a diagnostic naming the labeled form. D-LOOPSTATE1's labeled idiom stays untouched.

options.name: A loop else block
options.detail: Python's answer: an else block on the loop that runs when no break fired. It reads like the body's sibling, but it is a new construct, its firing rule famously confuses readers, and the found value still needs a binding that escapes the block.
options.technical: A new grammar production on `loop`. The else block cannot hand a value to a surrounding binding without further scoping rules, so the flag pattern often returns anyway.

options.name: Keep the labeled idiom only
options.detail: No change. D-LOOPSTATE1's labeled loop with `Val` and `None` written by hand stays the one spelling. Everything is explicit, and the simple one-source search pays two extra loop lines and a label for it.
options.technical: No change. The teaching gap is docs and one example file.

comparisons.note: for-else is the construct option B copies. Even its fans look up the firing rule.
Iterator::find returns Option, and the miss is handled by the caller — the same shape as option A's mandatory route, but only on iterator chains.

recommendation.why: The search gets one obvious spelling whose miss is written on the same statement, and the mandatory route means the type story has no silent inference in it.

whyNot.reason: A new construct with a memorized firing rule, doing what `??` already does, and its block still cannot hand back the found value.
It taxes the most common search with a wrapper loop, a label, and hand-written `Val` and `None` for no added safety.

recommendation.tradeoff: The route can sit far from the subject when the body is long. Accepted: the route is mandatory, so the reader always knows to look for it, and the labeled idiom remains for anything more complex.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft typed the loop as optional with an optional route. The revision made the route mandatory so exhaustion is always answered in writing.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a result-typed search loop and a find method. The method exists either way as a library line, and fallible break values already unify, so neither changed the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of A and C is the design itself: the labeled idiom stays for nested searches, and A covers the single-source case. Recorded on both options.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned with its block-sibling readability and honest scoping notes. Option C gained its strongest case: everything on the page, nothing new to teach.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The audit attacked the type-at-a-distance inference, the comprehension look-alike, and the skip route grabbing the wrong loop. The repairs are in option A: mandatory route, arrow forms unchanged, and the two control routes rejected after the brace.

decisions.title: Multi-head functions: one coverage proof, and how far to unify
decisions.gist: Which proof checks a multi-head function, and whether its surface becomes table sugar.
decisions.lesson: S83 lets one function name carry several heads, dispatched by argument shape. The `if` table does the same elimination, and the isomorphic audit asked twice for this ballot. The adversarial audit added a blocker the first draft missed: S83 heads are a second pattern dialect. They use bare names where arm heads require a leading dot (D-ENUMDOT1), plus typed sub-bindings no arm head has. So the safe unification today is the proof, and the surface desugar is a follow-up with the dialect question named.
decisions.story: Marco publishes a geometry package. Multi-heads make his API docs read one case per line, and he likes that. His reviewer asks which error fires when a new Shape variant leaves a hole, and the answer is a second rule beside E0307, with its own copy to learn.

options.name: One proof now, surface later
options.detail: Coverage and overlap of multi-heads are checked by the table's proofs: E0307 for a hole, the unreachable-arm lint for a shadowed head. One error copy instead of two. The surface stays exactly as it is. Whether it later becomes literal table sugar is a named follow-up, which must first reconcile the head dialect with the leading-dot law and the declined parameter destructuring.
options.technical: Sema routes S83 coverage through the table's exhaustiveness engine; declaration order becomes arm order for the overlap lint, which makes head order meaningful and is said out loud in the diagnostic. The E0307 message gains a multi-head variant so it never points at a brace the user did not write. The dialect questions (bare heads vs D-ENUMDOT1, typed sub-bindings vs D-PAT6) are explicitly out of scope and named for the follow-up.

options.name: Full desugar now
options.detail: Define the form as table sugar immediately. This forces the dialect answer in the same ruling: heads either gain leading dots and lose typed sub-bindings, or the desugar quietly blesses a second pattern dialect. It also turns unordered dispatch into ordered first-fit in one step, which can change meaning where group heads overlap.
options.technical: Heads desugar in declaration order to arms over a synthesized subject. Requires ruling the head dialect against D-ENUMDOT1 and D-PAT6 now, inventing a subject for heads over unrelated types, and defining multi-parameter heads as tuple subjects.

options.name: Keep it fully separate
options.detail: No change. Multi-heads keep their own dispatch and coverage rules beside the table's. Two elimination mechanisms stay in the language, with two proofs to teach, document, and keep aligned.
options.technical: S83 stands as its own mechanism with its own exhaustiveness rule and diagnostics.
options.code:
fn area(Circle(r: Float)) => Float = 3.14 * r * r
// checked by S83's rule; the table's E0307 never sees it

options.name: Retire multi-heads
options.detail: One spelling remains: write the table. The mechanism count drops the most, but API surfaces lose the one-case-per-line signature style, and every existing multi-head migrates for a win the proof unification already delivers.
options.technical: S83 is retired with a teaching diagnostic and a formatter rewrite to the table form.

comparisons.note: Function equations are defined as sugar for one case expression — the end state option D wants, reached only because the two spellings share one pattern dialect.
comparisons.code:
area (Circle r) = 3.14 * r * r
area (Rect w h) = w * h

comparisons.note: Multi-clause functions are one of the community's best-loved surfaces, and clause order is meaningful there — the ordered-dispatch model option A's lint adopts.
comparisons.code:
def area({:circle, r}), do: 3.14 * r * r
def area({:rect, w, h}), do: w * h

recommendation.why: It delivers the whole user-visible win — one coverage proof, one error copy — without ruling the dialect question in a hurry or blessing a second pattern dialect by accident.

whyNot.reason: It forces the dialect and subject-synthesis questions in one ruling, and silently converts unordered dispatch to ordered first-fit where group heads can shadow.
Two proofs for one idea is the fragmentation this audit exists to remove.
It pays the biggest migration to delete a surface the proof unification already tames.

recommendation.tradeoff: Declaration order becomes meaningful for the overlap lint before the surface is formally sugar. Accepted: the lint says so in its message, and the follow-up ballot settles the surface with the dialect on the table.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft recommended full sugar. The adversarial audit surfaced the second pattern dialect and the ordered-dispatch change, and the recommendation moved to the proof-only scope.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested restricting multi-heads to public API files. That is a style lint under any outcome and folded out of the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The proof-now, surface-later shape is itself the hybrid of full sugar and full separation. Option D preserves the original full-sugar path as a real menu entry.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option D was steelmanned with the Haskell precedent and its honest prerequisites written down. Options B and C gained their strongest cases: independence and the smallest language.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack: the proof move alone might still change meaning where heads overlap. The repair is the ordered-overlap lint that names head order in its message, and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Single-line function bodies: = or ::
decisions.gist: Which symbol attaches a one-line body to a function.
decisions.lesson: A concise function is `fn area(r: Float) => Float = 3.14 * r * r` (D-ARROW-CONTROL1). Definitions elsewhere are moving to `::`: aliases (D-ALIAS-OP1) and module instantiation (D-CONF-GENSPELL1) both made the switch. The owner asked whether the function body should move too, since the line binds a name to its logic. The split under test: `::` defines a thing; `=` fills a slot inside a thing being defined — defaults, discriminants, reassignment.
decisions.story: User reads three one-line definitions in a row: an alias with `::`, a module with `::`, a function with `=`. The function is the odd one out, and he has to remember why.
decisions.inWild:
alias Parsed<T> :: T ? AppError            // ratified, D-ALIAS-OP1
module int_cache :: cache<Int>(64)         // ratified, D-CONF-GENSPELL1
fn area(r: Float) => Float = 3.14 * r * r  // today, D-ARROW-CONTROL1

options.name: :: defines, = fills
options.detail: The one-line body binds with `::`, matching every other one-line definition. The rule becomes teachable in one sentence: defining a named thing uses `::`, filling a slot inside a definition uses `=`. Reassignment, parameter defaults, field defaults, and enum discriminants are slot-fills and keep `=`. Every existing single-line function migrates by formatter.
options.technical: Amends D-ARROW-CONTROL1=A. S83 multi-heads move with it (`fn area(Circle(r: Float)) => Float :: 3.14 * r * r`). Unchanged `=` sites: reassignment (S2), parameter defaults (S61/D-NARG1), field defaults (D-FIELDDEF1=C), enum discriminants (D-META-CONST1=A), index write (S39/D-API-STORE1). The parser is unambiguous: after a return type, `::` can only open a body. Named honestly: D-ALIAS-OP1's rejected option kept the fn `=` on purpose, and ratifying this overrides that recorded reasoning.

options.name: Keep =
options.detail: No change. The body keeps `=`, the spelling D-ALIAS-OP1's own reasoning chose to preserve when aliases moved. The cost is the story above: three one-line definitions, two symbols, and a rule that only history explains.
options.technical: No change. D-ALIAS-OP1's rejected-option text stands as the recorded rationale: the alias move was argued precisely so the fn body `=` could stay.
options.code: fn area(r: Float) => Float = 3.14 * r * r

options.name: Retire the single-line form
options.detail: Braces only: every function body is a block. The symbol question disappears, and every concise helper pays two braces and a line for it. The measured corpus is full of one-line helpers, so this taxes the common case to dodge a one-token choice.
options.technical: D-ARROW-CONTROL1's `= expression` production is removed; formatter rewrites to braces.

comparisons.note: Every definition uses `=`, uniformly — the opposite consistency. The lesson is that one symbol for definition reads well; which symbol matters less than using it everywhere.
Expression bodies use `=` while properties use `=` too, but locals use different keywords — a mixed record that never settled a define-versus-fill split.
comparisons.code: fun area(r: Double): Double = 3.14 * r * r

recommendation.why: One reading for every one-line definition: name, shape, `::`, meaning. The fill-sites keep `=`, so the split is one teachable sentence instead of a history lesson.

whyNot.reason: It preserves the last definition still spelled `=`, and the reason it survived was an argument about aliases, not about functions.
It deletes a loved concise form and taxes every small helper to avoid answering a one-token question.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every existing single-line function migrates, and D-ALIAS-OP1's recorded rationale is overridden by name. Accepted: the formatter does the whole migration, and the overridden reasoning is quoted here rather than silently dropped.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the `::` body, keeping `=`, and braces-only, and recommended `::` for the define-versus-fill split the ratified alias and module moves already started.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested dropping the operator entirely and reusing the arm arrow for bodies. Both collide with existing grammar or overload an arm token, so both folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid — `::` for functions, `=` elsewhere — is option A itself, since defaults and discriminants are slot-fills by the stated law. No separate entry needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned with D-ALIAS-OP1's own recorded reasoning, quoted rather than paraphrased. Option C gained the honest note that it ends the symbol debate permanently.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack: migration churn across every example and golden, plus overriding a recorded rationale. Both costs are named in the tradeoff, the formatter owns the churn, and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The statement test-bind: subject == pattern ?? route
decisions.gist: How one line tests a shape, binds its names, and exits on the miss.
decisions.lesson: S31 already lets `==` test a pattern and bind names inside an `if` head. In statement position that power is missing, so breaking down a result costs an arm table even when the miss should simply leave. This ballot makes the statement form law: subject first, the test spelled `==`, the miss answered by a written `??` route that must leave. It replaces S74's pattern-left refutable bind, which is ratified but has zero code.
decisions.story: Kofi validates a request: parse the id, load the record, serve it. Each step is one test and one exit. Today each test is an arm table, and the happy path drifts one indent to the right per check.

options.name: Test, then a route that must leave
options.detail: The statement reads left to right: the subject, the shape it should have, and the written answer for the miss. The route must leave the surrounding flow, which is exactly why the bound names are safe afterward. Inside a loop, `?? next` is the skip, written out loud. A test with no route binds nothing.
options.technical:
The grammar already parses this shape: `==` builds a pattern test at any expression site, and the fallback operator wraps it at the loosest rung. New written law: the route must diverge (`return`, `break`, `next`, `panic`). A value route is illegal because the bound names would be unproven. Names survive the statement only when the route is present. E0405 gains one named exception: a pattern-test left side with a diverging route. A plain value test (`x == 5` with a route) is legal and binds nothing.

Amends S31 (binding scope extends past the statement when the route diverges), S74 (the unbuilt pattern-left form is retired; card #1652 re-points here), and D-FAIL-BIND1. Ambient `err` reaches these routes only when the missed subject carried a failure value, as in an `.Ok` test over a fallible type. A pure shape miss has no `err`, and using it is a compile error that says why. Byte patterns ride the same engine.
options.code:
parse_id(raw) == .Ok(id) ?? return reject(err.message)
load(id) == .Ok(rec) ?? return reject(err.message)
serve(rec)

version == "v{major:Int}.{minor:Int}" ?? return usage()
use(major, minor)

loop r, readings {
    r == .Ok(reading) ?? next
    record(reading)
}

options.name: Keep S74's pattern-left bind
options.detail: Build the ratified spelling as written: the pattern sits left of `::` and the route follows. The adversarial audit found three problems. The shape before the subject reads backwards, the failure is invisible until the route, and the leading dot, quote, and bracket forms collide with shipped statement grammar.
options.technical: Requires new statement-start dispatcher arms ordered before the scope-member statement (D-DOTSCOPE1) and string-literal statements. This is the S74 text made real, unchanged.
options.code:
Val(n) :: maybe_port() ?? return
