.Ok(rec) :: load(id) ?? return reject(err.message)

options.name: Arm tables only
options.detail: No statement form. Every shape test stays a table, which is always explicit and always exhaustive-checked. The cost is the rightward drift in the story above, multiplied by every check in every validation path.
options.technical: No change. Card #1652 closes as will-not-build with an S74 amendment retiring the promised form.

comparisons.note: guard-let is the closest precedent for option A: the test is announced, the else block must leave, and the bound name survives because it did.
comparisons.code:
guard let id = parseId(raw) else { return reject() }
serve(load(id))

comparisons.note: let-else gives the same guarantee with the pattern on the left — the order option B uses and the audit rejected for Jet.

recommendation.why: It is the S31 test everyone already reads, allowed to stand alone, with the miss written on the line. Subject first, spoken left to right, and the grammar parses it today.

whyNot.reason: The shape arrives before the subject, the failure is invisible, and the leading-token forms collide with shipped statement grammar.
It keeps the rightward drift that makes validation code hard to read, which is the whole cost this ballot exists to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: `==` now sometimes binds in statement position, and `??` accepts one non-fallible left side. Accepted: both powers are announced by visible tokens on the same line, and the diverging-route law keeps every surviving binding proven.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the statement test-bind, the S74 pattern-left form, and tables-only, recommending the test-bind for its reading order and zero new parse rules.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a dedicated try-bind sigil and a keyword form. The sigil fixed nothing about ordering and added a fourth bind operator, so both folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid keeping S74's spelling for enum shapes only would run two orders for one construct. It was dropped as the exact disease this slate treats.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned as the ratified text made real, with its parser costs written down. Option C gained the honest note that tables stay canonical for two-sided handling.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The audit attacked `Bool` left sides, the plain value test, and binding scope. The repairs are written law: diverging routes only, no route means no binding, and the E0405 exception is named.

decisions.title: One crossing law for every value that enters Jet
decisions.gist: One law for every value that enters Jet from outside.
decisions.lesson: Jet checks foreign values in five separate ways: typed literals, wire decode, foreign calls, manifests, and dependency bytes. Each was ratified alone and stops at its own border. This choice decides whether the spec states one shared law: every crossing names its schema, and every crossing leaves a fact. With the law, a future boundary feature must land in a named cell of one grid instead of minting a sixth mechanism.
decisions.story: Priya builds a payments service in Jet. In one week she asks three questions: where should AVRO support live, how do I trust this new dependency, and why does a Java call skip the rollback check. Today each question has a different owner, a different answer shape, and no shared rule to appeal to.

options.name: Adopt the law and the grid as spec law
options.detail: The spec gains one section: a crossing happens at comptime, build, link, or run time, and every crossing must name its schema and leave its fact. New boundary features must name their cell. Existing ratified rules become recorded instances of the law. Gain: one place to reason about every boundary. Loss: a new feature that fits no cell needs an owner ruling first.
options.technical: Grid rows: comptime (literal), build (manifest, dependency), link (foreign signature), run (wire data). Columns: schema named by, checked by, evolves by, fact left. Recorded instances: D-UNIFYLIT1, D-VALIDATE-DECODE1, D-MIGRATE1, D-FACT-FLOW1/HOME1, D-JPK-TRUSTROOT1, E0119, E1204.

options.name: Keep five per-plane laws
options.detail: Each area keeps its own rules and evolves alone. Gain: no shared constraint to maintain. Loss: the divergence bill keeps growing. The audit found six hand-rolled JSON escapers, a duplicate JSON parser, and a transaction law that trusts every foreign runtime — each grew in a gap between two planes.
options.code:
// Status quo. The next format, binder, or taint feature
// picks its own shape, and the audit table gains a row.

options.name: Record the grid as guidance only
options.detail: The grid goes in the docs as advice, not law. Gain: zero constraint on future work. Loss: guidance without force is how the current drift happened — every divergent mechanism in the audit was written next to a ratified rule that already covered the job.
options.code:
// docs/spec gains an informative section.
// A feature may still ship outside the grid without an owner ruling.

comparisons.note: WIT is one typed contract for every boundary; both sides are generated from it. It is the closest shipped version of one crossing law, but scoped to wasm only.
comparisons.code:
// WIT
record repo { name: string, stars: u32 }

comparisons.note: CUE unifies types, values, and validation into one operation, but never reaches FFI or provenance. It proves one law is possible and that stopping halfway caps the value.

recommendation.why: The law is one sentence, and every ratified boundary rule is already an instance of it. Adopting it converts future boundary design from open debate into a cell lookup, the same way I8 works for mechanisms.

whyNot.reason: The five planes drifted already; the audit table is the bill. Keeping them separate keeps paying it.
Guidance without force produced the six JSON escapers and the duplicate parser. Advice does not stop a sixth mechanism; law does.

recommendation.tradeoff: A genuinely novel boundary feature that fits no cell must wait for an owner ruling before it ships. That is accepted: a crossing the grid cannot name is exactly the case the owner should see first.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared adopting the law, keeping per-plane laws, and guidance-only, and recommended adoption because every ratified rule already instances the law.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a fourth option, adopting the law per-plane over time. It folded into A because staged adoption is A's implementation plan, not a different end state.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested law-plus-guidance: binding for new work, advisory for shipped code. That is what A already is — shipped divergence is defect cards, not violations — so no new option emerged.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B: independent planes can move faster without cross-plane review. That speed is real and is how the six escapers shipped.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with a feature that fits no cell: a capability handle crossing a process boundary. The grid names it (run-time crossing, schema = handle type, fact = authority), so A survived and the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Typed heads for URL, Path, and DateTime literals
decisions.gist: Compile-time checked literals for URLs, paths, and datetimes.
decisions.lesson: A typed head like SQL.{"…"} checks its text at compile time and encodes each interpolation hole safely. SQL, HTML, Sh, Regex, and byte patterns have heads today. URL, Path, and DateTime literals do not: the writer parses them at run time and unwraps a Result on text the compiler could have read. This choice decides whether those three domains join the head row, with the same hole law the other heads follow.
decisions.story: Marco writes his first Jet service. He types url.parse("https:/api.example.com") ?? panic("bad url") — one slash short. The compiler says nothing. The panic fires on the first request in production, hours after the typo was on his screen.

options.name: URL, Path, and DateTime heads with the shared hole law
options.detail: URL.{"…"}, Path.{"…"}, and DateTime.{"…"} join the head row. A bad literal is a compile error, and the value needs no Result unwrap. Holes follow the head law each head already teaches: a URL hole percent-encodes, a Path hole is one component so ".." cannot climb, a DateTime head takes no holes. Runtime strings keep the existing parse constructors unchanged.
options.technical: Rides D-UNIFYLIT1 (typed head only), D-DOTCTOR3 (universal head), and D-CORE-PATH1 (#1577 Path type; strings stay accepted everywhere). Validation runs in sema like E0152 does for Regex. No amendment to any ratified decision.
options.code:
base :: URL.{"https://api.example.com/v2"}     // typo => compile error
log  :: Path.{"/var/log/{service}.log"}         // hole = ONE component
t0   :: DateTime.{"2026-08-07T12:00:00Z"}

user :: "ada/../etc"
p :: Path.{"/data/{user}.json"}   // hole encoded: no path escape

options.name: URL head only
options.detail: Only URL joins the row now; Path and DateTime wait. Gain: the highest-injury case ships first. Loss: the head row stays uneven, and Path literals — the second most common checked-text domain in real programs — keep the runtime ceremony for no stated reason.
options.code:
base :: URL.{"https://api.example.com/v2"}
log  :: path.parse("/var/log/app.log") ?? panic("bad path")  // still ceremony

options.name: Keep runtime parsing for all three
options.detail: Status quo. Gain: nothing changes. Loss: the language checks literal SQL at compile time but not a literal URL, and no principle explains where that line sits.
options.code: base :: url.parse("https://api.example.com/v2") ?? panic("bad url")

comparisons.note: Library interpolators like uri"…" validate at compile time via macros. The value is proven; the cost there is macro authorship, which Jet's head rail already paid.

recommendation.why: The head mechanism exists, the hole law generalizes cleanly to all three domains, and each new head deletes a panic-unwrap from the beginner path. One change closes the whole row.

whyNot.reason: Shipping one head leaves the row uneven and re-opens this decision twice. The Path hole law also carries real safety: one-component holes end path traversal by construction.
Compile-time knowledge checked at run time with a panic is the exact ceremony D-UNIFYLIT1 removed for SQL and HTML.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three more head grammars live in sema and must match the runtime parsers exactly. That is accepted: the grammars already exist in core.url and friends, and I9 parity tests pin them together.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the full row, URL-only, and status quo, and recommended the full row because the mechanism and the hole law already exist.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested more heads: Email, UUID, SemVer, MIME. They folded out: this ballot stays at the three domains with shipped runtime parsers, and D-BOUND-SINK1 opens the rest to libraries.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested heads that return Result instead of failing the compile. That weakens the point — the literal is known now — so the options stayed as drafted.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: runtime-only parsing keeps one code path for literals and dynamic strings. The uniformity is real and costs a production panic per typo.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with dynamic-looking literals: a URL assembled across lines and a Path with a hole per segment. Both fall to the existing rule — heads take literals, runtime strings take constructors — so A survived.

decisions.title: Typed head bodies own their escapes
decisions.gist: Backslashes inside a typed head are literal text.
decisions.lesson: Jet's plain-string escape table has four entries and runs before a typed head ever sees its text. So the checked pattern Regex.{"\d+"} is a lex error, and the writer must type \\d. The head then validates a pattern the writer never wrote. This choice decides who owns escapes inside a head body: the plain-string table, or the head's own grammar. It amends only the D-UNIFYLIT1 head-body lexing; plain strings are untouched either way.
decisions.story: Ana ports a log filter to Jet. She types Regex.{"(\d+)-(\d+)"} straight from the old code and gets E0001 on the first backslash. She doubles every one, the pattern still reads wrong a week later, and she files the bug the audit found waiting.

options.name: Head bodies are raw: the head grammar owns every escape
options.detail: Inside Type.{"…"}, a backslash is a literal character, and the closing quote keeps today's rule. This ballot changes backslash handling only. Brace lexing is untouched, and each head's hole policy stays its own ratified law — Regex keeps refusing interpolation entirely (D-REGEX-LIT1, E0152), named here so nothing shifts silently. Gain: checked text is typed once, correctly. Loss: a head body can no longer use \n to mean newline; multiline head text uses the """ form.
options.technical: Amends D-UNIFYLIT1's body lexing: the ESCAPES table (Syntax/math_layout.rs:318) stops applying inside head bodies. Hole lexing and per-head hole policy (D-REGEX-LIT1/E0152 for Regex) are explicitly untouched. E0152-style validation is unchanged and now sees the written text verbatim. Plain "…" and '…' keep the 4-entry table.
options.code:
digits :: Regex.{"(\d+)-(\d+)"}      // reads as written
win    :: Path.{"C:\logs\app.txt"}   // no doubling (Path head is D-BOUND-HEAD1)
cmd    :: Sh.{"grep -E \d+ {file}"}  // pattern survives intact
// Brace lexing and hole policy: unchanged by this ballot.

options.name: Add a raw-string spelling for all strings
options.detail: A general raw literal such as r"…" joins the language, usable anywhere. Gain: raw text everywhere, not only in heads. Loss: a second string spelling for every string, when the pain lives only where text is checked — and D-UNIFYLIT1 just spent a ballot deleting extra literal spellings.
options.code:
digits :: Regex.{r"(\d+)-(\d+)"}    // two spellings compose now
note   :: r"C:\logs"                 // raw strings leak into all prose text

options.name: Status quo: the plain table applies inside heads
options.detail: Nothing changes. Gain: one lexing rule for all quoted text. Loss: every checked pattern with a backslash is written doubled, which is exactly the class of silent transcription error typed heads exist to end.
options.code: digits :: Regex.{"(\\d+)-(\\d+)"}   // forever

comparisons.note: Raw string literals ("""…""") were added mainly so regex and JSON could be pasted verbatim; the demand came from checked text, not prose.
Tagged templates give the tag the raw segments (String.raw) precisely because the tag, not the string rules, knows what a backslash means.

recommendation.why: The head already owns validation of its body; owning the escapes is the same principle finished. Checked text reads as written, and no new spelling enters the language.

whyNot.reason: It solves head pain by adding a language-wide spelling, the exact move D-UNIFYLIT1 reversed. Raw prose strings have no demonstrated need in the corpus.
Doubled backslashes in compile-checked patterns are transcription errors waiting to validate — the pattern checked is not the pattern the writer read.

recommendation.tradeoff: Head bodies lose \n and \t as spellings for control characters. That is accepted: multiline head text has the """ form, and a literal tab in checked text is rare enough to write in the runtime constructor.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared head-owned escapes, a general raw string, and status quo, and recommended head-owned escapes as the smallest change that ends double-escaping.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-head opt-in (each head declares raw or cooked) and a lexer flag. Both folded into A: no shipped head wants cooked bodies, so the choice would be dead weight.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested A plus B together. B adds nothing A does not already give inside heads, and its whole surface lies outside them, so the hybrid dissolved.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: one escape rule for every quoted region is genuinely easier to teach. It still makes the checked pattern differ from the written one.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with a literal close-quote in a head body and with brace-heavy regex text. Quotes keep today's rule, and the ballot was narrowed to backslash handling only — brace lexing and Regex's no-interpolation law (D-REGEX-LIT1) are named untouched, so A survived.

decisions.title: Libraries declare their own checked text types
decisions.gist: A library can declare a checked text type like SQL has.
decisions.lesson: The typed-head list is closed: SQL, HTML, Sh, Regex, and byte patterns, all stdlib-owned. A library that handles CSS selectors or GraphQL gets plain String — no compile check, no safe holes. D-META-DSL1 ratified library-declared block languages on the marker rail, still unbuilt. This choice decides whether that rail also opens text heads, and how a function demands checked text. One prior note diverges: the 2026-07-28 audit's F9 recorded types, not markers, for user heads; both shapes are on this ballot.
decisions.story: Rosa maintains Jet's most-used CSS library. Users hand her selectors as String, and the top three bug reports are malformed selectors that a compile check would have caught. She reads the SQL head source, finds the list is closed, and files the feature request this ballot answers.

options.name: Open text heads on the ratified marker rail
options.detail: The marker rail D-META-DSL1 ratified for blocks gains a text target: a library declares a head with a comptime check and a hole encoder. Users then write Selector.{"…"} exactly like SQL.{"…"}. A sink needs no registry — a function that takes Selector is a sink, because only the checked head or an audited .raw() can construct one. Gain: every text domain gets the SQL treatment, and the planned sink-registration mechanism is deleted, not built.
options.technical: Extends D-META-DSL1 from [.Block] to [.Text] on the same marker grammar. check runs at comptime over $body; hole names the encoder each interpolation passes through. Construction rails, .raw() audit gate, and E0149 behavior copy the shipped TypedText law verbatim.

options.name: A dedicated text type declaration form
options.detail: A new declaration form, for example text type Selector { … }, owns checked text separately from markers. This is the shape the F9 audit note recorded: a library-declared distinct String type with a comptime validator — types, not markers. Gain: a head is an ordinary nameable type, and the declaration reads as one. Loss: a second declaration mechanism beside the marker rail that D-META-DSL1 later ratified for the sibling job, which I8 counts as duplication.

options.name: Keep the head list closed to the stdlib
options.detail: Status quo. Gain: every head is stdlib-audited. Loss: user domains keep plain String forever, and the safety story of typed text stops at the five domains the stdlib happened to ship.
options.code: fn select(root: Node, pattern: String) => [Node]   // forever

comparisons.note: Any library can define an interpolator (sql"", css""), and the good ones validate at compile time via macros. Adoption proved the demand; macro authorship difficulty capped it. Jet's marker rail is the pre-paid version of that cost.
PEP 750 t-strings exist because f-strings gave libraries no interception point. The fix was structural: hand the library the segments and holes. Jet's head law is already that structure.

recommendation.why: One ratified rail gains one target and the whole text-domain space opens. Sinks fall out of the type system for free, so a planned mechanism dies instead of being built.

whyNot.reason: B is the F9 note's recorded shape, and it still loses here. D-META-DSL1 ratified the marker rail for declaring a language after that note, so B would be a second declaration form beside a ratified one. Every text-only feature B could grow fits the marker body too.
It caps typed text at five stdlib domains. The injection class this mechanism kills does not stop at the stdlib's domains.

recommendation.tradeoff: A badly written library check can reject valid text or pass bad text, and the compile error carries the library's name, not the stdlib's. That is accepted: it is the same trust users already extend to a library's runtime validation, moved earlier.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the marker rail, a dedicated declaration form, and the closed list, and recommended the marker rail because D-META-DSL1 already ratified it for blocks.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested derive-based heads on Codable and capability-scoped heads that only the declaring package may use. Both folded into A as marker-body details, not distinct end states.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested A with B's named-method surface inside the marker body. The marker grammar already names check and hole, so the hybrid was A restated.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B with its true provenance: the F9 audit note recorded types-not-markers as the direction, and B is that shape done honestly. It also strengthened C: stdlib-only heads audit to one standard, which is real and is why Rosa's users file selector bugs.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with a malicious head whose check passes everything and whose hole encodes nothing. The .raw() parity rule repairs it: an identity hole is spelled .raw() and lands in the audit ledger, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Boundary values carry an origin fact until a typed decode clears it
decisions.gist: Outside data is marked at entry; decoding it into a type clears the mark.
decisions.lesson: The ratified fact plane gives Jet one flow store where taint spreads silently and one gate word, #Scrub, where it clears. Nothing yet says who writes the first taint fact or what clears it without ceremony. This choice decides both: boundary functions seed an origin fact, and a successful typed decode clears it, because a value that just proved a schema cannot be raw attacker text. Only the audited raw escapes then refuse origin-marked strings.
decisions.story: Leo demos his first Jet web app. Short on time, he passes the request body straight into SQL.raw to skip the head. Nothing warns him. The demo works, ships, and becomes the injection postmortem — the one class of bug every taint system in history was invented to stop.
decisions.inWild:
body :: net.get(endpoint)?          // attacker-shaped text, unmarked today
q :: SQL.raw(body)                   // compiles: the audited escape trusts anyone
db.run(q)?

options.name: Seed at the boundary, clear on decode, gate at raw
options.detail: net.*, fs.read*, env.*, process output, and FFI marshalling mark what they return with an origin fact. The fact spreads silently, free of ceremony, as the fact law already rules. json.decode<T> and every typed construction clear it — the schema check is the laundering. SQL.raw, HTML.raw, and Sh.raw on an origin-marked string become a compile error naming the flow path. Beginners type nothing new; the unsafe demo path is the only path that changes.
options.technical: Instances D-FACT-FLOW1 (taint shares the one flow store) and D-FACT-HOME1 (origin rows in the registry). Clearing rides D-VALIDATE-DECODE1: a decode that returns Ok constructs a value garbage could not build. #Scrub (D-TAG-SURFACE1) stays the word for hand-written sanitizers. jet inspect gates lists every raw site and scrub. One typed-settings row on the D-CONF rail refuses seeding project-wide — proposed spelling settings: { origin_facts: off }; the final key is the owner's.

options.name: Opt-in per project
options.detail: Everything in A, but seeding starts off and a settings row turns it on. Gain: zero behavior change for existing code. Loss: the writer who most needs it — the beginner pasting request bodies into raw — is exactly the writer who never turns a safety setting on.
options.code:
// pkg.jet
settings: { origin_facts: on }   // Leo never writes this line

options.name: No origin facts
options.detail: Status quo. The taint plane stays ratified and empty: #Scrub exists, nothing seeds what it would clear. Gain: nothing to tune. Loss: the one bug class typed heads cannot catch alone — trusted-looking text handed to an audited escape — stays open, and the fact ledger stays a ledger of nothing.
options.code: q :: SQL.raw(body)   // compiles forever

comparisons.note: Taint mode died because laundering was a regex touch, not a proof — any match cleared the mark. Clearing on typed decode is the repaired version: only a real schema check launders.
$SAFE levels were removed in Ruby 3.0: runtime flags with propagation gaps were unenforceable. Compile-time flow facts on one ratified store avoid both failure causes.

recommendation.why: It connects two planes the owner already ratified — taint flow and typed decode — and the connection is the parse-do-not-validate lesson: laundering must construct a value garbage could not build. The beginner path gains safety and zero ceremony; only raw escapes tighten.

whyNot.reason: A safety default that ships off protects the people who least need protecting. Leo never finds the setting.
It leaves the ratified taint plane as an empty ledger and the raw escapes as unaudited injection doors.

recommendation.tradeoff: Code that intentionally forwards raw external text — a proxy, a log shipper — must decode to bytes, match, or carry #Scrub once at the sanitizer. That is accepted: those are exactly the sites an auditor wants named in the gate ledger.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared default-on seeding, opt-in, and status quo, and recommended default-on because decode-clears makes the safe path the zero-ceremony path.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-root granularity (net on, fs off) and runtime taint. Granularity folded into A's settings row; runtime taint was dropped — it is the mechanism that failed twice elsewhere.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested A seeded only for net. The flow store makes extra roots free, and fs and env text reach the same sinks, so narrowing bought nothing and the full seed set stayed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: zero facts means zero false positives, and typed heads already stop naive interpolation. True — and the raw escapes remain open doors, which is the story's exact bug.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with false positives: a config value from env.get used in Sh.raw for a trusted script. The repair is one #Scrub on the loader or decoding to a typed setting, both one line, and the flow-path error names them; the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Published schemas keep unknown fields across a round trip
decisions.gist: A wire-stable type keeps fields it does not recognize.
decisions.lesson: #PublishedSchema types have a migration chain: old data decodes forward through named steps. They lack the other half of safe evolution: decode newer data with an older binary, re-encode, and the newer fields vanish. Protobuf proved which rule makes evolution safe in both directions — unknown fields survive the round trip. This choice decides which types get that rule. It extends D-MIGRATE1-4; the migration chain itself is unchanged.
decisions.story: Ivan runs a rolling deploy. For twenty minutes, half the fleet runs the old binary. Old replicas decode v2 records, touch one field, and write them back — minus the v2 field they never knew about. The corruption is silent, spread randomly across the store, and discovered a week later.

options.name: #PublishedSchema preserves by default; plain Codable keeps the drop
options.detail: Wire-stability is what the marker means, so preservation attaches to the marker. Unknown fields ride the value invisibly and re-emit on encode. Plain #Codable types stay cheap and keep today's drop; #DenyUnknownFields stays the strict refusal. The spectrum reads refuse, drop, preserve — one word each. Gain: rolling deploys stop eating data. Loss: published values carry a hidden holder for unknowns.
options.technical: Extends D-MIGRATE1-4. The holder lives beside the migration bookkeeping decode_traced already carries for these types. Encode emits unknowns after known fields, preserving their relative order per the DataTree ordered-Object law. Field markers and E2412 semantics unchanged.

options.name: Preserve on every Codable type
options.detail: All decoded structs keep unknowns. Gain: one rule, no tiers. Loss: every struct in every program pays a hidden holder for a guarantee only wire-stable types promised, and in-memory types that never re-encode pay it for nothing.
options.code:
#Codable
struct Point { x: Int, y: Int }   // now carries an unknowns holder too

options.name: A separate opt-in marker
options.detail: A new #Preserve marker adds the holder to any type. Gain: fully explicit. Loss: the writer who needs preservation is the one who forgot the marker — Ivan's replicas were not going to carry it — and the marker count grows for a property #PublishedSchema already implies.
options.code:
#[PublishedSchema, Codable, Preserve]   // three markers to be safe on the wire
struct UserRecord { id: Int, display_name: String }

options.name: Status quo: drop everywhere
options.detail: Keep today's behavior. Gain: no holder anywhere. Loss: the migration chain protects reads from old data while writes from old binaries corrupt new data — half an evolution story.
options.code: json.encode(rec)   // v2 fields silently gone

comparisons.note: proto3 briefly dropped unknown-field preservation and reversed course in 3.5 — real deployments corrupted data exactly the way this ballot's story does. The reversal is the strongest field evidence available.
Reader and writer schemas resolve explicitly, but both must be present, forcing an external registry service. Preservation-in-the-value avoids the registry by carrying what it does not understand.

recommendation.why: Preservation attaches to the marker whose meaning is wire stability, so the guarantee lands exactly where it was promised and nowhere it was not. The industry precedent reversed onto this rule after shipping the alternative.

whyNot.reason: It taxes every struct in every program for a wire guarantee most never made.
Opt-in preservation fails its own story: the forgotten marker is the corruption. #PublishedSchema already names the intent.
It leaves the migration chain protecting one direction while the other direction corrupts.

recommendation.tradeoff: Published values grow a hidden holder, and equality of two published values can differ by unknowns the program cannot see. That is accepted: decode_traced already exposes migration state for these types, and the holder is inspectable the same way.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared marker-scoped preservation, universal preservation, a new opt-in marker, and status quo, and recommended marker-scoped because wire stability is the marker's meaning.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested schema-registry resolution (the Avro shape) and version tags in the payload. Both were dropped: each forces out-of-band infrastructure the in-value holder makes unnecessary.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested A plus an opt-out (#DropUnknown on a published type that wants cheapness). Folded into A's technical note as a possible escape, not balloted — no story demands it yet.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened D: no holder means values are exactly their fields, and equality is transparent. That transparency is real and is what the old replica uses to destroy data.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with unknown-field collisions after a rename migration: an unknown named like a future field. The migration chain runs before preservation and owns renames, so the collision resolves by chain order; the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: jet bind reads data schemas, not only language headers
decisions.gist: One command turns a sample file into a typed Codable struct.
decisions.lesson: Jet already answers how a foreign schema becomes Jet types — for languages. The C++ binder reads a clang AST and writes a Jet module with content-addressed provenance. A JSON sample, a CSV header row, and a SQL DDL file are foreign schemas too. Today a writer transcribes them into a struct by hand, and every transcription error ships silently. This choice decides whether the binder verb accepts data schemas.
decisions.story: Sam integrates a partner API. He copies the sample response into a struct by eye, misses two optional fields, and mistypes one Int as String. Nothing fails until the partner's data hits the wrong field three weeks in. The sample file that would have generated the struct correctly was in his repo the whole time.

options.name: jet bind accepts data schemas and writes a visible module
options.detail: jet bind json sample.json --type Repo writes bindings/repo.jet: an ordinary #Codable struct with the sample's hash in its header. Same verb for csv, sql DDL, xml, and proto. The file is committed and owned like any source; regeneration is explicit, and drift from a new sample shows as a normal diff. Gain: transcription errors die, and the FFI and data worlds share one verb. Loss: a generated file can go stale until someone reruns the command.
options.technical: Extends the shipped binder pattern (jet inspect bind cpp; content-addressed provenance over inputs). Output is plain Jet source on the R11 rail — nothing generated-only. Respects D-NAME-FILES1=C: a visible file, no invisible import. Inference rules (optionality from absent fields, Int vs Float from tokens) are recorded in the file header.

options.name: Comptime schema import, no file on disk
options.detail: The schema is read at compile time — the F# type-provider shape. Gain: never stale, zero files. Loss: types appear from nowhere, which breaks the ratified rule against invisible imports, and every build needs the sample present, which is the exact CI brittleness that kept type providers from spreading.

options.name: No format binders; keep hand-written structs
options.detail: Status quo. Gain: nothing new to maintain. Loss: every external schema is transcribed by eye, and the audit's row-4 bug class — silent drift between the wire and the struct — stays open.
options.code: // Sam keeps typing structs from samples, by hand.

comparisons.note: Type providers proved literal-as-schema-import works and that build-time connectivity makes it brittle. A checked-in sample plus an explicit command keeps the power and drops the brittleness.
sqlx checks queries against a database at compile time, then added offline mode with a checked-in cache because CI kept breaking. The cache file is the lesson: put the schema snapshot in the repo.
comparisons.code: let r = sqlx::query!("select name from repos");

recommendation.why: The binder mechanism, its provenance stamping, and its mental model already exist for languages. Extending the verb to data schemas kills the hand-transcription bug class with zero new machinery and no invisible types.

whyNot.reason: Invisible types contradict D-NAME-FILES1=C, and build-time sample reads recreate the F# CI failure this design exists to avoid.
The schema is already in the repo as a sample; asking a human to re-type it is asking for row 4 of the audit table.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bound module can lag its sample until regeneration. That is accepted: staleness is a visible diff away, while B's freshness costs invisible types and network-dependent builds.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared explicit binding, comptime import, and status quo, and recommended explicit binding because the binder pattern already ships for languages.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added live-endpoint binding (jet bind url) and IDE-triggered regeneration. Both folded into A as later conveniences over the same generated-file substrate.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested A plus a staleness check: the build warns when the sample's hash differs from the header stamp. That strengthened A and is recorded in its technical notes as the drift surface.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B honestly: never-stale types are a real win in fast-moving schemas. It still ships invisible types and network-coupled builds, which two ratified walls reject.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with a lying sample — optional fields present everywhere, so inference over-narrows. The header records each inference and the file is hand-editable source, so the repair is an ordinary edit; the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: A foreign call inside #Transact needs a declared undo
decisions.gist: Transactions refuse foreign calls that cannot be rolled back.
decisions.lesson: #Transact promises rollback: on failure, the block's effects unwind. The compiler enforces this for Net, FS, and Exec — an irreversible effect inside the block is E0746. The sixteen foreign-language effects are not in that set. So a call into a live Java or Perl runtime — which can charge a card or send mail — passes silently, and rollback cannot undo it. This choice decides whether foreign calls join the irreversible set, and what makes one legal. It amends the D-TXN2-era irreversible set, which today is exactly Net, FS, Exec.
decisions.story: Nadia wraps order placement in #Transact: reserve inventory, charge the card through the company's Java billing client, insert the order. The insert fails, rollback runs, inventory is restored — and the customer is still charged. The compiler that refuses a bare net.post inside the block waved the Java call through.

options.name: FFI joins E0746; #Undo(inverse) makes a call legal
options.detail: The FFI root becomes irreversible by default — the compiler cannot see the foreign body, so it must not assume it can unwind one. E0746 fires with the same fixes Net has today: hoist the call out of the block, or declare the contract. The new rung is #Undo(inverse) on the binding: name the compensating call, and #Transact registers it on the rollback path like an on_rollback hook. Gain: the rollback promise becomes true. Loss: existing foreign calls inside transactions stop compiling until they declare or hoist.
options.technical: Extends is_irreversible_effect (Effects.rs:594) from Net|FS|Exec to include the FFI root of D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1. #Undo rides the ratified rollback machinery (D-ROLLBACK-TRAIT, on_rollback hooks) — the inverse runs in reverse order with other rollback actions. No new transaction mechanism.

options.name: Warn only
options.detail: The same analysis, surfaced as a warning. Gain: nothing stops compiling. Loss: the program that loses money still ships, and a warning on silent money loss is a postmortem with earlier timestamps.

options.name: Status quo: foreign calls pass silently
options.detail: Keep the irreversible set at Net, FS, Exec. Gain: no migration for existing code. Loss: #Transact's central promise is false for every one of the sixteen foreign runtimes, and the falsehood is silent.
options.code: charge_card(order)?   // compiles, cannot unwind, says nothing

comparisons.note: The saga pattern made compensating actions the standard answer for un-undoable external steps: every forward step names its inverse. #Undo is the saga step, checked by the compiler.

recommendation.why: It makes the transaction promise honest by the same rule the block already applies to Net. The fix vocabulary — hoist or declare the inverse — is the industry's proven answer to exactly this problem.

whyNot.reason: A warning does not protect Nadia's customer; the charged-but-unordered state still ships. E0746 is already an error for Net for the same reason.
It keeps a silent false promise at the exact point programs move money.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing transactions with foreign calls break until each call hoists or declares #Undo. That is accepted: every such site is a live bug today, and the error text names both fixes.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared joining E0746, warning, and status quo, and recommended joining because the block already refuses bare Net for the same reason.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested per-language reversibility declarations and a pure-FFI carve-out for foreign calls that declare no side effects. Both folded into A: a pure foreign fn already carries no FFI-root obligation under the effect law, and per-language defaults are #Undo's granularity done worse.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested A with B's grace: error in new code, warning in existing code via edition gate. Recorded in A's migration note as the rollout path, not a separate end state.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: some foreign calls are read-only and harmless in a transaction. True — and unknowable from the signature, which is why the default must not guess.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with a failing inverse: refund_card itself throws during rollback. The ratified rollback machinery already defines failure-during-rollback behavior, and #Undo inherits it unchanged, so the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Dependency provenance gets a read surface and a default posture
decisions.gist: You can read where every dependency's bytes came from, and choose what to require.
decisions.lesson: jetpack's trust machinery is ratified and typed: TUF roles, publisher identity, build attestation. Live verification is deferred, and no command shows any of it — provenance nobody can read is provenance nobody has. Integrity is the one enforced layer today: bytes must match the locked hash. This choice decides the read surface and the default posture for the layers above integrity. It implements D-JPK-TRUSTROOT1=D; the trust model itself is not reopened.
decisions.story: A supply-chain CVE lands on the front page. Mia's CTO asks the reasonable question: who built our dependencies, from what commits, and can we prove it. The honest answer today is that the data model for the proof exists in the compiler's source code and nowhere Mia can point a terminal.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet inspect provenance textkit
tower: unknown inspect target 'provenance'
# the TUF types are in crates/jetpack/src/TrustRoot.rs — and that is where they stay

options.name: Verify and show by default; require by manifest choice
options.detail: jet inspect provenance prints each dependency's chain: locked hash, transparency-log entry, publisher identity, build attestation — each line marked enforced, verified, or recorded. Integrity stays enforced always. Everything above it is verified and shown when present, and required only when the manifest's authority block says so. The same row is the refusal switch. Gain: the chain becomes readable today and enforceable per project. Loss: an unattested dependency still resolves by default.
options.technical: Implements D-JPK-TRUSTROOT1=D (attaches the deferred live verifiers) on the authority-block rail (#1570). The ratified D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1 trust vocabulary is { default, ci, services } with allow/prompt/deny; the require: row (values none | logged | attested) is a named amendment adding new vocabulary to that block. Exact spelling is the owner's. E1204 hash enforcement unchanged.

options.name: Require attestation by default
options.detail: Unattested dependencies fail resolve unless the manifest lowers the bar. Gain: the strongest default. Loss: most of today's ecosystem is unattested, so nearly every project's first resolve fails on day one. The practical lesson from npm and Go is that adoption grows from visible-by-default, not mandatory-at-birth.

options.name: Tooling only: show, never enforce
options.detail: The inspect surface ships; no manifest row exists. Gain: zero resolve behavior at stake. Loss: the project that needs enforcement — the one Mia works at — has a report and no lever, and the deferred verifiers stay deferred with nothing pulling them live.
options.code:
$ jet inspect provenance textkit   // readable
// and no way to make any of it required

comparisons.note: Provenance shipped as a visible badge first; registries and orgs then ratcheted requirements. Visibility created the demand that made enforcement adoptable.

The checksum database is enforced silently for everyone — the layer analogous to Jet's E1204 — while identity and build proof stayed out-of-band. Jet already matches the enforced layer; this ballot adds the readable ones.

recommendation.why: It turns typed-but-dead trust machinery into a chain anyone can read today and any project can require tomorrow, on the authority rail the owner already ratified for exactly this kind of choice.

whyNot.reason: It breaks nearly every resolve in an ecosystem that is not attested yet, and the precedent shows visibility-first is what makes requirement adoptable later.
A report without a lever leaves the highest-stakes projects exactly where the story starts: able to describe the gap, unable to close it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The default accepts unattested dependencies, so a project must opt into the stronger posture. That is accepted: the posture is one manifest row, and the inspect output names every dependency that would fail it before the switch is flipped.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared verify-and-show, require-by-default, and tooling-only, and recommended verify-and-show with a manifest requirement lever.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested review attestations (the cargo-vet axis) as a fourth layer. It folded out as future work — a different proof with its own ecosystem, and the chain surface can add its line later without a new decision.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested B-for-new-projects, A-for-existing. That is A plus a template default, recorded in A's notes for the jet new scaffold rather than balloted separately.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C: shipping read-only first is a smaller change and still answers Mia's CTO. It answers the question and still cannot act on the answer.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's require row with a broken registry log — attested deps failing resolve during a log outage. The posture check reads locally cached attestations pinned in the lock, so an outage degrades to the cached proof; the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Tier parity: resolve I9 against the interpreter carve-out
decisions.gist: Decide once whether the interpreter tier must match AOT exactly, because two ratified texts currently disagree.
decisions.lesson: Invariant I9 says every tier preserves one meaning for every feature. A later ratified verdict, D-VERDICT-1254-1, says in full: "Full JIT/AOT parity required, but the user-visible law is byte-identical default-run behavior. Interpreter-tier parity is a lower concern; implementation may close gaps or route around the interpreter." Both are law today, and the open question is only the interpreter tier. The gap is not abstract: the interpreter silently skips view-range bounds checks (card #1616). One text must win.
decisions.story: A teacher demos Jet with jet run. A student indexes past a view's end. On the teacher's laptop, nothing happens; the interpreter skips the check. Compiled for homework submission, the same program stops with a bounds error. The student's first lesson about Jet is that it disagrees with itself.

options.name: Full parity, no carve-out
options.detail: The interpreter is a first-class tier. Every safety check and every semantic holds there. D-VERDICT-1254-1 is superseded and says so with a link. The jit_gaps ledger and card #1616 become blocking work.
options.technical: Supersedes D-VERDICT-1254-1. I9 text unchanged. Every Prelude semantic reachable from deopt calls the same Prelude symbol; the one-home guards from D-ONCE-LAW1 enforce it.

options.name: A named carve-out (amends I9)
options.detail: This option amends I9 to permit one guarded exception registry. The interpreter may lag, but only on surfaces named in that list, and never on safety checks. I9's text names the list's home. Anything not listed must match, and silent new gaps still fail.
options.technical: I9 text amended to cite an interpreter-exceptions registry. Safety checks (bounds, overflow, unsafe gates) are never listable. The list ratchets: entries carry a removal condition.

options.name: Demote the interpreter to a dev shim
options.detail: Accept the verdict's direction fully: the interpreter is a development convenience, not a semantic tier. jet run warns when deopt runs code whose meaning is unproven there. I9 text shrinks to AOT, JIT, and web.

recommendation.why: Safety is rank one and the interpreter is the tier beginners touch first through deopt. A skipped bounds check there is a memory-safety story, not a performance story. One meaning everywhere is also the cheapest rule to guard.

whyNot.reason: A listed carve-out is a standing ledger of differences, and this audit shows ledgers of allowed drift grow until someone closes them as done with 48 entries still inside.
A permanent warning teaches every beginner that jet run is not really Jet. That trades the first-hour experience away to save engine work, which the constitution forbids weighing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Full parity makes some future features land slower, because the interpreter path must ship in the same change. That is the do-it-right rule already written in the philosophy.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft framed the contradiction, offered full parity, a named carve-out, and demotion, and recommended full parity on the safety rank.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered deleting the interpreter tier entirely and JIT-only dev. Both collapse into option C's honesty question and were folded there.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested full parity for safety checks plus a listed lag for everything else. That is exactly option B, so no new option was added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the never-listable safety rule and a removal condition per entry, and strengthened C with an explicit user-visible note instead of silence.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with the cost of blocking features on interpreter work and with deopt surfaces that genuinely cannot apply. The existing owner-ratified carve-out mechanism in I9 already handles true cannot-apply cases, so A survives without a standing lag list.

decisions.title: Retired spellings: the enforcement mechanism
decisions.gist: Pick what happens when code uses a retired spelling, so renames stop living forever.
decisions.lesson: Greenfield law says a replaced form is deleted in the same change. Nothing enforces it. The ratified entry file run.jet has zero adopters; the retired main.jet has 94. The ratified manifest name has 7 files; the retired one has 45. A retirement today ships as a memo. This ballot makes it ship as code: an error, a rewrite, and a ratchet test.
decisions.story: The owner ratifies run.jet as the entry file. Three weeks later a new contributor copies an example, names the file main.jet, and everything works silently. The ratified decision exists only in the ledger. Nobody is wrong, and the migration never happens.
decisions.inWild:
$ ls my-app/
main.jet   pkg.jet        # both retired names, both accepted in silence today
$ jet run my-app/main.jet
Hello!                    # no notice, no nudge, forever

options.name: Hard error with a fix line
options.detail: A retired spelling is a compile error with what, why, and fix, and jet fix performs the rename on demand. Old trees stop building until touched once. The strictest reading of greenfield law.
options.code:
$ jet run my-app/main.jet
Error [E13xx]: `main.jet` was retired; the entry file is `run.jet`
 Why: one canonical entry name (D-VERDICT-678-1)
 Fix: run `jet fix --rename-entry` to rename it
// E13xx is provisional; the real code is assigned at registration
$ jet fix --rename-entry
renamed: main.jet -> run.jet

options.name: Auto-rewrite with a notice
options.detail: jet fmt and jet fix rewrite retired spellings mechanically and print what they did. The compiler accepts the old form for one release window and says so each time. That window is a compatibility exception, so greenfield law requires this option to carry an owner-ratified carve-out naming its exact scope and removal condition. Errors appear only where a rewrite cannot be mechanical.
options.code:
$ jet fmt
rewrote: pkg.jet -> package.jet   (retired name, D-ECO-FILEROOT1)
$ jet run my-app/main.jet
note: `main.jet` is retired; this build accepted it and renamed guidance applies

options.name: Both, split by category
options.detail: Pure renames auto-rewrite with a notice. Retirements that change meaning or structure hard-error with a fix line. Every retirement declares its category when it lands, and both roads end at the same ratchet: a test asserting the retired form's in-repo count is zero.
options.technical: A retirement row: {old, new, category: rename|semantic, error code, rewrite rule?, ratchet test}. The row is the one home; loader silence is no longer a possible outcome.
options.code:
// retirement row (proposed):
retire main.jet -> run.jet        category: rename    rewrite: yes   ratchet: 0 files
retire payload:{} -> name:/version:  category: semantic  error: E1206   ratchet: 0 files
$ jet fmt        # renames just happen
$ jet build      # semantic retirements stop the build with the fix

comparisons.note: Editions pair a hard boundary with cargo fix, which rewrites mechanically; retired forms do not linger silently inside one edition.

recommendation.why: Renames and meaning changes deserve different force. A rename that a tool can perform should never cost a human a build break, and a meaning change should never be rewritten silently. One row shape carries both and ends at zero either way.

whyNot.reason: Hard-erroring a pure rename makes the tool ask a human to do what the tool can do itself.
A notice on a semantic change lets a program's meaning shift under a formatter run, which is exactly the silent move the fact law forbids.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every retirement must now declare its category and ship its row. That is one line of ceremony per retirement, paid by the person retiring, not by users.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft offered hard error, auto-rewrite, and the category split, recommending the split because renames and meaning changes deserve different force.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested grandfathering old trees permanently and a telemetry-driven deprecation clock. Permanent grandfathering is the current silent failure with paperwork; clocks without enforcement decay, so neither joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed C is itself the hybrid of A and B and checked it stays coherent: one row shape, two forces, one ratchet.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with jet fix on demand and B with a one-release acceptance window, making both their strongest honest selves before judging.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked C's category field: who decides rename versus semantic? Repair: the retirement row is part of the retiring change and reviewed with it, and a wrong category is a normal review finding, not a new mechanism.

decisions.title: The corpus law: say it once, with a guard
decisions.gist: Adopt one law for the whole corpus: every truth has one home, every other appearance is rendered from it, and each law ships with a guard.
decisions.lesson: The audit found 18 cases where one job is implemented by several hand-kept copies: two schedulers, three effect-root lists, four copies of one error message, two decision ledgers. Each copy is kept in sync by comments or habit. The fact law you ratified already forbids this for program facts. This ballot extends the same rule to the compiler, its tables, its messages, and its records.
decisions.story: An agent fixes the deadline error text in the scheduler. Three other copies keep the old wording. The test suite stays green, because every test only checks that the text exists somewhere. A month later, two tiers print different errors for the same failure, and nobody knows which one is law.

options.name: The law plus mandatory guards
options.detail: Every unified truth registers its home, the surfaces rendered from it, and a guard test. A registered truth without a guard fails lint. New second copies fail the build. This is the fact-law row shape, applied to the corpus itself.
options.technical: A truth row: {name, home, renderers[], guard}. Guards are cheap uniqueness tests: assert one definition site, or diff derived output against the home. tower lint gains a corpus-law pass that fails a row with no guard.

options.name: The law as doctrine, guards optional
options.detail: Adopt the one-home rule as written policy. Guards are recommended, not required. Reviewers enforce the rule by reading. No registry, no lint pass. Lighter to run, but the audit shows review alone did not stop the existing hundred copies.

options.name: Per-slate policing only
options.detail: No corpus-wide law. Each ratified slate keeps policing its own area, as the report slate and fact slate do today. Cross-domain forks, like one error text living in four crates, stay nobody's job.

comparisons.note: rustc generates its diagnostics index and its option tables from single declarative homes; a second copy cannot drift because it does not exist.
comparisons.code: // rustc: declare_lint! / diagnostic structs -> rendered docs, JSON, and checks from one source

recommendation.why: The audit is the proof: doctrine without guards produced about one hundred copies, four live forks, and a green test suite through all of it. A guard turns the next fork into a red build the same day.

whyNot.reason: Doctrine alone already failed. AGENTS.md forbids parking work in jit_gaps.txt, and the file holds 48 entries.
The worst forks cross slate lines. Four copies of one error text span three domains, so per-slate policing never sees the whole animal.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every future unification must also write its guard row. That is one small test per truth, and it is the only thing that has ever kept two copies equal.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared mandatory guards, optional guards, and per-slate policing, and recommended mandatory guards because the evidence shows reviews alone missed a hundred copies.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested two more shapes: a one-time cleanup sweep with no standing law, and generating all code from one schema. The sweep decays like jit_gaps did, and full generation is a build-system rewrite folded into option A's guard idea.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried doctrine now, guards later. It collapsed into option B, because a guard promised later is a promise, and the audit is a museum of expired promises.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a quarterly audit cadence and C with a named cross-slate owner. Neither repair catches a fork the day it lands, which is the job.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with guard rot: a weak guard passes while meaning drifts. Repair: a guard must diff behavior or count definition sites, never just check existence, and A survives with that rule in the row shape.

decisions.title: One word, one mechanism: stream and yield
decisions.gist: Give the words stream and yield exactly one meaning each in Jet's spec and docs.
decisions.lesson: The word stream names six unrelated things today: the generator type Stream<T>, a codec reader mode, file-line iteration, the Event type's description, a future analytics type, and scheduler internals. The word yield is a suspension keyword, yet the spec also calls eager list-building loops yielding loops. No user spelling is wrong; the vocabulary is. A newcomer cannot ask what Jet means by streaming and get one answer.
decisions.story: A newcomer reads that encoding supports streaming, finds Stream<T> in the reference, and writes a codec loop expecting yield to work inside it. It does not; codec readers are a different machine with the same name. Their mental model breaks on a word, not on a rule.
decisions.inWild:
fn count() => Stream<Int> { yield 1 }        // a real Stream: suspends
reader :: json.reader(file)                   // the spec calls this streaming too
loop line, handle.lines() { }                 // and this
ev :: event.new<Int>()                        // "a typed occurrence stream" — also this

options.name: Stream<T> owns the word
options.detail: Only the generator type is called a stream. Codec modes are readers and writers, which their API already says. Events are events. Eager loops become collecting loops. One spec page defines the vocabulary and every other page links it. Zero user spellings change.

options.name: Rename the type, free the word
options.detail: The generator type becomes Seq<T> or Flow<T>, and stream becomes the umbrella word for all values-over-time surfaces, with one page mapping the family. A real user spelling changes, and every existing example migrates under the retirement mechanism.
options.code:
fn count() => Seq<Int> { yield 1 }   // renamed type
// "streaming" now legally describes readers, events, and Seq alike

options.name: Glossary only
options.detail: Keep all current wording and add a glossary page that disambiguates the six uses. Lowest churn of the three: no prose sweep, no doc lint, and readers of older material meet no renamed terms. The six meanings stay live, with the page as the map.
options.code:
// docs/spec gains one page: the six senses of "stream", each linked to its mechanism
// existing prose untouched; new prose free to use any sense

recommendation.why: The generator type is the only surface where the word does work: it names a language mechanism with suspension law behind it. Everything else already has a better word in its own API, so prose just starts using those words.

whyNot.reason: It spends a real breaking rename to buy an umbrella word, and umbrella words are how six meanings happened.
A glossary documents the collision without ending it, and the next spec page re-collides.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some prose becomes slightly longer, saying reader or collecting loop where stream used to blur. That is the cost of one meaning per word.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared narrowing the word, renaming the type, and a glossary, recommending narrowing because every other surface already owns a better word.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested banning the word entirely and renaming Event to Topic. Banning punishes the one legitimate owner, and the Event rename is out of scope here, so neither joined.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested narrowing plus a glossary page, and folded it in: option A already includes the one vocabulary page, so no separate option exists.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with real candidate names and C with a linked glossary that costs nothing and breaks nothing. C is the right pick for an owner who values zero churn over one-word-one-meaning.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with enforcement: prose rules rot. Repair: the vocabulary page is a truth row under D-ONCE-LAW1, and a doc lint flags the retired senses, so A survives with teeth.

decisions.title: One spelling to request a derived capability
decisions.gist: Pick the single way a type asks for a built-in capability like Comparable, and end the second spelling.
decisions.lesson: Today a struct can request Comparable two ways: a marker before the type (#Comparable) or a body line (derive Comparable, D-USERDERIVE1). Both fill the same field; the parser proves they converge. The same keyword also means something else entirely: derive T.Trait { } defines a provider (D-METADERIVE1). One job with two spellings, and one keyword with two jobs.
decisions.story: A reviewer reads two structs in one file. One says #Comparable above its name; the other says derive Comparable inside its body. They check the compiler to learn whether these differ. They do not — and the keyword they just studied means definition, not request, three files later.
decisions.inWild:
#[Printable, !Debug]
struct Visible { value: Int }        // marker spelling

struct Score {
    points: Int
    derive Comparable                 // body-line spelling, same effect
}

derive Money.Wire { ... }             // same keyword, different job: defines a provider

options.name: Marker requests, keyword defines
options.detail: #Comparable and friends are the one request spelling. The body line derive Comparable retires through the retirement mechanism, with fmt rewriting it to the marker. The derive keyword keeps only its provider-definition meaning from D-METADERIVE1. Amends D-USERDERIVE1; keeps D-METADERIVE1.
options.code:
#Comparable
struct Score { points: Int }          // the one way to ask (bare form; #[A, B] only for two or more, D-MARK-STACK1)

derive Money.Wire { ... }             // the one thing `derive` means
// jet fmt rewrites:  derive Comparable  ->  #Comparable

options.name: Body line requests, marker narrows
options.detail: derive Comparable inside the body is the one request spelling, keeping requests next to fields. Markers keep every non-derive rule (#Layout, #State) but stop carrying derive names. The keyword then means request in a body and define at top level, split by position. Amends the marker table's derive rows.

options.name: Keep both, document equivalence
options.detail: Both spellings stay and the spec states they are one feature with two entry points, like inline versus external methods. Zero migration for the shipped corpus, and authors keep the adjacency choice per type. The reviewer's question from the story stays a live question.
options.code:
// status quo, plus one spec sentence:
// "#Comparable and `derive Comparable` are the same request."

comparisons.note: One spelling: the attribute. No body-line alternative exists, so the question never arises.

recommendation.why: Markers already carry every other declaration-site rule, so requests join the family the reader already knows. The keyword then has one meaning, and fmt can migrate the corpus mechanically.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the keyword meaning two things by position, which is the exact one-word-two-mechanisms defect this slate exists to end.
The structural-flexibility rule covers where code lives, not two spellings of one request; I8 calls that a second mechanism.

recommendation.tradeoff: Types with many derives stack markers above the name rather than lines in the body. The bracket list form keeps that compact.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared marker-only, body-line-only, and keep-both, recommending marker-only because markers already own declaration-site rules.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a third spelling, deriving inside an impl block, and folding requests into trait syntax. Both add mechanisms rather than delete one, so neither joined.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested marker-only requests while keeping the body line as fmt-rewritten sugar. That is option A with the retirement mechanism doing exactly that, so it folded in.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the adjacency argument for long files, and C with the structural-flexibility precedent for one feature with two entry points. Each now states its best honest case.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with the distinct-type wrinkle, where capability markers set booleans instead of derives. Repair: that unification is the type slate's row and A only fixes the spelling, so A survives scoped.

decisions.title: The plugin package kind gets its own word
decisions.gist: Stop using the word wasm for two unrelated mechanisms: the browser compute bucket and the sandboxed plugin kind.
decisions.lesson: Two mechanisms share one word. #Target(Wasm) marks a function for the browser's compute bucket inside a web package. target: plugin compiles a whole package into an isolated Component Model guest — its point is isolation, not the instruction set. A user searching the spec for wasm gets two disjoint stories with disjoint diagnostics.
decisions.story: A developer builds a browser app with #Target(Wasm) functions. Later they want a safe third-party extension point and find target: plugin described as wasm too. They assume the two compose, spend an afternoon, and learn the only shared thing is the compiler's internal ISA choice.
decisions.inWild:
#Target(Wasm) fn crunch(rows: List<Row>) => Stats { ... }   // browser compute bucket

// package.jet of an extension:
name: "mathkit"
target: plugin        // sandboxed guest, loaded by core.plugin — also called wasm in docs

options.name: Rename the kind to sandbox
options.detail: target: sandbox says what the mechanism is for: an isolated, capability-free guest. The wasm word stays only where the browser bucket genuinely means the browser ISA. The old kind name retires through the retirement mechanism. Amends D-PLUGIN1 naming.

options.name: Rename the browser marker instead
options.detail: #Target(Wasm) becomes #Target(Compute), pairing naturally with #Target(JS) as the view bucket. The plugin kind keeps its name and the word wasm leaves the marker surface. Amends the web partition marker vocabulary.
options.code:
#Target(Compute) fn crunch(rows: List<Row>) => Stats { ... }
#Target(JS)      fn render(s: Stats) => Html { ... }

options.name: Keep both, add a disambiguation page
options.detail: Both names stay and the spec adds one page separating the stories. No manifest migrates and no term anyone has learned changes. The word keeps two meanings, with the page as the boundary marker.
options.code:
// docs: one page, two sections — the browser bucket and the sandbox kind,
// each naming the other as "not this"

recommendation.why: The plugin kind's user-facing promise is isolation, so its name should say sandbox; nobody chooses it for the instruction set. The browser bucket genuinely is the wasm target, so its name stays truthful.

whyNot.reason: It renames the surface that was telling the truth and keeps the name that was not.
A page that explains a collision preserves it, and search still returns two stories for one word.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing plugin manifests migrate one field value under the retirement mechanism's rename category.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared renaming the kind, renaming the marker, and documenting both, recommending the kind rename because isolation is that mechanism's actual promise.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested renaming both surfaces and folding plugins under the web partition. Renaming both fixes a collision that one rename already ends, and the fold is false: the mechanisms share nothing but an ISA.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested sandbox as the kind plus Compute as the marker. It adds a second rename without removing a second collision, so it folded back to A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the Compute/JS symmetry argument and C with its zero-migration guarantee. C is the right pick for an owner who wants no manifest churn this epoch.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with ecosystem expectations: developers search for wasm plugins. Repair: docs keep the word as an implementation note on the sandbox page, so discovery survives while the surface name tells the truth.

decisions.title: One policy ladder for every audited escape
decisions.gist: Give the three audited escape markers one org-policy ladder, and retire the one-off --allow-impure flag.
decisions.lesson: Three markers share one shape: write a reason, step off the safe path. Behind them sit three unrelated depths. #Unsafe has a five-scope, six-mode policy ladder with an org file. #Impure has a single CLI boolean. #Nondeterministic has nothing. The shared audit ledger is already ratified (D-FACT-GATE1, card #1571); this ballot decides only the policy half.
decisions.story: A team lead forbids unsafe code org-wide with the policy file and believes the org is locked down. A contractor's build script passes --allow-impure, and comptime code reads the network during builds. The lead never sees it, because the org file governs one marker of three.
decisions.inWild:
#Unsafe("pointer stays local") { ... }        // governed by org policy file
#Impure("reads a feature flag") { ... }        // governed by a CLI bool, invisible to policy
#Nondeterministic("samples entropy") { ... }   // governed by nothing

options.name: One ladder for the family
options.detail: The unsafe policy ladder generalizes: one policy surface names all audited escapes, with the same five scopes and modes. The one-off --allow-impure spelling retires, replaced by one family flag the org file can refuse — solo scripts need no policy file. A beginner still writes one marker and one sentence.
options.technical: PolicyKey::Unsafe generalizes to per-gate keys sharing one PolicyValue shape and one resolution order (Organization, Package, Module, Function, Block). The env-var org hook covers the family. All three land in the ratified gates ledger.
options.code:
// org policy file, after:
#Policy(unsafe: .Forbid, impure: .GateOnly, nondeterministic: .Default)

$ jet build --gate impure=allow      // the per-invocation escape, one spelling for the family
$ jet build --allow-impure
Error [E21xx]: `--allow-impure` was retired; use `--gate impure=allow` (org policy may refuse it)

options.name: Ladders per marker, shape shared
options.detail: Each marker gets its own policy key and file section, all using the same six-mode shape, but set independently with no shared default. More knobs, same coverage, and a lead must remember to set all three.
options.code:
#Policy(unsafe: .Forbid)
#Policy(impure: .Forbid)          // forgotten? impure stays open
#Policy(nondeterministic: .Forbid)

options.name: Ledger only, ladders stay uneven
options.detail: Ship the ratified gates ledger and stop there. Visibility becomes uniform; control stays three different shapes. The contractor story remains possible, now with better logs.

recommendation.why: The family shares one meaning, so it should share one control surface. One ladder makes the org file the whole answer to who may step off the safe path, which is what a lead actually asks.

whyNot.reason: Independent knobs with no shared default recreate today's hole: the marker you forgot is the one the contractor uses.
Seeing an escape is not governing it; the audit's missing-exit standard requires the refusal switch, not only the ledger.

recommendation.tradeoff: The org policy file gains two fields, and the old flag spelling retires with a teaching error pointing at the family flag.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one ladder, per-marker ladders, and ledger-only, recommending one ladder because the family shares one meaning.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested folding taint scrubs and #Transact undo declarations into the same ladder. Both are different shapes, propagating facts rather than scoped escapes, so the family stayed three.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested one ladder with per-marker overrides. That is what option A already is: one default surface whose fields may differ per gate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C by pairing the ledger with a CI query teams could alert on. It remains observation without refusal, but it is C's strongest honest form.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with policy-file blast radius: one bad org file could block builds org-wide. Repair: the existing six-mode vocabulary already includes permissive modes, and scope resolution keeps local overrides where policy allows, so A survives.

decisions.title: One decision ledger
decisions.gist: Pick the one home for ratified decisions, because the spec and Tower currently disagree about what the law even is.
decisions.lesson: The spec cites about 927 decision IDs as law. Tower holds 505 records. 675 cited IDs have no Tower record, and 253 Tower IDs appear nowhere in the spec. The drift linter scans a directory that now holds a README. Verdicts can silently contradict each other with no supersession link; the comptime keyword was ratified immutable one day and retired the next, both records still standing. Nobody can query whether an ID is current law.
decisions.story: An agent drafts a proposal and cites a ratified decision it found in the spec. The dedupe reviewer cannot verify it: the ID has no Tower record, no status, no date. Hours go to archaeology that a one-line query should answer — this audit paid that cost repeatedly, today.
decisions.inWild:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs decision show D-MEM1
not found                       # yet the spec cites D-MEM1 as ratified law in 30 places

options.name: Tower is the home; the spec renders
options.detail: Every spec-cited ID gets a Tower record in a one-time import, with status and source span. The spec keeps its prose, but a decision block's canonical fields come from the store. The lint walks docs/spec and fails on any ID with no record. Supersession links become mandatory on verdicts.
options.technical: Import builds records from spec citations with status ratified-by-spec until reviewed. tower lint --docs gains a spec-walking pass. decision add gains a required supersedes field when the same surface is re-decided.
options.code:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs decision show D-MEM1
D-MEM1  ratified  source: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2210  supersedes: —
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs lint --docs
E_DRIFT: docs/spec/spec.md:1180 cites D-XYZ9 — no record

options.name: The spec is the home; Tower links
options.detail: The spec's declaration of itself as canonical stands. Tower records become pointers into spec spans, and the lint verifies every Tower ID resolves to a live spec citation and the reverse. Queries answer from the index the lint builds.
options.code:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs decision show D-MEM1
D-MEM1 -> docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2210 (indexed; spec text is the record)

options.name: Two ledgers with a sync guard
options.detail: Both stay authoritative for their halves, and a guard fails when an ID exists in one and not the other. The 675-and-253 gap becomes a burn-down list. Ends silent drift without moving either home, and keeps two write paths forever.
options.code:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs lint --docs
E_SYNC: 675 spec-only ids, 253 tower-only ids — sync required before merge

recommendation.why: Law you cannot query is folklore. Tower already has status, dates, options, and ratification mechanics; the spec has prose. Give the structured half the record and the prose half the rendering, and the one query works.

whyNot.reason: A 5,900-line prose file as the record means status and supersession stay regex archaeology forever.
