Two write paths is the disease this whole slate treats; a guard makes the symptom loud without curing it.

recommendation.tradeoff: A one-time import of several hundred spec-cited IDs, each landing with a source span and a provisional status until touched.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared Tower-as-home, spec-as-home, and guarded dual ledgers, recommending Tower because the record needs queryable status and supersession.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a third store, one file per decision in git, and generating the spec from Tower entirely. The per-file store is Tower with worse tooling, and full generation is a later step A does not preclude.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced A's final shape: Tower holds the record while the spec keeps the prose and renders canonical fields, which is the workable middle of A and B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a built index making spec spans queryable, and it stands for an owner who wants prose primacy preserved exactly as declared today.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's import quality: 675 records minted from citations could be noise. Repair: imported records carry a provisional status and their source span, so review happens lazily and nothing is invented.

decisions.title: One verb per job in Core collections
decisions.gist: Make one verb mean one job across List, Map, and Set, and bless the constructor spelling the corpus actually uses.
decisions.lesson: Today replace means three jobs: swap-by-value on List, upsert on Map, canonical-swap on Set. Remove-and-return is pop on Map but take on Set. The API law documents Type.from_x() conversions, yet bare .from() is the most common real form, with 32 call sites and no rule blessing it. Each inconsistency is small; together they mean nobody can guess a collection API without reading it.
decisions.story: Someone who just used map.pop(key) writes set.pop(value). It does not exist; Set spells the same job take. Their fix is a search through two API pages for a distinction that carries no meaning.
decisions.inWild:
displaced :: prices.replace("eggs", 3.99)   // Map: upsert, returns displaced
swapped  :: names.replace("Bob", "Rob")     // List: swap first equal value
back     :: seen.take(id)                    // Set: remove-and-return
gone     :: prices.pop("eggs")              // Map: remove-and-return — same job, other verb

options.name: Adopt the verb table
options.detail: One table fixes the family. The verb pop means remove-and-return on every collection, matching the verb beginners arrive knowing. The verb replace keeps only the List swap meaning, and Map upsert stays add per the ratified storage law. Bare .from() is written into the naming law as the conversion constructor. The from_x() shape stays reserved for source-qualified variants. Retired verbs go through the retirement mechanism.
options.technical: Amends the storage-verb table around D-API-STORE1 and the D-STDRUBRIC1 constructor idiom list. Both IDs are spec-only today with no Tower record; B9's amendment lands wherever B8 homes the decision record. The verb table is a truth row: stdlib docs, CLI verb choices, and future API review render from it.
options.code:
gone :: prices.pop("eggs")      // one verb, every collection
back :: seen.pop(id)
names.replace("Bob", "Rob")     // replace = swap, List only
Set.from([1, 2, 3])              // bare .from blessed in the law it already dominates

options.name: Match the substrate
options.detail: Align verbs with Rust's std where they differ, so people arriving from the backend's own ecosystem guess right: pop, insert, and HashSet's take and replace keep Rust's meanings. Consistency comes from the neighbor language rather than from an internal table.
options.code:
prices.pop("eggs")               // Rust's verb, kept
seen.take(id)                    // Rust's verb, kept
seen.replace(v)                  // Rust's canonical-swap, kept — three meanings stay

options.name: Document the map, change nothing
options.detail: Keep every verb and add a cross-collection table to the docs. Nothing ships, nothing renames, and no golden output changes. The guessing failure stays, with a shorter search.
options.code: // docs table: "remove-and-return: Map.pop / Set.take" — a legend for the maze

comparisons.note: pop means remove-and-return on dict, list, and set alike; one verb, one job, and beginners guess right.

recommendation.why: Guessability is the beginner surface: one verb per job means the second collection you learn is free. The table picks pop because the ballot's own evidence shows it is the verb people arrive knowing. The table also becomes the review rubric, so the next API cannot reintroduce a synonym.

whyNot.reason: It imports Rust's own inconsistencies, and Jet's users are not required to know the backend exists.
A legend for the maze leaves the maze; the audit's standard is deleting the second spelling, not mapping it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing code using the retired verbs migrates through the retirement mechanism's rename category, mechanically.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an internal verb table, Rust alignment, and documentation-only, recommending the table because guessability is the beginner surface.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass swept the wider verb space, including has, add, and open across modules. This ballot stays scoped to collections where the collisions are proven, and the table's later rows carry the full-surface sweep.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested the table with Rust's verbs as tie-breakers when jobs match. That rule folded into A: where meanings already agree, nothing changes anyway.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B for FFI-heavy users who context-switch into Rust daily, and C for owners who want zero golden churn. The adversarial pass then forced A to justify its verb pick against the Python comparison, which flipped the choice to pop.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A's original take pick with the ballot's own Python row and story, and A now picks pop. It also attacked churn: the retirement mechanism's rename category makes each migration one fmt run.

decisions.title: The at-sign: build it, reassign it, or state the reservation
decisions.gist: Decide the at-sign's future: fulfill its reservation, narrow it, publish it, or make @ the one word for both at-a-place and at-compile-time.
decisions.lesson: The at-sign has one ratified, working meaning: the package-reference source separator, as in textkit#1.2.0@vendor (D-JPK-REF1). It also carries a documented reservation for locations and sources, with no feature behind it. Meanwhile the dollar sign is ratified as the compile-time mark and the fact-read spelling (D-FACT-READ1: T.$range, $build.profile). That dollar surface is law without code today. A respelling now is cheap; the same change later is a corpus-wide break. Option D amends the dollar law; the others leave it alone.
decisions.story: A language-curious expert hits the reserved-sigil error, goes looking for the location feature it advertises, and finds nothing: no type, no roadmap card, no design note. The reservation is a promise only the error message remembers.

options.name: Design the promised feature
options.detail: Mint a design card for locations and sources as a real typed surface, with @ as its sigil, homed to the epoch that owns distributed and packaging work. The reservation gains a due date and a designed shape. No syntax ships until that design ratifies.

options.name: Narrow the reservation to the packaging meaning
options.detail: The packaging separator becomes the sigil's whole official meaning. The location promise is withdrawn from the teaching error and the reserved-space docs. This amends the reservation text only, never D-JPK-REF1 itself. A future location feature would need to claim new space on its own merits.

options.name: Keep the reservation, publish it
options.detail: The reservation stays, and it becomes a visible row: jet inspect reserved lists it with its written condition for minting, and the teaching error links there. The promise becomes auditable and falsifiable instead of living only inside an error string.
options.code:
$ jet inspect reserved
@   live: package-reference source separator (D-JPK-REF1)
    reserved: locations, addresses   condition: distributed-execution design epoch

options.name: @ is the word at: place and compile time
options.detail: Prefix @ becomes the compile-time mark and the fact-read spelling, replacing $ everywhere: @config, T.@range, @build.profile. Infix @ keeps its ratified at-a-source meaning unchanged. The location reservation folds into the same word: a future at-a-machine feature rides @, so where and when share one story. This amends D-FACT-READ1's spelling half and the ratified comptime-mention mark — the read semantics stay, the glyph changes. The dollar sign is freed; its next job is D-ONCE-DOLLAR1's question.
options.technical: Amends: D-FACT-READ1 (spelling only; the one-mark-per-registered-plane law stands) and the $ comptime-mention rule. Untouched: D-JPK-REF1 semantics. Migration: mechanical respell of the shipped $ surface (comptime splices, the layout selector) via the retirement mechanism; the fact-read organs are unbuilt, so most of the change is spec text.

recommendation.why: One word carrying one meaning — at — across place and time is the strongest use of the glyph, and the packaging surface already teaches it. The swap is near-free today because the dollar read surface is law without code; that window closes as the fact organs land.

whyNot.reason: It spends design effort on the location half alone, before its epoch, and leaves the when-versus-where split standing.
It quietly forecloses the distributed future to save one ledger row, and the at-compile-time reading dies with it.
Publishing the reservation is honest but spends nothing and unifies nothing; it is the right floor, not the best ceiling.

recommendation.tradeoff: The comptime mark attaches to every mention of a comptime name, so a heavier glyph raises visual density in comptime-heavy files — and two fresh ratifications get their spelling amended.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft mis-read the sigil as unused; review rebuilt it around D-JPK-REF1 and scoped the question to the reservation's unfulfilled half, recommending publication.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the owner-raised swap: prefix @ as the compile-time mark, unifying at-a-place with at-compile-time. It also re-tested freeing @ as an identifier character and decorator use; both still lose.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed D is itself the unifying hybrid. It keeps B honesty about the live packaging meaning, keeps A path to the location future, and adds the when reading under one word.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C as the epoch-rule floor that spends nothing, and A as the only option that delivers the location promise on its own. Both stand for owners weighing those highest.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked D with glyph density on every comptime mention and with amending two fresh ratifications. The density cost is real and accepted in the tradeoff; the amendment is named, and the unbuilt read surface makes the migration window genuinely cheap now.

decisions.comment: This also must replace the macro expansion $[…]$ which would become @[…]@

decisions.title: The ratified UI-tree spelling was never built: ship it, amend it, or decide with the architecture
decisions.gist: Decide what happens to the ratified dot-construction UI spelling that no shipped code uses.
decisions.lesson: The spec ratifies typed dot-construction for UI trees, spelled .Button.{ label: "OK" } (recorded as D-UITREE1, which itself has no Tower record). Nothing was ever built: no Button type exists, and every shipped example and test uses the function-call surface, ui.box and ui.button. A reader trusting the ratified text writes code that does not compile. Separately, card #1588 is an open evaluation of one canonical UI architecture. This ballot decides the spelling's fate.
decisions.story: A developer reads the ratified decision text, writes .Button.{ label: "OK" }, and gets a parse error. They check the examples, find ui.button("OK"), and now hold two official answers: the ratified one that fails and the shipped one the spec does not teach.

options.name: Build the ratified spelling
options.detail: The dot-construction tree ships in the UI epoch: nameable widget types, .Button.{ } construction, and migration of the function-call examples. The ratified text becomes true. Until it ships, the spec marks the spelling unbuilt.

options.name: Amend the text to the shipped surface
options.detail: This ballot amends the ratified decision: the function-call constructors become the recorded UI surface, and dot-construction for UI trees is withdrawn. The spec tells the truth today, and a future architecture may still propose a new surface through its own ballot.
options.code: tree :: ui.box([ui.button("OK", on_click: done)])   // now also the ratified story

options.name: Mark unbuilt now, decide with the architecture
options.detail: The minimal gate ships immediately: the spec marks the spelling ratified-but-unbuilt so no reader is misled. The spelling decision itself waits for card #1588's architecture evaluation, because the tree syntax should serve whichever architecture wins. This ballot then reopens with that evidence.
options.code:
// spec, today: ".Button.{ } is ratified and unbuilt; the shipped surface is ui.*"
// spelling decided together with the #1588 architecture result

recommendation.why: The tree spelling and the UI architecture are one design surface, and the architecture evaluation is already open. Deciding the spelling first risks deciding it twice; the honest gate costs one spec sentence now.

whyNot.reason: It spends a future epoch's design budget now, before the architecture it must serve is chosen.
It ratifies the stopgap surface as final while the evaluation that could justify something better is still open.

recommendation.tradeoff: The spec carries an admitted unbuilt marker for a while, which is the truthful state anyway.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared building now, amending to the shipped surface, and deferring with a gate, recommending the gated deferral tied to the open architecture card.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested deleting the UI-tree promise entirely and building a third spelling. Deletion is option B with less honesty, and a third spelling multiplies the defect, so neither joined.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass confirmed C already combines A and B: it ships B's honesty sentence now and preserves A's build path for the epoch.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with the do-it-right principle and B with the spec-tells-the-truth-today principle. Both stand as real picks for owners who weigh those highest.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked C as a decision that just re-queues itself. Repair: C names its reopening condition, the #1588 evaluation result, so it cannot drift as an unowned deferral.

decisions.title: One naming lexicon for every surface, or one per tool
decisions.gist: Decide whether the ratified naming and abbreviation law also governs CLI verbs, flags, manifest keys, and file names.
decisions.lesson: Inside .jet source, naming is law: plain English words, a closed abbreviation list, fixed acronym casing. Outside it, nobody governs. jetpack says uninstall where the stdlib says remove. Some CLI verbs are kebab-case and some are smashed together. dry-run is a flag on one command and a subcommand word on its sibling. The abbreviation list allows len and fmt but the CLI ships deps, pkg, a11y, semindex, and sbom unexamined. The audit found the same concept named differently on two surfaces repeatedly.
decisions.story: A user who learned remove from the collections API types jetpack remove and is told the verb is uninstall. The language taught them a word; the tool speaks a different one.
decisions.inWild:
names.remove("Bob")        // the stdlib verb
$ jetpack uninstall http    # the tool verb for the same job
$ jet fix --dry-run         # preview as a flag
$ jet codemod dry-run plan  # preview as a word

options.name: One lexicon, every surface
options.detail: The ratified source-naming law extends to CLI verbs, flags, manifest keys, and tool file names. One blessed-abbreviation list and one acronym table govern all of them, rendered from one home per the corpus law. Violations retire through the retirement mechanism, mechanically where possible.
options.code:
$ jetpack remove http       # the stdlib verb, everywhere
$ jet fix --dry-run
$ jet codemod --dry-run plan   # preview is a flag, one spelling
// deps:, a11y, sbom: each either joins the blessed list by ballot or renames

options.name: Two lexicons, both written
options.detail: Source keeps its law; the CLI and manifests get their own written convention honoring command-line tradition, including its short verbs and abbreviations. Each lexicon has one home and a guard, but they are allowed to differ, and the remove versus uninstall split becomes official.

options.name: Per-tool freedom
options.detail: No new law. Each tool keeps naming as it likes, and review taste is the only guard. Zero migration and zero new rules, at the cost of the story's collision staying permanent and ungoverned.
options.code: // status quo: the next tool picks its own verbs

comparisons.note: One naming voice across the language, standard library, and go tool subcommands; gofmt-era users never meet a second lexicon.
comparisons.code: $ go mod tidy   // plain words, one casing, tool and library agree

recommendation.why: The beginner meets Jet as one product, and every second lexicon is a second thing to learn. The source law already works; extending its reach deletes a whole class of collisions the audit proved are live.

whyNot.reason: It writes the collision into law: the same job keeps two official names, and every future surface must pick a side.
Ungoverned naming is how uninstall, a11y, and dry-run-the-word happened; keeping it guarantees more.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some familiar command-line spellings rename or must earn a place on the blessed list by ballot.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one lexicon, two written lexicons, and per-tool freedom, recommending one lexicon because the beginner meets Jet as one product.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested aliasing both verbs everywhere and a lexicon for verbs but not flags. Universal aliases are two spellings with extra steps, and a half-scope lexicon leaves the flag collisions standing.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested one lexicon with a short blessed-exception list for entrenched command-line terms. That is option A as written, since the blessed list already exists for exactly this.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the unix-tradition argument, and it stands for an owner who wants the CLI to feel native to shell users first. C gains zero-churn honesty.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with ecosystem familiarity: users expect sbom and a11y in security and web tooling. Repair: the blessed list takes new rows by ballot, so familiar terms can earn their place explicitly instead of by drift.

decisions.title: The hash glyph's four jobs: keep them positional, or rename the colliding one
decisions.gist: Decide whether # keeps four position-split jobs, or the interpolation selector stops borrowing marker names.
decisions.lesson: One glyph does four jobs, split by position: applied-rule markers (#Debug before a type), fixed-size lists ([T#4]), package version pins (textkit#1.2.0), and interpolation format selectors ("{x#Fixed(2)}"). Three never collide in a reader's mind. The fourth does: {u#Debug} borrows the literal marker name Debug, but is not a marker, is never checked against the marker table, and carries its own error codes. Same glyph, same word, two judgment systems.
decisions.story: A learner who just wrote #Debug above a struct writes "{user#Debug}" in a string and reasonably believes it is the same feature. When their custom marker works in one position and not the other, the error text has no shared vocabulary to explain why.
decisions.inWild:
#Debug
struct User { name: String }      // a marker: judged by the rule table

print("{user#Debug}")             // a format selector: same word, different machine
prices :: [Float#4]                // a size: third job
deps: { textkit: "lib#1.2.0" }    // a pin: fourth job

options.name: Keep four jobs, write the one law
options.detail: All four spellings stay. The positional split becomes written law in the canonical syntax file and the reserved-space listing, and the selector's docs stop calling its arguments markers. The dot glyph already carries nine positional jobs under ratified law, so the precedent is established.
options.code:
// unchanged surface; Syntax.rs and jet inspect reserved record all four jobs
print("{user#Debug}")   // documented: a format selector, not the #Debug marker

options.name: The selector stops borrowing #
options.detail: Interpolation selectors move to a spelling that cannot be mistaken for a marker, such as a colon: {x:Fixed(2)}, {user:Debug}. Markers, sizes, and pins keep #. The one genuine mind-collision is deleted, and the format language gains room to grow without shadowing marker names. Migrated mechanically per the retirement mechanism.
options.code:
print("{user:Debug}")
print("{distance:Unit(km)}")
print("{x:Fixed(2)}")   // format language, visibly not the marker plane

options.name: The size separator moves instead
options.detail: Fixed-size lists respell ([T * 4] or similar) and # keeps rules, pins, and selectors. This trades the low-confusion job away while keeping the high-confusion pair, so it only wins if the size spelling has independent problems.
options.code:
prices :: [Float * 4]
print("{user#Debug}")   // the marker-name collision remains

comparisons.note: Format specs live after a colon inside braces, a lane that never collides with decorators or attributes.

recommendation.why: Three of the four jobs never share a reader's headspace; the selector does, because it borrows the marker plane's own names. Moving it to a colon deletes the one real confusion and matches the format-spec lane every mainstream language already teaches.

whyNot.reason: The dot precedent covers positions that never swap names; {u#Debug} versus #Debug shares the word itself, which documentation cannot un-collide.
It spends a migration on the job nobody confuses and keeps the one people do.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every interpolation selector in the corpus migrates once, mechanically, under the retirement mechanism.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared documenting the four jobs, moving the selector, and moving the size separator, recommending the selector move because it deletes the only name-level collision.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested retiring selectors entirely in favor of method calls inside interpolation. That trades a format language for expression noise in every string, so it did not join the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested keeping # while banning marker-name reuse in selectors. A name-ban inside one spelling is a lexicon patch on a structural collision, so it folded into A's honest form.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened A with the dot-glyph precedent and ratified positional law, and C with a genuine check of the size spelling. A stands as the zero-churn pick.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked B with churn and with colon overload risk in future format specs. The migration is mechanical under the retirement mechanism, and the colon lane is reserved to selectors alone, so B survives.

decisions.title: The dollar sign's next job, if the at-sign takes compile time
decisions.gist: Decide what the freed dollar sign does next; this only takes effect if D-ONCE-AT1 picks the swap.
decisions.lesson: If D-ONCE-AT1 chooses option D, the at-sign becomes the compile-time mark and the dollar sign is freed. Prime one-character syntax space is scarce: today only a handful of glyphs remain unclaimed. This ballot decides whether the dollar sign is reassigned at once or held with a published reservation. If D-ONCE-AT1 picks any other option, this ballot closes as moot and the dollar sign keeps its ratified compile-time job.
decisions.story: A maintainer sees the swap land and asks what the dollar sign now means. The honest answers are nothing yet, or a new job chosen deliberately — not a leftover glyph that three parser paths still half-recognize from its old life.
decisions.inWild:
// after the swap, these are the candidate futures for $:
home :: env.$HOME              // config surfaces read the environment
names.map(f => f.upper())       // today
names.map($.upper())            // or: a shorthand parameter
emit { fn get_$name() = $body } // or: $ stays only inside emit templates

options.name: Publish the reservation, assign later
options.detail: The dollar sign goes into jet inspect reserved with the candidate jobs named and a minting condition: each candidate arrives by its own ballot when its feature area reaches design. Nothing is spent on speculation, and no parser path keeps a half-meaning.
options.code:
$ jet inspect reserved
$   reserved: unassigned (freed by D-ONCE-AT1=D)
    candidates: environment access, shorthand parameter, template splice
    condition: the owning feature area reaches its design epoch

options.name: Environment and config access
options.detail: The dollar sign reads the environment in config surfaces: $HOME in env.jet and deploy files, matching decades of shell folklore exactly where config authors expect it. Ordinary program code does not use it, keeping the glyph rare by design.

options.name: Shorthand closure parameter
options.detail: The dollar sign becomes the implicit parameter in short closures: names.map($.upper()), pairs with $1 and $2 for arity two. A large everyday ergonomic surface — deliberately the opposite of a rare job, for an owner who wants the glyph earning daily rent.
options.code:
names.map($.upper())
scores.filter($ > 90)
pairs.sort_by($1.age <=> $2.age)

options.name: Template splice only
options.detail: The dollar sign returns to its original job and nothing else: splices inside comptime emit templates, where shell and template folklore already point. Outside emit blocks it becomes free space again, reserved and published as in option A.
options.code:
emit { fn get_$name() => $ty = self.$field }
// outside emit: $ is reserved, listed, unassigned

recommendation.why: The epoch rule: freed space is spent when a feature area earns it, not the day it opens. A published reservation keeps every candidate alive, and each future assignment arrives with its own design evidence.

whyNot.reason: Environment access is real but belongs to the config domain's own design pass, where its typing and audit story live.
A daily-ergonomics surface deserves its own worked design against Jet's existing closures, not a rider on a glyph swap.
Keeping a half-job alive re-creates the situation this slate exists to end: one glyph, one leftover meaning, three parser paths.

recommendation.tradeoff: The glyph sits idle for a while, visibly, in the reserved listing.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared reserving, environment access, shorthand parameters, and splice-only, recommending the published reservation under the epoch rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested currency and unit literals and a pipeline hole marker. Units already ride #UnitFamily and the pipeline design is unstarted, so both fold into the reservation's candidate list.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested splice-only plus a published reservation for the rest, which is exactly option D as written, so no new option was added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with the config-folklore fit and C with the daily-rent argument. Each stands as a real pick for an owner who wants the space earning now.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A as deferral dressed as discipline. Repair: the reservation row names its candidates and its minting condition, so every deferral is falsifiable and owned.

decisions.title: select() element types: one generic door or an Int-only law
decisions.gist: Pick whether select can receive from a channel of any type, or is Int-only and says so.
decisions.lesson: Sema accepts `.recv(rx)` on any `Receiver<T>` and only asks that the arms agree on T. Both runtime doors take i64: `jet_scheduler_select_int_channels` and its timed twin. The Cranelift bridge calls the same door. So a `Receiver<Str>` select is a promise the runtime cannot keep. The gap is undocumented today. This ballot picks which side becomes the truth.
decisions.story: A user builds a task group with a `Str` channel for log lines. The checker accepts the select and says nothing. The value then has no door to come through at run time.
decisions.detail: Sema: crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerTaskGroup.rs, `infer_taskgroup_select` at line 698 and `infer_select_recv` at line 769. Runtime: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Scheduler.rs:2422 and crates/jet-codegen/src/SchedulerHost.rs:139. Cranelift: crates/jet-jit/src/Concurrency.rs:807 calls the timed Int door. Whatever wins must hold on AOT, `jet run`, and the interpreter per I9, with the meaning in the Prelude.

options.name: Generic select on any T
options.detail: Widen the scheduler door to a type-erased channel handle, so select carries any element type. Sema keeps its current promise, and the doc comment becomes true without any new restriction.
options.technical: One Prelude function takes erased handles and returns the winning arm plus its payload slot. Emit, Cranelift, and interpreter marshal only.
options.code:
(tx, rx) :: tasks.channel<Str>()
tx.send("log line")
line :: g.select().recv(rx).wait()   // Str, Float, or a struct: all work
print(line)

options.name: Int-only, rejected in sema with a diagnostic
options.detail: Sema errors on a non-Int element type with what, why, and fix. The doc comment states the restriction. Users tag work with an Int and read the payload after the select.

options.name: Scalars now, aggregates rejected
options.detail: The door carries a tagged 64-bit value, so Int, Float, and Bool all work. Aggregates such as `Str` and structs are rejected in sema with the same diagnostic shape as option B.
options.code:
(tx, rx) :: tasks.channel<Float>()
temp :: g.select().recv(rx).wait()    // ok: Int, Float, Bool

(tx2, rx2) :: tasks.channel<Str>()
g.select().recv(rx2).wait()
// Error [E13xx]: `select` carries scalars only; `Str` is not one

recommendation.why: The bug is a silent promise, not a missing feature. The smallest complete fix makes the checker say what the runtime already does. It costs one diagnostic and one doc line, and it holds on every tier at once.
recommendation.tradeoff: Users who want a typed select must send an Int signal and read the payload after. That is one extra line, and it is visible instead of silent.

whyNot.reason: A type-erased scheduler handle is new runtime machinery on three tiers to serve a case nobody has hit yet.
A scalar tier is a third rule to teach, and it still rejects the `Str` case the report actually names.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft offered a generic door and a sema rejection, and recommended the rejection because it closes the silent promise now.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested auto-boxing every payload and a compiler-inserted Int tag channel. Both hide a type change from the user, so neither joined the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced option C, which serves scalars through a tagged word and rejects the rest.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option A a single Prelude entry so the tiers stay marshalling only, and gave option B a fix line that names the workaround.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether option B blocks a real program. Any payload still arrives through `rx.receive()` after the select, so the pattern stays available.

decisions.title: The print family: which spellings survive
decisions.gist: Five print spellings greet a beginner today. Choose the surviving set.
decisions.lesson: The first hour of Jet shows ambient print, io.print, io.println, io.sprint and io.repr with no stated difference. I8 wants one mechanism with a small beginner surface. No ratified decision picks the survivors; D-ONCE-VERB1 rules collection verbs only.
decisions.story: The corpus audit found the five spellings introduced together in examples/features/io/io_surface.jet:5-7 as a sweep. A beginner cannot tell which one to reach for. The say-it-once law asks for one home per job.
decisions.inWild: Python ships one print with an end parameter. Rust splits print and println. Swift ships one print that ends the line. Each language that kept many spellings teaches them forever.
decisions.detail: Sources: examples/features/io/io_surface.jet:5-7; BUILTIN_PRINT at crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_surface.rs:173; jet_std_io_sprint at crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/IoLineStream.rs. D-PRELUDEX1 ratified the qualified io.* spelling under #NoPrelude, so the ambient survivor keeps a qualified twin. Interpolation "{x}" already builds strings, and "{x=}" already labels values, which covers sprint and much of repr.

options.name: One print, line-ending, with its qualified twin
options.detail: Ambient print(x) prints x and ends the line. io.print is its #NoPrelude twin per D-PRELUDEX1. io.println and io.sprint retire by fmt/fix rename; sprint callers become "{...}" interpolation. io.repr retires; repr output comes from the "{x=}" selector or a repr format selector. Example: print("hi") replaces io.println("hi"); s := "{user}" replaces io.sprint(user).
options.code: print("done: {n}")

options.name: The print/println pair
options.detail: print(x) writes without a newline; println(x) ends the line, matching Rust and C. io.sprint and io.repr retire the same way as option A. Beginners learn two verbs on day one. Example: print("loading"); println(" done").
options.code: println("done: {n}")

options.name: Keep all five and teach them
options.detail: The five spellings stay. The io_surface example and the docs gain one table naming each job. No retirement ships. The beginner surface stays five wide.
options.code: io.sprint("{n}")

recommendation.why: One verb with the newline included is the beginner default every survey of first programs supports. Interpolation already covers string building and labeled debug output, so the other spellings are second homes.
recommendation.tradeoff: Printing without a newline needs an explicit io call or a later ballot. Rust habits expect println, and option A retires that muscle memory.

whyNot.reason: Two verbs double the day-one surface to serve the rarer no-newline case, which the qualified io form can carry instead.
Five taught spellings for one job is the exact coat the say-it-once law deletes.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft carried the one-verb option and the Rust-style pair, and recommended one verb because the newline default serves the first program.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tried an end parameter on print, Python style. It adds a named argument to the day-one verb, so it stays out of the menu and waits for a real need.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced option C, keep and teach, as the no-retirement floor.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option A its migration route: fmt/fix renames through the #1718 retirement table, and interpolation absorbs sprint and repr callers.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked what breaks without a no-newline print. Progress meters do; the qualified io form or a later ballot carries them, and the ratchet counts the survivors.

decisions.title: Lower-level Core doors: fold into one ladder or ratify the split
decisions.gist: Pick how a lower-level Core API relates to its friendly sibling, so `expert` stops being an unexplained second door.
decisions.lesson: `core.crypto.expert.hkdf_sha256` takes raw bytes. Its `core.crypto` sibling takes typed keys. Neither door mentions the other, and no decision governs the split. One split already has a rule: `core.random` against `core.crypto.random`, ratified as D-RANDSPLIT1 and taught by an example. Card #1579 makes layering law and grandfathers nothing, so the two shapes cannot both stand.
decisions.story: A user reaches for HKDF, finds two functions with one name, and picks the one whose arguments compile. Nothing tells them one door is the lower rung. They ship the raw-bytes call by accident.
decisions.inWild:
use core.crypto as crypto
use core.crypto.expert as expert

key :: crypto.hkdf_sha256(...)     // typed keys
raw :: expert.hkdf_sha256(...)     // raw bytes, no cross-reference, no rule
decisions.detail: Sema routes all three module names together: crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/core_call.rs lines 179 and 366. `core.http.client` is a ratified builder (D-HTTPLIB2=B, D-HTTPLIB4=B, D-HTTP-CLIENT2=A) but still states no rung boundary against `core.http.get`. Evidence: card #1725 and the xcut-ladder tables in docs/proposals/corpus-say-it-once.md.

options.name: One module, two rungs
options.detail: Fold the lower-level function back into its base module under a name that says what it gives up. The `expert` module goes away, so there is one import and one page per subject.
options.code:
use core.crypto as crypto

key :: crypto.hkdf_sha256(key: k, salt: s, info: i)      // default rung
raw :: crypto.hkdf_sha256_bytes(key: kb, salt: sb, info: ib)  // lower rung
// core.crypto.expert is retired; imports move in one change

options.name: Keep the split, ratify and teach it
options.detail: Two modules stay. Every split carries a decision id, a cross-reference line in both doors, and one golden example showing the same result through each. This copies the rule D-RANDSPLIT1 already sets for random.
options.technical: The layering law gains one row shape: base module, lower module, decision id, example path. A split without a row fails the layering check.

options.name: No rule; each module states its own shape
options.detail: Nothing changes in the code. Layering stays a per-module habit, and the four drifts on card #1725 close as documentation only.
options.code:
use core.crypto.expert as expert
raw :: expert.hkdf_sha256(...)   // unchanged: no cross-reference, no example, no rule

recommendation.why: The precedent already exists and works. D-RANDSPLIT1 keeps two doors and makes the boundary teachable, and the same row closes every other split at once. No API is deleted and no caller moves.
recommendation.tradeoff: Each split costs a decision id, two doc lines, and one example. That is paid by the person who adds the split, not by users.

whyNot.reason: Folding raw-bytes calls into the friendly module puts the sharp tool in the beginner's first import.
That is today's silence with paperwork, and card #1579 rules out grandfathering.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft offered folding into one ladder against ratifying the split, and leaned on the random precedent.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a compiler-enforced rung attribute on every Core item. That is a new mechanism for a four-case problem, so it stayed out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass checked whether some subjects fold and others split. Mixing both leaves users guessing which shape a subject uses, so it was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option A a name suffix that states the cost, and gave option B a row shape the layering check can read.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked who decides that a split is worth keeping. The answer is the ballot for that split, reviewed with the change that adds it.

decisions.title: policy.auto_derive: a deny entry or its own boolean
decisions.gist: Pick whether refusing auto-derive is spelled on the generic deny list or stays a private boolean key.
decisions.lesson: Five project-wide refusal switches exist in five shapes. `policy.lints.deny` is the one generic list, ratified as D-LINTPOLICY1=A, and it takes lint codes. `policy.auto_derive` is an `Option<bool>` with its own parser, its own malformed-value diagnostic, and its own codegen check. Card #1570 collapses the authority keys but has not landed. The question is which surface auto-derive uses.
decisions.story: A team wants to refuse auto-derive across the project. They already deny lints by code in one list. They then learn that this one refusal lives somewhere else, in a different shape.
decisions.detail: policy.auto_derive is a bespoke boolean beside the general lint policy. Owner law (2026-08-07): config surfaces take names, never codes — see card #1748. Any migration lands on the NAMED deny list (deny: [auto_derive]), not a code.

options.name: Migrate to the named lint deny list now
options.detail: auto_derive registers as a named lint; policy.lints.deny: [auto_derive] replaces the boolean via the #1718 retirement rename. Depends on #1748 (named lint selection in config). Example: policy { lints { deny: [auto_derive] } }.
options.code: deny: [auto_derive]

options.name: Wait for the #1570 authority block
options.detail: Keep the boolean until the one authority block in the package manifest ships, then fold the knob into it. One migration for users instead of two.
options.code: policy { auto_derive: false }

options.name: Keep the boolean as a stated exception
options.detail: Ratify the boolean as the one blessed policy toggle and record why it stands outside the lint plane. No migration ships.
options.code: policy { auto_derive: false }

recommendation.why: One policy plane with named entries reads clearly and deletes a bespoke boolean. The named deny list is the general mechanism the say-it-once law points at.
recommendation.tradeoff: Option A waits on card #1748 landing named lint selection; the boolean survives until then.

whyNot.reason: The authority block has no landed design date, so the coat survives indefinitely.
Blessing a bespoke boolean beside a general mechanism contradicts I8 and the say-it-once law.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft offered migrating now, waiting for the authority block, or keeping a documented exception, and recommended migrating now.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a general manifest key-to-lint mapping table. That is a mechanism for one key, so it stayed out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass checked accepting both spellings for a window. Two live spellings for one refusal is the exact drift this card closes.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave option B a single combined migration note, and gave option C a stated reason on the spec page.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether a lint code fits a build behaviour. Lint codes already name behaviours the build refuses, so the shape holds.

decisions.detail:
Retired by owner order, recorded by Main. The import placeholder cited docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3975. The live text, Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:5056-5058 on dev (4593-4595 on master), is a truncated sentence about a core.linalg ring package with Vec2/3/4 and Mat3/Mat4 aliases over a generic Vec<N>/Matrix<M,N>, tracked by #293. No Core/linalg exists.

Superseded by D-LINALG1, ratified 2026-10-01, which is the live law for fixed vectors and matrices. The Linear algebra section of Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md (line 2412 on dev, 1786 on master) specifies Vec2/3/4, Mat3/Mat4, column-major storage, dot, cross, matmul, transform, transpose and a left-to-right reduction order. The generic tensor and matrix layer shipped as core.compute through cards #443, #1137 and #1118, all done. Card #293 is the core.math libm audit and never owned a matrix layer. Whether Vec2/3/4 become aliases of a number-parameter Vec<N> belongs to card #3505 under D-CONSTGEN1 and D-CONSTGEN2.

Follow-up repository edit, not part of this record: repair the truncated spec sentence to cite D-LINALG1 and core.compute.

decisions.title: Package store folders: name and version first, full fingerprint last
decisions.gist: Should the recovered store-folder rule stand as written, with every folder name ending in the full fingerprint?
decisions.lesson: A fingerprint is a hash that identifies exactly what was built, including its dependencies. The lock file records each package's true identity, and folder names exist for people reading the store. A shortened fingerprint never changes which package the lock selects, but two different builds of one version could then claim the same folder.
decisions.explainer:
This ballot restores an approved rule whose text was lost. The recovered rule says each store folder is <name>-<version>-<full-fingerprint>. The full fingerprint tells apart builds of the same name and version. The lock file entry, never the folder name, is the identity used for correctness.

The one difference from today's code is the fingerprint length. Toolchain pin folders keep 8 hex characters, and package folders keep 12. Option A brings both to the full fingerprint, as the rule says. Option B amends the rule to a shortened fingerprint.
decisions.story: Ana lists her package store and sees fastfetch-2.1.0-3fa9c2d1e0b7. She wants to know whether that folder holds exactly the build her lock file names. With the full fingerprint, the folder name itself answers that.
decisions.inWild:
# Spack default layout: name and version first, then the full 32-character build hash
# (hashes below are illustrative, not real builds)
opt/spack/linux-ubuntu22.04-x86_64/gcc-11.4.0/zlib-1.3-<32-char hash>
# Nix and Guix: the 32-character base-32 hash first, then name and version
/nix/store/<32-char hash>-firefox-118.0
decisions.detail:
Why this is open again. D-PM1 was ratified on 2026-06-13 as one of D-PM1 to D-PM8. Card #1735 imported it as a spec-only placeholder citing docs/spec/philosophy.md:306 and docs/spec/roadmap.md:127. Those lines were later removed, and commit 27cf90eda deleted the source plan. The owner asked for this ballot to be open for review with its real text.

Recovered text, from git show 27cf90eda^:docs/plans/jetpack-jetos/unified-ecosystem.md, section 10: "D-PM1 — Store path layout: Content-addressed store with human-readable names first: <store-root>/<name>-<version>-<full-fingerprint>/. The full plan fingerprint disambiguates when the same name+version could differ."

The recovered text continues: "Identity for correctness is always the lockfile entry, not parsing the directory name. Phase 1 stores source trees only; Phase 2 adds compiled artifact cache." The phases are history. The same section says U1, U2 and U10 renamed jet.toml, jet.lock and ~/.jet/store to pkg.jet, .jet/lock and the hangar store. It says the architecture stands.

The same section defines the fingerprint as covering the whole dependency ancestry: change a deep dependency and every identity above it changes, old and new coexist, and nothing is mutated in place. Invariant PM-I2 says the store is append-only and the fingerprint is verified on creation and on demand.

Live code that follows the rule, on the dev branch on 2026-10-10. HangarRoots.jet:174 documents fastfetch-2.1.0-<fp> with name and version first and fingerprint last. Realized.jet:51, HangarListing.jet:286-290 and StoreIntegration.jet:42 cite the same rule. HangarListing.jet:289-290 says never hash-first, and that the lock file, not the folder name, is identity. Lock Schema.jet:1 cites D-PM1 and D-PM3.

The mismatch. JetPin.jet:86-90 names toolchain folders jet-<version>-<fp> with the first 8 hex characters of sha256 over version and platform. HangarListing.jet:309-313 names package folders with the first 12 hex characters of a sha256 fingerprint. The rule says the full fingerprint, which is 64 hex characters for sha256.

Why the mismatch matters. Identity still comes from the lock, so the wrong package is never selected by a folder name. But 8 hex characters are 32 bits and 12 are 48 bits. Two different builds of one name and version could share a folder, and a deliberate collision at 48 bits is within reach of a determined attacker. PM-I2 would then have to refuse or detect it.

How other stores name folders. Spack's documented default install layout ends in name-version-hash with the full 32-character hash. Its leading architecture and compiler parts vary by Spack version [INFERENCE: from Spack documentation, not checked against a live install]. Nix and Guix put a 32-character base-32 hash of 160 bits first, then the name and version. The Go module cache uses module@version and relies on go.sum for verification.

Out of scope. D-PM2 to D-PM8 and PM-I1 to PM-I8 are not reopened. Restoring section 10 as a live page under Docs/spec/packaging is a documentation step after ratification.

options.name: As written: full fingerprint
options.detail: The recovered rule stands unchanged. Every store folder is <name>-<version>-<full-fingerprint>, and the lock file entry stays the identity used for correctness. Toolchain pin folders and package folders both move to the full fingerprint, so a folder name always matches the fingerprint in the lock file.
options.technical: JetPin.jet trust_pin_object_id and HangarListing.jet store_short_entry_id stop truncating the sha256 hex. store_expected_entry_id then expects full-length ids, so existing hangar folders are renamed in one cutover, and the store verify path checks the full fingerprint. Restore section 10 of the deleted plan as a live page under Docs/spec/packaging.
options.code:
<store-root>/fastfetch-2.1.0-<64 hex fingerprint>/
<store-root>/jet-0.9.0-<64 hex fingerprint>/
// identity for correctness: the .jet/lock entry, never the folder name

options.name: Amend: a shortened fingerprint
options.detail: The rule is amended so folder names end in the first 12 hex characters of the fingerprint, as package folders do today. Toolchain pin folders move from 8 to 12 characters. The lock file stays the identity, and the store must detect two builds that claim one folder.
options.technical: Amends D-PM1's path text. JetPin.jet moves from 8 to 12 hex characters. The store adds an explicit check that refuses a second build whose short id collides with an existing folder of different full fingerprint.
options.code:
<store-root>/fastfetch-2.1.0-3fa9c2d1e0b7/
<store-root>/jet-0.9.0-a41c09d2e3f1/
// identity for correctness: the .jet/lock entry, never the folder name

comparisons.note: The module cache names folders by module and version and verifies content through go.sum.

recommendation.why: It is the rule you approved, the code already follows its name-first order and lock-file identity, and the full fingerprint removes any chance that two builds share a folder.
gains: The approved rule is restored word for word.
A folder name matches its lock-file fingerprint exactly.
No two different builds can share a folder.

losses.loss: Folder names grow from about 30 to about 80 characters.
losses.mitigation: Name and version stay first, so store listings still sort and read by package name.

whyNot.reason: A shortened fingerprint lets two builds of one version claim the same folder, and it needs a new collision check.

recommendation.tradeoff: Longer folder names, for names that match the lock file exactly.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by BallotRework on 2026-10-10 from the recovered plan text; validated offline with validate.mjs. No Tower write was made.

Submit with decision reopen first, so the stored import record moves to the current ballot process, then decision update with this file and --ready. Card #1735 is done, and a done card never shows the decide lane, so move it to deciding until the owner rules.

After ratification of A: toolchain pin and package folder ids use the full sha256 hex; existing hangar folders are renamed in one cutover; store verify checks the full fingerprint. Run the Jetpack store and trust tests, including StoreIntegration and the pin tests.
decisions.situation: When Jetpack installs a package, it keeps it in a store folder named for the package and version, ending in a fingerprint, a hash of exactly what was built. You approved this rule in June, but its text was lost when a planning document was deleted, so the board shows only a placeholder. The code follows the rule, except that folder names shorten the fingerprint to 8 or 12 characters instead of the full hash. This vote restores the rule and settles that length; we recommend the rule as written, with the code moving to the full fingerprint.

surface.gist: Should the recovered store-folder rule stand as written, with every folder name ending in the full fingerprint?
surface.lesson: A fingerprint is a hash of exactly what was built. The lock file says which build is used; folder names are for people. Today's code shortens the fingerprint in folder names.

current.note: Folders shorten the fingerprint to 12 or 8 characters.

wild.note: Name and version first, then the full build hash.

options.name: As written: full fingerprint
options.gist: Restore the approved rule; folders end in the full hash.
gains: Matches the approved rule word for word.
Folder names match the lock file exactly.

options.name: Amend: shortened fingerprint
options.gist: Keep 12 characters and add a collision check.
gains: Shorter folder names.
losses: Two builds could claim one folder.

recommendation.why: It is the rule you approved, and the full fingerprint means no two builds ever share a folder.
gains: The lost rule is restored as written.
Folder names match lock entries.

losses.mitigation: Name and version stay first, so listings still read by name.

whyNot.reason: Short names can collide and need extra checks.

recommendation.tradeoff: Longer folder names, for names that match the lock file.

attempts: Keep a 12-character prefix; rejected because two builds of one version could then share a folder.
Keep name and version first so people read and sort by name, and let the full hash prove the build; kept.

decisions.title: What a keyless --no-sign publish does to registry metadata
decisions.gist: When an unsigned publish may skip the registry metadata refresh.
decisions.lesson: A publish writes two trust records. The package author's signature is optional with --no-sign; D-PKGSIGN1 ratified that choice. The registry metadata chain uses the registry root key and protects every consumer. A publisher without a key or pin cannot refresh it. Today, keyless --no-sign fails with E2607 even when a new registry has no chain. A publisher-side skip would break resolution for pinned consumers on an established registry.
decisions.story: Sam starts a private registry for a game-jam team. He publishes the first package with --no-sign; no root key exists, and no consumer has a pin. The command fails with E2607 even though the registry has no chain. Ada runs the same command without a key on her company's signed registry. A silent metadata skip there would break her teammates' resolution of older signed versions.
decisions.inWild:
Sam's release script runs this command:

$ jet publish game-core --no-sign

The new registry has no checkpoint or sparse metadata, so the command succeeds. Against the company's established signed registry, the same command fails with E2607.

options.name: Registry-side gate
options.detail: Skip the metadata refresh only when the registry repository has no checkpoint and no sparse metadata. This identifies a never-signed registry. Established chains always refresh. Ada fails closed with E2607, while Sam's first publish works.
options.code:
$ jet publish game-core --no-sign --registry jam
published game-core 0.1.0

$ jet publish game-core --no-sign --registry company
error[E2607]: registry metadata chain cannot be refreshed

options.name: Always require a chain
options.detail: Every publish requires a signable root key. --no-sign still creates or uses a local registry key for the metadata layer, but it leaves the author signature empty. Sam must run keygen once.
options.code:
$ jet keygen --registry jam
created registry root key
$ jet publish game-core --no-sign --registry jam
published game-core 0.1.0

options.name: Retire keyless registries
options.detail: Unsigned registries are unsupported. --no-sign leaves only the author signature empty on an otherwise signed chain. The keyless test path is deleted.
options.code:
$ jet publish game-core --no-sign --registry jam
error: unsigned registries are unsupported

recommendation.why: A lets Sam publish the first package to a registry with no chain. It still protects established registries because the repository must lack both a checkpoint and sparse metadata before refresh is skipped.

whyNot.reason: B makes Sam create a root key before the first publish. It rejects the new keyless registry even though no metadata chain exists to refresh.
C removes keyless registries and deletes their test path. It avoids the edge case by banning the use case instead of checking registry state.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds a registry-repository check before refresh can be skipped. The check must treat either existing artifact as an established chain.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compares a registry-side gate, a required chain, and retired keyless registries. It recommends A because it permits a new empty registry without weakening an established chain.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a publisher-side skip, a local pin check, and a manual override. Those tactics do not distinguish a new registry from an established one, so they stay inside the three main options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested option A with option B's local key creation. That still requires Sam to create a key, so it adds no value to the recommended gate.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each option on its own terms. A protects old signed versions, B gives every registry a signed chain, and C removes an unsafe deployment class.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested missing checkpoints, stale sparse metadata, and a keyless publisher on an established registry. A fails closed in the established case and skips only an absent chain, so it remains the recommendation.

decisions.title: Where a contributor's secret values may live
decisions.gist: Which storage places the Jet vault supports for secret values.
decisions.lesson: Jet projects declare named secrets, and the vault stores the values in one encrypted file inside the repository. Some people and companies do not allow secret values in git at all, even encrypted. Other tools let each contributor keep values in a store they already use, while the project only declares names. This choice decides which storage places Jet supports.
decisions.story: Riley joins a Jet project at a company that forbids committing secret material to git, even encrypted. The project declares three API keys. Riley already keeps every credential in the company password manager. Today the vault offers only the in-repo encrypted file, so Riley cannot use it at all.

options.name: Repo vault only (today's law)
options.detail: The one place a value can live is the encrypted file in the repository, shared through git and unlocked per recipient. Zero setup for new contributors, and it works offline. People who must not put secret material in git cannot use the vault at all.
options.technical: Status quo D-JPK-SECRET1=A: .jet/secrets.age, age-style recipients file, memory-only decrypt at activation, every read carries the Secret effect.
options.code:
$ jetpack secrets set stripe-dev sk_live_x
ok: stored in .jet/secrets.age
$ git add .jet/secrets.age   # encrypted, committed, shared
# policy shops: no path forward

options.name: Blessed provider fleet
options.detail: Jet ships native backends for common stores: the repo file, the system keyring, and major password managers. Each contributor picks one, and the project only declares names. Every backend is code Jet must build, test, and keep working on three platforms forever.
options.technical: Per-backend native integrations (keyring APIs, manager CLIs or APIs), a provider registry, and per-platform CI coverage for each backend.
options.code:
$ jetpack secrets provider use bitwarden
$ jetpack secrets get stripe-dev
ok: fetched from Bitwarden
# Jet now owns Bitwarden, 1Password, Vault, keyring... code

options.name: Repo vault plus system keyring
options.detail: Two built-in places: the shared repo file, or the contributor's own system keyring. This covers the no-secrets-in-git rule with no third-party code. People who live in external password managers must copy values into one of the two by hand.
options.technical: One extra native backend: Secret Service on Linux, Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows. No external-manager integrations.
options.code:
$ jetpack secrets provider use keyring
$ jetpack secrets set stripe-dev sk_live_x
ok: stored in the system keyring (repo untouched)
# password-manager users: copy values in by hand

options.name: Repo vault default plus one command bridge
options.detail: The repo file stays the beginner default with nothing to configure. An expert may declare one provider command, per project or per user; Jet runs it to fetch a named value into memory. Any store works through this one mechanism, including keyrings and password managers. The command runs only after the existing trust prompt.
options.technical: One provider contract: the command receives the secret name, prints the value on stdout, and a non-zero exit fails activation with a registered diagnostic. Keyring and manager recipes ship as documented presets, not code paths. Values never touch argv, logs, or the hangar.
options.code:
# default: unchanged
$ jetpack secrets set stripe-dev sk_live_x   # → .jet/secrets.age

# expert, per user: any store through one contract
$ jetpack config set secrets.provider "bw get password jet/{name}"
$ jet run
trust: this project fetches secrets with `bw ...` — allow? [y/N] y
ok: stripe-dev fetched (memory only)

comparisons.note: One declared contract, 27 provider backends; each contributor picks their own store. The contract idea is the lesson; maintaining the fleet is the cost.
Encrypted values live in git and contributors hold keys. Same shape as Jet's vault today, and the same objection from no-secrets-in-git shops.
Plaintext files outside git: easy, leaky, and unshareable. The thing both Jet's vault and SecretSpec exist to replace.
comparisons.code: STRIPE_KEY=sk_live_x   # sits in plaintext on every machine

recommendation.why: One extra mechanism serves every external store, so the vault keeps its zero-setup default while the no-secrets-in-git rule stops excluding whole companies.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the vault unusable for anyone whose policy forbids secret material in git.
A backend fleet is permanent upkeep across three platforms, and every backend invites behavior drift.
It serves keyring users but still shuts out password-manager and central-vault users.

recommendation.tradeoff: A provider command is arbitrary code that can read secrets. That is accepted because it runs only after the existing first-entry trust prompt, and the beginner default never runs one.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the status-quo repo file with a native provider fleet and recommended one generic command bridge over per-vendor backends.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested SOPS-file import, per-secret provider pins, and a hosted Jet secrets service. They folded into the fleet and bridge options because the storage place is the only real axis.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the keyring from a native backend into a documented bridge preset, so option D covers option C's use case without a second code path.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option A with its offline and zero-drift virtues and credited option B with first-run polish that a raw command cannot match.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the bridge as a secret-stealing vector and a beginner trap. The trust prompt, the untouched repo-file default, and a registered failure diagnostic repair both, so D stands.

decisions.title: Compose secret values from named inputs
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet composes secrets and when it resolves the inputs.
decisions.lesson: Secret composition builds a value from named secrets and literal text. A template is a pattern with placeholders. Store-time composition resolves it during a write. Read-time composition resolves it when code asks for the value. Store-time data can become stale after rotation. Read-time data stays current but repeats work. Missing inputs must fail without revealing values. The vault stores flat name/value pairs and reads one name. This choice changes source surface and audit record. References: docs/research/2026-07-24-devenv-parity.md:199 and crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:10-14,147-149.
decisions.story: Maya runs a service with separate DB_HOST, DB_USER, and DB_PASSWORD names. She wants DB_URL for a local tool, but rotation must not leave an old assembled value in the vault. The owner must choose whether Jet owns that dependency graph or Maya writes the assembly in ordinary Jet code.

options.name: No composition
options.detail: Keep secrets as a name list. Jet adds no composed-secret surface. The user reads each part with core.crypto.vault.get and assembles the result in normal code. This keeps the vault flat and leaves composition policy with the application. References: crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/jetpack_config.rs:1-5, crates/jetpack/src/CLI/realize.rs:623-626, and crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:142-149.
options.technical: A declared missing name fails activation with E1263. An undeclared read keeps the current Option behavior and returns no value. Composition happens in user code at read time. Jet encrypts only the named parts through crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs:303-357. It does not store a composed value. There is no composition audit event. Any application audit event names the output and input names only. Errors, logs, fixtures, snapshots, and ballot text contain no secret values.

options.name: Materialize at store time
options.detail: Add a command that resolves named inputs and writes the result as a normal vault entry. The user reads DB_URL through the same existing secret path. This is simple to inspect as one stored name, but rotation leaves DB_URL stale until the user composes it again. References: crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs:360-371,303-357 and crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:10-14,147-149.
options.technical: The compose command fails before writing if any input is absent. It reports E1263 with the missing input name and leaves the store unchanged. Resolution happens once at compose time. The composed pair is encrypted in .jet/secrets.age with the other pairs. A later source rotation does not change DB_URL. The audit event records compose DB_URL from DB_HOST, DB_USER, and DB_PASSWORD at a store revision. It records names only. Errors, logs, fixtures, snapshots, and ballot text contain no secret values.
options.code:
jetpack secrets compose DB_URL --template DB_URL_TEMPLATE --from DB_HOST,DB_USER,DB_PASSWORD
template: postgres://{DB_USER}:{DB_PASSWORD}@{DB_HOST}/app
result: stored encrypted entry named DB_URL
missing input: E1263 no secret named DB_PASSWORD
rotation: DB_URL keeps its old assembled value until compose runs again
audit: compose DB_URL from [DB_HOST, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD]

options.name: Compose in the read API
options.detail: Add a core.crypto.vault.compose call that takes a template and explicit input names. The caller keeps control of the final read, while Jet supplies one shared composition rule. This avoids stale stored results, but each caller repeats the template and dependency list. References: crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:142-149 and crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/core_calls.rs:258-271.
options.technical: A missing input returns no composed result and reports E1263 with that input name when the caller requires the result. Resolution happens on every read. Jet stores only the source pairs and derives the composed value in memory. Each read audit event names DB_URL and its input names. Rotation changes the next read. Errors, logs, fixtures, snapshots, and ballot text contain no secret values.

options.name: Declare a read-time composition
options.detail: Extend the environment secret declaration with a named template and its input names. Code still calls core.crypto.vault.get for DB_URL, so beginners get one named secret and experts can inspect the dependency list. Activation can validate the graph before any value read. References: docs/research/2026-07-24-devenv-parity.md:199, crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/jetpack_config.rs:1-5, and crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:21-44,488-490.
options.technical: The compiler checks template shape, input names, duplicate names, and cycles. Activation checks that every referenced input exists. A missing input fails closed with E1263 naming the missing input. Resolution happens on every get read. Jet encrypts only source pairs and derives DB_URL in memory. The plan and each read audit event name DB_URL and the sorted input names. Rotation changes the next read. Errors, logs, fixtures, snapshots, and ballot text contain no secret values.

comparisons.note: Docker Compose interpolates named inputs when it evaluates a configuration. That resembles read-time declaration, but it does not define encrypted vault storage or Jet activation.
Kubernetes commonly keeps secret references separate and lets the application assemble a connection string. That resembles no composition and keeps dependency policy in application code.

recommendation.why: D gives beginners one named read and gives experts an explicit dependency list. It fails closed before activation, reflects rotation on the next read, and records names without values.

whyNot.reason: A pushes the same template and missing-input rules into every application. It also gives activation no shared dependency graph or composition audit event.
B leaves a stored composed entry stale after any source rotation. The user must remember a second compose action before the result changes.
C shares the read mechanism but repeats templates and input lists at every call site. Activation cannot know dependencies unless source declarations repeat them.

recommendation.tradeoff: D changes the current name-list shape and makes dependency names part of project source. It accepts that visible policy because it keeps values encrypted, keeps rotation current, and gives activation one auditable graph.

reviewPasses.base: The draft compares no composition, store-time materialization, imperative read-time composition, and declarative read-time composition. It covers missing inputs, storage, rotation, and name-only audit records.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested command-only composition, automatic environment variables, and encrypted template files. Those choices either hide dependencies or add a second source of truth.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The synthesis pass combines D declarative dependency graph with C read-time derivation. It keeps one named read while preserving explicit expert control over inputs.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Cooperative review strengthened each option on its own terms. A protects simplicity, B gives materialized portability, C gives call-site control, and D gives shared activation policy.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Adversarial review tested missing inputs, source rotation, stale stored results, template cycles, audit leakage, and repeated declarations. D keeps names visible and values out of every error and audit path.

decisions.checkInstructions: After ratification, implement only the selected surface and update criterion 4. Keep all diagnostics and audit records name-only.

decisions.title: Define secret metadata and activation rules
decisions.gist: Choose which metadata a secret carries and what activation checks.
decisions.lesson: Secret metadata describes a secret name without storing its value. Required means activation must have an entry. Optional means absence is allowed. Allowed environments limit where code may request the name. Rotation policy states when a value needs review. A compiler can check declarations and metadata shapes. It cannot prove an encrypted store contains a value because the vault opens at runtime. This choice sets the source contract and missing-secret response. References: crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:21-44,488-490 and crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:142-149.
decisions.story: Leon shares one env.jet across laptop, CI, and production. CI needs API_KEY, but a local preview does not. Today every listed name is checked the same way at activation. Leon needs metadata that keeps optional local work alive without allowing a required CI run to start with a missing secret.

options.name: Keep names only
options.detail: Keep the current secrets name list. Every listed entry remains required at activation. The compiler checks list syntax, but it cannot check local store presence before a run. Missing API_KEY shows E1263 at activation, not check time. No description, optional flag, allowed environment list, rotation policy, default, or generator policy exists. References: crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/jetpack_config.rs:1-5, crates/jetpack/src/CLI/realize.rs:623-626, and crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:21-44,488-490.
options.technical: validate_declared_secrets calls Secrets.get for each name and returns E1263 on the first absent entry. The current get path returns an Option after reading the encrypted store. The compiler sees names only. Activation remains the only missing-entry check. The error names API_KEY and contains no secret value. Errors, logs, fixtures, snapshots, and ballot text contain no secret values.
options.code:
env.dev {
    secrets: ["API_KEY"]
}
check: syntax only
activate: E1263 no secret named API_KEY
timing: activation only
output: name only, never a secret value

options.name: Declare a full typed schema
options.detail: Make each secret a typed declaration in env source. Carry description, required or optional status, allowed environments, rotation policy, per-profile default, and generator recipe. The compiler checks field types, duplicate names, environment labels, policy conflicts, and generator shape. Activation checks the selected environment and required store entries. Missing API_KEY shows E1263 at activation with the name only. References: crates/jetpack/src/CLI/realize.rs:623-626, crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:21-44,488-490, and crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:142-149.
options.technical: A known active profile lets the compiler reject an invalid allowed-environment rule. A dynamic profile defers that check to activation. Required false permits absence. Rotation can warn or fail at activation according to the declared policy. The compiler still cannot prove local ciphertext contains API_KEY. Reuse E1263 for a missing required entry and name the environment. Errors, logs, fixtures, snapshots, and ballot text contain no secret values.

options.name: Add activation metadata beside the name list
options.detail: Keep the env source as a name list. Add a typed metadata command that writes non-secret records to .jet/secrets.meta. Activation reads required status, allowed environments, rotation, descriptions, defaults, and generator recipes from that record. The compiler still sees names only. Missing API_KEY shows E1263 at activation with the name only. References: crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs:29-42,252-306, and crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:21-44,488-490.
options.technical: The metadata record becomes a second project input beside .jet/secrets.age. Activation checks its fields and then checks required store entries. The compiler does not cross-check the metadata file, so mismatches appear at activation. A missing required entry reports E1263 with API_KEY and the active environment. Descriptions and rotation state can appear in names-only inspection. Metadata files, errors, logs, fixtures, snapshots, and ballot text contain no secret values.
options.code:
env.ci {
    secrets: ["API_KEY", "PREVIEW_TOKEN"]
}
jetpack secrets metadata set API_KEY --required --allowed-environment ci --rotation 90d --description "CI credential" --default-profile none --generate none
file: .jet/secrets.meta
activate: E1263 required secret named API_KEY is missing for environment ci
output: name only, never a secret value

comparisons.note: Kubernetes commonly declares a secret name and key separately from the workload. Availability is checked when the workload starts, which resembles activation metadata more than compiler proof.

The parity note names required, default, description, and generated value as the missing Jet metadata surface. This ballot adds allowed environments and rotation because activation needs policy boundaries.
comparisons.code:
required: true
description: CI credential
default: none
generate: none

recommendation.why: B puts policy beside the name that uses it. The compiler can catch malformed declarations and profile conflicts before a run. Activation still fails closed for a missing required name and uses a name-only E1263.

whyNot.reason: A cannot express optional local secrets, allowed environments, rotation policy, or per-profile generation. Every listed name stays required and every store check waits for activation.
C gives activation useful policy but hides it from the compiler and creates a second project input. A stale or mismatched metadata record is found only when activation starts.

recommendation.tradeoff: B changes the current name list into a typed source schema and keeps local store presence as an activation check. It accepts that boundary because ciphertext is not available to the compiler and all missing-secret output stays name-only.

reviewPasses.base: The draft compares the current name-only model, a full source schema, and activation metadata beside the name list. It covers compiler checks, activation timing, and name-only missing errors.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested inferred requiredness, environment variables as metadata, and a global policy file. Those choices hide ownership or weaken the link between a name and its rule.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The synthesis pass combines B's source schema with C's activation checks for local store presence. It keeps static policy visible while preserving the runtime trust boundary.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Cooperative review strengthened each option on its own terms. A preserves the current surface, B gives static policy checks, and C keeps source syntax small with runtime metadata.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Adversarial review tested missing required names, optional local names, profile mismatch, stale metadata, rotation, generated policy, and value leakage. B keeps policy visible and errors name-only.
