decisions.checkInstructions: After ratification, implement only the selected metadata model and update criterion 5. Register or reuse the missing-required diagnostic. Keep every error and log name-only.

decisions.title: Program allocator: how a program swaps or wraps its memory allocator
decisions.gist: How a Jet program names the allocator that serves every allocation in it.
decisions.lesson: Every program needs memory while it runs. An allocator is the part that hands out that memory. Most programs never think about it and use a hidden default. Sometimes you want to swap it or wrap it: count every byte, cap total use, trace leaks, or use a faster allocator for a game. Rust calls this the global allocator. Jet has scoped allocators (arenas, fixed buffers) but no way to change the allocator for a whole program.
decisions.story: Last night a test program looped and quietly ate 34 gigabytes. The machine ran out of memory and the kernel killed every agent session on it. Overnight work was lost. A capped wrapping allocator would have stopped that program in seconds with a clear error. User wants every Jet program to be able to name such an allocator — the same power Rust's global allocator gives, in one clean Jet spelling.

options.name: Profile fact in package.jet
options.detail: The package file names the program allocator, the same way freestanding targets already name theirs. Code does not change. Beginners never see it. The build dossier shows it, so audits see exactly which allocator shipped.
options.technical: Extends the ratified D-TARGET-ALLOC1 typed profile fact from freestanding profiles to hosted programs. The fact names any value whose type implements the core allocator trait. Sema validates it; codegen routes the program heap through it on every tier (I9). Absent fact = hidden default, unchanged.

options.name: Marker on one binding in the entry file
options.detail: A marker names one binding as the program allocator, like Rust. The choice lives in code, so it travels with the source and needs no package file. Sema rejects two markers or a marker outside the entry file.
options.technical: New ratified marker (I7) valid on one top-level binding in the entry module. Duplicate marker and wrong-placement diagnostics required. Same allocator trait and tier-parity rules as option A.

options.name: Scoped allocator block
options.detail: A block makes everything inside it allocate through a named allocator, like Jai and Odin contexts. Wrapping run() covers the whole program. Fine control, but the ambient rule must answer hard questions: what happens across task boundaries, stored values, and returns.
options.technical: Ambient allocator as dynamic scope. Needs defined behavior for values that outlive the block, task spawn inheritance, and interaction with arenas and #Region. Highest semantic surface of the four.

options.name: No program allocator — scoped only
options.detail: Keep today's surface: hidden default plus explicit arenas and fixed buffers where you choose them, like Zig's explicit style. Honest and simple, but there is no way to wrap every allocation, so caps, counting, and leak tracing stay impossible program-wide.
options.technical: Status quo. D-REGION1 arenas and D-FIXED-BACKING1 fixed buffers remain the only user-facing allocators.

comparisons.note: One attribute on one static swaps the program allocator.
No global. Every function takes an allocator argument; maximum honesty, maximum ceremony.
An implicit context carries the allocator; blocks override it in scope.
Replace global operator new and delete anywhere in the program; powerful and famously easy to get wrong.
comparisons.code: void* operator new(std::size_t n) { return my_alloc(n); }

recommendation.why: Freestanding Jet already names its allocator as a typed profile fact (D-TARGET-ALLOC1, ratified). Extending that one fact to hosted programs keeps one mechanism for every target (I8). The allocator is a whole-program shipping fact, so it belongs beside the program's other shipping facts, visible in the audit dossier. Beginners never touch it; experts get swap, wrap, cap, and trace with one line.

whyNot.reason: It hides a whole-program fact inside one source file and adds a new marker plus placement diagnostics. Once freestanding uses profile facts, a marker is a second mechanism for the same fact.
An ambient scoped allocator must answer escape, storage, and task-boundary questions that arenas and #Region already answer. It duplicates Jet's existing scoped tier at high semantic cost.
It leaves counting, capping, and tracing impossible program-wide. Last night's crash is the direct cost of that gap.

recommendation.tradeoff: Swapping allocators means editing package.jet, not just code. A quick experiment touches configuration. That is one clear named line, and the choice stays where audits can see it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a package profile fact, a Rust-style entry marker, a scoped ambient block, and the status quo. It recommended the profile fact because freestanding targets already ratified exactly that shape.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also weighed a build flag, linker-level interposition, and per-package allocators. The first two folded into option A as spellings of the same fact; per-package allocators were dropped for creating two heaps in one program.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested profile fact plus scoped block together, but arenas and #Region already are Jet's scoped tier, so it collapsed back to option A. Wrapper composition (mem.Counting.over) was kept so one fact also covers wrapping.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each option: the marker is greppable and mirrors Rust habits, the block matches Odin and Jai practice, and the status quo is Zig's honest explicitness. Each option now shows its best real form.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked option A on custom allocators, test harnesses, and config friction. The fact accepts any user allocator value, tests set it in their env profile, and the recommendation survived unchanged.

decisions.title: The CLI system: the program struct, shared flags, and the standard pack
decisions.gist: How a program declares its commands and shared flags, and how much the common case gets for free.
decisions.lesson: A program with subcommands wants three things: add a command with almost no ceremony, declare a shared flag once, and get standard behavior such as --verbose and --version for free. Today each subcommand needs its own struct, an enum variant, and a dispatch arm; nothing is shared and nothing is free. This choice picks the whole shape, so the most common cases carry the least friction.
decisions.story: Priya builds a deploy tool: plan, apply, rollback. Today that is three structs, one enum, and a three-arm dispatch before any logic. She wants --verbose everywhere, so she types it three times and rollback drifts. A teammate runs `deploy --verbose apply` and gets an unknown-subcommand error. Adding a fourth command means touching four places.

options.name: Each command declares its own
options.detail: Keep today's law. Every subcommand struct lists every flag it accepts, including repeated ones. Nothing is shared, nothing is free, and nothing is hidden. The cost is the ceremony the story shows: struct plus variant plus dispatch arm per command, duplication of shared flags, and silent drift.
options.technical: No change. D-CLIFLAG1 stands: no root flag namespace; argv before the subcommand token must be the subcommand name.

options.name: App struct with a command enum field
options.detail: The entry takes one #CLI struct. Its scalar fields are the shared flags; one enum-typed field is the subcommand. Shared flags parse before or after the subcommand word. Per-command ceremony stays: each new command is still a struct, a variant, and a dispatch arm.
options.technical: E1308 extends: the entry parameter may be a #CLI struct containing exactly one enum-of-#CLI field. Shared scalars parse anywhere in argv; variant fields parse after the token. A shared-versus-variant name collision is a compile-time error.

options.name: The bare map registry
options.detail: The program is a map from command names to functions; each function's parameter list is its flags. Adding a command is one function and one line. But shared flags need a separate mechanism, inline member docs move to parameters, and the map is a second program shape next to the struct everyone already knows.
options.technical: #CLI on a registry binding of function values declares the entry. The literal is read at compile time; each callable must have CLI-mappable parameters. Shared flags arrive through a hoisted #CLI struct parameter.

options.name: Marker registration on each function
options.detail: Each command function carries its own marker, Cobra-style. No registry at all — the marker is the registration. The cost is a scattered surface: no single place lists the program's commands, ordering is unclear, and discovering the full shell surface means reading every file.
options.technical: #Command(name?) on a top-level function registers it as a subcommand. Command list order follows declaration order across files, which imports can reshuffle.

options.name: The program struct: fields are flags, callable members are commands
options.detail: One #CLI struct is the whole program. Scalar fields are shared flags with the same #Doc and = defaults as today. A callable member is a command: bind an existing function with =, or define a method whose self reads the shared flags. The member name is the command word; member #Doc is its help summary. #CLI(Standard) grants working --verbose, --quiet, --color, and --version with automatic wiring. One-command tools skip the struct entirely: parameters on fn run are the flags. Growth never rewrites: signature, then struct, then members.
options.technical:
Member kinds split at compile time: scalar fields become root flags parsed anywhere in argv; callable members become subcommands named by their lowercased member name. A method's self is the parsed shared-flag struct, read-only. A bound function may declare one parameter of the struct's type to receive shared flags; its remaining scalar parameters, S61 `= expr` defaults, and parameter #Doc define that command's flags.

#CLI(Standard): --verbose/-v and --quiet/-q drive core.log level, --color=auto|always|never honors NO_COLOR, --version prints the package version. Bare #CLI keeps only auto --help. jet inspect expand shows every inferred piece.

Flag-versus-command name collisions and callable members inside #Codable structs are compile-time errors. Callable members are not data: never constructed, serialized, or positional. Zero arguments or root --help prints the command list with member #Doc summaries and exits 0 (existing orientation law).

E1308 extends to param-direct entry: fn run(path: Path, threshold: Int = 100) maps parameters as flags. Amends D-CLIFLAG1: the enum subcommand form is deleted (greenfield). The dossier, embedded schema, and completions carry command names and summaries; signature changes surface in the existing breaking-shape report.

comparisons.note: A struct declares configuration and lists subcommand types in one place — the closest prior art for option E's program struct.
Function signatures become CLI flags with defaults and help from annotations — the parameter mapping options C and E share.
A plain dict of callables becomes the whole CLI — option C's map, but untyped and runtime-reflected.
Imperative AddCommand registration plus PersistentFlags — option D's scatter with extra ceremony; the video mine that raised this ballot.

recommendation.why: The program struct keeps the struct surface Jet already ratified and absorbs the registry into it. Fields are flags, callable members are commands, and one #Doc and one = expr rule serve every member kind. The most common actions become the cheapest: one signature for a one-command tool, one member per new command, one marker argument for the standard pack. Shared flags reach commands through self with no injection mechanism to learn, and the whole shell surface is one readable struct.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the ceremony and the silent drift the story shows, and root-position flags stay errors.
It fixes shared flags but keeps struct-plus-variant-plus-dispatch ceremony for every command, so the most common action stays the most expensive.
The map is a second program shape whose shared flags and member docs need separate mechanisms the struct already owns.
Scattered markers leave no single place that lists the program, so the shell surface becomes implicit and hard to audit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Struct members now come in two kinds, data and callable, and the derive must keep them apart from construction, serialization, and positional filling. That is accepted: the kinds are visually distinct in source, every misuse is a compile-time error, and the payoff is one struct that is the whole program.

reviewPasses.base: The draft was rebuilt twice: first around a bare map registry, then, on owner direction, around the program struct. The final menu ranks five shapes by friction on the most common actions.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested auto-discovery of public functions, an imperative add() builder, and manifest files, and kept marker-per-function as option D. The rest folded away: implicit surface, runtime ceremony, or truth split across files.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass produced the recommendation itself: option B's struct and option C's registry fuse into E, where callable members are the registry entries. Owner review resolved the member-kind question to both bound and method forms and deleted the standalone map.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C with compile-time map checking and B with the Standard pack, which composes with any winner. C still splits shared flags from commands; B still pays per-command ceremony.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked E: flag-versus-command name collisions, callable members leaking into #Codable serialization, self mutation expectations, bound-function signature drift, and positional ambiguity. Compile-time collision and serialization errors, read-only self, the existing breaking-shape report, and named-value-wins repair those, so E survives.

decisions.title: Command files: which mark makes one
decisions.gist: Which mark, if any, sets a command file apart from every ordinary Jet file.
decisions.lesson: Four commands can be replaced by a function of the same name: run, build, dev, and test. That function may live in any file. A command file is the optional home for one of them, and it sorts where its name puts it. This choice picks the mark that name carries. D-ONCE-AT1 already reserved `@` for locations, addresses, and sources, and left the location half to a later ballot. The underscore ladder gives none, one, and two their own meanings: ordinary, disabled, machine space.
decisions.story: Ravi joins a team and opens a package with thirty files at the root. He wants the entry point and the build override. He scrolls the listing, misses run.jet between record.jet and streams.jet, and greps for `fn run` instead. In Python he would have seen __init__.py at the top without looking.
decisions.inWild:
// today — the two files a reader wants are scattered
README.md
api.jet
billing.jet
package.jet
queue.jet
run.jet
streams.jet

// option A — `@` is 0x40, above every letter
@build.jet
@run.jet
README.md
api.jet
billing.jet
package.jet

// option B — `_` is 0x5F, below every capital
README.md
__build.jet
__run.jet
api.jet
billing.jet
package.jet

options.name: `@` marks a command file
options.detail: The four optional homes are `@run.jet`, `@build.jet`, `@dev.jet`, and `@test.jet`. `@` sorts above every letter, so the set opens each listing. Every tool still sees them: `ls`, `rg`, `fd`, and a `*.jet` glob all match. Jet already reads `@` as at a location, and a filename is a location. Gain: one mark, already taught, visible everywhere. Loss: `@run` renders as a mention in Markdown and chat, so prose needs backticks.
options.technical: Mints the location half of D-ONCE-AT1, which that decision left to a later ballot. Prefix `@` on a filename names a command location. Infix `@` stays the package-source separator under D-JPK-REF1, and prefix and infix never meet. At package root, `@` is legal only in front of a command name; `@notes.jet` raises an error. The underscore ladder keeps its identifier-only meaning, so `__` never becomes user-typeable on files. Amends D-VERDICT-678-1: `run.jet` loses reserved status.

options.name: `__` marks a command file
options.detail: The four homes are `__run.jet`, `__build.jet`, `__dev.jet`, and `__test.jet`. The underscore ladder extends to filenames: none is ordinary, one is disabled, two is machine space. Gain: the ladder already exists, and readers coming from Python know the shape on sight. Loss: `_run.jet` and `__run.jet` differ by one character and mean opposite things, and `__` gains a second user-typeable meaning.
options.technical: Amends D-NAME-SIGIL1 so machine space covers compiler-recognized files as well as generated symbols. Identifiers stay forbidden. At package root, `__` is legal only in front of a command name. The disable rule keeps matching exactly one leading underscore, so `___run.jet` disables a command file. Sorts below capitals, so `README.md` still opens the listing. Amends D-VERDICT-678-1: `run.jet` loses reserved status.

options.name: No mark; plain names and a homing lint
options.detail: The names stay ordinary words: `run.jet`, `build.jet`, `dev.jet`, `test.jet`. A lint asks a package with several files to home each override in the matching name. Gain: nothing renames, and a beginner's first file stays a plain word. Loss: the files sort into the middle of the listing, so the surfacing that started this choice never arrives.
options.technical: No ladder or sigil amendment, and no change to any ratified spelling. Adds the homing lint plus four conventional filenames as documentation-level convention. `run.jet` keeps the status D-VERDICT-678-1 gave it. Command functions stay discoverable wherever they are declared.

comparisons.note: `@` names a repository address: `@rules_go//go`. The mark reads as at this source, which is the same word Jet gives it.
`__init__.py` and `__main__.py` sit in the interpreter's dunder namespace. They sort near the top, and the spelling still feeds a tutorial industry.
`build.zig` is a plain-name command file at the root. Every Zig reader knows it, and it still sorts under b like any other file.

recommendation.why: `@` sorts above every letter and stays visible to `ls`, ripgrep, fd, and shell globs. It carries a meaning Jet already teaches, so the rule costs one character and no new concept. It also leaves the underscore ladder untouched.

whyNot.reason: The mark works, but `_run.jet` and `__run.jet` differ by one character and mean opposite things. It also gives `__` a second user-typeable meaning that the ladder did not have.
Plain names home the code without surfacing it. `run.jet` still hides between `record.jet` and `streams.jet`, which is the itch that opened this decision.

recommendation.tradeoff: `@run` reads as a mention in Markdown, chat, and issue trackers, so every mention in prose needs backticks. A URL escapes it to `%40`, which shows up in registry and raw links. Scaffolds and the missing-command diagnostic must carry the one-sentence rule so the mark never needs a tutorial.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a marked command file against plain names and against tooling alone, and found that only a mark puts the four files at the top of every listing.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a leading dot, bang, tilde, capitals, and a command directory. A dot hides the file from `ls`, ripgrep, fd, and `*.jet` globs, bang and tilde fight shells, capitals sort unreliably, and a directory buries the entry.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a command directory holding many named entries. It was dropped because `#Job fn` under D-JPK-TASKRUN1 already names extra entry points, so a third naming mechanism would break I8.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C with scaffold comments and a `jet map` listing, and strengthened B with a diagnostic that names the disabled twin. Both improve, and neither gains sort-to-top surfacing.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on mention rendering in Markdown and chat, on URL escaping to `%40`, and on the visual echo of infix `package@source`. Backticks cover prose, command files are never fetched by name, and prefix never meets infix in the grammar.

decisions.title: Command functions: override or requirement
decisions.gist: What run, build, dev, and test do when the matching function is absent.
decisions.lesson: Each of the four commands can be replaced by a function of the same name. D-BUILDENTRY1 already rules that `jet build` runs `fn build` when it is defined, and the batteries pipeline when it is not. This choice decides whether the other three follow that same law, and what a file argument on the command line selects. It also decides what happens when two files define the same command.
decisions.story: Mara writes one file and types `jet test`. Nothing overrides anything, so she expects the stock harness to find her checks and run them. A month later her team adds `fn test` to start a database first. Same command, same file, one extra step and no new rule to learn.
decisions.inWild:
// no command function anywhere — every command still works
jet run    → runs the file
jet build  → standard compilation
jet dev    → watch, then re-run run
jet test   → stock harness over every #Test

// a file argument names the target, not the lookup
jet build main.jet   → the package override, scoped to main.jet
jet test parser.jet  → the stock harness, scoped to parser.jet

options.name: One law: every command function is an optional override
options.detail: An absent function means stock behavior. Run executes the file, build compiles it, dev watches and re-runs run, and test runs the stock harness. A file argument sets scope, not lookup, so a package override still applies when you name a file. Two definitions of one command raise an error. Gain: one sentence covers four commands. Loss: `run.jet` gives up its reserved status.
options.technical: Generalizes D-BUILDENTRY1 to run, dev, and test. A command function is discovered by declaration across the package, which matches D-JPK-FILENAME2 and the shape of E1239. A duplicate raises a new error listing every file that declares it, and lint policy can soften it to a warning. Amends D-VERDICT-678-1 so `run.jet` is an ordinary filename. Only a `fn build` inside the named file outranks the package override.

options.name: The entry is required; the other three are optional
options.detail: A package must declare `fn run` or be a single script file. Build, dev, and test keep their stock behavior when nothing overrides them. Gain: `jet run` never has to guess what a package meant. Loss: two rules where one would do, and a library package must declare an entry it will never run.
options.technical: Keeps the reserved-entry half of D-VERDICT-678-1 and generalizes D-BUILDENTRY1 to dev and test only. A package with no `fn run` and no script body raises a missing-entry error even when it ships no executable. Duplicate handling matches option A.

options.name: No search; an override counts only in a declared home
options.detail: A command function counts only inside its own command file or `package.jet`. A `fn build` written in `util.jet` is ordinary code and nothing calls it. Gain: resolution is one file lookup, and no scan can surprise a reader. Loss: the command file stops being optional, so a one-file script can never override its own command.
options.technical: Replaces package-wide discovery with a fixed lookup table of command files plus `package.jet`. Duplicates become impossible by construction, so the duplicate error is not needed. The command-file mark stops being optional for any project that overrides anything.
options.code:
// util.jet
fn build(b: BuildContext) { … }   // ordinary function, never called by `jet build`

comparisons.note: `build.zig` is the only home for the build graph, and a project without one cannot be built by the build command at all.
Every command works with no user code, and `build.rs` is a pure addition. Nothing is required before it is wanted.
comparisons.code: cargo test   // works with zero configuration

comparisons.note: A missing script is an error, so each command a project wants must be written out before it will run once.
comparisons.code: npm run dev   // fails without a dev script

recommendation.why: One sentence covers four commands, and it is the sentence D-BUILDENTRY1 already ratified for build. Nothing is required before it is wanted, so a single file and a large package obey the same rule. A file argument never silently drops the project's own override.

whyNot.reason: A library package gains a required entry it never runs, and a reader learns two rules instead of one. The guess it prevents does not happen, because a missing entry already has a stock answer.
A single-file script could not override its own build or test, which is the case the optional design exists to protect. It also makes the command-file mark mandatory.

recommendation.tradeoff: Without a command file the compiler scans the package to find each override, where a command file is a direct hit. `run.jet` loses reserved status, so D-VERDICT-678-1 needs that amendment recorded. Scaffolds ship a commented example override rather than a copy of the real default, so a generated project never freezes today's build logic.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one uniform override law against a required entry and against explicit homes only, and found the uniform law already half-ratified in D-BUILDENTRY1.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a manifest script table, a registration call inside `package.jet`, and per-command rules kept as they are. Each adds a second place to look for the same answer, and none removes a rule.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a required entry with optional everything else, which is option B. It was kept as an option rather than folded, because the entry question is genuinely separable from the other three.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review added the scoping rule that keeps a package override alive when a file argument is present, and the duplicate error modelled on E1239. Both fixes belong to every option.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on scan cost and on the silent-override risk when a stray `fn dev` sits in an unrelated file. The duplicate error removes the stray case, and a command file removes the scan.

decisions.title: FFI namespaces use the one import form
decisions.outcome: No separate import grammar for FFI. Single import stays c.lib; multiple libraries use c.[lib1, lib2], the same .[ ] form every other namespace uses.
decisions.comment: No separate import grammar for FFI. Single import stays c.lib; multiple libraries use c.[lib1, lib2], the same .[ ] form every other namespace uses.

decisions.title: Close cards before milestone review
decisions.outcome: A card closes when its nonempty observable exit criteria are all met with concrete evidence, its patch is integrated into the milestone stream, and no known blocker contradicts the evidence. Do not require a per-card reviewer or duplicate proof. At the milestone boundary, run one composed targeted test sweep and one fresh-context review of the integrated milestone diff; reopen owning cards and criteria for findings, fix and review the correction delta, verify criteria, then explicitly verify the milestone.
decisions.comment: A card closes when its nonempty observable exit criteria are all met with concrete evidence, its patch is integrated into the milestone stream, and no known blocker contradicts the evidence. Do not require a per-card reviewer or duplicate proof. At the milestone boundary, run one composed targeted test sweep and one fresh-context review of the integrated milestone diff; reopen owning cards and criteria for findings, fix and review the correction delta, verify criteria, then explicitly verify the milestone.

decisions.title: The four frozen epoch-3 cards: which ones stay
decisions.gist: Decide which of the four frozen epoch-3 cards belong in epoch 3.
decisions.lesson: Four epoch-3 cards are frozen. A frozen card is owner-only. No agent may plan it, home it, or close it. Two of them were frozen by an old instruction that a later ratified decision has since answered. One was deferred by an owner verdict. One is held back on purpose as the last card of the epoch. Epoch 3 cannot finish while any of them sit in the owner lane.
decisions.story: User asks for epoch 3 to run start to finish with no further owner input. An agent sweeps the board and reaches the four frozen cards. It cannot touch them, so it stops and asks. That single stop is the thing this ballot removes.
decisions.inWild:
$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs card update '#1462' --milestone e3-bucket-1 --by architect
tower: card #1462 is frozen — owner-only until the owner moves it out

$ node plugins/tower/tower.mjs card list --epoch e3 --phase frozen
#480   E3-UL9: mobile native UI (iOS/Android) + app-store pipeline
#677   Typed project compile-latency budgets
#775   Proposal: checked transaction regions (rollback on failure)
#1462  Full suite red: seven truthfulness checks fail on master

options.name: All four run in epoch 3
options.detail: Unfreeze every card and build all four inside epoch 3. Epoch 3 then also carries phone and tablet apps, store signing, and a parked language proposal. That is a large addition to an epoch already holding more than two hundred open cards.
options.code:
# Owner runs four unfreeze commands, then agents work them like any other card.
tower card update '#480'  --phase ready --by owner
tower card update '#677'  --phase ready --by owner
tower card update '#775'  --phase planning --by owner
tower card update '#1462' --phase ready --by owner

options.name: Split by whether the design is settled
options.detail: Build the two cards whose design is settled. Move the two that are not out of epoch 3. Compile budgets and the red test suite stay. Phone and tablet apps and the rollback proposal leave.
options.code:
# Settled, so they stay:
tower card update '#677'  --phase ready --by owner   # D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1 = C
tower card update '#1462' --phase ready --by owner   # plan and criteria already written

# Not settled, so they leave:
tower card update '#480' --epoch e11 --phase ready --by owner
tower card update '#775' --epoch e11 --phase planning --by owner

options.name: All four leave epoch 3
options.detail: Move every frozen card to a later epoch. Epoch 3 closes on the cards that are already moving. Nothing is lost, but the red test suite then stays red inside epoch 3, and no card holds the fix.
options.code:
tower card update '#480'  --epoch e11 --by owner
tower card update '#677'  --epoch e11 --by owner
tower card update '#775'  --epoch e11 --by owner
tower card update '#1462' --epoch e11 --by owner

options.name: Split, and run the test-suite card last
options.detail: Same split as option B, with one added rule. The red-test card runs as the final card of epoch 3, after every other card lands. Its own log already asks for this. That keeps agents from fixing the same test twice.
options.technical: #1462 moves to bucket 4 with the highest workOrder in the epoch. Its exit criterion stays: `cargo test --test truthfulness` passes with no weakened check and no grown allowlist. #677 moves to bucket 2 and implements D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1 outcome C.
options.code:
# Settled work joins the buckets:
tower card update '#677'  --phase ready --milestone e3-bucket-2 --by owner
tower card update '#1462' --phase ready --milestone e3-bucket-4 --workOrder 9999 --by owner

# Unsettled work leaves:
tower card update '#480' --epoch e11 --phase ready --by owner
tower card update '#775' --epoch e11 --phase planning --by owner

$ tower card list --epoch e3 --phase frozen
(no cards)

comparisons.note: Rust moves an unfinished feature to the next train rather than holding the release. The train ships on its date.
comparisons.code:
feature not ready -> next milestone
release date -> fixed

comparisons.note: Work that misses the merge window waits for the next cycle. Nothing sits half-in.
comparisons.code: merge window closes -> queue for next cycle

recommendation.why: It clears the owner lane completely, keeps the work whose design is already ratified, and records the order the red-test card needs. Epoch 3 then has no card an agent cannot touch.

whyNot.reason: It adds phone and tablet apps and store signing to epoch 3, which an owner verdict already deferred on 2026-07-13.
It makes the right split but leaves the red-test card unordered, so a worker may run it early and repeat the same fix later.
It leaves the failing test suite inside epoch 3 with no card that owns the fix, so the epoch would close on red.

recommendation.tradeoff: Compile-latency budgets stay in epoch 3 and add real work. That is accepted because the owner already ratified their design as outcome C.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keeping all four, splitting them, and moving all four out. It recommended the split, because two cards have ratified designs and two do not.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested deleting the two parked cards and merging them into later epoch umbrellas. Both were dropped because they lose the mined design work with no gain.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review added the run-last rule for the red-test card, taken from that card's own log. It became option D.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the all-in option by noting that mobile work has three ratified design decisions and a written seven-slice plan. The 2026-07-13 deferral verdict still outranks that readiness.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what happens if the truthfulness suite fails for a cause outside epoch 3. The card's criteria already allow splitting such a cause into its own card, so option D survives.

decisions.title: How a user caches a pure function's results
decisions.gist: How a Jet user reuses a slow function's past answers.
decisions.lesson: A slow function called twice with the same input does the same work twice. Keeping past answers removes the second run. Jet has the bounded Cache collection, so a user can build that store by hand today. The hand-built version puts a lookup and a save inside every function that wants it. This choice decides who owns the store and how a user asks for one.
decisions.story: Priya builds a shipping quote page. Every quote calls a rate lookup that walks a large table. The same few zones repeat all day, so the same slow lookup runs again and again. She wants the repeat lookup to be free without a store, a check and a save inside her rate function.

options.name: A marker on the function
options.detail: You write one marker above a pure function. Jet keeps one store for that function and answers repeat calls from it. The body stays about its own job. The name does not change, so existing callers and recursive calls are served too. A size argument sets the limit.
options.technical: `#Memo` prefixes a `fn` whose effect row is empty. Sema rejects any other function with a registered code. The key is the argument tuple and reuses the existing hashable check. The store is one `Cache<K, V>` per function, bound 128, least-recently-used eviction; `#Memo(bound: none)` removes the limit. `name.cache()` reports hits, misses, size and bound. A return type of `Iter<T>` is rejected, because a stored iterator is spent after one read. Semantics live in one Prelude part that AOT, the JIT and the interpreter call.

options.name: The caller keeps the store
options.detail: No new syntax. Core gains one helper on Cache that looks up a key and computes the value when it is missing. The user makes the store, names it and decides its size. The store is plain code the user can read, share between functions and clear.
options.technical: Add `Cache.get_or_add(key, compute)`. It returns the stored value, or calls `compute(key)`, stores the result and returns it. Nothing checks purity, because the store is ordinary data. Nothing checks the key beyond the existing `Cache<K, V>` hashable bound. A recursive function must call itself through the store by hand.

options.name: Jet decides on its own
options.detail: No user surface at all. Jet stores results for pure calls it judges slow and repeated. Nobody writes a store, a marker or a size. The cost is that memory use and speed change without anything in the source saying so, and the user cannot turn it off for one function.
options.technical: The compiler picks memoized call sites from a cost model over pure calls. Storage size, eviction and lifetime are compiler policy. Reproducible builds need that policy pinned, or two builds of one source differ in memory use. There is no per-function opt-out and no report.

options.name: A memo value in Core
options.detail: No new syntax. Core gains one function that takes a pure function and returns a caching version of it. The user binds that version to a new name and calls it. The store rides along with the new name and can be reported on or cleared.
options.technical: `core.memo(f, bound: n)` accepts an `fn(K) =[]=> V` and returns `fn(K) =[]=> V` with an attached `Cache<K, V>`. Purity is a type bound, so an impure argument fails at the call. The original name keeps its old behaviour, so recursive calls inside `f` are never served from the store.

comparisons.note: A decorator on the function, keeping the name. The store is bounded at 128 by default and reports hits, misses and size. A second unbounded decorator was added later for one job, which is the wart to avoid.
A library function wraps a function and returns a caching one under a new name. This is option D. Recursive calls inside the original still miss the store.
comparisons.code:
(def fast (memoize zone-rate))
(fast 3)  ; walks the table
(fast 3)  ; answered from the store

comparisons.note: Nothing in the standard library. Users reach for an outside crate that adds an attribute above the function, which is the shape of option A.

recommendation.why: The marker keeps the function's name, so every existing caller and every recursive call is answered from the store with no other edit. Jet already proves a function is pure with the empty effect row, so the one rule that makes stored answers safe is checked by the compiler instead of written in a comment.

whyNot.reason: The store, its size and its lifetime go back into the user's code for every function that wants caching, and a recursive call inside the function still runs the slow path.
A store nobody asked for spends memory nobody can see, and no reader of the source can tell whether a call was answered from it.
The stored answers live under a new name, so recursive calls and every existing caller keep running the slow path until each one is edited.

recommendation.tradeoff: A marker is new user-typed syntax, so it needs a registered spelling, a formatter rule and its own diagnostics. Jet accepts that cost because the marker family already exists, and every other option puts the bookkeeping back into function bodies.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a marker, a caller-held store and an automatic compiler store. It recommended the marker because the function keeps its name, so recursion and existing callers are covered.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the Core memo value that Clojure uses. It folded per-argument keys, time-based expiry and a shared store between functions into the marker's arguments rather than padding the menu.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a marker that also hands back its store. The marker now reports hits, misses, size and bound, so the expert path needs no second mechanism beside it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the caller-held store with a get_or_add helper and gave the automatic option a size limit. Both still hide the store or repeat it in every function.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the marker with recursion, unhashable arguments, lazy returns and unbounded growth. The empty effect row, the existing hashable check, a stated refusal for Iter returns and a bounded default answer each attack, so the marker stands.

decisions.title: A computed field that is slow: how a user asks for the answer to be kept
decisions.gist: How a user asks Jet to keep the answer of a slow computed field instead of working it out on every read.
decisions.lesson: A computed field is a formula over its sibling fields. D-FIELDPOL1 makes it run again on every read, which is always correct and never stale. When the formula is slow, every read pays. The only fix today is to add a second plain field and fill it by hand, which is the bookkeeping computed fields removed. D-MEMO1 already answers this for functions with a `#Memo` marker. This choice picks the field spelling, and must agree with that one.
decisions.story: Mara models a supply route. Her `Leg` struct has a computed `distance` that walks a road graph. A report reads `distance` inside a sort, so the same walk runs thousands of times and the report takes a minute.

options.name: Keep it, and clear it when a source changes
options.detail: You mark the field. Jet keeps the answer after the first read. When any sibling the formula reads is written, the kept answer is dropped and the next read works it out again. Nothing can go stale. Mara marks one field and her report is fast.
options.technical: `#Memo` prefixes the field. The compiler already knows which siblings a computed field reads, because D-FIELDPOL1 orders them and rejects cycles. The same set drives the clear. A write to any of them clears the kept answer. `.{ }` copies and patches start empty. The formula must be pure, the same rule `#Memo` sets for a function.

options.name: Keep it, and never clear it
options.detail: The same marker keeps the answer, but nothing ever drops it. It is simple and fast. A patch that changes a source leaves the old answer in place, so a field can report a number that no longer matches its own formula.

options.name: A second arrow says it is kept
options.detail: No marker. A different arrow spells the kept form: `=>` works it out each read, `==>` keeps it. The struct reads as one table with no prefix. It costs a new arrow that a reader must learn, and it does not match the function spelling.

options.name: Nothing new; write it down by hand
options.detail: Jet adds no surface. A user who needs the answer kept adds a plain field and fills it in the constructor. It is honest about the cost and adds nothing to learn. It also returns the bookkeeping that computed fields removed, and the hand-filled field can go stale with no warning.

options.name: Keep it, and let the user say when to clear it
options.detail: The marker keeps the answer, and the user names the siblings that should clear it. It gives exact control for a formula that reads something the compiler cannot see. It also lets a user name the wrong set and ship a stale field.
options.technical: `#Memo(on: [from, to])` names the clearing set. With no argument, the set is every sibling the formula reads, which is option A's rule.

comparisons.note: Python keeps the answer forever and clears nothing. Its own documentation warns that the object must not change.
Swift has a lazy stored property that runs once. It never clears, and it cannot appear on a value type that gets copied and patched.
comparisons.code: lazy var distance: Double = shortest(from, to)

comparisons.note: Vue keeps a computed value and drops it when a source it read changes. That clear-on-source-change rule is the same one option A uses.

recommendation.why: Mara marks one field and gets the speed, and no reading can ever disagree with the formula. The compiler already tracks the sibling set, so the rule needs nothing new to be exact.

whyNot.reason: It lets a field report a number its own formula no longer produces, which is the silent wrong answer Jet refuses by default.
It adds a second arrow for a job a marker already spells on functions, so one idea would have two shapes.
It returns the hand bookkeeping that computed fields removed, and the hand-filled value can go stale with no warning.
It puts the clearing set in the user's hands, so a wrong list ships a stale field that reads as deliberate.

recommendation.tradeoff: A write to any source clears the answer even when the formula would return the same number. That is accepted because a correct field beats a slightly faster one.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keeping the answer with clearing it against keeping it forever, and recommended clearing, because a computed field must never disagree with its own formula.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the second-arrow spelling, the do-nothing option, and a user-named clearing set. It dropped a time-limit option, because a clock cannot tell whether a source changed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested folding the user-named set into the recommendation as an expert door. It stayed a separate option, since the automatic set is already exact and a second spelling would weaken it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the do-nothing option by noting that a hand-filled field is visible and costs nothing to learn. It still returns the bookkeeping computed fields were built to remove.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked about a formula that reads something outside the struct, which the compiler cannot track. Option A already requires a pure formula, so that case is refused rather than silently kept.

decisions.title: What an automatic fix promises before a tool applies it
decisions.gist: How much Jet promises about an automatic fix.
decisions.lesson: Jet reports can carry a machine-applicable edit. Editors and `jet fix` apply those edits, and coding agents apply them in a loop without a person reading each one. Today the report says nothing about how much to trust an edit. A rename and a guess look identical. This choice decides what Jet promises when it offers a fix, and what a tool may safely do with that promise.
decisions.story: Priya is porting a 40-file service to Jet. She starts an agent, closes her laptop, and lets it run overnight. The agent applies every fix Jet offers, rechecks, and repeats. In the morning she needs two things: the errors are gone, and nothing was silently changed into something she did not mean. She never reads the individual edits.
decisions.inWild:
# The agent's overnight loop. It never reads the fix sentence.
while jet check src/ --json > reports.jsonl; do
  jq -c 'select(.fix_edits | length > 0)' reports.jsonl | apply-edits
  [ $? -eq 0 ] || break
done

# Two reports from one run. Which of these is safe to apply unread?
{"code":"E0102","what":"nothing named `pirnt` exists here",
 "fix_edits":[{"new_text":"print"}]}

{"code":"E0311","what":"this value is used after it moved",
 "fix_edits":[{"new_text":"value.copy()"}]}

options.name: Four grades, the vocabulary Rust already uses
options.detail: Every edit carries one of four words: safe, may-be-wrong, has-placeholders, or unknown. Tools choose which grades they apply. Gain: a reader who knows Rust knows this at once, and tools written for that model port over. Loss: three of the four words mean some version of 'do not trust this', so the tool author still has to pick a policy Jet never states.
options.technical: Adds `applicability` to `jet.report/v1` with the closed enum `safe`, `maybe_incorrect`, `has_placeholders`, `unspecified`. Amends D-REPORT-MACHINE1. `jet fix` applies `safe` only. Every grade needs a registry entry and a golden.

options.name: One class: an edit exists only when it is always right
options.detail: Jet offers an edit only when applying it is correct every time. A repair that depends on what the author meant carries no edit at all. The fix sentence still teaches the person what to do. Gain: no grades to learn, and no tool ever has to choose a policy. Loss: helpful-but-uncertain suggestions become prose only, so an agent cannot act on them mechanically.
options.technical: No new field. The rule moves to the raise site: a checker attaches an edit only when the repair is determined by the program, not by intent. `fix_edits` stays as specified. A guard test fails any diagnostic that attaches an edit for an ambiguous repair.
options.code:
{"code":"E0102",
 "fix":"did you mean `print`?",
 "fix_edits":[{"new_text":"print"}]}

{"code":"E0311",
 "fix":"copy the value, or move the later use above this line",
 "fix_edits":[]}

$ jet fix src/
src/a.jet: applied 1 fix

options.name: Two words: safe and suggested
options.detail: An edit is either safe to apply unread or a suggestion a person should look at. Tools apply safe edits and show suggestions. Gain: one bit, easy to explain, and it keeps uncertain suggestions usable by an editor. Loss: 'suggested' hides real differences — a placeholder to fill in and a plausible guess get the same word.
options.technical: Adds `applicability` to `jet.report/v1` with the closed enum `safe`, `suggested`. Amends D-REPORT-MACHINE1. `jet fix` applies `safe`; `jet fix --suggested` prompts. Editors show suggestions as code actions.

options.name: Safe means proved: applying every safe edit always makes progress
options.detail: Same two words as C, but 'safe' becomes a promise Jet keeps and tests. Applying every safe edit and rechecking must reduce the report count and must never add a new problem. A loop that runs to zero is guaranteed to end. Gain: an unattended agent can trust the loop, not just the edit. Loss: a repair that cannot be proved to make progress ships as a suggestion until someone proves it.
options.technical: Adds `applicability` with the closed enum `safe`, `suggested`. Amends D-REPORT-MACHINE1. Adds a conformance property: for any source, applying all `safe` edits and rechecking yields strictly fewer reports and introduces no report absent from the previous round. Fixture-proved per release; a violation is a release blocker.
options.code:
{"code":"E0102","applicability":"safe",
 "fix_edits":[{"new_text":"print"}]}

$ jet fix src/ --loop
round 1: applied 12 fixes, 31 reports remain
round 2: applied 9 fixes,  4 reports remain
round 3: applied 0 fixes,  4 reports remain
stopped: 4 reports need a person (suggested, not safe)

comparisons.note: Four grades. They are advisory: nothing promises the repair loop ends, and `cargo fix` can apply an edit that leaves new errors behind.
`gofmt -r` and `go fix` apply only rewrites that are correct by construction. There is no grade because nothing uncertain is ever offered.
comparisons.code: $ go fix ./...   # rewrites only what it can do exactly

comparisons.note: One bit: a rule is fixable or it is not. Fixes are applied in rounds until nothing changes, with a round cap when a pair of rules disagree.
comparisons.code: $ eslint --fix src/   # loops internally, caps at 10 passes

recommendation.why: It is the only option that promises something about the loop rather than about one edit. An agent working unattended needs to know the run ends and never goes backwards. That promise is testable, so Jet can hold itself to it every release.

whyNot.reason: Four words describe Jet's confidence but promise nothing about what happens after an edit is applied. Three of them mean 'do not trust this', so each tool still invents its own policy.
One class is honest and needs no vocabulary, but it throws away every uncertain repair. An editor can show a suggestion safely, and this option gives it nothing to show.
Two words are the right shape, but 'safe' stays an opinion. Without a proved progress rule, a safe edit can still add a new problem and a loop can run forever.

recommendation.tradeoff: A repair nobody has proved to make progress ships as a suggestion, so `jet fix` starts narrower than it could. That is the right way round: the promise is only worth having if it always holds.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared Rust's four grades against a single always-right class. It recommended the four grades because they are familiar and let editors show uncertain repairs.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the two-word option and the proved-progress option, then checked Go, which offers nothing uncertain, and ESLint, which loops in capped rounds. That surfaced the real question: the loop, not the label.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined the two-word vocabulary with the always-right discipline and added the progress property. The result became option D, and the recommendation moved there because a promise about the loop beats a label on an edit.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each loser: Rust tooling ports to option A unchanged, option B needs no tool policy at all, and option C gives editors a real suggestion path. All three remain honest choices.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the progress property with edits that conflict inside one round and spans that shift after an earlier edit. Stating the property over a whole round, with spans reapplied against the round's starting text, repairs both attacks.

decisions.title: Hardened profile: runtime checks for #Unsafe islands and foreign-code edges
decisions.gist: How Jet checks its trusted unsafe islands and foreign-code edges while a program runs.
decisions.lesson: Safe Jet is proven at compile time. The exceptions are the trust boundaries: #Unsafe regions and calls into C, C++, or Rust. A wrong region or a misbehaving foreign library corrupts memory silently, exactly as in Rust. Today nothing watches those boundaries at run time. This decision picks where runtime watching lives, what it covers, and what it costs.
decisions.story: Priya ships a Jet image service. One #Unsafe region wraps a C decoder for speed. A rare frame makes the decoder write four bytes past its buffer. Every test passes. Production corrupts a neighboring allocation about once a week, and the crash appears far from the cause. Priya needs the toolchain to catch the bad write at the boundary, in CI, before shipping the fast build.

options.name: Hardened profile: instrument only the islands
options.detail: A named profile, for example jet test --profile hardened, adds runtime checks only inside #Unsafe regions and at foreign-call edges. Raw pointer operations get bounds, liveness, and alignment checks. Memory that foreign code can touch comes from a quarantining allocator, which catches use-after-free and overflow at the edge. Safe Jet runs unchanged, so cost tracks the unsafe surface and is near zero for typical programs. Beginners never see it; experts turn it on with one flag on test, build, or run.
options.technical: Reuses the ratified D-MEM-SENTRY1=A sentry machinery; the profile is the opt-in spelling of the same mechanism (I8). D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1 amendment: each recorded obligation compiles to a runtime assertion in this profile and stays a static audit record elsewhere. Edge checks assert the E0702 boundary contracts. Reports carry region name, reason string, and the failing check, and land in jet inspect unsafe and the dossier. Failures are registered diagnostics with snapshots (I4); never raw sanitizer output (I2).
options.code:
$ jet test --profile hardened
FAIL image.copy_rows
  E31xx: raw write past block capacity inside #Unsafe("copy decoded rows...")
  at src/image.jet:42 — dst.cap = 4096, attempted write = 4160 bytes
  This test passes in the normal profile. The region's stated reason does not hold.

options.name: Always on under jet test, no new profile
options.detail: No new flag. jet test always instruments the islands; jet build and jet run never do. Everyone gets the protection in CI for free, which matches how practitioners use such tools. The loss: no way to reproduce a hardened run outside tests, no hardened soak of a long-running service, and FFI-heavy suites change timing with no visible cause.
options.technical: Same island instrumentation as option A, attached unconditionally to the test runner. Expert opt-out through a package policy key. No run-tier spelling exists, so a bug that only appears under real traffic cannot be watched.
options.code:
$ jet test
FAIL image.copy_rows
  E31xx: raw write past block capacity inside #Unsafe("copy decoded rows...")

$ jet run --profile hardened server.jet
error: no such profile — hardened checks exist only under jet test

options.name: Whole-program hardened build
options.detail: Instrument the whole program the way Fil-C and the Zig proposal do: every allocation and every pointer, safe code included. This also catches the two things island checks miss: compiler bugs, and foreign writes that land in safe memory through pointers Jet never saw. The cost is what the competitors pay: several-fold slowdown everywhere, a changed runtime layout, and giving up Jet's edge that safe code is already proven.
options.technical: All allocations go through the checking allocator; all pointer arithmetic is checked, generated code included. Instrumented artifacts get a distinct ABI; mixing profiles across a foreign boundary is rejected at link time.
options.code:
$ jet build --profile hardened
note: whole-program hardened build; expect 2x-6x slowdown

$ jet run --profile hardened server.jet   # every allocation checked, safe code too

options.name: Document sanitizer passthrough, build nothing
options.detail: No new mechanism. Jet documents one supported way to run the generated artifact under AddressSanitizer or valgrind, with symbols mapped back to Jet names. Cheapest to ship. The report quality is the foreign tool's, not Jet's: generated-code frames leak through, checks are whole-program and slow, and nothing understands #Unsafe regions, reason strings, or obligations.
options.technical: A jet test --sanitize=address wrapper builds with the sanitizer runtime and maps symbols. Diagnostics remain sanitizer text, so the front end cannot fully own them; rustc and the generated layer stay visible in stacks, which strains I2.
options.code:
$ jet test --sanitize=address
==91234==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
  #0 0x55d2 in jet_image_copy_rows_h8f2 (generated)
  #1 0x55d1 in __jet_main ...   # generated frames, no region names, no reasons

comparisons.note: The race detector is a named instrumented build mode: opt-in per invocation, tolerable overhead, first-class reports. The closest shipped precedent for option A's shape.

Whole-program capability checks at 1x-4x (Fil-C), or checks plus garbage collection with an ABI break (Zig proposal). Both pay everywhere because neither language has a static safe/unsafe partition to scope the checks to.
comparisons.code: $ zig build -Dsafety=full   # proposed: checks + GC, whole program

comparisons.note: Miri interprets unsafe code but covers neither FFI nor production binaries. Practitioners fall back to external sanitizers whose output is shaped by rustc, not by the source language.
comparisons.code: $ cargo +nightly miri test   # no FFI; interpreter speed

recommendation.why: Option A watches exactly the code Jet already distrusts, under every command, at a cost that tracks the unsafe surface. It turns the reason string on #Unsafe from a promise into a checked claim, and it reuses the ratified sentry machinery instead of adding a second mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Test-only coverage cannot soak a real service or reproduce a production report, and the mechanism is identical, so withholding the profile spelling saves nothing.
A whole-program slowdown surrenders the proven-safe edge and copies what competitors already do; island checks catch the same boundary bugs for a fraction of the cost.
Sanitizer output names generated symbols, not regions or reasons, and puts rustc's layer back in front of the user; that is a documented workaround, not a product.

recommendation.tradeoff: Island-scoped checks cannot catch a foreign write that lands in safe memory through a pointer Jet never saw. The quarantining allocator narrows that hole at the edge. Closing it fully is exactly option C's whole-program price, which remains available later if evidence demands it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an island-scoped profile, a whole-program build, and documented sanitizer passthrough, and recommended the island profile because its cost tracks the trusted surface.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added always-on-under-test as option B, and examined per-region opt-in attributes and a CI-only environment switch. Both folded into A and B because they only respell where the same checks turn on.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tried A plus automatic enabling of the profile under CI test runs. That survives as a default-behavior note for A's implementation card, not a separate option, because it composes freely after ratification.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the losers: D gained symbol mapping back to Jet names, and C gained reuse of the island allocator. D still cannot name regions or reasons; C still pays everywhere.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with false positives from legal raw tricks inside #Unsafe and with C libraries that free memory across the boundary. A per-region suppression with a mandatory written reason, audited in jet inspect unsafe, repairs both without weakening the default.

decisions.title: Shipping runtime checks for unsafe islands and foreign edges
decisions.gist: Choose how CI watches unsafe code and foreign memory before release.
decisions.lesson: Jet proves safe code at compile time. An `#Unsafe("reason")` gate marks raw or foreign memory; the compiler records the boundary but cannot prove its promise. Typed obligations name facts such as `valid_ptr`, `aligned`, and `no_alias`. A runtime sentry checks accesses against allocation bounds, liveness, and alignment. FFI means a call to C, C++, or Rust across Jet's boundary. Quarantine gives foreign code tracked allocations, so a bad write faults instead of corrupting Jet's heap. Hardened mode turns checks on at trust boundaries. Safe Jet adds no checks.
decisions.story: Maya maintains a parser that calls a C tokenizer. Her fuzzing tests can exercise a bad `#Unsafe` index or a foreign write only by leaving Jet's toolchain and using a whole-process sanitizer. She wants CI to run the same tests with island checks, fix each located fault, and ship the normal artifact after the checks pass.
decisions.inWild:
# package.jet
deps: .{ tokenizer: c.tokenizer#1.4 }

# src/parser.jet
#Unsafe("C tokenizer writes only within this buffer") {
    tokenizer.next(buffer, length)
}

$ jet test src/parser.jet
test result: ok

$ jet test src/parser.jet --profile=hardened
Runtime fault [R0801]: raw access used an address outside `buffer`
  --> src/parser.jet:4, in #Unsafe gate
 Why: tokenizer wrote 8 bytes past the live allocation.
 Fix: repair the index or foreign contract, then rerun this profile.
 obligation: valid_ptr = false
 foreign: tokenizer = fenced
exit: 1
decisions.detail:
Derived plan: ratify one complete contract. Then implement the selected profile through the shared Prelude sentry and fence seams. Prove normal and hardened runs across every applicable execution tier. Register actionable reports, update the audit and dossier projections, and measure safe-only overhead.

Owner gates: I8 approves the new runtime-hardening mechanism. I7 approves any new command or blessed profile name. D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1 decides whether runtime evidence supplements or discharges typed obligations. D-MEM-SENTRY1's existing I9 carve-out covers dev and hardened sentries. A new tier needs another owner ruling. D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 already fixes `harden: true` as all-foreign-dependency containment. Any narrower meaning must name an amendment.

D-BUILDPROFILE1 governs `--profile=<name>`; reuse must not create a second profile axis. D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1 owns the typed `policy:` field. D-FFI-UNIFY1 and D-FFI-CAP1/E0702 stay the FFI contract. D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1 stays separate; the fence must not become the program allocator. I1 remains in force. I4 is a mandatory implementation gate for new reports, not an owner choice. I6 remains unchanged because this design adds no dependency.

options.name: Built-in `--profile=hardened`, dual proof, and a full foreign fence (recommended)
options.detail: Use the existing named-profile selector on `jet build` and `jet test`. The built-in name turns on sentries for every `#Unsafe` operation and uses the existing all-foreign-dependency fence. Required static obligations still appear and pass. Runtime evidence records whether each asserted obligation held on this run. Safe Jet has no added checks. Gain: one CI command tests the shipping shape and names the gate, operation, obligation, and foreign component. Loss: vendor code inside the fence can run slower.
options.technical: Reuse D-BUILDPROFILE1's `--profile=<name>` selector and D-MEM-GUARANTEE1's `harden: true` containment meaning. Extend `jet test` to accept the same selector. Amend D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1 only to record runtime evidence; missing static assertions remain E3107. Complete D-MEM-SENTRY1's named hardened tier and use its existing I9 carve-out. D-FFI-CAP1 and E0702 keep their current access modes. The selected profile fences every foreign dependency. Add no allocator and no external dependency.
options.code:
$ jet test src/parser.jet
test result: ok

$ jet test src/parser.jet --profile=hardened
Runtime fault [R0801]: raw access used an address outside `buffer`
  --> src/parser.jet:4, in #Unsafe gate
 Why: tokenizer wrote 8 bytes past the live allocation.
 Fix: repair the index or foreign contract, then rerun this profile.
 obligation: valid_ptr = false
 foreign: tokenizer = fenced
exit: 1

$ jet build src/parser.jet --profile=hardened
built parser (hardened; foreign dependencies fenced)

options.name: Composable `--harden`, runtime discharge, and an edge-only fence
options.detail: Use a separate `--harden` modifier that composes with `--profile=release`, `--profile=debug`, or a package profile. In this mode, the runtime witness may discharge `valid_ptr`, `aligned`, and `no_alias`; a missing postfix assertion is allowed only there. Quarantine covers allocations and access modes visible at each FFI call. Foreign internal allocations remain trusted. Gain: teams can test any optimization profile and pay only at exposed edges. Loss: an untested path keeps no runtime evidence, and this mode cannot claim whole-binary containment.
options.technical: Add a new command flag under I7 instead of adding a blessed profile. Amend D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1 so runtime discharge is legal only for this mode; normal builds retain E3107. This is narrower than D-MEM-GUARANTEE1's `harden: true`, so that existing meaning stays unchanged and the new report must not say `fenced` for foreign internals. D-MEM-SENTRY1's I9 carve-out covers sentries only; no engine may add policy.
options.code:
# package.jet
policy: .{ unsafe: .Obligations }

# src/parser.jet
#Unsafe("C tokenizer writes only within this buffer") {
    tokenizer.next(buffer, length)
    // no static postfix assertion
}

$ jet test src/parser.jet
Error [E3107]: `tokenizer.next` is missing `valid_ptr`
 Fix: add a typed assertion or select the hardened modifier.

$ jet test src/parser.jet --profile=release --harden
Runtime fault [R0801]: raw access used an address outside `buffer`
 obligation: valid_ptr = runtime-failed
 foreign boundary: watched
 foreign internals: TRUSTED
verdict: exercised boundary only

options.name: Manifest `harden: true`, static obligations, and no new command
options.detail: Keep activation in the package manifest. `policy: .{ harden: true }` makes ordinary `jet test` and `jet build` use release sentries and the existing fence for every foreign dependency. Typed obligations keep their current static discharge law; runtime faults remain execution evidence, not a substitute. Gain: the shipping guarantee is versioned with the package and cannot depend on a CI command. Loss: a one-off hardened run needs a manifest change, and every foreign dependency pays the fence cost.
options.technical: Reuse D-MEM-GUARANTEE1=A without a new command flag or profile name. Do not amend D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1. `harden: true` means all foreign dependencies are contained; `contain: [deps]` remains the narrower explicit allowlist when a package does not claim the whole-binary guarantee. D-BUILDPROFILE1 stays optimization-only for this choice. D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1 remains separate.
options.code:
# package.jet
policy: .{ harden: true }

# src/parser.jet
#Unsafe("C tokenizer writes only within this buffer") {
    tokenizer.next(buffer, length)
        assert valid_ptr, aligned
}

$ jet test src/parser.jet
Runtime fault [R0801]: raw access used an address outside `buffer`
 obligation: valid_ptr = false
 foreign: tokenizer = fenced

$ jet build src/parser.jet
built parser (hardened)

comparisons.note: Rust sanitizer workflows instrument an artifact or whole process. They do not make the `unsafe` block or foreign allocation scope a first-class profile.
Zig debug checks cover broad language operations and release removes them. Jet can keep safe code statically proven and spend runtime cost at named trust boundaries.
Fil-C shows that checked foreign code can use tracked pointers with an ABI change and runtime cost. Jet can scope that cost to its named islands.

recommendation.why: Option A gives CI one explicit profile, preserves compile-time obligations, and reuses the already-ratified all-foreign-dependency fence. It adds runtime evidence without changing safe Jet or the normal release artifact.

whyNot.reason: B lets untested code pass the static obligation floor and leaves foreign internals trusted. It helps edge diagnosis, but it cannot support a whole-binary shipping claim.
C is reproducible, but it requires manifest edits for a one-run check and does not give the requested command-level profile. It also keeps runtime evidence separate from obligation discharge.

recommendation.tradeoff: Option A accepts the cost of fencing every foreign dependency in hardened builds. The report must show that cost and each component's status, while normal builds remain unchanged.

hybrid.synthesis: Option A keeps static proof, adds runtime evidence, and uses the existing all-dependency fence.

harvest.use: Keep the spelling.
Keep composition as a later extension.
Retain package harden as a shipping floor.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared a named profile, a modifier, and package policy. It kept profile spelling, obligation discharge, and FFI scope in each complete option.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested whole-program checking, garbage collection, sidecar isolation, and sanitizer-only workflows. Those choices either duplicate safe Jet's static proof or leave named islands unprotected.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept the modifier's profile composition and the package policy's reproducibility. It rejected both as the primary surface because they add a second activation story or remove the requested one-command test.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave the losing options their strongest use: B fits debug-plus-release matrices, and C fits repositories that make shipping policy declarative. Neither loses its stated boundary or evidence cost.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: GPT. Adversarial model family: Claude. The adversarial pass attacked false confidence from untested paths, foreign code that writes through a borrowed buffer, and accidental allocator replacement. The ballot labels exercised evidence, foreign trust, and the separate program allocator gate.

decisions.checkInstructions: Implement one shared profile fact. Route sentry and fence decisions through Prelude functions on every applicable tier. Keep engines as adapters. Prove the normal pass, the hardened fault report, audit projections, and safe-only overhead.

decisions.title: Storing a read-only view: semantic copy with a visibility ladder
decisions.gist: What happens when a program stores a zero-copy view in a list, struct, or cache.
decisions.lesson: A view is a zero-copy look into a string or list. Today a program cannot store one anywhere: the compiler rejects the store with E2307 and its fix text says to write `~` and copy. So the most common memory error demands a fix the compiler could apply itself. This choice decides who applies that fix: the language, a source rewriter, or the user. Write-through views (ViewMut) keep the error under every option, because a copy there would break write-back.
decisions.story: Ana writes her first parser. She splits each line with `.before(":")` and pushes the pieces into a list. The compiler stops her, tells her to sprinkle `~` on every push, and she does it without understanding why. Her file now has eleven sigils that all mean 'the compiler made me'.

options.name: Language semantic plus visibility ladder
options.detail: Storing a read-only view stores a copy. That is what the construct means, on every tier, with nothing injected into the file. Experts climb rungs. `jet audit copies` lists each copy with its size. The editor can show ghost `~` hints. `jet fmt --explicit-copies` writes real sigils on request. `policy: .{ copies: .Explicit }` in package.jet restores the error project-wide. Gain: the most common memory error stops existing and behavior stays fully predictable. Loss: a reader of plain source does not see the copy until they ask a tool.
options.technical: Amends D-MEM-VIEWRET1 boundary behavior: a read-view store lowers to the same code as an explicit `~` store. E2307 retires for read views and stays for ViewMut. D-SHAPE-COPY1 is untouched: `~x` remains the only copy spelling; the semantic inserts no second spelling. The package policy key rides D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1 and only tightens. The compiler never edits user source; `jet fmt --explicit-copies` is the invited, deterministic materializer.
options.code:
cache :: [ha, hb]          // works: a store IS a copy

$ jet audit copies
cache.jet:6  `ha` stored into `cache` as a copy (5 bytes)

$ jet fmt --explicit-copies   // you invite the ink
cache.jet: 2 copies written as `~`

# package.jet — perf-strict projects refuse the magic
policy: .{ copies: .Explicit }

options.name: Compiler writes the sigil into your file
options.detail: On compile or format, the toolchain inserts a real `~` at every view store, so the file always shows every copy. Gain: plain source is always explicit. Loss: your diff grows characters you did not type, agents get edited out from under themselves, and `~` stops meaning 'the author chose this'. It also breaks the toolchain norm that no command modifies user source uninvited.
options.technical: Would need a mandatory format-on-build step and a rule for code the formatter cannot reach (generated sources, patches in review).

options.name: Keep the error
options.detail: E2307 stays as shipped. The user types `~` at every store. Gain: every copy is author-written and visible in plain source forever. Loss: the beginner's first parser still fails on the language's most common memory error, and the fix remains mechanical typing the compiler already knows.
options.technical: No change. Probe P04j documents today's behavior on both tiers.

comparisons.note: Stored borrows force lifetime parameters onto every enclosing type; most users call `.to_owned()` by hand — option C's world with more ceremony.
comparisons.code: struct Tok<'a> { s: &'a str }   // the annotation tax Jet avoids

comparisons.note: Substrings share the backing array silently: convenient like option A, but with no receipt, no refusal switch, and surprise retention of large buffers.
comparisons.code: tok := line[0:3]   // keeps all of `line` alive, invisibly

recommendation.why: The store keeps one meaning everywhere: it behaves exactly as if the user wrote `~`, because that is the defined semantic. Beginners never meet the error. Experts get a receipt, a manual spelling, and a project-wide refusal.

whyNot.reason: A build that rewrites source churns diffs and review, and a machine-inserted `~` no longer tells a reader the author chose that copy.
It keeps the most common memory error alive to demand typing the compiler already prints in its own fix text.

recommendation.tradeoff: Plain source hides small copies until a tool is asked. We accept this because the copies are cost-only facts with a ledger, and `policy: .{ copies: .Explicit }` restores full visibility where cost is the product.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the language semantic, source injection, and today's error, and recommended the semantic because it removes the error without changing any meaning.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested copy-on-write strings, implicit gc promotion, and editor-only ghosts as full options. All three were folded away: copy-on-write hides cost worse than a ledger, the owner rejected silent gc at checkpoint, and ghosts alone need an IDE.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass moved the best part of option B into option A: `jet fmt --explicit-copies` gives B's always-explicit file to anyone who wants it, on request instead of by force.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened option C: its error text now names the store, the owner, and the exact fix, which is the strongest honest version of keeping the wall. It still fails the beginner on their first parser.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked hidden cost on hot paths and ViewMut ambiguity. The policy key restores the error for perf-strict projects and write-through views never copy silently, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: Capability sigils across the FFI boundary
decisions.gist: Whether an expert can lend or give memory to foreign code without copying it.
decisions.lesson: Today every FFI crossing copies: E0702 bans `&` and `^` in extern signatures, and each side frees its own copy. That rule is a perfect beginner floor and kills cross-boundary double-frees by construction. But it is also the only tier: no lending, no ownership handoff, no way to hold a handle that C allocated. This choice decides what the expert tier looks like above that floor.
decisions.story: Mo embeds Jet in an audio engine. Every 100 MB sample buffer he passes to a C DSP routine is duplicated first, once per call, on the real-time thread. He reads the E0702 fix text, drops the sigil, and ships the copies because there is nothing else to type.

options.name: The same three sigils, checked across the border
options.detail: `&` lends for exactly one call: the foreign side may read, must not keep, and no copy happens. `^` gives ownership away: the foreign side owns and frees it, and the Jet name dies. `#Close(fn)` puts a returned foreign handle on Jet's `close(^)` protocol, so the foreign free runs exactly once or the program does not compile. Gain: zero new vocabulary and zero-copy crossings, with who-frees-what written in the signature.
