$ rustlings hint intro1

comparisons.note: The official tour runs in the browser against a remote sandbox. It gives a good first hour, but it is not the local toolchain, and no bridge leads from a local compiler error back into the tour.
comparisons.code: ## tour.golang.org — browser only; the `go` CLI has no learn verb

comparisons.note: Elm bet everything on teaching compiler errors plus a written guide, with no exercise runner. The errors are loved, but learners still assemble their own practice path.
comparisons.code: ## elm-lang.org/docs — guide and famous errors; no `elm learn`

recommendation.why: Jet already owns the two pieces learners love: teaching diagnostics and a 42-millisecond watch loop. `jet learn` joins them into one offline path that is always the same version as the compiler. The Rust evidence is direct: the loved mechanic is the hint inside the watch loop, and the failure is that it lives outside the toolchain.

whyNot.reason: A browser track breaks the loop this decision exists to protect: it can drift from the installed compiler, its hints are not the live diagnostics, and it vanishes offline.
Rust ran this experiment. Strong compiler errors without an ordered practice path still cost learners three outside resources and a mentor.
A registry pack recreates the rustlings failure: the pack and the compiler version apart, hints quote errors the installed compiler does not print, and the first fetch needs a network.

recommendation.tradeoff: The toolchain now carries a curriculum, and every language change must update its exercises. That cost buys a live gain: the exercise suite runs in CI as end-to-end proof that the teaching diagnostics still teach.

decisions.title: How Jet enforces the panic law in libraries
decisions.gist: How the compiler makes libraries follow the panic law.
decisions.lesson: Stdlib law L2 says a function returns `T ? E` for expected failure and panics only for programmer error. Today nothing checks this. A library can stop the whole program on bad input, and no surface reports it. Jet's own examples corpus holds 842 `panic(` calls, and flagship serde examples model `?? panic("bad json")`. Rust tried opt-in lint walls, and unwraps still spread through README examples. This ballot picks the one route that enforces the law.
decisions.story: Priya maintains confkit, a small config library that other teams embed. Her parse_port stops the process on a bad value. An on-call engineer's service dies at 3am because one environment variable held "abc". Priya wants the compiler to tell her, before release, which of her functions can stop someone else's program.

options.name: Function-level #NoPanic proof marker
options.detail: You mark a function #NoPanic. The compiler then proves that the body and every reachable callee cannot stop. A panic call, an unproven trap, or an unmarked callee is a compile error. The gain is a caller-visible guarantee on exactly the functions that promise it. The loss is a second wall mechanism: Jet already has the =[!E]=> prohibition arrow for "this call graph never does X", so a new marker adds a parallel spelling.
options.technical: A new attribute plane beside #Pre and #Post. Obligations: no reachable panic, #Todo, require, or unproven E30xx trap site. Refinement facts (#1549) and #Pre facts discharge obligations under D-FAIL-TIER1 proof-keyed erasure. A callee needs the marker, or the checker reproves its whole body. The proposed diagnostic code E0755 is new.

options.name: Refinements only, no new wall
options.detail: No new surface. Refinement types such as Int(0..100) (#1549, ready) prove panic sites away where authors adopt them. Bounds and range facts move into signatures, trap checks erase, and runtime values convert fallibly. The gain is safer signatures with no annotation ceremony, and faster code where proofs land. The loss is that nothing obliges a library to adopt them. A panic on expected failure still compiles silently, so law L2 stays an honor system.
options.technical: Rides #1549 (D-TYPE2-SPELL1) and D-FAIL-TIER1 unchanged: a range proof removes a check, the unproven case keeps it. Enforcement pressure comes only from the L2 review rubric in docs/spec/stdlib-api-laws.md, which reviews stdlib additions but never third-party or example code. jet prove --lens refinements already grades the evidence.

options.name: jet check policy wall with a panic budget
options.detail: A package sets a panic budget in package.jet, and jet check fails the build when the count of panic sites grows. This generalizes the shrink-only continuous-integration gate proposed for the examples corpus (#1903) to any package. The gain is a wall that covers a whole corpus at once and is easy to read. The loss is that a count cannot tell a legal programmer-error panic from an illegal expected-failure panic. The wall also lives beside the compiler, the exact place where Rust's clippy walls decayed.
options.technical: Extends the D-JPK-POLICYSURFACE1 policy: namespace, next to lints: { deny: [...] } and effect budgets. Host and org policy narrows, never widens. The count is syntactic: explicit panic( sites per package, budget shrink-only in continuous integration. Trap sites, #Todo, and require are not counted, so the wall misses implicit stops entirely.

options.name: Panic joins the effect tree as a deniable row
options.detail: Panic becomes a row that the shipped prohibition arrow and the manifest deny list already know how to enforce. A signature writes =[!Panic]=>. A package writes effects: { deny: [Panic] } in package.jet, and E1220 already names a panicking dependency. The compiler proves that denied scopes cannot stop: expected failure must become T ? E, and programmer-error stops must move behind #Pre or refinement facts that callers prove. One mechanism covers one function, a whole package, and its dependency graph.
options.technical: Reuses D-PROP1/D-PROP2 (=[!E]=>, E0749) and the D-AUTHORITY-MEM1=B denial precedent (deny: [Mem.Alloc]). Adds one denial-only row and amends the D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1 closed table by this ballot. Discharge: refinement proofs (#1549) and #Pre facts under D-FAIL-TIER1 proof-keyed erasure; jet prove --lens refinements shows the evidence. A #Pre on a denied function transfers the stop obligation to callers: a denied caller must prove it, an undenied caller keeps the runtime check at the call site (D-FAIL-TIER1 blame rule).

comparisons.note: The no_panic crate enforces panic freedom with a linker trick, outside the type system. Clippy's unwrap_used wall is off by default, and the Don't Panic video shows unwraps spreading through README examples anyway.
comparisons.code:
# clippy.toml walls are off by default; the video's own errata corrected this
# [lints.clippy]
# unwrap_used = "deny"        # opt-in, per crate, decays

#[no_panic]                    // third-party crate; enforced by a linker trick
fn parse_port(raw: &str) -> u16 { raw.parse().unwrap() }

comparisons.note: SPARK mode proves absence of runtime errors for marked units. Obligations come from contracts, and the prover erases checks. This is the discharge model option D borrows.
Error unions !T force callers to handle expected failure, which matches T ? E. But @panic and unreachable compile anywhere, and nothing proves a call graph panic-free.

recommendation.why: Denial rides surfaces Jet already ratified: the =[!E]=> prohibition arrow, the manifest deny list, and proof-keyed erasure. One spelling scales from one function to a package to its dependency graph. Enforcement is at compile time, so denied code pays nothing at runtime and often runs faster, because proved checks erase. And it enforces exactly law L2: expected failure is forced into T ? E, while programmer-error stops stay legal behind contracts that callers prove.

whyNot.reason: It gives the same guarantee as option D but mints a second wall mechanism beside the shipped =[!E]=> arrow. Two spellings for "this call graph never does X" breaks I8.
Proofs without an obligation enforce nothing. A library that panics on bad input still compiles silently, so law L2 stays an honor system. That is the failure Rust already demonstrated.
A count cannot tell a legal programmer-error panic from an illegal expected-failure panic, so it blocks the wrong sites and excuses implicit traps. Walls outside the compiler decay, as clippy's did.

recommendation.tradeoff: Denial is only as strong as the prover. Some code that never stops in practice cannot be admitted yet, and it must return T ? E, add facts, or stay undenied. We accept this because that escape shape is the shape law L2 prefers anyway.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a #NoPanic marker, a refinements-only route, and a jet check budget wall. It recommended the marker for its caller-visible, per-function guarantee.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review searched the ratified record and found the shipped prohibition arrow =[!Net]=> (D-PROP1) and the manifest denial precedent deny: [Mem.Alloc] (D-AUTHORITY-MEM1=B). It added option D, which spells the same guarantee in those existing surfaces.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review folded the marker's function guarantee, the budget wall's package scope, and the refinement proofs into option D: one denial row, discharged by proofs. The recommendation moved from A to D.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each loser on its own terms. Option B gained the L2 review rubric as an adoption path, option C gained the shrink-only budget #1903 needs anyway, and option A gained whole-call-graph checking with #Pre discharge.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked D where the prover is too weak: denied code that never stops in practice may not compile. The repair names three exits (return a fallible result, add facts, stay undenied) and records the D-AUTHORITY-ROOTS1 amendment by name, so D survives.

decisions.title: Expanded multi-line print for nested values
decisions.gist: How a person asks for a readable multi-line print of a nested value.
decisions.lesson: Today every value prints on one line, however deep it nests. A two-level struct already prints as a 117-character line. Reading state while debugging means scanning that line by eye. Python added an expanded pretty-printer for exactly this pain, and Rust ships {:#?}. Jet's interpolation selector set is closed, so adding a spelling is an owner choice.
decisions.story: Mara is debugging her game's level tree. She prints the world object to see which group holds the broken invader. The whole tree arrives as one endless line, and she starts counting brackets by hand.

options.name: :Pretty selector on the existing rail
options.detail: You write {value:Pretty} in any interpolation, next to :Debug and :Fixed. The value prints indented, one field or element per line. Beginners find it where they already found :Debug. Experts get the same text as a string through core.fmt.pretty when they need to route it elsewhere. One formatter produces both.
options.technical: Selector lowers to one Prelude formatter (jet_fmt_pretty) shared by AOT, JIT, and interpreter (I9). Output is deterministic and width-independent: indent two spaces per level, one field/element per line, stable across runs. E0914's valid set grows by one. core.fmt.pretty(value) => String is the same function exposed for expert use.

options.name: A second print verb: print_pretty
options.detail: You call print_pretty(org) instead of print(org). No new interpolation spelling. The cost: a second print verb splits the print surface, and the expanded form cannot be mixed into a larger message the way a selector can.
options.technical: New ambient prelude function print_pretty(value). Same one Prelude formatter underneath. Interpolation stays unchanged, so "world: {org}" can never opt in.

options.name: Library function only: fmt.pretty
options.detail: You import core.fmt and print the returned string. Experts get full control. Beginners pay a use line and a nested call for a one-off debugging look, and nothing next to :Debug hints that the option exists.
options.technical: core.fmt.pretty(value) => String only. No selector, no ambient verb. Discovery relies on docs.

options.name: Make nested printing multi-line by default
options.detail: print(org) itself becomes multi-line once a value nests or passes a length threshold. No one has to ask. The cost: output shape now depends on the value's size, every existing golden and log line changes, and scripts that parse one line per print break.
options.technical: Default Debug rendering switches on a nesting/width heuristic. Thresholds become observable behavior that must be specified, snapshot-tested, and kept identical across tiers forever.

comparisons.note: pprint gained expand=True because nested one-liners were unreadable; expansion is opt-in, never the default.
The alternate debug selector {:#?} sits beside plain {:?} in the same format-string rail.

recommendation.why: The selector rides the rail the owner already ratified for Debug and Fixed, so the person who found :Debug finds :Pretty in the same error message. One Prelude formatter serves the beginner spelling and the expert string function, so there is still one mechanism.

whyNot.reason: A second print verb splits one surface into two, and the expanded form can never join a larger interpolated message.
A use line plus a nested call is real ceremony for a debugging one-off, and nothing at the point of pain reveals that the function exists.
Output shape would depend on value size, breaking every golden, log parser, and agent that relies on one stable line per print. Python deliberately kept expansion opt-in.

recommendation.tradeoff: The closed selector set grows by one name, and the expanded shape becomes specified output that snapshots must bless once. That is acceptable because the shape is deterministic and shared by every tier.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a selector, a second print verb, a library function, and a changed default, and recommended the selector for discoverability beside :Debug.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a width-aware terminal formatter and a jet repl-only pretty mode. Both were folded away: width-aware output is nondeterministic, and repl-only help abandons scripts and logs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review merged the selector and the library function into one option: the selector lowers to core.fmt.pretty, so both facets share one formatter. Option A now carries that shape.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened D with a heuristic spec and B with message composition via a helper, and strengthened C's docs path. D still changes every existing golden; B still splits the verb.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with selector-set creep and golden churn. The set grows by one, the shape is opt-in so no existing golden changes, and E0914 already teaches the set, so A survives.

decisions.title: Map keys beyond scalars: which types may be a map key
decisions.gist: Which types may be a map key.
decisions.lesson: Today a map key must be Int, String, Bool, Char, or a payload-free enum. Keying on a pair or a small struct is everyday work: caches, grid coordinates, dedupe rows. Jet maps are ordered trees, so a wider rule means deep field-by-field compare, not hashing. This ballot picks how far the key rule widens.
decisions.story: Ana builds a permissions service. She wants one cache from a (user, resource) pair to an allowed flag. Jet rejects her struct key with E0502, so she glues both names into one string. A teammate later picks a separator that appears inside a user name, and lookups silently collide.
decisions.detail: The rule decides which key types the checker accepts for [K:V] maps. Equality and order for accepted keys are deep value semantics in one Prelude path on every tier (I9). Jet's map is an ordered tree (Arc over BTreeMap), so this ballot promises ordering and equality, never hashing. Set elements (E0506) are a separate, later choice.

options.name: Recursive rule: composites of key-eligible fields
options.detail: A key is Int, String, Bool, Char, a payload-free enum, or a tuple or struct whose fields are all key-eligible, recursively. Float, views, functions, lists, maps, sets, Shared, and payload-carrying enums stay out. Beginners key on pairs and small structs directly; the E0502 error names the field that disqualifies a composite. Loss: Float coordinates still need scaling to Int or a formatted String.
options.technical: Checker predicate extends is_map_key_type recursively, consulting the type registry for struct field types; named tuples check members in canonical order. Comparison is derived structural Ord/Eq on generated key types, flowing through the one JetMap (Arc<BTreeMap>) Prelude path on all tiers (I9). No hash path is introduced.

options.name: Scalar keys only (status quo)
options.detail: E0502 stays as shipped: keys are Int, String, Bool, Char, or a payload-free enum. Nothing new to learn, build, or test. Loss: every pair or struct key becomes a hand-glued string or nested maps, and separator collisions become silent lookup bugs the type system never sees.
options.technical: No checker or Prelude change. is_map_key_type stays syntactic; both E0502 sites keep the current copy.

options.name: Any ordered type, Float included
options.detail: Every value type gains key status through one total ordering, Float and containers included. No key shape is refused. Loss: the map's idea of equal splits from `==` — the map treats NaN equal to NaN and -0.0 different from 0.0, while `==` says the opposite. Container keys also hide big per-lookup comparison costs.
options.technical: Float keys order by IEEE-754 totalOrder; lists, maps, and sets compare lexicographically. Same single Prelude path; the change is checker-side plus derived orderings for every value type.

comparisons.note: Tuples are dict keys out of the box, and the frozen-dict push (Python 3.15 talk) exists because people key on compound values constantly.
BTreeMap accepts any Ord key; a derived struct key is one attribute line. f64 is excluded because it is not Ord — the same Float line option A draws.
Comparable structs are map keys, and floats are allowed — so a NaN key becomes an unreachable entry. This is the trap option C invites.

recommendation.why: The recursive rule covers the everyday cases — pairs, coordinates, small structs — with one teachable sentence: a key is a scalar or a composite of keys. It keeps Float out, so the map's idea of equal never splits from `==`.

whyNot.reason: It keeps everyday keys illegal, so people hand-glue strings and inherit the separator-collision bugs the type system was supposed to prevent.
It legalizes NaN and -0.0 keys, where the map's equality quietly disagrees with `==`, and lets big container keys hide their per-lookup cost. Go ships float keys and NaN entries are a famous trap.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some real shapes stay refused: Float coordinates must scale to Int or format a String, and a list key needs converting to a tuple or struct. The E0502 message must also name the disqualifying field, or the recursive rule will confuse.

reviewPasses.base: Drafted three rules — recursive composites, scalar status quo, and any-ordered-type — around one shared cache-and-grid program, recommending the recursive rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Tested two more designs: an opt-in per-type key marker and a hash-based rule. Both were dropped — the marker duplicates what recursion already grants, and JetMap is an ordered tree, so a hashing promise would be false.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tried recursive composites plus Float behind an explicit opt-in marker; rejected because it adds a second key mechanism for a case that Int scaling already serves.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanned B as zero-cost and honest, and C as matching what the ordered tree can already do; C's strongest form still splits map equality from `==` on NaN and -0.0.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on deep-key copy cost, error clarity, and future Set widening: value semantics already copy on insert, the plan adds a field-naming fix line, and E0506 stays a separate card. A survived.

decisions.title: Flatten helpers on lists: run at once, or stay one-pass
decisions.gist: Decide whether flatten and flat_map on a plain list run at once, like map and filter already do.
decisions.lesson: On a plain list, map and filter run at once and hand back a list. Their siblings flatten and flat_map instead hand back a one-pass stream, so printing the result is an error. Two rules live on one receiver, and people must memorize which helper follows which. This choice amends ratified law D-CORE-EAGER1=A. That law says: "The rest of the D-ITERTOOLS1 adapter ledger stays on Iter". The ballot asks whether flatten and flat_map on a list leave that ledger and join the run-at-once set.
decisions.story: Priya cleans survey answers. Each page of the survey gives her a list of numbers, so she holds a list of lists. She writes nested.flatten() and prints it, exactly the way she printed nested.map(...) a minute earlier. The map call worked. The flatten call stops her with error E0112 and tells her to add .to_list() first. She has no way to guess which helpers need the extra step, because both sit on the same list.

options.name: Run at once, like map and filter
options.detail: flatten and flat_map on a plain list build the flat list right away and hand it back. Printing just works, and a filter chained after flat_map stays a plain list step. Writers who stream huge data opt out with .lazy(), the same switch map and filter already use. The gain is one rule for every helper on a list. The loss is that the flat list exists in memory at once unless the writer asks for .lazy().
options.technical: Amends D-CORE-EAGER1=A. The amended sentence is: "The rest of the D-ITERTOOLS1 adapter ledger stays on Iter". It gains the carve-out: "except flatten and flat_map on a concrete List, which join map and filter in the eager set". Iter receivers keep lazy flatten/flat_map, so .lazy().flatten() still defers. The adjacent-fusion clause of D-CORE-EAGER1 applies unchanged: callback order and count are identical either way. Golden proof runs on JIT and AOT (I9).

options.name: Keep the split; teach it in the docs
options.detail: flatten and flat_map keep handing back a one-pass stream, exactly as ratified. The fix is teaching only. The docs row where the eager rule is taught gains the split. The E0112 advice ("materialize it first: add .to_list()") is copied there, so readers meet it before the error does. The gain is zero change to ratified law and no new memory cost. The loss is that the trap stays: two rules on one receiver, and every new reader must memorize which helper follows which.
options.technical: No law change. D-CORE-EAGER1=A stands as written. Docs work only: the D-LOOPMAP1 teaching row in docs/reference/core-library.md and examples/features/collections/lazy_iter.jet name flatten/flat_map as one-pass and show the .to_list() fix. The E0112 message itself already gives the fix; this copies it to where people read first. Card #1972 criterion 1, second arm.

options.name: Split the pair: flatten at once, flat_map one-pass
options.detail: flatten runs at once because it takes no callback; flat_map keeps handing back a one-pass stream because it takes one, like scan and filter_map do. The gain is that the no-callback helper stops erroring on print. The loss is a new trap inside one family: map(f).flatten() would run at once while flat_map(f) — the same computation in one word — would not. That is harder to memorize than today's split, not easier.
options.technical: Amends D-CORE-EAGER1=A for flatten only; flat_map stays on the Iter ledger. Creates the identity break map(f).flatten() : List versus flat_map(f) : Iter for the same elements in the same order. No other language surveyed splits these two helpers across regimes on the same receiver.
options.code:
fn run() {
    nested :: [[1, 2], [3], [4, 5]]
    print(nested.flatten())                       // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

    orders :: [[10, 25], [40], [5, 60]]
    print(orders.map(o => o).flatten())           // [10, 25, 40, 5, 60]
    big :: orders.flat_map(o => o)                // one-pass stream
    print(big.filter(n => n > 20))                // still E0112
}

comparisons.note: Lists have no flatten method. The common idiom is a nested comprehension, which builds the flat list at once. The lazy spelling, itertools.chain.from_iterable, is a separate opt-in name — laziness is the marked case, like option A.
comparisons.code:
flat = [x for row in rows for x in row]   # eager, prints fine
lazy = itertools.chain.from_iterable(rows)  # explicit lazy opt-in

comparisons.note: Iterator flatten and flat_map are lazy and need .collect(), like option B — and unused lazy adapters need a must_use warning to catch the mistake. But the eager path exists under a different name: concat() on a slice of vectors flattens at once.
comparisons.code:
let flat: Vec<i32> = rows.iter().flatten().copied().collect();
let flat2 = [vec![1, 2], vec![3]].concat();  // eager, no collect

recommendation.why: The argument that ratified eager map and filter applies here with more force. flatten has no callback, so there is nothing to defer except the middle list. flat_map runs its callback once per element in the same order either way. Option A removes the last two-regime helpers from the list receiver, so one rule covers the whole family, and .lazy() stays the single opt-in for streaming.

whyNot.reason: Docs teach the memorization instead of removing it. The receiver still carries two rules, the print error still lands on beginners first, and a filter after flat_map still silently changes regime.

It trades one split for a worse one: map(f).flatten() would run at once while flat_map(f), the same computation in one word, would not. A family whose members disagree is harder to learn than today's rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: With option A, the flat list exists in memory all at once, so very large nested data pays that cost unless the writer types .lazy() first. We accept this because map and filter already made exactly this trade under D-CORE-EAGER1, and the opt-out is one short word at the front of the chain.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared eager, status quo plus docs, and the flatten-only split, all grounded in live probes of today's binary. It recommended eager because the ratified map/filter argument transfers directly.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested making the whole Iter ledger eager and making print materialize streams itself. Both were dropped: file and channel sources must stay one-pass, and a print that silently spends the only pass hides real consumption bugs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review promoted the flatten-only split into full option C instead of a footnote, so the owner sees why the asymmetry loses. It also confirmed .lazy().flatten() keeps the streaming path for experts under option A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option B to its best form: copy the exact E0112 fix line into the docs row and the lazy_iter example. Even at its best it leaves two regimes on one receiver.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked option A with huge nested lists and callback-order worries. Order and count are unchanged by eagerness, fusion still applies, and .lazy() names the memory-safe path, so the recommendation held.

decisions.title: How the dev tiers run a columnar list
decisions.gist: How `jet run` and the interpreter read a struct stored as columns.
decisions.lesson: A columnar struct is stored one array per field instead of one record per item. This is a memory layout choice, and its ratified promise is that the code you write does not change. Today only the compiled build can read that layout. The fast dev loop and the interpreter cannot, so they quietly fall back to slower execution. This choice decides how they read it.
decisions.story: Priya writes a particle simulation and marks her struct columnar for speed. She runs it with `jet run` while editing, and it works. She never learns that the fast path silently gave up, because the answer is correct either way. Her edit loop is slower than it should be, and no message says why.

options.name: One shared column store in the Prelude
options.detail: The Prelude owns the column store and the read that pulls one item out of it. Every tier calls that same code. The compiled build stops generating its own private layout. Gain: one meaning for columnar on every tier, and the fast loop keeps working. Loss: the compiled build gives up a layout tuned per struct, so its speed may drop a little.
options.technical: Add a Prelude struct-of-arrays object holding one typed column per field, plus one gather symbol taking a column set and an index and returning the record. AOT emit, the Cranelift host and the interpreter ambient all marshal into that symbol. Retire the per-struct generated `__jet_<S>_columns` type and its `from_aos` and `gather_at` helpers from `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Items.rs:496-622`.

options.name: Teach the other tiers to read the generated layout
options.detail: The compiled build keeps generating its own layout per struct. The fast loop and the interpreter learn to read that same shape. Gain: the compiled build keeps its tuned layout and its current speed. Loss: the shape is described in two places, so the two can drift apart. A drift shows up as a wrong number, not as an error.
options.technical: Publish the generated column layout as a described record shape the JIT and the evaluator can look up, then add a gather in each engine that walks it. The layout stays authored by codegen, so the engines depend on a generated artifact rather than a shared symbol.

options.name: Convert to plain records when a tier cannot read columns
options.detail: When the fast loop meets a columnar list, it copies it into ordinary records once, then runs normally. Gain: small change, and every tier gives the right answer with no shared store to build. Loss: the copy costs time and memory on entry, so a large list may be slower than the plain layout the user was trying to beat.
options.technical: Materialize the columnar list into array-of-structs form at the tier boundary, then lower the loop with the existing list path. Requires no new shared symbol and no engine-side column reader.

options.name: Write down that columnar is compiled-build only
options.detail: Keep today's behaviour and record it as a deliberate limit. The fast loop drops to slower execution for columnar code, and says so. Gain: no new machinery, and the honest limit is visible instead of silent. Loss: a ratified feature works on one tier only, and the fast loop stays slow for the exact code that asked for speed.
options.technical: A named tier-parity carve-out naming columnar layout as compiled-build only, plus a message when a tier declines it so the fallback is not silent. This is the only option that needs an invariant carve-out.

comparisons.note: Rust has no built-in columnar layout. Libraries build it, and every reader uses the library's own accessor rather than its own copy of the shape.
Zig ships a multi-array in its standard library. One type owns the columns and hands out an item, so callers never address a column directly.
comparisons.code:
var list: std.MultiArrayList(Particle) = .{};
const p = list.get(i);

comparisons.note: Arrow makes the column layout an open format with one specification. Many languages read the same bytes, and none writes its own private version.

recommendation.why: One store and one read give columnar a single meaning, so all three tiers answer alike by construction rather than by matching effort. It also removes the reason a tier declines the layout, which is what makes the fast loop slow for the code that asked for speed.

whyNot.reason: It writes the layout down twice. A drift between the two readers prints a wrong number instead of failing, which is the exact failure this project has been digging out all epoch.
The copy taxes the case columnar exists to speed up. A user who chose the layout for large data pays most.
It keeps a ratified feature working on one tier. It also needs an invariant carve-out, which is a cost the other options do not ask for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A shared store may be slower than a layout tuned for one struct, so the compiled build could lose a little speed. That is acceptable because a correct fast loop on every tier is worth more. A tuned path can be added later behind the same shared read.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a shared Prelude store against teaching each engine to read the generated layout. It recommended the shared store because one store cannot disagree with itself.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added converting to plain records on entry, and writing the limit down as compiled-build only. It also tested deleting the layout feature, which was dropped because the layout is already ratified and shipped.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested a shared store plus a tuned path for the compiled build. It was folded into the recommendation as a later addition, because a tuned path behind one shared read stays one mechanism.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the copy-on-entry option with a size limit and a cache. It still taxes large data, which is the case the layout exists to serve.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review added a field to the struct and asked which option prints a wrong number. Only the two-readers option can, so the shared store remains the recommendation.

decisions.title: How a program passes a core-library error out of a plain fallible function
decisions.gist: Whether the standard library declares one conversion for its own error types.
decisions.lesson: A fallible Jet function is written `fn run() ?`. Its failure value has one type. When a library call fails with its own error type, something must say how that becomes the function's failure. Today the program must declare that itself, once per error type, in every program. This choice decides whether the standard library declares it once instead.
decisions.story: Sam writes a twenty-line script that fetches a URL and prints the body. The fetch can fail, so Sam writes `fn run() ?` and passes the failure up with `?`. The compiler stops and asks for a declared conversion from the network error. Sam did not define that error and does not want to name it.

options.name: The standard library declares the conversion for its own errors
options.detail: The standard library ships one declaration covering its own error family, so passing a library error out of a plain fallible function works with no extra code. Gain: the short program above compiles, and no one copies the same declaration into every project. Loss: the conversion is invisible in the program text, so a reader cannot see where it came from.
options.technical: Ship `impl <CoreError> => Err` once for the core error family on the existing D-ERR-CONV rail, injected the way `Prelude/Units.jet` already is (see `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Bundle/Units.rs`). No new syntax, no new trait, no new compiler arm, and one source for every tier to lower.

options.name: The program names the error types it passes up
options.detail: Keep today's rule. A function that passes a library error up names that error in its own return type. Gain: the reader sees exactly which failures a function can produce, and nothing is added behind their back. Loss: every such function repeats the list, and a new call site can force the list to change.
options.technical: Keep the ratified explicit rule. The 28 affected examples move to typed or union error returns, following `examples/features/net/http_readiness.jet:5`, which already spells `fn run() ? NetError | RangeError | TaskFailure`.

options.name: The program declares the conversion once per project
options.detail: Keep today's rule and let a project write the conversion one time in one file, then reuse it everywhere. Gain: short signatures, and the conversion is written down somewhere a reader can find. Loss: every new project still writes it, so the same lines exist in every project rather than in every function.
options.technical: No language change. The declaration is ordinary user code in the project root module, relying on the existing declared-impl rule.

comparisons.note: Rust ships a blanket conversion into a boxed error, so a short program passes library errors up with no declaration. A program that wants named failures opts into its own type instead.
Go has one error interface, so any library error satisfies any error return. The cost is that a signature says nothing about which failures are possible.
Swift marks a function `throws` without naming the error type, so a library error passes up untouched. Typed throws were added later as an opt-in.

recommendation.why: The declaration is the same in every program, so writing it once in the library is the one-mechanism answer. It also fixes the beginner path: the twenty-line script compiles, while an author who wants named failures still writes them and gets exactly today's behaviour.

whyNot.reason: It is correct today and stays available, but on its own it makes the short script name a type its author never chose. It also leaves 28 shipped examples needing per-file unions.
It moves the repetition from every function to every project without removing it. A rule that every project must restate is a library gap, not a project decision.

recommendation.tradeoff: Option A makes one conversion invisible in the program text. That is acceptable because it is the library's own error family, not the author's, and an author who wants the failure named still writes the named form. If the invisibility ever bites, `jet inspect` can show the conversion rather than the rule being reversed.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a library-shipped conversion against keeping the explicit rule, and recommended the library conversion because the declaration is identical in every program.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the per-project declaration, and tested inferring the union automatically. Inference was dropped because a signature that changes when a callee changes is worse than either option here.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept the library conversion and asked whether a project could refuse it. That is already possible by naming the error type, so no separate opt-out is needed.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the explicit rule with better diagnostic text naming the exact impl to write. It still leaves the same line copied into every program.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review asked what happens when two library errors reach one function and whether a report loses detail. The failure carries the original report either way, so no detail is lost, and the library conversion remains the recommendation.

decisions.title: Analytics query surface: SQL text, typed methods, or both
decisions.gist: How a Jet program asks a question of a CSV file or an in-memory table: SQL text, typed method calls, or both.
decisions.lesson: The owner set a bar: meet or beat DuckDB's core loop. That loop is: point a SQL query at a data file, get typed rows back, inside your own process. Jet can already decode a CSV file into typed records and store data in columns. But Jet has no query surface over files. This ballot picks only the shape of that surface. One shared engine sits behind it no matter which shape wins.
decisions.story: Mara does revenue reports. Every week she gets an orders export as a CSV file. Today she opens a Python notebook, imports DuckDB, and writes one SELECT to sum revenue per customer. She wants that same one-step loop in Jet, without leaving her program or losing type checking.
decisions.detail:
What exists today. `SQL.{"…"}` is the checked SQL text head; D-UNIFYLIT1=A retired the old `sql"…"` prefix. The live marker row is `marker SQL(row: Type = none, @sites: [.Block])` at Prelude/Markers.jet:97. The old row at line 118, `marker Sql(@sites: [.Block], @retired: "#SQL")`, is retired. D-BOUND-SINK1=A lets a library declare a checked text head with a comptime check and per-hole rules. Lists already carry `filter`, `map`, `group_by`, and `sum`.

Not decided here: where the engine comes from. A vendored engine or a new format reader such as Parquet is an I6 owner gate. That gate is raised separately, before any code depends on it. This ballot decides the query surface only. One engine serves that surface either way (I8).

options.name: Checked SQL text over files and values
options.detail: You point a checked SQL query at a CSV path or an in-memory list. Typed rows come back. The query text is checked at compile time against the record type's fields. A typo in a column name is a compile error, not a runtime surprise. This is DuckDB's exact loop, plus the schema check DuckDB cannot give. Loss: SQL text is a second spelling for sums and filters that method calls can also write.
options.technical: Reuses the ratified `SQL.{"…"}` head (D-UNIFYLIT1=A) and the checked-text-head law (D-BOUND-SINK1=A). New Prelude fns `csv.query<T>(path, q)` and `[T].query(q)` marshal to one `jet_*` engine entry (I9). Dialect scoped to project / filter / aggregate (sum, count, min, max, mean) / group / order / limit. Unknown column: registered diagnostic in Prelude/Diagnostics.jet plus a tests/ui compile-fail pair (I4). `{value}` holes stay bound parameters per the existing SQL taint rail.

options.name: Typed method calls only (no SQL text)
options.detail: No SQL dialect enters Jet. You load the file into typed records, then chain the list methods that already exist: `filter`, `group_by`, `map`, `sum`. Every column name is a field access, so every typo is an ordinary compile error. Gain: nothing new to learn, no query dialect boundary. Loss: you cannot paste a SQL query from docs, a teammate, or an assistant and run it. The owner's DuckDB bar is exactly that paste-and-run loop.
options.technical: New Prelude fn `csv.load<T>(path)` = read + `csv.decode<T>` in one step. Aggregation runs over the existing list surface (Core/Collections.rs `jet_list_group_by`, `sum`, `filter`); the columnar substrate (Core/ColumnList.rs, D-SOA1) accelerates it underneath. No new user-typeable surface, so no I7 decision is spent.

options.name: Both doors: SQL text plus a dedicated builder
options.detail: Ship option A's checked SQL head and also a dedicated query-builder API, over one shared engine. SQL text is the paste-and-run beginner door. The builder is the expert door for queries assembled by program logic. Loss: two query surfaces for one job. Jet's list methods already cover the typed door, so the dedicated builder mostly duplicates them. I8 says one mechanism per job; this option must show the builder adds real power, and today it does not.
options.technical: One engine (one I9 entry) with two front ends: the comptime SQL checker lowers to the same logical plan the builder constructs. The builder would be a new API (`orders.query().group(…).agg(…)`) over `[T]`/`JetColumnList<T>` — parallel to the existing `filter`/`group_by` surface.
options.code:
// Door 1 — SQL text (same as option A):
totals :: csv.query<Order>("orders.csv",
    SQL.{"SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer"})?

// Door 2 — dedicated builder over the same engine:
totals2 :: csv.load<Order>("orders.csv")?
    .query()
    .group(o => o.customer)
    .agg((customer, rows) => (customer: customer, total: rows.map(o => o.amount).sum()))
loop t, totals2 -> print("{t.customer}: {t.total}")

comparisons.note: The bar itself. One line of SQL at a file path, in-process, fast. But an unknown column fails at runtime, and rows come back as untyped tuples.
comparisons.code:
duckdb.sql("SELECT customer, SUM(amount) FROM 'orders.csv' GROUP BY customer").fetchall()
# typo a column name -> Binder Error at runtime

comparisons.note: Ships both doors: an expression builder and a SQL context over the same engine. Column names are strings either way, so typos fail at runtime.
comparisons.code: pl.scan_csv("orders.csv").sql("SELECT customer, SUM(amount) FROM self GROUP BY customer")

comparisons.note: C# ships two surfaces for one engine: method chains and a SQL-like comprehension syntax. The comprehension door decayed; style guides now prefer method chains. A caution for option C's second door.
comparisons.code:
orders.GroupBy(o => o.Customer)
      .Select(g => new { Customer = g.Key, Total = g.Sum(o => o.Amount) })

recommendation.why: Option A is the competitor loop itself, made safe: SQL text at a file, typed rows out, and a column typo fails at compile time. Jet's list methods already serve the typed expert path, so no second query API is needed. One engine, one new door, and the compile-time schema contrast lands head-on.

whyNot.reason: Builder-only misses the owner's bar. DuckDB's loop is pasting SQL at a file; a method chain cannot run a pasted query from docs, teammates, or assistants.
The dedicated builder duplicates the list methods Jet already has, so the second door adds surface without new power (I8). C#'s decayed comprehension syntax shows where that door leads.

recommendation.tradeoff: SQL text becomes a second spelling for sums and filters that method chains can also write. We accept this because the head reuses the existing checked SQL rail, the engine stays single, and paste-and-run SQL is the exact bar the owner set.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a checked SQL head, typed methods only, and both doors. It recommended the SQL head because it is DuckDB's own loop plus a compile-time schema check.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a LINQ-style comprehension syntax, a dataframe type, and a CLI-only `jet query` command. All three were folded out: new grammar, a result shape the card bans, and a door programs cannot call.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept one shared engine under whichever door wins, so a builder can bolt on later without a second engine. Option A's technical notes now name that engine contract.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B — no dialect, no parser, every typo an ordinary field error — and gave C its honest two-audience case. B still cannot run pasted SQL.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked dialect creep (joins, windows) and the cost of a SQL checker in sema. Scoping the dialect to project, filter, aggregate, group, order, and limit repaired it; the recommendation stands.

decisions.title: Time literal suffixes end at week
decisions.outcome: Add week as the only new Time literal suffix, a fixed 7-day scale on the ns carrier. Calendar-dependent units (month, year, decade, century, millennium) never become literal suffixes; they stay in the checked Period and date API.
decisions.comment: Add week as the only new Time literal suffix, a fixed 7-day scale on the ns carrier. Calendar-dependent units (month, year, decade, century, millennium) never become literal suffixes; they stay in the checked Period and date API.

decisions.title: Compact act-on-error form for Result and Optional
decisions.gist: Pick the compact way to act on a failed Result or Optional and then bail out.
decisions.lesson: Jet already spells most failure handling compactly. Postfix `?` passes a failure up. `??` gives a fallback value, and a `??` block may run statements before that value. `?? return` bails out at once. One case has no compact form: run a statement on the error, then bail out. Writers who hit it fall back to a five-line `if` block with a re-extraction, or copy `?? panic(…)` from the examples. Every option below keeps `?` and `??` as they are.
decisions.story: Priya writes a CLI that syncs inventory counts. When a fetch fails she wants one log line, then a clean exit. `?? return` cannot log first. A `??` block cannot exit. The five-line `if` block feels like punishment, so she copies `?? panic("bad fetch")` from an example. Her tool now crashes with a bug report instead of exiting cleanly.

options.name: Finish the `??` block: tail value or real exit
options.detail: The `??` fallback block keeps its statements and its ambient `err`. Its last line becomes either a plain value or a real exit: `return`, `return expr`, `break`, `next`, or `panic(…)`. A value fills in for the failure. An exit leaves the function or loop for real. Today's special reading, where a tail `return x` means the block's own value, is retired; the bare tail value stays the value form. No new operator, keyword, or binder. `?? return`, `?? next`, and `?? break` become the empty-block case of the same rule.
options.technical:
Parser: `parse_or_fallback_block` accepts a diverging tail and drops the return-as-block-value reading (crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Expressions/binary_unary.rs). Sema: a diverging block types the binding at the payload type, exactly like `?? return` (CheckerInfer/fallible.rs). E0003 still fires when a block neither yields a value nor diverges; its fix text already teaches the bare tail.

`err` stays ambient only in fallible fallbacks (D-FAIL-BIND1). D-CHOOSE-TEST1 pattern-test routes gain the same block form and must still diverge. I9: lowering reuses the shipped OrFallback::Block TIR path plus the `?? return` route lowering; no engine-side logic.

Migration: examples/features/errors/ambient_err.jet re-spells one tail; tests/ui/qq_block_fallback.jet flips from E0003 to valid and is re-blessed.

options.name: `else` handler on `?`: observe, then pass the failure up
options.detail: Postfix `?` grows an optional `else { … }` clause. The block runs on failure with ambient `err`, for one log line or a metric. The failure then travels up exactly as `?` does today, with the same conversion and the same journey. The block cannot cancel the failure and cannot supply a value. The act-then-bail-out case stays unsolved, so the five-line `if` block, or a second new form, would still be needed beside it.
options.technical: New optional clause on the Try expression, run before propagation on every tier. A note and an `else` may sit on the same call — `f()?("note") else { … }` — which puts two handler surfaces on one hop. Overlaps ratified law: D-FAIL-CTX1 notes already attach context to a hop, and #2044 redesigns the report trail for visibility.

options.name: Guard binding: `ok name :: expr else { … }`
options.detail: A new binding keyword in the Swift guard style. `ok body :: fetch(url) else { … }` binds the payload on success. On failure the else block runs with ambient `err` and must leave the function or loop. It reads top-down and the keyword is easy to search for. It is a third bind-or-bail grammar beside the `??` fallback and the pattern test `r == .Ok(x) ?? route`. It covers only bindings; an effect call such as `save(x)` gets nothing.
options.technical: New statement grammar: `ok NAME :: expr else BLOCK`, optional only for fallible and optional right-hand sides. The else block must diverge (same check as D-CHOOSE-TEST1 routes). Unlike Rust's `let … else`, the block can read the error through ambient `err` (D-FAIL-BIND1 extended to this position).

options.name: Method combinators: `.if_ok(…)` / `.if_err(…)`
options.detail: Prelude methods take a closure, run it on the matching side, and hand the outcome back for chaining. Good for pipelines and familiar from Rust's `inspect_err`. A closure cannot make the surrounding function return, so every bail-out still needs `?`, `??`, or an `if` block around the chain. Control flow hides in the middle of call chains, and branching gains a second mechanism beside the ratified arm table.
options.technical: Two Prelude methods on the one outcome carrier (D-FAIL-CARRIER1): `if_ok(fn(T))` and `if_err(fn(E))`, both returning the receiver unchanged. No grammar change. Effect typing follows the ordinary closure rules; the closure cannot use `return`, `break`, or `next` against the enclosing function or loop.

comparisons.note: Zig's `catch |e| { … }` block runs statements on the error and may return for real. This is option A's shape, and Zig users rate it among the language's best ergonomics.
`let … else` is option C's shape. Its famous gap: the else block cannot see the error value. Jet's ambient `err` avoids that gap in every option here.
`inspect_err` is option D's shape: observe in a chain, then still need `?` to leave.
`guard let … else` is option C with a required exit, checked by the compiler the same way D-CHOOSE-TEST1 checks a diverging route.
`if err != nil` is the five-line before shape this ballot exists to shrink. Go accepts the boilerplate as a feature; Jet's corpus answered it with `?? panic(…)` instead.

recommendation.why: A closes the one measured hole — act on the error, then leave — by finishing a block that already ships. It adds no operator, keyword, or binder. The existing routes become the empty case of one rule, and the 360 `?? panic(` teaching sites gain an honest replacement that is just as short.

whyNot.reason: It keeps the failure moving up, so act-then-bail-out stays unsolved and a second form would still be needed. The ratified `?` note and the #2044 report redesign already cover most observe-only needs.

It repeats option A's diverging block under a new keyword: a third bind-or-bail grammar beside `??` and the pattern test, against the one-mechanism law. It also covers only bindings, not effect calls.
A closure cannot make the surrounding function return, so none of the 309 `?? return` or 360 `?? panic(` sites can move to it. It also hides branching inside call chains.

recommendation.tradeoff: A tail `return x` inside a `??` block changes meaning from block value to real function return. The repo holds exactly two such spellings, both migrated by this card, and the bare tail stays the value form. Greenfield law forbids keeping both readings, so the flip is accepted.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft worked the card's three candidates plus a guard binder on one shared program, and measured 360 panic fallbacks, 309 bare early-return fallbacks, and one value-only fallback block. Finishing that block, option A, closes the measured gap, so A became the recommendation.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested Go-style two-value binding, a try/catch statement, `?.`-style ok-chaining, and expression-position deconstruction. All were folded: two-value binding breaks the one-carrier law, try/catch duplicates `??`, ok-chaining duplicates postfix `?`, and the arm table already deconstructs in expression position.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested one clause doing both observe-then-propagate (B) and act-then-exit (A), and rejected it because merging propagation into `??` blurs the ratified `?` versus `??` split. A's technical notes instead name `return err` for propagate-after-effect when the error types align.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened each loser: B gained the conversion argument, since a plain `return err` skips the `?` conversion rail. C gained Swift's top-down readability and a searchable keyword, and D gained pipeline chaining with Rust `inspect_err` precedent; all three still leave the measured gap.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A's silent meaning flip of a tail `return x`; only two in-repo spellings exist, and payload and return types disagree in most wrong programs, so sema catches them. The hidden-control-flow attack inverted, because today's block-value `return` is the surprising reading, so A survived and the tradeoff records the flip.

decisions.title: Call arguments: positional when unambiguous, named to deconflict
decisions.gist: When a call may use bare arguments and when the compiler makes you write parameter names.
decisions.lesson: Jet calls can write arguments bare, in order, or with names. Today the API author picks zones that force one form or the other. This choice sets the default culture: bare calls everywhere they are unambiguous, or names everywhere on complex APIs. It also decides what happens when one bare call could match two function bodies.
decisions.story: Priya knows `clamp` by heart and calls `clamp(v, 0, 100)` a hundred times a day. Her import of a C++ settings library exposes two `put` overloads that both take two strings. One bare call is muscle memory; the other is a coin flip about which body runs.

options.name: Bare when one binding exists; names only to deconflict
options.detail: A bare argument list is legal whenever exactly one binding exists after zones, defaults, and the variadic tail. Names stay required in exactly three places: a `*` zone, skipping a default, and a call that matches two bodies. The ambiguous call is a hard error that prints every candidate and the labeled rewrite. The editor always shows parameter names as ghost text, so nobody retypes them.
options.technical:
Bare arguments fill parameters left to right in declaration order (S61 E0768/E0769 unchanged). Defaults fill unbound trailing slots; arity then must match (E0766). Types check after binding and never reroute it (E0112). Remaining bare arguments pack into a final `...T` (D-VARIADIC1).

When one name resolves to several callable bodies (collapsed C++ overloads, D-CPP), a bare call must bind exactly one; two or more is the new sema error E0772. User code keeps one definition per name (D-CAP10), and S83 heads dispatch on enum variants, so E0772 fires only on interop surfaces today. The language server serves call-site parameter-name inlay hints from the semindex, on by default (precedent: D-REF3).

options.name: Named-first: complex APIs force labels with `*` zones
options.detail: Keep S61 exactly as it is and steer every multi-parameter public API toward a `*` label-only zone. Callers then type names at every call site, every time. Source stays self-documenting without an editor, and the two-body case cannot arise because every call is named. The cost is a permanent typing tax on APIs people already know.
options.technical: No compiler change. A style rule plus a standard-library sweep adds `*` after the first parameter of multi-parameter `pub` functions. E0769 already rejects bare arguments in the label-only zone. Inlay hints stay type-only, since names are in the source.

options.name: Bare always; first declaration wins; a lint warns
options.detail: A bare call is always legal. When two bodies match, the first declared one runs and an advisory lint flags the call. Nothing ever blocks a build. The danger: reordering declarations in an imported header silently changes which body runs, and advisory warnings ship to production.
options.technical: The binder ranks candidates by declaration order and picks the first that binds. A new advisory lint (L-family) marks any call where a second candidate also binds. No hard error exists for ambiguity; CI may promote the lint per package policy.

comparisons.note: Bare arguments by default; the `/` and `*` zone separators are the exact spelling S61 borrowed. Keywords deconflict when the author or caller wants them; editors show name hints as ghost text.
comparisons.code:
connect("db.internal", tls=False)
def clamp(value, /, low=0, high=100): ...

comparisons.note: Argument labels are required by default and `_` opts a parameter out. This is option B's named-first world, priced at every call site in the language's whole ecosystem.
comparisons.code:
func clamp(_ value: Int, low: Int, high: Int) -> Int { ... }
clamp(v, low: 0, high: 100)

comparisons.note: Overloads resolve by types and arity only. An ambiguous call is a hard compile error, never a silent first-wins pick — the precedent for E0772 over option C.
comparisons.code:
put("theme", "dark");
// error: call of overloaded 'put(const char*, const char*)' is ambiguous

recommendation.why: Bare calls match how people use APIs they already know, so the common case costs zero typing. The compiler steps in only where two bodies could run, which is the one real danger. Ghost text supplies every name without anyone retyping it.

whyNot.reason: It taxes every call to every complex API forever, to solve a readability problem the editor already solves. That fails the beginner pass: ceremony without necessity.
A first-wins pick can silently run the wrong body after an unrelated declaration reorder. An advisory lint does not stop that build from shipping.

recommendation.tradeoff: Outside an editor — diffs, review, pastebins — simple calls show bare arguments without names. We accept this because `*` zones remain available wherever an API author decides names are load-bearing.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the three regimes on one program, wrote the deterministic-mapping rule, and ran the beginner and expert passes: bare-by-default serves beginners, zones and E0772 keep expert control.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested arity thresholds (labels above N parameters), a per-package strictness setting, and forced labels on adjacent same-type parameters. All three folded away: thresholds are arbitrary, settings split the language into dialects, and same-type adjacency is reader ambiguity that ghost text already answers.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review layered option B's label-only sweep on top of A and rejected it, because S61 zones already give authors that power per API. A absorbed one part: the E0772 fix line prints a ready labeled rewrite, borrowing B's self-documenting call shape at exactly the ambiguous sites.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B — named calls document diffs with no editor, and a library upgrade can never create new ambiguity — and strengthened C with a build-breaking CI mode. B remains a per-call tax; C's wrong-body danger still ships by default.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A where an overlay upgrade adds an overload and breaks a legal bare call; E0772 repairs this mechanically by printing each candidate with its labeled rewrite. Plain-terminal readers without ghost text keep `*` zones for load-bearing names, so A survived.

decisions.title: Accept #2044 — Runtime error report redesign: root cause first, then the trail
decisions.gist: Close #2044, or bounce it back to building.
decisions.detail:
1. Report leads with the root error (what/why/fix grade), then the propagation trail with source frames; repeated frames dedup — met (PROOF (2026-08-19, builder f30728f4d): jet run examples/features/errors/error_context.jet now prints 'Error: file not found' FIRST, then ' Trail [E3002] (3 hops via ?, origin first):' with three numbered frames carrying their notes. Consecutive-identical frames still collapse and now carry a repeat count. Three order copies were found and deleted (Outcome.rs held the order, and the generated wasm store plus the JS projection each concatenated journey+report themselves); all now call one jet_journey_compose. Seven error goldens blessed from real runs (commit ac2c0a19d) and the whole delta reviewed byte by byte.)
2. Real terminal state matrix proven: tty vs pipe, ANSI vs NO_COLOR, narrow widths; snapshots for each (I4) — met (PROOF cargo test --test terminal 12/12 ok (23.4s, 2026-08-19, builder 1c761ea67). Criterion was 0 percent satisfied before, not partly: the report emitted no ANSI, read no NO_COLOR, read no tty state and read no width, so a pipe, a colour terminal, NO_COLOR and a 40-column terminal all received identical bytes - and the real example's hop lines are 85 and 90 columns, so they already soft-wrapped mid-path at 80. Four matrix fixtures now exist (tests/cli/error_report_pipe.txt, error_report_tty_ansi.txt, error_report_tty_no_color.txt, error_report_tty_narrow40.txt). One design constraint shaped it: Outcome.rs is include_str!'d verbatim into every generated program, so it may use std only - facts go in, policy lives in the one renderer, detection happens in exactly one place, so no per-tier variant can exist and the crate's existing colour ladder now calls that same detector instead of spelling NO_COLOR itself.)
3. Same report shape on every execution tier: AOT, default jet run, jet dev deopt (I9) — met (PROOF (2026-08-19, builder at the closure_ops caller commit): all three legs of examples/features/errors/error_context.jet now print the byte-identical report - jet run, jet run --release (AOT), and jet run --interpret each emit 'Error: file not found' then ' Trail [E3002] (3 hops via ?, origin first):' with the same three numbered frames and notes. Before the fix --interpret printed the root cause with NO trail block. Root cause was not a missing adapter: the hop store is a thread_local and the TIR evaluator runs every interpreted program on a spawned jet-tir-eval worker, so hops were recorded in the worker while the report edge drained the caller's empty list after the join. The same boundary covered the JIT whole-program deopt edge; mid-run deopt was never affected because it stays on the JIT's own thread. Fixed as marshalling - Foundation still owns the list, the collapse and the rendering, and adopting replays carried hops through the same collapse. A cross-tier snapshot test was added, which the trail example had never had; that absence is why the divergence shipped.)
4. Before/after comparison on real failing examples shows the actual error is findable first; owner visual acceptance on look-and-feel — met (Before/after on the real failing example examples/features/errors/error_context.jet. BEFORE (its blessed golden at the time): three 'error propagated from: ...' lines first, then 'Error: file not found' LAST - one line said what broke, three near-identical lines said where it passed, and the failure sat at the bottom. AFTER: 'Error: file not found' first, then ' Trail [E3002] (3 hops via ?, origin first):' with the three frames beneath it. Seven error goldens moved accordingly and every delta was reviewed byte by byte. Owner visual acceptance on look-and-feel is the only remaining gate; nothing machine-verifiable is outstanding.)

decisions.title: Structure is a fact plane: liveness, lifecycle, and edges under the fact law
decisions.gist: Whether facts about a program's own structure join the one fact registry, or stay separate checks.
decisions.lesson: Jet holds facts about values, rights, effects, and time under one ratified law: one home, silent tightening, one written word to loosen, one ledger (D-FACT-LAW1). The audit on card #2052 found structure truths with no home: whether a name is used, what stage an API is in, which import edges are legal. This ballot decides where those truths live. The follow-up ballots (D-STRUCT-LIVE1, LIFE1, EDGE1) decide each surface; this one decides the substrate.
decisions.story: Mara's team has a wiki page: 'delete dead imports, don't import the DB layer from UI, use parse not decode'. None of it is checked. A new agent session breaks all three rules in one afternoon, and review catches one of them. Mara wants the compiler to hold the rules the way it already holds effects.

options.name: One plane: structure facts join the fact registry
options.detail: Liveness, lifecycle stage, and edge legality register as fact rows with a stated safe direction and a gate word. Every bypass lands in the one gate ledger. `jet inspect structure` reads the rows the same way `jet inspect gates` reads gates. Users get one mental model: the compiler learns structure facts for you, never forgets one, and every exception is one written word.
options.technical: Rows: liveness (safe direction = referenced; gate = `_name`), lifecycle (safe direction = fewer promises announced, more warnings honored; gate = policy allow), edge (safe direction = fewer edges; gate = manifest rule edit, on the record). All rows erase at runtime (I3). Drift guard from D-FACT-LAW1=B applies: a row that states no direction or gate fails the build of the compiler itself.
options.code:
$ jet inspect structure app/
liveness   app/main.jet:3  use core.files   unused — remove, or mark `_files`
lifecycle  store.decode    retiring 1.2     replacement: store.parse
boundary   app.api → core.files   DENIED by package.jet boundaries[0]
gates      _files (main.jet:3)    1 use

options.name: Lints only: verdicts without registry rows
options.detail: Ship the same warnings and errors, but as ordinary diagnostics with no fact rows, no ledger entries, and no inspect lens. Simpler to picture. The cost: suppressions are invisible to audit, and the structure story cannot be asked for. Each verdict becomes its own small system — the fragmentation the fact law was ratified to end.

options.name: External analyzer: keep the compiler out of it
options.detail: Leave structure checking to a separate tool, the way Java leaves it to ArchUnit and Python to import-linter. The compiler stays smaller. The cost: a second source of truth about the program, a second config surface, and no I4 diagnostics contract. Every peer that took this road ended with rules teams do not run.
options.code:
$ jet-structure check .   # hypothetical side tool
# separate install, separate config, separate output format

options.name: Decline: structure stays folklore
options.detail: No new checks. Wikis, review comments, and agent prompts keep carrying the rules. Nothing changes for any current program. The four audit losses to clippy, eslint, ArchUnit, and rust's deprecated attribute stay open.
options.code:
// status quo: jet check prints "ok" over dead imports, dead functions,
// silent layering breaks, and un-deprecatable APIs

comparisons.note: Rustc holds unused checks in the compiler with one suppression spelling (`_x`, `#[allow]`); architecture rules live nowhere. Jet can hold both in one registry with one audited gate story.
comparisons.code:
warning: unused variable: `dead`
  = note: `#[warn(unused_variables)]` on by default

comparisons.note: Architecture rules are a test-library bolt-on. Teams that skip the test suite skip the rules. Compiler-held rules cannot be skipped silently.

recommendation.why: The fact law already answers every hard question these checks raise: where the truth lives, how it tightens, how a bypass is spelled, and where the bypass is recorded. Registering structure rows buys the ledger, the inspect lens, and the drift guard for free, and keeps one mental model for beginners: Jet learns facts for you.

whyNot.reason: Plain lints rebuild the pre-fact-law world: each verdict becomes its own small system with invisible suppressions. That fragmentation is what D-FACT-LAW1 was ratified to end.
A side tool is a second source of truth with no I4 contract. The peer evidence is uniform: bolt-on analyzers get skipped, which is why this gap exists in every mainstream language.
Declining keeps the four measured losses open, and agents keep eroding structure that no oracle defends.

recommendation.tradeoff: The fact registry gains three row kinds whose subjects are names and edges rather than values. That widens the registry's job description, and we accept it because the law's own text already names scopes and the build as fact subjects.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared registry rows, plain lints, and declining, and recommended rows because the ledger and inspect lens come free.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the external-analyzer option, since ArchUnit-style tools are the real incumbents. It stayed a losing option: every one of them is skippable and un-contracted.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested lints-first-rows-later as a staged hybrid. Rejected: staging is implementation shape, not a distinct final design, so no option was added.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B (it can reuse the `_name` gate and policy walls) and C (it could ship in-repo and versioned). Both still lack the ledger, the lens, and the diagnostics contract.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on registry bloat and beginner noise. Each row has a subject, a safe direction, and a gate word, and warnings never fail builds, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Liveness verdicts: unused imports, bindings, functions, and unreachable exports
decisions.gist: Which dead names the compiler reports, and how a user silences one.
decisions.lesson: Today Jet says nothing about dead code. A probe this run passed `jet check` with an unused import, an unused function, and an unused binding in eleven lines. Every mainstream toolchain reports these. Dead code also costs agents directly: they pay tokens to read names the compiler already knows are dead. The suppression spelling already exists — the underscore ladder (D-NAME-SIGIL1) makes `_name` the human mark for internal or discarded names. This ballot is a scope dial, not a design contest: it decides how far one verdict family reaches.
decisions.story: An agent refactors Priya's service across forty edits. Each edit orphans an import or a helper. Nothing ever says so. Three weeks later a quarter of the file is dead weight, every future agent reads all of it, and Priya cannot tell live code from fossil without tracing by hand.

options.name: Full family: file-local dead names plus unreachable package exports
options.detail: Four verdicts: unused import, unused binding, unused private function, and a `pub(package)` or application-target export nothing reaches. All are warnings under the override law — they never fail a build unless a team wall says so. Renaming to `_name` or deleting is the whole fix. Library `pub` items are exempt by definition: their consumers live outside the build.
options.technical: File-local verdicts need only the existing resolver. The export tier needs a new package-wide reference pass over the explicit import graph. ApiFreeze snapshots only the package's own public surface (verified in Sema/ApiFreeze.rs), so no existing data shortens that pass. The tier applies only where the consumer set is closed: `pub(package)` items and application (payload) targets. Never fires on library `pub`. Policy names: unused_import, unused_binding, unused_fn, unreachable_export.
options.code:
warn: import `files` is never used
  fix: remove it, or name it `_files`
warn: `attempts` is never read
  fix: remove it, or name it `_attempts`
warn: `retry_once` has no callers in this package
  fix: remove it, or name it `_retry_once`

// team wall, package.jet:
policy: .{ lints: .{ deny: [unused_import] } }

options.name: File-local only: imports, bindings, private functions
options.detail: The same verdicts without the export tier. Everything is decidable inside one file's resolver output, so no reachability question exists. The cost: exported-but-orphaned code — the largest and longest-lived kind of dead weight — stays invisible.

options.name: Imports only
options.detail: Report only unused imports, the least controversial verdict. Smallest possible step. Bindings and functions keep rotting silently, which is where most of the measured waste sits.
options.code:
warn: import `files` is never used
// everything else: silence

options.name: Decline
options.detail: No liveness verdicts. Jet stays the only modern toolchain that says nothing about dead code. Scratch scripts stay perfectly quiet, which is the one honest gain.
options.code:
$ jet check main.jet
ok: `main.jet` has no problems   // including the dead third of it

comparisons.note: Unused imports and locals are hard errors. Users hate the interruption mid-edit; the ecosystem grew `_ = x` idioms to fight the compiler. Jet's warning-plus-underscore keeps the teaching without the fight.

Warnings by default, `_x` to silence, deny-able per project. Widely considered the right default. This is option A's shape, minus the export tier rustc lacks (dead pub detection needs external tools there).
comparisons.code:
warning: unused variable: `attempts`
help: if this is intentional, prefix it with an underscore: `_attempts`

recommendation.why: Dead exports are the dead code that matters most and lasts longest. Jet is unusually able to catch them: imports are explicit, wildcards are banned, and the graph is closed for package-fenced and application code. The family is one law — every declared name is reachable or carries the `_` mark. One law teaches better than a shrinking subset, warnings never block anyone, and the fix is one rename with one obvious repair.

whyNot.reason: Stops exactly where the value is highest. File-local rot is annoying; orphaned exports are the fossils that survive for years.
Unused bindings are the most common dead name in the corpus and the cheapest to detect. Reporting only imports leaves most of the waste.
Keeps the one hygiene loss to every peer toolchain, and keeps paying agent tokens for names the compiler knows are dead.

recommendation.tradeoff: The export tier needs a new package-wide reference pass whose incremental cost is unmeasured, and it can mislabel code kept for future use inside an application. We accept both because the `_name` mark and the policy allow are one written word each, and library `pub` is exempt by scope.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed the four-verdict family with `_name` as the one suppression, over file-local-only, imports-only, and decline.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested hard errors (Go's model) and silent auto-deletion. Both folded: errors fight users mid-edit, and silent deletion changes programs without a verdict.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested pairing every verdict with a `jet fix` edit. That strengthened all options rather than creating a new one, so the fix note moved into A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B (no reachability analysis needed anywhere) and D (scripts stay noise-free). Both remain weaker than A on the audit's measured waste.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked the export tier: library `pub` has zero in-repo consumers by design. Repaired by scoping that tier to `pub(package)` items and application targets, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: One lifecycle ladder: user-facing #Deprecated and the end of the Core-only table
decisions.gist: How a library tells its users an API is going away.
decisions.lesson: A Jet name already climbs a ladder: `_name` internal, `pub _name` soft-public (L0601), `pub` stable with its shape frozen by ApiFreeze. The ladder has no top: nothing marks an API as retiring. Core keeps that power in a duplicated two-row table — canonical in jet-pkg-model Manifest.rs, mirrored in Sema/Edition.rs — live for exactly two cbor items, and no package can use it. Amendment note: this ballot opens the Core-only E2001/E2002/L2001 deprecation area to every package.
decisions.story: Ana ships a config library. Version 1.2 renames `decode` to `parse` because the old name collided with a family verb. She cannot say so in code. Her options today are a comment, a changelog, and hope. Every consumer learns about the rename when `decode` disappears and their build breaks with no pointer to the replacement.

options.name: The full ladder: #Deprecated marker, both Core table copies deleted into it
options.detail: Any package marks any `pub` item `#Deprecated(since: "1.2", use: "parse")`. Consumers get one warning carrying the replacement; `jet fix` applies it when the replacement is a plain rename. Core's two rows become ordinary markers on `cbor.encode` and `cbor.decode`. Both table copies — jet-pkg-model Manifest.rs and the Sema/Edition.rs mirror — are deleted in the same change, per the greenfield law. One mechanism, top to bottom of the ladder, same for Core and everyone.
