options.technical: Marker registers in Prelude/Markers.jet (law zero). Warning rides the live L2001/E2002 path (today emitted from CheckerCoreLib/core_call.rs via the hardcoded table); that path re-reads the marker registry instead. `removed_in:` is optional and only binds when package editions are wired. ApiFreeze remains the enforcement half: removing the item later is the same named-delta error it is today. Policy names: deprecated_use (warn by default; deny-able; allow-able for vendored deps).

options.name: Marker only: users get #Deprecated, Core keeps its table
options.detail: Same user-facing marker, but Core's duplicated table (Manifest.rs plus the Edition.rs mirror) stays as a second mechanism. Users gain everything option A gives them. The compiler keeps two homes for one truth — three counting the marker — which the corpus law names a defect.

options.name: Manifest-declared deprecation
options.detail: Deprecations live in package.jet as data (`deprecations: .{ "decode": .{ since: "1.2", use: "parse" } }`), not at the item. Keeps source files untouched and the list auditable in one place. The cost: the truth sits away from the item, so readers of the source see nothing, and the fact law wants the word at the site.

options.name: Decline
options.detail: No user-facing deprecation. Libraries keep breaking consumers cold, or keep old names forever. Note the tension: keeping old names forever is what the greenfield law forbids Jet's own corpus.

comparisons.note: `#[deprecated(since, note)]` is available to every crate and is the single most-used evolution tool in the ecosystem. Note is free text; Jet's `use:` names the replacement, so the fix is typed.
comparisons.code:
#[deprecated(since = "1.2", note = "use parse")]
pub fn decode(bytes: &[u8]) -> Config { ... }

comparisons.note: Deprecation is a comment convention (`// Deprecated: ...`) that tools grep for. It works only because gopls chose to honor prose. A convention held up by one tool is the outcome to avoid.
comparisons.code:
// Deprecated: Use Parse instead.
func Decode(b []byte) (Config, error) { ... }

recommendation.why: The ladder completes with one marker in the registry every other marker already lives in, the warning window already spec'd, and the enforcement half already shipped as ApiFreeze. Core eating its own dogfood — its two rows becoming ordinary markers — is the proof the mechanism is honest. The replacement lands in the consumer's hands as a typed edit, which is the repair-determinism win agents need.

whyNot.reason: Keeps two homes for one truth. The corpus law (D-ONCE-LAW1) makes an underivable second copy a defect, and the second copy here is inside the compiler itself.
Moves the truth away from the item. Source readers see a healthy function, and the fact law's own words ask for the written word at the site.
Leaves libraries the choice between breaking consumers cold and hoarding stale names forever — both outcomes the rest of Jet's law system exists to prevent.

recommendation.tradeoff: The `removed_in:` field stays dormant until package editions are wired, so the ladder's last rung is warn-only for now. We accept a ladder with a soft top over no ladder, because ApiFreeze already makes removal a named, non-silent event.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed the site marker with a named replacement and recommended deleting the Core table into it.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added the manifest-declared option and tested runtime warnings (Node's model). Runtime warnings folded because Jet facts erase at runtime by law.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested marker-at-site plus a rendered manifest summary. Folded into A: `jet inspect api` renders the lifecycle table from the markers, giving C's auditability without its scattering.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened C (survives file moves without touching source) and D (pre-1.0 breaking with good notes is defensible). Both still lose on where the reader looks and on typed fixes.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked the edition coupling: `removed_in:` implies machinery that is staged, not wired. Repaired by making the field optional and warn-only until editions land, with removal staying on ApiFreeze.

decisions.title: Boundary rules: import edges as manifest policy
decisions.gist: Whether a package can declare which of its own modules may import which.
decisions.lesson: Every team past a certain size writes the same rule in prose: the UI layer never touches storage, the core never imports upward. No mainstream language can check it, so a whole tool family bolts it on (ArchUnit, import-linter, eslint-boundaries). Jet already constrains what a dependency may do — effect budgets in package.jet, with E1220 naming the offender (D-EFFBUDGET1). This ballot decides whether the same manifest can constrain the package's own import graph. The compiler already holds that graph completely: imports are explicit, wildcards are banned, cycles are errors.
decisions.story: Tom's team agreed in review: handlers call the store module, never core.files directly. Six months and two hundred agent edits later, eleven handlers read disk directly. Nothing objected at any point. The wiki page was correct the whole time.

options.name: A boundaries: key, shaped like effect budgets
options.detail: One manifest key lists denied (or exclusively allowed) import edges between module paths. A violating `use` is one error naming the edge and the rule, the way E1220 names a dependency. No key means no rules — today's behavior exactly. Policy narrows and never widens, per the ratified policy law.
options.technical: Edge = `{ from: "module.path", to: "module.path" }` with one trailing `*` subtree wildcard per side. Checked at import resolution; zero runtime presence. Rules bind the declaring package's own modules only — dependencies police themselves. Diagnostic names the edge, the rule index, and the two fixes: route through an allowed layer, or amend the manifest (one written line, on the record). Key style follows D-EFFBUDGET1's plain-brace effects spelling.

options.name: One merged rules surface for effects and imports
options.detail: Fold effect budgets and import rules into a single `rules:` key, since both are allow/deny edge policy. One law on paper. The cost: the two rule kinds bind different graphs — the dependency graph versus the package's own module graph — and a merged key hides which graph a rule touches. This option amends the ratified D-EFFBUDGET1 spelling.

options.name: Site markers on modules
options.detail: Declare constraints where the module is declared: `#NoImport(core.files)` on the module. The rule sits next to the code it governs. The cost: the architecture story scatters across files, and package-level policy already has a ratified home — the manifest, which only tightens (D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1).

options.name: Decline
options.detail: No import rules. Layering stays prose. Jet keeps parity with every other language here, and teams that care adopt review discipline or wait for an ecosystem tool that does not exist yet.
options.code:
// wiki: "handlers never import core.files"
// compiler: no opinion, forever

comparisons.note: The most-adopted architecture checker anywhere, and it runs only when the test suite runs. The demand is proven; the delivery mechanism is the weakness Jet can fix by holding the rule in the compiler.

The `internal/` directory is the one architecture rule Go ever added, retrofitted into the toolchain after conventions failed. Evidence that when a boundary rule matters enough, it ends up compiler-held.
comparisons.code: package foo/internal/db  // importable only from within foo/

recommendation.why: The compiler already holds the whole import graph explicitly, so the check is a table lookup at resolution time. The key mirrors a shape the owner already ratified for effects, so there is nothing new to learn: allow/deny, policy only narrows, the error names the offender and both fixes. No language owns this surface; it is a categorical win at near-zero conceptual cost, and absent the key nothing changes for anyone.

whyNot.reason: Merging hides which graph a rule binds — a dependency's behavior versus my own module edges are different questions, and D-EFFBUDGET1's spelling would be amended for a legibility loss.
Scatters the architecture story across module headers and creates a second home for package policy, against the ratified rule that the manifest is where policy tightens.
Keeps the most-requested architecture check in industry unexpressible, in the one language positioned to hold it natively.

recommendation.tradeoff: The manifest gains three small value kinds: record-literal rule rows, module-path strings, and one trailing subtree wildcard. We accept them because a rules list without record rows and subtree matching forces one bare string per module pair and rots as the tree grows.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed the sibling key with effect-budget shape and deny-first semantics, against merged-surface, site-marker, and decline options.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested directory-convention rules (Go's internal/) and a standalone rules file. The convention folds into the existing `_name` ladder; the file lost to the one-manifest law.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested manifest rules plus a read-only site echo. Folded into the inspect story: `jet inspect boundaries` shows per-module bindings without a second writable surface.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B (one edge-policy law is the deeper unification on paper) and C (locality helps single-module readers). Both still lose on graph legibility and the manifest's ratified role.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked rules-rot and allow-mode lockout. Repaired: a rule matching zero edges becomes a liveness warning, and deny-first is documented as the default posture, so the recommendation survived.

decisions.title: Policy authorship: who may mint a #Policy setting
decisions.gist: Whether users can author new policy settings for the ratified #Policy wrapper, or only apply the Core set.
decisions.lesson: Jet already has the one typed callable wrapper (D-CALLPOLICY1=E, D-CALLPOLICY2=C, shipped). `#Policy(retry(3), trace("users.load"))` sets a declaration default; `apply(retry(3), fn)` replaces the chain and preserves the whole checked contract. This ballot never touches that spelling. The door it examines: `PolicySetting` is a compiler-known type, so users apply policies but cannot author one. A team that needs `audit(...)` waits for a compiler release — the closed-table shape again. This ballot extends D-CALLPOLICY1's vocabulary and names that as its scope.
decisions.story: Sam's team passed a compliance review that requires an audit-log entry around every handler that touches billing. `#Policy(trace(...))` exists, but `audit` is not in the Core vocabulary. Sam's choices today: hand-write the audit call in forty bodies, or file a compiler feature request and wait a release cycle for Core to bless a setting Core cannot even know about.

options.name: User-declared settings through checked marker bodies
options.detail: A package declares a policy setting the way it declares a marker, with an ordinary checked body — the machinery D-META-USER1=A already ratified for markers that emit additive items. The setting's wrapper body is normal Jet: its effects add to the wrapped function's row visibly, and the wrapped contract is preserved by the same law apply() already enforces. Beginners keep applying; authors get one declaration site; every team's cross-cutting concern gets a first-class home.
options.technical: A declared setting names its parameters (typed, defaulted like any signature) and a wrap body that receives the callable. The body may observe arguments and results and may add its own effects; it may not edit the wrapped signature — the preserved-contract rule of D-CALLPOLICY2 is the invariant. Settings are nominal and package-scoped; applying an unknown setting stays an error naming the declaring package. No AST access, no signature edits, no macro.

options.name: Core-grown vocabulary: one ballot per setting
options.detail: The set stays compiler-known; it grows by owner ballot the way the prelude grows (D-PRELUDE-LAW1's discipline). Every setting is vetted, uniform, and documented once. The cost: Core cannot know a team's concerns — `audit`, `tenant_scope`, `cache_for` — so the most common cross-cutting needs keep living as pasted body code, and every request waits a release.

options.name: Closed on purpose
options.detail: The vocabulary stays exactly today's Core set, permanently. Policy behavior remains something the compiler authors and users only select. Maximally uniform and auditable; every concern outside the set is hand-threaded forever, and the closed-table defect this audit found twice becomes a wall kept on purpose.

comparisons.note: Decorators won because policy authors and policy users are different people: any team can mint one. They lost every type guarantee. Jet's version keeps authorship AND the preserved checked contract apply() already enforces.
User-authored wrapping needs proc macros — untyped token expansion Jet's walls forbid. The demand routes through the one hole in Rust's type story; Jet can serve it with a checked body instead.
comparisons.code: #[instrument]  // tracing's proc macro rewrites the fn

recommendation.why: The wrapper law is already ratified and its preserved-contract invariant does the safety work; authorship is the only missing half. Option A reuses the checked marker-body machinery that already ships (D-META-USER1) and keeps the application spelling identical, so beginners see nothing new. The two closed-table findings of this audit — deprecation and this — argue the same way: a vocabulary users need grows where users are.

whyNot.reason: Core cannot enumerate other people's concerns. Every real need waits a release, so the pasted-body reality this surface exists to end persists between ballots.
Keeps the closed-table defect as policy. The mechanism's whole value — one home per concern — stays unreachable for exactly the concerns teams actually have.

recommendation.tradeoff: User wrap bodies put user code around every application site, so a bad policy body can slow or log-flood every wrapped call. We accept it because the body is ordinary checked Jet — its effects surface in the wrapped row, and the preserved-contract rule caps what it can touch.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft of this ballot re-litigated the wrapper mechanism itself from a stale 2026-08-03 field audit; the fresh-context review caught D-CALLPOLICY1=E already ratified and shipped. This recast asks only the authorship question.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested user-extensible `#Context` keys as the authorship vehicle and a trait-based policy interface. Context keys thread state, not behavior, and ride any outcome; a trait interface duplicates the marker-body machinery D-META-USER1 already ratified.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested A-plus-B: user settings in packages plus a vetted Core set. That is not a hybrid — it is option A, since Core is a package and its settings stay vetted by ballot regardless.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B (uniform vetted vocabulary, zero user-authored behavior injection) and C (smallest possible surface, nothing to audit). Both are honest walls; both leave the measured pasted-body corpus exactly as it is.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on effect honesty and wrapper misuse: a policy body that swallows errors or hides latency. Repaired — the body's effects join the wrapped row visibly, the preserved-contract rule forbids signature edits, and an application stays one written mark at the site.

decisions.title: Say it once, in programs: @loop reaches marker bodies, impl items, and test blocks
decisions.gist: Whether the existing template loop can generate registry rows, impls, and benches from one written table.
decisions.lesson: Jet's corpus law says every truth has one home and every copy is rendered (D-ONCE-LAW1), and Jet programs cannot obey it in three positions. The stdlib is the proof. Units.jet repeats a 24-row prefix block across 31 of 32 families (~700 of 910 lines). Errors.jet hand-writes 13 identical impls; one bench file unrolls a 4×3×2 matrix into 24 blocks. The ratified template machinery (D-META-CODE1) stops at type members. This ballot decides whether it reaches marker bodies, impl items, and test blocks, naming two extensions as amendments.
decisions.story: A contributor adds the Luminance family (candela per square meter) to Jet's unit catalog. The new family is one concept. Today it means hand-writing the same 24 prefix rows a 32nd time, and review must confirm by eye that every exponent matches the other 31 copies. One typo'd exponent ships until a golden test happens to touch it.

options.name: Templates reach the three positions (two named amendments)
options.detail: The existing `@loop` becomes legal inside marker bodies, at top-level impl-item position, and inside test and bench declarations. Loop sources must be written literal tables or comptime-pure values — closed lists a reader can see, never reflection over open sets. The checker sees each generated declaration one by one, exactly as derive templates already work. Two forms exceed today's ratified law and are adopted as named amendments: loops over a closed written type list, and declaration names built by interpolation inside marker bodies.
options.technical:
Amendment 1: `@loop E, [BrowserError, …]` adds a closed-type-list comptime binding kind; D-GENMOD-VALUE1's value set does not contain types today. Amendment 2: `unit("{p.name}ohm", …)` admits comptime-computed declaration names in marker bodies. Both stay inside S26's intent: no type is created or selected at a use site, each impl head names a written type, and the impl set stays closed. Intent is not law, so this ballot carries the amendment text.

Coherence: generated impls obey the ordinary orphan rule at the expansion site. `jet inspect expand` covers these expansions (spec.md:3710). Family-specific unit rows stay hand-written; the loop replaces only the mechanical 24.

options.name: Stdlib-internal expansion only
options.detail: The compiler gets a blessed expansion path for its own Prelude files; user programs get nothing. The 700 lines die, but the capability is hoarded — the same closed-table defect this audit found in the deprecation machinery, repeated in the metaprogramming layer.
options.code: // Prelude builds shrink; a user's 24-case bench matrix stays hand-unrolled

options.name: Parameterize each DSL instead
options.detail: No loops. Each registry surface grows its own knob: `#UnitFamily(..., prefixes: si.all)`, `#Bench` accepts a case table, error families get a derive. Every knob is small and safe. The cost: N bespoke mini-features doing one job — the many-coats shape the one-mechanism invariant exists to prevent — and the next DSL starts at zero again.

options.name: Decline
options.detail: The three positions stay literal-only. The stdlib keeps its 700 pasted lines, review keeps confirming 28 copies are identical by eye, and user registries inherit the same ceiling as they grow.
options.code: // the Luminance family lands as 24 more hand rows; exponent typos ship

comparisons.note: This exact pressure produced `macro_rules!` tables in every large crate — untyped token expansion that Jet's walls forbid. The demand is real; the question is whether Jet's typed loop answers it before users hit the wall.
Comptime loops generating declarations from written tables is Zig's signature move, and it stays fully checked. Closest existing shape to option A.

recommendation.why: One ratified mechanism reaching three more positions beats three bespoke knobs and beats a hoarded compiler-only path. The lists stay written at the site, so nothing becomes less auditable. A visible table and shape is strictly more reviewable than 31 hand copies that merely claim to be identical. The stdlib's own ~700 lines are the acceptance test.

whyNot.reason: Repeats the closed-table defect inside the metaprogramming layer: the compiler keeps a power users are denied, and user registries hit the same wall unfixed.
N mini-features for one job is the many-coats shape I8 exists to prevent, and every future DSL starts the fight over.
Keeps measurable, review-hostile duplication in the compiler's own source while the corpus law calls that a defect.

recommendation.tradeoff: Marker bodies stop being purely literal: a reader may now meet a loop where rows used to be. We accept it because the loop's source table is written at the same site and `jet inspect expand` renders the rows on demand.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed extending @loop to the three measured positions against stdlib-only, per-DSL knobs, and decline.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested build-step file generation and runtime case tables for benches. Both folded: generation loses provenance and review locality; runtime tables lose per-case compile-time identity.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested adopting loops plus a #Bench case-table knob as sugar. Folded: once loops reach the position, a knob is a second spelling for the same rows.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened C (each surface gets a designed, minimal vocabulary) and B (the stdlib is where all three measured offenders live). Both remain subsets of A's coverage.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on the S26 wall and on auditability drift, and the attack landed: type-list loops and interpolated names exceed ratified template law. Repaired by naming both as explicit amendments in the ballot instead of claiming S26 compliance, with loop sources restricted to literal tables named at the site.

decisions.comment: With this decision, we need to reverse the decision made earlier today to erase @if and collapse to if.

decisions.title: keep(x): a benchmark sink the optimizer must respect
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a keep(x) helper that stops the optimizer from deleting benchmarked work.
decisions.lesson: An optimizing compiler deletes work whose result is never used. A benchmark loop often computes a value and drops it, so the release build can erase the loop and report near-zero time. Jet's harness already protects each region's final result, but values dropped inside the body have no protection. A lazy resource, such as a file that is read only when touched, can also defer its cost past the timer. This choice decides how a bencher marks a value as truly used.
decisions.story: Mara benchmarks her log scanner before a launch post. The release optimizer sees her hit counter is never read and deletes the whole scan. Her chart says the scanner takes half a nanosecond per file. Both perf talks mined for this card ended on this exact trap: one benchmark measured integer division instead of loops, another was wrong by 2000x because a lazy file was never loaded. Mara needs one obvious way to say: this value counts.

options.name: keep(x): an always-available Prelude sink
options.detail: keep(x) is a tiny Prelude function that returns its argument and forces the optimizer to treat the value as used. It works anywhere: inside a measured region, in warm-up code, in every execution tier. It belongs to no harness, so it survives the ratified move from #Bench to .measure with no second migration. The cost is one more always-available name, and a stray keep() outside a benchmark does nothing.
options.technical: Signature keep(x: T) => T, a generic identity. One jet_keep kernel in a PRELUDE_PARTS file wraps std::hint::black_box for AOT; the interpreter ambient, Cranelift host, and comptime bind the same symbol with identity behavior (I9). Sema registers the name in the core call tables and the core-surface ledger absorbs it. No new diagnostics: misuse reuses the existing arity and type errors, so no I4 row.

options.name: No new name: document the result-threading pattern
options.detail: Ship no function. The bench docs teach the existing escape: thread every computed value into a checked result, because the harness already protects each region's final result. Zero new surface and zero naming cost. But the pattern only works when the bencher can state an expected value, the check itself joins the timed work, and nothing can force a lazy resource during warm-up. Every bencher must rediscover the trick or copy it from the docs.
options.technical: Docs-only change: the optimizer-trap catalog lands in the spec bench section and the core-library reference. The generated harness already wraps each region body call in std::hint::black_box (Codegen/mod.rs), so a value that reaches an assertion survives. Values with unpredictable results, such as timings or random inputs, have no honest expected value to assert.

options.name: keep(x) only inside measured regions
options.detail: The sink exists, but the checker rejects keep() outside a measured region with a new error. This keeps benchmark vocabulary out of production code, so no reviewer ever meets a stray keep(). It costs a new diagnostic with its own catalog row, and it forbids the second real use: forcing a lazy resource in setup code before the timed region starts. That setup-forcing gap is exactly the 2000x lazy-file lie from the perf talk.
options.technical: Same Prelude kernel as option A, plus a sema scope check tied to measured-region lowering and one new diagnostic (code, message, and docs row per I4). The scope check must move with the harness when D-CLAIM-BENCH1 retires #Bench for .measure, so the restriction is a second thing that migration can break.

comparisons.note: std::hint::black_box(value) is a stable identity function the optimizer treats as opaque. It lives in the standard library and works everywhere, not only inside a bench harness.
benchmark::DoNotOptimize(value) forces the value to exist and benchmark::ClobberMemory() flushes pending writes. Both live in the benchmark library, the harness-scoped shape option C mirrors.

testing.B.Loop (Go 1.24) keeps loop results alive automatically. Older Go code assigned results to package-level sink variables by hand — option B's pattern, and a documented source of wrong benchmarks.
Blackhole.consume(value) is injected into benchmark methods by the harness. Outside JMH there is no equivalent, and hand-rolled sinks are famously unreliable across JIT versions.

recommendation.why: A tiny always-available identity sink fixes both measured lies from the perf talks: dead in-loop values and lazy costs deferred past the timer. It belongs to no harness, so it survives the ratified retirement of #Bench in favor of .measure without a second migration. One kernel serves every execution tier, which keeps the I9 parity story trivial.

whyNot.reason: The pattern only works when an expected value exists, the check itself joins the timed work, and nothing can force a lazy resource during warm-up. Every bencher must rediscover the trick, and the two perf talks show experienced people failing exactly there.
It buys a new diagnostic and its catalog row to forbid a harmless no-op. It also blocks forcing lazy resources in setup code outside the region, which is the exact shape of the 2000x lazy-file lie.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more always-available Prelude name. A stray keep() in production code does nothing and misleads no one, but reviewers must learn to read past it, and the core-surface ledger grows by one entry.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an always-available sink, a docs-only pattern, and a region-scoped sink. It recommended the always-available sink because it alone survives the ratified .measure migration and covers warm-up forcing.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a #Keep marker, a build flag that disables elision in bench builds, and a volatile-write intrinsic. All three were folded away: the marker adds syntax weight, and the other two slow every region body instead of one value.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of A plus a lint hinting at keep() outside measured code was tested and dropped. Jet's lint surface is accessibility-only today, and the hint adds machinery without preventing any measured lie.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with a worked expected-value recipe and C with a precise diagnostic sketch. B still cannot handle unpredictable results or lazy warm-up; C still forbids setup-code forcing.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack ran random-input results against B and the lazy-file warm-up against C; both fail where A holds. Against A it tried name collision — no live keep exists in the Prelude surface, core call tables, or spec — so the recommendation survived intact.

decisions.title: Development evidence: one act, one receipt
decisions.gist: Whether every development act must leave a receipt, and every project claim must render from receipts.
decisions.lesson: Most verbs keep no record of what they proved. Warm `jet build` and `jet test` recompute everything (~33 s measured on hello-world). Status ledgers are written by hand; one claimed zero parity gaps while 51 failures existed. This choice decides whether evidence becomes one law for the whole toolchain or stays a per-verb habit.
decisions.story: Mara closes a card as done because her tests passed yesterday. Overnight a teammate's change stales that result. The board still says done, and the bug ships. Mara never lied — the project had no memory.
decisions.inWild:
$ time jet test math.jet     # 33.2 s — warm rerun, nothing changed (live probe)
$ ls crates/jet-debug/src/Dap.rs   # DAP server shipped in code
$ tower card show '#12'      # 'Native debugger: DAP framing and state-machine core' — still phase: ready
# tests/jit_gaps.txt once declared zero gaps while the jit_coverage_audit observer found 51 (e3 handoff, card #1663)

options.name: One law, four clauses
options.detail: Every act leaves a receipt bound to its locked input closure. Every project claim renders from receipts, or it prints not-recorded. Unchanged inputs never pay twice. Every receipt names its witness. Speed and honesty come from the same record.
options.technical: Receipt base = the D-ECO-RECEIPT2=A chain verbatim: exact inputs, planned actions, produced output digests, activation proof, parent generation. This ballot amends it with two new fields: evidence rows (the .jetproof shape with the four ratified grades — proved, passed, observed, met) and the witness. Store: extension-less content-addressed objects under .jet/ and the Hangar (D-ECO-RECEIPTSTORE1=A); no new .jet<kind> is minted, so D-ARTIFACT-EXT1's closed family is untouched. Also extends D-ONCE-LAW1 (rendered truths) and D-PROVE-SEM1 (summaries derive from evidence) from one verb to every act. All three extensions are named amendments.
options.code:
$ jet test
14 passed · wrote receipt 4c22 (closure a1b2c3, grade: passed)
$ jet test        # nothing changed
14 hold from receipts · 0.08 s
$ jet explain receipt 4c22   # closure, witness, evidence rows

options.name: Evidence law without the speed clause
options.detail: Acts leave receipts and claims render from them, but each verb decides for itself whether to reuse prior work. Honesty lands now; the warm tax survives wherever a verb skips reuse.
options.code:
$ jet test
14 passed · wrote receipt 4c22
$ jet test        # still recomputes: reuse is this verb's choice
14 passed · 33.1 s

options.name: Cache law without the evidence clause
options.detail: Never-pay-twice applies to every verb, but results stay in a private cache. Ledgers, cards, and status stay hand-written, so the lying price stays.
options.code:
$ jet test        # warm: fast now
14 passed · 0.1 s (cache hit)
$ cat tests/jit_coverage_audit   # still hand-written, still able to lie

options.name: Decline: keep per-verb records
options.detail: `.jetproof`, API snapshots, budget baselines, and hand ledgers stay separate formats. Every verb keeps its own memory or none. Both measured prices stay.
options.code:
$ time jet build   # 34.3 s warm, zero changes
$ jet test --json  # E2102: unknown flag — results still die in the terminal

comparisons.note: Proves never-pay-twice at monorepo scale with a content-addressed action cache. It has no claim grades and no rendered project status, and its config language is a famous cost.
comparisons.code: bazel test //...   # cache hits are instant; 'what is true' still needs bazel query archaeology

comparisons.note: The store is the inputs-to-output law working in production for twenty years. It stops at bytes: no test grades, no claim ledger, no review surface.
comparisons.code: nix build   # same closure, same path — but 'do the tests still hold?' is not a Nix question

comparisons.note: Evidence exists but lives in web logs: unreadable by tools, expiring, and disconnected from the inputs that produced it.
comparisons.code: # 'Did CI pass for exactly this tree?' — answered by re-running the workflow

recommendation.why: The waiting price and the lying price have one root: acts keep no record bound to inputs. One record fixes both. Three ratified laws (D-PROVE-SEM1, D-BUILDCACHE1, D-ECO-RECEIPT2) already state its clauses locally; this option makes them one law before their implementation cards build three stores.

whyNot.reason: Splitting honesty from speed builds the same store twice and leaves the 33-second warm tax wherever a verb opts out.
Fast but still dishonest: ledgers keep lying because nothing forces them to render from evidence.
Keeps both measured prices and lets the open receipt, cache, and ledger cards build three more disconnected record formats.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every verb must hash its closure before answering. That bookkeeping is real, so the law carries a warm-answer latency budget (interpreter-tier bar, enforced by the budget machinery) rather than a hope.

reviewPasses.base: First draft compared the full law against evidence-only, cache-only, and decline, and recommended the full law because both measured prices share one root.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a fifth direction: evidence in the VCS (commit-status style, like GitHub checks). Folded into the comparisons because it reproduces the web-log defect — evidence disconnected from closures.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested adopting A while keeping hand ledgers during migration; rejected because a render guard with exceptions is D-ONCE-LAW1's known failure mode. Migration staging belongs to the implementation phases instead.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B by noting it still kills false green, and C by noting it alone erases the 45-90 minute golden wall. Both gains are real; each still leaves one price standing.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on closure-hashing overhead and receipt forgery; repaired with the budgeted warm-answer bar, and receipts being content-addressed store objects makes forgery store tampering, not text editing. The recommendation survives.

decisions.comment: But allow an override flag to force rerun

decisions.title: Claims leave receipts; ledgers render
decisions.gist: Whether test results, goldens, budgets, and API snapshots become one receipt kind, with status ledgers rendered from them.
decisions.lesson: `jet test` results die in the terminal; the only durable test record is written under `jet prove`. Goldens are blessed by hand with no record of what produced them — three were found blessed against wrong output. The hand-written parity ledger (tests/jit_gaps.txt) once declared zero gaps while its audit observed 51. This choice decides whether project claims get one durable, rendered form.
decisions.story: Rin, an agent, closes a card: the tests passed in its worktree. The orchestrator cannot tell that claim from a guess, so it re-runs everything — or worse, trusts it. Twenty-five real fixes later, the board recorded none of them.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet test
double doubles: pass · 1 passed        # then it is gone — no artifact, no JSON
$ git show -s --format=%s 8acbb3454    # fix(fmt,golden,budget): … — commit body: 'Three goldens were genuinely stale'
# tests/jit_gaps.txt once declared zero gaps while the jit_coverage_audit observer found 51 (card #1663)

options.name: All claim kinds, one receipt, rendered ledgers
options.detail: Test runs, golden blessings, budget baselines, API snapshots, and schema snapshots become receipt kinds in one store. The parity ledger and the feature manifest become rendered views, byte-compared in CI like llms.text. A hand-written second copy fails the guard.
options.technical: Receipt kinds embed today's payloads unchanged (.jetproof rows, .api snapshot, baseline content); receipts are extension-less Hangar objects (extends D-ECO-RECEIPTSTORE1=A), so D-ARTIFACT-EXT1's closed .jet<kind> family is untouched. Golden receipts record the producing closure and tier. Retires tests/jit_gaps.txt (the hand ledger) as a source of truth. The jit_coverage_audit observer and its both-direction ratchet (#1998) are kept and become the render guard; #1663 lands here. Guard = the D-ONCE-LAW1 mechanism applied to project-state ledgers — named amendment.
options.code:
$ jet test
14 passed · wrote receipt 4c22 (tiers: run,aot)
$ jet inspect parity      # rendered from tier-tagged receipts
run-tier: 511 hold · 0 stale · 3 not-recorded   # 'not-recorded' can never print as '0 gaps'

options.name: Test receipts only
options.detail: The most frequent act gains a durable record now. Goldens, budgets, snapshots, and ledgers stay as they are, keeping three bespoke formats and the stale-blessing defect class.
options.code:
$ jet test
14 passed · wrote receipt 4c22
$ # goldens: still hand-blessed, still no closure recorded

options.name: Rendered ledgers without a durable store
options.detail: Ledgers are generated by re-running their checks at render time instead of reading receipts. Honest at the moment of rendering, silent in between, and it pays the full compute price on every render.
options.code: $ jet inspect parity      # re-runs the tier matrix to answer: minutes, not milliseconds

comparisons.note: `jet inspect digest` renders llms.text from typed registries and CI byte-compares it. It is the one project ledger that has never lied. This ballot makes that pattern the norm.
comparisons.code: $ jet inspect digest   # rendered; a hand edit fails CI

comparisons.note: Snapshot review flow with explicit accept. Good accept ergonomics, but snapshots carry no record of the producing toolchain, so stale blessing survives there too.
Enforced API diff at publish: version numbers cannot lie about breaking changes. The same render-don't-declare move, applied to one claim kind.
comparisons.code: elm publish   # refuses a minor bump on a breaking diff

recommendation.why: Every lying surface in the evidence table is a hand-maintained copy of something an act already knew. One receipt shape plus rendered views deletes the class, and the in-repo digest pattern already proves the mechanism works.

whyNot.reason: Fixes the loudest gap but keeps the stale-blessing class and two lying ledgers, so the reconciliation audits continue.
An answer that costs minutes is an answer nobody asks; status must be a read, not a run.

recommendation.tradeoff: Golden and ledger workflows change: blessing writes a receipt, and editing a ledger by hand becomes a build failure. That is the point, and it is also the migration cost this option accepts.

reviewPasses.base: First draft set all-claim-kinds against tests-only and render-by-rerun, recommending all kinds because the lying surfaces span every kind, not just tests.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass looked for claim kinds the draft missed and added schema snapshots and bench measurements to A's scope; both already have solid homes that become receipt kinds unchanged.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested A-for-new-claims with legacy ledgers grandfathered. Rejected: a guard with a grandfather clause is how the parity ledger got here.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B as the correct first implementation slice and said so in the phases; strengthened C by noting render-by-rerun is exactly right for cheap checks and remains available under A for them.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A with receipt-spam and blessing-friction concerns; repaired via content-addressing (identical results dedupe) and one-command blessing that writes the receipt as a side effect. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: One project truth surface
decisions.gist: Where the one answer to 'what is true about my project right now' lives.
decisions.lesson: Answering that question today costs six verbs and two minutes of AOT recompute: check, test, prove, budget, audit, publish dry-run. With receipts the answer is a store read. This choice picks the surface that reads it.
decisions.story: Priya returns from a week off. She wants one screen: what still holds, what went stale while she was away, what was never proved at all. Today she runs six commands and reconstructs the answer in her head.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet check && jet test && jet budget check && jet prove run.jet
# four verbs, ~100 s warm, and still no answer about publish safety or staleness
$ git status   # the muscle memory this question deserves

options.name: New flat verb: jet status
options.detail: One daily-frequency verb, no arguments, one screen: the closure, then each claim family with its grade, freshness, and receipt. Never runs work; only reads. `--json` emits one machine line per row.
options.technical: Amends D-CLI-SURFACE1=B (closed verb family) by its own frequency rule: daily verbs ring flat. Rows render from receipts; a family with no receipts prints not-recorded. --json emits one versioned status object per row — status data in D-REPORT-LAW1's sense ('status lines stay plain'; command status envelopes remain status data per D-REPORT-MACHINE1), never a jet.report/v1 report.
options.code:
$ jet status
closure  a1b2c3 · 2 files changed since receipt 9f41
check    ok        current
claims   14 hold   current            (receipt 4c22)
proofs   2 proved  STALE — parser.jet changed
budgets  3 met     current
publish  0 breaks  current against v1.2 API

options.name: Inside the project group: jet project status
options.detail: The truth table lives under the existing `jet project` group verb. No closed-family amendment, but the most-asked question in development sits one word deeper than `git status` trained every developer to type.
options.code:
$ jet project status
# same table, one word further away

options.name: Under the proof verb: jet prove --status
options.detail: Evidence questions live with the evidence verb. Coherent for experts, but it hides the beginner's first status question behind a verb most beginners have not met.
options.code:
$ jet prove --status
# same table, behind the proof verb

options.name: Decline: status stays composed
options.detail: Users and agents keep composing check, test, budget, prove, and publish dry-runs. Receipts still speed each verb up; no single surface exists.
options.code: $ jet check && jet test && jet budget check   # still the status ritual

comparisons.note: `git status` is the most-typed command in development because it answers state without doing work. That is the exact contract this verb copies: read, never run.
Has no status verb; 'is everything ok' is `cargo check && cargo test` recomputed. The absence is the pain this ballot removes.
comparisons.code: cargo check && cargo test   # the ritual

comparisons.note: `bazel query` can answer anything and beginners can answer nothing. Expert-only status is a known failure shape.

recommendation.why: The question is daily at every echelon, and D-CLI-SURFACE1's own law rings daily verbs flat. Read-only-from-receipts keeps it instant and honest, and gives agents the loop state in one JSON read.

whyNot.reason: Buries the most frequent question one level deep, against the ratified frequency rule itself.
Couples the beginner's first question to the expert's proof vocabulary.
Keeps the six-verb ritual and leaves agents re-running suites to learn what a table could say.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more flat verb in a deliberately small ring. Accepted because the frequency rule that closed the ring is the same rule that admits this verb.

reviewPasses.base: First draft set a flat verb against group placement, proof placement, and decline, recommending the flat verb on the frequency rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested an always-on TUI dashboard and editor-only status (LSP). Folded both into renderers of the same rows rather than competing homes.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested flat verb plus `jet project status` as an alias. Rejected: D-CLI-SURFACE3 kills silent aliases; one spelling only.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B by noting `jet project` already exists and stays coherent; strengthened C by noting experts asking evidence questions will find prove natural either way.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A with 'status lies when receipts are sparse'; repaired because sparse families print not-recorded in so many words, so the surface is honest about its own blind spots. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Review as a product: meaning, authority, evidence
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a review verdict that joins semantic diff, authority diff, and receipt diff.
decisions.lesson: Code review has no owner anywhere in Jet — no verb, proposal, or card. Reviewers re-derive facts the compiler holds: what changed in meaning, what gained authority, which claims went stale. Every ingredient ships today (structural diff, blast radius, gate ledger, receipts); this choice decides whether they join into one verdict.
decisions.story: Omar reviews a 400-line change. The forge shows him lines. He wants three answers: what changed in meaning, does anything new touch the network, and do the claims that held before still hold. He reconstructs all three by hand, slowly, or approves on vibes.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet diff a.jet b.jet
E2104: currently requires --structural      # and only two single files
$ # authority delta: jet inspect gates, per file, joined by hand
$ # claim delta: nothing — test results were never recorded

options.name: New verb: jet review <ref>
options.detail: One verdict over a base ref: meaning (semantic diff with blast radius), authority (gate and effect delta), claims (receipt diff: new, stale, held). Human-readable screen and one JSON object. Works project-wide, not per file.
options.technical: Amends D-CLI-SURFACE1=B (new verb). Joins jet diff --structural, jet inspect impact, jet inspect gates, and the receipt store; adds no new engine. JSON rides jet.report/v1 framing.
options.code:
$ jet review origin/main
meaning    2 fns changed, 1 signature (blast: 7 callers)
authority  no new gates · no new effects · no new deps
claims     +2 new · 1 held-at-base now stale · 0 deleted
evidence   13 hold at both ends · 2 await this machine's witness

options.name: A mode of diff: jet diff --review
options.detail: The same verdict as a flag on the existing diff verb. No closed-family amendment, but a review is not a diff of two files — it is a project-level judgment over meaning, authority, and evidence, and a file-diff verb misnames it.
options.code:
$ jet diff --review origin/main
# same output, spelled as a diff mode

options.name: Decline: ship the ingredients only
options.detail: Structural diff, impact, gates, and receipts each stay reachable alone. Forges and scripts compose them. Review stays unowned in Jet, and the join is rebuilt differently by every team.
options.code:
$ jet diff --structural a.jet b.jet && jet inspect impact … && jet inspect gates …
# per file, joined by hand, no claim delta

comparisons.note: Owns review network effects and inline comments, and is structurally blind to semantics and evidence — it diffs text. Jet cannot beat the network; it can ship the verdict no forge can compute.
comparisons.code: # PR view: lines added, lines removed. Meaning: unknown. Claims: unknown.

comparisons.note: Proves one slice of this verdict (API breakage) is checkable and loved. It stops at the public API and knows nothing of authority or tests.
Enterprise review with verified-vote plumbing. It bolts evidence onto text review from outside; the join lives in CI scripts nobody shares.
comparisons.code: # 'Verified +1' — a bot vote standing in for a receipt diff

recommendation.why: Review is the largest unowned surface in the lifecycle, and Jet is uniquely placed: it already holds all three planes the verdict needs. One verb makes the join canonical for humans, agents, and forges alike.

whyNot.reason: Misnames a project-level judgment as a file diff and inherits diff's two-single-files shape in users' heads.
Leaves the highest-value join to be rebuilt badly and differently by every team and every forge integration.

recommendation.tradeoff: A new verb in the closed ring for an act that is daily for teams but absent for solo beginners. Accepted: the verb is inert until a base ref is named, so the beginner surface gains zero ceremony.

reviewPasses.base: First draft set a review verb against a diff mode and decline, recommending the verb because the join is a judgment, not a file diff.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested review-as-forge-plugin (ship a GitHub app instead). Folded into comparisons: the verdict must exist in the toolchain first; forges render it.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested verb-plus-flag coexistence. Rejected under D-CLI-SURFACE3: one spelling per act, no silent aliases.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened C by acknowledging teams with entrenched review stacks will consume the JSON directly, verb or no verb; strengthened B by noting diff already has JSON plumbing.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A with 'review without inline comments is not review'; repaired by scoping honestly — this is the verdict, not the conversation, which stays on the forge that renders it. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Witnesses: whose receipts count, and what CI is
decisions.gist: Whether receipts are signed by who ran them, shared over the existing cache rails, and accepted only per trust policy.
decisions.lesson: Team caching, CI, and merge protection are unowned today; CI is a consumer Jet serves with exit codes. Receipts make them one question: whose evidence do you accept? Signing and revocation rails exist for package artifacts (D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1), and trust domains exist for remote builders (D-JPK-REMOTE1). This choice decides whether receipts ride them.
decisions.story: A CI machine spends an hour proving the tree green. Dana pulls the same tree and her laptop spends the same hour proving it again, because the CI run left nothing her toolchain can read, verify, or trust.
decisions.inWild:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — 200 lines of YAML re-deriving what jet already knows
$ jet test   # locally: recomputes everything CI just proved; trust not expressible

options.name: Full witness model
options.detail: Every receipt names and signs its witness. `jet verify --cold` replays every act from the lock with no reuse and countersigns — that command is CI, on any machine you choose. Receipts share over existing cache bindings; acceptance is trust policy; the default is local-only.
options.technical: Amends D-CLI-SURFACE1=B: `jet verify` is a new flat verb. The ballot settles the word against the ratified store spelling `jet hangar verify` (D-CLI-STORE2=A); precedent: `jet check` and `jet os check` coexist. Trust rides ratified rails: signing, read-time verification, and revocation per D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1=D; trust domains per D-JPK-REMOTE1=D. No new trust mechanism. Default receipts policy .LocalOnly keeps D-TELEMETRY1=A's posture: nothing shared without an explicit binding. Merge protection = require a countersigned receipt for the merged closure.
options.code:
$ jet test
14 hold (11 yours · 3 countersigned by ci@team) · 0.1 s
$ jet verify --cold        # what the CI machine runs; there is no pipeline DSL
wrote 31 receipts, countersigned
$ jet explain receipt 31a0 # witness chain, key, binding

options.name: Local witnesses only
options.detail: Receipts record who ran them but never leave the machine. `jet verify --cold` still defines CI's job, but its receipts cannot reach a teammate, so every machine re-proves the world.
options.code:
$ jet verify --cold   # green — and the proof stays here
$ # teammate: pays the full price again

options.name: Decline: share artifacts, not evidence
options.detail: The binary cache keeps sharing bytes as today. Evidence stays private per machine. 'Is my teammate's green my green' remains unanswerable in the toolchain.
options.code:
$ jet build   # may hit the shared artifact cache
$ jet test    # evidence: always recomputed, never shared

comparisons.note: Binary cache signatures are the working model: bytes accepted only from trusted keys. Jet extends the same trust shape from bytes to evidence.
Shares results at scale but trusts the cache endpoint wholesale; poisoned-cache incidents are the documented cost of trust without per-writer identity.
The not-rocket-science rule: never merge untested trees. Implemented as a bot because toolchains cannot express 'this closure has a countersigned green'. Receipts express exactly that.
comparisons.code: bors r+   # a bot vote where a store fact should be

recommendation.why: One trust question unifies team caching, CI, and merge protection, and the rails for it are already ratified for artifacts. Evidence is smaller and more valuable than bytes; sharing it under the same policy is the point of having receipts.

whyNot.reason: Defines CI honestly but wastes it: every machine still re-proves the world, so an hour of proof buys one machine's confidence.
Keeps the strange asymmetry where a team shares compiled bytes but cannot share the fact that tests passed.

recommendation.tradeoff: A countersigned lie is a signed lie: a compromised witness key poisons trust until revoked. Accepted because per-writer identity plus revocation is strictly stronger than today's alternative — trusting a cache endpoint or a CI log wholesale.

reviewPasses.base: First draft set the full model against local-only and decline, recommending full because the trust rails already exist and evidence sharing is the payoff.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested transparency-log countersignatures (sigstore-style public witness). Folded into A's future room: the receipt shape carries it; the default posture does not require it.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested artifact-sharing-plus-local-evidence as a middle option; it is option C's real content and was merged into C's steelman.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B for the solo developer and the air-gapped site, where it is not a compromise but the correct end state; A's default equals B until a binding is added.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A with key compromise and with 'CI without pipelines cannot express deploy stages'; repaired because revocation rides the existing key rails and staged delivery is jet deploy's ratified territory. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Production runs leave receipts
decisions.gist: What a production crash leaves behind for the developer who must fix it.
decisions.lesson: `jet report` bundles version and policy only — nothing that helps diagnose a failure. `jet inspect live` needs a pre-armed process. A production crash today arrives as a prose ticket. The replay rail (D-JREPLAY1) is ratified and shipped, but nothing in production feeds it.
decisions.story: A service crashes at 3am. The operator files: 'it crashed, logs attached'. Noor spends the morning reconstructing which build, which inputs, which code path — facts the crashed process knew perfectly in its final millisecond.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet report
wrote local report bundle to .jet/reports/<sha>   # version, target, policy — no evidence
$ jet inspect live 4123
error: start the program with --observe or attach to jet dev   # too late now

options.name: Crash receipts, observed runs, evidence-carrying reports
options.detail: A crashing release binary writes a crash receipt: the report frame, the closure digest, and a replay capture. `jet report --attach` ships it in the support bundle. Long-running services may opt into periodic observed-run receipts. Everything stays on the machine unless the operator ships it, and a project can refuse recording entirely with one typed setting.
options.technical: Crash path emits the ratified Stop report (D-FAIL-BREACH1) plus a D-JREPLAY1 capture into the receipt store. `jet debug --replay <receipt-id>` is a proposed extension of the ratified `--replay=NAME` spelling (D-RUN-RECORD1); the capture format itself is unchanged. D-TELEMETRY1=A kept verbatim: no network, no default shipping. Recording itself is refusable project-wide with the typed setting `receipts: .Off`, for fleets that forbid on-host artifacts. Observed-run receipts reuse the inspect-live snapshot bound (≤1 MiB).
options.code:
# in prod, crash:
wrote crash receipt 8a3f (.jet/reports/8a3f): report frame · closure · replay capture

# back home:
$ jet debug --replay 8a3f     # the crash, replayed on the developer's machine

options.name: Crash receipts only
options.detail: The crash moment is covered; healthy-run observation stays out. Smallest surface, and the 3am ticket still becomes a replayable fact.
options.code:
wrote crash receipt 8a3f
$ jet debug --replay 8a3f

options.name: Decline: reports stay thin
options.detail: `jet report` keeps carrying version and policy. Production failures keep arriving as prose, and the shipped replay rail keeps waiting for an input that never comes.
options.code: $ jet report   # version, target, policy — the morning of archaeology stays

comparisons.note: Made crash context table stakes — by phoning home. Jet's law is the opposite: the same context, written locally, shipped only by the operator's hand.
comparisons.code: Sentry.init(dsn=…)   # evidence leaves the building by default

comparisons.note: Crash dumps with process state made 'it crashed' an analyzable fact decades ago. The lesson: the process is the best witness of its own death.
The classic path: heavyweight, host-dependent, and disconnected from source closures. A typed replay capture is the same idea with the toolchain's knowledge kept.

recommendation.why: The replay rail is ratified and shipped; production is its missing producer. Crash receipts turn the worst debugging session — remote, cold, prose-mediated — into the same replay loop developers already have locally.

whyNot.reason: Right first slice, but leaving observed-run receipts unspecified invites ad-hoc service instrumentation to grow beside the store instead of in it.
Keeps the shipped replay rail starved and the support bundle useless for the one case support exists for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A crash receipt can contain sensitive runtime state. Accepted under the existing posture: local-only by law, safe-locals redaction rides the ratified report frame, and shipping is always a human act.

reviewPasses.base: First draft set full production receipts against crash-only and decline, recommending full with observed runs behind explicit opt-in.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested exporting to OpenTelemetry and Prometheus as part of this ballot. Excluded deliberately: exporters are an observability-platform question, named future territory in the proposal.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested crash receipts now plus a later observed-run ballot; folded into A by marking observed runs opt-in, which contains the same staging without a second ballot.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B as the privacy-maximal choice; strengthened C by noting some fleets forbid any on-host artifacts — and noting policy can express that refusal under A too.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on secret leakage into captures and disk growth on crash loops; repaired because safe-locals redaction is already law in the report frame and content-addressed receipts dedupe a crash loop. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Never pay twice: receipt reuse on every verb
decisions.gist: Which verbs must reuse prior work when inputs did not change.
decisions.lesson: D-BUILDCACHE1=A ratified an automatic action cache, scoped to `fn build` actions, and it is unbuilt. Meanwhile every AOT-path verb pays ~33 s warm with zero changes, and the golden suite pays 45-90 minutes of mostly identical compiles. This choice decides how far the automatic cache law reaches.
decisions.story: Ben renames one function and runs `jet test` to see if anything broke. He waits 33 seconds for an answer his machine computed an hour ago. He starts running tests less often. The bugs arrive later, bigger.
decisions.inWild:
$ time jet build          # 34.3 s — warm, zero changes
$ time jet test math.jet  # 33.2 s — same test, same result as an hour ago
$ time jet budget check   # 34.1 s — on hello-world
$ time jet prove run.jet  # 33.1 s burned BEFORE noticing rustc is missing

options.name: Every verb, with a latency budget
options.detail: Build, test, prove, budget, bench measurement, image, and doc rendering all consult and write the receipt store. A warm no-op verb must answer within the interpreter-tier bar (0.05 s class), enforced as a typed budget. `--fresh` refuses reuse per call.
options.technical: Cache key = the D-BUILDCACHE1 key verbatim and in full: inputs, outputs, argv, env, caps, tool digest, target, policy, toolchain, compiler version, and generated source hashes. The probe cost itself lands under D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1 machinery. Generalizes D-BUILDCACHE1=A beyond fn build — named amendment.
options.code:
$ jet build
ok: build/run current (closure a1b2c3, receipt 9f41) · 0.09 s
$ jet test --fresh        # institutional distrust, per call
recomputing all 14 claims …

options.name: Build and test first, others follow
options.detail: The two highest-frequency verbs adopt reuse now. Prove, budget, bench, image, and doc keep recomputing until a follow-up ballot. Lower risk of a bad key hiding a real change, smaller first win.
options.code:
$ jet test    # fast
14 hold from receipts · 0.1 s
$ jet budget check   # still 34 s on hello-world

options.name: Keep the ratified scope
options.detail: The automatic cache stays inside `fn build` actions as D-BUILDCACHE1 wrote it. Verb-level speed comes from separate per-verb optimizations, each designed alone.
options.code:
$ jet build   # fast only when the project defines fn build actions
$ jet test    # 33 s warm, forever, unless its own optimization card lands

comparisons.note: Task-level build cache: correct-key reuse across a team. Its lesson is key discipline — a missed input in the key produces wrong reuse, which is worse than slow.
comparisons.code: gradle test --build-cache   # FROM-CACHE tasks are instant

comparisons.note: Brought task caching to JS monorepos and made warm no-ops feel instant. Its hash covers declared inputs only, so undeclared inputs cause famous stale-cache bugs.
comparisons.code: turbo run test   # cache hit: replayed logs, 0 s

comparisons.note: Compiler-invocation caching bolted on from outside. It shows the ceiling of external caching: it cannot see project claims, only compiles.

recommendation.why: The key is already ratified down to env and tool digest; only its reach is undecided. Reaching every verb makes warm-equals-instant a property of the toolchain, not of whichever verbs got optimization cards.

whyNot.reason: Leaves budget, prove, and bench paying the full tax, and schedules more ballots to decide what the law already implies.
Keeps the measured 33-second warm tax on every AOT verb for projects that never write fn build — which is nearly all of them.

recommendation.tradeoff: A wrong cache key silently reuses a stale result, which is worse than recomputing. The key therefore stays the ratified maximal one, `--fresh` exists on every verb, and any wrong-reuse class found in practice is a stop-ship defect, not a tuning note.

reviewPasses.base: First draft scoped reuse to all verbs versus the two hottest verbs versus the ratified fn-build scope, recommending all verbs under one budgeted bar.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass considered daemon-resident warm state (a compiler server) as a fourth direction. Folded into A's technical note: a daemon is an implementation of the same law, not a different law.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested B-then-A staging as a standing option. Rejected: it is a rollout order, not a design; phases belong to the implementation shape.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened C by crediting that fn-build actions are where multi-tool pipelines live, so its scope is not trivial. Strengthened B as the honest minimal-risk step.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A with the wrong-reuse scenario, an undeclared input hiding a real change; repaired because the ratified key includes env and tool digests and --fresh is universal. Wrong reuse is classed as a stop-ship defect, and the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: The cone law: verdict latency scales with the edit
decisions.gist: Whether re-verdict cost after an edit must scale with the edit's blast radius, never with program size.
decisions.lesson: Receipts (D-DEVR-TWICE1) erase cost when nothing changed. When something did change, every CLI verb still re-derives the whole program; only the editor path is incremental. At toy scale this is invisible (0.05 s `jet check`); at real scale it is the wall every large codebase lives behind. This choice decides whether bounded re-verdict becomes a budget-enforced law.
decisions.story: Ada's project grew from 2 files to 200. Her one-line edit still re-checks all 200 through the CLI, while her editor answers instantly from the incremental engine. Same compiler, two speeds — because only one path has a law.
decisions.inWild:
$ vim src/parser.jet          # one-line edit in one function
$ jet check                   # re-runs the whole front end
$ jet run --release           # regenerates and recompiles one monolithic program
# the blast-radius engine already exists: jet inspect impact <file> <symbol>

options.name: Every verb, budget-enforced
options.detail: Check, test, run, and dev re-verdict only the edit's cone: the definitions the blast-radius engine names. Typed latency budgets pin the bound per verb, so a super-linear regression is a red budget, not a slow afternoon. The guarantee covers the CLI, the editor, and the dev session equally.
options.technical: Rides the incremental query engine (already live for LSP), `jet inspect impact` (D-IMPACT1), and D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1=C machinery (card #677). That budget grammar is ratified as closed: per-verb latency rows are new entries in it, a named extension this ballot carries. AOT side lands via per-part compilation artifacts, starting from the content-addressed Prelude/Core rlib card. Contradicts nothing; D-BUILD-DEFAULT1 profiles unchanged.
options.code:
$ vim src/parser.jet && jet check
ok: 3 definitions re-checked (parse_line's cone) · rest current · 0.02 s
$ jet explain check           # why the cone was 3: signature untouched, 2 callers

options.name: Budgets on check and dev only
options.detail: The two tightest-loop verbs get the law; test, run, and build keep whole-program behavior until later ballots. Smaller guarantee, and the loop breaks the first time a user leaves `jet check` for `jet test`.
options.code:
$ jet check    # bounded by the cone
$ jet test     # still whole-program between receipts

options.name: Decline: incrementality stays an implementation detail
options.detail: The engine keeps improving where engineers happen to work on it. No law, no budget, no promise — and the editor-versus-CLI speed split stays permanent.
options.code: $ jet check    # fast or slow depending on the year

comparisons.note: The canonical two-speed split: the editor answers incrementally while cargo check re-derives. Users learn to distrust one or the other. The lesson: incrementality that is not a product law forks the toolchain's word.
comparisons.code: # IDE: instant squiggle · terminal: 40 s cargo check

comparisons.note: Full incremental compilation as a platform property — the reason Visual Studio feels instant at massive scale. Proof the law is achievable when the compiler owns it end to end.
comparisons.code: // same compiler serves editor and build

comparisons.note: In-place binary patching is its announced endgame for the same reason: bounded re-verdict is the only thing that keeps big programs interactive.

recommendation.why: The two-speed split (instant editor, whole-program CLI) is already visible in Jet, and it only widens with program size. One law with typed budgets keeps every surface telling the same truth at the same speed, and the budget machinery to enforce it is ratified and building.

whyNot.reason: Guards the loop until the user runs a test, then breaks it exactly where confidence matters most.
Keeps bounded latency a matter of luck, and permanently forks editor truth from CLI truth.

recommendation.tradeoff: Cone tracking adds bookkeeping to every verb, and a wrong cone is worse than a slow one. The bound is therefore conservative — over-approximate cones are legal, under-approximate cones are a stop-ship defect — and the budgets police only the latency, never the correctness.

reviewPasses.base: First draft set every-verb budgets against check+dev-only and decline, recommending every-verb because the split the law removes is between verbs.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested a resident compiler daemon as its own option; folded into A's technical note because a daemon is one way to meet the budget, not a different law.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested budgets-without-cone-guarantee (pure observability). Rejected: a budget with no architectural commitment just documents the wall.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B as the honest first slice and said its verbs are where the loop lives today; strengthened C by conceding incremental work continues regardless.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A with the wrong-cone scenario and with comptime edges that widen every cone; repaired by making under-approximation a stop-ship defect and letting `jet explain` name the widening edge. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Debugging is a query over a recorded run
decisions.gist: Whether any recorded run answers backward questions: why is this value X, when did this place change.
decisions.lesson: Debugging reconstructs causality backward, but every tool samples forward: breakpoints, prints, re-runs. Jet's recording rail is ratified and shipped (D-JREPLAY1 under `jet prove`), and Part I's crash receipts feed it from production. Time-travel is deferred to Epoch 6 (D-TIMETRAVEL1=C). This choice decides the substrate law those two facts point at.
decisions.story: Noor replays the 3am crash. She can step forward from the start, again, like it is 1985. What she wants to type is: why is total zero. The recording holds the answer; no surface asks it.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet debug run.jet           # forward stepping, interpreter evaluator
> step
E0956: static mylib.greet isn't supported by the current evaluator yet
# and for a crash in prod: a prose ticket, logs attached

options.name: Adopt the query law now
options.detail: Any recorded run — local, test, or crash receipt — answers `why <expr>` (the backward slice of writes and decisions that produced a value) and `when <place>` (the write timeline). This is a named amendment: `when` sits inside the per-variable-history territory D-TIMETRAVEL1=C deferred to Epoch 6 and D-RUN-RECORD1=A re-affirmed as deferred. Option A pulls the query surface over existing recordings forward; reverse-step execution and the standalone always-on history engine stay on the Epoch 6 schedule.
options.technical: Rides D-JREPLAY1=A capture and `jet debug --replay`. Amendment scope, exactly: queries run only over an existing recording (opt-in flag, crash receipt, or claim run); no always-on history, no reverse-step, no new recorder. Epoch 6's engine then lands as a richer query engine over the same recordings, built once. Queries read the replay, so live-process overhead is zero and I9 is untouched (the replay is tier-tagged).
options.code:
$ jet debug --replay 8a3f
> why total == 0
total = 0   because sum(items) ran over []      service.jet:41
items = []  because parse(csv) dropped 14 rows  service.jet:22
> when order.state
.Open   service.jet:12   ·   .Stale   service.jet:87   ← last write

options.name: Crash-replay queries only
options.detail: `why` and `when` exist only for crash receipts. The worst debugging session gets the best tool; everyday test failures keep forward stepping.
options.code:
$ jet debug --replay 8a3f    # queries work here
$ jet debug run.jet          # and nowhere else

options.name: Decline: wait for Epoch 6
options.detail: Time-travel arrives on its deferred schedule with whatever substrate it builds then. The risk the deferral already took: the recorder and the query engine get designed twice.
options.code: # until then: step, print, re-run

comparisons.note: Record-and-query debugging exists and its users call it life-changing; it stays niche because it fights the OS from outside. A language owning every execution tier can make determinism a property instead of a heroic capture.
The time-traveling debugger proved the UX at language scale — for a pure language. Jet's effects are typed facts, which is what makes replay of effectful programs a design instead of a hope.
The world's actual debugger. Every print is a hand-built answer to one `when` query, paid for by a re-run. The query law is printf with the re-run removed.

recommendation.why: The recorder is ratified and shipped, the crash producer is in this slate, and the deferred Epoch 6 engine needs exactly this substrate. Naming the amendment now means recording and querying are designed once, and the everyday test failure gets the same power as the 3am crash.

whyNot.reason: Splits debugging into two grammars and reserves the good one for the rarest case.
Repeats the known cost of deferred substrates: Epoch 6 would mint a second recorder next to the ratified one.

recommendation.tradeoff: Recording effectful runs has real overhead, so recording stays opt-in rather than always-on; the law governs what a recording answers, not when one is made. And option A knowingly pulls part of a deferred territory forward — the amendment is named so the owner re-decides that scope, never inherits it silently.

reviewPasses.base: First draft compared adopting the query law now against crash-only and wait-for-E6, recommending now because the substrate exists and the deferral names no substrate.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested live-process queries (attach and ask). Folded out: `jet inspect live` stays stats-only by design, and queries over a replay dominate on safety and determinism.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested `when` without `why` (timelines are cheaper than slices). Kept both: a timeline without causality reproduces printf archaeology.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B as the minimal privacy surface; strengthened C by conceding E6 could still unify — at the price of a second recorder in the interim.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on recording overhead, slice explosion, and silent trenching of the D-TIMETRAVEL1=C deferral; repaired with opt-in recording and bounded slice depth. Option A is restated as a named amendment, with reverse-step and always-on history kept in Epoch 6, so the recommendation survives.

decisions.title: #Todo is a typed goal; jet fill proposes candidates
decisions.gist: Whether the checker talks about #Todo sites — expected type, effects, candidates — and whether a fill command proposes checked code.
decisions.lesson: `#Todo` ships today: it compiles and stops if reached. At that site the checker knows the expected type, the allowed effects, and every fact in scope — and says nothing. Meanwhile agents and beginners fill gaps with dummy values to keep the checker quiet, which hides the gap from every later reader. This choice decides whether the gap becomes a first-class, talked-about goal.
decisions.story: Kim sketches five functions to shape a program, bodies later. Today she invents fake return values so `jet check` passes, and one fake survives to production. What she wanted was to write `#Todo` five times and have the compiler keep score.

options.name: Goal card + fill
options.detail: `jet check` prints a goal card per `#Todo`: expected type, allowed effects, in-scope values. Goal cards are advisory rows: the exit code never changes, they summarize past a handful, and a project switch silences them. `jet fill` proposes ranked candidates found by signature search over the prelude and deps; every candidate already passes checking before it is shown. Runtime behavior is untouched — programs with goals still run and stop on reach.
options.technical:
Goal reporting is sema output (I3), advisory class per D-REPORT-SEV1. Candidates come from the semindex signature search (shares D-DEVR-FIND1's engine), filtered by the site's type, effects, and facts. Proposed code is ordinary term-level Jet that re-enters ordinary sema — never AST injection (D-METAMUTATE1), never a new type (S26). The `fill` spelling is open: a flat verb amends D-CLI-SURFACE1=B, or it rides `jet fix` as a fix kind.

Word choice is carried by this ballot. 'Hole' already names interpolation slots (D-PARSESTR1, D-META-CODE1) and #Todo itself (E3011/E2902 row text, D-TOOL2). Either keep 'hole' as shipped, or adopt 'goal' and rename the E3011/E2902/D-TOOL2 text, examples, and spec mentions via the D-ONCE-RETIRE1 mechanism.
options.code:
$ jet check
goal: parse_row's body   needs Row ? ParseError   (pure)
  in scope: line: String · Row.{...} · ParseError.{...}
$ jet fill run.jet:2
  1. Row.{ cells: line.split(",") }              passes check
  2. line.take_pattern("{a},{b}") → Row.{...}     passes check

options.name: Goal card only
options.detail: The checker reports every goal's type, effects, and scope; nothing proposes code. Honest and small, and the agent still has to invent the candidate the toolchain could have ranked.
options.code:
$ jet check
goal: parse_row's body   needs Row ? ParseError   (pure)

options.name: Decline
options.detail: `#Todo` stays a runtime stop the checker never mentions. Gaps keep being papered over with dummy values that outlive the sketch.
options.code: return Row.{ cells: [] }   // the fake that ships

comparisons.note: Typed holes (`_`) print the expected type and relevant bindings, and users call them the best teaching feature the compiler has. They never left the checker: no fill, no ranking.
comparisons.code: f = _   -- Found hole: _ :: Row, relevant bindings: line :: String

comparisons.note: Holes plus expression search (`:ps`) is compiler-driven development — the workflow this ballot imports. It works because candidates are checked before they are shown.
Fill without a checker in the loop: fluent candidates, no guarantee they type-check, no effect discipline. Jet's version inverts it — only checked candidates are ever shown.
comparisons.code: // suggestion compiles? unknown until you try

recommendation.why: This is the highest-leverage agent feature in the slate: one goal, one typed target, ranked candidates that already pass sema — repair determinism made concrete. Beginners get sketch-and-run with the compiler keeping score, using a marker they already have.

whyNot.reason: Stops one step short of the payoff: the toolchain knows the candidates and makes the caller guess anyway.
