Keeps the dummy-value pattern that hides unfinished work from every reader, human and machine.

recommendation.tradeoff: Ranked fill can propose plausible-but-wrong code with full confidence. Accepted because every candidate is type- and effect-checked before display, the human or agent still chooses, and the goal stays visible until filled — unlike the dummy value, which vanishes into the diff.

reviewPasses.base: First draft compared goal-card-plus-fill, goal-card-only, and decline, recommending the full feature for repair determinism.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested example-directed synthesis (give input/output pairs at the goal). Folded into the fill engine's future room via D-DEVR-FIND1's example search rather than a separate mechanism.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested fill living only in the editor (LSP code action). Folded in: the LSP action and the CLI spelling share the fix engine already, so the surface choice stays an open detail inside A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B by noting GHC shipped exactly that for a decade to great love; strengthened C by conceding #Todo already beats most languages' TODO comment.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on candidate explosion and on walls (does fill create types or macros?); repaired by bounding candidates to checked signature matches and confirming fill emits ordinary term-level code into ordinary sema. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Discovery by contract: jet find
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships search by type signature, by effect, and by input/output example.
decisions.lesson: The costliest beginner hour is 'what is this called'; the costliest agent tokens are directory listings and doc dumps. The developer knows the shape of what they need — a String in, a Path out — not its name. Jet's semindex holds every signature and effect as typed facts. This choice decides whether shape becomes searchable.
decisions.story: Ravi has a String and needs a Path. He greps the core-library page for 'path', reads four entries, and asks an assistant, which lists a module. Ninety seconds for a question the type system could answer exactly.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet inspect semindex run.jet     # name-keyed index: great if you know the name
$ jet inspect search json          # E1340: no local discovery index — package names, not signatures
# nothing anywhere answers: what takes a String and gives a Path?

options.name: Full find: signature, effect, example
options.detail: `jet find "String -> Path"` unifies against every visible signature. `--effect FS.Read` filters by the typed effect rows. `--example '"a,b" -> ["a","b"]'` runs pure candidates at comptime against the example and returns the ones that reproduce it. One read-only verb, human and `--json` output.
options.technical:
Signature search = unification over semindex rows (D-SEMINDEX1), prelude and deps in scope. Effect filter reads the same rows `jet inspect` renders. Example search evaluates only pure candidates in the comptime interpreter with the standard fuel bound — no effects run, S26 untouched. Flat verb amends D-CLI-SURFACE1=B; option C avoids the amendment.

Naming settlement carried by this ballot: `find` asks code by shape and contract; `search` stays the package-catalog word (`search`/`info` per D-JPK-DISCOVER1). Pre-existing drift noted for its own card: the live binary teaches `jet inspect search` while D-CLI-SURFACE1=B lists `search` flat.
options.code:
$ jet find "String -> Path"
core.files.Path.from(s: String) -> Path ? PathError
$ jet find --effect FS.Read "read a csv"
core.data.csv.read(path) =[FS.Read]=> Table ? CsvError
$ jet find --example '"a,b" -> ["a","b"]'
String.split(sep)   (reproduces the example)

options.name: Signature search only
options.detail: The Hoogle core, nothing else. Effect and example search wait. Smallest slice of the win, and the two Jet-only searches — the ones no other language can copy — are the ones deferred.
options.code:
$ jet find "String -> Path"
core.files.Path.from(s: String) -> Path ? PathError

options.name: Under inspect: jet inspect find
options.detail: The full feature, grouped under the expert namespace. No closed-family amendment — and the beginner who needs it most never discovers it there.
options.code: $ jet inspect find "String -> Path"

options.name: Decline
options.detail: Discovery stays names, docs, and guesswork. The digest keeps serving agents a full surface dump instead of one answer.
options.code: $ grep -i path docs/reference/core-library.md   # the ritual

comparisons.note: Signature search, beloved for two decades, still confined to Haskell because no other toolchain holds full typed signatures. Jet holds signatures, effects, and a safe evaluator.
Type-directed find over a content-addressed codebase shows the search is a natural consequence of the compiler owning the index.
Name-and-README search at ecosystem scale: the counterexample. Shape is absent, so ranking is popularity, and typosquats ride it.

recommendation.why: Signature search alone is proven and loved; effect and example search are the two rungs only Jet can build, because effects are typed facts and comptime can safely run pure candidates. Shipping all three makes discovery a contract question at every echelon, including the agent that should spend one query instead of a thousand tokens.

whyNot.reason: Defers exactly the two searches that are Jet-unique and leaves the agent's effect-scoped questions unanswered.
Hides the beginner's most-needed answer inside the expert namespace.
Keeps the ninety-second ritual and the token-burning surface dumps.

recommendation.tradeoff: Example search can only ever cover pure candidates, so its answer set is honest but incomplete. Accepted: it says so in the output, and the signature rung covers the effectful rest.

reviewPasses.base: First draft set the full verb against signature-only, inspect-grouped, and decline, recommending the full flat verb.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested natural-language-only search (ask the digest). Folded into the words argument of `--effect`: free text ranks within shape matches, never replaces them.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested find-inside-fill (D-DEVR-HOLE1) as one surface. Kept separate spellings over one engine: a goal site queries implicitly; a human queries explicitly.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened C by noting inspect already owns semindex and dossier, so grouping is coherent; strengthened B as the proven-value core.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on unification cost over big dep graphs and on example-search fuel abuse; repaired with the semindex's existing incremental index and the standard comptime fuel bound. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Refactors carry their meaning
decisions.gist: Whether toolchain-executed refactors record semantic ops that diff, merge, review, and blame consume.
decisions.lesson: A rename touches 47 lines, so the diff shows 47 edits, a concurrent change conflicts, blame loses the definition's history, and reviewers burn attention on churn. The tools that executed the rename — jet fix, codemod plans, LSP rename — knew exactly what it meant and threw that knowledge away. Structural merge already keys on stable definition IDs. This choice decides whether refactor meaning survives into the collaboration surfaces.
decisions.story: Omar renames parse_row to parse_line while Dana fixes a bug inside it. Git shows Dana a 47-line conflict wall. The two changes touch different things — one the name, one the body — and no tool can say so.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet merge --structural base ours theirs --out merged.jet
conflict: fn:module:base::run (overlapping_edit)   # stable IDs exist and stop at file scope
# a rename executed by jet fix leaves no record that it WAS a rename

options.name: Record and consume
options.detail: Every toolchain-executed refactor (jet fix, codemod plan, LSP rename) records its semantic op beside the text change. Diff, merge, review, and blame consume ops plus stable definition IDs: a rename renders as one line, merges clean against body edits, and blame follows the definition. Hand edits stay plain text forever; every surface keeps a --text view.
options.technical: Ops are additive metadata riding codemod plans (D-CODEMOD1 already replayable) and the semindex stable-ID space structural merge uses. No VCS is replaced: ops travel with the change (in .jet/, shareable like receipts). Consumers: jet diff/merge (shipped, extended), jet review (D-DEVR-REVIEW1), blame view via semindex history.
options.code:
$ jet review origin/main
meaning   renamed parse_row → parse_line (47 sites)   ← one line
          1 fn body changed (blast: 2 callers)
$ jet merge --structural …    # rename + body edit: no conflict, different subjects

options.name: Record only
options.detail: Ops are written now; diff, merge, review, and blame learn to read them later. Preserves the knowledge before more of it is thrown away, delivers no visible win yet.
options.code: $ jet fix --rename parse_row parse_line   # op recorded; surfaces unchanged

options.name: Decline
options.detail: Refactors stay text churn. The 47-line conflict wall, the burned review attention, and the lost blame history remain the daily tax of keeping code well-named.
options.code: # git: 47 changed lines, 1 conflict, blame reset

comparisons.note: Industrial evidence that rename-aware history pays at scale — built as a whole VCS because the language toolchain underneath held no semantic identity. Jet holds it already.

The radical endpoint: definitions are content-addressed, renames are metadata, conflicts on names cannot exist. Jet's bounded version keeps files and text as ratified, and moves only refactor meaning.
comparisons.code: # Unison: rename = update one name mapping

comparisons.note: Rename detection by similarity heuristic at diff time — guessing after the fact what the toolchain knew for certain at edit time.

recommendation.why: The knowledge already exists at edit time and the consuming surfaces (structural diff/merge, review) are in this slate; recording without consuming wastes the one moment the meaning is certain. Review attention moves from churn to substance, which is the scarcest resource in team development.

whyNot.reason: Preserves the data and delivers none of the payoff, betting a later ballot re-finds the motivation.
Keeps taxing exactly the behavior — renaming things well — the codebase most wants to encourage.

recommendation.tradeoff: Ops are one more artifact traveling with a change, and a stale op (edited by hand after recording) could lie. Accepted: ops are advisory over text — the text is always the truth, an op that no longer matches its text is dropped with a note, and every surface keeps the --text view.

reviewPasses.base: First draft compared record-and-consume, record-only, and decline, recommending record-and-consume because the consumers are already in the slate.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested the full Unison model (content-addressed definitions, names as views). Rejected as out of scope: Jet's source model keeps files and manual named imports (D-NAME-FILES1=C and the file-tree name law), and the bounded version captures the collaboration payoff without reopening them.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested ops stored in git commit trailers instead of .jet/. Folded into A's technical note as a transport detail, not a design fork.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B as the reversible, zero-risk first step; strengthened C by conceding git's heuristic rename detection covers the easy cases today.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A with the stale-op lie and with op spam from bulk codemods; repaired by making text authoritative (mismatched ops drop with a note) and batching bulk plans into one op. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Speculative acts: try, verdict, roll back, remember
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a transaction for edits: apply in an overlay, re-verdict affected claims, roll back by default, keep on demand.
decisions.lesson: Agents and careful humans need 'would this break?' without dirtying the tree. Today that costs apply, run, revert — with the tree exposed in between and nothing remembered after. The pieces exist: overlay-aware semindex, codemod apply/undo, affected-claim selection from the receipt store. This choice decides whether they join into one transaction.
decisions.story: Rin, an agent, has a candidate fix and one directive: never leave the tree dirty. It applies the fix, the suite half-runs, the session hits a limit, and the next agent finds a mystery tree. The fix was right; the transaction was missing.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet inspect codemod plan.json --dry-run   # shows the edits, runs nothing
# to learn if claims still hold: apply, jet test (33 s), git checkout -- .
# interrupted between apply and revert = the mystery tree

options.name: Full try verb
options.detail: `jet try <plan|patch>` applies in an isolated overlay, re-runs only the claims the change reaches, answers with a verdict, rolls back, and writes a speculative receipt so the result is remembered. `--keep` lands the change when the verdict is clean. The tree is never dirty, even on interruption.
options.technical: Rides overlay-aware semindex open (shipped), codemod apply/undo (D-CODEMOD1), affected-claim selection and receipts (Part I). Try receipts are marked speculative: no ledger or status row counts them as project truth. Flat verb amends D-CLI-SURFACE1=B. Distinct from the runtime rollback-regions draft, which governs program state at run time, not tree state.
options.code:
$ jet try fix-plan.json
2 claims re-checked · 1 breaks: parse rejects empty (E3001 parser.jet:12)
rolled back · wrote speculative receipt 6b09
$ jet try fix-plan.json --keep     # clean verdict → land it

options.name: Agent-only flag: codemod --try
options.detail: The same transaction under `jet inspect codemod`, JSON output only. Agents get the primitive; humans keep the apply-run-revert ritual and the closed verb family is untouched.
options.code:
$ jet inspect codemod plan.json --try --json
{"verdict":"breaks","claims":[…],"receipt":"6b09"}

options.name: Decline
options.detail: Speculation stays manual. Every 'what would break' costs a dirty tree and a full-price test run, and interruptions keep manufacturing mystery trees.
options.code: $ git stash && … && git stash pop   # the ritual, with its failure modes

comparisons.note: --nobuild/--check_up_to_date answer 'is it affected' but nothing runs claims against a hypothetical edit; speculation requires a second workspace.
The manual transaction: a second checkout per speculation. Works, costs a cold build per worktree — the exact tax Jet's own agent fleet measured at 15-20 minutes.
The model being imported: apply, check invariants, commit or roll back, keep the log. Fifty years of proof that speculation needs a transaction, not discipline.

recommendation.why: This is the convergence primitive the agent fix-loop needs: card c0kbzrub ('Prove the agent fix loop converges') proves the loop, and try makes each iteration safe and cheap. Part I's affected-claim selection makes the verdict fast enough to sit inside that loop, and humans get the same 'what would break' answer without ritual.

whyNot.reason: Builds the full transaction and then hides it from every human who wants the same answer.
Keeps manufacturing dirty trees and full-price speculation, the two costs the agent fleet already measured.

recommendation.tradeoff: An overlay is not the real tree: comptime probes of the filesystem could diverge between try and keep. Accepted with the guard that `--keep` re-verdicts on the real tree when the closure hash differs, so a divergent overlay can never land a stale verdict.

reviewPasses.base: First draft compared the full verb, the agent-only flag, and decline, recommending the verb because both audiences ask the same question.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Breadth pass tested try-servers (a resident speculation daemon) and multi-candidate racing (try N plans, keep the best). Both folded into A's future room: batching is an argument shape, not a new mechanism.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Tested B-now-A-later staging; rejected as a rollout order, not a design — the JSON surface in A already covers the agent path on day one.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Strengthened B by noting the closed verb family is a real cost and agents are the primary consumer; strengthened C by conceding worktrees plus discipline do work at small scale.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A with overlay-reality divergence and speculative-receipt pollution; repaired with the re-verdict-on-keep guard and the speculative marking that keeps try results out of every truth surface. The recommendation survives.

decisions.title: Drop the leading dot from literal constructors
decisions.gist: Whether literal constructors keep the dot before their braces, as in `Point.{x: 1}`, or lose it, as in `Point{x: 1}`.
decisions.lesson: Every Jet construction carries a dot before its braces, as in `Point.{x: 1}` and `[Int].{1, 2, 3, 4}`. The dot marks that a brace opens a value, not a block. It is one universal rule, yet it is ceremony on every construction, and no peer language writes it. The corpus holds about 3,500 dotted constructions. This choice decides whether the dot stays, goes everywhere, or goes only after a named head. The variant selector `.Tls13` stays in every option.
decisions.story: Priya ports a Go service to Jet. Her fingers type `Config{host: h}` and the compiler answers E0320: 'named construction has a dot before the brace'. She fixes it, then hits it again in the next file, because every language she knows — Go, Rust, C, TypeScript — writes construction without a dot. Reading back her finished config code, she sees `.{` on nearly every line and asks what the dots are buying her. The honest answer today is: they buy the parser one guaranteed token, and they buy her nothing.

options.name: Keep the dot everywhere (status quo)
options.detail:
No change. Every construction keeps its leading dot, including named structs, list and map literals, enum payloads, and anonymous records.

The gain is one law with no position limits. Because `.{` can never open a block, constructions parse inside `if` and `loop` headers, where dotless braces would be ambiguous.

The loss is permanent ceremony. Every construction pays two extra characters, and each new writer meets error E0320 by muscle memory.
options.technical: Ratified law: D-DOTCTOR1/2/3, D-UNIFYLIT1, D-BINPAT1, D-BOUND-HEAD1. Parser: `.{` and `Type.{` are accepted even where `allow_struct_lit` is false (card #1441, Parser/Expressions/binary_unary.rs:618-627), so construction works inside every control header. Dotless `Type { }` stays teaching error E0320 with parse recovery (primary.rs:422-438).

options.name: Drop the dot everywhere
options.detail:
The owner's sketch. Named heads write `Point{x: 1}` and `[Int]{1, 2, 3, 4}`. Enum payloads write `.Password{username: u}`. Anonymous records write `{port: 8080, on: true}`.

Code then reads like every peer language. The reflex that E0320 punishes today becomes the correct spelling.

Three costs follow, each with a fixed answer. Brace literals stop parsing inside control headers, so you add parentheses or bind first. A headless brace is a record only when its first token is a field name or a string key. Statement-position destructuring keeps working through one bounded look-ahead to `::`.
options.technical:
Grammar law. `Ident{`, `[T]{`, `[K:V]{`, `[T#N]{`, `.Variant{`, and `alias.Type{` in value position are construction heads.

The existing `brace_body_looks_like_fields` probe already separates field bodies from element bodies (Parser/Expressions/collections_structs.rs:127). Lowercase unit heads such as `px{100}` parse by the same head-adjacent rule, which is safe because trailing blocks were retired (D-TRAILBLOCK2, E0335).

Header positions keep `allow_struct_lit=false` (ptr_tuple.rs:433-447), and the card #1441 dot carve-out is deleted. A header construction then needs parentheses. A fallback brace after the coalescing operator stays a block unless it is field-led. `.{ id, sev } :: x` respells as `{ id, sev } :: x` through a save-and-restore probe.

options.name: Drop the dot after a head; keep `.{ }` when headless
options.detail:
Named heads lose the dot, so you write `Point{x: 1}`, `[Int]{1, 2, 3, 4}`, and `.Password{username: u}`.

The headless record keeps its dot as `.{port: 8080, on: true}`. Headless destructuring and dispatch patterns keep it too. The head token anchors the parse, so the dot survives only where a bare brace is genuinely unclear.

This is Zig's split. The gain is that the risky headless cases never change, so no field-led rule is needed. The loss is two spellings for one idea, and a record changes spelling when it gains a typed head.
options.technical: Headed forms follow option B's head-adjacent grammar. Headless `.{` keeps today's grammar unchanged, including card #1441 header parsing for the `.{` form only; headed forms in headers need parens. Amends the headed halves of D-DOTCTOR1/3, D-UNIFYLIT1, D-BINPAT1, D-BOUND-HEAD1, D-UNINIT-SENTINEL2; leaves D-DOTCTOR2 (`.{ }` inferred), S74 destructuring, and dispatch-arm struct heads untouched. Formatter auto-fix migrates headed sites only (~85% of corpus occurrences).

options.name: Retire brace construction; construct with parentheses
options.detail:
Construction becomes a call shape. You write `Point(x: 1, y: 2)`, `[Int](1, 2, 4, 8)`, and `.Password(username: u)`. The anonymous record becomes the existing named tuple `(port: 8080, on: true)`.

Swift and Python work this way. Parentheses never open a block, so construction parses in every position with no restriction and no probe.

The loss is large. Jet's ratified rubric separates the inert literal `Type.{ }` from a call that may run code. That distinction dies, and every list and map literal respells.
options.technical: Amends D-API-CTOR1's literal/call split and the whole D-DOTCTOR family. Named arguments at construction sites reuse S61 named-argument grammar. `[Int](…)` requires a new head production because a bracket type followed by `(` currently has no meaning. Named-payload enums already parse `(…)` (binary_unary.rs:693-705); only named fields inside are new. Typed text heads become one-argument calls; validation stays in sema. Uninit becomes `Int(uninit)`. Empty collection: `[T]()`.

comparisons.note: Dotless struct literals, with exactly the restriction option B adopts: a struct literal cannot appear in an `if`/`while`/`match` header; you add parentheses or bind first. Decades of use show the rule is learnable and rarely hit.
comparisons.code:
let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };
if p == (Point { x: 1, y: 2 }) { }   // parens required in the header

comparisons.note: Dotless composite literals for structs, slices, and maps — the closest match to Jet's whole literal family. Go bans composite literals in statement headers unless parenthesized, the same escape hatch as option B.

The split option C proposes: a named head is dotless (`Point{ }`), and only the headless inferred literal keeps a leading dot (`.{ }`). Jet already declined Zig's inner `.field = value` spelling (D-DOTFIELD1); this is only about the head.
comparisons.code:
const p = Point{ .x = 1, .y = 2 };
const q: Point = .{ .x = 1, .y = 2 };  // headless keeps the dot

comparisons.note: No struct literal at all — construction is an initializer call with named arguments, which is option D. Braces stay reserved for closures and blocks, so Swift never has the brace ambiguity; the price is that data and code construction look identical.

recommendation.why:
Option B gives Jet the spelling every programmer already types. One rule covers it. A brace after a head, or a field-led brace in a value slot, builds a value.

The ambiguity the dot solved is real but small, and it lives only in control headers. Rust and Go have proven the parenthesis escape there for decades.

The parser already owns every tool the change needs. The header restriction exists, the field-body probe exists, and the formatter already carries the E0320 rewrite machinery pointed the other way.

whyNot.reason: The dot taxes every construction forever to buy convenience in the rare header case. Every new writer types the dotless form first and is corrected by E0320; keeping the dot keeps that permanent friction.

Two spellings for one idea. A record changes its dot when it gains or loses a head, so readers must track position, not meaning. It also keeps the dot in the manifests and config files where it is most visible and least loved.

It erases the ratified literal-versus-call distinction (D-API-CTOR1): today `Type.{ }` is inert data and `Type(…)` may run code. Merging them hides that difference, and it forces the largest respell of all — every list and map literal in existence.

recommendation.tradeoff: B accepts three costs. Brace literals no longer parse inside control headers, so you parenthesize or bind first. A headless brace must be field-led to be a record. The migration touches corpus, docs, snapshots, and teaching text at once, so it must ship as one formatter-driven cutover.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keeping the dot, dropping it everywhere, and dropping it only after a head, using one shared program. It sized the blast radius at 521 dotted sites in examples, 2,211 in tests, and 764 in docs.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added parenthesized construction as option D and rejected a whitespace rule, because whitespace-significant grammar breaks under reformatting. A `#{ }` record head was also rejected, since `#` already carries three ratified jobs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested dropping headed dots now and keeping `.{ }` for records until manifests migrate. It was rejected as option C with an expiry date, so C's field-led insight was folded into option B instead.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning found real strength in A, which has no position limits at all, and in C, which quarantines every parser risk to sites that never change. Option D also composes with existing named-tuple grammar rather than a brace probe.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack pass hunted grammar breaks in option B and found each one answered, because a fieldless selector never takes a brace and a fallback brace is never field-led. Statement-start destructuring also survives through the bounded look-ahead probe the parser already uses elsewhere.

decisions.title: One arrow for callables, arms, and lambdas
decisions.gist: Whether every arrow in Jet becomes one spelling.
decisions.lesson: Jet has three arrow spellings today. `=>` gives a function its result type and writes a lambda. `->` picks a dispatch arm, a one-line body, or a loop item. `=[IO]=>` adds an effect ceiling. A ratified rule split callable syntax from control syntax on purpose. This choice asks whether one arrow now serves all three jobs, and what that split was buying.
decisions.story: Priya teaches a two-day Jet workshop. On day one she explains that `=>` hands back a value. An hour later a student writes `->` in a dispatch arm and asks why the arrow changed. Priya answers that one arrow means results and the other means selection. Half the room writes the wrong arrow for the rest of the day. The compiler catches each one, but the lesson time is gone.

options.name: Keep three arrows (today's rule)
options.detail: Nothing changes. `=>` means a value comes back. `->` means one branch or item is selected. `=[IO]=>` marks the effect ceiling. Readers can tell a result from a selection without reading further. New writers must learn which arrow each position wants, and the compiler teaches them by rejecting the wrong one.
options.technical: Status quo: OP_CALLABLE_ARROW `=>`, OP_ARM_ARROW `->`, EFFECT_ARROW_OPEN/CLOSE `=[` / `]=>` (crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs:135-153). Ratified by D-ARROW-CONTROL1=A (card #1209), D-LOOP-STMT-ARROW1=C (card #1453), D-BODY-ARROW1. Zero migration.

options.name: One arrow `:>` everywhere
options.detail:
Every arrow becomes `:>`. Function results, dispatch arms, loop bodies, and lambdas all read the same. The effect ceiling becomes `:[IO]>`.

There is one arrow to learn and one to type. Readers lose the instant cue that told a result from a selection, and every arrow in the repository and in user code changes.
options.technical:
Retires `=>`, `->`, `=[`, and `]=>`. Adds one token `:>` plus the effect form `:[Effects]>`.

Fallible spellings compose unchanged, as in `fn read() :> String ?`. Migration covers 1,716 `=>` sites, 977 `->` sites, and 123 effect arrows across in-repo `.jet` files. The formatter, grammar files, editor packs, and arrow-quoting diagnostics move in the same change.

options.name: `:>` for arms and lambdas; keep `=>` for results
options.detail: Arms, one-line bodies, and lambdas take `:>`. A function result keeps `=>`, and the effect ceiling becomes `:[IO]>`. The result arrow stays distinct, so a signature still reads differently from a branch. Two arrows remain, so the workshop question does not fully go away.
options.technical: Retires `->`, `=[`, `]=>`; keeps OP_CALLABLE_ARROW `=>`; adds `:>` and `:[Effects]>`. Migration touches 977 `->` sites and 123 effect arrows; the 1716 `=>` sites stay. D-ARROW-CONTROL1's callable/control split survives in weakened form.

options.name: One arrow, but reuse `=>`
options.detail: Everything unifies on the arrow Jet already has. Arms, loop bodies, and lambdas take `=>`, and the effect ceiling becomes `=[IO]=>` unchanged. Writers learn one arrow and no new symbol enters the language. Existing code that uses `=>` keeps working, so the change is smaller.
options.technical: Retires `->` only; keeps `=>` and the current effect arrow. Adds no token, so no new Syntax.rs sigil row. Migration touches 977 `->` sites. Risk: `=>` then means both result and selection, and `if x == { 200 => ... }` reads like a lambda table to readers from other languages.

comparisons.note: Two arrows, split the way Jet splits them today: `->` for a result type, `=>` for a match arm.
One arrow for both jobs. Results use a colon, and `=>` covers arms and lambdas.
One arrow, `->`, introduces every clause body. Readers never choose between arrows.
comparisons.code:
label(N) when N rem 15 =:= 0 -> "FizzBuzz";
label(N) -> integer_to_list(N).

comparisons.note: No arrow at all. Results are bare types and cases use a colon, which shows a fourth path exists.

recommendation.why:
One arrow removes a rule that readers must hold but that no program needs. The compiler already knows whether a position wants a result or a branch.

Spelling that difference twice gains the reader nothing. `:>` also frees Jet from the `=[IO]=>` bracket sandwich, which is the least readable token in the language today.

whyNot.reason: The split it protects is taught by compiler errors, not by reading. It spends beginner attention on a distinction the machine never needs.
It keeps two arrows, so a writer still has to ask which arrow a position wants. It pays most of the migration cost for part of the gain.
Reusing `=>` for arms makes a dispatch table look like a table of lambdas. It also keeps `=[IO]=>`, the form readers report as hardest to scan.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet accepts one large mechanical migration and the loss of an at-a-glance result cue. That is acceptable because the compiler enforces the distinction, the formatter performs the rewrite, and the language is still greenfield.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared today's three arrows with the owner's single `:>` form and recommended `:>`, because the arrow choice is decided by position and the compiler already knows the position.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a colon-only result form as in Go, an arrow-free layout rule, and per-context words such as `then`. Those became option D and the Go comparison, because none of them changed who decides the arrow.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option C, which unifies arms and lambdas but keeps `=>` for results. It survives as a real design because the result arrow is the one arrow a signature reader scans for.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Steelmanning option A named what the split buys, because a reader sees at once whether a line returns a value or selects a branch. It also confirmed that the fallible spellings compose with `:>` without a new rule.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack pass found four risks in `:>`, namely a crowded colon family, the characters `:[` inside map types, comparison-like reads in generic argument lists, and a 2,800-site migration. Each is answered by pinning `:>` to arm, body, and signature positions and by landing the formatter rewrite in the same change.

decisions.title: Teaching foreign keywords
decisions.gist: Choose how the compiler teaches a wrong-language keyword.
decisions.lesson: Users often bring declaration, binding, loop, or import words from another language. The compiler can name the current Jet form at the error site, group those messages by family, or keep compile errors generic and teach through a separate command.
decisions.story: Ravi knows three languages and writes `fun`, `var`, and `import` in a new Jet file. He needs the first error to name the Jet form, not blame the line for computing an unused value.
decisions.inWild:
```jet
fun add(a: Int) => Int { a }
var x: Int32 = 1
import core.text
```

The current baseline reports E0003 for these foreign declaration and binding shapes. The choice decides whether that code also teaches the family and replacement.

options.name: One shared teaching code
options.detail: Use E0003 for every recognized foreign keyword. Keep one registry row, but make What, Why, and Fix name the word and its Jet replacement.
options.technical: The committed loop teaching already uses E0003 (`crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Statements/control.rs:1739-1754`). The registry defines E0003 as one generic statement row (`crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:8`, `docs/spec/diagnostic-rows.md:9-11`). It is not a family row. It is not a per-keyword row. One foreign-word table exists at `crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Statements/control.rs:16-28`. Extend that table for imports. Do not add a second one. The generic false cause is emitted at `crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Statements/control.rs:2568-2577`.
options.code:
```jet
fun add(a: Int) => Int { a }
var x: Int32 = 1
while ready { print(ready) }
import core.text
```

Rendered diagnostics:
```text
Error [E0003]: `fun` is a function declaration keyword; Jet writes `fn`
 Why: Jet uses one function declaration spelling so every declaration has one shape
 Fix: replace `fun` with `fn`

Error [E0003]: `var` is a foreign binding keyword; Jet writes `:=`
 Why: Jet puts binding mutability on `:=` or `::`, not on a declaration keyword
 Fix: write `name := value`

Error [E0003]: `while` is a foreign loop keyword; Jet writes `loop`
 Why: Jet uses one loop form for finite and conditional iteration
 Fix: write `loop condition { … }`

Error [E0003]: `import` is a foreign import keyword; Jet writes `use`
 Why: Jet brings modules into scope with `use`
 Fix: write `use "core.text";`
```

options.name: One code per family
options.detail: Use one code for declarations, one for bindings, one for loops, and one for imports. Tools can filter families, but the registry gains four public rows.
options.technical: Use new family rows E0068 for declarations, E0069 for bindings, E0080 for loops, and E0081 for imports. Those codes are absent from the current diagnostic registry. The existing loop behavior is E0003, so this option changes the shipped code and snapshots for the loop family.
options.code:
```jet
fun add(a: Int) => Int { a }
var x: Int32 = 1
while ready { print(ready) }
import core.text
```

Rendered diagnostics:
```text
Error [E0068]: `fun` is a foreign declaration keyword; Jet writes `fn`
 Why: Jet uses one function declaration spelling so every declaration has one shape
 Fix: replace `fun` with `fn`

Error [E0069]: `var` is a foreign binding keyword; Jet writes `:=`
 Why: Jet puts binding mutability on `:=` or `::`, not on a declaration keyword
 Fix: write `name := value`

Error [E0080]: `while` is a foreign loop keyword; Jet writes `loop`
 Why: Jet groups loop words under one loop family
 Fix: write `loop condition { … }`

Error [E0081]: `import` is a foreign import keyword; Jet writes `use`
 Why: Jet uses one import family for module loading
 Fix: write `use "core.text";`
```

options.name: Teach only through `jet explain`
options.detail: Keep compile diagnostics generic and teach wrong-language words through a dedicated explain command. This avoids more compile branches, but the first error does not show the fix.
options.technical: The parser keeps the one foreign-word table as an explain lookup, but it does not change E0003 at the source site. The generic E0003 row remains at `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:8`. The syntax record pauses old-spelling teaching in `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:58-64`, so this option needs an owner amendment.
options.code:
```jet
fun add(a: Int) => Int { a }
```

Compile output:
```text
Error [E0003]: this line computes a value but doesn't do anything with it
 Why: only calls, bindings, assignments, and `return` are allowed here
 Fix: use the value, e.g. `x :: ...` or `print(...)`
```

Follow-up:
```text
$ jet explain keyword fun
`fun` is not a Jet keyword.
Jet writes `fn` for a function declaration.
```

comparisons.note: Zerolang's benchmark report names the wrong-language failure with PAR100 and shows the parser treating Rust's `fn` as an ordinary name. It reports the parse location rather than teaching `fun` as a replacement.
Rust's parser reports the token and expected grammar when a programmer writes a foreign word. It does not promise a cross-language replacement, so the error stays tied to Rust grammar.

recommendation.why: E0003 already owns the loop teaching path and its registry row is generic. One shared code keeps the table and tooling small while family-specific What, Why, and Fix text gives the beginner the needed replacement.

whyNot.reason: Family codes help filtering, but four public rows split one teaching mechanism and force a code change for the shipped loop diagnostics.
A separate explain command hides the replacement at the moment of failure. Beginners often stop after the first compiler error and never run a second command.

recommendation.tradeoff: E0003 cannot classify foreign words by code in tools. The diagnostic text and the one lookup table carry the family detail, while the code remains compatible with the current loop path.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared one shared code, four family codes, and a separate explain surface. It kept the current E0003 loop path visible in each choice.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested one code per keyword, warning severity, and compiler suggestions without a replacement. Per-keyword codes duplicate the table, and warnings leave the false cause in place.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested E0003 with structured family data and family-specific text. That keeps one public code while giving tools and people more detail, so it strengthens option A rather than adding a fourth choice.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened family codes with stable names and strengthened explain-only teaching with an automatic follow-up hint. Both still add a second public surface or hide the first fix.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested code filtering, snapshot churn, paused teaching law, and the first-error workflow. Shared E0003 with exact family text survives those attacks with the least surface change.

decisions.title: Expected-fail test declaration
decisions.gist: Choose how a test records a known failure.
decisions.lesson: A known bug needs a test that runs and fails without making the suite red. The suite must turn red when the bug is fixed. This choice also decides where the bug reason lives.
decisions.story: Mina maintains a parser with one known bug. She wants its regression test in every run, but she wants the test to fail loudly when the parser starts working.

options.name: Typed #Test argument
options.detail: Put the expected-fail state beside the test name. A typed field can carry a bug reason and can gain checked values later. It adds one owner-gated marker field.
options.technical: Add `xfail: String` to the existing `#Test` marker. The marker currently declares `name: String` and `faults: [Effect]` at `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:88-90`. The test marker is registered at the `.Test` site in `crates/jet-foundation/src/Policy.rs:1517-1533` and `crates/jet-foundation/src/Policy.rs:1605-1616`. The field is new syntax under I7.
options.code:
```jet
#Test("map parser rejects duplicate keys", xfail: "card #2107") {
    require_eq(parse("{a: 1, a: 2}"), none)
}
```

Failure output:
```text
test map parser rejects duplicate keys ... xfail
test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 1 xfailed; 0 xpassed
```

Unexpected-pass output:
```text
test map parser rejects duplicate keys ... XPASS
error: unexpected pass in expected-fail test `map parser rejects duplicate keys`
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 xfailed; 1 xpassed
```

options.name: Reserved name prefix
options.detail: Reserve `xfail:` at the start of a test name. It needs no marker field, but names become runner commands and tools must parse the convention.
options.technical: The runner strips `xfail:` before reporting the test name. A name prefix is not typed by the marker registry. The existing `#Test` name is a `String` argument at `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:90`.
options.code:
```jet
#Test("xfail: map parser rejects duplicate keys") {
    require_eq(parse("{a: 1, a: 2}"), none)
}
```

Failure output:
```text
test map parser rejects duplicate keys ... xfail
test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 1 xfailed; 0 xpassed
```

Unexpected-pass output:
```text
test map parser rejects duplicate keys ... XPASS
error: unexpected pass in expected-fail test `map parser rejects duplicate keys`
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 xfailed; 1 xpassed
```

options.name: Separate #XFail marker
options.detail: Stack a dedicated marker with `#Test`. The state is visible and separate, but the language gains a second marker and a second registration row.
options.technical: Add a new `#XFail(String)` marker at the `.Test` site. The existing registry reads every marker declaration from `Prelude/Markers.jet` through `crates/jet-foundation/src/Policy/MarkerSource.rs:19-32`; this option adds a second rule.
options.code:
```jet
#XFail("card #2107")
#Test("map parser rejects duplicate keys") {
    require_eq(parse("{a: 1, a: 2}"), none)
}
```

Failure output:
```text
test map parser rejects duplicate keys ... xfail
test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 1 xfailed; 0 xpassed
```

Unexpected-pass output:
```text
test map parser rejects duplicate keys ... XPASS
error: unexpected pass in expected-fail test `map parser rejects duplicate keys`
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 xfailed; 1 xpassed
```

options.name: Reuse `.expect_fail` region
options.detail: Wrap the known failure in the existing region member. This avoids new syntax, but it changes a region contract into a whole-test contract only by convention.
options.technical: Today `.expect_fail` belongs inside `#Test` and takes an optional E30xx stop code (`crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/math_layout.rs:685-702`, `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/ScopeMembers.rs:757-770`). The runtime catches the region stop at `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs:460-485`. A clean region already fails. It reports `expected this region to fail, but it passed` at `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/emit/statements.rs:1930-1973`.
options.code:
```jet
#Test("map parser rejects duplicate keys") {
    .expect_fail(E3010) {
        require_eq(parse("{a: 1, a: 2}"), none)
    }
}
```

Failure output:
```text
test map parser rejects duplicate keys ... pass
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 skipped
```

Unexpected-pass output:
```text
FAIL map parser rejects duplicate keys
Error: expected this region to fail, but it passed
```

comparisons.note: `pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True)` keeps a failing test expected, but makes an unexpected pass fail the suite.
The repo research records `xfail` and `unexpectedPasses` as named test results. It does not give Jet a source spelling to copy.
Rust `#[should_panic]` asserts that a test panics. It does not record a known bug, and an unrelated panic can satisfy it unless `expected` narrows the message.

recommendation.why: A typed field keeps test identity, reason, and runner state in one marker. It preserves the strict unexpected-pass rule without turning names or regions into hidden protocol.

whyNot.reason: A name prefix is easy to miss in editors and cannot carry a checked marker type. It makes names part of the runner protocol.
A separate marker makes the state clear, but it duplicates the test marker surface and adds another registry row for one test property.
A region expects one runtime stop, not one test defect. Reusing it would blur two scopes and would not cover failures outside the region.

recommendation.tradeoff: The owner must approve one new typed `#Test` field. A reason string is less strict than a closed bug reference, so later work may type the reason without changing the marker shape.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared a typed marker field, a name convention, a separate marker, and the existing region member. It kept strict unexpected-pass failure in every whole-test option.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a test-file prefix, a command-line allowlist, and a manifest entry. Those choices either hide state outside the test or add a second configuration surface, so they were dropped.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested a typed marker field combined with `.expect_fail`. The two scopes carry different failure contracts, so the typed field stays whole-test and the region member stays region-only.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the losing choices. The prefix gets a reserved separator, the marker gets a reason, and the region gets a stop code, but each still loses one clear source of truth.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested a fixed bug, a wrong failure, a flaky failure, and a test with several regions. A strict typed field can reject an unexpected pass and keep the other cases visible, so the recommendation remains A.

decisions.title: Last expression returns; the `::` function body retires
decisions.gist: Whether a function's value comes from the last expression of its block, retiring the `fn … :: expr` body form.
decisions.lesson: Two questions were bundled. Where a value comes from is separate from what may introduce a body. `:>` already gives arms and control bodies a brace-free one-expression form, so last-expression-returns does not put braces on a pattern table. The clutter lands somewhere else entirely: a headless literal return becomes a double brace.
decisions.story: Jet writes the return type in the signature, so an implicit trailing value is checked against a declared type rather than inferred from it. Languages burned by implicit return are the ones that infer the return type; Jet cannot be, because `fn f() :> Int` already said what must come out. That makes the last-expression rule safe here in a way it is not elsewhere, and it makes a REPL cell, a notebook cell and a function body obey one rule.
decisions.inWild: Rust, Ruby, Kotlin, Scala and Haskell all return the last expression; Rust marks discard with a trailing semicolon. Python, Go and C require an explicit return. Notebook and REPL environments universally echo the last expression of a cell, which is the alignment the owner is asking for.
decisions.detail: Measured over 600 shipped examples: 230 `:: expr` bodies, 739 block bodies, 62 brace-free arms, 250 braced arms, 221 brace-free control bodies, 212 explicit returns. Migration of the 230 sites is mechanical and `jet fmt` can perform it, the same playbook that just moved 444 files for D-LIT-DOT1=B.

options.name: Last expression returns; retire `::`; a returned literal names its head
options.detail: A block yields its last expression. `fn f(x: Int) :> Int { x * 2 }` is the short form, `return` means early return only, and `::` goes back to meaning exactly one thing: bind a name to a value. Arms, control bodies and lambdas keep `:>` and stay brace-free, so pattern tables are untouched. Where a function returns a headless literal today, it names the head instead: `fn make() :> Point { Point{x: 1, y: 2} }`, which avoids the `{ {…} }` double brace and reads better besides.
options.technical: Parser: a function body is a block; the block's trailing expression becomes its value when the declared return type is not Unit. Retire the `::` body arm with a teaching diagnostic pointing at the brace form. Formatter must keep `fn f() :> Int { x * 2 }` on one line, and rewrites the 230 `::` sites. Sema already knows the declared return type, so a trailing value of the wrong type is an ordinary mismatch, not a new check.

options.name: Last expression returns; keep `::` as a second short form
options.detail: Adopt the last-expression rule for blocks but leave `fn … :: expr` in place. Nothing migrates and no literal-return question arises, because `:: {x: 1}` is unambiguous. The cost is that two spellings mean the same thing, which is the inconsistency the proposal set out to remove, and every reader and tool must know both.
options.technical: Parser gains the trailing-expression rule; the `::` arm stays. No corpus migration. Violates the spirit of I8 by keeping two mechanisms for one meaning.

options.name: Last expression returns; retire `::`; accept the double brace
options.detail: As A, but a headless literal return is written `fn make() :> Point { {x: 1, y: 2} }` rather than naming the head. Keeps the inferred-literal convenience at the cost of a shape most readers will misread on first encounter.
options.technical: As A, minus the head requirement. The parser must disambiguate an inner brace in trailing position as a literal rather than a nested block.

options.name: Keep the current design
options.detail: `::` stays the single-expression body form and `return` stays mandatory for a value from a block. No migration, no REPL/notebook alignment, and the two-form inconsistency remains.
options.technical: No change.

decisions.comparisons: A and C differ only in how a headless literal return is spelled. B avoids all migration but keeps two ways to say one thing. D declines the REPL and notebook alignment the owner named as a motivation.

recommendation.why: Jet declares the return type in the signature, so a stray trailing value is a type error rather than a silent return. That makes the last-expression rule safe here. It also gives a function body, a REPL cell and a notebook cell one rule.

whyNot.reason: Keeping `::` beside the brace form leaves two spellings for one meaning. That is the inconsistency the proposal set out to remove, and I8 asks for one mechanism.
A headless literal in trailing position reads as `{ {x: 0, y: 0} }`. Most readers will misparse the double brace, and naming the head costs one word.
Doing nothing declines the REPL and notebook alignment the owner named. It also keeps `return` doing two jobs, early exit and ordinary result.

recommendation.tradeoff: You give up the shortest one-line body. `fn double(n: Int) :> Int { n * 2 }` is four characters longer than the `::` form, across 230 sites. You also make the formatter load-bearing: if it does not keep a short body on one line, this change manufactures the clutter it set out to avoid.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared retiring the body form, keeping it, and doing nothing. It checked each against the arm surface and found that no option puts braces on a pattern arm.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tried a Rust-style trailing semicolon for discard, a separate `yield` word, and inferring the return type. All three were dropped as worse than the options here.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of A and B was considered: retire `::` everywhere except a literal return. It was rejected because a survivor rule for one shape is harder to teach than naming the head.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass asked what the options share. Every one keeps `:>` as the brace-free marker for arms, control bodies and lambdas, so the pattern table in the sample is identical in all four.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass found the collision with D-LIT-DOT1=B. A headless literal in trailing position is ambiguous with a body block, which is why option A names the head.

decisions.checkInstructions: Read the four options and pick one. The question is only how a function body produces its value and whether `::` survives as a body form. Pattern tables and control bodies keep `1 :> "one"` under every option.
decisions.comment: Owner ratifies the RULE only: a block yields its trailing expression, and return narrows to early return. The surface question — whether the single-expression body form retires, and whether the return type and the body arrow swap places — is deliberately split out to its own ballot rather than decided here.

decisions.title: Where the return type sits, and what `:>` means
decisions.gist: Whether the return type moves off the arrow so `:>` means one thing everywhere: the body follows.
decisions.lesson: Uniformity is not one body form. It is the same two forms everywhere: `:>` for one expression, braces for many. Today `:>` carries a type in a signature and a value in an arm.
decisions.story: Measured over 600 shipped examples: 427 signatures declare a return type, 34 carry an effect ceiling, and 641 declare nothing. So 461 signatures change, against 387 arm, lambda and control sites that already read `:>` as the body marker. The swap also removes a collision D-LIT-DOT1=B created hours earlier: after `:>` the parser is in value position, so a headless literal body needs no second brace.
decisions.inWild: Go writes `func f(x int) int`, juxtaposing the return type. Rust, Kotlin, TypeScript and Haskell put an arrow or colon before it. No mainstream language moves the arrow onto the body, so this is unfamiliar outside Jet while being more consistent inside it.
decisions.detail: D-BODY-LAST1=B already ratified that a block yields its trailing expression. This ballot decides only the signature shape and whether the `::` body form retires. Every option keeps pattern tables identical, because arms are introduced by `:>` and not by the signature.

options.name: Return type after a colon; `:>` is the one body arrow
options.detail: The return type takes a colon, exactly like a parameter or a field. Then `:>` introduces a one-expression body and braces introduce a block, matching arms, lambdas and control bodies. The effect ceiling takes the body-arrow position as `:[IO]>`. The `::` body form retires and `::` goes back to meaning only bind-a-name.
options.technical: Parser: the return type parses after `)` behind a colon, and `:>` plus `:[IO]>` become body introducers at function level. Retire the `::` body arm with a teaching diagnostic and a fixture. `jet fmt` rewrites 461 signatures and 230 bodies.

options.name: Return type juxtaposed; `:>` is the one body arrow
options.detail: As A, but the return type sits bare after the parameter list. One fewer sigil per signature, and the shape Go users already know. The cost is that a type appears with nothing introducing it, the only such place in Jet.
options.technical: As A, except the return type is parsed by juxtaposition after `)`. Unambiguous, because no statement may follow a parameter list.

options.name: Keep the arrow on the type; bodies are always braces
options.detail: The signature does not change. A one-expression body uses braces and relies on the ratified trailing-expression rule. The `::` form retires. Smallest change, but `:>` keeps two jobs, and a headless literal return must name its head to avoid a double brace.
options.technical: Retire the `::` body arm only. No signature migration. `jet fmt` rewrites 230 bodies.

options.name: Keep both the arrow and the `::` body
options.detail: Only the trailing-expression rule lands. Nothing migrates, and two spellings for a one-expression body remain.
options.technical: No further change.

decisions.comparisons: A and B differ only in whether a colon or juxtaposition introduces the return type. C keeps the signature and pays with a double brace on literal returns. D changes nothing beyond the ratified rule.

recommendation.why: It gives `:>` exactly one meaning across the language: the body follows. It also removes the literal-return collision, because after `:>` the parser is in value position and a headless literal simply works.
recommendation.tradeoff: You pay unfamiliarity. No mainstream language puts the arrow on the body, so a newcomer reads the signature twice. You also migrate 461 signatures, though the formatter performs it.

whyNot.reason: Juxtaposition is terser and Go users know it. It makes the return type the only unannounced type in Jet, which costs more than the sigil it saves.
It leaves `:>` carrying a type in one place and a value in another. It also forces a head onto every literal return to avoid a double brace.
Two spellings for one body remain, which is the inconsistency this discussion set out to remove.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared moving the return type, keeping it, and doing nothing. It confirmed that pattern tables are byte-identical under all four options.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tried inferring the return type, splitting `->` for types from `:>` for bodies, and a trailing where clause. Each added a token or weakened the checking that makes trailing returns safe.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid was considered: a colon for the return type but braces always and no body arrow. It was rejected because it discards the brace-free line the owner asked to keep.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass noted that 641 of 1102 signatures declare no return type. The most common shape, `fn run() { … }`, is untouched under every option.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked where the effect ceiling goes. `:[IO]>` reads well before an expression body but sits oddly before a brace, and 34 sites depend on that answer.

decisions.checkInstructions: Read the four code samples. They are the same program, so the only difference is the surface. Decide where the return type sits and whether `:>` becomes the single body arrow.

decisions.title: `?` for absence, `!` for error
decisions.gist: Whether the error separator in a type becomes `!`, freeing `?` to mean only absence.
decisions.lesson: `?` currently does four jobs, and two of them sit in the same position. `Int?` is an optional and `Int ? String` is a result, so a reader can fairly read the second as an optional Int. That collision is the defect; the operators are less confused than the types.
decisions.story: Measured over 600 shipped examples: 18 optional types `T?`, 145 result signatures `… ? E`, 179 postfix propagations `x?`, 760 fallbacks `??`, and zero uses of `!!`. So the error separator is the small, contained surface and the fallback operator is the large one. `!` as an infix appears nowhere in real code today.
decisions.inWild: Zig makes exactly this split: `?T` is optional and `E!T` is an error union, with `orelse` and `catch` as separate fallbacks. Swift writes `T?` and uses `throws`. Rust names both in the type. Kotlin's `!!` means force-unwrap, a different meaning from any option here.
decisions.detail: D-SIG-SHAPE1=B already puts the return type bare after the parameter list, so a signature reads `fn read_config(path: String) Config ! IOError`. `!` is unambiguous in type position — there is no boolean not there — and `!=` stays a single token.

options.name: Split the type only
options.detail: The error separator becomes `!`: `Config ! IOError`. `?` keeps its other jobs — optional type, postfix propagate, and `??` fallback. This removes the one genuine ambiguity, where two different meanings share the type position, and leaves the 939 operator sites alone. 145 signatures migrate.
options.technical: Parser and formatter accept `T ! E` in return position and retire `T ? E` with a teaching diagnostic. `jet fmt` rewrites 145 sites. No change to postfix `?` or `??`.

options.name: Split everything: `!` is the error rail end to end
options.detail: `!` marks error in the type, in propagation, and in fallback: `Config ! IOError`, `files.read(path)!`, and `… !! panic(…)`. `?` becomes purely about absence. This is the fullest answer and the largest migration. The operator half is not mechanical. Deciding whether an existing `??` becomes `??` or `!!` needs the type of its left side. That rewrite must run after sema, not in the formatter.
options.technical: As A, plus postfix `!` for error propagation and `!!` for error fallback. Roughly 1084 sites, of which the 760 `??` uses require type-directed classification.

options.name: Split the type and the fallback; one propagate operator
options.detail: `Config ! IOError` and `!!` for error fallback, but postfix `?` stays the single propagation operator because it can already tell from the type what to do. Keeps the visible `?`/`!` parallel the owner is after without a second propagate sigil.
options.technical: As A, plus `!!`. About 905 sites, and the `??` split still needs type information.

options.name: Keep `?` for both
options.detail: No change. `Int?` and `Int ? String` continue to share the type position, and `!!` stays unused.
options.technical: No change.

decisions.comparisons: A fixes the ambiguity for 145 sites and touches nothing else. B and C also split the fallback, which costs a type-directed rewrite of 760 sites. D leaves the collision in place.

recommendation.why: The collision worth removing is in the type position, where `Int?` and `Int ? String` mean different things with the same sigil. The operators do not have that problem: `??` on an optional and `??` on a result both mean the same thing, supply a value when there is none.
recommendation.tradeoff: You give up the full `?`/`!` symmetry, and `!!` stays unused. If the symmetry itself is the goal rather than the ambiguity, take C.

whyNot.reason: A second propagate sigil buys little: `x?` already knows from the type whether it is unwrapping absence or an error. It also costs the largest migration.
Reasonable if the parallel matters for its own sake. The 760-site fallback rewrite needs sema, not the formatter, which makes it a much bigger change than A for a smaller gain.
Leaves a reader unable to tell an optional from a result by looking at the type, which is the whole complaint.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared splitting the type, splitting everything, splitting type plus fallback, and doing nothing. It counted every site of each form first.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered a keyword such as `throws`, naming the error type only in the signature, and inferring it. Each either hides the error type or adds a word where a sigil already works.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid was considered: split the type now and split the fallback later if the asymmetry grates. That is option A with option C held open.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass noted that every option keeps `??` working on optionals, so the 760 most common sites are untouched under A.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether `!` collides with boolean not. It does not in type position, and `!=` remains one token; postfix `x!` and prefix `!x` are distinguishable.

decisions.checkInstructions: Read the four samples — the same program each time. Decide whether `!` takes over the error rail, and if so how far it goes.
decisions.comment: Absence keeps the question mark and nothing else. A fallible type is written T bang E, for example Config bang IOError. Call sites do not change: the coalescing and propagation forms keep their current spelling. A second call-site sigil was considered and rejected as too much new surface to teach for the distinction it buys.

decisions.title: The one arrow's glyph: -> or => or keep :>
decisions.gist: Pick the glyph Jet uses for its one arrow.
decisions.lesson: Jet has one arrow. It marks every callable body, dispatch arm, loop body, lambda, conversion declaration, and migration verb (D-ARROW-UNIFY1=B). The glyph today is `:>`. It was easy to type, but on the page it reads as noise and sits inside a crowded colon family (`::`, `:=`, `:`, `:[IO]>`). This ballot changes only the ink; the unification stays. The live surface is fully on `:>` — spec prose still showing `=>` forms is recorded drift. The effect row's fate is D-EFFECT-ROW2's own question; fused spellings per winner are priced there.
decisions.story: Ana reviews a pull request at the end of the day. The diff has forty arrows: function bodies, arm tables, loop bodies. With `:>` her eye keeps stumbling — the glyph looks like a typo of a type annotation. She wants the arrow to disappear into the reading, the way `->` does in Rust, or to say something, the way `=` says 'outputs'.

options.name: `->` everywhere
options.detail: The light arrow. It reads as 'maps to / yields' and vanishes into the line, which suits dense arm tables. It is the arrow most programmers' eyes already skip over (Rust, Swift, Haskell). Every arrow position respells with it, including `impl Source :> Target` and the migration verbs.
options.technical: Respells every OP_UNIFIED_ARROW site. Amended spellings: D-ARROW-UNIFY1=B, D-LOOP-STMT-ARROW1=C, D-SIG-SHAPE1=B, D-TRAILBLOCK2=A and D-ONELINE-BODY1=B examples, D-FAIL-CONV1=A's `impl` rail, and the D-MIGRATE rename/change verbs. I7 Syntax.rs rows and the generated editor grammar migrate in the same change. L0507, E0335, E0992, E0068 fix text and UI snapshots re-bless. `jet fmt` migrates the corpus once; `:>` and `=>` become teaching diagnostics with no alias.

options.name: `=>` everywhere
options.detail: The heavy arrow. The `=` inside it says 'outputs / binds', which matches what the arrow means in Jet: something is yielded. A generation of JS/C#/Scala programmers reads `=>` as 'body follows'. The cost is visual weight: in a forty-arrow diff, `=>` is louder than `->`. The respell breadth is identical to option A.
options.technical: Same amendment and migration list as option A; only the glyph differs.

options.name: Keep `:>`
options.detail: No migration, no re-bless. The glyph stays cheap to type. But the owner's own reading verdict — it looks sloppy — stands, and the colon family stays four members deep. Every future reader pays the crowding forever, while the migration cost is paid once.
options.technical: No spelling change. The drift cleanup card still lands (stale `->`/`=>` in spec prose and fixtures).

comparisons.note: Uses `->` for function results and `=>` for match arms. Two arrows, two jobs — readers report no confusion, but Jet's one-arrow law removes the split entirely.
comparisons.code:
fn double(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2 }
match code { 200 => ok(), _ => log(code) }

comparisons.note: `=>` is the lambda arrow. A generation of programmers reads `=>` as 'function body follows'.
No arrow at all; readability comes from keywords and braces. Evidence that arrow weight is a real reading variable, not decoration.
comparisons.code: func double(n int) int { return n * 2 }

recommendation.why: The arrow appears more often than any other sigil in Jet — every body, arm, and loop. The glyph that wins is the one the eye skips: `->` carries the 'yields' meaning with the least ink, which serves reading in exactly the dense arm tables Jet leans on.

whyNot.reason: `=>` says 'outputs' nicely and its migration is no larger, but it is visibly heavier in exactly the arm tables Jet leans on, and that weight is paid on every line forever.
Keeping `:>` saves one migration and nothing else. The glyph reads as a typo beside `::` and `:=`, and the owner has already rejected it on the page.

recommendation.tradeoff: One full-corpus respell: sources, snapshots, docs, I7 rows, and the editor grammar re-bless once. Accepted: the migration is mechanical fmt work, and the reading cost of `:>` is paid on every future line.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared `->`, `=>`, and the status quo with one worked program per glyph. It recommended `->` for the lowest reading weight in arm tables.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested `|>`, `>>`, a keyword, and Unicode arrows. All folded out: bar collides with D-SHAPE-PIPE1=C, keywords bloat tables, Unicode fails the typing floor.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A split — `=>` for callable bodies, `->` for arms — was tested and rejected. It re-adds the two-rule tax that D-ARROW-UNIFY1=B deleted.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B got its strongest case: `=` reads as 'outputs' and JS/C# familiarity is huge. Option C got the real re-bless cost of any respell.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The attack rechecked the live arrow surface: conversion rail and migration verbs are already on `:>`, so no option gains a hidden compatibility edge. No live `-` digraph conflicts exist; the familiarity claim for `->` holds at the same position in Rust, Swift, and Haskell.

decisions.title: One callable shape: a function is a named lambda
decisions.gist: Make every callable — function, lambda, code argument — one grammar shape.
decisions.lesson: Today the callable concept wears seven costumes. A braced function has no arrow, a one-line function has one, and effects fuse the arrow into `:[IO]>`. A lambda always has one, a function type has none, and a lambda cannot state a return type at all. A reader re-derives the rule at every site. This ballot picks the one shape: interface facts sit before the arrow, and the body sits after it.
decisions.story: Sam is three weeks into Jet. He knows `fn double(n: Int) Int :> n * 2`. He writes a braced version with the same marker — it parses, then `jet fmt` silently deletes his arrow. He asks which shape is real. Today's answer is 'the one fmt leaves behind, which depends on body form and effects'. That instability is the bug.

options.name: Arrow iff a success value is declared
options.detail: One rule: the arrow appears exactly when a non-unit success result is declared, and everything left of the arrow is the complete interface. Unit functions — plain or fallible — keep bare braces, so the beginner case and the ratified unit-fallible law both gain zero ceremony. Braced value-returning functions gain the arrow, which also kills the `Rect {` type-or-literal squint. Lambdas are the same shape minus the name and the slot-known types; their arrow is the lambda's body marker as today.
options.technical: Amends D-SIG-SHAPE1=B (braced value bodies gain the arrow) and subsumes D-BODY-ARROW1=B. D-FAIL-UNIT1=A is explicitly preserved: `fn save(path: String) ! IOError { … }` stays arrowless. Grammar: `[fn name] ( params ) [Return] [! Error] [:[Effects]] ARROW body`; ARROW present iff Return is non-unit or the callable is a lambda. Function types stay arrowless (no body). `task { … }` stays outside this grammar as D-CONC-SPAWN1=D's task-specific lowering. Shown in the ratified `:>` glyph; the glyph follows D-ARROW-RESPELL1.

options.name: Arrow always
options.detail: Maximum uniformity: every callable body, including unit functions, takes the arrow. One rule with zero exceptions — but the beginner's first function pays for it: `fn greet() -> { … }` adds a mark that buys the beginner nothing. Ceremony creep on the lowest rung.
options.technical: Same grammar as A but arrow unconditionally required between interface and body, including unit functions and unit lambdas.

options.name: Keep today's split
options.detail: No change: braced functions drop the arrow, expression bodies take it, effect rows keep their ratified fused spelling, and fmt keeps stripping a marker the parser accepts. The seven-costume table remains the callable chapter.
options.technical: No grammar change. D-SIG-SHAPE1=B stands as ratified.

comparisons.note: Functions and closures are two shapes (`fn f(n: i32) -> i32` vs `|n| n * 2`). Readers manage, but Jet can do better: one shape means the lambda chapter is one sentence.
Expression bodies (`= expr`) and block bodies are visually distinct on purpose; the style guide leans on that distinction. Evidence that a visible yield marker helps readers.
comparisons.code:
fun double(n: Int): Int = n * 2
fun greet() { println("hi") }

recommendation.why: One shape with the arrow meaning 'yields' gives the reader a single invariant that holds at every site, and it costs the beginner nothing — the unit function is untouched. It deletes six costumes and one real ambiguity (`Rect {` vs `Rect{`).

whyNot.reason: Buys one fewer exception at the exact place Jet must stay ceremony-free: the first function a beginner ever writes.
Keeps the seven-costume table and the re-derive-at-every-site tax that triggered this audit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Braced yielding functions gain three characters (` -> `). Accepted: the mark is the reader's guarantee boundary, and the corpus migration is one mechanical fmt pass.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed arrow-iff-success-value with unit bodies bare. It recommended that over arrow-always and the status quo.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a body keyword, Kotlin's `=` bodies, Python's `:`, and mandatory braces. Each collides with ratified law or kills one-line forms, so all folded out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Arrow-iff-yield plus an optional arrow on unit functions was tested and rejected. Optionality re-creates two spellings of one thing (I8).
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was strengthened: zero exceptions is genuinely the simplest statement. Option C was strengthened: zero migration during an active epoch.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacks tested `Rect :> {` against type-literal parsing, multi-head functions, unit-fallible signatures, and forced annotations. Positions stay distinct, S83 heads fit, D-FAIL-UNIT1=A is preserved by name, and inference law is untouched.

decisions.title: The effect row stands alone, outside the arrow
decisions.gist: Write effects as their own interface fact instead of deforming the arrow.
decisions.lesson: Today the effect row and the arrow are one fused token: `fn bump(n: Int) Int :[IO]> { … }`. The fusion has three costs. A unit function with effects is forced to carry an arrow it otherwise would not have. The function type drags a body arrow into type position where no body can follow (`f: fn(Int) Int :[]>`). And every arrow-glyph candidate needs a fused variant — the exact `=[IO]=>` form the arrow-unify ballot called unreadable. Unfusing makes effects a plain interface fact between the error and the arrow.
decisions.story: Priya writes a callback type: `f: fn(Int) Int :[]>`. Her reviewer asks what the trailing `>` points at. Nothing — there is no body in a type. The glyph is there only because the effect row physically contains an arrow.

options.name: Standalone `:[Effects]`
options.detail: The row keeps its spelling and loses the fused `>`. It sits with the other interface facts: return type, then `!` error, then `:[Effects]`, then the arrow if the callable yields. Types carry the same fact with no fake arrow. Unit functions with effects stay arrowless.
options.technical: Amends D-SHAPE8=A: EFFECT_ARROW_OPEN/CLOSE (`:[` / `]>`) become `:[` / `]`. Open rows keep `..E` inside the brackets (`:[Log, ..E]`). Prohibitions and `via` unchanged. Interface order fixed: Return, `! Error`, `:[Effects]`, then the body arrow when one is due. Shown in the ratified `:>` glyph; the glyph follows D-ARROW-RESPELL1.

options.name: Keep the fused arrow
options.detail: No change. The row stays inside the arrow: `:[IO]>` today, or the fused variant of whichever glyph D-ARROW-RESPELL1 picks (`-[IO]->` or `=[IO]=>`). The type-position dangle stays.
options.technical: D-SHAPE8=A stands; the fused token respells with the arrow choice.

options.name: Word form: `uses IO`
options.detail: Spell effects as a word clause after the error: `fn poll(url: String) Response ! NetError uses IO -> { … }`. Most readable to a cold reader, but it mints a keyword, breaks the visual rhyme with effect rows in types, and makes dense signatures longer.
options.technical: Mints contextual KW `uses` (I7 row). Type position: `fn(Int) Int uses IO`. Retires `:[` / `]>` entirely.

comparisons.note: Effect rows sit in the type between params and result (`(int) -> io int`) — a fact in the interface, not a decoration on an arrow.
comparisons.code: fun bump(n : int) : io int { println(n); n + 1 }

comparisons.note: Abilities appear in braces inside the type signature, positionally, not fused to any glyph.

recommendation.why: Effects are a guarantee, so they belong with the guarantees. Standalone `:[IO]` keeps the ratified spelling readers already know, fixes the type-position dangle, and frees every arrow candidate from a fused monster.

whyNot.reason: Keeps a body arrow in type position pointing at nothing, and taxes the arrow ballot with fused variants nobody defends on the page.
A new keyword for a solved spelling; it breaks I7 economy and reads worse in dense callback types than the bracket row.

recommendation.tradeoff: One character of separation (` `) replaces the fusion, and every effect-row snapshot re-blesses. Accepted: the re-bless rides the same migration as the arrow respell.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed the standalone row and recommended it over the fused status quo.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the `uses` word form and tested effects-before-params and a marker form. The last two folded out for burying or colliding with the marker plane.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Standalone row plus a word-form sugar was tested and rejected as two spellings of one fact (I8).
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B's best case is zero re-bless during the epoch. Option C wins only on first contact and loses on every dense callback type after.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacks tested `:[` tokenization against type colons, the open, empty, and prohibition rows, and independence from the arrow ballot. `:[` stays one token, every row form is unchanged inside the brackets, and the unfused row parses identically under any glyph winner.

decisions.title: Lambdas may state their whole interface
decisions.gist: Let a lambda write a return type, error, and effect row when its author wants them visible.
decisions.lesson: A lambda today can annotate its parameters but physically cannot state a return type, error, or effect row — the AST has no slot for them. Usually the call slot supplies those facts. But a lambda stored in a binding has no slot, and its author has no way to make the contract visible. Under the one-callable shape this is not a new mechanism: it is the same grammar with the front matter omitted.
decisions.story: Marco stores a parser step: `parse :: raw -> raw.trim().to_int()`. Six weeks later a reader wants to know: can this fail? The answer lives in the body's `?` chain. Marco wanted to write the contract on the interface, where readers look first. The grammar refused.

options.name: Full parity, inference unchanged
options.detail: A lambda may write any suffix of the interface — return type, `!` error, `:[Effects]` — in the same order and shape as a named function.
