Nothing becomes required that was not required before: slot inference stays the default, annotations stay optional. Beginners never see the upper rungs.
options.technical: Extends S46/S47: lambda grammar gains the optional Return / `! Error` / effect-row slots from the callable production. AST Lambda gains result/error/effects fields (today absent, crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/expressions.rs:256-336). D-LAMBDA-INFER1 untouched: annotation required only where no expected type exists. Shown in the ratified `:>` glyph and fused `:[IO]>` row; spellings follow D-ARROW-RESPELL1 and D-EFFECT-ROW2.
options.code:
nums.map(n :> n * 2)                          // rung 0: unchanged
parse :: (raw: String) Int ! ParseError :> {   // stored lambda, visible contract
    raw.trim().to_int()? "parsing {raw}"
}
on_tick :: () :[IO]> flush()                   // effects visible where the author wants

options.name: Params-only (status quo)
options.detail: Lambdas keep parameter annotations only. A stored callable that needs a visible contract must become a named `fn`. Cheap rule, but it forces a name and a promotion for what is a spelling need, and it keeps the one-shape law half-true.
options.technical: No grammar change.

options.name: Required interface on stored lambdas
options.detail: Any lambda bound with `::`/`:=` must write its full interface. Maximum explicitness at every storage site — and ceremony creep everywhere a two-line helper closure is bound locally. The beginner rung pays.
options.technical: Same grammar as A plus a sema rule: Lambda in a binding initializer without expected type requires Return (and `!`/effects when inferred non-empty).
options.code:
double :: (n: Int) Int :> n * 2   // forced even for this
// double :: n :> n * 2           // E: stored lambda must state its interface

comparisons.note: Closures elide types because context supplies them; named functions are explicit because they are interfaces. Rust readers report the boundary works; Jet adopts the same boundary but keeps one grammar.
comparisons.code:
let g = |n| n * 2;
fn f(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2 }

comparisons.note: Arrow functions may annotate a return type when the author wants the contract visible; most call-site lambdas do not. The optionality is used and liked.

recommendation.why: It completes the 'function is a named lambda' law with zero new mechanism and zero new ceremony: pure capability, opt-in, on the exact shape the reader already knows.

whyNot.reason: Keeps the promotion tax and leaves the one-shape law with a documented hole.
Converts a reading aid into a beginner toll at every local closure binding.

recommendation.tradeoff: The lambda AST and sema grow interface slots that most lambdas never use. Accepted: the slots are the same checked fields named functions already carry.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed full parity with inference unchanged and recommended it over the status quo.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a cast-style ascription escape and contract-in-binding. Both folded out: the first moves the contract off the interface, the second collides with D-BIND-BARE1=A.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Parity plus a lint nudging stored lambdas toward annotations was tested. The lint was kept out: style policy should follow corpus data, not precede it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option C was steelmanned: every stored callable reads like an interface at review time. The cost stands — local two-line closures are the common case.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacks tested double errors on disagreeing annotations and `!`/`:[` precedence in lambda position. Both resolve to the existing declaration grammar with no new ambiguity.

decisions.title: Parentheses required when arm atoms mix with boolean guards
decisions.gist: Make a mixed dispatch arm head show the grouping the compiler uses.
decisions.lesson: In a dispatch table, a bare atom desugars against the subject: `if n < { 48 | 45 && ready -> 2 }` means `((n < 48 || n < 45) && ready)` (D-IFDIST1=A). The desugar is invisible, and `|` binds tighter than `&&`. A probe against today's binary confirms the trap: `grade(46, false)` silently falls to `else`. Pure atom arms, pure predicate arms, and pattern-plus-guard arms are all honest on the page; only the atom-plus-boolean mix hides the real predicate.
decisions.story: Lena ports a pricing rule: 'tier 2 when under 48 or under 45 and the account is ready'. She writes `48 | 45 && ready -> 2`, reads it back, and cannot say which grouping runs without opening the spec. Her reviewer cannot either. The compiler knows; the page does not.

options.name: Require parens on the mix
options.detail: When distributed atoms and `&&`/`||` meet in one arm head, the atom group must be parenthesized: `(48 | 45) && ready`. A new diagnostic carries a machine-applicable fixit that inserts the parens the compiler already assumes. Pure atom arms and pure predicate arms are untouched.
options.technical: Amends D-IFDIST1=A: bare-atom lists may not appear as a direct operand of `&&`/`||`; the atom group takes parens. New E-code with MachineApplicable fixit; UI snapshot per I4. No runtime or lowering change — the required spelling is the current desugar made visible.

options.name: Keep and document
options.detail: The mix stays legal; the book and `jet explain` teach the precedence. Zero migration, but the trap stays armed for every cold reader, and the probe shows real values silently rerouting.
options.technical: No grammar change. Docs and explain text gain the precedence rule.
options.code: 48 | 45 && ready :> 2   // still legal; reader must know | binds tighter

options.name: Forbid the bare-atom/boolean mix
options.detail: An arm head may not combine bare distributed atoms with `&&`/`||` at all. Structural pattern guards (`.Err(e) && e.fatal`) stay legal — they contain no bare atoms. The mixed case must be rewritten as an explicit-subject predicate (`n < 48 && ready`), repeating the subject and comparison the table header already states. Strongest reading guarantee; the price is subject repetition exactly where parens would have sufficed.
options.technical: Amends D-IFDIST1=A: an arm containing bare distributed atoms rejects `&&`/`||` operands entirely; the diagnostic teaches the explicit-subject predicate rewrite. Pattern guards unaffected.
options.code:
48 | 45 :> 2            // atoms: legal
n < 48 && ready :> 2    // predicate: legal, subject written out
.Err(e) && e.fatal :> die(e)   // pattern guard: legal, no bare atoms
// 48 | 45 && ready :> 2  // E____: rewrite as atoms or as an explicit predicate

comparisons.note: Match or-patterns plus guards read unambiguously because the guard is keyword-fenced: `1 | 2 if ready =>`. The `if` keyword is the visible boundary Jet's mix lacks.
comparisons.code: match n { 1 | 2 if ready => a(), _ => b() }

comparisons.note: PEP 572 banned several walrus placements purely 'to avoid user confusion' — precedent for requiring parens exactly where a compact form hides grouping.

recommendation.why: It makes the page and the compiler agree at the exact spot they diverge today, costs two characters, and arrives with a fixit so the repair is one deterministic edit.

whyNot.reason: Documents a live trap instead of disarming it; the probe shows the misread producing wrong values, not style complaints.
Preserves every capability but forces the subject and comparison to be restated in prose predicates where two parentheses already make the grouping honest.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing mixed heads break until the fixit runs. Accepted: the corpus contains few, fmt/fixit migrates them mechanically, and each break is a site where a reader was already exposed.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed required parens with a fixit, against keep-and-document and a full ban.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a Rust-style guard keyword and reversed `|` precedence. The keyword collides with guard heads; the precedence change silently rewrites ratified semantics.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Parens-required with a lint-only first release was tested and rejected. Greenfield law ships the final form once.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned for expert table authors who know the rule. Option C was steelmanned as the strict form: pattern guards survive it, and its real price is subject repetition in rewrites.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacks confirmed `.Err(e) && e.fatal` stays legal under both A and C and that the fixit preserves the current desugar exactly. The rules key only on bare atom lists meeting boolean operators.

decisions.title: One rule for subject shorthand: method heads and a nesting fence
decisions.gist: Make `.member` shorthand follow one rule in loops and call slots, and fence it out of nested scopes.
decisions.lesson: Two ratified features share the bare `.member` spelling. The loop's implicit subject accepts method heads: `loop words if .len() > 1 -> .len()` runs today (D-LOOP-SUBJECT1=A). The call-slot shorthand accepts member heads only: `words.map(.len())` fails with E0302 plus E0104, and neither error names the real rule (D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A). Same spelling, two verdicts — a false rhyme, probed live. Separately, prior art (Kotlin's style law) marks nested implicit scopes as the point where the shorthand stops being obvious.
decisions.story: Noor writes `words.map(.len())` after reading `loop words if .len() > 1` two lines above. The compiler answers with a struct-field error and an arity error. She concludes the shorthand is unpredictable and stops using it — including where it genuinely reads better.
decisions.inWild:
words :: ["x", "yy", "zzz"]
active :: loop words if .len() > 1 :> .len()   // runs today
lens :: words.map(.len())                      // E0302 + E0104 today

options.name: Widen to method heads, add a nesting lint
options.detail: A `.method(args)` head chain becomes legal in call slots, matching loops: one rule everywhere the shorthand exists. A new lint, selector `subject_shorthand_nesting`, fires when shorthand appears inside another shorthand scope and shows the named-binding rewrite. Locally allowed with `#[allow(subject_shorthand_nesting)]`; projects refuse or promote it through the `policy.lints` deny table. Deletes a rule instead of adding one; E0302/E0104 stop firing on a form readers expect to work.
options.technical: Amends D-SUBJECT-CALL1=A: the chain grammar becomes `.segment[(args)] [.segment[(args)]]*` with method or member segments in any position. Lowering unchanged (one-parameter lambda). New registered L-code (next free L05xx) with selector `subject_shorthand_nesting`, UI snapshot per I4, MachineApplicable rewrite to a named binding. Local `#[allow(subject_shorthand_nesting)]`; package `policy.lints.deny = ["subject_shorthand_nesting"]` promotes it to a wall. Shown in the ratified `:>` glyph.

options.name: Narrow loops to member heads
options.detail: Loops adopt the call-slot rule: member heads only. One rule, achieved by deleting a working, readable form (`if .len() > 1`) that real examples use today. Consistency by subtraction.
options.technical: Amends D-LOOP-SUBJECT1=A: implicit-subject guard/body chains reject method heads; teaching diagnostic points to a named binding.
options.code: active :: loop w, words if w.len() > 1 :> w.len()   // the only spelling left

options.name: Keep the split, teach it
options.detail: Both rules stand; E0302/E0104 get rewritten to name the member-head rule and suggest the lambda rewrite. Cheapest, but the false rhyme stays: the same glyph sequence keeps two verdicts by position.
options.technical: Diagnostic text change only; both decisions stand as ratified.
options.code:
lens :: words.map((w) :> w.len())   // the taught rewrite
active :: loop words if .len() > 1 :> .len()   // still legal in loops

comparisons.note: Official conventions: use `it` in short, non-nested lambdas; declare parameters explicitly in nested ones. The nesting fence is the tested boundary, adopted by option A's lint.
comparisons.code:
ints.filter { it > 0 }.map { it * 2 }   // fine
// nested: declare names explicitly

comparisons.note: Key-path literals in function position (`\.name`) accept property chains but not method calls — the same member-only cliff option B would generalize; Swift users routinely hit it and rewrite to closures.
comparisons.code:
users.map(\.name)      // fine
// users.map(\.name.uppercased())  // needs a closure

recommendation.why: One rule replaces two, the rule matches what readers already assume, and the one real hazard prior art identifies — nesting — gets a targeted fence instead of a blanket ban.

whyNot.reason: Buys consistency by deleting the more useful half of the feature and rewriting working corpus code.
Better error text on top of a false rhyme is still a false rhyme; every new reader re-discovers the split.

recommendation.tradeoff: Widening lets longer computations hide the subject in call slots. Accepted: the nesting lint plus the existing named forms bound the damage, and the loop surface has run this way without incident.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed widening plus the nesting lint, against narrowing and keep-plus-teach.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested an explicit `it` keyword and free-standing method references. The first was already rejected in c0xsk2wa; the second is its own ballot-sized feature.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Widening without the lint was tested and rejected. Kotlin's evidence is that the win needs the nesting fence.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned as one crisp grammar everywhere. Option C was steelmanned as a two-string fix; neither answers the probe's reader.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacks tested argument-position ambiguity for `.len()` and lint reach over ratified single-level chains. The parse is unique, the lint fires only inside another shorthand scope, and its allow/deny paths use the ratified lint controls.

decisions.title: Default values: the default rides the type
decisions.gist: Decide how parameter and field defaults are spelled.
decisions.lesson: Locals bind with one typed-value atom: `version :: Float{0.1}` (D-BIND-BARE1=A). Parameters and fields declare a slot and dangle the default after `=`: `timeout: Int = 30` (D-APILABEL1=A). That is the only place Jet writes type here, `=`, value there. The owner asked for a binding-consistent shape without keywords or a split sigil, covering every edge. Probes fixed the constraint: optional and capability defaults are live today, and neither has a binding-glyph spelling because suffixed and marked type heads do not exist in expression position.
decisions.story: Sam learns `version :: Float{0.1}` in chapter one: the typed value is one atom. In chapter three he meets `timeout: Int = 30` and asks why the atom split. The slot plane needs the type first — but nothing stops the value from riding the type the same way it rides in a binding.

options.name: Keep `name: Type = value`, teach the fill law
options.detail: No spelling changes. The fill law gets stated where beginners meet it: `::` defines, `:=` defines mutable, `=` fills an existing slot. Familiar to every Swift, TypeScript, and Python reader. The cost: the one place in the language where a typed value is written as two separated pieces stays.
options.technical: No grammar change. Doc and diagnostic-text additions only.
options.code:
fn connect(host: String, /, *, timeout seconds: Int = 30, tls: Bool = true) String { … }
struct Server { port: Int = 3000 }

options.name: The default rides the type: `name: Type{value}`
options.detail: The default fuses into the annotation using the same `Type{value}` atom bindings already use. One law: `name :: Int{3}` — the name owns the typed value; `name: Int{3}` — the slot ships holding it, caller may override; `name: Int` — the slot ships empty, caller must fill. Sigil never splits, type stated once, `=` retires from the declaration plane (reassign and extern fill remain). Every edge closes: `Int?{None}` and `^Int{first}` parse in slot grammar because the annotation position already reads a type.
options.technical: Amends D-APILABEL1=A (parameter default spelling) and the field-default row including D-CLI-GLOBAL1=E's `=` binding form; narrows D-CHOOSE-FNBODY1=A's fill scope to reassignment and extern slots. Slot grammar: `name ':' [cap-mark] Type [suffix] [ '{' default-expr '}' ]`. Evaluation unchanged: the default is constructed per call when the argument is omitted; references stay left-to-right. Labels, zones, variadics, fn types, trait signatures, uninit law: untouched. Call-site and literal fills keep the use-side colon (`f(force: true)`, `Rect{width: 3}`).

options.name: Binding-glyph defaults: `name :: Type{value}`
options.detail: A defaulted parameter becomes a `::` binding the caller may override, and required params keep `name: Type` — required versus optional shows at the glyph. Honest holes, probed: optional and capability defaults have no expression spelling. `Int?{None}` is E0003 as an expression, and the `^` mark has no home there. So this option needs new expression grammar, or it keeps the `=` form for exactly those edges — two spellings of one fact.
options.technical: Would amend D-APILABEL1=A and mint new expression heads for suffixed and marked types, or carve out annotation-form defaults for optional and capability cases (I8 pressure either way).

comparisons.note: Both spell defaults `name: Type = value`. Familiar, and both live with the split atom; neither has a typed-value literal form to fuse into.
The language already owns the fused atom: `version :: Float{0.1}`. Option B extends the atom to the slot plane instead of importing a foreign shape.
comparisons.code:
version :: Float{0.1}
port: Int{3000}   // same atom, slot plane (proposed)

recommendation.why: One typed-value atom (`Type{value}`) now covers both planes, the sigil never splits, and `=` leaves the declaration plane. The probed optional and capability edges close inside existing slot grammar — no new expression heads, no keywords.

whyNot.reason: Keeps the only two-piece typed value in the language and the extra `=` role, purely for arrival familiarity.
Fails closure: the probed optional and capability defaults need new expression grammar or a second retained spelling — overhaul or duplication, not streamlining.

recommendation.tradeoff: Braces replace the bare `= literal`, so `Int{30}` reads as construction to Swift and TypeScript eyes, and default-bearing snapshots re-bless once. Accepted: a default is a construction, and the atom is already Jet's native spelling.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared keep, binding-glyph defaults, and default-rides-type after probing the optional and capability edges. It recommended rides-the-type for closure without new grammar.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a keyword form, `:=` in slots, and fused value-riding on the binding glyph. Keywords add ceremony, `:=` lies about mutability, and the binding glyph fails the probed edges.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid keeping `= value` for literals and `Type{value}` for edges was tested and rejected as two spellings of one fact (I8).
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option A was steelmanned on arrival familiarity, the strongest real argument against B. Option C was steelmanned as the required-versus-optional scan win at the glyph.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacks tested slot-grammar parsing for suffixed and marked heads, literal-fill confusion at use sites, and evaluation order. The annotation position already reads a type, use-side fills keep their own colon, and per-call construction is unchanged.

decisions.comment: Owner picked default-rides-type in chat after the full binding-map review and directed direct ratification. Defaults fuse into the annotation as the Type{value} atom: name: Int{30}; optional Int?{None} and capability ^Int{first} close in slot grammar; = retires from the declaration plane (reassign and extern fill remain); field defaults including D-CLI-GLOBAL1 CLI flags respell the same way.

decisions.title: Failure surface as suffixes: Success? Error! in signatures
decisions.gist: Spell the return facts as type suffixes: `?` for maybe-absent, `!` on each error type.
decisions.lesson: Today `?` is a suffix (`Int?` means maybe absent) but `!` is an infix separator: `Int ! ParseError`, with unions grouped as `T ! (E1 | E2)` (D-ERRSIGIL1=A, D-UNIONTYPE1=A). The two marks read differently, and the combination cannot be written at all: `fn find() Int? ! E` is a parse error today (probed: E0003). This ballot makes both marks suffixes with one reading: each type in the return zone declares its own role. `Int?` — a value, maybe absent. `IOError!` — a possible failure.
decisions.story: Dana writes a cache lookup that can miss (absent) and can also fail (backend down). Today the signature cannot say both; she smuggles the miss into an error variant and callers lose the distinction. She wants to write what she means: `fn get(key: String) Entry? StoreError! { … }`.

options.name: Role suffixes; unions by repetition
options.detail: The return zone is a sequence of suffixed types. One optional success (`Entry?` or plain `Entry`), then any number of error types, each marked `!`. Repetition is the anonymous union: `DbError! TimeoutError!` means either failure. Unit-fallible drops the success type: `fn save(path: String) IOError! { … }`. Bare `!` stays the default-error shorthand. Every fact reads left to right with its role on its own type.
options.technical: Amends three spellings. D-ERRSIGIL1=A: the fallible mark moves from infix separator to error-type suffix. D-UNIONTYPE1=A: error unions respell as suffix repetition, while `|` keeps its arm-alternative and pattern roles. D-FAIL-UNIT1=A: unit-fallible becomes `Error!` alone, and bare `!` remains the default-error row. Grammar: return zone = `[Type[?]] [Type!]*`. Works in every type position: aliases, fields, fn types (`fn(String) Entry? StoreError!`). Under D-CALLABLE-ONE1 the arrow follows the last suffix. Shown on the ratified braced baseline.
options.code:
fn get(key: String) Entry? StoreError! {          // absent and failure, both visible
    row :: db.fetch(key)? "fetching {key}"
    row
}
fn pick(n: Int) Int DbError! TimeoutError! {       // anonymous union by repetition
    load(n)? "loading"
}
fn save(path: String) IOError! {                   // unit-fallible: error suffix alone
    write(path)? "saving"
}
fn run() ! { … }                                   // default-error shorthand, unchanged
alias Fetched :: Entry? StoreError!                // same spelling in any type position

options.name: Suffix with one `!` on a union group
options.detail: Same suffix reading, but multiple errors stay a `|` union with one mark: `Entry? (DbError | TimeoutError)!`. Keeps the ratified union spelling and a single failure mark per signature. The parentheses are the price: the common two-error case gains a bracket pair that option A does not need.
options.technical: Amends D-ERRSIGIL1=A and D-FAIL-UNIT1=A as in option A. D-UNIONTYPE1=A survives with explicit parens: `(E1 | E2)!`; a bare `E1 | E2!` is rejected to keep grouping visible (consistent with D-ARMHEAD-PAREN1's reading law). Grammar: return zone = `[Type[?]] [UnionOrType!]`.

options.name: Keep the infix separator, fix the hole
options.detail: `T ! E` stays as ratified yesterday; the grammar gains the missing combination `T? ! E`. Cheapest change, but the two marks keep two different grammars — one suffix, one separator — and the combined form reads as three disconnected marks in a row.
options.technical: D-ERRSIGIL1=A and D-UNIONTYPE1=A stand. The signature grammar accepts an optional-suffixed success type before `!`; today's E0003 at that position becomes legal syntax.

comparisons.note: Error unions use `!` with the error side BEFORE the mark and success after: `anyerror!u32`. Jet's suffix keeps success first, which matches how signatures are read: what you get, then how it fails.
The combined case is spelled by nesting: `Result<Option<Entry>, StoreError>`. It works and is famously noisy; the suffix form states the same three facts in three marks.
Typed throws separates the channels: `func get(key: String) throws(StoreError) -> Entry?`. A keyword for one channel, a suffix for the other — evidence both channels deserve first-class spelling.

recommendation.why: One reading covers every case: each type in the return zone wears its role. It fills the probed hole (`Entry? StoreError!`), makes multi-error signatures flat, and turns yesterday's two grammars into one suffix rule.

whyNot.reason: Same reading, but the common multi-error case pays a bracket pair for a grouping repetition already makes unambiguous — there is nothing in the group to misread.
Fixes the hole while keeping two grammars for two sibling facts, and the combined spelling `Entry? ! StoreError` reads as punctuation soup.

recommendation.tradeoff: Yesterday's D-ERRSIGIL1=A infix spelling migrates again, one day after ratification. Accepted: the corpus on `T ! E` is hours old, and the suffix form is the one the infix ballot never had on its menu.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft proposed role suffixes with union-by-repetition, against a grouped-union suffix and the ratified infix separator.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested keyword channels (`throws`, `fails`), a `Result`-style generic, and Zig's error-first order. Keywords and generics re-add the ceremony D-ERRSIGIL1 removed; error-first reads backwards against Jet's signature order.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid allowing both repetition and one grouped `!` was tested and rejected: two spellings of one union (I8).
reviewPasses.cooperative: Option B was steelmanned: one mark per signature is a real scanning aid. Option C was steelmanned: it is the smallest diff that fills the hole and touches no ratified spelling.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacks tested the bang suffix against expression negation, its parsing inside generics and fn types, and the cost of re-respelling a day-old law. Type and expression positions stay disjoint, the sequence parses with one token of lookahead, and the infix corpus is hours old.

decisions.title: Source-loop binding keyword: loop x in xs
decisions.gist: Source loops spell the binding-to-source join with the keyword in; the clause comma there retires.
decisions.lesson: A source loop walks a collection and names each item. Today the name and the collection are joined by a bare comma, so the reader must already know the grammar rule to tell which is which. The keyword in makes the sentence read aloud: loop user in users.
decisions.story: A first-hour learner reads loop n, 0..10, 2 and sees three comma-separated things with three different jobs: the name, the range, and the stride. Nothing on the page says which is which. With loop n in 0..10, 2 the name and source are joined by a word, and the one remaining comma can only mean the stride.
decisions.inWild: Python, Rust, Swift, and Kotlin all spell this join as in; JavaScript uses of; Go uses range. No mainstream language ships a bare binding-comma-source header.

options.name: Keyword in
options.detail: The binding-to-source join is the keyword in. Two-name bindings keep their parens: loop (key, value) in map. The stride stays the optional comma third clause and becomes the only comma in the header. The guard keeps its ratified comma-less if. Infinite, conditional, bindingless-subject, and explicit-state loops are unchanged. in is a reserved keyword with an I7 Syntax.rs row. The retired comma form gets a teaching diagnostic. Expression-position membership, x in xs, is rejected with a teaching diagnostic pointing at .contains(x); no membership operator ships.
options.technical: Amends D-LOOP-COMMA1=A. D-LOOP-GUARD1=A, D-LOOP-SUBJECT1=A, D-LOOP-STMT-ARROW1=C, and the stride clause of S19 are untouched. Syntax.rs LOOP_CHANNEL_DRAIN respells to loop value in receiver.

options.name: Keep the clause comma
options.detail: Retain loop x, xs as ratified by D-LOOP-COMMA1=A. Shortest spelling; the header stays purely positional.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: for user in users reads aloud with no grammar knowledge.
Comma-joined header, but the range keyword still marks the source role.

recommendation.why: The comma there is role-overloaded: it joins binding to source, separates the stride, and also appears inside the (key, value) tuple. The keyword gives every source loop a natural-language reading, makes the remaining stride comma unambiguous, and matches the reading-first direction of the ratified 2026-08-21 slate. The guard clause already uses a role word; this finishes the header.

whyNot.reason: Position-only roles force the reader to know the rule before the line reads at all, and the two-stride form stays cryptic.

recommendation.tradeoff: in becomes a reserved word and costs two characters on the most common statement form. Users coming from Python will try membership x in xs; the teaching diagnostic routes them to .contains(x) instead of adding a second mechanism.

decisions.shortAuthorizedBy: Owner: Ok let's amend to use in. Skip the whole balloting process I want to directly confirm and proceed with making this change via card. Let's point at the .contains method.

decisions.title: Signed nixpkgs index selects and proves package identity
decisions.gist: Record how Jetpack trusts a signed index to name a nixpkgs package.
decisions.lesson: Jetpack must know which store path a nixpkgs name points at before it can fetch anything. It reads that from a signed index that records one channel, one revision, one system, and the attrs it can prove. Jetpack refuses an index whose manifest, target, signature, or canonical record fails verification. It also refuses an attr the index does not cover, rather than guessing.
decisions.story: Ana asks for ripgrep. Jetpack looks it up in the signed index, checks the signature, and gets an exact store path. When she asks for an attr the index does not carry, Jetpack says so plainly instead of failing later.
decisions.detail:
Retired by owner order, recorded 2026-10-10 by Main. This was an orphaned draft with no options, no recommendation and no situation; its text described behavior already in place, not an owner choice.

Settled by D-VERDICT-2157-1, ratified 2026-08-25 on card #2157, which is done with all exit criteria met. Jetpack gets a local unofficial catalog with no keys: explicit opt-in, never a silent fallback from a failed signature, and marked unverified in the lock and Hangar receipt. Every signed-path rejection stays: forged, stale, cross-system, duplicate and ambiguous records. The hardcoded test key is deleted, and official signed publication waits for a real registry.

The draft's lesson, one channel, revision and system per index, refusing a bad manifest, target, signature or canonical record and refusing uncovered attrs, is already law and built. A later owner ruling on #2157 made jetpack the public source and nixpkgs migration provenance only. The open items, key ceremony and custody, the immutable publication URL, signer rotation and the catalog operator, belong to card #2199, which should raise a fresh ballot at its key-ceremony step.

options.name: Retired: settled by D-VERDICT-2157-1
options.detail: The owner retired this draft. The signed-path rules it described are ratified by D-VERDICT-2157-1 and built on card #2157; official signing and key custody are deferred to card #2199.
options.technical: No rule of its own remains.
options.code: // superseded: see D-VERDICT-2157-1; signing ceremony on #2199

decisions.comment: Owner order 2026-10-10 ~20:25 (ask answer). Superseded; evidence in the Retired option.

decisions.title: Local unofficial catalog now, signed publication deferred
decisions.outcome: Jetpack gets a local unofficial package catalog that needs no keys and carries no signing guarantee, so local use works today. It is explicit opt-in and never a silent fallback from a failed signature. Packages realized through it are marked unverified in the lock and the Hangar receipt. Every rejection on the signed path stays. The hardcoded test key is deleted rather than promoted. Official signed publication, key custody, the publication URL, rotation and the operator are deferred until a real registry exists.

It is explicit opt-in and never a silent fallback from a failed signature. Packages realized through it are marked unverified in the lock and the Hangar receipt. Every rejection on the signed path stays. The hardcoded test key is deleted rather than promoted. Official signed publication, key custody, the publication URL, rotation and the operator are deferred until a real registry exists.

decisions.title: How should Jetpack phase out Nix while keeping a local fallback?
decisions.gist: Choose how Jetpack imports missing packages without Snix or Tvix.
decisions.lesson: Jetpack should own package selection, builds, caches, storage, and execution. Nix remains useful only as a temporary translator for packages Jetpack has not imported yet. The package source is named `jetpack`: a bare package ref means `package@jetpack`.
decisions.explainer: The signed index (card #2157) covers a fixed set of attributes. Overlays and custom flakes need real evaluation, so this choice decides the long path.
decisions.story: Ana runs a package that Jetpack already knows and sees no compatibility work. She later asks for an uncovered package. Jetpack uses her local Nix once, imports the evaluated build graph, then uses Jetpack on later runs.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack use ripgrep
  resolve  ripgrep@jetpack
  ready    signed Jetpack package

$ jetpack use uncommon-tool
  resolve  uncommon-tool@jetpack
  miss     package is not in Jetpack
  fallback local Nix · pinned nixpkgs revision
  import   closed build graph into Jetpack
  ready    uncommon-tool@jetpack

options.name: Jetpack first, local Nix import on a miss
options.detail: Bare refs and `@jetpack` use the Jetpack catalog first. If a package is missing and local Nix is available, Jetpack evaluates that exact pinned package once, imports its closed build graph, and then realizes it through Jetpack. No Snix or Tvix code or binary is used.
options.technical:
Amends D-JPK-REF1: `name` canonicalizes to `name@jetpack`; `@nixpkgs` retires with a fix to `@jetpack`. Resolution checks native recipes, the signed catalog, and verified caches before local Nix.

Fallback uses an exact Nix executable, version, nixpkgs revision, system, and attr. It imports the closed graph, hashes, losses, and proof into a Jetpack recipe and lock. Jetpack owns all later work. Offline mode never shells out. CI needs explicit policy. No Snix or Tvix artifact enters Jet.
options.code:
// both refs mean the same source
ripgrep
ripgrep@jetpack

$ jetpack use uncommon-tool
  miss     uncommon-tool@jetpack
  fallback /run/current-system/sw/bin/nix 2.35.2
  pin      nixpkgs b5aa0f… · x86_64-linux
  import   drv graph + outputs + hashes
  ready    uncommon-tool@jetpack

$ jetpack use uncommon-tool
  ready    locked Jetpack import · no Nix call

options.name: Published Jetpack catalog only
options.detail: Bare refs still mean `@jetpack`, and Snix/Tvix remain absent. Only centrally imported, signed packages are available. A local catalog miss fails and waits for the next catalog publication.
options.technical: Jet-owned infrastructure may use Nix to generate the signed catalog. User machines never invoke Nix. Unsupported refs get one request path and exact coverage report. Jetpack owns every product operation.
options.code:
$ jetpack use uncommon-tool
  error    uncommon-tool@jetpack is not in the signed catalog
  fix      request it or add a native Jetpackage recipe

options.name: Jet-owned native Nix translation only
options.detail: Bare refs mean `@jetpack`, and no external evaluator runs locally or centrally. Jet expands its clean-room translator until it can evaluate the required nixpkgs and configuration corpus.
options.technical: `jet-nix-eval` implements every admitted Nix semantic and lowers the result into Jetpack. Unsupported semantics fail closed. Snix/Tvix and installed Nix are never invoked.
options.code:
$ jetpack use uncommon-tool
  evaluate native Nix compatibility
  import   closed graph into Jetpack
  ready    uncommon-tool@jetpack

recommendation.why: A makes Jetpack the default and final system while preserving a practical escape hatch for the shrinking set of missing packages. It avoids a permanent Nix engine and every Snix/Tvix licence boundary.

whyNot.reason: The central catalog keeps user machines clean but blocks immediately when its published coverage misses a package.
A full clean-room evaluator removes the temporary Nix tool but rebuilds the system Jetpack is trying to retire.

recommendation.tradeoff: A missing package may invoke installed Nix once on a local machine. The command must announce that fallback, use exact pins, record a proof, and never make Nix part of later realization.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared local one-time import, central-only publication, and a full native translator. It recommended local import after a Jetpack miss.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested Snix linking, a GPL subprocess, live Nix delegation on every run, and source-to-source translation. The owner rejected Snix/Tvix, and repeated delegation would never phase Nix out.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combines the signed central catalog for the common path with local Nix only for uncovered packages. Every successful fallback enlarges Jetpack state instead of creating a permanent parallel path.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened central-only publication for reproducibility and native translation for complete independence. Their coverage delay and engineering cost remain larger than a pinned one-time fallback.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested ambient channels, changed Nix versions, offline use, CI, malicious outputs, repeated fallback, and source-name drift. Exact locks, visible receipts, policy gates, and import-once reuse contain those risks.

decisions.title: Literal suffixes for numeric carriers
decisions.gist: Choose whether a number may carry a suffix naming its core carrier type, and how that fits the open unit-suffix namespace.
decisions.lesson: A literal suffix attaches a type to a number where it is written. D-UNITLIT1 already resolves 500ms against in-scope #UnitFamily members, and D-DIMENSION-OPEN1=D says the compiler holds no dimension-name table. Measured today: bare 3 reaches Int, so takesint(3) compiles. Bare 3.4 is a Decimal and takes(3.4) into a Float parameter fails E0112. Float is the one core carrier with real friction. The prelude spells units out as inch and farad, so f, i, j and k are unclaimed.
decisions.story: Nora writes a helper taking a Float. She writes takes(3.4) and sema rejects it, saying the argument must be a decimal number and her Decimal is wrong. The spelling that works is Float{3.4}, which the message never names, and she repeats it at every call site. Her integer code needs no such ceremony, because takesint(3) already compiles.

options.name: Reserve core-carrier suffixes by commonality
options.detail: Reserve a small set of one-letter suffixes for the most common core types, ranked by how often they appear in real code. Float takes f. Units yield the letter and use two or three letters instead, so inch becomes in and farad stays spelled out. Suffix length becomes inversely proportional to commonality.
options.technical:
Sema checks the reserved carrier set before in-scope family members. A family declaring a reserved name is rejected where it is declared, naming the collision.

This adds a small compiler-owned name table and so amends D-DIMENSION-OPEN1=D, which states the compiler holds no dimension-name table. The amendment must be explicit. No name is taken from users today, because the prelude spells inch and farad out in full.
options.code:
3.4f -> Float
3    -> Int, unchanged
3.4  -> Decimal, unchanged
500ms -> Milliseconds, unchanged
#UnitFamily(Length, base: meter) { in }  -> inch keeps a two-letter suffix

options.name: Carrier suffixes in a separate lexical slot
options.detail: Give carriers a spelling the unit namespace cannot produce, using a separator before the letter. The unit namespace stays fully open and no name is reserved.
options.technical:
The lexer separates a carrier suffix from a unit suffix before resolution, so there is no precedence rule and no reserved-word table. A family may still declare f.

The cost is one more lexical form to teach, and a spelling less terse than a bare letter for the most common case. The separator must not be confusable with a float exponent, which D-UNITLIT1 reserves for e plus digits.
options.code:
3.4_f -> Float
500ms -> Milliseconds, unchanged
#UnitFamily(Capacitance, base: farad) { f } -> still legal

options.name: Fix inference only, add no suffix
options.detail: Treat the gap as missing inference. A decimal literal is accepted where a Float is expected, matching the integer literal behaviour that already works. Float{3.4} stays for positions where nothing constrains the literal. This spends no syntax budget.
options.technical:
Sema gives a numeric literal a pending carrier and settles it from the expected type at the use site. E0112 fires only when no expected type exists, or the target is not a numeric carrier.

This removes the call-site ceremony and the Int and Float asymmetry. Bare bindings and generic arguments still need Float{3.4}. It does nothing for complex or vector literals.
options.code:
takes(3.4) -> accepted, settles as Float
x :: 3.4   -> Decimal, unchanged
Float{3.4} -> still needed where nothing constrains the literal

options.name: Fix inference and reserve core suffixes
options.detail: Do C and A together. Inference removes the ceremony wherever an expected type exists, and a reserved one-letter suffix covers the positions inference cannot reach. Also reserve i, j and k for imaginary and vector components, which are a separate construction rather than carrier selection.
options.technical:
Two mechanisms, named separately in the spec. A carrier suffix selects the carrier for the same numeric value. A component suffix builds a different value, so 3i is Complex{0, 3}. Conflating them under one word would hide that.

Inference lands first and is the larger ergonomic win. The reserved set stays at f, i, j and k, all unclaimed today. This still amends D-DIMENSION-OPEN1=D and must say so.
options.code:
takes(3.4) -> accepted by inference
y :: 3.4f  -> Float, explicit where nothing constrains it
z :: 2 + 3i -> Complex
q :: 1 + 2i + 3j + 4k -> Quaternion

recommendation.why: D fixes the measured defect and the ergonomic gap in the right order. Inference removes most ceremony and closes the Int and Float asymmetry, which is the actual bug. A reserved one-letter suffix then covers bare bindings and generic arguments, and i, j and k claim unused names for complex and vector work before a unit family takes them.
recommendation.tradeoff: D reserves four names and so amends D-DIMENSION-OPEN1=D, which says the compiler holds no dimension-name table. It also introduces two kinds of suffix, carrier and component, which must be taught as separate ideas.

whyNot.reason: A alone leaves the Int and Float asymmetry in place, so takesint(3) works while takes(3.4) still needs a suffix or a wrapper.
B keeps the namespace fully open but spends the terseness on the most common case, which is exactly where friction should be lowest.
C is the right first step and is included in D, but it leaves bare bindings and generic arguments verbose and does nothing for complex or vector literals.

reviewPasses.base: The draft compares reserving core suffixes, a separate lexical slot, inference alone, and inference plus reserved suffixes. It covers resolution order, what each option costs a beginner, and which names are free today.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested letting any type claim a suffix, and changing the default decimal literal type from Decimal to Float. The first makes ambiguity routine; the second silently changes the meaning of existing code.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The synthesis pass is option D itself: inference first for the common path, then a reserved suffix for positions inference cannot reach, with component suffixes named as a distinct mechanism.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Cooperative review strengthened each option. A gained a declaration-time collision error, B an exponent-safety rule on the separator, C the two E0112 wording fixes, and D the carrier and component split.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Adversarial review attacked reserving names against D-DIMENSION-OPEN1=D, and attacked C for leaving bare bindings verbose. Reserving survives because no prelude unit claims these letters and commonality justifies the amendment.

decisions.title: Naming the automatic channel tier
decisions.gist: Name the tier that moves a package pin on its own, and settle whether the shipped #latest spelling stays the manual tier.
decisions.lesson: Channel markers already exist: a source may be declared #latest, #main or #vN.x, and jetpack update re-resolves a channel and moves the lock. The owner wants three tiers on one axis, decided by who moves the pin. Pinned never moves. The current #latest moves only when the user runs update. A third tier moves on its own, as an explicit per-package opt in. This decision names that third tier and settles whether the existing #latest spelling stays as the manual tier.
decisions.story: User runs omp, which releases often. Today it comes from the NixOS user profile, so every release costs a system-config edit and a rebuild. He wants omp marked so it updates itself, while a pinned toolchain never moves and an ordinary #latest source moves only when he asks.

options.name: #auto beside #latest
options.detail: Add #auto as the third tier and keep #latest meaning the manual pull. The axis is who acts, and the two words say it: latest is a thing you fetch, auto is a thing that happens. Shortest to type and the least ambiguous to read aloud.
options.technical:
Sema accepts #auto wherever #latest is accepted, on a source or a package entry. jetpack update moves #latest entries; a scheduled or hooked path moves #auto entries and propagates the resulting pin into the manifest. jetpack outdated labels all three tiers.

The risk is that #latest and #auto both suggest newest, so a reader may not infer which one moves by itself without reading the docs once. The words are short enough that the pairing is easy to memorise.
options.code:
rustc@nixpkgs          // pinned
#latest jq@nixpkgs     // manual
#auto omp@releases     // automatic

options.name: #rolling beside #latest
options.detail: Name the third tier #rolling, borrowing the established packaging meaning of a rolling release: continuously current without a release event. Carries ecosystem resonance for anyone arriving from pacman, Arch or a rolling distro.
options.technical:
Identical mechanics to A; only the keyword differs. The advantage is that rolling already means continuously moving to a whole audience, so the contrast against a fetched latest is carried by prior art rather than by documentation.

The cost is that rolling describes the upstream cadence in common usage, not who triggers the move, so a strict reader could argue the word names the wrong thing.
options.code:
rustc@nixpkgs           // pinned
#latest jq@nixpkgs      // manual
#rolling omp@releases   // automatic

options.name: A named ladder: #pin, #latest, #auto
options.detail: Make all three tiers explicit keywords rather than leaving the pinned tier implicit. A reader sees the tier on every entry and never has to know that absence means pinned.
options.technical:
Adds #pin as an explicit marker for behaviour that is already the default. That is redundant for the common case and makes the beginner surface noisier, which cuts against the dual-facet mission.

It does buy uniformity and greppability: a policy audit can find every entry's tier without reasoning about absence. Consider whether #pin is accepted as an optional emphasis rather than required.
options.code:
#pin rustc@nixpkgs      // explicit
#latest jq@nixpkgs      // manual
#auto omp@releases      // automatic

options.name: One marker with a mode argument
options.detail: A single marker takes the tier as an argument, for example #track(manual) and #track(auto), instead of one keyword per tier. Adding a future tier costs an argument rather than a keyword.
options.technical:
This keeps the keyword surface at one and makes the axis explicit in the source: every entry that moves says #track and names how. It is the most extensible shape.

The cost is ceremony on the common case, and it retires the existing #latest spelling, which is already shipped and used. Under the greenfield rule that migration is allowed, but it is churn for readability rather than capability.
options.code:
rustc@nixpkgs                 // pinned
#track(manual) jq@nixpkgs     // manual
#track(auto) omp@releases      // automatic

recommendation.why: A keeps the shipped #latest spelling meaning what it means today. It adds one short word for the new tier. The deciding axis sits in the two keywords: latest is fetched, auto happens. It is the smallest change that expresses all three tiers, and the pinned default stays silent so the beginner surface stays quiet.
recommendation.tradeoff: Both #latest and #auto read as newest, so the difference between them has to be learned once. B fixes that with prior art but names the upstream cadence rather than who triggers the move.

whyNot.reason: rolling conventionally describes the upstream release model, not who moves the pin, so it names the wrong axis even though it reads well.
an explicit #pin marker is redundant with the default and makes every ordinary entry noisier for an audit benefit that tooling can provide instead.
it retires a shipped spelling and adds ceremony to the common case, buying extensibility this axis is unlikely to need beyond three tiers.

reviewPasses.base: The draft compares one new keyword beside the shipped one, a prior-art keyword, a fully explicit ladder, and a single parameterised marker. It covers reading clarity, the beginner default, and migration of the existing #latest spelling.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a global policy file and a per-source default with per-package overrides. Both move the tier away from the entry it governs, so a reader can no longer see what moves by looking at the line.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The synthesis pass keeps A and takes one idea from C: #pin is accepted as optional emphasis for a reader who wants every tier stated, without becoming required.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Cooperative review strengthened each option. A gained the optional #pin emphasis, B gained a documentation note about cadence versus trigger, C narrowed #pin to optional, and D gained a named migration for existing #latest sources.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Adversarial review attacked A for two keywords that both mean newest, and attacked D for churning a shipped spelling. A survives because the pairing is short, learned once, and leaves the default silent.

decisions.title: How should a user open Canvas?
decisions.gist: Choose the one command that opens Canvas.
decisions.lesson: Canvas is a visual lens on the resident dev session. The command should say that relation clearly. A second watch loop or hidden automatic browser would split one development act into two models.
decisions.story: Maya edits a native game. She wants the graph beside the running program without pretending that the game is a web target.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev game.jet --canvas
watching game.jet
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:43127/session/…

options.name: A flag on `jet dev`
options.detail: Use `jet dev <source> --canvas`. Canvas is visibly a lens on the dev session. Plain dev stays terminal-only. The command is longer than a new verb.
options.technical: The existing dev dispatcher starts one resident session. The flag attaches the Canvas control host and browser client to that session.
options.code:
$ jet dev game.jet --canvas
watching game.jet
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:43127/session/…

options.name: A `jet canvas` command
options.detail: Use `jet canvas <source>`. The command is short and easy to discover. It must still create or attach to a dev session, so the verb hides that shared lifecycle.
options.technical: `jet canvas` becomes a canonical top-level command. It calls the same dev-session constructor and changes only the initial lens.
options.code:
$ jet canvas game.jet
watching game.jet
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:43127/session/…

options.name: Canvas opens for every dev session
options.detail: Plain `jet dev <source>` always opens Canvas. Beginners get the visual tool with no flag. Terminal users pay a browser launch and local server they did not ask for.
options.technical: Canvas becomes an unconditional dev-session client. A new opt-out would be required for headless and terminal use.
options.code:
$ jet dev game.jet
watching game.jet
Opening Canvas…

$ jet dev game.jet --no-canvas

recommendation.why: A states the true model: Canvas is one optional lens on `jet dev`. It preserves the quiet terminal default and avoids a second lifecycle verb.

whyNot.reason: The short verb hides that Canvas owns a dev session and creates two entry stories for one act.
An automatic browser and server burden headless, remote, scripted, and terminal-only work.

recommendation.tradeoff: The user types one flag. That cost keeps the command model honest and the plain dev loop quiet.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a dev flag with a new command and recommended the flag because Canvas shares the dev lifecycle.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested automatic opening and an editor command. Automatic opening became option C; an editor command duplicated the same hidden session problem as option B.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested keeping both `jet canvas` and `jet dev --canvas`. It was removed because two canonical spellings would split help, scripts, and teaching.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the new verb as the shortest discoverable form. It still hides the session relation that controls reload, tests, and debugging.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested remote terminals, headless runs, browser failure, and repeated invocation. The optional dev flag survives without adding an opt-out or second lifecycle.

decisions.title: How should Canvas choose its target and local endpoint?
decisions.gist: Choose how Canvas runs without a web target or required port.
decisions.lesson: Canvas edits checked source and projects a dev session. The program target decides how the program runs, not whether Canvas exists. The browser client still needs a safe local transport.
decisions.story: Noah opens Canvas for a command-line parser, then for a web app. He expects the same graph and no port setup in either project.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev parser.jet --canvas
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:43127/session/…

$ jet dev site.jet --target=web --canvas
App: http://127.0.0.1:8080
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:43128/session/…

options.name: Target-neutral loopback host
options.detail: Canvas always uses a Jet-owned loopback control host. The operating system selects a free port. `--canvas-port` is an expert override. The program target stays independent.
options.technical: Bind `127.0.0.1:0` by default and read the assigned port. Use a session secret and strict origin checks. A non-loopback host needs explicit unsafe network exposure policy.
options.code:
$ jet dev parser.jet --canvas
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:43127/session/…

$ jet dev parser.jet --canvas --canvas-port=9001

options.name: Native desktop shell
options.detail: Canvas opens in a first-party desktop window and needs no TCP port. Browser deployment and remote use need another transport or product.
options.technical: Embed the existing HTML and JavaScript in a native webview. The webview protocol replaces HTTP locally but requires a platform shell and packaging path.
options.code:
$ jet dev parser.jet --canvas
Canvas: native window
# no local URL is available

options.name: Keep Canvas inside web dev
options.detail: Canvas remains a route on `jet dev --target=web`. The existing port scan stays. Native, game, service, and library projects still cannot use Canvas directly.
options.technical: No host split. Canvas routes remain owned by `WebHost` and share its target and listener.
options.code:
$ jet dev parser.jet --canvas
Error: Canvas needs `--target=web`

$ jet dev parser.jet --target=web --canvas

recommendation.why: A keeps the existing browser surface, removes the false target dependency, and makes the port an implementation detail. It also supports remote forwarding without a second product.

whyNot.reason: A desktop shell removes ports locally but adds a platform product and still needs a transport for remote use.
Canvas source editing has no web-only meaning, so this keeps the exact restriction the card must remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: Canvas still starts a local HTTP service. Loopback binding, a session secret, and strict origin checks bound that risk.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft separated the program target from the Canvas transport and recommended an automatic loopback host.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a native shell, static files, Unix sockets, and the current web route. The shell and current route remain distinct options; static files cannot support live transactions.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combined a loopback host with an optional desktop wrapper. The wrapper is only a later client, so it does not change option A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the desktop shell with zero visible ports and native packaging. It still leaves remote and browser use needing another transport.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested port collisions, hostile origins, remote hosts, and multiple sessions. Port zero, session secrets, and loopback-only defaults repair those risks.

decisions.title: How should Canvas share a session with app dev servers?
decisions.gist: Choose how app preview and Canvas share one dev session.
decisions.lesson: A web app may own routes, middleware, and a port. Canvas also needs a control transport. They must share source, revisions, debugging, and last-good state without forcing one server to own both jobs.
decisions.story: Iris runs a custom web server on port 3000. She opens Canvas, edits a handler, and expects the preview and graph to move to the same accepted revision.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev app.jet --server=dev --canvas
App:    http://127.0.0.1:3000
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:43127/session/…
Session: 7f2a · revision 19

options.name: One session, separate listeners
options.detail: The app server and Canvas control host use separate listeners but one resident session. App routes stay fully customizable. Canvas never reserves paths in the application.
options.technical: One session broker owns revisions, transactions, last-good artifacts, debugger state, and client leases. Target adapters and listeners subscribe to that broker.
options.code:
App:    http://127.0.0.1:3000
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:43127/session/…
Session: 7f2a · revision 19

options.name: One listener with reserved tool routes
options.detail: The app and Canvas share one host and port. Jet reserves `/__jet/*` for tools. One URL is simple, but custom routing and middleware must never intercept the reserved namespace.
options.technical: The dev host multiplexes app traffic and tool protocols. Every custom server must implement or delegate the reserved route contract.
options.code:
App:    http://127.0.0.1:3000/
Canvas: http://127.0.0.1:3000/__jet/canvas
# `/__jet/*` belongs to Jet

options.name: Separate Canvas session
options.detail: Canvas starts its own compiler, watcher, and transaction state beside the app dev server. Each product stays isolated. Source revisions, reload, state, and diagnostics can disagree.
options.technical: Two independent session engines watch the same project. Coordination relies on file changes rather than shared semantic state.
options.code:
App session:    revision 19
Canvas session: revision 18
Warning: Canvas waits for its own rebuild

recommendation.why: A shares every semantic fact that must agree while keeping application networking independent. It works for custom web servers and for targets with no app server.

whyNot.reason: Reserved routes push Jet policy into every custom server and can collide with middleware, proxies, and user routes.
Two sessions can disagree on revision, last-good code, state, diagnostics, and debugger position.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users may see two local URLs for web work. Clear labels and automatic browser opening make that cost small and honest.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared shared and separate server topologies and recommended one session with separate listeners.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested reverse proxies, one process with two ports, embedded panels, and file-only coordination. These reduce to the three session and listener models shown.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept separate listeners but added one session broker and preview bridge. That complete combination became option A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened one-listener mode with a reserved namespace and delegation contract. It still burdens every custom server.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested stale revisions, custom middleware, two browsers, target switches, and compile failure. A shared broker with separate listeners contains each failure.
