decisions.title: How should expert code select modular arithmetic?
decisions.gist: Choose one safe low-friction arithmetic policy system.
decisions.lesson: Jet exact Int arithmetic does not overflow, and fixed-width arithmetic traps by default. Hashes, checksums, ciphers, codecs, and hardware protocols need modular arithmetic. The expert opt-in should expose that intent once without weakening division, shifts, conversions, indexing, or bounds.
decisions.story: Ravi ports Murmur3. The safe default protects ordinary code. One visible policy boundary lets reviewers compare the modular algorithm with its reference.

options.name: Lexical `#Arithmetic` policy
options.detail: Beginner code keeps exact Int and checked fixed-width arithmetic with no annotation. Experts select `.Wrapping`, `.Checked`, or `.Saturating` on a function or block. An inner marker overrides an outer policy.
options.technical: `#Arithmetic(mode)` is a registered marker for functions, methods, and blocks. It changes fixed-width add, subtract, multiply, negate, and power overflow only. Division by zero, shift counts, conversions, indexing, and bounds remain checked. Sema records policy provenance on each operation; all tiers call the same Prelude operation. Innermost scope wins.

options.name: Arithmetic policy follows a value type
options.detail: Beginner defaults stay unchanged. Experts convert values to `Modular<U32>` or `Saturating<U32>`, use ordinary operators, then leave through an explicit checked conversion. Policy follows values across helper calls.
options.technical: Core adds transparent policy wrappers with same-width operators and no implicit conversion to or from the base type. Layout, ABI, serialization, and generic bounds remain distinct unless an explicit adapter proves them.

options.name: Type-owned policy operations and pipelines
options.detail: Beginner defaults stay unchanged. Experts select policy per operation through `.wrapping_*`, `.checked_*`, and `.saturating_*` methods. Core adds byte and rotation helpers so ports stay readable without a lexical mode.
options.technical: No ambient arithmetic policy exists. Every overflow-sensitive operation names its behavior. Checked and saturating pipelines use the same type-owned APIs. General Core helpers own endian loads and rotations.
options.code:
h = h.wrapping_mul(c1)
h = h.rotate_left(15)
h = h.wrapping_mul(c2)
h = h.bit_xor(h >> 16)

recommendation.why: A charges one explicit marker only to the rare modular region. It keeps the algorithm readable, allows nested checked islands, and leaves every unrelated safety check intact.

whyNot.reason: Policy-carrying types are precise across helper calls but add conversions at constants, parameters, returns, Core methods, and foreign boundaries.
Per-operation methods give maximum local precision but repeat the same policy across arithmetic-heavy algorithms and obscure reference code.

recommendation.tradeoff: A lexical policy changes several operators inside its visible scope. Source markers, hover, semantic tokens, and inspect output must make the active mode unmistakable.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared lexical policy, policy-carrying values, and type-owned operations. It recommended one lexical marker for modular algorithms.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested new wrapping operators, unsigned wrap-by-default, package-wide modes, and target-machine behavior. Each added punctuation, weakened safety, or made meaning nonlocal.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combined the lexical marker with type-owned Core helpers and the existing shared Prelude operations. It adds no second arithmetic engine.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened value wrappers for cross-function policy and per-operation methods for exact local review. Their routine conversion and repetition costs remain higher.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested nesting, generic code, division, shifts, conversion, indexing, target differences, and mixed policies. Narrow semantics and innermost precedence contain those risks.

decisions.title: How should Jet make failure safe without routine ceremony?
decisions.gist: Choose the complete beginner and expert failure model.
decisions.lesson: Programs can fail even when authors do not plan for failure. Jet must preserve one structured report without making every function repeat an error type or propagation mark. Experts still need closed error contracts, automatic conversion, and a proof that a function cannot fail.
decisions.story: Mara writes a config loader on her first day. It reports useful failures with no ceremony. A library author later narrows the same function to a stable public error domain.

options.name: Implicit structured Error, typed expert opt-out
options.detail: Every function has the structured Error route by default. Sema removes it when impossible. Plain calls propagate automatically. Experts use `#Error` types, prefix contracts, unions, declared conversions, and `!Never` without changing the beginner path.
options.technical: Amends D-ERRSUFFIX1, D-FAIL-UNIT1, D-ERRSIGIL1, D-FAIL-CARRIER1, D-FAIL-CONV1, and D-BUILD-FAIL1. Type roles are prefix forms: `?Success`, `!Error`, and `!(E1 | E2)`. Bare postfix propagation `?` retires; `?(text)` keeps journey context. A named type may wear `!` only when marked `#Error` or built into Core as an Error type. One declared `Source -> TargetError` conversion applies automatically. `!Never` requires sema proof that the route is unreachable.

options.name: Infer the exact typed error set
options.detail: Beginner source also omits error syntax and propagation marks. Sema infers the concrete closed union from reachable calls. Experts pin or name the inferred set before publishing an API.
options.technical: Function interfaces carry inferred error unions. Hover and inspect show them. Public functions must accept a generated interface change or declare a named `#Error` contract. Body edits can change private function types and dependency hashes.

options.name: Require explicit typed contracts
options.detail: Every fallible function writes one `#Error` type or union. Plain calls still propagate automatically, but source always states the failure boundary. Tooling can generate the signature.
options.technical: No implicit default Error route exists. Sema rejects a reachable failure when the function has no explicit `!Error` contract. `!Never` remains the explicit infallible form.

recommendation.why: A prices friction by frequency. Every program gets structured failure handling automatically, while experts can narrow, convert, inspect, prohibit, and publish exact contracts through the same route.

whyNot.reason: Exact inference preserves types but lets ordinary body edits change interfaces and rebuild boundaries without a written public choice.
Explicit contracts are stable but charge every function for a failure channel Jet must support regardless.

recommendation.tradeoff: Beginner source does not show the default Error route. Hover, diagnostics, receipts, and `jet inspect` must make the route and its proof status fully visible.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared one implicit Error route, exact inferred unions, and mandatory explicit contracts. It recommended the implicit route with typed opt-out.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested public Result wrappers, a throws keyword, effect-row errors, and optional postfix propagation. Each added a second carrier or repeated default behavior.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass joined the lowest-friction default with the strongest expert tools: `#Error`, prefix contracts, named unions, automatic declared conversion, and `!Never`.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened inferred unions as maximally typed beginner magic and explicit contracts as maximally visible APIs. Their interface churn and routine ceremony remain larger costs.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested public API stability, hidden control flow, conversion ambiguity, optional success, unit failure, and impossible failure. Inspection, sema conversion checks, and `!Never` contain those risks.

decisions.title: How should a short Result handler fit on one line?
decisions.gist: Choose the compact exhaustive Result handler.
decisions.lesson: A one-sided Result test already fits on one line. Handling both cases uses an arm table. The formatter needs a compact form that keeps ordinary enum patterns and visible exhaustiveness.
decisions.story: Asha parses one setting. Success stores the value; failure records the message. Both actions are short, but the current table takes four lines.
decisions.inWild: if parsed == { .Ok(value) -> save(value), .Err(error) -> warn(error) }

options.name: Comma-separated short arm table
options.detail: A fitting arm table may put its arms on one line with commas. Long or commented arms stay vertical. Result uses ordinary `.Ok` and `.Err` patterns, not a special handler.
options.technical: Comma becomes an optional arm separator only inside a one-line arm table. The formatter inserts it when collapsing and removes trailing ambiguity. Sema and TIR stay on ordinary arm-table paths.
options.code: if parsed == { .Ok(value) -> save(value), .Err(error) -> warn(error) }

options.name: A two-branch Result operator
options.detail: Add a dedicated success and error form. It is short and names both roles. Result handling gains syntax that ordinary enums do not share.
options.technical: A new expression grammar binds success and error payloads. It lowers to the same carrier split but needs new parsing, formatting, diagnostics, and teaching.
options.code: parsed ? value -> save(value) ! error -> warn(error)

options.name: Keep vertical arm tables
options.detail: Keep the current four-line canonical form. It is clear and already exhaustive. Common short handlers remain visually heavy.
options.technical: No grammar or formatter change. One-sided tests stay the only one-line Result form.

recommendation.why: A makes the existing exhaustive mechanism compact without giving Result a private control-flow language. The same form helps any short enum dispatch.

whyNot.reason: A dedicated operator duplicates ordinary enum patterns and adds dense punctuation that is harder to scan.
The vertical form is clear but keeps four lines for two tiny exhaustive actions.

recommendation.tradeoff: Commas gain one formatting role inside short arm tables. The parser must keep that role local and unambiguous.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a compact arm table, dedicated punctuation, and the current vertical form. It recommended the compact table.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested fold methods, callbacks, else-pattern syntax, and tuple destructuring. Each either hides control flow or duplicates the arm table.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept vertical layout for long arms and used commas only when the whole table fits. This preserves readability at both sizes.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the dedicated operator as the shortest spelling. Its punctuation still creates a Result-only branch mechanism.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested nested calls, commas in arguments, comments, value arms, and missing cases. Local parsing and formatter width rules repair those risks.

decisions.title: How should a build entry declare its failure type?
decisions.gist: Choose the default failure contract for `fn build`.
decisions.lesson: A build entry must return a `BuildPlan`. BuildContext operations fail with structured build errors. The entry is already a recognized compiler hook, so Jet can supply that common error contract or require it in source.
decisions.story: Morgan writes a small package build. The happy path should name the plan, while an expert build can add a domain-specific failure.

options.name: Implicit `BuildError` for build entries
options.detail: A recognized `fn build` writes only `BuildPlan`. Jet supplies `BuildError!` as the default failure domain. Experts can declare a wider explicit error union.
options.technical: The special entry contract is `fn(BuildContext) BuildPlan BuildError!`. Source may write `BuildPlan CustomBuildError!`; sema includes BuildError through declared conversion or an explicit union.

options.name: Always write `BuildError!`
options.detail: Every build entry writes `BuildPlan BuildError!`. The contract is fully visible and uses ordinary suffix rules. Small package builds repeat a type fixed by every BuildContext operation.
options.technical: No entry-only defaulting. Sema requires the ordinary explicit signature and validates exact BuildContext error propagation.

options.name: Use the generic default error
options.detail: Build entries write `BuildPlan Error!` or the bare default form if it remains legal. Build-specific cases become report details rather than a stable public BuildError domain.
options.technical: BuildContext errors convert into the global default report. Callers and tooling lose exhaustive BuildError cases.

recommendation.why: A gives the recognized entry a safe useful default and keeps `BuildPlan` in the success position. Experts can expose more errors without changing the beginner form.

whyNot.reason: The explicit type is honest but repeats a contract already fixed by BuildContext on every ordinary build entry.
A generic report hides stable build cases that tools, tests, and custom error conversion can use.

recommendation.tradeoff: The source omits one error type on a special entry. Hover, docs, and diagnostics must always show the expanded contract.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared implicit BuildError, explicit BuildError, and the generic default error. It recommended the recognized entry default.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested a `build` keyword, a BuildResult wrapper, and body inference. Each adds a second entry or failure mechanism.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept the beginner default and allowed an explicit wider union for experts. This complete pair became option A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened explicit BuildError because source alone shows the whole contract. Expanded hover and generated docs give option A that visibility.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested custom errors, no BuildContext use, generated build files, and ordinary functions named build. The default applies only to the recognized entry shape.

decisions.title: How should code read tracked origin?
decisions.gist: Choose the one public surface for tracked origin.
decisions.lesson: `#Track` stores a compiler fact. Jet now reads compiler facts with `@`, but the old example calls `.origin()` like a runtime method. Keeping both surfaces makes one fact look like two mechanisms.
decisions.story: Sofia tracks a calibration value. She wants to print its source note and inspect the same typed fact in tooling.

options.name: One `.@origin` compiler fact
options.detail: Read `value.@origin` at comptime. It returns typed origin data that code may embed or print. Remove `.origin()` and the longer `.@track_origin` name.
options.technical: Rename the registered TrackOrigin fact to Origin. The value contains tracked, source, line, column, and ambiguity fields. Sema owns it; runtime output embeds a folded value.

options.name: Keep `.@track_origin` only
options.detail: Remove `.origin()` but keep the precise existing fact name. It distinguishes `#Track` provenance from input-origin and attribution facts. The common read stays longer.
options.technical: The registered fact name and type remain TrackOriginInfo. The runtime method retires.

options.name: Keep fact and runtime method
options.detail: Use `.@track_origin` for compiler work and `.origin()` for runtime text. Each phase has a direct surface. Users must learn why two reads of one metadata source differ.
options.technical: Both surfaces share sema data, but codegen keeps a runtime string operation for `.origin()`. Tooling exposes the typed fact separately.

recommendation.why: A follows the one fact-read law and uses the short name the owner expected. Typed data can still be folded into runtime output without a runtime-looking method.

whyNot.reason: The precise name avoids one collision, but it preserves needless wording on the primary origin fact.
Two public reads make one compiler fact look like separate compile-time and runtime mechanisms.

recommendation.tradeoff: `origin` must be documented beside input-origin and attribution facts. Its typed fields must make that distinction clear.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared the short fact name, the current long fact name, and the duplicate method. It recommended one short fact.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested `@provenance`, a free `origin(value)` function, and reflection-only access. Each either broadens the meaning or breaks the fact-read law.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept one typed fact and allowed ordinary comptime folding to print it at runtime. That removes the need for a second method.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the long name because it separates Track from input origin. Typed fields and documentation can make that distinction without a long public name.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested untracked values, copies, moves, branches, mutable bindings, and runtime printing. A typed optional or ambiguous fact handles each case.

decisions.title: What complete lifecycle should a durable send expose?
decisions.gist: Choose the beginner send and expert delivery audit model.
decisions.lesson: A durable send outlives one stack frame and may cross retries, restarts, retention, dead letters, and cancellation. An immediate enum mixes operation history with lifecycle state. Jet needs one identity that beginner code can use safely and experts can control and audit.
decisions.story: Priya submits an order. The common statement waits until durable acceptance. The expert path keeps a handle, watches delivery, and proves what happened after a restart.
decisions.inWild:
orders.send(order)

delivery :: orders.send(order, key: order.id)
delivery.wait(.Delivered)
receipt :: delivery.receipt()
events :: delivery.events()

options.name: Authority-owned stable Delivery handle
options.detail: `send` returns a must-use Delivery handle. A bare statement consumes it by waiting for durable acceptance. Binding it enables wait, retry, cancel, status, receipt, and event history. Dropping an unconsumed handle is a compile error.
options.technical: The service authority owns delivery after acceptance; dropping an observed handle never cancels it. Public states are Pending, Accepted, Delivering, Delivered, DeadLettered, and Cancelled. Duplicate idempotency keys return the same identity. Retention, attempts, deadlines, and idempotency are typed facts. Rejection and unavailable authority use the normal Error route. `receipt()` returns a signed immutable snapshot; `events()` returns the ordered append-only lifecycle.
options.code:
// common: continue after durable acceptance
orders.send(order)

// expert lifecycle control
delivery :: orders.send(order, key: order.id)
delivery.wait(.Delivered)
receipt :: delivery.receipt()
events :: delivery.events()

options.name: Caller-owned linear Delivery task
options.detail: `send` returns a must-use Delivery task owned by the caller. A bare statement waits for acceptance. A bound task must be joined, stored, detached, or cancelled. Dropping it cancels before scope exit.
options.technical: Delivery lifetime follows structured task ownership. Explicit detach transfers ownership to the service authority and produces a durable identity. Receipts and events begin at detach or acceptance. Restart recovery requires a stored or detached handle.
options.code:
orders.send(order)

delivery :: orders.send(order, key: order.id)
delivery.detach()
receipt :: delivery.receipt()

options.name: Immutable operation receipts with queries
options.detail: A bare send waits for acceptance and returns no retained handle. Expert send returns an immutable receipt for that operation. Later status, retry, cancellation, and history use authority queries by receipt id.
options.technical: Receipt variants describe Accepted, Duplicate, Delivered, Retained, DeadLettered, Cancelled, or rejected operation results. Authority queries reconstruct current state and event history. The receipt is a snapshot, not a live identity.
options.code:
orders.send(order)

receipt :: orders.send_receipt(order, key: order.id)
status :: orders.delivery_status(receipt.id)
events :: orders.delivery_events(receipt.id)

recommendation.why: A makes one stable identity carry the whole durable lifecycle. The common statement is safe and short, while experts get precise control, signed evidence, and restart-safe audit without a second query vocabulary.

whyNot.reason: Caller ownership fits ordinary tasks but makes a durable service operation cancel when an unrelated local scope ends unless explicitly detached.
Snapshot receipts are durable evidence but force every later action through a separate authority query keyed by an id.

recommendation.tradeoff: A bound Delivery handle is must-use and requires flow checking on every path. That cost applies only when code opts into lifecycle control.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared authority-owned handles, caller-owned tasks, and immutable receipt queries. It recommended the authority-owned identity.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested fire-and-forget unit sends, event streams without identity, synchronous delivery, and hidden global status. Each lost safety, control, or restart correlation.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass joined a stable handle with signed snapshots and append-only events. The handle controls live work; receipts prove durable history.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened linear tasks for structured ownership and receipt queries for simple persistence. Their cancellation and split-vocabulary costs remain larger.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested ignored handles, duplicate keys, rejection, partition, crash windows, retention, cancellation, dead letters, and replay. Must-use flow and authority ownership give each case one rule.

decisions.title: When does a function block return its final expression?
decisions.gist: Choose the function tail-value rule.
decisions.lesson: Jet already has value expressions and value arm tables. A block can either require `return` or yield its last expression. One rule must cover functions, methods, lambdas, and nested value blocks.
decisions.story: Eli writes a status label as one exhaustive arm table. He wants the table value to be the function result without repeating `return` in every arm.

options.name: Every value block yields its tail expression
options.detail: The last expression of a value-expected block is its value. Functions, methods, lambdas, fallback blocks, and nested blocks share one rule. A semicolon or statement tail yields unit.
options.technical: Sema gives each block an expected type and checks its final expression. Explicit `return` still exits early. TIR receives an ordinary block value; engines add no policy.

options.name: Only a sole expression returns
options.detail: A function block returns its expression only when that expression is the only top-level item. Any setup statement requires explicit `return`. The common branch-table case is short, but blocks gain a special count rule.
options.technical: Parser or sema checks the number of top-level items before allowing an implicit result. Nested blocks keep existing rules.

options.name: Keep explicit returns in braced functions
options.detail: Every braced function path uses `return`. A short expression body after the arrow remains the only implicit result form. Control flow is explicit but repetitive.
options.technical: No semantic change. The lint may still replace branch returns with `return if ...` and one trailing `else`.

recommendation.why: A gives blocks one compositional value rule and removes repeated returns from branch tables. It matches the existing bare-value tail in fallback blocks.

whyNot.reason: Counting top-level items creates a special case that breaks as soon as a setup statement is added.
Explicit returns keep value tables wrapped in control-flow noise and make functions differ from other value blocks.

recommendation.tradeoff: A final expression can become observable after an edit. Type checking and explicit unit tails must make that change clear in diagnostics.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared general tail values, a sole-expression exception, and explicit returns. It recommended one value rule for all blocks.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested automatic return of the last statement and a function marker. Statements do not always have values, and a marker would make ordinary block meaning opt-in.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept explicit early `return` while making only the natural tail expression the block value. This is option A, not a separate mechanism.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened sole-expression return as the exact owner example with smaller blast radius. Its item-count rule remains brittle and hard to teach.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested unit functions, trailing assignments, comments, unreachable tails, divergence, and added setup code. Expected block types and unit diagnostics contain the risks.

decisions.title: How should a marker declare its legal sites?
decisions.gist: Choose one legal-site clause for all marker declarations.
decisions.lesson: A marker has ordinary arguments and a list of legal targets. Jet currently writes that list as `@sites` inside parameters for most markers, but text heads use `on [...]`. Both forms describe the same registry fact.
decisions.story: Tariq publishes two rules. One applies to types and another to checked text. He expects their declarations to differ only in the site list.

options.name: Use `on [...]` after parameters
options.detail: Ordinary arguments stay in parentheses. Every marker then writes `on [sites]`. Registry metadata is no longer disguised as a parameter.
options.technical: Grammar: `marker Name [ ( params ) ] on [ Site, ... ] [ body ]`. Inheritance, repeatability, and status stay registry facts or gain separate named clauses by later ballot.
options.code:
marker Inline(mode: InlineMode{.Hint}) on [.Function, .Method]
marker Pattern on [.Text] { check @body; hole escape(@value) }

options.name: Use `@sites:` inside parameters
options.detail: Every marker, including text heads, keeps sites in one metadata parameter list. The form already covers generated Prelude rows. It mixes callable arguments with declaration metadata.
options.technical: Grammar keeps reserved metadata parameters such as `@sites`, `@inherits`, and `@repeatable`. The `on` text-head clause retires.
options.code:
marker Inline(mode: InlineMode{.Hint}, @sites: [.Function, .Method])
marker Pattern(@sites: [.Text]) { check @body; hole escape(@value) }

options.name: Infer sites from first use
options.detail: Marker declarations omit legal sites. The compiler records the first applied target or derives sites from body operations. Libraries become shorter, but errors and interfaces depend on use order.
options.technical: The registry stores inferred sites after checking a package. Published marker interfaces must serialize those inferred facts.

recommendation.why: A separates user arguments from declaration metadata and gives every marker the same readable site clause. It also matches the owner-preferred text-head form.

whyNot.reason: Reserved metadata inside parameters makes a declaration look callable and preserves the divergence the owner noticed.
Inferred sites make published interfaces depend on use order and delay errors until application.

recommendation.tradeoff: The Prelude marker registry gets a broad source migration. Greenfield policy makes this a clean one-time cutover.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared `on`, metadata parameters, and inference. It recommended the explicit clause outside parameters.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested per-site keywords, decorators on declarations, and separate registry files. Each spreads one fact across more syntax or files.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept ordinary parameters and moved only legal sites to `on`. Other registry facts remain data until a real user surface needs them.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened `@sites` as the least parser work and current generated form. It still reads as a callable argument.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested no-argument markers, many sites, bodies, text heads, generated rows, and future site kinds. The `on` clause handles each without ambiguity.

decisions.title: How should typestate mark a terminal state?
decisions.gist: Choose whether no outgoing transition is a valid final state.
decisions.lesson: Many protocols end in Confirmed, Closed, Completed, Failed, or Cancelled. A state with no outgoing transition can be intentional or accidental. Jet must decide whether absence is enough or needs an explicit final mark.
decisions.story: Ari models an order. Confirmed orders can be inspected and audited, but they never transition again.

options.name: No outgoing transition means terminal
options.detail: A state with no outgoing transition is a valid terminal state. No warning appears. Separate checks still report states that no path can reach.
options.technical: Remove unconditional L0151. Reflection derives `terminal: true` from the checked transition graph. Methods may still require the terminal state.

options.name: Mark terminal states explicitly
options.detail: The declaration labels final states. An unmarked state with no outgoing transition keeps a warning. Readers can tell intent from the state list, but Jet adds syntax.
options.technical: Add a terminal modifier or marker in the state declaration. Reflection stores declared terminal status and checks that no outgoing transition contradicts it.
options.code:
state Order { Draft, terminal Confirmed }
// or the ratified equivalent

options.name: Keep the dead-end warning
options.detail: Every state needs an outgoing transition or a local warning suppression. The checker catches accidental omissions, but normal final states create routine warning policy.
options.technical: Keep L0151 and its current trigger. Projects may allow or deny it through lint policy.
options.code:
state Order { Draft, Confirmed }
// Warning L0151: Confirmed has no outgoing transition

recommendation.why: A treats a normal graph property as normal. Reachability checks still catch genuinely unused states, while terminal methods remain legal and useful.

whyNot.reason: An explicit final mark repeats information the transition graph already proves and adds syntax to every closed protocol.
The warning makes intentional final states look suspicious and teaches users to ignore or suppress a common false alarm.

recommendation.tradeoff: A missing outgoing transition no longer warns by itself. Reachability, tests, diagrams, and explicit transition review must catch accidental final states.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared implicit terminal states, explicit final marks, and the current warning. It recommended the graph-derived rule.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested naming conventions, a `#Terminal` marker, and lint heuristics. Each is a weaker version of explicit marking.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept silent graph-derived terminals and separate unreachable-state checks. This catches a real defect without warning on a valid end.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened explicit marking as visible intent and typo protection. It still repeats a fact the compiler can derive exactly.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested accidental omissions, cycles, self-loops, read-only terminal methods, reopenable resources, and failure states. Separate reachability and transition checks cover the defects.

decisions.title: How should libraries define checked text types?
decisions.gist: Choose one honest type model for domain-checked text.
decisions.lesson: SQL, patterns, selectors, paths, and templates can reject invalid literal text and encode interpolated values for their domain. A value such as `Pattern{"..."}` is a nominal type, not a marker. Libraries need the same checker at compile time and runtime, plus an audited raw escape.
decisions.story: Mei publishes a route-pattern library. Users construct Pattern values, pass them through APIs, and cannot accidentally supply an unchecked String.

options.name: Ordinary nominal type plus CheckedText trait
options.detail: Declare a normal String-backed nominal type. Implement the standard CheckedText trait once. Users get compile-time checked literals, encoded holes, validated dynamic construction, typed sinks, reflection, and an audited raw escape.
options.technical: The same pure `check(text)` function runs at compile time for known literals and at runtime for `Type.from(text)`. `encode_hole` handles each interpolation. Construction returns the nominal type. Raw unchecked construction requires a reasoned audited or unsafe gate. The trait is nameable, hoverable, implementable across modules, and shared across all execution tiers.

options.name: Dedicated checked text declaration
options.detail: Use one declaration that creates the nominal type and owns its checker and hole encoder. Library code is compact and focused. Jet gains a declaration kind beside ordinary nominal types and traits.
options.technical: `checked text Name` lowers to a String-backed nominal type plus compiler-known construction hooks. The checker still runs on all tiers, dynamic construction validates, and raw construction needs an audited gate.

options.name: Ordinary type plus `#CheckedText` derive
options.detail: Declare a normal String-backed nominal type and apply a marker that names checker and encoder functions. Users get the same construction behavior. Library authors use a derive-style rule instead of a trait impl.
options.technical: `#CheckedText` is a registered type marker. It validates the named callables and synthesizes the CheckedText implementation, dynamic constructor, reflection, and raw gate. Advanced customization requires marker fields or a manual generated impl escape.
options.code:
fn check_pattern(text: String) !PatternError -> …
fn escape_pattern<T>(value: T) String -> …

#CheckedText(check: check_pattern, encode_hole: escape_pattern)
Pattern :: distinct String

recommendation.why: A says exactly what exists: Pattern is a type with a reusable contract. It needs no special declaration or marker exception, and one pure checker guarantees compile-time and runtime parity.

whyNot.reason: The dedicated form is compact but adds a declaration mechanism for behavior ordinary types and traits can already model.
The derive is concise but pushes advanced control into marker parameters and generated behavior instead of the normal trait seam.

recommendation.tradeoff: Library authors write a type declaration and an impl. That one-time expert ceremony keeps every library user on the shortest safe construction path.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a trait, a dedicated declaration, and a derive marker. It recommended an ordinary type plus a standard trait.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested sink registries, expected-type string coercion, compiler-owned names, and unchecked wrappers. Each hid the type boundary or closed the library surface.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept the ordinary trait and generated its routine constructors and reflection from the impl. This preserves expert control without user ceremony.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened the dedicated form for compact library code and the marker for derivation. Their new syntax and customization seams remain weaker.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested dynamic text, hole types, imports, generics, raw bypass, diagnostics, runtime layout, and tier parity. One pure trait contract covers each case.

decisions.title: Where should a type declare its typestates?
decisions.gist: Choose the source home for a type state machine.
decisions.lesson: States belong to one type and resolve as `Type.State.Name`. A separate `state Order` declaration repeats the type name and looks like a competing declaration. The source should make ownership unmistakable.
decisions.story: Dina opens the Order model. She wants its fields, states, and transitions to lead back to one type definition.

options.name: A `state` section inside the type
options.detail: Structs and other eligible types declare `state { ... }` inside their body. Ownership and namespace are visible in one place. The type body gains one reserved section.
options.technical: The parser stores a state section on the owning type item. It is allowed once. Qualified paths remain `Type.State.Name`; transitions may live in any impl.

options.name: Keep a companion declaration
options.detail: Keep `state Order { ... }` beside the type. Sema requires an existing owner and treats the declaration as an extension, not a second type. Large state machines can stay outside field bodies.
options.technical: A companion state item resolves its owner by semantic identity. Missing, duplicate, and cross-module owners are errors. Tools link both declarations.
options.code:
struct Order { id: Int }
state Order { Draft, Confirmed }

options.name: Use a fact enum plus a type marker
options.detail: Declare `OrderState` as an enum and attach it to Order with a marker. States become ordinary names, but the owner and state set use two public declarations and an extra name.
options.technical: `#StateMachine(OrderState)` attaches one compile-time enum fact domain. Marker arguments use enum variants. Runtime construction of the fact enum must remain unavailable or erased.

recommendation.why: A puts the state set where readers look for the type and removes the apparent namespace collision. Transitions stay in impl blocks, so large behavior does not crowd fields.

whyNot.reason: Semantic linking can make the companion safe, but the repeated declaration head still looks like two Orders.
A separate enum and marker add a second public name and more ceremony for facts that already belong to the type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Type bodies gain a reserved `state` section. Formatter and tools must present it clearly beside fields and nested declarations.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared an in-type section, a checked companion, and a fact enum attachment. It recommended the in-type section.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested a type-header clause, impl-owned states, and transition-only inference. The header crowds signatures, impl ownership fragments facts, and inference hides the full set.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept states in the type and transitions in impl blocks. This preserves local ownership without centralizing behavior.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened companion declarations for large generated machines and partial modules. Tool links help, but the source still repeats the type head.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested generics, forward references, multiple modules, generated code, empty states, and nested types. One optional in-type section gives deterministic ownership.

decisions.title: How should Jet price effects vocabulary for beginners and experts?
decisions.gist: Choose source spelling, plain-language tooling, and authority flow together.
decisions.lesson: Effects describe what code may do. Authority describes what the application grants. Beginners should not write either list when sema can infer it. Experts need a short lexical boundary, a first-class handle, exact policy, and auditable receipts.
decisions.story: Kai writes a network call with no ceremony. Jet infers the effect and asks at the application boundary. A plugin host later narrows authority and passes a typed handle.

options.name: Short `#FX` in source, plain words everywhere else
options.detail: Beginner source writes no effect row or marker. Sema infers effects and asks for approval at the application boundary. Experts use short `#FX` scopes and typed Authority handles. Tools use full plain words.
options.technical: `#FX(Net)` narrows a lexical scope. `#FX(grant: FS, Net)` also binds an Authority handle and cannot widen outer authority. Interactive approval supports once or project scope; non-interactive and CI runs require declared policy. Reports use `required_effects`, `granted_effects`, and `authority`. Every grant leaves a receipt. Effect rows remain the explicit expert assertion surface.

options.name: Use Effects as the one public word
options.detail: Beginner inference and boundary approval stay the same. Experts write `#Effects`, pass an Effects handle, and configure `effects:`. One familiar word covers both requirement and grant.
options.technical: Tools distinguish required, granted, denied, and observed Effects by field names. The same Effects type represents a requested set and a granted handle with role metadata.

options.name: Use Authority as the one public word
options.detail: Beginner inference and approval stay the same. Experts write `#Authority`, bind Authority handles, and configure `authority:`. The grant model is clear, but source no longer names the effect relation directly.
options.technical: Effect rows still list Net and FS requirements. `#Authority` supplies or narrows grants. Diagnostics use authority for both scope and value.

options.name: Keep Ability and `#Abilities`
options.detail: Beginner inference and approval stay the same. Experts use the existing Ability menu, Abilities value, and `#Abilities` marker. One plain vocabulary remains consistent across source and tools.
options.technical: Confirm D-AUTHORITY-WORD2. Browser and CLI keep abilities names. Reports distinguish required and granted abilities.

recommendation.why: A prices words by where they appear. Experts get the short repeated source marker, while beginners and operators read complete terms in prompts, diagnostics, policy, and receipts.

whyNot.reason: Effects is familiar but makes a requirement and an authority handle look like the same role.
Authority names the grant precisely but makes the frequent lexical source boundary long and indirect.
Abilities is plain but remains long in expert source and less direct than effects in diagnostics and inspection.

recommendation.tradeoff: Source and tooling use different spellings for the same boundary. Generated docs and hover must always expand `#FX` to “granted effects” and link it to Authority.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared frequency-priced FX with uniform Effects, Authority, and Abilities vocabularies. It recommended short source and plain tooling.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass also tested Rights, Grants, Caps, Permissions, Power, and FX everywhere. Each added policy jargon, revived retired terms, or forced an abbreviation onto beginners.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass deliberately combines `#FX` for expert source with effects and authority in prose and data. This is frequency pricing, not two semantic mechanisms.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened each uniform vocabulary for search and consistency. Their source friction or role confusion remains larger than the naming split.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested first-run prompts, CI, nested scopes, bound handles, manifests, JSON, browser protocol, search, and audit receipts. Explicit role fields keep the split coherent.

decisions.title: Boundary law: jet acts on code, jetpack acts on environments
decisions.outcome: Any verb that reads or executes Jet source belongs to the jet binary. Any verb that acquires, pins, realizes or exposes what your code needs belongs to jetpack. There is no exception. Consequently jetpack dev, jetpack test, jetpack fmt, jetpack build, jetpack run and jetpack enter are deleted, and the hangar verb is removed from the jet binary.
decisions.comment: Any verb that reads or executes Jet source belongs to the jet binary. Any verb that acquires, pins, realizes or exposes what your code needs belongs to jetpack. There is no exception. Consequently jetpack dev, jetpack test, jetpack fmt, jetpack build, jetpack run and jetpack enter are deleted, and the hangar verb is removed from the jet binary.

decisions.title: jet env forwards to jetpack env rather than owning it
decisions.outcome: jetpack env is the canonical spelling for entering a project environment. jet env becomes a documented thin forward to it, one implementation with two entry points, so the ratified shell auto-activation hook keeps working while the boundary law holds: jet acts on code, jetpack acts on environments. Bare jetpack is reserved for a future interactive TUI and must not enter an environment. jetpack tool run is deleted as the arity-1 case of jetpack use with a trailing command.
decisions.comment: jetpack env is the canonical spelling for entering a project environment. jet env becomes a documented thin forward to it, one implementation with two entry points, so the ratified shell auto-activation hook keeps working while the boundary law holds: jet acts on code, jetpack acts on environments. Bare jetpack is reserved for a future interactive TUI and must not enter an environment. jetpack tool run is deleted as the arity-1 case of jetpack use with a trailing command.

decisions.title: Shell prompt label reads jetpack
decisions.outcome: The visible prompt label inside a Jetpack shell is jetpack, not jet. The environment belongs to jetpack under the boundary law, so the prompt names the tool that owns it. This amends the D-JPK14 default.
decisions.comment: The visible prompt label inside a Jetpack shell is jetpack, not jet. The environment belongs to jetpack under the boundary law, so the prompt names the tool that owns it. This amends the D-JPK14 default.

decisions.title: Accept #2189 — jetpack env and jetpack use: the two shell verbs
decisions.gist: Close #2189, or bounce it back to building.
decisions.detail:
1. jetpack env with no argument enters the default env module, and jetpack env <name> enters that module positionally — met (`env_enters_default_and_positional_modules`)
2. jetpack env -- <cmd> runs in the project env and exits with the command's status — met (`parse.rs:189`, `run_enter_dev.rs:1590`, `Shell.rs:657`; `Shell::tests::run_command_returns_child_status` passed.)
3. jetpack use <pkgs> yields a shell containing exactly those packages both inside and outside a project directory, proven by a test that runs it in each — met (`tests/jetpack_tool.rs:182`, passing focused test `use_ephemeral_execs_inside_and_outside_project_without_path_projection`)
4. jetpack use <pkgs> -- <cmd> runs once and leaves nothing on PATH or in the tools profile afterwards — met (`crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs:371,527`; `use` skips project profile/native PATH projection.)
5. jetpack tool run is removed and its help, tests and docs no longer mention it — met (no matches in `tests/` or `docs/`; help lists only install/list/uninstall; `prepare_flag_retired.stderr:1` preserves E1353 coverage.)
6. jet env forwards to jetpack env with identical behaviour, and the D-ENVHOOK1 auto-activation hook still activates on cd — met (jetpack tool run is retired and answers E1353. Verified by running the binary.)
7. bare jetpack does not enter any environment — met (`crates/jetpack/src/CLI/parse.rs:402`; fresh binary exited `0` and printed `jet env` help.)
8. The --prep flag on env and on use materializes the closure and exits without entering, and a following entry performs no download — met (`run_enter_dev.rs:1571`, `run_enter_dev.rs:1651`, `Store.rs:1747`, passing test `use_prep_materializes_then_entry_reuses_the_package`)
9. Owner rules on what bare jetpack does before any TUI code is written — met (`crates/jetpack/src/CLI/parse.rs:397-402`; bare `./target/debug/jetpack` prints help and exits `0`, without entering env.)

decisions.title: Refs are spelled package@source#version and the prefix tier form is deleted
decisions.outcome: Every package reference is written package@source#version. The hash slot answers which version and accepts a literal version or a policy tier such as auto or latest. The prefix spelling, for example the tier written before the name, is deleted; the same meaning is written omp@releases#auto. Plain refs such as ripgrep@nixpkgs are unchanged. The old parse path is removed with no fallback parser retained.
decisions.comment: Every package reference is written package@source#version. The hash slot answers which version and accepts a literal version or a policy tier such as auto or latest. The prefix spelling, for example the tier written before the name, is deleted; the same meaning is written omp@releases#auto. Plain refs such as ripgrep@nixpkgs are unchanged. The old parse path is removed with no fallback parser retained.

decisions.title: Jet never acquires; jetpack confirms every download
decisions.outcome: A jet verb that needs the project environment while outside it fails with a coded diagnostic and acquires nothing. jetpack env and jetpack use enter silently when the closure is already materialized and confirm once, showing package count and total bytes, when anything must be downloaded. The yes flag skips that prompt. A non-interactive run that would need a download and has no yes flag fails naming the flag, and downloads nothing.
decisions.comment: A jet verb that needs the project environment while outside it fails with a coded diagnostic and acquires nothing. jetpack env and jetpack use enter silently when the closure is already materialized and confirm once, showing package count and total bytes, when anything must be downloaded. The yes flag skips that prompt. A non-interactive run that would need a download and has no yes flag fails naming the flag, and downloads nothing.

decisions.title: jetpack update is scoped by the current directory
decisions.outcome: jetpack update determines its scope from the current directory: inside a jetpack project it updates that project. Narrowing flags select dependencies only or tools only, and the default covers everything in scope. It prints one plan naming every moving source with its before and after identity, package count and download size, then applies after a single confirmation. The outdated verb survives separately.
decisions.comment: jetpack update determines its scope from the current directory: inside a jetpack project it updates that project. Narrowing flags select dependencies only or tools only, and the default covers everything in scope. It prints one plan naming every moving source with its before and after identity, package count and download size, then applies after a single confirmation. The outdated verb survives separately.

decisions.title: Installed tools are projected as shims
decisions.outcome: Every tool installed by jetpack is projected as a jetpack shim rather than a hardlink into a read-only store object. The shim execs the real binary for normal use, and when the tool attempts to update itself the shim refuses the in-place write cleanly and offers to move the declarative pin instead. The accepted costs are that jetpack sits in the execution path of every installed tool, and that which reports the shim path.
decisions.comment: Every tool installed by jetpack is projected as a jetpack shim rather than a hardlink into a read-only store object. The shim execs the real binary for normal use, and when the tool attempts to update itself the shim refuses the in-place write cleanly and offers to move the declarative pin instead. The accepted costs are that jetpack sits in the execution path of every installed tool, and that which reports the shim path.

decisions.title: No shim: detect tool drift on the next jetpack command
decisions.outcome: There is no shim. Installed tools keep their current projection and jetpack detects drift on its next command, reporting the installed and pinned versions and offering to move the declarative pin. A managed tool that cannot rewrite itself gets a registered jetpack diagnostic naming the tool and the exact command, never a bare permission error. Detection must add no closure resolution, no network call and no full-binary hash to a normal command. Non-interactive runs never prompt.
decisions.comment: There is no shim. Installed tools keep their current projection and jetpack detects drift on its next command, reporting the installed and pinned versions and offering to move the declarative pin. A managed tool that cannot rewrite itself gets a registered jetpack diagnostic naming the tool and the exact command, never a bare permission error. Detection must add no closure resolution, no network call and no full-binary hash to a normal command. Non-interactive runs never prompt.

decisions.title: Progress shows an aggregate phase line and per-package rows
decisions.outcome: Realization displays one live aggregate line carrying the current phase with counts, transferred bytes and total bytes, plus one settled row per package as it completes. Byte totals grow honestly as the closure is discovered rather than being fabricated. Output degrades to deterministic plain lines with no terminal, under NO_COLOR, and when piped, and live regions are erased before any diagnostic.
decisions.comment: Realization displays one live aggregate line carrying the current phase with counts, transferred bytes and total bytes, plus one settled row per package as it completes. Byte totals grow honestly as the closure is discovered rather than being fabricated. Output degrades to deterministic plain lines with no terminal, under NO_COLOR, and when piped, and live regions are erased before any diagnostic.

decisions.title: Store plumbing is grouped under the hangar verb
decisions.outcome: The hangar verb groups everything that manipulates the store rather than the project. It absorbs the former top-level cache, shared-store, vendor, clean and list verbs. The name hangar is kept because it is the existing user-facing name for the object store, so no new word is coined. The doctor verb stays top-level because it is what a stuck user runs first.
decisions.comment: The hangar verb groups everything that manipulates the store rather than the project. It absorbs the former top-level cache, shared-store, vendor, clean and list verbs. The name hangar is kept because it is the existing user-facing name for the object store, so no new word is coined. The doctor verb stays top-level because it is what a stuck user runs first.

decisions.title: Whether a Jet diagnostic carries a link
decisions.gist: Choose whether error messages point at a web page for more detail.
decisions.lesson: Jet treats every diagnostic as a product. Each one has a registered code, a what, a why, and a fix, plus a snapshot test. Owning a domain makes it possible to give each code a page. The question is whether the error text itself should carry that address, since the text is the most read thing the compiler produces and every character in it competes for attention.
decisions.explainer: Roughly nine hundred codes exist, and the pages would be generated from the same source that produces the messages.
decisions.story: Ana hits an error she does not understand. The message already tells her what happened, why, and what to do. A link would offer more, but only if she is online and only if it says more than the message already did.
decisions.inWild:
# A Jet diagnostic today
Error [E1272]: 28 packages lack a supported Nix compatibility output
 Why: `cargo@default` and 27 others need a pinned compatibility output.
      Jetpack does not invoke an installed Nix executable for realization.
 Fix: provide a pinned fixture or verified Hangar output, or replace the
      package with a native source or adapter.

options.name: No link in the message; publish the pages anyway (recommended)
options.detail: Every code gets a generated page, reachable by searching the code or by a documented address, but the terminal text stays exactly as it is. The message must remain sufficient on its own, which is the existing standard and the reason the diagnostics are good. Cost: a user who wants more has to know the pages exist.
options.code:
Error [E1272]: 28 packages lack a supported Nix compatibility output
 Why: ...
 Fix: ...

# and separately, generated:
jet-lang.dev/e/E1272

options.name: Append a link to every diagnostic
options.detail: Each message ends with its address. Maximum discoverability, and a user can always go deeper. Cost: one more line on every error in every build log forever, and it invites messages to get lazier over time because the page can carry the explanation.
options.code:
Error [E1272]: 28 packages lack a supported Nix compatibility output
 Why: ...
 Fix: ...
 More: jet-lang.dev/e/E1272

options.name: Link only where the page adds something the message cannot
options.detail: A link appears only for codes whose page carries a worked example, a migration table, or a long explanation that does not belong in a terminal. Keeps the common case clean and spends the line only where it pays. Cost: a rule someone must apply per code, and inconsistency that users may read as arbitrary.
options.code:
Error [E0112]: type mismatch
 Why: ...
 Fix: ...

Error [E1272]: 28 packages lack a supported Nix compatibility output
 Why: ...
 Fix: ...
 More: jet-lang.dev/e/E1272   (migration table)

recommendation.why: The message being sufficient on its own is why Jet diagnostics are good, and a link is the easiest way to erode that.
recommendation.tradeoff: Discoverability of the pages depends on search rather than on the message itself.

whyNot.reason: A line on every error forever is a large permanent cost, and it creates steady pressure to move explanation off the terminal and onto the web.
Spending the line only where it pays is the most defensible middle, but it needs a per-code judgement that will drift as nine hundred codes evolve.

reviewPasses.base: Every diagnostic already carries a registered code, what, why and fix text, and a snapshot test, so the source material for generated pages exists without new authoring.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The largest version would add per-code playground links, version-specific pages and localisation. None of that changes whether the terminal text carries an address, which is the only owner decision here.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid could omit links in machine output and include them in human output. That is worth doing under any option, since machine consumers should never receive prose.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Rust and Elm both point at longer explanations, and both are frequently cited as having good errors, so a link is not evidence of a weak message.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The strongest case for option B is that a user who does not know the pages exist will never find them. The mitigation is naming the pages in the help output and the docs rather than in every error line.

decisions.title: What case Jet uses for UI chrome
decisions.gist: Choose the case for labels, headers, summaries and buttons.
decisions.lesson: Jet prints two kinds of text. Chrome is a label: a command summary, a section header, a column heading, a button. Prose is a sentence that explains something. This choice covers chrome only. Today there is no rule at all, so the same kind of label appears in three different cases depending on which file it lives in, and the output reads as unmanaged.
decisions.explainer: Prose sentences inside diagnostics are decided separately, in D-CASE-PROSE1.
decisions.story: User runs a command, reads the help, hits an error, and opens the Canvas. Every one of those surfaces labels things differently today. He wants them to look like one product built by people who care.
decisions.inWild:
# The same kind of text, three different cases, all shipping today

$ jetpack --help
environments:                          # header, lowercase
  jetpack env    enter the default project environment    # summary, lowercase

$ jet --help
  jet build [args]    Create a native executable          # summary, uppercase

# Canvas toolbar
Fit graph | Start debug | Developer                       # sentence case

options.name: Title Case for all chrome (recommended)
options.detail: Every label capitalises each significant word: command summaries, section headers, column headings, buttons, menus, tabs and panel titles. Small words such as a, an, the, of, to, in, for, and, or stay lowercase unless they begin the label. Identifiers, flags, paths, refs and type names always keep their own case wherever they appear. Cost: title case needs a small-word list and a rule for hyphenates, so the checker is more than a first-character test, and long summaries read as heavier than sentence case.
options.code:
environments:  ->  Environments:
  jetpack env    Enter The Default Project Environment
  jet build      Create A Native Executable
Canvas:  Fit Graph | Start Debug | Developer

options.name: Sentence case for all chrome
options.detail: Capitalise only the first word, plus anything that is a proper noun or an identifier. One rule, trivially checkable, and it matches what most modern tooling does. Cost: it is what Jet half-does today, so it will feel like no change was made, and it does not read as deliberate the way title case does.
options.code:
environments:  ->  Environments:
  jetpack env    Enter the default project environment
  jet build      Create a native executable

options.name: Title Case for headers and buttons, sentence case for summaries
options.detail: Short chrome that acts as a label gets Title Case; a summary that is really a description gets sentence case. Follows the shape of the text rather than its location. Cost: a per-string judgement about whether something is a label or a description, which is exactly the kind of judgement that produced the current 50/50 split.
options.code:
Environments:                  # header, Title Case
  jetpack env    Enter the default project environment
Canvas:  Fit Graph | Start Debug

recommendation.why: It is the only option that visibly changes every surface, which is what the owner asked for, and one rule applied everywhere is enforceable.
recommendation.tradeoff: Title case needs a small-word list and hyphenation rule, so the enforcement check is more work than a first-character test.

whyNot.reason: Sentence case is easier to enforce, but it is close to what half the tree already does, so the result would not look deliberate.
Splitting by label versus description is defensible in isolation, but it needs a per-string judgement and that judgement drifting is exactly how the current split happened.

reviewPasses.base: Counted in the shipped tree: jetpack help descriptions are 86 lowercase and 0 uppercase, jet help summaries are 0 lowercase and 109 uppercase, and all 8 jetpack section headers are lowercase.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The largest version would restyle every string including machine output and log lines. Machine output is parsed and must stay byte-identical, so it is excluded under every option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Option C is the hybrid. It is rejected not because it is wrong but because it needs a judgement per string, and unenforceable judgement is what produced today's inconsistency.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Existing labels in the Canvas toolbar are already close to title case, so that surface moves least.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The strongest case against title case is that long command summaries read heavily. The mitigation is shortening summaries, which is worth doing anyway, rather than choosing a weaker rule.

decisions.title: What case a diagnostic uses for its three lines
decisions.gist: Choose the case for the problem line, the why line and the fix line.
decisions.lesson: Every Jet diagnostic prints three parts: a one-line statement of the problem, a why, and a fix. The why and the fix are sentences. The problem line is arguable: it reads like a headline but it is written like a sentence. Today none of this is decided, so across 854 diagnostics the problem line starts lowercase 283 times and uppercase 235 times.
decisions.explainer: The owner said some diagnostic sentences are better in sentence case, so this is separated from chrome.
decisions.story: Ana hits an error. The first line tells her what went wrong, and two more tell her why and what to do. She should not be able to tell which developer wrote which diagnostic.
decisions.inWild:
# Two shipped diagnostics, opposite conventions

Error [E1276]: `--offline` forbids network access
 Why: `ripgrep@default` is not in the hangar and --offline forbids fetching.
 Fix: drop `--offline`, or realize the object before going offline.

Error [E2604]: Integrity check failed for `jq` `1.8.2`
 Why: The cached artifact failed race-safe pre-consumer revalidation.
 Fix: Re-run `jet store fetch` after `jet clean`.

options.name: Sentence case for all three lines (recommended)
options.detail: The problem line, the why and the fix each capitalise only their first word, plus proper nouns and identifiers. They are sentences and they read as sentences. A line that begins with an identifier, a flag or a quoted code fragment keeps that fragment's own case and does not get force-capitalised. Cost: the problem line stays visually similar to today for the 235 rows that already start uppercase, so the improvement there is consistency rather than appearance.
options.code:
Error [E1276]: `--offline` forbids network access
 Why: `ripgrep@default` is not in the hangar.
 Fix: Drop `--offline`, or realize the object first.

options.name: Title Case the problem line, sentence case the why and fix
options.detail: Treats the problem line as a headline, matching the chrome rule, while the explanation stays prose. Makes the first line scan quickly in a wall of build output. Cost: a headline that begins with a flag or an identifier looks broken, and roughly a third of the 854 rows begin with exactly that.
options.code:
Error [E1276]: `--offline` Forbids Network Access
 Why: `ripgrep@default` is not in the hangar.
 Fix: Drop `--offline`, or realize the object first.

options.name: Title Case all three lines
options.detail: Maximum consistency with the chrome rule and the most visually deliberate. Cost: it makes explanatory prose hard to read, and it mangles any sentence containing a path, a flag or a type name, which most diagnostics do.
options.code:
Error [E1276]: `--offline` Forbids Network Access
 Why: `ripgrep@default` Is Not In The Hangar.
 Fix: Drop `--offline`, Or Realize The Object First.

recommendation.why: All three lines are sentences, and roughly a third of them begin with an identifier or a flag that must keep its own case.
recommendation.tradeoff: The problem line will not look as visually distinct as a Title Case headline would.

whyNot.reason: A Title Case headline scans well, but a large share of problem lines begin with a flag, an identifier or a quoted fragment, and those look broken when title-cased.
Title casing explanatory prose harms readability and mangles the paths, flags and type names that appear in most why and fix lines.

reviewPasses.base: Counted across 854 diagnostic rows: the what-line starts lowercase 283 times and uppercase 235 times; the why-line 367 against 405. Every row also carries a UI snapshot, so any change re-blesses hundreds of snapshots.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The largest version would rewrite the wording of every diagnostic, not just its case. That is a separate and much larger piece of work and must not be smuggled into a case change.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Option B is the hybrid between chrome and prose. It is rejected on the measured share of rows that begin with a code fragment.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Rust, Elm and Swift all use sentence case for diagnostic prose, so option A is also the least surprising to anyone arriving from another toolchain.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The strongest case for option B is that an error headline is chrome, not prose, and the owner explicitly wants chrome in Title Case. The counter is that the line is a full clause with a subject and a verb, which is a sentence regardless of where it sits.

decisions.title: Accept #2203 — Ratify one case law for every user-facing surface
decisions.gist: Close #2203, or bounce it back to building.
decisions.detail:

decisions.title: Sealed verification manifests for warm-store admission
decisions.gist: Hash every hangar object once at admission, seal the digest with per-file identity tuples, and re-hash only entries whose identity drifted. Full re-hash stays available through jetpack hangar verify.
decisions.explainer: Option A: trust sealed manifests. Full-hash each object once at admission, atomically seal its digest plus sorted per-file (inode, size, mtime) tuples, re-hash only changed, missing, or malformed entries, and report every reuse, re-hash, and self-heal decision for expert audit. Option B: always re-hash. Preserve the current cryptographic proof on every admission; simple trust story, keeps the observed multi-minute warm-store cost. Option C: time-limited proof cache. Trust a previous full hash until a fixed expiry; simpler metadata, but a timer can miss changes before expiry and adds a policy knob.
decisions.story: A warm jetpack env re-hashed every already-verified object on every run. The measured cost on this machine was minutes of pure sha256 over a 6.2 GB store before a single download started. Verification work should be proportional to what changed, not to what exists.
decisions.inWild: Git trusts stat identity for its index and re-hashes on drift. Nix re-verifies on demand with nix-store --verify rather than per use. Cargo and most package managers verify at fetch time and trust the store afterward.
decisions.detail: Manifest lives beside the object under the hangar, written under the hangar lock at admission or self-heal. A stat-identity match returns the sealed digest; any miss, drift, or parse failure falls back to a full canonical re-hash and reseals. jetpack hangar verify ignores manifests and remains the full cryptographic audit; doctor reports manifest reuse decisions. Known tradeoff: an in-place rewrite that preserves inode, size, and mtime evades stat detection; the explicit verify verb is the audit escape.
decisions.rec: A. It matches the owner posture from the 2026-08-26 interview (trust sealed manifests), targets the measured latency directly, and keeps the expert full-proof path explicit.
decisions.comment: Owner chat verdict 2026-08-27: nix-equivalent time is the minimum bar; jetpack must beat nix on every package-management operation. Sealed manifests (A) become the default; full cryptographic re-hash remains explicit via jetpack hangar verify. Measured context: warm nix develop 17.6-25.1s on this repo; nix does no content re-hash on use.

decisions.title: Apply docs garbage collection and the canonical docs layout
decisions.gist: Choose which documents stay active and which leave.
decisions.lesson: An active document is a current input for users, tools, or owner decisions. A fold moves durable law into its canonical home before its old file leaves. A delete removes a source with no current owner or consumer. An archive keeps history outside active navigation. A hold keeps a live source until its gate, consumer, contradiction, or owner question closes. This split lets readers find current law without losing needed evidence or open choices.
decisions.story: Rina maintains Jet's language docs while several finished design papers still look current. She needs a contributor to find the spec, a maintainer to find live plans, and an owner to see open choices. A cleanup pass must preserve hard consumers and move only durable law.

Python uses accepted PEPs for decisions and separate historical records for rejected or superseded proposals. A reader can distinguish rule from discussion.
Git keeps project history in commits while the working tree presents current files. A hidden archive serves a similar navigation goal for finished docs.

recommendation.why: A follows the accepted docs cleanup shape and the census evidence. It leaves current law, live gates, open choices, and hard consumers visible while removing finished duplicate reports.

whyNot.reason: B preserves every stale source in active navigation. Folding content does not remove duplicate status claims or the search cost that caused the cleanup.
C preserves history, but the 67 moved files still enlarge the archive and remain easy to mistake for active evidence. The census already identifies durable sources that need to stay.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts deletion after each fold and consumer update. History remains in Git or the existing archive policy, while active docs keep one clear role.

decisions.gist: Choose which document owns each surface truth.
decisions.lesson: A source of truth is the one place that owns a rule or inventory. A pointer explains where readers should look without copying the rule. A generated projection renders source data for another audience. A hand-written guide can teach meaning, but it must not become a second syntax or inventory source. This split matters because one changed constructor, command, or diagnostic can otherwise leave several current-looking copies behind.
decisions.story: Leah changes Jet's constructor spelling after an owner decision. The syntax record uses Build{...}, but a typed diagnostic row, an error page, and llms.text still show Build.{...}. She needs one edit to update every projection and one test to catch stale copies.

comparisons.note: An OpenAPI document can generate client and server views. The schema owns the wire shape, while generated files are outputs rather than competing contracts.

decisions.title: Consolidate feature examples into curated suites
decisions.gist: Choose how feature examples become curated suites.
decisions.lesson: An executable example is language evidence that a tool can run. A suite is one program that carries one user goal through related mechanisms and prints one stable result. A check proves a compiler error, target, host, harness, or gate that is not an honest portable story. A golden is expected output paired with a source path. That path is also a proof identity in tests and manifests. A merge therefore needs a map that keeps each old behavior, special channel, and consumer visible.
decisions.story: Maya maintains Jet examples while an agent repairs compiler regressions. She wants a beginner to find one useful story, while the team keeps target, web, FFI, and diagnostic proofs. The current topic tree gives each tiny case a path, but it hides related behavior and lengthens every repair search.

decisions.title: Set the repository root and session artifact law
decisions.gist: Choose how the root and session artifacts stay clean.
decisions.lesson: A root allow-list names intentional project entries. An ephemeral entry may exist during a build or session, but it is never source and is never tracked. A session cache stores reports, probes, and logs outside the repository for one run. An ignore rule blocks accidental tracking, but it does not delete a tracked file. A growth bound rejects oversized durable state before it consumes memory or disk.
decisions.story: Noah runs Jet's parity and browser checks from one checkout. Each run creates reports, probes, target trees, and timing files. He needs the next agent to see project files at the root, find evidence in the lane cache, and avoid trusting a 2.0 GiB lock or a stale generated tree.

comparisons.note: Cargo writes build output under target and lets each checkout own a target directory. Jet extends this boundary to reports, probes, and named session targets.
Bazel separates source trees from output bases. The same separation keeps generated and session output away from Jet's root source map.

C keeps the current boundary even though the hygiene report already found repeated probes, logs, caches, generated trees, and cwd timing output.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts explicit output paths and a layout check for every session. In return, root files, durable state, and disposable evidence remain distinguishable.

reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass checked root entries, worktrees, Cargo output, Zed output, .claude artifacts, .cache runtime files, .jet state, and timing reports. It kept product roots and separated disposable output.

reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked root src duplication, tracked cache files, unbounded lock provenance, alternate worktree roots, and cwd timing writes. It added explicit lifetime and size rules.

decisions.title: What jet run does with a web-targeted program on the native tier
decisions.gist: Whether running a web app natively errors, stays silent, or serves it.
decisions.lesson: A Jet web app mounts a browser tree. Ratified D-WEBDEFAULT1 makes native jet run ignore an inferred web target, so the program executes against a null backend, prints nothing, and exits 0. The gauntlet flagged that silence as a false success: the user typed run, saw nothing, and got no signal. This ballot picks the native-run behavior for web-targeted source.
decisions.story: Ines finishes her first counter app from the web tutorial. She types jet run main.jet like every other example taught her. The terminal prints nothing and returns 0. She assumes Jet is broken and files her first bug in her first hour.

options.name: Reject with a teaching diagnostic
options.detail: Native jet run on web-targeted source stops with a registered error naming the target and the two real paths: jet dev for the live loop, or jet build --target=web. Nothing silently executes against a null backend. Dual-target programs keep native runs by declaring a native target explicitly.
options.technical: New registered diagnostic with what/why/fix and UI snapshot (I4). Detection uses the same inference D-WEBDEFAULT1 already performs at Source/main.rs:3327-3351; the change replaces silent-ignore with the error. Explicit #Target(Native) or a manifest target keeps native execution.
options.code:
$ jet run main.jet
Error [E13xx]: this program targets the web
 Why: run() mounts a browser tree; the native tier has no browser
 Fix: use `jet dev main.jet` for a live preview, or `jet build --target=web`

options.name: Auto-serve: run becomes dev for web source
options.detail: Native jet run on web source starts the same local preview jet dev provides: build the web bundle, serve it, open the browser. One command works everywhere, and the beginner never learns the difference. It also makes run long-lived and network-bound for these programs, which surprises scripts and CI that expected a process that ends.
options.technical: run detects the web target and delegates to the dev server path (#2235/#2236 infrastructure). Requires Browser/Net authority; noninteractive contexts refuse per the normal authority flow.
options.code:
$ jet run main.jet
Serving web preview at http://127.0.0.1:5199 (ctrl-c to stop)

options.name: Keep silent-ignore as ratified
