options.detail: No change: native run executes against the null backend and exits 0. Preserves D-WEBDEFAULT1 exactly and keeps the measured false success: the beginner's first web run stays a blank terminal.
options.code:
$ jet run main.jet
$ echo $?
0

comparisons.note: Web tooling never pretends a browser app ran headless; the entry command starts a dev server.

recommendation.why: The measured harm is silence. A teaching error removes the false success, costs one line to read, and routes the beginner to the two commands that actually work, without making run long-lived.

whyNot.reason: Serving changes run into a long-lived network process for one class of source. Scripts, CI, and the harness lose the finite contract, and authority prompts appear where a build error was expected.
It keeps the exact failure the gauntlet measured: exit 0, empty output, no signal. A first-hour user cannot distinguish it from a broken install.

recommendation.tradeoff: Dual-target programs must name a native target explicitly to keep running natively. That one line is acceptable to end silent false success for everyone else.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared reject, auto-serve, and status quo, and recommended reject because it ends silent false success with the smallest behavior change.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a warning-plus-run hybrid and a config default. A warning still exits 0 silently for pipes, and a config default hides policy in a file nobody reads.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review examined reject-then-offer: error first, flag to serve. That is option A plus jet dev, which already exists, so it folded into A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened auto-serve with a --no-serve escape and strengthened status quo by documenting the null backend. Neither removes the surprise for scripts or the silent zero.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked reject on dual-target workflows and headless testing. Explicit native targets and the existing test harness paths keep both working, so the recommendation holds.

decisions.title: Grow the interpolation selector family: hex, width, padding, and integer precision
decisions.gist: Which formatting selectors the braces gain beyond Fixed and Debug.
decisions.lesson: Jet ratified one formatting rail inside string braces: a value plus one selector, like {price:Fixed(2)}, each mapping to one core.fmt function (D-FMT-INTERP1). The gauntlet measured what the current set cannot spell: hexadecimal with zero padding, column width and alignment, and Fixed on integers. Jet programs hand-rolled these in three entries and paid up to 19 extra lines each against Python and Rust. This ballot picks the selector set that closes the gap while keeping the closed, named-selector shape.
decisions.story: A worker printing a binary file checksum needs sixteen hex digits with leading zeros. Python writes one format code. In Jet they build a byte array by hand, shift eight times, and call a hex encoder: ten lines for one number.

options.name: Minimal trio: Hex, Pad, and integer Fixed
options.detail: Add exactly what the measurements demanded: {n:Hex(16)} for zero-padded lowercase hex, {s:Pad(20)} and {s:PadLeft(8)} for columns, and Fixed widened to accept Int. Smallest new surface; scientific notation, percent, binary, and fill characters stay function calls.
options.technical: Three selector rows in the closed set. Hex(n) lowers to fmt.hex zero-padded to n digits; Pad and PadLeft lower to fmt.pad_right and fmt.pad_left with space fill. Fixed(Int) converts exactly then formats. E0914 fix text lists the new set. I7 rows plus UI snapshots per selector.
options.code:
print("fnv {hash:Hex(16)}")
print("{name:Pad(20)} {qty:PadLeft(5)}")
print("sum7 {total:Fixed(6)}")

options.name: Full family in one ruling
options.detail: The trio from option A plus {x:Sci(3)} scientific, {x:Percent(1)}, {n:Bin} and {n:Oct}, and a fill argument for padding. One ballot settles formatting for years and every selector still maps to one core.fmt function. The cost is a wider closed set to name, teach, snapshot, and keep on every tier.
options.technical: Nine selector rows, each one-to-one onto an existing or new core.fmt function. Every selector must run identically on every tier (I9) before it ships. Unknown selectors keep the registered E0914 error listing the valid set.
options.code:
print("fnv {hash:Hex(16)}")
print("growth {rate:Percent(1)}")
print("mass {kg:Sci(3)}")
print("flags {bits:Bin}")
print("{name:Pad(20, '.')}")

options.name: No new selectors; methods only
options.detail: Keep the current set and spell everything else as core.fmt calls inside the braces, like {fmt.hex(hash, 16)}. Nothing new to ratify, and the measured losses stay. The hex line stays a wrapper call, and the ratified one-value brace shape must bend to allow call expressions.
options.code:
use core.text.fmt as fmt
print("fnv {fmt.hex(hash, 16)}")

comparisons.note: The colon mini-language covers all of this in one dense grammar. Jet already rejected that grammar for named selectors; this ballot decides how much of its power the named set carries.
Same mini-language family as Python, plus Debug formatting. Rust users coming to Jet expect hex and width to be spellable inline.

recommendation.why: The owner goal is Python-class brevity with better methods. The full family closes every measured and every foreseeable formatting loss in one ruling, keeps one mechanism, and each selector stays a named, teachable word instead of punctuation.

whyNot.reason: The trio closes today's three losses and leaves scientific, percent, and binary to return as the next audit's finding. A second ballot later costs more than deciding once.
Methods-only keeps the measured ten-line hex loss, and letting call expressions into the braces breaks the ratified one-value shape for a worse read.

recommendation.tradeoff: Nine selectors are more surface to snapshot and keep tier-identical than three. That is acceptable because each is a thin sugar over one core.fmt function and the set stays closed with a registered error naming it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a minimal trio, a full family, and methods-only. It recommended the full family because one ruling settles the formatting surface.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested reopening the colon mini-language and a user-extensible selector registry. Both lose: one was already rejected by ratification, and open extension breaks the closed teachable set.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review considered the trio now with the rest pre-approved later. That is the full family with extra ceremony, so it folded into option B.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened methods-only by allowing whitelisted fmt calls in braces. It still reads as a call, still needs a grammar exception, and still loses the density users expect.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the family on tier drift and selector creep. Per-selector I9 snapshots gate shipping, and the set stays closed with E0914 naming it, so the recommendation holds.

decisions.title: Ambient basics: what a manifest-less program may do without asking
decisions.gist: Whether printing and reading arguments need permission paperwork.
decisions.lesson: Jet programs declare effect authority in package.jet, and undeclared effects stop noninteractive runs with E1803. The gauntlet measured the floor: printing needs IO and Mem.Alloc, and reading arguments adds Exec, so a two-line hello with an argument cannot run without a manifest. Every peer language runs such programs immediately. This ballot decides the default authority for programs with no manifest, while keeping expert deny and audit control intact.
decisions.story: A student's first program prints a greeting with their name from the command line. In Python it just runs. In Jet the terminal demands an authority block before hello can print, and the student has learned policy vocabulary before variables.

options.name: Ambient basics for manifest-less programs
options.detail: A program with no package.jet gets a fixed tiny grant: stdout and stderr, argument reading, and allocation. Files, network, processes, and everything else still require authority. A manifest, when present, overrides everything, and a manifest deny always wins. Beginners run their first programs immediately; auditors know exactly what the implicit floor is because it is one fixed, documented set.
options.technical: Scope: only when no package.jet resolves. Grant set: IO limited to stdio, Exec limited to argv reading, Mem.Alloc. Any other effect keeps E1803. jet inspect reports the ambient floor explicitly. Spec text names the set; changing it is a new ballot.

options.name: Scaffold grants instead: jet new writes the effects it uses
options.detail: No ambient change. jet new writes an authority block covering what its generated code needs, so scaffolded projects run immediately. Bare single files keep demanding a manifest for hello-with-arguments, which keeps the measured first-hour wall for everyone who starts from a plain file, the way every tutorial and every gauntlet worker did.
options.code:
$ jet new hello && cd hello && jet run run.jet -- world
hello, world
$ jet run ../bare.jet -- world
Error [E1803]: application authority is undecided for `IO, Mem.Alloc, Exec`

options.name: One-shot interactive approval becomes the noninteractive default too
options.detail: Keep the effect floor, but a noninteractive run of a manifest-less program proceeds and prints a one-line notice of what it exercised, instead of stopping. Nothing is silently granted forever: the notice names the effects each run. Automation stops failing, but every CI log gains noise and the boundary between approved and unapproved becomes a log line rather than a rule.
options.code:
$ jet run hello.jet -- world
notice: ambient effects this run: IO, Mem.Alloc, Exec
hello, world

comparisons.note: Also permission-gated, but stdout and argv are always free; only files, network, and env need flags. That floor is widely considered the usable line.
comparisons.code:
$ deno run hello.ts world
hello, world

comparisons.note: No authority system; everything is ambient. Jet's differentiator is the gate on real capabilities, not on printing.

recommendation.why: The safety product is gating files, network, processes, and memory tricks. Printing and reading argv carry no capability a shell did not already give the process, so gating them buys audit noise, not safety, and costs the first hour.

whyNot.reason: Scaffolds help projects but the measured wall was bare files: tutorials, gists, and every quick script still die on hello. The first-hour failure stays for exactly the people it hurts most.
Proceed-with-notice makes the boundary a log line. Auditors lose the hard rule, CI gains noise, and the set exercised can drift run to run.

recommendation.tradeoff: There is now one implicit grant set to know about. It is acceptable because the set is tiny, fixed, documented, reported by jet inspect, and a manifest always overrides it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared ambient basics, scaffold grants, and proceed-with-notice, recommending ambient basics because it removes the measured wall without weakening real capability gates.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested gating nothing, per-user global grants, and environment-variable overrides. All three blur audit boundaries far more than one fixed documented floor.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined A and B: ambient basics for bare files plus honest scaffold grants. B's half is ungated template work already planned on the card, so the ballot stays about A.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C with a quiet flag and machine-readable notices. It still turns a rule into telemetry and still surprises auditors.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A with exfiltration-via-stdout and argv-as-secret scenarios. Both exist identically in every gated language today because the shell owns those channels, so the floor adds no new capability.

decisions.title: A written allow list adds to the beginner floor
decisions.situation: Every Jet program may print, read input, allocate memory and read its own arguments without asking. That floor exists so a first program runs at once. Today, the moment a package writes any permission list, the floor disappears. A package that only denies running other programs also loses printing, and most allow lists repeat the floor by hand. The vote decides whether a written list adds to the floor; we recommend that it adds.
decisions.gist: Should writing an allow list keep printing and arguments, or take them away?
decisions.lesson: Every program may print, read input, allocate memory and read its arguments without asking. That small set is the beginner floor. Today, writing any permission list in a package erases the floor, so the list must repeat it. This vote decides whether a list adds to the floor instead.
decisions.story: Sam's script prints a report. Sam adds one line to forbid running other programs. The next run refuses to print, and the fix asks Sam to list printing again.
decisions.inWild:
deno run --allow-net=api.example.com app.ts
# console.log and Deno.args need no flag
# https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/

options.name: The list adds to the floor
options.detail: The floor (IO, Mem.Alloc, Exec.Args) holds for every program. A written allow list adds rights to it. A floor right leaves only through deny, and deny still wins over every allow. Amends D-AUTH-AMBIENT1=A, whose option text says a manifest overrides everything, and spec.md 'Application authority'.
options.technical: EffectProjection.jet:62-72 and its CLI copy Cli/Authority.jet:158-171 seed the ambient set for every policy, then add allow and subtract nothing; denied stays checked first. The E1803 fix text loses 'list every effect the program needs' (DiagnosticRows.jet:7404). jet fix removes floor entries from existing allow rows. Evidence: 138 of 187 single-line allow rows in .jet files restate IO and Mem.Alloc; probe p2 (deny: [Exec] only) refuses print with E1803.
options.code:
authority: { allow: [Net] }
authority: { deny: [IO] }

options.name: The list replaces the floor
options.detail: Keep today's rule. A package with any allow or deny entry receives exactly its allow list. The floor survives only when the block writes neither list.
options.technical: No code change. The E1803 Why and Fix keep the warning that a written block replaces the default.
options.code: authority: { allow: [IO, Mem.Alloc, Exec.Args, Net] }

comparisons.note: Output and arguments are always available; --allow-* flags only add. https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
With the permission model on, stdout still works; --allow-fs-read adds file reading. https://nodejs.org/api/permissions.html

recommendation.why: The floor carries no power a shell has not already given the process. Repeating it is noise, and losing it by writing a deny is a trap.
gains: Shorter lists that name only real additions.
Adding a deny never breaks printing.

losses.loss: A reader must know the floor to read a list completely.
losses.mitigation: The floor is three fixed rights, written once in the spec, and deny removes any of them.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the trap where denying processes also stops printing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Lists stop being self-contained, in exchange for never repeating the floor.

surface.gist: Should writing an allow list keep printing and arguments, or take them away?
surface.lesson: Every program may print, read input, allocate memory and read its arguments without asking. That small set is the beginner floor. Today, writing any permission list in a package erases the floor, so the list must repeat it. This vote decides whether a list adds to the floor instead.

current.note: Writing a permission list replaces the floor. Denying only processes also stops printing.

wild.note: Deno programs always print and read their arguments; each flag adds one permission on top. See https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/.
wild.code:
deno run --allow-net=api.example.com app.ts
// console.log and Deno.args need no flag

options.name: The list adds to the floor
options.gist: Allow adds rights; a floor right leaves only through deny.
gains: Lists name only what the program really adds.
A deny list never removes printing by accident.
losses: Removing printing needs an explicit deny entry.

options.name: The list replaces the floor
options.gist: Keep today's rule: any written list is the whole policy.
gains: The written list is the complete policy.
losses: Three in four lists repeat the floor by hand.
A deny-only list silently stops printing.

recommendation.why: The floor carries no power a shell has not already given the process. Repeating it is noise, and losing it by writing a deny is a trap.
gains: Shorter lists that name only real additions.
Adding a deny never breaks printing.

losses.loss: A reader must know the floor to read a list completely.
losses.mitigation: The floor is three fixed rights, written once in the spec, and deny removes any of them.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the trap where denying processes also stops printing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Lists stop being self-contained, in exchange for never repeating the floor.

decisions.title: SIMD by default: auto-vectorization with an opt-out, and wider portable lanes
decisions.gist: Whether Jet speeds up loops with vector instructions automatically, and how experts control it.
decisions.lesson: Modern processors run the same math on 4 or 8 numbers at once, and compilers can often rewrite plain loops to use this for free. Jet ratified small portable vector types, F32x4 and F64x2, with element-wise math and reduce (D-SIMD1, D-SIMD2). The gauntlet measured the remaining gap: scalar expert Jet nbody runs 3.05ms; the C and Rust references run 1.55ms and 1.66ms with wider vectors. This ballot decides whether vectorization becomes a safe compiler default, and whether the lane family grows wide enough for experts.
decisions.story: Maya ports a particle simulation to Jet. Her inner loop is plain float math over arrays. In C her compiler vectorizes it silently and she never thinks about it. In Jet today the same loop runs scalar. She has no wider lane type to reach for. Jet reads as the slower language even though nothing in her code asked for less speed.

options.name: Auto-vectorize by default, opt-out only
options.detail: The compiler emits vectorizable shapes and enables vector instruction selection everywhere it can prove safety. A function or block can opt out with a directive when exact scalar behavior matters. No new types. Experts who need guaranteed vector width still have only F32x4 and F64x2.
options.technical: Codegen emits loops in shapes LLVM can vectorize through rustc, and enables a portable baseline feature set per target. Opt-out spelling `#Scalar` on fn or block, registered in Syntax.rs (I7). Float semantics stay IEEE and ordering-sensitive reductions stay scalar unless proven safe, so results never change.

options.name: Auto-vectorize by default, plus a complete portable lane family
options.detail: Option A, and the ratified lane family grows from F32x4 and F64x2 to the full portable set: F32x8, F64x4, plus integer lanes I32x4, I32x8, I64x2, I64x4, U8x16, U8x32. Same ratified surface shape: constructor, splat, index, element-wise ops, reduce, from_array and to_array. The compiler picks real instructions per target and falls back cleanly where a width is not native. Beginners never see lanes; experts close the last 2x by hand where the auto pass cannot.
options.technical: Extends the D-SIMD1 closed type set; operator overloading stays restricted to built-in lane and linalg types (D-SIMD2, E2510, E2511). Lowers to rustc portable SIMD-capable shapes or explicit intrinsic calls in generated Rust behind the same I2 wall. Raw arch intrinsics remain behind #Unsafe as ratified. I9: lane types evaluate identically on every tier; interpreter uses the same Prelude implementations.

options.name: Explicit lanes only, no automatic pass
options.detail: Grow the lane family as in B, but never vectorize automatically. Every speedup is code someone wrote. Predictable, and the beginner default stays slow: the gauntlet loops stay scalar unless rewritten, so plain Jet keeps losing to plain C on plain code.

comparisons.note: Both auto-vectorize plain loops at default optimization levels, and both offer explicit vector paths. This is the baseline Jet is measured against.
comparisons.code:
// gcc -O3 vectorizes this silently
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = a[i] * b[i] + c[i];

comparisons.note: Ships a generic @Vector(len, T) type with element-wise operators, plus LLVM auto-vectorization by default.
comparisons.code:
const V = @Vector(4, f64);
const sum = @reduce(.Add, a * b);

comparisons.note: No user SIMD surface and weak auto-vectorization; it loses the same gauntlet kernels by similar margins.
comparisons.code: // no vector types; plain loops only

recommendation.why: The owner goal is winning on plain code and on expert code at once. The automatic pass makes beginner loops fast with zero ceremony, and the wider lane family gives experts the same ceiling C and Rust experts have, inside the safety rails already ratified.

whyNot.reason: Auto-vectorization alone cannot close hand-tuned gaps like nbody, because the reference implementations use shuffles and reciprocal square root patterns no automatic pass finds. Experts stay capped at F64x2.
Explicit-only keeps every plain loop scalar. The language that claims safe speed by default would ship slow defaults and demand rewrites for wins peers get for free.

recommendation.tradeoff: The automatic pass adds compile work and a new class of codegen surface to keep correct. That is acceptable because results are bit-identical by rule: any loop where vector math could change observable results stays scalar unless the user opts in explicitly.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared three shapes: automatic vectorization alone, automatic plus a full lane family, and explicit lanes only. It recommended the combined option because one mechanism serves the beginner default and the expert ceiling.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also weighed raw intrinsics as the primary surface, a numeric-array trait pass like NumPy, and doing nothing until the Rust backend is replaced. Raw intrinsics stay behind #Unsafe as already ratified; an array-programming layer is a separate future decision; waiting loses measured ground now for no gain.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review merged the original two-option split into option B, since a lane family without the automatic pass or the pass without the family each solve half the measured problem.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C by noting its predictability for audit-heavy shops, and strengthened A by keeping its surface minimal. C still leaves plain code slow by default, and A still caps experts below the C reference.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the combined option on float determinism, compile time, and tier parity, and each attack is answered by a rule now written into the option. Ordering-sensitive reductions stay scalar unless proven safe, the shape pass bounds compile cost, and lane types share one Prelude on every tier.

decisions.title: Bytes literals: how a program spells raw byte text like a file magic
decisions.gist: How to write the bytes of a short ASCII tag in source.
decisions.lesson: Binary formats begin with fixed magic bytes, and network protocols and tests compare short raw byte strings constantly. Jet has [U8] lists and string types but no literal that means the bytes of this ASCII text. The gauntlet's binary parser spelled a four-byte magic check as four numeric reads compared against 74, 71, 66, 49. Every peer spells it as one comparison against a bytes literal. This ballot picks Jet's spelling, the one syntax gap the brevity analysis found.
decisions.story: Rye writes a PNG sniffer. The header is eight known bytes. In Rust that is b"..." and one compare. In Jet today Rye either types eight numeric literals in a [U8] list or reads a comment explaining what 74 means.

options.name: b-prefix literal: b"JGB1"
options.detail: The Rust and Python spelling. A b before a string literal makes a [U8] value of the ASCII bytes; escapes like \x00 allowed, non-ASCII characters rejected at compile time. Familiar to switchers, one character of ceremony, and greppable. Adds a new literal prefix to the grammar.
options.technical: Grammar: prefix b on string literals produces [U8#n] with compile-time length; \xNN escapes; non-ASCII code points are a registered compile error. Equality against slices and lists works through existing [U8] comparison. I7 row plus snapshots.
options.code:
magic :: reader.read_bytes(4) ?? return Err("short magic")
if magic != b"JGB1" -> return Err("bad magic")

options.name: Typed literal body: [U8]{ "JGB1" }
options.detail: Reuse the ratified typed-literal head instead of a new prefix: a string body inside a [U8] literal means its ASCII bytes. No new sigil and it reads like every other typed literal, at the cost of more characters and a less familiar spelling for switchers.
options.technical: Extends typed-literal body rules: [U8]{ string } and [U8#n]{ string } accept ASCII strings with \xNN escapes; length mismatch on the sized form is a compile error. No grammar prefix added.
options.code:
magic :: reader.read_bytes(4) ?? return Err("short magic")
if magic != [U8]{ "JGB1" } -> return Err("bad magic")

options.name: No literal: a stdlib conversion
options.detail: Spell it as a conversion call like Bytes.ascii("JGB1"), checked at compile time when the argument is a literal. Zero grammar change, and every use pays a call wrapper that peers do not, in exactly the hot binary code where brevity was measured worst.
options.code: if magic != Bytes.ascii("JGB1") -> return Err("bad magic")

comparisons.note: b"..." byte string literals; the direct model for option A.
Same b-prefix; switchers carry the muscle memory.
No prefix needed: string literals are byte arrays already. Jet's strings are validated text, so it needs an explicit spelling.

recommendation.why: The b-prefix is the spelling both major switcher populations already know, and it is one character. It keeps byte data visibly distinct from text exactly where confusing them is dangerous.

whyNot.reason: The typed-literal body is consistent but seven characters longer, unfamiliar to every switcher, and reads as a conversion rather than a literal in scanning-heavy binary code.
A checked call is still a call: it costs the wrapper everywhere, reads as runtime work, and leaves Jet the only language in the comparison without a byte literal.

recommendation.tradeoff: A new literal prefix is one more lexer rule and one more thing the tutorial names. That is acceptable because it is one character carrying an unambiguous, widely known meaning.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the b-prefix, a typed-literal body, and a checked conversion call, recommending the b-prefix for switcher familiarity and scan-time clarity.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested hex-only literals, char lists, and making plain strings coerce to bytes. Coercion blurs the text and bytes boundary Jet deliberately keeps; the others cover less.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review considered shipping B now since the head exists, adding A later as sugar. Two spellings for one literal violates one-mechanism, so it folded.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C with comptime evaluation guarantees. It still reads as a call and still costs the wrapper at every site.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked A on non-ASCII confusion and prefix creep. Non-ASCII rejects at compile time with a registered error, and the prefix set stays closed, so the recommendation holds.

decisions.title: Spell the Duration total-in-unit call
decisions.gist: How a program asks a Duration for its total in one unit.
decisions.lesson: Duration ships a method registered as in(unit). Nobody can call it: 'in' is the loop keyword, so a.in(.Seconds) is a parse error. A shipped call that cannot be typed is dead surface. This choice picks the spelling every program will use to turn a Duration into a number of seconds, milliseconds, or any other unit.
decisions.story: Priya writes a build timer. She has a Duration from subtracting two instants and wants one number: total milliseconds for a log line. She reads the docs, types elapsed.in(.Milliseconds), and gets a parse error about loops. There is no working spelling for the thing the docs promise.

options.name: Rename to total(unit)
options.detail: The call becomes elapsed.total(.Milliseconds). One word says what you get: the whole duration, as one number, in that unit. No grammar change. Beginners never meet the reserved-word trap. The loss: the docs and the registry rename a shipped name, and 'total' must also be taught next to the per-part accessors so nobody confuses total seconds with the seconds component.
options.technical: Registry rename in the Core time module; same Prelude implementation on every tier (I9). Matches the exact/calendar split law from the Temporal-parity plan: total() is exact-time only; calendar units keep their Period path.

options.name: Rename to in_unit(unit)
options.detail: The call becomes elapsed.in_unit(.Milliseconds). It keeps the documented 'in' flavor, so old docs read almost right. The loss: it is a two-word name for a one-word idea, and it reads like a workaround for the keyword rather than a name anyone would pick fresh.
options.code: print("build took {elapsed.in_unit(.Milliseconds)} ms")

options.name: Allow 'in' as a method name after a dot
options.detail: The grammar treats 'in' as an ordinary name when it follows '.', so a.in(.Seconds) works as documented. The gain: the documented spelling ships unchanged. The loss: 'in' now means two things, and every reader must know which one applies from position alone. Editors, formatters, and error messages must special-case it. One keyword with two meanings is a standing tax on beginners.
options.technical: Parser carve-out: 'in' after '.' in a postfix position lexes as an identifier. Touches grammar, tree-sitter, tmGrammar, formatter, and E0003 fix text.
options.code:
print("build took {elapsed.in(.Milliseconds)} ms")
// works, but 'for x in xs' and '.in(' now share one word

comparisons.note: Temporal.Duration.total({ unit: 'seconds' }) is the exact-total call; per-unit fields stay component parts.
timedelta offers total_seconds() only; every other unit is manual division, which users complain about.
std Duration uses as_secs(), as_millis(): a per-unit family instead of one call with a unit argument.

recommendation.why: total(.Unit) says exactly what comes back: the whole duration as one number in that unit. It needs no grammar change, it cannot collide with the loop keyword, and it lands on the same name Temporal proved in the wild.

whyNot.reason: in_unit is a workaround name. It exists only because 'in' is taken, and it reads that way forever.
Giving 'in' two meanings taxes every reader and every tool to save one name. The beginner surface pays daily for a one-time rename.

recommendation.tradeoff: Programs must learn that total(.Seconds) and the seconds component are different questions. That is accepted: the split is real, and the name makes the difference teachable.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared rename-to-total, rename-to-in_unit, and a grammar carve-out, and recommended total for clarity and zero grammar cost.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a per-unit method family (as_millis style) and computed properties. Both multiply surface for no new power, so they were folded into the comparisons rather than kept as options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tried shipping total() while also allowing .in( as an alias. Two spellings for one call violates the one-mechanism law, so the hybrid was dropped.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option C: the carve-out is small and precedented in other grammars. It still leaves one word with two meanings in every reader's head, which the beginner pass rejects.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked total() with the component-confusion case: does total(.Seconds) round? The answer is documented exact conversion with fractional result where the unit demands it, matching Temporal; the confusion risk is a docs line, not a design flaw.

decisions.title: What a mutating method call on an indexed element means
decisions.gist: Whether m[k].push(v) changes the map, is rejected at compile time, or stays as it is.
decisions.lesson: Jet programs keep lists inside maps and lists inside lists. Today a mutating call on an indexed element behaves three different ways. lists["x"].push(3) silently changes nothing on any tier. outer[0].push(9) changes the list on the default tier but silently changes nothing on release. A mutation that vanishes with no error is silent data loss, the class the owner declared fatal. One rule must cover every container and every tier.
decisions.story: Maya builds a word index for her site search: a map from word to the list of page ids. For each page she writes index[word].push(page_id). The program runs, prints no error, and her index ends up with the first page only. She ships a search that cannot find most pages and has no idea why.

options.name: Reject every read-modify use of an indexed slot
options.detail: A mutating method call on an indexed element becomes a compile error, like compound assignment already is. The error teaches the total-update spelling: read the value, change it, store it back. Nothing silent remains, but common nested updates need three lines.
options.technical: Extend the S17/E0163/E0164 sema family: a method requiring `&self` may not take an indexed read (`m[k]`, `l[i]`) as its receiver. New registered diagnostic with fix text `v := m.get(k) ?? []; v.push(x); m[k] = v`. UI snapshot per I4. Default-tier list mutate-through behavior is removed so one rule holds everywhere.

options.name: Indexed slots are real places for assignment and mutating methods
options.detail: m[k].push(v) mutates the element inside the container, on every tier. A missing key stops the program loudly, exactly like reading m[k] today. Compound arithmetic (m[k] += 1) stays rejected with its ratified teaching text, because it hides a default-value question that push does not have.
options.technical: Lower an indexed receiver of a `&self` method as a place projection (get-mut style), not a temporary copy. The same lowering fixes #2262 nested index assignment. Missing map key = the existing indexed-read runtime stop. E0163/E0164 stay ratified and untouched. One Prelude lowering per I9; interpreter, AOT, and JIT share it.
options.code:
index["jet"].push(7)      // grows the stored list, all tiers
outer[0].push(9)          // [[1,2,9],[3]], all tiers
outer[1][0] = 5           // nested assignment works (#2262)
counts["a"] += 1          // still E0164 with the total-update fix

options.name: The full place family, arithmetic included
options.detail: Indexed slots become real places for everything: assignment, mutating methods, compound assignment, increment. One rule with no exceptions, but it reverses the ratified E0163/E0164 verdicts and brings back the trap they teach against: counts[word] += 1 panics at runtime when the word is missing.
options.technical: Retire E0163/E0164 (S17 partial reversal, owner-only). All indexed lvalue forms lower through place projection. Missing key = runtime stop at the read. Migration: the existing fix-text spellings keep working.
options.code:
counts["a"] += 1     // works when "a" exists, stops the program when missing
index["jet"].push(7)  // works

comparisons.note: d[k].append(x) mutates the stored list; a missing key raises KeyError at the read. This is the behavior most newcomers expect.
Mutation through a map needs an explicit mutable lookup, so the copy-versus-place question never hides.
obj[k].push(v) mutates because everything is a reference; nothing is ever copied, and nothing is ever loud.

recommendation.why: B makes the written intent true: a push into a container element changes the container, on every tier, and a missing key stops the program the same way a bare read does. It also fixes #2262 with the same lowering and keeps both ratified compound-assignment verdicts intact.

whyNot.reason: A turns the most common nested update into a three-line ritual and contradicts #2262, which already treats nested index assignment as intended behavior.
C reverses ratified E0163/E0164 and revives the missing-key arithmetic trap they were ratified to teach against, for no gain B does not already deliver.

recommendation.tradeoff: B accepts one asymmetry: index[k].push(v) works while counts[k] += 1 stays a compile error with teaching text. The asymmetry is principled — arithmetic needs a default for a missing key; push does not.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared loud rejection, real places for methods, and the full place family, and recommended real places because the written intent becomes true on every tier.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested two more shapes: an explicit borrow spelling (&m[k]).push(v), and container-provided update closures (m.update(k, fn)). Both were folded in — the borrow spelling is option B's lowering with extra ceremony, and update closures can ship later as library sugar under any option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of A and B (reject on maps, mutate on lists) was drafted and discarded: two rules for one spelling is exactly the inconsistency this ballot exists to remove.
reviewPasses.cooperative: A was strengthened with a precise fix-text recipe and C with a migration note showing the ratified fix spellings keep working. Both are honest, complete designs after this pass.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested whether place projection opens a new alias window and whether the missing-key stop adds a failure class; both match today's bare-read window and stop. B survives; recommendation unchanged.

decisions.title: What invalid bytes mean when they become text
decisions.gist: Whether decoding invalid UTF-8 fails loudly by default or silently substitutes replacement characters.
decisions.lesson: Turning bytes into a String meets invalid data: a stray 0xFF, a cut-off multibyte character. Today Jet silently swaps each bad sequence for the replacement character � and reports nothing. The hex decoder also silently ignores surrounding whitespace. Data changes shape with no signal and no written rule. This choice picks the default and names the explicit alternative. A sibling policy ballot, D-STDLIB-OPTPARAM1 on card #2322, decides the standing rule for variant spellings; option D below shows this surface in that shape and names its cost.
decisions.story: Priya ingests customer CSV exports from an old system that mislabels its encoding. Jet decodes the bytes, silently replaces every accented name with �, and her deduplication merges 'García' and 'Garcés' into the same mangled key. The corrupted names reach production before anyone sees an error.

options.name: Strict by default, lossy by name
options.detail: String.from_bytes returns a failure on the first invalid sequence, naming its byte offset. A sibling, String.from_bytes_lossy, does today's replacement on purpose and says so in its name. Dirty data cannot change shape unless the program either handles the failure or spells 'lossy'. Hex and base64 decoders follow the same rule: exact input or a loud failure.
options.technical: from_bytes: Bytes -> String!DecodeError; the error carries offset and byte. from_bytes_lossy: Bytes -> String, U+FFFD per Unicode substitution of maximal subparts. hex.decode rejects whitespace and odd length. One Prelude implementation per I9; registered diagnostic text snapshotted per I4.

options.name: Lossy by default, strict by name
options.detail: Today's replacement behavior becomes the documented default: decoding never fails, and bad sequences become �. A named strict variant returns a failure for callers that need exactness. Beginner code never meets a decode error, but silent shape change stays the default, which the owner's zero-tolerance rule calls fatal.
options.technical: from_bytes stays total with documented U+FFFD semantics; from_bytes_strict returns String!DecodeError. Hex keeps whitespace trimming, documented.
options.code:
text :: String.from_bytes(raw)          // never fails, may substitute
exact :: String.from_bytes_strict(raw)?  // loud

options.name: Strict only
options.detail: One function, always a failure on invalid input. Programs that want replacement write the loop themselves. Smallest surface, but real-world dirty data makes every caller re-implement the same lossy loop, and most will do it worse.
options.technical: from_bytes: Bytes -> String!DecodeError. No lossy sibling.
options.code: text :: String.from_bytes(raw)?  // the only path

options.name: One from_bytes with a defaulted mode option
options.detail: One method: from_bytes(raw, mode) with .Strict as the default and .Lossy as the named option. To fit one signature both modes must share one result type, so even lossy calls return a failure-typed String that never actually fails. One name to find, but the type no longer proves that lossy cannot fail — the cost of unifying modes that change the result shape.
options.technical: fn from_bytes(raw: Bytes, mode: DecodeMode{.Strict}) String!DecodeError; enum DecodeMode { Strict Lossy }. Lossy never returns the failure arm. This is the exact boundary case the #2322 policy's sibling clause exists for.
options.code:
text :: String.from_bytes(raw)?                 // strict default
text :: String.from_bytes(raw, mode: .Lossy)?   // the ? never fires

comparisons.note: Strict by default; substitution is an explicit opt-in argument.
No default at all: the caller must pick the strict or the lossy function by name.
Conversion never fails and silently substitutes; a known source of quiet corruption bugs.

recommendation.why: A matches the project's zero-tolerance rule for silent data change: the default is exact or loud, and the lossy path exists, works, and announces itself in its own name. Both personas are served — beginners get a safe default with a one-line fallback, and experts get the exact behavior they spell.

whyNot.reason: B keeps silent shape change as the default, which is the exact fatal class this sweep exists to remove; documenting a silent default does not make it loud.
C removes the safe named escape and pushes every real-world program to hand-roll a worse lossy loop.
D forces the lossy mode to wear a failure type it can never produce; modes that change the result shape are the policy's own stated boundary for keeping siblings.

recommendation.tradeoff: A makes quick scripts over dirty data one line longer. That line is the entire point: it is where the program admits the data may change shape.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared strict-default, lossy-default, and strict-only, and recommended strict-default with a named lossy sibling because silent substitution is the fatal class.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a substitution-count return, a mode flag, and a streaming decoder. The count folded into A's error detail; the flag makes one spelling mean two things; streaming waits for a streaming reader.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of A and B (strict in checked builds, lossy in release) was drafted and discarded immediately: it is a tier-divergence machine, the exact I9 breach this sweep kept finding.
reviewPasses.cooperative: B was strengthened with documentation and a strict sibling, making it a coherent Go-style design; C was strengthened with a worked fallback recipe. Both remain honest options.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass checked caller breakage and beginner weight. No callers exist because from_bytes compiles nowhere today (#2306), and the one-line fallback keeps beginner code short, so A survives. A later policy pass added option D and found it blunts the type-level guarantee, reinforcing A.

decisions.title: How bitwise OR is written in an expression
decisions.gist: Whether x | y becomes a legal expression, stays assign-only, or the assign form is retired too.
decisions.lesson: Jet ships bitwise AND (&), XOR (~|), NOT (!), and shifts as expressions, and even ships the OR-assign form x |= y — but the expression x | y does not parse. OR is the only bit operation you cannot write in a formula. The pipe character already has a ratified job in type position (union types), which is why expression position was left empty.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a permissions module. He writes flags :: READ | WRITE and gets a parse error pointing at the pipe. He discovers flags |= WRITE works, so he writes a temporary variable and two statements for every mask he builds, and his port fills with noise the original did not have.

options.name: Admit infix | in value position
options.detail: x | y parses as bitwise OR wherever a value is expected. Type position keeps its ratified union meaning; the two positions are grammatically distinct. The surface becomes complete: every bit operation has an expression form and an assign form.
options.technical: Add BinOp::BitOr (already in the AST, spelled |) to the value-expression grammar. Precedence pins (a | b) == c — the | tier sits above comparisons, avoiding the C trap. Parser disambiguates by position exactly as D-UNIONTYPE1 anticipated. Syntax.rs decision row per I7; fixtures both tiers.
options.code:
mask :: READ | WRITE | EXEC
keep :: (bits & !mask_out) | forced_on

options.name: Assign form retired; OR becomes a named method
options.detail: Remove the stranded x |= y and make OR a named method, so the pipe means union types and nothing else. Consistent, but it demotes one of the four basic bit operations to a method while &, ~|, <<, >> stay operators — a new asymmetry replacing the old one.
options.technical: Retire |= (S17 row update, owner-only), add Int.bit_or. Migration: mechanical rewrite of in-repo |= uses.
options.code: mask :: read.bit_or(write).bit_or(exec)

options.name: Keep today's shape, but write it down
options.detail: x |= y stays, x | y stays illegal, and the spec says why (pipe is reserved for union types). Zero parser work, but the asymmetry every porter trips on becomes permanent documented law.
options.technical: Spec note plus an E0003 fix-text at a pipe in value position suggesting the |= two-step, or ~| where XOR was meant.
options.code:
mask := READ
mask |= WRITE   // the documented spelling

comparisons.note: Every mainstream language spells bitwise OR as infix |; ports and examples assume it.
The XOR precedent: when ^ was taken by power, XOR got a new operator (~|) rather than a method — operators stayed operators.

recommendation.why: A completes the operator family with the spelling every peer language and every porter already assumes, and the value/type position split is exactly the disambiguation D-UNIONTYPE1 already relies on. The assign form |= stops being a stranded exception.

whyNot.reason: B solves the asymmetry by amputating: one of four basic bit operations becomes a method chain while its three siblings stay operators, and every mask expression reads worse.
C freezes a trap as law; documentation does not stop the parse error every porter hits first.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts a small permanent parser duty: value-position and type-position pipes must stay unambiguous as the grammar grows. Today's grammar already makes that split, so the cost is vigilance, not redesign.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared admitting infix |, method-only OR, and documented status quo, recommending infix | because it completes the operator family with the universal spelling.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a fourth spelling: a new tilde-family operator for OR, leaving pipe untouched. Rejected as a menu entry: it invents a nonstandard glyph for the one operation where every language agrees, the opposite of the ~| case where ^ was genuinely taken.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of A and C (admit | only inside parentheses) was drafted and discarded: position-dependent legality is harder to teach than either pole.
reviewPasses.cooperative: B was strengthened with its real virtue — the pipe means exactly one thing forever — and C with a concrete E0003 fix-text improvement that ships value either way.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass found one real flaw: naive C precedence would parse a | b == c as a | (b == c). Repaired by pinning the | tier above comparisons; A survives with that repair.

decisions.title: Freestanding profile selection migration
decisions.gist: How old freestanding builds move to typed profiles.
decisions.lesson: A typed profile carries board assumptions. A hosted single-file program should remain free of profile syntax. The old flag still exists in current callers, so migration needs one rule.
decisions.story: Tess maintains sensor firmware and a hosted command-line tool. Her firmware scripts use `--freestanding`, while new projects use typed profile modules.
decisions.detail: Choose migration behavior only. The typed profile law, `#Target` marker law, and no-`no_std` law are already ratified.

options.name: Compatibility alias with migration notice
options.detail: Keep `--freestanding` as a temporary alias for a canonical no-OS profile selection. New source uses typed profiles. Old scripts keep working while the tool teaches the replacement.
options.technical: `targets:` selects the typed profile. `#Target(...)` remains the source partition marker under D-MARK-TARGET1 and does not become a second profile selector. The alias supplies no providers and cannot bypass profile validation.
options.code:
$ jet build firmware --freestanding
notice: `--freestanding` is a compatibility alias
fix: select `targets.firmware` with a typed no-OS profile
built: firmware

options.name: Retire the flag immediately
options.detail: Reject `--freestanding` and require a named typed profile now. The surface becomes smaller at once, but existing firmware scripts stop before their profile facts can be migrated.
options.technical: The error must name the typed profile route. No second `no_std` flag is added.
options.code:
$ jet build firmware --freestanding
Error: `--freestanding` is retired
Fix: declare a typed target profile and select it through `targets:`

comparisons.note: Rust uses target and no-std conventions, but Jet already ratified typed target profiles and no `no_std` flag.
Zig selects a target triple while allocator choice remains explicit in code.

recommendation.why: A protects existing callers without preserving two semantic models. The alias can disappear after an adoption ratchet reaches zero.

whyNot.reason: B breaks current callers before they can move their board facts into typed profiles.

recommendation.tradeoff: The compiler carries one temporary alias and one migration message. It never carries a second target or allocator model.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a temporary alias with immediate retirement.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a second no-OS flag and a board file. Both duplicated the typed profile surface and were removed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid keeps the alias only as a resolver to typed profiles. It adds no parallel provider or validation path.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The retirement option now gives a direct profile fix and preserves the no-flag rule.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked selector conflicts, hosted single files, and stale aliases; the acceptance terms reject silent overrides.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose alias or immediate retirement. Confirm that typed profiles remain canonical, `#Target(...)` remains a marker, no `no_std` flag is added, conflicts are explicit, and migration has an adoption ratchet. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-LAYER1 and D-FREESTAND-FACTS1.

decisions.title: Prelude partition boundary
decisions.gist: Where core, alloc, and hosted Prelude parts stop.
decisions.lesson: The Prelude mixes pure values, allocation, operating-system calls, and report rendering. A freestanding build needs a transitive closure, not a short import list.
decisions.story: Maya writes a packet decoder for a board with no heap. She wants fixed byte operations and structural checks, but not an accidental text formatter or file helper.
decisions.detail: Choose the semantic boundary for the emitted Prelude closure. The one-source and one-tier-meaning laws remain fixed.

options.name: Strict semantic split by allocation and OS
options.detail: Keep allocation-free carriers and operations in Core. Put owned strings, vectors, maps, and allocating encoders in Alloc. Put OS adapters in Hosted. This gives the smallest useful no-heap closure.
options.technical: Core contains scalar and fixed-value operations, allocation-free structural equality, the generic Outcome carrier when its type arguments fit, structural debug traversal, and error discriminants. Alloc contains owned `String`/`Vec`/map operations, encoders returning owned values, owned Path values, materialized debug text, and allocated report text. Hosted contains filesystem, network, process, terminal, ambient OS time, and OS scheduler adapters. Outcome allocation, thread-local state, and report sink are separate implementation parts with unchanged semantics.
options.code:
module board.sensor_v1 {
    target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4
    allocator: board.none
}

bytes :: [1, 2, 3]
text :: encoding.hex(bytes)
Error: `encoding.hex` returns owned text and requires `alloc`

options.name: Coarse whole-module promotion
options.detail: Keep each Core module intact and promote a module when any helper allocates or touches the OS. This is easy to classify, but useful pure operations inherit the largest requirement.
options.technical: `core.encoding`, `core.files`, `core.term`, and mixed Outcome or debug modules move as whole units. No helper-level closure table is needed.

options.name: Per-call target-specialized parts
options.detail: Split each callable by its exact allocation and provider needs. This maximizes Core coverage, but makes the registry and audit explain many small parts that can change independently.
options.technical: Every generated Prelude callable carries a target requirement. The same public module may contain Core, Alloc, and Hosted callables without a stable module-level classification.
options.code:
bytes :: [1, 2, 3]
text :: encoding.hex(bytes)  // call-specific target requirement
checksum :: encoding.crc32(bytes)  // a different requirement

comparisons.note: Rust uses core, alloc, and std as separate library layers.
Zig passes allocators through APIs and keeps OS access in standard-library modules.
comparisons.code:
const bytes = try allocator.alloc(u8, n);
const file = try std.fs.cwd().openFile(path, .{});

comparisons.note: Go compiles a broad runtime into ordinary binaries, which hides freestanding closure costs.

recommendation.why: A gives a board the largest honest Core subset without inventing a second semantic Prelude. It makes allocation and OS edges visible in the closure.

whyNot.reason: B promotes pure helpers with unrelated hosted or allocation-heavy siblings, shrinking useful freestanding code.
C creates unstable fine-grained classifications and a larger audit surface for one public module.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires a maintained part ledger. The ledger is the price of a small beginner-safe Core closure and one semantic source.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared strict semantic, whole-module, and per-call partitioning.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested an all-hosted Prelude and a public target annotation on every function. Both added ceremony or destroyed the useful Core closure.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The strongest hybrid keeps strict semantic parts while allowing module-level audit views. It remains Option A rather than a second partition rule.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The coarse option now states its clarity benefit and its real loss of pure coverage.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked mixed Outcome, owned debug text, and transitive helpers; the acceptance list assigns each boundary explicitly.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose strict semantic, coarse module, or per-call partitioning. Confirm the transitive closure, Core and Alloc ownership, Hosted adapters, Outcome split, and one-source tier parity. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-LAYER1, D-FREESTAND-ADMIT1, D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, and D-FREESTAND-ALLOCAPI1.

decisions.title: Target fact vocabulary
decisions.gist: Which typed facts name available target services?
decisions.lesson: A target fact states what the selected machine provides. An effect states what code may do. An Authority value states which rights a scope holds.
decisions.story: Rina ports a packet service from Linux to a board. The board has a UART and timer, but no filesystem or socket stack. She needs the compiler to name each difference without hiding it in a triple.
decisions.detail: Choose the typed vocabulary for machine availability. Effects and Authority remain separate semantic rights under current law.

options.name: Closed typed profile fields with provider identities
options.detail: Recommended. A closed fact menu names machine services. Each present fact names a provider and provenance. Effects and Authority continue to describe permission and semantic use.
options.technical: The fact menu covers runtime layer, allocator, startup entry, vector table, panic report, memory, linker, IO read/write, wall and monotonic time, zone data, and sleep. It also covers crypto entropy, scheduler, sockets, filesystem, browser DOM, GPU, FFI, MMIO, and volatile access. Each fact is registered, typed, nameable, and auditable. Provider identity and digest are required when present. Missing facts stay explicit.

options.name: Provider handles only
options.detail: Profiles name providers, and sema discovers their services from provider interfaces. This reduces profile fields, but a reader must inspect each provider to learn which fact is missing.
options.technical: Provider interfaces must expose a typed service set and stable digest. Unknown provider services cannot satisfy admission. The profile does not list each service directly.

options.name: Use effects and Authority for availability
options.detail: Target profiles grant existing effect and Authority paths such as IO.Write and Time. This uses one rights tree, but it conflates permission with physical provision.
options.technical: Target facts become positive rights. A profile would grant roots that currently describe code effects. This risks making a granted right look like a board implementation.

comparisons.note: Rust combines target configuration, cfg predicates, allocator choice, and platform traits.
Zig exposes target data and explicit allocators, while platform interfaces remain ordinary values.
comparisons.code:
const target = builtin.target;
const allocator = board_allocator();

comparisons.note: WASI worlds list imports and exports that a host must provide.

recommendation.why: A makes the machine contract visible to beginners and experts. It prevents a triple from silently claiming a UART, clock, entropy source, or browser.

whyNot.reason: B hides the missing service behind provider inspection and weakens the target dossier.
C confuses permission to use a service with the fact that hardware supplies it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The closed menu grows through ballots. That governance cost is safer than silently accepting an unknown provider claim.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared closed profile fields, provider discovery, and rights-based availability.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested arbitrary fact maps and target-triple inference. Both were rejected because unknown values would weaken admission.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid keeps provider identities inside closed typed fields. Provider interfaces may supply details, but only registered facts affect admission.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The provider-only option now exposes stable service sets and digests, making its inspection benefit concrete.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked fact growth, effect conflation, and triple inference; the closed registry and separate rights model repair those risks.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose closed typed fields, provider-only discovery, or rights-based availability. Confirm one registered fact plane, explicit absence, provider identity and provenance, no triple inference, and separate effects and Authority. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-SELECT1 and D-FREESTAND-ADMIT1.

decisions.title: Core owned-output policy
decisions.gist: How no-heap Core APIs handle owned text and vectors.
decisions.lesson: The allocator and failure contracts are already ratified. One remaining choice is the boundary for Core APIs that return owned `String` or `Vec` values.
decisions.story: Maya writes a no-heap decoder. She wants a checksum in Core, but she also wants a convenient text encoder for hosted tools. The two results have different storage needs.
decisions.detail: Choose the Core result boundary only. One program allocator, fixed backing, and `AllocError` semantics remain ratified.

options.name: Owned results belong to Alloc
options.detail: Recommended. Core APIs return fixed values, views, or caller-owned buffers. APIs that create owned `String` or `Vec` live in Alloc. This keeps Core strictly heap-free.
options.technical: D-ALLOC-PROGRAM1=A keeps one typed program allocator fact. D-FIXED-BACKING1=A keeps lexical `Fixed.new` and borrowed `Fixed.over` with no heap fallback. D-ALLOCFAIL1=A gives `try_` operations `T ! AllocError`; plain allocation keeps its hosted abort default.
options.code:
module board.sensor_v1 {
    target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4
    allocator: board.none
}

encoded :: core.encoding.hex(bytes)
Error: owned text requires `alloc`
Fix: use a fixed-output Core operation, or select an Alloc profile

options.name: Caller-buffer Core operations
options.detail: Keep selected encoders and formatters available in Core by requiring caller-owned fixed storage. Alloc provides convenience wrappers that return owned values. This preserves more no-heap functionality, but adds buffer sizing and overflow handling.
options.technical: Core operations accept genuine fixed-size storage and return a count or a typed size error. They never use a hidden allocator. Alloc wrappers use the single program allocator and the existing `AllocError` family.

comparisons.note: Rust keeps allocation-free core APIs separate from alloc collections and string builders.
Zig commonly passes an allocator or caller-owned buffer to APIs.
C library APIs often expose caller buffers and explicit lengths.
comparisons.code: int snprintf(char *dst, size_t n, const char *fmt, ...);

recommendation.why: A keeps the Core boundary simple. Owned results have one obvious home, while fixed-output needs remain possible through later Core APIs.

whyNot.reason: B preserves more Core calls but charges every caller for capacity, sizing, and overflow details.

recommendation.tradeoff: No-heap users move owned encoders to Alloc or use fixed buffers. The boundary is visible and never hides a heap call.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared alloc-only owned results with caller-buffer Core operations.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested hidden target allocators and arena-only ownership. Hidden allocators violate the Core layer, and arenas remain the existing scoped mechanism.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid keeps Option A as the public boundary and permits Option B's fixed-buffer forms as explicit APIs, not a second owned-result rule.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The caller-buffer option now states its useful checksum and formatter cases with explicit sizing errors.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked hidden allocation, fixed-buffer escape, and tier drift; the locked allocator and failure laws block each failure.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose Alloc-only owned results or explicit caller-buffer Core forms. Confirm one program allocator, fixed backing without heap fallback, `T ! AllocError`, plain hosted abort behavior, and tier parity. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-LAYER1, D-FREESTAND-PRELUDE1, and D-FREESTAND-FACTS1.

decisions.title: Output and panic sinks
decisions.gist: How output and reports reach targets without standard streams.
decisions.lesson: `print`, `input`, terminal reports, and panic reports assume a normal host. A board needs an explicit path for bytes, input, and failure reports.
decisions.story: Maya deploys a sensor that has a UART but no stdout. A malformed packet must be reported, and normal output must keep its call order.
decisions.detail: Choose the target output and panic provider contract. Report identity and target-native failure routing remain ratified.

options.name: Reject missing sinks at sema
options.detail: A program may use output, input, terminal, or panic reports only when the target declares the needed sink. Pure code still builds. Boards without a sink lose useful report paths.
options.technical: Reachable `print`, `eprint`, `input`, terminal, and report operations require their corresponding target facts. Missing facts are compile diagnostics. Hosted defaults remain hidden.

options.name: Typed byte and report providers
options.detail: Recommended. Targets declare typed byte sources and sinks. The shared Prelude serializes output, maps input failure to `IOError`, and sends structured reports to a panic-capable sink.
options.technical: `IO.Read` and `IO.Write` are target facts. `Panic.Report` is required when a reachable panic or runtime stop exists. A sink receives the canonical report record or its canonical bytes. Writes preserve Prelude call order. Sink failure enters the registered runtime failure path; no bytes are silently dropped.
options.code:
module board.sensor_v1 {
    target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4
    io_write: board.uart_tx
    io_read: board.uart_rx
    panic_report: board.report_uart
}

print("packet ready")
line :: input("command") !IOError

options.name: Bounded report and output buffer
options.detail: Targets provide fixed storage instead of a live stream. Output and reports remain available for later inspection or flush, but finite capacity creates a visible overflow boundary.
options.technical: The profile declares a fixed backing size. Calls append complete frames in order. Overflow is a registered stop; truncation and silent discard are forbidden. A host adapter may drain the buffer without changing report meaning.

comparisons.note: Embedded Rust commonly passes a `Write` implementation or uses a panic handler.
Zig exposes writers and readers as explicit interfaces.
Board logging and queues are supplied by the board port, not by the CPU triple alone.

recommendation.why: B gives firmware a real output path while keeping the target contract explicit. It lets hosted, board, and web adapters share one Prelude report.

whyNot.reason: A makes a no-stream board safe but removes useful diagnostics when a UART or equivalent sink exists.
C makes every output path manage finite storage and adds flush lifecycle semantics that a typed sink already supplies.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every target that reaches output or panic must name a provider. That requirement prevents silent loss and makes the report path auditable.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared sema rejection, typed providers, and fixed buffering.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested silent discard and host-only logging. Both were rejected because they lose reports or hide target assumptions.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid keeps typed providers as the semantic choice. A fixed buffer may implement that provider, but it is not a second report model.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The rejection option now preserves pure programs and gives an exact missing-sink fix.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked interleaving, report recursion, sink failure, and buffer overflow; ordering and complete-frame rules repair them.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose sema rejection, typed byte and report providers, or bounded buffers. Confirm read and write facts, panic reporting, call order, complete frames, provider failure reports, no silent discard, and one report renderer. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, D-FREESTAND-PRELUDE1, D-FREESTAND-DIAG1, and D-RTFAIL1.

decisions.title: Time providers on freestanding targets
decisions.gist: Which time operations need a target provider?
decisions.lesson: Calendar arithmetic can be pure. Wall time, monotonic measurement, zone data, and sleeping need different services. One clock value cannot honestly stand in for all of them.
decisions.story: Rina schedules sensor samples and measures radio latency. Her board has a timer but no calendar database or wall clock.
decisions.inWild:
duration :: Duration.seconds(5)
clock :: Clock.new(0)
wall :: Clock.system().now()
instant :: Instant.now()
time.sleep(duration)
// The target profile must distinguish these operations.
decisions.detail: Choose the target time-provider matrix. Pure calendar, Duration, deterministic injection, and distinct time types remain fixed by current law.

options.name: Separate pure, injected, and ambient provider facts
options.detail: Recommended. Pure calendar and duration operations need no provider. Injected Clock is deterministic. Wall, monotonic, zone data, and sleep each require their own declared service.
options.technical: Pure `Duration`, `Period`, calendar arithmetic, and parsing remain provider-free. D-DET1 injected `Clock` and `Rng` remain reproducible and do not read the machine. Ambient wall time requires `Time.Wall`. `Instant` requires `Time.Monotonic`. Named zones require `Time.ZoneData`. Sleep requires `Time.Sleep` plus the scheduler contract.
options.code:
duration :: Duration.seconds(5)
clock :: Clock.new(0)
clock.wait(duration)       // deterministic, no target clock
wall :: Clock.system().now()
Error: `Clock.system` needs Time.Wall

options.name: One composite clock provider
options.detail: Require one target Clock provider for wall time, monotonic time, zone data, and sleep. This is simple to explain, but a board with only a timer must provide unrelated services.
options.technical: The composite provider must state which suboperations it supports. Unsupported suboperations still produce a target diagnostic, so the apparent single fact contains a hidden matrix.

options.name: No ambient time in freestanding profiles
options.detail: Allow pure calendar work and injected Clock only. Freestanding profiles reject wall time, monotonic measurement, zones, and sleep, even when a board could supply them. This keeps the first profile small but blocks useful firmware.
options.technical: The no-ambient rule is a profile-wide prohibition. A later target decision would be needed to admit a real timer or zone provider.
options.code:
duration :: Duration.seconds(5)
clock :: Clock.new(0)
wall :: Clock.system().now()
Error: ambient time is unavailable in this freestanding profile

comparisons.note: Rust separates `Duration`, `Instant`, `SystemTime`, and timezone crates.
comparisons.code:
let elapsed = start.elapsed();
let wall = SystemTime::now();

comparisons.note: Zig separates monotonic, timestamp, and sleep interfaces.
Swift uses distinct clocks and calendar values.

recommendation.why: A preserves the ratified distinct time types and lets each target provide only what it owns. It keeps deterministic tests free from host time.

whyNot.reason: B overstates what a board clock provides and hides the missing subservice inside one provider name.
C discards valid monotonic and timer hardware that firmware needs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Profiles contain several time facts. The extra rows prevent a timer from pretending to be a calendar, zone database, or sleep scheduler.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a separate provider matrix, one composite clock, and no ambient freestanding time.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested host tzdata discovery and target-triple clock inference. Both were rejected because they hide provenance or provider absence.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The composite option's supported-subservice matrix was folded into Option A's explicit facts.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The no-ambient option now states its useful deterministic path and its firmware cost.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked fake epochs, zone leakage, timer-only boards, and sleep cancellation; explicit facts and no fallback repair them.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose separate facts, one composite clock, or no ambient freestanding time. Confirm pure and injected operations, wall and monotonic facts, zone data, sleep and scheduler linkage, missing-provider diagnostics, no fallbacks, and tier parity. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, D-FREESTAND-SINK1, D-FREESTAND-SCHED1, D-TIME-CALENDAR1, and D-DET1.

decisions.title: Freestanding scheduler model
decisions.gist: Which scheduler can a freestanding target expose?
decisions.lesson: The task model already defines groups, channels, cancellation, deadlines, and task failure. A freestanding target still needs a scheduler that honors those meanings without OS threads.
decisions.story: Maya runs packet work and periodic sampling on a board. She may have cooperative callbacks, timer interrupts, or a board runtime, but no operating-system thread pool.
decisions.detail: Choose the freestanding scheduler provider model. Task vocabulary, failure values, cancellation points, and tier parity remain ratified.

options.name: Profile-selected scheduler provider
options.detail: Recommended. A target selects cooperative, interrupt-driven, board-runtime, or no-scheduler mode. Each provider implements the same task contract and declares its wait and I/O behavior.
options.technical: D-TASKRUNTIME1=A, D-CONC-SCHED1=A, D-CONC-FAIL1=A, and D-CANCELMODEL1=C remain fixed. A provider must define task launch, wait points, cancellation, deadlines, blocking I/O, and cleanup. A no-scheduler profile rejects task APIs.
options.code:
module board.sensor_v1 {
    target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4
    scheduler: board.cooperative
    timer: board.systick
}

job :: tasks.spawn(sample_packet)
result :: job.join() !TaskFailure

options.name: Cooperative scheduling only
options.detail: Use explicit cooperative waits for every freestanding task. This is easy to simulate and audit, but it cannot directly model interrupt-driven work or board supervisor runtimes.
options.technical: Tasks yield at channel, timer, join, and I/O waits. A board must turn interrupts into queued events before Jet code runs.

options.name: Interrupt or board runtime only
options.detail: Use a board scheduler or interrupt dispatcher as the required task provider. Hardware integration is direct, but host simulation and simple boards need a larger provider.
options.technical: The provider owns ISR boundaries, queueing, timer delivery, cancellation, and cleanup. Direct user code in an interrupt remains prohibited unless separately typed and audited.

options.name: No scheduler in freestanding profiles
options.detail: Reject tasks, channels, timers, and blocking waits on no-OS targets. Synchronous Core code remains available. This is smallest, but it removes structured concurrency from firmware.
options.technical: Sema reports a missing Scheduler fact for every reachable task or wait operation. Raw polling is not an implicit replacement.

comparisons.note: FreeRTOS supplies a board scheduler and interrupt-to-task boundary.
Rust async code needs an executor, which may be cooperative or interrupt-backed.
Go hides an OS-thread-backed scheduler behind goroutines.

recommendation.why: A keeps one task meaning while allowing each board to choose the smallest honest runtime. It makes no-scheduler targets safe and explicit.

whyNot.reason: B cannot express boards whose work arrives through interrupt or supervisor queues.
C makes host simulation and small synchronous boards pay for a hardware runtime.
D gives up structured firmware concurrency even when a board can provide it safely.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every scheduler provider must preserve one cancellation and wait contract. The provider choice becomes visible in the target dossier.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared a selectable provider, cooperative-only, board-runtime-only, and no-scheduler model.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested async-await syntax and hidden polling. Both add a second task model or hide blocking behavior, so they were excluded.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The provider option absorbs cooperative and board implementations while preserving one task and failure contract.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative-only option now states its interrupt queue boundary and simulation benefit.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked ISR reentrancy, cancellation during I/O, deadline waits, and busy polling; provider obligations close each gap.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose a profile-selected provider, cooperative-only, board-runtime-only, or no scheduler. Confirm one task and failure contract, wait-point cancellation, interrupt boundaries, blocking I/O behavior, no busy polling, dossier identity, and tier parity. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, D-FREESTAND-TIME1, D-FREESTAND-TIER1, and D-FREESTAND-SINK1.

decisions.title: Startup and linker contract
decisions.gist: Which typed facts own startup and low-level target wiring?
decisions.lesson: Memory, linker provenance, allocator, panic, MMIO, and volatile rules already have ratified homes. Startup entry, vector data, and provider ownership still need one contract.
decisions.story: Tess boots a Cortex-M image. The board needs a reset symbol, vector table, ABI, memory map, panic route, and UART region before generated code can run.
decisions.inWild:
module board.sensor_v1 {
    target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4
    entry: reset
    vector: board.vector_table
    startup: board.startup
    linker: board.linker.generated
    memory: board.memory
    allocator: board.fixed
    panic: board.abort
}
decisions.detail: Choose startup and provider ownership. Memory, linker generation and hashes, allocator, panic, MMIO, volatile, and audit laws remain fixed.

options.name: Typed startup provider with generated glue
options.detail: Recommended. The profile names entry, vectors, ABI, and a startup provider. Jet generates startup glue and linker input from typed facts, while expert file overrides remain hashed.
