options.technical: D-TARGET-MEMORY1=A, D-TARGET-LINKER1=A, D-TARGET-ALLOC1=A, D-TARGET-AUDIT1=A, and D-FLAGSHIP-MMIO1=A stay fixed. Startup provider identity, entry symbol, vector table, ABI, and placement are typed facts. C ABI and alternate conventions follow D-CABI-PLATFORM1=A. Raw pointer, volatile, MMIO, and FFI use require `#Unsafe` under S58.
options.code:
module board.sensor_v1 {
    target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4
    startup: board.cortex_m4.startup
    entry: reset
    vector: board.cortex_m4.vectors
    linker: board.linker.generated
    memory: board.memory
}

options.name: Hashed user startup artifacts
options.detail: Experts supply startup assembly or C and a linker file. Jet validates hashes, ABI declarations, symbols, and memory facts. This gives vendor control, but the profile explains less generated intent.
options.technical: `startup` and `linker` accept file inputs only with explicit hashes and provenance. The target dossier records exact files. The generated Jet Prelude still uses the same semantic providers.

options.name: Pinned external board package
options.detail: A board package owns startup and vector implementation. The profile pins its package identity and digest, while Jet validates the typed interface. This supports vendor ecosystems, but adds a package boundary to boot trust.
options.technical: The package must expose typed entry, vector, ABI, memory, panic, and provider facts. Its generated artifacts enter the target cache key and dossier. No package may add a second task or Prelude meaning.

comparisons.note: Rust commonly combines `#[entry]`, a vector table, a linker script, and a panic handler.
Zig exposes target-specific startup and linker controls through build configuration.
CMSIS supplies vendor startup files and vector tables as target artifacts.

recommendation.why: A keeps boot assumptions typed and auditable while still allowing existing hashed file overrides. Generated glue gives beginners a coherent path.

whyNot.reason: B makes vendor files the primary semantic source and weakens the profile's readable target contract.
C adds a boot package trust boundary before its provider interface and update law exist.

recommendation.tradeoff: Vendor-specific startup providers need typed adapters. The target dossier records the provider, so boot trust stays inspectable.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared typed generated startup, hashed user artifacts, and pinned board packages.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested toolchain defaults and triple-derived startup. They were excluded because triples cannot imply providers.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The provider option keeps hashed file overrides and permits pinned board packages as providers, without changing the semantic contract.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The file option now states exact symbol, ABI, hash, and dossier obligations.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked vector mismatch, stale linker files, unsafe leakage, and boot trust; pre-codegen validation and provenance repair them.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose typed generated startup, hashed user artifacts, or a pinned board package. Confirm entry, vectors, ABI, memory and linker law, provider provenance, pre-codegen validation, `#Unsafe`, dossier identity, and one semantic Prelude. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-SELECT1, D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, D-FREESTAND-TIER1, D-FREESTAND-ARTIFACT1, and D-CABI-PLATFORM1.

decisions.title: Wasm target profile split
decisions.gist: How browser, WASI, and no-OS Wasm profiles differ.
decisions.lesson: Browser Wasm has a DOM and JavaScript boundary. WASI has sockets and files through a component host. No-OS Wasm has neither unless a profile supplies it.
decisions.story: Priya ships a browser dashboard and a WASI service. A third team wants a deterministic no-OS Wasm module with no browser or WASI assumptions.
decisions.detail: Choose the no-OS Wasm grouping only. Browser and WASI server contracts are ratified and must not be reopened.

options.name: Separate browser, WASI, and no-OS profiles
options.detail: Recommended. Keep three explicit profile identities. Browser uses DOM and JavaScript providers. WASI uses sockets, files, and its component host. No-OS Wasm names only its own providers.
options.technical: D-WASM1=A owns browser effect inference and module target controls. D-WASISRV1=A makes `wasm32-wasip2` a first-class server target with `wasi:sockets`, no AOT-only exception, and shared network Prelude semantics. No-OS Wasm receives no browser or WASI provider implicitly.

options.name: One Wasm profile with provider variants
options.detail: Use one user-facing Wasm family and choose browser, WASI, or no-OS providers inside it. This reduces profile names, but a generic Wasm target can hide incompatible host boundaries.
options.technical: The profile identity must still include the exact triple and provider set. Browser, WASI, and no-OS calls remain sema-distinct. This option changes the selection surface, not the provider contract.

options.name: Defer no-OS Wasm
options.detail: Keep the ratified browser and WASI targets. Record no-OS Wasm as unsupported until a startup, allocator, output, and execution contract exists. This avoids a partial profile, but delays deterministic Wasm firmware.
options.technical: Browser and WASI remain governed by D-WASM1 and D-WASISRV1. No-OS Wasm receives a clear unavailable-target diagnostic rather than a preview carve-out.
options.code:
$ jet build firmware --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown
Error: no-OS Wasm is not a supported target profile
Fix: choose the browser profile or the WASI server profile

comparisons.note: Browser Wasm uses JavaScript bindings and DOM APIs, not WASI sockets.
WASI Preview 2 defines component worlds and socket imports for server hosts.
TinyGo separates WebAssembly browser, WASI, and bare-metal targets.

recommendation.why: A makes each host boundary visible and prevents browser or WASI services from leaking into no-OS Wasm. It matches the two ratified web target contracts.

whyNot.reason: B makes a generic Wasm label carry three incompatible startup and host models.
C delays a useful no-OS target instead of defining its provider boundary explicitly.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users see three profile names. The names prevent a target triple or generic Wasm label from implying the wrong host.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared separate profiles, one provider-family profile, and no-OS deferral.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a browser-plus-WASI mixed profile and a preview no-OS target. Both hide or normalize incompatible host boundaries.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The provider-family option now requires exact triple and provider identity, while the recommendation keeps separate profile names.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The deferral option states a useful unavailable-target message and preserves the two ratified web targets.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked DOM leakage, WASI socket assumptions, allocator identity, and tier exceptions; separate profiles and explicit facts close them.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose separate profiles, one Wasm provider family, or no-OS deferral. Confirm browser and WASI laws stay closed, no-OS providers are explicit, profile identity includes exact inputs, mixed hosts are rejected, and all applicable tiers share one Prelude. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, D-FREESTAND-SINK1, D-FREESTAND-START1, D-FREESTAND-TIER1, D-WASM1, and D-WASISRV1.

decisions.title: Prelude artifact and cache identity
decisions.gist: How target Prelude artifacts are keyed and audited.
decisions.lesson: A target-specific Prelude may be compiled from a source closure or cached as a linked artifact. The cache must never turn packaging into a second semantic implementation.
decisions.story: Maria builds firmware for two boards and runs the same program in the interpreter and AOT compiler. She wants reuse, but a cache hit must prove it used the same target facts and Prelude closure.
decisions.detail: Choose target Prelude packaging and cache authority. The existing explainable action-cache law remains the base identity contract.

options.name: Compile only the selected source closure
options.detail: Each target artifact compiles its selected Prelude source closure directly. This is transparent and simple, but repeats compilation when the closure is unchanged.
options.technical: The closure digest still enters the normal action key. No separately linked target Prelude artifact is accepted as a semantic input.
options.code:
prelude.kind = "source-closure"
prelude.key = hash(closure, target_facts, providers, linker, tier)

options.name: Separately linked target Prelude artifact
options.detail: The target uses a separately linked Prelude artifact as its normal input. This can reuse work, but the artifact must carry complete semantic identity or it can hide a stale provider.
options.technical: The artifact key includes the canonical source closure, target facts, provider identities, linker inputs, tier parity facts, compiler ABI, rustc identity, profile flags, environment, and runtime dependency key.

options.name: Source authority with artifact cache projection
options.detail: Recommended. The source closure remains the semantic authority. A linked artifact is an optional cache projection with the full identity key. A miss recompiles the same source closure.
options.technical: This extends R8 and D-BUILDCACHE1 without making an artifact a second source. The dossier records the source digest, artifact key, and all target and tier inputs. Artifact validation may reject and rebuild from source.
options.code:
prelude.authority = "source-closure"
prelude.cache = "linked-artifact"
prelude.fallback = "recompile-source-closure"
jet explain-build firmware --why-rebuilt

comparisons.note: Cargo and rustc cache rlibs and generated artifacts from source and target fingerprints.
Go's build cache reuses compiled package objects by action identity.
Zig caches target-specific objects while source and target settings remain build inputs.

recommendation.why: C keeps source as the one semantic authority and still reuses target-specific linked work. A cache miss has a complete same-source fallback.

whyNot.reason: A gives up safe reuse even when the exact closure and target facts are unchanged.
B risks making a stale artifact look like a semantic source unless the cache contract is treated as a hard identity.

recommendation.tradeoff: The key and dossier carry more identity fields. That cost buys explainable reuse and prevents provider or tier drift.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared source-only compilation, linked artifacts, and a source-authority cache projection.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a shared target-independent artifact and provider-selected fallback. Both were rejected because they omit target identity or alter semantics.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The source-authority projection is a real hybrid. It keeps A's truth source and B's reuse without making the artifact authoritative.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The linked-artifact option now states the complete key and a hard cache miss rule.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked stale providers, linker changes, tier mismatch, and compiler coupling; the required key and source fallback repair them.

decisions.checkInstructions: Owner check: choose source-only compilation, linked artifact authority, or source-authority artifact projection. Confirm the full closure, target, provider, linker, allocator, panic, tier, compiler, environment, and dependency key; confirm same-source cache misses and dossier parity. Dependencies: D-FREESTAND-PRELUDE1, D-FREESTAND-FACTS1, D-FREESTAND-START1, D-FREESTAND-TIER1, D-FREESTAND-SEAM1, and D-BUILDCACHE1.

decisions.title: Target admission diagnostics
decisions.gist: How missing target facts appear to users and tools.
decisions.lesson: A missing allocator, sink, clock, scheduler, entropy source, or provider must stop clearly before codegen. Current rows cover some cases, but their old wording assumes `--freestanding`.
decisions.story: Maya builds the same decoder for a board and a hosted test. The board lacks a clock provider. She needs one report that names the operation, target, missing fact, and fix.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet check sensor.jet --target=board.sensor_v1
Error E33xx: `time.now` needs target fact `Time.Wall`
  target: board.sensor_v1
  fix: declare a wall-clock provider, or use injected `Clock`
decisions.detail: Choose target-fact diagnostic code granularity. Registered reports, one human and JSON renderer, and rustc isolation remain fixed.

options.name: One common target-unavailable diagnostic
options.detail: Use one registered code with a typed missing-fact kind. The human frame stays consistent, while JSON carries the exact target, operation, provider, and call path.
options.technical: All new target admission failures use one E33xx row. Existing E3301, E3303, E3304, and E3305 require an explicit retirement or scope decision. The row has target, layer, missing fact, provider, operation, source span, call path, and fix fields.
options.code:
Error E33xx: target fact missing
  what: `time.now` needs Time.Wall
  why: `board.sensor_v1` declares no wall-clock provider
  fix: declare one, or use injected Clock

options.name: Dedicated registered rows by fact family
options.detail: Recommended. Keep existing rows for their owned cases and add registered rows for missing sinks, clocks, schedulers, entropy, and providers. Each error teaches the direct fix.
options.technical: E3301, E3303, E3304, and E3305 are amended to name the selected profile and layer rather than hard-code `--freestanding`. E3302 remains target-triple or toolchain absence. New E33xx rows are registered for new target-fact families.
options.code:
Error E33xx: `time.now` is unavailable for target `board.sensor_v1`
Why: target fact `Time.Wall` has no provider
Fix: declare `Time.Wall`, or use injected `Clock`

Error E3303: allocator fact is missing
Fix: select a typed allocator profile

options.name: Keep current rows and target data
options.detail: Reuse E3301, E3303, E3304, and E3305 while leaving new missing facts in `TargetMachineError` data. This avoids new codes, but users receive inconsistent detail and some failures are not registered reports.
options.technical: TargetMachineError remains internal data for new provider failures. No new UI snapshot or stable `jet explain` row exists for those failures.
options.code:
Error E3301: API is unavailable in `--freestanding`
// This wording is wrong for a typed profile and misses clock or scheduler facts.

comparisons.note: Rust diagnostics often name an unsatisfied trait or target configuration at the source call.
comparisons.code: error[E0277]: the trait bound BoardClock: Clock is not satisfied

comparisons.note: Zig reports target-specific unavailable declarations during compilation.
comparisons.code: error: dependency on libc requires a hosted target

comparisons.note: Missing component imports are boundary errors, not silent host fallbacks.

recommendation.why: B preserves direct teaching for existing allocator and socket cases while making every new fact a registered report. It fits the I4 registry and current rows without forcing one generic code to explain every fix.

whyNot.reason: A reduces code count but makes one generic row carry many unrelated fixes and requires retiring current rows.
C leaves new target failures as unregistered data and keeps misleading flag-based text.

recommendation.tradeoff: The diagnostic registry gains several fact-family rows. Each row has one clear fix and one stable human and JSON shape.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared one common row, dedicated fact-family rows, and current data errors.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a diagnostic per provider instance and rustc forwarding. Provider-instance codes duplicate rows, and rustc forwarding violates I2.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The common row's shared JSON fields were folded into dedicated rows. B keeps one record shape without forcing one code.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The common-code option now gives a compact stable frame and names its migration cost.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Luna. Adversarial model family: Claude. The rival pass attacked code sprawl, stale E3301 wording, JSON drift, and rustc leakage; the ledger and shared renderer repair them.

Confirm registered ownership, direct fixes, typed target and provider fields, shared human and JSON rendering, rustc isolation, pre-codegen failure, and no duplicate rows. decisions.title: What regex replace means
decisions.gist: Whether Regex.replace changes every match, only the first, or refuses to exist without a suffix.
decisions.lesson: Today the same Regex.replace call changes every match on the default tier and only the first match on release. Both cannot be right; one program must mean one thing. Jet's own String.replace already changes every occurrence, matching Python. This choice pins what the regex spelling means everywhere. A sibling policy ballot, D-STDLIB-OPTPARAM1 on card #2322, now decides the standing library rule for variant spellings; option D below is this surface's shape under that rule.
decisions.story: Tom sanitizes user posts: a card-number pattern replaced with dots. In development every card number disappears. In the released build only the first one does, and the rest go out in plain text. Same program, different data, discovered in an incident review.

options.name: replace means every match; replace_first is the exception
options.detail: The short name does the safe, expected thing: every match is replaced, agreeing with Jet's own String.replace and with Python. The rarer intent gets the longer, self-describing name. The existing default-tier behavior is already correct under this rule.
options.technical: Regex.replace(haystack, template) replaces all non-overlapping matches left to right; Regex.replace_first(haystack, template) replaces at most one. $n templates unchanged. One Prelude implementation per I9.
options.code:
re.replace(post, "•")        // every match
re.replace_first(post, "•")  // exactly one

options.name: replace means first; replace_all is the exception
options.detail: Follows Rust and JavaScript: the short name replaces one match, and the common sanitize-everything intent needs the longer name. It contradicts Jet's own String.replace, so the same verb would mean two different things one call apart.
options.technical: Regex.replace = first match; Regex.replace_all = all. String.replace keeps replacing all.
options.code:
re.replace(post, "•")      // one match only
re.replace_all(post, "•")  // every match

options.name: No bare replace: both intents must be spelled
options.detail: Only replace_all and replace_first exist. Reading any call tells you exactly what happens, the same philosophy as the ratified zip verdict. It costs one syllable forever on the most common call, and it leaves Jet's short String.replace as an inconsistency anyway.
options.technical: Remove bare replace from the regex surface; ship replace_all + replace_first.
options.code:
re.replace_all(post, "•")
re.replace_first(post, "•")

options.name: One replace with a defaulted mode option
options.detail: One method: replace(haystack, template, mode) where mode defaults to every match and .First is the named variant. The owner's proposed library shape (card #2322): one name to find, the option space visible in the signature, and the safe behavior as the default. Resolves identically to A at simple call sites.
options.technical: fn replace(haystack: String, template: String, mode: ReplaceMode{.All}) String; enum ReplaceMode { All First }. Uses ratified D-CALLPOS1=A defaults + named arguments; no new syntax. One Prelude implementation per I9.
options.code:
re.replace(post, "\u2022")               // every match (default)
re.replace(post, "\u2022", mode: .First)  // exactly one

comparisons.note: re.sub replaces every match; the count argument is the explicit limiter.
comparisons.code:
re.sub(pat, '•', post)        # all
re.sub(pat, '•', post, count=1)

comparisons.note: replace is first-only and replace_all is separate; a recurring source of half-sanitized output bugs.
String.replace with a plain regex replaces one match; the g flag or replaceAll changes all — a famous footgun.

recommendation.why: A gives the short spelling the safe meaning and keeps one verb one meaning across Jet. If the owner ratifies the option-parameter policy (D-STDLIB-OPTPARAM1=B), option D is the same safe-default design in the policy's shape and becomes the preferred pick.

whyNot.reason: B makes the same verb mean all on String and first on Regex, and it inherits the exact half-sanitized-output footgun Rust and JavaScript are known for.
C pays a permanent naming tax on the most common call and still leaves the short String.replace inconsistent with its own rule.
D is A wearing the option shape; it only loses if the owner rejects the option-parameter policy on #2322, so the two ballots should be picked together.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts that a Rust or JavaScript arrival may expect first-match and get all-match. A mistake in that direction removes too much instead of leaking data, which is the survivable direction.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared all-first, first-all, and explicit-only naming, and recommended all-by-default because it agrees with String.replace and fails safe.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added a count-limited form (replace with an optional limit) and a callback-template form. The limit was folded into A as a compatible later extension of replace_first; the callback form is a separate surface card, not a naming choice.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid of A and C (bare replace = all, plus both explicit names as aliases) was tested and rejected: two spellings for one meaning violates the one-mechanism rule for no reader gain.
reviewPasses.cooperative: B was strengthened with its strongest argument — ecosystem familiarity for Rust and JavaScript arrivals — and C with the ratified zip precedent for verb explicitness. Both are real designs.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass tested large-input cost (the same card requires linear-time matching) and future count arguments (replace_first can grow one compatibly). A survives; recommendation unchanged. A later policy pass added option D (root + mode option) and confirmed it preserves the safe default.

decisions.title: How the standard library spells operation variants
decisions.gist: Whether variant behavior lives in one root method with an option parameter or in sibling methods.
decisions.lesson: Many library operations come in near-identical flavors: replace all or first, decode strict or lossy, read bytes little- or big-endian. Today each flavor tends to become its own method name, so the byte codec plan alone wants about 24 names. Jet already ratified the needed call machinery: defaults fill after supplied arguments, and named arguments deconflict (D-CALLPOS1=A). This choice sets the standing rule for how every future surface spells its variants. Full study: docs/audits/optional-args-stdlib-2026-08-28.html.
decisions.story: Ana learns Jet and wants to mask the first card number in a post. Her editor's completion list shows replace, replace_first, replace_all, and she pauses to diff three documentation entries. In the option world she finds one replace, reads its signature, and writes mode: .First without leaving the call site.
decisions.inWild:
// sibling world (today's drift)
clean :: re.replace_first(post, mask)
value :: bytes.read_i16_le(buf)
name  :: s.trim_start()

// root + options world (same programs)
clean :: re.replace(post, mask, mode: .First)
value :: bytes.read_int(buf, width: .W16)      // endian .LE, signed true default
name  :: s.trim(edges: .Start)

options.name: Sibling methods stay the house style
options.detail: Each variant keeps its own name. Reading any call names the exact behavior with no defaults to know, matching the ratified zip verdict's philosophy. The cost is namespace growth (24 codec names), three documentation entries where one would do, and a completion list that makes newcomers diff method names.
options.technical: No policy change. #2304 and #2297 resolve among their sibling-name options; #2310 ships the full name matrix.
options.code:
re.replace_first(post, mask)
bytes.read_i16_le(buf)
s.trim_start()

options.name: One root method with a defaulted option parameter — new surfaces
options.detail: When variants share the same subject and the same result shape, the common safe behavior is the default and the variant is a named enum option. Siblings remain only when the result type changes, when a mode is a safety cliff the call site must spell, or when signatures genuinely differ. Ratified verb families (zip) stay as ratified.
options.technical: Rule text enters the spec's stdlib design section. Boundary: same subject + same result shape + every mode safe -> option parameter with the common case as default; otherwise siblings. Uses only ratified machinery (D-CALLPOS1=A; Type{default} parameter defaults; dot-variant enums). Comptime and generic-module value parameters keep their no-defaults rule.
options.code:
fn replace(pattern: String, with: String, mode: ReplaceMode{.All}) String

s.replace(p, w)               // common case, zero ceremony
s.replace(p, w, mode: .First) // variant named at the call site

options.name: Root + options everywhere, retrofitting ratified verb families
options.detail: Option B's rule, plus the owner amends ratified verb verdicts such as the zip family into one root with an option (ends: .Strict default, .Shortest, .Pad(x)). Maximum consistency, but it reopens D-ZIPLEN1=D. That verdict exists so the dangerous case cannot hide behind a short spelling, and an option default is such a hiding place unless the default is the loud one.
options.technical: Requires explicit amendment of D-ZIPLEN1=D / D-ZIPPAD1=E; migration of any shipped verb spellings in one change per greenfield law.
options.code:
a.zip(b)                    // .Strict default: unequal lengths stop loudly
a.zip(b, ends: .Shortest)   // the dangerous case, named
a.zip(b, ends: .Pad(0))

options.name: No standing rule; decide per surface
options.detail: Every new surface argues its own shape in its own ballot. Maximum flexibility, but the library drifts into a mix of both styles, which is the current state this ballot exists to end.
options.technical: No spec text; per-card decisions continue.
options.code: // whatever each ballot picks

comparisons.note: One function with keyword options is the house style; count and errors are the exact pattern proposed here.
comparisons.code:
re.sub(pat, mask, post, count=1)
raw.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')

comparisons.note: API design guidelines prefer one base name with labeled parameters and enum options; siblings are reserved for genuinely different operations.
Uses sibling names (replace / replacen, from_utf8 / from_utf8_lossy) largely BECAUSE it lacks default arguments — a constraint Jet does not share.

recommendation.why: B delivers the owner's goals: one discoverable name, a small namespace, options taught by the signature. It keeps the honest sibling boundary for result-type changes and safety cliffs, and it touches no ratified verdict. The codec matrix alone collapses about 16 reader names into one method.

whyNot.reason: A grows the namespace combinatorially and makes newcomers diff method names to find behavior that one signature could teach.
C buys marginal consistency by reopening a ratified verdict whose safety reasoning still holds; retrofit can be proposed later per family if wanted.
D is the status quo that produced the drift; it guarantees a permanently mixed style.

recommendation.tradeoff: B accepts that the default variant is invisible at simple call sites. The boundary clause contains the risk: any mode that is a safety cliff may not ride an option default and must stay a spelled-out sibling or the loud default.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared house-style siblings, forward-only root+options, full retrofit, and no rule, recommending forward-only root+options for discoverability without touching ratified verdicts.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested two more shapes: builder chains (replace(p,w).first()) and per-variant free functions. Builders were folded out as heavier than an enum option for flat variants; free functions duplicate the method namespace problem.
reviewPasses.hybrid: A hybrid making the option parameter positional rather than named was tested and rejected: a bare .First at a call site loses the self-labeling that makes the pattern readable.
reviewPasses.cooperative: A was strengthened with its best case — the ratified zip reasoning that call sites must name dangerous behavior — and that reasoning was imported INTO B as the safety-cliff boundary clause. C gained a concrete amendment path.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass asked whether an invisible default recreates the silent-drift class this sweep hunted. It does only when a mode changes data safety, and the boundary clause forbids exactly that, so B survives with the boundary clause load-bearing.

decisions.title: Cost transparency: what surfaces a hidden expensive operation
decisions.gist: How Jet tells you when an innocent-looking line does expensive hidden work.
decisions.lesson: Jet's value semantics sometimes do hidden work. A view stored into an owned slot copies (D-MEM-COPYSEM1). A shared collection clones its spine on write, and a huge Int falls back to slow big-number math. Each choice is safe and usually right. But inside a loop, one hidden copy can turn a linear-looking function into a quadratic one. This decision picks how Jet makes such costs visible, so performance stays predictable, not just fast.
decisions.story: Priya ports her team's log pipeline to Jet. It benchmarks great on samples, then times out on a 2GB file in production. The slow line looks identical to every fast line around it. She has no way to see that it copies a string per iteration, so she concludes Jet is unpredictable and ports back.

options.name: Standing law, loop lint, and a cost view
options.detail: Three parts. A standing law: no construct ships a new invisible super-linear cost without a matching surface. A lint: a hidden copy, clone, or representation fallback inside a loop gets a registered advisory naming the exact repair. A cost view: jet explain --cost annotates each line with its hidden allocations, copies, and fallbacks. Beginners see nothing until a real cliff exists; experts get a per-line ledger on demand.
options.technical: Lint facts come from TIR lowering, where copy and clone insertion already happens; no second analysis. Cost-view rows are tier-labeled. The law lands in performance-budget-decisions.md and binds future ballots: a new hidden cost names its lint or cost-view row at ballot time.
options.code:
$ jet check pipeline.jet
L2510 pipeline.jet:4  this push copies the String view into an owned slot, once per loop turn
  fix: bind the copy once outside the loop, or keep views with [View<String>]

$ jet explain --cost pipeline.jet
4  out.push(log.lines().first())   copy String (view -> owned)   repeats: per iteration

options.name: Loop lint only
options.detail: Ship the hot-loop hidden-cost lint and stop. Cheapest path to catching the worst cliffs. But there is no per-line ledger for code the lint does not flag, and no standing rule, so the next feature can quietly add a new invisible cost.
options.code:
$ jet check pipeline.jet
L2510 pipeline.jet:4  this push copies the String view into an owned slot, once per loop turn
  fix: bind the copy once outside the loop, or keep views with [View<String>]

options.name: Optimizer removes the cliffs, no surface
options.detail: Spend the effort on codegen: hoist clone-on-write out of loops, keep small strings inline, widen the fast Int path. Real cliffs get rarer and code stays clean of tooling. But some costs are semantic and cannot be optimized away: a copy demanded by D-MEM-COPYSEM1 must happen, and big-number fallback must exist. Those stay invisible.

options.name: Hidden loop copies become teaching errors
options.detail: Inside a loop, a hidden copy is an error until you write the explicit ~ copy. Nothing expensive is ever silent. But the common case gains a marker it did not need before, which is ceremony creep: beginners writing a 10-item loop now meet a memory lesson.

comparisons.note: Copy-on-write cliffs are famous and invisible; finding one requires Instruments profiling. This is the failure mode Jet inherits by default.
comparisons.code:
var out: [String] = []
for log in logs { out.append(String(log.prefix(while: { $0 != "\n" }))) }

comparisons.note: Costs are visible in the source: an owned copy is a written .clone() or .to_owned(). Predictable, but every reader pays the ceremony everywhere, not only where a cliff exists.

recommendation.why: Option A keeps the beginner page clean, catches real cliffs where they bite, gives experts a full per-line ledger, and binds future features so the guarantee survives new ballots.

whyNot.reason: Without the law and the cost view, unflagged code stays illegible and the next feature can reintroduce invisible cliffs.
Semantic copies and big-number fallback cannot be optimized away, so the worst surprises stay invisible; optimizer work is complementary, not a substitute.
It taxes every ordinary loop to prevent a cliff most loops do not have, which is ceremony creep on the common case.

recommendation.tradeoff: A new advisory lint and a new explain mode must be built and kept honest against TIR changes. That cost is accepted because predictability is the trust product; effort is expendable.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a standing law plus surfaces, a lone lint, optimizer-only work, and mandatory explicit copies, and recommended the law with both surfaces.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested runtime profiling hooks, a cost budget per function, and IDE-only inlay hints. Profiling and budgets already exist in the performance-budget system, and inlay hints are a rendering of the same cost facts, so none earned a separate option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass merged optimizer work into A's law: a cost the optimizer provably removes needs no lint row. That keeps the ledger small and stops A and C from being rivals.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened D: scoping the error to profiled hot paths only would cut its ceremony. It still gates a beginner's ordinary code behind a memory lesson, so it stays behind A.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on lint noise in tiny loops and on the ledger going stale against TIR changes. Repairs: the lint fires only when the copied value can exceed a small fixed size, and cost-view rows are snapshot-tested against lowering.

decisions.comment: Owner adopts A AND C together: the transparency surfaces ship, and the optimizer is a first-class killer feature, not a fallback. Hybrid clause stands: a cost the optimizer provably removes needs no lint row; everything semantic that remains gets the lint and the cost view.

decisions.title: Runtime failures: product bar or best effort
decisions.gist: Whether a crash at runtime gets the same product quality bar as a compile error.
decisions.lesson: I4 makes every compile-time diagnostic a product: registered code, what/why/fix text, snapshot test. Runtime failure has no such bar. A panic in a deployed Jet service today can print free-form text. A stack trace can show generated Rust frames the user never wrote. This decision picks the bar for panics, traps, and traces on every tier.
decisions.story: Marcus runs a Jet order service. At 3am it crashes. The trace names jet_out.rs and mangled runtime frames, none of which appear in his code. He cannot tell which of his functions failed, and his on-call notes say to restart and hope. His postmortem recommends moving off Jet.
decisions.inWild:
What Marcus sees today when a list index is out of range in fn pick_order:

thread 'main' panicked at 'index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 7', jet_out.rs:412
stack backtrace:
   0: jet_rt::list::index_fail
   1: jet_out::__jet_fn_pick_order
   2: jet_out::main

Not one line of this names his file, his function spelling, or a fix.

options.name: Invariant: every runtime failure is a product
options.detail: Extend I4's bar to runtime. Every panic and trap has a registered code with what/why/fix text. Stack traces show Jet frames only, mapped through source maps; generated Rust never appears on any tier, which extends I2 to runtime. All of it is snapshot-tested. I9 requires the same failure text and trace shape on AOT, JIT, and interpreter. E2-M12 implements under this law.
options.technical: Trap sites already flow through Prelude functions, so registered text lives there once (I9). Frame mapping uses the existing codegen source maps. Snapshot coverage rides the existing UI snapshot harness; a runtime failure with no snapshot does not ship.
options.code:
runtime error R0210: list index out of range
  what: index 7, but orders has 3 items
  where: orders.jet:31, fn pick_order
  fix: check idx < orders.len(), or use orders.get(idx) and handle .None
  trace: pick_order (orders.jet:31) <- handle_request (server.jet:88) <- run (run.jet:5)

options.name: Spec guideline, no invariant
options.detail: Write the same goals into the spec and let E2-M12 implement them without invariant status. No enforcement teeth: a new trap site with lazy text or a leaked Rust frame is a bug like any other, not a stop-and-fix. History says the teeth are what made I4 work.
options.code:
runtime error: list index out of range at orders.jet:31

Better than today, but nothing forces the what/why/fix shape or blocks a new failure surface that skips it.

options.name: Traces only
options.detail: Mandate Jet-frame-only traces, since leaked Rust frames are the worst confusion, but leave panic text free-form. Cheapest credible fix. The 3am reader gets the right file and function, yet still no what/why/fix, and text drifts per trap site.
options.code:
panicked: index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 7
  trace: pick_order (orders.jet:31) <- handle_request (server.jet:88) <- run (run.jet:5)

comparisons.note: Backtraces are opt-in, noisy, and show internal frames; panic text is free-form per call site. Widely tolerated, never loved.
comparisons.code: thread 'main' panicked at src/main.rs:31: index out of bounds

comparisons.note: Stack traces are legible and name user frames, which is why teams accept them; but the text explains nothing and suggests no fix.
comparisons.code: java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 7 out of bounds for length 3

recommendation.why: Compile-time diagnostics are Jet's strongest asset; the same bar at runtime is a differentiator no incumbent meets, and invariant status is what kept the compile-time bar from eroding.

whyNot.reason: Without teeth, coverage erodes exactly the way pre-I4 diagnostics did; a guideline cannot stop a lazy trap site from shipping.
It fixes the trace and leaves the message: the reader learns where, but not what went wrong or how to fix it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every current and future trap site must carry registered text and a snapshot, which is real ongoing work. Accepted: effort is expendable, the 3am experience is not.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared invariant status, a spec guideline, and traces-only, and recommended the invariant because enforcement is what made the compile-time bar hold.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested crash-dump artifacts, structured JSON failure output for machines, and automatic error reporting. All three are E2-M12 implementation shapes under whichever bar wins, not separate bars, so they folded into the options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass gave A its rollout ladder from C: traces land first, registered text follows, the invariant gates only what has shipped. A stays one coherent option with a staged path.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B: a spec section plus a review-checklist line is nearly free and catches most drift in review. It still cannot block a merged lazy trap site, which the invariant does.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on panic-path binary size and on snapshot brittleness across tiers. Repairs: registered text lives once in Prelude so size cost is one table, and tier snapshots share one golden with a tier label.

decisions.title: Megaproject scale canary: which program anchors it
decisions.gist: Which real 20-50k line program becomes Jet's standing scale probe.
decisions.lesson: The largest real Jet program is about 650 lines. Language flaws that only appear at scale — compile time stacking on rustc, error cascades, editor latency, refactoring pain — are invisible to the current workflow. Card #217 already requires a dogfood portfolio before self-hosting; this decision picks the one flagship-scale anchor program inside that portfolio and instruments it with continuous scale measurements. Ratifying this ballot picks the program only: the owner separately says when building starts.
decisions.story: The first professional team adopts Jet and their codebase passes 30k lines in month two. Whatever breaks for them at that size breaks in public, with their patience as the budget. The megaproject exists so an agent fleet hits those walls first, in private, with unlimited patience.
decisions.inWild:
What the canary measures continuously once built, gauntlet-style:

cold build            full compile from clean
warm build            incremental after a one-line edit
lsp latency           completion and diagnostics percentiles on the open buffer
error cascade         diagnostics quality after one seeded breaking change
refactor task         timed rename/move across packages

Every regression class mints a Tower card.

options.name: Port the Tower board to Jet
options.detail: A real web product the owner uses every day: HTTP service, live board UI, persistence, validation, SSE updates. Exercises services, concurrency, web UI, and long-lived state — the shapes professional teams build. Runs as a read-only shadow against board snapshots; it never writes the canonical store, and any switchover is a separate owner decision. Daily use means drift and papercuts get noticed immediately.
options.technical: Shadow law: the Jet port reads exported snapshots of plugins/tower/.tower, never the live files, honoring the standing one-server rule. Parity is measured against the Node app's rendered state, which doubles as a Jet-versus-Node comparison on a real program.
options.code:
tower-jet/
  package.jet
  src/
    model/      cards, decisions, lanes, archive law
    store/      snapshot read, journal replay
    server/     http service, sse, json api
    board/      web ui, focus mode
    lint/       board-health checks
  tests/        parity suite vs Node renderings

options.name: Grow the Jet site into a docs platform
options.detail: Expand site/generate.jet (650 lines today) into the full docs platform: spec rendering, diagnostic browser, searchable stdlib reference, playground. Builds on working Jet code and produces public-facing value. But it is mostly one shape of program — static generation plus templating — so it under-stresses services, concurrency, and long-lived state.
options.code:
site/
  package.jet
  src/
    generate/   existing generator, grown
    spec/       decision-log renderer
    diagbrowse/ all 854 diagnostics, searchable
    search/     index build + query
    playground/ web-target compile service

options.name: Port a toolchain piece: jet fmt or jetpack
options.detail: Compiler-shaped Jet: parsing, trees, arenas, index handles. This is exactly the code shape self-hosting needs, so it doubles as an early e11 down payment. But it front-runs the e11 readiness gate that card #217 guards, and its single shape misses services, UI, and persistence.
options.code:
fmt-jet/
  package.jet
  src/
    lexer/      token stream
    tree/       arena ast, index handles
    print/      canonical style, fixpoint law
  tests/        byte-parity vs shipped jet fmt on the example corpus

options.name: Game or media vertical slice
options.detail: The e11 epoch already names a game/media dogfood slice: real-time loop, assets, FFI into raylib, performance pressure. Strong stress on a dimension the other options miss. But it is the least like what professional teams ship first, and its quality bar is visual, which machines verify poorly.
options.code:
game-jet/
  package.jet
  src/
    loop/       fixed-step simulation
    render/     raylib ffi
    assets/     deterministic loading (card #238)
    net/        lobby service

comparisons.note: Cargo and rustc themselves became the scale canaries; every compile-time complaint in the world got filed against real code first.
The compiler is written in TypeScript and was for years the largest TS program; scale pain hit the team before users.

recommendation.why: A is a real multi-shape product — service, UI, persistence, concurrency — that the owner exercises daily, and its Node twin gives a free honest Jet-versus-incumbent comparison.

whyNot.reason: One program shape: static generation under-stresses services, concurrency, and long-lived state, which is where professional teams live.
It front-runs the e11 readiness gate card #217 guards, and its compiler shape misses services, UI, and persistence.
Its quality bar is visual and machine-verified poorly, and it is the least like a professional team's first Jet program.

recommendation.tradeoff: The board is live infrastructure, so the port must stay a read-only shadow with parity tests until a separate owner decision. Accepted: the shadow law is written into the option itself.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared the board port, the docs platform, a toolchain port, and a game slice, recommending the board port for shape breadth and daily dogfooding.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested a synthetic generated megaproject and porting an existing open-source app. Synthetic code stresses nothing real; a foreign port imports foreign architecture, so neither earned an option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass ordered instead of merged: the portfolio in card #217 still wants multiple shapes later, so losing options remain future portfolio entries rather than parts of a chimera anchor.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened D with a headless deterministic-replay mode, making more of it machine-checkable. Its first-team relevance gap remains.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A on shadow-parity cost and on the one-server data-loss history. Repairs: parity runs against exported snapshots only, and the shadow law forbids any write to the canonical store without a new owner decision.

decisions.comment: Owner adopts two anchors: A (Tower board port) AND the jetpack port from option C. Both are dogfood anchors under the same scale-metrics rig. fmt is not selected. Build still waits for explicit owner go.

decisions.title: Team policy surface: where a tech lead sets project ceilings
decisions.gist: Where a team writes and enforces its project rules: allowed effects, unsafe use, expert features, dependencies.
decisions.lesson: Professionals adopt a language as a team, and a tech lead's first question is whether the toolchain can enforce team rules. Jet already has package-level contain and harden keys (D-MEM-GUARANTEE1), but no general policy surface. Without one, every team invents an unofficial style-guide dialect and enforces it by hand in review. This decision picks where such rules live and what enforces them. A project with no policy block must stay exactly as ceremony-free as today.
decisions.story: Elena leads eight engineers on a payments service. Her rules: no #Unsafe outside the audited module, no network effects in the domain layer, no new dependencies without review. Today her only tools are code review vigilance and hope; one tired approval ships a violation.

options.name: Policy block on the existing package keys
options.detail: One policy section in package.jet, extending the same key family as contain and harden. It sets effect ceilings by module path, an unsafe allowance, an expert-surface ceiling, and a dependency allow list. Sema and lint enforce it with registered diagnostics, so a violation is a build result, not a review catch. jet inspect guarantees shows the effective policy and every grant. No policy block means no new behavior anywhere.
options.technical: Proposed spelling, final shape at implementation ballot: policy: .{ effects: [module path -> ceiling], unsafe: .Deny | .Paths([...]), expert: .Deny | .Allow, deps: .List([...]) }. Enforcement reuses the existing effect-checking and marker machinery in sema; no second checker. Diagnostics get I4 registration and snapshots.

options.name: Tool config file, outside the language
options.detail: A lint profile file, like clippy.toml, read by jet lint only. Easy to add and easy to ignore: it guards nothing unless CI runs lint, it cannot use sema's effect facts as guarantees, and jet inspect guarantees cannot vouch for it. Rules drift from the code they govern.
options.code:
jet-lint.toml (proposed):

[policy]
domain_effects = []
unsafe_paths = ["src/audited"]

$ jet lint --policy
warning: src/domain/settle.jet uses IO.Net

options.name: No surface: review and CI scripts
options.detail: Teams keep enforcing rules with code review and homegrown CI greps. Zero language cost. Every team pays the same tax separately, greps miss what sema would catch for free, and the tech lead's first evaluation question gets the answer no.
options.code:
ci.sh (per team, homegrown):

if rg -l 'http\.' src/domain; then
  echo "domain layer may not use the network"; exit 1
fi

Misses aliased imports, wrapped calls, and every future effect the grep never heard of.

comparisons.note: The closest prior art: a crate-level attribute makes unsafe a hard error for the whole crate. Teams use it precisely because it is in the language, not in a config file.
Permission flags gate effects at run time per invocation. Strong idea, wrong layer for teams: the rule lives in whoever types the command, not in the project.
Config-file rules drift and get disabled inline; every large team carries a graveyard of eslint-disable comments.

recommendation.why: A makes team rules build results backed by sema's real effect and marker facts, extends an existing key family instead of adding a mechanism, and costs solo users nothing.

whyNot.reason: A config file outside the language cannot use sema's guarantees, is skippable, and drifts from the code it governs.
It answers the tech lead's first question with no, and makes every team rebuild weaker enforcement by hand.

recommendation.tradeoff: The package schema grows one section that solo beginners will never touch. Accepted: the section is invisible until written, and teams are the adoption unit for professionals.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an in-language policy block, a lint config file, and no surface, recommending the policy block because enforcement rides sema facts.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested per-file pragmas, a separate policy.jet file, and workspace-level inheritance. Pragmas scatter the rules they should centralize; the separate file and inheritance are placement details of A, folded into its technical shape.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass moved B's best part into A: lint-severity policy rows are allowed, so a team can stage a rule as advisory before making it a build error.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened C with a curated official CI recipe, which would help small teams. It still cannot see effects sema sees, so it stays weakest.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Attacked A as a second permission system beside contain/harden and as monorepo pain when policies nest. Repairs: A is defined as the same key family with one merge law, and workspace nesting reuses the existing package merge table.

decisions.title: Quantitative proof window for Jet's professional handoff
decisions.gist: How much clean differential and red-team evidence Jet needs before professional handoff.
decisions.lesson: The triple gate is already ratified. This choice sets only the clean fuzz window and the fresh-context red-team quota. A useful threshold must prove time, volume, and public-surface breadth without risking this workstation.
decisions.story: Mara evaluates Jet for a production service. A million repeated easy cases look impressive but never touch an obscure Core row. She needs one number that proves sustained, broad pressure and one repeatable adversarial session.
decisions.inWild:
$ scripts/agent/hardening-rig.mjs status
HANDOFF  NOT READY
conformance  1,104 / 1,104 covered; 0 hidden
fuzz         day 9 / 14; 6,820,441 / 10,000,000 cases
row floor    100 required; lowest row 73
red-team     8 / 8 fresh lanes; 0 new P0
open P0      0

options.name: Balanced time, volume, breadth, and eight fresh lanes
options.detail: Require 14 consecutive clean days, 10,000,000 valid differential cases, and 100 valid mutations for every eligible public callable. Then run eight fresh Luna-max lanes in four waves of two. Every exclusion stays counted and owner-ratified.
options.technical: A silent-data finding resets the clean window. A semantic change invalidates both the window and red-team result because their target commit no longer matches.
options.code:
fuzz_window_days = 14
valid_cases = 10_000_000
min_cases_per_eligible_row = 100
red_team_lanes = 8
red_team_concurrency = 2

options.name: Thirty clean days only
options.detail: Require 30 consecutive clean days and eight fresh lanes. Do not require total cases or a per-row floor. This proves elapsed exposure but can pass during idle or narrow cycles.
options.technical: The dashboard still shows case and row counts, but they do not gate readiness. A slow machine or skipped domain can consume the whole month without failing this option.
options.code:
fuzz_window_days = 30
valid_cases = advisory
min_cases_per_eligible_row = advisory
red_team_lanes = 8

options.name: One hundred million cases only
options.detail: Require 100,000,000 valid cases and eight fresh lanes. Do not require a minimum clean duration. A fast narrow burst can finish quickly, so elapsed stability has no force.
options.technical: Every eligible row still needs one valid case through conformance, not through fuzzing. Hot pure functions can dominate the volume while expensive effectful rows stay lightly stressed.
options.code:
fuzz_window_days = none
valid_cases = 100_000_000
min_cases_per_eligible_row = none
red_team_lanes = 8

options.name: Light balanced gate
options.detail: Require seven clean days, 1,000,000 valid cases, ten valid mutations per eligible row, and four fresh lanes. This reaches a result sooner. It gives much less pressure to rare boundaries and cross-domain interactions.
options.technical: The same invalidation and exclusion rules apply. The lower row floor makes one lucky pass much more important than repeated behavior across distinct inputs.
options.code:
fuzz_window_days = 7
valid_cases = 1_000_000
min_cases_per_eligible_row = 10
red_team_lanes = 4
red_team_concurrency = 2

comparisons.note: SQLite combines independent harnesses, differential engines, millions of tests, boundary checks, fuzzing, and mutation testing. Its release soak uses large volume instead of one green suite.
comparisons.code:
SQL Logic Test: 7.2 million cross-engine queries
TH3 release soak: about 248.5 million tests

comparisons.note: libFuzzer records seeds and corpora, supports fixed run counts, and enforces an RSS limit. It treats a reproducible input as the durable unit, not a prose success claim.
The silent-data sweep found P0 defects after existing examples and tier gates were green. A bind-and-discard UUID probe also passed while the value-consuming call failed.
comparisons.code: coverage without a consumed value = no proof

recommendation.why: Option A makes time, volume, and breadth constrain each other. It gives every eligible callable repeated pressure, keeps execution concurrency at two, and adds eight independent attack lanes.

whyNot.reason: Elapsed time can pass while the runner is idle or one domain receives almost no valid cases.
Pure hot rows can produce the volume in a burst while rare effectful and boundary rows remain weakly tested.
Ten mutations per row and four lanes are too small for a professional handoff claim after Jet's observed silent-data defect rate.

recommendation.tradeoff: Option A takes longer and spends more local compute. The bounded two-core runner, 8GiB memory ceiling, and two-lane red-team cap keep that cost below the workstation safety limits.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared balanced, time-only, volume-only, and light gates. It recommended the balanced gate because no single measure proves sustained breadth.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested CPU-hours, code coverage, unique paths, mutation score, and agent-hours. These remain dashboard facts because each can reward narrow work or unstable instrumentation.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combined time, volume, per-row breadth, and a fixed red-team quota. That complete combination became option A rather than a fifth overlapping choice.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B with visible advisory counts and C with conformance coverage. Both still lack one force that A makes mandatory.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial pass attacked A with expensive effectful rows and workstation risk. Eligible-row classes, owner-visible exclusions, batching, and a two-core resource cap keep the gate strict without making it unsafe.

decisions.comment: Owner chose the balanced time, volume, breadth, and eight-lane gate in chat.

decisions.title: Typed CLI entry becomes the canonical input recipe
decisions.gist: Which spelling a program with fixed inputs should normally use to read them.
decisions.lesson: Jet already ratified a typed entry: a #CLI struct becomes the entry parameter, and the compiler generates parsing, defaults, help, and metadata. Real code ignores it. A lexical sweep finds 79 lines touching process.argv(), most of them hand argument handling, and jetpack itself carries a 120-line hand parser. This choice picks the recipe that docs, first examples, scaffolds, and our own dogfood teach.
decisions.story: Mara writes a small report tool. She copies the nearest example, so she writes argv length checks, an index-one read, a usage panic, and a hand Int.parse. Her tool has no help text, and a wrong invocation prints whatever her panic string says. The typed entry she never saw would have generated the parsing, the validation, and the help.

options.name: Typed entry is the canon; builder and raw argv are explicit escapes
options.detail: Docs, first-contact examples, scaffolds, and dogfood show the #CLI entry for every fixed-shape program. The core.args builder stays as the expert floor for irregular or dynamic grammars. Raw process.argv() stays for true passthrough. The ratified flag-only rule for defaulted fields stands, so the parser has one binding rule and wrong invocations become teaching errors.
options.technical: No compiler change. The recipe is safe only with an exact failure contract, so acceptance pins it. Unknown options exit 2 with usage. Surplus bare values exit 2 with usage; card #2372 is a prerequisite. The named form always beats any positional reading. Generated help works on AOT and default jet run. Migration: dogfood/jetpack cli/main.jet, the agent workload adapters, and fixed-shape gauntlet entries move to #CLI; parse_or_exit is the documented process-boundary call for builder code.

options.name: Canon plus positional promotion for defaulted fields
options.detail: Everything in option A, and defaulted scalar fields may also fill from bare values in declaration order. This is the strongest form for tools whose positional order is the user-facing interface: greet Ada works with no flag, and the named form stays available. The cost is a second binding rule. A stray token near a mistyped flag now binds to a defaulted field instead of erroring. The parser must also define how required and defaulted fields interleave in the queue.
options.technical: Amends the ratified flag-only rule D-CLI-POS1. Required fields keep declaration-order filling; defaulted fields would join the queue after required ones. Named always beats positional.

options.name: Keep raw argv as the taught floor
options.detail: Examples and docs keep teaching process.argv() first, and the typed entry stays an advanced chapter. Nothing migrates. The gain is zero churn. The loss is that every new program keeps paying the length-check, index, usage, and conversion tax the compiler already knows how to remove, and agents keep reconstructing command schemas from control flow.
options.code:
args :: process.argv()
if args.len() != 2 -> panic("usage: tool INPUT")
input :: args.get(1) ?? panic("missing input")
value :: Int.parse(input) ?? panic("bad integer")

comparisons.note: argparse gives typed values and help, but it is a parser object beside main. Jet's entry parameter is the schema itself.
clap derive is the same idea as #CLI, but it is a third-party choice. Jet ships it as the entry contract with compiled metadata.

recommendation.why: The typed entry already exists, is ratified, and generates what every hand parser rewrites badly: validation, help, defaults, env fallback, and a queryable schema. Making it the taught default fixes the corpus-wide friction without any new mechanism, and the pinned failure contract makes wrong invocations teach instead of drift.

whyNot.reason: Its convenience is real, but it reopens a ratified rule and trades one binding rule for two. A strict error that names the flag teaches the fix; a stray token that binds silently does not.
It keeps the most common program shape on the most error-prone path and leaves our own package manager as a 120-line counterexample.

recommendation.tradeoff: Defaulted fields stay flag-only, so greet Ada errors instead of greeting Ada. The error names the fix, which we judge better than ambiguous silent binding.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared canon-plus-escapes, positional promotion, and the status quo, seeded by four lanes of corpus evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a fourth option, new entry sugar with no struct, and folded it into A because #CLI already covers it without new syntax.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved strict surplus rejection out of the options and into a shared prerequisite, card #2372, since every option needs it.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C by naming its real constituency, passthrough grammars, and strengthened B with a defined binding order.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review fixed an invalid one-marker bracket spelling in the example and replaced an unsupported flag-typo story claim. It rescoped the argv count as a lexical signal, moved the exact failure contract into option A's acceptance, and forced an honest steelman of positional promotion.

decisions.title: Machine-plain decimals: what Fixed(n) prints
decisions.gist: Whether {x:Fixed(2)} prints 1234.50 or 1,234.50.
decisions.lesson: The Fixed selector formats a number with a fixed number of decimals. Today it also inserts digit-grouping commas, for floats and for integers. That default is right for a human report and wrong for delimiter-sensitive output: files, protocols, logs, and diffs. Two gauntlet entries already strip the commas back out with replace. Peer languages print plain digits by default and make grouping the opt-in.
decisions.story: Deniz writes a tool whose numeric summaries feed a downstream parser that splits on commas. The sums come out as 1,234.50, so every large number silently grows an extra field. He discovers the workaround only after the corrupted output ships: format, then replace the commas with nothing.

options.name: Fixed(n) prints plain digits; Grouped(n) carries the current behavior
options.detail: Fixed(2) prints 1234.50, safe for machines and unsurprising to anyone arriving from another language. Human grouping moves to a sibling selector, Grouped(n): same precision argument, same error behavior, output identical to today's Fixed(n). Every golden that shows grouped output migrates in the same change.
options.technical: Both formatter kernels change. jet_fmt_decimal for floats and jet_fmt_decimal_int for integers stop grouping, and grouped variants keep the current behavior. Grouped(n) is ratified here as a full selector row: registry entry, one core.text.fmt mapping, precision argument, the same errors as Fixed, proven on every tier per I9. Acceptance inventories and migrates every affected golden and snapshot.

options.name: Keep grouped Fixed; add a plain sibling
options.detail: Fixed(2) keeps printing 1,234.50, so every existing report, golden, and external consumer keeps its exact bytes. A new plain selector covers machine output. This is the zero-risk path. The loss is that the shortest spelling stays the dangerous one. Every file, log, or protocol author must know the longer sibling exists, and the failure mode is silent field corruption, not an error.
options.technical: Adds a plain fmt kernel and its selector row beside the current grouped default. No golden churn anywhere.
options.code:
print("{sum:Fixed(2)}")   // 1,234.50 - still unsafe near delimiters
print("{sum:Plain(2)}")   // 1234.50

options.name: Fixed(n) takes a grouping argument
options.detail: One selector with a second argument: Fixed(2) plain, Fixed(2, group) grouped. The selector family already has argument-bearing members such as Hex(n) and Pad(n, fill), so this fits the ratified grammar. The real downside is that a positional boolean reads as configuration instead of intent, and the Fixed signature changes for every existing caller anyway.
options.technical: Extends Fixed's registry row with an optional grouping argument. Migration cost equals option A's, since the default flips or every grouped caller edits its call.
options.code:
print("{sum:Fixed(2)}")          // plain
print("{sum:Fixed(2, group)}")   // 1,234.50

comparisons.note: The plain form is the default; grouping is the explicit comma flag.
Rust's formatter never groups; grouping requires a crate. No peer groups by default.

recommendation.why: A default must match the most likely destination, and formatted decimals flow into files, protocols, and diffs far more often than typeset reports. Plain digits make the short spelling the safe one and delete a silent-corruption workaround our own gauntlet entries already carry.

whyNot.reason: It preserves every existing output byte, which is its honest strength. But it leaves the default corrupting machine output silently, and safety by longer sibling is the wrong direction for a beginner surface.
It fits the grammar but pays option A's full migration anyway, and a positional boolean states intent worse than two named selectors.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every golden and report that shows grouped output changes bytes once, and any external consumer of current Jet output sees the new form. That is a real one-time output change, accepted because the grouped bytes were the unsafe ones.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared flipping the default, adding a plain sibling, and a grouping argument, with the gauntlet workaround as evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested locale-aware grouping and rejected it: Jet output must not vary by machine locale on the default path.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review confirmed A already contains B's mechanism as its Grouped sibling, so no separate hybrid option exists.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B by naming its real virtue, zero output change, and C by citing the one-name discoverability gain.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review caught the second grouping kernel for integers, corrected a stale claim that selector arguments break the grammar, and repaired an unsupported CSV-column story. It also forced the tradeoff to state the output-byte change honestly.

decisions.title: DataTree scalar access and unordered equality
decisions.gist: Which helpers dynamic JSON values get for reading scalars and comparing documents.
decisions.lesson: DataTree is the dynamic value a program gets when it parses JSON without a schema. Tower, our largest dynamic-data program, wrote two divergent scalar-to-text ladders with conflicting rules, one of five functions and one of eight. It also wrote one hundred lines of recursion to compare two documents while ignoring object key order. Document comparison recurs in every program that inspects foreign JSON, and today it has no spelling at all.
decisions.story: Priya syncs a board snapshot against a server reply. She wants one line: are these two documents the same, ignoring the order keys arrived in. Instead she copies a page of recursive comparison from another file, and the two copies have already started to drift.

options.name: Ship equal_unordered and a fully specified scalar to_text
options.detail: DataTree.equal_unordered(other) compares two documents with object key order ignored and array order respected. DataTree.to_text() returns the text of a scalar leaf and nothing for anything else. Ordinary == stays order-sensitive, and the method names make the two policies explicit at the call site. Truthiness ships nowhere: which values count as true is a policy of the source domain, and even tower's own two truthiness ladders disagree with each other.
options.technical: equal_unordered: objects compare as key-to-value maps with recursive equality and insertion order ignored; arrays compare element-wise in order. Numbers are variant-sensitive, so Int(1) does not equal Float(1.0), matching the untyped parse projection; Float NaN never equals anything. to_text: Text returns itself; Int and Float render exactly as interpolation renders them; Bool renders true or false; Null, arrays, and objects return nothing. Tower's five-function ladder retires onto it; the eight-function ladder mirrors JavaScript display rules and stays domain code.
options.code:
if !left.equal_unordered(right) -> return false

label :: (tree.field("title") ?? DataTree.Null).to_text() ?? "untitled"

options.name: Ship equal_unordered only
options.detail: Only the comparison ships. It is the helper with a single honest contract and a hundred-line duplication behind it. Scalar reads keep their ladders, on the argument that each program's coercion policy differs anyway, as tower's two ladders show. The loss is that the most common single-leaf read keeps needing a match or a helper for every scalar variant.
options.technical: Same equality contract as option A, nothing else.
options.code:
if !left.equal_unordered(right) -> return false
// scalar reads stay hand-matched

options.name: Decline; keep explicit matching
options.detail: No new methods. Every program keeps writing its own comparison and scalar ladder. The gain is a smaller surface. The loss is one hundred duplicated lines in our own dogfood today, drifting copies, and a comparison job with no discoverable spelling.
options.code:
// status quo: copy semantic_equal between files
if !semantic_equal(~left_value, ~right_value) -> return false

comparisons.note: Dict equality ignores insertion order natively, so the gap never shows up there. Jet objects deliberately preserve insertion order, so the unordered comparison needs an explicit name.
No built-in deep equality; every project imports or writes one. That is the failure mode Jet can avoid.

recommendation.why: Unordered comparison has one honest answer and a hundred-line reimplementation proving demand. Scalar text has one honest answer once it is pinned to the same rendering interpolation already uses, and the pinned contract is in the option. Truthiness has no single honest answer, so it stays out.

whyNot.reason: It reads tower's divergent ladders as proof that no shared coercion exists, but the divergence is display policy; the scalar-only, interpolation-matching contract in A is neutral and covers the common leaf read.
Declining keeps a proven, drifting, hundred-line duplication in our own dogfood and gives the comparison job no discoverable name.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two equality spellings exist, ordered and unordered, and the difference must be taught. The method name carries the policy, which is the point.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft bundled equality, scalar text, and a possible truthiness helper, seeded by the tower ladders.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a json.equal_unordered free function and folded it into method spelling on the value itself.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review split scalar coercion into its own option so the owner can take the comparison alone.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened C by conceding surface-size discipline and B by granting that coercion policies genuinely differ across domains.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review found tower's second ladder is eight functions with rules conflicting with the first, which killed the truthiness option outright. It forced the equality contract to pin variant-sensitive numbers and NaN, and the coercion contract to name every variant's output.

decisions.title: Delimited records: delimiter and framing options on the CSV engine
decisions.gist: How a program reads tab-separated and other delimited text without hand framing.
decisions.lesson: Jet has a real CSV engine with parse, decode, reader, and writer entry points, but only for commas. Tab-separated files are everywhere in tooling. Five of our agent workload adapters frame them by hand: split on newline, count lines manually, skip the header, skip blanks, split each line on tab, and validate field counts. Hand framing also silently breaks on quoted fields that valid delimited files may contain. A probe confirmed core.encoding.tsv does not exist.
decisions.story: An agent ports a log-processing task. In Python it wrote csv.reader with a delimiter argument and enumerate for line numbers. In Jet it maintains a counter, a header flag, and a blank-line branch, and the header bug it introduces survives until a human reads the output.

options.name: One engine gains delimiter, header, and blank options plus a record contract
options.detail: The existing CSV entry points, parse and reader, gain named options: delimiter, header, and skip_blank. Comma stays the default, so existing callers are untouched. Iterating the parse yields records that expose their fields and the physical source line where the record starts, so error messages stay exact. Raw split remains the override for malformed-input recovery and unusual protocols.
options.technical: The options parameterize the one existing engine; quoting, CRLF handling, and multiline quoted fields keep the current RFC-4180 reader semantics, and the delimiter changes only the field separator. Record lines are physical start lines, so a quoted multiline record reports its opening line; a skipped header is still line one. Malformed-field policy is the engine's current policy, unchanged. Acceptance migrates the five hand-framing workload adapters onto the options and proves each framing job, header, blanks, counts, and line numbers, is covered.

options.name: A tsv facade over the same engine
options.detail: A core.encoding.tsv module whose functions call the shared engine with the tab delimiter fixed. No duplicate implementation, so no drift. The gain is a discoverable name for the most common non-comma case. The loss is that a name per delimiter does not scale: semicolons, pipes, and exotic separators still need the option form, so the facade adds a module without removing the mechanism underneath.
options.technical: Thin forwarding functions only; the engine work of option A happens anyway.
options.code:
use core.encoding.tsv as tsv
loop row in tsv.parse(text, header: true) { ... }

options.name: Line-framing helper only
options.detail: A text-level helper that yields numbered, optionally header-skipping and blank-skipping lines, leaving field splitting manual. Smaller addition, useful beyond delimited data. The loss is that field splitting, quoting, and count validation stay hand-written in exactly the programs that motivated this, so quoted fields keep breaking silently.

comparisons.note: One csv module, delimiter as an argument. This is the exact shape option A adopts.
encoding/csv exposes a Comma field on the reader; tab support is configuration, not a second package.

recommendation.why: Delimited parsing is one mechanism, and every peer treats the delimiter as a parameter of it. Parameterizing the existing engine erases the five hand framings, fixes their silent quoted-field breakage for free, and generalizes past tabs with one argument.

whyNot.reason: Honest as a facade, it still adds a module name per delimiter while the option form must exist anyway; the discoverability gain does not pay for the extra surface.
It stops one step short: the motivating programs still hand-split fields, so quoting stays broken and most of the friction survives.

recommendation.tradeoff: The CSV entry points gain named options and a record contract, growing their signature surface. The comma default keeps every existing caller unchanged.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared extending the CSV surface, a tsv twin, and a line-framing helper, seeded by five workload adapters.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a full typed-record decoder over delimited text and deferred it: typed decode already exists for CSV and can gain the same delimiter option later.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved record line numbers from a separate idea into option A, since exact errors were half the motivation.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review rebuilt B as a facade over one engine, removing the drifting-twin strawman, and strengthened C by noting framing helps plain text too.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review caught that the draft extended a csv.rows entry point that does not exist, so the ballot now targets the real parse and reader surface. It forced the RFC-4180 interplay, the physical-start-line meaning, and the adapter-by-adapter migration proof into the option.

decisions.title: HTTP message-level text and typed JSON request bodies
decisions.gist: Whether HTTP messages get direct text reads, typed JSON request bodies, and request-free route handlers.
decisions.lesson: Reading a response as text is the most common HTTP client operation, but every example spells it through the body wrapper with a hand-passed byte limit.
