Sending typed JSON has an expert path, encode with json.to_string and pass the string, but the shortest visible example hand-writes an escaped JSON literal. Fixed routes must also name and type a request parameter they never read. Three last-mile gaps in an otherwise coherent surface, each independently decidable.
decisions.story: Jonah calls a weather API. He wants the reply text, so he writes resp.body().text with an eight-megabyte limit he copied from an example, unaware the runtime already caps bodies at one megabyte. Then he posts a reading by pasting an escaped JSON string, one brace away from a malformed payload. The typed encoder was two modules away, and the example did not use it.
decisions.inWild:
// examples/features/net/http_rest_service.jet:34 and http_web_defaults.jet:44-46 (real)
print(resp.body().text(8 * 1024 * 1024) ?? "invalid body")
sent :: post.header("origin", "https://app.example")
    .body("{{\"city\":\"Reno\",\"degrees\":31}}")

options.name: Message projections plus request-free route handlers
options.detail: Received messages gain a direct text read: resp.text() on a response and req.text() on an incoming server request. Both default to the runtime's shared one-megabyte body cap, and the explicit limit form stays available. The client request builder gains json(value), which encodes any Codable value with the existing typed encoder and sets JSON framing. Routes additionally accept a zero-argument handler as sugar for an ignored request. body() and body(String) remain the expert floor.
options.technical:
text() delegates to the existing body text read with the shared cap (JET_HTTP_MAX_BODY_BYTES, one megabyte, HTTPMessage.rs:4), the same cap the defaulted JSON decode already enforces. Consumption and error behavior are exactly body()'s. The client builder does not gain text(); it is a writer.

json(value) reuses the typed encoder and must not create inference ambiguity with the decode-side generic, which keeps its type argument. Zero-argument handlers adapt to the existing handler shape at registration. Surface inventory: one method on response, one on server request, one on the client builder, one registration-time adaptation.
options.code:
print(resp.text() ?? "invalid body")
sent :: post.json(Reading{city: "Reno", degrees: 31})
mux.get("/ok", () -> Ok(http_server.response(200, "ok")))

options.name: Message projections only
options.detail: text() on received messages and json(value) on the builder ship; route signatures stay as they are. This takes the two projections with industry-proven shapes and leaves the routing sugar, which touches handler registration rather than messages, for its own day. Fixed routes keep their unused, typed parameter.
options.technical: Identical projection contracts to option A, no handler adaptation.
options.code:
print(resp.text() ?? "invalid body")
sent :: post.json(Reading{city: "Reno", degrees: 31})
mux.get("/ok", (_req) -> Ok(http_server.response(200, "ok")))

options.name: Decline; the wrapper is the surface
options.detail: No additions. body() stays the single spelling for every read, which keeps one API name and keeps the byte limit an explicit per-call decision, a genuine resource-policy virtue. Typed request encoding keeps its two-call spelling through json.to_string. The loss is that the most frequent operations stay one hop longer than in every peer client, and the visible examples keep teaching hand-escaped payloads.
options.code:
print(resp.body().text(1024 * 1024) ?? "invalid body")
sent :: post.body(json.to_string(Reading{city: "Reno", degrees: 31}))

comparisons.note: requests puts text and json directly on the message; nobody touches the raw body for the common case.
reqwest is the same shape: text() and json() on the message, bytes() as the floor.

recommendation.why: The projections are the two most frequent HTTP operations, currently one wrapper hop and one hand-passed constant longer than needed. The zero-argument handler removes a dead parameter from the most common route shape. All three reuse existing machinery under proven peer spellings, and the expert floor is untouched.

whyNot.reason: A defensible stopping point, but the dead request parameter is the same last-mile ceremony as the wrapper hop. Deferring it buys nothing, since the adaptation is registration-time sugar over the existing shape.

Its per-call-limit discipline is real, but the runtime already enforces the shared cap underneath, so the explicit constant is ceremony that documents a limit the caller does not actually control alone.

recommendation.tradeoff: The default text limit becomes stdlib policy, pinned to the existing shared one-megabyte cap, rather than a per-call decision. The explicit limit form remains for anyone who cares.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft bundled the three last-mile projections found across 38 body-text call sites and the client example.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested streaming and bytes projections and left them on body(), which already serves them well.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review checked that json(value) and the generic json decode coexist without inference ambiguity and recorded that as an acceptance term.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review rebuilt C around its honest virtue, explicit resource policy, and split the projections from the route sugar so B is a real stopping point.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review broke the bundle into separable choices and replaced a hand-escaping strawman with the real json.to_string expert path. It pinned the default limit to the existing shared one-megabyte cap with citations, restricted text() to received messages, and corrected the surface inventory.

decisions.title: Unit scalar scaling preserves the unit
decisions.gist: Whether a unit-tagged value can be multiplied by a plain number without losing its unit.
decisions.lesson: Unit families tag values so quantities from different families cannot mix. Same-family addition works. But scaling by a plain count, the most common unit operation, is rejected today; a fresh probe confirms every scalar form is E0127, in both operand orders and for division. Real code erases the unit with raw(), converts, multiplies, and rewraps, which forces boundary ceremony into every formula and leaves the value unprotected mid-computation. This ballot covers linear quantities only: affine points and nominal currency keep their own ratified law.
decisions.story: Ana computes an order subtotal: price times quantity. The natural line is rejected, so she writes the erase-convert-rewrap chain from the example. The chain is explicit, but it is three calls where peers write one operator, and inside it her value is a bare float that the family can no longer guard.

options.name: Scalar multiply and divide preserve the unit
options.detail: For linear unit-family quantities and deltas: unit times a plain number, in either operand order, yields the same unit; unit divided by a plain number yields the same unit. Affine points are excluded, matching their ratified algebra. A plain number divided by a unit stays rejected, since that would be an inverse unit. raw() and the from_ constructors remain the explicit boundary for deliberate erasure and conversion.
options.technical: Scalars are Int plus the family's backing numeric type; a bare decimal literal follows the normal literal rules for that backing type, so a Decimal-backed family accepts a decimal literal scalar. Division by zero and overflow follow the backing type's existing rules. Delta scaling is included; point scaling stays E0127.
options.code:
fn subtotal(price: Usd, qty: Int) Usd -> price * qty

half :: fare / 2          // still Usd
bad :: 2 / fare           // rejected: inverse unit

options.name: Scalar multiply only
options.detail: The conservative slice: multiplication in both operand orders ships with option A's scalar and exclusion rules, and division stays rejected. This fixes the cited subtotal without deciding division's zero and rounding questions. The loss is that halving a fare still needs the erase-rewrap chain, and the asymmetry, multiply works, divide does not, must be taught.
options.technical: Identical rules to option A minus division.
options.code:
fn subtotal(price: Usd, qty: Int) Usd -> price * qty
half :: Usd.from_float(fare.raw() / 2.0)   // division still manual

options.name: A scale method instead of the operator
options.detail: No operator change; linear quantities gain scale(n). Scaling reads as a deliberate named operation, and the library can surface rounding and overflow policy at one auditable seam. The loss is that the most common arithmetic on units stops looking like arithmetic, and formulas with several scalings become method chains.
options.code: fn subtotal(price: Usd, qty: Int) Usd -> price.scale(qty)

options.name: Status quo: erase, convert, rewrap
options.detail: Nothing changes. Every scaling crosses the explicit raw() boundary. The gain is zero semantic surface growth and a visible audit point at every scaling. The loss is three calls of ceremony for the most common unit operation and an unprotected window inside every formula.
options.code:
fn subtotal(price: Usd, qty: Int) Usd ->
    Usd.from_float(price.raw() * Float.from_int(qty))

comparisons.note: Units of measure allow scalar scaling natively; only unit-changing products need a declared result unit. Option A adopts the scalar half of that behavior.
comparisons.code: let subtotal (price: float<usd>) (qty: float) = price * qty

comparisons.note: Branded number types lose the brand on any arithmetic, forcing rewrap ceremony. That is the shape Jet currently requires explicitly.
comparisons.code: const subtotal = usd(price as number * qty)

recommendation.why: Scaling by a count is what linear unit values are for. Closing multiply and divide over the unit keeps the tag alive through whole formulas instead of forcing an erasure boundary into each one. The excluded cases, points, inverse units, and cross-family mixes, keep their current rejections.

whyNot.reason: Its caution is real, but division by a count inherits the backing type's existing division rules, so deferring it buys no safety and leaves a taught asymmetry.

A named method makes ordinary arithmetic read as an API call and pushes multi-term formulas into chains, taxing the common case. Its policy-seam virtue matters only if scaling ever needs custom policy, which the backing types already define.
It keeps three calls of boundary ceremony on the most common unit operation and an unprotected bare-number window inside every guarded formula.

recommendation.tradeoff: The operator table for unit families gains scalar rules, and the linear-versus-affine distinction now shows up in what multiplies. Same-unit ratio, unit divided by unit, stays a future decision.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared operator scaling, a named method, and the status quo, seeded by the unit_family example.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested full dimensional algebra, unit times unit with derived units, and deferred it as a separate future decision.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review added scalar division to the lead option after finding the same erase-rewrap chain for halving, and later split multiply-only out as its own option.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened the scale method with its auditable-policy-seam argument and the status quo with its visible-audit-point argument.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review disproved the claim that unit-times-unit is always rejected, since nominal currency multiplication compiles by ratified design, so the ballot now scopes to linear quantities. It also excluded affine points, pinned decimal-literal scalars, added the multiply-only option, and reframed raw() as an explicit boundary rather than a silent lapse.

decisions.title: Typed digests canonical: delete hex-string _bytes aliases
decisions.gist: Whether the hash functions whose names end in _bytes, but return hex text, survive.
decisions.lesson: The crypto surface has typed digests: sha256 takes bytes and returns a Digest256, which renders hex with hex() and yields raw bytes with bytes(). Beside them sit sha256_bytes, sha512_bytes, and blake3_bytes, which despite the name return a hex String. The reference table meanwhile still documents the typed entry points as returning strings, contradicting the compiler. A name that promises bytes and delivers text is a trap for exactly the code, key derivation and wire protocols, where the difference corrupts silently.
decisions.story: A developer derives a key and reaches for sha256_bytes because the KDF wants bytes. The function hands back 64 hex characters, the KDF accepts any string, and the derived key is wrong on every machine, discovered only when another implementation disagrees.

options.name: Delete the aliases; the typed digest is the one path
options.detail: sha256_bytes, sha512_bytes, and blake3_bytes are removed. Hex output is the digest call plus hex(); byte output is the digest call plus bytes(). Every consumer migrates in the same change, per greenfield law. That covers the dogfood call site, the example and fuzz callers, the conformance fixtures, the sema registrations, the Prelude functions, and the reference table whose current rows contradict the compiler.
options.technical: Remove the three fixed signatures, their module registrations (fixed_sigs.rs, module_items.rs:748-760), and their Prelude functions. Migrate the known invocations: dogfood/tower/run.jet:2928, the example and fuzz callers, and three conformance fixtures. Correct docs/reference/core-library.md:789-798, which still types the digest entry points as returning String. Update the surface ledger and goldens in the same change.
options.code:
actual :: crypto.sha256("abc".bytes()).hex()      // hex text, explicitly
key_material :: crypto.sha256(input.bytes()).bytes() // real bytes for byte APIs

options.name: Rename to _hex and keep both spellings
options.detail: The aliases survive under honest names: sha256_hex and siblings. The lying name disappears, but every hash keeps two permanent entry points returning different shapes. Under greenfield law a kept parallel spelling is a compatibility exception, which requires an owner-ratified carve-out naming its scope and removal condition; this option is that request.
options.code:
print(crypto.sha512_hex(abc))
digest :: crypto.sha512(abc)

options.name: Make _bytes actually return bytes
options.detail: The names stay and become true: sha256_bytes returns the raw digest bytes. Every current caller, all of whom use it for printable hex, silently changes behavior, and the surface still carries two entry points per hash beside the typed digest that already offers bytes().
options.code:
raw :: crypto.sha256_bytes(abc)   // now real bytes
print(crypto.sha256(abc).hex())   // hex moved here

comparisons.note: hashlib has one entry point per hash; the digest object offers digest() for bytes and hexdigest() for text. Representation is a method, not a function name.
Sum256 returns a byte array; hex is an explicit encoding step. The name never promises what it does not return.

recommendation.why: The typed digest already carries both representations honestly as methods, so the aliases add nothing but a lying name in the one domain where the lie corrupts silently. Greenfield law says delete the replaced form and migrate every consumer now, including the reference rows that currently contradict the compiler.

whyNot.reason: It fixes the lie but requests a permanent compatibility carve-out for two entry points per hash, which the one-mechanism invariant exists to prevent.
It silently changes the behavior of every existing caller and still leaves a duplicate entry point beside a digest type that already offers bytes().

recommendation.tradeoff: Hex output costs an explicit hex() call and byte output an explicit bytes() call, and expected strings in goldens migrate once. That buys a surface where names never misstate the returned type.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared deletion, honest renaming, and honest behavior, seeded by the fixed-signature evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review checked for other representation-lying names in the crypto surface and found none; the scope stays three functions.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested rename-then-deprecate and rejected it: greenfield law forbids the deprecation tail.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened B as the churn-free path and C as the reading that takes the names at their word.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review caught the draft's own example teaching the representation mistake it condemns, so the byte path now spells bytes() explicitly. It also replaced a wrong consumer count with an enumerated inventory and surfaced a reference-table row that contradicts the compiler.

decisions.title: Small stdlib holes: ascii fold, path containment, file walk, args view
decisions.gist: Whether four small, dogfood-proven helper gaps ship as stdlib methods.
decisions.lesson: Four independent one-call jobs have no stdlib spelling, and real code fills each hole badly. Jetpack folds ASCII case with twenty-six replace calls in a security-relevant path law. Four separate sites implement path containment as normalized-prefix checks, three named helpers and one inline. Every file-processing walk repeats the same directory filter. Every raw argv consumer re-skips the program name. Each gap is small; together they are the texture of daily friction.
decisions.story: A reviewer reads jetpack's store path law and finds the letter Z on line thirty-three of a case-folding helper. The law is right, but no reader can verify twenty-six replacements at a glance, and the next program will copy it with a typo.

options.name: Ship all four
options.detail:
String.to_ascii_lower() and to_ascii_upper() fold ASCII letters only and leave every other code point untouched. The upper twin ships as the symmetry pair; the corpus evidence is lower-folding.

Path.is_within(base) answers containment lexically on normalized components, so slash direction and partial-name prefixes cannot lie. It never touches the filesystem; security callers canonicalize first, and its documentation says so. fs.walk_files(root) walks like fs.walk but yields regular files only. process.args() returns a fresh list of the arguments without the program name; argv() keeps the full vector.
options.technical: to_ascii_lower is not Unicode to_lower; both remain, with distinct documented contracts. is_within compares normalized component sequences, resolving dot and dot-dot segments lexically; symlink truth requires explicit canonicalize, per its docs. walk_files inherits walk's error, ordering, and symlink policy. args() returns a new List of String, the same element type argv() returns; it is a projection, not a borrow.

options.name: Ship only the two correctness-sensitive helpers
options.detail: to_ascii_lower and is_within ship, because hand-rolling them risks wrong behavior, not just length: a missed letter or a naive string prefix is a security bug. walk_files and args() stay local patterns, since their hand-rolled forms are verbose but correct. The loss is that the two most repeated conveniences keep their ceremony, and the walk filter keeps being copied.
options.code:
return Ok(name.to_ascii_lower())
if !path.is_within(store_root) -> return Err(PathLaw.Escape)

options.name: Decline all four
options.detail: The surface stays smaller. Jetpack keeps its twenty-six lines, four containment sites keep drifting, walks keep their filter, and argv keeps its index tax. The audit's evidence says these are the exact spots where real Jet code got longer and harder to audit than peers.
options.code: folded = folded.replace("A", "a") // and 25 more

comparisons.note: The standard library ships the ascii fold and component-aware containment; the walk comes from the ecosystem, and env::args still includes the program name, an index tax Jet can drop.
casefold is Unicode-wide, a different contract from the ASCII-only fold proposed here, and the universal args view is spelled as an index hack.

recommendation.why: Each helper has one honest contract, a proven hand-rolled counterpart in the corpus, and an exact deletion target in dogfood. Shipping all four removes real audited-by-eye risk and daily ceremony without any new mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Its correctness line is principled, but the walk filter and argv skip are the highest-frequency copies in the corpus, and declining them preserves most of the measured ceremony.
It preserves twenty-six-line case folding in a security path law, which is exactly the audit finding this ballot exists to fix.

recommendation.tradeoff: Four names join the surface, to_ascii_lower must be taught beside Unicode to_lower, and is_within must be taught as lexical with canonicalize as the symlink-truth step. The distinct contracts justify the pairs.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft bundled the four dogfood-proven gaps with their exact hand-rolled counterparts as evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review checked the declined-names record, D-STR-DECLINE1, and confirmed none of the four was previously declined.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested folding args() into the CLI recipe ballot and kept it here: it serves raw-argv experts regardless of that outcome.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review built option B as the strongest honest subset for an owner who weighs surface growth heavily.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review added a fourth containment site, downgraded is_within to an explicit lexical contract with canonicalize named for symlink truth, and pinned args() as a fresh list. It also rewrote comparisons that oversold peer parity and flagged the upper-fold evidence gap now acknowledged in the option.

decisions.title: How much must plain jet check prove?
decisions.gist: Choose whether jet check proves one file, the default output, or the complete project without execution.
decisions.lesson: Plain check currently stops after front-end projection. Real package failures can remain in imports, Core closure, TIR, or another output until run or build.
decisions.story: A developer runs jet check on a file inside a package and gets success. The next jet run fails because a reachable module or tier lowering was never checked.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet check src/main.jet
checked app: entries, graph, Core closure, TIR, JIT, interpreter, AOT
$ jet run
# no new compiler-side failure
decisions.detail: Every option is read-only. Check never executes user code, invokes rustc, links, generates sources, runs actions, or mutates locks.

options.name: Full static project proof
options.detail: Resolve the owning project and every declared runnable output. Validate imports, reachable Core closure, canonical TIR, and every applicable execution-tier lowering. Preserve isolated single-file checks.
options.technical: Reuse the build front end and checked bundle with execute false and inspect-only true. Apply edit-cone and receipt reuse laws. Missing project context names the canonical root import.
options.code:
$ jet check .
checked default, worker, web: graph + Core + all applicable tiers

options.name: Prove the default output only
options.detail: Resolve the project but check only its canonical default output and native tiers. Named outputs, web, and plugins remain the responsibility of their build commands.
options.technical: The default output gets graph, Core, TIR, interpreter, JIT, and AOT checks. Other outputs are not part of a plain check verdict.
options.code:
$ jet check .
checked default output

options.name: Keep front-end-only check
options.detail: Preserve current semantic and preflight behavior. TIR and tier failures remain deferred until run or build.
options.technical: No new pipeline work. The command cannot promise that a checked program reaches any execution tier.
options.code:
$ jet check src/main.jet
semantic checks passed

comparisons.note: cargo check proves the selected package graph through code generation analysis without producing a final linked program.
go test and go vet follow package imports. A file-local success is not treated as a complete project verdict.

recommendation.why: A makes check the one trustworthy pre-execution verdict. It reuses the canonical build front end, catches every known failure class, and honors one-bundle tier parity.

whyNot.reason: B leaves named outputs and selected web or plugin targets outside the ordinary project verdict. Those are common release-time surprises.
C preserves the observed failure: check succeeds before the compiler reaches a broken Core closure or tier lowering.

recommendation.tradeoff: A performs more static work. Edit-cone and receipt laws bound repeat cost, while deterministic output must state exactly which outputs and tiers were proved.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared complete project proof, default-output proof, and the current front-end-only command.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered execution, rustc, linking, generated sources, and actions. Those violate a static check contract and were excluded.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass combined project graph checks with default-only lowering. That became B, but it still leaves named output failures deferred.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B's lower repeat cost and C's stable command meaning. Neither supports a trustworthy full-project verdict.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review required arbitrary-depth imports, all outputs, exact no-side-effect boundaries, missing-context teaching, and reuse of the existing front end.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use the existing build front end and checked bundle. Prove entry, graph, Core closure, and tier-lowering failures; clean run/build follow; read-only behavior; and receipt reuse.

decisions.title: Public typed package model for Jet tools
decisions.gist: Choose where Jet tools read package, lock, and resolved profile facts.
decisions.lesson: Jet already parses these files into typed Rust models, but Jet programs cannot inspect them. A public read surface must preserve spans and provenance without exposing secrets or adding another parser.
decisions.story: A Jet tool needs package identity, resolved dependencies, outputs, and profile facts. Today it must shell out or parse compiler-owned files again, losing source spans and compiler truth.
decisions.inWild:
facts :: compiler.package(package_source, lock_source, profile_source) ?? return Err(PackageRead.Invalid)
print(facts.package.name)
print(facts.profile.fingerprint)
decisions.detail: The surface is immutable and source-backed. It performs no filesystem, network, provider, lock mutation, or package resolution work. Every exposed path stays logical and package-relative.

options.name: Deepen core.compiler
options.detail: Add one immutable typed package model to the existing compile-time-only core.compiler seam. Reuse jet-pkg-model and jet-env-model. Keep runtime rejection and the existing compiler callback.
options.technical: Accept source values through existing literal and embed boundaries. Return package, lock, and resolved-profile projections with logical origins, byte spans, declaration order, and typed causes. Redact secrets and reject escaping paths.
options.code: facts :: compiler.package(package_source, lock_source, profile_source) ?? return Err(PackageRead.Invalid)

options.name: Add core.package
options.detail: Expose the same immutable typed model through a new Core module. Naming is clearer, but Jet gains another registry surface and another execution-tier seam.
options.technical: The data and safety contract matches A. The new module still delegates to existing parsers and must not depend on jetpack.
options.code: facts :: package.read(package_source, lock_source, profile_source) ?? return Err(PackageRead.Invalid)

options.name: Keep it Rust and CLI only
options.detail: Expose public Rust APIs and a CLI projection, but no Jet API. This avoids Core growth, yet Jet tools still cannot consume the typed model directly.
options.technical: jet-pkg-model and jet-env-model become the only public seam. CLI output remains a serialization boundary.
options.code: $ jet inspect package --json

comparisons.note: cargo_metadata exposes one typed read model for package and resolve facts. It does not ask each tool to parse Cargo files.
go list exposes resolved package facts through one toolchain-owned model. Consumers do not implement module parsing.

recommendation.why: A deepens an existing compiler-only seam and keeps one typed parser authority. It has the smallest I6 and I9 surface while letting Jet tools consume compiler truth.

whyNot.reason: B adds a new module and parity seam for data already owned by core.compiler. The naming gain does not justify the second public home.
C cannot satisfy the Jet dogfood witness. Jet tools would still shell out or rebuild a loose projection.

recommendation.tradeoff: core.compiler gains more methods and records. Strict projection and redaction rules keep compiler internals, credentials, absolute paths, and mutable operations out.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass compared the existing compiler seam, a new package module, and a Rust-only surface.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass considered filesystem and network operations. Those belong to package tooling, not a pure read model, and were removed.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass tested a core.package alias over core.compiler. It was rejected because greenfield law forbids two public homes for one mechanism.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass strengthened B's naming advantage and C's smaller Core surface. Neither lets Jet tools reuse the existing authority with less total machinery.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT. The rival review required exact spans, declaration order, secret redaction, logical paths, no Core-to-jetpack edge, and no write or network surface.

decisions.checkInstructions: Use one immutable typed model. Prove real manifest, lock, and profile reads; typed source errors; secret redaction; path boundaries; no new dependency; and applicable tier parity.

decisions.title: Agent skill and model-routing source of truth
decisions.gist: Where Jet keeps agent rules, skill routing, and model choices.
decisions.lesson: Jet now has overlapping project skills, global managed skills, and vendor plugin skills. Several define the same delegation, burndown, review, and model-routing rules differently. This choice sets one maintained authority and keeps task-specific skills narrow.
decisions.story: User corrects an orchestrator after it launches too many expensive workers and stops before integration. The next orchestrator must learn that correction from one maintained place instead of choosing among stale skills.
decisions.inWild:
Request: Burn down epoch 4.

1. Read docs/agents/owner-guidance.md.
2. Select the domain workflow named there.
3. Use the approved host and model route named there.
4. Integrate, prove, and close under the same owner rules.

options.name: One owner guide
options.detail: Make docs/agents/owner-guidance.md the only owner-edited control file for shared agent conduct and model routing. Keep agent-memory.md only for project state and technical traps. Keep orchestration.md only for mechanics, with no owner policy or model choices. Repo task skills keep domain steps. Retire .claude/skills/burndown. Keep tower-burndown as a thin Tower adapter. Disable jet-fast-burndown and milestone-burndown inside Jet without deleting their global installations.
options.technical: AGENTS.md loads a compact preflight and keeps I1–I9 above the guide. Model routing exists only in owner-guidance.md. Dispatch loads one named adapter profile and stops when that profile is missing, stale, conflicting, or unknown. Migration maps every trigger and unique rule. A generated lock records active repo, managed, plugin, vendor, and cache inputs. The owner edits only the guide. Vendor files stay read-only, and rollback restores the prior activation map.

docs/agents/owner-guidance.md       # policy, adapters, routing, retirement table
AGENTS.md                           # invariant-safe universal preflight
docs/agents/agent-memory.md        # project state and technical traps only
docs/agents/orchestration.md       # mechanics only; capability names, no models

options.name: Policy plus adapter registry
options.detail: Keep stable owner policy in owner-guidance.md and changing model mappings in agent-adapters.md. Keep agent-memory.md for project state and orchestration.md for mechanics only. Retire or disable the same duplicate burndown skills as option A. Domain skills keep their distinct task steps.
options.technical: AGENTS.md loads both control files and keeps I1–I9 above them. A generated lock versions repo, managed, plugin, vendor, and cache inputs. Dispatch stops on a missing, stale, conflicting, or unknown adapter. This gives policy and runtime data separate files, but User must edit two shared-control surfaces.

docs/agents/agent-adapters.md       # models, commands, paths, limits
AGENTS.md                           # loads both under I1-I9
docs/agents/agent-memory.md        # state and traps only

~/.omp/agent/managed-skills/*       # disable Jet duplicates
scripts/agent/skill-drift.*         # generated versions and gate

options.name: Tower-first workflow
options.detail: Make tower-burndown the main implementation workflow. Keep owner-guidance.md for shared corrections and a small model-routing file for non-Tower work. Keep agent-memory.md for state and orchestration.md for non-Tower mechanics. Retire the project burndown skill and disable duplicate managed burndown skills inside Jet.
options.technical: Tower owns worker limits, worktrees, proof, integration, and closure for tracked work. A small routing table covers research, review, HTML, gauntlet, and Codex tasks. A generated lock blocks stale or conflicting adapters. This choice keeps strong Tower safety but spreads shared control across several files.

plugins/tower/skills/tower-burndown/SKILL.md # main workflow
docs/agents/model-routing.md                  # non-Tower models

~/.omp/agent/managed-skills/*burndown*        # disable inside Jet

options.name: Keep skills, add drift checks
options.detail: Keep the current distributed skills and authority files. Add governed keys for concurrency, closure, worktrees, model routes, and output duties. Keep agent-memory.md for state, but retain shared conduct in owner-guidance.md, orchestration.md, and task skills.
options.technical: The gate snapshots repo, managed, plugin, vendor, and cache inputs. It blocks dispatch when an active source is unknown, stale, or conflicts with another source. This has the smallest migration, but shared rules still require edits in several places and every snapshot refresh preserves that duplication.

Keep agent-memory.md for state and generate orchestration routing from the same manifests. Retire or disable duplicate burndown skills through the manifest.
options.technical: Continuous integration regenerates the guide and checks its input versions. Dispatch stops when generated output is stale. Agents read one file, but User edits several source files and must regenerate the view before a change becomes active.

comparisons.note: Today, five burndown sources and several task skills carry overlapping orchestration or model rules. The same request can select different worker counts, worktree rules, proof duties, or models.
comparisons.code:
Policy sites: 5 burndown sources
Model routes: Luna, Sol, Haiku, Sonnet, general-purpose, default
Normative edit sites: distributed

recommendation.why: A gives shared conduct and model routing one owner-edited source while keeping domain skills narrow. It adopts D's fail-closed drift checks, so stale managed, plugin, vendor, or cache inputs cannot silently regain authority.

whyNot.reason: B gives stable policy and changing adapters separate files. A keeps the same enforced boundary inside one file, so User has one shared-control editing surface instead of two.
C is strong for Tower work, but it makes Tower assumptions govern non-Tower research, review, HTML, gauntlet, and Codex routes.
D detects conflict well, but shared conduct and model choices still have several edit sites. Snapshot refresh also preserves duplication instead of removing its cause.
E gives one reading surface but not one editing surface. Changes still start in several inputs and require generation before agents can use them.

recommendation.tradeoff: A puts stable policy and changing adapters in one file. Enforced sections, one routing table, a generated version lock, and fail-closed dispatch keep that choice bounded.

reviewPasses.base: The base draft compared one guide, a split adapter registry, a Tower-first workflow, and the current distributed design with drift checks.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested deletion, vendor mirroring, generated manifests, and lint-only enforcement. It kept a generated-view choice and folded smaller tactics into the other options.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept distinct domain skills under option A. It added option D's fail-closed drift gate without adding a second owner editing surface.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave every option explicit file dispositions, input version checks, and cold-agent failure behavior. It also made each option's owner editing cost visible.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: OpenAI. Adversarial model family: Anthropic. The rival review rejected draft A because it omitted live authority files, retirement choices, and fail-closed checks for stale adapters. The revision keeps A only after naming every disposition, one routing home, invariant precedence, version checks, and cold-agent failure behavior.

decisions.title: Put Package facts inside a single source file
decisions.gist: Choose how one Jet file declares its Package facts.
decisions.lesson: Today, one Jet file is complete only while default Package facts are enough. This ballot chooses how that file can declare a name, dependencies, capabilities, targets, or build settings without package.jet. G is today's behavior; A–F are proposed replacements.
decisions.explainer:
All options change only how Package facts are enclosed. They keep package.jet's fields, values, defaults, dependency resolution, capabilities, targets, builds, Package graph, and lock behavior. A deps key is the local dependency name used after use. The @ characters inside a quoted dependency coordinate are plain text.

For A, the inline declaration is the first non-comment construct in the entry source file. It appears once per Package, before every use and declaration. Other source files cannot add or override Package facts. More than one inline declaration, or an inline declaration beside package.jet, fails before dependency resolution. No source wins or merges; the diagnostic names every conflicting location.

Outside strings, @fact reads a fact known before the program runs; it does not create that fact. B would also make @package introduce a declaration. C would make @field assign Package fields. A leaves @ unchanged.

To extract A, copy only the package block's body into package.jet at the Package root. Delete the wrapper and leave every use and program declaration in the entry file. The reverse operation inserts the wrapper after leading comments but before every use or declaration, then removes package.jet in the same tool operation. If that placement is unavailable, the tool fails without changing either file.

Inline and extracted forms normalize to the same Package facts and dependency graph. The wrapper and manifest path do not change the lock key or resolved versions. Package locks remain in .jet/lock. One-file means one authored file to share; Jet may still keep generated lock and cache data.
decisions.story: Maya shares one run.jet file that fetches weather data and prints a report. The program needs one dependency and network access. She wants one file now, without blocking a later move into a larger Package.

options.name: Native package block
options.detail: Start the file with one package declaration. Its body uses the same fields and values as package.jet. Tools can parse it as Jet and move it unchanged into package.jet later.
options.technical: package is a declaration, not a runtime value. Only one may appear, before other declarations. An inline block and package.jet are mutually exclusive. Both produce the same Package model, graph identity, and lock identity.

options.name: Marked package block
options.detail: Use @package to mark the block as compiler input. The marker makes the special role visible. It also gives @ a new declaration role beside its existing compile-time read role.
options.technical: The body and migration rules match option A. This expands @ beyond known-value reads such as @build and @name, so the syntax must distinguish reading a fact from declaring Package facts.

options.name: Marked fields
options.detail: Prefix each Package field with @. Small files avoid a wrapper, and each special line is visible. Larger manifests repeat the marker and turn one Package declaration into many directives.
options.technical: Each allowed Package field is one contiguous top-of-file @field directive. Repeated, late, or unknown fields fail. Extraction removes each @ and writes the fields in source order as one package.jet body.

options.name: Typed Package value
options.detail: Declare Package facts with Jet's normal typed binding syntax. This reuses familiar grammar. It also looks like a runtime value that users could rename, pass, or construct more than once.
options.technical: Only the top-level binding named package with declared type Package supplies compiler facts. It appears once and cannot be read or passed at runtime. Any other Package value is ordinary program data.

options.name: Bare Package fields
options.detail: Allow recognized package.jet fields directly at the file top. This is the shortest form. A reader must know where metadata stops, and those names cannot be ordinary declarations in that prefix.
options.technical: Only a contiguous prefix of recognized package.jet field names is metadata. Each appears once. A recognized name there is never a user declaration. Repeated, late, or unknown metadata fields fail.

options.name: Comment front matter
options.detail: Place a fenced package.jet document inside comments. Existing tools can scan text before parsing Jet. Users must learn a second embedded format, and language tools need two parsers for one file.
options.technical: The exact // ---package opener is the first non-comment line, and // --- closes it. Every body line starts with //. Missing, repeated, or late fences fail. Fence-like text elsewhere is ordinary text.

options.name: Reserved directive lines
options.detail: Write one reserved line for each Package setting, like .NET file-based apps. Each line is easy to add independently. Package configuration becomes a separate directive language beside Jet declarations.
options.technical: A contiguous top-of-file prefix accepts directives such as #:name, #:dep, and #:capability. Repeated, unknown, or late directives fail. Extraction translates the directives into one package.jet body.
options.code:
// Package header only; the complete unchanged program is shown above.
#:name weather-report
#:dep http ./deps/http
#:capability Network

options.name: Keep package.jet separate
options.detail: Keep source files free of Package facts. The current model stays simple for tools. A program that needs one dependency or capability stops being a single-file program.
options.technical: This keeps today's behavior. Scripts stay file-free only while defaults are enough. The first explicit Package fact requires package.jet at the Package root.

comparisons.note: PEP 723 standardizes fenced TOML comments. uv makes the workflow popular and now supports uv lock --script. The praised result is a shareable file; complaints target comment fences, hidden metadata, and project promotion.
RFC 3502 uses ---cargo TOML front matter. It praises format reuse and easy migration. It records unclear defaults, hidden locks, cache concerns, and tooling rollout as costs.
.NET 10 uses reserved top-of-file directives such as #:package and #:property. This keeps one source file, but each project setting becomes a separate directive outside normal C# declarations.

Kotlin uses file annotations such as @file:DependsOn. The marker is explicit and editor-visible, but package configuration becomes annotation-shaped compiler input rather than one coherent manifest value.
Sourcegraph indexed 10,811 PEP 723 matches across 1,670 repositories, 1,215 .NET directive matches across 109, and 145 Cargo-script matches across 22. These are matches, not users.
comparisons.code: Queries: context:global archived:no fork:no lang:Python '# /// script'; lang:C# '#:package'; lang:Rust '---cargo'. Results may include docs, tests, examples, and shard-limited counts.

comparisons.note: uv had 89,288 GitHub stars and 182,502,668 recent-month PyPI downloads. Two Hacker News PEP 723 stories received 640 and 247 points. These signals do not isolate feature usage.
The 93-post PEP 723 discussion had 8,791 views and 265 likes. Participants praised low boilerplate, debated namespacing, warned about pyproject confusion, and demanded a clear promotion path.

recommendation.why: A keeps the proven one-file workflow without embedding package.jet text inside comments. It gives Jet one native declaration, one Package model, exact editor error locations, and a body that moves unchanged into package.jet.

whyNot.reason: B is explicit, and Kotlin proves @ can introduce annotations. Jet already gives @ one different law: outside strings it reads compile-time facts. The package keyword avoids making the same mark mean both reading and declaring.
C is brief for one field, but repeats syntax as Packages grow. It fragments one Package value and forces a directive grammar for every current and future field.

D reuses binding syntax but is not an ordinary binding: the reserved package value cannot be read, passed, shadowed, or rebound. A parses as a declaration from the start and never promises those binding operations.
E is shortest, but hides the boundary between Package facts and user declarations. It reserves field names and gives parsers, readers, and tools less structure.

F copies the market leader's comment fence rather than its useful one-file workflow. It needs comment scanning and a second embedded grammar, with weaker editor locations and more edge cases than native Jet syntax.
H is proven workable by .NET, but every Package field needs a second directive grammar and translation rule. A keeps the complete package.jet body as native Jet data instead.
G preserves today's split, but breaks Jet's single-file promise as soon as a program needs one dependency, capability, target, or build setting.

recommendation.tradeoff: A reserves one declaration keyword and adds one source-file construct. Existing source that binds package must migrate in the same clean cutover; Jet keeps no compatibility alias. That visible cost avoids expanding @, runtime bindings, or comment grammar.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps uv's self-contained workflow, Cargo's unchanged promotion path, and .NET's explicit compiler-owned boundary. It replaces their secondary metadata syntax with Jet's native Package body.

harvest.aspect: One native declaration keeps the Package whole.
harvest.use: Use it as the canonical source form.

harvest.aspect: A visible marker prevents accidental runtime interpretation.
harvest.use: Keep the visibility through the package keyword, not @.

harvest.aspect: The body should look like normal typed Jet data.
harvest.use: Reuse Package field and value grammar without creating a runtime binding.

harvest.aspect: package.jet and inline source should share a body.
harvest.use: Make split and merge move the body unchanged.

harvest.aspect: Tools should find metadata before running user code.
harvest.use: Give the native declaration a fixed top-of-file position.

harvest.aspect: Large Packages deserve a dedicated manifest.
harvest.use: Keep package.jet as the extracted form, never as a requirement for one-file programs.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass framed the choice as preserving one-file Packages without inventing a second Package model.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass added keyword, @ block, @ fields, typed binding, bare fields, comment front matter, and status quo as distinct final designs.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept the market leader's self-contained workflow, Cargo's promotion path, and an explicit compiler boundary while replacing secondary metadata syntax with native Jet.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave every option its strongest real benefit and named its concrete grammar, tooling, migration, or semantic cost.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: InlinePackageBeginner. Skill: rli5. The pass exposed an unclear baseline, incomplete migration example, and missing common placement, conflict, lock, and @ rules; the revised ballot now teaches each before comparison.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: OpenAI. Adversarial model family: Anthropic. A survived, but the pass exposed inconsistent dependency grammar, a missing .NET-style directive option, and stale locking language. The revision adds that option, unifies examples, and replaces rhetoric with concrete grammar costs.

decisions.title: Pass first-class SQL values to database sinks
decisions.gist: Choose whether database calls accept one checked SQL value or separate text and parameter lists.
decisions.lesson: SQL is a value that stores executable query text plus its bound inputs. Checked means interpolation inputs become database parameters, never pasted text. A sink is a call that sends SQL to a database. Today, every sink splits SQL into ordinary String text and [DBValue] inputs. This ballot chooses the permanent boundary.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner glossary:

- String is ordinary text. SQL is executable database text plus its ordered bound inputs.

- SQL{"... {id} ... {name} ..."} stores template "... ? ... ? ..." and inputs [id, name] in that order. User input never becomes query text.

- :: binds a value. [T] means a list of T values. result ?? panic("message") stops if result is an error.

- DBScope is an open database connection with access authority, row policy, and user identity attached.

- query reads many rows. query_one reads at most one. execute changes rows. live keeps a query result updated.

- transaction runs a group together or rolls all of it back. migrate records a named schema change. prepare asks the driver to compile a statement.

Safe edit rule: put changing values in an SQL hole. To add a name filter, change SQL{"... WHERE id = {id}"} to SQL{"... WHERE id = {id} AND name = {name}"}. Holes bind values only, not table or column names.

Dynamic identifiers require a program-owned allowlist and then SQL.raw for the complete statement. SQL.raw is an explicit, audit-visible escape; the compiler does not prove its runtime text safe. Never pass untrusted text to it.

Universal rule under A: each single-statement DBScope sink takes one SQL. A grouped transaction or migration takes [SQL]. Ordinary String fails with E0149. Group operations stay db.transaction(scoped, label, statements) because they coordinate one scope and several statements.

SQL is not a database connection and performs no effect by itself. DBScope remains the receiver for single-statement calls because it carries database access, row policy, and identity.

A hole-free statement still uses SQL{"..."}. Query builders return the same SQL value as a literal. The public db.params helper disappears. Template inspection remains read-only for audit output.

Prelude owns the SQL plan through AOT, JIT, and interpreter execution. Runtime layers preserve its template and input order. The final driver seam may rewrite placeholders and allocate the driver parameter array. Tier-parity tests must prove identical template, input order, errors, policy, transactions, and migrations.

This ballot does not turn CSV into checked text. CSV is structured data with parsing and encoding rules. HTML and Sh already retain their checked types at their sinks.
decisions.story: Maya inserts a user-supplied name, reads the row, and groups two setup statements. She wants the compiler to keep executable SQL distinct from ordinary text through every database call.

options.name: Typed SQL at every sink
options.detail: Make query, query_one, execute, and live accept one SQL value. Make transaction and migrate accept [SQL]. Each {hole} remains a bound input inside that value.
options.technical: Plain String arguments fail with E0149. SQL.raw(text) remains the explicit audit-visible escape. Query builders return SQL. db.params is removed. Runtime layers preserve the plan until final driver marshalling.
options.code:
id :: 7
name :: "Ada"
changed :: scoped.execute(SQL{"INSERT INTO person (id, name) VALUES ({id}, {name})"})
row :: scoped.query_one(SQL{"SELECT name FROM person WHERE id = {id}"})
// changed is 1; row contains "Ada". A plain String is E0149.

options.name: SQL value executes itself
options.detail: Keep one SQL value, but put query and execute methods on SQL. The SQL value receives a DBScope when it runs.
options.technical: DBScope still supplies database access and row policy. The method direction changes, so executable text appears to own the effect even though the scope grants it.

options.name: Keep text plus parameters
options.detail: Retain today’s API. Each call receives ordinary String query text and a separate [DBValue] input list. Checked SQL must be split before use.
options.technical: This matches common database drivers. Any String can reach execution, and callers can pair text with the wrong inputs or order.

options.name: Prepare a DBStatement first
options.detail: Convert SQL into a connection-bound DBStatement, then pass that statement to query and execute. Preparation is always visible and may fail.
options.technical: A DBStatement works only with the DBScope that prepared it. It adds another plan type and a preparation step, although Jet already caches prepared statements.

comparisons.note: Kysely's sql template tag returns a RawBuilder that carries substitutions as database parameters. The object can execute directly with one database argument; sql.raw is the explicit unchecked escape.
comparisons.code:
sql<Person[]>`select * from person where id = ${id}`.execute(db)
// Source: https://kysely-org.github.io/kysely-apidoc/interfaces/Sql.html

comparisons.note: SQLx query! returns a query object with checked bind arguments, then fetches or executes it against a connection. Its strongest checking requires literal SQL plus a build-time database or offline metadata.
comparisons.code:
sqlx::query!("select * from account where id = ?", id).fetch_one(&mut conn).await?
// Source: https://github.com/launchbadge/sqlx/blob/main/src/macros/mod.rs

comparisons.note: Prisma generates a typed query value and passes that single value to $queryRawTyped. It protects parameters and result types, but needs separate SQL files, generation, and an active database.
jOOQ keeps values as bind parameters inside its query model, renders prepared statements by default, and can inline only when asked. The query object is the unit passed toward execution.
The postgres crate accepts a Statement or raw String as one argument and a separate parameter slice as another. This flexible driver boundary resembles option C and keeps raw text executable.
comparisons.code:
client.query("SELECT name FROM person WHERE id = $1", &[&id])?
// Source: https://docs.rs/postgres/latest/postgres/struct.Client.html#method.query

comparisons.note: Python's sqlite3 API uses SQL text plus a separate parameter collection and warns against string formatting. It is simple, but the language type system does not distinguish executable SQL from String.
comparisons.code:
cur.execute("SELECT name FROM person WHERE id = ?", (id,))
// Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#how-to-use-placeholders-to-bind-values-in-sql-queries

recommendation.why: A completes the safety promise SQL already makes. One value owns template-to-input ordering from interpolation through execution. DBScope remains the visible database access and policy receiver.

whyNot.reason: B preserves one value, but makes executable text look like the effect owner. For each single-statement call, scoped.query(sql) keeps database access and row policy visible as the receiver.
C accepts ordinary String and asks every caller to preserve the pairing between text and inputs. That defeats checked SQL at its most important boundary.
D helps when users control preparation lifetime or reuse. Jet already caches prepared statements, so mandatory DBStatement adds another plan type without new control.

recommendation.tradeoff: A amends D-DBDRIVER1 and D-DBMIGRATE1. Every database caller migrates at once, db.params disappears, and query builders must return SQL. Final driver marshalling may rewrite placeholders and allocate its parameter array.

hybrid.synthesis: A keeps Kysely’s parameter-carrying value, SQLx’s query-object boundary, and Jet’s policy-bearing DBScope receiver for single statements. Group operations stay module calls because they coordinate one scope and several SQL values.

harvest.aspect: One SQL value preserves binding order.
harvest.use: Use it at every executable database sink.

harvest.aspect: The plan should remain first-class until execution.
harvest.use: Pass SQL intact, but keep DBScope as receiver.

harvest.aspect: Backend adapters ultimately need template text and parameters.
harvest.use: Split them only inside the final marshalling adapter.

harvest.aspect: Prepared statements should be cached and reusable.
harvest.use: Keep transparent runtime caching without a mandatory second type.

reviewPasses.base: The base pass traced SQL from typed interpolation through every current database sink and found the value dismantled at the last boundary.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass compared typed sinks, methods on SQL, split arguments, mandatory prepared statements, partial adoption, and compatibility overloads.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid pass kept one parameter-carrying SQL value, the policy-bearing DBScope receiver, and transparent prepared-statement caching.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative pass gave split driver arguments and explicit preparation their strongest portability and lifecycle cases before rejecting them for Jet's public surface.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: TypedSqlBeginner. Skill: rli5. The pass found undefined terms, an out-of-order example, incomplete option behavior, and no new-sink rule. The revision adds a glossary, ordered examples, option outcomes, a safe-edit rule, and one universal sink law.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: OpenAI. Adversarial model family: Anthropic; agent TypedSqlCaveRival found zero-copy, receiver, raw-escape, and hole-limit defects, all repaired with explicit I9 proof terms.
